## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each biblical book and in which places of their works. An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection is single, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.*

### Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The *Patrology* has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold at 1,200 francs per thousand volumes; the Greek-Latin at 1,800 francs per thousand. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# Volume Three of the Works of Saint Peter Damian in the Cajetan Edition

## Containing Various Minor Works

[Col. 0009]

# Cajetan’s Dedicatory Letter

To the Most Blessed Father in Christ, Paul V, Supreme Pontiff, Dom Constantine Cajetan, abbot of Saint Barontus of Cassino, everlasting happiness.

Sacred writings and the monuments of the saints, most blessed Father, are ordinarily of such value and character that, even if they seem to lie for a long time in darkness, wrapped in silence, and erased by oblivion, they nevertheless—because of their reputation, their reputed sanctity, and the excellence of their heavenly teaching—retain perpetual light in darkness, a tongue in silence, and memory in oblivion. In this mystical heaven of the Church they can be hidden like the sun, but never perish.

For the supreme pontiffs who govern this Christian world, moved and impelled by the Spirit of God, cause its sun to rise and shine after night and setting; and this is all the more glorious and divine because they accomplish it through a weak and insignificant instrument. This has certainly happened to me through you, most blessed Father, who ordered me to devote myself to these sacred monuments of literature and, through the perpetual fountain of your generosity, aroused me not to neglect anything in this undertaking, but to make the labor of my vigils visible and to seem, if not to attain, at least to follow and scent out your abundant favor toward me.

When, therefore, I had devoted this care and diligence to the minor works of Blessed Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, which had lain hidden in the dark bosom of antiquity—so that I might gather what was scattered, arrange what was disordered, and divide it into four volumes—after the first and second had already been published and received so kindly under your great and singular patronage, this third and next-to-last volume, also bursting forth from the same darkness, comes into the light like a brother jealous of their glory. When it sees the day, it considers nothing greater than to see your days and to live and rejoice with you.

Therefore, most blessed Father, do not cease to receive and cherish it, especially because it is the offspring of your son—namely, of that cardinal who deserved so well of the Apostolic See and the Christian commonwealth. While he was still alive, Alexander II called him, in writing, “the eye and immovable foundation of the Apostolic See,” already approving his sanctity and teaching by apostolic judgment. He burned with such zeal for piety and religion that, through speech, books, and example, he knew how to plant virtues in people’s souls and uproot vices, strengthen the minds of the good, and break the audacity of the wicked. Seeing him advance beyond the powers of nature, not only in the private but also in the universal Church—sometimes by exhorting, sometimes by teaching, sometimes by governing and protecting, sometimes by active work—the common people proclaimed him blessed with unanimous agreement and one voice.

The authority of the Benedictine order will also be pleased, for it glories so greatly in this disciple and teacher of its own that, almost disregarding its numerous ancient and modern pledges, it welcomes Peter Damian and caresses him as though he were its only son. It sees in him the splendor of its ancient family especially renewed, together with the merits of the labors he undertook always for the Roman Church. It also recalls in the name of this Peter his most holy namesake, Peter, prince of the apostles, who established that same Benedictine people in his own see through so many centuries, so that it might restore the Church in troubled times.

For Peter the deacon expressly records (*Treatise on the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, from the Cassinese Library, manuscript in my possession) that Peter himself, prince of the apostles, seeing the ship of his Church tossed by the storms of the wicked, hastened to Benedict as his most vigorous avenger and sought for himself a tranquil seat at Cassino:

> “I am going,” said the most holy Peter when certain pilgrims met him, “to my brother Benedict, so that with him I may celebrate the day of my passion; for my Church is being overwhelmed by various storms.”

Who, then, seeing that all things were held in common by Peter and Benedict through their brotherly love and association, would not hope that Benedict himself, through his own people, would assume Peter’s place for many successive centuries, as he had also done before?

[Col. 0011] Events indeed confirmed the matter itself. From the time when Saint Benedict, having established his choir, introduced his disciples into the basilicas and other churches of the City, down to the year 1144, they continuously customarily held the supreme pontificate, while the clergy itself created and elected the pontiffs. If afterward, with the succession interrupted, some—such as Sylvester II, Clement II, and others—were raised to that supreme dignity who were not from the Roman clergy, there is nevertheless no doubt that they were members of the Benedictine order.

Moreover, we venerate or revere as outstanding in every virtue the sixteen later pontiffs who governed God’s Church for a hundred years, added to nearly one hundred and fifteen earlier ones, all of them either enrolled among the saints or distinguished by every kind of virtue. What shall I say of the number and greatness of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, when in that period scarcely anyone—or only a few—rose to such eminence from the Benedictine cloisters?

I say nothing of the innumerable multitude of this holy offspring throughout the whole world. I do not recount how much Italy, England, Germany, Belgium, Gascony, Bohemia, Hungary, Swabia, Gothia, and Poland owe to the many apostles sent there by the Benedictines; nor, finally, how much the West Indies owe to Bartholomew Buylt, a monk of Tarragona and Montferrat, who was delegated by Alexander VI as the first apostle there nearly fifty years before Blessed Brother Xavier was sent there by Blessed Ignatius.

I do not relate how many martyrs and virgins it has produced in every age and of every sex, how many confessors in every rank, how many pastors throughout all the Churches, and how many distinguished teachers in every academy. Yet in Peter Damian it now sees all these things, once divided among its members, joined and united by a singular benefit of God; and although it cannot converse with him living in the flesh, it does not cease to admire him breathing through his writings.

Since these are the principal reasons, most blessed Father, why you should receive the teaching contained in this book with no less patronage and esteem than the works of others, I shall nevertheless add one final reason, which I do not doubt will also please you. For if it is permissible to pass and descend from the Benedictine head to its members, I find myself the last of them—not through myself (for I feel how useless and insignificant I am), but through my ancestors, whom I would not deny to have borne some name and distinction in service of the Apostolic See.

For the most ancient house of the Cajetani, to which I belong though unworthy, having migrated from Rome and Gaeta—whose principality it had held for nearly five hundred years—to Pisa, did not forget the devotion of its ancestors toward the Roman pontiffs. There it more than once defended them loyally and fearlessly against the violence of the emperors of that time and the arrogance of many people, and for a long time preserved their authority intact. The magnitude of its merits may be inferred from the fact that, from that time onward, this one Cajetan family, enlarged by so many and such great titles and honors of the Apostolic See, surpassed almost all the other families of the Pisan commonwealth; for, among other distinctions, it shone three times with the dignity of the cardinalate.

Furthermore, it is established that from the same family, which long before had made Rome its homeland, some obtained the supreme pontificate, several reached the cardinalate at different times, and others were also entrusted with the prefecture of the Roman commonwealth, Campania, and the Patrimony. Among them, the dukes of Gaeta and Fondi, and the counts of Ceccano and Signia, as well as the princes of Vico, descendants of the same house, enjoyed hereditary rights over several cities and towns. Leonardo Aretino, a most distinguished man, bears witness to this together with the ancient Annals, recording that they undertook very many labors for the Roman pontiffs.

But now, saying no more about the services rendered to your predecessors, I shall turn favorably to your own affairs, trusting that your favor toward me will never diminish but rather increase. Know, most blessed Father, that the family of the Orsini, most noble in birth and achievements, joined its loyalty and strength with the assistance and courage of my family in defending the liberty of the pontiffs, so that together they might win for the Holy See the glory of shared danger and labor. To confirm this harmony of piety and virtue by the powers of nature, they often bound themselves together by mutual marriages.

Thus these two plants, grafted into and intertwined with one another, began to produce the splendor and name of both the Cajetan and Orsini families. Among them—leaving aside for now the later Cajetani—was that John, most distinguished senator of Rome, who, although born of an Orsini father, wished to be called Cajetan after his mother Perna, of the dukes of Gaeta and kin of Gelasius II. He was followed by another John Cajetan, son of the great Matthew Orsini, senator of the Romans, and of Perna of the same Cajetan family; by a certain divine character of his morals he shone forth as Nicholas III when elevated to the pontificate.

Finally, to pass over many other examples supplied by this lineage, all the Orsini princes who survive today owe their origin to Napoleon Cajetan, son of that same great Matthew.

Therefore, most holy Father, since I recognize that through the Benedictine order and through my ancestors I belong entirely to the Apostolic See, you have bound me so closely to yourself by singular beneficence that I have believed it my rightful duty, as a benefit and inheritance, to expose my life for the glory and dignity of your name. May almighty God preserve you unharmed for a very long time as the support of his Church.

[Col. 0013]

# Cajetan’s Preface

[Col. 0013A] Since there are especially two things, diligent Reader, that can exalt and illuminate the writings of a sacred teacher—the first, innocence and integrity of life; the second, the fidelity and authority of orthodox teaching—I do not doubt that you will find both in Peter Damian, a most holy and learned cardinal.

If you look at the life he lived on earth, you would call it wholly heavenly and angelic, and therefore worthy of being enjoyed by the Church Militant for overturning the vices of his time, conquering errors, building virtues, and restoring morals. For all who had seen him say and do marvelous things in speech, work, and example, who had recognized his marvelous piety toward God and human beings, his incredible wisdom, his submission joined to power, his renunciation joined to riches and wealth, and his purity joined to resistance against the incentive and enticements of the flesh, proclaimed him blessed with one voice. Believing him almost an angel, they could not determine from which supreme hierarchy of spirits this being had descended to earth.

If the common opinion and acclaim of the people contain some element of truth and divinity, what could be more glorious and divine than to be commended by the testimony of one who represents God on earth? For Alexander II called the living Damian in a letter “his eye and the immovable foundation of the Apostolic See.”

Truly he was an eye; truly he was the foundation of the Church. In him, as in the firmament of justice, immortal light and the fixed stars of every virtue shone forth, making him more precious than purple and more visible to God and human beings. God Almighty, looking down from the lofty throne of his glory upon this bright and burning lamp, which had been content to lie hidden beneath the bushel of the Benedictine order, placed it upon the candlestick of his Church, in a high and eminent position. From there it might shine conspicuously with the light of miracles and holiness, and thus provide assistance to the Apostolic See, an example to the cardinals, a rule to pastors, and finally a saving way for all others.

This was Peter Damian, most gracious Reader. If, while he lived, the people—refreshed by the nourishment of his heavenly teaching, astonished by his miracles, and strengthened by the example of his life—proclaimed him holy and blessed, and if the supreme pontiff glorified him with the encomium you have seen, there is no reason for you to doubt his sanctity after death or to investigate more closely by what manner and at what time Peter Damian was enrolled among the saints. For across so many centuries we have found no evidence anywhere except the irrefutable testimony of the two Churches of Ravenna and Faenza, whose entire force and truth rest upon ancient custom and immemorial tradition.

[Col. 0014A] First, the most holy man’s native city, Ravenna, celebrates him throughout its city and entire diocese with an inviolable feast and a double office.

Then Faenza, where he died and left the sacred remains of his body, from the time when it was freed from the siege of the Gauls through the singular patronage of this saint, resolved to celebrate him—whom it had already long before received as one of its four protectors—together with the other three in an annual inviolable feast. It venerates him with the same celebration and office, namely on 22 February; but because that day is occupied by the feast of Saint Peter’s Chair at Antioch, it is always transferred to the following day. On that day a solemn procession proceeds with the clergy, religious orders, and a retinue of magistrates from the Major Church to the church of Saint Mary of the Angels, [Col. 0014B] where the body is deposited.

Moreover, in almost every year in which the order for reciting the office excludes this feast, the following is inserted: “The twenty-third day of February: yesterday was the double feast of Peter Damian, bishop and confessor of Ravenna.” By this same order he has also been placed and invoked from ancient times in the Litany with the holy bishops who were confessors and with the other heavenly beings. I have also discovered that in the most ancient registers and memorials of those same Churches—especially Ravenna and Faenza—the name of Damian was perpetually numbered among the saints.

The tomb of this most blessed doctor also commends his sanctity. It was constructed nearly three hundred years ago of white marble, in an elevated and lofty place behind the high altar, [Col. 0014C] with, among other words, the following inscription carved in the marble:

> In the year of the Lord 1353, on 13 April, the body of Saint Peter Damian, doctor in Sacred Scripture and bishop of Ostia, and legate of the Apostolic See, was translated.

There is also this inscription:

> Christ’s confessor Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia and most holy cardinal, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

Although this tomb is extremely ancient, that devout people worship, kiss, and embrace it with living and renewed devotion, and experience his assistance as present in their affairs. Therefore they rightly honor it with votive tablets and gifts that are hung there, as well as with burning lights. On the feast of this holy man, the image attached to the tomb is dressed in episcopal vestments and visited by a large crowd. All these things are confirmed by authentic testimonies [Col. 0014D] of the aforementioned Churches and city, which were sent to me.

No less weight is added by the testimony of several religious men, who attest clearly and with their own eyes that, when this tomb was opened about twenty years ago, Peter Damian’s body was found incorrupt. Lest anyone suppose that their eyes had been deceived, [Col. 0015A] the monks themselves, who examined the whole matter most carefully, affirm that this man of God was of small bodily stature. At that time they removed one arm from him so that, together with the other relics of the saints, it might be displayed at solemn feasts on the high altar, as has customarily been done down to the present day.

Finally, there is the authority of ancient and modern writers who do not hesitate to call this Peter, our own, distinguished for the praise of holiness and teaching. Whenever they wish to insert one of his sayings into their writings and sermons, they preface it with the title “saint.” If all these things seem insufficient, the same reason for doubt would arise concerning many saints whom the private or universal Church nevertheless celebrates, since nothing other than ancient custom and tradition supports their testimony and reputation.

As for the teaching of this holy man, Reader, impress this upon your mind and understand that it is equal in weight and value to the monuments of the ancient Fathers. Through it orthodox faith is strengthened, Catholic religion illuminated, piety kindled, human error and impiety vanish, and the way to heaven is fortified and shown.

Moreover, this doctor of ours is uniquely and singularly worthy of praise because, in an unaffected and simple style, he knew how to weave together abundant and varied instruction, from which teachers of different disciplines may draw useful and necessary things as from springs. For this reason we have devoted no small amount of industry and labor to arranging these pearls individually in their proper places, which the holy doctor customarily poured forth as time, place, and circumstance required.

Since we had given the first volume of minor works, containing what may be called political matters, to those concerned with public affairs, and the second, in which passages of Sacred Scripture are expounded, to preachers, we assign this third volume—which contains the disputatious theology carried on with heretics and schismatics—to scholastic theologians.

Lest those who delight in the pursuit of learning seem to be deprived of their pleasure, we shall reserve the fourth and final volume, containing poems of various kinds and sacred prayers, for learned men themselves. Yet no one should think that he can extract his entire subject from this volume in a perfectly systematic way, because the holy man did not treat these varied topics expressly, as we have said. Nor was the mind of so great a man ever set on commending his teaching to human applause, but rather to the common salvation and above all to the glory of God.

Therefore, I ask you to receive with gratitude and joy our intention of serving everyone, and never cease to pursue with all your strength the teaching of this most holy man as we present it in his writings, and to imitate his life through it. Farewell.

[Col. 0015]

# Certain Corollaries Concerning the Praise and Sanctity of Blessed Peter Damian

## I. Pope Leo IX, in a diploma granted to him while he was still alive

[Col. 0015C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It belongs to the authority of the Apostolic See to establish what is lawfully ordered and, concerning what has once been offered to God, to provide that it be preserved unshaken in the future, lest what the devout piety of those who came before has begun be overturned—God forbid—by the sacrilegious rashness of those who come after.

Therefore we assign to you, Peter Damian, prior of the hermitage called Ocri, situated in Saxon territory, and to your successors, the hermitage itself; and we decree that this hermitage remain in its present condition and endure forever. Nor shall any mortal, whether of low or high rank, ever be permitted to reduce this hermitage to secular ownership or to subject it entirely to any monastery.

Indeed, we do not refuse to allow the aforesaid place to become a monastery in itself, if that should seem appropriate; but we absolutely prohibit its being subjected to the jurisdiction of another monastery. For we are not unaware that such subordination is often, without doubt, the destruction of a place.

We also decree that the parish church of Saint Mary, situated in the place called Vineole, shall be held by the aforesaid hermitage in perpetuity. It shall also hold peacefully and quietly whatever estates it now possesses [Col. 0016C] or may acquire in the future, without unjust harassment by anyone.

Nor shall anyone be permitted to burst violently into the hermitage by a hostile attack, or to expel the servants of God who dwell there, or harass them by plunder; the rights of the faithful laymen who are patrons of the hermitage, and who founded it for the remedy of their souls, are nevertheless preserved.

If anyone should prove to be a violator of this apostolic decree of ours and, unless he comes to his senses, should scorn to make amends in every respect as an open enemy of God, let him know without doubt that he will be bound by the chains of anathema.

## II. Alexander II, in an apostolic letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning Blessed Peter Damian, who was carrying out a legation in those regions, speaks in these magnificent terms

[Col. 0016D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, if they obey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If you were carrying out what belongs to your office, you would have expelled not the abbot but the sorcerer Rainald from the monastery of Saint-Medard, which he invaded by simony, after he had been condemned by Peter, bishop of Ostia, and by you in councils according to due process, as has been reported to us.

But if, out of greed, love, or fear of some powerful person, you refused to accomplish this, then you placed all these considerations above the fear of almighty God and gave no consolation of returning to the dispersed monks. Consequently, the wickedness of that same Rainald is multiplied and increased.

We have taken care to command these things because some of the dispersed monks came to us weeping and lamenting, while others sent sorrowful letters, requesting the justice of Saint Peter and our consolation on account of such injustice. Therefore, by our authority, we confirm the sentence of the aforesaid Peter and of you; we anathematize Rainald and those who agree with him; we place the monastery itself under interdict for as long as he remains there; and we command you to do the same.

## III

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We return due thanks to your fraternity because, in the expulsion of Ivo, condemned by us for having invaded the Church of Chartres by simony, you showed yourself ready and diligent; and because, so that another worthy and suitable man might be canonically substituted for him in that Church, you gave counsel to our dearest son Philip, king of the Franks. We invite your prudence to offer fitting thanks on this matter to him and to his nobles.

Let your fraternity also know that we have admonished our brother, the archbishop of Sens, to excommunicate, by our apostolic authority, the invader of the Church of Orléans. For it is clear that he obtained the bishopric by simony and, to conceal the wickedness of his offense, incurred perjury at the synod of Chalon and deceived our brother Peter, bishop of Ostia, by whose authority that synod was held.

Moreover, to increase his crimes, he wholly rejected the letters of our apostolate by which he had been summoned to have these matters examined. Therefore, by apostolic authority we admonish your charity to offer yourself as a companion and helper to the aforementioned archbishop of Sens in condemning the invader of Orléans, disregarding the fear and favor of everyone.

## IV. Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, later Pope Victor III, in a letter sent to him

To Lord Peter Damian, venerable bishop, Desiderius the abbot sends the grace and salvation of God.

Since it has become sufficiently clear that you love this monastery of Saint Benedict, which I seem to govern, more than all the other monasteries founded in the surrounding region, we promise you—with all our brothers praising and gladly consenting—that I, Brother Desiderius, together with the entire congregation of this holy monastery, shall annually commemorate the anniversary of your death.

We also desire that our successors faithfully observe the same practice, just as we most dutifully celebrate the memory of our predecessors, the abbots who have recently departed from this light. It seems entirely worthy and honorable to us, to whom you show such great love and benevolence, that we should return some benefit, so that, as you have begun to love us, you may always love us while you live, and your love may grow in us, while you expect to receive from us some devotion and affection beyond the ordinary.

But if anyone should violate this promise of ours, whether among those living with us or among those who succeed us, let him be presented guilty before the judgment seat of Christ.

*[Note: [Col. 0017D] In accordance with this holy promise of Abbot Desiderius and his monks, Cassino commemorated the memory of the famous Peter Damian every year. For we saw the following noted in their Calendar, which is read after the Martyrology: “On the eighth day before the Kalends [Col. 0018D] of March died the venerable Lord Peter, bishop of Ostia.” The title “venerable,” which was customarily given to men distinguished for holiness, is especially clear from the same Cassinese Calendar.]*

I, Desiderius the abbot named above, have signed.

I, Brother Rainerius, have signed.

## V. The inscription carved in marble on the tomb of Peter Damian

His tomb is still illuminated with pious lights and visited by crowds, especially by those who come seeking the healing, through contact with it, of illnesses of the head. The letters of this inscription, now worn away there because of the use of candles but formerly intact, were sent to me by Jerome Rubeus, a most learned man and my dearest friend.

> In the year of the Lord 1354, on 13 April, the body of Saint Peter Damian of Ravenna, doctor in Sacred Scripture, bishop of Ostia, legate of the Apostolic See, and member of the Order of Saint Benedict at the Hermitage of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana, was translated into this present ark by the Reverend Father Lord Matthew of Callio, abbot here.

### Beneath the same ark

> When one thousand three hundred and fifty-four years had passed,  
> and April’s thirteenth dawn had passed,  
> the clergy translated you, learned in sacred Scripture,  
> bishop of Ostia, whom the cardinalate adorns.  
>   
> O Peter Damian, may the Cross at the community of Fonte  
> Avellana bless you, so that at last, as legate  
> of the Apostolic See, you are now enclosed by this stone.  
>   
> Abbot Matthew, born at Callio, undertook this work.

## VI. Votive inscription preserved in the cathedral church of Faenza

The cathedral church of Faenza still retains and preserves this inscription on one of its columns, from the time when God, through the merits of the saints Savinus, bishop and martyr; Aemilianus, bishop and confessor; Terentius, deacon; and Peter Damian, freed that city from the siege of the Gauls.

In gratitude and fulfillment of its vow, the same city resolved to celebrate Peter Damian—whom, together with those same saints, it had long before received as its patron—with all of them in an annual inviolable feast.

[Col. 0018D]

> When the danger of slaughter, destruction, and flame from the Gauls threatened the city, the entire people of Faenza vowed that, if almighty God would avert the ruin, they would celebrate the office on the feast days of the saints Savinus, [Col. 0019A] Aemilianus, Terentius, and Peter Damian no less solemnly than it was customary and proper to celebrate it on Sundays. [Col. 0020A] This he did. 1512.

[Col. 0019]

# To the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Scipio Borghese, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Major Penitentiary and Librarian of the Apostolic See

Dom Constantine Cajetan, abbot of Saint Barontus of Cassino, sends every kind of salvation, prosperity, and happiness.

[Col. 0019B] Just as those who have lain for a long time in darkness, when at last they emerge into the light, cannot suddenly look upon the light itself but need some preliminary aid by which they may endure its splendor without fear or injury, so this third volume of the minor works of Blessed Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, has experienced the same thing.

Because it has until now lain hidden in the darkness and dust of antiquity, and is now coming into the light—especially so that it may behold the eminent light of our most holy Lord Paul V, your uncle—it asks for your protection and your name, most illustrious Cardinal Scipio. Supported by you, it will not fear to come before the presence of so great a prince.

For discerning people will understand how many ornaments of virtue and learning correspond to your name; they esteem it so highly that they place it alongside the name of its author. It therefore seeks you, approaches you, and embraces you as its guide, so that you may not disdain to lead it by the hand to its destination. It is not forgetful that this is also owed to you by duty, since it is the offspring of that man who was once joined to you by fraternal dignity and whom, like the others who flourished in the Church of God through heavenly teaching and piety, you never cease to follow and imitate.

And I also, whose work presents him—such is your great kindness—I do not doubt that you will look upon graciously and receive more favorably as one who serves you. May God Almighty always protect your Eminence, prosperous and safe within his Church.

# Various Minor Works of Saint Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church

[Col. 0019]

## 1–2. First Minor Work: On the Catholic Faith, to Ambrose

### Argument

He discusses clearly the essence of the Trinity—that is, the distinction of the Persons and the unity of substance—the true humanity and divinity of Christ, the procession of the Holy Spirit, the incorrupt virginity of the Blessed Virgin, and finally the mysteries of the whole orthodox faith. He demonstrates what the faithful must believe and what they must hold according to the tradition of the universal Church and the judgments of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0019C] To Ambrose, beloved son of holy hope, Peter, a sinful monk: the truth of the orthodox faith.

You ask, dearest son, that I write something to you about the catholic faith and briefly run through at least a few of those matters which the Fathers explain at greater length. For you hope, as you say, to be instructed more effectively and to have this impressed more firmly upon your memory if what has been published in the pages of ancient [Col. 0020C] teachers is now brought forth from our own mouth, as though from a household storehouse. For although what is mixed may come from a single cask, the hand that offers it in a familiar manner is nevertheless more pleasing. And often the medicines provided by those who recognize the illness of our weakness through the fellowship of constant familiarity benefit us more. For [Col. 0021A] since you are very well known to me through the unanimous affection of brotherly love, you trust that I will apply the healing salve especially where I know the sinews of your faith to waver somewhat less firmly in the strength of certainty. And you act irreproachably in seeking to establish, as it were, the foundation of faith amid the very beginnings of your new conversion, so that upon it the structure of your secure work may rise like the machinery of a spiritual building, never destined to fall. Certainly your request is worthy of praise; and what is demanded is not idle, but supremely necessary. Therefore, because the holy persistence of your devotion asks for something just, it does not deserve rejection of its petition. For without faith we can neither live in Christ nor please God at all by any action. Both apostolic and prophetic authority bear witness to this. For the voice of the Apostle [Col. 0021B] says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11). 3 Through the prophet, however, it is said: “But the righteous person lives by faith; but if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him” (Habakkuk 2; Hebrews 10).

Therefore, according to both testimonies, we cannot please God unless we hold to the correct rule of true faith. Faith is the origin of virtues; faith is the foundation of good works; faith is the beginning of all human salvation. Whoever does not walk carefully along the path of faith must necessarily be caught in the snare of error. Consequently, even if someone appears to undertake an institution of good works, without right faith he can in no way belong to the fellowship of the children of God. And whoever does not know how to walk by faith will never be able to attain to vision; and, to conclude everything briefly, without right faith no one attains the grace of justification or earns eternal life. Let us now, therefore, approach the living heart of the matter and the center of the subject proposed, with the very one of whom we are speaking as our guide.

## CHAPTER I. What Must Be Believed

First, then, whoever wishes to be a true and perfect catholic must believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all visible and invisible things. He must also believe in his only-begotten Son, namely the Word, the power and wisdom through whom all things were created. He was not created, but begotten before the ages; true God in every respect, like the Father, and of one substance with the Father, [Col. 0021D] although he is a different person. He is not later in time, lower in dignity, or weaker in power; rather, he was begotten wholly as great as the one who begot him. And although the Son is affirmed to have been begotten by the Father, no time is assigned to him, any more than to the Father. For whoever confesses the Father to be eternal must necessarily affirm the Son to be coeternal with him. Indeed, since [the text has *qui*; read *quia*, “since”] the Father always existed before the ages, without any beginning whatsoever, he always had the Son. For the Father could not have been eternally Father if he did not eternally have a Son.

He must also believe in the Holy Spirit, truly God, proceeding from the Father and the Son together, and always equal to both in substance, power, will, and eternity. [Col. 0022A] He certainly does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify creation, as certain people impiously and perniciously understand; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both. For the Father begot such a Son that, just as the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, so also he proceeds from the Son.

Therefore, dearest son, believe consistently and firmly that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one sole and true God, almighty, eternal, immutable, and impassible. For the only substance or essence that is immutable and entirely without any alternation of change is the substance that is God. To this substance, indeed, being itself—which is where the word “essence” derives its name—belongs supremely and most truly. To this supreme and unique substance properly and uniquely belongs the name [Col. 0022B] which the Greeks call *ōn* [ὤν], “the one who is,” and which in Latin is *est*, “is.” Hence 4 the Apostle also says: “There is no ‘is’ and ‘is not’ in him, but ‘is’ is in him” (2 Corinthians 1). The Lord himself likewise says to Moses: “I am who I am. And: Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3).

Accordingly, when we call God’s substance one, simple, and invisible, but distinguish the Trinity in its names, and confess one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we must understand absolutely that each one singly is God and that all three together are one God. Each one singly is a full, perfect, and eternal substance; all three together are equally one simple substance. Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit said together are not something greater or fuller than any one person of the same holy Trinity when named individually. For almighty God, through the immensity of his nature, both fills and contains all his creation. Therefore the Father fills all that exists, the Son fills all that exists, and the Holy Spirit fills all that exists, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God.

For this reason, my son, when you happen to persist in litanies or prayers, do not do what certain simple people do more out of ignorance than unbelief: invoke the name of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit once, but repeat the name of the holy Trinity more often, as though it were something greater and deserving greater reverence. That would imply that, just as a multitude of saints is greater than one saint, so—God forbid—the whole Trinity were something greater than one person of that same holy Trinity. This is rejected by the piety of the faithful and not admitted by the rule of orthodox faith.

Without any doubt, we must believe that the Father is fully and perfectly God, the Son is fully and perfectly God, and the Holy Spirit is fully and perfectly God. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one full and perfect God. Nor do the three named together signify anything greater than any one of them, whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, named individually. For the same greatness exists in each person named individually [Col. 0023A] as exists in the whole Trinity named collectively. Otherwise, although the Father is rightly called God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, each one singly would be an imperfect God if God seemed fuller in the three than in one person. But this is far from the piety of the faithful, who ascribe neither anything greater nor anything lesser to the simple nature of the divinity.

Since the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, God must in no way be called “threefold,” because, since he cannot be diminished, there is also no way in which that same perfection of the supreme Trinity could increase. Therefore, whether the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is called the full and perfect God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are also the full and perfect God. Hence God is to be called triune, not threefold.

Moreover, in this holy Trinity there is no succession of time, no distinction of magnitude, and no variation of rank. Nothing there is older in time, nothing differs in quantity, nothing surpasses in honor; rather, the whole essence of the divinity is of such a simple nature that, apart from the names indicating the property of the persons, whatever can be said essentially of one person may equally be understood of all three. It should certainly be noted that the human being was created not in the image of one person, but in the image of the whole Trinity. Hence Scripture does not read, “Let me make in my image,” but: “Let us make the human being in our image” (Genesis 1).

## CHAPTER II. The Heresies of Arius and Sabellius Are Refuted

[Col. 0023C]

As, in confuting Arius, we confess that the substance of the whole Trinity is one and the same, so likewise, while avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons, not confused with one another and clearly expressed, each according to its own property. For God the Father is not, as heretical impiety imagines, Father when he wishes, Son when he wishes, and Holy Spirit when he wishes. Rather, each person is distinguished from the others by a certain property, so that the Father is always Father and never Son or Holy Spirit; the Son is always Son and never Father or Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0023D] is never Father or Son, but always the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it is not merely the bare diversity of names that must be considered; the property of the persons must be distinguished with precision.

The Father’s proper characteristic is that, among all things that exist, he alone is from no other. Thus he alone is recognized as the person of fatherhood, but he is not alone in the essence of deity. The only-begotten Son of God has as his proper characteristic that he alone is from the one alone—that is, he alone is substantially and essentially begotten from the Father. This is the Son’s property.

The proper characteristic of the Holy Spirit is that he proceeds simultaneously from the Father and the Son. He is, of course, consubstantial and coeternal with both, of the same immensity and power, of the same will and inseparable nature. For he is in no respect lesser than those from whom he proceeds; rather, together with them he is worshiped as truly almighty God and equally adored with them. He remains wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son; he proceeds wholly from the Father and wholly from the Son. He remains in them in such a way that he always proceeds from both; he proceeds in such a way that he remains inseparably in them. With them he possesses both the natural and coessential fullness of unity and the unity of fullness.

This is that supreme love by which the one begotten is loved by the one who begets and loves his begetter. Therefore there are no more than three: essentially undivided, yet distinguished by a threefold property. One is the lover of him who is from him; one is the lover of him from whom he is; and one is the love of whom it is said: “God is love” (1 John 4). This is the supreme, ineffable, and incomprehensible Trinity—not, I say, of one God, but one God.

One person does not turn or change into another; rather, what each is remains continually and unstained, without any change. For the prophet says: “The word of justice shall go forth from my mouth, and it shall not return” (Isaiah 45). What does “it shall not return” mean? It prevents a Sabellian from saying that the one who is Father is also Son, or a Patripassian from saying that he is Father when he wishes and Son when he wishes. The word that has gone forth does not return, because the Father is always Father and the Son is always Son.

## CHAPTER III. The Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Col. 0024C]

We also believe that the Son of God, whom God the Father begot from his own substance before the ages, assumed a true human being of our nature and came forth from his mother’s womb while preserving inviolate virginity. For he who was God from God and almighty from the Almighty was not later in time, not inferior in majesty, not unlike in glory, and not divided in essence; the same only-begotten and eternal Son of the eternal Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

He assumed humanity without changing the divinity in any respect. He substantially united to himself true flesh and a true soul, so that, according to his humanity, by dying he might destroy death and overcome the devil, who held the power of death. That uniquely wonderful and wonderfully unique birth must not be understood in such a way that, through the novelty of the creation, the property of the human race was taken away. The Holy Spirit gave fertility to the virginal womb; nevertheless, the reality of the body proceeded from the condition of the mother’s nature, and the spirit of rational life immediately animated it.

For we condemn Apollinaris, who claims that the Savior assumed not the mind of a human being but only a soul without reason. He teaches that the divinity alone could suffice to provide a mind and infuse the counsel of rational wisdom. This is undoubtedly equivalent to saying that our Redeemer was not a human being, but merely possessed the limbs of a human body. Brute animals have soul and body, but they do not have reason, which belongs properly to the mind.

But if the Manichaeans are detestable because they deny that he had a true body, the lowest element in a human being, how much more must those be condemned who affirm that he did not possess what is best in a human being? Therefore, far be it from us to believe what reckless blindness and arrogant verbosity have fabricated. Far be it, I say, that the Son of God assumed something less from human nature, or that in flesh, soul, or sensation the humanity assumed by him was unlike ours. Apart from the sole stain of sin—which is not natural to those for whose sake he was assumed—we confess him to have been wholly like us.

For this reason he is called the mediator of God and human beings: because, just as he is true God, so he is true human being, possessing with the Father the same nature in divinity and possessing with his mother a human substance differing in nothing. From us he possessed, even unto death, the penalty of our iniquity; from God the Father he possessed immutable justice. He is the one “who was crucified from our weakness, but lives from his own power” (1 Corinthians 13).

He experienced death through participation in human feeling, a death he had willingly accepted, without losing the power of his nature through which he gives life to all things. He himself is both the author and the work of the author, because he offered himself as priest and sacrifice; and the same one hung upon the cross as the victim of sweet fragrance. With the property of each nature preserved, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. To pay the debt of our condition, inviolable nature was united to passible nature, so that one and the same mediator of God and human beings could die according to one nature and could not die according to the other.

## CHAPTER IV. How the Son Alone Assumed Flesh and Endured Death

But here, son, a thought may perhaps creep upon you and object, as though by logical consequence: Since the Son is believed to be of one substance with the Father and of inseparable nature, how could the Son, without the Father, assume the form of humanity or alone endure the outrage of suffering?

Because this is divine and inaccessible, and what proceeds from the ineffable substance cannot be grasped through visible evidence, catholic teachers often explain it by examples drawn from visible things. Hence blessed Augustine also says: “One thing is the soul and another is reason; and yet reason is in the soul. The soul is one, but the soul does one thing and reason another. The soul lives, and reason understands; life belongs to the soul, wisdom to reason. Yet neither is the soul without reason nor reason without the soul. Although they are one, the soul alone receives life and reason alone receives wisdom. So also the Father and the Son, although they are one and there is one God, flesh belongs to Christ alone, just as wisdom belongs to reason alone, although it does not depart from the soul.”

Again he offers another example: “In the sun, heat and radiance are in one ray, but heat dries and radiance illuminates. Although heat does one thing and radiance another, they cannot be separated from one another. So the Son assumed flesh and did not abandon the Father. In a lyre, too, although art, hand, and string are unquestionably cooperating, only one sound is heard. Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together cooperated in Christ’s humanity, but the Son alone assumed humanity.”

If this also perhaps troubles you—how Christ’s body could have been true if it came forth from his mother’s womb while virginity remained intact—look at what is readily before your eyes and infer immense things from the smallest. The ray of the sun penetrates a mirror in such a way that, passing through its obstruction with imperceptible subtlety, it nevertheless does not in any way impair its solidity; and it is seen within as it appears outside. Thus, when it enters and when it exits, it does not shatter the mirror, because the mirror remains intact both at its entry and at its exit.

If the sun’s ray does not break a mirror, could the omnipotence of the Redeemer at his birth not preserve the integrity of a virgin? Virgin integrity gave birth incorruptibly, just as it conceived inviolate. He who was born from her is true and complete God, just as he is true and complete human being. There is no falsehood in this union, since human lowliness and divine sublimity are joined to each other. For just as God is not diminished by condescension, so humanity is not consumed by dignity.

Each nature acts according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh naturally carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to injuries. Yet the creature was not changed into divinity, nor was divinity changed into a creature. The person of the mediator of God and human beings consists from two natures and in two natures in such a way that, after the Son of God became human, neither did the fullness of divinity consume the human nature, as heretical blasphemy asserts, nor did divinity pass over into the essence of humanity.

When God assumed humanity, his divine nature remained altogether immutable and impassible. It is “from two natures” because he united both indivisibly; it is “in two natures” because he preserved both incorrupt. The only-begotten Son of God, assuming a perfect human soul and flesh, is consubstantial with the Father in the form of God and consubstantial with his mother in the form of a servant.

Nor, because he shared in human weakness, did he thereby become a participant in our sins. He assumed the form of a servant without the contamination of servitude; he did not diminish the divine but exalted the human. What was assumed from the Lord’s mother was nature, not guilt. He could not contract sins of his own, since he came to cleanse the sins of others.

The distinct property of the human and divine nature is therefore known to remain undivided in him: although we see that the Word is naturally one thing and flesh another, we nevertheless confess one Son of God, both Word and flesh. He is true God and true human being: God in that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1); human being in that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). God in that “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid.); human being in that “he was made from a woman, made subject to the law” (Galatians 4). The infancy of a child is shown in the humility of the cradle; the sublimity of the Most High is declared in the voices of angels.

## CHAPTER V. How the Persons Are Distinguished in the Trinity

When arguing about this supreme matter, it is necessary both to maintain a discriminating caution and to weigh the substance carefully. We are compelled to distinguish the persons in the divinity, while we dare not separate the divine substance. We believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be three persons, while confessing one simple and altogether inseparable essence. Conversely, in Christ we affirm two complete and perfect substances, divinity and humanity, while asserting that he has only one person.

It is not lawful to say “another” of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since all have one and the same nature; but only “another person,” since there is no doubt that the persons in them are distinct. In Christ, however, it is not proper to say “another,” since there is only one person of God and human being; but “another thing” must be said, since there is a twofold nature of different substance.

On the other hand, Bishop Nestorius and the archimandrite Eutyches, together with Dioscorus, contend with one another in this disagreement: the former declares Christ to be a mere human being, while the latter attribute to him only the nature of divinity. The holy Church rightly took care to exclude them from her thresholds, so that, shut outside alone and without harm to the many, they might be compelled to quarrel with one another.

We, however, understand the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation without hesitation in such a way that, although God and human being are truly believed to be one person in him, the nature of divinity and the nature of flesh are nevertheless not one nature in him. Divinity in Christ could not be the same thing as flesh, nor flesh the same thing as divinity; rather, each nature—divinity and humanity—remained immutable and unconfused in its own property. We therefore confess that the Son of God assumed human substance, that is, true flesh and a rational soul, in the unity of person, not in the unity of nature.

The mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, therefore, just as it did not make Christ’s person double, likewise did not make the assumption of human nature common to the holy Trinity. The property of each substance remained, while the indivisible unity of person likewise always endured. That assumption of the form of a servant belongs solely to the person of the Son; nevertheless, it took nothing away from the fullness of divinity and diminished nothing of inexhaustible majesty.

Hence, in one and the same Redeemer, the truth of human nature shone forth and the eternal immutability of divine power remained. In Christ, therefore, we speak of a distinction of natures, not of person; in the holy Trinity, we confess a distinction of persons, not of nature.

Although, as a human being, he lay hidden within the narrow confines of a single small body, yet as God he governed the creatures of all visible and invisible things. The one through whom all things were created is not one person and the one who was created human another; the creator and the creature are the same; the physician and the medicine are the same; the priest and the victim are the same.

The immensity of divine greatness is such that we understand him to be within all things but not enclosed, outside all things but not excluded. He is interior so that he may contain all things; exterior so that he may encompass everything by the immensity of his unbounded greatness. By being exterior he is shown to be the creator; by being interior he is demonstrated to be the governor and ruler of all things.

## CHAPTER VI. How the Word Is Begotten by the Father

Some people, wishing to investigate the mystery of divine generation, are deceived by fantasies of bodily thoughts. “Did almighty God,” they ask, “take a wife, since he begot offspring?” But from our own weakness we can gather what we ought to contemplate in the depth of the hidden divine work.

First, a plan arises in the heart of an architect, so that the building of the future house may be constructed. The hidden heart generates the plan, so that the structure of the house may rise through the various lines of its walls and corners. The plan is therefore like a son of the human heart: it breaks forth outward for the construction of the building, yet nevertheless remains wholly in the heart of the one thinking.

If, therefore, a building is raised through a plan that is, as it were, the son of the heart, what should we think of the Son of God, the Word through whom all things were created? If the human heart can generate a plan without a mother, how much more could the almighty Father, from himself alone, ineffably beget the Word?

When the Word assumed human limbs, he did not abandon the mysteries of the paternal divinity; and when he was clothed with the veil of our flesh, he was received in the virginal womb but not enclosed. And why should this be surprising in the case of the Word of God, when even this speech which we utter with the tongue of flesh flows so richly into the senses that the heart of those listening receives it but does not enclose it? For if it were not received, it would instruct no one; if it were enclosed, it would not come to others.

Much more fully and, so to speak, more ineffably, the Son of God came to us through the mystery of the Incarnation, while nevertheless remaining with the Father in divinity. Assuming true flesh from the womb of a virgin, he wished to unite both natures in such a way that the one who truly was God would be true human being, and that the one who was human would undoubtedly be God. That assumption was such that it made God human and the human divine.

When the form of God assumed the form of a servant, both are God and, because of the humanity accepted, both are true human being. Although each of the saints may have deserved to attain exceptional grace from God, no one could be joined with God into one person. But the soul and flesh of Christ together with the Word are one Christ, one Son.

To establish a distinction between the multitude of all the saints and the author of the saints and of all holiness, blessed Paul the Apostle says: “In many parts and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Hebrews 1).

But it is one thing for God to speak through the mouths of the prophets and another for him to speak through the Word who is coeternal and consubstantial with him before the ages. One thing is the Word in flesh, another the Word made flesh. One thing is God in a human being, another God-human. One thing is the minister of the Word, another the teacher. 11 One is to be called the author of faith, another its preacher.

Moreover, it is one thing to receive the Holy Spirit through prophetic grace and another to possess him substantially by nature (Matthew 3). Although the Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, the divinity of the Redeemer could not receive him, since according to the essence of divinity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

It is therefore established that Christ received the Holy Spirit in his human soul, not in the divinity according to which he is one in nature with that same Holy Spirit. Thus the eternal divinity of the Son with his complete humanity, and that same complete humanity of the Son with his eternal divinity, are one person in the holy Trinity—and this person is not adoptive but proper, not merely titular but consubstantial and perfect.

He himself, wholly in his divinity and humanity, is the only-begotten and true Son of God; and likewise, wholly in his divinity and humanity, he is the true son of a human being—not merely titular, as the Spanish heresy impiously and recklessly presumed to assert. It claimed that the Son of God was true God in his divine nature but titular or adoptive in his human nature, as though there were two persons in Christ: true Son of God through divinity but adoptive through humanity.

Yet it is certain, according to the rule of catholic faith, that the only-begotten Son of God assumed human nature into the unity of his own person, with the property of each substance preserved, but with the unity of person remaining altogether undivided and simple. Therefore there are not two Christs or two Sons; rather, God and human being are one Christ, one Son in a unique sense.

The divinity of the Word did not come to the blessed Virgin by local movement. Rather, through the mystery of his ineffable power, the Son of God filled the womb of his mother in order to be born, while nevertheless remaining in the unity of the paternal divinity. He came to us to take away from us what he found in us and to offer on our behalf what he took from us.

The divinity of the Word could neither be divided into parts nor separated from the Father; rather, he is wholly everywhere and perfect everywhere. Thus he did not abandon the Father when he descended to the Virgin, just as he did not abandon the world when, victorious over death, he ascended into heaven. Hence he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

He speaks on earth and confesses that he is in heaven, because when he descended from heaven he nevertheless remained in heaven. And just as he is the Son of Man who is said to have descended from heaven, so he is the Son of God who is seen bodily in the flesh.

## CHAPTER VII. In Christ the Divine and Human Nature Manifested Themselves

In Christ, therefore, there is both unity of person and two natures, always unconfused and distinguished by their properties. One nature in him derives its origin from the virginal womb; the other is coeternal with God the Father, without any beginning whatsoever.

One is the nature by which he wailed in the cradle; the other is that through which he was worshiped by the Magi (Matthew 2; Luke 2). One is the nature by which he advanced in age and wisdom; the other is that by which he himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 13). One is the nature by which, after the exhaustion of a forty-day fast, he hungered while fasting (Matthew 4); the other is that which angelic sublimity immediately served through the duty of submission.

One is the nature by which he slept in the boat and was awakened by the disciples (Mark 4); the other is that by which he commanded the storms and winds. One is the nature by which, shedding tears, he mourned his dead friend; the other is that by which he recalled his soul from the underworld and raised the four-day-old corpse unharmed from the tomb (John 11).

One is the nature by which he was sorrowful unto death (Matthew 26); the other is that by which he declares that he has power to lay down and take up his soul (John 16). One is the nature by which he was able to tread with dry feet upon the swelling sea and its rough waves (Matthew 14); the other is that by which, fleeing into Egypt, he avoided Herod’s savagery.

One is the nature by which he shone like the sun when transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17); the other is that by which, when the vision departed, only the form of human weakness remained (Matthew 2). Moreover, one nature in him is that concerning which it is said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2); the other is that concerning which, as another prophet bears witness, it was said: “You are my servant, because in you I shall be glorified” (Isaiah 49).

According to one nature, the voice says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109); according to the other, it says: “It is too little that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the borders of Israel” (Isaiah 49).

There is therefore one substance or person in Christ, but not one substance or nature. Although the divine substance is one thing and the human substance another, in Christ the Son of Man must in no way be believed to be one person and the Son of God another.

From the very beginning of the Lord’s incarnation, God passed into humanity and humanity into God, so that the one who was born from God the Father before the ages might truly be the Son of Man and truly human, and the one who was born of a virgin at the end of the ages might truly be the Son of God and truly, without doubt, God.

We therefore rightly confess two births in Christ: one from the Father, without beginning, without time, eternal and in every respect coeternal with the Begetter; the other from his mother’s substance within the course of time. [Col. 0031A] Divinity and human condition came together in Christ, so that the Word might become flesh and flesh might pass into God, and so that one Emmanuel might arise from both substances, one who would be a suitable mediator of God and human beings.

In him the natural rights of each retain their proper force, as do the sublimity of divinity and the humility of flesh. Therefore it was not another but one and the same person who exercised two operations, and each form or nature, in communion with the other, performed what was proper to it: divinity sharing in the works of flesh, and flesh sharing in the works of divinity.

Thus the same one is God and human being in one subsistence or person, while the distinct property of each substance is preserved and the nature remains such that the union neither divides nor confuses either of them. The Word is Word and not flesh; flesh is flesh and not Word. Yet the operation of flesh and of the Word is one, because the person of God and human being is one.

Hence John says: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen, what we have contemplated, and what our hands have touched concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1). Yet no one can see God, much less touch him with his hands, except through the mystery of the human being united to him.

Divinity was united to humanity so inseparably that, after once receiving it into the unity of person, it never afterward departed from it in any respect. God made human being came forth from his mother’s womb; God made human being hung upon the wood of the cross. The same God-human, according to flesh alone, lay in the tomb; the same God-human, according to soul alone, descended into the depths of the underworld. The divinity that assumed both natures at the conception did not separate itself at death from either substance of the human being it had assumed.

Who, then, is he through whom the world was made? Jesus Christ—but in the form of God. Who is he through whom the world was redeemed? Jesus Christ—but in the form of a servant. Who was abandoned in hell? Jesus Christ—but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, destined to rise again? Jesus Christ—but in the flesh alone. Thus, in each of these particulars Christ is present, and in all of them there are not two Christs, but one Christ. Therefore the one and the same Christ is seen with both natures enduring, naturally performing what belongs to each substance; and each substance, in communion with the other, was doing what was its own, according to the essential quality or natural property implanted in each. We must therefore weigh everything carefully, so that the full humanity may be believed to have been assumed into God, and the full divinity understood to have been united to humanity. Our sole concern in this is to render to God what belongs to God, and to humanity what belongs to humanity.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born from the dove, in whose form he appeared

Accordingly, since a question is often raised concerning this subject, there is no small difference between the assumption of the dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit was seen, and the assumption by which the Son of God deigned to appear in the reality of flesh (Matt. 3). For some have tried to persuade others that the Son of God was not born from a woman, just as the Holy Spirit was not born from a dove (Mark 1). “That dove,” they say, “was not born from an egg, although it was physically seen by human eyes” (John 1). To them those who rightly believe reply that we read of the Holy Spirit appearing to John in the form of a dove precisely where we find that Christ was born from a woman (Luke 3). We must not believe the Gospel in part and refuse to believe it in part. If we believe the Gospel, then, that the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove, we must also believe that our Redeemer was born from a virgin. [Col. 0032B]

But why is the Holy Spirit in no way recognized as having been born from a dove, whereas Christ is recognized as having been born from a woman? The reason is undoubtedly that the Holy Spirit did not come in order to redeem doves by his appearance as a dove, but in order visibly to signify spiritual love and innocence through this form. The Son of God, however, who came both to raise up our fallen nature and to renew it, grown old in original vices, ought naturally and essentially to assume, in the unity of his person, that which he came to liberate through the mystery of his passion and resurrection.

Yet we do not say this in such a way as to acknowledge that our Redeemer alone assumed true flesh, while the Holy Spirit merely put on an imaginary form. For just as it was not fitting for the Son of God to deceive human eyes, so it was altogether unfitting for the Holy Spirit to counterfeit anything by falsehood. For, just as the one is truth, so the other is likewise the Spirit of truth. Both bodies, therefore—the body of the dove and the human body—were in the reality of their essence just as they were seen by human eyes. But that form of a dove, after it had fulfilled the ministry of usefulness that was required, came to an end; whereas the Lord’s body remained forever in the stable unity of the Word that had assumed it.

We must therefore confess that the true God Emmanuel exists from two substances, without confusion and without division; and for that reason we must truly assert that the blessed Virgin is the Mother not only of a human being but also of God. For naturally and bodily she gave birth to the flesh that the Word of God had become. [Col. 0032D] Let us also confess that the Word is naturally and substantially co-born with the flesh, and that there is one Christ; but rather, together with that flesh and soul, that he is the true God, truly one, and the natural Son of God. We must never presume to assert that the assumed human being ought to be co-adored or co-glorified with God the Word, as though one were to be worshiped in the other. For this is what the superadded syllable “co-” leads one to understand. Let us instead worship Emmanuel, namely the true God and human being, with one simple act of adoration.

This is also found inserted among the Anathemas of Blessed Cyril:

> “Nor should we say that God operates in the human being, as though one were the person seen externally and another the one operating internally. Rather, let us worship one God: the human being subject to our eyes, and the majesty hidden within. For this is why he is mediator: because he is the same true God and true human being, possessing one divine nature with the Father and not a different human substance from his Mother. In both natures the same one is the Son of God, assuming what is ours and not losing what is his own; renewing humanity in a human being, while always remaining unchangeable in himself.”

According to the form of God it was said: “He begot me before all the hills” (Prov. 8)—that is, before all times and temporal things. According to the form of a servant it was said: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (ibid.). According to the form of God he said: “I am the truth and the life” (John 16); according to the form of a servant: “I am the way” (ibid.). For the statement that “the Word became flesh” does not mean that the divine nature was changed into flesh, but that flesh was assumed by the Word in the unity of the person. The bodily birth from his Mother took nothing away from the divine majesty, added nothing to it, and changed nothing from it into something else. For just as the unchangeable substance could in no way be converted into another, so it could neither be diminished nor increased. [Col. 0033B]

Recognizing, then, the indications of each nature, we adore both the Word in the human being Christ and Christ the human being in the Word. For the Word made flesh is one Christ in two essences; in him there is nothing belonging to either nature that is not also characteristic of both. The same one is in the form of God who is seen in the form of a servant; the same one is subject to suffering in our weakness and inviolable in divine power; the same one remains incorporeal while assuming a body; the same one is not divided from the throne of the Father’s majesty and yet was crucified on the wood by the impious.

It is certain that both substances converged in one person; therefore the one and the same person ascended victorious over death above the heights of heaven and yet does not abandon the universal Church until the consummation of the age. Since each nature remains in its own properties, such a communion of unity has been made between them that whatever is there of God is not separated from humanity, and whatever is of humanity is not divided from divinity.

When he was conceived in the womb of the virgin, the power of the Word was absent neither from soul nor from flesh for even a moment. Nor was the garment formed or animated before the heavenly King put it on; rather, through him and in him that temple of the human body began to exist, so that the Son of God might essentially unite it to himself. For the Son of God came to be conceived in the virgin’s womb, and there, as it is written, Wisdom built the house of his body (Prov. 9).

Nothing, therefore, had yet been begun there concerning the creation of the offspring that was to come; but after the Word had entered into the unity of himself, the new human being received its beginning. Two natures converged in the one person of Christ: divine power for the performance of wondrous works, and the weakness of humanity for enduring sufferings. Yet both were God by the power of the one who assumed, and both were human by the humility of what was assumed.

[Col. 0034A] We must therefore beware lest, deceived by those things that must be referred to the form of a servant—that is, the form of humanity—we believe the majesty of the Son to be inferior to the Father. To show that the Son of God is not a distinct person, nor from another person, he says together with that form: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14); and yet with the same form he also says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). God certainly says, “The Father is greater than I,” on account of our weakness; and the human being says, “I and the Father are one,” on account of divine power.

## CHAPTER IX. Christ assumed human nature, not a human person

A question arises: since the Son of God is believed to have assumed nothing less than humanity, but the whole and complete human being, why is it asserted that God made human has only one person? For how did he assume the whole human being if he did not assume a human person? Or, if the Son of God, who is one person within the Trinity, is joined to a human person, how is it said that the substance of God and the substance of humanity have come together in one person? [Col. 0034B]

When I investigated this carefully and diligently sought what the Fathers understood on this matter, I found that Alcuin wrote to the emperor Charles that “the Son of God did not assume a human person, but a nature.” According to his judgment, then, the person of the Son assumed the essence of humanity without a human person.

But the great Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and an exceptionally learned teacher of the Christian faith, uses these words in an explanation contained in one of his sermons (see the Scholia at the end of the work):

> “This,” he says, “wondrous birth of the holy Virgin truly brought forth in one offspring one person, truly human and truly divine, because the two substances did not retain their properties in such a way that a distinction of persons could exist in them. Nor was the creature assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that he was the inhabitant and it the dwelling-place; rather, one nature was joined to the other.”

This is indeed expressed clearly and balanced with the utmost caution in the suspension of its words. Emmanuel, God with us, is always one person in the holy Trinity; just as he could never be diminished from the fullness of his power, so he could not be increased through the union of the humanity he assumed. Here, then, is the person. For the present, these examples may suffice; it is left to your diligence to discover whether any Catholic teacher has written about this matter with greater refinement. [Col. 0034D]

## Epilogue

This epilogue announces matters in a new form so that it may summarize what has been said above. But since, in mystical and profound subjects, the lengthy style dulls the minds of inexperienced hearers, and often, while attempting to illuminate the mind, obscures it, we are concerned for your inexperience, my dearest son, and do not wish to prolong you in these matters, so that, having traversed them briefly in summary, you may grasp them more firmly.

For although the strength of a lively intellect is powerful in you, consideration must be given to the inexperience of your conversion, lest, if the burden of a lengthy discussion is placed upon your shoulders, your still-tender strength fail under the load before it has learned to carry it.
