Since we are also concerned for your weakness, we append an epilogue at the end, so that you may find the matters previously expressed in fuller language now gathered into one place and, as it were, apprehend them more easily—not so much as repetitions as additions.

Believe, then, my son, that God is one substantially and three personally. Although these persons are distinguished by their own properties, they are in no way divided in their works. We never perceive the distinction of the persons more clearly and plainly than when we recall the baptism of the Lord. For we see—and, as though presented with a divine spectacle, contemplate—that at the waters of the Jordan the indivisible Trinity of the divine persons is being commended to us.

When that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world had been baptized, the heavens were immediately opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. Then the voice of the Father thundered: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). We therefore have the Trinity clearly distinguished: the Father in the voice, the Son in the human being, and the Holy Spirit in the dove.

This holy Trinity, then, just as it is distinguished in its names, so in this passage, as far as the literal sense is concerned, appears to be divided in its operation. It cannot be said that the Son, who was seen in the form of a servant, is the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor that the voice which came from heaven is the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor that the dove is the Father or the Son, since the Gospel itself testifies: “The Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove” (ibid.).

But right faith, true faith—uncertain not through presumptuous opinion but strengthened by the testimony of Scripture, not wavering through heretical recklessness but founded rather upon apostolic truth—plainly indicates that whatever is done divinely is performed inseparably by the whole holy Trinity. For although the Son alone was born from the Virgin Mary, the Son alone was suspended on the cross, and he alone rose from the dead, nevertheless the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together brought about the entire mystery of the divine Incarnation, passion, and resurrection.

That the Father sent him—that is, ordained that he should become incarnate—the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4). [Col. 0035D] The Father sent the Son, and the Holy Spirit also sent him. The Son himself declares this through the prophet, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, and to proclaim release to captives and opening to those who are shut up” (Isa. 61).

The Apostle also speaks of the Son: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2).

Although, then, the Son alone became incarnate, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together brought about the Son’s incarnation. The Father also brought about the Son’s passion, as it is said: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8). The Son did so as well, as it is said: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2).

The Holy Spirit also did so, concerning whom it is written: “The Spirit of wisdom is benevolent and did not release the accursed from his lips” (Wis. 1). Christ is called accursed because he hung upon the cross; concerning him the Apostle says: “Christ, in order to free us from the curse of the law, became a curse” (Gal. 3). The Spirit, therefore, did not release the accursed from his lips, because he permitted Christ to undergo all the punishments of passion and death that he had foretold through the mouths of the prophets.

The Father, moreover, brought about the Son’s resurrection, as it is said: “Therefore he exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2). [Col. 0036B]

The Father, then, raised the Son, awakening him from the dead and singularly exalting him above all. Christ also raised himself, as he says figuratively of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). Furthermore, to show clearly that he himself was the author of his passion and resurrection, he expresses it briefly in a single statement: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10). He repeats this elsewhere: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (ibid.).

That the Holy Spirit too, together with the Father and the Son, is the author of the resurrection, the Apostle testifies, saying: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8). [Col. 0036C]

For if we are to be given life at the end because of the Spirit dwelling in us, it is clear that the Holy Spirit has already done in the head of the Church what he will do in its body.

The same understanding must be maintained in every respect concerning miracles and all other works: whatever appears to belong specially to one person must without doubt be believed to be accomplished by the whole holy Trinity. The powers and signs that Christ displayed were performed inseparably by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Hence the statement: “The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works” (John 14). Hence also what he says concerning the Holy Spirit: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11).

This incomprehensible Trinity is confined neither by the limits of brevity nor extended by spatial breadth. It is absent nowhere, always and everywhere present, and present inseparably. It is neither greater in one part nor less in another, but wholly present everywhere, always undivided. The Father is from no one; the Son from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit from both.

Many among the Greeks, because they are unable to find what they regard as clear authority for this in the Lord’s sayings, believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son (see the Scholia). Blessed Jerome too, following their doctrine, says in his exposition of the faith: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the true God proceeding from the Father.” Here he was silent about the Spirit proceeding from the Son. The Creed of the Council of Nicaea likewise contains the words: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds properly from the Father, and is true God, as is the Son.”

## CHAPTER X. That the Holy Spirit unquestionably proceeds from the Son, just as from the Father

We, however, instructed by the teachings of the blessed doctors Augustine and Gregory and of other Catholic Fathers, believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together. So that the faith of believers may not henceforth be forced to waver, we shall not hesitate to add a few testimonies from Scripture.

Both prophetic oracles testify and apostolic authority confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Isaiah says concerning the Son: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he will kill the wicked” (Isa. 11). Concerning him the Apostle also says: “The Lord Jesus Christ will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 8).

The Savior plainly made known that this Spirit proceeds from him when, in the presence of his disciples, he breathed upon them: “Receive,” he said, “the Holy Spirit” (John 20). John, moreover, says in the Apocalypse: “A two-edged sword came forth from the mouth of Jesus” (Rev. 1). The Spirit, therefore, which he breathed there from his lips is certainly the sword that here proceeds from his mouth.

The Father also says to the Son through the prophet: “My Spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have placed in you, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your offspring, from now and forever” (Isa. 59). The Apostle says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). And to the Galatians: “Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4).

Blessed Peter likewise indicates that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Son as well as to the Father when he says: “The prophets searched and investigated this salvation, who prophesied of the grace destined for you, searching into what time or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ who was in them signified, when he foretold the sufferings destined for Christ and the glories that would follow” (1 Pet. 1).

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15). Since Christ himself is the truth, he undoubtedly taught that the Spirit was his own when he declared him to be the Spirit of truth.

John says: “By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us from his Spirit” (1 John 4). In the Book of Blessed Job it is also written: “He will hear the sound in the terror of his voice, and the sound proceeding from his mouth” (Job 37). Here the mouth of the Father is undoubtedly to be understood as the Son, while the sound proceeding from his mouth is the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit is rightly called a sound, because he came upon the Apostles with a sound and, from the heart that he fills, immediately bursts forth into the words of holy preaching (Acts 2). That the Son is to be understood as the mouth of the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from this mouth, the Psalmist testifies when he says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 33/34).

We judge it superfluous to offer examples that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, since we see them abounding throughout so many pages of Scripture. Such is the statement: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians the Apostle says: “He who confirms us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; he who sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1). In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians he says: “Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us” (1 Thess. 4).

Moreover, that the Father poured out the Holy Spirit upon the disciples is written in the Epistle addressed to Titus: “Through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (Titus 3). That the Son also poured out this same Spirit is written in the Acts of the Apostles. Peter says concerning Christ: “Exalted at the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he poured out this gift, which you see and hear” (Acts 2).

That the Father and the Son together poured out the same Spirit is proclaimed by the oracle of Joel in the words of both: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2).

Although, as we have said, many among the Greeks do not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, blessed Athanasius, bishop of the see of Alexandria, nevertheless says the following in his book written against Arius:

> “I believe,” he says, “in the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son; and I believe that the Spirit, the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father, belongs both to the Son and to the Father, because he also proceeds from the Son, as it is written in the Gospel that through his breathing he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20).

Saint Cyril also says against Nestorius concerning this very procession of the Holy Spirit:

> “Although the Spirit is in his own substance his Spirit, there is no doubt that he is the Father’s, so that the property of the person may be understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, yet he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth. Hence he proceeds from him in the same way as from God the Father.”

Blessed Ambrose also says among many other things:

> “For the Spirit is not sent as though from a place, nor does he proceed as though from a place, when he proceeds from the Son.”

Augustine likewise writes against the heretic Maximinus [Maximus]:

> “You ask me,” he says, “if the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is also from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son?”

He immediately adds:

> “Behold, I answer, whether you understand or do not understand: the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father; but the one is begotten, the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he is begotten; the other is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both.”

A little later he says:

> “The Spirit, then, belongs to both, proceeding from both.”

To conclude our position on the authority of this eminent doctor: in that holy Trinity there is one Father, who alone essentially begot the one Son from himself; one Son, who alone was essentially born from the one Father; and one Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Since a very great multitude of ancient and modern writers agrees concerning the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son, and since examples abound sufficiently through almost every page of sacred Scripture, we consider it superfluous to heap them up here, when you yourself can find more than enough of them.

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 0039B]

This discussion of the Catholic faith, dearest son, is sufficiently appropriate both for me, who have almost completed the course of the race, and for you, who have recently entered the training-ground of spiritual warfare. The sublimity of such an incomprehensible and incomparable subject should be sought by a new soldier amid the very beginnings of combat; yet no one who has not been worn and trained in sacred discourse ought readily to respond concerning it.

The former must establish the foundation of right faith upon which he may build the structure of good works; the latter must, through the discipline of a long way of life, discern subtly the secret of the heavenly mystery. For faith is both the beginning of those who act well and the consummation that perfects the virtues.

As the Apostle says concerning Christ: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3). Conversely, concerning the same one the Prophet says: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117/118). For the one who is placed beneath as a foundation, like the base supporting a building, presides over the Church as its summit and highest hinge.

May almighty God, dearest son, establish your feet upon the rock of the Catholic faith, so that he may also raise the sharpness of your mind to the summit of his contemplation.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## SCHOLIA

“This,” he says, “wondrous birth of the holy Virgin truly brought forth in one offspring one person, truly human and truly divine.”

This is a statement of Saint Leo (*Sermon 3, On the Nativity of the Lord*). It should first of all be noted that Damian’s reading differs somewhat from the words of Saint Leo himself, who has the following: “For this wondrous birth of the holy Virgin truly brought forth in one offspring one nature, truly human and truly divine.”

Nevertheless, I would believe that the meaning is the same, and that, for the sake of easier explanation, our cardinal expressed Saint Leo’s meaning in other words—unless we should rather say that Damian encountered another copy of Saint Leo in which he spoke in this way.

As for the words that follow below, where Saint Leo says, “But in such a way that one nature was mingled with the other,” they can offend no one’s ears, since Saint Leo, a vigorous defender of Catholic doctrine [Col. 0040A] in so many sermons and letters, and especially in that celebrated Encyclical to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople (Leo, Letter 10, formerly 12), used this phrase in order to refute the heresy of Nestorius. He says:

> “For nature was not so joined to nature that there might be a confusion of both, as certain heretics impiously said.”

For Nestorius maintained—and Saint Thomas also writes this in the Third Part, question 2, article 6, in the body of the article—that the Word was united to the flesh according to indwelling, as though the Word of God dwelt in that human being as in a temple.

Therefore Saint Leo, expressly refuting this, after saying, “Nor was the creature assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that he was the inhabitant and it the dwelling-place,” immediately adds: “But rather, one nature was joined to the other”—that is, united; namely, human nature was assumed by the Word for hypostatic union.

Saint Leo himself explains how this statement is to be understood in the letter cited above:

> “With the property of each nature therefore preserved, and with both converging in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity; and, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature.”

“ The Father is from no one, the Son from the Father alone, the Holy Spirit from both.” Many among the Greeks, because they are unable to find what they regard as clear authority for this in the Lord’s sayings, believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son.

The Greeks who contend that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son cannot appeal to authorities, either of the Fathers or of the councils, which at any time assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; this phrasing perhaps occurs in the passages of both the Council of Nicaea and Jerome that our cardinal cites.

For from the declaration of the Fathers, following the discussion held at the Council of Lyons under Gregory X and at the Council of Florence under Eugene IV, it is clear that, from what is said in sacred Scripture concerning the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father, it consequently follows that he also proceeds from the Son. For Christ, explaining himself, says: “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16).

In this sense the Council of Florence cites Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, and Cyril in his Letter to Nestorius, following Didymus and Athanasius. In the letters of union, chapters 6 and 7, it demonstrates that all the expressions of the Greek doctors where they speak of the procession of the Holy Spirit have the same meaning: namely, that they judged the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Son as well as from the Father.

Nor should it be believed that Saint Jerome wholly disagreed with this position, since throughout his short works he speaks of the procession of the Holy Spirit in the Catholic sense and with the phrase customary among the Latins.

Thus, to omit other examples, writing to Hebidia (Jerome, Letter 150, question 9, near the end), he says:

> “When the Lord says, ‘I will send you another Paraclete’ (John 14), he shows himself to be the Paraclete who is called the Comforter. Hence God the Father is understood by this name, the God of mercies and of all consolation. But if the Father is the Comforter, and the Son is the Comforter, and the Holy Spirit is the Comforter; and if believers are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, which signifies God; and if one name of divinity and Comforter belongs to them, then they also have one nature.”

A little later he adds:

> “Nor did the prophets prophesy without the Holy Spirit; and by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host; and whatever belongs to the Father and the Son belongs likewise to the Holy Spirit; and when the Holy Spirit is sent, he is sent by the Father and the Son. In one place he is called the Spirit of God the Father, and in another the Spirit of Christ.”

[Col. 0041]

## 23–24. SECOND WORK. *ANTILOGUS AGAINST THE JEWS*, TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN HONESTUS

### Argument

He composed this little book for the refutation of the Jews. In it he proves, by numerous testimonies from sacred Scripture, those things that they impiously deny: namely, the Trinity of persons in the divine essence; that Christ, whom they call the Messiah, was God and human being, and that he has already come into the world. Finally, he closes off all the evasions by which they might craftily attempt to oppose Christians.

[Col. 0041A] To the most illustrious Lord Honestus, a man according to the darkness of this Egypt, Peter, the least servant of the monks: perpetual love in Christ.

Dearest friend, recently you sent us, through our brother Leo, words of entreaty, asking that we write something for you by which you might often silence the mouths of disputing Jews with rational arguments and, when they enter into controversy concerning Christ, overcome them with the clearest testimonies of sacred Scripture.

But if you desire to be a soldier of Christ and to fight manfully for him, seize rather the weapons of a distinguished warrior against the vices of the flesh and the stratagems of the devil—the enemies, that is, who never die—than against the Jews, who have now been almost wiped from the earth.

Nevertheless, I do not at all disparage this undertaking; indeed, I judge it right also to satisfy your request. For it is disgraceful for a churchman to remain silent through ignorance before those who are outside and make accusations; and for a Christian, unable to give an account concerning Christ, to withdraw defeated and confused while enemies insult him.

To this may be added the fact that the harmful ignorance and blameworthy simplicity often found in this matter not only suggest boldness to unbelievers but also generate error and doubt in the hearts of the faithful.

Since this knowledge certainly belongs wholly to faith, and faith is unquestionably the foundation of all virtues, when the foundation is shaken, the entire structure of the building soon threatens to collapse headlong. Yet it must be understood that a Christian should not enter this contest for the sake of empty glory or merely out of a love of disputation, but rather because he hopes that, through the grace of conversion, he may be able to benefit the mind of the one who is arguing. Hence Paul says: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Cor. II). And to Titus: “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes about the law; for they are useless and empty” (Tit. II).

When someone initiates a dispute concerning this matter, he should be admonished not to exasperate his opponent with abusive quarrelling or the arrogance of pride, but to soothe his mind with kindly charity and the most patient seriousness, so that a stony heart—which, covered with overflowing bitterness, might otherwise become even harder—may perhaps be softened into belief by the restrained sweetness of words. Thus the same Apostle, after saying to Timothy, “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions” (2 Tim. II), immediately added: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with all restraint those who resist, lest God perhaps grant them repentance for acknowledging the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (ibid.).

But since almost all the books of the Old Testament bear witness to Christ, setting aside a multitude of words, we shall take care to present a few clearer testimonies of the prophets, by which, with God’s help, you may nevertheless gain victory over every madness of Jewish perversity and over their bombastic inventions. And because an arrow is shot more directly if the target into which it must be fixed is first set opposite it, we introduce here the Jewish combatant himself, so that the darts of our words may not drift away uselessly into the air, but may instead reach a definite object at which they have been aimed.

## 25. In the name of the Lord, the actual contest begins

Say, then, O Jew—for while you deny the Trinity, you consequently fail to understand unity—if, as you assert, God is one in person, to whom did he say: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I)? For if there were one person in the Godhead, he would not say “Let us make,” but “Let me make.” If there were three substances, he would not say in the singular, “our image,” but rather “our images.” Since, therefore, “let us make” asserts threeness, while “our image” declares unity, it is most clearly established that God, one in essence, consists of three persons.

Come, Jew, continue through the forests of divine speech; walk with me, turn over attentively the pages of your Law. Will you find anything in them that differs from this assertion of ours? Listen to what your Moses says again: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created man, he made him in the image of God; male and female he created them” (Gen. I). Why is it not said that God created man in his own image and likeness, but that God created man in the image of God, unless it is so that the person of the Father and that of the Son may be clearly distinguished? Similar is what is again said through the same Moses: “The Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building” (Gen. XI). And a little later it adds: “Come, let us descend and confuse their language there” (Gen. XI).

You see, therefore, that “the Lord descended” declares the one essence of the Godhead, while “come, let us descend” teaches that there are three persons. Ask Abraham also why he saw three and worshiped one. For it is written: “The Lord appeared to him as he was sitting in the valley of Mambre at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day” (Gen. XVIII); then it adds: “When he had lifted up his eyes, three men appeared to him, standing near him” (ibid.). Behold: although it was first said that the Lord appeared to him, when the matter is explained it does not say that one man appeared to him, but that three men appeared to him. Here it is plainly shown that the one who appeared to him is both one in the substance of the Godhead and three in persons.

Abraham’s own words also testify to this, when he says: “Lord, he said, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant; but I shall offer a little water, and let your feet be washed, and rest beneath the tree” (ibid.). There corresponds most fittingly to this what is written about Lot: when two angels were leading him out of Sodom, which was soon to be overthrown, Lot said to them: “I beg you, my Lord, because your servant has found favor before you” (Gen. XIX). A little later it adds: “Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (ibid.). For when the Lord is said to rain from the Lord, it is plainly evident that both persons—the Father, that is, and the Son—are signified.

For this reason he says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Why does he recall himself as the God of only these three fathers, and not also of the others? Was he not also the God of Enoch? Was he not the God of Noah and of countless other righteous men? What, I ask, is the reason that, having passed over the other fathers, he calls himself the God of only three men, unless it is to show that he, who is one in substance, is three in persons?

The prophet Isaiah also explicitly taught this Trinity of persons and unity of nature when he said that he had seen seraphim crying out: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. IV). To display the Trinity of persons, “holy” is said three times. But to make it apparent that the Trinity is one substance, he is declared to be not “the Lords of Sabaoth,” but “the Lord.”

David, likewise holding this understanding, says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXIII). For the Word of the Lord is the Son of the Father.

But to show that the same heavens were created by the whole Trinity together, the divinity of the Holy Spirit is immediately added: “And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (ibid.). Concerning this Spirit it is read elsewhere: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job XXVI). In another psalm the same David says: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI). Although he had named God three times, in order to show that this one is one, he added: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him” (ibid.).

And so that we may show another blessing of God, similar to the one which the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of David, let us turn to the book of Numbers. There it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses,” saying: “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus you shall bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you; may the Lord turn his countenance toward you and give you peace” (Num. VI). And to make clear that there is one God, whose name is invoked three times over the people, it immediately adds: “They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I shall bless them.”

Behold, O Jew: as we pass through and examine almost all the books of your Law, we find most appropriately both the unity of the divine essence and the Trinity of persons. And if we wished to gather for the affirmation of this doctrine all the testimonies available to us from your books, our tongue would perhaps fail first, before we lacked examples.

But since the entire argument of your party is chiefly directed toward striving to deny that Christ is God or the Son of God, let the course of our present argument now proceed along this path. I would not have you, as is your custom, transform yourself through deceitful evasions into a monster of many forms, like a slippery serpent seeking to escape one’s hands once captured. Rather, let all the inner recesses of your understanding be opened to comprehension; let your heart cast off its ancient veil of ignorance; let the ears of your mind attend watchfully. When you cannot reasonably oppose me, let silence overcome you, so that, if possible, he who provides me—a plainly ignorant man—with the material of arguments for establishing his truth may himself also pour the light of his wisdom into the darkness of your mind, so that you may believe.

# A REPLY AGAINST THE JEWS, TO HONESTUS

## 27. CHAPTER ONE. Concerning Christ, who is the Son of God

Let us begin, then, and confidently implore the help of the one about whom we speak, saying: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; and let those who hate him flee from his presence” (Ps. LXVII).

We read, believe, and prove that God the almighty Father begot the Word from himself before all ages. But if you, Jew, insist on denying this, you are unquestionably shown to be fighting against the very God whom you claim to revere. For he himself says: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. XLIV). Concerning this Word another prophet says: “The word of the Lord is powerful and strong; who will be able to comprehend it?” (Isa. LV). Isaiah speaks of it again when he says: “So shall be the word that goes forth from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I have willed, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it.” Certainly, if he were speaking of a transitory word, he would not announce that it would return to him or accomplish anything.

By the power of this Word the earth was founded, the heaven with its luminaries was made firm, and the sea was spread out in its basin. Concerning it, as was said above, we read: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII). This Word, begotten from the Father before the ages, willed at the end of the ages to become man in the Virgin’s womb.

Concerning the incarnation of this Word Habakkuk says: “Before his face the Word shall go, and he shall come forth into the fields” (Hab. III). What this Word is, however, is found a little farther on, when he says: “But I shall rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus” (ibid.). Hence Isaiah also cries out most explicitly: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son; and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted ‘God with us’” (Isa. VII).

Concerning him the same prophet says elsewhere: “The Lord loved him; he shall do his will in Babylon, and his arm among the Chaldeans. I, I have spoken and I have done; I have called him, I have led him, and his way has been made straight” (Isa. XLVIII). Immediately, in the person of the Son himself, it adds: “Draw near to me and hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time before they came to be, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit. Thus says the Lord God, the Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, teaching you profitable things, guiding you in the way in which you walk. If only you had attended to my commandments,” and what follows (ibid.).

Hear also the testimony of the prophet Micah concerning Christ: “It shall be,” he says, “in the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared on the summit of the mountains, and exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths; for from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples, and shall rebuke strong nations even afar off” (Mic. V).

Isaiah uttered this not merely with the same meaning, but in almost the same syllables. Nor are we reluctant, to strengthen the force of our assertion, to write again what the Holy Spirit willed to repeat through the mouths of two prophets. He says: “It shall be,” he says, “in the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it, and peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths; for from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples” (Isa. II). A little later it adds: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord” (ibid.).

For it is not reasonably believed that one prophet borrowed this statement from the other, since both prophets are known to have prophesied at the same time and under the same kings.

And if all these witnesses to the truth are still not sufficient for you, Jew, hear also your Baruch saying: “This is God,” he says, “and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to his servant Jacob and to his beloved Israel. Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III).

For if Christ, as you assert, is not God, show me from your books when, after the Law had been given to Jacob, God was seen on earth and lived among human beings. But since you will not be able to find this, you must admit that you have been convicted on every point.

But lest I seem to overcome you by my own words rather than by the examples of the prophets, let Daniel also come forward and bear witness concerning Christ: “When the Holy of Holies comes,” he says, “the anointing shall cease. You will say: ‘The Holy of Holies has not yet come; the Messiah has not yet come; but he is to come—show the anointing’” (Dan. VI). But if, as is true, your anointing has ceased—for you no longer have a temple, a king, or priests—acknowledge that the Holy of Holies has come, of whom Isaiah says: “I am God, calling the bird from the east and the man of my will from a distant land. I have spoken, and I shall bring it about; I have created him, and I shall make him. Hear me, hard of heart, who are far from righteousness: I have brought my righteousness near” (Isa. XLVI).

Let the patriarch Jacob also come forward: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

If, then, you have lived for a thousand years and more without a king and have lain beneath the feet of the nations, where do you now await the expectation of the nations? From the time when you said to Pilate, crying out, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX), you have had no king; and because you refused to hear the King of kings, you lost your kingdom together with your homeland.

Moses had foreseen this well when he said: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from his people” (Deut. XVIII). The same Moses says again: “For the Lord will give you a fearful heart, failing eyes, and a soul consumed by sorrow; and your life shall hang before you. You will fear night and day and will not believe in your life” (ibid.).

But when was your life hanging before you, except then, when, shaking your heads before the cross, you said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XVII; Mark LXV)? The Son of God himself most clearly speaks this through the mouth of David, saying: “All who saw me scorned me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads. He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he desires him” (Ps. XXI; Luke XXIII).

In the same psalm he shows more clearly than daylight the wounds made by nails in his hands and feet, saying: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (ibid.).

If you do not know, Jew, that was your ox, which was then sacrificed before you on the altar of the cross; but because of the merits you brought upon yourself, you have not yet eaten from it. Concerning it Moses speaks against you in Deuteronomy, saying: “Let your ox be slaughtered before you, and do not eat from it” (Deut. XXVIII). That was the ass, concerning which he says again: “Let your ass be seized in your sight and not returned to you” (ibid.). Rightly, by way of figure, our Redeemer is called an ass, since, in order to receive the burdens of our depravity, he in a manner offered his back; for as the prophet says: “He himself bore our sins” (Isa. LIII). There it suitably adds: “Let your sheep be given to your enemies, and let there be no one to help you” (ibid.).

Who these sheep are, from whom the synagogue ought to have received help, is clearly explained when it adds: “Let your sons and daughters be given to another people, your eyes seeing it, and failing at the sight of them all day long, and let there be no strength in your hand.” The holy apostles, who are called sheep because of their innocence, are sons of the Israelite people, since they derive their origin from its lineage. They are given to another people when, in response to the persecuting Jews, they say: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations. But although you saw these things, you did not see; and although you heard, you did not understand” (Acts XIII).

The same Moses rightly reproaches you for this even to the present day, saying: “The Lord has not given you a heart capable of understanding, eyes capable of seeing, or ears capable of hearing, even to this present day” (Deut. XXVIII). He also invokes the same punishment against you, saying: “May God strike you with madness, blindness, and fury of mind; and may you grope at midday as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness, and may you not direct your ways” (ibid.). And Isaiah says: “Hear, hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not recognize it. Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and close its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes, hear with its ears, understand with its heart, be converted, and I heal it” (Isa. VI).

Do you want yet another testimony of Isaiah concerning Christ? “I,” he says, “raised him up for righteousness, and I shall direct all his ways. He himself shall build my city and release my captives, not for a price or for gifts, says the Lord of hosts. Thus says the Lord: The labor of Egypt, the trade of Ethiopia, and the Sabeans; lofty men shall cross over to you, and they shall be yours, and they shall walk behind you. Bound in fetters they shall proceed, and they shall worship you and supplicate you. Only in you is God, and there is no God besides you. Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior” (Isa. XLV).

Speak, Jew; answer: who is the one who says, “I raised him up for righteousness”? But if you do not know, continue; turn your eyes to the end of the preceding statement and see that it says, “the Lord God of hosts.”

But if you now know that God is speaking, consider also to whom he is speaking. Go down, then, to the end of the following line and see what is said: “Only in you is God, and there is no God besides you. Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior.” If, therefore, the one who speaks is God, and the one to whom he says, “You are God,” is God, it is unquestionably established that the person of the Father speaks to the Son.

For the fact that it does not simply say, “You are God,” but “In you is God,” and “You are a hidden God,” clearly designates the humanity of our Redeemer. For in Christ Jesus, as our Apostle says, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” And when it says, “The labor of Egypt, the trade of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans; lofty men shall cross over to you, and they shall worship you” (Col. II), it openly announces that all the nations of the Gentiles are to be converted to the faith of Christ.

Hence a little later it adds: “Turn to me and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth, because I am God and there is no other. I have sworn by myself: the word of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth and shall not return; for every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall swear” (Isa. XLV).

Immediately the Father himself, who is speaking, bears manifest testimony concerning the Son when he adds: “Therefore in the Lord they shall say: ‘My righteousnesses and my dominion belong to me.’ To him they shall come, and all who oppose him shall be confounded. In the Lord all the seed of Israel shall be justified and shall be praised” (ibid.).

Similar is what is said elsewhere through the same prophet: “It is too little,” he says, “for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and convert the remnants of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX).

Christ is called a servant because he assumed the form of a servant. Hence, from the perspective of his humanity, he entreats the Father in the psalm, saying: “Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you” (Ps. LXXXV). For who is this one who both confidently affirms that he is holy and humbly entreats that he be saved, except the one whom the Lord promises through Isaiah will come, saying: “My righteous one is near; my Savior has gone forth” (Isa. LI)?

Behold: so that both the weakness of humanity and the power of divinity may be shown in the one Mediator of God and human beings, the one who there had asked salvation for himself is here declared to be the Savior.

Concerning him the same Isaiah bears witness elsewhere, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous shoot; and he shall reign as king, and he shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness on the earth” (Jer. XXII). Then he adds: “In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteous one’” (ibid.).

This is the righteous one for whose coming the same prophet burns and yearns with all his innermost being, saying: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened and let it bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise at the same time. I, the Lord, created him” (Isa. XLV). And elsewhere: “Would that you would tear open the heavens,” he says, “and descend; the mountains would flow down before your face, as in the burning of fire they would melt and burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies” (Isa. LXIV). And again: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like splendor, and her Savior is kindled like a lamp” (Isa. LXII).

Habakkuk also bears witness to the same coming of Christ, saying: “And the Lord answered and said to me: Write the vision on boxwood clearly, so that the one who reads it may grasp it; for the vision is still for its appointed time, and it shall arise at the end and not be in vain. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. II).

Let the prophet Obadiah also come forward to bear witness to Christ: “For just as you drank,” he says, “upon my holy mountain, all shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and they shall be as though they did not exist. And on Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy; and the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed them. The house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble” (Obadiah).

For what should be understood by the house of Jacob and Joseph except the Church of Christ? And what by the house of Esau except the people of the unbelieving? The house of Jacob and Joseph therefore became fire, because the holy Church, inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, kindled the formerly cold hearts of carnal people toward the love of God; and thus, from desire for the present age toward desire for the Creator, it burned up the house of Esau like stubble. Concerning this fire Truth says in our Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Christ, who is the cornerstone

Tell me this also, O Jew: who is this stone which the Lord promises that he will place in the foundation of Zion? Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, I shall place in the foundation of Zion a tested stone, a cornerstone, precious, founded upon a foundation” (Isa. XXVIII).

Who, I ask, is this stone except the one of whom David sings: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. CXVII)? And if your stony heart thinks that Isaiah meant a material stone, hear what follows: “Whoever falls upon it shall be shattered; but whomever it falls upon, it shall crush.” For it is plainly proved that a stone placed in the foundation of a wall cannot fall upon anyone.

This is certainly that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. II)—namely, Christ, begotten from an incorrupt virgin without the act of human coupling.

Hear yet another testimony which the same Isaiah offers concerning Christ, saying: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

What could be clearer than what David sings concerning Christ in the psalm? “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

Could David himself be called the Son of God, or, established upon the throne of only the Israelite people, could he possess all the kingdoms of the earth? Since, therefore, this prophecy cannot be seen to fit David, a mortal king, it follows that it must unquestionably be believed to have been spoken concerning Christ, the Son of God.

Concerning this eternal David Isaiah says: “I shall make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David. Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you shall run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you” (Isa. LV).

Had David not already departed from this life when the prophet said these things? How, then, could it be said of him that he would call the nations and that nations would run to him, when he, having been stripped of his body, no longer remained among mortals? Since, therefore, it is recognized that this prophetic oracle of promise could in no way have been spoken concerning David, who had already died, it remains that it must be believed to have been uttered concerning the one who had not yet come.

Again, through Zechariah the Lord pronounced a very clear judgment concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the nations, saying: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place an offering is sacrificed and presented to my name, a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal. I). And a little later: “And on that day, says the Lord of hosts, I shall destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and they shall no longer be remembered; and I shall remove from the earth the spirit of the false prophets and the unclean spirit” (ibid.).

Say also, Jew: of whom do you understand it to have been said when you read: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI)? Who is this king who is the father of the king’s son? Is it David, the father of Solomon? But read the psalm in order and see what follows: “And he shall endure with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation.” Could it truthfully be said that Solomon would endure forever, when he held the reins of the kingdom for scarcely forty years?

Read further, continue through the entire psalm, and consider how it is found to be alien to Solomon, especially where it says: “He shall free their souls from usury and iniquity” (ibid.). For how could Solomon free souls from iniquity, since he himself later turned to iniquity after first embracing righteousness? And to whom does that statement belong except God alone: “May his name be blessed forever”?

The psalm continues and says: “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all the nations shall magnify him.” Long ago God had promised this same thing to Abraham, saying: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI). And elsewhere to David: “The Lord swore truth to David and will not frustrate it: ‘From the fruit of your womb I shall place upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI).

In the Second Book of Kings it is also written: “These are the last words which David, son of Jesse, spoke: the man to whom the Christ of Jacob was appointed spoke” (2 Kings XXIII).

In the Book of Chronicles: “And the word of the Lord came to David through Nathan the prophet, saying: Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: I announce to you that the Lord will build you a house. When you have completed your days and go to your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall be one of your sons, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house, and I shall make his throne firm forever. I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and I shall not remove my mercy from him as I removed it from the one who was before you. I shall establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be most firmly established forever” (1 Chron. XVII).

## CHAPTER III. The errors of the Jews are refuted

Who could be so foolish, who so insane, as to believe that all these things were fulfilled in Solomon? For how is it to be understood of Solomon when it says: “After you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall be one of your sons, and I shall establish his kingdom” (2 Kings VII)? How, I ask, could this be said of Solomon, who was not born after David’s death, nor began to reign then, but reigned while his father was still alive?

What, then, is meant by the statement, “After you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you,” except that Christ is signified in this promise, who was to be raised up not before David’s death but long after his departure? He would build a house for the Lord—not from walls made by human hands, but from living and precious stones, that is, from holy and righteous people.

This too, which follows, must be considered: “His house shall be faithful, and his kingdom shall endure forever before me” (ibid.). Who could understand this as spoken of Solomon, when one reads that his house was filled with foreign women? How could Solomon’s house have been faithful to God, when it was full of Gentile women and of those who worshiped idols? He himself, seduced by them, fell into idolatry; good at the beginning, alas, he had a bad ending. Or how can his throne rightly be called most firmly established forever, when it is evident that no king from Solomon’s seed is found anywhere today?

It is necessary, therefore, Jew, that you admit that all these things—which you see cannot possibly correspond to Solomon—fit Christ in every respect. Zechariah also bears witness concerning him, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Behold, a man whose name is Rising, and beneath him he shall rise, and the temple of the Lord shall be built. He himself shall build the temple; he himself shall bear glory; he shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a priest upon his throne” (Zech. VI).

And again: “Behold,” he says, “I shall bring my servant Rising, for behold the stone which I have given before Jesus” (Zech. III). Upon the one stone are seven eyes, by which seven holy gifts of the Spirit are signified.

And if all these examples of the prophets still do not convince you, consult also Psalm Eighty-Eight and consider the Lord’s manifest promise to David concerning Christ: “I have sworn,” he says, “to David my servant: I shall prepare your seed forever, and I shall build your throne for generation after generation” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And a little later: “I shall place his hand upon the sea and his right hand upon the rivers. He shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’ And I shall make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. Forever I shall preserve my mercy for him, and my covenant shall be faithful to him. I shall establish his seed forever, and his throne like the days of heaven.”

And again: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall endure forever, and his throne shall be like the sun in my sight, and like the full moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

Examine carefully, then, all these promises made to David, and either show a king from David’s offspring preceding him upon his throne, or necessarily confess that everything was foretold concerning Christ and fulfilled in him.

Continue further and examine another psalm. Who is the one of whom it is said: “The mother of Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’?” (Ps. LXXXVIII.) Who is this Most High who is also called a man, and who is the Most High? Search, examine, and turn over, if you please, all the pages of sacred speech, and consider that “Most High” is everywhere spoken of God; nowhere is it found spoken of an ordinary human being.

It remains, therefore, that when “Most High” and “man” are joined together, one person is understood to be called both God and man. Of him it is wonderfully said that the one who was born in her—that is, in Zion—himself founded her. For a city must first be founded, and only afterward can a man be born in it. But who can first construct a city and afterward emerge from his mother’s womb within it? Who, I ask, except our Redeemer, who deigned to become what he had made?

What will you now attempt to object to these things, Jew? With what shameless audacity of mind will you be able to oppose such clear, such evident, such divine assertions? Granted that, in your blasphemy, you say that Christ could have fabricated lies about himself: if he were not God, could he nevertheless, before he was born, have foretold himself through the mouths of others?

I also take pleasure in hearing how you understand the following: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the king” (Psalm XLIV). Who is that king to whom God speaks of his works? Perhaps you will say to me: David. But read the sixth psalm in sequence and understand the truth of its meaning. Descend a little farther and ask—not me, but the Lord himself—who is the king to whom he himself speaks of his works. Hear what God himself says to the king mentioned above: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (ibid.).

If, then, the one who speaks is God, and the one to whom the speech is directed is God, it follows that it is not the temporal David but the Son, coeternal with the Father, who is truly “mighty in hand,” that must be understood.

Nor do I think that the following passage, which you likewise interpret as referring to David, should be passed over in silence: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm CVII). If, as you assert, this is to be understood of David, how can what follows be applied to David?

“With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” And again: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Therefore, if you cannot bend what follows to an interpretation concerning David, you are compelled also to affirm that what precedes was spoken of Christ, to whom it most evidently applies.

Concerning him Isaiah plainly declares, saying: “On that day there shall be a root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; the nations will entreat him, and his tomb will be glorious” (Isaiah XI). The root of Jesse stands as a sign for the peoples when Christ impresses the seal of the cross upon human foreheads. His tomb, moreover, is so glorious that, apart from the glory which we, the redeemed, offer him with all our inmost being because of his death, we also see that the very place, radiant with miracles, summons the whole world to the contemplation of his glory.

## CHAPTER IV. Christ Is Confirmed to Be Truly the Son of God

Now, amid so many prophetic oracles and so many most evident testimonies of the saints, will you, Jesus son of Sirach, remain entirely silent? Will you, too, among the others, offer no testimony concerning Christ? Let your most eloquent wisdom now come forward and introduce into the whole world the stronger Jesus—namely, the fountain of paradise—with his four rivers under the figure of the evangelists:

“Moses,” he says, “gave the law in the commandments of righteousness, as an inheritance to the house of Jacob and as a promise to Israel. He appointed David his servant to raise up from him a most mighty king, seated upon a throne of honor for ever. He fills, like Pishon, with wisdom; like the Tigris, in the days of new growth; he fills, like the Euphrates, with understanding; he multiplies, like the Jordan, in the time of harvest; he sends forth instruction like light, and, standing forth like Gihon in the day of vintage” (Sirach XXIV).

Behold, good Jesus, one testimony concerning Christ. Give us another in turn:

“In his word,” he says, “the wind was stilled; by his thought he appeased the abyss; and the Lord Jesus planted him. Because of him the end of the journey was completed, and in his word all things were brought to completion” (Sirach XLIII).

We shall say many things and shall fail for lack of words. He himself is the consummation of words. In all our glorifying, what will we be able to accomplish? For he is almighty above all his works; the Lord is terrible and exceedingly great, and marvelous is his power. However greatly you may glorify the Lord, his magnificent majesty will still surpass it and remain wonderful. Blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, for he is greater than every praise. Exalting him, be filled with strength; do not weary yourselves, for you cannot attain it. Who has seen him and declared him? And who has magnified him as he was from the beginning? Many things greater than these are hidden, for we have seen only a few of his works.

Whoever considers the order of Scripture can doubt that all these things plainly apply to our Redeemer? Let Jesus add a third testimony concerning our Savior, so that, as I might say, every word may stand on the testimony of two or three—indeed, of several testimonies. He says:

“Christ cleansed his sins, exalted his horn for ever, gave him the covenant of kings, and the throne of glory in Israel” (Sirach XLVII).

If, then, Christ—who according to the flesh derived his origin from David—cleansed David’s sins, exalted David’s horn for ever, and bestowed upon him the throne of glory, it is altogether clear that he is the Son of David and that he is also David’s creator. The reader will recognize that these words are spoken of David if he passes through the preceding text with a continuous glance.

Let Isaiah continue to bear witness concerning Christ:

“I will place a lion over those who have fled from Moab and over the remnant of the land. Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah XVI).

From this people of the Moabites came forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world and rules throughout the earth. For the one who is called a lion because of his strength is himself proclaimed a lamb because of his gentleness. The rock of the desert is understood as Ruth, who, left desolate by the death of her former husband, bore Obed from Boaz; from their stock, too, Christ descended.

When, therefore, I intermingle the statements of the prophets here, now bringing forward the testimony of one and now returning to the words of another whom I had already left, I do this out of weariness—or rather, for the purpose of avoiding satiety—lest, if several testimonies of one prophet were heaped together at once, they should produce disgust in the listeners. I also make a point of giving the prophets’ names with each individual testimony, so that, if anyone should happen to seek the place where something is said, it may easily be found and calumny avoided.

Let Daniel come forward once again as a witness and bring into the midst what he learned concerning Christ. But first let him relate what King Nebuchadnezzar saw after he ordered the three boys to be thrown into the furnace of fire:

“Behold,” he says, “I see four men walking loose in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Daniel III).

Behold, Jew, you have the Son of God. Why do you continue striving to deny the Son of God? Speak; answer. What could have been expressed more clearly or more plainly concerning the Son of God than to say “the Son of God”? If you can now offer no objection and find no escape, surrender; humbly hand yourself over to the victor, and confess that you have been defeated and utterly overcome.

Now let Daniel himself say what he saw concerning Christ, the Son:

“I was watching in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days. They presented him before him, and he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Daniel VII).

And again, in his eighth vision, the same Daniel says:

“Know, therefore, and listen attentively, and understand: from the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks, and the walls shall be rebuilt in the distress of the times. And after sixty weeks Christ shall be slain, and there shall not be his people, who will deny him” (Daniel IX).

What could be said more openly or explicitly concerning Christ’s death than this statement: “Christ shall be slain”? No mystical figure is hidden here, no obscure meaning, but rather an open account, although a history of future events is now being narrated.

To this same Daniel, the angel Gabriel had also said a little earlier:

“Give heed to the word and understand the vision: seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to an end, sin may receive its conclusion, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (ibid.).

If you doubt the predetermined number of years, read Tertullian, and you will plainly find that four hundred and ninety years elapsed from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, until the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, ruler of the Roman Empire. Seventy weeks unquestionably amount to four hundred and ninety years.

You say, however, that Christ has not yet come and that you still await his coming. But who can doubt that this number of years has elapsed since Daniel’s time, when I know that one thousand and forty years have already been added to that total?

It is therefore utterly shameless, after so long a period has been added to the prophetic number, still to assert that the Savior’s coming is future. At the time when the Lord lived among human beings, the malice of the Jews could perhaps oppose the truth by claiming that it doubted whether so great a period of time had been completed. But now, when such a multitude of years has grown beyond the number mentioned above, who can claim to doubt the fixed number, when he can scarcely calculate the additional stretches of time that have accumulated?

Again, Isaiah speaks most plainly of Christ’s passion and death, saying:

“Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? He will rise up like a tender shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has no form or beauty; we saw him, and there was no appearance in him, and we desired him despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness. His face was as though hidden and despised; therefore we did not esteem him.

“Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows; and we considered him as a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded because of our iniquities, crushed because of our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we were healed.

“All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned to his own way. And the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all.

“He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth. He was taken away from distress and judgment. Who will declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living; because of the crime of my people I struck him.

“He will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity and there was no deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. If he gives his life for sin, he will see a long-lived offspring; and the will of the Lord will prosper in his hand, because he handed over his life to death and was counted among criminals. Yet he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors, that they might not perish.”

Do you still wish to hear other, ever clearer testimonies concerning Christ’s death, expressed without any obscurity at all? Hear, then, what Solomon asserts concerning the Jews plotting against Christ and deliberating his death:

“The ungodly said among themselves: ‘Come, let us ensnare the righteous man, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works; he reproaches us for sins against the law and denounces against us the sins of our discipline. He professes to have knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God. He has become for us a condemnation of the thoughts of our souls.

“He is burdensome even to behold, because his life is unlike that of others and his ways are altered. We are considered by him as triflers, and he withdraws from our ways as from uncleanness. He declares the latter end of the righteous blessed and boasts that he has God as his father.

“Let us see, then, whether his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him; then we shall know what his end will be. For if he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies. Let us question him with insult and torture, so that we may know his reverence. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for, according to his words, he will be regarded.’

“These things they thought, and they went astray, for their wickedness blinded them. They did not know the mysteries of God, nor did they hope for the reward of righteousness, nor did they judge rightly the honor of souls” (Wisdom II).

And Jeremiah says:

“The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins; to him we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lamentations IV).

And through blessed Job, the Lord himself, placed in his passion, complains, saying:

“My wrinkles bear witness against me, and the liar rises up against my face, contradicting me. He also gathers his fury against me; threatening me, he gnashes his teeth at me. My enemy has looked upon me with terrifying eyes.

“They opened their mouths against me; reproaching me, they struck my cheek; they were satisfied with my sufferings. God has shut me up with the wicked and delivered me into the hands of the impious. He surrounded me with his spears and pierced my loins; he did not spare me and poured out my entrails upon the earth” (Job XVI).

All these things, utterly foreign to blessed Job himself, are found to have been fulfilled in Christ with the clearest evidence.

[Col. 0057A] Behold the one who, after such a manifest light of examples, still needs testimonies: it remains for him to demand the light of a lamp in order to contemplate the sun shining at midday. For when you see before you, Jew, the rays of so many heavenly stars shining forth, I marvel what such dense darkness of blindness can still occupy even empty eye-sockets. This clear light of truth could not be hidden even from the man who had lost the eyes of his heart in the darkness of gloomy greed—namely, Balaam, who, while he preferred the light to the disdain of others,* walked himself in darkness. If, then, Jew, you do not wish to have the guidance of those who see along the way of truth, at least, being blind, follow this blind man as your guide.

[Col. 0058A] Hear, therefore, what he himself says:

“Balaam son of Beor said; the man whose eye is closed said; the hearer of the words of God, who knows the doctrine of the Most High and sees the vision of the Almighty, who, falling, has his eyes opened, said:

“‘I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A STAR SHALL RISE from Jacob, and a scepter shall arise from Israel; he shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth. Edom shall be his possession, and Seir shall become the inheritance of his enemies; but Israel shall act courageously. One shall arise from Jacob who will rule and destroy the remnants of the city’” (Numbers XXIV).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0057]

## 41–42. THIRD LITTLE WORK. A DIALOGUE BETWEEN A JEW WHO QUESTIONS AND A CHRISTIAN WHO RESPONDS IN OPPOSITION. TO THE SAME HONESTUS

### ARGUMENT

He refutes the obstinacy of the same Jews with still greater force by resolving certain sophistical questions that they frivolously raise against Christians. All of these depend upon the question why, if Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law are neglected by Christians. He therefore shows that the precepts of the Mosaic Law were mystical and prophetic signs of future things, and that for this reason they reached their fulfillment in Christ.

[Col. 0057B] Now, concerning certain ceremonies about which you often inquire with excessive scrupulousness and over which you raise disputes through the loquacious circumlocutions of your questions, let a brief discourse be woven between us in the form of an inquiry and response, so that, once you have been satisfied concerning everything, you may either be compelled to surrender, having been convicted, or depart in confusion, ashamed of your disgraceful unbelief. Come, then.

### Question 1. If Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why is a Christian not circumcised in the flesh?

### Response

Rather, a Christian no longer circumcises himself for this very reason: what was prophesied through circumcision has been fulfilled by Christ. The stripping away of carnal life, which had been represented in the Old Law, is now seen to have been completed in Christ’s resurrection; and what we expect to occur in our own resurrection is already signified in the mystery of sacred baptism. Carnal circumcision is therefore rightly despised as superfluous, since the spiritual circumcision for which it had gone before as a sign is now celebrated.

### Question 2. Why does a Christian omit observing the Sabbath, if Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it?

### Response

We do not observe the Sabbath for this reason: what was then presented beforehand in figure, we now see fulfilled through the manifestation of the reality. In Christ we keep the true Sabbath of spiritual rest when we place our hope in him alone and rest in him with the full love and devotion of our hearts, so that we cease from every servile work of vice and from ambition for earthly things. He himself calls us to celebrate this Sabbath when he cries:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

We therefore consider the observance of the carnal Sabbath superfluous, since we now celebrate the true and saving Sabbath for which it was instituted.

### Question 3. If Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian disregard the distinction of foods that the law commands to be observed?

### Response

Rather, this distinction of foods is not accepted by Christians for the very reason that what was signified by it is fulfilled by Christ. The uncleanness that was then avoided in foods is now rejected in human conduct. For just as all holy and righteous people are transferred into the body of Christ, so the wicked and unrighteous are rejected by him as unclean foods.

Therefore, after the Truth itself, which was being signified, arrived, the shadow of the sign rightly ceased.

### Question 4. If Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian not take care to offer God a sacrifice of the flesh of animals?

### Response

Such a sacrifice is not offered by Christians for the very reason that whatever was performed typologically in those victims is truly fulfilled in the offering of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John I). Since all those things possessed no saving purpose except that they should unanimously point toward this sacrifice of ours, and since the whole variety of ceremonies designated this one thing, after the unique victim appeared, the manifold shadow that preceded it vanished.

For who does not know that those sacrifices were imposed upon the disobedient people chiefly so that they would not fornicate with idols, rather than offered to God as though he himself desired them?

### Question 5. If Christ came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian not observe the unleavened bread that the law prescribes?

### Response

The visible and bodily unleavened bread is disregarded by Christians for this reason: once the leaven of the old life has been purged away, the new mixture is fulfilled spiritually. At that time it was a precept of the written law; now it is a testimony. After what was signified arrived, that which signified it passed away.

[Col. 0059B]

### Question 6. If Christ came to fulfill the law, why does a Christian not celebrate Passover with the blood of the paschal lamb, when the law itself determines this so emphatically?

### Response

Here the same answer must be given as was already stated above: after the true Lamb who was being signified is recognized as having come, the one who signified him is judged superfluous. With his blood we no longer anoint wooden or stone doors; rather, we seal the innermost parts of the human being.

### Question 7. If Christ did not abolish the law, why does a Christian not celebrate the new moon commanded by the law?

### Response

The Christian also refrains from celebrating it for this reason: Christ fulfilled the whole purpose for which it was once celebrated. The solemnity of the new moon signifies that a new creation is to be made in a human being, concerning which the Apostle says:

“If anyone is therefore in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians V).

### Question 8. If Christ came not to abolish the law, why does a Christian not observe those baptisms of washings that the law prescribes?

### Response

These things do not deserve the observance of Christians because they were then shadows of future things, whose evident fulfillment we now possess. For we have been buried with Christ through baptism into death (Romans VI), so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.

### Question 9. If the law was fulfilled by Christ and not abolished, what reason is there for Christians not to celebrate the solemnity of the Feast of Tabernacles?

### Response
