The tabernacle of God is the fellowship of the Christian people. Since that tabernacle prefigured the holy Church, the sign is disregarded after what had been prefigured has come. It would not be called the tabernacle of testimony unless it bore witness to something that was to be revealed in its proper time as the truth.

What was then enacted in a figurative command is now seen present and revealed as testimony. When what was signified is already seen, what signified it is judged altogether superfluous.

### Question 10. If Christ did not wish to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian not observe the seventh year of remission?

[Col. 0060A] Or even the Truth and Wisdom of God, who, while teaching the angels in heaven, also came to teach human beings on earth, commanded his disciples to understand spiritually what he had first ordered to be observed carnally under the shadow of enigmas.

### Response

The seventh day is commanded to be kept as a day of rest so that eternal rest might be signified through it. The same is true of the seventh year and of the Jubilee, which, through the cycle of years repeated seven times by the number seven and increased by one unit to reach fifty, indicates the secure rest of perpetual blessedness.

When the Jubilee begins, trumpets are sounded, and everyone returns to his own possession, because, as the Apostle says:

“The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible.”

For each person to return to his own possession means that he will immediately receive back his body incorruptible. Then Adam will return to the ancient earth of his flesh, in which he first dwelt; then Noah, Abraham, Moses, and all the others will receive their own possession, when their bodies are restored to them incorruptible.

Our Redeemer, therefore, who opened the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the mysteries of Scripture, did not wish the Jubilee, the seventh year of remission, or the other ceremonies of legal observance to be kept carnally.

After he caused all these things to be understood spiritually, the legal commands are truly fulfilled when they are carried out according to the spiritual understanding for which they were instituted. At that time, when they were observed carnally, they were empty—namely, a shadow and image of the reality, not the reality itself.

Do you wish to hear how they were empty and vain, and not the truth itself but examples of the truth? Hear what the Lord says to Moses in Exodus:

“There shall be poles on both sides of the altar for carrying it. You shall not make it solid, but empty and hollow, just as it was shown to you on the mountain” (Exodus XXVII).

What Moses saw on the mountain is the holy Church; it is the very truth of the reality. That tabernacle constructed in the desert is its shadow and image, made according to its model.

A human being exists, for example, according to whose image a seal is made; but in the relationship of representation, the human being is called the reality and truth, while the seal appears only as the likeness and form of the reality.

After the fullness of time came, Christ fulfilled these things by commanding that they be presented spiritually. Hence it happened that, after the Lord’s coming, that earthly Jerusalem, with its temple, fell in total ruin and was utterly overthrown, so that only the holy universal Church might shine throughout the world.

As the evangelist relates, when some people spoke about the temple, saying that it was adorned with beautiful stones and gifts, he said:

“These things that you see—days will come when not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matthew XXIV; Matthew XIII; Luke XXI).

That Jerusalem was formerly a great royal city in which a famous temple had been built for God. But after the one who was the true temple of God came and began to disclose the mysteries of the heavenly Jerusalem, the earthly city was destroyed, where the heavenly one had appeared, and not one stone remained upon another in that temple.

Previously there was a high priest who purified the people with the blood of bulls and goats. But once the true High Priest came, who would purify believers with his own blood, that former priest was nowhere to be found, nor was any place left for him.

Previously there was an altar and sacrifices were celebrated. But when the true Lamb came, who offered himself as a victim to God, all those things, established as they had been for a time, ceased like shadows. For this reason divine providence brought it about that the city itself, the temple, and all those things were overthrown together, lest someone still immature and nursing in the faith, if he saw them continuing, should be astounded by the ritual of the sacrifices and the order of the ministers and be carried away by the sight of those various forms.

But, taking thought for our weakness and seeing his Church multiply, God caused all those things to be overthrown and entirely removed, so that, once the shadows and figurative images had ceased without hesitation, the old might remain; and, after the material temple had been overthrown, the Church alone might reign throughout the world.

## Epilogue

But now, after so great a cloud of witnesses, Jew, I shall provide you with an epilogue. Beginning with the origin of Christ’s humanity and proceeding through the stages of time to its consummation, I shall place the prophetic testimonies before your eyes, if you have them, so that, gathered as if into a single view, you may briefly see what you previously observed me setting forth at length and in scattered form.

For Jeremiah testifies that the Son of God was going to assume our humanity, saying:

“The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah XXXI).

If he were speaking of an ordinary man, the word “new” would be superfluous, since what is customary is seen everywhere in the human race. But that this woman would be a Virgin, through whom the Son of God would come forth, as through a heavenly gate, from the bosom of the Father into our public realm, Ezekiel shows when he says:

“He turned me toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, which faced east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate that you see shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, for it shall remain closed forever’” (Ezekiel XLIV).

Blessed Mary the Virgin is always closed, because both before childbirth and after childbirth she remains forever undefiled. Concerning her David also sings, saying:

“He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm XVIII).

That he would be a little child in the substance of humanity, so that he might make us great through the power of divinity, Isaiah bears witness, saying:

“For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and the government has been made upon his shoulder. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His rule will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace. He will sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now and for ever” (Isaiah IX).

For when he declares that the one whom he had previously described as a child would afterward be called Mighty God and Father of the age to come, he plainly manifests him as both God and man.

Isaiah says again:

“The wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the sheep will dwell together, and a little child will lead them” (Isaiah XI).

Through the inmost organs of holy charity, the wolf will dwell with the lamb, because those who were predators in the world rest peacefully with the gentle and meek. The leopard lies down with the kid because the one who was marked by the varied stains of his sins consents to be humbled together with the one who despises himself and confesses that he is a sinner.

And it is added:

“The calf, the lion, and the sheep will dwell together,” because the one who prepares himself through a contrite heart as a daily sacrifice to God, the other who raged like a lion through cruelty, and the one who perseveres like a sheep in the simplicity of his innocence have come together in the folds of the holy Church.

The little child leads these animals because he who was made a little lower than the angels daily kindles us invisibly through inward desire, lest our hearts cling to earthly things. Through the charity that he grants us, he does not permit us to fix our minds in this world. His leading us is precisely this: to kindle us continually toward his love, lest, when we love one another in return, we remain in mind in this exile.

Malachi the prophet also announces that he would be brought to the temple, saying:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face. And immediately the ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts; and who will be able to contemplate the day of his coming?’” (Malachi III).

That he would still be a little child and would be led down into Egypt and brought back from there, Hosea reveals when he says:

“As morning passes, so the king of Israel will pass away, because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son” (Hosea XI).

That he would come to Jerusalem seated upon a donkey, Zechariah declares, saying:

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, righteous and Savior, himself poor and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey. I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be destroyed. He will speak peace to the nations, and his power will be from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Zechariah IX).

That he would rebuke the Jews and correct their wickedness, Isaiah declares when he says:

“He will not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears. He will judge the poor in righteousness and rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked. Righteousness will be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins” (Isaiah XI).

Moreover, Isaiah announces that he would be baptized in the Jordan when he says:

“Let the desert rejoice, and let the solitudes of the Jordan rejoice, and my people shall see the height of the Lord and the majesty of the Lord” (Isaiah XXXV).

And shortly afterward:

“I will open rivers upon the mountains, and I will cleave the mountains and confound the thirsty land without water” (Isaiah XLIV).

That he would be handed over by one of his disciples is testified by the Lord himself, who complains through the mouth of David, saying:

“For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm XL).

And again:

“If my enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would certainly have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance” (Psalm LIV).

That he would be sold for silver, Amos bears witness, saying:

“For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he sold the righteous for silver” (Amos II).

That it would be for thirty pieces of silver, Zechariah enumerates, saying:

“They weighed out my wages at thirty pieces of silver” (Zechariah XI).

And because those same pieces of silver were thrown down by Judas after he had received them, the same prophet also explains this in detail when he adds: “And the Lord said to me: ‘Throw it to the statuary, the splendid price at which I was valued by them.’ And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord, to the statuary, the splendid one” (ibid.). A little later, concerning the condemnation of the Jews, he adds: “They will look upon me,” he says, “whom they pierced, and they will mourn with a mourning like that for an only son, and they will grieve as one grieves at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. XII). There also he plainly foretells the marks of the nails in the Lord’s hands, when he says: “And it will be said: ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he will say: ‘With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me’” (Zech. XIII). There is further added: “Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man joined to me, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (ibid.).

But that he would be hung upon wood Jeremiah makes clear, saying: “Lord, you have shown me, and I have understood; you have shown me their designs, and I was like a gentle lamb being led to the slaughter. And I did not know that they had devised plans against me, saying: ‘Let us put wood in his bread, and let us wipe him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more’” (Jer. XI).

That his garments were divided by lot he himself testifies through the mouth of David, saying: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. XXI). That he would be given gall for food and vinegar for drink, the same David testifies when he says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). But that he would be spat upon and pierced with spears, Jeremiah (?) indicates, saying: “Wicked men rose up against me without mercy; they sought to kill me, and they did not spare spitting in my face, and they wounded me with their spears.”

[Col. 0064A] Concerning his descent into hell and the deliverance of the saints, Hosea speaks in this manner: “From the hand of death I will free them; from death I will redeem them. I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell” (Hos. XIII).

But that he would rise on the third day, and at no other hour of the day than at dawn, the same Hosea openly proclaims, saying: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike us and will cure us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. We shall know, and we shall follow on to know the Lord. His going forth is prepared like the dawn, and he will come to us like the seasonal and late rain upon the earth” (Hos. VI).

But concerning the law of the New Testament, which he was to spread throughout the world, he promises through Jeremiah, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with your fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, the covenant which they annulled, although I was their master, says the Lord. But this will be the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts; I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Jer. XXXI).

[Col. 0064C] That he would ascend into heaven and send the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, David briefly comprises in a single verse, saying: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV). For Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive because by the power of his incorruptibility he swallowed up our corruption; and he gave gifts to men because, when the Spirit had been poured out from above, he granted his disciples various gifts of heavenly graces.

And Joel says: “And it will be after this: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your elders will dream dreams, and your young men will see visions. Moreover, upon my servants and handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit” (Joel II).

Concerning this same outpouring of the Spirit Isaiah testifies, saying: “Do not fear, my servant Jacob, my chosen one, whom I have chosen; for I will pour water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry ground. I will pour out my Spirit upon your offspring and my blessing upon your descendants” (Isa. XLIV).

But concerning the baptism which he was to command to be carried out throughout the world, he promises through Ezekiel, saying: “I will pour clean water over you, and you will be cleansed from all your impurities; and from all your idols I will cleanse you” (Ezek. XXXVI).

[Col. 0064D] But that he himself would judge the world, the Psalmist testifies. After first saying, “The Lord has reigned from the wood,” he adds at the end concerning the same Lord who reigned from the wood: “He will judge the world with justice and the peoples with his truth” (Ps. XCV).

Now then, Jew, since the testimonies of sacred Scripture do not draw you to faith in Christ, if the statements of all the prophets, so clear and evident, do not move you, I wish, setting aside the examples of the prophets, to contend with you by reasoning alone, [Col. 0065A] and briefly to examine with you, at the conclusion of this little work, a single small question, so that nothing that might be fitting for your conversion may appear to have been left unattempted by our efforts.

Come, then, answer me: what more serious sin are your fathers known to have committed, by which they might have kindled God’s anger more fiercely and provoked his vengeance against themselves more sharply? “Murmuring,” you will say, “idolatry, and fornication.” I agree with you in this, and I judge that those three offenses of theirs were the more condemnable; nevertheless, all these things did not suffer an irrevocable punishment under the justice of the merciful God.

For, to return to the history of your antiquity, concerning the murmuring it is read in the Book of Numbers: “Because the whole congregation cried out and wept that night, and all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness! Would that we might perish, and that the Lord would not bring us into this land, lest we fall by the sword and our wives and children be led away captive.’ And they said to one another: ‘Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt’” (Num. XIV).

Yet on account of this—the monstrous sin of murmuring—the divine vengeance did not rage against them for more than forty years, as the Lord is read to have said to them: “Your sons will wander for forty years and bear the iniquities of their fathers, until your corpses are consumed in the wilderness, according to the number of the forty days during which you inspected the land. A year will be reckoned for a day, and for forty years you will bear your iniquities” (ibid.).

[Col. 0065C] Likewise, for the calf which they worshiped beside Mount Sinai, we know that no more than twenty-three thousand men were slain by the sword, as is read in the Book of Exodus. Moses said to them: “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh, and go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses, and on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell. And Moses said: “You have consecrated your hands to the Lord, each one in his son and his brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. XXXII).

For the fornication which they committed with the daughters of the Midianites, likewise no more than twenty-three thousand men fell by the sword, as it is again written in the Book of Numbers: “And the plague ceased among the children of Israel, and twenty-three thousand men were killed” (Num. XXV).

What, then, is the reason that God is read to have exacted such a brief vengeance for the sins of your fathers, while this servitude of yours and your dispersion throughout the whole world have already been prolonged for so many centuries? Read also your Josephus (*The Jewish War*); there you will find that, as vengeance for the death of Christ, which Titus carried out together with Vespasian, ten times one hundred thousand of the Jewish people fell by the sword, and eleven times one hundred thousand were led away captive. After this, whoever among you remained, spared by the devouring sword, you appear to be subjected in servitude beneath the feet of all nations.

[Col. 0066A] Indeed, your fathers—whoever were led into captivity—even while placed in that exile were never entirely deprived of the company of the prophets, so that they might continually intercede for their sins, always recall the law of the Lord to their memory, and bring them great consolation amid their present calamities, while announcing to them the fixed time of their future return to their homeland.

As it is said through Zechariah: “The angel of the Lord said: ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.’ And the Lord answered the angel who spoke in me with good words, words of consolation” (Zech. I).

And through Jeremiah: “All these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years; and when the seventy years have been completed, I will visit the king of Babylon” (Jer. XXV), and the rest.

[Col. 0066B] It is therefore clear that, although your fathers were often struck by divine vengeance, they were nevertheless sometimes restored and refreshed by abundant consolations. But you, placed in such prolonged calamities from the passion of Christ to this very day, see no prophet anywhere among you on earth; nor do you hear at all a message divinely sent to you announcing future prosperity.

What, then, is this incurable guilt of yours? Whence comes such irremediable punishment upon you? Whence, I ask, except that you killed Christ, the Son of God, and after the deed had been carried out refused to return to the fountain of life? For this deepest abyss of your iniquity surpasses the measure of every crime and exceeds the enormity of every offense.

[Col. 0066C] Moses clearly foresaw this sin of yours when, angry against you, he said: “Gather to me all the elders of your tribes and your teachers, and I will speak these words in their hearing, and I will call heaven and earth against them. For I know that after my death you will act wickedly and quickly turn aside from the way that I have commanded you, and evils will overtake you in the final time, when you do evil in the sight of the Lord, provoking him through the works of your hands” (Deut. XXXI).

Now then, Jew, hear my counsel, so that you may have as propitious the God whom you have angered: lay aside the clothing of the old man and receive the sacrament of the new grace. Let the blessings of Garizim please you, so that you may escape the curses of Hebal (Deut. XXVII). [Col. 0066D] Abandon the error of Jewish blindness and direct yourself toward the truth of evangelical grace. Be entirely confident of pardon if, having turned to faith in Christ, you are washed in the water of holy baptism.

But since perhaps I have more influence with your heart by praying to God than with you by preaching, may the God of your fathers cast away from your heart the ancient veil of ignorance and, dispersing the darkness of error, flood you with the new light of his knowledge. He promises this through his prophet, saying: “If the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, the remnant of Israel will be saved” (Isa. X; Hos. I; Rom. IX).

## Epilogue

Behold, dearest brother Honeste, you yourself perceive that, while I strove to take account of your weakness, I did not concern myself with presenting the colored blossoms of rhetorical eloquence or the sharp arguments of dialecticians. Apart from the fact that I do not wish to follow the trappings of secular wisdom—for I know that, being occupied with secular affairs, you are unable to read through many things—I did not wish to burden you with lengthy distinctions of arguments.

Therefore, while I set before you almost bare examples from Scripture, I sent them into the quiver like a bundle of arrows. And because an abundance of responses is supplied by opposing statements, I have indeed furnished weapons; but as to how you should pour yourself forth invincibly, or how you should wield your shield, since the battles have not yet begun, I have not been able to teach you fully.

[Col. 0068A] You therefore have before you the things necessary for such a conflict. Use what has been prepared, as you decide to put it to use.

May almighty God, dearest brother, mercifully protect you from the ambushes of invisible enemies and lead you, unharmed from such a struggle, to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0067]

## 51–52. FOURTH LITTLE WORK. A SYNODAL DEBATE BETWEEN THE KING’S ADVOCATE AND THE DEFENDER OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

### Argument

In this little book the defender of the Roman Church and the advocate of King Henry are introduced disputing with one another. The cause of their dispute was this: a bad custom had become established, namely, that the Roman pontiff could not be elected unless he had first been confirmed by the emperor. Since at that time Henry III was a child and was still under guardianship, a pontiff was elected without his consent. When this was brought forward as a charge by Henry’s legates, all their objections are refuted in this debate, so that the royal advocate, gradually compelled by arguments and defeated, is brought over to the opposing opinion.

The debate is represented as having taken place before a synod of bishops who had assembled in order to pronounce judgment on this matter. The holy author addresses the antipope Cudalou in the following words.

[Col. 0067B] “But regarding this you boast and vaunt yourself: ‘The king and my imperial mother choose me; the royal majesty has raised me to this dignity.’ But since on one side the royal court protects its chosen man, while on the other the Roman Church defends its own bishop, already established upon the throne, it is fitting that a multitude of holy and prudent priests should assemble and, examining this question under the authority of canonical law, decide it.

“And since, as we hope, the Council of Osbor will shortly take place, let us now stage here, as it were in a painted tablet, a preliminary representation of that same council. According to Daniel’s vision (Dan. VII), let the thrones of the fathers be set up, let the court sit, let the books be opened, and let the question requiring a solution be brought forward.

“Let the defender of the Roman Church introduce his allegations from this side; from the other side let the royal advocate produce the arguments of his own party. Let Parma be silent with its heresiarch; let only the royal advocacy and the Roman Church speak against one another. Let the minds of the holy priests be attentive, so that they may weigh what is to be said on both sides and, when the case has been pleaded, cast their vote for a judicial sentence.

“Come, then: let the defender of the apostolic see begin; then let the royal advocate present whatever arguments he thinks appropriate.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“Since Your Beatitude, venerable fathers, is debating the matter of the apostolic see, you do not fail to understand that the issue before us concerns all the churches. When this see stands, the others stand; but if this one, which is the foundation and basis of all, is overthrown, the condition of the others must also collapse.

[Col. 0068B] “Every other church—whether the dignity of a patriarchal see, the primacy of a metropolitan church, the chairs of bishoprics, or the dignities of churches of whatever order—was established by a king, an emperor, or some ordinary human being, and each one fixed for itself, according as its will or power allowed, the rights of particular prerogatives.

“But the Roman Church was founded by that one alone and immediately raised upon the rock of the faith at its birth: the one who entrusted to the blessed keeper of the keys of eternal life the rights of both earthly and heavenly rule (Matt. XVI). It was therefore not any earthly decree, but the Word through whom heaven and earth were created, through whom, finally, all the elements were made, who founded the Roman Church. It enjoys his privilege; it is supported by his authority.

“Thus there is no doubt that whoever has taken away the right of any church commits injustice; but whoever attempts to remove from the Roman Church the privilege handed down to it by the supreme head of all the churches undoubtedly falls into heresy. While the former is marked as unjust, the latter must certainly be called a heretic.

“For he violates the faith who acts against the church that is the mother of faith, and he proves rebellious against the church which he is known to have placed before all the churches. Since, therefore, Your Holiness unquestionably recognizes these things, show, as noble and excellent sons of the Roman Church—not just any sons—the compassion of piety toward your mother, and judge whether she ought to be destroyed by choosing a pontiff for herself.

“It is astonishing if the canonical force attributed to lesser churches did not permit this one church alone, which is the head of all, to exercise it.”

[Col. 0068D]

### Royal Advocate

“Your lengthy declamation has secured attention, goodwill, and receptiveness—and this more according to the custom of a judicial court than according to the rule of a synodal council. In such a place we should not be greatly concerned with the elegance of painstakingly composed speech, but rather with the purity of a living judgment.

“To lay our complaint before the holy priests, it is enough for us to say that you enthroned a pope without the consent of our lord the king, plainly to the injury and contempt of royal majesty.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“We can neither deny nor ought to deny that the pope’s ordination took place; but in every way we repel the king’s alleged injury. Let us first see, if it pleases you, whether a pope could have been made without the king, and afterward let us discuss the king’s injury.”

[Col. 0069B]

### Royal Advocate

“We know with complete certainty that those who are determined by canonical authority to obey a pontiff after he has been ordained ought to choose him when he is ordained. But since the pope is the universal pontiff, not only the Roman people but also the Roman emperor, who is the head of the people, owes him obedience.

“It must therefore be judged proper that the people should choose a pope without his head and obey one whom the emperor did not choose. It is therefore established that, unless the assent of the Roman king has been given, the election of the Roman pontiff will not be complete.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“According to the terms of your argument, then, it must be stated that neither Stephen, nor Sixtus, nor Cornelius, nor, finally, Clement, nor Sylvester, nor blessed Peter the apostle himself, deserve the papal name, since they were not elected by emperors in their respective times.”

### Royal Advocate

“Gentile kings cannot be brought forward as examples for the election of which we are speaking. Since they were ignorant of the Christian faith, they could not ordain a pontiff for Christians. Christian princes, however, always elected Roman pontiffs.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“Whoever lies in ordinary conversation is called a liar; but whoever utters falsehoods in the presence of venerable priests undoubtedly incurs the crime of sacrilege. You said that Christian princes always elected Roman pontiffs. Review with me the histories of ecclesiastical antiquity; diligently examine the catalogue of the Roman bishops. When you find that only very few received royal consent in their election, admit that you have uttered an obvious lie.

“For which king elected Damasus the Spaniard, son of Antonius? Which elected Innocent, the Albanian, son of Innocent? Which, finally, elected Zosimus the Greek, son of Ebramius? Which further elected Leo, son of Quirianus, from Tuscany? Which elected Hilary, son of Crispinus, from Sardinia? Which elected Celestine, son of Priscus, a Roman citizen? Which elected Boniface or Anastasius, likewise Romans? I would add many more, unless I were to cause weariness.

[Col. 0070A] “But lest you think that I lack material because I stop their enumeration, which emperor elected Simplicius of Tibur? Felix, a Roman by nationality? Gelasius the African, son of Valerius? Symmachus, son of Fortunatus, from the province of Sardinia? Hormisdas, son of Justus, a Campanian by nationality; John, Tuscan by rank; Felix, Samnite by nationality; Boniface, son of Sigibald; Mercurius, son of Projectus; Agapitus, a Roman by origin, son of Cordianus?

“Which king is read to have given his consent to the election of any one of these, when in their times Christian princes are read to have ruled the Roman state—namely, Valentinian the Elder; Valens, his brother, who was killed in battle against the Goths near Adrianople; Gratian, who was slain by the tyrant Maximus; Valentinian the Younger, who was killed by his own count at Vienne; then Arcadius, Honorius, Theodosius; that John who was killed at Ravenna; Valentinian III, who was slain on the Campus Martius; Marcian, Leo, Majorian, Severus, Anthemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Zeno; that Nepos who was killed at his own villa near Salona; Augustulus, Anastasius, Justinus, and the other Roman emperors, whom I pass over to avoid a sprawling style?

“Give me, then, one of those whom we have enumerated who either sought a bishop or, as a ruler, gave assent in the election, and I will surrender and declare you worthy of the laurel. Otherwise, if you cannot do so, you must admit that you have been completely defeated in this matter.

“But as for the fact that the emperor Maurice is read to have given his consent to blessed Gregory, and a very few other princes to the promotion of certain others: this was dictated by the disturbances of the times and the terrible storm of wars.”

### Royal Advocate

“If to lie is to speak against one’s mind, it is rash to accuse me so brazenly of lying, since I thought that I had spoken not falsely but truly. Nevertheless, I do not deny that I have been overcome in this point as well.”

### Defender of the Church

“But so that this very matter may become still clearer, and so that you may recognize more plainly for yourself that you have lost this ground of combat, read the edict of the emperor Constantine, where he established the apostolic see as having primacy over all the churches in the world. After the founder had raised a basilica above the body of blessed Peter, and after he had built the Lateran palace in honor of blessed Saviour, he immediately established the dignity of the Roman Church through the wording of an imperial rescript.

“There he offered to blessed Sylvester and his successors that, in royal fashion, they should be crowned on the head with a golden crown and assume the other insignia of royal dress (see the notes at the end of the little work). But blessed Sylvester took for his own use the ornaments which he judged appropriate to the priestly office; the crown, however, and the other things that appeared more ambitious than mystical, he omitted.

“Constantine also granted him the Lateran palace, which until then had been a royal court, by perpetual right, and handed over the kingdom of Italy to be governed. For these too are the words of that king himself: ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘we have judged it fitting that our empire and the power of the kingdom be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that a city be built in the province of Byzantium, in the best location, bearing our name, and that our empire be established there; for where the principate of the priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly emperor, it is not right that an earthly emperor should have power there.’

[Col. 0071A] “You have heard that an earthly emperor has no power in the Roman Church. How, then, could a priest not be elected without the discretion of one who has no power there? He himself departed for Constantinople, as though he would reign perpetually in a second Rome.

“Much later, the emperor Theodosius began the basilica of blessed Paul; when he died, his son Honorius completed that same basilica to its very end. These men likewise confirmed the privilege of the Roman Church. How, then, would they retain for themselves a prerogative in the election of the Roman pontiff, when they did not at all strive to subject the Roman Church to themselves, but rather to place it first; not to command, but to obey; not to excel, but to be subject?”

### Royal Advocate

“I entirely agree, and I consider the matter settled by what you say. But suppose that royal majesty cannot now claim this on the basis of the custom of the ancient princes. Nevertheless, you cannot deny that my lord the king’s father, the emperor Henry of blessed memory, was made patrician of the Romans and received from them the right of precedence in the election and ordination of the pontiff.

“Moreover, something even more authoritative is added: Pope Nicholas granted my lord the king this privilege, which had already descended to him by paternal right, and further confirmed it in the text of a synodal decree. Since no private individual ought to be deprived of his right until, after the matter has been examined, a judicial sentence has been pronounced against him, how has royal majesty lost this prerogative of its dignity—a prerogative which it received through the generosity of the apostolic see and inherited through the paternal right of imperial rank? How, I ask, did he lose without judgment the place of dignity he had acquired in the Roman Church, when he did not offend the Roman Church?”

[Col. 0071D]

## 56. Defender of the Roman Church

“We too defend this privilege for our unconquerable king, and we fervently desire that he may always possess it in full and unimpaired. Yet the Roman Church is a much nobler and more exalted mother of the king than his mother according to the flesh.

“The former gave birth to him so that, through her transmission, he might return to dust; the latter gave birth to him so that she might make him a co-heir of Christ, who reigns without end. We all know clearly that the king, although of excellent character, is still a child. What wrong, then, does the Roman Church do if, while her son was still underage and still needed a guardian, she herself assumed the office of guardian and fulfilled the right that belonged to him?

“For who does not know that a child is ignorant of how to choose a priest? Often the mother bursts into the judge’s tribunal, summons witnesses, calls in notaries, and through formal attestations and, in addition, duly authenticated written records, transfers all the rights of her property to her son. Meanwhile, until he reaches the growth of youthful age and becomes capable of reason, she administers everything and orders everything; thus she arranges, according to her own prudent care, the patrimony that is already another’s right.

“Is she for that reason to be said to be taking away what was granted to her son? Rather, she is more truly said, as I think, to be serving the cause of piety, because what her still inexperienced son could have squandered and wasted, she preserves—properly arranged for herself, carefully retained, and rationally ordered.

“A carnal mother therefore helps her son in earthly matters; and should Mother Church not offer help to her royal son in spiritual gifts? Let the cunning that deserves punishment be silenced: it condemns what it ought to have praised and seeks to accuse the one who deserves a title of glory for her good deeds.

“Furthermore, because of changes in circumstances, the order of affairs often has to be changed. For when the Roman Church appointed a pontiff for itself, such fuel of discord had inflamed the citizens into sedition, and such envy and hatred had disturbed the hearts of the tumultuous people, that we could not possibly await a response from royal clemency from lands so far away.

“Unless a bishop were ordained as quickly as possible, a destructive sword would rage among the people, inflicting mutual wounds, and no small slaughter of Roman citizens would take place.”

### Royal Advocate

“Assert whatever you wish and argue whatever pleases you, provided it remains certain that what the pope granted, what he established by decree, and what he confirmed in writing could in no way have been changed.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“What wonder is it if the decrees of a human being, still surrounded by the frailty of the flesh, are changed, when even almighty God—who knows, of course, all things that are to come—changes those things which he himself establishes? For sometimes he diminishes something of what he promises, or even withdraws it altogether; sometimes he threatens evils and does not inflict them.”

### Royal Advocate

“Let the things you have proposed be demonstrated by examples from Scripture. What, then, is something that God ever promised and diminished?”

[Col. 0072D]

### Defender of the Roman Church

“If it has not escaped your memory, you can recall that the Lord said to Noah: ‘My Spirit will not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days will be one hundred and twenty years’ (Gen. VI). But since Scripture records that Noah was then five hundred years old when the Lord spoke these things to him, and that he was already six hundred when the cataclysm broke out, it is plainly evident that twenty years were subtracted from the number previously prescribed.

“God therefore reduced the span of life which he had promised to the human race, because the guilt of their perversity had increased.

“The Holy Spirit also promised Judah through the patriarch Jacob, saying: ‘The scepter will not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent’ (Gen. XLIX). Yet we do not read that men from the tribe of Judah always held the leadership over Israel in the time of the Judges, nor are kings from that same tribe found to have held the principate until the coming of Christ.

“It is therefore established that almighty God often diminishes what he has promised to man, because man has not fulfilled what he owed to God.”

### Royal Advocate

“Show also where God promised some good thing and did not effectively fulfill it.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“Recall that the Lord says to Josiah, king of Judah: ‘Because you saw the words of the book, and your heart was terrified, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words concerning this place and its inhabitants, and you tore your garments and wept before me, therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your tomb in peace’ (IV Kings XXII).

“Yet a little later Scripture says: ‘In his days Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates, and Josiah went to meet him, and he was killed at Megiddo when he saw him’ (IV Kings XXIII).

“It is also said to Zedekiah, king of Judah, through Jeremiah: ‘Hear the word of the Lord, Zedekiah king of Judah. Thus says the Lord to you: You will not die by the sword, but you will die in peace; and according to the burnings of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so they will burn for you; and “Alas, lord,” they will mourn for you, because I have spoken this word, says the Lord’ (Jer. XXXIV).

“Whoever examines the sequence of history will never be able to discover how this could have happened. For after he had once been captured by the king of Babylon and carried off to Babylon, he is never afterward read to have been released from his bonds.

“By a just judgment, therefore, God sometimes withdraws from man the good things he has promised, when rebellious man refuses to keep his commands.”

### Royal Advocate

“Explain also how God does not inflict what he has threatened.”

### Defender of the Roman Church

“No one who frequents the threshold of the Church is ignorant that Jonah, sent by the Lord to Nineveh, cried out, saying: ‘Yet forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown’ (Jonah III).

“But because that city turned to God with all its heart, it was by no means destroyed by the overthrow of ruin according to the Lord’s threatening sentence.

“Although almighty God is not only truthful but truth itself, while the purpose of his counsel remains inviolate, he often changes the external order of his judgment according to the quality of human merit, whether good or evil, so that one corrected from wickedness may escape what God justly threatens, while one who has fallen into guilt may in no way receive the good things he promises.

“Hence he says through Jeremiah: ‘Make your ways and your practices good, and hear the voice of the Lord your God; then the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you’ (Jer. XVII).

“Hence also the Lord says to Eli through a man of God: ‘Speaking, I spoke that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now, says the Lord, far be this from me; for whoever glorifies me, I will glorify, but those who despise me will be dishonored’ (I Kings II).”

### Royal Advocate

“You have rightly and completely supported everything you proposed with clear testimonies from Scripture. Now return for a little while to what came before and, in accordance with the terms of your undertaking, give an account of the injury done to the lord king.”

“You allege civil war and invoke impending danger in defense of your argument. ### Royal Advocate
[Col. 0074D] This is certainly clear and obvious. But what portent, what trickery you are nurturing under this thread of argument, I do not know.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

Remove the trickery and understand the truth. You fear me as though I were laying snares for you; hear Paul bearing truthful witness concerning his fellow apostle Peter: “Before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.” We therefore see that Peter was not rigid, but discerning. For he feared that the Jews might, through the occasion provided by the Gentiles, fall away from the faith of Christians; and, so as not to lose the flock entrusted to him, he imitated the example of the good shepherd. [Col. 0075A] For he became as a Jew to the Jews, so that he might win the Jews. Thus Christ appeared in the form of sinful flesh, so that he might free humanity from sins; and although he did not doubt that the law of Moses was to be abolished, nevertheless, out of consideration for brothers who were still inexperienced and weak, he temporarily maintained the shadow of the law, so that he might eventually lead them forward to a perfect knowledge of the fullness of truth. In this, therefore, blessed Peter gave us a rule of discernment: that at times, where it causes no great harm, we should deviate slightly from the path of strictness, so that we may be able to care for the weak.

**Royal Advocate**

Since you say that Peter at times observed the Jewish law, why do you not also say what is read in the same Epistle—namely, that Paul rebuked him to his face? [Col. 0075B] “I opposed him to his face,” he says, “because he was blameworthy.” And he said to him: “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Galatians II). Since, then, you mentioned the former, why did you suppress the latter in silence?

**Defender of the Roman Church**

What Peter did out of compassionate mercy, Paul rebuked in the exercise of disciplinary authority. Peter acted by dispensation, in order to remove a stumbling block from the weak; Paul corrected this, so that anyone indiscriminately might not bring it forward as an example. From Peter let us learn to be discerning when danger threatens; from Paul’s words let us be instructed, so that in matters of soundness our life may serve rectitude with exceptional devotion.

**Royal Advocate**

[Col. 0075C] I certainly commend the explanation you have given; but since you have proposed the teaching of the two apostles, it is strange that, leaving Paul aside, you have brought forward Peter alone as an example.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

Do not, brother, run childishly—indeed, do not fly—but proceed. For the gravity of the matter requires that the delivery of speech also be measured. Hear next Paul as well, setting before our eyes the golden guideline of discernment and as the author of that same compassionate dispensation. For, as the history of the Acts of the Apostles testifies: [Col. 0075D] “Paul traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches, and came to Derbe and Lystra. And behold, there was a certain disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing widow, but his father was a Gentile” (Acts XVI). To come to the point, the Apostle circumcised him because he feared the Jews—indeed, the Jews who were in those regions. Why, then, did he circumcise a faithful man who was not a Jew, who was in fact uncircumcised but Gentile by nationality, unless he was serving the purpose of discernment, lest the Jewish faithful, falling into scandal, should withdraw from the faith?

[Col. 0075D] This also comes to mind now: at one time, following the custom of the Nazarenes, he grew his hair in fulfillment of a vow; and after he had sailed to Syria, while staying at Cenchreae, he shaved his head in accordance with the commands of the law. Luke, the sacred writer of the History, further reports: [Col. 0076A] “When we had arrived,” he says, “in Jerusalem, the brothers gladly received us; and on the following day James and all the elders who were with him, having approved his Gospel, said to him: ‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealous for the law. But they have heard about you that you teach the Jews who are among the Gentiles to depart from Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom. What, then, is to be done? Certainly the multitude must assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you: we have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take them, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; and everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk observing the law.’ Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having been purified with them, [Col. 0076B] entered the temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification, until the offering was made for each one of them” (Acts XVIII and XXI).

[Col. 0076B] Why, then, did Paul shave his head according to the ceremonies of the Jews, practice going barefoot, offer sacrifices, and, while destroying the law, observe the precepts of the law? Why, I ask, did he do all these things, unless so that scandal might be removed from those who had become believers from among the Jews? He assumed the form of illness in order to take away diseases from the sick; he observed the ceremonies of the law, concerning which he nevertheless says in his Epistle: “The things that were gain to me, these I have counted as loss, and for the sake of Christ I regard them as refuse” (Philippians III). He circumcised a man, and yet he cries out with terrifying force: “I tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” [Col. 0076C] (Galatians V). What greater sin—or worse—could there be than to lose Christ, violate the rule of the Christian religion, introduce the rites of the Jewish law, and attack the new grace of the Gospel? And yet the Apostle Paul is seen to have done these things outwardly, so that, at the very beginnings of the new faith, tender minds might not suffer scandals.

For, as far as outward appearances are concerned, Cerinthus and Ebion are found to have done scarcely anything worse than Paul. They believed in Christ, but were anathematized by their parents for this sole reason: that they mingled the ceremonies of the law with the Gospel of Christ; and thus they confessed the new in such a way that they did not alter the old. But behold: when it is said that James and all the elders gave this counsel to Paul, then all the disciples likewise did what Paul did; both the one who acted and those who gave the counsel to act share the same merit in this matter.

If, then, the very princes of the world—whose laws are obeyed not only by earthly kingdoms but even by the heights of heaven—did not hesitate, for the sake of a very few men who were then present, to ascend into such a perilous undertaking, why should it not have been permitted to us, who are certainly little ones and lie far beneath their footsteps, to come to the aid of the innumerable multitude of the city of Rome? But why speak of the apostles’ having avoided scandal for the weak and newly converted, when their own teacher and Lord, under whose authority all ages are subjected, also forestalled scandal for the Jews as an example for our imitation? [Col. 0077A] “Simon,” he says, “from whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute—from their own sons or from strangers?” When he replied, “From strangers,” he immediately added: “Then the sons are free. But so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the fish that first comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matthew XVII).

Therefore, to soften the strictness of rectitude and to maintain the virtue of discernment, if Peter is not sufficient for you as an example, join Paul to him as well. But if neither of them is sufficient for your shameless obstinacy, be ashamed to advance beyond Jesus through the foolishness of your insolent speech: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans X).

[Col. 0077B] **Royal Advocate**

We do not reject the virtue of discernment, approved by so many testimonies of Scripture; but heaven forbid that there should be any virtue so sublime or so pre-eminent that, in our zeal to maintain it, we ought to fall into the abyss of anathema. Since everything prescribed to us by divine law undoubtedly tends toward this end—that eternal fellowship may unite us with our Creator—if, God forbid, it should happen that we depart from him through a sentence of cursing, what virtue, what discernment, what pious compassion, as it is called, could compensate us for so incomparable a loss? Surely, if virtue is desired solely so that fellowship with almighty God may be acquired, what kind of virtue will that be which drives us away from communion with the divine household?

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0077C] Explain clearly why you pursue this argument, since its implications are hidden from us.

**Royal Advocate**

The text of the synodal decree, which blessed Pope Nicholas established with the consent of the entire council, to which he added a clause in his own hand, and which the venerable and celebrated assembly of so many bishops confirmed by its subscription, could not, according to custom, be free from the bond of anathema. Therefore, out of compassion—or condescension, I do not know what you call it—for the raging populace, you ought by no means to have entangled yourselves in such insoluble bonds of a sentence. It is ridiculous to rescue someone so overwhelmed by the abyss of the sea that the rescuer himself is compelled to remain beneath the surging heaps of foaming waves.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0077D] When you speak so imprudently, you fight against me in the manner of blindfolded gladiators (see the scholia). They fight with their eyes always closed: they wound others, certainly, but do not know how to protect themselves from wounds. You say that we must by no means fall under anathema, even if through this we might be able to assist weak brothers. Behold, you have brandished the sword and attempted to inflict a wound, but you did not see where to place the shield before yourself. Have you already forgotten what I said above—that blessed Paul says in his Epistle: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians V)? [Col. 0078A] And yet what he so strictly forbade, he himself fulfilled out of charity toward weak brothers, so that they might not suffer scandal. What greater or worse anathema could anyone undergo than to be denied the benefit of Christ because of his condemnation for guilt? For whoever does not benefit from Christ is undoubtedly under anathema; and to become anathema is nothing other than to be expelled from fellowship with Christ, in whom all nations are blessed.

If, then, Paul did not fear undergoing this anathema out of charity toward his brothers—indeed, he wholly escaped it, when he circumcised not just any man but a Christian disciple—tell me, I ask, where have you lost the eyes of your heart, when you assert that what the Apostle did ought not to be done? For he himself says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” [Col. 0078B] (Romans XV).

63 **Royal Advocate**

It is plausible that, just as Paul, his fellow apostle, rebuked Peter for his renewed adoption of Judaizing, so likewise he rebuked himself after he had circumcised the disciple; nor will I ever be persuaded otherwise, unless perhaps something of the kind can be found in his words.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

So that no blemish of doubt may remain in your mind, and so that no darkness may henceforth confuse your heart concerning this matter, hear what that same Paul says to the Romans: [Col. 0078C] “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart; for I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kindred according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Romans IX).

Behold: since Paul was not compelled by necessity as we were, he freely and voluntarily desires to be accursed for his brothers; yet you set before me an anathema to be feared, when you see that I was both bound by an altogether unavoidable necessity and inclined by zeal for charity, so that so great a multitude of brothers might not fall. Hear also what Moses says when he pleads for the people of Israel: “I beseech you, Lord: this people has committed a great sin; they have made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, erase me from your book which you have written” (Exodus XXIII). [Col. 0078D] This will indeed be fulfilled when he says to the reprobate at the judgment: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew XXV).

Behold: on the one side Paul desires to become accursed for his brothers; on the other Moses asks to be erased from God’s book for love of the people he was leading. And only the Roman Church, which teaches piety and charity in a special and principal way throughout the whole world, dares not rescue her sons—whom she daily generates through the mystery of holy baptism—from imminent dangers and swords already brandished on every side?

[Col. 0079A] “Cursed is the man,” Saul said, “who eats bread before evening, until I have avenged myself on my enemies” (1 Samuel XIV). In this curse, as we read, Jonathan fell; but charity, by which he had bravely fought for the people, delivered him from the sentence of impending death. Do you wish to hear what the same Apostle says even about Jesus himself, the author of every blessing? “Christ,” he says, “to free us from the curse of the law, became a curse” (Galatians III).

If, then, the very author of eternal blessing, in order to release us from the bond of the curse, did not disdain to submit to a curse; if all the saints of either the New or the Old Testament, while imitating the example of their head and desiring to assist weak brothers in dangers, in no way shrank from undergoing the sentence of anathema—why do you strive to charge me with a single sin and fail to see that charity brought this about, charity which covers a multitude of sins? (1 Peter IV.) How can the sentence of any human being bind me, when charity itself, which is God [Col. 0079B] (1 John IV), sets me free? Let the one who imputes a human anathema be ashamed, since through the grace of charity he is, with me, a recipient of eternal blessing. 64

**Royal Advocate**

Whenever truth itself has failed someone struggling in a dispute, it is foolish to persist obstinately through evasions and subtleties; it is ridiculous to linger any longer over more prolix words. As for the bond of anathema, by which I had until now thought you bound, you have extricated yourself from it so skillfully that nothing further can be brought against you, and nothing reasonable can be opposed to you on this point. Nevertheless, I still see that material remains which I may, not without cause, bring forward against you as an objector.

You say that, being constrained by necessity and confined within a brief interval of time, [Col. 0079C] you were altogether unable to await the consent of the royal majesty in the election of the pontiff. This is plainly frivolous. For it is established that approximately three months elapsed between the death of Pope Nicholas of holy memory and the Kalends of October, when this man succeeded him. Let us see, then, whether during so long a delay—namely, a period of three months—you could not have obtained from the royal court a written receipt for the pragmatic sanction.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

Behold, you compel me to bring forth in common speech what I had resolved to pass over in silence out of reverence for the imperial palace. But in accordance with the urgency of your demand, let your excellent deed now be brought into the open—a deed unheard of throughout all the ages. [Col. 0079D] For the governors of the royal court, conspiring against the Roman Church with certain, so to speak, holy bishops of the Teutonic kingdom, convened a council in which you condemned the pope as though by a synodal sentence and, with utterly incredible audacity, presumed to annul everything that had been established by him. In this you not only judged but prejudged the matter, and even voided—if I may say so—the privilege that the aforesaid pope had conferred upon the king. For when everything he had established is destroyed by your sentence, whatever had been granted by him to the king is consequently abolished as well.

But far be it from us that, because of the insolence of any man, the king—who, so far as we are concerned, was innocent—should lose something belonging to his [Col. 0080A] right; and we do not permit the one whom, by God’s authority, we await with all our wishes for the imperial height to suffer harm to royal dignity on account of another’s guilt.

But to run through the whole history of our unheard-of calamity: Cardinal Stephen, a priest of the apostolic see, a man distinguished by such gravity and the splendor of such integrity, and finally adorned—as is by no means obscure—with such flowers of virtue, was sent to the royal court with apostolic letters. He was not admitted by the court officials; instead, for nearly five days, to the injury of blessed Peter and the apostolic see, he remained shut out before the doors. As was fitting for a serious and patient man, he bore this calmly; but he could not fulfill the office of legate that he held.

Thus he brought back the mystery of the council, closed and sealed, which he had been carrying, because the punishable rashness of the courtiers did not permit him to be presented before the king [Col. 0080B] and prevented him from delivering it. In this audacity of unexpected presumption there would seem to be such abundant material for argument that it could surpass the eloquence of Demosthenes and exceed the resources of Ciceronian ability. Therefore, if we wished to pursue our injury more rigorously, we could justly allege that you deprived the Roman Church—and yourselves—of this gift, since you gratuitously inflicted an insult upon it through your prejudice.

For he violates the bond of friendship who gratuitously assails a friend with the annoyance of an offense. [Col. 0080C] The Lord also says to the Jews through Jeremiah: “Behold, I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, the covenant which they made void” (Jeremiah XXXI). He therefore makes the covenant of a benefit void who first violates the sacrament of friendship.

Nevertheless, the Roman Church does not wish to exaggerate what she has endured; rather, she desires to persevere in the gift that she generously bestowed upon the royal dignity.

**Royal Advocate**

You rightly and reverently ascribe innocence to our lord the king; but in transferring blame, by contrast, to the administrators of the public court, you seem unjust. Whatever was done against you in such circumstances was prompted by the imperial command of the royal mother, not by the exercise of our own freedom.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0080D] I too shall answer you according to the hardness of your heart. For I say that at times it is a sin to obey the words of almighty God.

**Royal Advocate**

At this assertion the human mind is shaken, and the ear of Christian piety cannot bear it.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

Since you marvel at this so greatly, I shall add the following as well: because one man readily obeyed God, he perished utterly; another, because he scorned to obey, rose to a fuller abundance of grace.

[Col. 0081A] **Royal Advocate**

What you say is highly incredible. Nevertheless, if you wish to prove your statement by examples, tell me: who ever obeyed God and therefore perished?

**Defender of the Roman Church**

You are not unaware that the Lord said to Judas Iscariot, who had already taken counsel to betray him: 66 “What you are doing, do quickly” (John XIII). Later also, when Judas had presumed to approach him with a kiss, he added: “Friend, why have you come?”—with “complete it” understood. But because the wretched man obeyed these words effectively, he perished irrevocably.

**Royal Advocate**

Now that you have supplied the reasoning for this proposition, supply the reasoning for the other as well: who, specifically, rejected obedience to almighty God and thereby merited more abundant grace?

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0081B] If you please, recall what the Lord said to Jeremiah: “Go to the house of the Rechabites, speak to them, and bring them into one of the chambers of the treasury in the house of the Lord, and give them wine to drink” (Jeremiah XXXV). Shortly afterward the prophet adds: “I placed before the sons of the Rechabites cups full of wine and goblets, and I said to them: ‘Drink wine.’ They replied: ‘We will not drink wine, because our father Jonadab commanded us, saying: You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons, forever.’” [Col. 0081C] Therefore Jeremiah later said to them: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: There shall not fail to be a man from the offspring of Jonadab son of Rechab standing in my presence all the days.”

Behold: the one who obeyed wrongly, having completed the service of obedience, ran to the noose; these fortunate disobedient men earned the perpetual presence of their Creator. This also bears upon what was said above: when we elect a pope without the king’s consent, you ought not immediately to judge what was done outwardly, but rather carefully to consider with what spirit and intention it was done.

**Royal Advocate**

These arguments are familiar to us and never fail, because they are brought forth from your storehouses; for we can always commit an offense in performing an evil deed, and, since the inner motive is hidden, we must flee for protection to the purity of the mind.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0081D] Do you think that things must always be judged according to their outward appearance and the surface of words? For what is more discordant, judging by the clamor of words, than the statement that God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit delivered up the mediator between God and humanity? Behold: Judas delivered up Christ, and God the Father delivered him up as well. Does this not seem to be, as it were, a similar action? Is Judas therefore a betrayer, and God the Father a betrayer?

**Royal Advocate**

How do you prove that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit delivered up the Savior?

67 **Defender of the Roman Church**

Hear the Apostle saying: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” [Col. 0082A] (Romans VIII). Solomon also says: “Though you are righteous and dispose of all things justly, you condemn even him who ought not to be punished” (Wisdom II).

That the Son delivered himself up, the same Apostle says: “He loved me and delivered himself up for me.” And that the Holy Spirit also delivered up the Son, Wisdom bears witness, saying: “The Spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and he will not release the accursed from his lips” (Wisdom I). Among the ancients, all who hung upon a tree were called accursed. But Christ, as the Apostle says, became a curse in order to free us from the curse (Galatians III). The Holy Spirit did not release the accursed from his lips, because he did not prevent the things he had spoken through the mouths of the prophets concerning Christ’s passion; rather, he permitted all of them to be fulfilled upon him without diminution.

[Col. 0082B] Therefore, according to you, who judge not by the intention of the heart but always by the outward appearance of the deed: if the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son himself delivered himself up, and the Holy Spirit also did so, what evil did Judas commit? The delivering-up was done by the Father, by the Son, by the Holy Spirit, and by Judas. One action was performed by several, but the same action must be distinguished according to its agents. What almighty God did out of charity, Judas did out of desire to acquire money. What God did as a remedy for our salvation, Judas did to fulfill the wish of insatiable greed.

[Col. 0082C] You see, then, that we must not attend merely to what a person does, but carefully examine with what spirit and will he does it. For if we weigh only outward things, we find that the Lord and Savior himself both said what he forbids and acted differently from what he commands.

“Whoever,” he says, “says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew V); and yet on the day of his resurrection he himself said to two men speaking doubtfully about him: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe!” (Matthew XXV.) He had also said on the mountain to his disciples: “If someone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew V). But when he was in his passion, he not only did not offer the other cheek to the servant who struck him on the cheek, but added: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John XVIII.)

[Col. 0082D] And how can what Luke says about him be true—“He began to do and to teach” (Acts I)—if he did not fulfill what he taught? But undoubtedly we must understand that he commanded this for the preparation of the heart, not for an outward display of action. For how could he, who had resolved to be crucified in his entire body for the salvation of humanity, have been unprepared in heart to be struck on the other cheek?

Paul too, when struck on the face at the command of the high priest, said: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII). To those of limited understanding, this seems to be an insult in the words, but in meaning it contains the mystery of a prophetic oracle. For a whitewashed wall is hypocrisy, presenting under this name the dignity of the priesthood while hiding within the foulness of muddy wickedness. Yet he wonderfully preserved what belonged to humility. For when they said to him, [Col. 0083A] “Do you insult the high priest?” he replied: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people’” (Acts XXIII). Here it is plainly shown with what tranquility he spoke the words that appeared to have been uttered in anger.

What else are we taught by these testimonies of Scripture except that we must not always judge judgments according to bare words, but must examine with what spirit and intention of mind they are spoken?

**Royal Advocate**

You illuminate the doubts you raise brilliantly through the examples you bring forward. But I ask you to return for a moment to what came before and explain openly why you accuse us of having inflicted prejudice upon you, when we obeyed the royal authority.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0083B] Properly, plainly, orderly, and appropriately: after every objection of your side has been refuted, not by rhetorical arguments, not by oratorical embellishments, and finally not by dialectical syllogisms, but rather by the reasoning of living and evident truth, it is now fitting, in turn, to discuss—at least briefly—your excesses.

Indeed, the condemnation of the pope is so grave and inexplicable that it must be dealt with not by human judgment but solely by divine judgment. Our kings are excused both by the weakness of their age and by the frailty of their sex; guilt is not attributed to them, but is rightly charged to their counselors. Passing over the other perversities, why did you presume, with Rome unaware, to elect a reprobate man as Roman pontiff?

**Royal Advocate**

[Col. 0083C] We certainly made the election, as is evident; but we were induced to do so much earlier by Count Gerard and other Romans, as they were called, who persisted tirelessly in urging it. The abbot of the monastery called Clivus Scauri was also involved. Therefore, the election of the Roman pontiff was made not, as you claim, with Rome unaware, but with Rome present and requesting it.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

You work in my favor by testifying that you joined yourself to Gerard, who stood under anathema. For, leaving the abbot and the others aside for the moment, let us say only of Gerard that he was not a man of the Church and in no way belonged among the faithful of Christ. [Col. 0083D] For this one person alone was subject to anathema and a curse from nearly all the pontiffs who presided over the Roman Church in their respective times. Finally, shortly before he died, because of a duke and an archbishop of the English, whom he attacked as they were returning from the threshold of blessed Peter, stripped, and robbed of goods amounting to as much as one thousand pounds in Papiensis currency, he was excommunicated in a plenary synod presided over by Pope Nicholas and, with the lamps extinguished, condemned to perpetual anathema.

Let the holy synod therefore weigh whether the election carried out by him and his accomplices can rightly be considered valid—he who had been so terribly and irrevocably cut off from the Church’s entrails by the evangelical [Col. 0084A] and canonical sickle that not even at death was he restored to the title of Christian. And was it fitting that the Roman Church should be ordained through him—he who had always been her bloody enemy and had always persecuted her with deadly violence? And how can anyone ordain the supreme Church whose threshold he is not permitted to approach?

The Lord cries out to Israel: “Anathema is in your midst, Israel; you cannot stand before your enemies until the one who has been defiled by this crime is removed from among you.” And why? Because Achan son of Carmi had taken from the anathema of Jericho only two hundred shekels of silver, a golden bar of fifty shekels, and a scarlet cloak; and for this paltry sum, the perpetrator of the crime was not only stoned but also buried beneath heaps of stones.

If, because of that man, who had fraudulently committed only one sacrilege, Israel was about to fall before the face of its enemies, how will the Church stand if she is ordained through a man entangled in so many crimes? Especially since he also chose as bishop such a man—before the testimony of the world a cesspool of every vice, a false bishop, an apostle of Antichrist, an adversary of Christ, the soul of maidens, a trafficker in churches [Note: [Col. 0083D] He means Cadalous the antipope.].

Which of these, then, will seem preferable under a just examination? The one whom a single man, condemned by the perpetual anathema of a curse, elected; or rather the one whom the cardinal bishops unanimously called, whom the clergy elected, whom the people desired—not at the ends of the earth, but within the walls of Rome and in the very bosom of the apostolic see?

**Royal Advocate**

After so many arguments have been given by you, we might perhaps agree, if it were proper for the royal majesty to change a judgment once issued. For a blemish resembling inconstancy is impressed upon princely glory if any decree of its establishment is lightly annulled.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

[Col. 0084D] Who does not know that God is greater than a king? And yet he does not blush to say: “It repents me that I made Saul king” (1 Samuel XV); and through Samuel he announces to him: “The Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king over Israel” (ibid.). If God asserted that he repented, although he knew all future things, should a human being, who does not know what he himself will be like, be ashamed to change his judgment for the better?

70 He was made from good into evil; this Cadalous, on the other hand, from the evil that he already was, is daily becoming worse in the manner of the devil.

**Royal Advocate**

How recklessly you speak now, when you assert that the devil can become worse, although he is certainly so evil that he cannot be worse.

**Defender of the Roman Church**

I am lying if I cannot support what I have proposed with testimonies from Scripture. For, as Isaiah bears witness, the proud one said [Col. 0085A] at the beginning of the world: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV). But Paul says: “He will come at the end of the world, opposing and exalting himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians II). Since he then desired to be like God, at the end of the world, having become worse, he wishes to appear as though superior.
