From this it is plainly gathered that the devil can still fall into worse things, because *diabolus* (“devil”) is interpreted as “the one flowing downward.” Cadalous is named from *cadere*, “to fall,” and signifies the ruin of the people; in their very names the two appropriately correspond to one another.

Tell me, then, how this man will be pontiff—he whom not the Roman people but one man with his accomplices elected; and that man not a Roman but a suburban, [Note: [Col. 0085D] Gerard is the lord of Galeria; Galeria is a small town situated near the City and is therefore called suburban;] and not a son of the Church but a cursed and anathematized man. [Col. 0085B] Will he, in your judgment, be a pontiff who sold his own [church] in order to obtain the Roman Church? Who killed Romans by the edge of the sword in order to become Roman Pontiff?

You say that I ought not to have elected a pontiff without the king’s consent, and that I ought not to have regarded it as something of the highest importance that the people should not perish. Behold: on one side, blessed Augustine was placed over the Church of Hippo while Valerius was still alive; on the other, Ambrose was ordained bishop on the eighth day after he had been baptized, having received all the ecclesiastical orders. In both cases, the order of canonical authority was abandoned for no other reason than to provide for the salvation of the people.

And you tell me that, in preserving the people, I ought not to have consulted the king himself, so that glory might come to him from giving the consent of a single letter. For how would he later become Roman emperor if at that time the Roman people had destroyed one another with mutual wounds?

Moreover, since in establishing the pontiff the Roman Church did not withdraw from royal charity, this is also shown by the fact that, although her clergy abounded in religious and wise men, she elected not one of her own but the man who was to the king as a member of his household and a familiar associate.

**Royal Advocate**
Whoever stubbornly resists the truth after it has been revealed and made evident is rightly judged an adversary of almighty God, whose unquenchable wrath he provokes against himself (1 John 5), if he obstinately and arrogantly attacks the truth, which is God himself.

To bring your argument, as it were, to a conclusion: when the question arose between us whether the Roman pontiff could be elected without the king’s assent, you reviewed the catalogues of histories, gathered together such a multitude of Roman emperors and pontiffs, and set before me, as it were, a cloud of witnesses, that, on seeing them, I would scarcely have wished even to make the slightest further gesture against you in this matter. As for the anathema established by Pope Nicholas—where, as I now frankly admit, our entire argument had concentrated the force of its victory—your assertion cleansed itself by such unconquerable testimonies of Scripture, 71 and by such clear examples, sometimes from the blessed apostles and sometimes from the Lord and Savior himself, that it taught us what we had hitherto not known and powerfully released you from the bond of that sentence.

Then, concerning the injury to my lord the king—which, as we said, inflamed us more fiercely against you—your speech so vigorously cleared itself that it became evident from the plainest indication that, when the Roman people elected a pontiff for themselves, they had served the royal majesty above all; they had not, as was alleged, taken away its privilege, but rather strengthened it, since they raised to the summit of the apostolic see not a priest from the Roman Church, but one from the royal court.

Finally, what shall we say about the election of the bishop of Parma? Shall I speak, or shall I remain silent? But, according to Scripture, “Who can restrain a conceived word?” (Job 4). Certainly, where naked truth is visible, it is a shameful disgrace if one serves the fiction of deceit. We know plainly and clearly that Gerard was under anathema, and we do not fail to recognize that this bishop was drawn into this affair chiefly at his instigation. Thus, to speak in this way: a tree that springs from the poisoned root of anathema must by every means be uprooted before it bursts forth into a harmful fruit, as the Truth bears witness when he says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3).

**Defender of the Roman Church**

Your Beatitude, venerable Fathers, has heard that he who examines hearts has united us in a contest of words. For he saw that we were not contending out of malice, but devoting ourselves to the search for truth (Ephesians 2); therefore he deigned to quiet the quarrel that had arisen between us and to breathe his concord into us. For our peace, which made the two one, fused the hearts of both into a single understanding.

Let us give thanks to him who first allowed our fisherman’s little boat [Note: *Sagena* is frequently used by the holy Doctor for “little boat.”]—Peter—to be endangered by the violence of the winds and the storms of the waves. But behold: when he returned and stretched out his hand, he raised Peter, commanded the winds (Mark 6), and restrained the dangers of the sea. At once the sea, which had been rising into heaps, is overwhelmed; the storm of the tempest is calmed; the whirlwind of the winds is subdued; and the golden face of heaven grows clear.

**Conclusion of the Speech**

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us henceforth—on the one side, counselors of the royal court, and on the other, ministers of the apostolic see—join together in this single endeavor, laboring so that the supreme priesthood and the Roman empire may likewise be united, lest the human race, which you see governed through these two in both its aspects, be divided into factions, as recently happened through Cadalous. Thus may the summits of the world converge in the union of perpetual charity, so that the lower members may not be broken apart through their discord.

Just as these two powers—namely, kingship and priesthood—have been brought together by a divine mystery in the one mediator between God and human beings, so may these two exalted persons be joined to one another with such unanimity that, by a kind of bond of mutual charity, the king may be found in the Roman pontiff and the Roman pontiff in the king—while, of course, the pope’s own privilege remains secure, a privilege which no one but he is permitted to usurp.

For the rest, let the pope himself restrain offenders by secular law whenever the case requires it; and let the king, together with his bishops, issue decisions concerning the condition of souls, with the authority of the sacred canons having been declared. Let the former always preside as a parent by paternal right; let the latter, like a unique and singular son, rest in the embraces of his love.

Attalus, indeed, king of Asia, and Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, loved the Roman state so greatly that, when each of them died, he left the Roman people as his heir. How much more ought the rulers of the holy Church to agree with one another in mutual charity, since they have been charged above all to preach charity to the Christian people! Thus, from the concord proceeding from their piety, may the holy universal Church rejoice, and through the twofold zeal of both, may the discipline of the Christian religion flourish anew.

But as we draw the little boat of our fisherman away from the gaping abyss of Scylla, and lead Peter’s successor, submerged with faltering step in the faith, toward peaceful shores, let us sing a pious *celeuma*—a sailors’ song—to our Deliverer:

> We praise you, O God; we confess you, O Lord.
>
> Divine vengeance awaits you,  
> O ruin of Cadalo’s people,  
> to pierce your midst with a dreadful blow.
>
> High-flying one, you follow Simon,  
> Simon who seeks the stars;  
> the Tartarean abyss will likewise swallow you up.
>
> Blessed be the name of the Lord.

**Scholia**

“Constantine the Emperor offered to blessed Sylvester and his successors that they might, in royal fashion, be adorned on the head with a golden crown and assume the other insignia of royal dress. But blessed Sylvester took for his own use those ornaments that he judged appropriate to the priestly office. The crown, however, and the other things that seemed more ostentatious than mystical, he omitted.”

When the holy cardinal says that Saint Sylvester rejected the insignia of sovereignty offered by Constantine the Great, but chose for himself those ornaments that would adorn the dignity of the pontificate, he does not seem to depart from the truth. For what was the ardent piety of that same Constantine, newly converted above all to the Christian faith, if not such that he wished to confer all the splendors of empire upon the supreme pontiff? Yet Saint Sylvester showed singular prudence in selecting only those things that signified the summit and height of spiritual power.

The same point is found in the chapter “Constantine” of Distinction 96, in these words:

> “We have now handed over to blessed Sylvester and all his successors the Lateran palace of our empire; then the diadem, namely the crown of our head, together with the *phrygium*, and also the shoulder-cloth, that is, the band which customarily encircles the imperial neck.”

And after several intervening words:

> “But the most blessed pope, over the crown of the clergy that he wears for the glory of the most blessed Peter, did not permit himself to use a crown made of gold; but with our own hands we placed upon his most sacred head the *phrygium*, radiant with its white brilliance and signifying the Lord’s resurrection.” 73

Platina speaks of Saint Sylvester’s mitre in this way:

> “Eugene IV himself carried Saint Sylvester’s mitre, brought to Rome from Avignon, from the Vatican to the Lateran.”

Half of this mitre—or of another mitre belonging to the same Saint Sylvester—made of green, figured velvet, on which is painted an image of the Son borne in the lap of the most blessed Virgin and surrounded by winged childlike figures and stars, is honorably preserved among the relics at Saint Martin in the Mountains in Rome.

Nor would I have you understand this in such a way that the ornaments of pontifical dignity were first introduced into the Church at that time, whatever Aimonius, Sigebert, or others may say (AIMONIUS, *History of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 24; SIGEBERT, *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 550). For what Constantine, detesting the vanity of the pagans, appears to have granted to blessed Sylvester, the most holy predecessors of Sylvester evidently laid aside because of the savage and repeated persecution of other emperors.

For James, son of Alphaeus, surnamed Justus and also called the brother of the Lord, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by Peter, prince of the apostles, as Chrysostom very properly observes (CHRYSOSTOM, *Homily 87 on John*). He was accustomed to wear on his head a plate or golden band, as Epiphanius, Jerome, and nearly all the other ecclesiastical writers have handed down (EPIPHANIUS, *Heresies* 29 and 78; JEROME, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under James, and *Letter to the Galatians* 2; EPIPHANIUS, *Heresies* 29).

Epiphanius gives the following explanation of this matter:

> “He was permitted to wear a leaf, or band, upon his head, just as the trustworthy men Clement and Eusebius, mentioned above, testified in their commentaries: ‘Jesus Christ is therefore a priest, as I have said, forever according to the order of Melchizedek; and likewise a king according to the order from above, so that he might transfer priesthood together with the law. From the seed of David, because of Mary, he sits upon the throne forever, and there shall be no end of his kingdom. For it was necessary that he should now transfer the order both of priesthood and of kingship.’”

And after several intervening words:

> “He granted the kingdom to those placed under him, so that it might not be said that he proceeded from lesser things to greater; for his throne remains, and there shall be no end of his kingdom. He sat upon David’s throne, so that he transferred and bestowed upon his servants—that is, the pontiffs of the Catholic Church—the kingdom of David together with the pontificate.”

You will find more on these matters in the same Epiphanius.

As a sign, therefore, of the royal priesthood—for Peter calls it by this name (1 Peter 2)—it is reasonable to believe that not only James but also the other apostles were accustomed to wear such an ornament upon their heads (POLYCRATES, *Letter to Pope Victor*, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 23; JEROME, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Polycrates).

For although these things are not written concerning each individual, what we have seen regarding James seems sufficient to demonstrate the truth of the matter: John the Evangelist also used such an ornament for his head. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, testifies to this in a letter to Pope Victor, writing among other things:

> “John also is included, he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, who was a priest and who wore the golden band. This was a kind of head ornament that was transferred to the greater and more perfect priesthood of the Christian law, having once been granted by God to the priests of the ancient law. For sacred Scripture says: ‘You shall make a plate of pure gold, and upon it you shall engrave, in the work of an engraver, “Holy to the Lord.” You shall fasten it with a violet-blue cord, and it shall be upon the turban, projecting over the forehead of the high priest’ (Exodus 28, 29, and 39; Leviticus 8).”

Josephus accurately describes what the head ornament of the high priest was like (JOSEPHUS, *Antiquities*, book 3, chapter 8). He shows that not only was there a golden plate, but that the mitre was also adorned with a golden crown arranged in three rows. His words are:

> “He wore a cap—for so he calls the *cidaris*, or common mitre, likewise worn by the other priests—over which there rose another woven covering variegated with violet-blue. A golden crown in three rows encircled this, in which golden stones could be seen, like those we see on the herb called among us *daccharus*, and among Greek herbalists *hyoscyamus*.”

The divine Scripture also seems beautifully to have implied this very point in the words:

> “A golden crown upon his mitre, marked with the sign of holiness” (Ecclesiasticus 45).

For although the other priests were permitted to use the *cidaris*, or mitre, adorning the head with a golden plate was, as I said, peculiar to the high priest alone. Since this ornament of the mitre was covered with three golden crowns, it is rightly called a crown also in sacred Scripture. [Note: The most ancient monuments of the City have taught me that Saint Peter too was represented holding three keys in his hand.]

Since nearly all the ornaments of the high priests of the Old Law were transferred, with the supreme priesthood, to the Roman Church by the strongest right, it also seems worth knowing that Boniface, supreme pontiff of that same Church—apart from the salutary institution of the Jubilee, to be celebrated every hundredth year—was the first to restore to the use of the Roman pontiffs a tiara of this kind, commonly called the *regnum*, distinguished and adorned with three crowns. His predecessors had previously worn the same tiara marked by only one crown. [Note: Marcus Antonius Mazatonius wrote a booklet on the three crowns of the Roman pontiffs.]

This was Boniface VIII, born of the noble and ancient family of the Gaetani, son of the knight Livifredus and of a niece of Alexander IV. As Archbishop Antoninus of Florence, renowned for holiness and learning, testifies among others, he was a great champion and a defender of the rights of the Church. Because of the protection of the apostolic see, which he undertook with the greatest courage against those who occupied its territories and possessions, and brought steadfastly to completion, he made himself subject to countless calumnies from ill-wishers.

[Col. 0089]

**75–76. FIFTH OPUSCULUM: THE EVENTS AT MILAN, CONCERNING THE PRIVILEGE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, TO HILDEBRAND, CARDINAL ARCHDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH**

**Argument**

This opusculum is entitled *Concerning the Privilege of the Roman Church*. It is a brief account of what happened to that most holy doctor during his legation at Milan, when, sent by the apostolic see against the clerics of that Church—who were at once Nicolaitans and Simoniacs—he undertook to defend the rights of the Roman Church no less than chastity.

[Col. 0089B]

To the lord Hildebrand, venerable archdeacon, Peter, sinful monk, sends the affection of his most sincere devotion.

Only he clearly understands how much force the privilege of the Roman Church possesses for preserving the rule of canonical equity and justice, and how much vigor it contains for regulating the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, who is accustomed to labor in ecclesiastical affairs. Whoever is inexperienced in this privilege undervalues it; whoever is practiced in it embraces it. For just as one who knows nothing of battle does not care about weapons, so, conversely, the person eager to win the titles of victory in the customary manner girds himself avidly with weapons.

I would not inappropriately compare the privilege of the Roman Church with weapons. For while this one Church, made the head of the whole Christian religion through the chair of blessed Peter and presiding over all the Churches throughout the world, is supported like a commander before the battle line by the ranks of the faithful and fortified by the authority of a special prerogative, it both cuts off with the Gospel sword the necks of those who resist the truth and unites the entire army of Christ for unconquerable combat in the unanimity of one charity and one faith.

You, weighing this subtly, as well as many other matters, frequently asked me out of charity—which surpasses all things—to review the decrees and deeds of the Roman pontiffs, to extract carefully here and there whatever seemed specially to belong to the authority of the apostolic see, and to bring it together, by the art of a new compilation, into the unified form of a small volume.

When I, neglectfully, treated the urgency of your request as worthless and judged it more a matter of superstition than necessity, it came about, as I believe, by divine providence that, while serving as legate of the most blessed Pope Nicholas, I should visit the city of Milan.

There was indeed a sufficiently turbulent revolt between the clergy and the people on account of two heresies, namely the Simoniac and the Nicolaitan. Nicolaitans are called those clerics who associate with women contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical chastity. They plainly become fornicators when they enter into unions of shameful commerce; they are rightly called Nicolaitans when they defend this deadly pest as though by authority. A vice becomes a heresy when it is confirmed by the assertion of a perverse doctrine.

Why say more? After we had been received with the reverence due to the apostolic see and had announced the affairs that had brought us there, on the following day, at the instigation of certain clerics, a murmur suddenly arose among the people: the Ambrosian Church ought not to be subject to Roman laws, and the Roman pontiff possessed no right to judge or regulate that see.

“It is exceedingly disgraceful,” they said, “that the Church which under our forefathers always existed in freedom should now, to our shame and disgrace, be subjected to another Church—God forbid!”

At last the uproar of the crowds grew louder, and people gathered from different quarters at the episcopal palace. Then bells rang out; the enormous bronze trumpet that is there resounded; the whole city thundered with clamors. Everything threatened me with death, so to speak, and, as some of my friends often reported to me, certain people thirsted for my blood.

The fire of this conflagration was increased especially by the fact that, when the clergy of the entire Ambrosian diocese had assembled as though for a synod, I was seated—or rather presiding—in their midst, with the most reverend archbishop of Milan on my left. I was also accused of having placed on my right Anselm, bishop of Lucca, distinguished for prudence and holiness.

It is unnecessary to commit to writing all that the roaring people may have said at this point; it can readily be understood for itself. Indeed, as soon as the lord archbishop was reminded of our presiding position, he promptly offered—indeed, volunteered—that, if I ordered it, he would sit without objection on the footstool beneath our feet.

Let those who wish say that this was done with a less than simple intention. We, however, attribute it not to the irritation of the zealous people, as is reported, but to reverence for the apostolic see.

To come to the point: I ascended the pulpit and, when the people had scarcely been quieted, began with these words.

**Sermon**

Let your charity know, dearest brothers, that I have not come here for the honor of the Roman Church, but to seek your glory and, with its help, to provide for your salvation and the grace that is in Christ, if you permit me.

For what honor from a mere human being does she need—she who has received praises and proclamations from the Savior’s own mouth? What province, moreover, is found outside her authority throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, when at her discretion heaven itself is both bound and loosed?

Every person—whether king, emperor, or one of any other condition—who establishes the summit of a patriarchate, the primacy of a metropolitan see, the chairs of bishoprics, or the dignity of Churches of any order, fixes the rights of special prerogatives for himself according to his will or ability. But he alone founded the Roman Church and raised it upon the rock of the faith that was then coming into being (Matthew 16)—he who entrusted to blessed Peter, the Keybearer of eternal life, the rights of both earthly and heavenly rule.

It was therefore not any earthly decree, but that word by which heaven and earth were made and by which all the elements were finally created, that founded the Roman Church. It possesses his privilege; it is supported by his authority.

Hence there is no doubt that whoever takes away the right belonging to any Church commits an injustice. But whoever attempts to remove from the Roman Church the privilege handed down by the very supreme head of all Churches undoubtedly falls into heresy. The former must be called unjust; the latter, heretical. For the one who acts against the mother of the faith violates the faith, and he is found rebellious against the one whom he knows to have placed her before all Churches.

To leave aside other matters and come to what is now at issue: your holy devotion must not be unaware that, just as the blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, consecrated the Roman Church by their blood, so, at the very beginnings of the faith as it was arising, they won this Ambrosian Church for Christ through their disciples.

For the distinguished martyr Nazarius, as the Scriptures testify, received baptism by the authority of Peter from Linus, his successor; afterward, together with blessed Celsus, he was crowned with martyrdom in this holy city. The holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius are also known to have had the blessed apostle Paul as their teacher and instructor, as blessed Ambrose himself attests:

> “These are the men,” he says, “who, following my admonitions, rejected their estates and riches and followed in the footsteps of our Lord.”

Therefore, just as our Savior sent his disciples two by two before his face (Luke 19), so, in a certain sense, each holy apostle sent two preachers of the holy faith from his own teaching into this city.

Since, then, the authors of your salvation came forth from the discipline of the Roman Church, it follows, in accordance with the order of equity, that the Roman Church is the mother and the Ambrosian Church her daughter.

So that no one may doubt that this order between the two sees—the Ambrosian and the apostolic—arose not recently but existed from ancient times, when blessed Ambrose grieved that this filth of the Nicolaitans stank in this city to the ruin of many and could not restrain it by himself alone, he immediately sought the help of the apostolic see. The pope who then presided, Siricius, sent three persons—a priest, a deacon, and a subdeacon—to correct and punish this crime.

Together with these men, therefore, the most blessed pontiff cast out from this city’s little boat, as from a bilge swarming with worms, those whom he could not correct. Hence blessed Ambrose himself professes that in all things he follows the holy Roman Church as his teacher.

Search your Scriptures, therefore, and inquire diligently by whatever means you wish. If you cannot find within yourselves what we are saying, accuse us of falsehood. But if you can, do not resist the truth; do not savagely attack your mother. Rather, rejoice always to be refreshed by the solid nourishment of heavenly teaching from whose breasts you drank the milk of apostolic faith.

**How Beneficial the Argument Proved**

When these arguments concerning the prerogative and primacy of the apostolic see had been given, the people became entirely well disposed and unanimously promised that they would carry out whatever I should enjoin.

Then I clearly perceived how much it matters, in ecclesiastical affairs, to know the privilege of the Roman Church, and how rightly your holy prudence had requested this—not idly. With God’s assent, we shall strive to fulfill it, provided that we first arrange the order of what happened in this matter.

Why delay with many words? That very large gathering of the clergy was present. Everyone was questioned collectively and individually, and scarcely anyone among so many who had been promoted to an order without payment could be found.

For the genuine—or rather disordered—and unavoidable rule of that Church was that whoever approached to be ordained to any order, or even to the episcopate, first had to pay a fixed sum without any dispute. How many cares afflicted me, how many stings of thought wearied me, and how many sighs I drew from the depths of my heart cannot be explained even by an eloquent tongue.

To profane the churches of so extensive a diocese and so noble a city with sacred rites appeared, in a certain sense, to be the overthrow of the Christian religion. Yet it was contentious to show leniency to a few when nearly all shared the guilt; nor did it seem lawful to issue a different sentence against them when the cause was one for all.

This also increased our anxieties, because unless this matter received some kind of decision, unless the quarrels of the raging people were calmed—even at the cost of great human destruction—we would have no peace.

**On Reconciling Heretics**

Then, amid many debates, the sentence of Pope Innocent came forward, discovered among the ancients: when many commit a sin, it goes unpunished.

There also returned to memory the distinction that the holy pontiffs and authoritative founders of the canons established concerning the Donatists, the Novatians, and others who had been ordained among various heresies.

Nor did we overlook the fact that Pope Leo IX, within the memory of our own age, ordained anew many Simoniacs and those improperly promoted.

As we considered and discussed these and many other matters, there also came into our hands what the distinguished Pope Leo I wrote to Bishop Januarius:

> “Having read the letter of your fraternity, we rejoice with you over the vigor of your faith, which we formerly knew, and over the fact that you vigilantly discharge pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flock, lest the wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep (Matthew 7) tear the simple apart with bestial savagery. Thus not only do they themselves make no progress through correction, but they also corrupt what is sacred.
>
> “Lest this viperous deceit prevail, we have judged it necessary to admonish your affection, making clear that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics and schismatics and has in some way defiled himself by the contagion of heretical communion, then repents, is retained in Catholic communion without a lawful profession of satisfaction.
>
> “For it is most salutary and completely filled with the usefulness of spiritual medicine that priests, deacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and who, having once been admitted to the Catholic faith, now seek to return again, should first confess without ambiguity both their own errors and the authors of those errors as condemned.
>
> “Thus, when their perverse opinions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope will remain, lest any member be violated by association with such people, since their own profession will everywhere begin to oppose them.
>
> “With regard to them, we also command that the following constitution of the canons be observed: they should consider it a great benefit if, after every hope of promotion has been taken away, they remain permanently in the position in which they are found, provided that they have not been defiled by a repeated baptism.
>
> “The one who judges that such persons should be promoted to the sacred orders does not incur a light offense before the Lord. If promotion is granted to the innocent only after a rigorous examination, much less ought it to be permitted to one who is suspect.”

The same Leo also instructed Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning the reception of heretics:

> “Let those who condemn their evil deeds with full satisfaction, and who choose rather to accuse themselves than to defend themselves, rejoice in the unity of peace and of our common fellowship, so that what has been received against the Catholic faith may first be condemned by a fitting anathema.
>
> “Otherwise, in the Church of God, which is the body of Christ, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true pontiff reconciles us in the reality of our nature and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us. Therefore the grace of our communion must neither be denied harshly nor granted rashly.”

Writing likewise to the bishop of Aquileia, he says:

> “Let them condemn in explicit declarations the authors of their proud error, and let them detest what the universal Church abhorred in their doctrine. Let them declare, in full, open, and written professions made by their own hand, that they embrace and approve in all respects every synodal decree which the authority of the apostolic see has confirmed for the eradication of the Simoniac heresy.”

Nor did we overlook the fact that Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, is reported to have given his primate the following advice concerning a priest ordained for money, on the authority of the Council of Toledo. After introducing certain other matters, he added:

> “Therefore you shall not reordain the deposed man, but shall restore his orders to him through the instruments and vestments belonging to those orders, saying: ‘I restore to you the order of doorkeeper, and I restore you to that order,’ and so forth, ‘in the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’
>
> “Finally, you shall gladden him with a blessing, concluding in this way: ‘May the blessing of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, descend upon you, so that you may be restored in the priestly order and offer acceptable sacrifices of praise for the sins and offenses of the people to almighty God, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever.’”

Nor did this escape our memory: blessed Pope Gregory, as a dispensation, permitted the newly converted English for a time to enter marriages forbidden by the canons.

That apostolic distinction was also recalled to our minds by which those recently converted from paganism to the faith were burdened with nothing more than the requirement to abstain from what had been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from fornication.

Thus, placed in difficulty because we could not correct the evils of that Church by the authority of the canons alone, we at least strove to put an end to its corrupt practices and to provide, for the future, an order of promotion without payment.

From that time onward, therefore, we exacted an inviolable promise of promotion without payment: first through written documents, then by hand, and finally by the sacrament of the Gospel. The promise, set down in writing, is here simply transcribed as it is preserved among us.

**Promise of the Archbishop of Milan**

Wido, by the grace of God archbishop of the Church of Milan, to all the faithful of Christ, to the clergy and people of that same Church, eternal salvation in the Lord.

Your holy devotion, dearest brothers and sons, is not unaware how reprehensible, detestable, hateful to God, disgraceful, and perverse this custom was—and how condemned by the authority of all the holy canons—which had long taken root in this holy Church that, by God’s command, I serve; nor how it had drenched the souls of the innocent with the contamination of a deadly and pestilential leprosy.

This was the condemned and always to be condemned venality of the Simoniac heresy, and the destructive commerce of this kind that customarily prevailed in this holy Church: whoever approached to be promoted to the clerical orders was required, as though by a fixed rule of condition, to pay twelve coins for the subdiaconate, eighteen for the diaconate, and finally twenty-four upon receiving the presbyterate.

In this way Simon Magus—alas, what grief!—had made this holy Ambrosian Church into a workshop of his perversity. He possessed the moneybag, hammers, and anvil, as a moneychanger and minter of iniquity; he forged nothing other than the common peril of all souls.

But in our times, because our merciful and compassionate Savior grieved that his people, whom he had redeemed with his loving blood, should perish under this wasting sickness, he stirred your minds in agreement through the grace of the Holy Spirit visiting you, as though to confront and bravely resist the ravenous and poisonous dragon.

Thus, when certain people from among us approached the apostolic see, the holy and God-worthy Pope Nicholas learned of the enormous danger threatening this land and sent the lord Peter, bishop of Ostia, to suppress and utterly eradicate this crime.

[Col. 0095C]

Therefore, dearest brothers, in the sight of almighty God and of his Son Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and of the Holy Spirit, who especially condemns and destroys this pest, under the testimony of all the angels and all the saints of God, in the presence of the aforesaid lord Peter, bishop, and also of the venerable lord Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and of all of you, I condemn, detest, and judge reprehensible this perverse custom of commerce that has until now prevailed in this Church, and every Simoniac heresy.

Moreover, I bind not only myself but also all my clerics who now exist and all our successors, and I fasten them with the unbreakable bond of the firmest promise, so that neither I, nor any successor of mine, nor an investigator, nor a *Rodolarius*, nor anyone of this kind may take anything from those being promoted to ecclesiastical orders.

But if, at the persuasion of the devil, either one of us who now exists or one of our successors who will come after us should become a violator of this most salutary promise and presume, through this pestilential commerce, to take anything in the conferral of orders, then both the giver and the receiver, together with Simon, the author of this heresy, shall be bound by the perpetual bond of anathema. Separated from the fellowship of almighty God and all the saints, they shall be condemned with Judas and Caiaphas, with Dathan and Abiram, under the terror of eternal damnation.

We likewise condemn the heresy of the Nicolaitans, and we promise, insofar as it lies within our power, under the same testimony as above, to keep not only priests but also deacons and subdeacons away from the shameful association of wives and concubines.

So that this may be believed more truly, we confirm it by signing with our own hand together with our clerics, and we order the impression of our seal to be affixed.

Moreover, adding this and promising inviolably under the bond of the same pledge, we promise that neither we nor our dependents shall take anything at all from abbeys being established, chapels or any churches being invested, ordained, or handed over, bishops being promoted, the most holy chrism, or the consecration of churches.

May the Holy Spirit, who is the author of the holy chrism, release us and our successors from every bond of the aforesaid curse, while granting that we may steadfastly fulfill this most salutary constitution—he who lives with the Father and the Son forever and ever. Amen.

I, Wido, by the grace of God archbishop of the Church of Milan, have confirmed, strengthened, and subscribed this pledge made by me. Odalderic, vicedominus, and priest, have subscribed. Griberius, priest, have subscribed. Arderatus, priest, have subscribed. Atto, priest, have subscribed. Ariprandus, unworthy deacon, have subscribed. Ardericus, deacon, have subscribed. Ambrosius, deacon, have subscribed. Acto, deacon, have subscribed. Adam, subdeacon, have subscribed. Lyprandus, subdeacon, have subscribed. Landulfus, subdeacon, have subscribed. Acto, subdeacon, have subscribed, and the others subscribed.

## The Archbishop’s Oath

[Col. 0096C]

Afterward the same archbishop approached the holy altar and, in the presence of the lord of Lucca, swore into my hand, saying:

“If I do not faithfully observe these provisions concerning the eradication and utter destruction of the heresy of Simony and of the Nicolaitans, may I be excommunicated and anathematized by almighty God and all the saints, and may I be found separated from the fellowship of all Christians.”

Likewise his vicedominus and chancellor, and all the other clerics who were present, placed their hands in mine and spoke these same words of excommunication and anathema.

Then Arnulfus, the archbishop’s nephew, an honorable and prudent cleric, came forward. The archbishop held one of his hands, while Arnulfus placed the other upon the holy Gospel, and he swore, saying:

“My lord Wido the archbishop, who is here, will henceforth faithfully observe what he has promised concerning the chastity of clerics, for as long as he lives. Moreover, he will never consecrate a cleric of any order in his diocese, except monks, unless before his promotion he makes him swear what is written in this little document. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.”

## The Form of the Oath of Those Who Are Promoted

For receiving ecclesiastical orders, whether through me, through a person acting on my behalf, or by any device whatsoever, I have neither given nor promised anything, nor will I give anything by means of promises. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.

## The Archbishop’s Penance

[Col. 0097A]

After this had been done, the lord archbishop immediately prostrated himself upon the pavement with complete humility and begged that penance be imposed upon him for this abominable transaction of venality. Although he had not himself been the first originator of this crime in that Church, he had nevertheless not eradicated it as he ought to have done. He therefore imposed upon himself one hundred years of penance and assigned a specified sum of money as its redemption for each year.

## The Oath of the Archbishop and of the People, Which Was the Same

We entered the greater church together and ascended the pulpit. Then, before a large crowd of the city’s people and clergy, I made his cleric swear, touching the holy Gospels, that the archbishop himself, for as long as he lived, would strive, insofar as he was able—except for the giving of his own property, if he did not wish to do so—to uproot these two heresies, namely those of the Nicolaitans and of the Simoniacs, with every effort and all his strength, sincerely and faithfully. Thus he would permit neither a priest, nor a deacon, nor a subdeacon to have a woman together with his order; and he would utterly prohibit every commercial transaction of venality in the conferring of ecclesiastical sacraments.

A very large part of the people, not only those of the city but also those of the suburbs, had already taken this same oath against the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. Their multitude, it is said, exceeded a thousand.

When these matters had thus been carried out, and after we had considered the judgments of the holy Fathers whom we mentioned above, as well as those of others whom we omitted for the sake of brevity, it seemed good to us that all those clerics, after receiving penance, should be reconciled during the solemn celebration of Mass, receiving the vestments from the bishop’s hand, just as we related above that Bishop Fulbert had advised. First, however, they were to read before the holy altar what is written below.

## The Oath of the Clerics

I, Arialdus, called a deacon of the chapel of the archbishop of Milan, declare in this document, which I have written with my own hand, that I hold the faith which the seven holy councils confirmed by evangelical and apostolic authority, and which the most blessed Roman pontiffs have expounded in the clearest preaching of the truth given to various people.

I also anathematize generally all heresies that raise themselves against the holy catholic and apostolic Church, and specifically and by name the heresy of Simony, which attempts to introduce into that very Church the accursed venality of sacred orders or offices.

Likewise I anathematize the equally detestable heresy of the Nicolaitans, which shamelessly barks that the ministers of the sacred altar ought, or are permitted, to use wives freely, just as laymen do.

Therefore, since in these days these two heresies—the heresies of the Simoniacs and the Nicolaitans—are more grievously harassing and attacking the Church of God, I declare that all Simoniacs and Nicolaitans, together with their doctrines, authors, and adherents, are worthy of eternal anathema, swearing by the holy *homoousion* (consubstantial) Trinity.

## The Penance of the Clerics

The penance of the clerics was as follows. Those, namely, who had merely submitted to the rule established by the devil, so that some of them scarcely recognized that this was a sin, received five years of penance. In this manner, throughout the entire year, in summer as well as winter, they were to fast for two days each week on bread and water; during the two Lents of the year, namely those preceding Christmas and holy Easter, they were to fast for three days each week.

Those who had given more were assigned seven years of penance, distinguished by the same amount of fasting. After the seven years, for as long as they lived, they were to fast on Friday.

Anyone who could not easily fast was permitted to redeem one of these days each week, provided that he recited one psalter, or half a psalter together with fifty *metanoeae*—prostrations or acts of penitence—or fed one poor person and, after washing his feet, gave him a coin.

Furthermore, the lord archbishop promised that he himself would send all of them far away for the sake of prayer, whether to Rome or to Tours. The archbishop himself was planning to set out for the venerable tomb of Saint James, which is in Spain.

After these men had been reconciled in this manner, it was decreed that the office should not immediately be restored indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those who appeared to be learned in letters, chaste, and honorable in the gravity of their conduct. For the others it was sufficient that, by divine grace, they had once more been grafted into the holy Church, from which until then they had been cut off by the sickle of divine judgment.

Even those to whom the right to minister was restored were not reinstated in their lost office on the basis of their old ordination, which had been obtained through evil commerce; rather, they were restored on the basis of that most effective authority of the blessed chief of the apostles, which he suddenly exercised toward blessed Apollinaris, saying: “Rise,” he said, “receive the Holy Spirit, and likewise the episcopate.”

We have briefly set out the entire order of that inquiry conducted in the city of Milan. Yet we still do not know whether it pleases the judgment of the Apostolic See. For if we have erred in anything, we gladly approach Peter’s teaching to be corrected, and we do not fear the disgrace of retracting.

For this is, so to speak, that smith’s workshop over which presides the one who was called the son of a smith; to whose rule every coin is rightly brought back, and according to whose straight line whatever has been distorted anywhere is restored.

Whether I have erred in reconciling those men, I do not know. But I hope for one thing through the mercy of almighty God: after the many kinds of oaths by which the archbishop confirmed these promises; after the solemn oaths given by so numerous a people through the Gospel; and certainly after the oaths of all the clerics, spoken before the holy altar in writing and with their own mouths—these two heresies have been so worn down in that Church by the measures of prudent coercion that, with God as their author, they will not in our time be restored to renewed conflicts.

Nevertheless, let the Apostolic See examine these matters for reconsideration among its own judgments, and let it determine by the censure of its authority whether they deserve to be corrected with a point or with a file.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0099]

## 85–86 THE SIXTH LITTLE WORK: THE BOOK CALLED *GRATISSIMUS*, TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

### Argument

In this treatise he demonstrates at length that those who have been consecrated by Simoniac bishops should not be consecrated again; he confirms this by many arguments and by the authorities of the holy Fathers.

At that time, however, controversy over this question was being conducted in a council of bishops. For this reason he writes here to the archbishop of Ravenna, so that together with the others he may persuade the Roman pontiff of this position, lest the innocent be punished together with the guilty—namely, by being deposed from the ecclesiastical orders which they had received without any commerce or purchase.

## Verses on the Simoniacs

[Col. 0099A]

God condemns the pestilential thrones  
by overthrowing Simon’s smithy-anvil  
and the caves of the mint:

For afterward the thief creeps through byways,  
and the shepherd seeks the accessible doors  
with a free step.

But when the criminal dealings of the traffickers are absent,  
and the saleable talent does not swell  
the heavy moneybag,

the dealer does no harm,  
because no commerce is defiled.

For what harm can moneyed men do  
where coins cannot injure?

Or what harm can a foul hand  
do to tree-grown plants?

Often a sick physician has given a life-giving remedy;

slave-traders have produced a fighter, and the blind have begotten one who sees;

a foul and evil woman  
has borne a handsome nobleman;

nor should offspring be assigned  
to their fathers’ crimes.

Each person is burdened by his own,  
and no associate is held by another’s stain.

[Col. 0099B]

To the venerable Henry, bishop of the see of Ravenna, Peter, the most humble servant of the life-giving cross of Christ, sends greetings in the same Lord.

Since, with God as author, you have recently undertaken the priesthood, I thought that no gift could be offered you more appropriate than one concerning what has been done by priests.

I do not think that your holiness is unaware of how great a debate has already taken place for three years in three Roman councils concerning those who have been consecrated freely by Simoniacs, nor of how perplexing and confused the uncertainty has been, and how it is debated daily in those regions. This is especially so since, as the uncertainty has increased, matters have proceeded to the point that it is known that some bishops have consecrated again clerics ordained by those men.

For this reason many brothers, with the urgent insistence of what I might call presumptuous charity, make a familiar demand of me and compel me, so to speak, with forceful entreaty: that in such a crisis I should not hesitate to provide assistance, or at least write something concise, and explain what I think about this judgment.

I resisted this for a long time, hoping that I would first receive permission from the most blessed bishop of the Apostolic See, who was said to be passing this way shortly. For I judged that it would be proper to handle any ecclesiastical matter only if the prince of the Church himself granted me authority to treat it.

But when I recalled that the venerable pope, at the most recent synod, had earnestly entreated all the bishops, in the name of God, to pray together for God’s mercy, so that he might reveal to those who were wavering what ought to be decided concerning this scrupulous matter, I judged that I would entirely obey his command if, whether by praying or by writing, I could, with grace from above shining upon me, untie so difficult a knot in the Church.

Therefore, faithfully hoping in him who opens the book and releases its seals (Apoc. VIII), I shall set out upon the path toward resolving this question. Since I do not possess an abundance of speech, in the spirit of the obedience assigned to me, I who do not know how to speak shall at least attempt to gesture through signs.

## [THE BOOK CALLED *GRATISSIMUS*, TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP]

[Col. 0100]

## 87 CHAPTER I  
### That although Christ distributes his gifts through many, the fullness of all grace nevertheless remains in him

[Col. 0100B]

It is plainly established that Christ Jesus, the mediator of God and humanity, ordered his Church from the very beginning of human redemption in such a way that, through the ministers of his word, he distinguished the gifts of his charisms, while nevertheless retaining principally in himself the fullness of all graces.

For the one who says to the apostles, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (I Cor. IV), also declares: “In the breast of Jesus are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Coloss. II).

But if all the treasures are in the breast of Jesus, and nothing is excluded, what then remains to be stored in human earthen vessels? Rather, what he possesses wholly by nature, they possess through grace by participation in him, according to their measure.

For concerning them it is said: “The one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII); but concerning the only-begotten Son John the Baptist says: “God does not give the Spirit by measure.” And again: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I).

Since, therefore, all the righteous draw from that one fountain the source by which they live, they must always return to him with thanksgiving, and they must not believe that they can receive the gifts of heavenly grace from anyone other than him who bestows them, from whom it is certain that these gifts flow.

For those who think themselves indebted for divine light not to God but to a human being, as though dried up by the irrigation of their own fountain, must necessarily wither as they fail; nor can they flow within themselves while they forget to draw the abundance of their growth from the original fullness of the fountain.

Hence it is not improperly said through Solomon: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers emerge, they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccles. I).

The evangelist Luke mystically describes this course and return of spiritual rivers when he says: “When Jesus had summoned the twelve apostles, he gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases, and he sent them to preach the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

Behold the rivers’ going forth. Then he adds: “And the apostles, returning, told him everything they had done” (ibid.). Behold the rivers’ return.

“Therefore, to the place from which the rivers emerge, the rivers return,” because all the elect acknowledge without doubt that they are indebted to the one from whom they had drawn everything that flows spiritually through them.

Hence Paul also says: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all.”

Indeed, by placing the Spirit first, then adding the Lord, and finally God, he shows the holy Trinity, namely, that the one God is unquestionably the author of all graces. For he himself distributes his gifts, discerning the merits of individuals and the diversity of their works by a hidden providence.

## 88 CHAPTER II  
### That the priest ministers outwardly, but God consecrates invisibly

[Col. 0101C]

Therefore it must be believed with complete faith that Christ delegates to his ministers the office of ecclesiastical consecration in such a way that he nevertheless retains principally with himself the sacrament of all orders. He grants servants the ministry of promoting fellow servants, but he does not transfer to anyone the right or power of consecrating.

Although bishops may appear to consecrate through the office of administration entrusted to them, he truly consecrates who invisibly gives the Holy Spirit.

For one person prays, and another hears. One asks, and another grants the requests.

Who would dare compare himself with Peter and John? And yet it is said of them: “They were sent to Samaria; laying hands upon those who had been baptized, they prayed for them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII).

Therefore the Holy Spirit descended upon the believers not through their generosity but through their ministry, and consequently not because they gave, but because they prayed (Hebr. IX).

For there is one great priest, one supreme pontiff, who entered once for all—not into any ordinary holy of holies, but into heaven itself—to appear before the face of God for us.

From him, as from a certain summit, the whole priesthood is distributed through the members of the Church; everything that is sacred is propagated ineffably.

Therefore, when he sent his disciples to baptize, he did not transfer to them the power of the sacrament, but imposed obedience upon them; he made them not the authors of baptism, but its ministers.

For when he says, “Go into the whole world; baptize all in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII), he clearly shows that they themselves were not the authors of baptism; rather, unquestionably, the author was the one in whose name they baptized.

Hence John the Baptist also says: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes’” (John XI).

And yet the evangelist John says: “Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did.”

Behold, the Lord does not baptize, and yet it is said of him: “He is the one who baptizes,” because whoever performs the ministry of baptizing is nevertheless the one who effects the sacrament of its inward power.

## CHAPTER III  
### That just as there is one who baptizes, so there is one and the same who principally consecrates

[Col. 0102B]

If someone should perhaps object to me that baptism is one thing—the regeneration of humanity—and the dignity of ecclesiastical consecration another, we nevertheless hold concerning consecration everything that we believe concerning baptism in this respect.

Since baptism is the origin and beginning of the entire ecclesiastical sacrament, and since baptism belongs to God and not to humanity, so plainly all ecclesiastical consecration belongs especially to him from whom the fullness of all blessings has flowed.

Of him the Apostle says: “He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephes. I).

For neither baptism itself nor any consecration whatsoever would be called something great, if not because of the Holy Spirit, who is given through those acts.

For, as it is said, what is water except water? But the word is added to the element, and, when the Spirit descends, it becomes a sacrament.

Since, therefore, the whole greatness of both kinds of sanctification consists in this—that the Holy Spirit is received both by those who are baptized and by those who are consecrated—just as baptism is attributed not to human virtue or power but to God its author, so likewise every ecclesiastical consecration must in every respect be referred to him, since the many-formed grace of God operates in both: in the one case so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins, and in the other so that they may be advanced to the orders of spiritual dignities.

The former, stripped of their old self together with its acts of error, put on the new person; the latter, as priests of God, are clothed in righteousness.

The former, like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit; the latter strive to attain the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.

In the former he works so that they may become children by adoption; in the latter, so that they may be ministers and stewards of God’s ministries.

For the former are reborn through the Spirit; the latter, by the same Spirit’s ordering, are advanced so that they may already generate children of God (Ephes. IV; Coloss. III; Ps. CXXXI; I Pet. II; Ephes. IV; Rom. VIII; Gal. IV; Ephes. I; I Cor. IV).

## CHAPTER IV  
### That the Lord received together with baptism the rights of the priesthood

Therefore sincere and complete faith holds that, just as baptism is not polluted by the stain of corrupt ministers or violated by the guilt of another’s crime, so likewise priestly consecration is not polluted or violated.

However criminal the one who consecrates may be, and however entangled in crimes, the one who is consecrated is not thereby struck by any loss of the sacred office, nor deprived of any portion of heavenly grace.

For the mystery of consecration is propagated from one person to another not on the basis of the priest’s merit but through the office which he performs. In the consecrator, one must not consider how he lived, but only attend to the ministry which he received.

For just as there are many who perform the office of baptizing, yet there is one who baptizes, so, although there are many priests, there is nevertheless one who properly and especially consecrates.

In that dove which descended upon the Lord after his baptism (Matt. III; Mark I; Luke III; John I), he himself received both the sacrament of baptism and the rights of the true priesthood, when the oil of gladness was poured over him, concerning which the Psalmist sings (Ps. XLIV): “God, your God,” he says, “has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

It is proved that our Redeemer received the ministry of the priesthood together with baptism because, once baptized, he immediately began to preach, choose disciples, and shine forth through new miracles—things which he is certainly not read to have done before that time, if the sequence of the Gospel text is examined carefully.

Hence the holy Church took the norm of this institution from its own head and faithfully preserves it, so that, following the example of the Lord himself, it does not admit anyone to the priesthood before the age of thirty.

For unless it held a firm faith that the Lord received the priesthood together with baptism, why would canonical authority so strongly forbid anyone to aspire to priestly insignia before the age at which he himself was baptized?

Indeed, why would the example of the Lord’s age be applied to receiving the priestly dignity if it were not believed that at that time the Lord received baptism together with the priesthood?

Just as he received baptism, so too, in respect of his humanity, he received the priesthood for our salvation; and in him, insofar as he is God, he is the author and consecrator of both sacraments.

Concerning him the Apostle says: “Where our forerunner entered for us, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. VI).

For the holy Apostles themselves are not found to have been consecrated by the Lord anywhere other than in the reception of baptism. Yet they are not plainly read to have been immersed in the water of baptism; rather, they carried out the obedience imposed upon them when they were commanded to baptize believers in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, since the Lord said to them, “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now,” it is clear that they received the mystery of perfect baptism and, at the same time, of complete consecration when the Holy Spirit came upon them in the diversity of tongues.

Since, therefore, at the very beginning of human redemption both kinds of sacrament appear to have been received together, either from the Lord or from the apostles, it is clear that baptism is the foundation and beginning of ecclesiastical consecration, so that the one known to hold primacy in baptism must unquestionably also be believed to be the author of consecration.

## CHAPTER V  
### That, since no one dares to be rebaptized, there is no reason why anyone should be consecrated again

If this is so, I do not see what reason there is that one baptized even by a heretic is not rebaptized, while one promoted by a Simoniac, as is said, should either be deposed or consecrated again.

For if baptism given by a murderer, adulterer, or even heretic is to be considered valid, on account of the Gospel statement, “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John I), there is absolutely no reason why, in consecrations also, we should not return to the same author of both sacraments and likewise say: “He is the one who consecrates.”

Did that dove come upon the mediator of God and humanity with the power to baptize, but not with the power to consecrate? (Matt. III; Mark I.)

For what does the one who is baptized receive except the Holy Spirit? And again, what does the one who is consecrated receive except the Holy Spirit?

Therefore, if someone baptized by any wicked person is not rebaptized because he is believed to have received the Holy Spirit—not through that person’s merit but through that person’s office, and not from that person but from Christ, of whom alone it is specifically said, “He is the one who baptizes” (John I)—and if the one who is consecrated likewise receives nothing other than the same Holy Spirit, and receives it from Christ himself, then what difference is there in this respect between the baptized and the consecrated? It is not apparent at all.

Since, therefore, their cause is one, their judgment should be the same, unless perhaps the Spirit given in consecrations is to be considered one Spirit and the Spirit bestowed in baptism another.

But who would presume this with sacrilegious recklessness, when the Apostle plainly cries: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV)? And again: “If the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or you receive another Spirit whom you did not receive, or another Gospel which you did not receive, you would rightly tolerate it” (II Cor. XI).

To this it must be added that, as canonical authority testifies, rebaptism is forbidden precisely so that the name of the holy Trinity in which the person was baptized may not appear to be annulled.

If this is the reason why no one should be rebaptized, to whom could it more clearly apply than to anyone ordained by a Simoniac? Such a person consecrates not only in the name of the holy Trinity, but also observes the entire order of catholic consecration.

For although a Simoniac becomes a heretic through his perverse commerce, he is nevertheless catholic in faith; and his condemnation seems to arise more from ambition than to pertain to unbelief.

Even if Peter’s sentence hurled against Simon is examined carefully, Simon’s faith itself is not found to have been innocent: “May your money be with you for destruction,” he said, “because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts VIII).

For when he says, “You thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money,” he clearly shows that Simon’s faith was then such that, if he paid the price, he would not unreasonably have received the Holy Spirit as a purchase for performing miracles.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That if an ordination is catholic, it is also valid

The Simoniacs of the present age, however, because they do not hope that they can become renowned through miracles, do not desire the Holy Spirit or his gifts. Rather, inflamed by ambition to obtain positions of authority, they pant only for the summit of dignity.

Thus, insofar as they are sound in faith, they are nevertheless ensnared in the snares of Simoniac condemnation by the smithworks of the mint.

This heresy is read to have had two authors: one pestilentially emerging under prophetic teaching (IV Kings V), the other under apostolic teaching (Acts VIII). Gehazi, namely, appears to have been the master of those who sell; Simon, meanwhile, appears to have been the author of those who buy.

Therefore, just as their followers do not differ in error, so they do not differ in condemnation. Yet if a catholic ordination is performed for them, they perfectly receive the office of sacred dignity, to which they approach without deserving it.

For the Holy Spirit is of the same power when he is sold together with his grace as when he is given freely; and divine power does not lose the effect of its own authority on account of the commerce of human perversity.

Indeed, when our Savior had been sold and the sum of the most pestilential talent was already swelling the traitor’s purse, he restored the ear cut off from the servant Malchus amid the very hands of his persecutors (John XVIII; Luke XXIII; Matt. XXVII; Mark XV).

Thus he plainly showed how great his power was over those whose hands held him.

That he did not perform miracles for the demanding Herod was a matter of his dispensation, not a defect of power. The one who desired them was unworthy; the one from whom they were expected did not lack the efficacy of power.

Moreover, after he had been suspended upon the cross and given up his spirit, while the earth was shaken, the sun darkened, the veil was divided, the stones split, and the dead rose, all these things clearly testify that he was no less powerful while placed amid sufferings than he is now exalted at the right hand of the Father’s glory.

In the same way, therefore, we must also believe concerning the Holy Spirit: his power is one and the same both when he is seen to be subjected, in a certain sense, to venality and when he is bestowed through the free laying-on of hands.

Thus, just as our Redeemer, while he was being sold and suffering, could not fail in his majesty (John XIII), so the Holy Spirit, even though the bitterness of venality intrudes, does not suffer any loss of his own power.

Although any priest may appear to perform an outward action, it is Christ himself, the true Priest and supreme Pontiff, who distributes his gifts to those approaching their various ends.

These gifts come to some for salvation and to others for condemnation. Yet what is given is wholly good, although the one who receives it may be guilty.

For a good physician would not administer poison to a sick person.

Was that morsel which the Lord offered to Judas not good? Yet what was a means of salvation became for him the material of condemnation, because the one who was not at peace received the instrument of peace.

We all also know plainly that the sacrament of the Eucharist, which we receive from the most holy altar, whether we are righteous or sinners, is certainly good. The good person does not receive it better, nor the wicked person worse.

And yet the Apostle says that the unworthy person “eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. XI).

If, therefore, what the unworthy person receives is also the body of the Lord, it is clear that a good thing is turned to destruction for the wicked, although it was provided for the good person’s salvation.

Nor should it be called an evil thing because it causes harm; nor did it cease to be a sacrament because an accursed person received it. Rather, it must be affirmed that the same thing became an occasion of death for the unworthy person which was prepared for the good as a remedy of salvation.

It must therefore be believed without doubt that, if the consecration of any ecclesiastical order takes place within the catholic Church, namely in the unity of orthodox faith, so that faith is right in both cases, whatever is given to the good through the good is also effectively given to the wicked through the wicked.

For this sacrament does not depend upon the merit of the one who ministers or is about to minister, but upon the order of ecclesiastical institution and the invocation of the divine name.

And since, just as there is one who baptizes, so unquestionably there is one and the same who consecrates, it is through Christ’s abundant kindness that the one who receives obtains what he does not deserve.

For “he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V). What is surprising, then, if he pours the rain of his grace even upon a sandy shore? What is new if the rays of his splendor strike even the eyes of the blind?

Then they too may rightly sing what that wretched Balaam sang:

“A man,” he said, “whose eye has been closed, declared it; a hearer of the words of God declared it, one who knows the teaching of the Most High and sees the vision of the Almighty, who, falling down, has his eyes opened” (Num. XXIV).

## CHAPTER VII  
### That Balaam was a Simoniac, and nevertheless did not lose the spirit of prophecy

[Col. 0106D]

Behold, then: how could this son of avarice have perceived such great wonders and proclaimed so explicitly and clearly the redemption of the world, which was still far in the future, if he did not possess the presence of the Holy Spirit? For, as that outstanding teacher says: “Who knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him?” (1 Cor. 2). So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God—especially since the same Scripture says: “When the Spirit of God rushed upon him, he took up his parable” (Num. 24), namely, what we have just quoted. We say, then, that the Holy Spirit is not given through a simoniacal gift.

[Col. 0107A]

Is it not recognized that the Simoniacal heresy was already active in this Balaam? Was he not trying to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit when, in expectation of payment, he brought forth the oracle of his divination? For Scripture testifies that the elders of Moab were asking him, “holding in their hands the price of divination” (Num. 22). And again, it says, Balak son of Zippor sent other messengers to him, saying: “Do not hesitate to come to me. I am prepared to honor you, and whatever you wish, I will give you” (ibid.).

He was burning with the heat kindled by his love of money, and yet through him the Holy Spirit spoke profound mysteries. Balaam and Balak, finally, are both shown to have been openly opposed to God, and both hostile to God’s people; one was eager to buy the gift of divine grace, the other to sell it. Nevertheless, the secret of prophetic revelation was uttered by one, though he was unworthy, and heard by the other, though he had no claim to it. [Col. 0107B] And, so that we may marvel even more at the generosity of the divine gift, Balaam tried to curse, yet against his will he blessed instead: “I was brought to bless,” he said; “I cannot prevent the blessing” (Num. 23).

A bridle of divine power rested upon his mouth, and he could not direct the thrust of his tongue elsewhere than where the presiding Holy Spirit bent it. His tongue fought against his will, and the turbulent brine conceived by his condemned mind could not flow out through the channel of his mouth. Therefore, since he could not hurl curses at God’s people as had been requested, he turned to schemes of deception and placed before them a stumbling block through the Midianite women.

[Col. 0107C] If, then, even the man who desired to curse could not obtain the ability to curse, what else can this signify concerning Simoniacs, when the mind certainly agrees with the blessing of the tongue? But since he had irreverently abused the office of prophetic dignity, with what end, finally, did he conclude the prerogative of the grace bestowed upon him? [94] For after the victory over the Israelite people had been accomplished, Scripture immediately adds: “They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword” (Num. 31).

Thus, whether Simoniacs or any other criminals apply themselves to receiving ecclesiastical ministries, they receive the gift of heavenly grace through the generosity of the giver, yet they do not escape the fitting recompense of their own transgression. What was provided for the worthy unto salvation is turned for them into destruction. [Col. 0107D] From the very source by which others grow stronger in pursuing the rewards of life, they fall into the peril of eternal death.

Certainly, whoever passes with watchful attention through that page of sacred Scripture which speaks about the aforementioned Balaam cannot doubt that this unhappy man was, in truth, a Simoniac in every respect—except that Simon had not yet existed, from whom he could borrow that detestable name—and that he possessed the grace of prophecy for sale, yet that the Holy Spirit manifestly spoke through him. And, what is no less astonishing, although his heart was already burning with the fires of desire, God is nevertheless found to have spoken to him familiarly, both by day and by night.

[Col. 0108A] And lest anyone perhaps believe that he possessed the Holy Spirit to a lesser degree because Moses calls him a diviner, examine carefully the words of that same history. You will find, as Moses plainly testifies, that when he saw Israel dwelling in tents, the Spirit of God immediately rushed upon him (Num. 24), and at once stirred him, as a true prophet, to utter an oracle. Thus he is called both a diviner and a prophet: the heavenly grace had raised him to prophetic dignity, while his own depravity disfigured him with the shameful name of diviner.

Here we must consider how deep and subtle God’s judgment is—or rather, how fearful God is in his counsels concerning the sons of men (Ps. 65)—since that pitiable man neither lost, because of the wickedness of his guilt, the grace he had once acquired, [Col. 0108B] nor, because of the very grace he usurped, could he, though unworthy, avoid the sentence of divine vengeance. What wonder, then, if almighty God, who always remains what he is and does not know change, still preserves the ancient laws of his judgment and maintains the same rule of accustomed discernment, so that what he did in Balaam he likewise does today in those who resemble him: granting his gifts to the unworthy through the generosity of his mercy, yet striking them, in accordance with the severity of his justice, with the punishment they deserve?

## CHAPTER VIII. How the prophetic spirit seized the reprobate Saul and his attendants

It is also not obscure that when Saul sent executioners to seize David, and when, according to the truth of the history, [Col. 0108C] they saw with him a company of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of the Lord also came upon them and they began to prophesy. When Saul sent other men a second and a third time, the prophetic [95] Spirit likewise seized them. Finally, as Scripture testifies (1 Sam. 19), Saul himself went angrily to Ramah; but before he arrived, the Spirit of God also came upon him, and he prophesied all day long, naked, with the others before Samuel.

What wonder, then, if wicked people receive, to increase their condemnation, the gifts of God of which they are unworthy, when even Saul—whom God had rejected and whom a demon had already been accustomed to torment frequently—was not only permitted to receive the Spirit of God for a time, but also [Col. 0108D] to prophesy for a longer period along with his attendants?

He was moved by the gall of anger and inflamed at once by the heat of envy and hatred; and, not to linger over the matter, he had been irrevocably enslaved to the evil spirit, empty of God. Yet when he approached the place of the prophetic choir, the divine Spirit suddenly rushed upon him and, leaping upon him like fire upon material laid before it, took possession of him.

It should not, therefore, seem incredible that in the holy Church—which is unquestionably the throne of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, and the receptacle of all heavenly charisms—the unworthy person also receives that sacrament of grace with which he is not in agreement either in intention or in the merit of his life. For the merit belongs neither to the person who gives nor to the person who receives; the benefit belongs to the supreme giver. [Col. 0109A]

It is not written, “The Spirit breathes where there is one worthy,” but rather: “He breathes where he wills” (John 3), so that spiritual grace, which is granted through ecclesiastical institution, may clearly be attributed more to the divine will than to human merits.

Indeed, the Holy Spirit does not always come on account of merits, but he always remains in each person according to merits, namely for salvation. Hence what the Truth says: “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

[Col. 0109B] For when he promised that he would come to the one who loved him, and immediately added that he would also make his dwelling there, it is plainly evident that God dwells in some, while he lodges as a guest in others. Similar, too, is what he says: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). It is as though he plainly said: “He will indeed come upon others, but upon this one he will rest, because he is worthy.”

For, as was also said before us, the Holy Spirit, when reconciled and appeased, grants rest to those who are gentle and humble of heart; but, when opposed and hostile to the harsh and proud, he agitates them with the restlessness signified by those tiny gnats under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8), thereby confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them.

[Col. 0109C] Appropriately, then, in the third place—where the plague of gnats is introduced—the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Holy Trinity, is said to have been opposed to restless people.
