Jehu experienced this restlessness. Moved by divine zeal, he burned fiercely to avenge God’s enemies, especially the worshipers of Baal; yet he did not abandon the golden gods worshiped by Jeroboam (2 Kings 10).

## 96 CHAPTER IX. What the teachers think about baptism and the Eucharist of the Lord’s body

(1, q. 1, c. “Thus, however,” etc., continuing with “Is it not…”)

Three principal sacraments are regularly celebrated in the holy Church [Col. 0109D]: baptism, the saving mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, and the ordination of clerics. [Col. 0110A] Concerning baptism, blessed Augustine, in his exposition of the Evangelist John, and concerning the Eucharist of the Lord’s body, Paschasius, in his book, argue in such agreement that they testify that these mysteries are neither made better through good priests nor worse through wicked ones.

Whether these sacraments are celebrated by thieves, adulterers, or even murderers, they differ in no respect from the mysteries consecrated by holy priests. Whoever has devoted attention to the books mentioned above does not doubt that this has been explained and settled in greater detail.

There has not been equally frequent discussion concerning the ordinations of clerics because, once those two sacraments had been clearly explained, doubt found no room for hesitation about the third. Now, however, human curiosity, exceeding its proper limits, introduces a new question into the world and, by directing its gaze too intensely at the clear light and seeing less, attempts to bring darkness upon it.

“How,” they ask, “is the grace of the Holy Spirit either given through the wicked or received by the wicked?” They fail to notice that the grace of the Holy Spirit is received in the very order of ecclesiastical dignity. Whether an unworthy person confers it or an unworthy person receives it, the Holy Spirit, who orders the rights of his Church, determines that it is valid.

As blessed Jerome says (Book I, Against Jovinianus): “Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not names of merits but of offices.” It is as though an army commander, even if the tribune himself were degenerate or promoted some degenerate person into the rank of his military service, nevertheless, for the preservation of military order, determined that everything done should remain valid. The person who has not yet expelled that tribune from the dignity of his own rank does not overturn the statutes of the tribunate.

[Col. 0110B] But, on the other hand, behold, the Gospel cries out: “He who does not enter through the door but climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” (John 10). Let the one who crept in secretly by another way certainly be accused of theft and robbery; nevertheless, the one who admitted me through the door did not make me a participant in his crime.

Let him therefore suffer the punishment for the crime he committed, provided that the prejudice of another’s guilt does not entangle me and that another’s fault does not make me liable to condemnation when the purity of my own innocence makes me free.

As for the claim that an unworthy person cannot receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, it is unquestionably established that the Lord’s body, [Col. 0110C] consecrated on the sacred altars through the ministry of a holy priest, is brought to life and sanctified by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that it may give us life and sanctify us. As it is said in the venerable secret prayers of the Mass: “Through him, Lord, you always create all these good things, sanctify them, enliven them, and bless them.”

It is not believed that it can give life in any other way than through the Holy Spirit, since, as the Truth testifies (John 6), it is the Spirit who gives life. I ask, then: when a holy priest offers to some wicked person the heavenly gift that has been brought to life and sanctified by the power of the Holy Spirit and, to speak boldly, is truly full of the grace of that same divine Spirit, does the Holy Spirit therefore abandon the Lord’s body, departing in disgust as though nauseated by the filth of a foul vessel?

[Col. 0110D] But if this is so, how is it true that the Apostle says that the one who receives unworthily “eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body”? (1 Cor. 11.) For if, when the Spirit departs, it is no longer the Lord’s body but simply ordinary bread, the one who receives no sacrament does not incur judgment. But if it seems absurd and impious to separate the Holy Spirit from Christ’s body on account of unworthy communicants, it should not seem difficult to accept that wicked people also can receive the Holy Spirit for outcomes corresponding to the merits of the worthy.

[Col. 0111A] Hence blessed Augustine says the following in his exposition of the Epistle of the holy Apostle John (1, q. 1, “Many”): “A wicked person can possess baptism; a wicked person can possess prophecy.” We find that King Saul, who persecuted holy David, possessed prophecy: he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and began to prophesy (1 Sam. 10, 18, 19, 23). A wicked person can also receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. For it was said concerning such people: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

A wicked person can possess the name of Christ—that is, a wicked person can be called a Christian. Concerning such people it was said: “They polluted the name of their God” (Ezek. 36). Therefore, a wicked person can possess all the sacraments; but to possess charity while remaining wicked is impossible.

[Col. 0111B] If, according to the judgment of so great a teacher, a wicked person possesses all the sacraments, how foolishly must we laugh at those who shamelessly babble that a Simoniac does not possess the sacraments?

Let us hear what the same renowned teacher says elsewhere on the same matter (q. 11, “Questions of the New and Old Testament”), so that the view he held in the question we are examining may become known all the more clearly the more frequently it is expressed. When he was speaking about Isaac’s blessing of his son (Gen. 27), he added:

“The will of a just man is good as far as his conscience is concerned; as far as foreknowledge is concerned, he is free from adverse consequences, for God alone judges what is to come. Accordingly, Isaac, being just, thought that his elder son ought, in accordance with present human judgment, to be blessed first; but God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger son deserved the blessing, so that in the blessing it might be shown [Col. 0111C] that the benefit belonged not to the human being but to God. For it is the dignity of office, not the merit of the person, that God’s blessing follows.

“Finally, God said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron the priests: ‘You shall place my name upon the sons of Israel; I, the Lord, will bless them’ (Num. 6). Thus grace, transmitted through the ministry to those ordained, may flow into human beings; neither the priest’s will can hinder or assist it, but the merit belongs to the one who seeks the blessing.”

Let us observe from this how great the dignity of the priestly order is (1, q. 1, “It was said”). Among other things, it was said of the most wicked Caiaphas [98], the slayer of the Savior: “He did not say this of himself, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied” (John 11). This shows that the Spirit of grace follows neither the person nor the dignity, but the ordination transmitted through the institution. Thus, although someone may be of good merit, he cannot bless unless he has been ordained to perform the ministry; but it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing.

These words of the blessed man—blessed Peter Damian, the author of this book—are so plain and so clear that whoever, after once attending to them, still prepares to contend obstinately with a stubborn mind is shown to be attacking not Peter, who is nothing, but rather the great Augustine.

For what could be clearer than the statement that in a priest’s blessing the benefit belongs not to the human being but to God; that it is the dignity of office, followed by God’s blessing, and not the merit of the person; and, finally, that the Spirit of grace follows neither the person nor the dignity, but the ordination transmitted through the institution?

[Col. 0112A] And truly, what does it matter to me what merit my ordainer possesses, provided that what he perhaps purchased is freely bestowed upon me? Through the doorway by which he himself crept in secretly, may he introduce me—an exile—as a citizen, an outsider as a member of the household, and a hired laborer as an heir. I do not highly value from whom I am advanced, but to what I am advanced.

It is therefore established that, just as the two matters mentioned above—the sacrament of baptism and the saving sacrament of the Eucharist—are made neither better through the good nor worse through the wicked, so likewise is the ordination of clerics.

## CHAPTER X. How the Holy Spirit is given not on account of the merits of priests but through their ministry

[Col. 0112B]

Was that Caiaphas, finally, worthy to be the one through whom the Holy Spirit would speak the mystery of Christ’s life-giving death? For when he had said, “It is better that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” (John 11), the Evangelist immediately added: “He did not say this of himself, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied” (ibid.).

He received the prophetic spirit for a moment—not so that he himself might understand what he prophesied, but rather so that he might incite his fellow conspirators more eagerly to hasten the Lord’s death. He saw for us, not for himself, and opened the hidden treasure of wisdom which he himself did not know.

[Col. 0112C] Caiaphas is not entirely unrelated to the Simoniacs, if the sequence of ancient history is examined attentively. Thus, as Eusebius of Caesarea relates in his Ecclesiastical History (Book I, chapter 10; and Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, Book I, chapters 18 and 19), let the same words be set down here:

“By that time, legal provisions had ceased through violence and ambition. The honor of the high priesthood was bestowed on no one for the merit of his life or lineage, so that by then they were changed through annual successions.”

Then, citing Josephus as evidence (Antiquities, chapter 3), he testifies that within the space of a single four-year period four high priests succeeded one another, each holding the priesthood for approximately a year:

“Valerius Gratus,” he says, “having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ishmael, son of Baffi, as high priest. But not long afterward, removing him as well, he replaced him in the high priesthood with Eleazar, son of the high priest Annas. After a year he also removed him from office and entrusted the ministry of the high priesthood to a certain Simon, son of Camphus; but he too held it [Col. 0112D] for no more than a year [99], after which he received Joseph as his successor, who was also called Caiaphas.”

Behold: Caiaphas is understood to have received the priesthood neither freely nor lawfully. After others had been removed and men had been appointed by force, he himself had slipped into the place of another’s dignity. Yet, though unworthy, he received the spirit of prophecy.

Hence blessed Jerome says in his Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew (Book IV, chapter 26): “Moses, by God’s command, had ordered that high priests should succeed their fathers and that the succession of lineage should be maintained among priests.”

Josephus reports (Antiquities, Book XVIII, chapter 8) that this [Col. 0113A] Caiaphas had purchased his one-year high priesthood from Herod. To put it this way, light was placed in the hand of a blind man—not so that he might see it, but so that he might minister it to others. He received the prophetic spirit not on account of his merit but through the ministry he held.

For kingship and priesthood are known to have been instituted by God. Therefore, although the person of the administrator may be found wholly unworthy, the office, which is certainly good, is sometimes accompanied by appropriate grace.

Hence Nebuchadnezzar, after he had thrown the three youths into the burning furnace, although many others were present, was nevertheless alone able to see the fourth, whose appearance was like the Son of God (Dan. 3). The Holy Spirit must be believed to have opened the eyes of his mind, so that he alone might see what was hidden from the others and might even recognize willingly what he had seen.

[Col. 0113B] Hence Pharaoh saw a dream through which he forestalled the coming famine, lest Egypt, unable to endure hunger, be destroyed (Gen. 41). Hence Abimelech merited the oracle of divine speech and heard that he should return Sarah to her husband lest he suddenly die (Gen. 20).

For although some kings and priests are reprobate in the notable merit of their lives, they are nevertheless found to be called gods and anointed ones because of the sacrament of the ministry they have received. Hence the law commands that a Hebrew slave be brought before the gods—that is, presented to the priests (Exod. 21). Elsewhere it says: “You shall not revile the gods” (Exod. 22), that is, you shall not disparage the priests.

[Col. 0113C] Hence Saul, although he had already been cast down from the stronghold of the royal throne by the divine sentence, was nevertheless still called the Lord’s anointed until his death (1 Sam. 24, 26).

The law also commands that every firstborn male be called holy to the Lord (Exod. 22). But if the merit of each person is carefully considered, will Esau rightly be called holy? Of him, indeed, the divine voice says: “Esau I hated” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9).

Will Amnon be holy, who, when he shamefully burned with desire for intercourse with his sister, stained the sword of his brother Absalom—the avenger of the incestuous crime—with his own blood? (2 Sam. 13.) Can Manasseh or Ahaziah rightly be called holy, when one of them, as Scripture testifies, worshiped the entire host of heaven (2 Kings 21), while the other, consulting Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, about the duration of his life, ended his life in the despair of his unbelief (ibid. 1)?

For it is one thing to be holy on account of the merits of one’s life, and another to be called holy on account of the ministry of one’s office.

## 100 CHAPTER XI. It is not surprising that the Holy Spirit is received from the unworthy, since the Son of God was also seized by the impious

[Col. 0113D]

The merit of holiness is not transferred to another, but the order of ministry is extended to many, as ecclesiastical institution requires. In this matter one must distinguish not who possesses the office of consecration, but what he possesses.

The sacrament of grace is one thing; grace itself is another. Almighty God indeed gives grace even through the wicked, but he gives grace to them only through himself.

As has been said, God often grants his Spirit, from the generosity of his mercy, even to those whom he nevertheless rejects on account of the merit of their corrupt conduct. [Col. 0114A] Did those who will come before the Judge’s tribunal not unquestionably possess the Spirit of God, saying: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matt. 7:22.) To them the reply is immediately given: “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (ibid.).

[Col. 0114B] Since they testify both that they possessed the spirit of prophecy and that they nevertheless undergo the sentence of rejection, it is plainly shown that in some people the Holy Spirit is not excluded on account of the wickedness of their life, nor is a condemnable life excused on account of the Holy Spirit whom they irreverently abused.

For just as, according to the Lord’s testimony, “you do not know where the Spirit comes from or where he goes” (John 3), so you cannot know why he sometimes comes even upon reprobate people and through them declares the judgment of his will.

When the Apostle says, “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2), who can judge the Holy Spirit if he does not shrink from descending upon the wicked by some mysterious discernment known only to himself? He did not even wish to rescue from the hands of the impious the Son of God who is of one essence and coeternal with him.

Hence Solomon says: “For the Spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and he will not free the accursed from his lips” (Wis. 1).

[Col. 0114C] The Holy Spirit is rightly called benevolent because he repays those who deserve evil with good and bestows the gift of his grace upon those deserving punishment. But who must be understood here by the “accursed” except our Redeemer, who, in order to free us from the bond of the curse, did not himself refuse to submit to curses?

Hence Paul says (Gal. 3): “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’ (Deut. 21), so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, and so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

The Holy Spirit, therefore, did not free the accursed from his lips, because he effectively fulfilled, at the proper time through the accomplishment of events, all the punishments of the Lord’s passion and death that he had previously foretold concerning Christ through the mouths of the prophets. [Col. 0114D] He would, in a certain sense, have freed him from his lips if he had failed to fulfill through the order of events what he had declared concerning him in prophetic oracles.

Here we must note how profoundly and mystically the judgments of the two teachers agree. What one said—“The Spirit will not free the accursed from his lips”—is the same as what the other asserted: “so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” And to show concerning what curse the wise man was speaking, he immediately added: “For God is the witness of his kidneys, the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue” (Wis. 1).

Because the unity of the Father and the Son is inseparable and of one essence, the Father is rightly asserted to be the witness of the Son’s kidneys and the searcher of his heart. The Son himself, who is power and wisdom, is believed to differ from him by no inequality and to be separated from him by no division.

[Col. 0115A] The Father is also the hearer of his tongue, as the Son himself testifies: “Father,” he says, “I thank you because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me” (John 11).

Therefore, the Spirit did not free the accursed from his lips because God is the witness and searcher of his heart and the hearer of his tongue. It is as though he plainly said: “The Son of God endured the punishments of the passion because the Son himself, who with the Father and the same Holy Spirit possesses one will and one providence, decreed that this should happen for the salvation of the human race.”

Concerning him the Apostle says: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2).

[Col. 0115B] To return, then, to our subject: what wonder if the Holy Spirit sometimes comes upon reprobates, since the Son, who shares the same nature and power with him, handed himself over into the hands of the impious and did not disdain not only to be subjected to their blows but also to suffer the cruelty of death inflicted upon him?

## CHAPTER XII. How the gift of God is not polluted by any contamination of its ministers

If the ray of this visible sun suffers no darkness from any gloomy pit and is not defiled by the filth of any sewer, what wonder if the supreme and unbounded Spirit touches certain dark or filthy hearts with his radiance and nevertheless remains in his own cleanliness and purity?

[Col. 0115C] Whatever crime the one who consecrates may be guilty of—whether pride, lust, murder, or even Simony—he himself is polluted and, without doubt, covered with the deadly leprosy. But the gift of God that passes through him is polluted by no stain and defiled by no contagion.

What flows through him is pure; it passes clean and clear toward the fertile earth. The holy Church is a garden of delights and a spiritual paradise, watered by the streams of heavenly charisms.

Let us suppose, then, that wicked priests are in a certain sense stone channels. Nothing grows in stone channels, but the water flowing through them pours itself into fertile plots. [Col. 0115D] Even if many reprobate priests successively arise through the changes of time, so that both those who consecrate and those who are consecrated are found equally unworthy, that living fountain is nevertheless not restrained from flowing through the grove of the Church until the end of the age, so that not only the priestly order but all who are reborn in Christ may drink the cup of their salvation.

[102] Through priests, baptism and chrism are bestowed, and the entire ministry of the ecclesiastical sacrament is performed. If the wickedness of priests could restrain divine gifts, then, when they transgressed, the whole human race would necessarily recoil from divine benefits.

But if people received heavenly gifts while those priests stood firm, yet could obtain them in no way once the priests had fallen, they would necessarily attribute the cause and the entire power of their salvation not to God but to the priests. [Col. 0116A] But far be it from us that an evil minister should be able to harm me where the Lord is certainly good, or that a malicious herald should harm me where the judge is benevolent.

The dove does not recoil, nor does it grow nauseated at the ministry of any filthy person, so long as the one upon whom the whole dove descended alone retains the primacy of consecration. For the unity of the Church stands through this: Christ retained with himself the power of consecrating and transferred the rights of consecration to none of his ministers.

If consecration proceeded from the merit or power of a priest, it would in no way belong to Christ. But although the bishop lays on his hands and speaks the words of blessing through the ministry entrusted to him, it is certainly Christ who consecrates and sanctifies through the hidden power of his majesty.

Hence God commands Moses in a divine voice: [Col. 0116B] “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: ‘May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you; may the Lord turn his countenance toward you and grant you peace’” (Num. 6). Immediately it adds: “They shall invoke my name over the sons of Israel, and I will bless them” (ibid.).

It is therefore the priests’ task to invoke the divine name over those who are to be consecrated; but it belongs to God himself to bless inwardly. The external order of consecration is assigned to ministers, but the efficacy of consecration itself is reserved for the Lord alone.

Hence he himself said in Exodus: “I am the Lord who sanctifies you” (Exod. 31). If, then, it is the Lord who sanctifies, why should we fear that the guilt of some punishable servant might [Col. 0116C] obstruct him?

## CHAPTER XIII. How neither the minister of the word nor the minister of the sacrament can obstruct the gifts of God
The Apostle complains that certain false brothers preached Christ insincerely out of envy and rivalry (Phil. 1). But what follows from this? Does he decide that they are to be forbidden? Hear, then, what follows: “For what does it matter,” he says, “provided that in every way, whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed? And in this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice” (ibid.).

Christ has ministers of the word, and likewise ministers of the sacrament; among both kinds there are some faithful and good, others wicked and treacherous. Yet the sacrament is not received better from the good, nor worse from the wicked. The ministers are different, but what is provided is one and the same. The author of the gifts is wholly good, and what he gives contracts no stain from the service of his ministers. The stream flows pure, and the leprous hand of the one drawing it is of no account when what is taken up is clear and limpid. What difference, then, does it make for the moment whether the minister is good or evil, provided that the one who is always the same is the principal author either of the word or of the sacrament?

In the display of miraculous signs, in prophetic utterances, and also in the possession of the virtues of religious devotion, the grace of the Holy Spirit is diminished or increased. Thus Elisha asked his master, saying: “I ask that a double portion of your spirit come upon me” (2 Kings 2). This request is recognized as having been fulfilled in Elisha’s miracles, in which there is certainly both greater power than in Elijah’s signs and a twofold number of them—something that anyone who carefully considers their histories knows.

But this diversity does not occur in the grades of ecclesiastical office. One man is not more a presbyter than another, nor more a deacon, nor more anything else of this kind. In the former matters, the faith and devotion of the one asking are taken into account; here, only the order of ecclesiastical institution is observed.

Let us hear what the Lord says about wicked preachers: “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do everything they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23). If the wickedness of any priest does not prejudice the word that is given through him to those who hear it, how could it harm the sacrament, which is bestowed with God, not man, as its author? Both the one who preaches and the one who consecrates are ministers, not donors.

Hence it often happens that the teacher has one tongue, but his words bear fruit in different ways within the minds of his hearers: one person’s heart grows numb with an icy coldness, while another’s spirit, upon hearing the word, immediately burns with the fire of divine love. How, then, do words proceeding from one mouth, and striking the ears of many without distinction, reach the inner recesses of their hearts in different ways—unless it is because one is the person who ministers outwardly through the office of the tongue, while another is the one who, by his own power, dispenses the preacher’s words throughout the inward parts?

Therefore, whether in distributing words of instruction or in conferring ecclesiastical gifts, the priest does not employ his own powers, but merely carries out the office of the administration entrusted to him. Otherwise, if these things proceeded from the priest’s merit, they would certainly empty divine grace of all its faith.

## CHAPTER XIV. That Moses did not give of his own spirit to the seventy men, but God did so.

For a human being does not give what is divine. There is one God who makes good use even of the wicked, and who alone bestows his gifts through the good and also through the wicked. Therefore the gift of divine grace is neither diminished by the administration of the wicked nor increased at all by the service of the good.

This is clearly understood if the account of sacred history is recalled. For the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers and leaders; and you shall lead them to the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and make them stand there with you, so that I may descend and speak with you. I will take from your spirit and give to them” (Num. 11).

Here it must be noted that he did not say, “You shall take from your spirit and give to them,” but rather, “I will take and give,” so that he might plainly show that one human being does not give the Holy Spirit to another, but that he alone distributes the gifts of his grace as he wills. Hence a little later it is added: “And the Lord descended in the cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men” (ibid.).

The Lord is said to have given the men something of Moses’ spirit so that it might be clearly taught that both those who ordain and those who are ordained ought to have one spirit. Thus the rulers of the Church should not hold differing opinions among themselves, from which—God forbid—schisms or destructive heresies might arise; rather, they should all teach one thing harmoniously and live together in unity of spirit.

Moreover, just as those seventy whom the Lord appointed after the apostles (Luke 10), and likewise approximately as many others whom he wished to assist Moses in bearing the burden of the people, prefigured presbyters, so Moses first, and afterward the apostles, appear to have possessed the dignity of bishops. And just as the former could not receive the Holy Spirit from the apostles, nor the latter from Moses, so without doubt the same must be thought concerning bishops and the other ranks of ecclesiastical dignity: namely, that the one almighty God, who distinguished them through different grades of office by the administration of his governance, alone also poured out the grace of his Spirit upon each one as he himself knew.

For in that giving of the Spirit Moses could claim no privilege for himself beyond what the divine voice commanded him: that he should choose the men, lead them to the entrance of the tabernacle, and stand there with them. This was the whole extent of Moses’ task. What, then, could Moses recognize as belonging to his own power in this gift of God, when, moreover, two of those who had been enrolled remained in the camp, as Scripture testifies, and did not come to the tabernacle, yet, without Moses’ knowledge, received the Spirit equally with the others?

In the statement that something was taken from Moses’ spirit and given to others, Moses must not be thought to have suffered any loss of his spirit. It is like a material borrowing light from a burning lamp: the lamp is not thereby diminished through any loss of its own brightness.

## CHAPTER XV. That those who come to be consecrated already possess the Holy Spirit.

As there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so likewise there are seven orders of ecclesiastical dignity. As for the fact that others are placed above all these grades—namely, patriarchs, archbishops, and bishops—they do not so much receive a new order from these as appear to be elevated more excellently within the same priesthood.

Since a priest is so called because he gives what is sacred, that is, because he offers sacrifice to God, what more sublime or eminent can be found in the Church than the priesthood, through which the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is offered?

Although those men each enjoy certain privileges according to their particular ministry, because they share with the other priests what is greater than all these things, they too rightly retain with them the name of priesthood (*dist.* 21, c. “Clericos”). Accordingly, when the ministers of the Church are promoted to these grades, they must not be thought to receive the Holy Spirit newly and suddenly, as though that heavenly inhabitant then began for the first time to visit them as empty houses. Rather, those whom he already inhabits are brought, through a greater grace, to the advancement of a higher grade.

Otherwise, how could anyone receive him anew when undertaking offices, since the grades themselves are regularly conferred at measured intervals of time (*dist.* 75, c. “Ordinationes”), and baptism—to which the first gift of the Spirit is attributed—appears to have been received long before?

The same distinction is also unquestionably observed in the apostles: they received again the Holy Spirit whom they already possessed, and aspired to pass from grace to grace, increased by their own advances.

Without prejudice to the mystery—which divine providence is understood first to have secretly effected in their hearts—they are read as having received the Holy Spirit twice through manifest gifts: first, when the Lord breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20); second, when the appearance of fiery tongues came upon them (Acts 2).

Nevertheless, even before these unmistakable signs of the gift, namely, from the very beginnings of their calling, they are known to have been divinely inspired. For how could they have cast aside everything they saw bodily and hastened toward invisible things at the command of a single voice, unless the grace of the Holy Spirit had already shone into their inward eyes?

Hence Paul also says: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). Although this apostolic statement had not yet been written, it was nevertheless already unquestionably true. They would never have entrusted themselves to Christ’s discipleship so as to belong to Christ if they did not already possess the first fruits of his Spirit.

Thus the gift of divine generosity, which he had already given to his faithful, he gave again and again, so that by repeating his gift he might kindle their cold and barren hearts more fervently and flood them more abundantly. In this way, in this very way, human nature—which had been consumed by the long squalor of harmful antiquity—was to be restored to the bloom of new life through the successive stages of its growth.

Therefore, if, according to what has been set forth above, no one could be established in any lower grade, or even be baptized, without the Holy Spirit, whoever is promoted to the priestly office does not receive the Holy Spirit anew, but receives an increase of the Spirit whom he already possesses.

Just as one soul is diffused through all the members of the body, so the universal Church is enlivened by one Holy Spirit of God. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12). For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.

Yet although the soul is one and gives life to all the members, it does not administer one and the same power to every member. To some, as though by a kind of prerogative, it grants what it does not impart to others. Thus, while the other members live through it in common, the eye receives from it not only the power to live but also to see; the ear, to hear; the heart, to understand; the nose, to smell; the tongue, to speak. Although the same soul is in no way different, it nevertheless assigns different functions to the individual members.

So too the Holy Spirit, while granting faith to all who have been reborn in Christ, pours life, as it were, into all the members of the Church, just as it is said by the divine voice: “But my righteous one shall live by faith” (Heb. 10). When, therefore, he promotes some to the ministries of ecclesiastical dignity, he grants them special gifts as though they were certain superior members.

Furthermore, the soul does not distinguish whether its eyes are clear, its ears crooked [perhaps: “sonorous”], or its nostrils [properly formed]; whether these organs are beautiful or ugly, it assigns to each its proper function. In a certain sense, therefore, it seems not to consider what kind of members they are, but rather the places in which they have naturally been set.

Likewise, when the Holy Spirit confers the sacrament of spiritual grace, he considers not so much the merit of the life as the function of the office entrusted to the person’s grade. Thus, for the moment, it is not especially relevant whether the members of the Church are arranged in a deformed or honorable manner; what matters rather is where they have been placed. We must consider not so much their merits as their positions, especially since the Apostle says: “God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed” (1 Cor. 12).

Yet it often happens that the very members to which the more important functions of the senses are assigned are found subject to deformity, while the other members are conspicuously adorned with beauty. Those other members, to be sure, share in their functions for the common benefit, yet they themselves admit no blemish whatsoever of the former members’ deformity. Hence the same Apostle says: “Our unseemly members have greater comeliness” (ibid.).

Thus clerics ought to regard what they possess in a special way as belonging no more to themselves than to the common usefulness of the entire Church. Consequently, if they are unworthy, they owe to others the privilege by which they are placed above them, but they do not escape the judgment of the guilt under which they lie.

If they undertook the priestly ministry only for their own sake, people would not unreasonably dispute their merits. But since that grace is bestowed for the common salvation of all, one should consider not to whom it is given, but for whom it is given.

Moreover, the Truth says: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15). From this vine different branches grow: some are eventually to be cut off, while others are to be preserved perpetually for the production of fruit. Yet until the evangelical or canonical pruning knife approaches those that are to be cut off, whatever they produce is not separated from the fruit of the good branches but is treated without distinction.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the most wicked bishops whose ordination nevertheless remained valid.

This is why all the ordinations performed by Liberius—who was a heretic and a partisan—are known to have been preserved immovably in the stability of their status (see the scholia at the end of the treatise).

Liberius, deceived by the error of treachery, is known to have subscribed to the Arian heresy, and through his transgression the most abominable crimes were committed. Many priests and clerics were also killed through his wickedness, while the remaining Catholics were expelled not only from their churches but even from their own places.

Liberius, having thus become an apostate, survived for six years. Nevertheless, whatever he did concerning ordinations remained fixed and valid in the stability of its force.

What shall I say about Pope Vigilius? Wicked and impious as he was, no bishop presumed to annul anything that he established by ordaining. Know, finally, that this was Vigilius: he first plotted against Pope Boniface so that, while Boniface was alive, he might sacrilegiously seize the apostolic see. But when the senate resisted him, he could not carry out his unlawful and wicked attempts.

Later, by his customary machinations, he attacked Pope Silverius in order to deprive him of his apostolic dignity. Silverius, immediately perceiving this, convened a synodal council, where, by the authority of the Holy Spirit and apostolic power, he cast Vigilius away in chains as truly a Simoniac and an invader of the Church.

Nevertheless, Vigilius, as his sacrilegious mind had conceived, wickedly condemned the aforementioned Pope Silverius through imperial power, money that he supplied, and the assistance of false witnesses. He clothed him in monastic garments and sent him into exile at Pontiae, sustaining him with the bread of tribulation and the water of distress. There that blessed pope, becoming a confessor, died and was buried; at his tomb some sick people were healed.

Vigilius, meanwhile, entangled in the bonds of a deserved anathema and moreover guilty of homicide, established himself as pope through his wicked daring.

But, O immeasurable mercy of divine clemency! Vigilius, who had already been given over to guilt, was preserved for repentance. He refused to enthrone Anthimus, the heretical patriarch whom he had promised to reconcile. For this reason, after being thrust into a long exile and worn down by dreadful afflictions, he received things worthy of his deeds and, finally expelled far from his homeland, died in peace in the Lord.

Nevertheless, as has been said, his ordinations remained forever in their own stability.

These matters that we have related concerning Silverius and Vigilius are recorded partly in the synodal decree of Silverius himself and partly in the papal register.

If, then, the decrees of such disgraceful bishops are not annulled, how could the hands of a Simoniac harm an innocent man whom his own judgment does not condemn? How could another’s wickedness separate from divine grace one whom his own life commends to God?

For the Holy Spirit is given through one by whom, without doubt, he is not possessed.

But so that the assertion of our weakness may win the confidence of those who hear it, let blessed Augustine also serve as a suitable witness (*Against Parmenianus*, book 2, chapter 11). For in addressing the Donatist Parmenianus, he says:

“As for what is read in the Book of Wisdom—‘The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will remove himself from thoughts that are without understanding’ (Wis. 1)—this must be understood in such a way that he is absent from that person’s salvation, but does not abandon the ministry through which he works the salvation of others. Hence the Apostle says: ‘If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship’ (1 Cor. 9). It is as though he said: It benefits those to whom I dispense it, not me, who perform the act.”

The eminent teacher also speaks in this way in his exposition of the Gospel of blessed John:

“Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15). Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the baptism with which you have been washed,” but rather, “because of the word that I have spoken to you”? Is it not because even in the water the word cleanses? Remove the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself also being, as it were, a visible word.

He had said the same thing when he washed the disciples’ feet: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash except his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13). Whence does water possess such great power that it touches the body and cleanses the heart, except through the action of the word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.

For even in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, and another the abiding power—that is, the word of faith that we preach. The Apostle says: “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10; Isa. 8).

Hence it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 13). And in his Epistle blessed Peter says: “Baptism now saves us—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God” (1 Pet. 3). This is the word of faith that we preach, through which baptism is undoubtedly consecrated so that it can cleanse.

Christ is the vine with us, and the Father is the cultivator; Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her. Read the Apostle and see what he adds: “That he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Eph. 5).

Cleansing, therefore, would not be attributed to the flowing and unstable element unless the word were added. This word of faith has such power in the Church that through the believing, offering, blessing, and baptizing Church it cleanses even a tiny infant, however unable he may yet be to believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

All this is accomplished through the word of which the Lord says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 12).

According, therefore, to the judgment of this blessed man—or rather, according to the saving teaching of our Redeemer himself—the mystery of every sacrament rests not on the merit of the one who consecrates, but on the word of the consecration. What is concealed in the consecration by merit is therefore not to be weighed heavily; rather, one must consider what descends through the words upon the person who is to be consecrated.

The same man also says in his exposition of Psalm 10:

“What, then, is the righteous man? If Caecilian offended you, what did Christ do to you? He who sent his betrayer—whom he called the devil, who even before the Lord’s betrayal could not show faithfulness concerning the Lord’s money-box—with the other disciples to preach the kingdom of heaven, in order to demonstrate that the gifts of God reach those who receive them with faith, even if the one through whom they receive them is like Judas.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Anatolius and Polychronius, who, after wicked beginnings, were converted for the better and showed themselves worthy of their orders.

Why, then, does the empty rashness of human beings boast that another person’s contagion can defile the purity of the innocent, and that the crime of traffickers can overwhelm those who have no knowledge whatsoever of the transaction, when those who began badly often finish well, and sinister beginnings lead to good outcomes through the satisfaction of a reformed life?

But so that we may confirm by an example what we have put forward in words, it is well known that when Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, had been sent into exile because of his Catholic position, Anatolius was ordained by the heretics in his place while Flavian was still alive.

To him holy Pope Leo speaks as follows:

“When your predecessor, Flavian of blessed memory, had been expelled for defending the Catholic truth, it was not without reason believed that those who ordained you seemed, contrary to the provisions of the holy canons, to have consecrated one like themselves. But God’s mercy flowed abundantly, guiding and strengthening you in this, so that you might make good use of bad beginnings and show that you had been advanced not by judgment but by God’s kindness. This must truly be understood in this way, provided that you do not lose the grace of the divine gift through an evil confession.”

Furthermore, what shall I say about Polychronius, the bishop of Jerusalem? As is found in the papal records, while arrogantly asserting that Jerusalem was the first see and stubbornly declaring himself the supreme pontiff, he also fell into the abyss of the Simoniac heresy. He would not promote clerics without money, nor would he accept less than ten pounds of gold from the dedication of any church, which he wickedly treated as a commercial transaction.

What more need be said? At last Sixtus, bishop of the Roman see, convened a council and, together with seventy-six bishops, condemned him as deposed from his own see. He assigned him only three church estates by right of usufruct.

Nevertheless, he ordered that Polychronius’s place be preserved intact, suspended his ordination, and left a certain bishop named Theodolus as his vicar in the see. After nine months, when the city of Jerusalem was oppressed by a famine, Polychronius sold the very estates that he had received for use and legally distributed their price to the poor.

When Sixtus learned this from the deacon Priscus, who accused the bishop and charged Polychronius with a pious crime—for he said that Polychronius had not been permitted to dispose of the Church’s goods, which he had received only for temporary use—the holy pope rejoiced greatly and immediately reported the pious deed to Augustus Valentinian.

Then, after a synod had been convened, the Roman pontiff and Valentinian presiding together, they began to deliberate what ought fittingly to be done with Polychronius, who, distributing everything amid the poverty of his deposition, had laudably imitated the evangelical widow praised by the Redeemer (Mark 12; Luke 21).

Accordingly, the following decision was issued with appropriate judgment: “He is not to be deprived who, by piously giving away her livelihood, followed the widow.”

Thus Polychronius, who had deservedly lost his rank through pride and greed, later became generous and humble and recovered for himself the insignia of his former dignity.

If holy conduct could excuse Anatolius—who, as stated above, was ordained while the bishop was still alive, after that bishop had been deposed, and moreover by heretics—and if a single act of almsgiving could restore the plainly Simoniac Polychronius to his former honor, how can it be said that one promoted by a Simoniac will in no way obtain the fruit of the honor he received?

## CHAPTER XVIII. That miracles are often performed even through unworthy priests.

Indeed, what wonder is it if almighty God permits the priestly office to be propagated in his Church through wicked ministers, when through those same ministers he also frequently displays signs of power—not, to be sure, on account of the merit of a religious life, but because of the sacrament of the priestly mystery that has been received?

To touch briefly on a few examples out of many: there was a bishop of Fiesole named Raimbaldus, manifestly a Simoniac. Not only had he obtained the height of the episcopate through money, but he scarcely ever consecrated clerics or churches without payment.

In addition, he had one woman publicly and familiarly attached to him, as though she were his lawful wife; several sons and daughters of theirs still exist, bound together in marriage and multiplied by growing offspring.

Nevertheless, many miracles are reported to have been performed through this man. It is sufficient here to relate only one, so that from this single example the mind may gather what it may reasonably believe concerning the others that rumor has spread.

Rozo, called the choirmaster and a priest of the Florentine Church, a man highly educated in literary studies, related the following to me in the presence of a large gathering of his clerics and also of his most reverend lord, Bishop Gerard:

“Once a possessed woman was brought to the church of our bishopric. Perhaps the solemnity of the Finding of the Lord’s Cross was then being celebrated. When the offertory was reached—the part that says, ‘A most splendid man coming to Constantine’—the clerics, I do not know by what accident, were suddenly overtaken by forgetfulness of the melody.

“At once the woman, as though rushing to help those who had fallen into difficulty, sprang hastily into the midst, burst into a performance with an exceptionally powerful voice, and maintained the pattern of the sweet melody so skillfully that everyone marveled.

“When the demon was adjured to depart, he replied that he ought to be expelled only by Romulus. Hearing this, the woman’s companions hurried immediately to the church of Fiesole. There, before the altar of Blessed Romulus, they awaited divine mercy.

“But when the demon was questioned there as well, he replied that he would not leave unless Bishop Raimbaldus arrived. While the aforementioned bishop was making haste to come, the demon meanwhile said: ‘Woe! Look, the bishop is now mounting his horse; look, he is already in such-and-such a place; look, he is now passing before this or that house.’ Those who were taking note of the places found that everything was truly happening just as the lying spirit asserted.”

At last the bishop arrived, invoked the name of Christ, and immediately expelled the evil spirit from the possessed body. He sent the woman back to her own home free and unharmed.

At the same time, when the Simoniac plague was fatally spreading through the whole body of the Church and sprouting freely everywhere through all the ecclesiastical grades, there was a certain priest named Marinus. He was the father of the most reverend and honorable man Eleuchadius, who now presides over the monastery of blessed Mary, Mother of God and Ever-Virgin, established near the walls of the city of Faenza.

This Marinus did not hesitate to possess Eleuchadius’s mother publicly as though she were his legitimate wife.

Divine providence had bestowed such great grace upon this priest that, when he sprinkled the crops in the fields with water that he had sanctified, no plague of worms, caterpillars, or indeed locusts remained to damage the crops; rather, once the sanctification of the water had been sprinkled over them, all immediately departed in a body.

On another occasion, the master of that same priest Marinus, a man named Jeremias, was tormented by the hatred of a most serious quarrel with a rival who was related to him by family but entirely opposed to him in intention. Among his other fears arising from this hostility, he was afraid that some hostile enchantment might bewitch the keenness of his dogs, which were devoted to hunting. He therefore asked the aforementioned priest to sanctify by exorcism a bucket full of water and bring it to him, since he judged it very necessary for certain purposes of his own.

When Marinus, with simple intention, had carried out what was commanded, Jeremias—wise enough to do evil but entirely ignorant of the sacrament’s power—did not hesitate to cast pearls before swine. For the foolish man mixed the sanctified water with a *cantabrum* [the term is uncertain] and offered it to his dogs to devour, intending by this magic to prevent them from being bewitched.

But divine providence judged otherwise, and his plan was turned against him. He suffered the evil that he had wickedly wished to avert; and while he carelessly sought to protect the irrational animals, he injured his own soul instead.

When the dogs were admitted to eat, they had scarcely opened their eager mouths at the first attack and had not yet touched the savage food with their tongues when, after perceiving the odor with their nostrils, they all immediately fell dead to the ground.

Then doubly confounded—guilty of sin and struck by the loss of his property—he disclosed to the priest Marinus the entire sequence of events exactly as it had happened and tearfully begged that penance be imposed upon him for so great an act of daring and so great a sacrilege.

Marinus denied that he could arrogate to himself the judgment of such a great crime, and, though he was pressed with prayers from every side, he agreed to nothing else except that, if Jeremias truly sought penance, he must necessarily hasten to the summit of the apostolic see.

Compelled by necessity, Jeremias finally obeyed him and received from the Roman Church the judgment of penance that he had requested.

At another time, a certain girl whom the same priest Marinus had baptized was carried off by a wolf into the dense forests and secluded thickets, while many people pursued it. When her mother, beside herself with grief, ran after her, she suddenly encountered the priest Marinus. With great wailing, she expressed the sobs of her sorrowful complaint:

“Alas, alas, Father,” she said, “I could never have imagined that the daughter of an unhappy mother, whom you yourself drew from the sacred font, would be made the prey of bloody beasts and, becoming food for wolves, satisfy the jaws of their savage rapacity.”

The priest said to her: “Do not be afraid, woman. For if she truly is one whom I baptized, no beast will ever receive the power to devour her.”

Then, boldly and rashly, he foolishly added this as well: “For if I washed her in the bath of holy baptism and the beast has torn her apart, I shall no longer believe that God reigns in heaven.”

A marvelous event followed. After nearly four hours, at a distance of almost eight miles, the girl was found unharmed and safe among the forest thickets; beside her stood the innocent wolf. Just as the lion was not permitted to violate the corpse of the prophet returning from Samaria (1 Kings 13), so this wolf did not dare to injure the girl. So far as can be understood, it even appeared voluntarily to guard her.

No injury at all was found on the girl, except that her legs and arms appeared to have been bloodied by the spines of thorns and brambles.

There was also recently another priest in these parts, the brother of the most reverend Gerard, who now presides over the monastery of Saint Donatus, situated in the suburb of the town of Imola. This priest’s life was ordinary and almost secular, but he had obtained such great grace from the Lord that whenever someone was reported to him as having been bitten by a serpent, he immediately gave the messenger water that he had sanctified, so that the messenger might drink it.

After the water had been swallowed, the efficacy of divine power immediately became so evident that the person who had drunk it vomited out all the serpent’s venom, as though a snake had specifically bitten him; and the one who had been bitten returned entirely free of poison, with all his inward parts cleansed of the deadly fluid, safe and sound.

Another priest, too, was almost entirely insignificant, so much so that he possessed not even the slightest aptitude for secular wisdom; as for letters, he could scarcely spell them out syllable by syllable, and that in rustic stammering. Once, toward evening, a hawk carried off his hen [Col. 0126D]. This injury stirred him with the bitterest gall of anger—so much so, plainly, that he threatened the saint in whose name he governed the consecrated church: unless the saint restored to him his lost fowl, he would never again celebrate the ecclesiastical offices there. And as though the madness of his tongue were not fully sufficient, he even dared to cut [the object is omitted or corrupt in the source] with his hands, and began to beat the very altar with rods. What more is there to say? On the following morning the hen returned. Except for its wings and head, it had been stripped of all its other feathers, yet it brought back no trace of injury anywhere on its body. Thus it was clearly shown that, although the priest’s words were insane, divine mercy did not altogether reject them, since the hawk was not granted permission to swoop down to the hen’s destruction [Col. 0127A].

And what wonder is it if divine dispensation displays the powers of miracles through priests of whatever sort, provided that they are orthodox, when it often manifests signs of its power even through heretics themselves? For, to pass over other examples, what is read in the Tripartite History does not seem inappropriate if it is simply introduced in the same words:

“Meanwhile,” it says, “the fire which had broken out in the city of Constantinople gradually reached the baths called the Achilleae, and finally the place called Pelargus, so that it encompassed the church of the Novatians. Then Paul, their bishop, is said to have stood amid the flames before the church, entreating God that the church might not likewise be burned. That place was rescued, and to this day it remains unharmed; there, on the seventeenth day of the month of August, an assembly is celebrated among the Novatians. This place, therefore, is venerated at once by Christians and pagans.” [Col. 0127B]

But these signs of power, which divine dispensation works either through heretics or through priests of orthodox faith who are unworthy, do not free those priests—since such signs are granted not on account of the merit of any one of them but through their ministry—from the punishments they deserve, nor do they excuse them from the guilt they have committed before the strict Judge. For from the very source whence they hunt glory, they fall into the disgrace of shame; and the more they are exalted by the favor of flatterers, the more readily they plunge headlong into eternal damnation. Often, struck by a terrible death, such men make clearer than daylight how truly reprobate they were, though outwardly they appeared almost miraculous [Col. 0127C].

The Fesulan bishop whom we mentioned shortly before was of such depravity that even his lay brother, a man of honorable and modest life, did not deign to maintain any intimacy with him. Yet he shone so brightly with the powers of signs that, at the dedication of a single church, five demoniacs are consistently said, according to the testimony of all who reported it, to have been cured by him before the entire people. But because he became renowned not through his own miracles but through those of another, when he came to die he was marked out for punishment by the avenging fire of his burning body. For the fuel of a destructive burning arose pestilentially on his foot and seized the entire sole, shin, and thigh, together with the groin and genitals, so that, creeping onward, it reached his vital organs; and, like dry fuel for a log, consuming his inner organs, it burned him up with hidden vapors, so that he might already be kindled by the preliminary fire which a flame never afterward to be extinguished would consume. Bound by the excess of so intolerable and savage an illness, he is known neither to have undertaken fitting repentance nor to have wished to remove from himself the company of women, whose services he still shamelessly did not hesitate to use. [Col. 0127D]

Moreover, since our Redeemer says, “that he himself casts out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI), and the finger of God is unquestionably understood as the Holy Spirit, it is plainly recognized that demons are never expelled from human bodies except through the power of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0128A]. Hence it is manifest that, although that bishop was unworthy, although he was a Simoniac and stained with the filth of seductive lust, he could in no way have driven out demons if he had not possessed within himself the power of the Holy Spirit.

For Samson, too, who, contrary to the commands of divine law, consorted with prostitutes of a foreign nation, could never have escaped such exceedingly harsh bonds, nor alone slaughtered so many thousands of men, unless the strength of the Holy Spirit had fortified him (Judges XIV). Furthermore, that false prophet also possessed a prophetic revelation of the Holy Spirit: without it, he could not have persuaded the man of God returning from Bethel, through carefully contrived lies, to eat contrary to the divine command. He asserted:

[Col. 0128B]

“An angel,” he said, “spoke to me by the word of the Lord, saying: Bring him back with you to your house, so that he may eat bread and drink water” (III Kings XIII).

Immediately Scripture continues:

“He deceived him,” it says, “and led him back with him” (ibid.).

And shortly afterward:

“When they were sitting at table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet who had brought him back, and he cried out” (ibid.),

declaring, namely, the manner of his death, because he had been disobedient to the Lord’s command. Here it must be observed that Scripture first plainly accuses the man of having deceived his brother, yet immediately afterward it unequivocally affirms that the word of the Lord came to this same man and that he prophesied most truly. Certainly, if the sequence of the event is carefully considered, this deceiver is unquestionably shown to have been the murderer of an innocent man. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit did not refuse to come upon such a man; and at the very moment of his deceitful entrapment, while he sought to deceive through a lie, he was compelled to prophesy through an oracle of truth. (See the scholia.) [Col. 0128C]

Indeed, who does not know that the priest Eli was reprobate and condemned by the sentence of divine judgment both for his leniency and for the unrestrained license of his sons? Yet through his blessing Hannah’s womb was not barren, for he had invoked fertility upon her womb. Scripture says:

“Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, and said: May the Lord grant you offspring from this woman in return for the loan which you have lent to the Lord.”

Immediately afterward it adds:

“Therefore the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters” (I Kings II).

This blessing, therefore, was made effective not by the man’s merit but by the office of the priest; and what the minister’s personal condition lacked, the power of his ministry supplied.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That evil beginnings often lead to fortunate outcomes

[Col. 0128D]

What harm, finally, does a Simoniac do if he lays hands upon those being ordained, since he is able neither to take away what is possessed nor to prevent what is divinely increased? That gift of heavenly grace is brought forth invisibly not from the purse of the man laboring outwardly, but from the treasure of the one who presides invisibly. Even if the man who sows is a thief, the earth nevertheless, by God’s authorship, supplies strength for the crops to germinate. Though the hand that plants be filthy or leprous, the fruit gathered at the fullness of maturity is certainly clean. [Col. 0129A]

Often a beautiful offspring is born from an adulterous marriage, and from the obscene pleasure of parents there arises an attractive appearance in their children. Jacob fathered some sons by his legitimate wives and received others from concubines of servile condition; yet when both groups came to obtain the inheritance, they were granted equal rights in the distribution of their allotted portions (Genesis XXX). Pharez was born from a woman [the reading *theristrata* is uncertain] who had been exposed at the crossroads, yet he is found not least among the leaders of the Israelite clans (Genesis XXXVIII). Solomon is known to have originated from the woman who had belonged to Uriah, yet he held an incomparable primacy of the royal scepter (II Kings X; I Chronicles III). Obed certainly took his origin from Ruth the Moabite, but he merited having the excellent king David, that is, the great one, as his grandson. [Col. 0129B] Boaz, too, was fathered by Rahab the prostitute, yet he merited being counted in the royal catalogue of the Lord’s genealogy (Matthew I). (See the scholia.)

And why should I mention others? For the Mediator himself, God and man, took his origin from sinners, and from fermented dough he assumed unleavened purity without any infection of antiquity. Indeed, to speak more explicitly, from the very flesh of the Virgin, who was conceived in sin, there came forth flesh without sin, which moreover freely erased the sins of the flesh.

What wonder, then, if the powerful hand of the Lord, effective for whatever he wills, does in the Spirit who gives life what it is proved to do even in the flesh, which profits nothing? (John VI.) For if he causes evil beginnings to come to fortunate outcomes, and does this in earthly matters, how can we fail to believe that he acts in the same way, with a more generous dispensation, in spiritual sacraments? Surely, he who commands a tree not to know the contagion of a filthy planter—why should it be denied that those who are consecrated have no guilt at all from the wickedness of the consecrator? He who admitted bastards (*manseres*) alongside legitimate sons, and the sons of slave women alongside their masters’ sons, into partnership as though they were to receive an inheritance, and distinguished them from the others by no inequality—what wonder if he also causes those promoted by wicked priests to share equally in the dignity of priestly office with those ordained by good priests? [Col. 0129C]

This plainly does not happen through the merit of the consecrator but rather through the word of the living and abiding God. For by the word of God the Father it was said:

[Col. 0129D]

“Let the earth bring forth green plants, and those producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees making fruit according to their kind” (Genesis I).

And behold, this word remains inviolate even today, so that the yield of fruits does not imitate the diversity of the farmers, but in each kind its own proper seed is found in the grasses and its own proper seed in the fruits. That seed, in turn, is committed to the earth and afterward prepared not differently but according to the appearance of its own kind. If, therefore, through the power of the divine word, the earth returns what it receives in the same likeness, what wonder if that priestly blessing, which is cast into the soul of the person approaching like a seed, invisibly works priesthood through the breath of the Holy Spirit, and therefore it is no longer the image of the sower that must properly be sought in the fruit, but only, so to speak, the likeness of the seed that emerges? [Col. 0130A]

God also said to the animals: “Increase and multiply” (ibid.). Through the efficacy of this word, all living creatures continue to be produced to the present day—not, certainly, principally as new creations, but propagated by transmission from the same original seed.

[Col. 0130B]

Since, then, those words, once spoken, remain so immovably effective, what should we think of the words of priestly blessings, which are entirely sacred and divine and are therefore repeated outwardly whenever people are promoted, so that they may work the mystery inwardly? For if such power is asserted to reside in the words of enchanters that a serpent is broken as though struck by stones thrown at it, what wonder if a priestly blessing contains within itself the sacrament of divine power, through which the priest becomes what he is when it is applied to him? Are incantatory words, then, of greater power than those wholly efficacious and mystical words consecrated by the invocation of the divine name?

## CHAPTER XX  
### That reason does not permit the Holy Spirit to be given through a Simoniac in baptism but not in consecration

[Col. 0130C]

It is surely astonishing that those who shamelessly assert that Simoniacs can baptize effectively but can in no way consecrate should be so foolishly senseless. Although this has already been discussed briefly above, it does not seem out of place to explain it more fully. Let us therefore bring forward a Simoniac baptizing and likewise consecrating, and let us determine, if we can, why, when baptism administered through him is effective, consecration should come to nothing and, as they say, lose the power of the sacrament. [Col. 0130D]

Behold: after the first rudiments of faith which he has taught the catechumen, the one who baptizes immediately recites prayers over him, in accordance with ecclesiastical custom. These prayers were composed for this very purpose by priestly authority. Thus, through the grace of exorcism, he drives out the evil enemy who had exercised tyranny over the catechumen until then, and by invoking the Paraclete he introduces the Holy Spirit into him through pious prayers. But what else does the consecrator do except, likewise reciting the canonical prayers, invoke the same Holy Spirit over the one who is being advanced, and entreat that he may deign to descend upon him? Is not something greater accomplished through the baptizer than is exhibited through the office of the consecrator?

For it is more for the Holy Spirit to descend with new favor upon one in whom he had not previously been than to promote one in whom he already dwelt through faith to the order of a higher rank. Through the office of the catechist, or of the baptizer, the unclean spirit is expelled and a dwelling is prepared in the new human being for the God who is coming, as the words of that same exorcism testify. By the command of adjuration they say to the wicked spirit: “But you, flee, devil; for the judgment of God is approaching.” In consecrations, however, what is expelled is not something evil that had already been erased and seemed to be absent; rather, what is good and had been bestowed is increased through an accumulation of fuller grace. [Col. 0131A]

Is it to be believed, then, that one and the same person can accomplish what is greater but cannot fulfill what is lesser? Perhaps the contrary is said: that those rudiments of initiating faith contain things that are not employed in the mysteries of consecration, such as the salt placed into the newly converted, the water into which the person being baptized is immersed, and the chrism with which he is anointed. But these things, considered in themselves, are bare elements and are known to possess no secret of mystical dignity; through the priest’s prayer, however, and the invocation of the divine name, they conceive the sacrament of inward power.

The sacraments, therefore, whether of consecration or of baptism, consist not in material and earthly things but in the prayers of priests and the invocation of divinity—although in the consecrations of priests sanctified oil also appears to be employed. Since, then, one and the same Simoniac completes the order of canonical prayers in both cases and regularly invokes the name of the divinity in both, when the Holy Spirit is given through him in baptism, how is it that he is not given in priestly promotion? This does not penetrate the understanding of reason, nor does human judgment discern it. But the contrary is said: that a Simoniac cannot give what he does not possess.

[Col. 0131B]

Very well, then: what is the meaning of the fact that the priest breathes upon the face of the catechumen, saying: “Come out from him, unclean Satan; give honor to the living and true God; give honor to the Holy Spirit”? These words plainly show that through the priest’s breathing upon the person—through the hidden working, evidently, of the divine power’s mystery—the evil spirit is expelled and the Holy Spirit deigns to enter. If all this is likewise fulfilled through the breathing of a Simoniac, just as through the office of a good priest, why should what is conceded to be possible in one sacrament consequently be denied as possible in another? [Col. 0131C]

Even if baptism were, God forbid, administered for sale—although this is strongly contrary to the sacred canon—it is by no means to be believed that it lacked the mystery of full and perfect regeneration. Therefore the one who received baptism under such a payment of money is asserted neither to require rebaptism worthily nor to be judged deprived of the divine gift. [Col. 0131D]

If anyone should burst into such madness of obstinacy as to judge even the baptism of Simoniacs invalid, then not our own argument but the entire discipline of the Catholic faith would rise against it in general, and the universal Church would arm itself against the claim, since it seeks to overturn all the institutions of the holy Fathers.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### That attention must be paid to what is received, not from whom it is received

Perhaps, however, the objection is made that blessed Pope Gregory testifies concerning the condemnation of Simoniacs, saying:

“His blessing,” he says, “is turned into a curse, because he is promoted in order to become a heretic.”

[Col. 0132A]

We certainly approve this judgment and do not deem it permissible to dissent from it. The one who received what was good wrongly is cursed and is a heretic. What is received is good in itself, but it has become evil for the recipient. Thus the morsel—that morsel, namely, which was extended to Judas (John XIII)—did not become evil from being made out of something good; it became evil for the man who did not receive what was good well, because he received it unworthily. Therefore, if Judas had handed that same morsel to someone else, the sacred gift would not have contracted any stain in itself from the guilt of the giver, nor would any contagion necessarily have passed to the recipient.

Even today, if any unworthy person receives the Lord’s body from the most holy altar and hands it to another, what is received is unquestionably clean, and the gift of divine grace is not defiled by the stain of the corrupt minister. Though every wicked person eats and drinks judgment upon himself (I Corinthians XI), nevertheless what is eaten and drunk is the grace of God. For the grace of God tasted death, that is, the humanity of Christ. “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I). [Col. 0132B]

If, therefore, what is clean is itself unclean to the defiled, it must be admitted that priesthood, which for a good man is the cause of spiritual dignity, becomes for a Simoniac the material of condemnation: so that by that very thing one man is certainly a Catholic priest, while another is truly asserted to be a heretic.

[Col. 0132C]

Nor is it surprising that this occurs in spiritual matters, since the same difference can easily be found in bodily things. Often food that invigorates one person burdens another, and from the same medicinal antidote one person dies while another recovers. [Col. 0132C] There is one fire by which wax melts and earth dries at the same time; and the same candle that is consumed by fire is used to illuminate those who approach, while the light which it offers at the cost of its own destruction has been made an instrument for us to see amid darkness. What difference does it make to me, then, that the candle is turned to ashes, provided that the light I borrowed from it continues for me without failing?

Let the Simoniac burn, burn from the very source by which the Catholic is illuminated; and by the same light through which he ministers to others, let him himself move toward the darkness of his own ruin, so that what burns may perish, while what has been illuminated may live. The light of priests is indeed light for those who seek light; but for those who burn with the heat of ambition, it is a conflagration. What one possesses for the destruction of his own ruin, another receives for the advancement of increased salvation. [Col. 0132D]

Samson, to be sure, drew a honeycomb of honey from the mouth of a dead lion, and from the dry jawbone of a donkey he satisfied himself with flowing water (Judges XIV); but he tasted neither the donkey’s sluggishness in the water nor the beast’s ferocity in the honey. In both cases, what was taken tasted in the mouth according to its own nature. The source from which it had been taken made no great difference.

What wonder, then, if we think that something similar occurs with Simoniacs to what we see taking place in baptismal water? Through it we are reborn anew in Christ, although the same water, after the work has been completed, is poured out into a despised sewer.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That neither the Novatians are to be deposed nor the Arians baptized again

[Col. 0133A]

But let us now examine the sacred canons as briefly as possible. Although the explicit judgment on the question proposed is not frequently found in them, let us establish what ought to be held by comparing certain cases. We know that it was decreed by the Council of Nicaea that the Cathari who return to the Catholic Church are to be received in their orders merely by receiving the imposition of hands. Why is this, unless that class of heretics remained intact in the Catholic faith, although they went astray in certain other superstitions?

[Col. 0133B]

For it is known that Novatus, whose error they followed, had taught that one ought neither to communicate with those married twice nor to grant forgiveness, even after repentance, to those who had fallen during persecution. If, then, those who have already been ordained by these heretics are by no means to be deprived of their honor, for the reason that their consecrators do not waver in the faith, what are we to think about the ordinations of Simoniacs, who preserve almost all the regulations of ecclesiastical institution?
