Perhaps, however, it is objected that Simoniacs are not perfect in faith, since they sin against the Holy Spirit, whom they suppose can be purchased with money. We readily reply that, if this exacting severity of judgment is maintained, a certain kind of fault against the Holy Spirit is also found among the Novatians. [Col. 0133C]

Since forgiveness is granted to the penitent through the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of sins, it is unquestionably clear that the one who does not communicate forgiveness to those who have fallen and repented fights against the Holy Spirit.

But it is one thing to sin in the faith and another to depart from the faith. A soldier who has fallen weakly in the conflicts of war must be rebuked differently from one who, having renounced his military oath, has defected as a surrendered man to the camp of the enemy. The same punishment is not owed to the servant who sins in domestic matters under his master’s authority and to the one who has shaken off the yoke of servitude and chosen the right of a foreign master. Although these people appear to offend against the rule of faith in some respect, they do not do so to the extent that they should be accused, through heretical depravity, of denying the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0133D]

Therefore, when they return, hands are imposed upon them because they have sinned; but because they have not denied the Spirit, they are not deprived of the office of the priestly rank. The Arians, on the other hand, who openly and utterly impiously oppose the divinity of the Holy Spirit, cannot, when returning to the Catholic faith, continue in the dignity of the evil order they received. For, as their sacrilegious confession makes clear, they believe that the Father is creator, the Son a creature, and that the Holy Spirit is, damnably, a creature of a creature.

Since, therefore, they do not possess the power of the Holy Spirit in the faith—through which, evidently, every order of the Church’s dignity is perfected—the ordination performed among them is judged invalid by canonical decrees. [Col. 0134A]

But we believe it appropriate to insert here anything that Pope Innocent may have left concerning them in his Decretals, under his own words:

“We detest the Arians,” he says, “and other such plagues, because we receive their laymen who have been converted to the Lord under the appearance of repentance and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the imposition of hands; but it does not seem that we should receive their clerics together with any dignity of priestly ministry. For if we permit only their baptism to be valid—which is performed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—do we not therefore think that they possess the Holy Spirit from that baptism and those mysteries? Since their authors departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received, and they cannot give its fullness, which operates especially in ordinations; for through the faithlessness of their impiety, rather than through faith, I should say, they lost it. Nor can we deem their profane priests worthy of Christ’s honors, when we receive their imperfect laymen, as I have said, with the appearance of repentance, so that they may receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0134B]

In these decretal words it is plainly understood that in the promotion of clerics the faith of the one ordaining is rightly taken into account; from it, evidently, depends whether the ordination itself is judged valid or invalid. What the ordinator holds in faith, the ordained receives as a gift. Indeed, if the Arians had possessed the right faith, even if they had been entangled in the error of some other depravity, the consecration performed among them would not have perished. (See the scholium.)

[Col. 0134C]

Here it must be noted how great a reverence is owed to the invocation of the divine name, since even those baptized by men whose faith is condemned as so perfidious, if I may put it so, do not dare to rebaptize. Because their authors, as is said, did not possess the right faith for receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, hands are imposed upon them; but because they were immersed in water under the invocation of the Holy Trinity, they are not baptized again. Since, then, words spoken without faith under the heretical superstition of the Arians are not dared to be judged invalid, how can the consecration of Simoniacs lack force, when faith and the other sacraments of regular observance agree with it?

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### That the effect of consecration rests upon the foundation of faith

[Col. 0134D] Concerning the Donatists, too, we know that the Council of Carthage granted that whenever any of them intended to return to Catholic unity, he should be received with his honor if this appeared beneficial to Christian peace (Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, Book II, chapter 9). As we learned in the general enumeration of heresies, the Donatists were not led astray by a serious error of faith; rather, they formed a schism in anger because a certain Caecilian had been enthroned in the see of Carthage against their wishes, and they were cut off from ecclesiastical communion. Although it is certain that no one can receive the Holy Spirit except within the holy Catholic Church, nevertheless anyone ordained among them was not deprived of his honor if this served peace, because he persevered in the faith.

[Col. 0135A]

Since, then, a Donatist—who is unquestionably a schismatic and is proved to be alien from the gift of the Holy Spirit—can sometimes remain in the order of the honor he received, it is clearer than daylight that consecration is not the merit of the one ordained or of the one ordaining, but that the entire sacrament looks rather to the faith of both. Otherwise, whether a Donatist promotes a Donatist or a Novatian a Novatian to the rights of the clergy, what dignity of merit exists in either of them, such that one could give or the other receive the mystery of divine grace?

But between the evil parties—the giver and the recipient—there lies a good thing in the middle, which knows not to be deterred from its own nobility by the fault of either. If a leper gives gold to a leper, the gold certainly gleams and is not stained by any variation of rough hands. If a blind man hands a lamp to a blind man, the light, knowing nothing of blindness, does not admit darkness from the hands of those carrying it. [Col. 0135B]

Therefore, if the right faith is present—namely, if belief in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is correct—the consecration even of any unworthy priest is accomplished without distinction; nor does the gift of divine grace suffer any loss of its perfection because of the merit of the unworthy minister.

[Col. 0135C]

Hence the aforementioned Pope Innocent, when discussing the two heresies, namely the Paulianists and the Novatians, together, and explaining why he decreed that those coming from the Paulianists were to be baptized but entirely prohibited this in the case of the Novatians, gave them this reason in the following words:

“The Paulianists,” he said, “do not baptize at all in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; nor has any question concerning the unity of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit ever arisen among these”—namely, the Novatians.

And therefore, out of all the separated groups, this one alone was selected as the group to which this should be granted, because they committed no offense against the sacrament of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0135D]

These words of the venerable Innocent are so definitive and clear that they remove every scruple from our minds and unquestionably resolve the knot of the question proposed. If, then, the sacrament cannot be given through the Paulianists because they do not possess faith in the Holy Trinity, but can be given through the Novatians because, although they are heretics in another respect, they nevertheless retain the fullness of orthodox faith, it follows plainly that, if faith stands firm, consecration possesses force; nor is the action undermined by a fault when it rests upon the foundation of faith.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That bishops wrongly ordained possess the grace of consecration for others, though not for themselves

Let us therefore concede—or rather assert—that the Simoniac is a heretic, but that the Novatian is also a heretic, and the Donatist likewise a heretic. The Simoniac sins against the Holy Spirit because he purchases the gift of God; the Novatian certainly sins against the same Holy Spirit because, even after repentance, he despairs of forgiveness for those who have fallen; and the Donatist, too, sins against the Holy Spirit because he separates himself from the Church, outside which the Holy Spirit cannot be found. What reason, then, is there that, when the ordination of those others is decreed valid, the ordination of these men should be judged worthless—especially since we are not striving to ensure that Simoniacs remain in the honor they wrongly purchased, but rather that those ordained by them freely should not lose the place of their rank?

[Col. 0136A]

Here it must be observed how great is the difference in the condition of those about whom we are speaking. Donatists promote Donatists, and Novatians promote Novatians, who are entangled in the same errors; Simoniacs, however, ordain not Simoniacs but rather innocent and Catholic men. Thus the latter are not only subject to the objection that they were ordained by heretics; it would also have to be added that they themselves were likewise heretics. The former, however, are not subject to the heresy of Simony, even if they were regularly promoted by Simoniacs with every commercial transaction of venality removed, and even if they received the office of administration in the same churches where they had received the mystery of holy baptism. [Col. 0136B]

[Col. 0136C]

Whether such men are rightly excluded from their honors can easily be assessed from the authority of blessed Leo, if we do not hesitate to record here his decretal judgment in his own words. He says (*Distinction* 62, chapter “No Reason”):

“No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan. Since the question of an honor wrongly received often arises, who would doubt that nothing should be attributed to these men which is not shown to have been conferred? If, however, any clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in their churches, which belonged to their own bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding authorities, it can be held valid, so that they may remain in those churches; otherwise such an ordination must be considered void.”

Behold, by the authentic judgment of Pope Leo, those whom neither the agreement of the clergy nor that of the people elected, and whom the concord of the provincial bishops did not consecrate with the judgment of the metropolitan, are not counted among the bishops. Yet those who were ordained by them in their own churches by the judgment of the presiding authorities are not at all commanded to be deprived of the honor of the rank imposed upon them. This is so because the man who forced his way into the office of bishop through such great usurpation that almost everyone’s opposition was directed against him, and for whom what he received could be of no benefit—since he is not counted among the bishops—could nevertheless benefit others, so that those promoted by him would not be excluded from their own honors. [Col. 0136D]

But who would deny that a commercial transaction of venality could also have intervened there, where the summit of honor was seized through such obstinate and untimely ambition? Yet he possesses for others what he does not possess for himself, since he is permitted to consecrate others although he himself is not counted among the bishops. Often a second branch is grafted onto a sterile trunk; in what it produces, it preserves the rights not of the trunk but of its own nature.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### That those often ordained by impious heretics are not removed from their offices

[Col. 0137A]

What shall I say about the fact that ecclesiastical authority appears to come to the aid of those who were ordained by the most impious heretics, and that in promulgating judgments on this controversy it considers not so much the ancient faithlessness of those promoting them as the new faith and repentance of those who were promoted? Anyone who carefully studies the decrees of the pontiffs is not unaware that the same Pope Innocent whom we mentioned shortly above granted permission for all those who had been ordained by Bonosus the heretic before his condemnation to remain in their honors, provided that, having abandoned and condemned his error, they decided to join themselves to ecclesiastical unity. [Col. 0137B]

Bonosus, indeed, as is found in the same decrees, is recognized as having been a Photinian. The Photinians, however, deny that Christ, God, was begotten before the ages from the substance of the Father. Since they do not fear to deny the Son of God together with the Jews, they likewise incur with them a share in no different condemnation.

Since, then, those who are reported to have been consecrated not only by so pernicious a heretic but also to have been entangled in his errors are permitted to remain in the ranks they have received, it is readily understood what ought rightly to be judged concerning those who have been advanced by Simoniacs without themselves being guilty of simony.

Nor is that matter unlike what Pope Anastasius decreed concerning the heretic Acacius. His decretal judgments are so carefully arranged [Col. 0137C] and in every respect so consistent with our arguments that, even if everything we have written at greater length were lacking, they would fully suffice to establish the question now under discussion. Therefore, let us not hesitate to quote here at some length from his writing, so that what we say may appear to be drawn not from our own inventions but from the regulations of the Fathers.

For among other things he says (Distinction 19, chapter 1) to the emperor Anastasius:

“According to the custom of the Catholic Church,” he says, “let the most sacred heart of Your Serenity recognize that no portion of harm proceeding from the name of Acacius touches any of those whom Acacius baptized, or whom, according to the canons, he ordained as priests or Levites, so that perhaps the grace of the sacrament, handed down through an unrighteous man, might seem less firm. For even baptism bestowed outside the Church, whether given by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient no less undefiled, because that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution”; as is declared when it is said: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew XXIII).

For if the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through the most fetid places, are not defiled by any contamination from contact, how much more is the power of him who made this visible sun untouched by any unworthiness of the minister. Even Judas, although he was sacrilegious and a thief (John XXIII), was not rejected in whatever he did among the apostles according to the dignity entrusted to him; and the benefits given through an unworthy man suffered no diminution on that account. The Lord made this clear in the most manifest words: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do” (Matthew XXIII).

Whatever, therefore, any minister in the Church appears to perform for the advancement of human beings according to his office is wholly contained in the effect produced by the fulfillment of divine power. Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians III). A little later the same Anastasius says:

“Therefore he also, whose name we say ought to be withheld, by ministering good things badly harmed only himself. For the inviolable sacrament which was given through him achieved in others the perfection of its power.” [Col. 0138B]

Behold: this apostolic man is seen to have stood as though on our behalf and to have taken up our cause, so that he seems to have left us almost nothing to say concerning this question. Let them go, then, and impudently resist so great an authority. Nor will what seemed right to ancient rulers suffice these new censors, so that, while discretion is not maintained, even piety may be lost.

For some, while desiring to appear holier than they are, try to cut away what is corrupt in such a manner that they also attack and tear apart what is sound. And, in order to seem to persist sternly in the judgment of justice for the applause of men, they do not fear to stray cruelly from the path of piety.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That those whom Acacius ordained after his condemnation should not be deprived of their honors.

[Col. 0138C]

Let these men hear what the same pope decreed concerning those whom Acacius ordained after his condemnation; for I do not think they have read it, since it plainly conflicts with their rash judgment. Let them therefore hear the mercy of the Apostolic See and soften the harshness of their own examination.

After the matters we have already presented, he adds this:

“If,” he says, “the curious suspicion of some extends so far that, after the judgment pronounced by Pope Felix, they imagine Acacius to have acted ineffectively in the sacraments which he usurped, and therefore fear that those who received the mysteries imparted either in consecrations or in baptism may appear to have received divine benefits in vain, let them remember that the preceding treatment prevails equally in this matter. For he did this not without usurpation of the priesthood; yet, since the mysteries retain their power, the guilty person did not thereby harm others. For to him applies what is sung by David’s trumpet:

‘Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the head of those who walk in their sins’ (Psalm LXII).

“For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others. The authority of all heavenly Scripture testifies to this judgment, as it is also said through the Holy Spirit in the Prophet: ‘He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house’ (Psalm C).”

Thus, when he claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head when he was condemned; [Col. 0139A] for it was not the people, who thirsted for his gift in the ministries, who were excluded. Rather, that soul which had sinned was justly liable in its own person. The abundant teaching of Scripture everywhere bears witness to this.

What can now be said in response to these things? What cunning stratagem can prevail against them, or what arguments will be available to those who oppose the truth? Here the matter concerns one particular person, but the cause defined is universal.

We do not, however, present these matters as though we were standing on behalf of heretics, intending thereby to destroy the other judgments of the holy Fathers that impose stricter penalties upon them and their ministry. We present them so that, while the moderation of discerning judgment found among the earlier saints is observed, those who live now may likewise not exceed the bounds of upright examination through immoderate justice; lest what the Apostle says of certain similar people also appear to apply to them: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans X).

Those, therefore, who were advanced by a heretic condemned by the authority of the Apostolic See—[p. 125] do not fall from the administration of their rank; yet those who were consecrated by Simoniacs without themselves being Simoniacs are to suffer the danger of losing the honor they received? Surely this is a harsh sentence and an altogether inhuman judgment of indiscriminate examination: that those whom conscience declares innocent should be condemned by the punishment inflicted upon them, and that judicial severity should be extended against those whom no rashness in an alleged sacrilege accuses.

Where no crime has been committed, why should a penal punishment be imposed? Where there is no guilt, why should an innocent man be displayed as guilty? What would be judged prejudicial even in the courts of judges—why should it appear right in the council of holy priests?

Pious pontiffs customarily respond to the deposition of any single priest with a sigh from the depths of their hearts, covering their sorrowful faces with abundant streams of tears, while all those present are compelled by the impulse of pious compassion to share in the grief.

Behold: now almost the whole Church of Christ is deprived of priests by the reckoning of a single judgment; and, to make the situation appear tolerable, the entire body of priests is deposed collectively, and this is treated as a joke. Why is there not at least recalled what the divine voice cries out through Ezekiel:

“The soul that sins shall itself die. The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor the son bear the iniquity of the father. The justice of the just shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezekiel XVIII).

These men, greedy for the calamity of their brothers, strive and exert themselves toward this end: that a soul which has not sinned should perish, and that an innocent person should pay the penalty for another’s crime. They long for sons to be condemned for the iniquities of their fathers, for the righteous to be proscribed on account of the crimes of the wicked; and, to speak more plainly, they assign those who are not Simoniacs to the punishments of Simoniacs and condemn them for the commerce of men who are wholly ignorant of the crime of that accursed business.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the Simoniac heresy flourished down to the present time.

Who does not know that, until the reign of this most clement king Henry [Col. 0140A] and the pontificate of Clement, of revered memory, and of this most blessed apostolic Leo—under whose pontificate the holy Church now rejoices that it is governed—the deadly poison of the Simoniac heresy boiled over throughout the western kingdoms? What was commonly done was freely permitted and was not at all considered subject to avenging punishment; and what was agreeable to almost everyone was held as a rule, as though it had been decreed by a legal sanction.

What, then, did the man deserve? What did he do wrong who approached simply his mother Church, in which he had been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, and received there both baptism and the grace of consecration? It was not his responsibility to debate the character of the person who was to consecrate him. Therefore, when he found that the man presiding over his own Church in the episcopal chair was there, he rightly considered it proper to be advanced by him to the order.

What else could he do, when necessity required him to give his name in the profession of sacred service, while he was not permitted to migrate to the bishop of another diocese? Why are the ancient deeds or precepts of the holy Fathers not examined more carefully, so that when the judgment of censure is pronounced, the same line of discerning moderation may always be maintained?

For the aforementioned magnificent Leo also ordered that all clerics coming from heretics should indeed be received in the orders they had already attained, but forbade them to be advanced to higher ranks. We are content here briefly to cite the title of his decree, while referring those who have the leisure to the text itself to read what is written there at greater length:

“Every cleric,” he says (I, question 1, ‘If anyone of heretical’), “of whatever order, who, abandoning the Catholic faith, has joined himself to heretical communion, if he returns to the Church, shall remain in the rank he held, without advancement.”

Let us suppose, then, that Simoniacs differ in no respect from other heretics, and that through a schismatic sect they likewise withdraw far from ecclesiastical communion with them. Nevertheless, whoever has already been advanced by them to the priesthood or to other ranks is, by Leo’s judgment, decreed to remain there.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Here it is clearly proved that the Holy Spirit is received through Simoniacs.

But the opposing side says: Behold, Blessed Pope Gregory cries out: “If anyone,” he says (II, question 1, “Whoever”), “does not burn intensely, with due regard for his office, to correct the crime of the Simoniac heresy or of the neophytes, let him not doubt that he shares in the portion of him from whom this sacrilegious offense took its beginning.”

I agree, I say, and God forbid that I should hold a different opinion from this holy man. Indeed, each of the faithful should strive with all his strength to correct the offense of both plagues, and should burn with zeal for sound judgment so that Simoniacs, together with neophytes, may be deposed alike.

We therefore do not stand on behalf of Simoniacs, whom the authority of all sacred Scripture testifies must be condemned. Rather, as we gather from the many sanctions of the holy Fathers, we freely profess that those ordained gratuitously by Simoniacs ought rightly to be retained in their orders. Thus, whoever appeals to Gregory as evidence for his own case (Gregory, Homily on the Gospels) should not disdain, in reciprocal fairness, to admit Gregory’s testimony as well—and not merely some random testimony, but, as the saying goes, one that touches the matter itself to the quick—and should henceforth put an end to contentious verbosity.

Finally, when speaking in a certain homily about Simoniacs, he added:

“For who are those who today sell doves in the temple of God, except those who in the Church receive a price for the laying on of hands, through which laying on of hands the Holy Spirit is given from heaven?”

Behold: if it is decided that faith must be placed in the authority of this holy man, there is no reason to prolong the controversy of the dispute. What could be clearer, what more explicit, than the statement that the Holy Spirit who is sold through the laying on of hands is given from heaven? [Col. 0141B]

And, to impress the same point even more firmly and to instruct the slower understanding more fully concerning what had been said, he did not hesitate to repeat what he had plainly stated earlier, saying:

“Therefore the dove is sold, because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price.”

If, then, the Holy Spirit is received through that laying on of hands which is offered for a price, what less sacrament is found in Simoniacs than in priests advanced without payment? They are like vipers: they are themselves damnably watered by the fountain that they beneficially cause to flow for others, and, while they give birth to children, they themselves die.

For what is surprising if good ministers arise from evil ordainers in spiritual ministries, when something similar often occurs even in carnal generation? It is certain that children with sound sight are born from blind parents, and that offspring sound in limb and tall in stature may follow hunchbacked and disabled parents.

Clearly, neither is the virtue of those who ordain an increase to those who do not fear to walk by crooked ways; nor, again, does their wickedness harm those who proceed along the straight line of upright conduct.

For is Samuel known to have suffered prejudice because he was Heli’s disciple? (1 Samuel II, 3.) Or what benefit did it bring Nicolas that the apostolic election raised him to the rank of Levitical ministry? The former received the laying on of the apostles’ hands together with Stephen and perished (Acts VI); the latter lived together with the wickedness of Hophni and Phinehas. Yet it became known to all that Samuel was a prophet faithful to God.

Therefore it would have been fitting for those who are all consumed with zeal to depose everyone collectively to preserve at least the principle of the above-mentioned Innocent’s moderate dispensation. For when he was discussing those ordained by heretics, after much else he added:

“Whenever,” he says, “a sin is committed by peoples or by a crowd, since punishment cannot be exacted against everyone because of their number, it is customary to let it pass unavenged.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. That those who were advanced by Simoniacs shine through miracles.

Nor do I think I should silently pass over something that I hear repeated frequently by many who report it. What shall we say of certain venerable men whom we know beyond doubt to have been advanced to the priesthood by Simoniacs, and whom we know to have persisted continually in offering sacrifices until their death, while we now plainly see them shining with the distinguished power of miracles?

In our own time, blessed men—namely, Rondaldus of Camarina, Amitus of Ramibona, Guido of Pomposa, Firmanus of Fermo, and many others—flourished through their devotion to holy conduct. Over their venerable bodies, by the authority of a priestly council, sacred altars have been erected, where the divine mysteries are offered in response to the demands of miracles.

It is therefore plainly evident that the sacrifice offered by their hands has been sweet and acceptable in the sight of God; and through them the divine dispensation is made known with the clearest light. For the darkness of another’s perversity does not obscure anyone whom the radiance of his own religion and uprightness illuminates; nor does the guilt of those who advanced them overwhelm a place where the purity and innocence of the advanced men stand firm.

But when I was once discussing these matters with certain devout bishops, what Ubertus of Rimini—an exceedingly reverend and honorable bishop—reported now returns to my memory:

“My namesake predecessor, Bishop Ubertus,” he said, “paid nine hundred pounds of Pavia currency toward the purchase of the holy see, as the province bears witness. Yet afterward he consecrated Blessed Arduinus as a priest, through whom Almighty God displays so many astonishing miracles. When I immediately inquired whether that man of blessed memory had continued to offer sacrifice in sound health, he replied that Arduinus had diligently labored in offering saving victims until the moment of his final illness.”

Since, then, all those whom we mentioned above are said to have been consecrated by Simoniacs, yet remained in the offices they had received until the end of their lives and so pleased the divine judgment that the wondrous testimony of their merits bears witness to them, it is beyond doubt that purchase by those who promote does not prejudice the one promoted when the promoted man is unaware of the transaction’s venality; nor is the guilt of the seller transferred to one who is not held by the crime of the sale.

It might perhaps be regarded as tolerable in some measure if an assertion of falsehood confused only the order of the present life—unless it also entirely removed every hope and basis of Christian piety from the past age. For they say that what was then regarded as the Church was merely an ordinary house; that what was believed to be an altar was simply a stone; that priests and those seen to have been established in the other orders were altogether laymen and strangers to every power of the spiritual sacrament; that what was believed to be the body and blood of the Lord was simply bread and wine; and that no earthly substance had been infused with the power of the Holy Spirit.

Everything, then, would have been false, frivolous, and utterly removed from the truth of Christian redemption. It follows that our fathers—whether they knew these things to have been false or judged them to be false although they were true—all perished indiscriminately through an unavoidable necessity. For what benefit is there in recognizing a danger that one is not permitted to escape? Or how can anyone reach the fountain of truth if, even unknowingly, he eagerly wanders through crooked bends?

Could Simon alone extinguish the waters, like a barrier placed between God and human beings, and separate the human race from fellowship with its Creator? Far be it, far be it that a false man should sever what the true God and man has joined together. Far be it that human perversity should be able to overwhelm all people and erase divine benefits.

But what, I ask, shall we say about those whom, after their participation in that wicked commercial transaction, we see even today occupying the pontifical insignia for forty or fifty years? To say nothing of their predecessors, whether near or distant, whom the same thief produced elsewhere: all who were ordained at that time through the intrusion of these men have either already been removed from this life or have been withdrawn from the exercise of their offices by the obstacle of a dark old age.

It is therefore necessary that in their dioceses the sacred mysteries nevertheless be performed by those clerics who received their order from Simoniacs who are still alive. What, then, should be thought about these men? What must be admitted? [p. 129] Are we to believe that many thousands of people under them are perishing, deceived by an empty semblance of the sacrament from men who themselves do not possess the sacrament’s grace?

Should the people be told either to obtain priests from other dioceses or, themselves migrating, to receive the sacraments from those who were not ordained by Simoniacs? But behold, the sacred canons strongly resist this and repel from communion those who cross the boundaries of parishes without the bishop’s authorization.

When these people seek our advice, then, what counsel shall we give? According to the ineffectual logic of this supposed dispensation, native priests cannot impart the sacred mysteries to them, while canonical authority does not permit them to pass to outsiders. Thus, to the injury of the immensely generous divine mercy, an unavoidable necessity of perishing is imposed upon people who, shut in on every side, receive no help from any remedy of salutary refuge.

But we postpone pursuing these matters further. What is dreadful even to hear should, in the judgment of a sound mind, be left to be understood rather than read, so that the sober reader may recognize in a few words how great an impossibility entangles the authors of this doctrine.

## CHAPTER XXX. That rebaptism and reconsecration are equal crimes.

Since, then, in speaking of reconsecrations this matter has appropriately arisen, and since this alone remains at the end of our little work, let us not hesitate to treat, even briefly, this subject as well.

Certainly, anyone accustomed to tread the threshold of sacred Scripture has learned to weigh rebaptism and reconsecration on the same scale of judgment. For just as one who is rebaptized is shown to have stripped off Christ, whom he had put on, so one who is reconsecrated is plainly proved to have lost the Holy Spirit whom he had received. Since the divinity of the supreme Word and of the Paraclete is one, and their essence is undoubtedly the same, whoever loses the one will not have the other. Therefore, just as it is wicked for someone through the repetition of baptism to presume to drive Christ from himself, so it is likewise execrable for someone through reconsecration not to fear denying the Holy Spirit.

If we do not object to adding a brief passage from the decree of Pope Felix, where he speaks of those who have been rebaptized, we can there plainly gather what we ought also to think about reconsecration. Among other things he continues as follows (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Those whom”):

“Those,” he says, “who are known to have been bishops, priests, or deacons, and who, whether willingly or perhaps under compulsion, are shown to have suffered the loss of that one washing and to have stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of the honor they had received—for it is clear that no one could come to a second washing unless he had openly denied himself to be a Christian and professed himself to be a pagan—although this is universally to be execrated in everyone, is proved still more horrifying even to hear or speak of in bishops, priests, and deacons.

“But because the same most merciful Lord and Savior wishes no one to perish, it is fitting that, until the day of their death, if they repent, they should lie in penance. They must in every way be excluded from prayer—not only from that of the faithful, but even from that of catechumens—and lay communion is to be restored to them at death.”

In these words, then, we must carefully observe this point: if one who has been rebaptized is said to have denied Christ because, after receiving baptism, he denied himself to be a Christian, then the one who approaches for reconsecration is likewise convicted of having denied the Holy Spirit because, after consecration, he testifies that he did not receive the Holy Spirit.

The reconsecrated person, therefore, is not separated from the rebaptized person by a different condemnation, since both are joined in an equal offense of impiety—unless perhaps someone should assert that the former sins more wickedly, because Truth says:

“Whoever sins against the Father and the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matthew XII; Luke XII).

Indeed, if we examine the decrees of Catholic pontiffs with more careful precision, we find that some permission has been granted in the matter of rebaptism, whereas we see that reconsecration is wholly forbidden (I, question 1, “What certain men”; I, question 1, “If any”).

For if we do not allow the things said above to slip from memory, we observe that those baptized by the Paulianists and other heretics who do not possess the Holy Spirit ought regularly to be rebaptized. Yet this is not called repeating baptism, because the earlier, impure washing does not appear to have been baptism.

Those who come from any kind of heretics, however, cannot be reconsecrated at all, because the sacred canons entirely reject this. We are therefore greatly astonished that some people rave with such monstrous blindness that they contend that those ordained by Simoniacs must be consecrated again. They publish concerning the ordination of Simoniacs a decree that even those heretics find discordant who appear to possess not even the slightest trace of orthodox faith.

Among heretics, some possess the true faith and are to be received in their ranks; others lack the true faith and ought not to remain in the honor they hold.

And since we cannot drive away from Simoniacs the mark of heresy, let us clearly distinguish to which category of heretics they appear rightly assignable. They must either be said to possess the true faith, like the Novatians, or be held in the errors of unbelief, like the Paulianists or Arians.

But if they possess the true faith with the Novatians, then, just as those who come from the Novatians are ordered to be received in the honors they hold, so those ordained by Simoniacs ought not to be removed from the duties of the rank imposed upon them. If, however, they are entangled with the errors of unbelief together with the Arians or Paulianists, then, just as those who depart from them are in no way permitted to be reconsecrated—as we learned earlier, with Pope Innocent altogether forbidding it—so these men who have been advanced by Simoniacs cannot for any reason be consecrated again.

It remains, therefore, that whether they believe rightly or do not believe rightly, they ought not to be reconsecrated. Accordingly, in light of what has been said, those ordained by Simoniacs must either be said to believe Catholicly and therefore ought to remain in their offices, or be proved guilty of unbelief and thus lose what they received.

But who does not know that they not only persist in the solidity of orthodox faith, but that many of them also—[p. 131] truly Catholic men in every respect—flourish through devotion to holy conduct and the excellence of every virtue?

It follows, therefore, that they rightly remain in the honors they received, since holy conduct agrees in them with the integrity of faith. Let blasphemous rashness, then, be rejected; let unlawful presumption be restrained; and let those who argue that rebaptized people have stripped off Christ also execrate the claim that the reconsecrated, through an equal impiety, deny the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That just as no one may be rebaptized, so no one may be consecrated again.

Come, then: those who assert that people consecrated in whatever manner can receive a second laying on of hands should strive to confirm this not by their own assertions but by the testimonies of canonical authority.

Let them say, then: which of the holy Fathers presumed to teach this, or at least dictated that it should be presumed? And when the authentic pages of the ancients fail them as evidence, let them acknowledge themselves to be the necessary authors of this new doctrine.

Since this is nowhere found to have been commanded by the sanction of the teachers, it is found instead to have been expressly forbidden. For Blessed Pope Gregory asserted to John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, that just as no one may be rebaptized, so no one may be consecrated again, in these words (Register, book II, letter, chapter 32):

“But that,” he says, “which you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is exceedingly ridiculous and appears foreign to the judgment of your intelligence, unless perhaps that example is brought forward, on the basis of which even the man reported to have done something of this sort was judged. Let it be far from your fraternity to think in this way. Just as one who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order.”

[Col. 0146A]

These words clearly show that, just as Christ is stripped off in rebaptism, so in reconsecration the grace of the Holy Spirit is emptied out in the one who has been wrongly advanced. For what is that sacrilegious consecration except a double deposition? When one man is sacrilegiously consecrated, both are rightly deposed.

Hence it is not without reason that we read in the canons of the apostles (Distinction 68, chapter “Just as once”):

“If any bishop, priest, or deacon has received a second laying on of hands from anyone, let both him and the one who attempted to ordain him be deposed. For it is not possible for those baptized or ordained by such men to be either faithful or clerics.”

If anyone objects that Formosus, bishop of the Roman See, was reconciled after his deposition, let him know [Col. 0146B] that many priests were indeed reconciled, yet nowhere are they read to have been consecrated again for the same order.

For it is one thing for someone to be restored by a synodal judgment to the rights of an order he had lost; it is another to obtain through the mystery of consecration—which cannot be repeated—the grace of the Holy Spirit, especially since, in one who is deposed, although the external privilege of exercising his dignity is lost, the sacrament of the order once received nevertheless remains. So too, while the sacrament of regeneration remains in him, a person guilty of any crime is excommunicated, and he does not lack that same sacrament even if he is never reconciled to God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That it is false that anyone consecrated by a Simoniac differs in no respect from a layman.

[Col. 0146C]

Although we have said much about the impiety of reconsecration, nevertheless, so that the matter does not remain in doubt if the authority of historical events is not also brought forward, let us offer an example from ecclesiastical history (Eusebius, book X, chapter 15), so that the consecration of any priests may appear to have some reality, as the saying goes.

Let the same words be set down here:

At the time when Bishop Alexander was observing the day of the martyr Peter at Alexandria, and, after the solemn rites had been completed, was awaiting the clerics who were to come to his banquet, he saw from a distance, near the seashore, a group of boys on the shore, as is customary, playing at being a bishop and at the things customarily done in churches.

But when he watched the boys attentively for a long time, he saw them performing certain things that were more secret and mystical as well. Immediately disturbed, he ordered the clerics to be summoned to him and showed them what he himself had seen from a distance. Then he ordered them to go and bring all the boys, having seized them, into his presence.

When they arrived, he asked what their game was, what they had done, and how they had done it. As is natural for their age, they were frightened and at first denied it; then they disclosed the matter in order and confessed that they had baptized some catechumens through Athanasius, who had been made to play the role of a boy-bishop in that game.

Then he carefully inquired of those said to have been baptized what questions had been put to them and what they had answered, and likewise questioned the one who had administered the questions. When he saw that everything conformed to the rite of our religion, he is reported to have conferred with the council of clerics and decided that those upon whom water had been poured with the complete questions and answers should not be baptized again, but should receive what is customarily completed by priests.

As for Athanasius and those whom that game had appeared to have as priests or ministers, he summoned their parents and, under adjuration before God, handed them over to the Church to be nurtured. The account continues by relating that Athanasius was in fact made a bishop, just as he had been impersonated as one when a boy.

We have taken care to bring forward this example from antiquity against those who assert that consecration performed by Simoniacs is entirely nothing and contend that those ordained by them differ in no respect from laymen.

For if that preliminary performance—in which the boys had pretended to be priests or ministers—was regarded as so significant that the bishop, after summoning their parents and under adjuration before God, handed them over to the Church for nurture, and did not consider it right for them even to remain in the secular order, since they had fashioned themselves as clerics through the appearance of a mere imitation, how can they be said to differ in no respect from laymen when it is established that they received the mystery of consecration according to ecclesiastical custom from anyone whatsoever?

Only imitation separates those boys from laymen; yet false human vanity proclaims that those men who truly received everything according to the rule differ in no respect from them. “Whatever,” as the Apostle says, “was written was written for our instruction” (Romans XV).

And in his Moralia, if I remember correctly, Blessed Gregory is also found to have said that a Simoniac is placed between two dangers: whether he abandons the flock entrusted to him or remains in the honor wrongly received, he must escape the snares of sin. Without expressly defining either alternative, he merely asserts that the easier course should be explained as quickly as possible.

If, then, a Simoniac is a layman, as is said, in what, I ask, does he sin if he abandons the office of priestly dignity? If he does not possess the sacrament of priesthood in any sense, why is he separated with guilt from pastoral ministry, when he is not bound to it by the bond of the sacrament?

But tell me, brothers—I speak with your permission: if Simoniacs, or those ordained by them, differ in no respect from laymen, as you assert, why do the sacred canons decree that Simoniacs must be deposed in a synodal council?

If a layman is convicted of having usurped priestly authority, does he need a synodal proceeding and assembly in order to be solemnly deposed? Would it not be enough for him to be corrected by some private disciplinary measure, so that he might be broken from his presumptuous rashness even by simple words?

After his deposition, will a Simoniac be able to receive the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands, to bear secular military service, to take a wife, and safely to engage in commercial business? For although they lose the exercise of their office, they cannot nevertheless lose the sacrament of ordination.

Since, then, you necessarily admit that none of these things can properly apply to Simoniacs, while you do not deny that they suit any layman, you must confess that the two groups differ from one another in some respect, since you plainly see that different things belong to them.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What Innocent thinks about reconsecration.

[Col. 0148A]

Let us see also what the aforementioned Pope Innocent, although only in passing, recorded as his opinion concerning re-consecration. For in the decree that he writes to the bishop of Naissus, he says:

“In former times, if I remember correctly, I recall having sent letters of this kind both to Your Belovedness and to our brothers and fellow bishops Rufus and the others concerning the clergy of Naissus—namely, those who assert that before the condemnation of Bonosus they had been ordained by him both as priests and as deacons: that, if they wished to abandon and repudiate his error and be joined to the Church, they should gladly be received, lest perhaps those who might be worthy of recovering salvation should perish in that same error.

“But now, while I am established in the city of Ravenna on account of the very frequent needs of the Roman people, Germanius, who claims to be a priest, and Lupensius, who says that he is a deacon, having undertaken what was virtually an embassy on behalf of many such men, eagerly sought, through earnest entreaty, to express their own grievances. They assert that they retain the churches situated in the parishes of Your Belovedness, but that they have been unable to merit your communion, for this reason in particular: a certain man named Rusticus had received the priesthood through a repeated ordination, 134 and this has become no small impediment, since either they grieve that such a man is retained in the Church, or he thinks that he himself ought to sin against others in the same way as he recognizes that sin has been committed against himself.”

[Col. 0148B]

Here it is clearly recognized what opinion Innocent held concerning re-consecration, since he was endeavoring to restore to communion with their bishop those who, out of zeal for justice, grieved that a re-consecrated man was being retained in the Church. He reports that the man thought he himself ought to sin against others in the same way as the bishop who re-consecrated him had sinned against him: for, with the familiar zeal of the reprobate, he was attempting to entangle others in the snare of the same condemnation in which he himself had not feared to become entangled first. Hence they reasonably thought that such a man, as utterly damnable a heretic, ought to be driven from the Church—one who neither spared himself nor took precautions against endangering others.

[Col. 0148C]

But lest anyone accuse us of being entangled in an unwieldy volume, while complaining that perhaps more extensive examples from the canons have been mixed into this work, let him know beyond doubt that the reason is this: we cannot compel or persuade those with whom we are dealing to examine the sacred canons, despite our frequent exhortations and entreaties. For that reason we deem it fitting to set down here the judgments of the holy Fathers, so that we may place at least excerpts before their delicate and tender eyes; so that, when they consider what we think in the material we have brought forward, they may also yield to the authority on which we rely.

[Col. 0148D]

But so that it may be evident to them that everything proceeds in confusion, they also act against the canons in this respect: they receive all the grades simultaneously in re-consecration. Thus, when I learned about a certain man known to me who had recently been consecrated, I confess that I was horrified at the deed. What more need be said? At last I met the man.

“Was there already,” I asked, “anything in you from among those grades that you recently received from the bishop?”

“Absolutely nothing,” he replied. “Why would I receive them, if it were established that I already possessed them?”

“And so,” I added, “you differed in no way from a layman; indeed, you were entirely a layman.”

“Yes,” he said, “plainly a pure layman, since I possessed nothing from the clergy.”

“But if you were a layman,” I said, “and on the very day on which you were a layman you rushed into the rights of the priesthood, then by your own judgment you became a neophyte and therefore must unquestionably be deposed.”

At this he, confused, blushed; and because he could not weaken the necessity of the conclusion, he confirmed it by remaining silent.

This too appears to be a madness of no lesser kind: those who perform re-consecrations observe the fasts prescribed by the canons, but do not preserve the Sabbaths appointed for the conferral of sacred offices. Instead, in whatever month or on whatever weekday, they indiscriminately assume the office of an irregular ordination, as though the first consecration granted permission for this second consecration—so that, with the orders confused because they are conferred all at once, the established times may also be confused. Thus in re-consecration they permit what they themselves testify to be utterly absurd even in consecration.

135

## CHAPTER XXXIV. He addresses the bishops, so that through them discernment may be suggested to the supreme see.

[Col. 0149A]

[Col. 0149B]

Therefore, I ask you, devout pontiffs, rally against this impious doctrine with the divine fervor of holy zeal, and unanimously confront this new heresy now emerging for the first time. “Let the mouth of those who speak wickedness be stopped,” and let the hand of sinners not shake the foundation of the apostolic faith. Let ecclesiastical doctrine be preserved in its purity, and let it not be permitted to be harassed by the turbulent cunning of earthly sages.

[Col. 0149C]

The enemy rises by night to sow weeds throughout Christ’s field; you, during the day in which you walk, must eradicate the evil seed by the hoe of sound doctrine, root and branch (Matt. XIII). By night the Philistines fill Isaac’s wells with rubble; by day let Isaac hasten to empty them (Gen. XXVI). The nocturnal thief attempts to break into Christ’s sanctuary; let the tongue of his dogs be roused to bark salutarily. But if perhaps someone from your own order should come forward and presume to teach such abominable doctrines, you ought to rebuke him all the more harshly, since the one who ought to have been the Church’s protector is striving to attack it.

[Col. 0149D]

Suggest, therefore, to our most blessed lord the pope that he extend the force of ecclesiastical severity against the guilty in such a way that, according to the wishes of undiscerning men, the same sentence may not envelop the innocent. For judgment seems to be running wild when a sentence promulgated for a father’s crime is directed toward the destruction of his children. Let him, strengthened by divine power, destroy the Simoniacs, as he had already begun to do; but not so far as to permit their ordinations to be subjected to the immoderate judgment of certain people.

Rather, let the man who holds the keys of the Church in the place of Peter (Matt. XIII) himself rise above all against this new doctrine, and let a thrust of a worthy sentence strike down the introducers of depravity. Let the man who guides the net entrusted to fishermen strive, under this dispensation, to distinguish the bad fish from the good, so that he does not condemn the good along with them.

Let him therefore say to undiscerning men what the master of the household is said to have told his servants: “Lest perhaps, while you gather the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them” (ibid.). That is, let the weeds afterward be gathered into a bundle for burning, so that the wheat may be collected into the granary.

For when the blessed apostle struck Ananias and Sapphira with a sentence of deserved punishment (Acts V), did he also decree that vengeance should be taken upon their children or relatives? The sentence hurled against Simon himself did not extend to those who perhaps might have been able to extract some truth from him. For when it is said, “May your money be with you for perdition” (Acts I), the money is struck together with the trafficker; where the money is absent, the blow is not feared.

[Col. 0150A]

And so you also, venerable Fathers, together with the most blessed supreme pontiff, arrange everything with the equity of a discerning examination, so that you may be seen in your judgment also to preserve the rule handed down by so great a teacher. Let what is corrupt in the Church’s body feel the iron, while whatever is sound remains in the strength of its proper vitality. Let punishable excesses be punished in such a way that, while legal severity pursues guilt, 136 the immunity of innocence is preserved. Let the diseased tree be subject to axes, while the plants transplanted from it take root and grow together in the grace of their own vigor.

## CHAPTER XXXV. What Pope Leo finally decreed concerning those who were promoted gratuitously by Simoniacs.

[Col. 0150C]

Nevertheless, we do not believe it irrelevant to explain what the same venerable Pope Leo decreed concerning this matter. For when he had annulled all the ordinations of the Simoniacs by the authority of synodal force, a great tumult of sedition immediately arose among the multitude of Roman priests, so that it was said not only by them but by many bishops that nearly all the basilicas had been left without priestly offices, and especially that the solemn celebrations of Mass should be entirely discontinued, to the subversion of the Christian religion and the despair of all the faithful throughout the surrounding region.

What more need be said? After long volumes of debate on both sides, it was finally reported that Clement, the bishop of that see recently deceased and of revered memory, had decreed the following: Whoever had been consecrated by a Simoniac, while knowing at the very time of his ordination that the Simoniac to whom he had offered himself was promoting him, should now perform forty days of penance and then minister in the office he had received.

The venerable Leo immediately approved this judgment and ordered all such men thereafter to remain in the offices they had received under this penance. For even today you see some who, although they had been ordained by such men through the various grades, were advanced by the same supreme pontiff to the height of the episcopate.

Nor was this done improperly, because since canonical authority decrees (I, question 1, “If any bishop”): “Whoever has obtained a sacred dignity through money shall himself be deposed, together with his ordainer,” it is unquestionably clear that, in condemning the man ordained simoniacally and his ordainer, this canon immediately fixed the boundary of the judgment; nor did it extend the sentence to one who might have been promoted by such a man.

For if the author of this canon had considered that anyone promoted by a Simoniac should be deposed, then, after marking out the man himself and his ordainer, he would consequently not have been silent concerning those who could have been promoted by him. He would surely have said: “Let him and his ordainer be deposed,” and immediately added: “And whoever has been ordained by him.” Since he did not say this, he has not indicated that we should think it either.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Where Emperor Henry is raised up with glory worthy of praise.

[Col. 0151A]

Moreover, as we recall the deeds of the venerable pope, reason consequently urges us to turn our attention also to the distinguished praise of this great King Henry. After God, he himself rescued us from the insatiable mouth of the dragon; he himself, by the sword of divine power, truly cut off all the heads of the many-headed hydra of the Simoniac heresy.

He may rightly say, to the glory of Christ: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.” For until the time of his reign, the insatiable falsehood of priests—if I may put it so—was supplying the Babylonian Bel with expenses. But after this man, by God’s will, obtained his ancestral principate, the pious king immediately thrust a lump of pitch into the dragon’s jaws and, like another Daniel, extinguished the monstrous beast.

[Col. 0151B]

Pitch, which burns and constricts, may reasonably signify love of money. This love burns in the furnace of the miser’s heart in such a way that it restrains him from generosity in mercy and pious compassion. What, then, is it to throw a lump of pitch into the dragon’s mouth except openly to say with Peter: “May your money be with you for perdition”? (Acts VIII.) This is precisely what this prince declared when he overturned the seats of those selling doves, 137 drove out the money-changers, and refused to allow commerce to be conducted for profit in the temple of God.

Nor does it seem unrelated to this interpretation that Daniel is described as having mixed fat and hair with the pitch. For what do we understand by fat except the pleasure of the flesh? And what is signified by hair, which lies outside the bodies of animals, except external substance?

[Col. 0151C]

The king therefore mixed fat and hair with the pitch and thus broke the dragon, because, utterly detesting the Simoniac poison, he not only did not succumb to avarice, but in conferring ecclesiastical dignity he sought no gratification of the flesh or gain from external profit whatsoever.

Now that the dragon has been slain, cast down from heaven, and bound in the abyss by an angel with a chain—he who had formerly fought with Michael and had dragged a third of the stars after him (Rev. XII)—let us fittingly mock him with Isaiah: “O Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn, how have you fallen from heaven and collapsed to the earth, you who wounded the nations?” (Isa. XVI.)

[Col. 0151D]

Until the time of this Augustus, all the decrees of the canons that the Fathers had issued concerning this plague seemed already to have been erased from the memory of many by prolonged oblivion. But as soon as this man, like that celebrated Josiah of old, found the book of the Lord’s law, he tore his garments and grieved; he demolished the altars, cast down the abominable idols, and overturned all the sacrilegious superstitions of the former kings (IV Kings XXIII).

And because he refused to follow the rule of his predecessors, so that he might preserve the commands of the eternal King, divine providence granted him—something it had not permitted to most of his predecessors—that the holy Roman Church should now be organized at his command, and that no one at all should elect a priest for the apostolic see without his authority.

[Col. 0152A]

Indeed, if David deserved to bind the king’s daughter to himself in marriage because of the slaughter of the Philistine Goliath (I Kings XVII), why should it be surprising if this emperor also, victorious over Simon the heresiarch, received the holy Church, who is truly the daughter of the supreme King?

And to compare him, in some respect, not without reason with David: David desired water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which was held among the enemy ranks; but when it had been brought by his obedient soldiers, he refused to drink it and poured it out. 138 Hence it is immediately written: “He poured it out as a libation to the Lord” (II Kings XXIII).

If, then, the rejected water was transformed into a sacrifice to God, how much more precious a gift must the money he refused be considered? David poured out the water and made it a libation; this man likewise offered God a pleasing sacrifice when, for love of Him, he rejected not water but gold.

[Col. 0152B]

And because there were some endowed with royal thrones who feared that they could not administer the government entrusted to them unless they increased the public treasuries through the sale of churches, behold: almighty God, in whose hand are the victory of conquerors and the scepters of rulers, without the proceeds of this dishonorable acquisition, subjected many foreign nations to his faithful servant, subdued the tyrannical ferocity of his adversaries under his rule, and laid low before him the necks of swelling and proud enemies. He granted him to defeat barbarian peoples on every side and to tread upon the necks of rebels who had faithlessly submitted.

Thus it is plainly evident that victory comes from heaven and is not proved to depend upon monetary gifts, but descends from the generosity of heavenly grace.

[Col. 0152C]

This emperor therefore appears to have obtained a victory against the enemies of the Catholic Church not unequal to that of Caesar Constantine. The one crushed the doctrine of the Arian sect beneath the arms of orthodox faith; the other destroyed the plague of Simoniac heresy by trampling avarice underfoot. The one, a defender of the faith, prevented Arius from dividing unity; the other, a victor over desire, confronted Simon so that he might not possess the seat of pestilence in the Church.

Let others sweat to weave the triumphs of kings into historical prose, and to raise the distinguished titles of wars and their brave deeds through praises of elaborate beauty. To me, the victory mentioned above seems far nobler and incomparably more glorious: in it no human blood is poured out, no multitude of soldiers is diminished, but the entire Catholic Church, spread throughout all the regions of the Roman Empire, is freed from the bonds of ancient condemnation as from a horrifying and very deep prison.

[Col. 0152D]

Thus, rescued by God through this Augustus, she can sing to God with a free voice: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXXV).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The author inveighs against the Simoniacs.

[Col. 0153A]

I complain against you, Simoniacs, who have inflicted upon us the grievous labor of this night-watch. We defend our position, certainly, but only in such a way as to condemn you perpetually. We admit what is done through you in such a way that we regard you as abominable and worthy of the most extreme punishments of all the lost.

Judas, believing the Lord to be merely a man, sold Him (Matt. XXVII); but soon afterward he cast away the price of blood, destined to suffer a punishment he deserved. You, however, while having no doubt about the divinity of the Holy Spirit, attribute to Him a commercial sale and possess the profit of the sacrilege you have committed; although you ought to have been punished by vengeance, you profit from the crimes you have committed.

To whom, then, should I rightly compare you, who possess divine gifts not for yourselves but for others, and who turn into judgment and perdition for yourselves what comes to those others as an increase of salvation? 139 I see you plainly as like the Jews, who, profoundly ignorant of the divine law, have become scribes for Christ’s faithful throughout the world.

You also seem almost to take on the form of bees, which, while transmitting honey worked out to sweeten human throats, soon wither away themselves in the deprivation of a famine destined to destroy them.

[Col. 0153B]

Finally, consider, unfortunate and miserable men, into what monstrous abyss of perdition you have been plunged. Not only are your evil deeds evil, but even the good deeds performed by you have been made evil. For blessing has been turned into a curse, charisms into heresy, sacraments into sacrilege, honor into insult, and promotion into ruin.

To this is added the fact that you are liable to give an account for so many souls over whom you now appear to have been set. Heap up wealth now; crowd yourselves with swelling bands of attendants. Soon you will see all the armies of angels fiercely angry against you, and the ranks of apostles, martyrs, and all the saints rising dreadfully against you and joining together in a sentence of your condemnation with a judgment at once unanimous and equal.

[Col. 0153C]

You have offended Him, and consequently have Him as your enemy—Him whose offense is forgiven neither here nor in the future. Moreover, in the enormity of your bloody and most wicked crime, you surpass adulterers, exceed murderers, and rise above the crimes of robbers, sacrilegious persons, incestuous people, parricides, and nearly all other offenders.

Still this is not enough. For if the matter is weighed according to its true importance, the Jewish perfidy itself and every kind of heretical depravity do not equal your excesses. Night has arisen for you at midday, a storm in fair weather; the sky has become iron for you and the earth bronze, because you neither rise toward heaven beneath the weight of your wickedness nor conceal among human beings what, as conscience bears witness, has been committed.

[Col. 0153D]

Indeed, if even now, as the authority of the Fathers testifies (I, question 1, “Whoever”), blessing is turned into a curse for you when you appear to be blessed by the priest’s mouth, what will happen to you then, when the divine voice itself calls you accursed and rejects you, and the fury of the Judge casts you from His presence and hands you over to the executioners?

Then you will truly learn how costly is the bitter purchase of the honor formerly held, when it will already be necessary for the endlessly open Tartarus to swallow you and the cruel cauldron of Gehenna to enclose you. Then crackling and shrieking flame will consume your bones, irrigated with rich marrow. Then the devouring fire, as though belching from a furnace, will not cease to belch vapors through your mouths, eyes, ears, and nostrils.

[Col. 0154A]

Then, yes then, it will be fitting that you share a portion with that leader of yours, namely Simon the heresiarch. Since the paradise freely promised by Christ was not enough for you, let the hell purchased with money from the devil satisfy you.

Although I understand that you will rightly be judged more damnable than the author of your error and the president of the pestilential seat, so that you may fittingly precede in punishment the one whom you wickedly surpassed in guilt. For he merely wished to buy a heavenly gift, but did not attain the effect of his desire, which deserved to be struck down. You, however, both wished and accomplished; 140 you approached and insinuated yourselves. The structure was erected, and the coin came forth.

[Col. 0154B]

Finally, while he pretends to be God, he is shown to be a dog; while he is lifted up, he is overwhelmed; while he seems to climb to heaven, he falls into Tartarus. Accordingly, you also, while seeking high places, fall; while you are not content to appear equal to other human beings, despised alike by divine and human judgment, you hasten toward the likeness of unclean dogs.

But we are wasting our efforts if, in rebuking you, we attempt—as though prophesying—to restore dry bones to life. We must simply pray that, having laid aside your honor, you may put flesh and sinews back on and thus revive again through the breath of the Holy Spirit.

But now, having crossed the sea, we lower the sails while gripping the helm; for, with Christ as our guide, we see the shore and are approaching the harbor.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Where the completed work is brought to its conclusion for the bishop of Ravenna.

[Col. 0154C]

[Col. 0154D]

Finally I return to you, venerable father Henry, and return at the end of this little work to the one with whom I began. Please do not look here for the ornamented elegance of carefully labored diction, nor demand the sharpness of polished wit, but only rough simplicity and a poor little speech scarcely able to explain what it thinks.

For I proposed to set serious and necessary matters before the hearts of my brothers, more usefully than brilliantly, and not to serve the allurements of their ears with the seductions of empty words. You are not unaware that speech deliberately adorned drains the vitality from ideas, and that elaborate splendor weakens the force of what is said.

Let those serve grandiloquent and measured words who labor to win the favorable applause of men by the pleasant beauty of soothing speech. But we, who are commanded to walk with bare feet, ought not to write in buskins; and those upon whom the censorship of silence is imposed do not seem suited to the ragged profusion of luxuriant eloquence.

[Col. 0155A]

Therefore, dearest one, I offer these rustic compositions, written in a rough style, into your hands as though they were cheap fruits. Yet because the countryside has produced nothing better, please do not despise them. Since, so to speak, I am descended from the place—[Note: He means Ravenna as his native soil, referring to the holy doctor]—and you have attained the highest honor, I have chosen you above all as the person to whom I should entrust this little gift, so that, like a very small sheep to its own shepherd, I might bring forth fruit not of the belly but of the mind.

[Col. 0155B]

Finally, I know that your Church, like an apostolic senate, is adorned and strengthened not by a numerous but by a venerable and mystical college of holy bishops. Through their devotion it preserves the straight line of apostolic tradition and remains immovably established in the purity of the most sincere faith, so that, with every heretical depravity removed, it represents today that new Church which had existed under the apostles; indeed, it seems even to be bringing forth Nicaea itself, the seat of the faith.

From among these men, therefore, let Your Holiness select those whom you deem appropriate, and with them carefully investigate and prudently examine how far this work accords with Catholic faith and sound doctrine. If this book is found to be excusably open to criticism, 141 let your prudence correct it, and then show it also to the most blessed pope, if, as rumor has spread, it passes through your hands, so that what is despised because of the inept composition of its craftsman may be commended for the service of so great a labor.

[Col. 0155C]

But if, contrary to our belief, it appears everywhere so liable to erasure that it cannot be corrected before it is made publicly known, let devouring fire consume it. Here you may not inappropriately apply the following example: you have Aaron and Hur with you; if any question arises, refer it to them.

For I am not ashamed to erase what I write, so long as I am not ashamed freely to confess what I believe; thus the one who marks me as speechless may compensate by proving me faithful.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Added to the preceding little work.

[Col. 0155D]

I, rough and unlearned, wrote this little book in a state of scrupulous uncertainty; and, as can be seen at the end, [the supplied text breaks off: “of apostolic authority”].

In the time of the venerable Pope Nicholas—[Note: We placed at the beginning of the little work the letter of Leo IX, following the manuscripts written by hand]—this question was raised again and debated for a long time. But after many waves of controversy, and finally after the tangled and winding volumes of wavering questions, the matter was at last brought to this limit of judicial decision: those who had previously been consecrated gratuitously by Simoniacs were to remain in the honor of the dignity they had acquired; but those not yet promoted were thereafter not to have permission to be advanced by them to an order.

[Col. 0156A]

This provision was maintained so that, on the one hand, the entire ecclesiastical order would not collapse all at once through the severity of the sentence, and, on the other, the Simoniac plague would not gain force and strength in the conferral of dignities through the leniency of clemency—so that what was ratified in the past would be entirely prohibited for the future.

We, therefore, do not stubbornly assert our own arguments, but humbly obey synodal decrees. We follow the edict of the apostolic see, whether what has already been promulgated, or, if something still more refined and beneficial is to be established in the future, we profess our obedience to that as well. Just as, when the Gospel shone forth through the blessed apostles, we received the beginnings of the newborn faith, so thereafter let us hold every rule of life and belief handed down by apostolic men.

[Col. 0156B]

Moreover, that bishop of Ravenna to whom this little book was initially sent was recently promoted and therefore unknown to me; he was thought to possess knowledge of the Scriptures. But since I was unable to extract from him even the faintest spark of a solution concerning this question, I decided to be content with the authority of the apostolic see. Whatever synodal judgment has been established concerning this matter must unquestionably be authoritative for me and must certainly appear to be supported by the force of canonical authority.

142

## SCHOLIA

[Col. 0156C]

“Moreover, let the pontiff himself restrain delinquents by civil law whenever the case requires it; and let the king, together with his bishops, decide concerning the condition of souls on the authority of the sacred canons that have been promulgated” (*Ant. Flor. Chron.*, part III, title 20, chapter 7, paragraph 1).

In this passage one must certainly believe that, through the carelessness of scribes, an error has undoubtedly entered the manuscript copies. Since the holy doctor’s intention was to show the duties both of the supreme pontiff and of the king or emperor concerning the governance of peoples, it should not be thought that he wished to attribute to the king what belongs to the pontiff, since the two powers are distinct from one another by divine law, as is clear from chapter “There are two,” Distinction 96, and chapters “If the emperor” and “The usual,” *On Majorities and Obedience*.

[Col. 0156D]

Therefore, where Damian’s text says, “and the king with his bishops,” and so forth, it must necessarily be read: “and the pontiff with his bishops,” as anyone can see who carefully compares what precedes with what follows. The corruption of the text just cited also becomes especially evident from the fact that, after Damian himself had set down those words, he immediately added concerning the Roman pontiff: “Let the one, like a parent, always preside by paternal right; let the other, like an only and unique son, rest in the embrace of his love.”

“Unless, indeed, he had certain faith that the Lord received the priesthood together with baptism,” and so forth.
