Since it is absolutely certain that the priesthood is fitting to Christ as man, and that all gifts and charisms were bestowed upon Him at the instant of the hypostatic union, it cannot be maintained that Damian here reports Christ to have become a priest at His baptism—unless perhaps he wished to say that Christ’s priesthood was not conferred at baptism but began in some way to be manifested then.

This is like the way theologians interpret the words, “And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and men” (Luke II): not that Christ’s wisdom truly increased in the reality of the matter, since He had received it all at once, but that, as His age increased, it became much more conspicuous.

Saint Thomas likewise says (I part, question 22, article 2, reply to objection 3) that Christ’s human nature, when it was offered to God in the Passion, was sanctified in a new way, namely, as an offering then actually presented. For at that time it acquired the actual sanctification of a victim from the ancient charity and the grace of union, which had sanctified it absolutely as a victim.

[Col. 0157A]

“Although, therefore, they”—he means bishops—“each specially enjoy certain privileges according to their respective ministry, nevertheless, since they share with the other priests what is greater than all these things, they too, together with them, not undeservedly retain the name of the priesthood.”

Concerning these words I think it should be noted that the holy cardinal does not deny that the episcopate differs from the presbyterate by divine law, even though at first sight he seems to say that bishops are greater than presbyters because of certain privileges. For he establishes as much distinction between the former and the latter as exists between subjects and rulers.

[Col. 0157B]

Hence Saint Ignatius, in almost all his letters, often honors bishops with the title of ruler. Thus he writes to the Trallians:

“For what else is a bishop than one who is superior to every principate and power and who, insofar as is possible for a human being, has become an imitator of Christ God according to his strength? What else is the priesthood than a sacred assembly of counselors and assessors of the bishop? What are deacons other than imitators of the angelic virtues, who offer them a pure and blameless ministry—just as Saint Stephen did for blessed James, Timothy and Linus for Paul, and Anacletus and Clement for Peter? Whoever, therefore, does not obey these men is utterly godless and impious, despises Christ, and diminishes His ordinances.”

And to the Philadelphians:

“Let rulers obey Caesar, soldiers their rulers, deacons the presbyters, and presbyters the overseers of sacred things; let deacons and the rest of the clergy, together with the whole people, the soldiers, and Caesar, obey the bishop himself; let the bishop obey Christ, as Christ obeyed the Father. In this way unity will be preserved in all things.”

[Col. 0157C]

Saint Jerome confirms this same point, as can be found in Distinction 35, chapter “The rulers of the churches.” There is likewise the explicit judgment of Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 5. All the Scholastics in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, distinction 24, support them, especially Saint Thomas, II-II, question 184, article 6. Add to these the canonists, among whom Cardinal Turrecremata discusses the matter in book I of the *Summary of the Church*, chapter 69.

For this reason the Aetians were regarded as heretics by Epiphanius (*Heresy* 75) and Augustine (*Heresy* 53), because they denied that bishops were superior to presbyters.

[Col. 0157D]

“For even the holy apostles themselves are not found to have been consecrated by the Lord anywhere except in receiving baptism; yet they are not clearly read to have been immersed in baptismal water, but rather to have carried out the obedience imposed upon them, namely, to baptize.”

For clarification of this entire period, through the end of that chapter, and to avoid confusion, we state three things concerning the apostles that are absolutely certain.

First, the apostles were baptized according to the form and manner in which they were later commanded to baptize others, as Saint Augustine demonstrates at length in Letter 109, following Tertullian’s book *On Baptism*. There is also an ancient tradition received from Evodius, bishop of Antioch and successor of the apostles, preserved in Nicephorus, *History*, book II, chapter 3: Christ baptized only Peter with His own hands; Peter then baptized Andrew and the sons of Zebedee; those men baptized the remaining apostles; and Peter and John baptized the Seventy (Luke XXII).

[Col. 0158A]

This same point is gathered from chapter “When,” *On Consecration*, distinction 4, and from the gloss thereon. Cardinal Turrecremata is added to these authorities, and among many others also Augustine Triumphus, *On the Power of the Church*, question 84, article 4.

Second, it is certain that the apostles were consecrated as priests by Christ at the Last Supper, when, instituting the holy Eucharist, He commanded them to offer it as a sacrifice with the words: “Do this in remembrance of me.” The Council of Trent explicitly teaches this, session 22, chapter 1.

Third, I say that after the Resurrection the apostles were created bishops by Christ, when He appeared to them gathered together and, as John records, said these words: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John XXI).

Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theophylact, and many more recent authorities explain this passage in that way. Others, however, think that before the Ascension Christ created only Peter as a bishop; afterward, following the sending of the Holy Spirit, Peter consecrated only John as bishop, and these two consecrated James the son of Zebedee; and that it was subsequently decreed that no one should be ordained bishop except by three bishops likewise, as stated in chapter “Moreover,” Distinction 66.

Cardinal Turrecremata demonstrates this at length in chapter “In the New,” Distinction 21, article 3, and in book II, chapter 54, of the *Summary of the Church*; Cardinal Jacobatius does so in *On Councils*, book X, article 7; and others do likewise.

“Liberius is recognized as having been deceived by the error of treachery and having subscribed to the Arian heresy.”

What Damian says here—that Pope Liberius was a heretic—requires clarification, although he can be excused, since other highly eminent Fathers judged the same: Athanasius, *Apology* 2 and *Letter to the Solitaries*; Hilary, *Against Constantius*; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Fortunatianus; and Notker, the ancient monk of Saint Gall, in his *Martyrology*, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. In fact, Liberius himself gave occasion for the report that he had fallen into heresy, because, in subscribing to the formula of faith—which, properly understood, was Catholic—he nevertheless omitted the term “consubstantial,” used by the First Council of Nicaea; and for that reason he was commonly thought to have fallen into Arian perfidy. [Col. 0158B]

Yet that he was entirely free from every taint of Arianism and of any other heresy is especially clear from the firm manner in which he argued and acted with Emperor Constantius in defense of the Catholic faith, both before his exile, as may be seen in Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* I.21; Socrates II.29 at the end and IV.11; Sozomen IV.10 and 14; and Theodoret II.15, 16, and 17; and after his exile, when he wrote to the Macedonian bishops, in Socrates IV.11 and 12. [Col. 0158C] Sozomen IV.14 explicitly writes that these insults against Liberius were fabricated from the calumnies of the Aetians.

But when Damian also says that Liberius stirred up persecutions against the clergy, this must be understood properly. When, by order of Emperor Constantius, he was recalled from exile to Rome, and the clergy refused to receive him because, while he had remained in the East, he had subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius, the magistrates stirred up a persecution against the clergy of the Roman Church. Since this had happened on Liberius’s account, the blame was attributed to him.

In any event, how highly Liberius was esteemed for praise and holiness even after his death is taught especially by the most distinguished men: Ambrose, book III of the *Commentary on the Virgins*; Basil, Letter 74; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 75; and Bede, in his *Martyrology* on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, together with Wandelbert on the ninth day before the Kalends of that same month, publicly testify that the memory of Liberius was to be celebrated with that of the other saints on his annual feast day. [Col. 0158D] In addition to these writings, a full and eloquent defense of Liberius may be found especially in the works of the most illustrious cardinals, Baronius in the *Annals* and Bellarmine in the *Controversies*.

“Indeed, who does not know that the priest Eli was rejected and condemned by the sentence of divine retribution both for his leniency and for the unrestrained license of his sons?” [145]

Our cardinal’s approval of this judgment concerning Eli is not surprising, since it was also embraced by Tertullian, *On Modesty*; Jerome, book I, *Against Jovinian*; John Chrysostom, book II, *Against Those Who Condemn the Monastic Life*; Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 370 to Cyril; and Innocent III, in the chapter *Licet Heli*, *On Simony*. Nevertheless, the contrary opinion is also probable. It is defended by Alfonso de Madrigal in book I of *Kings*, chapter 4. [Col. 0159A] Perhaps this is what the Fathers themselves meant, since nothing more can be gathered from their words than that Eli perished by that kind of death because he had not rebuked his sons’ crimes.

“We observe that those baptized by the Paulianists and by other heretics who do not possess the Holy Spirit are regularly baptized.” [146]

What the holy Doctor asserts here concerning those baptized by the Paulianists and Cataphrygians—who are mentioned in chapter *Si quis* I, question 1—is true if they returned to the Church, according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea, since they neither believed that Christ was human nor confessed the Holy Spirit. Consequently, since their baptism was not conferred in the name of the Holy Trinity, those returning to the Catholic Church rightly had to be baptized. [Col. 0160A]

It must not, however, be generally held that those baptized by heretics are to be rebaptized, as the heresy of the Donatists impiously affirmed, against which Saint Augustine strenuously fought. Moreover, the scholastics in book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 4, single question, and Saint Thomas, part III, question 66, article 9, clearly demonstrate how true the doctrine is that those baptized by heretics in the form of the Church are not to be rebaptized. The same is taught in the chapters *De Arianis* and *Ab antiqua*, *On Consecration*, distinction 4. That our cardinal also embraced this opinion is made entirely certain by his words.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0159]

## 147–148. SEVENTH OPUSCULUM: THE GOMORRHIAN, TO LEO IX, ROMAN PONTIFF

### ARGUMENT

He laments the unspeakable and detestable crime into which men dedicated to God in his time were falling, and argues that they must be removed from the sacred orders as unworthy. He implores Pope Leo to restrain by his authority those who sin so shamefully.

### LETTER OF LEO IX, BY WHICH THIS LITTLE BOOK OF THE HOLY MAN IS CONFIRMED

[Col. 0159B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Peter the hermit: joy of eternal blessedness.

Your little book, which you have composed against the fourfold pollution of carnal contagion in an honorable style but with an even more honorable purpose, plainly commends the fact that, through pious struggle, your mind has reached the splendid and shining bed of chastity, dearest son. You have subdued the barbarism of the flesh, since you have raised the arm of the spirit against the obscenity of lust. This vice is truly execrable and separates one far from the author of virtues, who, being pure, admits nothing impure; nor can anyone belong to his portion who submits to filthy allurements.

The clerics, moreover, concerning whose most filthy life your prudence has argued both tearfully and reasonably, truly—and entirely truly—do not belong to the cord of his inheritance, since they remove themselves from it through their voluptuous pleasures. If they lived chastely, they would be called not only the holy temple of God but also the sanctuary itself, in which that conspicuous Lamb of God, radiant in snowy whiteness, is sacrificed, and through whom the foul plague of the whole world is washed away. [Col. 0159C]

Such clerics, although not by the testimony of their words, nevertheless by the testimony of their deeds, profess that they are not what they are considered to be. For how can one be or be called a cleric who, by his own choice, does not fear to defile himself? Since, moved by holy fury, you wrote what seemed necessary to you concerning such men, it is fitting, as you desire, that we interpose our apostolic authority, so that we may remove the scruple of doubt from readers and make it clear to all that, in our judgment, whatever this little book contains has met with our approval, being set against the devil’s fire like water. [Col. 0159D]

Therefore, lest the unpunished license of filthy lust spread abroad, it must be refuted by a fitting rebuke of apostolic severity, while some moderation must nevertheless be introduced into that severity. [Col. 0160B]

Behold, all those who are polluted by any of the four kinds of defilement mentioned above are, according to the judgment of equity, expelled from all the grades of the immaculate Church, both by the judgment of the sacred canons and by our own. Yet, acting with greater humanity, we trust in divine mercy and wish—and even command—that those who have emitted semen either with their own hands, or mutually with one another, or between the thighs, provided that they have restrained their desire, have not persisted in the practice for a long time or with many persons, and have expiated their shameful deeds through worthy penance, may be admitted to the same ranks which they had held while persisting in their crime, now no longer persisting in it. [Col. 0160C]

But hope of recovering their order is removed from those who have been stained by either of the two kinds of defilement you described, whether over a long period with themselves, or with others or with many, even for a short time; and especially from those who—and this is horrible to say and hear—have fallen upon their backs.

If anyone dares to judge or bark against this decree of our apostolic sanction, let him know that he acts at the peril of his order. For whoever does not prick vice but strokes it is rightly judged guilty of death together with the one who dies in vice. But, dearest son, I rejoice beyond words because, by the example of your conduct, you teach whatever you have taught by your eloquence. To teach by one’s deeds is greater than to teach by one’s voice. [Col. 0160D] Therefore, with God as author, you will obtain the palm of victory, and with God and the Son of the Virgin you will rejoice in the heavenly dwelling, enriched with as many rewards as those whom you have snatched from the devil’s snares and, in a sense, crowned.

## THE GOMORRHIAN, TO LEO IX

[Col. 0161]

### PREFACE

[Col. 0161A]

To the most blessed Pope Leo, Peter, the least of the servants of the monks, offers the service of due reverence. [149]

Since the apostolic see is known from the very mouth of Truth to be the mother of all the Churches, it is fitting that, whenever any doubt arises anywhere concerning what appears to belong to the care of souls, recourse should be made to it as to a teacher and, in a certain sense, a fountain of heavenly wisdom. Thus, from that single head, the light of ecclesiastical discipline may proceed, so that, once the darkness of uncertainties has been dispelled, the entire body of the Church may shine with the clear radiance of truth.

A very unspeakable and disgraceful vice has taken root in our regions. Unless the hand of strict correction confronts it as quickly as possible, it is certain that the sword of divine fury will soon rage terribly to the destruction of many. Alas, I am ashamed to speak; I am ashamed to disclose so foul a crime to sacred ears. But if a physician shudders at the poison of wounds, who will undertake to apply the cautery? If the one who ought to cure is nauseated, who will restore sick breasts to a state of health? [Col. 0161B]

This vice against nature spreads like a cancer until it reaches the order of sacred men. At times it rages like a bloody beast among Christ’s sheepfold with such audacious freedom that for many it would have been much more beneficial to be brought low under the yoke of worldly service than, under the pretext of religion, to be so freely enslaved to the iron rule of the devil’s tyranny—especially when this occurs to the scandal of others. For Truth says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18). [Col. 0161C]

Unless the vigor of the apostolic see intervenes as quickly as possible, there is no doubt that unrestrained wickedness, when someone attempts to restrain it, will be unable to desist from the force of its course.

## CHAPTER I. On the Varieties of Those Who Sin Against Nature

So that the entire matter may be laid out before you in order, this crime of wickedness produces four varieties. Some sin with themselves, others by the hands of others, others between the thighs, and finally others by completing the act against nature. Among these, one ascends by degrees, so that each later form is judged more serious than the preceding ones.

A greater penance is imposed on those who fall with others than on those who defile themselves by themselves; and those who complete the act are judged more strictly than those who are polluted between the thighs. The devil’s cunning devised these degrees of falling so that, the higher one climbs through them, the more readily the unhappy soul may be plunged into the depths of the infernal abyss. [Col. 0161D]

## CHAPTER II. That the Disordered Mercy of Rulers Does Not Restrain the Fallen from the Order

Those subject to this ruin often recover their senses through the generosity of divine clemency, come to satisfaction, and devoutly undertake the burden of penance, however heavy it may be; but they vehemently dread losing their ecclesiastical order. [150] [Col. 0162A]

Some rulers of the Churches, perhaps more lenient in this matter than is expedient, simply decree that, on account of the three degrees listed above, no one should be removed from his order. They do not refuse to degrade only those who are found to have fallen through the final act. Thus it happens that someone known to have fallen into this wickedness with eight or even ten other equally filthy persons nevertheless appears to remain in his order. [Col. 0162B]

This impious mercy certainly does not cut away the wound; it supplies fuel so that the wound may grow. It does not prohibit the bitterness of the illicit act once committed; rather, it grants license to commit it. A carnal person of any order fears and dreads being despised in the sight of men more than being condemned in the judgment of the heavenly Judge. Accordingly, he would rather endure any labor of strict and courageous penance than be exposed to the danger of losing his rank.

And while, through indiscriminate leniency disguised as discretion, he does not fear losing the status of his honor, he is encouraged both to attempt what he has not yet attempted and to persist longer in what he has rashly attempted against his will. Thus, so to speak, because he is not struck where he feels the sharpest pain, he lies softly in the mire of filthy obscenity in the place where he once fell.

## CHAPTER III. That Those Devoted to the Practice of Uncleanness Should Neither Be Advanced to the Order nor Remain in It Once Advanced

But, as it seems to us, it is entirely backward that those habitually defiled by this purulent contagion should dare either to be advanced to the order or to remain in the rank to which they have already been promoted. This is contrary both to reason and to the canonical sanctions of the Fathers. [Col. 0162C]

I do not assert this in order to pronounce a definitive judgment in the presence of Your Majesty, but to disclose the judgment of my own opinion. This crime is rightly believed to be the worst among other crimes, since Almighty God is always said to have hated it in the same way. When he had not yet placed restraints upon the other vices by legal command, he was already condemning this one through the strict judgment of vengeance.

To say nothing of the fact that he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah—two especially eminent cities—and all the neighboring regions by sending down sulfur and fire from heaven (Genesis 19), he struck Onan, the son of Judah, with premature death because of this unspeakable crime. [Col. 0162D] Scripture bears witness, saying:

“Onan knew that children would not be born to him, and when he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed upon the ground, lest children should be born in his brother’s name. Therefore the Lord struck him, because he had done a detestable thing” (Genesis 38).

It is also said in the Law:

“Whoever sleeps with a male as with a woman: both have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death. Their blood shall be upon them” (Leviticus 20). [151]

That one who has fallen into this crime should not be promoted to the ecclesiastical order, since the ancient Law commands that he be condemned to death, is attested by blessed Pope Gregory. In his letters to Bishop Passivus, he writes:

“Your Fraternity knows well how long Aprutium has been deprived of pastoral care. We sought for a long time someone who ought to be ordained, and we were unable to find anyone. But because Importunus is highly praised by me for his character, his devotion to psalmody, and his love of prayer, and is said to lead a religious life, we wish Your Fraternity to have him come to you and admonish him concerning his soul, so that he may grow in good pursuits. And if no crimes confront him which, according to the rule of sacred law, are punished by death, then he is to be ordained, either as a monk or by you as a subdeacon; and after some time, if it pleases God, he himself is to be promoted to pastoral care” (book X, letter 13). [Col. 0163A]

Here it is plainly gathered that whoever falls with a man—an offense which, as we have taught above, is punished by death according to the judgment of the ancient Law—even if he excels in honorable conduct, burns with devotion to psalmody, shines in his love of prayer, and leads an entirely religious life with an approved reputation, may indeed receive full indulgence for his guilt, but is in no way permitted to aspire to the ecclesiastical order.

For although that venerable man Importunus is first raised up with such fervent praise, crowned with so many signs of religious and honorable life, and adorned with so many commendations of virtue, it is nevertheless afterward said: “If no crimes confront him which, according to the rule of sacred law, are punished by death, then he is to be ordained.” [Col. 0163B]

It is therefore perfectly clear that no subsequent religious life restores to the reception of an ecclesiastical rank the man whom a crime deserving death had cast away. Nor can one rise to obtain the summit of honor who is known to have fallen into the abyss of mortal guilt. It is therefore clearer than daylight that whoever is proved to have fallen in the manner described—an act unquestionably a mortal crime—is promoted to the ecclesiastical order entirely against the norm of sacred law and entirely against the rule of divine authority. [Col. 0163C]

## CHAPTER IV. Whether, If Ecclesiastical Necessity Demands It, Such Men May Perform This Office

Someone may perhaps say that necessity is pressing: there is no person available to perform the sacred office in the Church; and a judgment previously pronounced at the prompting of divine justice is appropriately softened when circumstances require it. [Col. 0163D]

I answer briefly: Was necessity not also present when the pontifical see was vacant of a shepherd? For the benefit of one man, is a censure to be relaxed which remains unshaken when an entire people is deprived of its shepherd? What is not relaxed for the advancement of an innumerable multitude—will it be violated for the convenience of one individual? [152]

But let the excellent preacher himself come forward and make more clearly known what he thinks concerning this vice. For he says in the Letter to the Ephesians:

“Know this, understanding it: no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5). [Col. 0164A]

If, then, the unclean person has no inheritance whatsoever in heaven, by what presumption or rash arrogance should he obtain an office in the Church, which is likewise the kingdom of God? Will one who set aside the divine law by falling into crime not fear to despise it also by ascending to the office of ecclesiastical dignity? He spares nothing, since he does not fear to despise God in all things.

This law was evidently imposed especially upon those by whom it was violated. Paul bears witness, writing to Timothy:

“The law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and defiled, murderers of fathers and mothers, killers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine” (1 Timothy 1). [Col. 0164B]

Since, as has been shown, that law is laid down for men who lie with males so that they may not dare to profane the sacred orders, by whom, I ask, will this law be observed if it is despised especially by those for whom it was imposed?

And if someone is perhaps called useful, it is right that, the more wisely he flourishes in intellectual pursuits, the more carefully he should preserve the commands of authoritative sanction. For the better each person understands, the worse he sins. One who could prudently have avoided sin, had he wished to do so, will inevitably deserve punishment. As blessed James says:

“Whoever knows the good he ought to do and does not do it, for him it is sin” (James 4).

Truth also says: “From the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required.”

For if the order of ecclesiastical discipline is confused in any learned man, it is remarkable if it is preserved by an ignorant one. If someone experienced is brought disorderly into the order, he seems in some manner to pave for those who follow him—and, so to speak, for the simpler—the path of error which he himself has begun to tread with the swollen foot of pride. [Col. 0164C] He must be judged not only because he sinned, but also because, by the example of his own presumption, he invited others to imitate his sin.

## CHAPTER V. That Those Who Have Fallen into a Reprobate Mind Desire to Possess Sacred Orders after This Vice

Who could pass this by with deaf ears? Indeed, who would not tremble to the marrow at what the Apostle thunders concerning such men, like a powerful trumpet:

“God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves” (Romans 1). [Col. 0164D]

A little later he says:

“Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions. Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature; and likewise the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense which their error deserved. And because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (ibid.). [153]

What is it, then, that after so serious a fall they desire the eminence of ecclesiastical order so greatly? What are we to think or believe, except that God has given them over to a reprobate mind? Because their sins demand it, he does not permit them to see what is necessary for them. [Col. 0165A]

For the sun has set upon them—the one, namely, who rose above the setting of the sun (Psalm 67). Having lost their inward eyes, they cannot consider that the evils they committed through uncleanness are grave, nor how much worse it is to desire, against God’s will, to possess ecclesiastical dignity in a disorderly manner.

This proceeds according to the customary rule of divine justice: those who defile themselves with this most ruinous filth, struck by a judgment worthy of correction, fall into the darkness of blindness. As is read concerning those ancient authors of this foulness:

“When they were violently assaulting the just Lot and were already near breaking down the door, Scripture says, the men stretched out their hands, drew Lot inside to them, shut the door, and struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Genesis 19). [Col. 0165B]

It is clear that through those two angels who are said to have come to blessed Lot, the person of the Father and of the Son is not inappropriately signified. This is clearly shown by Lot’s own words to them:

“Please, my lord, because your servant has found grace before you, and you have magnified your mercy, which you have shown me by saving my life” (ibid.).

For one who speaks in this way to two persons as though to one singular person certainly venerates one substance in two persons.

The Sodomites, then, attempt to break violently into the angels, just as unclean men attempt to approach God through the offices of sacred order. [Col. 0165C] But these men are struck with blindness, because by the just judgment of God they fall into inner darkness, so that they cannot find the door; for, having been separated from God by sinning, they do not know by what way they may return to him.

Those who desire to approach God not through the winding paths of humility but through arrogance and pride plainly do not recognize where the entrance lies. Or, since Christ is the door, as he himself says, “I am the door” (John 10), those who lose Christ through sins, being unable to enter the dwelling of the heavenly citizens, do not find the door.

They have therefore been given over to a reprobate mind because, while they do not weigh the burden of their guilt on the scales of their own mind, they regard an exceedingly heavy mass of lead as the lightness of futile punishments. [Col. 0165D] What is said there—“They struck those who were outside with blindness” (Genesis 19)—the Apostle openly explains when he says, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind.” And what follows there—“so that they could not find the door”—he likewise explains plainly when he says, “to do what is not fitting.”

It is as though he said: so that they attempt to enter where they ought not. For one who, unworthy of the order, attempts to burst into the office of the sacred altar is doing nothing other than trying to enter, after abandoning the threshold of the door, through the impassable obstruction of a wall.

Because no free entrance lies open to their feet, such men, while promising themselves that they can reach the sanctuary, are forced by their presumption to remain frustrated in the outer vestibule. They may strike their foreheads against the stones of sacred Scripture, but they are in no way permitted to enter through the passage of divine authority. [Col. 0166A] While they attempt to enter where they are not allowed, they do nothing except pointlessly grope at a covered wall.

The prophetic saying appropriately applies to them: “At midday they will grope as in the night” (Job 5). Since they cannot cross the threshold of the straight entrance, they roll about in circles, wandering in the spinning madness of their error. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “My God, set them like a wheel” (Psalm 82), and again: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Psalm 11). Concerning them Paul also says, after the words quoted above:

“Those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1). [Col. 0166B]

Clearly, one who does not awaken at such a terrible thunderclap of apostolic denunciation is rightly judged not to be sleeping but dead. And since the Apostle intensifies the sentence of strict judgment with such zeal not against Jews who are in some sense believers, but against Gentiles who are ignorant of God, what, I ask, would he have said if he had seen such a wound festering in the very body of the holy Church?

What pain, what ardor of compassion, would have inflamed that devout heart if he had learned that this deadly plague was raging in the sacred order? Let the negligent rulers of clerics and priests hear this; let them hear it, and although they may be secure concerning themselves, let them fear being made participants in another’s guilt—those, namely, who connive at correcting the sins of their subjects and, through inconsiderate silence, give their subjects permission to sin. [Col. 0166C]

Let them hear, I say, and understand prudently that all alike are worthy of death: not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Spiritual Fathers Who Defile Themselves with Their Sons

O unheard-of crime! O deed to be mourned from the whole fountain of tears! If those who consent to such acts are to be punished by death, what punishment worthy of them can be imagined for those who commit these evils—deserving of the final condemnation—with their own spiritual sons? [Col. 0166D]

What fruit can now be found among the flocks when the shepherd has been plunged by so deep a fall into the belly of the devil? Who would remain under the authority of one whom he knows to have become so hostilely estranged from God? He makes a lover of a penitent, and the son whom he had spiritually begotten for God he subjects, through the uncleanness of his flesh, as a servant to the iron rule of the devil’s tyranny.

If someone violates a woman whom he lifted from the sacred font, is it not decreed without any hesitation that he must be deprived of communion and be compelled by the censure of the sacred canons to pass through public penance? [155] For it is written: “Spiritual generation is greater than carnal generation.”

It follows, therefore, that the same sentence should rightly strike both the man who has ruined a carnal daughter and the man who has corrupted a spiritual daughter through sacrilegious intercourse—unless perhaps the quality of the two crimes is distinguished in this way: both men, although they have sinned incestuously, have sinned naturally because they sinned with a woman; but the other man committed sacrilege against a son, incurred the crime of incest with a male, and dissolved the rights of nature. [Col. 0167A]

And, as it seems to me, it is more tolerable to fall into the crime of lust with an animal than with a man. It is judged much lighter for anyone to perish alone than to drag another with him into the danger of destruction. For miserable is the condition in which the ruin of one depends upon another, so that when one is extinguished, the other necessarily follows into death.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Those Who Confess Their Crimes to the Very Persons with Whom They Fell

[Col. 0167B]

So that the arguments of the devil’s contrivance may not remain hidden, but that what is secretly fashioned in the workshop of ancient wickedness may come into the light while I blush, I cannot allow this to be concealed: some men, sated with the poison of this crime, when they seem to return to their senses, confess to one another so that their guilt may not become known to others.

While they are ashamed before men whose guilt they themselves helped to produce, they become judges; and each one rejoices in granting the other, through an exchange of roles, the indiscriminate indulgence he desires to have granted to himself.

Thus it happens that they are penitents for great crimes and yet neither do their faces grow pale through fasting nor do their bodies waste away through emaciation. While the belly is in no way restrained from excessive nourishment, the mind is shamefully inflamed with the heat of its accustomed lust. Consequently, one who had not yet wept over his committed sins commits things still more grievous to mourn. [Col. 0167C]

But the command of the Law is that when someone is covered with leprosy, he be shown to the priests. He is not shown to priests but rather to a leper when an unclean man confesses a common wickedness already committed to another unclean man.

Since confession is manifestation, what does the man manifest who tells his hearer what the hearer already knows? Or how can that be called confession in which the one confessing manifests nothing except what the listener already knew long before?

And one who is bound to another by the shared bond of a completed iniquity—by what law or right can he bind or loose the other? For one who is himself entangled in bonds attempts in vain to release another. [Col. 0167D]

And one who wishes to become a guide for the blind must himself see, lest he become the cause of the follower’s downfall, as Truth says:

“If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15).

And again:

“You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not consider the beam that is in your own eye. Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7; Luke 6).

These evangelical testimonies make it perfectly clear that one who is pressed down by the darkness of the same guilt attempts in vain to call another back to the light of penance. [156] While, beyond his own strength, he does not fear causing another to perish by wandering, he does not escape together with the one who follows him from the pit of present ruin. [Col. 0168A]

## CHAPTER VIII. That, Just as the Sacrilegious Violator of a Virgin, So Also the Prostitutor of a Spiritual Son Is Rightly to Be Deposed

But now, whoever you are, carnal man, I address you face to face. Do you refuse to confess your sins to spiritual men because you fear that you must also cease from ecclesiastical rank? How much more salutary it would be to suffer temporal shame in the sight of men than to undergo eternal vengeance before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge!

Perhaps you say to me: “If a man falls with a man only between the thighs, he will indeed do penance, but out of regard for merciful humanity he ought not to be irrevocably cast down from his rank.”

I ask you: If someone has sacrilegiously violated a virgin, will he, in your judgment, remain in his rank? [Col. 0168B] There is no doubt that you would judge such a man worthy of deposition. It follows, therefore, that what you reasonably assert concerning a sacred virgin, you must also inevitably acknowledge concerning a spiritual son. Consequently, what you appear to assert concerning spiritual fathers, you must necessarily define in the same way concerning clerics.

This distinction must nevertheless be maintained: the act is judged worse in proportion as it is proved to be more contrary to nature through the identity of the sexes. Moreover, when excesses are judged, one must rightly have constant recourse to the will of the delinquent. The man who polluted male thighs, if nature had permitted it, would through the madness of unrestrained lust have perpetrated in a male everything that is done with women. He did what he could, proceeding even to what nature denied and fixing the boundary of his crime unwillingly at the point where the necessity of nature placed an impassable limit upon his ability. [Col. 0168C]

Since, then, the same law applies in both cases to sacred ministers and clerics, we must conclude that just as the sacrilegious violator of a virgin is rightly deposed, so also the prostitutor of a spiritual son must in every way likewise be barred from his office.

## CHAPTER IX. That the Person Guilty of the Same Crime Is Both the One Who Falls with a Carnal Daughter and the One Who Falls with a Daughter of Baptism

[The supplied source ends here.]

And so, for the discussion to turn once more to the sacred—that is, accursed—confessors: if any canonical presbyter has fallen with a woman upon whom he has imposed the judgment of penance even once, no one at all doubts that he is degraded by synodal judicial censure. But if a religious man falls with a religious man, with one, that is, for whom he either acted as judge in imposing penance or was himself judged in receiving it, will he not, justice dictating, lose the honor of his order? For by common usage one is called a “son of penance,” just as one is called a “son of baptism.” Hence it is also read concerning blessed Mark the Evangelist: “Because he is Peter’s son in baptism” (I Cor. I). And the outstanding preacher says: “For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize”; he says likewise: “For what is my glory before the Lord? Is it not you? For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I have begotten you” (I Cor. IV). Again he says to the Galatians: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

If, then, he begot and brought to birth who was not sent to baptize but to evangelize, and thereby to summon people to penance, it is fittingly said that the one who receives penance is a son, and the one who imposes penance is a father. Therefore, if what was said above is carefully considered, it is clearer than daylight that the one who fornicates with a carnal daughter or a daughter of baptism is guilty of the same crime as the one who commits an indecency with a son of penance. And just as the one who has fallen with the woman whom he carnally begot, or whom he received from baptism, or upon whom he imposed the judgment of penance, is rightly removed in every way from the order of which he is an administrator, so also the one who falls through impurity with a son of penance must in every way be separated from the order of which he is the administrator.

## CHAPTER X. On the apocryphal canons, in which all who place their confidence are completely deceived

[Col. 0169B]

But since certain dirges are found mixed into the sacred canons, in which lost men place their confidence through empty presumption, we set down some of them here, so that we may clearly demonstrate that not only these, but also all others written like them, wherever they may be found, are false and wholly apocryphal. For among other things it is said:

“A presbyter who has not professed the monastic vow, if he sins with a girl or a prostitute, shall do penance for two years and three Lents, always on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, with dry bread. If with a handmaid of God or a male, a fast shall be added—that is, five years—if it is habitual. Likewise deacons, if they are not monks, for two years; and likewise monks who are without rank.”

A little later it adds:

“If a cleric without the monastic vow has fornicated with a girl, let him do penance for half a year; if he is a canon, likewise; if frequently, for two years. Likewise, if anyone has sinned as the Sodomites did, some say ten years of penance; whoever makes a habit of it should be punished more severely. If he is in an order, let him be degraded and do penance as a layman. A man who has fornicated between the thighs shall do penance for one year; if he repeats it, for two years; but if he has fornicated in the rear, let him do penance for three years. If he is a boy, let him do penance for two years. If he has fornicated with an animal or beast of burden, let him do penance for ten years. Likewise, if a bishop sins with a quadruped, let him do penance for ten years and lose his rank; a presbyter, five; a deacon, three; a cleric, two.”

Many other false and sacrilegious contrivances of the devil are also found inserted into the sacred canons, which we would rather erase than write, and rather spit upon than impress such empty mockeries upon sheets of paper. Behold: carnal men place their confidence in these ravings, attribute faith to them as to apparitions in dreams, and deceive themselves with the security of a vain hope. But let us see whether these things agree with canonical authority, and whether they should be held or avoided; let the facts that bear witness make this known, rather than words.

## CHAPTER XI. A credible refutation of the canons cited above

Therefore, to return to the beginning of this deceitful chapter [Col. 0170A], it says: “A presbyter who has not professed the monastic vow, if he sins with a girl or a prostitute, shall do penance for two years.” And who could be found so dull, so insane, as to believe two years of penance adequate for a presbyter caught in fornication? For anyone who has touched even the slightest degree of knowledge of canonical authority, however superficially—and to say nothing of stricter judgments—plainly recognizes that at least ten years of penance are to be decreed for a presbyter fallen into fornication.

This two-year penance for fornication is judged to belong not only to no priests, but not even to laymen, for whom, running from this ruin toward satisfaction, a three-year period is prescribed. Then it adds: “If he has sinned with a handmaid of God or a male”—the presbyter is understood—“a fast shall be added, that is, five years, if it is habitual. Likewise deacons, if they are not monks, shall do penance for two years, as shall monks who are without rank.”

In the heading of this senseless opinion that I am expounding, I see and gladly attend to one point: namely, the statement, “If he sins with a handmaid of God or with a male.” Behold, good Sodomite, in that very writing of yours, which you love so singularly, which you embrace so eagerly, which you set before yourself like a shield of defense, you plainly see that whether someone sins with a handmaid of God or with a male makes no difference; the sin is judged equal and the sentence identical. You now have nothing with which to quarrel with me, nothing by which you can rightly dissent from my arguments.

[Col. 0170C]

But who could be so madly foolish, who could fall into such profound darkness of blindness, as to judge that five years of penance should be imposed for a fall with a handmaid of God—that is, a nun—or for a presbyter, or two years for a deacon or monk? Is this not the snare that lies in wait for the perishing? Is this not the noose of wandering souls?

And who could fail to condemn the statement: “If a cleric without the monastic vow has fornicated with a girl, let him do penance for half a year”? Who could possess such strength in the knowledge of sacred Scripture, who could be so ingenious in the sharpness of dialectical subtlety, as to presume to condemn a judicial prejudice so contrary to the law, and so laudably detestable in its authority? From the same source from which a three-year period is assigned to a layman, is a cleric ordered to do penance for half a year?

Blessed, then, are the clerics who fornicate, if they are judged according to the will of the Sodomites: for they desire to have measured back to themselves by the same measure with which they measure others. This author of error showed himself sufficiently eager to win souls for the devil: while he sought to destroy monks, he extended his doctrine of perversity even to the clerical order; and, being a murderer of souls, when he could not fill the stomach of his malice to the throat with the death of monks alone, he desired to sate himself from another order as well.

Now let us examine what follows:

“If anyone has sinned as the Sodomites did, some say ten years of penance; whoever makes a habit of it should be punished more severely; if he is in an order, let him be degraded and do penance as a layman. A man who has fornicated between the thighs shall do penance for one year; if he repeats it, let him do penance for two years; but if he has fornicated in the rear, let him do penance for three years.”

And since, as you yourselves assert, to sin as the Sodomites did is nothing other than to fornicate in the rear, why are your canons found to be so manifold and varied within almost a single verse, imposing the burden of ten years upon those who sin as the Sodomites did, but restraining the penitential lamentation of those who fornicate in the rear—for the same act—to less than three years? Are these not rightly compared with monsters, not produced by nature but constructed by human industry, some of which begin with horses’ heads and end in goats’ hooves? By what canons, by what decrees of the Fathers, do these mockeries agree—things that, being so discordant with themselves, resound with an even more horned brow? What authorities support things that tear one another apart?

“For every kingdom,” says the Savior, “divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house; and if Satan is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand?” (Luke XI.)

At one moment they appear to direct the judgment of strictness; at another, to display a kind of cruel mercy. And, like a chimerical monster, here the lion’s form thunders terrifically with threats, while there a worthless she-goat bleats humbly; by this diversity, as it were, of various forms, they provoke laughter rather than pierce the heart with penitential lamentation.

Similar in error also are the statements that follow:

“Whoever has fornicated with an animal or beast of burden shall do penance for ten years. Likewise, a bishop who sins with quadrupeds shall do penance for ten years and lose his rank; a presbyter, five; a deacon, three; a cleric, two.”

This is said even though the text had first stated plainly: “Whoever has fornicated with an animal or beast of burden shall be punished with ten years of satisfaction.” How, then, does it follow that penance for intercourse with an animal is assigned to a presbyter for five years, to a deacon for three, and to a cleric for two? From the point at which everyone—that is, any layman as well—is bound by the affliction of a ten-year period, a five-year term is assigned to the presbyter; that is, half the entire penance is relaxed.

With what pages of sacred eloquence, I ask, do these frivolous nightmares agree, when they so evidently attack themselves? Who would not consider, who would not plainly see, that these and similar things, fraudulently mixed into the sacred canons, are diabolical fabrications, devised by crafty machinations to deceive simple souls? For just as poison is fraudulently mixed into honey or into any especially delicious foods, so that while the sweetness of the food invites one to eat, the hidden venom may more easily pass into a person’s interior, so these deceitful and false inventions are inserted into sacred writings so that they may escape suspicion of falsity; they are, as it were, smeared with honey, appearing to be flavored with the sweetness of false piety.

But beware of these things, whoever you are, lest the song of the Sirens charm you with deadly sweetness, lest it plunge the ship of your mind into the depths of Scylla’s whirlpool. [Col. 0172A] Let the sea of the holy councils, perhaps advanced with austerity, not terrify you; let not the shallow sandbanks of the apocryphal canons, with their promised gentleness of waves, drag you down. Often a ship, fleeing stormy waves, has suffered shipwreck when it drew near the sands along the shore; and often, cleaving the deep sea, it has swum safely without loss of its cargo.

## CHAPTER XII. That these mockeries are rightly excluded from the number of the canons, since they do not appear to have a certain author

Yet who fabricated these canons? Who dared to sow such thorny, such barbed thistles of buckthorn in the purple woodland of the Church? It is clear, certainly, that all authentic canons have either been found in venerable synodal councils or promulgated by the holy pontiffs of the apostolic see. Nor is it permitted for just anyone to issue canons; that privilege belongs only to the one who is seen to preside in the chair of blessed Peter.

These things of which we are speaking—the spurious shoots of the canons—are known to have been excluded by the sacred councils and are plainly judged alien to the decrees of the Fathers. It follows, then, that those things should by no means be counted among the canons which appear to proceed neither from the decretal edicts of the Fathers nor from sacred councils. For whatever is not numbered among the species is without doubt judged alien to the genus.

But if the author’s name is sought, it cannot be called certain, since it could not be found uniformly in the various books. In one place it is written, “Theodore says”; elsewhere, “The Roman Penitential says”; elsewhere, “The Canons of the Apostles.” They are titled one way here and another way there; and since they do not deserve to have a single author, they unquestionably lose all authority. For things that waver under so many uncertain authors confirm nothing with certain authority. And it is necessary that things which generate the darkness of doubt in readers withdraw from the light of sacred Scripture, with every doubt removed.

Now that these theatrical ravings, in which carnal men placed their confidence, have been eliminated from the number of the canons and refuted by the transparent logic of argument, let us set forth those canons whose faith and authority we do not distrust in the least. For in the Council of Ancyra it is found:

## CHAPTER XIII. On those who fornicate irrationally—that is, who mate with animals or pollute themselves with males

[Col. 0172D]

“Concerning those who have acted, or are acting, irrationally: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, be deemed worthy of communion in prayers; then, after remaining in this communion for five years, they shall finally touch the sacramental offerings. Their life, moreover, shall be examined, what sort it was during the time of their repentance, and thus they shall obtain mercy. But if they have clung persistently to these crimes, let them spend a longer period in performing penance.

“Those, however, who, having completed twenty years of age and having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after undergoing twenty-five years of repentance, be received into communion in prayers; after remaining in it for five years, they shall finally receive the sacramental offerings. But if some, while having wives and having passed the fiftieth year of age, have committed such an offense, let them obtain the grace of communion at the end of life.”

Behold: in the very title of this venerable authority we plainly perceive that not only those who sin against nature by completing the act, but also those who pollute themselves with males by any method whatsoever, are in every respect compared with those who mate with animals. For if we look to the intervening words, we see that they were placed carefully and with a balance of great discrimination, where it says: “Those who mate with animals, or pollute themselves with males.” For if, by saying “those who pollute themselves with males,” it had wished to designate only those who sin against nature by completing the act, it would not at all have been necessary to put forward two words; it could have completed the statement of its intention with the single word “mate.”

Indeed, for brevity of style it would have been enough to encompass the whole sentence in one expression, saying: “Those who mate with animals or with males.” For both those who violate animals and those who violate males mate in one way. But since it says that some mate with animals, while others do not mate but pollute themselves with males, it is perfectly clear that at the end of the clause it pronounces judgment not only upon corrupters of males, but also upon those who pollute themselves in any manner.

It should be noted, moreover, that the edict of this constitution was established chiefly for laymen, as is easily perceived from what is added below:

“Those, however, who, having completed twenty years of age and having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after undergoing twenty-five years of repentance, be received into communion in prayers; after remaining in it for five years, they shall finally receive the sacramental offerings.”

If, then, any secular person guilty of this crime, after completing twenty-five years of penance, is admitted to communion in prayers but not yet to receive the sacramental offerings, by what reasoning will a religious man be judged fit not only to receive but also to offer and consecrate the sacred mysteries themselves? If he is scarcely permitted to enter the church to pray with others, how will it be granted to this man to approach the Lord’s altar to intercede for others? If the former, before completing such a lengthy period of penance, does not deserve to hear, how is the latter worthy to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass? If the one who sinned less—for example, proceeding along the broad road of the world—is unworthy to receive the gift of the heavenly Eucharist with his mouth, how will this man deserve to handle so terrible a mystery with polluted hands?

Let us see further what the same Council of Ancyra defined again concerning the same crime.

## CHAPTER XIV. On those who have formerly been polluted with animals or males, or who still waste away in this vice

[Col. 0174A]

“The holy synod commanded that those who have lived irrationally and have polluted others with the leprosy of an unjust crime should pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.”

Clearly, since it does not say, “those who have corrupted others with the leprosy of an unjust crime,” but “polluted,” which also agrees with the preface of the title itself, where it begins not with the corrupted but with the polluted, it is evident that, in whatever manner a man is polluted with a man through the heat of lust, he is commanded to pray not among Catholic Christians but among the demoniacs. Thus, if carnal men do not know how to assess for themselves what they are, they may at least be taught by those among whom they have been assigned to a common prison of prayer.

And certainly it is sufficiently fitting that those who, against the law of nature and against the order of human reason, surrender their flesh to demons through such foul dealings should share a common corner of prayer with the demoniacs. Since human nature itself wholly resists these evils and abhors the difficulty of a different sex, it is clearer than daylight that they would never presume to undertake things so contrary and alien unless wicked spirits possessed them completely—as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, so to speak. But once those spirits begin to possess them, they pour the Tartarean venom of their malignity through everything with which they fill the invaded breast, so that these men now eagerly desire not what the natural movement of the flesh demands, but what diabolical precipitation alone supplies.

For when a man rushes upon a man to perpetrate impurity, that is not the natural impulse of the flesh, but only the goad of diabolical compulsion. Therefore the holy Fathers vigilantly decreed that Sodomites should pray together with the possessed, since they did not doubt that both were invaded by the same diabolical spirit. How, then, should one who is separated from the congregation of the entire people and is commanded to pray only among demoniacs stand as mediator between God and the people through the dignity of priestly office?

But since we have taken care to produce two testimonies from one sacred council, let us also insert what the great Basil thinks about the vice now under discussion, so that “every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.” For he says:

## CHAPTER XV. On clerics or monks who are pursuers of males

[Col. 0174D]

“A cleric or monk who pursues adolescents or little boys, or who is caught in a kiss or in any shameful circumstance, shall be publicly scourged, shall lose his crown, and, after being disgracefully shaven, shall have spittle smeared upon his face. Bound tightly in iron chains, he shall be tormented for six months in the confinement of a prison; and for three days each week, until evening, he shall be fed on barley bread. After this, for another six months, living in isolation in a small enclosure under the custody of an elder in the spiritual life, he shall devote himself to manual labor and prayer, subject to vigils and prayers. He shall always walk under the custody of two spiritual brothers and shall thereafter be joined to young men in neither perverse speech nor counsel.”

Here let the carnal man carefully consider whether he can safely minister in ecclesiastical offices when sacred authority judges that he must be dishonored by such shameful and disgraceful insults. Nor should he flatter himself on the ground that he corrupted no one, since he sees written with complete clarity that anyone caught in a mere kiss or in any shameful circumstance is rightly subjected to all those disgraceful forms of discipline.

But if a kiss is punished with so severe a penalty, what does actual contamination with another deserve? For in punishing which crime, which most monstrous wickedness, would it not be enough to be publicly scourged, lose one’s crown, be disgracefully shaved, smeared with the filth of saliva, pressed for a long time in the confinement of a prison, and additionally constricted with iron chains? Finally, he is also ordered to be fed on barley bread, because one who has become “like a horse and a mule” (Psalm XXXI) is fittingly not restored with human food but fed with the grain of beasts of burden.

Moreover, if we neglect to weigh the gravity of this sin, it is nevertheless revealed most clearly in the very judgment of penance that is imposed. For whoever is compelled by canonical censure to undergo public penance is plainly judged unworthy of ecclesiastical offices by the manifest sentence of the Fathers. Hence blessed Pope Siricius also wrote, among other things:

“We were equally bound to provide this: just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman shall ever be permitted to obtain the honor of the clerical order. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they ought nevertheless to receive none of the instruments for administering the sacraments, since they had previously been vessels of vices.”

Since, then, blessed Basil commands that one guilty of this sin undergo not only harsh but also public penance, while Siricius forbids a penitent from holding the clerical order, it is plainly concluded that one who has been polluted with a male by the foulness of lustful impurity does not deserve to perform ecclesiastical offices. Nor are those fit to handle the divine mystery who, as it is said, had previously been vessels of vices.

## CHAPTER XVI. A deserved condemnation of unspeakable indecency

[Col. 0175D]

This vice, certainly, is comparable to no other vice, for it surpasses the enormity of every vice. This vice is the death of bodies and the destruction of souls; it pollutes the flesh, extinguishes the light of the mind, drives the Holy Spirit from the temple of the human heart, introduces the devil as the instigator of lust, sends the mind into error, entirely removes truth from the deceived mind, prepares snares for the one who is going, and, when he falls into the pit, blocks him from emerging; it opens hell, closes the gate of paradise, makes a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem heir to Tartarean Babylon, and makes a star of heaven fuel for the eternal fire. It cuts off a member of the Church and throws it into the devouring fire of burning Gehenna.

This vice attempts to overthrow the walls of the heavenly homeland and strives to restore the walls of burned Sodom, risen again. For this is what violates sobriety, kills modesty, strangles chastity, and slaughters virginity—which is irrecoverable—with the sword of the filthiest contagion. It defiles everything, stains everything, pollutes everything; and, so far as it is concerned, permits nothing to be pure, nothing free from filth, nothing clean:

“For all things,” as the Apostle says, “are clean to the clean; but to the polluted and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus I).

This vice expels a person from the choir of the ecclesiastical assembly and compels him to pray with the possessed and those afflicted by a demon; it separates the soul from God in order to join it to demons. This most pestilential queen of the Sodomites makes her subject, according to the laws of her tyranny, disgraceful to human beings and hateful to God. She commands him to wage unspeakable wars against God and to carry the military burden of the most wicked spirit; she separates him from the company of angels and, under the yoke of her own domination, takes captive the wretched soul in its nobility.

She strips her soldiers of the weapons of the virtues and exposes them to the arrows of every vice, so that they may be pierced. In the Church she humiliates them; in the forum she condemns them; in secret she defiles them; in public she dishonors them. She gnaws the conscience like a worm and burns the flesh like fire. She pants to fulfill pleasure, but at the same time fears that the matter may come to the center, emerge into public, or become known to human beings. For whom would that person not fear, when in fearful suspicion he dreads even the one who shares in the common ruin?

He fears lest the very one who sins with him become, through confession, a judge of the crime—not merely confessing without hesitation that he has sinned, but also consequently naming the person with whom he sinned—so that, just as one could not die in sin unless the other also died, so one may give the other an opportunity to rise when he rises.

The wretched flesh burns with the fury of lust; the cold mind trembles with the bitterness of suspicion; and in the breast of the miserable man a kind of Tartarean chaos already boils up. As many goads of thought as prick him, so many punishments and torments, in a manner of speaking, torture him. For once this most poisonous serpent has fixed its teeth in the unhappy soul, its senses are immediately taken away, memory is removed, and the sharpness of the mind is darkened. He becomes forgetful of God and even forgets himself.

For this plague empties the foundation of faith, weakens the strength of hope, dissolves the bond of charity, removes justice, undermines courage, takes away temperance, and dulls the edge of prudence.

And what more shall I say? Since it drives every wedge of the virtues from the court of the human heart and, as though the bars of the gates had been torn away, lets in the whole barbarity of vices. To this person the sentence of Jeremiah, spoken under the figure of earthly Jerusalem, aptly applies:

“The enemy,” he says, “has stretched out his hand to all her desirable things, because he saw nations entering her sanctuary, concerning whom you had commanded that they should not enter your Church” (Lamentations I).

Indeed, once this most savage beast has devoured someone with its bloody jaws, it binds him with certain chains away from all good works and drives him headlong, unbridled, through every precipice of the most wicked perversity. As soon as anyone has fallen into this abyss of ultimate destruction, he becomes an exile from the heavenly homeland, is separated from the body of Christ, is disgraced by the authority of the entire Church, condemned by the judgment of all the holy Fathers, despised among human beings on earth, and rejected from the fellowship of the heavenly citizens.

For him heaven becomes iron and earth bronze. He can neither rise there, weighed down by the burden of his crime, nor conceal his evils here for long in the hiding place of ignorance. Here he cannot rejoice while he lives, nor hope there when he dies, because both now he is compelled to endure the reproach of human mockery and afterward the torment of eternal condemnation.

To this soul the prophetic voice of lamentation aptly applies:

“See, Lord, that I am in distress; my belly is troubled; my heart is overturned within me, for I am full of bitterness. Outside, the sword kills, and inside, death is like it” (Lamentations I).

## CHAPTER XVII. A mournful lament over a soul given over to the filth of impurity

I—I lament you, unhappy soul, and from the depths of my heart I sigh over the fate of your destruction. I lament you, I say, miserable soul devoted to the filth of impurity, one to be mourned from the whole fountain of tears. Alas! Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes? (Jeremiah IX.)

Nor is this mournful voice brought forth by me now in sobs any less appropriately than it was then uttered from the prophet’s mouth. For I do not lament the stone fortifications of a turreted city, I do not complain of the overturned buildings of a man-made temple, nor do I mourn the multitudes of the common people who were led captive under the command of the king of Babylon. It is a noble soul that I mourn, created in the image and likeness of God and purchased with the most precious blood of Christ, brighter than many buildings and certainly preferable to all the heights of earthly construction.

I therefore lament the fall of a soul and the destruction of the temple in which Christ had dwelt. My eyes, fail from weeping; pour out abundant streams of tears; with continual sobs, let my mournful face be drenched in sadness. With the prophet, let my eyes shed tears day and night, and let them not be silent, because the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a very grievous wound (Jeremiah XIV).

For the daughter of my people has been struck by a most grievous wound, because the soul that had been a daughter of holy Church has been cruelly wounded by the weapon of impurity wielded by the enemy of the human race. She who in the palace of the eternal King was tenderly and gently nourished with the milk of sacred eloquence is now seen lying swollen and rigid amid the sulfurous ashes of Gomorrah, pestilently infected with the poison of lust.

“Those who ate delicately have perished in the ways; those who were nourished in scarlet have embraced dung” (Lamentations IV).

Why? The prophet continues and says:

“Because the iniquity of the daughter of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in an instant” (ibid.).

For the iniquity of a Christian soul surpasses the sin of Sodom, because a person now sins all the worse insofar as he also despises the commands of evangelical grace; and, so that he may find no remedy in evasive excuse, knowledge of the divine law continually accuses him.

Alas, alas, unhappy soul! Why do you not consider from how great a summit of dignity you have been cast down, from how great an adornment of splendor and glory you have been stripped?

“How the Lord in his fury has covered the daughter of Zion with darkness; he has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth; all her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion” (Lamentations II).

I, taking pity on your calamity and bitterly lamenting your disgrace, say:

“My eyes have failed because of tears; my inward parts are troubled; my liver has been poured out upon the earth over the crushing of the daughter of my people” (ibid.).

But you, refusing to consider your evils and taking courage from your crime, say: “I sit as queen, and I am not a widow!” I, pitying your captivity, cry out:

“Why has Jacob been led away like a servant, and Israel made a spoil?” (Jeremiah II.)

And you say: “Because I am rich, and have grown wealthy, and need nothing.” And you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked? (Revelation III.)

Consider, miserable one, how great a darkness weighs upon your heart; observe how dense a cloud of blindness envelops you. Has the fury of lust driven you toward the male sex? Has the rabidness of wantonness incited you toward your own kind—that is, a man toward a man? Did a he-goat ever leap upon another he-goat, driven headlong by lust? Did a ram ever rage against another ram in the heat of intercourse?

A horse grazes gently and peacefully with another horse at a single manger, yet when he sees a mare he is immediately carried away into the madness of lust. Never has a bull wantonly desired another bull out of love of mating; never has an ass brayed under the goad of lying with another ass.

Thus, what even brute animals dread, lost men do not fear to perpetrate. What is committed through the recklessness of human perversity is condemned by the judgment of irrational beasts.

Tell me, unmanned man; answer, effeminate human being: what do you seek in a man that you cannot find in yourself? What difference of sexes? What varied outlines of limbs? What softness? What tenderness of carnal allure? What charm of a slippery face?

Let the vigor of a masculine appearance terrify you, I beg; let your mind recoil from male limbs. For the function of natural desire is that each person seek externally what he cannot find within the confines of his own capacity. If, then, the handling of male flesh delights you, turn your hands upon yourself, and know that whatever you do not find in yourself, you seek vainly in another’s body.

Woe to you, unhappy soul, at whose destruction the angels grieve and the enemies exult with applause! You have become the prey of demons, the plunder of the cruel, the spoil of the impious:

“All your enemies have opened their mouths against you; they hissed and gnashed their teeth, and said: ‘We shall devour her. Behold, this is the day we were awaiting; we have found her, we have seen her’” (Lamentations II).

167 **CHAPTER XVIII. That the soul must therefore be mourned because it does not mourn**

For this reason I, with so many lamentations, mourn you, wretched soul: because I do not see you weeping. For this reason I lie prostrate on the ground on your behalf: because I see you, wrongly standing erect after so grave a fall, striving of your own accord even toward the summit of the ecclesiastical order.

But if you were to humble yourself, I, secure in your restoration, would rejoice with all the inward affections I have in the Lord. If a worthy contrition of a broken heart were to shake the hidden places of your breast, I would rightly rejoice in a triumph of unspeakable gladness.

Therefore you are especially to be mourned because you do not mourn; you need the grief of others because you yourself do not grieve over the danger of your calamity; and you are to be lamented with all the bitterer tears of fraternal compassion because you are perceived to be disturbed by no sorrow of your own. Why do you pretend not to weigh the burden of your condemnation? Why do you never cease, now plunging yourself into the depths of sins, now raising yourself into pride, to store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath?

That curse has come, it has come upon you—the curse that was hurled from David’s mouth against Joab and his household after the blood of Abner had been shed. That Gomorrian plague now lives in the dwelling of your body, the plague that condemned the house of Joab to the punishment of cruel murder.

After Abner had been struck down, David said:

“I am clean, and my kingdom forever, from the blood of Abner son of Ner. Let it come upon the head of Joab and upon all his father’s house; and let there never fail from the house of Joab one who suffers from a Gomorrian disease” (II Kings III).

The second translation has instead: “one who suffers from a discharge of semen, and a leper holding a distaff, and one who falls by the sword, and one who lacks bread.”

For the one who is defiled by the stain of a grave sin is drenched with leprosy. To hold a distaff is to abandon the strong deeds of a manly life and display the alluring softness of a feminine way of living. He falls by the sword who incurs the fury of divine indignation. He lacks bread whom the punishment of his own guilt restrains from receiving the body of Christ. For he is the living bread who descended from heaven (John IV).

If, then, after the emission of semen, you have become leprous and are compelled by the command of the Law to remain outside the camp, why do you still insist on obtaining even the first place of honor in that same camp? Did not King Uzziah, when he arrogantly wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense, after recognizing that he had been struck from heaven by the plague of leprosy, not only patiently submit to being expelled from the temple by the priests, but himself also hastened to go out quickly? For it is written:

> “When Azariah the high priest and all the other priests looked at him, they saw leprosy on his forehead, and they hurriedly expelled him”;

and immediately it adds:

> “But he himself, terrified, hastened to leave, because he had felt the Lord’s blow” (2 Chronicles 26).

[Col. 0179D]

If a king struck with bodily leprosy did not disdain to be driven from the temple by the priests, why do you, leprous in soul, refuse to be removed from the sacred altars by the judgment of so many holy Fathers? If he, having laid aside the authority of royal dignity, was not ashamed to live in a private house until his death, why are you ashamed to descend from the summit of priestly office, so that, shut away in the tomb of penance, you may strive to count yourself among the living as though dead?

And, to return to that mystical history of Joab: if you yourself have fallen by the sword, how will you raise another through priestly grace? If, because your merits demand it, you are in need of bread—that is, if you have been separated from Christ’s body—how will you be able to satisfy another with the provisions of the heavenly table? If you have been struck on the forehead by Uzziah’s leprosy—that is, if you are dishonored on your face by the mark of infamy—how will you be able to cleanse another from the flood of the crime he has committed?

[Col. 0180A]

Let swollen pride, therefore, be ashamed, and let it not vainly seek to raise itself above one whom the burden of his own guilt weighs down considerably beneath it. Let it learn to weigh its evils by careful reflection; let it learn humbly to restrain itself within the limits of its own measure, lest, while arrogantly usurping what it can in no way attain, it utterly lose even what true humility might have been able to hope for.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the office of an unworthy priest is the ruin of the people.

What is it, I ask, O damnable men of the flesh, that you pursue the summit of ecclesiastical dignity with such ardor for ambition?
