What is it that, with such desire for your own destruction, you attempt to entangle God’s people in the bonds of your ruin? Is it not enough that you plunge yourselves into the lofty precipices of wickedness, unless you also involve others in the danger of your downfall?

[Col. 0180B]

For if someone should perhaps come to us, asking us to intercede for him with some powerful man who was angry with him but unknown to us, we immediately reply: “We cannot come to intercede, because we have no acquaintance with him through friendship.” If, then, a human being is ashamed to act as an intercessor with another human being of whom he has no confidence, with what state of mind does someone seize the place of intercession before God on behalf of the people when he does not know, by the merit of his life, that he is familiar with God’s grace? Or how can he ask forgiveness from Him for others when he does not know whether He is reconciled to himself?

There is still another matter in this connection that must be feared even more anxiously: lest the one who is believed able to appease anger should himself deserve that anger through his own guilt. For we all clearly know that when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things.

[Col. 0180C]

Whoever, therefore, is still bound by earthly desires must beware lest, by more gravely kindling the anger of the strict Judge, he become—while delighting in the place of glory—the cause of ruin to his subjects. Let each person carefully measure himself, therefore, lest he dare to assume the place of priestly office while a condemnable vice still reigns within him; lest the one whom his own crime corrupts desire to become an intercessor for the faults of others.

Spare yourselves, then, spare yourselves, and fear inextinguishably kindling God’s fury against you. Do not further irritate by your very prayers the One whom you openly offend through your wicked conduct. Content with your own ruin, beware of becoming liable also for another’s destruction, so that, the more temperately you now fall through sin, the more easily you may one day rise again, by God’s mercy, when the hand of penance is extended.

[Col. 0181A] 169

## CHAPTER XX. That God does not wish to receive sacrifice from the hands of the unclean.

But if almighty God disdains to receive sacrifice from your hands, who are you to presume importunately to thrust it upon Him when He does not wish it? “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord” (Proverbs 21).

But you who are angry with me and disdain to listen to me as I write, listen at least to Him speaking to you through the prophetic mouth. Listen, I say, to Him preaching, thundering, rejecting your sacrifices, and publicly protesting against your services.

[Col. 0181B]

For the eminent prophet Isaiah—or rather, the Holy Spirit through Isaiah—says:

> “Hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah. What are your many sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened animals; and I have not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you come to appear before me, who has asked these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not offer sacrifice any longer in vain; incense is an abomination to me. New moons, Sabbaths, and other festivals I will not endure; your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me; I am weary of bearing them. And when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear. For your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1).

[Col. 0181C]

You perceive, therefore, that although the sentence of divine correction strikes all the evils of vice indiscriminately, it descends with particular force upon the princes of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah. Thus, if someone perhaps hesitates to believe human testimony concerning how deadly this vice is, the obstinacy of those who dispute may at least yield to the testimony of God.

But if someone objects to us that the prophetic speech continues, “Your hands are full of blood,” on the grounds that in the oracle of divine revelation this should be understood to mean homicide rather than the uncleanness of the flesh, let him know that in divine language all sins are called blood, as David testifies when he says:

> “Deliver me from blood-guilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Psalm 50).

[Col. 0181D]

Nevertheless, if we carefully examine the nature of this vice and recall the statements of the natural philosophers, we find that the emission of semen is produced from the origin of blood. For just as the agitation of winds turns seawater into foam, so the handling of the genitals arouses blood into seminal fluid.

It is not, therefore, rightly thought contrary to sound understanding if the statement, “Your hands are full of blood,” seems to have been spoken concerning the plague of uncleanness. And perhaps this was also why that vengeance against Joab proceeded from no other fault than that of shed blood: so that the one who had willingly shed another’s blood would be struck with a fitting punishment if he unwillingly endured the flowing of his own blood.

[Col. 0182A] 170

But since, by prolonged discussion, we have reached the point at which we have clearly demonstrated both that the Lord Himself rejects the sacrifices of the unclean and that He solemnly forbids them, why should we sinners be surprised if such men despise us when we admonish them? If we see the command of the divine voice treated as worthless by the hardened heart of the reprobate, what wonder is it if we are not believed, who are made of earth?

## CHAPTER XXI. That no offering of holiness is received by God if it is defiled by the filth of uncleanness.

Therefore, he who despises the venerable councils of the holy Fathers, who scorns the precepts of the apostles and of apostolic men, who does not fear to disregard the decrees of canonical sanction, and who makes light of the command of divine authority itself must at least be admonished to place the day of his calling before his eyes and to have no doubt that, the more gravely he sins, the more harshly he will be judged.

[Col. 0182B]

As it is said under the figure of Babylon by the angel:

> “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Revelation 18).

He must be admonished to consider that, as long as he does not cease to suffer from the disease of this vice, even if he is seen to do something good, he nevertheless does not deserve to receive a reward. No religious observance, no mortification, no perfection of life is judged worthy in the eyes of the heavenly Judge if it is defiled by the filth of such shameful uncleanness.

[Col. 0182C]

To prove that what is said is true, let the testimony of the venerable Bede be brought forward:

> “He who gives alms in such a way that he does not abandon his guilt does not redeem his soul, which he does not restrain from vices.”

That man proves this by his deed: an eremite who, together with a certain companion, had served God through many virtues received this thought from the devil: whenever he was stirred by lust, he should discharge his semen by rubbing his genital member, as though he were throwing phlegm from his nostrils. For this reason, at his death, he was handed over to demons, in the sight of his companion.

Then the same companion, unaware of his guilt but recalling his exercises in virtue, nearly despaired and said: “Oh, who can be saved? How did this man perish?” Immediately an angel standing nearby said to him: “Do not be troubled. Although this man did many things, he defiled them all through that vice which the Apostle calls ‘uncleanness’” (Romans 1).

[Col. 0182D]

## CHAPTER XXII. That all four modes enumerated above are against nature.

Let no one, therefore, flatter himself on the ground that he has not fallen with another, if he flows by himself through the contaminations of this lustful enticement. For this unhappy eremite, who was handed over to demons at the point of death, is shown to have polluted not another but to have destroyed himself through uncleanness.

Just as different branches emerge from a single vine-stump, so from one Sodomitic uncleanness, as from a most poisonous root, arise those four little branches that we enumerated above. Thus, whoever plucks the poisonous cluster from any one of them immediately dies indiscriminately, infected by its venom.

[Col. 0183A]

“For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them” (Deuteronomy 32).

For this serpent, which we are striving to break with the staff of our discussion, has four heads; and with whichever head’s tooth it bites, it immediately pours the entire venom of its wickedness into its victim.

Whether, then, someone pollutes himself or another in any manner—although the proper distinction must be maintained—he is nevertheless undoubtedly convicted of having committed the Sodomitic crime. For it is not read that the inhabitants of Sodom corrupted only others through the completed act; rather, it must be believed that, according to the impulse of unbridled lust, they practiced shameful acts in various ways, either against themselves or against others.

[Col. 0183B]

Certainly, if any place for pardon were granted in the downfall caused by this vice, to whom would remission more properly be owed than to that eremite who sinned through ignorance? He fell through the inexperience of simplicity; he believed that this was permitted to him, as though it were the obligation of a natural function.

Let the wretched learn, let them learn to restrain themselves from the plague of so detestable a vice; let them manfully tame the wantonness that panders to lust; let them repress the provocations of the flesh’s insolence; let them fear from the depths of their being the terrible judgment of divine severity, always recalling to mind that sentence of apostolic warning which says:

> “It is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10).

Let them also fearfully remember what the prophet thunders threateningly:

[Col. 0183C]

> “For in the fire of the Lord’s jealousy the whole earth shall be devoured, and by his sword all flesh” (Zephaniah 1).

If carnal people are to be devoured by the divine sword, why do they now love the flesh so damnably? Why do they yield so weakly to the pleasures of the flesh? This is surely the sword which the Lord threatens sinners through Moses, saying:

> “I will sharpen my sword like lightning” (Deuteronomy 32).

And again:

> “My sword,” he says, “shall devour flesh” (ibid.),

that is, “My fury shall swallow up those who live in the pleasure of the flesh.”

For just as those who struggle against the monsters of vice are supported by the help of heavenly virtue, so, conversely, those devoted to the uncleanness of the flesh are reserved solely for the judgment of divine vengeance. Hence Peter also says:

[Col. 0183D]

> “The Lord knows how to rescue the devout from trial, but to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment—especially those who walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness” (2 Peter 2).

Rebuking them elsewhere, he says:

> “They consider the pleasures of the day to be defilements and stains; they revel in their pleasures, overflowing with them, carousing with you at their feasts, having eyes full of adultery and never-ending sin” (ibid.).

Nor should those who have been placed in sacred orders glory if they live abominably. For the higher they stand and are conspicuous, the more deeply they lie when they fall. And just as they ought now to precede others in a life of holy conduct, so later they are compelled to endure more atrocious punishments. For, in Peter’s words:

[Col. 0184A] 172

> “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but, drawing them down with the cords of hell, he handed them over to Tartarus to be punished and reserved for judgment. And, reducing the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, he condemned them to destruction as an example of those who would act impiously” (2 Peter 2).

Why, after the blessed Apostle has recounted the precipice of the devil’s condemnation, does he immediately turn also to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, unless to show plainly that those who are now handed over to the vice of uncleanness are likewise to be condemned to eternal vengeance together with unclean spirits? And that those whom the heat of Sodomitic lust now torments will later burn with the flame of everlasting fire together with the author of all iniquity?

The apostle Jude also most aptly agrees with this sentence, saying:

[Col. 0184B]

> “The angels who did not preserve their own position of authority but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day. Likewise, Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, which in the same manner indulged in fornication and went after other flesh, are set forth as an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire” (Jude 1).

It is therefore clear that, just as the angels who did not preserve their own position deserved the punishment of Tartarean darkness, so those who fall from the dignity of sacred order into the abyss of carnal vice are rightly cast into the pit of everlasting condemnation.

And, to conclude everything briefly, whoever has defiled himself by contagion with the pollution of shameful conduct in any of the ways we distinguished above, unless he has been cleansed by the satisfaction of fruitful penance, will never be able to possess God’s grace, will never be worthy of Christ’s body and blood, and will never enter the threshold of the heavenly homeland. The Apostle John plainly declares this in the Apocalypse. Speaking of the glory of the heavenly kingdom, he adds:

[Col. 0184C]

> “Nothing defiled shall enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination” (Revelation 21).

## CHAPTER XXIII. An exhortation to a man fallen into sin, that he should rise again.

Rise, rise, I beg you; awaken, O man, who are weighed down by the slumber of miserable pleasure. Come back to life at last, you who have fallen before your enemies by a deadly sword.

The Apostle Paul is here. Hear him shouting, knocking, shaking, and calling out to you in clear and powerful words:

[Col. 0184D]

> “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will raise you up” (Ephesians 5).

When you hear Christ proclaimed as the resurrection, why do you despair of your own resurrection? Hear from his own mouth:

> “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even if he has died, will live” (John 11).

If Life, which gives life, seeks to raise you up, why do you continue to endure lying in your death? Beware, beware, therefore, lest the abyss of despair swallow you. Let your mind confidently presume upon divine mercy, lest it harden impenitently because of the greatness of its crime.

For to despair is not the part of sinners, but of the impious; nor does the greatness of crimes bring the soul into despair, but impiety. If the devil had such power that he could plunge you into the depths of this vice, how much more will the power of Christ be able to recall you to the summit from which you have fallen?

> “Shall not he who has fallen rise again?” (Psalm 40).

The ass of your flesh has fallen into the mud beneath its burden. There is a goad of penance to prick it; there is a hand of the spirit to pull it out manfully.

That exceedingly strong Samson, because he revealed the secret of his heart to a woman who wickedly flattered him, not only lost the seven locks by which his strength was sustained, but, having been made booty for the Philistines, also lost his eyes. Later, when his hair had begun to grow again, he humbly sought the help of the Lord his God, overturned the temple of Dagon, and killed a much greater multitude of enemies than before (Judges 16).

[Col. 0185A] 173

If, then, your shameless flesh deceived you by persuading you to softness; if it took away the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; if it extinguished not the light of your forehead but of your heart, do not lose courage, do not despair completely. Gather your strength again; shake yourself manfully; dare to attempt great things; and thus, through God’s mercy, you will be able to triumph over your enemies.

Certainly the Philistines were able to shave Samson’s hair, but not to pull it out. Likewise, although wicked spirits may for a time have driven the charisms of the Holy Spirit from you, they can in no way irrecoverably deny you the remedy of divine reconciliation.

How, I ask, can you despair of the Lord’s most abundant mercy, when he even reproved Pharaoh because, after sinning, he did not flee to the remedy of penance? Hear what he says:

> “I have broken the arms of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he did not plead that healing might be given him and strength restored to him to grasp the sword” (1 Kings 21).

What shall I say of King Ahab of Israel? After he had made idols and wickedly slaughtered Naboth the Jezreelite, he was finally humbled in part and therefore also received mercy in part.

For Scripture testifies that after he had received the terror of the divine threat, he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed. What followed?

> “The word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: ‘Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days’” (ibid.).

Therefore, if the penance of that man was not despised, although he is known not to have persevered fully, why should you distrust the abundance of divine compassion if you strive to persevere without tiring?

[Col. 0185B]

Establish for yourself, moreover, a continual struggle against the flesh. Always stand armed against the importunate madness of lust. If the flame of luxury burns in your bones, let the memory of the everlasting fire immediately extinguish it. If the cunning tempter places before you the slippery appearance of the flesh, let your mind at once direct its gaze toward the tombs of the dead and carefully consider what is pleasant to the touch or delightful to the sight that can be found there.

Consider, then, that the poison which now stinks unbearably, the corruption which breeds and feeds worms, and whatever dust or dry ash you see lying there were once joyful flesh, which in its freshness was subject to such passions.

[Col. 0185C]

Finally, let rigid sinews, bare teeth, the scattered structure of bones and joints, and the composition of all the limbs, monstrously dissolved, be weighed. Thus, thus, let the monster of a shapeless and confused image draw the delusion out of the human heart.

Consider, therefore, how dangerous is the exchange brought about by this reversal: for a momentary pleasure, by which semen is discharged in an instant, the punishment that follows does not end through the passage of thousands of years. Reflect how miserable it is that, because of one member whose pleasure is now satisfied, the entire body together with the soul is later tortured forever in the most atrocious fires.

[Col. 0186A]

Drive away impending evils with these and similar impenetrable shields of thought; erase past evils through penance. Let fasting break the pride of the flesh; let the mind, nourished by the food of constant prayer, grow strong.

In this way, therefore, let the spirit’s ruler restrain the subject flesh with the bridle of discipline and strive each day to hasten toward the heavenly Jerusalem by steps of fervent desire.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That contemplating the rewards of chastity is greatly beneficial for taming lust.

It is also worthwhile continually to look upon the rewards promised to chastity. Moved by their sweetness, you may pass with the free step of faith over whatever the cunning of the crafty tempter sets before you.

For if the happiness to which one does not attain without passing through difficulty is kept in view, what is endured in passing becomes light; and the hired laborer lessens the weariness of his work while eagerly awaiting the payment owed for his labor.

[Col. 0186B]

Consider, then, what is said through the prophet concerning the soldiers of chastity:

> “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56).

For eunuchs are those who restrain the unruly impulses of the flesh and cut off from themselves the accomplishment of wicked action.

Many of those who serve the enticement of carnal pleasure desire to leave behind them the memory of their name through the succession of offspring. They desire this with the whole affection of their minds because they do not at all consider themselves completely dead to this world if they extend the title of their name through the surviving growth of their descendants.

[Col. 0186C]

But celibates receive this same gift far more clearly and far more happily—the gift toward which those who have offspring, inflamed by the heat of such ardent ambition, strive—because their memory lives forever with Him who passes through no temporal condition but remains in eternity.

A name better than sons and daughters is therefore promised to eunuchs by the divine voice, because the memory of a name which the posterity of children could have extended for a brief span of time, they deserve to possess forever, without any obstacle of forgetfulness:

> “For the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psalm 121).

And again, in the Apocalypse, it is said through John:

> “They will walk with me in white, because they are worthy, and I will not erase their names from the book of life” (Revelation 3).

There it is said again:

[Col. 0187A]

> “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14);

and they sing a song that no one can sing except those 144,000.

Virgins sing a unique song to the Lamb because, with him, they rejoice forever before all the faithful, even in the incorruption of the flesh. Others who are righteous cannot sing it, although, placed in the same blessedness, they deserve to hear it. For through charity they gladly behold their exalted state, but they do not rise to their rewards.

Therefore, one must consider and turn over continually in one’s mind with every effort what a dignity and excellence it is to become greatest there where the highest happiness consists in being even last; to ascend the heights of privilege there where it is supremely blessed to preserve the laws of the homeland’s equity. Indeed, just as Truth testifies that “not all can receive this word in this age” (Matthew 19), so not all attain in the future to that glory of distinguished reward.

[Col. 0187B]

Consider these things, dearest brother—whoever you are—and many others of the same kind in the secret places of your mind. Hasten with all your strength to keep your flesh free from every plague of lust, so that, according to the teaching of the Apostle, you may know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thessalonians 4).

If you are still standing, beware of the precipice. But if you have fallen, confidently extend your hand to the hook of penance, which is everywhere at hand. Thus, although you were unable to live with Abraham far from Sodom, you may at least migrate with Lot when the destruction of the neighboring fire is already imminent.

Although you were not able to enter the harbor safely in the ship, let it at least be enough that you have escaped the shipwreck after passing through the waves. And although you did not deserve to reach the shelter of the shore without loss, may you rejoice, cast upon the sands after danger, to sing with a cheerful voice that proclamation of blessed Jonah:

[Col. 0187C]

> “All your breakers and your waves have passed over me; and I said: ‘I am cast away from the sight of your eyes’; yet I shall again see your holy temple” (Jonah 2).

## CHAPTER XXV. Where the author reasonably excuses himself.

But if this little book should come into the hands of anyone whose conscience does not support him and who perhaps dislikes what has been set forth above, accusing me as a betrayer and informer against a brother’s crime, let him know that I seek the favor of the inner Judge with the full attention of my purpose and that I do not fear the hatred of the wicked or the tongues of detractors.

[Col. 0187D]

I would rather be thrown innocent into a pit with Joseph, who accused his brothers before their father of a most serious crime (Genesis 37), than be punished with Eli by the vengeance of divine fury, because he saw his sons’ evils and remained silent (1 Samuel 2, 4).

For when the divine voice terribly threatens through the mouth of the prophet, saying:

> “If you see your brother acting wickedly and do not rebuke him, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3),

who am I to see such a deadly crime growing within the sacred order and, like a murderer of another’s soul, dare to await an accounting from divine severity while preserving the censorship of silence? And why should I begin to become liable for the guilt of one whose author I certainly was not?

[Col. 0188A]

And when Scripture says:

> “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48),

you urge me to place the sword of my tongue in the sheath of silence, where it may perish by itself as it contracts the rust of offense and may benefit no one because it does not pierce the faults of those who live wickedly.

To withhold the sword from blood is to restrain the word of correction from striking carnal life. Concerning this sword it is said again:

> “From his mouth came a sword sharp on both sides” (Revelation 1).

For how do I love my neighbor as myself if, seeing a wound by which I do not doubt that he is cruelly dying, I negligently allow it to rage in his heart? Seeing wounds of the mind, why should I neglect to heal them by cutting words?

[Col. 0188B]

The eminent preacher does not teach me this. He believed himself cleansed from the blood of his neighbors precisely because he did not spare their vices when they needed to be struck. For he says:

> “I testify to you today that I am innocent of the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20).

John did not instruct me otherwise. To him, by an angelic admonition, it is commanded:

> “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22).

That is, whoever receives the inner voice should also, by crying out, draw others there to which he himself is being drawn, lest, even when called, he find the doors closed if he approaches the one calling empty-handed.

Certainly, if you consider it right to rebuke me for rebuking others—or, so to speak, to accuse me of presumptuous accusation—why do you not rebuke Jerome, who disputes so mordantly against the various sects of heretics? Why do you not tear apart Ambrose, who preaches publicly against the Arians? Why not Augustine, who attacks the Manichaeans and Donatists with such stern controversy?

[Col. 0188C]

You say to me: “They were right, because they spoke against heretics and blasphemers; but you do not fear attacking Christians.”

To this I reply briefly: just as they endeavored to bring those who had gone out and were already wandering back to the fold, so it is also the intention of our work to prevent those who are still within from going out, however they may stand among us.

They said:

> “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

And we say: “They are indeed with us, but badly. Let us strive, if possible, that from now on they may be well with us.”

[Col. 0188D]

We add this also: if blasphemy is the worst of crimes, I do not know in what respect sodomy is better. The former makes a person go astray; the latter destroys him. The former divides the soul from God; the latter joins it to the devil. The former expels one from paradise; the latter plunges one into Tartarus. The former blinds the eyes of the mind; the latter hurls one into the abyss of ruin.

And if we strive to investigate carefully which of the two crimes weighs more heavily on the scales of divine judgment, a thorough examination of sacred Scripture teaches this more fully. There we find that the children of Israel, who blasphemed God and worshiped idols, were led into captivity, whereas the Sodomites were devoured by heavenly fire and sulfur (Genesis 19).

[Col. 0189A]

I did not put forward the holy teachers for the purpose of presumptuously comparing a smoking log with the stars. Indeed, I scarcely dare to mention such distinguished men with an unworthy mouth without offense. Rather, I say this: what they did by correcting and shaming vices, they also taught their successors to do. And if, in their time, this plague had arisen with such great freedom of shamelessness, we confidently believe that lengthy volumes of books against it would be seen written today.

Let no one, then, judge me while I dispute against a deadly vice. I seek not disgrace but rather the advancement of my brother’s salvation, lest, while persecuting the one who rebukes, he appear to favor the delinquent.

[Col. 0189B]

But, to use the words of Moses:

> “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me” (Exodus 32).

That is, let whoever recognizes himself as a soldier of God fervently gird himself to confound this vice; let him not cease to attack it with all his strength. Wherever it is found, let him strive to pierce and slaughter it with the sharpest darts of his words, so that, while the captor is surrounded by a dense battle line of wedges, the captive may be released from the bonds by which he had been enslaved. And while everyone’s united voice cries out in harmony against the tyrant, let the one who was being dragged away immediately be ashamed to become the prey of the raging monster. Let him who does not hesitate to be carried toward death when the testimony of many confirms it, return to himself and not delay in returning to life.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Where the discourse turns back to the lord pope.

[Col. 0189C]

Now, most blessed pope, at the end of this little work we turn back to you; to you we recall the point of this pen. To the one toward whom the beginning of the work is directed, its completed conclusion should rightly be brought.

We therefore ask and humbly implore that your Clemency—if it is permissible to say so—carefully examine the decrees of the sacred canons, which are nevertheless already very well known to you; that you summon spiritual and prudent men for consultation concerning this necessary investigation; and that you respond to us concerning these chapters in such a way as to remove every scruple of doubt from our breast.

[Col. 0189D]

We do not presume to say this because we are unaware that, with God as its author, your own profound expertise alone would suffice for this matter. Rather, when the testimony of sacred authority is brought forward, and when the matter is conducted with the agreement and judgment of many, let the complaint of perverse men—which perhaps might otherwise not blush to mutter in opposition—be silenced.

[Col. 0190A]

For a complaint is not easily brought against what has been established by the judgment of many. Often, however, a decision drawn by one person from the equity of the law is regarded by others as a prejudice.

178

Having therefore carefully examined the four varieties of this vice that we enumerated above, may your Blessedness graciously instruct me by a decretal letter:

- which of them makes a person liable to be irrevocably removed from the ecclesiastical order;
- to which prelate, through consideration of discretion, this office may mercifully be permitted;
- in which of the ways mentioned above, and with what degrees of culpability, each fallen person may be permitted to remain in ecclesiastical dignity;
- and in what manner, and with what degrees of culpability, someone who has been defiled must be compelled to cease from that office in the stated necessity.

[Col. 0190B]

Thus, from what is directed to one person, many who suffer from the same ignorance may be instructed, so that the lamp of your authority may dispel the darkness of our uncertainty and, so to speak, the sword of the apostolic see may tear out from the field of the wavering conscience the seed and root of every error.

May almighty God grant, most reverend Father, that during the time of your apostolate this monster of a vice may utterly perish and that the condition of the prostrate Church may everywhere rise again to the rights of its former strength.

## SCHOLIA

[Col. 0190C]

The command of the Law is that when someone is covered with leprosy, he should be shown to the priests. But the matter is shown not to priests but rather to a leper when an unclean person confesses to an unclean person the common wickedness they have committed together.

Concerning what blessed Damian writes in this little work, his intention should be considered rather than his words. For he does not mean that the confession of someone who confesses to a priest who was his accomplice is invalid because of a defect of authority, if that priest possesses a legitimate title and jurisdiction. Rather, he means that such a confession is fruitless and in a certain sense deceptive, because the penitent neither experiences the blush of shame nor can be stirred to contrition by one whose depraved example is present before his eyes.

The author weighs all these matters, as can be seen in the text, where he also says: “A confession made to a priest who was an accomplice is not made with that severity because of the easy forgiveness of the one who grants penance.”

[Col. 0190D]

Therefore, although all the Summists hold that such a confession is valid, they nevertheless do not approve of its being made except in a case of extreme necessity. So judge the Gloss on *Omnes*, canon 30, question 1; Sylvester, s.v. *Confessio*, 1, no. 17; and others.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0191]

## 179–180. EIGHTH OPUSCULUM. ON THE DEGREES OF KINSHIP. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CESENA, AND THE LORD ARCHDEACON OF RAVENNA

With a short dissertation on the same subject delivered by the author elsewhere.

### ARGUMENT

[Col. 0191] He attacks the experts in civil law who reckoned the degrees of blood relationship through the descending collateral line at excessive length, although canon law and divine law establish them at the fourth generation. Imbued with this faulty opinion, they did not hesitate to assert that marriage could lawfully be contracted between great-grandchildren. He demonstrates at length how absurd this is and how contrary it is to the tradition of the Catholic Church, and refutes the opponents’ position with numerous arguments.

[Col. 0191A] To the most reverend men in Christ, John, bishop of Cesena, and the lord archdeacon of Ravenna, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of a worthy obedience.

As you know, I recently visited Ravenna, and soon discovered that it was wavering, disturbed by the scruple of a perilous error. There was extensive debate concerning the degrees of consanguinity; and matters had already progressed so far that the wise men of the city, meeting together in response to inquiries from the Florentine couriers, had jointly replied that the seventh generation, fixed by canonical authority, ought to be understood in such a way that, after counting four degrees on one side of the family and three on the other, marriage might by law already be contracted.

To establish the absurdity of this backward argument, they also brought forward as evidence [Col. 0191B] what Justinian inserts in his Institutes (Book I, title *On Marriage*, paragraph “Between Them”): “But no one may marry his brother’s or sister’s granddaughter, although she is in the fourth degree.” From these words they drew certain misleading arguments, saying: “If my brother’s granddaughter is already separated from me by the fourth degree, consequently my son is five degrees, my grandson likewise six, and my great-grandson seven degrees distant from her.”

I resisted those who dogmatized in this way on the basis of bare words, and, as far as circumstances permitted, I wore down the emerging heresy, so to speak, with testimonies of canonical authority. But you were not content with this and decided that what I had expressed orally ought to be committed to writing, so that I might answer, with a simple summary, not merely a few but all who were wavering in this error [Col. 0191C].

## ON THE DEGREES OF KINSHIP

### CHAPTER I. That where there is a law of hereditary succession, there are no marital rights

[Col. 0191]

I gladly obey you in this matter as in everything else. Yet I see nothing at all that needs to be added to this discussion except what I recognize as having been handed down by our predecessors. They have dealt with the matter so thoroughly on every side that, if humility lends us sight, nothing further need be sought concerning it.

For what could be clearer than what Pope Calixtus asserted when he said: “We call those persons blood relatives whom divine and secular laws call blood relatives, who take an inheritance and cannot be rejected” [Col. 0192A].

Let those who judge in tribunals, who settle legal disputes, and who devote themselves to examining the decrees of the laws be asked: if nearer relatives are absent, are agnates up to the seventh degree not admitted either to an inheritance or to guardianship? But if by the right of consanguinity you are admitted to someone’s inheritance, how can you, as though a stranger, obtain his marriage?

Why, moreover, is such an elaborate diagram drawn among the sacred canons, terminating not only above and below but also on either side in six degrees, if—as they assert—the seventh generation is completed by counting three persons on one side and four on the other? The makers of the canons did not need to take precautions lest a grandmother’s tritavus—whose trineptis she is, of course—or the son of a trineptis, whose tritavus he himself is, should be joined in marriage. Nature itself does not permit the highest person to be joined to the lowest, even if the union had not been prohibited.

But when the holy teachers count the line of human consanguinity through so many degrees, they strive to prevent persons descending collaterally from joining one another up to the prescribed limit. Otherwise, once one reaches the great-granddaughter, who is the fourth person from the son on this side, and the great-grandson, who is the third on the other, why would one descend any further to count additional persons, if they were known to have no relationship to one another by any kinship?

Moreover, it would be burdensome and superfluous, in describing the degrees of genealogy [Col. 0192C], to introduce from outside persons who have no successive relationship to one another. But since we see that the lower degrees are named from the same person from whom the higher degrees receive their relational names—namely, that just as these are his son, grandson, great-grandson, and great-great-grandson, so those too are his great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-grandson—just as we can distinguish those born from one ancestor, so we judge it impious to separate as unrelated those born from one ancestor on either side.

For example, just as a trinepos (a sixth-generation descendant) cannot be called a stranger to the father who is his tritavus, so he is not found to be unrelated to the trineptis who descends on the opposite side from the same ancestor.

### CHAPTER II. That consanguinity, like the human body, terminates in six degrees

[Col. 0193A]

All these degrees are referred to an ancient origin in such a way that those who proceed from it do not abandon the relationship newly formed with one another. But, so that the matter may not extend to infinity, the holy teachers establish a suitable boundary: wherever the terms of succession can be found, kinship likewise continues.

Hence the custom arose of depicting the description of consanguinity under the figure of the human body. Just as the human body consists of six joints below and an equal number above—which are themselves also said to be lateral—so that the one in the middle is even called +*sexus*, as though “sixth”—something that can readily be observed from the second fingers of the hands or feet [Col. 0193B], so likewise that figure of human succession terminates in six degrees above and below, including those who come from the side, although, as a precautionary concession, a seventh generation is subsequently counted among them.

Whoever therefore wishes to sever the rights of kinship between those who descend from one person on both sides, even to the final degree, must also admit that the right limbs of a human being have no relationship at all to the limbs of the left side. To make what we are saying clearer, anyone who judges that a great-great-great-grandson is released from the bond of kinship with the great-great-great-granddaughter situated on the opposite side must maintain that there is no connection between the fingers with which I write and the joints of my left hand [Col. 0193C].

But the Apostle protests against this perverse assertion when he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, although they are many, are one body” (1 Corinthians 12). Therefore, just as many members come together through their participation in the whole, so that they are rightly called one body, so also the different persons who jointly proceed from one ancestor are without doubt one lineage.

### CHAPTER III. Why God created only one human being in the beginning

The law of marriage is therefore arranged under ecclesiastical discipline with such great skill, so that the bond of mutual charity may necessarily be maintained among human beings [Col. 0193D]—namely, so that, for as long as the order of succession continues, a reciprocal love of neighbor may be supplied by the very relationship of kinship.

But when the terms fail and the category of kinship comes to an end, the law of marriage immediately intervenes. It calls back, as though fleeing, the person who is moving farther away, and renews among new people the rights of the ancient affection.

Nor is it surprising that provision is made for charity in the begetting of human beings, since God, the creator of all things, appears to have provided for the same thing in creating them. For when, at the very beginning of nascent nature, he created not one but many of each of the other living creatures, as it is written: “God created the great sea creatures” (Genesis 1); and shortly afterward: “Let the earth bring forth cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds” [Col. 0194A] (Genesis 2), then he created not many human beings but one, and from his side he took a rib from which the woman was to be formed.

Why, when almighty God created several of the other living creatures, was he content to make one human being? From him, as though the potter lacked material, did he wish also to propagate the female sex? Was it not so that he might commend charity to human beings and bind them together in the unity of brotherly love, so that, corresponding to their own origin, they might in no way differ in mind when they were shown to be one body?

Hence Paul also says: “One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4).

[Col. 0194B]

Yet when the relationship of kinship grows distant, the flame of love grows cold through the fault of human perversity, as though the fuel of love had been removed. To restore the spark of mutual charity, the bonds of marriage subsequently come to its aid.

Indeed, because the time of the world unfolds through six ages and the life of humanity comes to an end, the very power of nature provides that brotherly love should be perceived within the human family up to the sixth degree of kinship and should, in a certain sense, emit among them the fragrance of natural fellowship. But when the hand of consanguinity, which had been drawing someone toward itself, fails, the hook of marriage appears at once to call back the fugitive.

### CHAPTER IV. That those who possess the right of inheritance also possess kinship by blood

[Col. 0194C]

To say nothing of the rest, I am at least astonished that experts in law could have become so foolish that, in calculating the degrees, they seem unable to see the figure set before their eyes [183]. While they make the fourth degree of a lineage the eighth, they fail to notice what their own laws also determine on this point.

But to make what we are saying reach its conclusion more easily, let us compare the sacred canons with the secular laws themselves. The Council of Meaux has this provision: “Concerning affinity of blood, it has been decided that it is to be observed through the degrees of kinship up to the seventh generation.”

Inheritance of property is likewise established by legal definitions so as to extend the succession of heirs up to the seventh degree. For they would not succeed unless they were entitled to do so by descent from the kinship.

[Col. 0194D]

According to this decree of the synodal judgment, then, whoever possesses the right of inheritance also possesses closeness of blood. For, as has been said, they would not succeed to an inheritance unless they belonged to the line of kinship.

But perhaps someone will reply that what these words command to be observed for seven generations has nothing to do with those who come from the side, but rather applies to those who descend in a direct line from the highest ancestor.

Yet if Scripture were to set a limit for such persons either for succession or for marriage, it would confine an infinite matter within narrow boundaries, as Justinian testifies when he says (Institutes, Book I, title *On Marriage*, paragraph “Therefore Not All”): “Marriage cannot be contracted between persons who occupy among one another the place of parents or children, such as between a father and daughter, a grandmother and grandson, and so on without limit” [Col. 0195A].

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that we must observe seven generations among those persons who come from opposite sides.

### CHAPTER V. He attacks the experts in law and confronts them with their own laws

Let us now inquire: at what degree can those descended from two full brothers succeed one another by inheritance?

I address you again, judges; I challenge you concerning your own law. I ask you, experts in law who examine legal rights and plead cases: Is the person who descends in the sixth place from one brother legally called to the inheritance of the person who proceeds in the sixth generation from the other [Col. 0195B]?

Certainly it cannot be denied that, if one of the two whom we have proposed dies intestate, and no nearer person exists, the other is admitted by law to his inheritance. And, so that you yourselves may approve what we are saying, let us again produce testimony from your own Institutes.

For it is said (Book III, title *On the Succession of Legitimate Agnates*, paragraph “Moreover”): “Among males, by the right of agnation, inheritance is taken both from one another, even if they are in the most distant degree.” Shortly afterward: “Males, moreover, are admitted to the inheritances of those women, even if they are in the most distant degree.”

If, therefore, inheritance is taken both from one another—not merely below or above—in the most distant degree, and if, as has been stated, no one can succeed an intestate person unless it is established that he belongs to the same lineage [Col. 0195C], it is utterly backward and confused to say that those who proceed in the fourth degree from full brothers may already contract marriage with one another, while those who come after them have not yet lost the right of hereditary succession.

One right removes the other: namely, whoever may succeed you by the right of inheritance, you may not join to yourself in a marital bond; and, conversely, wherever the right of marriage applies, the designation of heir ceases.

But perhaps you will say that “the most distant degree” may reasonably also be understood as the fourth, which among you is the eighth. Therefore, I ask you, return to your books and recall whether the lineage is really confined to this boundary, since perhaps the matter has slipped your memory.

For the same Justinian says above (Book III, title *On the Succession of Cognates*, paragraph “At This Point”): “At this point we must also necessarily be reminded that, by the right of agnation, someone is admitted to an inheritance even if he is in the tenth degree” [Col. 0195D].

Since it is therefore clear that no one is admitted to the inheritance of an intestate person unless he is joined to him by the right of kinship, how can the tenth-degree relative succeed to the inheritance by the right of agnation, while, according to you, the fourth degree may lawfully contract marriage with such persons—so that the tenth is regarded as a relative and the fourth appears to be a stranger?

And if it is already established by what has been set out above that those who are found in the fourth degree, both from one side and the other, are cognates and relatives, let us also hear what the Roman council judged concerning kinship: “If anyone takes in marriage a person from his own kinship, or one whom his relative had taken, let him be anathema.”

### CHAPTER VI. That generations proceeding on both sides from one ancestor ought to be counted simply

[Col. 0196A]

These few points ought already to have been sufficient, if those with whom I am dealing—being accustomed to litigation—knew how to raise only a few matters for controversy.

Let us therefore recall what I reported above, namely, that our legal advocates objected to us from their own laws: that no one may marry his brother’s or sister’s niece, although she is in the fourth degree.

[Col. 0196B]

When they repeatedly used these words to establish their own arguments, and then, by reasoning, assumption, and inference, constructed many kinds of sophistical arguments, I replied, being pressed into a corner, with the answer that occurred to me in that situation:

“This reckoning, which places the granddaughter of a brother or sister at the fourth degree from her paternal or maternal great-uncle, but counts the son of that paternal or maternal uncle, as you say, as fifth; his grandson as sixth; and his great-grandson as seventh from the granddaughter mentioned above, may indeed be found in the secular laws, since you insist so strongly upon it, but the sacred canons do not admit it.

“In truth, divine law does not count twice the lines of descent that proceed through different branches from one founder of a lineage. Although several descendants flow forth here and there, when they are considered generally from one ancestor, they are nevertheless enclosed within one generation [Col. 0196C].”

But since we are contending with the polished wit of the experts in law, let us also bring forward an expert in law as a witness for our side: Moses—not, certainly, a jurist to be rejected, but one who was highly learned both in drawing up judicial decisions and in promulgating laws themselves.

From the teacher we learn what opinion to hold concerning a disciple of no contemptible character. Let him therefore come and settle between us the dispute that concerns generation. For he says of Joseph: “And he lived one hundred years”; then he adds: “And Ephraim saw children to the third generation” (Genesis 50).

If he had agreed with our judges in counting generations, then, looking also to Manasseh, he would have asserted that Ephraim’s lineage was not merely the third but rather the sixth [Col. 0196D]. For immediately afterward he says: “The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees” (ibid.).

Since, therefore, the third generation of Ephraim and likewise the third of Manasseh are not extended because of any relationship between them, but each is simply called the third on its own side, as sacred Scripture bears witness, by what authority and novelty of doctrine is kinship now divided in such a way that the great-grandchildren of two brothers are taught to be separated from one another by eight degrees?

The Lord also says to Abraham concerning his descendants who would later go down to Egypt, with the same Moses as witness: “In the fourth generation they shall return here” [Col. 0197A] (Genesis 15).

Indeed, if the divine voice were to divide all the generations that returned from Egypt to the land of Canaan under Moses according to the opinions of our judges, it would have stated not the fourth generation but rather the thousandth, or certainly an even greater number.

Likewise, what is said through the Psalmist—“He remembered his holy word, which he commanded for a thousand generations” (Psalm 104)—does not refer to the multitude of generations that exist at one time in this life, but rather to those that succeed one another through longer ages.

For if the Prophet had wished “generations” here to mean the generations of individual parents, there is no day on which a thousand generations could not be found among the people of God. Therefore, commanding his word for a thousand generations would mean nothing more than giving a law to a people among whom there were a thousand fathers.

It is also written of blessed Job: “For he saw his sons, and his sons’ sons, even to the fourth generation” (Job 42).

Since Scripture does not say that Job saw the sons of his son—that is, a simple line descending from one ancestor—but rather “the sons of his sons,” and declares that all of them came, while he was still alive, not to four generations but individually to the fourth generation, it is perfectly clear that, by the authority of divine speech, the generations proceeding from brothers are not counted separately but simply.

The same is said of Tobit: “And Tobit saw the fifth generation of his sons” (Tobit 14).

You see, then, judges, what is being said: both “generation” and “the sons of his sons” [Col. 0197C]. In “the sons of his sons,” therefore, attend to the several lines of descent; but in the generation that is mentioned, count them all together as though they formed the order of a single succession.

For it is an idiom of sacred Scripture that the descendants of different brothers are comprehended as one generation, as though a succession descending from one man were being woven together. If I wished to gather here all the examples found in the sacred books, daylight would reach sunset before the examples came to an end [186].

You see, then, judges, that by counting wrongly you encounter the numerous witnesses of sacred speech who protest against you; and that, while introducing the filth of incest under the guise of marriage, you attempt to defile the purity of ecclesiastical chastity.

Let the vanity of earthly wisdom therefore be ashamed, and let it not scatter the thorns of error in the forest of the Church. Rather, let it restrain the arrogance of the perverse spirit and humbly submit itself to sacred authority. Let it not immediately believe whatever is suggested to it by the petulance of a luxuriant understanding acting as its flatterer; rather, let it regard as entirely authoritative whatever has been defined by the holy teachers.

### CHAPTER VII. Where he defeats his opponents with an unanswerable argument

After that scarcely navigable statement of Justinian, in which the niece of a brother is said to be in the fourth degree, a certain energetic, quick-witted, and sharp-tongued Florentine—keen in intellect, biting in speech, forceful [Col. 0198A] in argument—was, I think, insolently pressing me with the words of blessed Gregory. Gregory had commanded (Register, final book, letter 31) that the English should already be joined in the fourth or fifth generation.

“Although,” he said, “that holy man granted this by way of accommodation to a newly converted people, nevertheless, if consanguinity had to be avoided so carefully in marital union, permission to come together among such close relatives would certainly not have been granted. It is clear that he judged more moderately on this point of union, since, although they were inexperienced, he did not deny marriage in the fourth generation.”

Let us compare the two statements, that of Justinian and that of Gregory. Let us strike them against one another like two stones hurled at us from the enemy’s battle line, so that from their collision a spark may emerge which will show the light to those same adversaries of ours—not, out of respect, to say blind judges, but at least bleary-eyed and dim-sighted ones [Col. 0198B].

Listen, then, judges, and carefully attend to the words of both teachers. Here in the Church forbid that disorderly murmur with which you are accustomed to behave in the marketplace or tribunals. Let our dispute be settled not by the confused loquacity of the parties but by the reasoning of an attentive heart.

Let us therefore cry out together to the Lord and let both sides say to him: “Arise, O God, judge your cause” (Psalm 73).

Now then: your Justinian says, as has often been stated above: “Your brother’s granddaughter is already separated from you by the fourth degree.” You are one; your brother is the second; his son the third; and his granddaughter [Col. 0198C] is distinguished from you by the fourth degree.

If this is so, we need not weary ourselves by going any farther, since we can find more immediately what we judge necessary for the matter.

Since, then, as has been said, you are third from your brother’s son, your daughter is consequently also in the fourth degree from that same son of your brother—provided, of course, that what you assert, namely, that degree and generation are the same, is granted.

If this is indeed true, everything that Gregory permits to be joined in the fourth generation amounts to nothing other than his judging that the sons and daughters of two full brothers or of two full sisters may be joined in marriage.

But where is the fact that Gregory himself altogether forbids the son and daughter of two brothers or two sisters to be joined? Should we suppose that he contradicted himself, immediately decreeing that what he had prohibited should be done?

Who would believe this of Gregory, unless he were utterly deranged in mind? Nevertheless, let Gregory’s own writing come forward, and let the order of the passage itself show more clearly whether it is consistent with itself (ibid.) [Col. 0198D]:

“A certain earthly law in the Roman state permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister or of two full brothers or of two full sisters to be joined. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot grow from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that the faithful should now lawfully join one another in the fourth or fifth generation.”

Behold, the very sequence of the writing proves that the children of full brothers are not in the fourth generation, since the same authority by which they are forbidden to marry permits those who are in the fourth generation to enter into the bonds of marriage [Col. 0199A].

For if the children of full brothers stood in the fourth generation, what else would it mean to say “the children of full brothers must not be joined” and “people in the fourth generation may be united,” except that the statement would proceed as follows: “Cousins must both not be joined and be joined”? This would surely be considered ridiculous rather than authoritative.

Thus the same venerable teacher, after first stating, “It is necessary that the faithful should now lawfully join one another in the fourth or fifth generation,” immediately adds: “For they must altogether abstain from the second, as we have said above.”

Behold, we have battered against one another the stones hurled by the hostile hand, drawn out sparks, and obtained light. Let us therefore walk in the light of the Lord, lest darkness overtake us (John 12).

But if you perhaps ask me how that statement of Justinian can be reconciled, it is of no concern to us. We leave your matters to you and do not arrogate to ourselves expertise in another person’s office.

We do not omit only this point, which concerns us: the lowest do not always correspond to the highest, worldly things to sacred things, or human things to divine things. For while Justinian asserts that a brother’s niece is placed in the fourth degree, blessed Gregory, as is obvious, calls the sons and daughters of two brothers or sisters—which is certainly farther and more remote—the second generation.

### CHAPTER VIII. That the seventh generation is not found among great-grandchildren

[Col. 0199C]

This too is a very strong argument that the seventh and eighth generations are not completed, as you assert, among the great-grandchildren of full brothers. For the sacred canons prohibit this: as long as the line of consanguinity is recognized or retained in memory, no one should presume to take a wife from his own kinship.

Certainly, we see some people living today who rejoice in being made fertile even by the offspring of their grandchildren [188]. Do you therefore judge that the elder man, whose posterity has already extended to great-grandchildren, should enter into a marital bond with his full brother, who is likewise a great-grandfather, and give his brother’s great-grandchild in marriage to his own great-grandchild?

How absurd this is, how horrifying and contrary to nature it appears, requires no verbal exaggeration [Col. 0199D].

And what lineage could be so lowly that, even among close relatives, memory would not reach back to great-grandfathers? Especially since, even if the father of both full brothers were still alive—as we ourselves have seen—all those persons could legally be under his authority, and he could call them all his children according to the law.

What sort of situation would it be if a father contracted marriage with children who were, in some sense, very distant from one another, and joined in a nuptial union those among whom that same father was himself the father?

You see, then, that although you are sons of the Church, you introduce the rites of the Synagogue to the injury of the mother; and under the profession of the Christian name you anticipate the heresy of Antichrist.

For it is known that, when Antichrist comes, he will teach people to become Jewish and will place the ceremonies of the old man before the new laws of evangelical grace [Col. 0200A].

But you must not act in this way. Even if the darkness of ignorance has for a time crept over you, return at once to the pages of sacred speech as to a clear light; humbly lay aside the error of your own judgment, and return as quickly as possible to the path of right understanding.

You who hold the rod in the school amid crowds of clients should not be afraid to undergo discipline in the Church. You who plead cases as learned men in the tribunals should be content, in Christ’s oratory, to hear the judgments of one who teaches.

It is honorable that those who have been accustomed to preside as censors over human affairs should also show themselves humble in mystical and spiritual matters [Col. 0200B].

Therefore, whoever you are who intend to enumerate the degrees of kinship, do not attach one line to another in length, as thread to thread, but conclude the persons descending on either side by a single reckoning. Do not say, “Four generations on this side and four on that side make eight generations”; say instead that these persons stand in the fourth generation from one another.

### CHAPTER IX. That common kinship should be reckoned according to the degree of the preceding person

But if the numbers are unequal—so that one person is found in the sixth degree and the other in the seventh, or beyond—then, as it seems to me, one must immediately return to the preceding degree and decide with regard to it that such persons cannot come together in marriage [Col. 0200C].

Although someone may already exceed the boundary of kinship, it does not seem permissible for him to marry a woman whom the measure of her own line still confines within it. The entire body of kinship must first be completed on every side; only then should the bonds of marriage return.

But if anyone is uncertain about this judgment, let the apostolic see be consulted. For we consider it more honorable to learn by inquiring with others than to teach alone through ignorance; and where we ourselves are stuck, we judge it rash to strengthen others.

Nevertheless, because we must assign the calculation of generation according to the degree of the preceding line, this too is indicated by what we reported above, namely, that the Lord promised Abraham [Col. 0200D] that his sons would be freed from Egyptian slavery “in the fourth generation” (Genesis 25).

To give examples from the distinguished lines of the Israelite people, the royal and the priestly: the lineage of Levi was then the fourth, but the generation of Judah had already preceded it as the fifth.

Since, therefore, the divine voice specified not the longer but the shorter line of succession, it has, as we infer, established by its authority a rule for us in counting generations: a person is to be considered in the same lineage as another at the degree in which the person higher in his line is found.

### CHAPTER X. That one person must exceed the number when the degrees are counted

It should also be noted that, in counting the generations of kinship [Col. 0201A], one person must always exceed the number. For generation cannot arise from a single person. Generation occurs when one who has been begotten proceeds from the begetter.

Without seeking an example from elsewhere, what we still have before us is sufficient: Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; and Eleazar begot Phinehas (Numbers 26).

Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi; Phinehas entered the promised land. If you count from Kohath to Phinehas, you will find five persons, although, as the divine oracle bears witness, there ought to be four generations.

And because Moses testifies in Exodus that the children of Israel came out of Egypt in the fifth generation, let us also examine the order of the tribe of Judah [Col. 0201B]: “Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon” (Matthew 1).

Perez went to Egypt with his father Judah; Nahshon is described as having been the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness; and his son Salmon entered the promised land.

If, then, we count from Perez to Salmon, we find six persons, but according to Moses we count only five generations.

If anyone is troubled that Moses’ number does not agree with the number established by the Lord, that belongs to another matter. For now it is enough to know that both are recognized as true if they are referred, as stated, to different tribes [Col. 0201C].

That there are more persons than degrees is also clearly demonstrated in the very diagram of the canons, where it says that in the first degree the upper line contains father and mother, and the lower line son and daughter.

Since father and son are placed in one degree, it is undoubtedly clear that in the series of consanguinity there are more persons than degrees [190].

What is added there—that no other persons are joined to these persons—is equivalent to saying that they do not come transversely. For a brother and sister come transversely or obliquely to a grandfather and grandson, who are in the second degree; a brother and sister likewise come obliquely to a great-grandfather and great-granddaughter; the son and daughter of a brother or sister do so in turn, and so on with the others [Col. 0201D].

No other persons are joined to the persons who are father and son because the two together make one degree, and therefore no other persons similar to them can be found.

The Psalmist also testifies to this when he says: “Let his descendants be destined for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out” (Psalm 108).

For the one whose sons he curses to destruction, he vows that their name should be blotted out in one generation. By these words he plainly declares that father and son are not two generations but one generation and one degree.

After these, however, there are without doubt as many degrees as there are persons.

Therefore, whoever wishes, in contracting marriage, to pass beyond the seventh generation completely must, as it seems to us, count nine persons equally on both sides: eight persons, by whom seven generations are formed; and the ninth must be the person who enters into marriage [Col. 0202A].

But if, according to another definition, someone has chosen to be content with the sixth generation, we do not judge that a new austerity should be imposed upon the ancient canons.

Nevertheless, since some teachers decree that the sixth generation should be observed and others the seventh, the following distinction should be maintained in such cases: if the counting begins from sons, it should end at the sixth generation; but if it begins from grandsons, it should extend to the seventh.

In this way the opinion of the majority will be found to be one, although it appeared to differ because of an inequality in the wording.

### CHAPTER XI. That sometimes “degree” means one thing and “generation” another

[Col. 0202B]

It must not, however, be passed over that in these writings which speak of the relationship of kindred, *degree* is not always used in place of *generation*. Otherwise Justinian would by no means have placed the brother’s granddaughter [*neptem fratris*] in the fourth degree, as was said above—especially since four generations could not possibly arise from only four persons, for brother has no generation with brother, since neither begets the other. Hence, as it seems to me, those disputants whom we mentioned above are deceived by the difference in this term: namely, because it is sometimes found to signify a generation, and sometimes merely the position of a person. For it amounts to the same thing to say that the brother’s granddaughter is in the fourth degree as to say that she is in the fourth position.

If my litigants, who scarcely know how to grow calm [the wording is uncertain], do not hesitate to renew what they were then attempting to bring against me, let them repeat their charges in revived attacks, saying—not without a certain swelling of contentiousness: “Why do you weave such lengthy lines of affinity? Teach us also whether a great-grandson, as you assert, descending in a direct line to a great-granddaughter, possesses the right of kinship; by what name of relationship will they be reckoned among themselves? As cousins (*sobrini*), paternal cousins (*patrueles*), or cousins through paternal aunts (*amitini*)? But if they are not related to one another by any such name, how are they blood-relations, when they seem to be connected with one another by no designation of kinship?”

To them I reply: if the matter concerns names, something of this kind is often found, so that certain persons both possess a relationship of closeness and lack the designation of affinity.

And, to confirm what we are saying by the testimony of sacred authority, it is commanded in Leviticus: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife’s sister, nor of her daughter; you shall not take the daughter of her son or the daughter of her daughter, to uncover her shame, because they are her flesh, and such intercourse is incestuous” (Lev. XVIII). Behold: by the divine voice a stepfather is restrained from the daughter of his stepchild, whether male or female; and yet there is no term of affinity by which the two persons ought to be designated in relation to one another. Do you therefore think that persons of this kind ought to be joined in marriage contrary to the divine command, since no designation of relationship is found by which they can be named? But observe what is said at the end of the judgment: “Such intercourse is incestuous.”

In the Decrees of Pope Innocent it is likewise written: “No one shall take as a wife, down to the third generation, the widow of the father of his wife, the widow of the brother of his wife, the widow of the son of his wife, or the widow of the blood-relatives of his wife.” Yet among all these persons the designations of affinity are not found; nevertheless, marriage between them is prohibited.

But if you are still not satisfied with these arguments and continue attempting to oppose them, we shall take from your own chambers a defense to set against your own arrows. For your Justinian, after enumerating six degrees of kindred on every side, immediately adds (Institutes, Book III, title “On Completing the Degrees of Kindred”): “From these things it is clear how we ought also to enumerate the further degrees: for each person who is born adds a degree, so that it is much easier to answer in which degree someone stands than to identify anyone by the proper designation of kinship.”

If therefore the legislator himself enumerates degrees of blood relationship where he testifies that the names are lacking, what wonder is it if we, doing the same thing, assert that a right of relationship exists among those whose corresponding designations are not found?

Let what I have now said about kinship suffice, lest my poor style exceed the measure of brevity appropriate to it. Nevertheless, as I believe, if this is carefully considered, every complaint that had recently arisen concerning this matter will be quieted.

## CHAPTER XII. An Apology for the Longer Treatise

Someone may say that I have wandered too freely in words. But the safety of my neighbors matters so much to me that I do not consider it useless to kindle a pyre of many logs, by which a basilisk—even though a small one—must perish for the sake of the unharmed people. Nor is much water poured out in vain if the spark of a fire by which a city was destined to be burned is extinguished.

A cheap arrow is driven into the breast of a warrior, but before it can be removed, much labor and sweat are expended. Nevertheless, whoever accuses me of a ragged and overextended work should consider with whom I have to deal in this dispute; and then let him attribute to necessity what he had until now ascribed to verbosity. We judged it necessary to write these things down, lest the cancer that was creeping onward day by day through its growth should spread still more disastrously through the entrails of the Church.

But you, most serene and venerable men in Christ—namely, you who commanded me to undertake this work—resist the error of such great perversity with all authority, and vigorously confront it, lest a deadly leprosy spread through the body of the Church. Chastity is a particular virtue, which has flourished among the worshipers of God from the very beginning of the world and has continually increased little by little with the passage of time. Now, however, with the divine judgment already impending, when people ought altogether to be persuaded to cut away the pleasures of the flesh, they are even voluntarily encouraged to bind themselves in incestuous marriages.

Let sacerdotal authority therefore rise against such plagues, and let the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline oppose wicked presumption. Let no horn be given to the sinner; let no boldness be left to vanity. Let that Mosaic serpent still live in the Church of Christ (Num. XXI), which swallowed the serpents of the enchanters. I say, let spiritual prudence live, consuming the poisons of carnal cunning, so that those whom the unbridled freedom of their own will had released may be restrained by the judgment of canonical severity; and those whom the swelling of celebrated reputation had inflated may be weighed down by the gravity of an account rendered; and those whom the unity of faith gathers together may not be scattered by the rift of doctrine.

Thus, indeed, through your zeal, may they return to the harmony of sober understanding; and, having now been humbled, may they be reconciled in one spirit with the peace of the Church. Thus may the sluggish serpent cease to pour forth the venom of wicked doctrine, and may the Church of Christ thereafter remain whole in the purity of her modesty.

[Col. 0204B]

# A SHORT TREATISE ON THE DEGREES OF KINSHIP

## Argument

He consults a certain presbyter about the manner in which the degrees of kinship ought to be counted. For the customary practice—namely, counting in such a way that the first person is always in excess—does not seem so entirely safe to him that it would be wrong to depart from it, especially since certain passages of Scripture seem to stand in its way. He therefore asks that, in this uncertainty, the writer disclose his opinion.

To the lord S., a religious presbyter, Peter, a sinful monk: the indissoluble bond of charity.

A wise man advises: “Treat of holiness with a religious man, and of justice with a just man” (Sir. XXXVII) [Note: The sense of this passage appears contrary to the text, which reads: “Treat of holiness with an irreligious man,” etc.]. He also says afterward: “Be constantly with a holy man, whoever you know to observe the fear of God” (ibid.).

Therefore, venerable brother, recognizing you as such a man, I considered it fitting not to discuss earthly counsels with you, but rather to treat of a spiritual and ecclesiastical question. In the short work in which I disputed the degrees of kinship, I remember saying, among other things: “In counting the generations of kindred, one person must always be in excess.” Approving this as well, I added: “For a generation cannot arise from one person.” I also brought forward testimonies from Scripture by which this argument established that, when the generations of relatives have been counted, one person must always be found in excess. For example: where there are five generations, there must necessarily be six persons. Thus also, in other cases, the number of persons must exceed the number of degrees.

But as time passed, while reading, I encountered something in Scripture that persuaded me that this rule for counting kinship could be changed—especially since many laypeople complain that this definition contains a harsh and inhuman severity, and declare that they cannot obey us unless we consent, in some way, to relax the rigor of this law. This is the daily conflict; this is the reproach we endure without truce.

## [Short Treatise]

## CHAPTER I. What rule must be observed in counting generations?
