It therefore seems to us that we may, without blame, condescend to the weaknesses of the weak [read: *condescendere*] and decree that the number of degrees of kinship and of persons should correspond to one another, so that however many the persons are, so many generations should also be said to exist.

But lest this appear to be our own rashness rather than the authority of the holy Fathers, blessed Jerome, when attempting to resolve the question in Genesis where it says, “Whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance” (Gen. IV), declares that there are seven generations from Adam to Lamech, although only that many persons—namely, seven—are found. And, to set down the very words of so great a teacher: “This is the opinion of our elders: they think that Cain was killed in the seventh generation by Lamech.” He then adds: “For Adam begot Cain, Cain begot Enoch, Enoch begot Cainan, Cainan begot Mahalaleel, Mahalaleel begot Methuselah, Methuselah begot Lamech, who is the seventh from Adam.”

A little later he says: “This Cain, then, was killed in the seventh generation and, according to another edition, paid the penalty for his crime; here, I think, nothing obscure remains.”

In these words of the most learned man it is plainly shown that, although from Adam to Lamech there are only seven persons, they nevertheless constitute seven generations. Blessed Gregory also does not disagree with this enumeration of generations. For in his exposition of blessed Job he declares Enoch to be the seventh generation, although only six persons who were his fathers are found before him.

These, indeed, are the words of the blessed man (Morals, X): “Enoch,” he says, “is born in the seventh generation among the elect,” because they seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of the final recompense.

And certainly, as the sacred history of Genesis clearly attests: “Adam begot Seth, Seth begot Enos, Enos begot Cainan, Cainan begot Mahalaleel, Mahalaleel begot Jared, Jared begot Enoch” (Gen. III).

Therefore, just as in the genealogy of Cain only seven persons succeeding one another are found from Adam to Lamech, so likewise through the succession of the elect only seven persons are counted from the same Adam to Enoch. But just as blessed Jerome testifies that Lamech is the seventh from Adam in the genealogy of Cain, so blessed Gregory testifies that Enoch is the seventh generation.

If, then, we do not shrink from following the example of such great men, it remains that as many generations should be said to exist as persons can be counted among the successors of any lineage.

## CHAPTER II. How there were fourteen generations from the Babylonian Captivity to Christ

Let us add something of greater weight, possessing the inviolable strength of authority. For after the evangelist Matthew had traced the line of Christ’s generation, he added this conclusion: “Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the Babylonian Captivity fourteen generations, and from the Babylonian Captivity to Christ fourteen generations” (Matt. XI).

Yet none of the three orders arranged in this pattern is found to enumerate more than fourteen persons who begot or were begotten. Indeed, if the matter is carefully considered, the third and final order is found to contain only thirteen persons.

On this point certain teachers, holding different opinions from one another, argue at length in order to show that there are fourteen generations here as in the other orders. Saint Jerome, for his part, asserts that there were two Jechonias, namely father and son; he says that the father was placed at the end of the second order and the son at the head of the third. But blessed Augustine says that one Jechoniah is counted twice.

If this is to be believed, I do not know how the assertion of the holy evangelist can be regarded as true when he says that from the Babylonian Captivity to Christ there are fourteen generations. For whether something that is one is counted twice, or as many times as one wishes, it nevertheless remains one. Even if something is said repeatedly, the essence of the thing is not increased, nor is the number multiplied, although the statement has been repeated.

I am plainly afraid to express the doubt that arises in me concerning the opinions of both teachers, lest I should seem—God forbid—to be angry in any respect with such illustrious teachers of the Church and champions of the truth.

I therefore do not dare dispute their venerable definitions; I simply set forth what seems to me. From the point at which it is said that, after the Babylonian Captivity, Jechoniah begot Shealtiel, up to the statement that “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary,” there are thirteen generations. Joseph is understood as the twelfth, and Mary as the thirteenth.

For if Mary were joined to Joseph in carnal intercourse, as a wife to a husband, there would rightly appear to be only one generation in both. But since Mary is in no way joined to Joseph, while the line of generation has been carried as far as Joseph through the succession of those preceding him, the generation suddenly leaps across to Mary, placed on the other side. As it turns back from its own line and passes into another, it forms a kind of angle.

From her was born the one who, according to the Apostle, is the cornerstone (Eph. II), and, as the Psalmist sings, “has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII). Nor is it inappropriate that one generation is assigned to Mary, since that generation is the origin of the one for whom all the preceding generations serve.

For while Joseph on one side descends from the straight line of propagated kinship, and on the other side Mary descends from another line of the same kinship, the passage itself from one line to another is the mystical sacrament of generation. Since Mary is not joined to Joseph in the flesh, the two do not constitute one generation; Joseph makes one generation, and Mary another.

Clearly, since the usage of Scripture does not preserve the line of kinship through women, Christ’s genealogy is carried forward through men. Yet in his birth no male substance is joined to it. Therefore, when Joseph is reached, the order of succession is not carried farther downward, but immediately turns across and passes laterally to the virgin. Thus, after the carnal generations, a spiritual generation takes place, so that something wholly unheard-of and singular may immediately follow. A spiritual generation takes place from Joseph to Mary; a singular one from Mary to Christ.

## CHAPTER III. How it is said that Ozias was begotten by Joram

But you say to me, whoever you are: how can there be said to be a generation between Joseph and Mary when Joseph himself did not beget Mary? And I, in turn, answer your inquiry with another question: Why does that same blessed evangelist Matthew, whose statement we are now discussing, say among other things, “Joram begot Ozias” (Matt. I), when he was not Ozias’s father, but rather the father of Ochozias?

For whoever reads through the history of the Fourth Book of Kings recognizes without doubt that Joram begot Ochozias, Ochozias begot Joas, Joas begot Amasias, and Amasias begot Ozias, who is also called Azarias by another name (IV Kings VIII).

Why, then, is Joram said not to have begotten Ochozias, whom he did beget, but rather Ozias, who stands fifth from him at a distance? If, therefore, a generation is said to exist between Joram and Ozias—not because Ozias was begotten by Joram, but because he was produced from him through the long transmission of an uninterrupted lineage—what prevents a generation from being said to exist between Mary and Joseph, who are certainly blood-relatives, through a certain force and mystery of the sacrament?

And if it cannot be comprehended how Christ is born from a virgin, what wonder is it if between his parents there appears to be a certain extraordinary and admirable generation, whose generation is singular, whose conception is new, and whose birth is found to be unheard-of?

We say these things, nevertheless, without prejudice to the authority of the holy teachers whom we mentioned above.

To return, then, to what we began after this digression: in this generation of the Lord the rule that we established elsewhere does not appear to have been observed—namely, that in counting generations one person should be provided in excess. If it were observed here, one additional person would necessarily appear to have to be added.

For in that line of kinship, arranged in a threefold enumeration, each of the three orders contains only fourteen persons, just as it contains fourteen generations. The multitude of persons does not appear to exceed the number of generations, since there the generations are nothing other than individual persons.

When one considers the matter and weighs it more carefully, it becomes plainly evident that the blessed evangelist, in counting the rule of kinship which we described above, not only did not observe it, but carefully avoided, deliberately rejected, and prudently excluded it.

For when, because of a definite mystery, he had decided to append fourteen generations in a threefold arrangement to the genealogy of the Lord, so as to show each person to be a generation, he removed from the order of the narrative the three kings mentioned above—namely Ochozias, Joas, and Amasias—and was content to set down as many persons as he counted generations.

Although he had an abundance of persons available, he plainly did not want a person to remain in excess of the generations, but wanted the number of generations and persons to correspond equally to one another.

Meditate carefully on these matters yourself, venerable brother, and discuss them diligently with your learned associates, so that, supported by their assistance, you may be able to give me a definite answer. Write back, therefore, whether, in counting the degrees of kinship, I ought to persist in what I described earlier, or whether I should rather adopt what I have recently discovered—so that, when you remove from me a doubt burdensome to many, many may in turn offer you, through me, a fitting expression of thanks.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0207]

# 197–198. NINTH OPUSCULUM. ON ALMSGIVING, TO MAINARD, BISHOP OF URBINO

## Argument

Above all other virtues he commends almsgiving. In praise of it the holy man gives free rein to his eloquence in this little work and pours out all the powers of his intellect.

To the lord Mainard, bishop of Urbino, of venerable holiness, Peter, a sinful monk, greetings in the Lord.

He who rests beneath a summer shade does not labor in battle at that moment, yet he nevertheless discusses battles not inappropriately. We do not rest idly if, while resting, we reflect upon labor—namely, upon the order by which either a sweeter fruit or a more abundant harvest may flourish.

He who dwells in a royal court examines all the gifts of his powers to see whether there is anything by which he might especially please royal eyes, and wherever he discovers that he is capable of more, there he strives to exercise himself more earnestly.

One person is stronger in war; another is wiser in counsel. One, when pleading cases, speaks publicly with brilliance and charm; another, unable to equal him in the urban elegance of eloquence, perhaps excels in the practice of composition, or even in bird-catching, or certainly in the art of hunting.

And, to come to our own subject, Moses says to the children of Israel: “Set apart among yourselves firstfruits for the Lord: let everyone who is willing and of a ready spirit offer them to the Lord—gold, silver, bronze, violet, purple, scarlet twice dyed, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins, acacia wood, and oil for preparing the lamps” (Exod. XXXV).

Since no one possessed everything, each person offered what he could and was more generous in that which abounded more plentifully for him, so that, while all offered what no individual possessed in full, the many might build one tabernacle for the Lord.

We too, who now establish a tabernacle in the desert of this life, hope to enter the land flowing with milk and honey and dedicate a temple in that heavenly Jerusalem under the rule of the true Solomon. That temple will not be made from various senseless metals, but from living stones; nor will it be adorned with the gleam of shining gems, but will radiate with the beauty of spiritual virtues.

By God’s generosity we can share in all good things, but we cannot possess all things equally. For even the holy Fathers who went before us to heavenly things, although by divine assistance they shared in all the virtues, are nevertheless not believed to have been equal in all of them.

Abraham surpassed the others in faith and obedience together; Isaac was adorned with the pure chastity of monogamy; “Moses,” as Scripture says, “was a very meek man above all the men who dwelt on the earth” (Gen. XV); Elijah was made illustrious by the authority of freedom (Num. XII); the fervor of zeal and vengeance established Phinehas forever as a priest in the sight of the Lord (Num. XXV); virginity raised John to recline upon the Lord’s breast (John XIII); and Peter was advanced by his preeminent love for the Lord to receive the rights of the chief shepherd (John XXI).

## [On Almsgiving, to Mainard, Bishop of Urbino]

## CHAPTER I. That one virtue should be chosen to which we may devote ourselves more fully

Although each holy person must necessarily flourish in all the virtues—for no single quality is truly a virtue if it is not joined to the other virtues—one virtue must nevertheless be chosen by each person above the others, so that the mind may cling to it more familiarly, serve it, so to speak, and not withdraw from its service.

We cannot exercise ourselves equally in all the virtues. But while we guard one more strictly, we make up in it what is lacking from the others; and while we continually embrace and hold it tightly, we possess, as it were, the whole body of the virtues through participation in a single member.

Which virtue, then, do I urge you to pursue more particularly? Fasting? But you will immediately reply: “If I wear down my body with immoderate fasts, I shall soon succumb to the labors imposed by the many affairs and journeys that confront me.”

“If I prescribe meditations upon the Psalms,” you will say, “I am hindered from constancy in prayer, since every day I am compelled and driven to answer the greetings of friends and to engage in conversation.”

“If I urge you to walk barefoot, according to the custom of the apostles; if I tell you to subdue your limbs with rough haircloth, after the manner of John; if finally I command you to go into exile, or to confine yourself in prison custody in the manner of penitents—you will plead that illness is at hand, or rather that you cannot endure so harsh a burden of bodily hardship.”

Since you still fear to afflict the members of your body—or rather, since through the severity of repentance you are not yet able to offer yourself as a sacrifice to God—stretch out your hand, I ask, to the things that surround you. Since you cannot give yourself, at least give what is yours.

If you were about to cut into human flesh, it is enough for me if you merely cut the hair; if you came as one who would sever hands, you are merciful if you cut off only the growth of the nails. The distance between a wound in human flesh and a wound in clothing is as great as the distance between a human being and his possessions.

In this way Abraham offered an animal so that he might preserve his son (Gen. XXII): he slaughtered a ram in order to safeguard the heir. In this way Michal placed an image in the bed in order to defend her husband from the swords of her father’s madness (I Kings XIX); and, so that David might truly live, she took pains to make him appear to be dying beneath a goatskin: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job II).

You too should exchange yourself for your possessions, and meanwhile make your possessions a sacrifice, so that afterward you may deserve to be received yourself as a burnt offering. For God does not receive an offering in such a way that he despises the one who offers it. Thus, whoever has become an offerer of his possessions can safely sing with the wife of Manoah: “If the Lord had wished to kill us,” she said, “he would not have received burnt offerings and libations from our hands” (Judg. XIII).

God receives almsgiving through the hands of the poor and preserves it for you, stored securely in that heavenly treasury. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal” (Matt. XVI).

For this reason almighty God constrains some by poverty and expands others through an abundance of riches, so that the latter may have from which to redeem their own sins, and the former may have from which to support their poverty. As it is written: “The ransom of a man’s soul is his riches” (Prov. XIII).

Daniel therefore says to Nebuchadnezzar: “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins with almsgiving and your iniquities with mercies toward the poor, if perhaps God may forgive your offenses” (Dan. IV).

Those who are rich are therefore commanded to be stewards rather than owners. They must not regard what they possess as belonging to their private right, since they did not receive these transitory goods for the purpose of luxuriating in them or spending them on their own uses, but in order to perform the office of administration while they remain in the stewardship entrusted to them.

Therefore, those who distribute aid to the poor return what belongs to others; they do not distribute their own. Hence, when the Lord commands almsgiving, he says: “Take heed that you do not do your justice before men, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI). He does not say, “your mercy,” but “your justice.” For the one who gives what is his own practices mercy; the one who returns what belongs to another practices justice.

Thus, when the Psalmist had first said, “He dispersed; he gave to the poor,” he did not say, “His mercy,” but, “His justice,” he says, “remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI).

When, therefore, we assist the poor, we unquestionably return what belongs to others; we do not provide what is ours. Nevertheless, in the sight of the gracious Judge we are judged merciful when we faithfully distribute these things, which are not ours but common to all. And when we justly return what belongs to others, we do not lack the reward of mercy before him who sees the innermost parts of the heart.

By contrast, those who now disdain to assist the poor are accused in the examination of the terrible judgment not so much of avarice as of theft; they are proved to have been not keepers of their own possessions, but rather robbers of what belongs to others.

To them the supreme Judge will say at the judgment: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. XXV).

It is as though he were saying: “Because you were unwilling to minister to your fellow servants what you received for their refreshment, may the cauldron of greedy Gehenna swallow you, whom the theft of another’s goods condemns through the burning passion of greed.”

And since what we have received for distribution in this life is alien to us, while the heavenly glory that we hope for is our own, that saying which the Lord speaks in the Gospel appropriately applies: “Since you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI).

He had certainly been faithful in what belonged to others who confidently said of himself: “The blessing of him who was perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow; I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; I was a father to the poor” (Job XXIX).

How faithful he had been in what belonged to others, and with what firm hope he could trust concerning his own things, when elsewhere also he proclaimed this about himself: “If I denied the poor what they desired, and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat of it—because from my infancy compassion grew up with me, and from my mother’s womb it came forth with me” (Job XXXI).

There he suitably adds: “If I despised a passerby because he had no clothing, or the poor man who lacked a covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (ibid.).

See how long this catalogue of mercies is, omitting absolutely nothing, meeting every kind of need, and, as though by healing, assisting every wound of want.

Moreover, when we come to the aid of the needy in their necessity, we fulfill both truth and mercy. Mercy, in that we compassionately sympathize with the destitute; truth—that is, justice—in that we provide them not with what is ours, but with what belongs to them.

Hence Solomon says in the Book of Proverbs: “Let mercy and truth not forsake you; bind them around your throat and write them on the tablets of your heart, and you will find grace and good discipline before God and men” (Prov. III).

Again it is written: “Mercy and truth prepare good things; in every good work there will be abundance” (Prov. XIV).

And lest sluggish indolence disparage the work of piety, but swift and ready devotion commend it, he says elsewhere: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you can give immediately” (Prov. III).

The hand of the miser trembles when he gives; and just as a sick person, shuddering at a bitter antidote, delays the drink, so this man delays giving something until later. The former is nauseated by the bitterness of the harsh drink; the latter fears poverty if he gives something. Therefore, although the time of necessity presses upon both the drinker and the giver, each reserves for the future, by inserting a delay, what he recoils from.

A generous and liberal spirit makes a person rich; fear and stinginess make him needy. Hence it is written: “The substance of the rich is a fortified city; the fear of the poor is their poverty” (Prov. X). Fear compels a base spirit to be needy, even though it may appear to overflow with an abundance of riches.

## CHAPTER II. What is the reward of almsgiving?

But you, beloved one, do not despise your brother in his present necessity if you desire God to assist you at the moment of your final necessity: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

Moreover, if you lend your money to a person at interest, you receive one percent; but if you give it to the poor, according to the divine commandments you will receive a hundredfold. And if this seems too little, eternal life is added to you.

Is it not therefore better for you to receive a hundredfold than to be content with one percent? Do not despise your neighbor if you do not wish to appear despicable before God.

Hence Solomon also says: “He who despises his neighbor sins; but he who has mercy on the poor will be blessed” (Prov. XIV). Immediately afterward it is added: “He who believes in the Lord loves mercy” (ibid.).

Clearly, if the one who believes in the Lord loves mercy, that person must be said not to believe who is convicted of not loving mercy. Why this person does not believe is explained by another saying from the same book, for it says: “He who has mercy on the poor lends to God, and he will repay him his due.”

Therefore he does not believe in the Lord who fears entrusting his goods to him, since he does not wish to present them to the needy. For if he truly believed in the Lord, he would not fear lending to him, as to a faithful debtor, the deposit of his resources [Col. 0213A]. But whoever doubts another’s faith unquestionably does not honor him, since it is written: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. III). And elsewhere it is said: “He who defrauds the needy reproaches his Maker; but he who has mercy on the poor honors him” (Prov. XIV). And again: “To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to God than sacrifices” (Prov. XXI).

For every almsgiver practices mercy when he sympathizes with the needy in their necessity; and he practices judgment when he bestows upon them not his own goods but theirs. Yet while in the present he supports another’s poverty, he prepares eternal riches for himself in the future. Hence it is written: “He who gives to the poor shall not lack; he who despises the supplicant shall suffer want” (Prov. XXVIII). [Col. 0213B] The rich man lays down what he gives to the needy and now, as a deposit of money lent, entrusts what he will receive in eternal life with multiplied interest. And the one who now becomes a creditor through mercy will afterward be a fortunate collector in the reckoning of repayment. Hence it is written: “The poor man and the creditor meet; the Lord enlightens both of them” (Prov. XXIX).

And concerning the strong woman—by whom either the holy universal Church or every faithful and devout soul is understood—it is said in Proverbs: “She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor” (Prov. XXXI). Immediately and appropriately it adds: “She shall not fear the cold of snow for her household, for all her domestics are clothed in double garments” (ibid.). Whoever is now clothed in the covering of a twofold charity, as though covered by a double garment [Col. 0213C], will in no way be constrained then by the cold of the future snow. And whoever is now inflamed by the ardor of charity will then know nothing of the penal chill of snow.

Concerning that snow, namely, the punishment to come, it is also said through blessed Job of the reprobate: “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat, and let his sin go even to the netherworld; let mercy forget him” (Job XXIV). For it is fitting that the one who in this life burned with the heat of carnal desire, but grew cold and numb, constricted despite the warmth of mercy, should there pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat—so that, just as here he sinned through two offenses, so there he may be tortured in hell by two punishments. And there, in turn, may mercy forget him who is proved never to have remembered mercy here.

Therefore, brother, send your riches on ahead of you [Col. 0213D], so that you may afterward live from them; let your resources go before you, so that you may possess them forever in that immortality. Remember what is written: “When the rich man sleeps, he will take nothing away with him; he will open his eyes and find nothing. Poverty will seize him like water; a storm will oppress him by night” (Job XXVII).

Let the counsel given through Solomon please you: “Cast your bread upon the passing waters, for after many days you will find it again. Give a portion to seven, and indeed to eight, for you do not know what evil may occur upon the earth” (Eccles. XI). And again: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest” (ibid.).

It is read in Genesis: “Isaac sowed in Gerar, and in that same year found a hundredfold” (Gen. XXVI). But how much more happily does he sow who, while supplying assistance to the needy, reaps wheat instead of oats, a measure instead of a handful, a heap instead of a grain: plainly purchasing heavenly things with earthly ones, eternal things with transitory ones.

Scripture says: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. XX). For who will boast that he has a chaste heart? But apply yourself diligently to almsgiving, and trust that through divine mercy you will be made clean. Hence the Savior says: “Give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI). For just as the heat of fire removes the rust from any metal, so almsgiving habitually cleanses the soul’s foulness.

Hence the wise man also says: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Eccles. III). [Col. 0214B] Immediately he adds: “And God is the observer of him; he will repay the kindness, remember him afterward, and at the time of his fall he will find support” (Eccles.). Then he continues: “My son, do not defraud the poor man of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor” (ibid. IV). And again: “Do not despise the hungry soul, and do not embitter the poor in his poverty. Do not afflict the heart of the needy, and do not delay giving to the distressed” (ibid.).

And there are many other things that this prophetic man strings together concerning the privilege of showing mercy to the poor. Before the Gospel had yet dawned, he extends, as it were, a priest in the Church, the course of a lengthy discourse. We do not think it necessary to enlarge upon all of them here together, lest we create weariness for our readers.

## CHAPTER III. Which almsgiving is the greater.

[Col. 0214C]

Although almsgiving is proclaimed throughout all the pages of sacred discourse, and mercy surpasses the other virtues and holds the palm among works of piety, nevertheless that mercy is preeminent which offers assistance to those who have recently fallen from abundance into want.

There are indeed some whom the rank of a more honorable lineage ennobles, but whom the straitness of their household resources constrains. Many are adorned with the titles of equestrian ancestry, yet are oppressed by the poverty of domestic necessity. The dignity of their lineage compels them to take part in the conversations of distinguished people: equal in their seating, but far unequal in their resources.

Although anxiety over domestic poverty torments them, even when necessity drives them to the utmost extremity, they do not know how to ask for food by begging. They prefer to die rather than beg publicly; they are ashamed to be recognized and afraid to confess their poverty. While others proclaim their destitution—indeed, sometimes exaggerating its extent so as to receive a more generous alms of consolation—these people conceal and disguise what they possess, lest some sign of their poverty disgracefully appear before human eyes.

Their need, therefore, is more to be understood than seen: it is more readily inferred from certain signs that emerge than detected through manifest indications. Concerning them the Prophet indicates how great the reward is, not openly but secretly, when he says: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor, etc. [Col. 0215A]” (Ps. XL).

We need no special understanding concerning poor people in rags and carrying little bags and pouches, whom we plainly see with our eyes. But we ought inwardly to understand those poor whose misery we cannot discern on the surface. “Blessed, therefore, is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.” And why is he blessed? “On the evil day,” he says, “the Lord will deliver him” (ibid.). Blessed is this promise: he who now assists the needy in their sorrow will afterward be delivered in the divine judgment; he who now has mercy on those suffering misery will then be rescued from the misery of calamity.

But let us hear further what the Psalmist continues: “May the Lord preserve him, give him life, make him blessed, cleanse his soul upon the earth, and not hand him over to the power of his enemy; may the Lord bring him aid” (ibid.). O how gloriously he trades who, in exchange for the mercy he displays to the poor, secures for himself the continual prayer of all Christendom! For the entire universal Church, spread throughout the whole world, daily entreats God for him, since it continually recites this psalm with daily devotion.

Add to this that this prayer can never come to be despised by divine clemency, since it was composed by the Holy Spirit, who is himself the forgiveness of sins. How could he not admit a prayer composed by himself? How could he fail to hear what he taught us to pray? Blessed, therefore—truly blessed—is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor.

Hence Moses—or rather, the Lord through Moses—says: [Col. 0215C] “If one of your brothers who dwells within the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God will give you, comes into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or draw back your hand; rather, you shall open it to the poor and lend him whatever you see that he needs” (Deut. XV). And elsewhere: “The poor shall not be lacking in the land of your dwelling; therefore I command you to open your hand to your needy and poor brother who lives with you in the land” (ibid.).

Almighty God knows that human frailty can never attain life by its own justice alone, but always needs mercy. Therefore, throughout all the pages of the sacred Scriptures, he praises almsgiving, proclaims mercy, and continually urges that the bowels of compassion be shown to the poor, so that while one human being has mercy on another, he may also obtain mercy from God for his own merits; and while he supports a sharer in his nature, he may deserve to have as his supporter the one who sustains him; and what he offers to his neighbor, he himself may also receive from God.

For just as the Creator of human beings predestined all the elect for the kingdom from the very origin of the world, yet commanded them to labor tirelessly for the attainment of that kingdom, so that what is freely granted by the Creator might be attained by human efforts, so it is necessary that we, who are to be saved through mercy by a compassionate Creator, should not neglect to distribute among our brothers the expenditure of our own compassionate humanity.

Hence Tobias says to his son: “Give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for thus it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you” (Tob. IV). Here he also establishes a measure of discernment and undoubtedly sets an authoritative rule for every amount of possession and substance. For he says: “As you are able, so be merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; if little, strive to share even the little willingly” (ibid.).

He explains why one ought to do this when he adds: “For you store up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity, because almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and will not allow the soul to go into darkness. Almsgiving will give great confidence before the Most High to all who practice it” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV. That one who does not provide alms either in deed or in intention cannot be dear to God.

[Col. 0216B]

To summarize the matter briefly, one who has neither the effect nor the intention of almsgiving will never be dear to God. That is, one who does not possess the means should possess the will; and while the abundance of household resources does not overflow, a generous spirit should not lose its riches.

For one who does not have food perhaps has a roof. If he cannot refresh the hungry with food, he can at least restore the exhausted through the service of hospitable humanity. Let him always remember the apostolic saying: “Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality” (Heb. XIII). For through this some, having received angels as guests, pleased angels.

Certainly, some people close their doors—and their hearts—to Christ’s poor, accuse them of theft, and, while withholding from them the humanity of hospitality through avarice, pretend that they suspect them of being thieves and fear loss to their household property. Sometimes they mockingly point to their plump faces and sometimes to their ruddy mouths; they charge such people, whose muscular arms and strong limbs are suited to agricultural digging, with offending God, though they could indeed support others through the exercise of their labor.

Such persons must greatly fear what was said through Moses to the Israelite people in Deuteronomy: “The Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth generation, shall not enter the assembly of the Lord forever, because they did not come to meet you with bread and water on the way when you went out from Egypt” (Deut. XXIII).

If those nations, which certainly did not possess the Law, are therefore irrevocably excluded from the Church of God because they neglected to meet even their enemies with the service of humanity, how terrible a sentence must those deserve who close their hearts to needy neighbors and do not extend charity to their brothers? These people were born from the font of holy baptism; with these they came forth from the womb of Mother Church. Yet while they share with them the table of the Lord’s body and blood, they deny them food that must be digested and passed out.

And with what conscience do we grow sluggish in distributing alms, when we rest in ecclesiastical peace, seeing that even the holy apostles—who had entered, as it were, into battle against the whole world—are recorded as having been concerned with this work of grace? If anyone could have been permitted to set aside this concern, surely they could have done so: they were intent on scattering the seed of the new faith and were engaged in so fierce a struggle against the world’s unbelief.

Yet no labor of persecution could restrain them from showing humanity to their brothers, and no urgency of preaching could hold them back from extending mercy to the poor. Hence Paul says to the Galatians: “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should preach the Gospel among the gentiles, and they among the circumcised; only that we should remember the works of mercy—which I was also eager to do” [Col. 0217B] (Gal. II).

He also says to the Corinthians: “Concerning the collections made for the saints: just as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also should do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside privately, storing up whatever may please him; and when I arrive, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry this gift to Jerusalem” (I Cor. XVI).

Such was the apostles’ generosity toward the poor that it is read in their Acts: “They broke bread around the houses, and took food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising the Lord” (Acts II). “Around the houses,” he says, not “inside the houses.” They do not follow the apostles’ example who, about to dine, fasten bolts and bars across their closed doors and secure the beams with locks, thus fortifying themselves against the poor as though against ranks of surrounding enemies during a siege.

## CHAPTER V. That the resources of children increase through their parents’ almsgiving.

Gerardus of Farvaldo was certainly one of the leading men of the city of Ravenna. I saw him long ago, when I was still a boy, though he was already of advanced and very old age. I often heard this related about him: when the people were suffering from poverty, so much so that severe hunger even killed some, he—although he already had descendants of grandchildren who would succeed him—sold some estates, even after cutting down the crops, and distributed to the needy whatever food he could.

At that time he himself ate with open doors, surrounded by a crowd of poor people. When the food had been consumed and he was still hungry, having nothing more to add either for himself or for them [Col. 0217D], he wept in compassion for them. His descendants still flourish in wealth today and possess more than their ancestral patrimonies had been.

Waldericus, moreover, who became a celebrated martyr while fighting against heretics, was—as Andrew, the venerable bishop of the Church of Spoleto, related to me—once visiting his mother’s house. He found a poor man before the door who complained that he had gathered a bundle of herbs but had been entirely unable to obtain salt from that woman with which to season the broth.

When the holy man entered his mother’s lodging and found a little salt in a vessel, he became exceedingly angry, seized the vessel with the salt, and scattered it through the street, to his mother’s reproach, saying that something which had been denied to Christ through avarice ought not to be eaten by a Christian at all. But shortly afterward, the vessel that she had put away empty was found, not without the astonishment of a miracle, to be full of salt.

Mainfredus, likewise, a margrave whose principality lay at the furthest boundaries of Liguria, was renowned, together with his wife, for his most fervent zeal in supporting the poor. Of him—leaving other matters aside—this one thing is commonly preserved in celebrated memory: on the very day of the most holy Resurrection, when his house shone like a royal palace with tapestries and purple decorations, lavish expenses abounded, and he was surrounded by a considerable crowd of clients in white garments, he ordered a magnificent banquet to be prepared.

After carefully arranging poor people at all the tables, he himself served as a steward with his servants. When they had been sufficiently filled, he himself, together with his servants, took whatever food remained, as though he were a private person, so that the Paschal solemnity might shine forth in the poor, while the private meal of the master of the house sustained him.

The man of God, my lord Leo, a venerable hermit who had by then spent nearly twenty years enclosed in a cell, also gave this remarkable testimony about him. When Leo himself was living with several brothers in the aforesaid margrave’s hermitage, the margrave’s wife had imposed this rule upon herself: whatever the hermits’ messenger requested as necessary, she would immediately double it with increased interest. If he perhaps requested five solidi, she would give ten; if he requested ten, she would immediately count out twenty.

But since I have forgotten, I certainly doubt whether I may have written this very thing elsewhere. Nevertheless, when something contributes to edification, it is better for it to be repeated in an account than erased through silence and forgotten.

Since, then, he was so generous in distributing alms to the needy, and since—if I remember correctly—he founded six or seven sizeable monasteries in his own legal possession and enriched them with estates and ornaments through munificent generosity, did his descendants therefore succeed him in poverty? Far from it. We see that his grandsons, boys of remarkable character, possess for the most part even the greater part of the kingdom of Burgundy. Moreover, their sister is known to have been endowed with a marriage portion by lawful marriage to our emperor.

Why, then, do we fear returning to God what he has bestowed—what is restored to us or to our heirs in this life, and increased in the glory of the heavenly kingdom through the interest of multiplied repayment?

## CHAPTER VI. That the abundance of temporal goods arises from almsgiving.

I consider it worthwhile to know this also, which Berardus, the margrave who died recently, often related. He said that a certain man in the lands of the Germans, from which he himself also originated, possessed an excellent estate belonging to him, abundantly rich in the produce of various kinds. He had twelve sons.

Meanwhile he began to consider what would happen after his death if he divided the inheritance of a single possession among so many coheirs. He said:

“I, who alone possess all this, live sufficiently and peacefully. But if so many claimants emerge, who will endure their rivalries? Who will bear the quarrels of jealousy and hatred arising among them? There cannot be unity of will where there is such manifold diversity of resources. Moreover, the tenants who are now content to obey one master will, not without grave injury to their peace, have to answer to a multitude of masters.

“Therefore, almighty God, I surrender to you whatever allodial property belongs to me; I choose you alone as heir of my possession. I commend my sons to you; do with them whatever is pleasing in your sight.”

Having said this, he immediately tied his glove to an arrow and, bending his bow with all his strength, shot it into the upper reaches of the vast sky. But soon the arrow fell back to earth without the glove, so that it might be shown by a clear sign that divine mercy had accepted the gift he offered in faith.

Then, made more confident and joyful by the offering of his gift, he handed over his possession to a certain church and secured it to himself in perpetual right through stipulations and confirmed agreements. Shortly afterward, his sons were endowed with such an abundance of flowing goods and so magnificently enlarged by such a wealth of estates and revenues that each of them surpassed the total of his father’s resources, and worldly prosperity smiled upon them in every respect.

Thus, he who received in heaven the investiture of the glove from his father’s hand poured down an abundant shower of his blessing upon the sons. Whatever, therefore, is given to God on earth is received in heaven [Col. 0219C]; and the reward is to be hoped for from the place to which the offered gift has gone before.

Hence the angel of the Lord said to Cornelius: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial before the presence of the Lord” (Acts X). O happy exchange, in which a human being becomes a lender and God almighty becomes a debtor! We may confidently demand from him a worthy repayment of our due if we strive to anticipate him with our gifts.

For I also remember that, in the time of Pope Gregory—he was the sixth of that name and was called Gratianus—what I am about to relate took place, as Bonizo told me, a very old man and rector of the monastery of Saint Severus situated near the old city.

The king of the Scots, then growing into the first flower of adolescence, succeeded his deceased father immediately in the rights of royal power. But when he carefully considered how fragile is everything that swells up in this world, how unstable what rises above others, and how quickly extinguished is everything that shines, although he was already married, he resolved to lay down the royal insignia for love of the heavenly kingdom: to change the crown for a hood and the purple for a cowl.

What more is there to say? He pretended to be devoted to prayer and undertook the journey to Rome. After completing his devotions at the thresholds of the apostles, without the knowledge of his entourage he secretly put on the monastic habit, and so secretly withdrew himself from the world together with the kingdom and cast both aside.

Soon afterward, struck by illness, he reached his final extremity and did not cease until his death to cry out these words, as though invoking the terms of a mutually agreed covenant: “Lord, I have done what you commanded; fulfill what you promised.”

Placed, as it were, in the vineyard, he demanded the coin because he knew that he had fulfilled the householder’s command. Although he had been hired at the eleventh hour, he demanded rest after his labor, and after completing the work he demanded his wage.

Let us not, then, hesitate to offer either ourselves or our possessions to God now, so that afterward we may be able to demand them back with full authority. And while we eat, let us not, by serving the needy sparingly, compel them to nibble as though they were abstainers, while we ourselves do not hesitate to consume laden platters. Nor should a measure by spoonfuls be applied to them, as some do, when pots and cauldrons scarcely suffice for us.

Fulcranus, the bishop of a certain region of Gaul—as the reverend Hugh, abbot of Cluny, related to me—was once asked by his steward what he wished to have prepared. He replied:

“Prepare according to the number of those dining, as you think appropriate. But for me alone present the finest pig, exceedingly fat and large, to the banquet-goers, so that no one may taste even the smallest lentil from it without my person being present.”

He therefore sat down to dine with the poor who were eating with him, consumed the entire victim with them, and offered no one else even the smallest morsel of meat.

## CHAPTER VII. Almsgiving benefits the dead and is hated by demons.

The same holy abbot related to me again that, while a certain man was traveling through various parts of the world in devotion to prayer, he came upon a desert where a certain holy brother lived in a cell. After some time, the hermit carefully asked the traveler whether he knew the monastery of Cluny.

Then he added: “I ask you, my brother, by the charity of God, that if you should perhaps happen to visit that venerable place, you tell the brothers and the abbot not to grow lukewarm in their devotion to almsgiving, but to persevere vigilantly and fervently in works of piety, as they are accustomed to do.

“For here hell burns with smoking flames, and from here the souls of the damned, as I have frequently heard, are plunged into Tartarus with great howlings and shrieks of weeping. But the prayers and almsgiving of that monastery strongly resist the evil spirits and rescue many from their hands like prey.”

After a long time the traveler came to the monastery and reported to the brothers, in order, what had been entrusted to him.

We are also sufficiently indignant at something that we do not doubt is done by certain people: they themselves lean against the raised platform of an elevated table, while the poor whom they feed sit on the bare floor among packs of dogs. They use cloths decorated with variegated embroidery, while food is placed in the laps of the poor.

Gothfredus, a most distinguished duke and margrave, told me that his own regional history records that the emperor Charles fought fifteen times against the king of the Saxons, who was still held in the error of paganism, and lost fifteen times. But after three further battles had been joined, Charles defeated him and finally secured him as a captive in victory.

On one occasion, while that same Charles was dining, enthroned—as was customary—on an elevated platform, while the poor whom he fed sat ignobly on the ground, the king, who was dining at a table far removed from the emperor, sent him this message through a messenger:

“While your Christ is said to receive himself in the poor, with what face do you persuade us to submit our necks to one whom you so despise and to whom you show no reverence of honor?”

The emperor, pierced in heart, grew ashamed, and was greatly alarmed that an evangelical sentence had proceeded from the mouth of a pagan. For the Lord says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

The emperor rejoiced that he had been rebuked in this way by one who, although he had not yet received the rudiments of the faith, was already proclaiming the fruit of faith—namely, works of mercy.

It must also be noted above all that washing the feet of the poor is most beneficial. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “If I, then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John XIII). And to establish this command with still firmer authority and impress it more deeply upon their minds, he added: “For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done, you also may do” (ibid.).

When the feet of the poor are washed in devotion to the one who gave this command, both the soul and the body of the person washing are certainly cleansed from sins. Hence Peter also says: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” [Col. 0221C] (ibid.).

Why, then, did Peter offer no other members of the body along with his feet except his hands and head? Because through these he expressed the works of the body and the thoughts of the mind: the head signifies the mind, while the hands signify the action of the whole body.

Moreover, Mainardus, the venerable bishop of Silva Candida, related to me that Pope Nicholas, of blessed memory, who departed this light in the Lord three years ago, never allowed a day to pass throughout the entire year without washing the feet of twelve poor people. If he did not happen to do it during the whole day, he completed this radiant work of piety at night.

But since I am granted to see more concerning the privilege of mercy and the dignity of almsgiving than I can express, I wish to exclaim briefly in its praise:

## CHAPTER VIII. Praise of almsgiving.

[Col. 0222A]

O power of almsgiving, which, like the stream of a well-watered spring, both washes away the defilements of sins and extinguishes the flames of burning vices! O blessed almsgiving, which draws the sons of darkness from the abyss of hell and brings those who have been adopted into the realms of heaven and the everlasting light!

You fly from the hands of the poor into heaven, and there prepare lodging for those who love you. If you are wine, you do not turn sour; if bread, you do not become moldy; if meat or fish, you do not decay; if clothing, moreover, you contract no age. You are continually preserved fresh and new, and as soon as your giver has died, you return to him immediately, multiplied.

You make those conspicuous who lie beneath the foulness of crimes [Col. 0222B]; you make saints from the condemned and Christians from pagans. Cornelius proves this, for his almsgiving ascended to the height of the divine presence (Acts X).

O rich almsgiving, which prepares for your lovers an unfading inheritance and the dignity of the heavenly court! O wondrous power of mercy, which cleanses the rust of every sin, mortifies the impulses of raging vices, and illumines the darkened minds of human beings with the splendor of heavenly grace!

You make God a debtor to human beings, so that they no longer seek the kingdom of heaven as though it belonged to another, but boldly seize it as though it were their own rightful possession. O blessed mercy, which indeed is born from misery, but produces true blessedness for those who carry it out!

You are a merchant more prudent than every huckster, purchasing heavenly things with earthly goods and exchanging eternal things for transitory ones. Happy are your transactions, in which lodging is given, a dwelling is received, a little bread is offered, a kingdom is received, a coin is extended, and the palace of heaven is acquired.

Among the other virtues, therefore, venerable brother, with which we do not doubt that the wisdom of your holiness flourishes, seize this one especially. Exercise yourself in works of piety; continually overflow with the bowels of mercy, so that you who now have mercy on Christ’s poor may afterward obtain mercy from Christ.

[Col. 0222D] Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0221]

# TENTH OPUSCULUM: ON THE CANONICAL HOURS. TO T. . . ., A MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN

## ARGUMENT

He explains the origin and mysteries of the canonical hours and enumerates their benefits. Therefore he urges a certain nobleman, to whom he sends this little book, not to neglect hearing the canonical hours or reciting them himself, and not to allow himself to be drawn away from so pious a work by any occupations. He also strongly commends to him the office of the Blessed Virgin.

[Col. 0221D] To my lord T. . . ., a most distinguished man, Peter, a sinful monk, sends prayers in Christ.

[Col. 0222D] While conversing with you, dearest friend, in the episcopal palace of Ravenna, I was suggesting to you certain precepts for living and urging you through various brief exhortations toward devotion to religion. At last the conversation reached the point at which I asserted that the seven offices of the canonical hours ought daily to be paid to God by all faithful Christians as a kind of service-obligation.

But what was then spoken by my flowing tongue, I judged it necessary to commit to writing, so that what you heard for a moment in simple words might not more easily slip away, but might cling more tenaciously to your memory, set before your eyes through the course of the moving pen.

## [ON THE CANONICAL HOURS]

## CHAPTER I. The effects of sins.

There are plainly seven principal vices (consult the scholia at the end of the opusculum), from which the other plagues of vices arise. These are pride, avarice, vainglory, anger, envy, lust, and sadness. Since these are the cause and origin of all evils, they are known to have effects corresponding to the same number: namely, seven criminal sins—adultery, murder, theft, perjury, false testimony, robbery, and blasphemy.

In these sins there is such certain and manifest death of souls that whoever dies caught in any one of them can in no way escape the sentence of eternal damnation.

Again, there are seven light and minor sins, into which not only the sinner but every just person falls daily, even if he seems already to stand upon the lofty summit of perfection. These are thought, ignorance, inconstancy, necessity, infirmity, forgetfulness, and inadvertence. Through these we continually offend in our daily conduct, and therefore against the wounds of sin we necessarily need the remedies of daily healing.

Hence it is written: “The just man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV). He is described as falling seven times and nevertheless being just because he does not cease to be just even while sinning, since he transgresses not deliberately but through human frailty.

Because of these seven light and minor sins, which we cannot avoid because of the weakness of human frailty, the devout teachers of the Church established, under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, that we should pay our vows to God seven times each day.

These seven offices of the canonical hours have been established in the bosom of the holy Church like seven baths of baptism, so that we may take care to cleanse the stains of the seven offenses that we contract through the daily conduct of this life by an equal number, so to speak, of streams of daily prayer. Thus the breeze of satisfaction may continually shake away the dust of corruptible life, and the frequent wave of poured-out prayer may wash away the mud of worldly conduct.

## CHAPTER II.

The hours of which we speak are these: Matins, namely Lauds, which are to begin between dawn and sunrise; then Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. It remains to say how many psalms the office of each hour contains, and why it neither falls below nor exceeds the prescribed number [Col. 0224A].

Matins, then, consists of five praises—namely, four psalms and one canticle. And fittingly, as the daylight breaks forth, we offer 213 praises to God, because under the appearance of outward light we await Christ, the Sun of justice, dawning in our hearts; and, as though the bridegroom were already arriving, the whole Church, rejoicing and exulting, goes out to meet him. Thus adorned with five praises, as though with an equal number of lamps received, and as though the cry of the final awakening had already been conceived in the ear of the heart—“Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him”—the evangelical saying is accordingly fulfilled in outward appearance: “Then all those virgins arose,” he says, “and trimmed their lamps” (ibid.).

That a canticle is added daily to the psalms in this office of morning praise seems to convey the mystery of both lives, namely the contemplative and the active. The Psalter, a vessel made in the form of a delta, is sounded by a plectrum striking its ten strings; but the canticle is expressed solely by the instrument of the voice. Therefore the former, because it requires the hands, signifies work and thus the active life; the latter, because it belongs to jubilation, signifies the contemplative life. And since we can scarcely persist in contemplation for even a little while, and then only intermittently and for a moment, whereas we are continually occupied in the conduct of active life, we rightly insert one canticle among several psalms.

For just as we ascend from the exercise of pious work to the summit of contemplation and, after the very brief [Col. 0224C] moment of inward vision, immediately turn back to the service of that same active life—so that our contemplation both begins from the active life and necessarily ends in it—in the same way we place the canticle neither before nor wholly after the psalms; rather, set between them on either side, we always place it next to last.

Moreover, because throughout the four seasons of the entire year we fatigue our body, itself likewise composed of four elements, by the exercise of action, we therefore sing four psalms in the celebration of this morning office. But because in the excess of contemplation we seek only one thing, which is unquestionably God, we fittingly sing one canticle as well.

That the canticle of Zechariah is also added at the end of the synaxis has a mystical significance: it is known to have been composed as the Old Testament was ending and the New Testament was already approaching, and it bears witness by the very time at which it is said that the night of vices has preceded and the day of virtues is approaching, as the Apostle declares (Rom. XIII). Let this brief preliminary treatment of Lauds suffice.

## CHAPTER III. Why the Creed is recited at Prime

The offices of Prime, Terce, Sext, and None likewise contain three psalms each; but in modern practice the catholic faith is fittingly added to the office of Prime—namely, the faith which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, is known to have transmitted with the greatest sincerity under the divine prompting of the Spirit. Since faith is the foundation and origin of the virtues, the canticle of faith, rightly joined to Prime, in a certain sense holds primacy over the entire day.

Indeed, the offices of the three hours—Terce, Sext, and None—are known to have come down to us from the teaching of the prophet Daniel. That holy man, as his own history testifies, turned toward Jerusalem in his upper room and offered the vows of prayer to the Lord three times a day.

Terce has, in addition, a privilege far more excellent: at that hour our Redeemer is read to have been crucified, according to Mark (Mark XV), and at that same hour the wondrous coming of the Holy Spirit refreshed the hearts of the apostles (Acts II).

Sext likewise is known to possess this privilege: at that hour Peter, standing above the upper room, prayed (Acts [Col. 0225B] X), and through the figure of various animals and reptiles learned by mystical revelation of the salvation of all the nations. At that same hour our Savior, as the other evangelists testify, was truly suspended upon the cross for the salvation of all (Matt. XXVII; Luke XXI).

Yet, lest anyone perhaps suppose that the holy evangelists, just as they appear to differ in the utterance of their words, also disagree among themselves in meaning, we say briefly that Mark asserts that the Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, while the other evangelists report him suspended at the sixth hour by the fastening of the nails. At the third hour they cried out, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him”; and thus the Jews crucified by their judgment the one whom the soldiers afterward fastened and hung upon the wood. Nor is the ninth hour deprived of its own title of honor, since the Lord is described as having given up his spirit at that hour, after completing the mystery of his Passion.

These hours, then, which are regarded as distinguished among the other hours of the day, and which, each with its own privileges, appear in a certain sense to be marked with the insignia of primacy amid a throng of special dignities, are separated from one another by an interval of the number three. Accordingly, when we offer the vows of praise at each of them, we demonstrate even through the course of time that we worship the one who remains one in the Trinity.

The fact that the same psalms are not sung at these four hours among the various orders of the Church—for among the clergy, the eighteenth after the hundredth [Col. 0225D] runs beneath the divisions of its sections, while in monasteries the canticles of the Steps follow their customary arrangement—proves, if we examine the matter carefully, that both practices are carried out fittingly. For since that lengthy psalm specifically directs the journey of those who are ascending, not only through its mystical sacrament but also because the way is frequently sounded upon the very surface of its words, while the Canticle of the Steps commends the stages of that same way, without losing the mystery of its depth, even through the transparent expression of its name, both are judged to have been harmoniously instituted for the completion of the office of those who proceed in the Church of God.

And because one does not differ from the other in variety of interpretation, whichever of them is sung does not depart from the straight line of concord. Prime, however, apart from Sunday, fittingly seems to begin the Psalter from its beginning, so that the origin of the day as it is born may also agree appropriately with the beginning of the book.

## CHAPTER IV. Why five psalms are said by the clergy and four by monks

Vespers does not have the same number of psalms among the various orders. Among the clergy it embraces five psalms, whereas among monks it is completed with only four. Yet neither practice is without reason, if it is investigated through a worthy inquiry.

The same explanation may reasonably be given for the five psalms of Vespers as was set out above for Matins. Since we know from the Lord’s own teaching that the judge of the human race will come at night (I Thess. V), but do not know at what hour of the night—whether at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning—because, as he himself declares, he will come like a thief, the holy Church of the elect rightly awaits her bridegroom in the office of evening praise just as in that of morning praise. She is suitably represented by the number of the five prudent virgins; and while she joins in song with five psalms, adorned with good works, she hastens joyfully to meet him as though with an equal number of lamps lit.

But the one who established four psalms is, unless I am mistaken, to be understood as having had this in view: just as there are four military watches, so likewise there are known to be four principal virtues—justice, fortitude, temperance, and prudence. In these we must remain continually watchful through the nocturnal darkness of this mortal life; and in the battle array of spiritual warfare, whose weapons we have sworn to bear, we must stand patiently in defense of our camp and fight without weariness. In this office of evening praise, therefore, we are instructed by the four psalms that we sing to keep vigilant guard over the four virtues.

The canticle of the Blessed Mother of God is also fittingly joined to the office of evening. For she, as though the long day of the past age had already run its course, precisely at the setting of the world as it grew toward evening, as soon as she conceived the light of the eternal Word in the flower of her blessed womb, immediately burst forth into a voice of divine praise: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” she said (Luke I).

In imitation of her, therefore, who is the mother of Christ, the whole universal Church, which is indeed the mother of Christians and carries in her mind the same light that she once bore in her womb, now that the day is growing toward evening magnifies God with worthy praise; and, giving thanks for the benefits bestowed, her spirit exults joyfully in God her Savior.

## CHAPTER V. Why three psalms are said by monks

Compline also varies according to this difference: among monks it consists of three psalms, whereas among the clergy it consists of four. The same explanation must nevertheless be given for the four psalms as was set out above for the office of evening praise: namely, that through the number of the fourfold psalmody we may be taught to take up, correspondingly, four weapons of the virtues. Armed with these, we may pierce the backs of thieving vices and repel the attacks of hostile spirits lying in wait.

Scripture describes such watches when it says: “Behold, around Solomon’s bed sixty strong men, among the strongest of Israel, stand guard; each has his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song I).

As for the three psalms, the Holy Trinity sufficiently supplies the required explanation: under its seal, Compline closes the day that has been completed. For just as the office of Prime, as stated above, is dedicated to faith in the Holy Trinity, so Compline is concluded with a confession of that same Holy Trinity, so that the one for whom the course of the entire day is understood to be a military service may also be the one in whom the closing of the completed daylight finally ends.

We have therefore touched briefly upon these offices of the hours of the day, so that we might explain more clearly for what purpose they were instituted and why they are concluded under a fixed reckoning of psalms. Whoever, then, offers these seven offices of the canonical hours daily to God with devotion—if he has kept wholly distant from those grave crimes, and has also restrained himself, insofar as human frailty permits and with the help of God who comes to his aid, from the seven lesser offenses enumerated above—will, as I confidently assert, be acquitted at the judgment of the fearful Judge from those things which he cannot avoid.

And because he does not now neglect to render to his Creator the appointed services of his bondage, he will then be able, with a free conscience and with blessed David, to sing in an eager voice: “Seven times a day,” he says, “I have given praise to you, Lord my God; do not destroy me” (Ps. CXIII).

## CHAPTER VI. That the Church’s prayer ought to be continual

Since the evangelical trumpet also rouses us to perseverance in continual prayer, saying, “We ought always to pray and never grow weary” (Luke XVIII), and the Apostle says, “Pray without interruption” (I Thess. V), ecclesiastical discipline has taken the greatest care to fulfill this command not only by day but also by night, so that the nocturnal vigils might be completed with twelve psalms.

It would indeed have been difficult for the sick, pregnant women, and people of every age and sex to rise during the intervals of the night and hasten to the Church just as they did by day.

Therefore, so that the discerning mistress, the Church, might moderate the labor, it was devised and established through a higher dispensation of counsel that, in accordance with the number of the nighttime hours, the order of the psalms should likewise proceed by twelves at the vigils. Thus the whole night might in a certain sense appear to have been spent in prayer, since one completed in prayer as many psalms as there were hours in the night.

The Prophet designates this nocturnal office when he says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet all these eight offices that have been described can also be distributed with equal proportion, so that four may suitably appear to belong to the night and four to the day: Vespers, Compline, Nocturns, and Lauds to the night; and Prime, Terce, Sext, and None to the day.

The very names of Vespers and Prime seem to support this assertion. Vespers is named from the evening star, which shines at the very beginning of night; and Prime, because the day begins from it, likewise makes this clear through the evident expression of its name. Since Vespers discloses the beginning of night, while Prime discloses the beginning of day, it follows that the offices are said to begin at one with the night and at the other with the day.

## CHAPTER VII. The penalty for exceeding the measure of food

This is plainly the twofold chariot in which the holy Church, now hastening toward the heavenly kingdom, is carried. Traversing in this chariot the journey of day and night, she is already joined in praising God to those of whom it is said, “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold” (Ps. LXVII), and later she will enjoy him through sight and through their blessed fellowship.

Concerning these it is certainly said through the Prophet: “They will not cease, night or day, to cry out, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Rev. IV).

Although the whole life of the just may reasonably be declared to be prayer, nevertheless we too, weak as we are, rightly trust that the command to pray always is fulfilled by us if we perform these canonical offices of ecclesiastical institution every day.

In Gaul, however, as we learned from the report of a particular man, the religious fathers of the monasteries, seeing that many of the brothers exceeded the measure of food handed down by the Blessed Benedict (chapter 39) and were unable to restrain themselves within the prescribed limit of the regular daily allowance, judged it prudent to add further psalms to each of the established offices of the hours, so that they might compensate by increasing the psalms for the excess of their more relaxed diet.

But perhaps you will object in irritation: “What have I to do, I ask, with the rule of monks? What concern is it of mine to learn things which it is not useful for us to know?”

Yet whoever undertakes to treat any subject must not satisfy only the person to whom he sends it; he must explain the matter by examining it from every side, so that one person may find the food he desires and another may not depart frustrated with an empty stomach.

Therefore, most noble and prudent man, never neglect these offices of ecclesiastical institution through any forgetfulness. Do not, occupied with however many secular concerns, pass over the sure remedy of your soul.

Moreover, if you can hear them in church from a priest, that is the safest course. Otherwise, whether you are riding out on horseback or are perhaps occupied with rural or any other labors, while you are at work, pay from the same tribute of the Lord to which you are enrolled whatever coin you have at hand. If there are psalms, let the appointed number be completed; if there is only one, let it be repeated as the canon requires.

But if you are entirely unacquainted with letters, you can fulfill what you desire by the Lord’s Prayer alone. Therefore, beloved, count these duties of Christian service not as a favor but as a debt, and attribute them wholly not to free choice but to necessity. Just as you do not cease to profess yourself a Christian, to imprint upon yourself the sign of the cross, and daily to invoke the name of the Lord, so do not at any time dare to pass over these duties because of obstacles presented by circumstances.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning a certain pious man devoted to the canonical hours

So that you may more readily heed these life-giving exhortations, I shall briefly explain what I recently learned while traveling to you.

In the suburb of Fano, namely three miles from the walls, there lives a certain man of moderate rank and means. Learning by chance that I was there, he hurried to me and, among other things, discreetly disclosed the purity of his chastity, which he maintained with his wife.

For a certain monk, who was in fact his uncle, had once declared that this man’s wife was related to him. Yet, because of his excessive simplicity, he was accustomed to call even some strangers his relatives.

The man gladly seized upon this saying and, after deliberation, remarked: “It is better to shine with the brightness of certain chastity than always to tremble under fear of uncertain incest.”

This man does not easily omit the canonical hours and ecclesiastical offices whenever he is able. For several years now he has also been accustomed to hurry on the principal feast days to the monastery of Saint Paternian, which is situated near the walls of that same city, and there to hear the nocturnal vigils.

He carries this out with such constancy that neither an inundation of rain accompanied by wind can restrain him nor the severity of winter hold him back. Often evil spirits cry out at him on the very road to frighten him and emit the din of a dreadful voice, but they show no visible bodily form.

A year ago, one night as he was hurrying to the aforesaid monastery, behold, wolves, dogs, and various monstrous creatures of raging animals formed a troop and rose up against him. Howling on every side and barking, they attacked him and tried to tear him with savage bites. At last he barely escaped from their teeth, stripped of both his cloak and his cap.

The signals for the vigils had not yet sounded. When he arrived and found the monastery doors still closed, he immediately prostrated himself in prayer before the threshold. After continuing in prayer for a long time, he finally arose and was greatly terrified to find the cloak and cap that he had lost lying beside him, thrown down there.

Whether this was done by angels, or whether the bloody robber, the devil himself, unwillingly returned what he had taken, may be questioned. Yet I would not unreasonably believe that the evil enemy himself was compelled to restore what he had taken and, to increase his own confusion and disgrace, was forced to serve the man whom he had injured.

## CHAPTER IX. How great is the efficacy of prayer

At another time, the same man of whom we are speaking was hastening in the silence of night to the aforesaid monastery. When he came to a stream that flowed across his path—called Argilla—which had swollen because its waters were then rising, he could not ford it.

He immediately devoted himself to prayer, and when the prayer was completed, wonderful to relate, he found himself transported to the farther bank.

I have related these things to you in order, most prudent man, so that I might clearly demonstrate how great is the care with which almighty God watches over those who reverently attend to the ecclesiastical offices.

Let your prudence therefore be ashamed to neglect the canonical hours, which you hear even holy rusticity celebrate with such glory. Indeed, whoever’s spirit burns somewhat more fervently with the love of God is moved even to this: not to regard it as burdensome to hear the hours of the Blessed Mother of God every day.

And since the opportunity has presented itself, I am not reluctant to write what else I have learned from this brotherly report, provided that you are not reluctant to hear it.

## CHAPTER X. How great is the efficacy of the hours of the Blessed Virgin

There was a certain cleric subject to many sins and especially polluted by the filth of carnal temptation. At last, seized by illness and brought to the point of death, he began, with his bowels trembling, to grow terrified and, as his conscience accused him, to fear the divine judgment from the depths of his being.

Finding in himself no hope based on any good work, he immediately turned entirely to seeking the help of the Blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and fled beneath her protection with the urgent anxiety of his heart, speaking approximately these words:

“I do not deny, O blessed queen of the world, that I have offended you in many ways. I have violated in my own body the seal of chastity and virginity, of which you are the mother. I am also wrapped in countless filthinesses of sin, and I am not found worthy to invoke with polluted lips you who are the sovereign of all purity.
