“Nevertheless, O gate of heaven, window of paradise, true Mother of God and man, you are my witness that I have given praise to you seven times a day and that, though a sinner and unworthy, I have not deprived you of the service of your praise at any of the canonical hours.”

When the cleric had uttered words of this kind, the most merciful Mother of God afterward appeared to him as he lay sick. She gently consoled him and announced that his sins had been forgiven through the generosity of divine mercy.

We nevertheless report this with trembling, because we do not know whether it truly occurred in accordance with the reliability of the account. But this we know beyond doubt: whoever diligently endeavors to perform every day the offices mentioned above in her praise acquires for himself, on the day of necessity, the mother of that very Judge as his helper and advocate.

Therefore, beloved, read through this little and unpolished work of writing by repeating it frequently. Pay attention not to how it is said but to what is said. Indeed, to put it so, take delight not in the straw or leaves of the words but rather in the marrow of their meaning.

Continually offer to God the obedience of the aforesaid hours, and diligently exercise yourself in the other pursuits of holy conduct as well, so that if you now, as a servant, have worn down the neck of your heart beneath his gentle yoke, you may afterward receive with glory, among the sons, your share in the inheritance of heaven.

## SCHOLIA

There are plainly seven principal vices, from which the other plagues of vices arise: pride, avarice, vainglory, anger, envy, lust, and sadness.

It is not surprising that the holy cardinal did not list gluttony among the capital vices, although according to the teaching of others he ought to have mentioned it—a fact that could not have escaped so learned a man. I nevertheless think that he did not remember gluttony because, farther below, among the lesser sins into which he says even every just person slips daily, he enumerates necessity and weakness. It is clear that gluttony is contained under these, since by its nature it is not a mortal sin.

It is evident that all the ways in which we sin through gluttony arise from frailty, since pleasure lies in ambush for us under the pretext of necessity. Thus teach John Climacus, *Steps* 14 and 15, and John Cassian, Book IX, chapter 7, *On the Spirit of Gluttony*. The latter appears to support our opinion when he says:

“Bodily weakness does not hinder purity of heart, if only those things are used which frailty, and not pleasure, demands.”

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0231]

# 221 222 THE ELEVENTH LITTLE WORK, THE BOOK CALLED *THE LORD BE WITH YOU*. TO LEO THE HERMIT

## ARGUMENT

He consults Leo, a hermit of wondrous holiness, about what should be thought concerning a certain doubt: whether, as some people believed, when someone recited the office alone in his cell, he ought to omit the phrases “The Lord be with you” and “Command, sir, that I be blessed” (*Jube, domne, benedicere*) as unsuitable to a single person. He says that he himself thinks otherwise for many reasons, yet takes refuge in Leo’s judgment. Finally, he pours himself out in praise of solitude.

To Lord Leo, enclosed by love of heavenly freedom, Peter, a sinful monk, whatever a servant and son may be.

Your Holiness’s prudence, beloved Father, does not fail to know that I regard you, above almost all mortals, not as some casual companion or friend, but as my father, my teacher, my master, and my chosen lord. I trust that through the urgency of your prayer I may find a place of mercy before the divine ears.

And what more shall I say? I have appointed you to be my angel, so that in doubtful matters, whatever counsel should proceed from your mouth for me as I hesitate and inquire, I might immediately accept without doubt as though the voice of a heavenly oracle were sounding in my ears through an angel.

Therefore, whenever some scruple concerning any matter creeps upon me, before I approach you for consultation I implore divine clemency within myself: that, making you as it were the instrument of his will, God may command me through your mouth what he decides I should do in the ambiguity before me.

Following this custom even now, I ask you to teach me about a matter concerning which many people frequently demand an answer from me. Certain brothers who follow the eremitical way of life often ask whether, when they live alone in their cells, they are permitted to say, “The Lord be with you” and “Command, sir, that I be blessed,” and whether, since they are alone, they ought to answer themselves according to ecclesiastical custom.

Some of them, reasoning among themselves, say: “Surely a blessing is to be sought from the stones or boards of the cell? Or should one say to them that the Lord be with them?” Others are afraid that, if they depart in any way from the order of ecclesiastical tradition, they will sin, as though they were diminishing the measure of divine service.

Thus, while a solution is sought from us, our equally uninformed mind is instead driven to inquiry. Surrounded by these narrow confines of questions, I return according to custom to my angel; I take the well-trodden path back to the fountain, not of Ciceronian eloquence but rather of divine wisdom.

## [THE BOOK *THE LORD BE WITH YOU*]

## CHAPTER I. Why holy simplicity is rightly preferred to the philosophers of the world

I reject Plato, who searches out the secrets of hidden nature, assigning boundaries to the circles of the planets and calculations to the courses of the stars. I make little of Pythagoras, who distinguishes all the climates of the spherical orb with his measuring rod. I set aside Nicomachus, whose fingers are worn down over calendars. I likewise turn away from Euclid, bent over the intricate study of geometrical figures. I declare all rhetoricians, with their syllogisms and sophistical quibbles, unworthy of this question.

Let the gymnosophists tremble, continually baring themselves through love of wisdom. Let the Peripatetics seek the truth hidden in the depth of the well. I seek from you the highest truth, namely that truth which has arisen from the earth, no longer lying ignobly hidden in a well, but manifested to the whole world and reigning in perpetual majesty in the heavens.

For what are the fabulous inventions of frenzied poets to me? What are the buskined tragedies of swelling tragedians to me? Let the crowd of comic writers cease to pour forth the poisons of lust from their clattering mouths. Let the crowd of satirists cease to burden its [uncertain: “clarnos”] with the bitter fare of captious detraction. Let not the orators of Cicero weigh out for me the carefully crafted words of elegant urbanity. Let not the rhetoricians of Demosthenes compose the crafty arguments of deceptive persuasion.

Let all those steeped in the dregs of earthly wisdom yield to their own darkness. Let those blinded by the sulfurous gleam of their murky learning offer me nothing. Let the simplicity of Christ teach me; let the true rusticity of the wise release me from the knot of my uncertainty.

For, in Paul’s words, “because the world through wisdom did not know God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I).

Therefore, let the letter that kills depart; let the life-giving Spirit stand beside us (II Cor. III). “The wisdom of the flesh,” as the same Apostle says, “is death” (Rom. VIII); but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God. It does not submit to the law of God; indeed, it cannot.

If the wisdom of the flesh cannot bend its neck beneath the law of God, how can the law of God penetrate eyes clouded by the smoke of pride?

Come, therefore, Father, quickly untie for me the knot of the question set before me. Do not allow a disciple of Christ’s humility to wander through the grandiloquent schools of swelling philosophers.

Let my angel tell me what the unlearned crowd of dialecticians does not know. Let wise ignorance tell me what foolish wisdom cannot grasp. Explain these matters wisely, dearest Father, so that once we have reached divine wisdom no one may thereafter find it necessary to debate their solution.

## CHAPTER II. Why one says, “COMMAND, SIR, THAT I BE BLESSED”

Perhaps you will first order me to untie the knot of this question in some fashion and afterward express your own judgment, following the practice of learned teachers who ask children what they think about whatever difficulty the proposed subject presents, so that they may first discover the disposition of their pupils through their own statements.

Accordingly, at your command I hesitate to express what I think about this doubt, subject, of course, to the faith, so that you may either correct what has been clumsily stated or approve by your authority what has been diligently resolved.

It does not, however, seem irrelevant first to try to show by what practice these expressions entered into use in the Churches; then, insofar as the grace from above grants the ability, to explain what seems to us concerning the matters proposed.

A reader, out of great humility, asks not to be blessed by the priest himself but by the person whom the priest has ordered, saying: “Command, sir, that I be blessed” (*Jube, Domne, benedicere*). The priest, in order to return an answer proportionate to such humility, does not delegate the duty of blessing to anyone beneath him; nor does he presume to give the blessing by himself. Rather, he requests that the blessing be bestowed by God, who is above all.

## CHAPTER III. Where “THE LORD BE WITH YOU” originated

The expression “The Lord be with you” is the priest’s greeting to the people. For he prays that the Lord may be with them, just as he deigns to say through the Prophet: “I will dwell in them” (Lev. XXVI). And to his disciples and all the faithful the Savior says: “Behold, I am with you” (Matt. XXVIII).

This word of greeting was not established by the recent invention of human judgment; rather, it is shown to have been taken from the ancient authority of sacred speech. If it is carefully investigated, it is found to have been used many times both in the singular and in the plural.

In the singular, as the angel says to the Blessed Mother of God: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke I). The angel likewise says to Gideon: “The Lord is with you, mightiest of men” (Judg. VI).

In the plural, as in the Book of Ruth Boaz greets his reapers, saying: “The Lord be with you” (Ruth II); and as in the Book of Chronicles a prophet sent by God is found to have greeted King Asa of Judah, returning victorious from battle with his army, saying: “The Lord be with you, because you were with the Lord” (II Chron. XV).

The Church, therefore, having received the priest’s salutary greeting, herself both greets in return and prays in greeting. She asks that, just as he desired the Lord to be with them, so he may also deign to be with him, saying, “And with your spirit”—that is, may almighty God be with your soul, so that he may be able to pray worthily for our salvation.

It should be noted that he does not say “with you” but “with your spirit,” so that everything carried out in the ecclesiastical offices may be understood to take place spiritually. And God is rightly desired to be with the human spirit, because rational man was created in the image and likeness of God in mind and spirit, and there he is capable of divine grace and illumination.

The episcopal greeting to the people, “Peace be with you,” or “Peace to you,” likewise did not arise from human reflection but flowed from the authority of sacred Scripture. In the Old Testament, an angel is found to have said to Daniel: “Do not fear, man of desires; peace to you; be strengthened and be courageous” (Dan. X). In the New Testament, the Lord is almost always read to have greeted his disciples in this way: “Peace to you” (Luke XXIII; John XX).

He commended this same form of greeting to those disciples when he said: “Into whatever house you enter, greet it, saying: Peace to this house” (Matt. X). It is therefore fitting that the successors of the apostles, namely the overseers of the Churches, should use this form of greeting, greeting the house of God, where all ought to be sons of peace, so that the greeting of peace, resting upon both those who greet and those who are greeted, may be fruitful for them all.

## CHAPTER IV. That, just as the rest of sacred Scripture is not subject to change, so neither is “THE LORD BE WITH YOU”

From what has been said above it is now clear that, just as prophetic Scripture, the chanting of the psalms, and even the grace of the Gospel came forth divinely for our knowledge, so too the expression “The Lord be with you” descends not from human judgment but from the authority of the Old and New Testaments.

Therefore, just as nothing is subtracted from or added to the authority of the divine Scriptures according to changing circumstances, but ecclesiastical custom is instead preserved in them, so likewise this priestly greeting is in no way subject to the contingencies of circumstances, so that it should sometimes be spoken and sometimes silently passed over. Even if several people are absent, it is unlawful for ecclesiastical tradition to be altered.

## CHAPTER V. That the holy Church is one among many and appears wholly in each individual
The Church of Christ is indeed bound together by so great a bond of mutual charity that, both in the many she is one, and in each individual she is, through the mystery, entire; so much so that the whole universal Church is rightly called the one bride of Christ, and each soul is believed, through the mystery of the sacrament, to be the full Church. For the whole Church was already prophetically present in Isaac’s nostrils when, speaking of the person of his one son, he said: “See, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field” (Gen. 27:27). And that needy woman who, at Elisha’s command, scattered a little oil like seed and soon gathered abundant produce as it overflowed into the vessels (2 Kings 4) plainly prefigured the Church.

If one diligently searches through the fields of sacred Scripture, one frequently finds the Church represented by the person of a single man or woman. For although the Church appears manifold because of the multitude of nations, she is nevertheless one and simple, united by the mystery of one faith and divine regeneration. And although seven women take one husband, a virgin nonetheless—and one—is said to be betrothed to that heavenly husband (Isa. 4:1). Concerning her the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

From these points, then, it is plainly gathered, as was said above, that when the whole Church is represented in the person of one human being, and the one Church is consequently called a virgin, the holy Church is both one in all and entire in each: in the many she is simple through the unity of faith, and in each individual manifold through the bond of charity and the diverse gifts of charisms—for all are from one.

## CHAPTER VI. Further concerning the unity of the universal Church

The holy Church, although diverse in the multiplicity of her persons, has nevertheless been fused into one by the fire of the Holy Spirit; and therefore, even if she appears divided into parts according to bodily location, the mystery of her inward unity cannot in any way be corrupted in its integrity. “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This Spirit, therefore, who is unquestionably both one and manifold—one in the essence of majesty, manifold through the various gifts of charisms—gives to the holy Church whom he fills the grace that she may be one in her universality and entire in her parts. Truth commended this secret of indivisible unity when, speaking to the Father about his disciples, he said:

“I pray not only for these, but also for those who are to believe in me through their word, that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one” (John 17:20–22).

If, then, believers in Christ are one, wherever a member appears to exist bodily, there also, through the mystery of the sacrament, is the whole body. And whatever properly belongs to the whole seems, in a certain manner, also to belong to the part; so that what the assembly of the Church proclaims together is not absurd if one person says individually, and what is rightly uttered by one may also be irreproachably spoken by many.

Hence, when we are assembled, we all rightly say:

“Bend your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor; preserve my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 85:1–2).

And when we are gathered individually, we appropriately sing:

“Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob” (Ps. 81:1).

Nor is it without reason that many of us say together:

“I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 34:1).

And often, when alone, we utter in the plural:

“Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together” (Ps. 34:3),

and many similar expressions. For the solitude of one person does not prejudice the plural words here; nor does the multitude of the faithful conflict with singularity there. Through the power of the Holy Spirit, who is present in each individual and fills them all, solitude is understood here as plural, and multitude there as singular.

## CHAPTER VII. If “The Lord be with you” is not said with reference to singularity, many other things must necessarily be omitted

Now let those who say, “Is a blessing to be sought from stones or the walls of a cell? Or should it be said to them, ‘The Lord be with you’?” answer me and tell me why those who are placed alone in the same cells say:

“Come, let us rejoice in the Lord” (Ps. 95:1).

Tell me, brothers—tell me, I ask, speaking with your permission—when you are alone, whom do you exhort? Whom do you invite to keep watch for the divine praises when you say, “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord,” or, “Come, let us adore the Lord, the King of martyrs”? This is indeed called an invitatory, and plainly for this reason: through it the people of the faithful are invited to praise God. But if you are then heard by absolutely no one, whom do you rouse with exhortatory words to rejoice in the Lord?

Come, I say, brothers, tell me further: if you do not look to the sacrament of ecclesiastical unity, but rather to the number of bodily persons present, to whom do you say:

“Rising at night, let us all keep watch”?

And to whom also:

“Refreshed in our limbs by sleep, let us all rise quickly”?

Why do you not certainly omit all the hymns and, finally, all the prayers that have been composed by teachers in the plural style—either passing them over in silence or forcibly reducing them to the singular number?

Moreover, when you come to the readings, since you consider it wrong to seek or give a blessing when no one is present, why do you read the homilies of the Fathers and the sermons of preachers? By the very manner of the reading, you seem to address the people and direct all your words, as it were, to a second person—that is, to hearers. To use the actual words of the homilies, whom, I ask, do you address when you say, “Listen, dearest brothers,” and what follows, when no brothers are there? If you wish, with the protesting style of the text, to bend these words forcibly to your singularity—and this is entirely impossible—you will now necessarily have to compose new ones in place of them.

Why also, when you have reached the prayers, do you say, “Let us pray,” when no one is there who ought to pray with you? Whom do you invite to the communion of prayer when you see that no one is present? And why, at the customary conclusion of the completed office, do you add, “Let us bless the Lord,” when no one is present to bless the Lord with you?

Consider these things, then, and many others too numerous to list, and observe the rule of ecclesiastical tradition uniformly, whether alone or with many. For if the teachers of the Church had judged it expedient, they would have handed down one order for individuals and another for many in the ecclesiastical offices. But, content to establish one order after removing all distinction, they taught us always to maintain one order through inviolable observance.

They foresaw that whatever is reverently offered in the divine services by any member of the Church should also be presented universally through the faith and devotion of all. For there is one Spirit of the Church, by whom one body is given life and preserved by Christ, its head. The whole Church, therefore, consists indeed of a structure of diverse members, but is unquestionably one body, founded upon the solidity of one faith and suffused with the one power of the life-giving Spirit. Hence the Apostle says:

“One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4:4).

It is therefore fitting that whatever is done individually in the sacred offices by any of the faithful should appear to be done unanimously by the Church herself through the unity of faith and the love of charity.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the sacrifice placed upon the altars is offered by men and women alike

This is why, in the very celebration of the Mass, after the words, “Remember, O Lord, your servants and handmaids,” it is shortly afterward added:

“For whom we offer to you, or who offer to you, this sacrifice of praise.”

These words plainly show that the sacrifice of praise is offered by all the faithful—not only by men but also by women—even though it appears to be offered specially by one priest. For what he handles with his hands in offering it to God, the multitude of the faithful commends with attentive devotion of mind.

This is also declared where it is said:

“Therefore, O Lord, we ask you graciously to accept this offering of our service and of your whole family.”

From these words it is clearer than daylight that the sacrifice placed by the priest upon the holy altars is offered generally by the entire family of God.

The Apostle plainly declares this unity of the Church when he says:

“One body, one bread, we who are many” (1 Cor. 10:17).

So great is the Church’s unity in Christ that throughout the whole world there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood. For just as the divinity of the Word of God is one and fills the whole world, so, although that body is consecrated in many places and on many days, there are not many bodies but one body of Christ.

And just as that bread and blood truly passed into Christ’s body, so all who worthily receive it in the Church undoubtedly become one body of Christ, as he himself testifies when he says:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:56).

If, then, we are all one body of Christ, and although we appear to be separated according to bodily appearance we cannot be separated from one another in spirit, since we remain in him, I do not see what harm there is if, as individuals, we also keep the common custom of the Church, from which we have never departed through the sacrament of indivisible unity.

When I alone speak the common words of the Church, I show that I am one with her and truly remain in her through the presence of the Spirit; and if I am truly her member, I appropriately fulfill the office of my whole body.

## CHAPTER IX. That the special function of any member is common to the whole body

In the human body, the eye, the tongue, the feet, and the hands naturally have different functions of their own. Yet neither do the hands alone touch themselves, nor do the feet walk for themselves, nor does the tongue speak for itself, nor do the eyes contemplate themselves. Rather, whatever each part of the body can do individually is shown to contribute to all in common.

And what is granted to each individual member by the distinct right of nature is judged to be done by the body itself—which is the whole of that member—so that it is not inappropriate to say that both the part performs the function of the whole and the whole performs the function of its part.

Hence Paul’s tongue truly says:

“I labor in the Gospel of Christ even to chains” (2 Tim. 2:9),

although his tongue itself is not bound. For, as the passage continues:

“The word of God is not bound” (ibid.).

And Peter ran to Christ’s tomb with John, although only the feet undertake the ministry of running (John 20:4). And Stephen saw the heavens opened, although seeing is properly the function of the eyes (Acts 7:56). And Isaac touched his son Jacob by feeling and touching him, although the capacity to touch or feel has been specially assigned to the hands (Gen. 27:21).

Whatever member is seen to do, therefore, is irreproachably said to be done by the body itself; and conversely, whatever the body does, the multitude of its parts consents to through cooperation.

## CHAPTER X. That the priest, a part of the ecclesiastical body, appropriately uses the words of the whole Church

What wonder is it, then, if any priest, who is unquestionably a part of the ecclesiastical body, alone fulfills the role of the Church that greets and returns the greeting, saying, “The Lord be with you,” and then responding, “And with your spirit”; if he alone again asks for and gives a blessing? Through the inward sacrament of unity, wherever there is one person of the same faith and fraternal devotion, that person is spiritually the whole Church.

There, the unity of faith neither admits solitude in one person nor allows a division of diversity among many. Indeed, what does it matter if a diversity of voices proceeds from one mouth, when, even if many tongues speak, one faith alternates between them?

The whole Church, as has already been said, is unquestionably one body. For, according to the Apostle:

“Just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Cor. 12:12–13);

and elsewhere:

“Together with his body, which is the Church” (Col. 1:24).

If, then, the whole Church is one body of Christ, and we are members of the Church, what harm is there if each of us uses the words of our body, that is, of the Church, since we are truly one with her?

Indeed, if many are one in Christ, each of us possesses in him what is wholly ours. Therefore, although we appear to be far removed from the Church through the solitude of our bodies, we are always most fully present in her through the inviolable sacrament of unity.

Thus what belongs to all also belongs to each individual; and what is specially particular to certain persons is likewise common to all in the integrity of faith and charity. Thus the people rightly cry:

“Have mercy on me, O God; have mercy on me” (Ps. 57:1),

and:

“O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 70:1).

And one person may rightly proclaim:

“May God have mercy on us and bless us” (Ps. 67:1).

Our holy Fathers judged this relationship and communion of Christ’s faithful to be so certain that they added it to the symbol of catholic profession and commanded us to repeat it among the very beginnings of the Christian faith. For as soon as we say, “I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Church,” we immediately add, “the communion of saints,” so that where we give God the testimony of our faith, there also we may consequently affirm the communion of the Church, which is one with him.

This, indeed, is the communion of the saints: that those who believe in one God are reborn through one baptism, confirmed by one Holy Spirit, and, through the grace of adoption, called to one eternal life.

Just as in Greek speech a human being is called *Microcosmus*, that is, “a smaller world,” because in material substance the human being consists of the same four elements as this universal world, so each of the faithful appears to be, as it were, a smaller Church. While preserving the mystery of the hidden unity, one person also receives all the sacraments of human redemption that have been divinely attributed to the universal Church.

If, then, it is beyond doubt that one person receives the common sacraments of the whole Church, why should he be forbidden to speak alone the common words of the Church, when the sacraments are plainly of much greater importance than words?

## CHAPTER XI. That the people of Israel built a structure to display their fellowship at the altar

If anyone should still arise as a slanderer of these arguments of ours, saying that what has been instituted for the common assembly of the faithful ought not to be appropriated by individuals, so that he may yield not merely to words but to reasons, we offer an example that we have learned from the authority of sacred Scripture.

It is well known, as is narrated in the book of Joshua, that the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, returning from the Israelites at Shiloh in order to enter the land of Gilead, their possession, built an altar of immense size in the land of Canaan.

When the people of Israel became gravely angry with them and took up arms against them, they were asked why they had rashly presumed to build an altar besides the altar of the Lord. They replied that they had done this not as an act of transgression but as a precaution for a future testimony:

“Lest,” they said, “your sons should say to our sons, ‘What have you to do with the Lord God of Israel? The Lord has placed the Jordan River as a boundary between us and you, and therefore you have no share in the Lord’; and by this occasion your sons might turn our sons away from the fear of the Lord” (Josh. 22:24–25).

If it is not clear to someone why we have brought this section of the history into the middle of our discussion, we shall briefly explain. The simplicity of certain brothers might be tested, so that they could in some way consider themselves separated from the fellowship of the faithful if, being placed in solitude, they did not dare to utter the common words of the Church in their prayers.

They therefore use the common words of the Church to show that they remain in ecclesiastical communion, and those very words satisfy the wavering mind, since they testify to the spiritual presence of the faithful.

Those men built the altar not for the use of sacrifices, but as a sign of their substitute fellowship with the Israelite people, just as they themselves say, as though already speaking in the person of their sons:

“See the altar of the Lord that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a testimony between us and you” (ibid. 22:27).

They did this as a testimony of their fellowship with Israel; we say these things as a sign of true ecclesiastical unity. They acted so as not to be despised by their brothers; we act so that we may not be tormented by our own thoughts. They built an imitation of an earthly altar; we display the reality of spiritual concord. They acted to show the testimony of their lineage; we act to preserve the inviolable sacrament of the new birth and fraternal communion.

## CHAPTER XII. Why a man married twice is entirely excluded from the priesthood, while one who has fallen into fornication is often restored to the order

Certain things are done in the Church that appear superfluous as far as the workings of human reason are concerned, but are divine if one looks to the inner sacrament of virtue. Who would not be astonished that canonical judgments have decreed that a man who has married twice may in no way be promoted to the priesthood, while a priest who has fallen into fornication may, after completing penance, be restored to the office of his former status?

Concerning fornication, the apostolic judgment is clear, for it is said:

“For neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

But concerning those who contract a second marriage, the text continues:

“A woman,” he says, “is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39).

The words of these two judgments plainly show that those who marry twice do not offend the rule of divine law, while fornicators are deservedly cut off from the kingdom of God because of the intemperance of their flesh (Heb. 9; Eph. 5).

What, then, is the reason that those who do not sin fall utterly from the hope of the priesthood, while those whom guilt excludes from the kingdom of God do not, if they repent worthily, lose their confidence in the ecclesiastical rank?

It is because, in those who are joined in a second marriage, attention is directed not so much to sin as to the sacrament of the Church. For Christ, who is the high priest of future goods and the true priest according to the order of Melchizedek, offered the lamb of his own body to God the Father on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the world. He is the husband of one bride, namely, the whole holy Church, who is unquestionably a virgin because she preserves the integrity of faith inviolate.

Thus every priest is commanded to be the husband of one wife, so that he may appear to bear the image of that supreme Bridegroom.

In those married twice, therefore, it is not the measure of sin but rather the form of the sacrament that is investigated. In their rejection, guilt is not punished; rather, the mystical rule of the true priesthood is guarded. Otherwise, how could something be counted among crimes that apostolic teaching permits to be done lawfully?

Moreover, the sacred canons mark as heretical, within the heresy of the Novatians, those who condemn second marriages.

To show, therefore, that we always preserve the mystery of ecclesiastical unity, we irreproachably use—even if the utterance of the words is not so necessary—

## CHAPTER XIII. That if “The Lord be with you” is rightly spoken between two persons, it may also rightly be said by one person alone

Now, preserving charity toward my brothers, I ask this as well: if two brothers are together, may one lawfully say to the other, “The Lord be with you”? For what is the reason that he speaks to one person in the plural, and that, setting aside the strictness of grammatical discipline, ecclesiastical custom is maintained?

As far as the art of speaking is concerned, a speech addressed to one individual would proceed with *tecum*, “with you,” rather than *vobiscum*, “with you all.” If, then, it is not permitted for someone to direct a plural word to one person, he must say individually, “The Lord be with you.” Anyone who crosses the threshold of the Church knows how far this departs from the rule of ecclesiastical institution.

For it is certain that neither the most blessed bishop of the apostolic see, when he privately offers service to God with a minister assisting him, nor any bishop or Catholic priest at all uses these words to another individual in that form.

But if the custom of venerable priests is praised, so that one person alone rightly says to another alone, “The Lord be with you,” and if this is neither discordant nor removed from the judgment of the ecclesiastical order, what objection is there if someone standing alone says the same thing? For just as that plural speech does not minimally correspond to one person as far as the letters are concerned, so it does not proceed between two persons as a plural expression.

Since ecclesiastical custom has such authority that every power of artificial eloquence humbly yields to it, and since the care is directed not greatly toward words but toward meanings, if the grammatical rule is rightly disregarded between two persons, it follows that it may also be irreproachably disregarded by one person.

Therefore, just as it belongs to ecclesiastical authority that “The Lord be with you” is rightly said between two persons, so it is not contrary to that same authority if the one who is alone says the same thing equally.

Finally, the same must be understood concerning its response, namely, “And with your spirit,” as well as concerning the blessing of the reader, which is to be sought and given individually. Here it is not properly the number of persons that is considered, but rather the sacrament of ecclesiastical unity: where neither unity excludes multitude, nor multitude violates unity.

For one body is divided among many members, and from diverse members one body is made complete. In the unity of the body, the multitude of its members is not confused; nor, in the plurality of the members, is the integrity of the one body violated.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the people of Israel maintained among themselves the rule of ecclesiastical unity

What wonder is it if this is said of the holy Church—that she is believed to be manifold in unity and one in multitude—when even carnal Israel, because he was united by lineage, appears already at that time to have maintained among himself the rule of this unity?

He sends messengers to the king of Edom who say:

“This is what your brother Israel commands” (Num. 20:14).

And elsewhere, when the king of Arad the Canaanite fought against Israel and, having taken spoils from him, emerged victorious, Scripture testifies that Israel, binding himself by a vow to the Lord, said:

“If you deliver this people into my hand, I will destroy his cities” (ibid. 21:2).

This is also plainly declared in the Book of Kings, when, upon David’s return to the kingdom, the Israelite people say to the men of Judah:

“I have ten parts with the king, and I am the firstborn; David belongs more to me than to you. Why have you wronged me, and why was I not informed first, so that I might bring back my king?” (2 Sam. 19:43).

If, then, that people, because they derived their origin from one stock—or rather because they held the worship of one God—speaks as one person in the singular, thereby testifying that it is one among many, what of the holy Church? She is sanctified and governed by one Spirit of God, instructed by the sacraments of one faith and one baptism, and called by the grace of adoption to receive the same inheritance. Surely she possesses such great communion among herself that individuals may use the words of all, and all may use the words of individuals.

This is also why, while engaged in the divine offices, we often sing in honor of one saint what we recognize to be appropriate to the whole Church together. Anyone who carefully examines the songs of the blessed Mother of God and of the other saints recognizes this without doubt.

## CHAPTER XV. That certain festivals are celebrated outside their proper time

The Church of Christ, who is the immovable pillar and has received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, is not subject to circumstances or numbers, but confines every manner of speech within the bounds of her law. She does not hunt after words but after souls.

Thus she does not attach great importance to the presence of bodies or to the divisions of time, but rather looks to the devotion and unity of minds. “She judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15).

This is why, in the most sacred solemnity of Easter, we say:

“O God, who on this day, through your Only-Begotten Son, having conquered death, opened for us the entrance to eternity,”

although we all know clearly that, according to the calculations of those who reckon dates, the Passover of the Hebrews—around which the Lord suffered and rose again—comes first; then, when the first Sunday thereafter occurs, the Easter festival dawns for us.

In the same sense we say “today” at the Ascension of the Lord and at holy Pentecost, although these festivals too are subsequently arranged according to the calculation of the paschal season.

The beheading of blessed John the Baptist is also celebrated in the month of August, although there can be no doubt that he was slaughtered by Herod at the time of the Lord’s Passion.

The same reasoning applies to the festival of Saint James and also to that of blessed Peter, which is called “of the Chains.” For since the Acts of the Apostles says:

“After Herod had killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, seeing that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter” (Acts 12:2–3),

and then adds:

“Now it was during the days of Unleavened Bread,”

and immediately continues:

“When he had seized him, he put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover” (ibid. 12:3–4),

it is without doubt clear that these events were carried out at one time of the year, while the solemnities established for their veneration were instituted later at another time.

For, as is well known, those festivals are celebrated around the end of July, at which time the Hebrew people are found to have celebrated neither the Passover nor that period of Unleavened Bread, if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. But because they could not be worthily venerated during the paschal solemnity, another time was provided by ecclesiastical arrangement for their observance.

I have spoken briefly about these sacred solemnities for this reason: that it might become plainly clear that the holy Church is not so constrained by the law of times as she restrains the seasons themselves according to her own will.

For the Church does not serve under the elements; rather, the elements themselves are subject to her and obey her. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles says:

“For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come—all are yours; and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. 3:21–23).

And, to show the greatness of the privilege of authority by which the holy Church excels, he says again to the same Corinthians:

“Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (1 Cor. 6:2–3).

## CHAPTER XVI. That in the Church one person rightly supplies the words of another

To return, then, to what was said above: what wonder is it if the holy Church, to whom such great power has been divinely granted, turns words that serve her to her own purpose, so that either individuals may speak the words of many or many the words of individuals?

Or what harm is there if things that properly belong to some are spoken by others?

Certainly we know that when children are catechized, the priest asks:

“What do you seek?”

There it is not the child but another who gives the reply in his place, saying, “Faith,” and the rest—things that properly concern the child—while another answers on his behalf.

If, then, in the very mystery of our regeneration, where the origin of the whole of human salvation is established, one person rightly speaks the words of another, what prevents another, in those ecclesiastical greetings or in blessings that are to be sought, from supplying by his response the place of the one who is absent?

The ability of one person to answer for another in the Church was not discovered by modern presumption; rather, it descends from apostolic authority. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians:

“But if you bless in the spirit, who supplies the place of the uninstructed person?” (1 Cor. 14).

Furthermore, if someone fears saying, “The Lord be with you,” or replying, “And with your spirit,” because of the absence of persons, he must also fear saying, “Let us pray,” and instead say, “Let me pray,” lest he appear to invite those who are absent to prayer.

And whoever considers it sacrilegious to ask for or give a blessing when no one is standing by should also beware of saying at the end of the reading:

“But you, O Lord, have mercy on us,”

and instead say, “Have mercy on me.”

But if this appears altogether inverted and altogether absurd, let the one who does not judge himself absent from the Church in mind and spirit not be afraid to utter the Church’s words alone. Let him not, by speaking, assert that he is divided from his own body when he professes himself specially to be its member. Since he is truly one with the Church of Christ, let him confidently fulfill the office of the whole, and strive rather to preserve the power of the ecclesiastical sacrament in these matters than to attend to the suitability of ordinary conversation.

## CHAPTER XVII. That almost everything done in the divine offices is arranged under mystical figures

For, as was said above, certain things are done in ecclesiastical observances that appear on the surface frivolous and light, but, when considered more subtly, are found to be supported by the weight of great significance.

To touch briefly upon a few among many examples: who, when he sees the priestly garments, would believe that there is anything worthy of admiration in them unless he understands that something is signified figuratively through them?

But if spiritual insight becomes clear, he notices why the sandals of clerics separate their feet from the earth while partly covering and partly leaving uncovered the upper parts of the feet. He also considers why the *poderis* descends as far as the ankles, why the *superhumerale* is always made of linen, and he weighs what the belt and the stole signify.

He likewise investigates why the dalmatic is square in the form of a cross; why the *casula* is to be placed over the other garments; and why the maniple is carried on the left side, with which, so to speak, the moisture of spiritual rather than bodily eyes or noses is wiped away.

Nor does he judge it to be without cause that the deacon who is not clothed in the dalmatic reads girded with the *casula*, or that the dalmatic itself has fringes on its left side.

Moreover, the custom by which the pallium is added to the pontifical garments was not maintained without purpose, just as in ancient times a plate was placed upon the forehead of the Pontiff for beauty and glory. On that plate the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, was written (Exod. 28), which was called “Holy to the Lord.” It consisted of only a few letters, but inwardly contained the power of a profound meaning.

But why should we pursue endless details, when almost everything performed in the divine offices under the Old or New Testament appears to be carried out through mystical figures and enigmas?

What do the entire arrangement of the tabernacle, the number of the Levites, the ceremonies of the priests, and, finally, even the present rites of the holy Church require, except that the power of spiritual understanding be sought in them?

To put it this way: mystery lies hidden in ministry, while through the exercise of external worship the sacrament of allegorical contemplation is grasped.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A brief epilogue to the completed little work

But leaving aside those matters that have been adequately explained by learned interpreters, let us briefly repeat what we undertook to discuss, so that it may become clearer.

The vice of arrogance is familiar to some readers, especially when someone possesses a certain elegance of eloquence. As an unrestrained tongue runs through the open fields of Scripture, a spirit of pride invades the heart devoted to popular favor; and while directing others along the path of the right road, it itself enters the side path of confused error.

This is also why, according to custom, the reader at table is told:

“May God remove from you the spirit of pride.”

Thus, so that humility may be placed against the arrogance that perhaps threatens at the very beginning of the reading, the blessing is rightly sought with so elaborate a form of submission that the one who is about to read is blessed not by the priest but by whomever the priest himself has appointed.

The priestly greeting is therefore given in the Church so that the priest may show that he is at peace with the entire congregation of the faithful. For in the Gospel the Lord commands, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father, who is in heaven, may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11). And again: “If you offer your gift at the altar,” he says, “and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you have come, offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

Thus, so that the priest may keep this command of the Lord not only in his heart but also display it through the outward form of the rite, before he offers the sacrifice of prayer to be poured out before God, he shows by the sign of mutual greeting that he is united with his brothers in unanimous charity. Therefore, whether they are present or absent, let him regard them as present with spiritual eyes, for whom he intends to pray; nor should he believe that those whom he includes together with himself in prayer are absent from him through spiritual fellowship. The gaze of faith, accordingly, directs itself toward the words of his greeting and receives what it perceives to be present nearby through spiritual presence.

Therefore, any brother who lives alone in a cell should not fear to utter the common words of the Church. Although local space separates him from the assembly of the faithful, the unity of faith nevertheless joins him in charity with everyone; and although they are absent through the masses of their bodies, they are present through the sacrament of ecclesiastical unity.

## CHAPTER XIX. Praise of the Eremitic Life

In the midst of these matters, I would like briefly to touch upon the merits of the solitary life and to make known what I think of the summit of the life mentioned above, praising it rather than debating it. The solitary life is truly a school of heavenly teaching and a discipline of divine arts. There God is everything that is learned; he is the way by which one advances and through which one reaches knowledge of the highest truth.

For the desert is a paradise of delights, where, like fragrant spices or gleaming flowers of aromatic plants, the perfumes of virtues breathe forth their fragrance. There the roses of charity flame with fiery redness; there the lilies of chastity shine with snowy beauty. With them, too, the violets of humility, content with the lowest places, are driven by no blasts of wind. There myrrh of perfect mortification exudes, and frankincense of unceasing prayer flows forth without failing.

And why should I mention each thing individually? Since there all the shoots of holy virtues gleam beautifully in diverse colors, and bloom incomparably with the grace of perpetual verdure. O desert, delight of holy minds and inexhaustible sweetness of inward taste! You are that Chaldean furnace where the holy youths restrain the power of the raging fire by their prayers and extinguish, through the ardor of faith, the globes of flame crackling against them; where bonds are burned, yet the limbs do not feel the heat, because sins are loosed and the soul is stirred to a hymn of divine praise, saying: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Daniel 3; Psalm 115).

You are the furnace where the vessels of the heavenly King are formed and, struck by the hammer of repentance and scraped by the file of salutary correction, arrive at perpetual brightness. In it, indeed, the rust of the worn-out soul is consumed and the rough dross of sins is cast away. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27).

O cell, apothecary-shop of heavenly merchants, in which the full store of those wares is kept by which possession of the land of the living is purchased! Blessed is the commerce in which heavenly things are exchanged for earthly, and eternal things for transitory. Blessed, I say, is the marketplace where eternal life is offered for sale, for the purchase of which even the smallest thing one possesses is sufficient; where brief affliction of the flesh buys a heavenly banquet, and scant tears produce everlasting laughter; where earthly possession is sold off and one reaches the inheritance of an eternal patrimony.

O cell, wondrous workshop of spiritual discipline, in which the human soul certainly restores within itself the image of its Creator and returns to the purity of its origin! There dull senses return to the sharpness of their acumen, and the unleavened bread of corrupted nature is restored in sincerity. You bring it about that faces appear pale through fasting, while the mind is fattened with the richness of divine grace. You bring it about that a person pure in heart sees God, although, wrapped in his own darkness, he previously did not know himself. You make a person return to his own beginning and call him back from the expulsion of exile to the height of his former dignity. You make a person established on the citadel of the mind see all earthly things flowing away beneath him, and see himself also passing along in the course of those fleeting things.

O cell, tabernacle of sacred warfare, battle order of a triumphant army, camp of God, “tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang upon you, every piece of armor of the strong!” (Song of Songs 4.) You are the field of divine battle, the spiritual arena of combat, the spectacle of angels, the wrestling-ground of wrestlers fighting bravely, where the spirit engages with the flesh and the strong is not overcome by weakness. You are the rampart of those running out on campaign, the fortification of the strong, the protection of warriors who do not know how to retreat.

Let the barbarian host of enemies roar all around; let siege sheds advance; let fire-tipped missiles be hurled; let the forest of flashing swords grow dense. Those who are in you, fortified by the breastplate of faith, rejoice beneath the unconquered protection of their commander and, already certain of the overthrow of their enemies, triumph. To them it is said: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent” (Exodus 14). Or, if there is only one enemy: “Do not be afraid,” he says, “for there are more with us than with them” (2 Kings 6).

O desert, death of vices and, without doubt, kindling and life of virtues! The law exalts you; prophecy marvels at you; and all who have reached the summit of perfection have recognized your praise. To you Moses owes the Decalogue of the law received twice (Exodus 24, 34); through you Elijah came to know the passing of the Lord (1 Kings 19); through you Elisha received a double share of his master’s spirit (2 Kings 2).

And what more shall I say? Since, at the very beginning of the world’s redemption, the Savior of the world made his herald a dweller in you, so that at the dawn of the coming age the morning star of truth might burst forth from you; after him the full sun, coming, might illuminate the world’s darkness with the rays of his splendor.

You are that ladder of Jacob (Genesis 28) which carries human beings to heaven and brings angels down to human assistance. You are the golden road that leads people back to their homeland. You are the racecourse that advances those who run well toward the crown.

O eremitic life, bath of souls, death of crimes, purification of the defiled! You purify the secrets of minds, wash away the filth of wickedness, and make souls reach the brightness of angelic purity. A cell is indeed a meeting place of God and human beings, a crossroads of those who live in the flesh and of those who dwell above. For the citizens of heaven gather there for human conversation; there it is not so much the tongue of the flesh that forms words as the fruitful secrets of minds that are disclosed without the din of speech.

A cell is the conscience of the secret counsel that God holds with human beings. O how beautiful is the sight of things when a brother established in his cell performs his nocturnal psalmody and, as though keeping military watch for the divine camps, stands guard! He contemplates in heaven the courses of the stars, while the order of the psalms passes through his mouth. And just as the stars that precede and follow one another reach the day by alternating their turns, so the psalms, proceeding from his mouth as though from a kind of eastern dawn, gradually run toward their completion in an equal procession with the stars.

The brother performs the service of his obligation; the stars carry out the duty assigned to them. He, by singing psalms, inwardly advances toward the inaccessible light; they, succeeding one another, restore for his outward eyes the visible day. And while both hasten toward their own completion by different paths, even the elements themselves somehow agree in serving God’s servant.

The cell is witness when the heart burns with the fire of divine love and when a person seeks the face of God with the urgency of perfect devotion. It knows when the human mind is drenched with the dew of heavenly grace and watered by the rains of overflowing tears through compunction. Even if tears do not burst from the bodily eyes, the bitterness of the heart is nevertheless not distant from waves of tears, because what is not gathered from the branch of outward circumstance is preserved in the ever-green root of the moist heart. It is enough for the mind to be tearful, even if it cannot weep continually.

The cell is a prison-workshop where precious stones are polished, so that afterward they may be placed in the structure of the temple without any sound of the craftsman’s hammer.

O cell, almost like the Lord’s burial place, which receives those dead in sin and makes them live again for God through the breath of the Holy Spirit! You are a tomb separating us from the troubled agitation of this life, but you open the entrance to heavenly life. Those who escape the shipwreck of the world’s waves find in you a harbor of tranquility. Those wounded in battle who have escaped the hands of their enemies recognize you as the chamber of a powerful physician.

As soon as a person withdraws with a perfect heart into the shade of your summit, every bruise of the wounded soul and every wound of the inner person is healed. Jeremiah had looked upon you when he said: “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth: he will sit alone and keep silent, because he will lift himself above himself” (Jeremiah 2).

For your inhabitant raises himself above himself, because the soul hungering for God lifts itself away from the sight of earthly things and suspends itself on the citadel of divine contemplation. It separates itself from the activities of the world and balances itself aloft on the wings of heavenly desire. And when a person eagerly strives to behold him who is above all things, he also transcends himself, together with all the abasement of the world’s valley.

O cell, wholly spiritual dwelling, which makes the proud humble, the gluttonous temperate, the cruel compassionate, the angry gentle, and the hateful ardent in fraternal charity! You are a bridle for the idle tongue; for lustful loins you provide a belt of shining chastity. You bring it about that the frivolous return to seriousness, that those given to joking refrain from buffoonery, and that the talkative bind themselves under the strict censure of silence.

You are the nurse of fasts and vigils, the guardian of patience, the teacher of the purest simplicity, wholly ignorant of deceitful duplicity. You cause Christ’s chain to restrain the restless, and those undisciplined in conduct to curb their own depravity. You know how to raise people to the summit of perfection and exalt them to the height of consummate holiness.

You make a person smooth and rounded, no longer differing from himself through any unevenness. You also make a person a square stone, suitable for building the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem: one who does not show himself changeable through fickleness of conduct, but remains always fixed in the gravity of holy religion.

You make people strangers to themselves and cause vessels of vices to flourish with virtues. You are black, but beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. You are the washing-place of the shorn ewes. You are like the pool in Heshbon. Your eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and sitting beside fullest-flowing streams (Song of Songs 1, 4, 5, 7).

For you are the mirror of souls, in which the human mind, looking carefully at itself, fills what is lacking, restrains what is excessive, straightens what is crooked, and orders what is deformed.

You are a bridal chamber in which the pledge of the Holy Spirit is bestowed and the blessed soul is joined in covenant with the heavenly Bridegroom. The upright love you; those who flee from you, deprived of the light of truth, do not recognize where they ought to set their steps.

“Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you” (Psalm 136), “if I do not set you at the beginning of my joy.” I also gladly sing this about you, with the same Prophet, in a cheerful voice: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it. How beautiful you are, and how lovely, dearest one, in delights!” (Psalm 131.)

In your figure, Rachel was adorned with the beauty of a lovely face (Genesis 20); and Mary chose the better part, which would never be taken away from her (Luke 19). You are a bed of spices, a fountain of gardens, a pomegranate. Although to those who do not know you, you may seem bitter in your rind, great indeed is what lies hidden within when one reaches the sweetness of the kernel.

O desert, refuge from the world’s persecution, rest of those who labor, consolation of those who mourn, refreshment from the heat of the age, rejection of sin, freedom of souls! David sought you when he endured the world’s evils and suffered the weariness of a timid and darkened heart: “Behold,” he said, “I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Psalm 54).

And why should I mention others? Since the Redeemer of humankind himself, at the beginning of his manifestation, deigned to visit you and consecrate you by his own dwelling. For after he had washed the water of baptism—in which he had been washed—as the Evangelist testifies, the Spirit immediately drove him into the desert: “And he was in the desert forty days and forty nights; he was tempted by Satan, and he was with the wild beasts” (Mark 1).

Let the world acknowledge that it is indebted to you, since it knows that from you God undertook to preach and perform miracles. O desert, dreadful dwelling for evil spirits! There the monks’ cells, like tents arranged in a military camp, are raised like the towers of Zion and like the fortifications of Jerusalem against the Assyrians and against Damascus. Indeed, since different duties are performed in these same cells by one spirit—here psalmody is sung, there prayer is offered, in another place writing is done, and in others various manual labors are pursued—who would not see that these divine words are suited to the desert, in which it is said:

“How beautiful are your tents, Jacob, your dwelling places, Israel: like wooded valleys, like gardens beside irrigated rivers, like tents that God has fixed, like cedars near the waters!”” (Numbers 24.)

And what more shall I say of you, O eremitic life, blessed life, garden of souls, holy life, angelic life, chamber of heavenly gems, court of spiritual senators! Your fragrance surpasses the scent of all spices; your taste, sweeter than dripping honeycombs and all honeys, sweetens the throat of the enlightened heart. Therefore, whatever is said about you does not equal the merits of your dignity, because the tongue of the flesh is utterly unable to express what the spirit invisibly senses about you; and what you taste in the inward palate and in the marrow of the heart, the bodily organ of speech has scarcely ever been able to explain.

Those who love you know you; those who delightfully rest in the embraces of your love recognize the praises of your glory.

Those who are ignorant of this cannot prevail to know you. I also confess that I am unequal to praising you, but I know one thing for certain, O blessed life, which I affirm about you without hesitation: whoever strives to persevere in the desire for your love is indeed your inhabitant, but God is his indweller.

The devil serves him through his temptations and groans because he is striving to reach the place from which the devil himself was cast down. Thus, victorious over demons, he becomes a companion of angels; an exile from the world, he is an heir of paradise; one who has denied himself, he is a follower of Christ.

And he who now walks in Christ’s footsteps will, when his course is completed, without doubt be raised to the glory of Christ’s fellowship. To say it confidently: whoever has maintained this solitary life for divine love until the end of his life, after departing from the dwelling of the flesh, will reach the ineffable building, the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

## CHAPTER XX. Conclusion of the Discussion, by an Apostrophe to the Hermit Leo

Behold, dearest Father, having been prompted by your fraternal inquiry, I have proposed to you the question that needed to be resolved; meanwhile I myself have not delayed to set forth what I thought—not, certainly, to teach others by assuming the authority of a teacher, but rather to explain clearly to you what opinion might be held of my incompetence.

For that reason, whatever has been contained in the foregoing discussions has been put forward not so much with the zeal of assertion as under a kind of suspension before your judgment. It is not a definitive sentence but a debate tested by reasoning. Therefore, dearest one, after carefully examining everything that we have arranged in whatever manner, if anything has been wrongly assumed, boldly erase it at once with the razor passed over it; or, if it perhaps accords with sound doctrine through your merits, confirm it by the force of your own authority.

I could indeed have compressed what was said at greater length into a shorter form; but, I confess, I was pleased to prolong the conversation afforded by your sweetness. For one gladly spends a long time grinding spices, especially when the fragrance of the one to whom the service is offered is sweet.

May almighty God, by hidden inspiration, command his servant Leo to pour out for me, miserable as I am, either tears or sighs three times each day.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0251]

## OPUSCULE TWELVE. AN APOLOGETIC WORK ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD. TO ALBIZO THE HERMIT AND PETER THE MONK

### Argument

In this little book he deplores with all the intensity of his soul the pitiable condition of religion in his own time, daily sliding into worse because of contempt for monastic discipline. He attacks monks who, although they profess to have renounced the world, are nevertheless held entangled in the world’s waves and affairs. He complains that among them the laws and institutions of the Fathers have no authority, since, despite the gravest sacrilege being threatened against those who keep money privately, individuals possess and openly seek it without fear.

He enlarges upon their frivolity and inconstancy, because they do not remain in their cells as they ought, but wander everywhere indiscriminately, with the result that they fall into the gravest sins. He detests their pride and arrogance: that they wear splendid garments and that they seek popular approval through simulated goodness. He then vividly describes and places before their eyes the external occupations and burdens of secular affairs with which they entangle themselves. Finally, he concludes by begging them that, if they care for their salvation, they should withdraw themselves entirely from the world and make it publicly clear by their actual conduct, not merely in appearance, that they have renounced the world.

## [AN APOLOGETIC WORK ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD]

### CHAPTER I. He Complains of the Decline of Monastic Discipline

Concerning contempt for this world, dearest brothers—namely, you venerable hermit Albizo, and you, Peter, formerly a rhetorician of the world but now a philosopher of Christ—we have often, as you know, been accustomed to discuss matters with a certain familiar devotion. We have grieved both over our own imperfection and complained about certain brothers of this sacred army who wander along precipitous paths.

For this world is daily rolling downward into such mire, becoming worse than itself, that not only does every order, whether secular or ecclesiastical, lie fallen from its proper state, but monastic discipline itself, so to speak, has been laid flat on the ground and languishes, having declined from that accustomed perfection of its lofty position.

Modesty has perished, honesty has vanished, religion has fallen, and, as though in an organized procession, the whole company of holy virtues has withdrawn far away. For everyone seeks his own interests (Philippians 2), and, having despised heavenly desire, greedily craves the earth. And because they do not cease to pant after it even at the very end of the world, like those carried ashore after the deep sea, they uselessly strike the earth with their oars while still hastening stubbornly to sail. Although the end of labor is unquestionably rest, those to whom a place of rest is freely offered wear themselves out in punishment through a superfluous zeal for labor.

### CHAPTER II. On Monks Who Return to What They Had Abandoned

Let it be so, then, that the children of this age toss about in the wave-tossed flood of secular storms and scatter the seeds in which they take greater pleasure, so that later they may reap not the harvests they would have wished. For what business is it of mine, according to the Apostle, to judge those who are in the world? (1 Corinthians 5.)

But we, who are called renouncers of the world and boast that we have escaped the shipwreck of earthly waves, why do we slide back again into it, as though violently swallowed by some whirlpool? Why, striving backward with retreating steps, do we return with an evil, fevered desire to those things that we despised for the love of God? Why are we not afraid to seek again, through the importunity of dishonorable ambition, what neither earthly law nor the authority of divine law had forbidden us to possess?

We ourselves acted so that things justly possessed by us would no longer be ours, and so that what had belonged to our right would emerge transferred into another’s ownership. What, then, was the purpose of bringing ourselves into such a dangerous contest, that now we must fight against the decrees of all human and divine laws, whose peace we had enjoyed? We began the war of our own accord, although we had not been provoked, and now we are not afraid to contend against the declarations of Holy Scripture.

### CHAPTER III. That Ananias and Sapphira Sinned Less Than Monks Who Possess Money

Who, I ask, compelled Ananias and Sapphira to renounce their own possessions? (Acts 5.) But because each of them retained part of the money for the supposed support of a long life, neither escaped the sentence of sudden death. And because they were by no means content to live according to the rule of those who had renounced possessions, they were compelled, in accordance with the punishment of transgressors, to breathe their last unhappily through a premature death.

Indeed, they were inexperienced and had only recently come to the faith; perhaps they had not yet fully learned the Gospel commandments, and the sacred books of the new teaching had not yet been publicly circulated for common use. Nevertheless, although they sinned with a certain simplicity at the very beginning of their faith, they were punished by a strict but merciful judgment only with the death of their bodies, as we believe.

But we, who know all the volumes of sacred speech, who keep before our eyes in constant examination the lives and precepts of innumerable holy Fathers who lived after that golden age of the apostles—what excuse can we offer before the tribunal of Christ? What argument of evasion can we find?

Behold, we not only abandoned far nobler profits and every kind of earthly gain, but also professed their perpetual renunciation not to a human being but rather to God. If, then, a coin is still enclosed in our purse, if any amount of money is reserved to the injury of the inner observer, what shall we say to him when we render our account? By what art of defense shall we cleanse ourselves?

To this is added the fact that they, with their faith still wavering, seemed unable to rely upon any ecclesiastical support, since at the very beginning of the Christian religion the churches themselves had not yet been constructed as material buildings.

But we, who see throughout the whole world such abundant church patrimonies that, while the world contracts daily through diminished possession, the Church expands most richly—if we store up carnal gain as provisions for the future, growing rich while providing for ourselves afterward, we show that we are empty of the treasure of faith.

Of this the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4). And while we break the pledge that we made with Christ, we can hope for no rewards from our conversion; rather, we ought to fear the punishments of violated faith.

For in an agreement made between two parties, the voice of a promise proceeds from both sides, so that whichever party keeps what was agreed receives the measure of the reward determined; conversely, whoever violates it incurs the loss resulting from the broken pledge.

In that agreement by which we entered into a covenant with our God, our voice was certainly this: that, following Christ, we promised to renounce the world and everything belonging to the world. The divine voice then responded accordingly: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

This is so if we keep the terms of the pledge we undertook. Otherwise, if we look back behind us, we soon hear the terrible oracle of divine threat: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

Behold, we have heard that those who renounce everything perfectly are promised not ordinary gifts but thrones—thrones from which they will become judges, who once feared being judged for their own excesses. Certainly, it was fitting that this change effected by the right hand of the Most High should take place, so that those who for Christ’s sake became poor through love of perfection might now, having become rich with him, sit together as senators of the heavenly court, as it is written: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Proverbs, final chapter).

### CHAPTER IV. That a Monk Cannot Possess Both Christ and Money

Whoever returns to the earthly things he abandoned by piling up whatever possessions he can, just as he is alien to the world from which he had resolved to strip himself, so too he is no longer fit for the kingdom of God, which he refused to possess although it was surely offered.

He is a foolish traveler: he can neither return to the place from which he irrevocably departed nor reach the destination to which he had intended to go. For when we renounced the world, we established God as our property; consequently, we became his property, so that he might be our portion and we, in a special way, his inheritance.

For we say: “You are my portion, O Lord” (Psalm 118). And he says to us: “You are the work of my hands, my inheritance, Israel” (Isaiah 19). Concerning earthly inheritance it is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Proverbs 20).

If, then, almighty God deigns to be our portion, what kind of wealth, I ask, will anyone be able to acquire that ought rightly to be piled above this unique treasure? That treasure is of such a kind that, if it alone is possessed, all riches can truly be possessed in it. For in the breast of Jesus “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2).

But if the one who possesses him wishes to heap other and foreign riches upon this treasure, he immediately disdains all fellowship with such a worthless and ignoble abundance. Unable to endure an unworthy companion, it is lost even while it is thought to be retained; and in this way it flies away from the frustrated possessor’s hands: “No one can serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6).

Therefore, monk, do you wish to store Christ in your little chest? First cast out the coin; for the two cannot suitably be joined in one receptacle. If you enclose both together, you will find yourself an empty possessor of one without the other. For the richer you are in the needy profits of the world, the more miserably you become empty of true riches.

Therefore, if there is money, let it immediately pass into the rights of others, so that Christ may find the chest of your heart empty. The great guest seeks to descend into the narrow space of your lodging, and for that reason he wishes to dwell alone and without companions. How can you attempt to introduce foreign associates to live with him in the small corner of your dwelling, when the vastness of heaven and earth cannot contain him?

Let earthly money give way—let it give way—where the heavenly treasure is admitted: “What fellowship does light have with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6.) What agreement has God with Mammon of iniquity? Let money therefore be cast away, subject to rust, moth, and theft. Let the chamber of the heart be vacant, so that it may be filled with heavenly commerce: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal” (Matthew 6).

### CHAPTER V. That It Is Better to Retain What One Has Than to Seek Again What One Has Cast Away

Money is more dangerous to the soul when it is acquired than when it is possessed as something freely supplied. In the latter case there is, in the earthly manner, legitimate possession; in the former, deadly ambition often rules. It would therefore have been healthier to possess what one had with a tranquil mind than to seek again what one had cast away, not without the anxious bitterness of troubled resentment.

Be ashamed, then, O soldier of Christ, to grow rich in perishable resources in this age, lest in the future you be compelled to beg forever, naked and destitute. For you swore an oath to the weapons of such a military service as seeks warriors who are naked and agile; but it excludes those who are laden and sluggish in God from the watches of the camp, exempting them from military pay.
