That warfare rejects one burdened with baggage and rightly, in shame, substitutes the equipped man before the proper time. It is not permitted for purses of coins to hang there where only cases of flashing weapons are seen. In a warlike battle line, one cannot safely serve inert money while fighting continually in densely packed ranks.

The man who is surrounded by a multitude of enemies and constantly awaits the missiles of weapons does not calmly count up a sum of solidi. Often in such circumstances, while a talent of some metal is being weighed, an unexpected arrow from a hidden enemy comes and is driven into the stomach of the one weighing it. Thus it happens that the man who seemed unable to suffice for himself alone without the support of household property now mourns that he and his possessions have been irrecoverably lost through a sudden disaster.

And the man who, poor with Christ, disdained to live in freedom is compelled to die damnably, rich without him but a slave to money.

Hear what the divine voice promises the rich: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation” (Luke 16). Do not overlook what James also says: “Woe to you who are rich; your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths, your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire” (James 3).

### CHAPTER VI. That the Greedy Man Who Worships Money Is More Truly Called a Money-Worshiper Than a Christ-Worshiper

Have you heard, I beg you, money-worshiper and monk, what the heat of greed produces for you? Have you heard to what end hoarded money leads? It is just that the flesh itself of the one whose mind now burns with carnal love in desire should afterward be burned in punishment.

Now the furnace of the mind is kindled by the invisible heat of desire; it is fitting that then, too, the material flesh should be endlessly consumed by the flames of fire.

Hear further, money-worshiper: when I call you a “money-worshiper,” I derive the name from the quality of your activity; I am not using the word as an insult against you. You worship coins, since you love money. And when the Lord says through the Prophet, “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 45), you offer to coins the worship of leisure that you ought to have offered to God, since you are at leisure in guarding them.

“For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matthew 6). Therefore, just as one who worships Christ is rightly called a Christ-worshiper, so one who serves coins by guarding them is not unjustly called a money-worshiper.

But perhaps I may be judged still to be following the inclination of my own heart in explaining this name, if I do not confirm its etymology by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. Truth itself says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6), as though it plainly said: No one can worship God and money at the same time.

The Apostle makes this clearer when he says: “But know this, understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—for he is a worshiper of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5). Thus, while he simply enumerates so many crimes and asserts that covetousness alone is the worship of idols, he teaches more clearly than daylight that the covetous person is a worshiper not of God but of money, and therefore of demons.

But while I linger too long in explaining the name “money-worshiper,” I turn the hand of my discussion—or rather, of my dissipation—away from pouring out the very heap of money. Having therefore satisfied you regarding your proper name, money-worshiper, listen attentively now to what I was going to say.

Hear, then, what Truth says about you and those like you: “It is difficult for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19). This sentence concerns those who possess riches according to the custom of the world. But those who, after casting everything away, have returned again to their vomit cannot, unless they repent, obtain the kingdom of heaven with any confidence, or even with difficulty.

### CHAPTER VII. That Even a Small Amount of Money Harms a Monk’s Soul Terribly
[Cols. 0257C–0258B]

But from this number of money-worshippers there will perhaps be some thick-headed person who will answer me as follows: “Why do you attack my wealth so sharply, when you see that I am content with a very small sum and scarcely have a few obols? Since I admit this in agreement with my own weakness, I am looking only to provide for a future necessity; I am not seeking to abound in riches. With the whole assembly of my brotherhood as witness, I receive nothing from my monastery’s resources, from the thread of the undergarment to the strap of my shoe; and if I completely empty myself of whatever little possessions are my own, how am I to live?” Behold our proprietor—or better, as before, our money-worshipper—uses poverty as his defense, so that he himself may appear irreproachably rich. With what disguises of argument does he cloak his deadly vice, so that, in a manner of speaking, a tomb full of foul corpses may gleam white beneath its coating of lime?

Come, brother: if you were permitted to expect some advantage from the monastery’s expenditures, would you not wear the garments as soon as they were provided, rather than receive profits in money, which you would keep to serve your purses? Why do you not use the same economy even with what is contributed by outsiders? That is, once any gift has been received, why not immediately purchase what is necessary, so that the poison of money does not linger with you? In this way the swift consolation of your need is advanced, and the leprosy of money does not sprinkle you with its foul spots.

Why do you applaud yourself as though secure because your money is little, when you do not deny that a *chalcus*—a small bronze coin—is forbidden to you just as the *as* itself is? When the whole of anything is prohibited to someone, he gains no escape for excuse from its tiny parts; and when everything has been surrendered, doubtless no part remains—especially since this is the nature of the human mind: when it is needy, it occupies itself with small things just as, when it is rich, it occupies itself with great ones. Whether you overflow with the costly inundation of riches or are pressed by the narrowest poverty of household goods, that saying cannot be changed: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. VI).

Croesus and Amyclas are indeed possessors of different kinds, but they display no different desires toward the things they enjoy. Although one measures out gold pieces and the other counts thousands, they are divided by the quantity of their resources, but they are held by no dissimilar love for what is individually available to each.

Moreover, if the tiniest mouse—or whatever small creeping creature—should by chance fall into the largest possible tub, would people not immediately rush together from every side with axes, pour out everything that it was, and, while everyone retched, feel sick with their stomachs threatening to vomit? If the thinnest drop of poison is poured into a broad pot of cooked vegetables, is not the entire dish judged utterly loathsome, however nourishing it might otherwise be?

If therefore very small evils so often corrupt the most abundant goods, how do you boast before your flattering conscience because what you possess in private ownership contrary to the purpose of your profession is little? For according to the Apostle: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V). And elsewhere: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccli. X). Our first parents, after all, did not gorge themselves at frequent banquets upon that forbidden fruit (Gen. III), by one taste of which alone they are read to have been corrupted; nor were they therefore entangled in the punishment of immediate retribution because they did not remain transgressors in their guilt for a longer time.

## CHAPTER VIII. How a monk can attain true riches [Cols. 0258C–0260C]

If therefore, brother, whoever you are, you take pleasure in acquiring resources with which you can meet a future poverty, prudently seek true riches and fear the want of true poverty. In view of that poverty, this poverty is very easily despised; in comparison with those riches, every abundance of earthly substance is scorned like shoreweed, which is trampled underfoot.

Therefore, if you truly strive to escape the misery of that most wearisome poverty, labor diligently in the field of your heart by sowing the finest crops. For the Apostle bears witness: “Whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. VI). And again: “Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in due season we shall reap, if we do not fail” (ibid.).

Hide in the fallow fields of your mind that highest and only grain—namely, the grain which, falling into the earth, died and produced much fruit (John XII). Let this be your treasure; let this be for you the abundance of crops of every kind. In it establish the end of your acquiring; in it place all your confidence for both lives. For the Lord is Lord of all, and rich toward all who call upon him (Rom. X).

Indeed, if you diligently strive to preserve that grain with suitable care, you will see the storerooms of your inner granary overflowing with talents of gold, silver, and every kind of wealth. You will also see your barns, through a new yield of grain, incomparably overflowing.

Cultivate that treasure, therefore, with vigilant concern continually; devote to it, with watchful diligence, night-long and day-long vigils. For in that one treasure you will be rich in all things and will be unable to lack an abundance of whatever is necessary for you.

In it you will possess the gold of divine wisdom and the silver of eloquence that builds up. In it, various beautiful and honorable garments: scarlet dyed twice, namely, of twofold charity; and the *colobium*—the sleeveless tunic—of shining chastity. In it, fine linen of patience; the fiery, double-woven cloth of divine fear; and the purple of royal dignity.

Since wool is dyed with the blood of the purple-fish so that it is turned into a purple color, whoever sits upon the throne of righteous judgment in such a way that he hastens, by violent rule, to put to death all the enticements of his flesh and the barbarity of his vices is rightly called a king and is clothed in the beauty of spiritual purple.

In it is the *diupisticum*—the garment or sign of ever-green hope—since you have been called to an undefiled, unfading inheritance, kept in heaven (II Pet. I). In it you will have the ring of faith, bracelets of perfected active work, and also ornaments for the right hand of contemplative speculation: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II).

And why should I promise you more, since in it you will enjoy the jewels of all virtues and the pearls of every spiritual gift? You will not lack herds of all clean and unclean animals, which will pass under the rod of your discipline.

The unclean herds of vices will be subdued under the rule of your authority; the clean ones, however, will fatten the belly of your inner person with the dishes of sweetest refreshment. A carefully tended flock of sheep with delicate wool will provide food of sweet innocence for your dishes. The flesh of domesticated fattened birds will not cease to increase within you the richness of divine love.

Every kind of bird will furnish a costly spiritual banquet upon the table of your mind; but the bull’s neck of pride will bellow beneath the yoke imposed by your authority. The unbridled freedom of equine lust will, under you, champ insatiably at the iron bit of the mouth’s bridle. All the beasts of vices and every monstrous creature of creeping things will tremble and fear the power of your dominion.

All these things will freely become your possession in this life, if you carefully strive to guard that precious and singular treasure of which we have spoken.

But in the life of true blessedness, what things, and how much greater things, will be given to you—it is not, I confess, within our strength to discuss, nor within our capacity to unfold. For a brief conclusion to an inexplicable matter, let it suffice to report this: those who have perfectly abandoned the world will receive “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (II Cor. II).

Therefore, carefully store in the chamber of your breast this treasure—namely, Christ our God and Lord, who became for us both redemption and price, himself the Promiser and the Reward, who is both the life of human beings and the eternity of angels.

Cast upon him every anxiety concerning every need. Take delight in him through the conversation of continual prayer. Refresh yourself in him with the vigilant feast of holy thoughts. Let him be your food; let him likewise be your clothing.

If it should happen that you also lack some external convenience, do not hesitate or distrust his faithful promise, by which he promises, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

He who commanded abundant streams of water to flow from that dry rock, for the thirsty ranks of the Israelite people (Exod. XVI); he who was able to provide heavenly manna for the hungry over long periods of time; he who commanded an innumerable multitude of quails to descend into the camp of those who murmured—will he be unable to provide what is necessary for one little man who is continually devoted to his service?

And he who preserved the garments of that innumerable crowd unharmed through approximately forty years—will it be difficult for him to replace worn-out old clothes with new garments for you?

We, certainly, who have the smallest faith, compel Christ to be sparing. The distrust of the fainthearted makes Christ poor; but full faith experiences him as rich and generous in his gifts.

Strive only to exercise yourself in what he commanded, and let no doubt whatsoever remain concerning what he promised. The creditor may be secure when the debtor is ready to repay. There is distrust without cause when he is the Promiser who never lies. The creditor walks securely when simple truth is held by its promise.

We have decided to touch briefly upon these matters concerning monks who possess property. Now, however, let us transfer the point of our discussion to those who take continual pleasure in traveling on horseback.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning monks who are continually wandering about [Cols. 0260C–0260D]

Nor do I think, dearest brothers, that it could have slipped from your memory that we have often lamented among ourselves, in harmonious familiarity, this ruin of monks as well; and that we have pitied, with fraternal affection, restless brothers who are perishing through the vice of wandering.

There are some who, while they were bearing the warfare of the world, had grown weary of running here and there beneath the yoke of human servitude, so much so that, from love of freedom, they resolved to pass over to the monastic leisure; but now they are so inflamed by the heat of their poisonous restlessness that, whenever no opportunity is offered for going farther afield, they seem to be confined in the horror of a dark prison.

This is doubtless brought about by the cunning of the ancient enemy. Those whom that most wicked rider still rides therefore he urges with the goads of restless wandering, so that they may both perish by returning to the vanity of the world and turn others away from taking the path of true salvation.

For there are very many people living in secular dress who, unless they flee under Christ’s leadership to this harbor of monastic discipline, utterly despair of being saved in any other way amid the stormy waves of the sea of the world.

## CHAPTER X. What laypeople say about worldly monks [Cols. 0261A–0261D]

But when they observe those who recently despised all that belongs to the world with great fervor now eagerly being drawn back into the whirlpool of secular affairs and wallowing in the muddy filth of the same pit from which they had escaped, amazement arises in those who watch, a sigh is drawn from the depths of their entrails, and despair is generated in their minds.

For each one lays this complaint against himself, saying: “Woe, woe! Where did I place my hope of salvation? Why did I decide, at the peril of my head, to enter that order? In scarcely a brief moment I almost lost body and soul together. I nearly threw myself into the fire with my eyes open and by my own will.

“For who ever sought the monastery with greater fervor? Who, as it seemed, hastened toward the warfare of Christ with more courageous constancy? But now, forgetful of everything he promised, he is continually occupied with earthly affairs; he handles the world and breathes the world. The habit of mortification makes him unlike me, yet he lives with me in no way unlike the world.

“Clearly, as is evident, he was able to change the outward appearance of his body, but his mind remained badly fixed in the state in which it had been. Why should I accuse those who incited his conversion? In military matters alone I have lost a fellow soldier; in the other earthly activities I have not lost a companion.

“With me he conducts lawsuits in the courts; with me he does not cease to plead before judges’ tribunals; with me, intrusively, he enters the halls of princes; with me he pours into their ears counsels of earthly profundity.

“But with what recklessness do I presume now to call him a companion, when I, who once habitually had him as a companion, now scarcely follow him as a female attendant in everything, though he barely goes before me?

“Certainly he gains so much glory among the people from his conversion that everyone rises when he arrives; whatever he brings, they believe as though it were a prophetic oracle, and they reverently offer him the service of their devotion.

“Clearly, as far as the flesh is concerned, his conversion is not believed to have been fruitless: because he did not lay aside secular dress together with his mind, the clever trafficker has acquired secular pomp in fuller measure.”

As detractors pour out these and similar murmurs, who could sufficiently enumerate how many opportunities for perishing in the world are created by the wandering of monks? For people more readily decide to perish even in secular dress than, by following the examples of the lost, to lose both worlds at once, as they say.

And truly it is not surprising that scandal arises in those who see this, since it is shown to be contrary both to God and to sacred authority. The Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has enlisted himself” (II Tim. II). The Lord himself also warns his disciples, saying: “Take care that your hearts not be weighed down by carousing, drunkenness, and the cares of this world” (Luke XXI).

## CHAPTER XI. That a monk’s wandering both drives out virtues and introduces a multitude of vices [Cols. 0262A–0263C]

From this poisonous root of restlessness so many offshoots of vices arise that, wherever it is known to flourish, the tree is stripped bare of every fruit of monastic perfection.

And just as the unripe figs of a fig tree cannot remain standing when exposed to the winds, so the fruits of good works cannot remain in such a person when the various temptations of the world blow through him from every side.

This vice is so violent that, once it has seized authority for itself in the monk’s breast, the choir of virtues, if it is present, soon departs for the most part; and certain monstrous vices break in as though into a prison belonging to them by right.

To mention a few examples out of many: a monk who is on a journey cannot keep his fast, because the hospitality shown to him does not permit it; he does not sing the psalms wisely, because the talkativeness of his traveling companions interrupts him; he does not devote himself to nocturnal vigils, because the solitude of seclusion is lacking; he does not labor at bending his knees, because the hardship of travel does not accord with the devotion of holiness; he is not at all confined by the discipline of silence, because, when causes frequently arise, he is driven, even unwillingly, into unbridled prolixity.

What shall I say? He has no time at all for reading or prayer, since pressing necessity dictates that he go outside himself and handle every earthly matter.

Charity is diminished in him, because the mind that receives the winds of so many secular activities grows cold from the fervor of inward love. His chastity likewise suffers loss, because sometimes the mind is pierced by the dart of desire through the appearance of the flesh that it contemplates outwardly.

The strength of patience is also broken. When one undertaking some task repeatedly encounters sudden events contrary to his wish, while hastening to complete his business, he does not bear them with equanimity, and then pours forth such words in impatience that, when he returns to leisure, he severely punishes himself with remorseful tears.

The rule of sobriety is not observed. When the banquet is furnished with more sumptuous foods, when the diligence of hospitality is displayed, he thinks it inhuman not to yield to the requests of those inviting him; and under the appearance of charity he also takes pleasure in indulging his belly gently.

At this point a doubt often arises in the mind of God’s servant: perhaps, in the very thing by which sobriety is being served, hypocrisy—an abominable vice—is also being served. Hence among some the measure of sobriety is utterly despised, so that even the appearance of hypocrisy may seem to be far removed.

But in this way discernment is not maintained in what is believed to be done discreetly. For the person who knows how to distinguish rightly is the one who knows how to separate virtue from vice; but whoever uproots the wheat together with the weeds undoubtedly does not understand the force of discernment.

Whoever, therefore, does not exceed the limit of sobriety solely out of regard for heavenly reward both tramples hypocrisy beneath the feet of his humility and confidently awaits the reward of guarded sobriety.

To speak further about the wandering monk: he does not possess the compunction of tears with which to mourn his sins. The dry mind that proceeds through the heat of earthly conduct, since it is not deemed worthy to be drenched by the dew of the Holy Spirit, withers; and, full of the mire of earthly thoughts, because, through grace as it is bestowed, it does not receive inwardly water for its head, it pours out no tears outwardly.

Sometimes, perhaps, he preaches while listeners surround him; but suddenly vain glory steals upon him and, emerging as though from ambush, kills the one who was healing others.

If, taking care to avoid this, he restrains himself under the discipline of silence, he is ashamed that he can accomplish nothing of what he came for. If he preserves, as is fitting, an appearance of deliberate gravity, he greatly fears that even here he may incur the reputation of hypocrisy as a pretender.

But if he relaxes himself, however slightly, from the rigor of his mortification into gentleness, he is even less secure, lest by his example he destroy others.

If at some point he wishes to restore the harmony of peace between people who are at odds, then, if he pursues the truth strictly, unity of reconciliation is not formed between them; but if he agrees to use lies, he does not escape the snares of sin.

When he wishes to rebuke sinners, he considers it no small fault to stir up against himself the hatred of so many of his neighbors. But to see and remain silent—what else does he judge this to be than consent to those acting wickedly?

These things concern those who burn with whatever spark of heavenly fervor. As for all who are cold, who, despising the camp of divine warfare, turn back through a crooked return to the millstone of worldly turmoil, let those who wish report how blameworthily they act and how inconsiderately they live.

It seems more prudent to us to mourn them with pious compassion than to record the deeds of their detestable way of life, lest with censorious writings we slander those to whom we ought to offer only the tears of compassion.

## CHAPTER XII. What evils the unhappy soul of a monk suffers when it returns to lower things [Cols. 0263C–0265A]

We state this plainly: the world has now been thickened with such dense nets of ambushes that whoever desires to live innocently in this holy order must most carefully refrain from advancing through it.

If he frequently treads its road, he does not escape the snares prepared by ambushes; and, like a tree stripped of the protection of its guarding bark, he will be able neither to bear the fruits of virtues nor to avoid the decay of vices as it gushes forth, as though in things continually being worn away.

When he returns to the enclosure of his own dwelling, a kind of compacted crowd of everything he has seen or heard accompanies him at close quarters, so that the uproar of busy affairs which he endured there in the body he suffers here in the mind with much greater force and much greater harassment.

Especially if he begins to devote himself more earnestly to prayer, behold the phantoms of thoughts; behold the images of the things he had seen. Thus, wherever he stands, he seems to himself to be attending theatrical games or sitting among those conducting a lawsuit in the forum.

The man indeed resists and, like flies flying around, tries to drive them away from the mouth of his mind. But as soon as they depart, they immediately return; as soon as they are repelled, they stand there again—like fugitives pursuing their own runaway, seeking to seize him and bring him back to the exercises of his former servitude.

Then the unhappy soul learns how much it has cost itself that it foolishly relaxed through the broad expanse of the world. It wastes away, dry, dark, and stony; hardened like a stone, it can neither break forth into streams of tears nor see the light, surrounded everywhere by darkness.

It strives to apply itself to the mysteries of the Psalms, but like eyes afflicted with dimness it is struck back by an intolerable light. It pants and strives with whatever strength it can toward higher things, but, weighed down by a certain burden of its own, it is forced to lie humbled in the depths.

The prophetic saying is appropriately applied to it: “He has placed me in darkness like those who have been dead forever; he has built against me, so that I cannot go out; he has made my fetters heavy. And when I have cried out and pleaded, he has shut out my prayer” (Lam. III).

It mourns, it is anxious, it pants; and because it is not even permitted to weep over its own misery, it is disturbed, filled with a more bitter anguish of pain.

At least it might be granted to pour out with the prophet this voice of weeping, in which it is said: “Therefore,” he says, “I weep, and my eye pours out water, because the comforter who restores my soul has gone far from me” (Lam. I).

But that unhappy soul, when it sees itself pitiable and yet cannot weep, sees how far it is from salvation, as though it had fallen into a certain pool of misery.

For since weeping is the only path by which a sinner can reach forgiveness, when it cannot mourn its guilt it seems to itself not yet even to have set foot upon the road by which it can reach pardon.

Something similar is said through the Prophet in the person of the imperfect: “My soul has desired to desire your justifications at all times” (Ps. CXVIII). Whoever does not yet desire the law of God—which is undoubtedly his justification—at all times, but desires to desire it, already looks toward it, however imperfectly, from a distance, but does not at all climb the heights of perfection.

Thus such a dark confusion comes upon the miserable mind that, wherever it turns, it sees itself still moving about in the world, although it unquestionably recognizes that the world exists without it.

It is with that world with which it is not itself; for the world which it abandoned by bodily departure it depicts with itself in the mind through fantastic imaginings.

Indeed, this calamity in the human mind is both sin and the punishment of sin. For it is just that each person should suffer unwillingly what he willingly admitted. The one who did not wish to confine himself within the secrecy of his order when he could have done so was therefore unable to be without the world even after he had left it.

The human mind, therefore, constrained by the necessity of such great destitution and want, grieves and groans and draws a sigh from the depths of its entrails, because it has lost the purity of its withdrawal through the vice of wandering and has again rolled itself in the mud of the world like a filthy swine (Prov. XXVI; II Pet. II).

Then it bitterly reproves itself for its lightness and inconstancy; it vehemently accuses itself of being wandering and deceitful; and it truly proves that God’s judgment is right and that he upholds the laws of equity, saying with the prophet:

“The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to await in silence the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man to bear the yoke from his youth: he will sit alone and be silent, because he has laid it upon himself” (Lam. III).

For if it had loved solitude, it would now rejoice at having been raised above itself; instead, it mourns because, going out into public, it sees itself lying prostrate beneath itself.

## CHAPTER XIII. That one who goes outside is compelled to associate with excommunicated persons [Cols. 0265A–0265D]

There is also another consideration which, even if the other impediments were absent, would by itself be sufficient to restrain monks from wandering through the world.

For at this time, who could find any gathering of secular people in which there was not someone who, on account of the expiation of his guilt, ought to undergo a judgment of excommunication?

For some time now all crimes have commonly arisen throughout the world; every evil of wickedness is now flourishing, and each day they spread more widely as they proliferate, the nearer the end of the world approaches.

Therefore it is impossible for a monk who goes out into public not to be compelled to associate either with excommunicated people or with those who are to be excommunicated—which amounts to almost the same thing.

He speaks with murderers, perjurers, incestuous persons, arsonists, and adulterers; and even if he recoils from them inwardly, he is often joined to them by a kiss and, when necessity demands, dines with them at the same table, while the Apostle cries out in opposition:

“If anyone who is named a brother is a fornicator, or unclean, or drunkard, or greedy, with such a person not even to eat” (I Cor. V).

Certainly it is sufficiently frightening and exceedingly contrary to propriety to have fellowship with those who are separated from God—especially for monks, who are joined to God by a particular and, so to speak, domestic familiarity, having renounced the world and being irrevocably assigned to divine service alone.

Just as one should avoid the very head of the reprobate, so also one should avoid his members, unless the cause of conversion requires otherwise. Here one act of rejection is owed to those for whom there one fire is prepared, as the Truth bears witness, when it says to those placed on the left:

“Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Since we see them making their way toward another homeland, we ought not to bind ourselves to them on the road by the glue of harmful companionship, lest those whom disordered love joins together also be enveloped together in the punishment of final retribution.

## CHAPTER XIV. That one ought to avoid not only the excommunicated but also those who are to be excommunicated [Cols. 0266A–0267B]

To make it even clearer how much the companionship of the wicked harms the good, we can gather the matter by this evident reasoning: some of them have recently been excommunicated by priestly sentence, while others have merely been deprived of communion according to the canonical judgment of the holy Fathers.

Concerning those who have recently been excommunicated, there is no doubt that everyone who shares in their fellowship receives a similar sentence of condemnation.

But concerning those who, because of crimes committed, are indeed to be condemned by canonical authority, yet have not apparently been cut off from ecclesiastical unity by the living voices of priests, some people are uncertain whether their companionship may safely be admitted.

But if we weigh the matter with more careful subtlety, we find almost no difference between them. Whether someone is rightly condemned by modern or by ancient Fathers, it is the same: the difference of times does not release one whom the same cause—the crime committed—binds, and the variety of ages does not prejudice the judicial calculation where one rule of refined equity dictates the sentence.

We shall demonstrate what we wish to establish more clearly if we set out the words of the Fathers who excommunicate, both ancient and modern.

The sacred canons say: “Whoever has done this or that is to be excommunicated.” Modern pontiffs likewise, when casting the sentence of excommunication, use almost the same words, saying: “That person who has done these things is to be excommunicated.”

Since their words are therefore the same, the sentence is likewise to be understood as the same; and since the entire judgment of the present holy pontiffs depends upon the definitions of the ancient Fathers, they presume to condemn no one except those whom they know already to have been condemned by the ancients.

They therefore do not condemn someone newly, but confirm an already issued sentence by following that of their predecessors.

We must conclude, then—see the scholia at the end of the little work—that just as one must beware of those whom modern synodal councils expel from ecclesiastical fellowship, so likewise one must avoid those whom the ancient Fathers decree should be removed.

This, therefore, is no small reason for restraining a monk from wandering through the world and making him steadfast in the corner of his withdrawal. For it is very miserable to be restrained from one’s own excesses yet to be stained by the spots of another’s guilt—to avoid committing a sin oneself and nevertheless suffer the punishments of another’s offense.

When we carelessly join ourselves in friendship to the wicked, we are bound by their faults. Thus Josaphat, who is praised with so many commendations for his former life, is rebuked as almost perishing through his friendship with King Ahab. The Lord says to him through the prophet:

“You give aid to the impious and join yourself in friendship with those who hate the Lord, and therefore you deserve the wrath of the Lord. Nevertheless, good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah” (II Chron. XIX).

We already differ from the one who is supremely upright precisely insofar as our life agrees with the friendships of the perverse.

Who would not be frightened by that apostolic voice which, warning us and calling us back from the companionship of the wicked, cries out:

“I charge you in the name of the Lord Jesus to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that we delivered to you” (II Thess. III).

If therefore we must carefully withdraw ourselves from all those whom we see not walking according to apostolic tradition, how many remain in that secular order with whom we can safely maintain the companionship of intimacy?

Moreover, whoever, having despised apostolic tradition, attempts to introduce another teaching, whether by dogmatizing or by living accordingly, does not deserve to enjoy the companionship of orthodox and religious men. The Apostle John also bears witness, saying:

“If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John XIII).

Instructed by these judgments of apostolic truth, we clearly establish that those who carnally form friendships with wicked men become participants in another’s guilt; and they are compelled to undergo with them the judgment of final retribution, although in this life they did not commit sin together with them.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning monks who take pleasure in expensive clothing [Cols. 0267B–0268A]

This vice, which we have already pursued, also familiarly besets the wandering monk, because he is never able to shake off from himself entirely the leprosy of vicious ownership, but always considers it necessary to retain with him, on the pretext of travel, however little it may be.

From this also arises the love of expensive clothing, lest, appearing in public, he should seem contemptible. Yet while the ornament of outward dress is sought, the entire arrangement of the inner person is scattered.

This madness, which is false, somehow so blinds the eyes of the perverse mind that it neither sees what constitutes honor among human beings nor considers by what means someone may appear more glorious before God.

Indeed, it is madness, and it is false. It is madness to despise in pride the judgment of the hidden Judge and to pursue the breath of human favor by softer clothing.

It is false because, by the very thing through which he offends the eyes of the heavenly Spectator, he also falls before the judgment of human opinion; and by the very thing through which he desires to appear more distinguished to people, he in some way exposes himself to the teeth of public criticism.

When the brightness of his clothing invites eyes to look at him, it also arms tongues to attack the wearer with the darts of insult.

For who sees a monk dressed in soft garments and does not immediately judge that he is empty of the divine Spirit and is aspiring to earthly rather than heavenly things?

The mind is inferred from the clothing, and the appearance of one’s intention is judged according to one’s outward adornment. This agrees with the authority of the Gospel, where it is said: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII).

Yet these people do not come to us in sheep’s clothing, since sheep’s clothing is the garment of humility and innocence, not of arrogance or plunder.

That garment is rightly called a garment of plunder which is purchased at the cost of two or even three garments. The crime of plunder is committed by one devoted to vain glory who spends alone on clothing his own body what he could have used to cover his brother together with himself.

Without doubt he commits plunder who, inflamed by the passion for empty honor, spends the cost of two garments on one and leaves his neighbor—whom he ought to have loved as himself—in nakedness.

But this is the difference between these newly enrolled monks and those hypocrites whom the Gospel censures: those hypocrites, as the Truth testifies, come to us in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matt. 7); these monks, however, swell inwardly with flanks bursting with the wind of vainglory, while outwardly they appear in the clothing of plunder, as has been shown, and thus arrogantly walk in the clothing of wolves. Therefore, when the Lord says to the Jews concerning John, “What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11), surely the monk who seeks the splendor of costly clothing [Col. 0268B] bears the service not of the heavenly King but of this world; and although he may seem outwardly to offer God the gift of his obedience, he is plainly convicted of truly serving vainglory by seeking human favor.

Moreover, if it is permissible to be dressed in soft garments under the pretext of obedience, to whom could this indulgence more liberally have been granted than to blessed John, who, endowed especially with the office of service, had come to turn the hearts of the fathers toward their children by a new preaching and to prepare a perfect people for the Lord Christ (Luke 1)? Could the Lord himself not have provided footwear for him, whose garments Gentile faithlessness alone divided among themselves? For if he had not lacked footwear, the sequence of sacred history would not have been silent about it.

## CHAPTER XVI. How, just as costly clothing provokes anger, so humble clothing moves God to mercy

[Col. 0268C]

The king of Nineveh, dressed in purple, deserved the destruction of his own city; covered with sackcloth, he appeased the movement of divine wrath by the humility of a contrite heart (Jon. 3). Hezekiah, too, adorned with royal dress, heard the terrifying threats of the king of the Assyrians and trembled; but as soon as he himself was clothed in sackcloth, and did not blush to send messengers to the prophet clothed in sackcloth, he received an oracle of imminent divine victory and hoped-for prosperity (2 Kings 19). This promise, as Scripture bears witness, quickly reached its fulfillment. For behold, the angel of the Lord struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians in a single night; then both sons slew Sennacherib himself, the king, with a parricidal but deserved sword (ibid.).

You see, then, how great is the difference before God between flowing and rough clothing. You perceive that cheap and despised clothing appeases as judge the one whom delicate clothing had deserved to experience as angry; and the one whom the former had rendered liable to punishment is commended by the latter as worthy of pardon. How significant the adornment of clothing is before God is clearly shown by that outstanding prophet among the prophets, Isaiah. At the command of the divine injunction he removed his clothing and went naked and barefoot for a period of three years. Let human pride, then, be ashamed; let the wretched mind corrupted by the plague of vainglory be confounded, when he—the instrument of God, the temple of the Holy Spirit, the herald of divine justice—did not hesitate to walk publicly naked. [Col. 0269A] And the unhappy man who has merited not even the slightest sign of divine intimacy seeks the superstitious adornment of a many-flounced garment; and while he puts on the cosmetics of badly colored clothing, he does not fear to turn himself away from the eyes of the heavenly Watcher, slippery and desirous of being looked at. Thus, since that garment of arrogance is despised under divine judgment, the one who wears it is consequently judged detestable as well.

But suppose, then, that Isaiah did indeed walk naked: when he was accustomed to go clothed, did he allow himself to be dressed in softer garments? Let us therefore question the very history of the prophetic narrative and hear what the divine voice commands him: “The Lord spoke,” it says, “by the hand of Isaiah son of Amoz, saying: Go, and loosen the sackcloth from your loins, and remove your sandals from your feet” (Isa. 20). For the one who is commanded to remove not some other kind of garment but sackcloth from his loins plainly declares how much the very plainness of his clothing meant to him. O how many gilded dining rooms there then were in the palaces of kings and princes of the earth! How many purple beds surrounded by painted domes! How many ornaments of the wealthy glittering with shining gems! How many ceilings furnished with cedar and cypress carvings! And yet, despising and contemptuously rejecting them all, almighty God deigned to build for himself a rational temple clothed in the deformity of sackcloth, and through him, as through an instrument, to reveal to mortals the mysteries of his secret counsel.

Let the newly enrolled monk learn, let him learn, how badly he makes his bargain: for by the very thing through which he seeks to appear distinguished in human eyes, he undoubtedly becomes filthy in the judgment of the heavenly Judge; by the very thing through which he is more earnestly honored by human beings, he is more despised by God. And while he provokes the eyes of those who gaze upon him to admiration, he withdraws himself, darkened, from the sight of divine grace.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning those who purchase the applause of the common people by the baseness of their clothing

Since, however, the opportunity to speak about the vanity of clothing has presented itself, just as we have briefly touched upon those who delight in soft garments, so let us also briefly discuss those who suffer from the same disease but are carried along by a different madness. For there are some [Col. 0269D] who purchase the favoring applause of the crowd by the deformity of cheap clothing; and they feed more pleasantly upon this delight if, while they seem despised because of their painstaking cultivation of ugliness, they fly gloriously through the mouths of boastful peoples. They rejoice that discussions about them are stirred up; they rejoice to be pointed out with a finger as something marvelous. These men, carefully arranged in their deformity, conspicuous in obscurity, contrive to appear exalted through humility. By the crafty cunning of diabolical cleverness they are lowered for the purpose of appearing lofty; they are disfigured for the purpose of shining as remarkable in the eyes of those who look upon them.

These men and the former group differ in what they spend, but they purchase the same rewards. Vainglory, as it were a certain merchandise, is placed in the middle, and various merchants approach it. Some bring cheap garments as the price from their purse; others strive to give back costly ones. But while each group labors on its own behalf, those who bring cheap clothing are immediately preferred to the other buyers. For the one who uses delicate clothing, as was said above, often exposes himself more broadly to the bites of detractors precisely where he thinks he is winning the breeze of favor. But the one who is content with the extremity of a cheap garment—and I am speaking of monks—whatever his intention may be, whether he does it wrongly or rightly, is usually commended to those who look upon him by the reputation of holiness; and the more deformed someone appears in outward dress, the more often he is judged worthy of reverence.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning David’s true humility

Nevertheless, whoever he is who hopes for the reward of heavenly recompense from the cheapness of his own clothing must continually trample under the feet of his mind every favor of human praise, as though it were muddy filth; and just as he presents himself to the eyes of those who look upon him, so must he judge himself within the secrets of his conscience. Hence, when Michal, the daughter of Saul, rebuked David, saying, “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and stripping himself as one of the buffoons might strip himself” (2 Sam. 6; 1 Chron. 15), he wished to show that the same humility flourished in his mind as was displayed in his body. He did not boil with anger or answer with words of arrogance, but humbly said: “As the Lord lives, I will play, and I will become even more worthless than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (ibid.).

In these words the pattern of true humility is set forth, since inward humility is demonstrated no less than outward humility. For some people, the more deformingly they abase themselves in their external appearance, the greater things they inwardly decide about themselves. They desire to appear one thing on the surface and to be understood as another in secret; and by the very thing through which they humbly abase themselves in public, they swell more arrogantly in private. David, however, in order to present himself as humble outwardly, says, “I will play and become even more worthless than I have been.” But to show the humility of his mind he adds, “And I will be humble in my own eyes,” as though he were plainly saying: “I will be humbled outwardly, so that I may offer others an example of salvation; and I will be humble inwardly, so that I too may persist in the root of that same saving humility.”

Whoever therefore walks so simply that he desires to be in the opinion of those who see him just as he presents himself in the deformity of his clothing truly bears Christ’s reproach and carries his cross, dead to the world behind him. He is rendered all the more illustrious in the divine sight the more despicable he is judged in human eyes; and in a fruitful exchange, the one whom outward clothing makes foul shines with inward grace.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the less perfect disdain soft garments, while the more perfect sometimes accept them indifferently

[Col. 0271A]

There are also some who, having long been accustomed to cheap clothing through the pursuit of a right intention, if it should happen that they are covered with garments however much softer, disdainfully reject them with the proud severity of a free humility. Just as others are ashamed to be clothed in ugly garments, so these are ashamed to be clothed in costly ones. They tolerate delicate dress and take pleasure in the roughness of despised garments; all bodily adornment becomes disgrace to them, and deformity becomes honor.

Esther had assumed the likeness of these people when she said: “You know, Lord, my necessity: that I abhor the sign of my pride and glory, which is upon my head in the days of my display, and I detest it like a menstrual rag and do not wear it in the days of my silence” (Esther 14). These people burn with the ardor of a holy desire, yet they are still struggling against the temptations of their passions. Others, however, have reached such a height of mortification that, having become almost insensible to both kinds of clothing, just as they habitually desire to be dressed in cheap garments, so also, when circumstances require it, they do not recoil at all from anything costly or bright. They contemplate both with a single gaze: soft garments do not dissolve their resolve, and rough ones do not afflict them.

Judith, too, had been an example of these people. Having used sackcloth until necessity demanded otherwise, she adorned her body with various ornaments of bodily beauty, as sacred Scripture testifies: “Judith removed her sackcloth, took off the garments of her widowhood, washed her body, anointed herself with the finest myrrh, arranged the hair of her head, placed a tiara upon her head, put on the garments of her joy, put sandals on her feet, took her bracelets, lilies, earrings, and rings, and adorned herself with all her ornaments” (Judith 10). With these ornaments, therefore, the holy woman both preserved true humility toward herself and did not lose the spirit of poverty with which she had been enriched.

## CHAPTER XX. Wandering has been an occasion of ruin for many

But while I desire to strip the wandering monk whom I had seized, dressed in costly garments, I lose him from the grasp of my own argument; and now, as he draws far away, I can scarcely see him, while I realize that only his clothing has remained in my hands. Let us therefore cast aside the clothing, pursue him swiftly, and, if possible, seize him and endeavor to make him stand still.

Let the monk devoted to the vice of wandering know, then, that unless he withdraws his foot from the world and steadfastly applies himself to serving God in a place of retreat, he will be able neither to attain the summit of perfection nor to preserve worthily the duties of his order. As long as Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, confined herself within her father’s tents, she preserved the rights of unviolated virginity; but when she went out to see the women of that region and entered the public place, her virginity immediately encountered an enemy, and she was shamefully prostituted to another’s lust (Gen. 34).

The Levite’s wife from the side of Mount Ephraim, so long as she remained indoors and occupied herself with household concerns, preserved the chastity of the marriage bed. But when, drawn by affection for her abandoned kinsmen, she returned to her homeland and parents, and then came back, she succumbed as prey to the madness of lust and many corruptions; and while she suffered the shipwreck of endangered chastity in the flesh, she also breathed out her spirit, harassed by disgraceful abuse (Judg. 19).

Tamar, the sister of Absalom, while she lived simply in her brother’s house, preserved the character of undefiled virginity; but when she undertook the duty of visiting her brother Amnon, son of David, she mourned that she had incurred the loss of her virginity, which had been seized from her (2 Sam. 13). At last, having learned that it was safer to remain than to go forth, she preferred, though late, secret leisure to harmful wandering.

And you, therefore, if you wish your soul to remain in the integrity of its virginity, if you consider it abominable to lie beneath foul and violent corrupters, seek secrecy, look for the retreat of solitude, firmly close your ears and eyes against the vanity of worldly affairs, and reject the conversations of carnal people, which are more likely to bring destruction than edification. For, according to Solomon, “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13).

Gather yourself, then, within the chamber of your conscience. Place the bars of censorial discipline upon all the doors of your house—that is, upon all your senses—so that no one may enter. A spring whose surroundings are closed off so that it cannot overflow rises upward in streams of water; conversely, one that is led away here and there through many channels is dried up as soon as more fervent heat settles upon it. Finally, if closed doors had stood in the way of David as he walked upon the terrace of the royal palace, he would never have burned with desire for Bathsheba as she washed herself (2 Sam. 17); but because he did not keep his eye under the guard of discipline, he too fell headlong after it into the immense chasm of gaping ruin. With his steps made slippery, he experienced the fall of his whole self because he relaxed the bridle of his gaze alone. To him that saying of Jeremiah most aptly applies: “My eye,” he says, “has plundered my soul” (Lam. 3).

If, then, so lofty a pillar of heaven fell so grievously because of the wandering of his eyes alone, what are we weak and little ones to think of ourselves, who run through the world and carry ourselves completely outside ourselves, occupying our sight, hearing, and every sense in drawing in the vanities of the world?

## CHAPTER XXI. How wandering cast Esau down, while Jacob’s steadfastness exalted him

What difference exists between monks who love secluded retreat and those who spread themselves through outward affairs is made abundantly clear to us in the two sons of Isaac. For it is written: “Esau became a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field; but Jacob was simple and dwelt in tents” (Gen. 25). The latter, prudently simple, cautiously carried out his advancement and received his brother’s birthright and his father’s blessing; the former, foolishly skilled in hunting, heard that he would live by the sword and serve his brother like a servant to his master. Yet if Jacob had not remained in the tents, he would undoubtedly have been deprived of the first blessing; and if Esau had not cast himself abroad through constant wandering, he would not have lost the privilege of his primacy. The one held the leisure of domestic quiet and, by the grace of God’s generosity, entered into another’s rights; the other, exhausted by the labor of hunting, lost even what rightfully belonged to him.

Those who travel throughout the world and boast that they serve the laws of obedience should cease to put forward the shield of excuse. Let them know that Esau too went out to hunt in obedience to his father’s commands; yet he neither deserved to offer food to his father nor to obtain the first fruits of the desired blessing. Whoever, led by habit and impelled by his own will, willingly carries out something pertaining to vice sins even if he seems outwardly to obey another’s orders. For when it is said, “Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting” (Gen. 27), it is plainly evident that Esau, in acquiring food for his father by the effort of hunting, obeyed his father’s command no more through obedience than he in some way paid tribute to his ingrained habit. Whoever therefore satisfies his own desire by running through the world and nevertheless claims that he obeys the commands of his superiors should know that God does not credit colored verbosity so much as he judges people according to their hidden conscience.

It should also be noted that some people, while they remain in the very condition of wandering, do not fall grievously; but when they return, as though drunk on some intoxicating liquor of worldly affairs, they roll into an immense precipice. They return with their eyes clouded by the smoke of worldly actions, and therefore, once restored to their own thresholds, they do not notice where they ought to place the foot of their work. Esau plainly indicates this. When he returned from the field and complained that he was extremely weary, he made a very ruinous bargain with his brother; and when he allowed an immoderate frenzy of hunger to rage within him, he sold the great dignity of the birthright for the cheap cooking of a small dish of lentils (Gen. 25).

Thus, indeed, thus does the person devoted to outward affairs abandon himself and afterward, recalled to inward things in body but not in heart, lose himself. It also happens to those who suffer from the vice of wandering that, with the eyes of their interior self covered in dust, they neither take precautions against falling into the pit of guilt nor afterward notice where they have fallen. Thus, while they neglect to consider carefully each of their offenses, they make light, through confused examination of the mind, of whatever it was that they had done wrong—not straining out a gnat, even though they swallow a camel.

Esau is also known not to have been free from this blindness, as sacred history relates. After saying, “Esau swore and sold his birthright,” it then adds: “And so, having received bread and the dish of lentils, he ate and drank and went away, making light of the fact that he had sold his birthright.”

## CHAPTER XXII. In these two brothers it is evident what difference exists between wandering and steadfast monks

In these two brothers, then (Gen. 27), it is plainly recognized how great a difference is understood to exist between monks who remain in place and those who wander. The former, unless he had spread himself outward as unstable and prodigal of himself, would never have lost the mystery of his father’s blessing together with the birthright; the latter, unless he had confined himself within the boundaries of his household, would have sat humbly below the prescribed limit of his subordinate position. The one, skilled and clever, slips away from the right of his privilege; the other, quiet and simple, rules with singular privilege over his subjected brothers. One, wearied by traversing forests and hunting grounds, is cast down from the dignity of his primacy; the other, enjoying leisure in a pleasant chamber, is divinely exalted to exercise sovereignty over peoples and tribes.

Let every monk, whoever he is, cease frequently to burst forth with Esau from the enclosures of his retreat; let him cease to entangle himself with worldly affairs under the pretext of obedience, lest he someday grieve with Esau as an exile from divine blessing, having taken him as the author of his harmful wandering.

Let him therefore present himself as domestic with Jacob; let him live simply with Jacob in the tents, so that he may refresh God, who is truly the Father of the elect and desires to feed upon the dishes of good works, not with the preparation of wild beasts but with that of a domestic flock—when he prepares for God a pleasant nourishment from the virtues of his conscience, not from the outward appearance of holiness. For God does not command the skins of sacrificial victims to be offered to him in sacrifice; rather, he commands that their inward parts be presented, together with the marrow. Hence, in setting forth the ritual of the sacrifices themselves, Moses commands: “After removing the skin, let them cut the limbs of the victim into pieces” (Lev. 1). This command is also found to contain a mystical meaning if it is examined more closely.

We remove the skin of the victim when we take away from the eyes of our mind the outward appearance of virtue. We cut its limbs into pieces when, distinguishing its innermost parts with subtle care, we consider them member by member, so that what appears outwardly sincere and solid may not inwardly be hollow with the hidden fault of vanity. David, however, promises that as a great gift he will offer God sacrifices filled with marrow, saying: “I will offer you holocausts filled with marrow, with incense and rams” (Ps. 68).

Whoever pours himself out pleasurably through the activities of worldly affairs removes the marrow and inward parts of his holocaust, and strives to burn only the skin of the victim, which is forbidden to be offered to God. But whoever desires to offer God a pleasant sacrifice should seek retreat and pursue the interior; he should preserve his soul whole and undefiled in its own virginity, and should not, by running through the brothels of the world, lay it beneath filthy corrupters like a prostitute.

Therefore, if he wishes to please the sight of the inward Bridegroom, let him not paint his eyes with cosmetic, like Jezebel (2 Kings 9)—that is, let him not cover himself with the cosmetics of worldly pomp—but, like Judith, let him anoint his limbs with the finest myrrh (Judith 10). Let him smear all the senses of his mind with the immortal oil of chastity, lest, falling through incontinence into death, he rot in the stench of lust.

Let the chaste soul therefore enclose itself in the chamber of holy Church, and thus rest continually in the bedchamber of the eternal King. Let it seek neither the affection of carnal relatives nor that of any companions, but delight in the embraces of the one true Bridegroom. For it is not without cause that it is written: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, for the King has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44).

In the chamber of this Bridegroom, then, let the holy soul sleep, free from every storm of worldly tumult; upon this author of its virginity let it burn with the torches of chaste love, singing and saying: “The King brought me into his chambers; we shall exult and rejoice in you” (Song 1). And again: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts” (ibid.).

But if an occasion of any kind should arise, so that the necessity of going out appears imminent, let him not immediately rush lightly into wandering; let him not cling greedily to family conversation; let his mind, fixed upon the world, not grow hot toward worldly vanity. Rather, let him deliberate slowly and gravely within himself, saying: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song 5).

## CHAPTER XXIII. How divine providence grants spiritual leisure to the good, while allowing the wicked to spread themselves through outward affairs

If, then, that singular Bridegroom perceives that this desire is present in a holy soul—for he is undoubtedly the Prince of peace—he grants it the free rest of spiritual leisure and arranges all the waves of emerging affairs around it in tranquil peace. Hence he says in the Song of Songs: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you do not awaken or rouse my beloved until she herself wishes it” (Song 2).

By contrast, to a reprobate mind, panting after worldly affairs, it is said through the prophet under the figure of Babylon: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. 47).

In this passage, I think, the human mind is called “virgin” not because it is undefiled but because it is unfruitful. And because Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” the unfruitful mind is rightly called the daughter of Babylon: in that it produces no good works and is ordered by no arrangement of right living, it is, as it were, begotten by confusion as its mother. But if “virgin” is understood not as unfruitful but as undefiled, then, after losing the state of salvation, what it once was is invoked to increase its confusion.

To this mind the divine voice fittingly says by way of reproach, “Come down.” The human spirit stands on high when it longs for heavenly rewards; but it descends from this state when, shamefully overcome, it subjects itself to the worldly desires that flow downward. To it is immediately and fittingly added: “Sit in the dust.” For descending, it sits in the dust, because, abandoning heavenly things, it becomes worthless in low places, sprinkled with earthly thoughts.

The words are then repeated with emphasis: “Sit on the ground.” It is as though the voice openly reproached it, saying: “Because you did not wish to govern yourself by a heavenly way of life, prostrate beneath yourself, humble yourself in earthly actions.” Hence it is necessarily added at once: “There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans.” For “Chaldeans” is interpreted as “fierce.” They are very fierce because, following their own desires, they do not know how to spare even their own moral character. Earthly desires are fierce: they make the mind hard and insensitive not only against the commandments of the Creator but often even against the blows of punishment.

But the daughter of the fierce has no throne, because the mind born from evil desires into love of the world and hardened by those same desires loses the seat of judgment when it subjects itself to earthly lusts. It presides over no throne within itself because it lacks the scrutiny of discernment. It is, as it were, driven from the session of its own judgment because it wanders through the desire for outward things.

It is clear that the mind that has lost the seat of counsel within scatters itself outward through innumerable desires. And because it neglects to do what it understands, it is also blinded so that it does not know what it is doing. Often, by the just judgment of God, it is abandoned to its own will and surrendered to the laborious services of the world beneath the desire it anxiously pursues.

Hence the passage appropriately adds: “For you shall no longer be called tender and delicate; take the millstone and grind flour” (ibid.). It is evident that parents spare their tender daughters and do not afflict them with hard and servile work.

Almighty God therefore calls someone a tender daughter when he recalls the beloved soul of each person from the laborious services of this world, lest, while it is burdened with outward actions, it become hardened away from inward desires. But the daughter of the Chaldeans is not called tender and delicate, because the mind devoted to evil desires is left in the labor of this world, which it anxiously pursues, so that outwardly it may serve the world like a slave, while inwardly it does not love God like a daughter.

Hence she is commanded to take up the millstone and grind flour. A millstone is driven in a circle, and flour is produced. Every activity of this world is a millstone: while it heaps up many cares, it turns human minds as though in a circle; and from itself it casts out what is like flour, because it continually generates the tiniest thoughts in a deceived heart.

Sometimes, however, a person who was believed to possess the merit of quietness is exposed when placed in some activity. Hence the passage immediately continues: “Uncover your shame; uncover your shoulder; reveal your legs; cross the rivers” (ibid.).

In the administration of work, shame is uncovered when a low and despised mind is recognized in the display of its actions, although previously, while quiet, it had been considered great. The mind uncovers its shoulder when it displays its work, which had been unknown. It reveals its legs when it shows toward which passions of desire for worldly gain it is eagerly inclined. It also crosses the rivers when it continually pursues the activities of this world, which flow daily toward their end; and while it abandons one thing and follows another, it proceeds as though always from river to river.

We have said these things to show where the mind lies when it has been shaken from the throne of holy intention and devoted to the vice of wandering: for if it ceases to long for those things that are above, it also continually falls beneath itself. It is fixed on high if, abandoning the love of temporal things, it is bound to hope in unchanging eternity.

Nor do we establish by these words that a monk should remain perpetually in his retreat with stubborn resolve and never agree to go out when urgent necessity demands it. Rather, we advise that he do so as much more sparingly and rarely as he knows that, by wandering through the world, he cannot live spiritually or attain the summit of perfection, even if he remains diligently watchful.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning hermits who are given to wandering

Among all the kinds of people who deviate from their purpose, there is one that displeases me greatly: some seem to have been admitted even among the most holy hermits, men tormented by the same disease of pestilential wandering. They are afflicted—as one may say—by Vertumnus, a certain kind of demon. Among the ancients, demons were called Vertumni when, through their prompting, people were made unstable by being placed in a state of dizziness.

Those people seem not unreasonably subject to these demons who remain in their cells only during the season of Lent but spend almost the entire circle of the year wandering here and there, and thus consume their lives in empty roaming. Sometimes seeking somewhat more remote places, and at other times coming out into public more frequently, they boast that they extend themselves into both forms of life, namely the contemplative and the active. Yet they are shown to produce the full fruit of salvation in neither. And while they applaud themselves for joining, with Jacob, the marriage of two wives in a special union, it is found that the judgment of their own opinion is turned against them.

For them, contrary to what is customary, Rachel becomes bleary-eyed and Leah barren: the one is dulled by impaired sight, the other struck by the punishment of sterility. Such people, running about in public and consequently regarded by the people as having a sinister reputation, cannot beget spiritual children for God; and, returning from the world like drunkards, they cannot penetrate the innermost places.

Whoever desires to reach that inaccessible light with the sharpness of the mind must necessarily purify the inner eyes from every stain of worldly action through prolonged periods of wandering, lest, while he raises his eyes to contemplate the heights, the dust of earthly conduct obstruct him, and he see rather the darkness he had left behind than grasp the light toward which he strives.

## CHAPTER XXV. How habit makes the cell sweet, while wandering makes it dreadful

To this is added the fact that for those who alternate their life under this instability of change, the life of retreat becomes more severe in proportion as they are held back by their ingrained habit of wandering. Thus the discipline of the hermit life seems to them an extreme difficulty, and the cell itself a horror. Habit makes the cell seem sweet to the monk; wandering makes it seem dreadful.

To wanderers the cell is a prison; to those who remain, it is a pleasant bedroom. Silence makes the persevering monk vigilant; sleep overwhelms the one who comes from outside. Sobriety strengthens a body accustomed to fasting; an excess of abundant feasts enervates it. Moderate wakefulness sharpens the edge of the human mind; repeated, doubled sleep dulls it. Frequent conversation produces hunger in the monk’s mind; secret retreat guards the soul in the rigor of its accustomed self-restraint.

Report of worldly affairs makes the soul subject to the passions of desire; constant meditation on sacred speech renders it dead to the world. Poverty is the monk’s security of mind; security is the mother of purity. Conversely, abundance of possessions produces the goads of anxiety; anxiety is the root of distress. Unwashed feet, neglected hands, unkempt hair—these are like an anchor keeping the monk continually in his cell; conversely, the careful arrangement of a delicate body is a snare and an occasion for going out into public.

Whoever, therefore, wishes the eremitical life to become sweet to him must certainly strive to persevere in it continually with steadfast mind; nor should he alternate between states if he wishes to bear the Lord’s yoke peacefully. For the eremitical life, when uninterrupted, is refreshment; when interrupted, it seems a kind of torment. Through continuous withdrawal the soul is also illumined, vices are exposed, and whatever had been hidden from a person about himself is brought to light.

When water is drawn from a fishpond after the obstructions have been removed, the fish left stranded on dry ground endure human sight; so, when the flood of earthly activity ebbs away from us, whatever was accustomed to swim beneath the depths of its rising storms is exposed. A hunter too blocks up the winding passages, encloses the haunts of the woodland with dense thickets, and artfully leaves the fleeing beasts a single entrance; there, gripping his brandished spear, he sets an ambush. Thus he shortens for himself the labor of the hunt: he quietly awaits, in industrious leisure, at the very threshold of the exit, the tracks of the swift animals that he could not have pursued through boundless spaces.

So we close off the channels of earthly activity against vices striving to emerge into the freedom of wicked action, as though we were laying an ambush for them in one place, because we fight continually against thoughts alone. Thus the bestial savagery of our vices is easily captured, while the single passageway of human thought is carefully guarded.

The bird-catcher likewise covers all the surrounding pools with dense branches and compels the birds, by an imposed necessity, to converge upon one place where sweet water may be drawn. While that single place is exposed for drinking, the devices of the traps arranged around it are enriched by the successful outcome of the hunt. Therefore, if we wish easily to cast snares for the mind’s various passions, let us dam the streams of worldly business and strive manfully against the assaults of thought alone, so that, when our vices, deterred from action, fly toward us only amid the fluctuations of thought, they may easily fall into the snares of holy prudence.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### How the monk is often deceived by the false promise of worldly people

[Col. 0279B]

It must be observed that the servant of God is often deceived through the members of this world, when he is importunately invited either to settle disputes among those at odds or to undertake some task—especially one supposedly useful for ecclesiastical purposes. They exaggerate the imminent danger and the common peril of many people, unless he proceeds. If he does go, they repeatedly assure him that everything will turn out according to his wishes and end happily.

For when the ancient enemy sees Christ’s soldier stationed in the battle-line of holy combat, he contrives to make him grow lukewarm in the fervor of his purpose by superficially shading over some greater good, so that, while the greater profit is being considered, the good already present may for a time be deferred, supposedly for the sake of proper administration.

But one who has frequently experienced the custom of the lying world prudently knows both to reject the fabrications of those offering empty suggestions and to guard himself rigorously from the exercise of fruitless labor. Among some people, the authority of an absent monk is weighty; but if he is present, he is judged to be of no importance. Often reverential honor is paid to the letters of some venerable man, while it is shown less devotedly to his person if he is present.

Among worldly people, indeed, every religious person is like a painting. If a painting stands at a distance, it is gazed upon eagerly and with avidity; if it is nearby, it is judged contemptible. So every spiritual person, when absent, seems frightening to the carnal, but when present, despised. The Apostle testifies that this happened to him when he says: “His letters are weighty and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Corinthians 10). Those whom he had terrified by the force and gravity of his letters found him contemptible in bodily presence.

But what wonder if this happens to any righteous men, when the Gospel narrative also asserts something similar concerning the very Head of the elect, namely our Redeemer? “When Herod,” it says, “saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him” (Luke 23). But let us see what end this great and long-standing desire, which Herodian falsehood had maintained for the absent Lord, reached when the opportunity of seeing him was presented. This is clearly shown when the text continues shortly afterward: “Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment, and sent him back to Pilate” (ibid.).

Behold: that malicious fox despised the one he had desired; he mocked the one he had wished to see; and because he had not sought life for the love of living, by sending him back to Pilate he remained in the death of his impiety.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### How the monk should guard himself from involvement in the world

Whoever, therefore, stationed in the battle-line of the heavenly army hastens toward the homeland above should strive to reject the promises of the world that falsely flatters; he should dread becoming entangled under any pretext in the snares of worldly affairs. He has an office assigned to him in his own service. Let him consider it sufficient if he can fulfill the prescribed duty of the obedience enjoined upon him.

Let him recall what is written: “Take care that your activities are not many” (Ecclesiasticus 11). Let worldly people be left to arrange worldly affairs. Let it be enough for the servants of God to show themselves dead to this perishing world. For just as it is absurd to prefer evil things to good, so it is foolish to judge what is best to be inferior to something good.

Mary, because she chose the better portion, considered it sufficient for herself; nor did she turn toward Martha’s good, namely frequent service (Luke 10).
