Moses, because he withdrew from human society and fasted for twice forty days, also deserved twice to receive the Law of the Lord written by the finger (Exodus 24). Aaron, however, who had been left to guard the people, is known to have fashioned idols (Exodus 32).

So, so indeed, it generally happens that one who is not content with his own affairs and goes forward to care for another’s salvation is compelled instead to endure danger to his own. When he stretches out a hand to another, as to someone struggling amid stormy shipwreck, the devouring wave also engulfs him and drags him headlong.

It is therefore safer, beneath the nocturnal darkness of this life, for us who stand on the shore to shine a light toward those being shipwrecked than to swim out to them in compassion at the peril of our own lives. In this way, guided by the indication of the straight course given through us, they may reach the haven’s safe harbor, while we, crossing over to them, are not swallowed by the abyss of the foaming sea.

On the summit of Mount Rephidim Moses was praying, while Israel fought in the valley under the leadership of Joshua. But if Moses had descended to the plain to aid his people, Amalek would undoubtedly have struck the backs of the Israelites who were fighting. If he had lowered his hands to take up weapons, after slaughtering his men he would have offered an easy victory to his triumphant enemies.

This is plainly recognized if the whole sequence of sacred history is carefully considered, where it says: “When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them a little, Amalek overcame” (Exodus 17). The hands of the one who prayed therefore strengthened the hands of those who fought; and because the former were stretched out toward heaven without weapons, the latter, fighting, obtained victory over their slain enemies. The battle was theirs, but the victory undeniably belonged to those hands, because in order that the fighters might conquer, the praying hands deserved to obtain it from God.

By contrast, Balaam son of Beor, who went out to battle with the Midianites, was slain by the sword among those whom he had determined to slaughter (Numbers 31). And rightly: one who is not content with his own duty is made subject to danger belonging to another. Unhappy man, he deserved to fall pierced by enemy swords among the ranks of combatants because, while remaining in peace, he could have announced through the oracle of prophecy the outcome of that very war.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On Elisha’s freedom and discretion

Elisha certainly did not follow King Joram of Israel as he hastened against Moab for battle; he considered it sufficient merely to predict to him the outcome of the war and the victory that would come after the enemies had been cut down (2 Kings 3).

But why do we say that he did not follow the royal camp into battle, when, even when Naaman came from the distant borders of Syria and humbly stood at the door of his house with horses and chariots, he did not deem it worthy to cross the threshold or open the door for him to enter, but instead sent word through a messenger about what had to be done?

Certainly Naaman possessed a wealth of worldly distinctions by which he might seem worthy of honor. As the history testifies: “He was commander of the army, a great man also with his lord, and honored” (ibid.). Through him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria. Moreover, as it is written, he was a strong and wealthy man. Even while engaged in that expedition, he was by no means lacking in material resources. For he had brought with him, as we read, ten talents of silver, six thousand gold pieces, and likewise ten changes of clothing. Although Scripture does not say what kind they were, who would doubt that, counted among substantial weights of gold and silver, they were precious?

How many today are considered members of the monastic order who, if so powerful and famous a man deigned to stand at their doors, would immediately hurry reverently to meet him, humbly beg him to enter, and utter words of flattery—not so much words that ought usefully to be fulfilled as words they would gladly hear? Even if they were asked so insistently, they would by no means refuse the gifts offered, especially if a somewhat larger community of brothers to be fed were present.

But Elisha, disciple of the Holy Spirit, rich in hope and wealthy in the treasure of faith, although he supported a hundred sons of the prophets under his discipline and teaching, despised money, rejected gifts, and commendably refused to receive repayment for the grace he had bestowed, lest he seem to sell, to the injury of the giver, what he had received freely.

When Naaman came, he did not rise—not arrogantly, but prudently—lest he show reverence to a foreigner who was still presuming upon earthly glory. For even then he displayed the image of apostolic dignity, which Paul later expressed when he said: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry” (Romans 11).

Is he to be considered a servant of humility, he who made Naaman stand arrogantly before his doors, when he allowed himself to be led from Mount Carmel, where he lived, by a woman, and not only accompanied but even followed the Shunammite woman? For when she said (2 Kings 4), “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you,” Scripture immediately continues: “He arose and followed her.”

Did he also reject abundant gifts with the pride of haughty arrogance, when he did not disdain charitably to accept cheap barley loaves from a certain man who came from Baal-shalisha?

But here, while we set forward the prophet’s obstacle, lest he be accused of proud exaltation, we open an entrance to a searching question against ourselves. An objection of this kind can be raised against what we have proposed: If so great a prophet both accepted loaves from the hands of the one offering them and consented to leave the wilderness at a woman’s entreaty, why should a monk either dare not frequent the world or be reluctant to accept gifts?

In brief response, we do not entirely cut off a monk’s permission to receive something; rather, we advise that he do so more moderately and with discretion, when fraternal devotion requires it. Let him accept whatever is necessary, as the prophet accepted the loaves he needed, but let him refuse what he judges superfluous, as Elisha refused the money.

As for the fact that Elisha descended from his mountain retreat to restore the Shunammite’s son to life, this should be regarded by monks of the present time more as something to venerate than to imitate. A monk may certainly return to the world by his own choice whenever he is able to raise a dead person to life.

That prophetic journey is clearly both filled with power, through the miracle of human resurrection, and typical, through the mystery of its inner meaning. It is not useless to add briefly what it signifies.

The boy sent by Elisha did not raise the Shunammite’s son with the staff. Elisha himself, however, came and stretched himself over the dead man; drawing himself together to his limbs, walking back and forth, and breathing seven times into the mouth of the dead man, he immediately restored him to living light through the mystery of compassion.

God, the author of the human race, grieved over us as over a dead child when, in pity, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he brought forth the terror of the Law, he sent the rod, as it were, through a boy. For God had held the rod of the Law when he said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die” (Exodus 20–21).

The Law, therefore, could not raise us from the death of sin; but God, by the breath of the grace of gentleness, mercifully raised us to the state of life. The boy could not raise the dead with the staff because, as Paul testifies, “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7).

But Elisha came in person and humbly stretched himself over the corpse, drawing himself together to equal the dead man’s limbs: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2).

He walks back and forth because he calls both Judea, which is near him, and the nations situated far away. He breathes seven times over the dead because the sevenfold grace of the Spirit inflames those lying in the death of sin for the reception of the divine gift. Immediately the living man rises, because the one whom the rod of terror could not raise is brought back to life by the spirit of love (2 Kings 4).

Who, then, would rightly dare to take the prophet’s journey as an example, when it is clear that he cannot equal either its power or its mystery?

Let Christ’s soldier therefore keep constant watch, protected by the breastplate of faith and stationed in the battle-line of the heavenly army. Let him always stand ready to fight before the camp of his commander, lest the hostile sword perhaps find him wandering outside the camp and consume him.

As long as Abner remained in the camp of his fellow soldiers, he was terrible to the ranks of his adversaries. But after he laid down his arms, he paid the penalty for the recently slain Asahel by the sword of an even less experienced soldier (2 Samuel 2).

If Uriah had been pleased to take lodging in his own house, he would undoubtedly have escaped the sentence of royal indignation and treachery. But because he preferred to sleep outside, in another’s quarters, rather than in his own bedroom, he carried to the commander besieging the city the letter that caused his death (2 Samuel 11).

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### How preaching in the present time is not as fruitful as it once was

[Col. 0283C]

There was once a time when the world needed those who announced good things. But the times have passed and slipped away in which a religious person could profitably advise worldly people and sow spiritual things, not without benefit, in carnal minds.

Now the unhappy regard the words of life as fables, and although they lend their ears to saving admonitions, they nevertheless avoid keeping them. If we turn the eyes of faith back toward the past, we find that the present age has degenerated from the former one like fruitful branches into barren shoots.

Who would not marvel that Nineveh, an exceedingly vast and incomparable city, was so easily converted from its wickedness at the voice of one man, and that an innumerable people—not only with children and women, but even with animals—was called back to repentance (Jonah 3)?

Who in the present time would dare prescribe a three-day fast, not to the weak in age or sex, but even to men themselves, so that they might neither drink water nor taste any food at all? Behold: among the Gentiles even brute beasts abstained from food for three days at the prophet’s voice, while under evangelical discipline human beings themselves disdain to fast beyond a single day.

They flocked unanimously to repentance at the preaching of one man; these people listen continually to crowds of preachers and in no way consent to obey.

Who would not also be astonished that all the men of Judah and Benjamin who had taken foreign wives, at the preaching of Ezra the priest, not only dissolved their unlawful marriages but also cast away all the offspring born from them (1 Esdras 10)?

Who does not know how great the love of men for their wives is, and how great the affection for children that binds a father’s heart? Who does not realize with what grief and bitterness human entrails could be torn apart in dissolving the double bond of this relationship? By what fire of most intense pain were paternal affection and marital devotion compelled to burn?

Yet because they possessed true piety toward God, they reduced the appearance of false piety to nothing. In order to be truly pious in spirit, they became laudably harsh toward flesh and blood. They armed themselves against the rights of nature so that they might faithfully serve the Author of nature. They forgot, in relation to their children, that they had been parents, so that they themselves might be reckoned heirs of the true Father; and in order to restore their covenant with heavenly peace, they severed the union of the marriage bed.

They do not know how to preserve fidelity to marriages where a better fidelity turns back toward its own author. To them what is said through Moses is appropriately applied: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize you,’ and who did not acknowledge his sons—these kept your word and observed your covenant” (Deuteronomy 33).

Who, I ask, could now dissolve incestuous marriages, however insistently he preached? Who could provoke, not a people, but even one person to repudiate an unlawful marriage? The sacred canons cry out; human laws exact punishment for such a crime; the preachers of the Church oppose it. Yet all these things produce laughter in ruined men, like old women’s tales, rather than piercing them with sorrow for correcting their abomination.

Moreover, as you know, this very year a synodal council was twice convened by the bishop of the Roman see, where once again all those in incestuous unions were deprived of ecclesiastical communion in accordance with the decrees of the canons.

But who among so many thousands of people has seen even one torn away from the abomination of that ill-fated union? Indeed, so that they might not be swallowed by the deeper chasm of one who justly cries out, which of them afterward ceased to tread the threshold of the Church? Or who, considering these things, withdrew from their companionship?

Thus the contagion of deadly leprosy spreads to everyone, because the bond of apostolic excommunication binds all their accomplices. Indeed, whoever is adorned with the titles of marital lineage, whoever is flattered by the ancestral beauty of an attractive form—especially if he abounds in the wealth of greater property, or if the character of growing offspring fills him with hope for future descendants—judges it more prudent to depart openly from God than to break apart the adhesive bond of so profitable a marriage.

If the opposite happens and he is struck by the calamity and distress of lust, the man himself fabricates a line of false kinship, invents through many arguments unheard-of names of great-grandparents, and summons certain old men as witnesses to this claim, although he knows that they have long since been removed from life.

Thus he himself, both accuser and defendant, brings the crime against himself, magnifies the offense, and seeks a means by which he may swim out of so dangerous a shipwreck.

Let the monk go now, then, abandon the saving leisure of his life, and consume his life by pursuing empty things under the pretext of winning souls. For what Simoniac has ever, at the prompting of our admonition, voluntarily laid down his office? What violent invader of another’s rights has restored to the patrimonies those driven from their paternal soil? What man surrounded on a battlefield by armed and warlike ranks, if he could meet them on equal terms, has returned home without bloodshed because an intervening obstacle of peace separated him from them?

What tax collector has forgiven a poor debtor the interest fixed in writing? What debtor has preserved the rights of good faith for the heirs of his creditor?

Everything is confused throughout the world; all decrees of piety and faith are shaken. Justice is sold by judges. Truth is darkened by legal experts beneath the shadowy color of sophistical argument. Laws are indeed for sale, and money justifies those who commit offenses.

Gold now presides over the senators themselves, judges in the tribunals, and like an emperor promulgates edicts of pragmatic sanction. For just as a king, in secret inner chambers, deliberates about the state of the kingdom and the sum of affairs, so gold, in a certain manner, lies hidden and issues its sentence publicly. It is enclosed in a small purse and, once business has been decided, places its judicial counters.

Often lying money shamelessly declares those whom the case condemns worthy of reward; conversely, it establishes as guilty before judges those whom conscience testifies to be innocent. Money assigns weight to the laws, and a false interpreter bends obscure judgments to its own understanding. Money softens the hearts of judges toward the rich with the oil of impiety; toward the poor, it drives them to exercise the severity of harsh punishment.

Now, therefore, avarice, the root of all evils, sprouts more luxuriantly and, like branches of a poisonous stock, spreads throughout the entire world the monsters of deadly vices.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### How all the monsters of vice now flourish more savagely

[Col. 0285D]

These are the times foretold by the apostolic oracle, when he predicts the future to Timothy: “In the last days,” he says, “there will be perilous times, and people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, without self-control, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3). After these words he immediately adds: “Avoid such people” (ibid.).

Was Timothy to live until the end of this world, when, as the Apostle enumerated the wickedness of people that would exist in the last days, he immediately added that he should avoid them? Or did he rather, in the person of one disciple, impose this command generally upon those whom he foresaw would still be appointed to office near the end of the age?

Since he does not say, “Preach to these people; announce the words of life to them,” but rather, “Avoid such people,” he certainly condemns the insolence of modern presumption and restrains the proud from fruitless preaching.

What do we monks say to this, who exceed the boundaries of our own measure and usurp for ourselves, arrogantly, the right to another’s office? If Paul prohibited a disciple specifically appointed to this task from preaching to the incorrigible, by what mark of audacity are we reproached, when, though no preaching office has been delegated to us, we thrust ourselves forward importunately and, putting our own salvation second, labor uselessly as though for the progress of others?

Let sterile concern for business yield, then—let it yield. Let it be judged superfluous to devote oneself to fruitless labor. Let the mind, gathered together within itself with all its strength, return to itself and keep vigilant for combat against its tireless adversaries.

Let charity overflow inwardly toward everyone, but let the mind judge it superfluous to extend itself outwardly for another’s salvation. Let it offer saving admonitions to those who come to it, but let it not lightly postpone the profits of its own quiet at anyone’s urging.

An imperial edict is delivered by a courier as he travels; sealed receipts are sent to us by the author of the apostolic see; a synod is convened, and the entire council’s principal responsibility is entrusted to religious men. Let the monk immediately comply only so far and reverently render honor to the sacred writings; yet let him regard the duty of this expedition as irrevocably foreign to him, saying within himself: “What have I to do with the kings of the earth? What have I to do with a synodal assembly? Let it be enough for me to persist in weeping over my sins; let it be enough for me to show myself dead to this world.”

Do not, I beg you, monks—do not, under the appearance of ecclesiastical compassion, burst into the courts of kings. Do not strike the ears of princes with tiresome importunity under the pretext of offering salutary advice. Believe one who has experienced this; believe one who has not been lightly wearied by devotion to this grace.

For we have often expressed to imperial majesty what seemed necessary to suggest; invited by the supreme pontiffs, we attended synodal councils. But whoever pursues such things in the present time seems to be sowing seed on sandy shores.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### How, in a synod, a monk does not dare to speak freely against the envy of bishops

Often, while stationed in synodal councils, we have seen certain men presiding among the priests who were savagely conscious of their own crimes—not merely unconcerned about themselves, but even shamelessly prepared to defend the crimes of others. As was reported, they had previously bought gifts with Simon (Acts 2), and later sold the gifts of divine grace with Gehazi (2 Kings 5).

Their power to devise excuses for sins was so great that, among their other evils, they seemed not merely defenders of the Simoniac heresy but rather its advocates. What monk would dare mutter against the envy of such men? Who would dare claim the right of freedom in order to reproach crimes or declare justice?

They would rage at once; they would immediately seize the weapons of harsh mockery against us; and, after beginning with abuse, they would command silence, complaining among themselves in this fashion: “We have assembled for this council in order to judge.”

But, O unprecedented presumption! We are subject to the judgments of the dead, and those who had been legally constituted under the laws of bishops have become their judges.

To such men one may sometimes reply: “Venerable Fathers and lords, just as the prerogative of judging has been specially granted to you, so it also belongs to the lesser members of the Church to bring together in common what they think. No authority of the canons forbids younger members from expressing what they believe beneficial to the Church, provided that the conclusion of pontifical judgment terminates the matters that have been debated.”

Whenever something of this kind, or anything similar, is humbly suggested to them, they do not accept it patiently. Whatever we say in the synod is wholly called a judgment against us in an arrogant accusation.

I have touched on these matters briefly so that any inexperienced person may learn from me how carefully it is necessary to keep oneself away from such people. From one person going ahead, one can gather whether an army following afterward may safely trust unknown waters.

Merchants immediately restrain themselves from the impulse of their own course when they see even one of their companions return from the market with nothing sold. A man often occupied with rural work has been deceived by a denied harvest; many have been restrained from cultivating barren fields.

When a searcher of the waves, frustrated by his labor, brings back his empty nets in weariness, he easily recalls those who have already been stripped bare from exploring the poor waters. So let it be enough that I have attempted such things—not for me alone, but for all my brothers—so that, when the labor of one is judged useless, caution may be provided not to one person but to many against the expense of superfluous work.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### How the monk should restrain himself from the world and always place God’s judgment before his eyes

[Col. 0287D]

Whoever, therefore, as a monk hastens to attain the summit of perfection should confine himself within the enclosures of his withdrawal and love spiritual leisure. But let him dread running through the world as though plunging himself into a lake of blood.

For the world is increasingly polluted day by day by the contamination of so many crimes that any holy mind is defiled by the mere sight of it. And while new evils are continually added to the old, what else is being done but, without doubt, preparing the way for Antichrist, so that, when he comes into the world near its end, he may enter freely without obstruction?

Since that way consists in nothing other than our scandals, the same consideration ought to restrain our footsteps which promises him the ability to take free steps [lacuna; surviving fragment: “tare”].

[Col. 0288A]

Let every brother, therefore, now be restrained within the narrow prison of his withdrawal, so that a house of infinite greatness may be prepared for him in heaven. Jeremiah says: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession! It is great and has no end; it is exalted and immeasurable!” (Baruch 3).

Now let him bind himself with the bond of divine fear, so that afterward he may obtain the right of true freedom. Resting in Christ, let him consider that he has nothing in common with the world, so that he may preserve not only in his heart but also in his very body what the Apostle John commands: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (2 John 2).

Let it be clear that Christ’s servant loves the world with no affection of the heart, and, to prove this, let him also disdain to frequent it with bodily footsteps. Let bodily abstinence itself confirm the hatred of the devout mind, so that the more someone is alienated from harmful knowledge of the world, the more closely he may be joined to God in intimacy.

Now let him keep his eyes fixed upon the earth, weeping and grieving, so that then, joyful, he may raise them to see him who will come in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty (Matthew 24), as it is written: “Look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21).

O how exceedingly brief these words are to pronounce, yet how infinite the meaning they contain when examined to the depths! For then the condemned, groaning with trembling hearts, will say: “Mountains, fall upon us, and hills, cover us from the face of the One seated upon the throne” (Luke 23).

Finally, “the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven” (Matthew 24). Then every eye will see him, including those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.

What human mind can conceive, what tongue can express, how great the joy of the elect will then be, how indescribable the happiness of the blessed, when, as the world falls into peril, they themselves cease thereafter to be subject to dangers and, with lamps lit, joyfully go out to meet the immortal Bridegroom who is coming! (Matthew 25.)

When the members of the world collapse to endure the punishments of infernal fire, they themselves rise happy to receive the rewards of inaccessible glory. When death suddenly cuts short the life of the former, glorious incorruption consumes the mortality of the latter, which has been swallowed up by the power of the resurrection.

Let the holy mind continually set before itself this singular spectacle, worthy of admiration throughout all ages. Let it paint before its eyes through constant meditation this terrifying image of the coming judgment. Let the chosen man already consider himself snatched before the Judge’s tribunal; let him fearfully reflect that, placed on trial, he is being pressed by divine questions to render an account.

Let him make himself a stranger to the world, so that he may cling more closely to God through the gift of a more generous grace. In this way, though dead, let him live; let him withdraw himself from earthly troubles; and, as though already placed in a tomb, let him rest sweetly in the sole desire of his Creator.

Thus let his life be hidden in God, so that, when Christ appears, he too may deserve to appear with him in glory (Colossians 3). Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### The author addresses the venerable monks Peter and Albizo

Now, therefore, dearest brothers—one a polished example of the coenobitic form of life, the other an example of eremitical conduct worthy of imitation—I turn the point of this pen back toward you, so that the conclusion of the little work already completed may end with those toward whom its beginning was directed.

You see how quickly this brief life passes; you see that this world now proclaims its approaching end through increasingly evident signs. For the earth, exhausted of its generative moisture, somehow endures the plow unwillingly, while it refuses to bear fruit for its cultivators. Like an aged womb, while the blood grows cold in the body as the womb withers, even if the desire to generate has not failed, it nevertheless does not rise to produce offspring.

Water likewise suffers sterility, so that the fisherman now finds his nets an expense without return, while the profit from a meager catch does not repay the hard labor expended upon the liquid element.

Nor will I pass over you, once-fruitful air, which now, because you do not produce results in the capture of birds through the various devices of snares, send the bird-catchers, frustrated by fruitless labor, back to agricultural work. Those whom formerly you directed toward high places in pursuit of your gifts, you now make subject to the earth that sustains them, so that they may remember to whom they owe the means of sustaining life. You, who once in your abundance commanded every coarser food to yield to your delights, now, withdrawing your hand from them, make cheap little vegetables fill the tables of the rich like carefully prepared feasts.

The world, then, as has been said above, like one already wearied by prolonged old age, clearly indicates through all its members that it is not extending the end of its course much longer. To this is added the fact that people now grow old in youth, and, while the beauty of youth is still flourishing, sprinkle their heads prematurely with gray hairs. Indeed, those whom their own age declares to be still green with the flower of immature beauty, the aged world, by a kind of violent exercise of authority, commands to appear decrepit along with itself. Hence it comes about that, just as the fruits of a hollow tree fall as soon as they have been produced, before they reach maturity, so [Col. 0289D] people die an untimely death, so to speak, before they arrive at the fullness of age.

Since, then, the world threatens that the sunset of its course is precipitously and already immediately impending before our eyes, and people too are daily carried away by premature death, what remains except that, in this brief moment in which we live, we should despise all things that are bound to fall as though they had already fallen, and hasten with the full desire of an ardent mind toward those things that endure? Behold, no slight rewards are set before those who are running, and the course of our journey is shortened each day. Let no stumbling blocks of the present life impede the path of our course; let no sluggishness born of carnal allurements entangle us in delays. [Col. 0290A] Let each person now direct the eyes of a discerning faith toward the promised rewards, and let him rise on the wings of sturdy hope above every obstacle of earthly perversity that stands in his way, as though casting off the bonds of brutish sluggishness. For behold, he who had called from afar now extends his hand to those who are drawing near; and, like a tender father strengthening little children who totter on wavering knees, he gently and kindly invites them into the embrace of his love.

Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of glory (Hebrews 4); let us seize the insignia of such great compassion. What would have been presumption—to seek what was not promised—let it be shame to refuse when it is offered. Let us now disdain to tread bodily so often the mire of this muddy world, whose love, by God’s inspiration, we have learned to trample underfoot with a free mind. Let bodily movement itself be restrained from him whom the soul does not love; let us judge him unworthy of the frequency of our visits who delights in triumphing over our ruin. Let bodily absence itself bear witness to the mind’s enmity; let that man not deserve our frequent passing-by whose sight our eyes have been accustomed to defile; and let him alone fall into the pits of his own ambushes who continually prepares the snares of deception for our footsteps. Thus, yes thus, let him mourn the failure of his fraudulent watchfulness while, as we rest in peace, the crafty ambusher investigates the entrance to our nocturnal departure.

Let the field of divine eloquence be sufficient for our wandering. Let us walk continually through this field and take delight in roaming about it. There it is permitted to run with free steps across the even plain of the sacred histories. [Col. 0290C] We can also, through the depth of mystical understanding, somehow climb there the heights of precipitous mountains. There we shall enjoy the sweet conversation of faithful friends; there is a varied display and an unceasing banquet of heavenly foods. Hungering for these dishes, let the faithful soul receive strength, nourished by the food of constant reading, and, fattened on the richness of the purest prayer, let it grow plump. Let the hunger of the world be left to those who disdain the world’s banquet. We, however, have learned to hunger for those dishes which are accustomed both to grant the hungry satiety with delight and yet do not know how to produce disgust in those who are satisfied. These dishes, indeed, pleasantly fill the stomach of our mind, yet owe nothing to the retreats of sewers. For they leave absolutely nothing of themselves for excretion; rather, they spread throughout the pores of all the veins and into the innermost parts of all the viscera, in order to provide strength. [Col. 0290D]

With these dishes of the heavenly table, then, let the attentive mind occupy itself without satiation; let the eye watch over them diligently; let the articulate tongue run through the words of the written page; let the heart understand what is read and turn over the secrets of the hidden mystery. Let the sacred animals continually ruminate this food through the practice of constant reconsideration; let it flow back repeatedly from the belly of knowledge into the throat of memory through repeated meditation. These dishes, I say, let the ever-fasting mind always hunger for; from them, though never satisfied, let it never withdraw. Rather, the more it is filled, the more eagerly let it again be inflamed with appetite for them. Let us so occupy all our senses with these life-giving foods [Col. 0291A] that, having become insensible to all the affairs of worldly causes, truly dead to the world, we may live for God alone. Thus may the author and instructor of this most blessed dish deem us worthy to enroll among those guests who shall deserve to hear from the mouth of Truth:

> “I appoint to you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one to me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

May almighty God, who is love (1 John 4), most beloved brothers, mercifully inspire your holy hearts, so that you may always deign to pray for me, a sinner.

## SCHOLIA

It must therefore be concluded that, just as we must beware of those whom the modern councils of synods exclude from ecclesiastical fellowship, so likewise we must avoid those whom the ancient Fathers decree should be cast out. At this point Blessed Damian seems to be speaking according to the custom of the Church that was observed in his own age. Before the Council of Constance, the faithful were universally forbidden to share in communion with excommunicated persons, according to chapter *Cautum est*, Distinction 11, Question 3, and chapter *Cum desideres*, as well as frequently elsewhere.

At the Council of Constance, however, through the Constitution of Martin V beginning *Ad evitanda multa scandala* (“To avoid many scandals”), which Leo X also confirmed at the Fifth Lateran Council, session 11, and which Martin Navarrus reports in his *Summa*, chapter 27, no. 36—an enactment still mentioned by Didacus Covarrubias in *Cap. Alma mater*, Part I, *Relectio*, paragraph 2—it was decreed:

> “The faithful are permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons, except for two classes: namely, those who have been formally denounced by name, or those who are notorious strikers of clerics.”

In accordance with this decree, we shall interpret the zeal and judgment of our doctor.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0291]

## 283–284. THIRTEENTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE PERFECTION OF MONKS. TO O. . . ., ABBOT OF POMPOSA, AND HIS COMMUNITY

### ARGUMENT

In this little book he performs, so to speak, the office of a teacher. After lamenting the corrupted customs and institutions of the monks of his own time, he instructs them toward perfection by means of highly salutary precepts: he carefully teaches what they ought to flee and what they ought to embrace, so that they may reach the desired goal of their labors and the palm of their struggles.

Indeed, almost the whole work is devoted to inviting them, after setting aside earthly desires, to love God ardently—not out of fear of punishments, but willingly—and to leading them, as though by the hand, to charity itself, the citadel of the virtues. Having opened this royal path as though it were a highway, he then turns to the other paths of the virtues: patience, humility, obedience, compunction, penance, and contemplation. Adorned with these virtues as with brilliant gems, the spirit of each monk appears beautiful and comely, not merely to the eyes of external observers but also before the gaze of the inward spectator.

After addressing everyone in general, he finally admonishes each one individually concerning his duty: abbots, provosts, and the rest, whatever their age, instructing them to live well and blessedly according to the rule prescribed by their predecessors.

[Col. 0291B]

To Lord O. . . ., venerable abbot, and to the holy community, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of most devoted servitude.

Although a poor little debtor cannot pay everything he owes, it is nevertheless an excuse to offer the very little that he possesses. Often a peasant who had borrowed money brought his creditor nothing more than a gift of vegetables, and soon returned freed by the written acknowledgment of his obligation. Thus I, who owe much to your kindnesses, send humble writings—humble, I say, because of my rusticity, not because of their own nature: for they are both faithful interpreters of the divine will and trustworthy repositories of ancient and recent deeds.

## [ON THE PERFECTION OF MONKS]

### CHAPTER I. On the Diminution of the Fervor of Holy Religion

[Col. 0291C]

You do not fail to know, my brothers—though I speak with a groan—to what a decline of holy fervor our order has fallen, indeed how it does not cease to fall more steeply each day: we have now almost carelessly forgotten all the commandments and seem content with the garment of this profession alone. For under the appearance of religion we live in a worldly manner, and, having violated the spirit of discipline, while we dissolve ourselves in the flow of allurements, we possess the name of monks in vain, like an illegitimate child who rejoices to be reckoned by his father’s name, although the degenerate condition of his birth excludes him by law from the inheritance.

Indeed, Ishmael and all the sons of Keturah were indiscriminately called sons of Abraham. But when the rights of succession were reached, the entire inheritance was handed over to Isaac, the legitimate son, while gifts alone were granted to the sons of the concubines. “An illegitimate shoot,” says Solomon, “will not strike deep roots” (Wisdom 4).

Please do not turn what I say into an insult against you. You know that fuel is properly piled up wherever at least a spark of fire seems to remain; but who blows uselessly upon a place where he sees that the heat has completely gone out? Unless I had greater confidence in you through the grace of Christ, I would judge it pointless to pursue you with the pen of exhortation while leaving the others aside. [Col. 0292C]

Therefore, my beloved, gather your strength with Christ’s help, and bear the service of him whose arms you have sworn to take up—not sluggishly, not weakly, but rather fervently and manfully. Thus the beginnings of your way of life, which still lie in a certain middle state, may not, God forbid, through negligence return to nothing, but may grow through the persistence of continual fervor toward the summit of perfection. Remember what is said to the angel of the Church of Sardis:

> “Be watchful, and strengthen what remains, which was about to die; for I have not found your works complete before my God” (Revelation 3).

Because he had not found his works complete before God, he declared even those things that had already been done well to be on the point of dying. For if what is dead in us is not kindled into life, even what is held as though still alive is extinguished. He loses what he had done who does not complete what must be done.

What good is it if a body begins to be formed in the mother’s womb and yet does not reach the fullness of natural growth? You are not unaware of the offspring concerning whom it is said:

> “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her anguish because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world” (John 16).

### CHAPTER II. That Unless Each Person Strives to Complete What He Has Begun, He Cannot Reach the Love of God

God plainly does not approve an abortive work. He examines the actions of persons and offices, conditions and orders on the scales of provident scrutiny, and he has different balances for each order. Had he not possessed a suitable balance for weighing the king’s deeds, and had he not weighed that man’s actions when he wrote upon the wall with the fingers of a hand:

> “Your kingdom has been weighed in the balance, and you have been found wanting?” (Daniel 5)

For this reason it was immediately added:

> “Your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (ibid.).

If almighty God therefore took both kingdom and life from that man for no other crime than that he found in him no fullness of such a good work as befitted a king, what are we to think of ourselves? Under a monastic profession we have promised to climb the heights of perfection, yet we still lie in the valley of our imperfection beneath the torpor of sloth. Why does a person not strive with all his strength to fulfill what lies before him? At least so that he may not lose everything he had acquired through earlier labor.

For no matter how far anyone has traveled, what does he gain, I ask, if he does not reach the appointed place? Moreover, if someone who was intensely hostile to a king could return to favor in no other way than by weighing out one hundred pounds of silver, certain that after paying the royal debt he would receive not only favor but also the insignia of some great dignity, would he not be foolish if he allowed the ninety-nine pounds already carried into the public treasuries to perish unless the single pound remaining from the account were paid? Is it not better that the small amount remaining be fully paid and that the man receive favor together with dignity, than that he lose both what was given and—what is more terrible—remain under the king’s displeasure?

Brothers, to speak confidently, we have given—yes, we have given ninety pounds of silver to our King Christ. For his sake we have abandoned possessions, rejected marriage, avoided the eating of meat, shuddered at the pomp and glory of the world, and exchanged the splendor of secular dress for a humble garment. These things are great, they are arduous, I confess, and they ought to be compensated by the gifts of heavenly reward. But something still remains by which the prescribed weight must be completed, so that we may deserve to be admitted into the treasury of the eternal King.

You ask what this is. It immediately occurs to me to answer you: obedience, love, joy, peace, patience, and the other virtues that the preacher to the nations enumerates (Galatians 5). But I want to touch on the matter briefly, so that it may more easily, and therefore more firmly, adhere to your minds. It is nothing other than fervor toward God and mortification of oneself.

For if the apostolic saying lived in us, in which it is said:

> “Always carrying in our body the mortification of Jesus” (2 Corinthians 6),

then, because carnal love would have no place within us in which to spread itself, all our delight would necessarily be transferred, suspended upon God. There our fire would leap up and live, because it would have no room within us in which to spread itself.

A prudent man, intent with great vigilance on guarding his salvation, constantly watches over the repression of vices with such care that, with the girdle of perfect mortification, he binds his loins and kidneys, his belly together with his sides, on every side. This happens when the itching appetite is restrained; when a forward tongue is curbed under silence; when the ear is closed to detraction; when the eye is forbidden to look upon unlawful things; when the hand is held back from striking rashly and the foot from wandering meaninglessly; when the heart is resisted so that it does not envy another’s prosperity, covet through avarice what is not its own, divide itself from fraternal love through anger, exalt itself arrogantly above others, consent with delight to tickling lust, or sink itself excessively into grief or dissolve itself in seductive joy.

Since the human mind cannot remain wholly empty, so as not to occupy itself with the love of some thing, when it is enclosed on every side by this wall of virtues, and is not permitted to expand around itself, it must necessarily be carried above itself.

### CHAPTER III. That It Is Necessary to Cultivate the Soil of Our Heart If We Wish to Rejoice in a Broad Possession

When, in this manner, our mind begins to rest in its Creator and already to taste something of that innermost sweetness, it immediately rejects whatever it judges contrary to the divine law and shudders at whatever differs from the rule of heavenly justice. From this true mortification is plainly born; from this it comes about that a person, carrying the cross of his Redeemer, appears dead to the world.

Thus he no longer rejoices in the foolishness of stories or allows himself to dissolve into idle words. Rather, he devotes himself to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; he seeks withdrawal and longs for a hiding place. He considers the workshops of those who converse to be the public marketplace of the monastery’s cloister; he delights in corners and searches out secluded places. And so that he may stand more freely in the sight of his Creator, he avoids human conversations as far as he is able.

[Col. 0295A]

After this man has overthrown the cities of his enemies, after he has trodden upon and destroyed the necks of kings hiding in a cave, after he has subverted maritime, level, and mountainous kingdoms, what remains except that he should possess the land of promise with Joshua the conqueror in tranquil peace?

Otherwise, what good does it do that, abandoning Egypt, we crossed the Red Sea after it was divided, if we are now confined for forty years in the desert and can neither return to the pots of meat nor enter, by right of possession, the land flowing with milk and honey? We sleep, we snore, and we waste away beneath the torpor of sloth.

It is rightly said to our reproach what Joshua is reported to have said to the seven tribes that still had no possessions:

> “How long,” he said, “will you languish in sloth and not enter to possess the land that the Lord God of your fathers has given you?” (Joshua 18).

A soldier is foolish, finally, if he strives to conquer but has not first determined to fight; he is excessively delicate if he tries to obtain victory before he goes forth to battle. The farmer is frustrated if, before sweating to sow, he desires to thresh, since it is certain that whoever wishes to gather grain must first uproot the thorns together with the briars.

And truly the divine voice says to sinful humanity:

> “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles” (Genesis 3).

But if this land is to be fruitful in crops, it must first endure the hoe and the plowshare, so that, cultivated through various afflictions and the disciplines of perfect penance, it may be adorned with the abundance of all virtues, like a rich yield of fruits. [Col. 0295C]

Joshua was figuratively urging the sons of Joseph toward this cultivation when, as they complained to him about the smallness of their allotted territory, he said:

> “If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and clear a space for yourself in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you” (Joshua 17).

To apply the matter, not inappropriately, to what lies closer to us: the man who decided to be content with the rule of Blessed Benedict alone has confined himself within the narrow possession of Mount Ephraim. But hear how the new Joshua urges you toward the mountain and commands you to hasten toward broader stretches of possession:

> “We have written this rule,” he says, “so that, by observing it to some extent, we may demonstrate that we have either integrity of conduct or the beginning of a monastic way of life.”

Behold Mount Ephraim. But because he recognizes that the possession here is narrow, he immediately sends the monks higher and also farther afield:

> “For those who hasten toward perfection,” he says, “there are the teachings of the saints, the conferences and institutions of the Fathers,”

and so forth. Since we know these matters to be very familiar to you, we judge it superfluous to set them down here.

### CHAPTER IV. On Those Who Imitate the Example of the Gibeonites

But would that, since we are tepid and degenerate and do not strive toward higher things, we would at least diligently plow the narrow places of this small mountain, so that no corner of the commandments within the same rule might lie hidden beneath negligence, where the plow of our labor and discipline has not furrowed. For whenever we see commands that are harder or however much higher, we fear to drive the plow of our sweat there, as though into a precipitous mountain or living rock.

We wish to be counted among the ranks of soldiers, but we do not care to possess the insignia of the virtues. Before the eyes of human beings we display an image of uprightness, but in the sight of the hidden Judge we neglect to possess the reality.

For some—what I cannot say without a groan—enter the order of the new religion in such a way that they never abandon the oldness of their former life. These are Gibeonites, not Israelites.

It is well known that the Gibeonites, terrified by fear of death, came to the Israelite people with fraud and cunning. They put on old garments and also carried dry loaves, wineskins, sacks, sandals, and everything else in a worn-out condition. After their lives had been spared by the treaty they obtained, their fraud was consequently exposed and recognized. Joshua, discovering the deception, condemned them under a curse and established them perpetually as water-carriers and woodcutters (Joshua 9).

Who, then, are the Gibeonites who pass over to the Israelites through fear of death, except those who flee to the service of God not from love of perfection but terrified by the enormity of their crimes? Some of them, however, changed in clothing but not in mind, carry dry loaves for food because they still do not know the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (2 Corinthians 5). They are covered with old garments because, still established in the old person, they do not know how to put on the new person, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth (Ephesians 4).

Finally, everything they carry appears old because they persist in the vices of their former life, not obeying the Apostle’s command:

> “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (ibid.).

Nor does this saying suit them:

> “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 1).

Coming superficially to newness, they remain in reality in their old state, because they do not display amendment and a new way of life in their conduct. Such people are punished with a curse and are in no way admitted to receive an inheritance with the Israelites. For they are not among those to whom it is said:

> “You have been called for this purpose, that you may inherit a blessing.”

The water, moreover, is insipid, and the wood is hard. They are therefore commanded to cut wood and carry water because, ignorant of the taste of spiritual understanding, they are occupied with the hard and insensitive tasks of external discipline. Thus they seem to confer some usefulness externally by serving the Church; but because they live in a servile manner, they cannot possess an inheritance among the Israelites.

### CHAPTER V. On Those Who Represent Those Appointed to Curse on Mount Ebal

Nevertheless, some of these people, if they have been frequently admonished, if the severity of correction is applied to them, if severe punishment is proposed for them, and if the terror of the dreadful Judge is finally held over them, pass from servitude to freedom and rise to take possession, with the others, of the rights of hereditary inheritance.

Their type was represented by those tribes that were appointed to pronounce curses, first at Moses’ command and then through Joshua’s execution of it. For Scripture testifies:

> “All the people, and all the elders, leaders, and judges, stood on either side of the ark in the presence of the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, the stranger as well as the native: half of them beside Mount Gerizim and half beside Mount Ebal. Those who stood beside Gerizim blessed the observers of the law, while those beside Ebal cursed the transgressors of the law” (Deuteronomy 27; Joshua 8).

What do those who perform the office of blessing signify except, unquestionably, those who flee to divine service not through fear of punishments but through hope of heavenly rewards and love of perfection, and who continually bless God through the works of a holy way of life?

And what do those who are placed there to curse signify except those who do not burn with love of perfection or breathe after the desire for heavenly glory, but observe only what is commanded in the law so that they may escape the punishments of Gehenna?

They were sent to pronounce curses so that, while they curse, they themselves may return to their conscience and, weighing the punishments established in Scripture for sinners, may restrain themselves from the perversity of sinning at least through fear.

This is plainly why the tribes appointed to bless are nobler, namely, the sons of wives, while those appointed to curse are ignoble, being sons of maidservants: Gad and Asher, Dan and Naphtali, among whom were Reuben, who had stained his father’s bed, and Zebulun, Leah’s youngest.

It should be noted, however, that all are reported to have stood around the ark of the covenant, because all—both noble and ignoble, and therefore both tepid and fervent in the love of God—do not depart from the holy Church.

This was commanded by Moses but was fulfilled much later in execution by Joshua. What is signified by Moses if not the Law? What by Joshua if not the Gospel? The blessing owed to the righteous and the curse to be inflicted on sinners had not only been foretold by the ancient Law; the grace of evangelical newness also makes it manifest.

Although these people are noble and therefore obtain the office of blessing, while those others are more ignoble and are terrified by the fear of the curse, nevertheless, because they fight together with one accord against their enemies and labor through a common exertion to claim the promised land for themselves, they are all admitted together to the allotments and become coheirs with one another under no different law.

Nevertheless, it is far more glorious to be found marked with the titles of the fervent and strong nobles than to be compelled to be branded with the ignobility of some softness or degeneracy.

Let us therefore flee Ebal and, even more, despise the Gibeonites, so that neither a servile condition may depress us, entangled in external things, nor the torpor of sloth carry us away among the ignoble sons, bound only by fear of Gehenna. Let us claim our inheritance with the weapons of the virtues, so that we may enlarge the boundaries of our possession through the sweat of continual cultivation.

But perhaps the slothful will reply that Scripture records the sons of Joseph saying:

> “We shall not be able to go up to the mountains, because the Canaanites who dwell in the plain use iron chariots” (Joshua 17).

They seek high things, but fear those who dwell in the depths, because they strive to hasten toward the citadel of the virtues but doubt that they can overcome the conflict with carnal vices. Yet they are not permitted to rest ignobly; instead, they are immediately answered:

> “You are a numerous people and possess great strength. You shall not have one allotment only; rather, you shall go up to the mountain and cut down and clear spaces for yourselves to inhabit, and you will be able to proceed farther” (Joshua 13).

Indeed, to give courage to the fearful, almighty God himself cries out:

> “I am the one who will wipe them from the face of Israel.”

And Joshua encourages the warriors of the heavenly army, promising them an easy victory over their enemies:

> “Do not fear or be terrified. Take courage and be strong, for the Lord will destroy all your enemies against whom you fight” (Joshua 10).

### CHAPTER VI. On Those Who, by Placing Perfection in Conversion Alone, Impose No Penance on Converts

Moreover, beloved, so that I may speak familiarly to you as accomplices and united friends in Christ, we know that a certain custom is maintained in many monasteries, and we humbly urge you to reject it.

Some superiors of the brothers, attributing more to the monastic rule than is expedient, impose no other penance on those who come from the world, even if they have fallen grievously, but merely command them to observe the common order of the monastery. Anyone who has understanding recognizes how inconsiderate, how inhuman, and how utterly undiscerning this is.

Such men place their hearers among the ignobility of the people of Ebal when they remove the fervor of penance; when, instead of teaching them to climb to higher things through love of perfection after the debt has been paid, they teach them to languish beneath the torpor of degenerate sloth, always bound by the terror of punishments and obligated by the security of a pledge. Thus they do not bless the Lord confidently with those who are beside Gerizim, but rather tremble at the darts of curses around Ebal with the sons of maidservants.

Whoever does this does not consider the difference between ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii. For if the law of discernment is observed, each person ought to be burdened with a heavier weight of satisfaction the more heavily he is burdened with offenses. A debtor who borrowed an ounce is released more easily than one who borrowed a pound; nor should the person who stole a sheep be punished with the same correction as the one who stole an ox.

For if we pay close attention, we find that even the apostles themselves, the leaders of our discipline and guides of Christian doctrine, had different degrees of labor among themselves according to the sins of their former lives.

Paul, because he took part in the killing of Stephen with cruelty (Acts 8), endured more sufferings than the others. Peter washed away the defilement of marriage with the blood of martyrdom (2 Corinthians 11) [see the scholia at the end of the work]. John, however, because he was chosen as a virgin (John 21), is loved more than all the others; and because he was taken from the world in childhood and did not commit grave sins, he departed not by suffering the punishments of martyrdom (1 Corinthians 15) but gently and peacefully, as though falling asleep.

And when that outstanding preacher says:

> “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 9),

when he chastises his body and subjects it to servitude (1 Corinthians 4), when he accepts nothing from the Gospel that he himself grants to others but lives by the labor of his own hands, when he labors more than all the others and yet fears that he has not attained the goal (Philippians 3)—if he, I say, amid such magnificent works of virtue, still does not trust himself in his apostleship, what do we, wretched and miserable people, presume so greatly about our monastic profession of sloth?

Certainly, whoever flees to this order of religion puts an end to his evil deeds.

But what does it profit to cease committing sins unless one also strives to erase those that have been committed through the satisfaction of strict penance?

But since perhaps I am not believed, let us inquire what Blessed Pope Gregory says about this in his *Pastoral Book*. He states:

> “Those who abandon their sins but do not mourn them must be admonished, lest they consider the offenses already relaxed which, although they do not multiply them by committing them, they nevertheless cleanse with no tears.”

These matters have been arranged there with such complete and evident reasoning that anyone who reads them carefully can no longer doubt this issue. We do not think it necessary to append them here, because we wish to avoid the weariness of excessive length.

And truly, how can someone be secure concerning the remission of his guilt if, coming to the place of penance, he does not observe penance?

But perhaps it is objected that, apart from what is common, the Rule does not command a special fast for anyone coming from the world. To this we readily reply that Blessed Benedict indeed issued his precepts for monks, but, while judging concerning sinners, he did not abolish the sacred canons; rather, he confirmed all Catholic writings.

He plainly gave converts precepts for living, but he did not grant sinners a penance. Otherwise, those who come to the monastic way of life in childhood, as well as those who are kept from grave offenses, could rightly murmur and complain if they were compelled to follow the same way of life as those burdened with crimes.

For if we should never fast differently or perform any other penance except what is prescribed in this holy Rule, why is it commanded there (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53):

> “Let the fast be broken by the prior for the sake of guests, unless it happens to be a special day of fasting”?

Come now: read, go through the text, turn over the pages, investigate carefully, and show where that special day of fasting—which is mentioned here in passing—is commanded by the authority of the holy teacher. When you cannot find it, necessarily confess that the holy man did not wish us to observe only what he himself wrote, and that, while establishing his own decrees, he did not cancel the edicts of the preceding Fathers.

But lest anyone attack me as though I were judging and disparaging the sacred order by detracting from it, we attribute so much to the holy profession that we acknowledge it to be, in the second place, after the apostolic order, and likewise to be second after baptism.

But I repeat what has been said: when the chief of the apostles says to certain people wishing to come to conversion,

> “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts 2),

with what state of mind can someone be secure who neglects to mourn his past sins, when the supreme shepherd of the Church believed that punishment should be added even to this sacrament, which principally remits sins?

The holy Rule has been arranged with such great art of discernment for those, and tempered with such a great balance of moderation especially for those, who freely abandon the world through spontaneous desire and love of perfection—not for those who, terrified by the enormity of their crimes, are compelled to flee it by necessity.

For these, I say, who come through love of obedience, not for those who are dragged by fear of Gehenna; for those who desire to increase grace, not for those who take precautions to avoid punishment.

This is clearly gathered at the very beginning of the book, if one carefully observes to whom the Holy Spirit directs his words.

I say “the Holy Spirit.” For the holy man, a cultivator of such great humility, did not immediately, as soon as he began to speak, usurp for himself the chair of a teacher and, above all, the privilege of a pious father, saying (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1):

> “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive the admonition of your loving father.”

Rather, he made his servant the instrument of his own voice—the one who likewise, at the opening of the beginning of his prophecy, began to cry out through Isaiah:

> “I have nourished and exalted sons” (Isaiah 1).

Let us therefore see, when he begins to write, to whom he directs his words and toward what class of people he directs the entire force of his ensuing discourse. For he says (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 1):

> “To you, then, my speech is now addressed, whoever you are: renouncing your own pleasures and intending to serve the Lord Christ, the true King, you take up the strongest and finest weapons of obedience.”

Thus, insofar as we can gather from the holy man’s words, this school of the Rule appears [Col. 0300D] to have been established more for learning obedience than for performing penance—not so as to exclude either sinners or the righteous, or to reject any one class of people, but because it directs all its force and purpose toward teaching the precepts of obedience.

Yet while writing these things, we know that we offend certain brothers—namely, those who think that both the absolution of crimes and the completion of virtue consist solely in conversion. For our part, let it suffice to reply that, in bringing these matters forward, we do not wish, in accordance with the Apostle, to lay snares for anyone, but only to urge what is good [Col. 0301A] (1 Cor. 7).

Why do I prolong this discussion so greatly? Since it does not seem irrelevant, I shall explain. A certain brother came to us from the monastery and confessed what he had committed while living as a layman. Accordingly, as it seemed to us on the authority of the sacred canons, seventy years of penance were owed him, if I remember correctly. He had already spent nearly seven years in the religious habit. When we asked how much penance he had by then performed for these sins, he replied that he had confessed everything to the abbot, but that the abbot had imposed no penance upon him beyond the monastery’s common observance, because he had declared that conversion alone was fully sufficient for the absolution of all his sins.

What shall I say? I confess that the matter greatly displeased me. I was appalled and horrified, and I declared [Col. 0301B] that the man had been deceived: clearly, he had not yet even begun the penance which through various forms of affliction he might already have brought to completion.

## CHAPTER VII. That it is better to do what is prescribed by authority than what is granted mercifully

As for you, dearest brothers, may these things and many others displease you—things which deceived men fail to recognize while believing themselves to be acting correctly. And so that, in other matters that ought not to be done, you may be able to correct them with free authority, take care yourselves to avoid what is abominable and point it out to others.

To return to my subject: the holy Rule has been made like a certain broad, capacious, spacious house, suitable for receiving every kind of person—children and old men, the strong and the weak, the delicate, and those differing in many ways through the unevenness of their characters. We must not therefore deceive ourselves with a vain sense of security, nor arrogate to our own supposedly licit use every concession of the Rule.

Although a public road lies open to all travelers, the traveler who attempts to occupy all of it with legs spread wide is indiscreet. The spring that flows in the middle belongs entirely to everyone; but the person who greedily desires to claim all of it for his own use acts insolently.

So, too, we speak about the relaxation allowed by the holy Rule, and we urge every brother concerned for his salvation to return to an awareness of his own capacity and, from the Rule’s concessions, to take for his own use not so much what is permitted as what necessity demands. For one thing is prescribed by authority, and another is mercifully granted [Col. 0301D]. What is prescribed cannot be neglected without sin; but what is granted is good if it is left undone, and not evil if it is fulfilled.

If we examine the words of the Rule itself carefully, we shall more easily approve what we wish to say. For when it says in one place (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 41):

> “Yielding to the weakness of the sick, we believe that one measure of wine per day is sufficient for each; but let those to whom God grants the ability to endure abstinence know that they will receive their own reward,”

what else does it say concerning wine for monks than what the Apostle says concerning the common marital embrace:

> “I say this by way of concession, not by way of command” (1 Cor. 7);

and immediately adds:

> “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (ibid.) [Col. 0302A].

294 The Apostle therefore wanted one thing and permitted another. He wanted all people to be as he himself was—that is, free from marital affairs—but because he could not persuade everyone to this, he permitted marriage, compelled by necessity. He judged it better that they lie as weak persons upon the marriage bed than that, falling into the abyss of lust, they break their necks.

Blessed, however, is the person who hears the Apostle prescribing what he wants, not pardoning what he does not want.

Thus, too, the author of the holy Rule, weighing matters with the balance of discretion, prescribes some things by authority and permits others, because necessity requires it on account of the weakness of the fragile [Col. 0302B]. For when he says (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 48):

> “Although we read that wine is by no means proper for monks,”

and elsewhere (chap. 49):

> “Although the life of a monk ought at all times to observe the discipline of Lent, yet because this virtue belongs to few,”

and many similar things, what else does he mean than this:

> “I show you lofty things, but because I see that your knees are still weak, I lead you along level ground. If strength of ability has come to anyone, let him leave behind the low things which I unwillingly allow and hold fast to the lofty things which I desire”?

Clearly, it is better for a soul to be saved in Zoar than to be consumed in Sodom by sulphurous fire. For it is better to marry than to burn (1 Cor. 7). But how much more glorious it is to climb into the mountains than to lie in the obscure lowliness of little Zoar.

[Col. 0302C] To return to what concerns us: certainly it is better to live even sluggishly in the spiritual order than to perish utterly in worldly life. But how much more excellent it is to destroy swiftly every monstrous form of vice and hasten with burning desire toward the summit of virtue than to sleep, during the time of laziness, in the mere security of the order one has undertaken.

It is as though the promulgator of the holy Rule were saying to his hearers:

> “In accepting what I grant, you do not sin; but in not accepting it, you have a reward. By accepting the mercy allowed, you do not incur punishment; but by relinquishing what has been permitted for God’s sake, you attain the crown. This applies to those who are not weighed down by a particular offense. Otherwise, whoever remembers having committed unlawful things must now, in a reversal of his former conduct, abstain from lawful things; and whoever arrogantly committed what was forbidden must now humbly renounce what has been granted.”

For many who live softly and pleasantly, whenever they are urged to undertake at least some small portion of the stricter way, immediately produce an argument in their defense. One of them says:

> “I live as I am commanded. By using what has been granted, I keep the commands of my law.”

Then, as though he wished to appear victorious in the dispute, he bursts into boldness:

> “Does the Rule,” he asks, “take away permission for these and similar things? Does it not grant me this and that?”

But whoever argues in this way has not yet learned to distinguish the author’s will from his concession. He does not understand that the author permits some things by way of indulgence and commands others by way of authority [Col. 0303A].

Such a man will die in the wilderness, because while he dwells ignobly in the pleasures of his flesh, he does not sweat through struggles of labor in order to obtain the land that is his by right. Or, like the Reubenites and the Gileadites, he is settled before crossing the Jordan and therefore does not deserve, after the triumph, to possess the land of milk and honey with the other tribes. He has set the limit of his intention: because, while still on campaign, he already believes himself to be living at home, he does not reach the allotted portion of his inheritance, where true rest and secure tranquillity are found.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the active and contemplative life under the figure of Leah and Rachel

[Col. 0303B]

Our entire conversion and renunciation of the world tends toward nothing other than rest. Yet this rest is acquired only if a person is first exercised through the various labors of struggle, so that afterward, when every tumult of disturbance has ceased, the mind may be transferred by the grace of contemplation to the investigation of the appearance of truth.

But since, as has been said, one reaches this rest only through labors and struggles, how can someone arrive at rest who has not yet descended into the very struggles established in between? How can anyone enter the royal palace if he has not yet crossed the arena that lies before its doors?

The person who has not learned to plant vines, who has not cut the shoots of the branches, who has never broken clods with hoes, who has not furrowed newly cleared fields with ploughshares—how will he be able, after threshing away the chaff, to store grain in the granary or carry wine away to the wine cellars through channels filled with must? [Col. 0303C]

It is not obscure that Laban had two daughters, of whom Jacob desired the younger in marriage. Yet he could not reach her embrace until, unknowingly and therefore unwillingly, he had taken the elder. But since I am speaking to those who know the matter, I need not labor over it with many words.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Who, however, is converted to God except in order that, having laid aside the blackness of sins, he may be whitened through the grace of forgiveness? Thus God himself promises, saying:

> “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow” (Isa. 1).

That fortunate sinner was asking for this when he said:

> “I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. 50).

Leah is interpreted as “the laboring one”; Rachel as “word,” or “the beginning seen.” Yet if we attend carefully to Scripture, we find that Jacob did not serve even a single day because of his desire for Leah; rather, he submitted to servitude throughout those entire weeks of years for Rachel alone. Moreover, he endured Leah herself for the sake of seeing Rachel.

For who turns to God in order to suffer labors and hardships and the struggles of temptations? Everyone who seeks God hopes and aims at this: that he may eventually reach rest and, in the joy of supreme contemplation, rest as though in the embrace of beautiful Rachel [Col. 0303D]—that is, that through the word he hears he may ascend to see the beginning he has sought.

Yet this person must first be exercised by the labor of various struggles before he reaches the sweetness of inner rest that he desires. He is first weighed down by servitude, so that afterward he may rightly be advanced to the honors of perfect freedom.

He serves for seven years under the grace of whitening when he keeps the seven commandments of the Decalogue that pertain to love of one’s neighbor: namely, first constrained by fear and therefore pressed beneath the yoke of servitude, he begins at least with the institutions of the ancient Law (Exod. 20)—honoring his parents, not committing adultery, not killing, not stealing, not bearing false witness, not coveting another’s wife, and not coveting his neighbor’s property [Col. 0304A].

When these have been properly observed, he is not immediately led, as he had hoped, to the delights of contemplation, so as to enjoy the long-awaited beauty of Rachel. Instead, Leah is unexpectedly placed beside him during the night, because amid the darkness of human ignorance he is assigned the endurance of labor. Yet from her he already receives numerous offspring, because through this labor he acquires abundant fruits of spiritual gain.

He therefore endures Leah in order eventually to reach the one whom he loves with perseverance. He is consequently urged to labor through another seven years, because it is certainly necessary for him to keep another seven commandments—but now somewhat more freely, not the legal commandments like a servant, but the evangelical commandments like a son-in-law: he must be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness (Matt. 5); merciful, pure in heart, and finally a peacemaker [Col. 0304C].

Indeed, if it were possible, a person would wish to endure no discomforts of labor, either by doing or by suffering them, but to reach immediately, at the very beginnings of his apprenticeship, the delights of beautiful contemplation. Yet this does not occur in the land of the dying, but in the land of the living. This seems to be signified by Jacob’s statement:

> “It is not,” Laban says, “the custom in our place to give the younger in marriage before the elder” (Gen. 29).

Nor is she improperly called the elder who is earlier in time. For in the education of a human being, the labor of good works comes before the rest of contemplation. Thus, when the two weeks have been completed—one belonging to the ancient Law, the other to evangelical grace—the embrace of the long-desired Rachel is at once attained [Col. 0304D]. For whoever desires to reach the delights of divine contemplation must first strive to carry out the commandments of both Testaments.

## CHAPTER IX. On Zilpah and Bilhah
