But since every chosen person, not content with the limit of his own perfection, also desires to beget children for God through spiritual fruitfulness, after Jacob entered into the marriage covenant with the two sisters, he did not refuse to take the maidservants also for the purpose of begetting a more abundant offspring (Gen. 30). And so that everything might be understood as overflowing with spiritual mysteries, the names of the maidservants themselves have also been expressed under mystical figures [Col. 0305A].

For Bilhah is interpreted as “the aged” or “grown old.” Since the human tongue cannot express the understanding of spiritual substance in bare words, the teaching of wisdom sometimes attempts to instruct its hearer through certain bodily likenesses. Bodily images are formed from the old life, devoted to carnal perceptions; their use is assumed for teaching whenever something is heard concerning the incomprehensible and unchangeable essence of divinity.

Rachel therefore preferred to receive children from a maidservant in some fashion rather than remain entirely barren. For the teaching of wisdom, or the grace of contemplation, makes known to its hearers, through knowledge of outward things or through the forms of visible realities, whatever is hidden concerning invisible things within the secrets of the mind [Col. 0305B]. Thus, in a certain sense, it receives children through a maidservant, when through the knowledge subordinate to it, it bears spiritual children for God.

Zilpah, however, is interpreted as “an open mouth.”

This maidservant therefore represents those whose mouths gape in preaching the evangelical faith, but whose hearts do not gape. Of them it is written:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15).

And concerning them the Apostle says:

> “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Rom. 2).

Nevertheless, from this maidservant Leah receives sons who will become heirs for others, because often, even through such preachers, the active life has adopted many children of the kingdom. Concerning such people the Truth says:

> “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).

And the Apostle says:

> “Whether Christ is proclaimed through pretense or in truth, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. 1) [Col. 0305C].

But let it be enough that we have prolonged our mention of sacred history this far, since it is not our purpose to expound the Scriptures sequentially. We judge that this one point must be considered: just as Jacob took all those women, from whom he begot sons, solely for the sake of Rachel, so whoever is established under the grace of whitening and desires to bear fruit for God through spiritual fecundity must, in everything he does, always strive toward the grace of contemplation.

## CHAPTER X. On those devoted to wandering who do not understand spiritual marriage

[Col. 0305D]

But what shall we say about these matters when we see certain people living in Laban’s house under such great torpor and negligent laziness that they neither seek the beauty of Rachel nor seem to exercise themselves in the labor of Leah?

These are plainly those who, established in monasteries, do not aspire to the grace of contemplation either through a more secluded life or through the constant practice of prayer, nor do they discipline themselves through the rigor of fasting and various labors. Such people are either entirely free from wives or content only with the embraces of maidservants, because they either enjoy the leisure of inert laziness or, if they do anything, do not direct it toward bearing the fruit of the active or contemplative life [Col. 0306A], but rather toward satisfying the desire of their own judgment and will.

These, finally, are the people who continually rush here and there with eager wandering to carry out every sort of business. Since they do not know how to rest, they wish to appear obedient; and so they obscure the disease of the vice from which they suffer beneath a covering apparently made of virtue.

They are not worn down by labors in order to obey; rather, they decide to obey their superiors so that they do not lose the opportunity to labor. They endure leisure and enjoy work. They consider wandering, restlessness, and turning the millstone of affairs to be a pleasant delight.

There are indeed certain paralytic souls 298 who rejoice in agitating themselves through frequent excursions. Whoever is bound by the weakness of bodily paralysis is often shaken by the interference of attendants and is thus revived by agitation [Col. 0306B].

These spiritual paralytics must certainly be said either to be joined only to maidservants, and therefore their children never attain the rights of inheritance; or, if they think they have free women rather than maidservants, they wish, so to speak, to join daughters to themselves because of the maidservants, in a perverse order. For they do not labor in order to obey; rather, they obey in order to labor.

Unlike Jacob, they do not refer the fruits of their works to the active or contemplative life. Whether they display something active in their work or utter something concerning contemplation in their words, they do not seek in these things the fruit of spiritual usefulness, but only pursue the decision of their own will [Col. 0306C].

## CHAPTER XI. On monks who eagerly desire to learn grammar

To speak with indignation, among this number are those who visit the crowd of grammarians and, abandoning spiritual studies, desire to learn the frivolities of earthly art. They hold Benedict’s Rule in little regard but rejoice to devote themselves to the rules of Donatus.

Disdaining knowledge of ecclesiastical discipline and yearning for secular studies, what else do they seem to do than leave a chaste wife in the bridal chamber of faith and descend to theatrical prostitutes? To put the matter plainly, delighted by the allurements of harlots, they divorce free women so that, having violated the marriage covenant, they may unite themselves to maidservants [Col. 0306D].

They abandon Laban’s wives—that is, his daughters—and go over to prostitutes in brothels, so that, like Bilhah, they may rightly seem to be witty about old things, and, like Zilpah, to be urbanely playful with empty talk.

Perhaps, however, they object that they labor over the trifles of external arts for this purpose: that they may advance more richly toward divine studies. Jacob certainly tolerated the embrace of the concubines at the request of his wives. Otherwise, those born from them would in no way have shared with the others in the rights of inheritance, if they had been subject to the disgrace of adulterous conception.

They therefore seek out and carefully consult the authority of the Fathers.

If sacred Scripture permits a monk to devote himself to these arts, let it now be said that a wife gives her maidservant to her husband for the production of offspring. But if Gregory, Jerome, [Col. 0307A] and the other holy teachers utterly reject these practices, let such men know that, deceived by an adulterous love of concubines, they stubbornly fight, as though against the marriage covenant without a covenant.

For we are not merely forbidden to devote ourselves to such empty teachings after receiving the sacred order; we are also commanded to cut away whatever is superfluous from the things we learned previously.

Hence the Law decrees through Moses that, for a woman captured in war and chosen by the victorious man for marriage, bodily excess is to be removed:

> “She shall shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured. She shall sit in your house and mourn her father and mother for one month; afterward you shall go in to her, sleep with her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. 21).

We shave the woman’s hair when we cut away the superfluous notions of rational discipline [Col. 0307B]. We also cut her nails when we sever from her every dead work of superstition. She is likewise commanded to remove the garment in which she was captured so that she may strip off the surface imposed upon her by stories and every kind of fiction and display the solid truth of genuine reason.

She mourns her father and mother because our mind considers the authors of the liberal arts dead and, in compassion, laments that they perished in error.

It is the custom of women to be cleansed each month through the shedding of their blood. After one month, therefore, we are commanded to enter this woman, so that we may take into marriage an art belonging to any discipline once it has been cleansed of every contagion of superstition [Col. 0307C]. Thus, having become Israelite, it may consequently pass into marriage with an Israelite and bring forth a suitably fertile offspring of spiritual works.

All these matters undoubtedly apply to those who are trained in the arts of liberal studies while serving in the secular campaign. But as for those who are not even permitted to speak with guests (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 53)—in whom Christ himself speaks and is received—who ought to open our mouths only when questioned and, when we are refreshed, do not dare to consult even the sacred reading itself: how could it be permitted for us insolently to burst into the theatrical schools of grammarians and, amid the clamors of market-day gatherings, exchange empty words with secular people?

We have said these things against monks entangled in the trifles of external arts, to show how far their vanity strays from the line of uprightness [Col. 0307D].

## CHAPTER XII. On the praise of tears

It is also beneficial that any brother who has abandoned the world with a perfect heart should unlearn the very things already familiar to him, if they are found to be harmful, and, insofar as he is able, consign them to perpetual oblivion.

Let him therefore no longer know how to argue about cooks; let him no longer be skilled at preferring richer foods to more refined ones; let him no longer know how to utter polished or deceptive words; let him no longer employ rhetorical ornaments for the purposes of ringing declamation; and finally, let him no longer force laughter from anyone through witty remarks and jests.

Let him love fasting, cherish the poverty of necessities, flee the sight of people, bind himself under the discipline of silence, withdraw from external business, guard his mouth from idle conversation, and seek the hiding place of his mind, where he may burn with all his strength to behold the face of his Creator. Let him long for tears and ask tears from God in his daily prayers.

The moisture of tears purifies the soul from every stain and makes fertile the fields of our heart so that they may bring forth the shoots of virtues [Col. 0308A]. Often the wretched soul, as though beneath a wintry frost, sheds the hair and leafy adornments of its beauty; when grace departs and it is left to itself, it remains entirely dry and seems stripped of the beauty of falling flowers.

But as soon as tears burst forth through the gift of the inward examiner, that same soul immediately grows green again. It is released from the cold of sluggish torpor and, like a spring tree growing warm through the stimulus of the south wind, is clothed again in the renewed flower of its virtues [Col. 0308B].

Tears that come from God approach the tribunal of divine hearing with confidence. Obtaining immediately what they ask, they trust in the certain remission of our sins. Tears are mediators in establishing peace between God and human beings, and in every uncertainty of human ignorance they are truthful and most learned teachers.

When we are uncertain whether something pleases God, we never grasp certainty better than when we pray with genuine tears. Then, whatever our mind has decided must be done, there will no longer be any need to doubt it again.

Tears wash away every contagion of impurity in the prostitute (Luke 7), and grant unclean hands (Matt. 27) the privilege of touching not only the feet but also the Lord’s head. Tears grant that the apostolic denier does not perish utterly after his fall but even obtains primacy over the other senators of the heavenly court.

Tears enabled David, after the deepest abyss of both adultery and murder (2 Sam. 12), not only not to lose his kingdom together with his life, but even to retain immovably, under oath, the promise of an heir to be born from him—an heir who would forever possess both the throne of his kingdom and the kingdoms of all the earth [Col. 0308C].

Through tears it was granted that, when Hezekiah was about to die, almighty God added fifteen years to his life and moreover freed him and the city of Jerusalem from the hands of the king of the Assyrians (2 Kings 20).

Through tears, divine mercy granted that Sarah, daughter of Raguel, should be mercifully released from the bond of shameful reproach and sent, through an angel, to the marriage chamber of a worthy husband under a nuptial covenant (Tobit 7).

Through tears Esther obtained that God rescue the Israelite people from the common danger of destruction and turn against Haman the sentence of the hanging he himself had prepared (Esther 14).

Tears likewise enabled Judith both to cut off the head of Holofernes (Judith 8–9) and not to lose the flower of her most chaste purity within the chamber of his lustful seduction.

What shall I say about the centurion Cornelius (Acts 10), who through the gift of tears deserved access to an apostolic visitation [Col. 0309A] and, immediately abandoning the error of paganism, was transferred into the newness of Christian rebirth?

What shall I recall about Susanna (Dan. 13), who, as soon as she fled for refuge to tears, was immediately snatched from the hands of those dragging her to death; the sentence of condemnation was turned upon the heads of the false witnesses, and thus, through the spirit of a young boy, innocent blood was freed?

If I should wish to run through all the gifts of tears, perhaps the day would end before the abundance of examples was exhausted.

These are the things that purify the soul from the stain of sins and strengthen the wandering heart in prayer. These are the things that give birth to joy from sorrow; and, while bursting forth through the eyes of the flesh, raise us toward the hope of heavenly blessedness.

For those tears cannot be despised in their petition which have great voices in the ears of the Creator. The man who frequently sent such voices to God and knew precisely what they could obtain said:

> “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication; give ear to my tears” (Ps. 38).

For when someone asks that his tears not be regarded with the eyes but be received by the ears, he plainly shows that tears contain voices [Col. 0309B]. When tears plead in the sight of a merciful judge, they hesitate at nothing; rather, they claim mercy for themselves as though it were any possession belonging to their own right, and confidently rejoice that they have obtained what they asked.

O tears, spiritual delights—sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, sweeter than every nectar! You refresh minds lifted up toward God with the delightful sweetness of an inward savor, and water dry, wasting hearts to their very marrow with a draught of heavenly grace [Col. 0309C].

The tastes and sweetnesses of earthly foods delight those who taste them on the surface of the palate, but they do not penetrate the inner organs. The taste of divine contemplation, however, fills, invigorates, and sweetens all our inward parts.

Tearful eyes terrify the devil. He dreads the force of bursting tears as though he were escaping hail from a storm cloud or the tempest of raging winds blowing from every side. For just as a swelling mass of foaming torrent, rushing upon it, cleanses the entire riverbed of its filth, so the course of flowing tears drives from the mind of the one who weeps both the seeds of diabolical cunning and every plague of filthy vices [Col. 0309D].

## CHAPTER XIII. That compunction arises from the love of God, and that divine love is increased again through compunction

This water flows from fire. Therefore, whoever desires to overflow with a flood of tears must first kindle the fire of divine love in the furnace of his mind.

We can express this more easily if we recall what the Second Book of Maccabees reports as having happened historically. Scripture says:

> “When our fathers were being led into Persia, the priests who were then worshipers of God secretly took fire from the altar and hid it in a valley where there was a deep and dry well. They concealed it there so that the place was unknown to everyone. After many years had passed, it pleased God that Nehemiah should be sent by the king of Persia. He sent the descendants of those priests who had hidden the fire to search for it; and, as they related to us, they did not find fire but thick water” (2 Macc. 1).

Among all these words, one point alone must be considered spiritually: first, fire is hidden in a deep and dry well of a valley, and afterward those searching find not fire but thick water.

A sincere and perfect mind that seeks God with purposeful intention is aptly signified by a deep and dry well in a valley. It is dry of the fluid pleasures of carnal allurements, deeply buried beneath the rubble of earthly desire, and founded in the valley of true humility [Col. 0310B].

Fire from the sacrifice is cast into this well when the flame of divine love is conceived in the mind of any chosen person and the devout soul is inflamed with heavenly desire. But this fire is turned into water, because from the water of divine love the compunction of tears is generated.

It should be noted that the account says that not merely pure water but thick water was found there. For what is thick water except the compunction of tears, unquestionably fattened by the richness of divine grace?

The Prophet was eager to be fattened by this richness when he said:

> “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62).

And through another prophet this same richness is promised:

> “Your soul shall delight in abundance” (Isa. 55) [Col. 0310C].

Again it is said:

> “May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become fat” (Ps. 19).

Nor should it be passed over that those who hid this fire are reported to have preserved it, not extinguished it completely. For the fire of divine love which we kindle on the altar of our heart, so that we may offer God a sweet sacrifice from the spices of good works, must always burn secretly within us at the beginning of our conversion, but must not spread outward through the flames of vainglory.

It is therefore preserved with its flames subdued, but it is not deprived of the force of its heat, so that it does not perish altogether but may afterward wonderfully turn from fire into water [Col. 0310D].

This water—the compunction of tears—does not merely purify us from the contagion of sins; it also commends our good works, so that they may please God. Every sacrifice of good works becomes more pleasing in the sight of the heavenly Judge when it is sprinkled with the tears of a contrite mind.

Hence the passage suitably adds:

> “The priest Nehemiah ordered the sacrifices that had been placed there to be sprinkled with that water, and the wood that had been laid upon them” (2 Macc. 1).

But when we drench the sacrifice of our works with the water of true compunction, a radiance immediately shines upon our minds and illuminates whatever was previously obscure or dark within them. A certain ray of inner light then reveals itself to us and suffuses all the hidden places of our soul with the new serenity of a joyful brightness [Col. 0311A].

Therefore, after the passage first says:

> “He ordered them to draw it up and bring it to him, and the priest Nehemiah ordered the sacrifices that had been placed there to be sprinkled with that water, and the wood that had been laid beneath them,”

the sequence of the narrative immediately adds:

> “This was done; the time came; and the sun, which had previously been hidden by clouds, shone forth. A great fire was kindled, so that everyone marveled” (ibid.).

Earlier we heard that water was found in place of fire; now, conversely, it is said that through the sprinkling of water a great fire was kindled. Thus water is born from fire, and fire is in turn generated from water.

For the grace of compunction arises from the fire of divine love, and again, through the compunction of tears, the ardor of heavenly desire is increased. Each depends upon the other and each in turn provides for the other: compunction flows from the love of God, and through tears our mind burns more fervently with love of God [Col. 0311B].

In every mind where this reciprocal alternation takes place, the entire foulness of its guilt is undoubtedly cleansed. Hence the passage suitably concludes:

> “Nehemiah called this place Nephthar, which is interpreted as ‘purification.’”

Our place, then, where sacrifice is offered and where, as has been said, the alternation of water and fire takes place, is the faithful soul. It is rightly called purification, because now it is refined by the fire of heavenly love, now cleansed by the tears of a contrite heart; like the waters of a second baptism, it is washed clean.

[Col. 0311C] Isaiah had deeply perceived these alternations of successive changes and the variety of spiritual transformations when he said: “Your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be like midday; and the Lord will give you rest continually, and will fill your soul with splendors, and will set your bones free” (Isa. XVIII). Behold, fire hidden in a well. But hear how this fire is changed into water; for immediately he adds: “And you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of waters whose waters shall not fail” (ibid.). Finally, so that you may know that this water is again changed into fire, and that through the grace of tears the fervor of divine love is kindled more intensely, he adds a little farther on: “Then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will raise you above the heights of the earth [Col. 0311D]” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIV. On Sylvester, Deceived by an Inundation of Tears

We do not think that what happened to us here should be passed over in silence. For, while we had been writing up to this point, the Lord’s festival came upon us, and the pressure of external affairs, as various duties emerged, restrained us from writing for a considerable time. Then a certain young man named Sylvester—he was not actually writing these things at my dictation, but, to speak of him as worthily as I can, was transferring what had been written on tablets onto sheets—was deceived by such great artifice of the wicked enemy that he suddenly burst into tears and scarcely restrained himself from an inundation of tears by night or day except during the hours of sleep and eating. [Col. 0312A] He entirely gave up wine and sustained himself on extremely restrained and very little food; he also allowed himself only the briefest amount of sleep.

Meanwhile the devil suggested to him that he should seek a retreat in a more remote desert, where he would see a human being either rarely or never again. When we offered him the possibility of confinement, he said that he absolutely did not wish to be shut in, but desired such a place that, as he entered and left it, he might be seen by no one, freely and in solitude. All the brothers unanimously opposed this obstinacy and plausibly declared it to be a trick and stratagem of the devil. But he, obstinate and unyielding, while putting his trust in his overflowing tears, remained irrevocably fixed in the resolve that he had conceived at the prompting of the evil spirit.

I think that the ancient enemy, having found a suitable opening for his deception, was thrusting before his eyes what Sylvester himself had written a little earlier in this work: that when we are uncertain about something—whether it pleases God or not—we never obtain certainty better than when we pray while truly weeping. For he did not notice what had been stated just before that verse: only those tears that come from God approach the tribunal of being heard; certainly not those suggested by the illusions of the crafty deceiver.

He also passed over inattentively the words “while truly weeping.” For he does not weep truly but deceitfully when false weeping is sent into him by the lying spirit from the beginning. The matter is not unlike what the blessed Pope Gregory also writes in his *Moralia* [Col. 0312C], saying:

“But these vices,” he says, “which the ancient enemy conceals under the appearance of virtues, the hand of compunction examines with great subtlety. For whoever truly grieves inwardly strongly foresees what ought to be done outwardly and what ought not to be done. If the force of compunction affects us in our inmost parts, every clamor of evil suggestion is immediately silenced. And if the heart truly grieves inwardly, the vices have no tongue against us.”

Behold this distinguished teacher, whose teaching is matched by the ineptitude of our own foolishness: he does not say, “if the heart grieves inwardly,” but “if the heart truly grieves inwardly.” He plainly indicates that one kind of grief is that by which the mind, inspired by God, is pierced with compunction, and another that by which, through the deceiver’s fraud, it imitates the tears of a contrite heart; that some tears are feigned by the spirit of falsehood and error, while others [Col. 0312D] are those by which the Spirit of truth cleanses the filth and rust of souls.

To return, then, to the order of our account: since he had previously been permitted to live in another solitude, he rashly cut himself off and wandered about in other places. Trusting only in his tears, he absolutely refused to give his consent to reasonable counsels. Nor did he in any way believe that he could be deceived, since daily compunction inundated him with frequent floods of tears.

Why say more? The egg that the asp was brooding in the nest of his breast finally burst forth as a familiar offspring. For he asked to see, for a short time, a book very dear to us. He secretly cut four gatherings from its middle and most carefully mutilated the clasps to the measure required for fastening the codex, so that we would suspect nothing of the kind. Then, terrified by the sting of conscience and standing before the door of his cell lest he be bound in fetters, he threatened to inflict a wound with a knife either on himself or on anyone who touched him. [Col. 0313A] Then it became perfectly clear that tears of this kind did not descend from heavenly dew but unquestionably welled up from the sewer of Tartarus.

We have told you this, my brothers, not to magnify the disgrace of a delinquent brother, but so that you may always strive to maintain caution and suspicion even regarding things that appear good in themselves.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Various Offices of the Monastery; First, on the Abbot

It is pleasing here to touch briefly on the various offices of the monastery and to set out, in the most concise manner, what it is fitting for each of their administrators to observe. First, therefore, venerable abbot, do yourself what you command, practice what you preach, and fulfill what you order. Let your life not disagree with your tongue; let your actions not appear different from your speech; let the authority of the superior not teach one thing while the conduct of the person living under that rule displays another.

Go out rarely, so that you may continually cultivate and water the seed of the word that you have sown. Let frequent movement outside not present you as a guest of the monastery; rather, let a prolonged and serious residence show you to be its inhabitant and member of the household. Let abstinence commend you when you preach fasting, and let the throat of one who eats not contradict the words of one who speaks. The hand teaches sobriety better when it brings food to the mouth under restraint than does the tongue of one who is eating. Moreover, it is preaching sufficiently lively and effective in the minds of the disciples to urge another’s mouth toward the tables while the one who urges it remains under the strictness of fasting. Direct the rod against offenders in such a way that you restrain the movement of anger in yourself under a strict discipline.

Meanwhile, while you threaten and shake the guilty with terrors, turn your eyes back upon yourself. Consider the measure of human weakness, and carefully reflect that you yourself could be corrected if a censor were present. Do not be surprised if some subordinate, perhaps transgressing, does not fulfill all the commands of your order, since human nature is so fragile that even the limbs of your own body cannot possibly obey you in every respect—*timibet* [printed reading; perhaps an OCR corruption] [Col. 0313D].

To make what we say evident, command your eyes not to be overtaken by weariness; command your heart not to lose itself in phantasms of thought; instruct your private parts in chastity, so that the provocations of lust may not at some time excite them; instruct your appetite in sobriety, so that it may not itch for more delicious foods; finally, command your whole body not to succumb when diseases attack. And when you have clearly proved that you can demand faithfulness from yourself in these matters but cannot obtain it completely, what wonder is it if you cannot find perfect obedience in all things among those whose persons and dispositions differ from yours?

Certainly, if you consider these things carefully within yourself, you will also bear with equanimity the excesses of your brothers’ weakness. If some larger patrimony should come to you, if you see that resources are available, if the house of God is enlarged [Col. 0314A], do not attribute it to your merits or efforts, but ascribe it solely to divine benefits. Bring before your eyes the times when you were a private person, and remember that these things had not come to you at all.

It is therefore clear that what you could not obtain without Christ is conferred not upon you but upon the Church of Christ. Do not recoil from eating at the brothers’ table; do not let private banquets delight you. Since you share the table of the altar with them, do not judge unworthy those who also share bodily food with you. Let the absence of one who eats privately therefore not generate suspicion, so that your reputation may not also suffer to the ruin of those who murmur or slander. Do not be greatly concerned with how precious the thing is that fills the latrine; concern yourself rather with that by which brotherly love in Christ may cohere through the bond of mutual affection [Col. 0314B].

Do not squander the monastery’s goods, nor seek to gain the favor of popular applause for yourself from the common benefit. For if we believe that the sins of those who enrich churches are forgiven, we must unquestionably also believe that those who diminish and squander them are bound by the chains of grave sacrilege; and they become subject to sins precisely where the others are found released from the bonds of sins.

Take care, when you are surrounded by the services of those who attend upon you and are sweetly flattered by the words of those who assent to you, lest—God forbid—your position of authority or the reverence paid to you itself become a form of seduction in your mind, and a thought that falsely caresses you flatter you as though you were worthy to have reached such a position. For the steward, the happier he is in the greater possession entrusted to him, the more wretched he is in rendering his account; and he must render an account of more things in proportion as he boasts of receiving greater things.

It is very much to be feared that what is said may be true (St. Benedict, *Rule*, chapters 2 and 64): “The abbot will have to render an account for all the souls entrusted to him, with the account of his own soul added.” Let us therefore consider how advantageous it now is for him to be struck with fear, since at the dread judgment he will come to be examined after already being wearied by the accounts of others. But since a teacher must teach more than learn, let these few words suffice for him who, established to speak of his own affairs, perhaps disdains to hear of those of others.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Prior of the Monastery

The prior of the monastery administers the office of his priorate diligently in this manner: if he does not differ from the will of his abbot; if, as far as lies within him, he confirms the hearts of all the brothers in sincere love for that same abbot.

Joseph, appointed over his master’s household (Gen. XXXIX), did not wish finally to draw another man’s wife into desire for himself, but taught her to remain in love for her own husband. That noble servant of Abraham also, so that he might faithfully provide a wife for his master (Gen. XXIV), that vigorous man set aside every office of human solicitude. He forgets his labor and so long a journey in order to serve his master alone in whatever he accomplishes while on the expedition.

Just as the abbot should provoke his sons to love of Christ through everything he does, so also the prior, lest—God forbid—jealousy arise, should strive to cherish the brothers unanimously in love for his abbot [Col. 0315A]. He should not show himself mild toward the faults of offenders in such a way as to make the abbot appear cruel; rather, he should rebuke every evil in the abbot’s absence so that, when the abbot returns, he may rest as though in the calm bosom of a safe harbor, amid the joy of spiritual brothers who rejoice.

Let him therefore maintain strict censure in correcting those who transgress, and not allow the discipline of the regular way of life to grow cold in his presence. Let him be strict in justice, so that the abbot may be seen to be kindly in gentleness; let him insist on exacting what the abbot may be able to pardon with fatherly compassion.

Moses, as a faithful servant, handed down the bare commands of justice; but Christ, as the truly compassionate Lord, tempered the harshness of the law. Aaron, however, who made himself pliable toward the transgressing people, manufactured idols together with them for their sacrilegious rites [Col. 0315B]. Just as a veil was hung before the ark of the covenant, so the prior should be, as it were, a covering for the abbot in all external affairs. The prior should always confront the dust rising from the road of the world; the abbot should continually persevere, like the ark of the Lord, in the purity of his splendor. The prior, made the abbot’s mouth like Aaron, should speak to the people; the abbot, like Moses, should enjoy divine addresses in matters pertaining to God.

Thus, each cooperating with the other in unity of spirit, let them nurture for God, if possible, such offspring that no posterity shall succeed it, enrolled in the right of the heavenly inheritance [Col. 0315B].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Announcer of the Hours

[Col. 0315C] Let the announcer of the hours know that no one in the monastery must flee forgetfulness more than he himself. For if he does not observe the appointed moment of any hour of the synaxis, whether it has been anticipated or delayed, he unquestionably disturbs the entire order of the hours that follow.

Let him therefore not spend time in stories, not mingle lengthy conversations with anyone, and not inquire what is being done by secular people. Rather, always intent upon the care entrusted to him, always watchful and always solicitous, let him continually meditate upon the necessity of the revolving sphere, which knows no rest, upon the passage of the stars, and upon the course of time as it slips away.

Let him make psalmody his habit if he wishes to have daily knowledge for distinguishing the hours, so that whenever the brightness of the sun or the variety of the stars cannot be seen because of the density of the clouds, he may measure out for himself, in the quantity of psalmody he has maintained, something like a clock.

Indeed, the custom by which people gather in church when the bells are rung descends from the mystical tradition of the ancient law, when the Lord commanded Moses: “Make for yourself two trumpets of beaten silver, with which you can summon the multitude when the camps are to move. And when you blow the trumpets, the whole assembly shall gather to you at the door of the tent of meeting” (Num. X). For just as the Israelite people then gathered at the tabernacle with trumpets, so now the people of the faithful hasten to church when they hear the ringing of the bells.

Nor is it inconsistent that they are said to move the camps, since camps are known to belong to the preparation for war. Hence a little later it is said: “When you go out from your land against enemies who fight against you, you shall sound the trumpets with loud cries, and remembrance of you shall be made before the Lord your God, so that you may be delivered from the hands of your enemies” (ibid.).

We hasten as though to battle, like camps, when, so to speak, we hurry to church to sing psalms or pray. There the princes of darkness fight savagely against us, attempting through the illusions of phantasms to turn wandering minds away from what flows from the lips.

And truly, what a beautiful image of military service this is, especially during the night hours, when the brothers, awakened as though by the sound of trumpets, form a column and, hastening as though in a drawn-up battle line, advance in astonishment to the preparation for divine combat [Col. 0316B]. The troop of boys leads; the band of young men follows like companies; and the old men, reading as they go, bring up the rear—the strength of the battle—guarding the rear of the entire army lest anyone fall behind or a stealthy enemy plunge in.

Add to this that a lantern is carried at the front of the battle, so that it may appear by a most fitting likeness to be the pillar of fire leading the people through the desert. Thus, indeed, thus Christ’s companies hasten to eat the heavenly manna; thus the true Israelite legions hasten to obtain the land flowing with milk and honey [Col. 0316B].

When the trumpets sound, they hasten to the tent of meeting so that there they may eat the banquet of the heavenly word and offer to God a sacrifice of praise and vows of good will. Hence it is fittingly added in the same place: “Whenever you have a feast on your festival days and at the beginnings of months, you shall sing over your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, so that they may be for you a remembrance of your God” (Num. X).

In these and similar words, therefore, the announcer of the hours should wisely understand how watchful and solicitous he must always be in the ministry assigned to him, lest through his negligence he confuse the ordinances of their order in so great a work [Col. 0316C].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Reader at Table

The reader at table should carefully consider how distinctly, clearly, and, finally, intelligibly he must read. For while he supplies nourishment to bodies, he provides food for souls. The Apostle said: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI).

Through others, then, food is offered to bodies, and it soon turns into corruption; through this man, divine utterances are ministered, and although heaven and earth pass away, they will not pass away. He should therefore read in such a way that, while the flesh is refreshed by its allotted provision, the soul also may be nourished by heavenly banquets.

Let him read not for the reader but for the hearer; let him not seek little whispers of his own reputation, but rather attend to the edification of another. Let him not care what people may say about the reader, but what can be understood from the reading [Col. 0317A].

Those who are eating should also be instructed to moderate their meal with sobriety, so that the noise of chewing may not block the passages of the ears. Let the hand, the mediator between mouth and table, move with restraint; let it restrain itself, suspended under the weight of the bridle, so that while earthly food is drawn through the throat, the hungry soul may not in any way be compelled to fast from divine nourishment.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Much Discernment the Steward Ought to Possess

The steward, since he is appointed as something like the father of the monastery, must carry out the office entrusted to him with such skill in administration that he both restrains his hand when opening and, when restraining it, opens it with discernment. Thus generosity in him should be frugal, and frugality generous [Col. 0317B].

Above all, care must be taken lest stinginess pretend to be frugality or extravagance pretend to be generosity. Often a vice disguises itself under the appearance of a virtue, and the more what is evil is seen as though it were good, the more difficult it is corrected.

A good administrator distributes what bodies need in such a way that he also attends to the health of souls, because by sparing he nourishes sobriety, and by giving he prevents the vice of murmuring from arising. Often, as a very prudent man says, generosity destroys generosity: namely, when goods are indiscriminately poured out upon those who do not need them, so that afterward there is nothing available to give to those who truly do need it.

Superfluities must therefore be denied to our own people, so that something may remain by which charity can be shown to outsiders. Nehemiah, in order to receive into the fellowship of his own table anyone arriving from the surrounding nations (II Esdr. V), considers it inhuman to spare his flocks; and he so restrains the provisions for his own people that he extends the service of charity also to strangers [Col. 0317C].

Tobias, when he suffered such poverty that his wife accepted wages from hired weaving (Tob. II), added even the little that he had, to divide it, so that he might offer at least some kind of consolation to his fellow captives. Though a stranger, he did not allow piety to be a stranger to him; though poor in possessions, he did not lose the riches of the most abundant charity.

When Abigail withdrew part of a magnificent banquet (1 Sam. XXV), she turned David’s sword away from her husband’s throat, where it was hastening in vengeance for the insult. Thus she cleverly stole food from her own people and, by distributing it to strangers, preserved their lives [Col. 0317D].

Paul also advises that on the first day of the week each person should set aside what seems appropriate, so that the Corinthians’ generosity might be sent to the saints in need at Jerusalem (1 Cor. XVI). Thus we ought to provide our own people with the provisions of daily sustenance while remembering, even when resources are available, to assist outsiders in their need.

Let the dispenser of the Church be not one who accepts persons but one who considers weaknesses; not a seeker of favor but a sustainer of another’s frailty. Let him give equal things to those who are equally in need, while the diversity of weakness that separates them should be distinguished by a measured distribution of administration. In this way every source of scandal is removed, if each member receives not what desire seeks but what necessity demands [Col. 0318A].

## CHAPTER XX. Admonition to the Boys

Since we embrace the whole body of this holy community as though with the outstretched arms of brotherly love, we think it appropriate also to distinguish the stages of age and to fit to each member, as it were, suitable garments of admonition.

To begin with those who are just starting: you boys must be instructed, because your age is now wax, and just as you are still tender in the smallness of your limbs, so you are also exceedingly pliable in the varieties of your character. The farther you are still from the branches of the Pythagorean letter, the easier it is for you either to be directed to the right or turned toward the slopes of the left.

But if a clay figure suffers some damaging defect in the hands of the potter, it is not healed unless it is corrected immediately; once it has hardened like stone, it cannot be remedied. If a shoot growing up from its first root bends crooked on any occasion, it never returns to straightness if it remains in that crookedness for too long; and because it is judged unfit to serve as a spear shaft, it is consigned as fuel to devouring flames.

Take care, therefore, that some fault of yours does not grow old together with the growth of your body, and that a knot of any perversity does not harden within you. Rather, be vessels made not for dishonor but for honor, prepared in the house of the Lord for every good work [Col. 0318C].

Certainly, if you wish to shine with the integrity of adults and to abound in virtues without the weariness of labor—something impossible for others—take up now the weapons of sobriety and fight with all your strength against the burning allurements of the flesh. At the very beginning of your military training, promise yourselves certain victory, with God standing for you, and, with the banner of the cross raised, boldly enter into an irreconcilable battle with hostile spirits.

Trample down pride; let anger be restrained; let envy be broken; let the tongue observe the discipline of silence; let meditation on the Scriptures extinguish the itch of appetite. As the tongue does not utter slander, so let the ear condemn it by refusing to hear it.

“Do not mingle in conversation with slanderers,” Solomon says, “for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both?” (Prov. XXIV.) This means both the person who slanders and the person who lends an ear to the slanderer. A brother’s sin must not be slandered, but it must not be concealed from the person by whom it ought to be corrected.

This is sometimes detected more easily by boys precisely because no suspicion of either knowing or reporting is held against them. Joseph accused his brothers before his father of a very serious crime (Gen. XXXVII); but from the source of the hatred he then endured, he later obtained authority over them. Ahimaaz and Jonathan hid near the spring of Rogel and brought word to King David so that he might flee as quickly as possible from Absalom (2 Sam. XVII). Abiathar and Zadok did through their sons what they could not do themselves. Often a fault is exposed through younger people and salutarily corrected by their elders.

You who are already somewhat older, do not argue improperly about the merits of your predecessors who perhaps live badly. Pay attention not to the path on which they walk but to whose office they hold, and obey them humbly in Christ. “We had fathers of our flesh as instructors,” says the Apostle, “and we respected them; how much more shall we obey the Father of spirits and live?” (Heb. XII.)

Samuel was taught by Eli what he should answer the Lord who called him (1 Sam. III); and although Eli was a reprobate priest, because Samuel obeyed him humbly, he immediately received an oracle of divine revelation. An evil spirit tormented proud Saul, and David did not refuse to serve him by playing the lyre (1 Sam. XVI) [Col. 0319B].

To extinguish the heat of lust, avoid the provocations of appetite as fuel—like tow, naphtha, pitch, and *malleola* [a combustible substance; the printed term is retained]. He who appeared as the fourth among the three abstinent boys in the fiery furnace (Dan. III) will also provide you with the refreshment of his Spirit, like a wind blowing dew.

In all things, therefore, cast off the toys of nursing infancy, and dedicate the beginnings of your training to the Lord through the nobility of your character. Follow him as your guide amid the contests of temptation; seek him as your guardian in the peace of prosperity.

Girded, therefore, with unconquerable weapons of virtue, say unanimously to Christ, your defender: “Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me; fight against those who attack me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to my help” (Ps. XXXIV). He will bring you to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of his age, and make you victors by his own strength. He will grant you to tread the necks of your enemies beneath your triumphant feet.

Read also the letter that we sent to our kinsman Marinus [Note: This is letter 26 of book VI of the letters of the holy Doctor.].

## CHAPTER XXI. Exhortation to Young Men and Adolescents

But you, adolescent youths, and you young men who are reaching maturity, need the more eager assistance of exhortations insofar as you endure the harsher battles of the fleshly fire [Col. 0319D]. Every hostile assault rushes upon you in a direct course; all the strength of the war rests upon you. Against you come the thickest hailstorms of every kind of weapon, and, with wicked spirits massed against you, the most turbulent storms arise in you together with the vices of the flesh.

Wars burn—burn in your bones; and like wandering Vesuvius or Etna, the furnace of your vaporous bodies belches forth globes of flame. Therefore, the more fiercely you are attacked, the more firmly you must stand guard over your protection. You must also take pains that those who never cease hurling missiles may themselves be exposed to missiles, and that those who long to inflict wounds may themselves feel wounds [Col. 0320A].

For either the enemy must be put to flight, or you must flee; either the back must be turned, or, conversely, the back must be yielded. Such is this battle that whoever does not cast down another is himself cast down, and whoever does not win gloriously is defeated shamefully.

Danger is everywhere, while the army of enemies surrounds you and a column of citizens at odds with you is joined to them; and while the battle line is drawn up for combat, the approaches to the camp are opened by seditious citizens. For the vices within us agree with the tempters in temptation and supply strength to wicked spirits.

Therefore, beloved, take up the weapons of sobriety, humility, patience, obedience, chastity, charity, and every virtue, and fight not for fields and cities, not for sons or wives, but for your souls, which surpass every affection of relationship.

Above all, so that your age may feel its strength, you must fast and pray, so that fasting may subdue the strength of the flesh and prayer may lift the soul to God. Yet it must be noted that some, while fasting indiscriminately, do not obtain the fruit of fasting: whatever they fast on one day, they compensate for on the next by filling themselves to their satisfaction. Thus the day of fasting becomes an ally of the following day; while today’s external food is scarcely digested, tomorrow’s abundance of preparation is eaten by the emptied stomach; and while something special and more lavish than ordinary fare is sought, all the storehouses of the pantry are attended to, not without weariness for the servants [Col. 0320C].

He therefore fasts well who, on the day of eating, is content with ordinary food—provided that, while he does not differ in the kind of food, he also does not exceed the amount eaten by those who dine each day. Yet do not, by attributing too much to fasts, abandon obedience, which is the golden road to heaven.

I shall speak of something I learned not from another’s report but saw with my own eyes. At Pomposia there was a certain brother named Raimbald, the brother of Peter, a most reverend man who now serves as abbot at Vicenza. This Raimbald had been accustomed to subdue his youth with frequent fasts and, as was evident in many matters at the beginning of his promising character, he displayed considerable excellence.

He was assigned the duty of serving a certain German recluse who, with his eyes gouged out and his right hand cut off, lived an arduous life beside the church. It was a rule of the monastery that none of those under enclosure should speak when going outside.

On one occasion Raimbald, while in the chapter house, complained bitterly that he could not possibly instruct inexperienced boys by signs to wash the servant of God’s clothes, and especially to tell them what food they should prepare for him. Finally, he asserted and declared that unless he broke silence, he would be entirely unable to fulfill the commands.

The holy man, however—Abbot Guido—strongly opposed him so that silence would not be broken and steadfastly maintained the judgment of his authority. At last, after much discussion, it came to this: Raimbald was ordered to cease from the administration and to rest [Col. 0321A].

But O swift severity of divine vengeance! Scarcely had half an hour passed when, placing his finger upon the place of his pain, Raimbald tearfully declared that he had been struck in the throat. What more is there to say? On the third day afterward, if I remember correctly, having made satisfaction and received the blessing of the holy Father, he died.

We have related this domestic example to you, beloved, so that you may remember that holy obedience must never be neglected out of confidence in any pious work or religious practice.

Moreover, be attentive amid the battles of your temptations, watchful and circumspect on every side, so that when the hour of temptation passes, what is suggested in thought may not immediately be completed in deed. Often in secular battles something occurs in a single moment that cannot afterward be corrected through any span of time. Conversely, whoever guards against the blow of a single wound gains an increase of a long life in the briefest instant.

You yourselves know what I mean: often someone suddenly falls into the abyss of sin and is necessarily compelled to mourn it throughout the whole of his life. At every point of temptation, therefore, one must carefully ensure that temptation itself does not reach its result. For if the evil action is delayed for a brief moment, one escapes; and while the momentary blow, so to speak, is discharged, an unharmed life is preserved for a long time afterward.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Novices

Those who are newly converted to the religious way of life must be admonished to undertake their first battles against appetite, so that when the belly is compelled to submit to the laws of sobriety, the flame of lust in the parts beneath the belly may consequently also be restrained.

Let the tongue be bridled not only from idle speech but also from the frequent conversational talk of the brothers, so that it may exercise itself more freely in prayers and divine praises insofar as empty verbosity does not weary it through the winding turns of its exchanges [printed: “ambagum vicissitudines”].

Let the eye constantly keep its gaze upon the pavement, while the mind is lifted to heaven by the machinery of burning desire. Let each substance consider its origin, so that the flesh does not doubt that it is the dust it sees, while the soul, raised toward what it has lost, sighs with eager and indefatigable longing [Col. 0321D].

Let scarcity, reduced to a thin allowance, commend ragged and rough garments; let cold commend garments that are cheap and despised. Let a hard bed be softened by sleep long delayed and then admitted in haste. For one who thinks only of the amount of rest granted considers the softness of the bed of little importance; and one who strives, intent upon prayer, to spend sleepless nights with Macarius does not long, like Sardanapalus, to float amid hanging feathers.

Let public places be abandoned; let the sight of people be avoided. Let them search out corners and penetrate the hidden recesses of more remote retreats. Secret prayers force heaven and seize indulgence, since they are often drenched in heavenly light amid darkness.

When insults are inflicted, let no insulting voice reply. Either let the bitterness of the person who abuses be sweetened by the restraint of the one who responds, or, if this cannot easily be achieved, let the discipline of silence at least restrain the tongue of the angry person, lest the quarrel pour forth savagely.

For a ship often sinks when it is driven by furious winds under full sail; but if the mast is lowered, all the force of the blasts must soon be poured out in vain. The arrow of insult does not find its mark when the mind of the insulted person lowers itself, as though bowed down, in humility.

Let the novice often attempt greater things, so that what is lesser may be made easy by comparison.

What I wish to say is this. Often turbid or lukewarm water is deliberately drunk, so that, once the craving for wine has been despised, only clear or cold water is judged sufficient. Often coarse “Cantabrian” bread is served, so that, while ordinary bread is desired, wheaten bread is not sought. Whoever is not satisfied with a patchwork quilt after cushions may satisfy himself with any straw, if he first rubs his bare body against the pavement. Whoever feels nauseated by oil after eating meat, so that a sober liquid may taste pleasantly in his throat, should live for a while on salted legumes. Whoever is delighted by the unusual transport of riding should confine himself within the narrow limits of his cell and thereafter regard the monastery cloister as a marketplace. Whoever, after the softness of a *gebellina* or *martorina*, finds a shorn ram’s wool distasteful [printed: *compedem*], if he puts on coarse cloaks, no longer distinguishes whether he is being warmed by the skins of strangers or of those at home.

Moses, in order to be content with the simple food of manna and not, together with the other Israelites, desire to sit over pots of meat (Exod. XXIV), fasted on the mountain from every food and drink through two successive periods of forty days. The sons of the prophets, so that they would not shrink from any little vegetable, did not refuse to cut very bitter colocynths into the pot (IV Kings IV). Daniel, when he was forced to live among the ravenous jaws of lions, learned thereafter not to fear the plots of wicked men (Dan. VI). Nebuchadnezzar, while enduring the senselessness of a brute animal and roaming, like the beasts, through the dense places of mountains and forests, was shaped so that he would not grow proud of the dignity of royal power (Dan. IV). David, when he was cast down from the height of the royal throne by his own son, was taught not to take vengeance on Shimei, a stranger, that is, on a foreign man (II Kings XV, XXIII). Isaiah, after walking naked and barefoot for three years, must certainly be believed not afterward to have sought to be clothed in superfluous or soft garments (Isa. XX).

Therefore, whoever wishes to make the exercise of any labor easy for himself should approach it fearlessly and attempt higher things, so that hardship may lighten hardship and, so to speak, nettles may be deemed tolerable when compared with thistles or bristling thornbushes. We do not say this so that one ought not to begin with the smallest things; rather, we say that while more difficult things are attempted, these same small things are lightened by comparison. Let the novice also take care of this: when, attempting arduous things, he enters upon a narrow path, as soon as he begins to be burdened beyond his strength, let him quickly return to a broader way. For if a needle is violently driven into something hard, unless it is withdrawn with discretion, it must break under compulsion; but if a tailor both pushes and withdraws it in the manner of cobblers, it will easily pierce whatever solidity resists it. So too, at the beginning of our way of life, while at one moment we strive and at another relax, now press violently through hard and difficult things and now loosen ourselves by relaxing, the way gradually opens, so that everything that had obstructed it may be passed through freely.

## CHAPTER XXIII

You also, holy elders, I must not pass over: the nearer you see the end of your own battle to be, the more necessary it is that you become cautious for the struggle. Hence it is clear that, if you now lose, you cannot afterward recover the titles of a victory once forfeited. Let your fervent spirit therefore now grow hot for brave action, and let youthful strength arise in old age to overcome the barbarity of vices. Surely you are already setting foot upon the threshold of the town; already you are approaching the leisure of the happiest rest, with only doors lying between.

Let sloth therefore be cast aside and laziness put down. Let not the memory of long labor already completed hold back those whom the sight of the reward now placed before their eyes invites. The seeker of gold, the deeper he digs out the veins of the earth, the more vigorously and fervently he girds himself to complete the work that remains. Nor does the labor already passed so much weaken his strength as the hope of a treasure now very near urge him to the work of removing the rubble. He longs in vain for breakfast who is hastening, as the bridegroom’s companion, to the wedding feast. For behold, the evangelical oxen and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready; moreover there is the herald’s voice: “Come to the wedding,” he says (Matt. XXII). Why then does one who approaches the wedding banquet to feast desire to anticipate his pleasures? Why does he wish to belch before he has reclined at table? Why does he fill himself with pigs’ husks when he is hastening to the banquet of angels? Why does he not now restrain himself from every hungry satiety of his pleasures, when the highest and perfect blessedness of heavenly glory awaits him? Why does he not now restrain his tongue from stories and empty loquacity, when he will behold the very Word through which all things were made (John I) in an immediate contemplation forever? Why does he not remove himself from the sight of men under the discipline of correction, when he is making his way to the court of the eternal emperor and of the heavenly senators? Why should he dread being covered with coarse garments when he is to be clothed in the robe of immortality?

Let us therefore not be reluctant to fast from all the delights of the world, so that we may deserve to overflow with the abundance of every heavenly delight; let our mind not cling to created things, but rather long for the embraces of the Creator. For anyone who, coming from far away, approaches the threshold of the palace is judged foolish if, intent upon buildings, he does not yearn for the king’s presence. Nor should the weakness of an exhausted body break us apart from the hope of acting bravely, because, if the spirit is present in the heart, it consequently supplies strength to the limbs from within. Hence Caleb, because he had fervently fulfilled God’s commands, said, vigorous with youthful strength: “Today I am eighty-five years old, as strong as I was at the time when I was sent to reconnoiter; the strength of that time remains in me to this day, both for fighting and for walking” (Josh. XIV). That is, both for resisting vices and for increasing in good works along the path of religious life. And in Deuteronomy: “Moses,” it says, “was one hundred and twenty years old when he died; his eye was not dim, nor were his teeth moved” (Deut. XIV). Hence also, in the blessing of Asher, he himself says: “Iron and bronze shall be his footwear; as the days of your youth, so shall be your old age” (Deut. XXXIII).

Therefore, beloved, do not, as though the vices had already been extinguished by fasts or vigils, lay down your weapons insofar as this is permitted. Do not, while you are still running in the stadium, indulge in enticing pleasures as though you were already secure. It is indeed familiar to old men to fast, and although weakness often desires food, the will implanted in nature agrees with fasting and sobriety. Barzillai the Gileadite is invited to rest: “Come,” King David says, “that you may rest securely with me in Jerusalem” (II Kings XIX). But he pleads the dullness of old age and declines the pleasure of royal banquets: “Can my senses,” he says, “still distinguish sweet from bitter, or can food and drink delight your servant? Can I still hear the voice of singers, male or female?” (Ibid.). From this one may judge how tranquil and certainly how well conducted this old man was. For how could he not be content with the poverty of his household if, when invited, he despised the delicacies of the royal table? How could he take pleasure in uttering idle words suited to laughter when he disdained to hear the voices of others’ melodies with chaste ears? And since he had refused to take pleasure even there, where at times the vessels of psalmody might resound, how could he have been able to rest where the entertainments and dances of actors make a din?

There are plainly some old men—a matter that must not be passed over—who, even after entering the religious order, are so occupied with fabulous old wives’ tales that they are harmful to themselves and appear deranged to their hearers. At one moment they weave together scraps of past events; at another they recount the decrees or victories of ancient kings; and thus they spend the day in the foolish recitation of childish trifles. It happens that, through a tongue dedicated to God, which salutary prayers do not occupy, ridiculous, empty, and superstitious chronicles are recited. While they fill their tongue with the poisonous dishes of stories—for loquacity is always hostile to fasting—they do not discipline their belly with the fitting moderation of sobriety.

Finally, we have an old man in the monastery of Sitria, named Mainard. When he was still wearing the military cloak, I urged him to become a monk. Since he had always been talkative and biting, he rose up, so to speak, in the form of a quarrelsome reply: “Behold,” he said, “my maidservants cherish and serve me everywhere with daily attentiveness, and thus I scarcely manage to keep myself going at all. How, then, shall I be able to take up the path of a spiritual discipline, when without any burden of discipline I can scarcely support myself on my feet?” Nevertheless, shortly afterward—through whose efforts I do not know—behold, he became a monk. Although already old and feeble, he began with such fervor that to elderly and mature men of sound judgment he became a marvel, but to the monastery’s slippery and wanton young men a subject of ridicule. Although they tore at him with slanders and gnawed at him with biting words, they could never bend him from the strictness of his purpose so far that he did not still complete four Psalters every day and, likewise, spend four days each week without any food or drink, in both summer and winter. He still observes this custom from his former practice: he devotes each month in such a way that during the first week of every month he eats nothing at all except on Sunday or Thursday. He has now, unless I am mistaken, been in the habit of holy life for twelve years, and he is here among the brotherhood.

There is also another man enclosed within the boundaries of his cell, namely Leo of Prezans, whom I remember having briefly mentioned in other little works of my composition. He is so decrepit that anyone who recalls the deaths of those whom he barely preceded in birth, and with whom he grew old while living alongside them, is himself an old man. Yet this man, despite the weakness and trembling heaviness of his body, never drinks wine except perhaps on two or three of the year’s principal festivals. Apart from Sundays, he never eats before the ninth hour; on two days of the week, when he lives more indulgently, he admits no dish at all besides one pottage. His order of prayer is arranged as follows: every day, whether in summer or winter, he completes one Psalter with its canticles and litanies before the Church’s nocturnal vigils; he chants a second Psalter for the dead, with nine readings, from dawn until the sixth hour; and he concludes a third Psalter with the *Gloria* again at the close of the approaching evening.

He possesses this grace, which I have never been able to detect in any man of however great a perfection: when he is psalmodizing, no thought ever intrudes upon him. Such purity of heart flourishes in him that, without any resistant disturbance, his mind thinks absolutely nothing that disagrees with what proceeds from the mouth of the psalmist. This too is greatly to be wondered at: the weariness of acedia never weighs down his eyes. Add also that, although because of the dimness of old age he cannot distinguish a person’s face, he distinguishes and reads letters; every day he goes through the Psalter twice by reading it.

This too is astonishing: while inside his cell, where the light is naturally rather dim, he distinguishes the letters of the written text; but when he goes outside, where the ability to see is freer, he does not recognize the characters. Thus he himself repeatedly confessed this to me when I questioned him carefully. He now endures no struggles of the flesh and suffers no wandering of the mind, even for a moment. Crucified, therefore, to this world, he scarcely perceives what is human; rather, wholly unleavened and wholly sincere, so to speak, he lives as an angel.

Behold, beloved, although many examples are available, I have set before you only two: one from the common life and the other from the solitary life. From these it is clearly gathered that, wherever the ardor of a fervent spirit has grown hot, old age does not grow sluggish in the pursuit of good works (Hebr. XII). Just as a living spirit, relying only on its ribs and not on feet, carries a serpent swiftly along for running, so divine love drives aged limbs through the pursuit of spiritual warfare. For we do not yet possess a lasting city, but seek the one that is to come (Gen. VIII); therefore we must not hope for rest here at any age. In the mire of this world the righteous labor, while the reprobate possess their rest. The raven and the dove, released from the ark, aptly signify this difference (Deut. V). The raven, settling upon corpses, did not return to the ark’s enclosure; the dove, however, returned because it found nowhere for its foot to rest. Here, where the wicked glut themselves with carnal pleasures, holy men cannot find where to place the foot of their desire for rest.

Hence also anyone discovered to have sinned is ordered by the commands of the Law to be beaten with forty blows. The number forty, in its mystery, comprehends this entire period during which the holy Church, spread through the four parts of the world, lives under the Decalogue of the Law. We are therefore beaten with the number forty when, in this time of repentance, we are chastised by blows. Every sinner, then, whether old or young, ought to be worn down by temporal punishments, so that, cleansed, he may be found worthy at the judgment. For no adversity of spirit there will be able to afflict those whom here, whatever their age or condition, the discipline of perfect repentance has struck.

## CHAPTER XXIV. In which he urges all together to the pursuit of charity

Now, dearest brothers, I address all of you in general (Phil. II); I adjure all of you by the name of Christ, before whom every knee is bent. Persevere in brotherly charity; unite unanimously in the pursuit of mutual love against the snares of the ancient enemy (Gen. VI). Let the whole structure of your holy activity be raised upon the foundations of charity; let every building you construct be joined together by the mortar of sincere love, from living stones of the virtues. The divine voice commanded that the ark, which preserved eight souls amid the waters of the flood, be coated inside and outside with pitch. The holy Church, which advances toward the glory of the resurrection, is similarly coated within and without with pitch, so that outwardly it may delight in brotherly sweetness and inwardly remain joined by the truth of mutual love. Whoever loves inwardly but outwardly disagrees with his brothers through the harshness of discordant behavior has pitch within but not without. Whoever, on the other hand, presents himself as affable on the surface and pretends friendship but does not preserve the truth of friendship in the secrecy of his heart, gapes open damnably within while outwardly holding together through the pretense of the pitch spread over him. Neither of these is rescued from the shipwreck of the flood, because neither is protected by the double pitch of charity, as God commanded.

But whoever shows himself lovable outwardly and preserves love inwardly displays outwardly, with the branches of the word, the fruit of beneficence; inwardly he fixes his root deeply because he loves from the marrow of his being. This man is coated with pitch both within and without (Gen. VI), because he is bound to his neighbors by the double mortar of charity. Moreover, since the ark is first commanded to be made from smoothed wood and then to be coated with pitch, we have described above, however briefly, how your wood ought to be smoothed and polished by the adze of repentance and discipline. Now, so that pitch may be added to the joined structure, we advise, as reason requires. Indeed, as long as people’s manners are harsh and uncultivated, the mortar of charity is applied to them in vain, since they quickly spring apart from one another when an even union of polished morality is not maintained among them.

Be smoothed, therefore, through the discipline of spiritual exercise; be coated with pitch through the harmony of brotherly charity. Yet this union cannot be perfectly fitting unless the ark is completed in a single cubit—that is, when one is set before many in the place of Christ. Unity makes many things fit together with one another, so that differing human wills may converge in the framework of charity and in the unanimity of a common spirit.

Therefore, beloved, if you wish to fit together with one another in the charity of Christ, obey with humble heart and close attention the one who presides over you in Christ’s place. Let there not be among you that talkative Ham who announces his parent’s nakedness and publicizes the obscenity of his father’s offense (Gen. IX). Let him, standing between two brothers, be counted neither among the first-fruits of the Israelites nor worthy of a place in the fullness of the nations (II Kings XX). Let there not be among you one who, scorning the shepherd, seeks a hireling; who listens to alien voices; who plays the hammers of discord in the furnace of hatred; who divides the kingdom of Israel by sowing schism. “We have no part,” he says, “in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.” Bees plainly produce honey together only as long as they remain under one leader. Cranes too, in accordance with their name, continue in orderly formation only so long as, by following one, they do not throw into confusion the sequence of letters on either side. As soon as Rome was founded, it could not have two brothers as kings at the same time; therefore it dedicated the first walls of its rising structure through fratricide. In the womb of Rebecca, who desired childbirth, Jacob and Esau, while they had not yet put on clothing beyond their mother’s womb, already, as though armored, engaged in battle (Gen. XXV).

Let the superior therefore embrace and cherish the brothers as sons, so that they too may show him the respect due from sons to a father. That saying of the orator Domitius is well known (Cicero, *De oratore*, book II, preface): “Why then should I regard you as a leader,” he says, “when you do not regard me as a senator?” This is not meant to be exacted from spiritual disciples, but to remove an occasion of murmuring from the weak. Let him love everyone, so that he may rightly be loved by everyone. Thus let shepherd and sheep (I John IV), leader and troops of soldiers, be united by one spirit in the practice of the virtues, so that charity, which is God, may hold primacy in them as their indivisible unity.

Behold, my beloved fathers and lords, I restrain the course of my running pen in deference to you, because I know that what is written is uncultivated and rustic. What is rightly despised for lacking the seasoning of salt may at least be commended by the economy of brevity. I therefore ask that you, who sometimes eat lupine beans after sea delicacies, do not disdain to glance, however briefly, at this little tablet after your sacred books.

## SCHOLIA

Peter washed away the uncleanness of marriage with the blood of martyrdom. Do not suppose that the holy teacher in any way condemns marriage, which is known to have been adorned by Christ the Lord with the honor of a sacrament; hence also Paul’s statement: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebr. XIII). The blessed Damian himself, whenever occasion presents itself, praises marriage in his writings, especially in book V, letter 11, addressed to the clergy of Faenza. By “the uncleanness of marriage,” therefore, he understands what someone contracts on account of married life: in it men are accustomed to devote themselves less fervently to divine matters, and for this reason the Apostle says: “He who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided” (I Cor. VII). Since they also more frequently encounter occasions for falling into vain offenses, it is not surprising that they contract uncleanness and are consequently bound to cleanse it away.

[Col. 0328D] Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## 321–322. FOURTEENTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE ORDER OF THE HERMITS AND THE RESOURCES OF THE HERMITAGE OF FONTE AVELLANA

### Argument

For the example and imitation of those who come afterward, he describes the rules and institutions of life that the hermits of Fonte Avellana used in his own time, and he earnestly adjures those who will come after him to use them and not decline toward a looser standard of life. He also begs them to remember him in their prayers after his death.

[Col. 0327D] When I carefully consider the fervor of your holy way of life, dearest brothers, I attribute it not to any human powers; rather, I give thanks to the one who works in you both the will and the accomplishment, according to his good pleasure. He is the fountain and origin of virtue; he is the inspirer of a good will. And what is surprising if he strongly strengthens the fragile vessels of your bodies to carry the cross after him, when he wonderfully balances all the granaries of the world upon light ears of grain? Stone buildings often collapse under their weight, yet the light sheaths of ears of grain, mixed with thin chaff, do not yield beneath the burden. What is surprising, I say, if he grants strength to the weak limbs of his servants, when he suspends the wines of every region everywhere in the thinnest skins of grapes? What more often flows laboriously from barrels carefully and arduously joined together, he preserves without diminution in a very slender rind, as in a faithful deposit; indeed, what there is frequently poured out drop by drop is here preserved, not diminished but rather increased through daily growth.

Who, however, could sufficiently narrate the greatness of the divine work when he sees the storehouses of the powerful and the supplies of kings enclosed either in stalks of straw or in clusters of grapes?
