Let us look at a leaf on a tree, trembling beneath the very frosts of winter, with the green of autumnal mildness consumed and already almost ready to fall, so that it scarcely clings to the little branch from which it hangs but displays the clearest signs of an easy fall. The blasts bristle; raging winds shake it from every side; the winter’s terror grows dense with the rigidity of thick air. And, to make you wonder still more, while the remaining leaves fall everywhere, the ground is strewn with them and the tree, having laid aside its foliage, is stripped of its beauty; only that leaf remains, enduring without support, and, as though the survivor of co-heirs, succeeds to the rights of its brother’s possession. What else is left to understand in considering this matter except that not even a leaf of a tree can fall unless it presumes upon the divine command?

What wonder, then, if, while the monastic order is already falling away for the most part, almighty God strengthens certain of his servants to endure the labor of various temptations—he who binds the leaves he wishes to the trees while the others fall? Hence, not undeservedly, blessed Job, that investigator of divine patience, says: “He does great things, and incomprehensible, and wonderful things of which there is no number” (Job XI). Therefore I give immense thanks to my Creator, who has willed that I hold an unworthy place of service in a community not of many but of good men, whom I must necessarily precede on their return to the homeland. Yet one should rejoice if I can keep pace with my brothers’ footsteps by an equal journey, so that fruit which is by no means gathered for me from broad land may seem to be more abundantly compensated by the yield of narrow fertility.

I wish, my brothers, to touch briefly upon the order of your way of life, so that what is now read in your living works may also be committed to writing and transmitted to the knowledge of those who will succeed us in this place. Thus, even if they do not happen to climb to higher things, let them at least strive faithfully to observe the same rule of life that they learn you to have maintained. Let those who succeed to the habitation also be heirs of the way of life; and when they see something specially written concerning the regular observance of this place, let them be ashamed if it should ever be erased through their failure to imitate it.

In this place, which is called Fonte Avellana, we generally live, more or less twenty monks in cells or in the obedience assigned to each one, so that all of us together, including converts and servants, scarcely or only slightly exceed the number thirty-five. The rule of life in our time is as follows.

From the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection until the holy day of Pentecost, you fast four days each week. Apart from Sunday, concerning whose reverence no one has any doubt, you take nourishment twice a day on Tuesday and Thursday. At that time, as you know, monks are not forbidden by the authority of the sacred canons to fast. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint John, fasting is observed on five days, with this provision: on Tuesday you have pottage at the ninth hour, while on Thursday you eat a second time. From the feast of Saint John until the Ides of September, a double meal each day is observed on Tuesday and Thursday; on the remaining four days the customary fast is kept. From the Ides of September until the Lord’s Pasch, fasting is kept without interruption for five days, except that the weaker brothers and those suffering from an imbalance of humors are mercifully assisted as necessity requires.

Let no rash person accuse me of lying when he considers that I am not speaking to outsiders but recounting these matters here in the presence of those who know them accurately. Certainly I would rightly blush if, among disciples of truth, I were to serve up a fiction of deceit while they themselves knew the facts.

Although I ought not to defraud those who will hear of this later of the matter’s fullness, I prefer to leave them what is true, preserving the truth, rather than boastfully assert what is not through empty persuasion. For behold, although I remain silent about those two forty-day periods that precede either the Nativity of the Lord or holy Easter, you know that there are some here who customarily pass through that entire double period in fasting, except on Sundays and on three solemnities: namely, Saint Andrew’s, Saint Benedict’s, and the Annunciation of the Lord. On the other festivals, which are indeed great but not so pre-eminent, whether during Lent or throughout the course of the whole year, the cellarer, together with those who live near the church, celebrates the twelve readings; if it seems appropriate to the prior, some merciful refreshment is provided for them. The others, however, who are stationed in their cells, content with three readings, preserve their fast according to custom, since they do not go outside at all.

We have called those people fasting who take bread with salt and water; when anything else is added beyond these, it is not called a complete fast. Some here used also to abstain from cooked food on Sundays during both forty-day periods, a practice that we have taken care to prohibit out of reverence for the holy day. The servants who are with us keep the customary fast three days each week throughout the whole year. During those two forty-day periods they properly observe four days, except those who are sent farther away on a journey.

As you know, for some time we refrained from wine, so that neither laymen nor outsiders who came here, not even at the Lord’s Pasch, drank anything here except water, and wine was kept here only for the sacrifice. But because those staying here began to fall ill and weaken, and some who desired to pass into the hermitage utterly shrank from observing this rigor, we mercifully yielded to brotherly—or, more truly, common—weakness and permitted wine to be drunk here with sober moderation. Since we cannot abandon it entirely with John, let us at least strive, with Timothy, the disciple of Paul, to administer it soberly and humbly to a weak stomach (I Tim. V). Since we cannot be altogether abstinent, let us at least strive to be sober.

Nevertheless, during the aforesaid two forty-day periods the custom has held that neither monks nor laymen are permitted to receive wine or even fish. Nor is there ever more than one pottage during those same forty-day periods, except on these four festivals: blessed Andrew’s, Saint Benedict’s, Palm Sunday, and the Lord’s Supper. On these most sacred days, fish and wine are received with thanksgiving.

[Col. 0331C] On Holy Saturday and on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, in order to lighten the labor of the ecclesiastical office, those who wish eat as much bread as they wish; neither laymen nor monks admit any other food at all. Only three octaves are celebrated each year in such a way that no one here is compelled to fast: the Lord’s Resurrection, holy Pentecost, and the Lord’s Nativity. But for some, because through lack of habit [printed: *desuetudinem*; read: *consuetudinem*] it is difficult to continue two meals throughout the entire week, when they humbly request it, they are mercifully permitted to fast to some extent.

It is the brothers’ custom on Sundays at all times, except during the two forty-day periods, to have two pottages; on the other days, only one. Let this suffice concerning fasts.

As for the other studies of spiritual exercise—what constant fervor, what solicitude, what watchful and active frequency there is—I fear to speak, lest I seem burdensome to men like myself, namely the slothful and negligent, and provoke some measure of their envy against me. Yet let me say this: such diligence is shown in the bending of knees, in disciplinary blows with brooms, and in other practices of this kind that, whenever a penitent of uncertain mind is commanded through these remedies to fulfill an imposed penance out of fear, a long penance is completed in a short time. The custom is nevertheless preserved that, if a person’s life is thereafter prolonged, the fast is not abandoned. Three thousand broom blows are customarily given for one year of penance, or twenty Psalters, or twenty-five Masses.

As for psalmody, the custom is that when two brothers live together in a cell, they complete two Psalters each day, one for the living and the other for the dead. The one for the living is said with those additions that blessed Romuald added; the one for the dead is said with nine readings, in three divisions of fifty psalms each. Whoever lives alone completes the entire Psalter for the living every day; for the dead, either half or the whole, according to what his strength permits. The canonical psalmody of the Hours is fulfilled here entirely and in due order, just as in the monastery.

This too must not be omitted among the other matters: in the cells, as truly as in the oratory, continual silence is customarily maintained. It is not permitted for anyone even to speak there for confession, except when the prior thinks it appropriate to grant novices and their instructors permission to speak for a short time. If they need to say anything, they go out to the church and make known whatever is necessary.

Another substantial part of the penance is that at all times, summer and winter alike, they use neither shoes nor boots in the cells; rather, it is customary for them always to remain with bare legs and feet, except those who are pressed by serious illness.

It is a monastic rule that those who are sent on a journey do not eat outside if they hope to return that same day. To this observance we add the following among ourselves: whether someone has gone out that day or the previous one, he must always return to the hermitage fasting.

As for the other observances of monastic discipline, whatever is maintained in a strict and regular monastery is likewise carefully and diligently observed here: prompt obedience, so that whatever is commanded is carried out with the greatest fervor; neither giving nor receiving anything without the prior’s order; possessing nothing of one’s own; maintaining silence while in the cloister adjoining the church, whether on feast days or at all inappropriate hours; not setting aside the regular custom in the chapter house, oratory, or refectory; not speaking with guests, and therefore not departing from the discipline of silence while coming from the cells to the church or returning from it; and many other matters of this kind, which we deliberately refrain from enumerating because we wish to avoid the tedium of a sprawling style.

I say nothing of voluntary lowliness and the roughness of clothing, of the hardness and austerity of beds, of the strict discipline of silence, or of the love of perpetual enclosure.

One thing plainly seems to surpass everything; one thing is rightly judged to stand out among all virtues practiced in holiness: there is such charity among the brothers, such unity of wills fused by the fire of reciprocal love, that each one believes himself born not for himself but for everyone; he possesses what belongs to another, and pours what is his own into everyone through an affection extended to all.

This also pleases me greatly, my brothers: if anyone among you appears weaker, you all immediately and eagerly inquire what he is suffering, so that he may not delay in relaxing his customary rigor. You press upon him not only by offering whatever necessities are required, but also by gladly and voluntarily offering yourselves to watch over him.

It is also worthy, in our judgment, not to pass over in silence that, whenever one of our brothers dies, each person fasts for him for seven days, receives seven disciplines consisting of a thousand strokes of the scourges, makes seven hundred *metanoeae* (prostrations), and chants thirty Psalters according to custom. In addition, for thirty continuous [Col. 0333B] days the solemn offices of Mass are specially celebrated for him. This rule of this place, therefore, is not set aside by any variation in one’s vows; this strict custom concerning the dead is always observed with complete and inviolable exactness. But if some novice, or someone overtaken by death in whatever manner, was unable to complete the penance imposed upon him, as soon as the matter has become known to the brothers, the entire penance is undertaken among them with great fervor, divided equally among them; and however great it may be, it is rapidly completed by various forms of affliction. Truly happy is the wealth of charity, which freely extends itself not only to the living but also follows the dead. Happy, I say, is that charity which comes to our aid there from the abundance of another’s good will, where the resources of our own works [Col. 0333C] fail; and when whatever we owe is strictly demanded from us, who have nothing with which to pay, the measure of our debt is completed from the abundance of fraternal charity.

Let these few remarks about the way of life now practiced in this wilderness suffice, so that from what has been briefly recorded it may be gathered what ought to be inferred concerning those things that have been passed over in silence. But behold, dearest brothers: while I report something about your virtues in your presence, I both fear and blush. I fear, of course, lest I offend you; I blush lest I seem to be serving flattery. Yet, as my conscience bears witness, the zeal of a good intention urges me to write this, and love for your fraternal well-being impels me, so that by writing such things I may not only advise you [Col. 0333D] but also provide more extensively for your successors. Indeed, I wish that you, on reading these things, may strive to persevere diligently in the good work you once began; and that they may learn from these matters what they ought to retain for imitation from us. Since, unless divine providence should determine otherwise, I hope that I shall soon have my grave in this place, I am no less concerned about the future religious observance of this place than I am attentive to the matters now being practiced here. Therefore, whoever you are, O prior, who will succeed me at whatever time in the administration of this place, I tearfully entreat you, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the dread of divine judgment; I solemnly adjure you by the name of the divine majesty: do not, together with those subject to you, turn away from the rule of this observance [Col. 0334A] or stray from the good path on which we now walk in this place. Be ashamed to become degenerate in your manner of life from the nobility of those whose dwelling you have succeeded. Far be it from you that, in your time, the tribute of divine service should appear diminished—the tribute that was customarily paid to God from the revenues of this place. For he who has leased his possession to new cultivators, assessed according to the ancient rent, rightly demands no lesser payment of the debt owed.

Therefore, do not take pleasure in walking along the broadness of the spacious way, since you are commanded to enter through the narrow gate that leads to life (Matthew 7). The way that leads to heaven is narrow, whereas the broad way plunges into hell. Do not, then, desire to descend from the eremitical strictness into monastic laxity [Col. 0334B] and, abandoning the law of the spirit, consent to the allurements and blandishments of the flesh. Those things are indeed good, but these are better. And what else is it to descend from better things to good ones, except to turn down from lofty things to lowly ones, to go backward from the straight course, to cool from the ardor of the spirit into harmful lukewarmness, and thus gradually to fall from sublime heights into destruction?

[327] Therefore, my successor, diligently examine these few things that I have written, and hold them as a kind of seal for imprinting the pattern upon your manner of life and that of your people. May this image never be corrupted in your keeping; may this salutary form never, through negligence in your time, be worn away—lest, God forbid, a counterfeit (*paracharaximus*) be produced in place of a coin by the debasement of the currency. Certainly you are not unaware that a fraudulent money-changer, who is convicted of having debased the coinage, is often punished by judicial sentence with the amputation of his hands [Col. 0334C].

But so that no room for excuse might remain with regard to observing these things, we have taken care to acquire possessions to the extent appropriate to the modest size of this humble place, so that you may support the aforementioned number of brothers, provided that the care required for their exercise is not lacking. We have also left a considerable number of books, so as to provide opportunities for meditation to our brothers who may deign to pray for us. We took care to correct, although only cursorily and therefore not exactly, the library of all the books of the Old and New Testament for you. You also have several books from the passions of the blessed martyrs; from the homilies of the holy Fathers; and from the commentaries of those who explain the allegorical meanings of Sacred Scripture—namely Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Prosper, Bede, Remigius, Amalarius, and, in addition, Haimo and Paschasius—as divine grace has smiled upon our labors. You may devote yourselves to these books, so that your holy souls may grow not only through prayer but also be enriched through reading. Of these codices, moreover, we corrected some as far as our ability allowed, so that we might open for you an entrance to understanding in the study of sacred discipline.

We also judged that a cloister should be built beside the church [328] with this intention: so that if anyone is still attracted by the long-established custom of the monastic order, he may have a place where, on the principal festivals, he can solemnly proceed according to custom. For this procession we also procured a sufficiently suitable silver cross [Col. 0335A]. With the same intention, and taking thought for the weakness of the frail, we acquired bells, *bechinia* [a term of uncertain meaning], and various utensils for the house of God. We also provided you with two beautifully gilded silver chalices, for this reason: so that when you wish to receive the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, you would not at all need to bring pewter or any cheaper metal to your lips. We likewise supplied conspicuous coverings for the most holy altar and costly ornaments for the celebration of the solemn offices of Mass.

We sought all these things, brothers, not without labor, so that we might remove the expense of labor from you; and so that your spirit might lift itself toward higher things all the more freely [Col. 0335B], the less it was burdened by the poverty of inadequate household resources in providing for itself [Col. 0336A]. Therefore I ask you, dearest brothers, whoever you may be who will succeed me in this sacred dwelling of this place: I who advised you before you had entered this life ask that you, in a pious exchange, now assist me, already dead, with your prayers; and I who prepared for you a place in which to live religiously ask that you acquire for me the opportunity to merit pardon. Behold, my brothers, I was what you are, and I have traversed what you are passing through. The things I abandoned are present before you; the place to which I have arrived is near. Thus run through the brief span of your mortality, so that, when the vain things that pass away temporally have slipped away, you may attain the good things that follow them and remain forever.

[Col. 0336B] Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0335]

## 329–330. THE FIFTEENTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE INSTITUTES OF HIS COMMUNITY. TO THE MONK STEPHANUS

### Argument

To a certain Stephanus, who had emigrated from a cenobium to the wilderness and desired instruction in the rules of eremitical life and conduct, he sets forth the regulations and way of life of the hermits over whom he presided. Meanwhile he intersperses highly salutary admonitions, so that he may gradually lead one still inexperienced and unacquainted with the method of this path to overcome the snares of the evil demon, endure all that is hard and harsh, and finally fulfill every requirement of the perfect hermit.

[Col. 0335C] To his dearest brother STEPHANUS, enclosed by the love of heavenly charity, PETRUS, the least servant of the cross of Christ, sends greetings.

Dearest son, we have received the desires expressed in your honorable request, by which you ask to be instructed in the rule of eremitical life through the lines of our admonition. Fleeing the spaciousness of monastic life, you immediately enclosed yourself, with fervent spirit, in the prison-like narrowness of a cell. Your request is plainly not to be despised, nor is the undertaking idle or foolish; indeed, if a competent executor could be found, it would be of no small benefit even to posterity. But since in our manner of life we lead no one along this path, we judge it rash to lead others by speech, as though we were guides or judges of the road. For it is perverse if the tongue takes up the rod of mastery over others like a teacher’s, when the person’s life still displays him as subject to the scourges. Yet since you have resolved, having trampled underfoot the judgment of your own will, to obey God in all things, it is certainly fitting that, out of fraternal charity, we should not sluggishly obey your requests as well.

Therefore, placed in a narrow position, while we wish both to satisfy your desires and yet do not dare to exceed the limits of our own measure, we think it safe and proper not to publish the precepts of this institution in their entirety. Let it suffice simply to explain what we observe and have experienced taking place in our community. We prescribe not so much what hermits ought to do by a general definition as we specifically report what is done in this wilderness, both with respect to the place and with respect to the person. Yet we do not believe that this will be fruitless for those who read it out of charity, since precepts indeed move people toward the summit of perfection, but examples compel them.

## ON THE INSTITUTES OF HIS COMMUNITY

### CHAPTER I. On the praises of the solitary life

Truly, brother, you have, as the saying goes, fixed the mark of the matter itself, since you have laudably chosen to return to God not by just any road but by the golden way. Human prudence did not impel you to this, but undoubtedly the divine Spirit stirred you. For this is the way that, standing out among the others that lead toward the heights, is eminent and lofty. Even now, by itself, it places the one who runs along it in his homeland; and it already in some fashion refreshes and consoles in rest the one who is still engaged in labor. This way, certainly, neither pricks the steps of those who travel it with the thorns of anxieties nor obstructs them with the mire of worldly affairs [Col. 0336D]. Moreover, this way is at once broad and narrow—but in such a manner that whoever walks along it accompanied by heavenly desire neither stumbles harmfully because of its narrowness nor turns aside from the line of straightness because of its breadth. For although it generally appears narrow or difficult to beginners, it is not immediately abandoned through fickle faintheartedness—unless, God forbid, faith should fail. To those who are accustomed to it and already approaching or clinging to perfection, however, the eremitical life appears a certain easy and, in a sense, broad way. Yet they never cease to carry the cross after Jesus, while they restrain their own wills and struggle against the assaults of temptations arising from their thoughts.

You have taken a wife, brother—not indeed one whom, like Jacob’s wives, sterility deprives of the begetting of offspring or failing eyesight [331] disfigures in the beauty of her face [Col. 0337A], but one who is both fruitful like Leah and beautiful like Rachel. This is so that your vision may become clear for seeing the Beginning, and so that many of your noble companions may imitate the example of your fervor.

This, certainly, is the woman of whom it is said: “For strength and beauty are her clothing” (Proverbs 31). The duty of solitary conduct is that a person should sweat in the strength of a great work to such an extent that he is always careful to display the purity of a beautiful soul. This is the woman, I say, of whom it is again said: “She put her hand to strong work, and her fingers grasped the spindle” (ibid.). That is, the suitable practitioner of this life expands himself through greater works out of the fervor of desire, yet is careful not to neglect even the smallest matters. She plainly claims for herself the dignity of both sisters of Lazarus: for with Mary she sits at the Lord’s feet and attends to his words, and with Martha she refreshes that same Lord with the varied banquets of holy virtues (Luke 19).

But why do I linger any longer in describing the merits of this holy life? To speak more briefly, there are many roads by which people go to God, and there are different orders within the whole community of the faithful. But among all these there is certainly no road so straight, so sure, so direct, and so free from all stumbling blocks of treacherous entanglement; for it removes nearly all the occasions through which one might sin and confers very great increases of the virtues by which God may be pleased. Thus, in a certain sense, it takes away the opportunities for wrongdoing and imposes the force of necessity upon persistence in good works. Whoever does not disdain to seek this out can find it expressed more fully in some other little works of our insignificance. To this holy and, as I truly confess, life-giving life, therefore, that saying of Solomon is not unfittingly applied: “Many daughters have gathered riches, but you have surpassed them all” (Proverbs 31).

### CHAPTER II. On the origin of the eremitical life

Nevertheless, the order of the subject requires that, before I touch upon the branches of this way of life, I diligently investigate the origin of the root itself and clearly explain who were the authors of this institution. I judge it fitting first to look upon the spring, so that afterward I may more securely draw water from its streams.

To pass over what is earlier, Elias began the pattern of this life in the Old Testament; Eliseus, however, enlarged it by increasing the fellowship of disciples. In the New Testament, Paulus and Antonius are believed to correspond to them in a similar proportion, since the truth of the accounts establishes that Paulus lived alone in the wilderness, while Antonius nourished many disciples in this profession. Yet it certainly should not be overlooked that Moyses, at the very beginning of the Law then promulgated, led the people through the deserts for forty years (Exodus 24); and that our Redeemer himself, when the grace of the Gospel had already begun to shine, consecrated the wilderness for an equal number of days. Mark bears witness, for after recounting the baptism he immediately added: “And at once the Spirit drove him into the desert, and he was in the desert forty days and forty nights, and he was tempted by Satan, and he was with the wild beasts” (Mark 1). John the Baptist also proved himself no ordinary advocate of this profession: he resolved, by no human strength, to live in the wilderness without human food (ibid.).

### CHAPTER III. On the twofold kind of hermits

Therefore, both from the very origin of this institution as it was coming into being and from the subsequent development of those who followed it, it is clearly gathered that the order of hermits is divided into two parts [Col. 0338B]. Some of them inhabit cells; others, wandering everywhere through the deserts of the wilderness, disdain to have fixed dwellings. Those who range throughout the wilderness are called *anchorites*; those who are content with cells are called *hermits* by the customary term. Thus a common name has become a particular one. Yet the brothers of the present time consider it arrogant to claim this title for themselves; rather, for the sake of humility, they gladly prefer to be called penitents.

The sons of Jonadab had already been the first members of the anchorites, for, as Jeremiah testifies, they did not drink wine or strong drink (Jeremiah 35). They lived in tents and had whatever shelters nightfall had compelled them to use. These, finally, are written about in the Psalm [Psalm 136] as having first suffered captivity under such a persecution [Col. 0338C], because the army of the Chaldeans, laying waste to Judaea, compelled them to enter the cities. Their reasoning was that they regarded towns as prisons and the solitude of the desert as the repose of a pleasant dwelling. But toward the holy anchorites, who at this time are either rare or nonexistent, we show only reverence; we turn the entire subject of this discussion toward the hermits.

### CHAPTER IV. With what diligence the temptations of the flesh and the devil must be resisted

Whoever, therefore, enters a cell to fight with the devil, and is stirred by the ardor of a fervent heart in the arena of spiritual battle, should direct the whole attention of his mind toward this: that he no longer feel the pleasure of the flesh even for a moment, but live dead both to himself and to the world. He should prepare his mind to endure calamities and miseries; devote himself to death for Christ; gird the loins of his mind with various weapons of virtue; and place every harsh and difficult thing before himself, so that when such things occur he may not, taken unawares, collapse weakly, but bear everything with equanimity.

Just as a river arises very small from the source of its spring but, through the course of a longer decline, is broadened by streams flowing into it from every side, so our inner man begins tenuous and, as it were, dry on the road of holy conduct; but gradually, through the growth of virtues, it grows strong, as though streams were running together toward it from all sides.

Whoever, therefore, strives to restrain the flow of a river must necessarily labor to carry obstacles near the entrance of its spring, so that where not yet a river but only a little stream is visible, it may easily be checked by barriers driven into it [Col. 0339A]. Whoever plans to hasten to a royal court goes out at the very beginning of his journey with only a few companions; afterward, as others converge, the number of his company increases. Finally, whoever lays an ambush for him does not hide far from the house from which he departs, so that, while the multitude of travelers has not yet gathered around him, he may not escape sudden attacks. We truly begin to hasten to our king when, still inexperienced and newly enlisted soldiers in spiritual warfare, we swear the oaths of our service. But because we are not yet surrounded by the ranks of spiritual pursuits and are not yet strengthened by the virtues of perfection, the aged enemy prepares his ambushes before the very threshold of our departure. There he arranges the deceits of his cunning, the arts and snares of his malice, the engines of his deceptions, and every device of his poisonous cleverness, so that he may block the still-thin stream of good works and extinguish the traveler before he is supported by the company of those journeying with him.

But amid these hailstorms of thick-flying arrows, amid these storms of wars that break upon him, let the soldier of Christ not waste away through fear or, broken by toil, fail; rather, fortified beforehand by the shield of unconquered faith, let him trust all the more surely in the nearness of God’s assisting breath the more fiercely he endures the battles of the combatants who attack him. Let him not doubt at all that, if he escapes unharmed from the crisis of the first temptation, then, strengthened and made powerful shortly afterward, he will prevail while his adversaries turn their backs and fall. For this reason the ambushing spirit pours out all the gall of its wickedness upon novices. It pours out every poison of its artful and deceptive cunning because it knows that, if it then loses the result of its perverse attempt, it will afterward have no opportunity to inflict harm. Indeed, he who could not trip his victim will later disgracefully suffer ruin; and he who does not prevail against the inexperienced will succumb to the practiced.

### CHAPTER V. On rest, silence, and fasting, especially necessary for hermits

It should be noted that, although all who hasten toward eternal things must possess every virtue of the soul, three external matters are especially appropriate to the purpose of the solitary life and must be maintained with distinctive observance above the others: namely, rest, silence, and fasting. The other instruments of righteousness generally exist only in devotion or habit, whereas these must be practiced with a certain familiar diligence. For just as it is the priest’s special duty to devote himself to offering sacrifices and the teacher’s to preach, so likewise it is the hermit’s duty to rest in fasting and silence.

Hence the saying is not found without reason among the ancient founders of this way of life: “Sit in your cell, and restrain your tongue and your stomach, and you will be saved.” The stomach must indeed be restrained, lest, while it is excessively filled with food, it infect all the other members with vices. The tongue is likewise confined, because, when released without discipline, it empties the soul of the strength of heavenly grace [Col. 0340A] and weakens it from the state of salutary strictness. Nevertheless, measure and discretion must be applied in such matters, lest what is undertaken without discernment be timidly laid down through intolerance as an unbearable burden.

As we promised above, then, let us briefly explain what rule of life is maintained in this wilderness, so that when you set it before the eyes of your consideration like a certain measure of living, whether you exceed it or fall short, you may be able to return to it with diligent attention and not go astray.

### CHAPTER VI. The rule of fasting and meals

From the Ides of September until the Lord’s Resurrection, fasting is customarily observed here on five days each week. From the octave of the Paschal feast until the sixth day of Pentecost, fasting is observed on only four days each week. This distinction is maintained so that, on account of the Lord’s Day, whose special reverence no one doubts, the brothers may eat twice on Tuesday and Thursday. At that time it is permissible to live somewhat more leniently, although the authority of the sacred canons by no means forbids monks to fast.

From the octave of Pentecost until the Nativity of Blessed John, a cooked dish is given to the brothers on Tuesday at the ninth hour, and on Thursday the meal is repeated. From the feast of Saint John until the Ides of September, two meals a day are observed on Tuesday and Thursday; on the other four days, fasting is kept according to custom. This is subject, of course, to the provision that if one of the brothers is seen to fall ill, he is immediately and mercifully assisted as necessity requires.

On the festivals of twelve lessons that occur from the Ides of September until the Lord’s Resurrection, the brothers eat only once, except on the solemnities of All Saints, Saint Martin, and Saint Andrew; during the week of the Lord’s Nativity; on the day of the Epiphany; and on Hypapante [the feast of the Presentation]. On these days the meal is repeated according to custom. On all other festivals they are content with only one meal.

It should be noted that not all the festivals celebrated in the monastery are also celebrated in the wilderness [Col. 0340D]. Those that are celebrated there are generally transferred so that they fall on either Tuesday or Thursday, except for the principal festivals, which cannot be transferred because of the reverence due to their dignity. On many festivals that are not especially important, whether during Lent or throughout the course of the entire year, the cellarer, together with those who live near the church, celebrates twelve lessons; and, if it seems good to the prior, some mercy in the form of a meal may be granted them, though very rarely. The others who are assigned to the various cells, since they do not come outside, remain content with three lessons and keep the customary fast.

By “fasting” we mean that they receive bread with salt and water. When anything else is added beyond these, it is not called fasting in the wilderness. During the two Lents [335] that precede either the Lord’s Nativity or holy Easter, there are some brothers here who pass the whole week fasting and live on bread and water every day except Sundays. Some brothers also abstain from cooked foods during both Lents not only on the various festivals but also on Sundays. We at first took care to prohibit this on Sundays, because of the excellence of the holy Resurrection, but afterward, compelled by fraternal entreaty, we permitted it. They eat fruits, the roots of herbs, and legumes soaked or even boiled.

We also do not pass over in silence the fact that, at the beginning of each of the two Lents, all the monks and laypeople alike strictly observe a three-day fast, so that those who cannot completely restrain themselves from taking food nevertheless live content with bread alone together with water.

It is customary for the brothers at all times to have two cooked dishes on Sundays, on account, that is, of the two Lents mentioned above, during which they are proved to be content with only one dish on every Sunday and on every feast of the saints. On the other days, when they live more leniently under a moderated fast, if they eat twice a day, two cooked dishes are prepared for them, one to be served to those dining at midday and the other to those dining in the evening. But if there is only one meal, there is likewise only one cooked dish.

When we recall that two cooked dishes are customarily prepared here on Sundays, it is clear that this was permitted outside the eremitical rule for the following reason: offerings of food are very rarely brought here by outsiders. But wherever the place is frequented by the devotion of the faithful, there is undoubtedly no doubling of the cooked dishes.

For this reason, in that wilderness which, with God as its author, we ourselves built on the flank of Mount Suavicinium, cooked food other than one dish is entirely unknown at every season. For some time we also abstained from wine, so that neither laypeople nor those arriving from outside, not even on the Lord’s Easter, drank anything here besides water; nor was wine kept here except for the sacrifice. But since those living here began to weaken through illness, and some who wished to pass over to the eremitical life seemed completely to recoil from observing this strictness, we mercifully yielded to the weakness of the brothers—or, more truly, to the common weakness—and allowed wine to be drunk with sober moderation.

Thus, what we cannot entirely abandon with John (Luke 1), we may at least remember with Timothy, the disciple of Paul, to spare an infirm stomach and minister humbly to it (1 Timothy). Since we cannot be completely abstinent, let us at least strive to be sober. Nevertheless, the custom has prevailed during the two Lents mentioned above that neither monks nor laypeople may receive wine or even fish, except on these four festivals: Saint Andrew, Blessed Benedict, Palm Sunday, and the Lord’s Supper. On these most sacred days, invited by the joy of the great solemnities, they receive fish and wine.

On Holy Saturday and on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, so that the labor of the church’s service may be relieved, those who wish eat all the bread [336]; they admit no other food at all, whether laypeople or monks. Only three octaves during the year are celebrated in such a way that no one here is compelled to fast: namely, the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection, the octave of holy Pentecost, and the octave of the Lord’s Nativity. Since it is burdensome for some, through lack of habit, to continue two meals throughout the entire week, they are permitted, out of mercy, to fast somewhat when they humbly request this. Nevertheless, both ecclesiastical tradition and the authority of the Fathers decree that one should fast during the octave of Pentecost. During the remaining octaves of whatever festivals, we maintain the ecclesiastical office as the regular order requires, but we do not change the established pattern of fasting.

### CHAPTER VII. On the discipline of the servants

So that the entire household of God may be maintained under regular custody and discipline, and each member may perform in the body the duty proper to its character, the servants who serve this place likewise do not depart from the way of life assigned to them. Throughout the course of the whole year they customarily fast on three days each week. During the two Lents they devote four days to fasting, except those who are sent on a distant journey. Wherever they go, moreover, they abstain from meat at all times; and, like the monks, they are likewise forbidden to possess anything as private property.

Some of them also rise earlier for the vigils at which the Psalter is heard, together with those brothers who live near the church. When they enter, they make this promise:

“I, brother N., promise obedience and perseverance for all the days of my life in this wilderness, which has been built in honor of God and of the holy Cross, for fear of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the remedy of my soul. If at any time I should attempt to flee or depart from here, may the servants of God who are here have the right, with the full authority belonging to them, to seek me out and recall me forcibly and under constraint to their service.”

They therefore place the sign of the cross at the head of this written promise and, after it has been read by one of the brothers before everyone, lay it upon the altar. The monks make no promise except the one customarily made in monasteries, with only the name “wilderness” substituted.

Indeed, for both monks and laypeople who wish to enter, everything hard and harsh is set before them: the extremity, or even nakedness, of their clothing; scarcity of food; rejection of their own will; the harsh severity of the strictest correction; insults; the persistence of rebukes, labor, and continual exhaustion. We neglect to pursue and enumerate these and many similar things because we remember that these same practices are carried out in monasteries according to established rule [Col. 0343A].

### 337. CHAPTER VIII. On the measure of bread and spiritual exercises

The measure of bread in the wilderness is the same as in the monastery, with this distinction: on days of meals, whether there is one meal or two, if a brother wishes to eat the whole portion, he is not compelled to submit to reproach. On days of fasting, however, since each brother has scales in his cell, he always weighs on them what he is going to set before himself for supper.

That measure has this form: with half a *quadra* added, it weighs half of a whole small loaf, the *quadra*, namely, remaining whole as a half. And so that no doubt may remain about this kind of measure, nine quail eggs—or three goose eggs—weigh exactly the same on balanced scales [Col. 0343B]. Let this suffice concerning fasts and the measure of foods.

As for the other practices of spiritual exercise—what sustained fervor is maintained here, what solicitude, how watchful and active the frequency—I fear to write, lest I perhaps seem, through vain exaltation, to boast of myself as one who dwells among them, even if I do not labor with them. Let me say only this: there is no small diligence here in genuflections, disciplines with scourges, and other such practices. Since you can learn these more clearly from the living voices of those who labor at them, dearest brother, it is not necessary to record everything here in writing.

### CHAPTER IX. On psalmody

[Col. 0343C]

The custom concerning psalmody is this: when two live together in a cell, they complete two Psalters each day, one for the living and the other for the dead. The one for the living is recited with those additions that Blessed Romuald appends; we too should not be reluctant to insert them, lest a novice perhaps complain that we have passed over matters he greatly needs to know.

After five psalms have been completed, this is immediately added:

“Glory to you, Trinity, one equal Divinity, both before every age and now and forever. Pray for us, all holy ones of God, that we may be made worthy of the promises of our Lord God Jesus Christ. Our Father.”

When these have been completed, the following is immediately added:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 123).

After another five psalms have been recited, this is then said:

“You, God the Father unbegotten, you, the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, the holy and undivided Trinity, with our whole heart and mouth we confess, praise, and bless; to you be glory forever. Amen.”

“Lord God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me. Let my enemies be put to shame and confusion, who seek my soul. Be my helper and deliverer, Lord; do not delay” (Psalm 69).

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

When this has been completed, “Our help is in the name of the Lord” is again said [Col. 0344A].

These additions are therefore always made alternately after each group of five psalms, until the Psalter has been completed together with the three Sunday canticles and the canticles for the entire week. Nor are the things that appear to have been added at the end of the Psalter neglected: namely, “We praise you, O God”; “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord”; the two Creeds; “Glory to God in the highest”; “Our Father,” together with the Catholic faith; and finally the litanies, with prayers, conclude all these matters in the customary manner.

The Psalter for the dead is recited with nine lessons, three lessons, that is, for each group of fifty psalms. But the brother who lives alone completes the entire Psalter for the living each day; as for the Psalter for the dead, he completes either half or the whole according to what his physical strength permits. The canonical psalmody of the hours, however, is performed here in its entirety and in due order, just as in the monastery.

### CHAPTER X. On the strictness of silence

[Col. 0344B]

This, among the other matters, must not be omitted: in the cells a continual silence is maintained, just as, in truth, in the oratory, according to custom. Nor is one permitted there to speak with another, even for confession, except if the prior should see fit to grant novices and their instructors permission to speak for a little while.

If they need to say anything, they come out to the church and make known whatever is necessary. For, as we have learned by experience, there is truly a great destruction of souls wherever conversation in the cell is freely permitted. While the sick brothers who visit one another under the pretext of confession briefly complete what they had begun, they soon extend themselves into other frivolous and idle matters, once freedom has been given to their shameless tongues. Suddenly forgetting why they had assembled, they soon slander their brothers, or even their priors; and those whom they ought to love sincerely and purely, they gnaw viciously with, so to speak, an envious tooth.

Then they pass on to secular affairs, and whatever is being done in the cities is discussed in the cell. Before long, rumor carries it to the ears of the common people, from which it has often already filled the hidden places of the mountains. Add to this that, when there are no witnesses present, the more secure they are from reproach, the more freely they pour forth whatever has gathered on their tongues. Thus it happens that those who had assembled in order to cleanse themselves sever themselves from one another all the dirtier, having accumulated the contagion of the tongue.

## CHAPTER XI. On Observance of Monastic Discipline

[Col. 0344D]

This too is no small part of penance: at all times, whether summer or winter, they use neither shoes nor boots in their cells; rather, it is their custom always to remain with bare legs and feet, except for those who are afflicted by a more serious illness.

It is a rule in monasteries (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 51) that those who are sent on a journey should not eat outside if they hope to return on that same day. To this observance we add among ourselves that, whether someone has gone out on that day or another, except on the principal feasts, he must always return to the hermitage fasting; otherwise, penance will not be lacking.

As for the other observances of monastic discipline, whatever is maintained in a regular and strict monastery is likewise carefully and diligently observed here: namely, prompt obedience, so that whatever is commanded may be carried out humbly and with the greatest fervor; neither giving nor receiving anything without the prior’s order; possessing nothing of one’s own; maintaining silence while in the cloister adjoining the church, whether on feast days or at all unsuitable hours; not setting aside the customary rule in the chapter-house, the oratory, or the refectory; not speaking with guests; and therefore, whether coming from the cells to the church or returning from it, not departing from the discipline of silence (St. Benedict, Rule, chaps. 5, 33, 54; 3, 55, 42, 52, and 53). We refrain from enumerating these matters, because we wish to avoid the tedium of an over-elaborate style.

## CHAPTER XII. On Piety toward the Dead

[Col. 0345B]

Nor do we think this should be passed over in silence: when one of our brothers who lives with us dies, each person fasts for him for seven days, receives seven disciplines with a thousand strokes of the scourge, makes seven hundred *metanoeas*—that is, prostrations—and, according to custom, chants thirty Psalters. Moreover, each priest celebrates seven Masses for him individually, apart from the fact that for thirty consecutive days the solemn rites of the Mass are celebrated communally for him in the assembly. This rule of our place is never set aside through any variation of custom; this practice regarding the dead is always maintained with strict and inviolable observance.

[Col. 0345C] If, however, some novice, or anyone else, prevented by death, has been unable to complete the penance imposed upon him, as soon as the matter becomes known to the brothers, the entire penance is undertaken with great fervor, divided equally among them; however great it may be, it is joyfully completed within a short time through various forms of affliction [the reading *ovanter* is uncertain].

Let these few remarks about the way of life now practiced in this hermitage suffice, so that from what has been briefly recorded it may be possible to gather what ought to be understood concerning the matters passed over in silence.

## CHAPTER XIII. Exhortation

These things, therefore, dearest son, which we have set before you concerning the way of life of our brothers, place carefully before your eyes and examine them. Weigh your own strength, as though on the scales of a strict examination, so that whether you fall short or rise above it, while continually contemplating the goal of the well-trodden path, you may not wander entirely into the byways of its winding turns.

A painter, too, sets an image before himself as a pattern for copying; yet he reduces everything to the measure of the panel at hand and composes the proportions of his borrowed work in conformity with it. You likewise should take these practices up for exercise according to the measure of your strength, which the Giver of heavenly gifts has infused into you. Know how much necessity compels you to lessen, or how much, through an increase of grace, you may be able to enlarge them in yourself.

Some people easily pass the entire week fasting; others endure even a two-day fast only with the greatest difficulty. Yet in performing these practices the two do not receive unequal merit: the strong person, who performs strenuous works, and the weak person, who does not leave undone the little that he is able to accomplish.

Therefore it is difficult to establish a definitive and common rule concerning fasts, lest we seem to force either the stronger to grow weak in their perfection or the weaker to attempt what exceeds their strength. “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7). For among our ancient Fathers, too, we read that there were many who, although living together in a common congregation, did not follow a common rule of life.

Let each person, therefore, consider his own strength and not deceive himself in vain; let him not mislead himself by feigned weakness. Rather, in accordance with what he sees himself capable of doing, let him bind himself under the laws of sobriety and the rigor of abstinence.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Those Who Have Bound Themselves to a More Rigorous Way of Life

Among us also there are some brothers who walk by a way of life quite different from what has been written here and bind themselves to a considerably stricter rule of living. Some never drink wine at any time or take vinegar in any form. Others do not eat eggs, milk, or cheese, nor even pork fat. Many despise mats as though they were soft bedding and are content to rest on papyrus mats, so that they entirely shun even the laying down of straw. Others reject the harshest hair shirts as though they were soft and delicate garments, and wear iron breastplates next to the flesh.

There is one who, throughout the entire year, is content with half a loaf not only on ordinary days but also on feast days and Sundays. This same brother, for about a year and a half, touched no food on five days of the week, being content to eat only on Sunday and Thursday. Even now, on Sundays and Thursdays, after the ninth hour, he refreshes himself with a single dish, so that he absolutely does not know a second course.

There is also one who, from love of continence and sobriety, has resolved to abstain not only from fruit but also from onions and leeks—in short, from all sharp-tasting vegetables. Another lives during both Lenten periods each day on garlic and a double handful of chickpeas; on Thursday always, and on Tuesday rarely, he eats bread alone. This man also continually girds his loins with an iron chain, lest he ever exceed the measure of a sober meal.

One of our elders confessed to me that, when he ate alone in his cell, he did not indulge himself with food as quickly as the itch of hunger demanded. Instead, by delaying and prolonging the meal, he would put into his mouth only crumbs, rarely and in tiny pieces, rather than pieces of bread. Thus, even amid the nourishment of the body, he afflicted himself more harshly through deprivation, so that the food itself seemed not so much to relieve him as to punish him; and refreshment seemed more properly to be called exhaustion, since it restored him not by delighting him but rather chastised him by afflicting him.

I rebuked a young man of ours, still of adolescent character, and chastised him with a particularly severe beating, because he lived each day on a square of Cantabrian bread. Only with difficulty did I finally obtain that it be enlarged to half a loaf. At that time he was wearing an iron breastplate beneath his garment and had taken no food at all from Sunday through Thursday; on the remaining three days of the week he lived on bread alone.

We have among us another brother, still young in age and a novice in his conversion, who is accustomed to complete the entire Psalter with his arms extended upward. After every fifty psalms he lowers his fatigued arms, but before he can finish even one longer psalm, he raises them again.

We also have another, already an elderly man bent with age, who chants two Psalters with his arms extended only once: one, namely, with the canticles and litanies and many prayers; the other for the dead, with nine lessons.

I shall speak of it, though who knows whether faith will be given to an assertion so faithful. Yet it is of little importance if human rashness accuses the one whom the highest Truth excuses from falsehood. This same old man, named Dominic, sometimes goes through nine Psalters in a single day continued into the night, meditating, while almost constantly striking his naked body with both hands armed with scourges.

It should be noted that, while he strives to complete this, he has no time to sleep, either by night or by day. Sometimes, however, as he bends his knees and lowers his head to the ground, sleep suddenly steals upon him while he is naked, and he is content with this alone. Once, in the intimacy of brotherly friendship, this brother complained to me that, although he often completed nine Psalters in this way by chanting them, he had never been able to reach a tenth.

I know a brother who admitted that he bent his knees while psalmodizing as many times as there were verses contained in the whole Psalter. The Psalter is said to contain nearly four thousand verses, as those who have devoted themselves to counting them maintain.

I do not pursue these matters at greater length because I fear offending those of whom I speak; and, cold as I am, I blush to live with men whose labors I do not share and to recount the fervor of others. I believe it fitting to leave such practices to strong and more perfect men, while tempering even the milder practices written above with the measured balance of discretion. Thus, while the more powerful are able to run with swift oars across the deep sea of virtue, the weak, skimming near the shore, will not be compelled to remain with their clinging boat in the sandy shoals.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Fasting of Hermits

Nevertheless, lest what we write seem entirely to waver, released from the law of a rule, we believe that every brother living in a cell, unless he is completely ill—so ill that he is confined to bed—can, with God’s help, very easily fast throughout the whole year, whether summer or winter, on three days each week, taking bread and water.

Since fasting on Saturday is also authenticated by canonical tradition, it should not seem burdensome for a brother to postpone his meal on Saturday until the ninth hour, so that he is refreshed only once that day. Nevertheless, by the concession of this institution of ours, he is not forbidden to take wine and a cooked dish. This applies in summer.

From the Ides of September until the joy of Easter, he should know that he must fast on four days each week. Yet if such great weakness should sometimes occur that even in winter, on Saturday, it becomes necessary to moderate the customary fast, he may do so with soaked legumes, the roots of plants, or even fruit. This is provided that, if he takes any one of these, he does not add another unless true necessity demands it.

Finally, for the faint-hearted, if necessity absolutely requires it, the same Saturday moderation that has been permitted in summer may be observed in winter.

As for the feasts celebrated in winter, on which we have stated that we customarily eat once a day, it is permitted to eat twice, as is the custom of coenobites. During the two Lenten periods, namely those preceding the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection, let the brother take a cooked dish on Tuesday and Thursday; on Sundays and principal feasts, and additionally on Thursday, let him also drink wine.

During a Lenten period, let the brothers be content with one cooked dish when they eat only once. When they eat twice, let them take one dish at midday and another in the evening. During the rest of the year, they should always have two. On Sundays and greater feasts, if means permit, we do not forbid a third.

## CHAPTER XVI. The Prior’s Discretion in Moderating His Subjects

We leave the discretion concerning the weak to the prior’s judgment, so that he himself may consider each person’s capacity and, according to what he sees to be advantageous for each, piously distribute food to them.

For we approve what Blessed Romuald is reported to have often said to his disciples: “Provided that a brother does not leave his cell, he may, in accordance with discretion, even be permitted to eat meat if such unavoidable necessity appears imminent.”

He added: “For it is almost the same thing to return from the hermitage to the monastery as to be carried from the monastic order back into the world.”

Therefore whoever presides over an eremitical brotherhood must carefully examine each person’s strength and supply what is necessary according to his capacity. If everyone is able to live according to the measure of one rule, that is best. Otherwise, if one or perhaps several are in need, let what the healthy do not require be offered secretly and discreetly to the weak with compassionate humanity, so that the strong may remain in the discipline of their rigor without the stimulus of envy.

Nor is it necessary that what misfortune imposes upon one person immediately become a rule for everyone, since the same brother who today asks to be helped through humane consideration may, perhaps strengthened in the following week, no longer require the services of that same humanity.

For Blessed Romuald himself, as his disciples customarily report, alternated the weeks of summer in such a way that he spent one week, from Sunday to Sunday, fasting on bread and water, while during the other week he ate a cooked dish on Thursday.

The same prior’s careful attention should also determine how much those who have converted fast.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Regulation of Sleep

For some people, not such harsh strictness as modest discretion is necessary concerning sleep. It is better to grant the flesh sleep through a measured form of provision and afterward keep fervent vigil in the praises of God than to drift about all day, yawning with half-asleep lips.

Indeed, even with our most recent predecessors it was not customary to sleep during the day at any time. We, however, sleep during the summer days; but, as we have certainly learned by experience, whatever progress we lose by sleeping during the day, we recover by rising earlier at night and applying ourselves more readily to divine service.

It should be noted that, before the office of the nocturnal assembly, if the night is still particularly deep or the vigils seem burdensome for any reason, it is permitted to return to bed. After the night office, however, it is entirely forbidden.

Therefore, so that this regular observance might be kept more easily, we have instituted that each day the signal should first sound for the vigils; then, when the Psalter has been completed according to custom—or as much of it as a consideration of the time permits—the signal should sound again and the nocturnal office be performed. Thus, near dawn, at the very time when accidie presses most heavily, it may find us standing and occupied with the canonical offices.

For at that time we must not yield to sleep or idleness, since it is the hour at which our Redeemer is known to have risen after destroying the power of death. If we sleep when, at the rising of the physical sun, our inner person ought also to await the unfading light, may that reproach not fittingly apply to us: “His disciples came by night, and while we were sleeping they stole him” (Matt. 28:13).

Care must also be taken that no one consent to sleep even for a moment at unsuitable hours. For if sleep frequently steals upon someone while he is sitting, or even standing, afterward, when he wishes to sleep, slumber withdraws from his eyes. Thus drowsiness produces wakefulness, and wakefulness produces drowsiness: the one who dozes later keeps unwilling vigil, while the one who keeps vigil too long necessarily dozes.

Something similar often happens to those who eat without discretion. Hence some foolishly delirious people complain excessively that they cannot eat supper, although this clearly results from the immoderate gluttony of their midday meal. If they did not exceed the limits of frugality at midday, they would not so greatly disdain the evening meal.

Therefore, if someone wishes to be able to eat supper and then have sleep come upon him as soon as he rests, let him eat lunch soberly and not admit the idleness of drowsiness.

Some people, however—and this must not be passed over—in order to sleep more securely at night and swell until satiated with the deep snorings of prolonged sleep, hurry to anticipate the psalmody while it is still day. Such people must be strictly forbidden to begin the psalms before they say Compline at its proper time.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Private and Public Psalmody, and on Other Exercises of the Hermits

[Col. 0350B]

Each brother should chant one Psalter every day. If he wishes to add a Psalter for the dead—whether the whole Psalter, half of it, or at least a third—or to omit it entirely, this should be left to that brother’s discretion, provided that he remembers to complete the entire order of psalmody, both for the living and for the dead, as it is practiced in monasteries.

On the four days on which we have decreed that they must fast, they are to maintain silence, unless some arising necessity commands otherwise. In the cells themselves they must never speak to anyone, unless they are completely enclosed there or are situated near the monastery.

Nor may one brother ever presume to eat together in a cell with another brother, whether from his own community or a stranger, or invite others to eat there. Indeed, even confession with another brother may not be conducted there in ordinary speech.

If two brothers live together in a cell, one should always preside and the other obey, according to the command of the common prior. If either of them is a novice, they may have permission to converse once or twice a week after Vespers. After he ceases to be a novice, however, they are henceforth to cease mutual conversation.

When coming from the cells or returning to them, they must always maintain silence, as was said above. When the signal sounds to assemble the brothers, whoever hears it must not have permission, while preparing himself, to remain in the cell longer than he can chant five psalms.

A diligent brother must take care not to wear out or handle carelessly things assigned for his needs or any utensils, such as clothing, tools, vessels, or similar objects. Above all, he should guard the holy books in such a way that he never keeps his hand upon the letters, never allows them to blacken with smoke, and never exposes them to the smell [or heat—*ardorem*, with *odorem* printed] of fire.

He should place beside him whatever he needs most familiarly, so that, whenever necessity requires their use, he himself may rise frequently to bring them out. Wandering must be avoided so thoroughly that it is not even permitted to walk about aimlessly within the cell itself. If he wishes, however, he may use shoes in the cell.

[Col. 0351A] Concerning *metanoeae*, disciplines, palm-strikings, the extension of the arms during prayers, and the other exercises of holy fervor, we bind no brother by any rule. Rather, we judge that these matters should be entrusted to his own prudent discretion. There are some for whom certain of these practices are unsuitable; therefore it seems safer and freer to offer a choice in such matters than to prescribe a definitive ruling of the rule.

They should shave their heads each month, except during the two Lenten periods, which must be passed without washing the head. If they are healthy, they should not use baths.

We have established these provisions, removing all rigor of austerity and applying the measured balance of such modest discretion, so that a brother concerned for his salvation will not recoil from a life-giving discipline; yet, if he fulfills these things fully, he may confidently rely upon the mercy of almighty God.

Nevertheless, this rule is to remain after our death; while we live, we do not permit the established practice to be diminished, by God’s gift.

Above all, care must be taken that no one, under the pretext of the eremitical life, evade the yoke of obedience. Rather, he should bind himself by a stricter law of obedience, since he knows that this institution surpasses the rule of the coenobites.

Often a brother is ordered to leave one cell and live in another, and is not permitted to carry away any utensil, even one he himself had prepared through his own labor. Often those who desire to rest in solitude are compelled to go out to perform some task. Sometimes the keys of the cells are removed from the doors and are not returned for a long time except on Sundays. Sometimes those who impose upon themselves strict restraint in food are compelled to live more leniently; and those who wish to eat are, on the contrary, compelled to fast.

Often a brother is ordered to go far away after the pack animals; often he is sent to the market to sell or buy. All these things, and whatever else is commanded by the prior, must be observed patiently and humbly, as though they had been commanded by God himself. Obedience commends our good works and excuses offenses arising from negligence.

Therefore, if our withdrawal or affliction is to be fruitful, it must always be seasoned with the salt of salutary obedience. Whatever branches of good work our life spreads forth must always grow together from the root of obedience.

In fact, we do not describe in detail all the precepts of this discipline, but deliberately omit many matters that frequently occur to us. Whatever has been said in the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whatever has been said in the institutions or conferences of the Fathers, we judge to belong to this discipline as well; nevertheless, we consider it superfluous to gather everything here into one place.

Furthermore, the cell itself and the long continuance of the life effectively instruct the one who perseveres, and in the course of time disclose through actual things what the tongue of the flesh, with its noisy words, cannot explain. Thus, selecting a few matters from many and touching upon them briefly, we pass over the rest and reserve a fuller knowledge of this holy discipline above all for the cell itself.

Let the brother merely persevere in the cell; it will teach its inhabitant the entire order of life more fully.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Not Receiving or Expelling Vain and Harmful Thoughts

Now let us briefly discuss, for the sake of concision, the matters that arise in the mind, so that we may equip the person struggling in spiritual combat against his own thoughts and various battles with weapons that cannot be overcome.

First, therefore, son, whoever prepares to join hands in combat with the invisible enemy, strive to fortify your mind through vigilant watchfulness against every assault of creeping suggestions. Just as you immediately cast into the fire the chaff and every bit of refuse that falls from the work of your hands, so likewise cast the movements of your thoughts upon God.

Since he himself is a consuming fire, hand over to him the superfluities of your heart to be consumed, remembering the apostolic saying: “Cast all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you” (Heb. 12; 1 Pet. 5). And the Prophet says: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. 54).

One of two things cannot be lacking to the person who fights courageously: either he must always resist suggestions attempting to enter, or strive to expel those that have entered. It is easier to break hostile attacks at the threshold than to drive them back after they have been admitted beyond the walls; it is safer to bar them before the doors than to force them out again after they have been admitted into the household.

Set temptation before yourself, therefore, as a serpent. If the serpent is driven away immediately at the entrance, everything remains unharmed: nothing is corrupted, nothing within is polluted. But if it is once admitted, even though it is afterward forced to depart with every effort, something, however little, of its poison or scales will necessarily remain.

Be vigilant, therefore, so that you may meet temptation at its first beginning, armed and ready (2 Cor. 10), and dash the small movements of emerging thoughts against the rock, which is Christ.

Believe one who has often experienced this: frequently we admit temptation as though we were merely deliberating, first making peace with ourselves on the understanding that we would drive it out as quickly as possible. But although we later expel that suggestion through an act of confession, and although we punish ourselves through the affliction of penance, I do not know by what means we remain unable for a long time to free ourselves from certain remnants of the pollution that has been expelled. By a just judgment, those who earlier allowed themselves to be tossed about willingly by an empty phantom are later pricked unwillingly by sharper goads of a biting conscience.

## CHAPTER XX. On Fleeing the Enticements of Gluttony

Since gluttony, first of all, is accustomed to brandish the weapons of its enticements against the undiscerning, rush fervently against this beast yourself and gird yourself with the weapons of continence.

It urges you to exceed the measure of your meal; but, holding the bridle of your body, never reach satiety. It perhaps suggests that you desire more sumptuous foods; but, once the service by which foods are put away has been completed, consider what follows.

If we judge rightly, it is almost the same madness to long for more exquisite dishes and to depict *anitergia*—privies or latrines—to be buried with them in pits. Both ambitions are equally ridiculous: just as a painting does not better wipe away the filth of excrement, so the human belly does not distinguish sweet foods from coarser ones.

The throat and palate indeed know the sweetness of foods, but they cannot enjoy it for long, because they immediately transmit to the stomach whatever has been crushed by the teeth. Thus, in turn, the palate, which tastes the foods, is abandoned by them in an instant, while the stomach, which does not taste them, keeps them longer.

The devil investigates what we judge more pleasant to eat. When this is offered, he urges us to cling to it so as to sharpen the appetite: while we plan to give it to no one and await the proper time for eating, our mind meanwhile becomes a meditation chamber for gluttony, a cauldron of food boiling over wickedly.

Therefore, to rid yourself of the material of this torment, throw away what is being badly kept; immediately the mind, freed from everything that weighed upon it, rises up.

Some people, although they do not desire more sumptuous foods, nevertheless, under the pretext of easing or having eased a fast, relax the restraint of food with reckless freedom. It is certain, however, that this immoderate intake of food strengthens the body less with power than it burdens it with mass, dulls the senses, induces torpor, and produces sleepiness. Since the body is frequently compelled to expel wind, swelling—or, to put it frankly, weakness—necessarily prevents the heart from remaining fixed in prayer or psalmody.

If, therefore, you expect strength for the performance of your tasks, never exceed the measure of tempered sobriety, because what is healthy for the body is clearly also a bodily ally of strength.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Loving Poverty and Meanness of Clothing

Be content also with poor and few garments. Accustom yourself always to be clothed in a light and very scant covering. At first this is not done without difficulty, but as habit advances and the practice becomes almost a second nature, the discomfort of the cold is easily mitigated.

Moreover, the scantiness of clothing and the poverty of food entirely drive every form of avarice from the monk’s heart. Why should I desire what adds nothing either to food or to clothing?

Thus, when we begin, we shrink with a certain fear from bare feet, scant clothing, the hardness of the bed, harsh food, drinking water, taking a cooked dish, and other things of this kind. But when we persevere and persist with patience, we regard them as entirely easy and tolerable. Frequency softens harshness; habit makes rigor acceptable.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Defining Nothing as Certain and on Discerning Thoughts

Do not find it burdensome to impose this habit upon yourself also: never decide with certainty that you are about to undertake or do something. Rather, if you recognize that it pleases God, make your plans with a certain condition, suspending your entire will upon God’s will.

Strive to act outwardly in such a way that the judgment of the heavenly disposition may always be present in your mind. Thus, if your effort is broken by the obstacle of some difficulty that meets it, your mind may immediately return to the judgment of divine providence.

Amid the fluctuating assaults of thoughts pouring in, make your mind like a net. Let it retain right counsels as fish, but let it allow vain thoughts to flow out and slip away, like whatever creeping things are abominable.

Discern your thoughts, and vigilantly observe not only what comes into your mind but also from where it comes.

Attend to what I am saying. Often the evil enemy recalls past sins to the mind so that you may again take pleasure in the same enticements. Often the divine Spirit does the same thing so that you may be pierced with compunction and tears. Since one and the same thought may tend toward different outcomes, the unwary mind often does not know what is happening around it.

Often a good thought is sent by the good spirit, namely, a thought of piety that ought to be carried out; but the cunning enemy falsely claims through crafty persuasion to be its author, so that the good may not be done because the deceived mind thinks it was suggested by the adversary.

Often, while we are chanting the psalms, we are attacked more fiercely by the devil under the appearance of dutiful thoughts, so that, while our mind considers itself to be thinking something pious, it may freely turn its eyes away from understanding what it is chanting.

[Col. 0354C] While we chant the psalms, we offer our God a sacrifice of praise. But destructive spirits fly around this sacrifice like harpies and defile it by injecting perverse thoughts, as though they were throwing dung into it. Or they utterly snatch it away if, by harassing us with temptations, they restrain us from prayer.

Just as sacrifices cannot please God if they have been snatched away from us, so those that have been polluted cannot please the author of purity. Therefore, we must likewise beware lest we either consent to fail in temptation or allow the attacking enemy to pollute our sacrifice with the foul contagion of thought.
