Whether you are devoted to meditation on the Scriptures or occupied with some work, frequently return to prayer. With your body prostrate on the ground, raise your mind toward heaven. Thus temptation leaves the heart, and troublesome accidie departs from eyes that have sat too long.

Do not, however, lie prostrate for a long time, because then the devil, as though the mind itself were lying down, hastens to attack more fiercely and supplies phantasms mixed with sleep to your thoughts. Whenever the hidden enemy sees the eyes of a drowsy person fluttering, he immediately fixes the dart of an evil thought in the wearied heart. The cunning plotter finds an opportune place for doing harm when, through the evidence of the outer eye, he detects that our mind is growing slack in its watchfulness.

Often extend your hands in prayer in the form of the saving sign, so that, while you strive to depict the image of the cross, you may rightly obtain forgiveness more easily from the Crucified One.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Against All Temptations, the Memory of Death and Burial Is Very Beneficial

In every struggle of the battle in which temptation provokes you, always strive to recall the grave to mind.

Perhaps anger lifts up your spirit: immediately direct your eyes toward the grave. All bitterness is soon laid aside when the prudent mind considers where human fury leads.

The spirit of pride inflates you: let the grave return to your mind. There, necessarily, we press down the swelling of the stiff neck, where we undoubtedly reckon ourselves to be ash and dust. “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?”

The flames of envy are kindled: look toward the grave and learn that, since we depart from this life so quickly, we envy others temporal goods in vain.

The incentives of lust burn: let the grave teach how quickly the freshness of the human body withers, how needlessly a bed of pleasure is spread for corruptible flesh, and what dreadful dwelling soon awaits its rest.

The itch of gluttony entices: immediately bring the grave back to mind and consider that, when we gently and tenderly nourish and distend our flesh, we are undoubtedly fattening food for worms. Thus it happens that the more we eat, the more are we eaten; while we pamper the belly softly, we nourish rich food for ungrateful guests.

The sting of avarice incites you: always hasten back to the tomb [Col. 0355C], and there learn that we who bring the very journey we are making to an end within so brief a span heap up in vain more provisions than our mortality requires.

If accidie or drowsiness weighs you down, let the tomb teach you to keep watch now for eternal rewards, since in it you must afterward rest for a very long time without any recompense. Thus, while you eagerly await the eternal rest of heavenly joy, you may now struggle with the momentary labor of your own sluggish indolence.

The splendor of clothing delights you: return to the tomb and consider how madly foolish are those who long to adorn a vile little handful of dust with ostentatious garments. They cover mud with gold and lay cleanliness upon filth because they do not understand the true ornaments [Col. 0355D] of the inner person.

Perhaps vainglory strives to lift you up: look toward the tomb and observe the end with which all human glory is closed: “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. IV). Your tongue itches to pour forth boastful or scurrilous words: let the tomb return to your mind and restrain you from criminal speech, and likewise from idle or joking chatter.

There you will be able to learn thoroughly how strictly it is fitting for us to withdraw from all the vanities of this life. And, lest I delay you by enumerating more examples, at every moment when a struggle arises, let this concern not leave you: immediately turn the eyes of your mind toward contemplating the tombs. Thus, while you consider yourself there to be unclean [Col. 0356A] and discarded dust, do not raise the neck of your heart in arrogance against the Creator; and while you clearly see that you will die, already present yourself to the vices that assail you as though dead.

Be equally vigilant that, whenever you sense a wicked thought approaching you, you hasten at once to sign your heart by extending your thumb. Thus, while the sign of the holy cross is impressed upon the very flesh, the inner person may immediately be roused with all its strength to fight against the perverse thought. In this way the mind, lifting the banner of triumph, may bravely confront its enemies and drive them from their proper dwelling while they are still lingering in the vestibule.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How you ought to confess

[Col. 0356B] But if, while at some time remaining in your cell, you sin by thinking or even doing something illicit, so that your terrified conscience gnaws at you however greatly, do not immediately go out for the sake of confession or break the strictness of your intended silence. Instead, confess meanwhile to God our Lord Jesus Christ, and offer him the following as a kind of pledge of your future confession:

“Lord Jesus Christ, eternal High Priest and minister of the holy things (Hebr. IX), and priest of the true tabernacle according to the order of Melchizedek, who offered to God the Father, for our sins, the holy and spotless lamb of your own body as a saving sacrifice, a fragrance of sweetness, and thus—not without blood—entered once a year into the Holy of Holies, that is, into heaven itself, to appear before the face of the Father [Col. 0356C]: I confess to you that I have fallen into this sin, which could not remain hidden from the eyes of your majesty. Therefore, both because of it and because of my countless other most serious sins, I am not worthy to raise my wretched eyes to heaven, or to enter your holy Church, or even to utter your blessed name with my polluted lips. Therefore, with tears, I beseech your immeasurable clemency—you who deigned to die for sinners and for those like me—that you mercifully forgive me this, and grant that I may attain true and fruitful repentance.”

If you still ask how you ought to confess alone at Prime or Compline, say this:

“I, most wretched and unhappy, confess before God, to you, holy and glorious Virgin Mary, and to you, all the saints of God: through my fault I have sinned exceedingly, through pride—in suggestion, delight, consent, thought, [351] words, and deed. Therefore I beseech you, most holy Mother of God, and all you holy and chosen ones of God, to deign to pray for me, a wretched sinner. Through the intercession of you all, may almighty God have mercy on me, forgive me all my sins, deliver me from every evil, preserve me, strengthen me, and make me steadfast in every good work; may God absolve me from every bond of my offenses, and may Christ, the Son of God, lead me to eternal life. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On those things that are useful for lightening the burden of eremitical austerity

[Col. 0357A]

Strive with every effort and with all your strength to attain to the grace of tears and to the perfection of contemplation. This is useful not only for acquiring a higher degree in that kingdom of blessedness, but also so that, in this very life you lead, all the dread of rigid austerity may depart, and whatever bitterness of severity and affliction had seemed harsh may be turned into sweetness.

When love has succeeded fear and freedom has succeeded servitude, necessity is turned into willingness, and, through the indescribable fire of charity, whatever had hitherto seemed rough and hard becomes sweet and pleasant [Col. 0357B].

The Israelite people, situated in the wasteland of the desert, could no longer return to Egypt, yet, because their merits impeded them, did not still enter the promised land. They were therefore forced to endure the weariness of labor and travel and the want imposed by various necessities (Exod.).

So too—indeed, so too—anyone who has already rejected the dark expanse of this world but, still bound by the sluggish idleness of torpor, does not strive toward the summit of perfection must necessarily endure many hardships and labors. Standing between the two, he enjoys neither the consolation, however slight, of worldly prosperity nor the light of heavenly contemplation. He has turned his eyes away from the world he abandoned, yet cannot see the light he seeks; he has nothing left in secular pleasure in which to rejoice, but does not taste the spiritual joy toward which he does not hasten with generous fervor.

Therefore one must either labor with all one’s strength toward perfection or endure many wearisome calamities and temptations. It is certainly hard to serve in the royal court; but after you have obtained the King’s favor and begun to cling more familiarly to his side, enter his chamber more frequently, stand in his presence, mingle mutual conversation, and attend his private counsels, then all the labor of that service becomes sweet and pleasant, and the troublesome business is judged sweeter than any rest.

You labor without labor, work without distress, and move about without vexation.

[Col. 0357D] Hasten, therefore, to destroy the passions of your vices, so that, admitted into the King’s chamber, you may cling to him like one of his household. Then the edge of your mind may turn more freely toward the Author of light, since the darkness of fantasies and vain thoughts does not obstruct it.

Often, while we are surrounded by a manifold siege of temptations, by the regard of divine clemency we are suddenly snatched into contemplation. Thus, as though inside a lodging, we look through hidden cracks upon the magnificent glory of the King, while our body remains outside and endures the storms of winds and the whirlwinds of pouring rains. In this way, as it were, only the eye enjoys the delights of royal pleasures, while the other limbs are exposed to blasts and torments [Col. 0358A].

Therefore, to make the labor of the journey lighter, one must direct one’s eyes toward the rest of the dwelling. Everything we do becomes light if the goal toward which we hasten is always before our eyes.

This also contributes greatly to easing the burden of eremitical austerity: if one imposes upon oneself for a time a shortage of food, dryness of drink, and certain other things contrary to the flesh. For when one afterward returns to one’s customary fare, one regards the rule of habit as a relaxation from weariness; and, by comparison, the flesh considers it no small gain to have added something to what had previously been enough for it.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the grace of tears may be acquired

[Col. 0358B] But since we have taught that one must devote oneself to tears, let us briefly explain next how one may attain that very grace of tears, insofar as their giver pours it forth.

If you seek not merely to grieve with a dry heart but also to overflow with an abundance of tears, remove yourself not only from the clamor of secular affairs but often restrain yourself from mutual conversation with your brothers. Cut away from yourself all the cares and anxieties of worldly activity, and hasten to remove them, like heaps of rubble and obstructions in a channel, from the breathing of the blocked spring.

For just as water coming from the abyss gathers in an underground cavern but, pressed down by barriers, does not flow out, so, when the depth of divine judgment is considered, sadness arises in the human heart; yet it does not flow forth through tears breaking out in weeping if the restraint of earthly actions stands in the way.

Sadness is indeed the material of tears. But, if you wish the vein of this spring to flow abundantly, strive to remove every obstacle of secular business. And, not to omit what I have often experienced myself, spiritual zeal, the discipline of those entrusted to one’s care, correction of offenders, and the address of holy preaching—although these things are holy and expressly commanded by divine authority—are nevertheless unquestionably recognized as impediments to tears.

If, therefore, you earnestly desire to attain the grace of tears, restrain yourself sometimes not only from earthly affairs but also from carrying out certain spiritual exercises. Remove malice, anger, hatred, and the remaining plagues of vices from the cave of your heart [Col. 0358D], lest, if an accusing conscience should happen to gnaw at you, your mind, emptied of its inner dew and moisture, wither in the dryness of fear, as Scripture says: “People will faint with fear” (Luke XXI).

Confidence in holiness and a conscience that bears witness to innocence irrigate the pure mind with certain streams of heavenly grace and dissolve it into tears; they soften the hardness of the squalid heart and open a channel for tears to flow. Let your conscience therefore be pure, clean, bright; let it be sincere, unleavened, and cleansed from every stain of spiritual wickedness. When compunction of heart hastens to break forth, let no barrier of a biting conscience stand in its way; nor let the chill of a proper fear bind the trembling heart [Col. 0359A], so that the water of tears, turned into ice, does not flow. Yet fear of sins can also sometimes produce the compunction of tears.

But servile fear is one thing, and spiritual grace another—the grace by which we offer to God, upon the altar of a contrite heart, sacrifices rich in their inmost substance, and healthfully burn a fat offering as a fragrance of sweetness.

If this grace of the Holy Spirit is lacking, even if someone strives to lift the mind toward heavenly glory, even if he recalls the punishments of Gehenna or past sins, or even remembers the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, tears nevertheless do not break forth, because the secrets of his mind have hardened through the demands of sins.

But you, like a prudent and diligent farmer, cultivate your field without ceasing. Plow the soil of your heart and body with the plowshare of holy discipline; break the clods of hardness bit by bit; strive to uproot the thornbushes of vices. Then, prepared each day, with your eyes raised toward heaven, await the abundance of the heavenly rain.

For the supreme Judge, that hidden observer who stands behind our wall, “looking through the window, gazing through the lattice” (Song II), even if for a time he withholds the water according to his provident dispensation, will, if he sees you acting so diligently and watchfully, soon irrigate the field with abundant showers of his own gifts. Then the field will be adorned with flowers of diverse virtues, so that what had previously seemed squalid and sterile will now be richly filled with the yield of overflowing crops.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On persevering in the manner of life that one has once undertaken

[Col. 0359C]

Moreover, steadfastly retain and constantly carry out the manner of life that you have once undertaken, lest, God forbid, you seem to differ from yourself with theatrical instability.

I do not want you to follow the example of ill-fated Icarus, who, now penetrating the heights and now descending to the depths with loosened wings, is hurled by the unbridled freedom of his inconstancy into the open depths of the sea. Take care lest wavering change make you, as the saying goes, many-colored; let the gravity of a uniform state be displayed instead.

Persevere, therefore, in what you have begun and hold to the straight line of your accustomed life. Do not let the diversity of an ever-changing life continually make you new; rather, let the habit of the rule once established on the foundation of holy constancy stabilize you, so that the practice of long habit may sweeten what human weakness and frailty reject as altogether bitter and harsh.

Present yourself everywhere conspicuous in the splendor of virtues and, so to speak, clothed in the uniform garment of holiness, to which no patch of any vice appears to have been sewn.

It is disgraceful and ridiculous if, while dressed in a purple garment, silk boots, and gilded shoes, you display, among all those ornaments, only the rustic cap of a shaggy ram.

What I wish to say is this: when, in the affliction of fasting, the severity of silence, and the harshness of an abject garment, you present an Antony, do not, in the lightness of laughter or the urbanity of witty banter [Col. 0360A], display a Democritus.

“For what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? What fellowship does light have with darkness? What concord does God have with Belial?” (II Cor. VI.) “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V).

Let the field of your soul therefore flourish with crops of virtues, so that the thorns of the brambles never bristle through negligence. Let uprightness on one side build up those who see it, so that, when vice rises on the other side, what has been built does not totter as though struck by a battering ram.

Be serious in your walk, mature in speech, slow to vengeance, swift to grant pardon to those who repent. In everything present yourself as an example of perfected virtue and, as the saying goes, make yourself smooth and round on every side, so that, afterward, bruised by the hammer of discipline, filed by repentance, and polished by holy struggle [Col. 0360B], you may be placed without ringing or clamor among the ranks of glowing stones.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What kind of person the superior of hermits should be chosen and should be

Since, for the sake of brevity, we have described as best we could how a hermit ought to conduct himself, let us briefly add at the end of this little work what kind of person it is fitting for the superior of hermits to be.

Nor should the order be called backward if the man who will be first in office is placed last in the description of the rule. He ought first to live in the same purpose before presiding over it, and the one who appears superior in governance ought to show himself the least of all.

Care must therefore be taken that the superior among the hermits not be chosen from the monastic order [Col. 0360C], even if he seems prudent and learned or trained in regular disciplines. Rather, a spiritual brother should be chosen from the very purpose itself—one who has already begun to live as a hermit and has learned by experience to fight against spiritual wickedness; one who recognizes the battles of another’s heart from his own heart, and what he hears from the mouth of one confessing recognizes from his own conscience, like a hand practiced for battle.

Strive, then, O superior—to address you directly—so that those whom you surpass by the office of superior you may also, if possible, surpass by however much in your life.

Preaching that is vivid and effective in the hearts of disciples is to provide nourishment for others while oneself persisting in the rigor of fasting. He preaches vigils excellently who, after the long course of psalmody, strikes the signal to awaken the brothers [Col. 0360D]. Most eloquently, while we are silent, we commend silence. He speaks profitably about the scantiness of clothing who disfigures himself by tearing his garments.

But one conspicuous in the splendor of clothing like a rich man preaches the hairs of camels in vain with John. The man who avenges an injury does not recommend patience. He who burns with eagerness to accumulate monetary gains does not extinguish the fire of avarice in another’s breast. He who is carried away by frequent wandering is considered a frivolous disputant when he speaks about the discipline of remaining in place. But he who continually inhabits his cell makes his whole body a tongue in praise of stability; and although his mouth is silent, his mute limbs cry out more effectively and more simply.

[Col. 0361A] Always have a witness to your life, one who can communicate your hidden good deeds to the brothers in an edifying report and can clear your reputation of sinister suspicion.

Lead your flock along easier paths; but meanwhile, as a discerning guide, point out the heights. Thus, while they attribute to your dispensation the fact that they live more leniently, and gird themselves more readily to climb the mountain of perfection because of the strict authority of the Fathers that they hear, let them be ashamed to grow dull in low places when they learn that their predecessors journeyed nobly through the heights.

Show yourself equal to those who walk along straight paths; but exercise the vigor of discipline zealously toward offenders. To preserve the purity of innocence within the conscience, do not lay down the rod of discipline. Yet let the word of correction proceed from your lips [Col. 0361B] in such a way that the sweetness of fraternal love remains in your breast.

Just as a hawk flies from the hand of its handler to catch birds, so let the voice of indignation proceed without indignation in your mind. An arrow wounds the one into whom it is fixed, but the bow from which it came knows nothing of the blood.

It must nevertheless be noted that a fragile mind is more easily broken away from perseverance in the desert even when the occasion provided is only a slight injury. A heavy burden is laid down with less deliberation the more the shoulder itself, which is burdened, seems in some way to advise it.

It is therefore easy to depart from the companionship of those among whom each person is ordered to enjoy daily want of food and to endure abundance only very rarely.

A measured art of discipline must therefore be used, lest the harshness of imposed correction overthrow those whom private affliction has weakened.

If the example of anyone acting bravely is from your own group, suppressing the person’s name, bring the example forward; but if it is an outsider, state his name. The examples of those living now encourage more effectively than those of the ancients. It is a source of great shame if men living in the same age as holy men are not found equal to them in some respect in the pursuit of upright conduct. Those others are strengthened by the innate nobility of their minds; these cannot excuse themselves by the weakness of different ages.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On those coming from the world to the desert

If someone wishes to turn from secular dress to the desert [Col. 0361D], do not, according to the custom of earlier superiors, advise him to begin with the monastery. Rather, if true and sincere devotion is evident, provide him in the desert he seeks with an entrance into conversion.

For, to speak with grief, many monasteries have fallen so far that those who enter them are found to be more vicious than those who have recently been rescued from the waves of the world’s shipwreck. Certainly, the mark of a coin is fittingly impressed upon simple metal; but once the coin has been falsified, it is difficult to correct it according to the truth of the minting rule.

Let the way in, then, be open to the person coming from the world, so that the form newly imposed may somehow be impressed upon simple [Col. 0362A] metal.

Once he has entered the cell, however, he should not immediately be permitted to fulfill the whole rule of the customary discipline. Let him seek for a long time what, having been found with difficulty, he will hold more dearly. Later, as time proceeds, let all the reins be relaxed for holy desire, and let him attempt whatever his mind longed for as arduous. Thus, in the very spirit of fervor, let him undertake to walk along the path of the higher way, from which he will afterward be ashamed to decline ignobly. Let him always keep the beginnings of his first undertaking before his eyes as an example, so that, if he has not climbed higher things, he will at least be ashamed to slip away from those with which he once began.

## CHAPTER XXX. On those who come to the desert from cenobitic life

But if it is someone from the rule of a monastery who hastens to the desert [Col. 0362B], judge certain superstitious strictures of monastic discipline, needless clangings of bells, the manifold harmonies of songs, the finery of ornaments, and other such things by a sober art of criticism. Suitably lessen their importance and depreciate them without condemnation, applying the Apostle’s words:

“In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any value, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. VI).

And again:

“The Most High does not dwell in things made by human hands” (Acts VII).

Also the words to Timothy:

“Bodily exercise is profitable for little, but godliness is profitable for all things” (I Tim. IV).

By these and similar teachings, suppress the esteem in which the monastic order is held with the balance of a modest correction, so that, while the structure of the customary life is demolished in the mind of the hearer, the building of the preferred solitude may be constructed [Col. 0362C]. Let him henceforth prepare himself firmly to stand, considering that until now he has lain prostrate.

But if, after long struggles of labor have been completed and the enticements of his chastened flesh have been subdued, he begins to see himself trampling upon the necks of certain vices as upon so many enemies, and begins to despise the past immoderately and to praise more freely the things now before him, then the praises of the cenobia must be proclaimed, and whatever is done in their disciples must be referred to the glory of God. The sacrifices of salutary obedience must be commended, so that, while the profession of communal life is exalted, any arrogance that may have crept in from the solitary way of life may be laid aside.

He must not swell with pride as though he possessed the privilege of a more perfect life, while he perhaps still does not equal many who walk with much greater sublimity in an inferior grade [Col. 0362D].

He should be admonished that, if something must perhaps be done, he should not therefore, like certain cenobites, chant hastily and then try, by a perverse exchange, to swim from the Psalter into business as though from the open sea to the shore.

The crafty enemy introduces anxiety of spirit; but the prince of peace seeks a quiet and humble mind in which he may rest.

Let him therefore answer the adversary who suggests stories while he is chanting:

“Be silent for the moment while I perform the office that is in my hands; afterward, if the matter requires it, make yourself known.”

But if the adversary presses more obstinately and persists with hardened determination [Col. 0363A], let him curse both the thing being sent and the one who sent it at the same time. Let him also add words to terrify him with threats, saying:

“Leave me, wretched man, and place before your eyes the terrible day of judgment, on which you will justly be condemned and afterward burned in everlasting avenging flames.”

This terror is highly effective for overcoming the struggle and escaping the cunning of the crafty enemy.

For this reason, too, after the prayers of the exorcisms, ecclesiastical tradition always adds:

“He who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.”

Thus, while the evil spirit is struck in temptation by such great fear, he may be driven out, terrified by God’s creature.

Instruct your fellow soldiers subtly with these and similar weapons, and, going before them in the battle line, teach them continually to fight against their adversaries [Col. 0363B].

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the virtue of patience, especially necessary to the one who presides

Although you ought to flourish in every virtue, since you have been placed over others as an example of virtue, devote yourself especially to the virtue of patience. Overcome every obstacle of every kind of adversity through patience.

Let patience make you a hard stone—or rather, an uncut diamond. The seal of a diamond impresses its form upon other stones, but it does not itself admit any image of another stone’s solidity.

If your mind likewise remains unchanged by any disturbance when adversities rush upon it, it does not receive the image of another stone, but rather impresses its own character upon others, converting whatever happens to adversity into its own good through the sweetness of the mind and the tranquillity of the spirit.

The chapter should be held with the brothers either never or rarely without your accusing yourself after the appointed metanoia. Even voluntarily, request that the discipline of the broom proceed against you, asking for it with sufficiently humble authority.

If you sense that either your own spirit or that of any brother has been wounded against you, do not rest until you strive to heal the wound of the mind, as the matter dictates—whether by correction, soothing, or even satisfaction.

We therefore extend our discussion of the superior’s office at greater length because, with divine grace leading the way, we do not doubt that the whole perfection of those subject to him depends upon his teaching.

What the stomach is in the human body, the superior is almost exactly that in a congregation of spiritual brothers [Col. 0363D]. For just as vigor and strength are spread through all the limbs of the body from the stomach’s receptacle, so the whole body of those living in the bond of charity is nourished by the well-administered office of the one who presides.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That this rule contains not the perfect and complete institutions of eremitical life, but certain lighter principles of this way of life

[Col. 0364A]

I beg you, my brothers, not to accuse me of laxity because you live by a stricter law than the one read here, nor to criticize me with reproaches for having moderated the austerity of the desert by a standard perhaps less severe than it should be.

When those carnal Israelites mournfully lamented the fall of Benjamin’s sons, who perished—though pardonably—while falling away, and grieved with bitter tears and wailings that one tribe had fallen from Israel, what should we do when we see that, among the remaining orders of ecclesiastical discipline, the number of those professing the eremitical life has diminished to such an extent that in many provinces of the earth we cannot doubt that it has been entirely wiped out?

Benjamin must therefore be spared—those outstanding and strongest warriors among the rest of the Israelites [Col. 0364B]—so that a pardonable and moderate discernment may multiply through the growth of posterity those whom strict severity, or rather human frailty, has destroyed. Thus the number of the tribes may remain complete, while moderated austerity preserves the tribe that seemed to have perished.

Nor has this escaped me: the holy apostles, who had been sent to preach Christ’s cross to the human race (Acts XV, XXI) and to instruct the adopted sons of every virtue through their teachings, commanded certain Gentiles, amid the very beginnings of the newly arising faith, only this: that they abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication.

By imposing the lesser things, they did not prohibit the greater, so that those who might have been frightened away by the harshness of the new teaching could eventually grow strong, invited by milder commands; and, like children still nursing, might begin with small and light matters, so that afterward, in mature age, they might courageously fulfill the more serious commands of divine law.

We too, who weave the toys of spiritual infancy and, so to speak, fashion the cradle of the hermit who is still nursing, lead the weak and those like ourselves along easier paths. Yet we do not forbid those who are readily girded from climbing the arduous mountain, so that the liquid of milk may nourish the still-weak in such a way that, when they have become strong and vigorous, the solidity of more substantial food does not repel them.

In this we trust in the goodness of divine clemency: whoever strives to carry out the things written in this little work, with the intention of advancing and progressing [Col. 0364D], will not be harmed by the second death, nor will his name be erased from the book of life. Rather, that Lamb, who sees him carrying his cross after him, will unquestionably enroll him as a coheir in the heavenly Jerusalem (Apoc. XX, XXI). Amen.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0365]

359–360. THE SIXTEENTH LITTLE WORK. AN INVECTIVE IN RHETORICAL DECLAMATION AGAINST A BISHOP WHO RECALLED MONKS TO THE WORLD. TO GISLERIUS, BISHOP OF AUXIMUM.

### ARGUMENT

He rebukes a certain bishop who had dared to assert that a monk might abandon, because of illness or other causes, the religious habit once assumed. He demonstrates at length how impious this is and contrary to the sacred canons and the decrees of the councils, and proves by the strongest arguments that it is not permissible to withdraw from the purpose of religion.

[Col. 0365A] To the lord Gislerius, bishop of Auximum, Peter, the least servant of the monks, sends the service of most fervent devotion.

You have not forgotten, most reverend bishop, that we have often jointly complained and often lamented with common distress over those reprobate men who, having despised the religious habit, have fallen back into the world.

Recently, when I happened to attend the Roman synod while you were suffering from bodily illness, I judged it appropriate to bring knowledge of this matter to the lord pope. He, being a most holy man, deeply grieved over the matter according to the innermost sincerity of the charity that flourishes in the temple of his breast, and immediately took care to apply a suitable remedy to the monstrous wound.

Since he could not find in those regions a man more suitable for carrying out this affair [Col. 0365B], he decided to send you his letters, so that you might address those transgressors according to the eloquence of your wisdom and recall those willing to obey to their original purpose; but those who proved rebellious were to be struck with the sentence of perpetual anathema.

I encountered the lord Guido, bishop of Numanum, at the aforesaid council. Since, as you know, he was said to provide encouragement for this vice, I confess my fault: I presumed to be harshly angry with him.

That man, worthy in humility and patience, and learned not only in sacred writings but also in the studies of the liberal arts, patiently endured my reproach. But, denying and detesting the charge brought against him and invoking God’s testimony, he repelled it most eloquently [Col. 0365C].

He even began voluntarily to direct the weapons of his words on my behalf—he who had hitherto been falsely said to be fighting against me.

But although that venerable man was found innocent, I nevertheless did not restrain the force of the dart I had already hurled. Instead, changing the name, I introduced another person with whom I might contend, so that anyone who wickedly aspires to the contest of this controversy may recognize that he is marked by this designation.

Although the author of this crime is not now manifest, while he strives for a time to remain hidden, he gains no immunity from the hiding place of his flight. Rather, let the armed order of argumentation block the opening of the dragon’s den, so that as soon as he emerges, he may suddenly strike against the sword awaiting him and be shattered.

Therefore, after that letter of supreme authority [Col. 0366A], receive this little work also. Then, like the son of Benjamin armed in each hand with a two-edged sword, rush into the crowded ranks of the enemy, so that the former, like a strong plowshare, may furrow the fields of the weed-filled breast in order to tear up the poisonous aconite by the roots.

Let this work, following like a cheap hoe, break the clods; or, to offer a more fitting example, let it, like an orator, convict those who are guilty of the manifest crime, while that authority, like a presiding judge, restrains them with the censure of canonical rigor.

But, with divine grace leading the way, let us immediately attack the one whom we strive to assail.

## INVECTIVE AGAINST A BISHOP WHO RECALLED MONKS TO THE WORLD

### CHAPTER I. That a sick monk is not permitted to return to the world

[Col. 0366B] Necessity requires me to write no little against you, venerable bishop Maure. I am compelled to cross the boundary of my rank and, though a priest, to oppose you with words that are not priestly. I am pressed and constrained on every side: to speak against a bishop is indeed proud, but to remain silent about such matters is to give consent.

Yet it is better that I alone appear arrogant than that a deadly vice, now beginning above all, should grow to the ruin of many. It is preferable to be rebuked in the judgment of bishops for the simplicity of my speech than to be condemned before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge for my silence.

Nearly two years ago, while I was hiding in the narrow corner of my cell, a sinister and sorrowful report was carried to me by spreading rumor [Col. 0366C]: namely, that certain ruined men, having turned after Satan, were abandoning the monastic habit with sacrilegious rashness and, in execrable apostasy, returning again to secular service.

It was said that they had been incited to dare this by your exhortations and supported in persevering in it by your authority, after falling into so deep an abyss of crime.

For you were reported to say that, unless someone had been tested according to the rule and over long periods of time, as the monastic rule commands, if he had entered the monastic order in another way—whether because of illness or for any other reason—he should have free power to return to the world.

I remember that at that time I sent you a brief letter concerning this matter and, with the humility that was proper, urged you to desist from this pestilential doctrine. [Col. 0367A] Recently, while staying at Auximum, I learned from many people that you nevertheless persist most obstinately in your intention and do not cease to proclaim the same doctrine against the authority of divine law and the norm of ecclesiastical custom. I am therefore greatly astonished how a prudent man, not altogether unfamiliar with literary studies, can advance so heedless, so perverse, and so harmful an opinion—one that is plainly opposed to the common salvation of humanity and seems to have been put forward for no other purpose than, beyond doubt, to close the gate of the heavenly kingdom against sinners. Tell me, I beg you, who discovered this opinion, unless it was the one who first drove the human race from the delights of paradise? Who, I ask, promulgated so cruel and impious an edict, unless he who plunged Cain the fratricide [Col. 0367B] into the abyss of despair and taught him to say—not in order to escape the danger of his ruin, but to fall more deeply into it—“My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon” (Gen. IV)?

What madness is this? What insanity? What cruelty? A man has free authority to dispose of his possessions, but has he no power to offer himself to God? He is able to hand over his property to human beings, but has he no freedom to return his soul to God? A man may push an animal that is about to fall away from the mouth of an open pit, but may he not rescue a soul that is soon to plunge into hell by the remedy of repentance? Moreover, if almighty God himself, who has been offended, is ready to receive the sinner, who is this person who restrains those wishing to run to that very fountain of mercy? If the Creator is ready to forgive sins, who is this man who prevents the sinner from converting? For what else is becoming a monk than converting? But whoever denies that a person established in bodily sickness can undertake the monastic way of life plainly and unquestionably asserts that such a person cannot convert. Once this is admitted, there can be no doubt that repentance—the hope of sinners and the one remedy for human salvation—is destroyed.

Behold, then, the sinner’s lost soul, condemned by an unopenable [sic] door to the gate of life, and every hope of human restoration torn away. But divine mercy cries out in opposition, saying: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XVIII); and again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should convert and live” (ibid. XXXV). And when he has converted and groaned in repentance, then he shall be saved. To offer a concise statement from canonical authority: whoever denies that repentance—even in the final breath of life—can abolish sins is a Novatian, not a Christian.

## CHAPTER II. Whether a sick person may put on the religious habit

Since, then, becoming a monk is certainly the same as converting, and the remedy of conversion rejects no hour and excludes no time, it is beyond doubt that a person established in sickness is not hindered by any obstacle of authority from converting whenever he wishes; likewise, he is rightly permitted to become a monk without any opposition. But since James says, “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death” (James V), of what murder is the person guilty who, on the contrary, dissuades the sinner from converting? Surely, unless I am mistaken, it is not the body—which will die at some time—that is killed, but the soul, which will live forever, that is slaughtered.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “a person suffering bodily illness is not prohibited from fleeing suddenly to the harbor of the monastic order; nevertheless, if he recovers, he may return to the habit of his former way of life.” But Truth itself cries out—indeed, cries out against so obvious a falsehood—when it says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX). It is fitting, then, that just as one who comes to God is fit for the kingdom of God, so one who withdraws from God should afterward be unfit for the kingdom of God. Such people, as we have learned by experience, do not remain at the same measure of evil at which they previously stood; rather, after returning to their vomit, they roll down more deeply into the abyss of iniquities. So it happened very recently to one who, as is reported, abandoned the habit of holy conduct at your urging. Then, scarcely after a short cycle of days had passed, he killed an innocent man with his own hands. In this evidently reprobate man we see fulfilled what we heard spoken from the mouth of Truth: that the unclean spirit who had earlier left him later returned, took with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself (Luke XI), and with all of them dwelt more pestilently in his familiar vessel; thus the last state of that man became worse than the first.

Certainly, if the laws of the world not only reject a deserter from earthly military service but also call him infamous, so that they do not even admit him to give testimony in a legal dispute, by what judgment, by what right, and with what countenance may one who had sworn allegiance to the arms of the heavenly Emperor, who had already put on the cloak of the heavenly army, who had girded himself with the belt of chastity, and who had received the gift of sacred speech from the commander of the soldiers himself now desert the camp of his own profession and, delighting in his own vomit, turn his mind back to the worldly vanities that he had despised, renounced, and condemned? We make a mortal covenant with a mortal being and keep it; we make a pledge to God and are not afraid to break faith. A man is held liable to another man for violating his undertaking; yet the man who tries to deceive the author of humanity is judged innocent? A deceitful debtor is constrained by his creditor; yet the person who withdraws himself from God is regarded as exempt? Surely a servant is not worthy of pardon who, having violated his faith, not only withdraws from his Lord but voluntarily joins himself to his enemy. That God is the enemy of this world, hear James saying: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James IV).

And to return to the matter at hand: will not the fellow servant who becomes the instigator of this escape be punished with the strict vengeance of the Lord’s judgment, and will not the penalty deserved by both be heaped together upon one head? Especially if the servant is accused of such fraud who had been placed in the position of ruler and appeared to preside over the others; who ought to have drawn outsiders into the service of his master but instead compels the household servants to depart; and who, so to speak, had the duty of restraining the violent attacks of marauding beasts against his master’s flock, yet himself strives to offer the innocent sheep to the bloody teeth of wolves.

## CHAPTER III. The lamentation of pernicious prelates

What shall I say about these things? Where shall I find consolation for my grief? I am compelled to cry out; I am compelled to pour forth the bitterness of my heart, so that I may say: O times, O morals, O iron age! An iron age, I say, in which gold is turned into dross and a vein of worthless tin falsely assumes the appearance of silver (Isa. XX; Ezek. XXX). In which the stones of the sanctuary have been cast at the head of every street (Lam. IV), and as is the people, so is the priest; as is the servant, so is his master. For who could be found so without a tongue that he would not at least burst forth into a lamenting cry over these things? Who is so iron-hearted, so stone-like, that his heart would not feel these wounds? The sword has indeed reached the soul.

The world plainly shows that it has fallen toward its end through ever-increasing ruin. And bishops, who ought urgently to draw souls to God, devote themselves to devising how people may withdraw from God’s service? The Judge is already drawing near, and the herald cries out that the citizens should flee? The whole of the human race is already being gathered before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge, and the priest orders people to scatter into worldly affairs? Alas! Has the priestly order been reduced to this: that those appointed to flood the world with the light of holy preaching themselves make every effort to blind people with the darkness of perverse doctrines? And those placed in the field of the Church to uproot all the thorns of error themselves are not ashamed to sow the prickly thistles of erroneous perversity? In former times, when the flourishing world still smiled upon people, the learned tongue of pastors drew very many away from it. Now, however, when the world most plainly reveals itself as contemptible, the Pastor of the Church invites people to return to it.

Every day we see people seizing what belongs to others, laboring zealously at wars, oppressing the needy, and concealing the snares of their schemes in the paths of their brothers. To sum up all the evils of the world in a brief expression, nearly everyone seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. II); yet we are not stirred against them by any zeal of charity, we do not oppose them with corrections, and we resist them with no contradiction. But if some exceedingly rare person from such a multitude of human beings, whether worn down by punishments or moved by the grace of divine inspiration, eventually turns to his Creator, we immediately turn him back through the blandishments of persuasive flattery; we bend the flowers of sacred speech to the perversity of our understanding, and thus teach one already devoted to divine service that he can return to the world’s mire. Often what the error of a person who misunderstands sees on the very surface of the text is overturned by the teacher’s intention, examined more subtly; and what seemed to be rightly understood in an isolated phrase is proved to be an error when the sequence of the continuous text is considered more carefully.

Now let Scripture itself, which speaks about monks, come forward, lest our opponent complain that he has been defeated merely by an argument concerning words. Let him not offer me the circles of his dialectical syllogisms; let rhetoric not pour into me the pleasing colors of its smooth persuasion; let no worldly wisdom, adorned with finery, suggest to me the blandishments of its refinement. Let the authority of the Fathers alone, bare and unadorned, present itself—those Fathers in whose breast almighty God, presiding as upon a tribunal and throne, willed to promulgate the decree of his sanction. Thus the person who attempts to contend may appear to be overcome not by the contrivances of quibbling words but rather by the very oracle of truth. And so that every avenue of evasion may be closed on every side, let him find that the very men whom the whole world possesses as judges and advocates are brought forward against him in the dispute.

## CHAPTER IV. What is undertaken voluntarily may not be abandoned without sin

Let the great Leo, then, first establish the decisive point of his authority and, as a truly invincible leader, himself carry the standard at the front line of battle. For among other things he says:

> “The monastic profession, undertaken by one’s own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what a person has vowed to God he ought to render. Therefore, whoever, having abandoned the profession of solitude, has turned to military service or to marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the better choice is a transgression.”

Here it should be noted that this most eloquent man does not say, as our bishop chatters, that the monastic profession must have been undertaken after a long period of delay. “The monastic profession,” he says, “undertaken by one’s own judgment or will cannot be abandoned without sin.” He therefore left no force to the passage of time or to delay, attributing everything to spontaneous will.

If, then, this profession cannot be denied to have been undertaken voluntarily, it must necessarily be affirmed to have been abandoned sinfully. The same applies to what that most eloquent man says about virgins:

> “Girls who have undertaken the profession and habit of virginity, not under the compelled command of their parents but by spontaneous judgment, if they afterward choose marriage, are transgressors, even if the grace of consecration has not yet come to them; for they would not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their profession.”

Do you hear, then, O bishop, that no importance is attributed to a lengthy conversion, nor even to consecration itself, but that all the strength of monastic perfection is reserved for spontaneous judgment?

The eminent Leo could have—and indeed ought to have—sufficed to refute the accusations of our litigant, if the latter could easily bend the rigid neck of his heart before sacred authorities. But since he perhaps still does not bend, let blessed Pope Gelasius also be called as a witness. For he writes, among other things:

> “Therefore, whoever among men or women has once voluntarily put on the religious habit—or whoever has done so; whether it be a man devoted to the church choir, or a woman, or one assigned to a monastery of girls—in either sex the transgressor must be compelled to return unwillingly to the profession: the man must be tonsured, and the girl must enter the monastery. But if, under any pretext, they wish to remain deserters, they are to be regarded by priestly judgment as excluded from the assembly of Christians, so that they have no place among them.”

Examine each word carefully, I beg you, weighing it in the balance of your mind, so that you may in no way deviate from the position of truth. Consider, then, what is said: “Whoever has once voluntarily put on the religious habit.” Behold: according to the meaning of the Gelasian decree, on whatever occasion, even if no delay in probation has intervened, whoever has once been clothed in the religious habit is entirely denied permission to return to the world.

## CHAPTER V. Whether children dedicated to God by their parents and clothed in the habit are bound to remain in religious life

Something similar is also found in the Council of Chalcedon, where we decree that those who have once been assigned to the clergy or have sought the life of monks are to come neither to military service nor to any worldly dignity; but those who attempt this, and do not repent so as to return to what they initially chose for God’s sake, are to be anathematized.

Let the Council of Toledo also add weight to the testimonies supporting our argument:

> “Let paternal devotion or a person’s own profession make someone a monk. Whichever of these has been alleged shall remain binding. Accordingly, we close the entrance by which such persons might return to the world, and we prohibit every return to worldly life.”

Again, much earlier in the same council, among other things, we read:

> “Therefore, if at any lesser age one or both parents have given sons or daughters, of either sex, either the tonsure of religion or the proper religious garment—even if these were received unwillingly or without their knowledge—and if they have not immediately rejected them when they saw them upon their children, whether in their own presence, before the Church, or publicly in the assembly, it shall never afterward be permitted to those children themselves to return to a secular habit. Rather, once it has been established that they have at some time had the tonsure or religious clothing, they are immediately to be recalled to the religious observance and habit and compelled, under strict discipline, to serve this practice.”

(See the scholia at the end of the work.)

If you wish, hear also what the Council of Tribur decrees concerning monks who abandon their profession:

> “Whoever, coming from secular life, has received penance, had himself tonsured, and then, transgressing, has again become a layman, must, once apprehended by his bishop, be recalled to the penance from which he withdrew. But if some prove obstinate with respect to the penance and, even after admonition, do not return, they are truly to be condemned before the Church by the sentence of anathema.”

Here we are expressly taught that this responsibility is imposed upon bishops not so that they may advise those who remain to leave the monasteries, but rather so that they may compel transgressors to return. But why should we complain about people who convert by their own voluntary judgment, when even those who are tonsured unwillingly are not permitted to return behind them?

Hence the following edict is also promulgated at the Council of Mainz:

> “Concerning clerics, we establish this: those who have hitherto been found tonsured, whether in the canonical or in the monastic order, without their consent, shall remain so if they are free persons.”

But perhaps you will answer me and, against so many authoritative judgments of the holy Fathers and so many statutes of venerable councils, will still raise the shield of a vain defense: “Let it be,” you will say, “that those who are offered by their parents should remain as they are; that those who convert voluntarily should not return to worldly affairs; and that those who are tonsured even against their will should now strive to persevere according to sounder counsel.” For what else is it than to see nothing with open eyes when confronted by the glittering spheres of the stars, if one doubts such clear statements of the holy Fathers?

But tell me, I beg you: is it to be endured, rather than denounced in free voices, when certain wicked rulers of monasteries—who demonstrably love neither God nor the salvation of souls—kindled by the goads of shameful profit, deceive simple people by smooth persuasion, enticing them with empty promises and drawing them into the monastery? Will such a conversion be considered upright, when inflamed greed has preceded the possessor rather than the possession? I answer without hesitation, and I firmly affirm that such people also must not be permitted to deviate from the profession they have begun. And so that the argument need not depend upon reasoning of my own, let us return once more to the Council of Mainz. After much else, it says:

> “This holy assembly has indeed decreed that bishops or abbots who, not desiring the harvest of souls but coveting avarice and shameful profit, have tonsured people by enticing and deceiving them, and by such persuasion have not merely received their possessions but rather stolen them, shall be subjected to canonical or regular penance, as followers of shameful profit. Those, however, who, enticed by empty promises or persuaded by any sort of schemes, have been deprived of their reason and, no longer knowing themselves to be masters of their possessions, have cut off their hair, must be compelled to persevere in what they have begun.”

But since every stratagem of a crafty litigant is fully refuted when whatever he can be thought capable of objecting is first beaten back as though by the heaviest battering rams of argument, perhaps you will not blush to say that blessed Gregory ordered a man to be withdrawn from a monastery and restored to his wife, even though he had already been tonsured.

We, however, answer you—not without reason—that an arrow shot at a stone sometimes strikes the one who directed it, and that often an incautious soldier is mortally wounded by the very weapon with which he tries to strike his adversary. For if you examine this example carefully, it is seen to stand on our side and is found unmistakably to support our arguments. To make what is said clear through the facts themselves, let us not hesitate to insert here something from Gregory’s letter:

> “Agathora, bearer of these documents, has complained that her husband was converted to the monastery of Abbot Urbicius against his will. Since this plainly pertains to the fault and disrepute of that same abbot, we instruct Your Experience to investigate the matter carefully, lest perhaps he was converted with her consent or she herself promised to change her way of life. If you discover this to be so, see that he remains in the monastery and compel her to change, as she promised.”

Here nothing is investigated concerning a lengthy conversion or the duration of probation. The sole command is that if he is proved to have been converted with his wife’s consent and promise, he must by every means be compelled to persevere in the same profession.

But as for what follows—“If none of these things is so, that is, if he was converted neither with his wife’s consent nor with her promise, let him be restored”—this also plainly supports our position. For when the reasons are enumerated on account of which the husband is ordered to be restored to his wife, no mention is found of a lengthy conversion. If that delay of prolonged conversion had been judged by so vigilant a man to possess any importance or force, he would certainly not have passed over it in silence while explaining the other matters. But what he left unmentioned, he commanded by eloquent silence to remain unmentioned.

## CHAPTER VI. What age is required for the consecration of virgins

But although you see such a dense cloud of witnesses set against your inventions that, like a slippery serpent, you are constrained by the strong hand of reason and are utterly unable to turn this way and that, perhaps you still seek a specific explanation concerning those who convert while ill. Yet if you carefully attend to everything said above, it is clear that you are needlessly questioning about the particular case what you are compelled to affirm about the general rule. For if conversion is judged valid not only for all who convert voluntarily but also for those who are compelled, including those who are despised, how could the same judgment not be preserved especially for the sick, who burn with an indescribable longing for this and demand it with great desire?

To say nothing of men, for whom no age prejudices the remedy of conversion and no period of life stands in its way, even virgins—whom it is not permitted to consecrate except on the principal festivals and after twenty-five years of age—may, when seized by illness, be fully consecrated and receive the sacred veil. In seeking testimony for this assertion, blessed Gelasius is the first to come to mind. He says:

> “The sacred veil is likewise not to be placed upon devoted virgins except at the Epiphany, during the white days of Easter, or on the birthdays of the apostles, and not before the age of twenty-five, unless perhaps, as has been said concerning baptism, it is not denied to those seized by grave illness who, fearing that they may depart from the world without this gift, implore it.”

You see, then, that the illness strengthens and excuses even that conversion which good health could have weakened and invalidated. To put it so: where the convert fell, there the conversion recovers its strength.

But if you perhaps accuse me of giving an example concerning women when you were asking about men, I do not want you to be unaware of what is read in the Council of Vernicri:

> “The same law shall apply to man and woman.”

And if you consider carefully what has been said, you will recognize that I did this not from necessity but from weariness, in order to strengthen the force of the argument more fully. Clearly, if we attempted to append all the testimonies of sacred Scripture that are found to agree with this assertion, the days might perhaps fail before the abundant supply of examples did. We have therefore postponed writing more of them precisely because we wish to avoid the tedium of excessive length. Accordingly, we send anyone who still shamelessly demands testimonies back to those assembled above, where the same rule embraces both the sick and the healthy and decrees that those converted not only voluntarily but also under compulsion, and even those persuaded by the schemes of a deceiver, must persevere in the same profession.

## CHAPTER VII. Whether widows may be veiled

The holy Fathers judged the monastic habit worthy of such veneration and such strict guardianship that, in almost whatever manner a person once put it on, he or she afterward had no permission to abandon it. And to establish what we say by testimonies, is it not very often forbidden in the sacred canons that a widow be veiled? To say nothing of the others, Gelasius says:

> “Let no pontiff presume to veil widows. Nevertheless, if she whom a pontiff is forbidden to veil should, under any impulse, place upon herself the sign of the sacred veil, she will no longer dare to remove it without any reconsideration.”

Hence we read in the Council of Orléans:

> “The synod has decreed that widows who, by their own spontaneous will, receive from the altar the veil of sacred conduct should remain in the same profession. For we judge that it is not lawful, after they have once consecrated themselves to the Lord under the veil, to permit them again to lie to the Holy Spirit.”

And again, elsewhere in the same council, after much else:

> “But we, supported by the authority of the Fathers, decree and freely judge in this holy assembly that if a widow has voluntarily placed a veil upon herself, even if it is not a sacred one, and has offered an oblation to God in the church among the veiled women, she must henceforth retain the habit of sanctity, whether she wishes it or not, even if she wishes to confirm by oath that she placed the veil upon herself on the understanding and for the purpose that she might later remove it.”

It is therefore clear that even that conversion which did not proceed lawfully and which ought not to have taken place at all is nevertheless not permitted to be violated after it has occurred, out of reverence for the sacred order. If, then, the holy Fathers strengthen a conversion that has taken place although they themselves forbade it from taking place, what, I ask, should be thought of that conversion to which they urge people by their exhortations and in which they admonish those who have entered it not to cease persevering?

So too, if you disliked a sudden conversion in any way, you could perhaps have objected to those who were converting that their conversion should be delayed, provided that you showed yourself in no respect to differ from the norm of the holy Fathers. But as for those who had converted, far be it from you to teach them to reconsider what has been done irrevocably.

And since the discussion has turned to women, why have we spoken of veiled widows, when even virgins who are not yet covered by any sacred veil are strictly forbidden to marry if they have at least pretended that they would remain in their virginal profession? Concerning them Pope Innocent writes:

> “Those who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always pretended to remain in the virginal profession, even though they were not veiled, are to be recalled if they should happen to marry, and they must perform penance, because their pledge was held by the Lord.”

For if the Apostle said that those who had departed from the profession of widowhood had condemnation because they had invalidated their first faith (1 Tim. V), how much more must this be said of those who have attempted to break their faith? And, following the words of the venerable Innocent’s thoroughly tested authority, if the Apostle declares those women blameworthy who merely dissolved their profession of widowhood, what should be said—what judgment should certainly be pronounced—upon those who abandon the world, cast away their possessions, voluntarily offer themselves to their Creator, submit themselves to another’s authority, and put on the habit of mortification and holiness so that they may appear wholly dead to the world?

That we now speak also of women is by no means, we think, outside the scope of the work undertaken. Apart from the fact that “the same law shall apply to man and woman,” our discussion extends also to the female sex because we fear that the vice which we now see arising improperly among men may at some time spread among women as well. Just as we strive to uproot it in men with the hoe of denunciation, so we forestall it in women, blocking the report of its birth, so that the ill-formed shoot may be compelled to die before it can be born; before it can burst into buds, may it wither within itself.

## CHAPTER VIII. Confirmation of the foregoing arguments

It is now pleasing to lead the mind back for a little to what was said earlier and, setting aside the examples of the Fathers, to debate with our opponent using his own assertions. Thus the man who is confounded by the grave and manifold authority of the canons may also be overcome with reasonable arguments of ours, so that the circle of argument may bind lying lips on every side and compel him forever to fall silent concerning such a perverse doctrine. Then it may rightly be said of us, “We have not raised up the horn of the sinner,” and of him it may rightly be sung with the Psalmist: “For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped” (Ps. LXII).

Come, then: what does this mean—“Unless someone has been put through the regular process and tested for the space of a year, even if he has converted through illness, he has an unrestricted freedom to relapse into the world”? Did the person who made this judgment concerning the healthy nevertheless make the same judgment concerning the sick? But what person, even one of unsound mind, does not see that no sick person, or one already near death, could possibly fulfill this observance? If, then, Saint Benedict included all people together in this sentence, it is plainly evident that he barred the way of conversion to the sick and wholly infirm, who are unable to rise to endure the required period. But who could bear even to suspect this of such a holy man, who not only remained entirely free from this and every plague of heretical perversity, but, filled with the Holy Spirit, was most clearly shown to be so by the testimony of so many signs? Who could endure the claim that he dragged people into despair through the heresy of the Novatians, when through the purity of sacred teaching he appears daily to restore so many human souls to the hope of eternal life? We must therefore acknowledge that the rule of this precept concerns the healthy and in no way applies to the sick.

But if someone, without bodily illness, came to the monastic order without probation, will our bishop nevertheless forbid him to turn back? Tell me, I beg you: have you ever read that the profession of the monastic life is a second baptism? Since it is plainly found in the sayings of the Fathers, it is no longer permissible to deny it. You also know that, by a decree of the ancients, it is again prescribed that longer intervals of time should extend toward the grace of baptism. To touch briefly upon the order of ecclesiastical instruction: just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism, beginning with the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entrance into the Church and continuing to the confirmation of the Holy Spirit through chrism. All these stages, as is more frequently practiced, ought properly to be completed over long intervals of time.

But if someone, setting aside observance of the lengthy intervening period, suddenly rushed forward to the fullness of baptism, would you, I ask, judge this baptism invalid? Would you teach that this person ought to disregard everything he had received and, in order to be saved, hasten again to the mystery of purification? Speak, answer: would you judge that this person could rightly repeat the washing of baptism because he had dared to leap precipitously toward baptism without the prescribed order? Why are you silent? Surely one so eager to speak would not fall silent in this way if he had anything reasonable to answer. But I do not doubt that you will firmly affirm that this baptism too is so valid and binding that whoever is reborn through it would unquestionably commit sacrilege and utter impiety if he were recalled again to the sacrament of the same rebirth.

It follows, then, that what you are compelled to think about the first baptism you must inevitably confess also concerning the second—that is, the monastic institution. And just as the first, once received, cannot in any way be repeated, so the second cannot be despised on any legal ground.

Nevertheless, tell me, I beg you: which saint, which ancient Father, was converted under the probation that you insolently assert? Was it Antony? Was it Paul? Was it Hilarion? Was even Saint Benedict himself—the man whom, as you mistakenly think, appears to prescribe these things—recorded to have reached the monastic order under observance of such a probation? Run through, please, all the histories of truthful antiquity. Since you cannot point to a single person tested over so long an interval, you must confess that you have been completely defeated and rightly lie exposed to the victor’s taunts.

Indeed, how can you pass over all the examples of the ancients and all the deeds of the Fathers with arrogant disdain and, rejecting everything, obstinately bind yourself to the center of a single sentence? For if those men are unquestionably holy, they must necessarily also be imitated. But if they are not to be imitated, they are not holy at all. You see, good litigant, where this learned opinion of yours leads. You are therefore compelled to confess either that our holy Fathers are not holy at all or that those who convert newly have no great need of probation.

Let the frantic tongue, then, be ashamed, and let the tongue that does not know how to be eloquent learn at least to be silent. It does not know how to say anything useful; let it at least know how to keep silent without causing harm. For this perverse speech creeps like cancer; unless it is cut away from one member by the sharpest instrument of correction, there can be no doubt that it will spread pestilentially to the healthy members of the Church.

## CHAPTER IX. Why probation is required of those coming to religious life
But perhaps you will answer these points by saying: “Why, then, is this probation prescribed generally, if it is not also to be observed universally?” And I ask you in turn: tell me, he who commands that someone come to conversion under this probation—where has he also decreed that one who comes in another manner should withdraw from monastic discipline? Since you will be unable to show this at all, it is fitting that you believe the statement was made, on account of wandering and double-minded men, more as a precautionary counsel than as an authoritative command. This is easily recognized if the beginning of the very sentence under discussion is read attentively. For he says (*Rule of St. Benedict*, chap. 58): “Let one who has newly come for conversion not be granted an easy entrance; but, as the Apostle says, ‘Test the spirit, whether it is from God’” (1 John 4).

From these words it is plainly understood that whoever approaches conversion, summoned by the divine Spirit, has no need at all of such a prolonged interval of probation. Remove the double spirit, and the trial immediately ceases. Let that Spirit knock which says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Rev. 1); if he is recognized, no delay is imposed upon him, no probation is required, but the door is opened at once to him who knocks. Indeed, as may be gathered from the apostolic example, the words placed there—“Test the spirit, whether it is from God”—show that this probation is more necessary for the one receiving than for the one coming: namely, so that the receiver may be able to discern by what spirit the person to be received is approaching. Probation is no longer useful where the one to be tested is clearly known. We light a lamp where we do not see what is hidden; but when what was concealed becomes visible, the lamp is immediately extinguished. Thus, where there is uncertainty about the mind of someone and about the spirit by which he is led, it is very necessary that he be tested. But where his conscience has become manifest and clear, the exercise of probation is pointless.

And since, as the author of that same little book of the Rule testifies, nearly all matters of this kind have been placed under the abbot’s judgment and authority, and since anyone who comes to conversion does so in the manner prescribed for him by the abbot, how shamelessly, how thoughtlessly, how senselessly would anyone assert that such a conversion should be judged invalid? Certainly the same Rule commands that the abbot’s table should always be shared with pilgrims and guests. But because, in our time, the religious superiors of monasteries do not do this, in order to restrain the gluttony of some and their luxurious banquets, are they, in your judgment, to be removed from their office? While these men carefully observe the intention of the holy teacher, they think little of following the surface of his words; while they ruminate upon the marrow of the life-giving Spirit, they trample underfoot the chaff of the letter that kills. But just as here you do not forbid the shell of the letters to be set aside for the sake of the flavor of understanding, so concerning a monk’s conversion you must necessarily affirm the same thing in due order.

But since we have raised an impregnable fortification from the squared stones of our arguments, it follows that, at the conclusion of this little work, we should firmly secure it with a kind of syllogistic key. For all who have assumed the habit of the monastic profession have been converted either by their own free choice, or by force, or through the crafty persuasion of deception. Those who were converted willingly either come to the monastery under probation, or, setting aside the difficulty of probation, rush in. But it has already been established above, by the manifold authority of the canons, that all who have been converted willingly, or under compulsion, or even through deception—whether tested or untested—are in every way compelled to persevere in the monastic order they have received, except those who have not obtained the consent and promise of a wife. It must therefore be concluded that all who have assumed the habit of the monastic profession, except those who were converted without their wife’s permission and promise, must in every way be compelled to remain in the order they began, however else they may have come to this purpose.

[Col. 0379A] Behold, as I think, you are surrounded by the testimonies of catholic Fathers and fortified on every side by manifold arguments drawn from evident truth, so tightly constrained that you can oppose nothing whatever to these points, nor in any way renew your former battles. Therefore surrender, and confess that you did not know what you said, and that in every respect you disapprove your own judgment; indeed, gird yourself with every effort of retraction against the things you rashly put forward, so that, with God as your author, you may be able to recall to the path of rectitude those who through you have fallen into error. Let your learned hand turn itself to the battle and wisely strive to stand for those whom it had stubbornly sought to attack, so that it may rightly be said of you, to the praise of God, together with Paul: “Is this not the man who was persecuting in Jerusalem all those who called upon this name?” (Acts 9).

[Col. 0379B] Spare, I beg you, my lips, whoever you are, venerable bishop; and if I have spoken anything harshly against you, if I have poured forth anything of bitter agitation, do not take it as a sign of arrogance, but charitably tolerate it as zeal for justice. For, provided that even one thorn of error can through my efforts be pulled from the forest of holy Church, I do not shrink from provoking the hatred of anyone who thinks wickedly of me. Nor should you be ashamed to correct your error through the rebuke of a younger brother, since you do not fail to remember that the least of the apostles himself withstood the prince of the apostles to his face (Gal. 2). And if perhaps you answer that Paul, although the least, was nevertheless a fellow apostle, whereas I am not a fellow bishop, hear at least what God says to human beings: [Col. 0380A] “Come,” he says, “and rebuke me” (Isa. 1). If God therefore invites human beings to rebuke him, it is entirely fitting that a person corrected by another person should bear the zeal of fraternal charity with equanimity.

## SCHOLIA

If, at any age below maturity, one or both parents have given their children, of either sex, either the tonsure of religious life or the proper religious garment, and, although the children were unwilling or unaware, have not renounced what they had assumed as soon as they saw it, but have allowed those same children to retain such things either in their presence or before the Church and openly in the assembly, then neither they nor their children will ever be permitted to return completely to secular dress. This is the decree of the Tenth Council of Toledo, which the holy teacher wished to cite here as the occasion required.

But although he appears to assert that children offered to monasteries by their parents must, once they have reached the age of discretion, thereafter persevere in them, understand this as arising from the duty of reverence they owe to the parents by whom they were offered.
