For it seems fitting that they should remain in the vocation they have begun, especially since they have already prepared for themselves, as it were, the habit and discipline of religious life. For, strictly speaking, parents cannot compel their children to enter religious life; indeed, children already offered may, when they reach the age of discretion, object if they wish to return to the world: *Decretum*, 10, q. 1, chap. 1, *Cum simus*; *De regularibus*; St. Thomas, *Quodlibet* 3, q. 5, and *Summa theologiae* II-II, q. 189; Cardinal Turrecremata, tractate 123 on the *Rule of St. Benedict*, chap. 59; Sylvester, s.v. “Religio,” q. 10; Council of Trent, session 25, chap. 15 and following. On this same matter see more in St. Bernard, *Letter 1 to Robert, his nephew*.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0379]

### 375–376 — THE SEVENTEENTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE CELIBACY OF PRIESTS. TO NICOLAS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

#### ARGUMENT

That the public licentiousness and wanton freedom of life among ecclesiastical men must be restrained; and that the nobler those who sin are, the more vigorously and freely they must be rebuked, he demonstrates by the outstanding example of Phinehas, who broke apart that knot of fornication. God so highly valued this deed that, among the other gifts bestowed for such a great accomplishment, he chose to reward Phinehas most justly by binding him with the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. By contrast, he warns through the downfall of the priest Eli what happens to negligent rulers who connive at the crimes of their subjects. Finally, inveighing sharply against fornicating priests and bishops, both with powerful arguments and with the authority of Sacred Scripture, he exhorts Nicholas, the supreme pontiff, to restrain those who sin grievously by canonical enforcement, lest, while he is excessively pious and indulgent toward others, he transfer another’s punishment upon himself.

[Col. 0379C] To Lord Nicholas, supreme pontiff, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the obedience due to his subjection.

Recently, when I was conferring with several bishops on the authority of Your Majesty, I wished to fasten bolts upon their holy thighs, so to speak, and attempted to apply the clasps of continence to the genitals of priests. But since this is a cause opposed everywhere, we confidently announce any other command of your constitution in the hope of carrying it out. Yet from them we can scarcely extort even the bare promise of this article, uttered with trembling lips. First, because they despair of being able to reach the summit of chastity; and then because they do not fear being punished by synodal judgment for the vice of lust. In our times a kind of established custom of the Roman Church is observed: with regard to the other concerns of ecclesiastical discipline, examination is undertaken as is fitting, but regarding the lust of clerics, silence is maintained for reasons of expediency, because of the taunts of secular people. This certainly deserves correction, lest precisely where the whole populace complains, the teachers of the Church should remain silent in judgment.

For if this evil were hidden, it might perhaps somehow be endured; but, alas, what a crime! After every sense of shame has been cast aside, this plague has burst forth into such audacity that the places where men fornicate, the names of their concubines, and even the names of their fathers-in-law, mothers-in-law, brothers, and every kind of relative fly through the mouths of the people. And, lest anything seem lacking to these assertions, the circulation of messengers, the lavish distribution of gifts, the jokes of those who laugh, and secret conversations bear witness; finally, when all doubt has been removed, swollen wombs and crying children provide evidence. Thus, to our shame, I do not know how what is shouted publicly throughout the world can be suppressed in a synod—not only so that those who sin may be branded with the infamy they deserve, but also so that those who ought to have been their avengers may themselves appear guilty.

## [ON THE CELIBACY OF PRIESTS]

### CHAPTER I. Phinehas deserved the covenant of an everlasting priesthood because he rose up in zeal for vengeance

Phinehas the priest was not covered by shame, for he seized an Israelite who was coupling with a Midianite woman in the sight of the whole assembly and pierced him through the genitals with a dagger (Num. 25). Yet we, accepting persons in opposition to the divine commandments, pursue the stains of lust among lesser priests, but among bishops—which is utterly absurd—we honor such stains by tolerating them in silence. But behold, when almost the whole Israelite people was falling through fornication with the daughters of Moab and initiating itself into the sacrilegious rites of Baal-peor, Phinehas, inflamed by the zeal of the divine Spirit, did not attack just any despised or lowly person as the defender of the divine law. Rather, he chose the more eminent and distinguished men among the people, whom he might kill in order to terrify the rest, as Scripture testifies when it says: “The name,” it says, “of the Israelite man who was killed with the Midianite woman was Zimri, son of Salu, a leader of a family and tribe of Simeon” (Num. 25).

If the woman’s nobility is asked about, it is found in what follows: “Moreover, the Midianite woman who was killed along with him was called Cozbi, daughter of Zur, a most noble prince of the Midianites” (ibid.). After recounting the history of the fornication and the deserved vengeance, why did Moses need to compose the genealogy of both fornicators and narrate that one was a leader and the other the daughter of a most noble prince, unless to teach that carnal enticements must be pursued more severely in eminent persons?

Hence the Lord himself, when the entire Israelite populace was held liable to the same crime, rose up in the fury of deserved punishment not against the people generally, but against the leaders alone. For in anger he said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them before the sun on gallows, so that my fury may be turned away from Israel” (ibid.). Moses likewise said to the judges of Israel, not to others: “Let each man kill his neighbors who have been initiated into Baal-peor” (ibid.).

Thus, when Phinehas, to avenge the common fornication of the whole multitude, attacked especially those who appeared to be leaders, the divine sentence likewise commanded that the leaders of the people be hanged on gallows; and Moses also commanded not just any lowly men, but the judges of Israel, to kill their neighbors as vengeance for the fornication. What is meant by all these things except that the guilt of adultery must be punished more harshly in persons of greater distinction? And whoever, moved by zeal, avenges such people earns without doubt the peace and favor of the heavenly Judge not only for himself but also for the people.

Hence the divine voice says: “Phinehas,” it says, “turned away my anger from the children of Israel, because he was moved by my zeal against them, so that I did not myself destroy them in my zeal” (ibid.). We have heard how, because of Phinehas’s anger, the Lord’s anger against Israel was appeased; let us now also hear how, through the movement of his spirit, he established perpetual peace for himself with the Lord: “Behold,” he says, “I give him the peace of my covenant, and it shall be a covenant of an everlasting priesthood for him and for his descendants, because he was zealous for his God and made expiation for the crime of the children of Israel” (1 Macc. 2).

The Lord gave him the peace of his covenant because, with every disturbance of the flesh quieted, he appointed him to live until the end of the world in the delights of paradise. For he is, unless I am mistaken, the prophet Elijah, who was taken up into heaven in fiery horses and a chariot while Elisha looked on (2 Kings 2). Whoever thinks that I am lying should rather rebuke Jerome, the interpreter of the divine law, who testifies to this in his book *Hebrew Questions*.

Moreover, it is plainly found that this same Phinehas survived into the time of King David and exercised the priestly office, as Scripture says: “These,” it says, “are the Korahites over the works of ministry, guardians of the vestibules of the tabernacle and of their families, guarding the entrance in shifts of the camps of the Lord. Phinehas, son of Eleazar, was their leader before the Lord” (1 Chron. 9).

[Col. 0382D] The name Phinehas was given to him by his parents, whereas Elijah is an added name arising from an event. For Elijah is interpreted as “The Lord is God,” and it is believed to have been imposed upon him for this reason: when he was carrying out the office of an embassy, he was sent by the Israelite people to the two and a half tribes—namely, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh—which had built an altar of enormous size. They gave him this reply in their defense: “The mighty God, the Lord himself knows whether we built this altar with any intention of transgression” (Josh. 22). From these words of those giving their account, he is said to have been called Elijah, though until then he was called Phinehas, so that their reply appears to have become his name.

It should also be noted that, as the most diligent Bede testifies in his chronicles, from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt until Elijah’s ascent to the summit of heaven, a calculation of six hundred and twenty years is found. Rightly, therefore, the man who suddenly inflicted death upon adulterers was granted a long span of life; and he who on earth was inflamed by the ardor of divine zeal was fittingly raised to heaven by fiery horses.

### CHAPTER II. Eli perished because, in a misguided kindness, he indulged his sinning sons

[Col. 0383A]

By contrast, Eli, because he knew his sons’ sins but did not rebuke them with the sharp reprimand they deserved, fell backward from his seat and died with his neck broken after those same sons had been killed by the Philistines in battle (1 Sam. 4). The ark of the Lord was also captured by the enemies, and first four thousand, then thirty thousand men were struck down by the Philistines.

He did rebuke them, and he did admonish them, but with a father’s gentleness and mildness, not with the severity or authority of a high priest: “Why,” he said, “do you do such things as I hear—such very evil things—from all the people? Do not, my sons; for the report I hear is not good” (ibid. 2). For Scripture testifies that he had heard that they slept with the women who watched at the entrance of the tabernacle (ibid.).

Thus he acknowledged as sons, to his own ruin, those whom he saw to be enemies of God; and those whom he ought to have struck with a hostile sword, he caressed with the gentleness of paternal affection. The faithful servant in the house of the Lord, Moses, the teacher of noble Phinehas, did not act so. Standing at the gate of the camp, he said: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him, and he said to them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his neighbor, and his friend” (Exod. 2).

After twenty-three thousand men had been killed, Moses said: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one in his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (ibid.). Just as those who correct faults are worthy of blessing, so likewise those who flatter sinners are liable to a curse, as it is said through the prophet: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). For he withholds his sword from blood who restrains himself from inflicting upon the reprobate the punishment of the fitting sentence. He is guilty of the deed who neglects to correct what he is able to correct.

Thus the man of God said to the aforementioned Eli, who is also thought to have been Phinehas: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you kick away my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honor your sons more than me?” (1 Sam. 2.) If Eli perished because of merely two sons whom he did not rebuke with the reprimand they deserved, along with them and with such a great multitude of people, what sentence do we suppose is deserved by those who sit in the court of the Church and on the seats of judges, yet remain silent concerning the crimes of wicked people that are not unknown? While they fear publicly disgracing human beings, they bring the commands of the divine law into contempt, to the insult of the heavenly Judge; and while they preserve for ruined men the office of honor they are about to lose, they cruelly dishonor the very author of ecclesiastical dignity.

Hence the divine voice also says to the same Eli, who had despised God by honoring his sons: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in low esteem.” Immediately afterward it adds: “Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house” (1 Sam. 2). It is as if he were saying openly: “Because through the dignity of pastoral office I gave you the arm of strength against my enemies, but you were unwilling to extend it against them for their punishment, now I will cut off your arm from you—that is, I will take away from you the vigor of the priestly summit—so that, although you had been appointed to fight for me, you will now have no hand even with which to defend yourself.”

Let us suppose plainly that Hophni and Phinehas are bishops, while Eli holds the place of a metropolitan. What worse thing can anyone do than to obey lustful bishops when he is able to correct them? Especially since the Lord says to the aforementioned Eli: “I announced to him that I would judge his house forever because of its iniquity, since he knew that his sons were acting disgracefully and did not rebuke them. Therefore I swore concerning the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house would not be expiated by sacrifices or offerings forever” (1 Sam. 3).

If all crimes are washed away by sacrifices and offerings, but false compassion in bishops alone does not obtain pardon, let him who avoids judging their evils consider how severe a sentence he makes himself liable to receive before the strict Judge. But since I do not dare even lightly to reproach the supreme prelate of the universal Church, I shall address briefly the one who sins.

### CHAPTER III. Against a priest devoted to lust

[Col. 0384C]

Why, priest, when you ought to give what is sacred—that is, to offer sacrifice to God—do you first sacrifice yourself as a victim to the evil spirit? For by fornication you cut yourself off from the members of Christ and make yourself a member of a prostitute, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (1 Cor. 6). And again: “Shall I take,” he says, “the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (ibid.) Far from it!

What, then, have you to do with the body of Christ, when through the lust of seductive flesh you have become a member of Antichrist? “What fellowship does light have with darkness, or what partnership does God have with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6.)

Do you not know that the Son of God chose such purity of flesh that he was conceived not even through marital chastity, but rather from a virginal enclosure? And, lest this seem sufficient—that the mother alone was a virgin—the faith of the Church holds that the man who was supposed to be his father was also a virgin. If, therefore, our Redeemer loved the integrity of blossoming chastity so greatly that he was not only born from a virgin’s womb but was also handled by a virgin foster-father, and this while he was still a little child crying in his cradle, by whom, I ask, does he now wish his body to be handled, when he reigns immense in heaven? If, when placed in the manger, he wished to be touched by pure hands, how much purity does he now wish to be present in his body, exalted as he is in the glory of the Father’s majesty?

Plainly, if a father incestuously corrupts his daughter, he is immediately cast out and excluded from the Church, deprived of communion, and either thrust into prison or sent into exile. How much more, then, must you yourself be cast out, since you do not fear perishing with your daughter—not a carnal daughter, which would be the lesser matter, but rather a spiritual one? For all the children of your Church are undoubtedly your children. And it is certainly clear that spiritual generation is greater than carnal generation.

Moreover, since you are the husband and bridegroom of your Church, as is shown by both the ring of betrothal and the staff of office entrusted to you, all who have been reborn in it through the sacrament of baptism are likewise bound to you by the relationship of children. Therefore, when you commit incest with your spiritual daughter, with what conscience do you dare to handle the mystery of the Lord’s body?

But perhaps you object that she was born long before you attained the episcopal dignity, or that she was baptized not in the episcopal city but in some parish—as though you had become the father only of those who were yet to be born, and your entire diocese were not your Church. Indeed, when the Lord says, “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7), what judgment will there be concerning you, who hand over your body—which has been sanctified through the conferral of consecration—not to dogs but to brothels? And since all ecclesiastical orders have been gathered together in you alone in a fearful mass, you defile them all without doubt when you pollute yourself by mingling with a brothel.

Thus you pollute in yourself the doorkeeper, the lector, the exorcist, and all the sacred orders that follow, for all of which you will have to render an account at the strict judgment of God. The Holy Spirit descended at the laying on of your hand, and you apply that hand to the genitals of prostitutes. God obeys your tongue, and you are not afraid to obey demons? Although you are seen conspicuously in ecclesiastical dignity, are you not ashamed to plunge yourself into the brothels of fornicators? And although you have been appointed a preacher of chastity, are you not ashamed to be a slave of lust?

The day will come—indeed, the night—when this lust of yours will be turned into pitch, with which everlasting fire will feed itself unquenchably in your entrails and consume your marrow together with your bones in an unfailing conflagration. Since you burn with the flame of lust, with what face and what audacity do you approach the sacred altars? Do you not know that the sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, were consumed by heavenly fire because they presumed to offer strange fire to the Lord? (Lev. 10; Num. 3.) The altars of the Lord receive not strange fire but only the fire of divine love.

Whoever, therefore, burns with the fires of carnal enticement and does not fear assisting at the sacred mysteries is undoubtedly consumed for the present by that fire of divine vengeance of which Scripture testifies: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Heb. 10). Just as he is now boiled in the flame of burning lust, so afterward he must be burned in the never-ending fires of the terrible Gehenna.

Moreover, unhappy bishop, are you not terrified that, by falling into the abyss of lust, you have incurred the heresy of the Nicolaitans? For Nicolaus, one of those whom the apostle Peter had consecrated as deacons, taught that clerics of every order should be bound in marital unions. What he taught in words, you, sitting in the seat of pestilence, invite people to do much more grievously by your example. Concerning this crime the divine voice says to the angel of the church of Ephesus: “You hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (Rev. 2).

And since the Apostle says, “No fornicator has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5), if you have no inheritance whatsoever in the kingdom of God—that is, in heaven—how do you obtain the dignity of preeminence in the Church, which is likewise the kingdom of God?

### CHAPTER IV. Exhortation to the supreme pontiff to exercise canonical authority against fornicating bishops

[Col. 0386B]

But you, my lord, venerable pope, who act in Christ’s place and succeed the supreme Shepherd in apostolic dignity, do not, through negligence, allow this plague to increase. Do not loosen the reins of rampant lust by conniving and dissembling. For this disease creeps like cancer, and its poisonous offspring stretches to infinity unless what grows evilly is cut away with the evangelical sickle.

Therefore, far be it from you that the sluggish torpor of an indulgent Eli should soften your holy heart; rather, let the zeal of noble Phinehas inflame you to avenge the crime. Let those who do not fear defiling the purity of ecclesiastical chastity be deposed, and, once cast down, let them deter those whom, while standing wickedly, they were provoking to the dishonor of shameful lust.

Let canonical authority therefore rise up for vengeance and restrain the crimes of wanton clerics, so that—God forbid—no stain of infamy may touch Your Beatitude and the customary brilliance of ecclesiastical discipline may shine forth. Your clemency does not fail to know that King Ahab of Israel, when he spared Ben-hadad, king of the Assyrians, with an ill-ordered compassion, provoked the sentence of divine anger against himself. To him the man of God said: “Thus says the Lord: Because you have released from your hand a man deserving death, your life shall be for his life and your people for his people” (1 Kings 20).

This same man of God, when he said to his companion, “Strike me at the word of the Lord,” and the man was unwilling to strike him, said: “Because you were unwilling to hear the voice of the Lord, behold, you will depart from me, and a lion will strike you” (ibid.). And when he had withdrawn from him a little, as Scripture testifies, a lion found him and struck him.

What else, then, is indicated by these words of sacred eloquence except that disordered compassion certainly deserves the anger of God, when it does not proclaim a sentence against the guilty according to the equity of strict justice? Rightly must the vengeance of the heavenly Judge overtake the one who has neglected to exercise discipline upon his subjects; and rightly is he handed over to that lion who goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5), because through the sluggishness of his torpor he restrains himself from inflicting the wound of repentance.

Thus let your noble spirit earnestly gird itself to remove the reproach of chastity; thus let it rise up vigorously and courageously to avenge the Nicolaitan heresy, so that, according to the promise made to Phinehas, almighty God may establish with you the peace of his covenant; indeed, just as Elijah, after symbolically slaughtering four hundred and fifty priests (1 Kings 18), may he bring you into heaven accompanied not by fiery horses but by angels.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0387]

### 383–384 — THE EIGHTEENTH LITTLE WORK: AGAINST INTEMPERATE CLERICS

A composition drawn from three other treatises of blessed Damian on the same subject.

## FIRST TREATISE

[Col. 0387B]

### ARGUMENT

To Peter, a distinguished cardinal, he adds, as they say, spurs to his running, when in a lengthy discourse he inveighs against the shameless life of clerics and exhorts him to undertake a thought worthy of his virtue: namely, that their intemperance must be opposed with all strength, so that it may, if possible, be restrained by some means. By the example of Phinehas and Moses he shows how pleasing this deed will be to God. He also furnishes him with many arguments and reasons, so that he may both defend chastity and destroy the lust of clerics through his speech.

To Lord Peter, archpriest of the Lateran canonry, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the bond of fraternal charity.

A missile is as powerful as the strength of the warrior. For however carefully it may be polished and sharpened, if the arm of the one who wields it grows weak, it does not carry away the spoils of a distinguished victory. But when the warrior is vigorous, triumph is sometimes won over enemies even with a blunt sword. Goliath, armed with a magnificent sword, not only lost his life but fell after being struck down (1 Sam. 17). Samson likewise killed a thousand Philistines with the worthless jawbone of a donkey (Judg. 15).

Hence, when Jether, Gideon’s firstborn, had been afraid to draw his sword, the kings Zebah and Zalmunna of Midian said to Gideon: “Rise yourself and fall upon us, for a man’s strength corresponds to his age” (ibid.). Therefore, since I am forging a hammer-like missile against the lust of clerics, I place it in no hands more suitably than yours. For I have always seen you burn inwardly with such zeal against their ruined morals that you might be judged not to need the fire of Phinehas or Elijah; so much so that they fear the reproach of your criticism more than they fear even a papal decree. For, like an outstanding dog guarding a royal palace, you attack nocturnal thieves with loud barking and seize them with your teeth, lest they burn the royal palace with the torches of their lust.

## [FIRST TREATISE]

### CHAPTER I. Why clerics ought to be chaste

You are not unaware that such a strict and rigorous rule of chastity is imposed upon priests, deacons, and subdeacons that, by the unanimous judgment of all catholic Fathers, they are completely cut off from contracting marriages. And it is entirely reasonable that, after bishops, the snow-white radiance of chastity should also flourish in these three orders, since they approach the sacred mysteries more familiarly. For because the Lord’s body was formed in the temple of a virginal womb, it now also seeks from its ministers the purity of continently chaste living.

Plainly, just as no male seed flowed into the conceiving divine Virgin, but the power of the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, so now the sacrament placed upon the altar is enlivened by that same power of the Holy Spirit; and it is necessary that a chaste and undefiled hand touch it. But since we have already discussed this theme at greater length elsewhere, first writing individually to Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, then to the bishop of Turin, and finally also to Countess Adelaide, assembling various examples from Scripture, I refer you, venerable brother, to those works and clothe you in them as in military armor; and I urge you to strive, like another Joshua, to overthrow the city of Jericho.

It remains, therefore, that I myself briefly attack those same clerics, so that what is kept in the furnace of the breast may escape through lips as through open cracks.

I address you, panders, wife-ridden men, and servants subject to the domination of women: why do you confound the laws of canonical sanction and violate the rule of ecclesiastical purity established by the holy Fathers? Shame upon you! You submit your necks to the laws of your lust and trample underfoot the decrees of the Holy Spirit proclaimed through the mouths of teachers.

Behold, through you the labor of the apostles is overturned, and the building founded by the teachers of the Church is plainly buried because you attack it. Thus it comes about that the law of the Church, which the clerical order is recognized to have established, is again destroyed in the opposite direction by that same order.

Amnon and Absalom were brothers, begotten by one father, but one destroyed the other (2 Sam. 3). Cain slaughtered Abel (Gen. 4)—the wicked, namely, the just. Often also the illegitimate kills the legitimate, as, according to Crispus, Jugurtha killed Hiempsal and Adherbal (Sallust, *The Jugurthine War*). In a certain sense illegitimate brothers kill legitimate brothers when those who profess to be clerics in name alone destroy the judgments of the holy Fathers. They seem to extinguish the very men whose sentences they do not fear to annul.

Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal, appears aptly to signify such men; Scripture reports that he was born from the concubine whom Jerubbaal had in Shechem (Judg. 9). He killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal—seventy men upon one stone. What, then, is signified by the seventy men except the scale of the Church’s preachers? Concerning them the evangelist Luke says: “The Lord also appointed seventy and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come” (Luke 10).

This order of preachers was also already symbolized in those concerning whom the Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people, and their teachers; and you shall lead them to the entrance of the tent of meeting” (Num. XI). That same mystical number is unquestionably recognized as applying to preachers when the Israelite people are said to have camped at Elim (Exod. XV), where there were twelve springs and seventy [Col. 0389B] palm trees. What, then, are the twelve springs unless they signify the holy apostles, who never cease to irrigate the aridity of the human heart with the streams of holy preaching? What, moreover, are the seventy palms unless priests of the lower rank are to be understood, those appointed throughout the world to proclaim the victories of Christ? The palm, after all, customarily crowns victors; and the number ten is reckoned sevenfold in them, because the Decalogue must be fulfilled through the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit.

Nor should it be passed over that, before that people came to Elim, it had camped the previous day at Marah (ibid.). There, since the water was so bitter that it could not be drunk, the wood that God pointed out was cast into it, and immediately it became sweet. [Col. 0389C] People shuddered to drink the deadly letter of the old law, which no one was able to fulfill, as though they were recoiling from salty waters because of their bitterness. But when the wood of the cross is applied to these waters, when the sequence of the Lord’s Passion is brought to bear, the sacrament of spiritual understanding is at once drunk with sweetness. Thus the people came from Marah to Elim: they rejected the horror of the bitter letter and rejoiced to hasten toward the sweetness of the apostolic springs and the fruits of the palms. Casting off legal servitude, they sought the sweet freedom of evangelical grace.

## CHAPTER II — Luxurious Clerics Compared with Abimelech

To return, then, to what we began: since the seventy men whom Abimelech killed signify the preachers of the Church, what are we to understand by Abimelech himself, who was their brother but a bastard, except luxurious and carnal clerics? Through the ecclesiastical order they have indeed become brothers of the catholic and holy bishops, yet through the degeneracy of their lives and the depravity of their ignoble deeds they are judged bastards. They kill their brothers when they destroy the judgments of the holy Fathers, when by living perversely they corrupt their decrees and ordinances. And this killing takes place upon one stone.

This stone is the Savior’s Church, of which it is said through Zechariah: “Behold, I will bring my servant the Orient, for behold, the stone that I have set before Jesus: upon one stone are seven eyes” [Col. 0390A] (Zech. III). This stone is most appropriately called one in both places, so that the unity of the Church may be commended. Concerning it the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, the only one of her mother” (Song VI).

What, then, are the seven eyes upon the one stone—apart, nevertheless, from any higher mystery, if such there is—except those seventy men, that is, holy teachers joined together in the unity of ecclesiastical peace and illumined by the charisms of the sevenfold Holy Spirit? Through these eyes the holy Church sees; through them she perceives where to place the foot of right action, so that, walking along the way of God’s commandments, she may not depart from the rule of uprightness.

Abimelech, therefore, a *manzer* and bastard, kills seventy legitimate brothers upon one stone when [the first] part of the clergy, degenerating from the nobility of ecclesiastical chastity, subjects itself obscenely to the laws of lust. While judging the sacred canons worthy of rejection, it slays their authors—holy men and therefore noble, the sons of Gideon, that is, of the Savior and the Church—with a kind of impious cruelty. For they have adulterated canons and certain novel quibbles of argument with which to attack them.

This is also signified in the siege of the tower of the Shechemites, when the narrative says of the same fratricide: “Abimelech, hearing that the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together, went up Mount Zalmon with all his people, and, having seized an axe, cut down a branch from a tree, carried it on his shoulder, and said to his companions: ‘What you see me doing, do quickly’” (Judg. [Col. 0390C] IX). Then it continues: “Therefore, cutting branches from the trees in rivalry with one another, they followed their leader; surrounding the stronghold with them, they set it on fire. Thus it happened that, through smoke and fire, about a thousand people, men and women alike, the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem, were killed” (ibid.).

It is not the place here to expound diligently the sacred figures contained in this history; for our purpose, it is enough to offer a brief preliminary treatment of the matter. The branches of the trees are brief statements from Scripture. When the lustful violently bend them to strengthen their own arguments, they extinguish numerous crowds of people with smoke and fire alike: with the smoke of error and the fire of desire, so that the flame of lust may set deceived minds of learners ablaze and the darkness of false doctrine may confuse them. These are the wares that were seen to emerge from Sodom and Gomorrah after their destruction: “Abraham,” Scripture says (Gen. XIX), “rising in the morning, where he had stood previously with the Lord, looked upon Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of that region, and saw smoke rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace.”

Moreover, when he besieged the town of Thebez with his forces, Abimelech appears to have represented the same conflict against chastity. “There was,” as Scripture testifies, “a lofty tower in the middle of the city, to which men and women together, and all the leaders of the city, had fled; its door was most securely closed, and they stood upon the roof of the tower behind its battlements” (Judg. IX). The city is the universal Church; the tower is the eminence of chastity. To it men and women had fled—that is, the strong and the weak—and also the leaders of the city, namely, the order of clerics, which holds primacy in the Church. Approaching the tower, Abimelech began to fight fiercely, and, drawing near the entrance, he tried to set it on fire.

## CHAPTER III — How Harmful the Intemperance of Clerics Is

In this way, then, impudent and undisciplined clerics attempt to set the tower of chastity ablaze, when they urge many to follow the example of their own lust and burning madness. Armed with fires, they attack the tower of chastity when they inflame the chaste with the destructive flame of their persuasion to incest. But what end is imposed upon this struggle? [Col. 0391B] What titles of victory does this battle win?

“Behold,” it says, “a woman cast down a fragment of a millstone from above, struck Abimelech on the head, and shattered his brain. He immediately called his armor-bearer and said to him: ‘Draw your sword and strike me, lest it perhaps be said that I was killed by a woman.’ And he, carrying out the order, killed him” (Judg. IX).

To avoid lingering over these words, this fragment of a millstone, which shattered Abimelech’s brain, is nothing other than that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. II), namely the Lord himself, who says of himself in the Gospel: “Whoever falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matt. XXI). The woman from whose hands it is thrown is the sacred law, which threatens the contemptuous violators of chastity with the sudden judgment of Christ. Concerning this it is said through Jeremiah: “Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer crushing a rock?” [Col. 0391C] (Jer. III.)

Abimelech’s armor-bearer is the devil, who supplies all who attack the tower of chastity with the weapons of lust and the sharp darts of luxury. Concerning these darts the Apostle says: “In all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one” (Eph. VI). And the prophet says: “There is Asshur with his weapons” (Ezek. XXXII). The woman struck him with the millstone fragment, but the armor-bearer killed him with the sword, because the devil slaughters with eternal death those adversaries of chastity against whom sacred Scripture directs the judgment of divine punishment. Thus the one who had been their assistant in battle becomes afterward their torturer in punishment, and the weapons he had supplied them against modesty are then, in accordance with their deserts, turned against their throats.

Let soft and incestuous clerics, degenerate from the native nobility of their order, now go forth; let them seize Abimelech’s weapons, kill legitimate brothers upon one stone, and strive to storm the tower of Thebes, that is, the fortress of chastity. Yet all their conflict ends in this: after the blow of the stone, they too are killed by the sword of their armor-bearer. Those who had extinguished their brothers with the sword upon the stone are crushed by the stone, so that they do not escape the sword: first, the weight of the divine sentence crushes them, and then the punitive blade of the evil spirit cuts them down.

Nevertheless, we do not overlook that Jerobaal may not unreasonably signify Christ and Abimelech the Antichrist. Just as the former is the son of a concubine, so the latter is the son of the rejected synagogue. By the seventy brothers whom Abimelech is said to have killed may be signified the nations of the seventy languages whom the Antichrist persecutes at the end of the age. But let us continue, as we began, to pursue the madness of the clerics.

These men, like the sons of Jacob, are indeed adorned with the title of paternal descent; but because they are bastards and degenerate, they derive their origin not legitimately from wives but rather ignobly, as though from concubines. [Col. 0392B] For as Scripture says: “Bastard shoots shall not strike deep roots” (Wis. IV). They are shown to be not the sons of Leah or Rachel, but rather of the maidservants Bilhah and Zilpah, through the servile labor of a sordid way of life.

Bilhah is interpreted as “aged” or “grown old.” By living carnally, these men testify that they proceed not from the newness of the spirit but from the seed of the carnal old man. Zilpah, however, in our language means “gaping mouth.” She is rightly called the mother of those whose mouth appears to go forth in preaching the truth, while their heart does not go forth; concerning them it is written: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

The Apostle also reproaches them as though addressing them personally: “You, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Rom. II).

For while they uphold the word of God with their lips, they tear it down by living reprehensibly. In speech they appear to descend from the most illustrious nobility of the patriarchs; in life they are proved to be propagated from the infamous line of a foul brothel. Abraham fathered one son from his wife and several from concubines, but while he was still alive he separated them far from himself. Those who served as offspring of a maidservant could not become coheirs with their brother. What, then, does Scripture say? “Abraham gave everything he possessed to Isaac; but to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts” (Gen. XXIII).

While Abraham was still alive, all of them boasted that they were Abraham’s sons; but when he bestowed the whole inheritance upon one, he clearly distinguished who truly possessed the name of son and who were marked by the disgrace of concubinage. Thus bastard clerics now appear to move about indiscriminately among Abraham’s legitimate sons, but afterward they are excluded from sharing the inheritance—those who meanwhile delight in women as though they were gifts received from their father.

## CHAPTER IV — The Clerics’ Perverse Objections and Their Refutation

But they say: Does the Apostle not say, “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (I Cor. VII)? “Behold,” they say, “these apostolic words are general; and since they grant everyone permission to marry, they do not appear to exclude us.”

To this I answer: If these words indiscriminately loosen the reins of conjugal incontinence, let the same freedom not be denied to bishops, monks, or even abbots. And since both sexes are bound by no different law, let holy virgins also be invited to enter into the bonds of conjugal intercourse. But what ears, worn smooth by ecclesiastical teaching, could endure this calmly without immediately recoiling in terror from such monstrous sacrilege?

Yet when some are questioned on this matter, they immediately take refuge in a defense of poverty, using it to set before themselves a shield of frivolous excuse: “We cannot do without the help of feminine diligence,” they say, “because we suffer from poverty in our household resources.”

To them we reply, conversely, that where provisions are scarcer, there a smaller household must be maintained; and a table not burdened with food should not be approached by more guests. Therefore poverty, in its need, must teach them to renounce the company of women and prevent them from begetting flocks of ravenous eaters and little children.

Yet with what audacity of mind do they not tremble to approach the divine mysteries, when David, before touching the bread of the Presence, reverently declares that he and his men have been clean for three days from contact with women? The priest Abimelech had said to him: “I have no ordinary bread, but only holy bread. If the young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat” (I Sam. XXI).

Here it should be noted that, when he says that those who were compelled to eat the holy bread must be especially clean from women, he plainly teaches that no contagion of guilt, no guilt whatever, is so contrary to the divine mysteries as illicit intercourse with women. If such great fear existed among the ancients even of the shadow of the Lord’s body, how much reverence is now owed to the reality itself? And if conjugal relations were restrained from approaching that bread, how much more must concubinage be kept away from this most holy mystery?

Ah, the crime! Hands appointed to arrange upon the heavenly table the life-giving food of angels do not fear handling the obscenities and filthy contamination of women. Those who are admitted among angelic choirs amid those dread sacraments immediately fall, as though tumbling from heaven, back into the embraces of feminine foulness; like unclean swine, they plunge into the muddy wallows of lust that breed worms. “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” (Isa. LXVI).

Heaven is opened; the highest and the lowest converge together as one; yet no one fears to thrust himself boldly into filth. The angelic powers stand trembling; divine power descends among the hands of those offering; the gift of the Holy Spirit flows in; that pontiff whom the angels adore does not withdraw from the sacrifice of his body and blood—and the man whom the fever of hellish lust inflames does not tremble to be present there.

If the man who was not clothed in wedding garments, bound hand and foot, is cast into the darkness of punishment (Matt. XXII), what may be expected for the man admitted to the heavenly banquet who is not conspicuous for the beauty of spiritual clothing but actually reeks, covered in the filth of sordid lust? If that man is punished with the gnashing of teeth and the weeping of eyes because he does not delight the eyes of the banqueters by the adornment of his clothing, what judgment awaits the man who, foul and stained, pollutes the purity of the nuptial feast as far as he is concerned, offends those reclining at table, and presumes to touch the King himself with filthy hands?

The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram when they quarreled against Moses and Aaron (Num. XVI). Korah, for this same reason, was consumed with two hundred and fifty men by a sudden blaze of fire descending from heaven. How, then, will this man live, who has offended not a human being but the Author of human beings—and offended him so bloodily and disgracefully?

Such clerics plainly send a message to the Lord, not with the clamor of words but with the tongues of their deeds and the intention of their vows: “We do not want this man to reign over us.” Concerning them he will later say: “Nevertheless, bring here my enemies, those who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me” (Luke XIX).

They delight in having Pharaoh’s power rule over themselves and refuse to have the God of Israel reign over them (Exod. I). But he overwhelms them with mud and bricks, because he compels them to labor amid muddy and filthy works. To these works are also mixed straw—that is, useless and unproductive actions, destined for unquenchable flames.

## CHAPTER V — Examples from Sacred Scripture Are Cited

The prophetic linen loincloth also most fittingly applies to these men, concerning which Jeremiah says: “The Lord said to me: ‘Go and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth, and place it upon your loins’” (Jer. XIII). A little later he says: “Arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a crevice of the rock.” When he had done this and hidden it in the Euphrates as he had been commanded, after many days the Lord said to him: “Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take the loincloth from there.” “And I went,” he says, “to the Euphrates and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, it had rotted, so that it was fit for no use.” And the Lord said: “So will I make the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem rot—this exceedingly wicked people who refuse to hear my words and walk in the perversity of their heart. And they will be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use” (ibid.).

What does the person of Jeremiah signify here except the Lord? What does the loincloth signify except the order of clerics? The whole Church is Christ’s garment, of whose members it is said through the prophet: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX). But just as the loincloth is close to the human body and adheres to it more tightly than the other garments, so the clerical order is joined more familiarly to divine service than other people are. As it says there concerning the Israelite people: “For as the loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I bound the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah to myself, says the Lord, that they might be my people, my name, my praise, and my glory; but they did not listen” (Jer. XIII).

To whom, I ask, can these words apply so aptly and explicitly as to clerics, who have been specially appointed to proclaim the name, praise, and glory of God? Just as Israel and Judah were God’s special people among all the nations of the earth, so clerics now adhere specially to Christ above all the members of the Church. These are the linen loincloth joined to the divine body by a closer familiarity. Linen reaches whiteness only through labor; and clerics, sometimes toiling over literary studies and sometimes ascending through certain degrees over intervals of time, are promoted with difficulty to the dignity of the sacred order.

Otherwise, if someone argues contentiously that this happened historically according to the sequence of Scripture and is not to be understood spiritually, how could Jeremiah, amid the innumerable nations of the Assyrians and Chaldeans besieging Jerusalem with massed forces, go out wearing a loincloth, hide it in the Euphrates, which flows so far away, and afterward, once a long period had passed, return almost safely and find it rotten, as Scripture testifies? Jerusalem was surrounded by a ditch, a rampart, fortresses, and such frequent defenses on every side. For when that same prophet once tried to leave for his village of Anathoth, situated three miles from the city, he was immediately seized at the gate, dragged before the authorities, severely beaten, and thrust into prison as a deserter or traitor to his country.

Since, therefore, it does not follow that this should be understood historically, there is no doubt that the mystery of a typological figure is present. Accordingly, in keeping with what has been said above, the choir of clerics is well expressed by the linen loincloth.

But what is signified by the command that this loincloth be placed in the Euphrates—that is, in a watery place—and in a crevice of the rock, that is, in darkness and shadow, except that part of the clerics which dwells beneath the shadow of pleasure and in the flood of lust? Concerning their leader the Lord says in the Book of Job: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secret place of the reed and in moist places. The shades cover his shadow; the willows of the torrent surround him” (Job XL). And to show how much he delights, together with his companions, in dwelling in the river, he immediately added: “Behold, he will absorb the river and will not wonder; for he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (ibid.).

As for the statement that it was placed in a crevice of the rock, this may suitably be understood as referring to the enclosure of the Church. Clerics are shut up, as it were, in a crevice of the rock when they are commanded to keep constant and diligent watch over their ministries within the thresholds of the Church.

The loincloth placed in a moist place rotted, because the prophet testifies concerning those who linger amid the streams of lust: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). Beasts rot in their dung when carnal and filthy people end their lives in the stench of lust. It was also found fit for no use, because the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

It is as though he openly says: Whoever, instructed by the rule of his order, once takes hold of the plow of chastity, but afterward, through the heat of lust, turns his eyes back toward Sodom—because he has now despaired of the mountains—shows that he has become wholly useless for the kingdom of God.

Thus, like the loincloth placed in a moist place, clerics rot when they stuff their swollen bellies with gluttony and drunkenness, when they flood themselves with the filth of lust and the muddy streams of luxury. In this way they become useless for every purpose, because the more they appear to flourish in the flesh, the more wretchedly they wither and grow obsolete in the foulness of their squalid soul. Concerning them the Psalm says: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pleasures” (Ps. XIII).

## CHAPTER VI — An Exhortation to Cardinal Peter

But you, venerable brother, armed with these and other weapons of Scripture, engage the camp of Midian; pierce Zimri and Cozbi, shamefully joining together in their place of intercourse, with the dagger of the divine word, so that with Phinehas you may deserve to receive the peace of the Lord’s covenant and the right of an everlasting priesthood: “Behold,” says the Lord, “I give him the peace of my covenant, and it shall be a covenant of an everlasting priesthood for him and for his offspring, because he was zealous for his God and made expiation for the crime of the children of Israel” (Num. XXV).

Let human hostility, therefore, not be feared when it is repaid by the peace of the divine covenant. For because Moses struck the Egyptian, he immediately lost Egypt as an exile; afterward, as though with interest increased, he obtained authority over the whole Israelite people: “For,” as Scripture testifies, “he saw an Egyptian striking one of his brothers; and when he had struck him, he hid him in the sand” (Exod. II).

You also, when you see an Egyptian—that is, the prince of darkness—striking one of your brothers, namely, someone of the clerical order, with the rod of lust, or rather, in a more fitting sense, slaughtering him with a deadly dart, immediately brandish the sword of the word and thrust yourself into the blow of the wound; kill the man who was punishing one of your own household, “reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine” (II Tim. IV).

But since, as the same Apostle testifies, “there will be some who will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables” (ibid.), do not cease, but do what follows: “But you,” he says, “be watchful in all things, labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry” (ibid.; the transmitted text reads *impie*).

Attract, then, those whom you can; but leave the contumacious and those rebelliously obstinate in mind amid the foulness of their obscenity. This is to bury the Egyptian in the sand. Sand is a loose and fragile earth, unable to hold the foundation of a rising building. Therefore the Church, which will never fall, is founded not upon sand but perpetually upon rock: “Upon this rock,” the Lord says, “I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

Those who are firm and steadfast in good works place their foundation upon the rock of the Church. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they beat against that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock” (Matt. VII).

But those who are fragile and dust-like, shaken like a reed by the blasts of carnal allurements (Luke VII), are unquestionably to be compared with the loose sand of the wasteland. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Not so the wicked, not so; but they are like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. I). And the Lord says: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they beat against that house; it fell, and its ruin was great” (Matt. VII).

Hence also in the Book of Kings: “All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of bronze, and the king cast them in the clayey ground of the plain of the Jordan” (III Kings VII). Since these vessels signify carnal people, they are said to have been formed not from gold but rather from bronze; and therefore they are cast not in the mountains but in the plain, because those represented by them do not climb the mountains of virtues but sink into the valley of carnal and luxurious life.

Nor are they wrought vessels but rather cast vessels, because they are not stretched out by the hammers of the cross and repentance; instead, they are loosened by the allurements of lust and dissolved by the flowing excesses of the most obscene pleasure. Therefore, just as the loincloth is placed in the Euphrates, so these vessels are described as cast beside the Jordan—not in solid and firm earth capable of holding the foundation laid upon it, but rather in clayey and sandy soil, which produces sudden collapse.

You, therefore, venerable brother, together with Moses, kill the Egyptian who strikes your brother, with the zeal of rigorous correction (Exod. II), and hide him as though in sand, in sandy minds, so that, dead, he may fill the clayey burial place of earthly minds and there give birth to the worms of desire. Thus may he cease to strike those who are truly Israelites with the lashes of their temptations.

It did not happen by chance that the Lord, the head of the elect, is buried in a rocky tomb, while the Egyptian, who signifies the devil, is buried in sand. The devil, whose name means “flowing downward,” claims for himself those who continually fall apart like sand toward ruin. But those who belong to Christ persist steadfastly in the solidity of their holy purpose.

A tomb, however, is the house of the dead. And because the devil is dead, being separated from God, who is true life, he unquestionably makes every mind he inhabits into a tomb. Hence the prophet says: “There is Asshur, and his graves” (Ezek. XXXII).

Let the Egyptian, then, struck by the blade of your sacred eloquence, perish, and let the burial place of sand enclose him, so that the Israelite people, with Pharaoh drowned and the standard of chastity going before them, may ascend with triumphant hymns to the promised land.

# SECOND DISSERTATION: AGAINST THE INTEMPERANCE OF CLERICS

## ARGUMENT

A man who was the most vigorous champion of ecclesiastical discipline, then almost collapsing, and the most holy lover and cultivator of chastity, attempts, with highly eloquent speech like a kind of trumpet call, to rouse and inflame nearly the whole world to defend and support chastity, which was being attacked by clerics.

For he writes to Cunibert, bishop of Turin, in whose jurisdiction he knew that the crime of so pernicious an example was being publicly tolerated, urging him to eradicate and remove this scandal from his Church. To persuade him of this, he leaves nothing unattempted. He gathers and examines every example and passage from both the New and the Old Testament. He also inveighs against the clerics themselves and against their mistresses, whom they falsely called wives, lucidly and gravely, as the matter required. In short, to sum it up in one word, he leaves no opportunity for it to appear that chastity lacked a champion.

To Cunibert, most reverend bishop, Peter, sinful monk, offers the service of devoted submission.

This is the rule of true charity and friendship: brothers should cherish one another with mutual affection in such a way that, if anything reprehensible exists in either, one does not conceal it from the other. That relationship is proved useful and honorable which, while bringing everything into the open, both corrects what must be corrected and preserves what is sound through mutual love of purity and sincerity. Thus, when the fault of the offender is corrected, more abundant grace is heaped upon the corrector.

Among the many flowers of virtue, venerable Father, with which the character of your holiness blooms, one, I confess, displeased me greatly. It both stirred me strongly against you then and now compels me to write this passage of my pen. You permit the clerics of your Church, whatever their rank, to be joined to wives as though by the right of marriage.

That this is obscene in the judgment of ecclesiastical purity, contrary to canonical authority, and certainly hateful to all the ordinances of the holy Fathers, your great prudence—such as is in you—must not be unaware. Especially since your clerics themselves, otherwise sufficiently honorable, are also decently instructed in literary studies. When they flocked to me, they appeared like an angelic choir and like the conspicuous senate of the Church.

## [DISSERTATION II]

## CHAPTER I — He Urges the Fallen Ecclesiastical Discipline and Chastity to Be Restored

After I learned of the hidden flood of this plague, light immediately turned for me into darkness and joy into sorrow, and my mind at once returned to that Gospel saying: “Woe to you,” he says, “scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of filth” (Matt. XXV).

What is this, Father? You keep watch over yourself alone, yet sleep with such sluggish security regarding those for whom you will first have to render an account? In all other persons whatever, the fruitfulness of chastity is not required; but in a bishop, chastity is rightly judged useless if it presents itself as sterile, so that it does not produce another chastity.

Especially since almighty God himself says through Isaiah: “Will I, who cause others to give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord” (Isa. LXVI). Here it should be noted that, since he says not “I cause women to give birth” (*alias parere facio*), but “I cause men to give birth” (*alios parere facio*), he expects the offspring of men and pastors of the Church.

A bad shepherd may lamentingly sing with the same prophet: “I have not labored in childbirth, nor given birth, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins to maturity” (Isa. XXIII).

Consider also carefully what is read in Leviticus: “Every animal that has its testicles crushed, bruised, cut, or removed, you shall not offer to the Lord” (Lev. XXII).

If, then, God so greatly hates sterility in brute animals that are offered to him through priestly ministry, how much more does he reject it in priests who offer sacrifice to him? Certainly, just as offspring of the flesh is required of those animals, so priests must cause shoots of holiness to grow in others.

Your chastity is approved before the divine gaze, then, if it extends and propagates itself into your clerics. Moreover, just as almighty God once chose the Levites from all the tribes so that through legal ceremonies they might govern the Israelite people, so in the New Testament he adopted clerics for himself as familiars, [Col. 0399C] to whom he might entrust ecclesiastical dignity.

For he says to Moses: “Bring the Levites before the tent of meeting, summoning the whole assembly of the children of Israel. When the Levites have been brought before the Lord, the children of Israel shall place their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the Levites as a gift before the Lord from the children of Israel, so that they may serve in his ministry” (Num. VIII).

Here it should be noted that, when he says, “The children of Israel shall place their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the Levites as a gift before the Lord from the children of Israel,” it clearly appears that the Levitical order is God’s gift, given by the people and offered to him as a sacrifice through the priest’s hand.

## CHAPTER II — Why Clerics Are Separated from the People
What, then, remains except that those who have already become a sacrifice to God should be free from the servile works of this world and devote themselves solely to the duties of divine service? For why are they separated from the people and made a special offering to God, unless it is so that they may follow a rule of life distinct from that of the people and persist continually in vigilant observance of the ceremonies of divine law?

Thus elsewhere he says: “I have taken the Levites from the children of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine” (Num. III). But since that law was given through a servant, whereas evangelical grace has been conferred through the Lord, it is necessary that one thing then be required of the Levites of the Synagogue and another now of the clergy of the Church.

For the former, in keeping with the character of the time, were permitted the rights of marriage; but the latter are commanded to be entirely removed from the embraces of carnal affection. Since at that time only the tribe of Levi had been chosen for priestly service, the propagation of offspring was necessary for preserving the office of priestly dignity, as the Lord says in Leviticus: “The priest,” he says, “shall take a virgin as his wife; he shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, lest he mingle the stock of his family with the common people of his nation; for I am the Lord who sanctifies him” (Lev. XXI).

But now, since the priesthood is freely chosen from the whole Christian people, and in the promotion of clergy it is not distinction of birth but solely the privilege of holiness that is sought, the rights of marriage cease, since the censure of the earlier command has been abolished, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “There is a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness; for the law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebr. VII). And shortly afterward: “But now Christ has obtained a ministry so much better, as he is also mediator of a better covenant. For if that first covenant had been without fault, there would certainly have been no search for a second” (Hebr. VIII).

This is directed against those who say that, if it were a sin for priests to marry, the Lord would never have commanded it in the old law. But those who say this undoubtedly either do not know what canonical authority decrees, or deceitfully pretend not to know it.

We, at any rate—all of us, naturally, who are ministers of the apostolic see—publicly proclaim this throughout all the churches: no one should listen to Mass from a priest, to the Gospel from a deacon, or even to the Epistle from a subdeacon whom he knows to mingle with women. And lest we seem to act improperly in this matter, we would append several statements of the Fathers, were we not restrained by the brevity appropriate to a letter. But since our words are not otherwise given credence, at least a few of their testimonies must be set down, so that from these which now come to memory they may infer how much authority the others possess, should they seek them in the actual books.

In the first place, then, let us hear what the apostle James wrote to the blessed Clement concerning this matter (Epist. 2):

“Ministers of the altar, priests or deacons, should be chosen for the Lord’s offices only if, before ordination, they have left their wives. But if, after ordination, a minister happens to enter his own wife’s bed, he shall not enter the thresholds of the sanctuary, nor become a bearer of the sacrifice; he shall not touch the altar, nor receive from those offering the holocaust the offering of the sacrifice, nor approach the portion of the Lord’s body. Let him bring water to the hands of the priests, close the outer doors, and perform lesser offices; but let him certainly not supply the vessel for the saving chalice.”

Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, likewise says among other things (Council of Carthage II, canon 2):

“It has pleased us that holy bishops and priests of God, as well as Levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, should be continent in all things, so that they may obtain simply what they ask from God; thus we too may preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself observed.”

Faustinus, bishop of the Church of Potentia [also: Pontiana], in the province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, said (Council of Carthage II, canon 2):

“It is pleasing that the bishop, priest, and deacon, and those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, abstain from their wives.”

All the bishops said:

“It is pleasing that chastity be preserved in all things and by all who serve at the altar.”

The Council of Carthage also says again (Council of Carthage V, canon 5):

“Moreover, when a report was made concerning the incontinence of certain clerics, even though they were readers, toward their own wives, it was resolved that bishops, priests, and deacons should, according to their own statutes, also abstain from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

The Apostolic Canons say:

“Concerning priests and deacons, divine law prescribes that those who are incontinent while placed in such offices shall be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor; nor shall they be admitted to such a ministry, which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.”

The same man mentioned above, namely the bishop of Carthage, says:

“We have heard, dearest brothers, that the incontinence of certain clerics, even though they are readers, toward their own wives is being retained. It has pleased us—and this has also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons, priests, and bishops, according to their own statutes, should also abstain from their wives, so that they may be regarded as though they did not have them. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.”

The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this except at a more mature age. The entire council said:

“We confirm that what your holiness has rightly regulated is holy and pleasing to God.”

But, to avoid weariness, it will be enough to introduce what has been decreed concerning subdeacons alone; once the measure required of them has been carefully examined, no one will be permitted to doubt concerning the higher orders.

In the decree of Pope Leo this is also found, among other matters (Pope Leo, Letter 82, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, canon 4):

“For although those outside the clerical order have free choice to pursue the union of marriage and the procreation of children, nevertheless, for the presentation of the purity of perfect continence, carnal marriage is not permitted even to subdeacons, so that those who have may be as though they had not, and those who do not have may remain unmarried.”

If this ought rightly to be observed in that order, which is fourth from the top, how much more must it be observed by the first, second, and third orders, so that no one may be considered suitable for Levitical honor, priestly honor, or episcopal excellence who is found not yet to have restrained himself from conjugal pleasure?

Pope Sylvester says in his decree (chapter 8):

“We permit no subdeacon to pass over into marriage, and we command that no one presume to do so by any transgression.”

The Council of Nicaea says (Apostolic Canons, 25):

“Concerning the unmarried who have been advanced to the clergy, we command that, if they wish, they may take wives—but only readers and singers.”

The blessed Gregory also instructed Peter the subdeacon, saying (Gregory, *Register*, book I, letter 42):

“Three years ago subdeacons of all the churches of Cilicia had been forbidden, following the custom of the Roman Church, to have intercourse with their wives in any way. This seems to me harsh and unsuitable: one who has not adopted the practice of such continence and has not previously resolved upon chastity should not be compelled to separate from his wife, lest—God forbid—he thereby fall into something worse.

“Therefore it seems to me that, from this day forward, all the bishops should be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised that he will live chastely, so that what was not sought through a prior resolve of the mind may not be forcibly demanded of the past, and what is to come may be guarded with care.

“But those who, after the same prohibition made three years ago, have lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and they are to be exhorted to remain in their good conduct. Those, however, who, after the prohibition was made, have refused to abstain from their wives, we do not wish to see advance to the sacred order. For no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been tested before he undertakes the ministry.”

## CHAPTER III — The Clergy’s Foolish Defense

But why do I go on assembling canons, when even those who fight against them with puffed-up necks cannot be ignorant of them? Once, when the fat bulls of the Church of Laon surrounded me with an armed conspiracy and many calves, tumultuously bellowing in a mad uproar, gnashed their teeth (Ps. XXI), as though to vomit a belch of gall into my mouth, they said:

“We have the authority of the Council of Tribur—if I have retained the name correctly—which grants those promoted to the ecclesiastical order the ability to enter into marriage.”

I replied to them:

“Your council, whatever name you wish it to bear, may retain that name; but I do not accept it if it does not agree with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.”

For they hunt up certain adulterated offshoots, as it were, of the canons and use them as authority by which they may empty the authentic force of the canons. But Solomon says: “For bastard shoots will not strike deep roots” (Wis. IV). Human inventions are far removed from the judgments that have been delivered through the Holy Spirit, and those who do not fear to oppose the sacred canons undoubtedly offend the Spirit himself, by whom they were promulgated.

Thus John says in the Apocalypse:

“If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share from the book of life, from the holy city, and from the things written in this book” (Apoc. XXII).

But lest anyone accuse us of bending the words of Sacred Scripture according to the wishes of our own will, claiming that these words do not at all apply to the sacred canons, let him hear what Pope Anacletus—the fifth, namely, from blessed Peter—says concerning violators of the canons:

“Those who voluntarily violate the canons are gravely judged by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were dictated. For those who, against these same holy canons, not compelled by necessity but willingly, as has been stated, either act insolently, presume to speak, or freely consent to those wishing to act, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.

“Such presumption is plainly one form of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, since, as has already been said, it acts against him by whose command and grace these holy canons were issued.”

Since, then, all the holy Fathers who established canons through the Holy Spirit agree with one another in undivided unanimity concerning the chastity to be preserved by the clergy, what can those hope for who blaspheme the Holy Spirit by satisfying the enticements of their own flesh?

Through the passing flow of momentary lust they purchase for themselves an unquenchable conflagration of eternal burning. Now they are soiled in the stench of lust; but then, handed over to avenging flames, they will be whirled about in a torrent of pitch and sulfur. Now, in the heat of lust, they give themselves over to Tartarus; then, plunged into the chaos of eternal night, they will endure without end the torment of savage Gehenna. Now they nourish within themselves the fire of desire; then they will feed the flames of an unfailing conflagration with the marrow of their own entrails.

And, O excessively unhappy and wretched men! By observing the laws of their rotten flesh, which is destined to be devoured by worms, they despise the laws of him who came from heaven and reigns over the angels.

Therefore the Lord says through the prophet to the wicked man:

“You have placed me behind your body” (Ezek. XXIII).

That is as if he were saying: “You guard the lust of your body as law, and you despise the commands of my law.” For the law of the human body is contrary to the divine law. Hence the Apostle says:

“I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII).

Those, then, place God behind their body who, despising the authority of the divine law, obey the enticements of their pleasures; and while loosening the reins of lust, they transgress the rule of discipline imposed upon them.

They do not know that, for the fleeting pleasure of a single act of intercourse, they are bargaining for a thousand years of burning, so that those who now burn with the flame of lust may then be consumed by the fire of vengeance.

But those who wallow in the filth of wanton desire—with what audacity of deadly presumption do they thrust themselves into the sacrament of the saving Eucharist, when the Lord says to the priests through Moses:

“Every man who approaches from your seed to the holy things that the children of Israel have offered to the Lord, while he has any uncleanness, shall perish before the Lord” (Lev. XXII).

Then it continues:

“A man of the seed of Aaron who is leprous or suffers an emission of semen shall not eat of the things sacrificed to me until he is healed” (ibid.).

If one who suffered the discharge of any uncleanness through bodily illness was not permitted to eat what had been offered, how can one who willingly remains in the contamination of lust be able to offer the sacraments to God?

Hence it is said in Leviticus:

“Every man who has a blemish from the seed of Aaron the priest shall not approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord or the bread of his God” (Lev. XXI).

Then it continues:

“He shall not enter within the veil, nor approach the altar, because he has a blemish and must not contaminate my sanctuary” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV — The Great Extent of the Continence of Priests and Levites Ministering under the Old Law

Let the prudent reader attend to how aptly that apostolic statement of James, set forth above, agrees with this divine law. If, then, at that time no one who had a blemish dared to enter the sanctuary, with what state of mind does anyone who now pollutes himself with women presume to minister at the sacred altars?

Certainly that tabernacle was only a shadow and an instrument of the image, whereas “the Church,” as the Apostle says to Timothy, “is the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III). And as he says to the Hebrews: “The Law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities” (Hebr. X).

Yet in that tabernacle—or temple—of the old law, when the Levites or priests were ministering, they did not have intercourse with their wives. For David, as we read in the book of Chronicles (I Chron. XXIII), established twenty-four lots of priests and an equal number of Levites, who were to perform their turns in the worship of the temple and minister at their appointed times according to the rites of the ceremonies. Until they had completed the period of their turn, they entirely abstained from rendering the conjugal debt.

The evangelist Luke also clearly declares this. Having first stated that Zechariah belonged to the division of Abijah and that he was exercising the priesthood in the order of his division before God, he shortly afterward says:

“It came to pass, when the days of his service had been completed, that he went to his house”; and immediately he adds: “After these days Elizabeth his wife conceived” (Luke I).
