It is therefore perfectly clear that the priests of that time were kept entirely free from rendering the conjugal debt until they had completed the period of their turn. Indeed, they continually remained in the temple until they had performed the duty assigned to their lot.

Thus Moses says to Aaron:

“Until the rite of the sacrifice has been completed, you shall remain in the tabernacle day and night, observing the Lord’s watches, lest you die” (Lev. VIII).

But now, since Scripture commands us always to pray, the ministers of the altar have no assigned turns, since without any interruption of time they offer the continual service of their ministry.

Moreover, the Apostle says:

“Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and the wife to her husband. Do not defraud one another,” he says, “unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Cor. VII).

If conjugal intercourse prevents laypeople from praying, in what way does it permit clerics to minister at the sacred altars? What time will they find in which they ought to devote themselves to marriage, when they are never free from the diligent service of the Church?

For to the Corinthians the Apostle says:

“He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But he who has a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (I Cor. VII).

Therefore everyone who is devoted to divine service must always attend with concern to the things that belong to God, lest he divide his mind through carnal affections. But how can one be concerned for and always attentive to the Creator whose heart is joined to his wife?

“Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are members of Christ?” (I Cor. VI.) And, to pass over many things that the same Apostle says on this subject lest I cause weariness, let me at least add this:

“Do you not know,” he says, “that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you?” (ibid.)

Concerning this temple he says elsewhere:

“If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III).

If, then, not only the soul but also our very body, which is seen and touched externally, is undoubtedly the temple of the Holy Spirit, how does one to whom carnal intercourse is forbidden not violate God’s temple when he makes himself a brothel of wanton lust, casts away the Holy Spirit in whom he had been sealed, and introduces into himself, in his place, the spirit of lust?

And when the same Apostle says to us:

“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed” (Eph. IV),

does not the one who excludes the Holy Spirit from the dwelling that belongs to him and admits its enemy—the author of lust—grieve the Holy Spirit unto his own destruction?

Why is it not recalled that the sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, when they brought strange fires to the divine altar, were immediately consumed by a fire sent from heaven?

“Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron,” he says, “having taken their censers, put fire and incense upon them, offering before the Lord a strange fire, which he had not commanded them to offer. And fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord” (Lev. X).

For what is it to offer strange fire to the Lord, if not to approach the most holy altars inflamed by the heat of lust?

And when Scripture says:

“Do not extinguish the Spirit” (I Thess. III),

these men, insofar as they can, extinguish the Holy Spirit who ought to burn within them, and offer strange fire when they approach the Lord’s altar with the flame of lust raging within them.

But suddenly the fire of divine fury is kindled against them, by which they are terribly consumed, as Scripture testifies:

“Now fire consumes the adversaries” (Hebr. X).

And certainly it is lawful that those who approach the sacred altars while polluted should perish by the sword of divine vengeance, since the Lord says to Moses:

“You shall teach the children of Israel to beware of their uncleanness, lest they die in their impurities when they have defiled my tabernacle, which is among them” (Lev. XV).

Shame upon us! The sons of Levi showed greater reverence toward the Synagogue than the ministers of Christ now show toward the Church. They disciplined themselves under the strictness of fasting when entering the tabernacle; these men are unwilling even to preserve the purity of chastity.

For the Lord said to Aaron:

“You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die. This is an everlasting command throughout your generations, so that you may have knowledge to distinguish between the holy and the profane, between the polluted and the clean” (Lev. X).

But now the ministers of the Church, who have Christ as their teacher—and Christ crucified—do not shudder at living amid the sweetness of their pleasures or at neighing wherever the itch of the flesh draws them, as the Lord says through Jeremiah:

“I filled them, and they committed adultery; in the house of the prostitute they indulged themselves. They became lustful stallions, each neighing for the wife of his neighbor” (Jer. V).

And again:

“For prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I found their wickedness, says the Lord” (Jer. XXIII).

But because they are now nourished by satisfying the pleasures of their desires, let them consider what will be repaid to them for having drunk in this sweetness:

“Behold,” he says, “I will feed them wormwood and give them gall to drink. For pollution has gone forth from the prophets of Jerusalem over the whole land” (ibid.).

Those who now live recklessly, who suck the marrow of carnal sweetness and are fattened, as it were, on the honey of wanton lust, deserve afterward to be made drunk with both gall and wormwood at the price appointed, so that just as they now water themselves with cups of pleasure, then, with their entrails filled with gall, they may become bitter.

Furthermore, what an audacious presumption it is that, although they cannot cease from obscene contamination, they nevertheless refuse to desist from carrying out the ministry to which they show themselves unworthy, when the Lord says to them through Isaiah:

“When you come to appear before me, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not continue to bring a sacrifice in vain. Incense is an abomination to me” (Isa. I).

Through Jeremiah he also rebukes them:

“Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba and sweet-smelling cane from a distant land? Your holocausts are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me” (Jer. VI).

And through Malachi:

“O priests,” he says, “who despise my name, and you say, ‘In what have we despised your name?’ You offer polluted bread upon my altar” (Malach. I).

And shortly afterward:

“Behold, I will cast the shoulder upon you, and I will scatter the dung of your solemnities over your faces” (Malach. II).

Again, through Isaiah:

“When you stretch out your hands,” he says, “I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear” (Isa. I).

Since, then, God himself declares that such an offering is rejected, why is it offered heedlessly? Hence he also says afterward:

“Your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear” (Isa. L).

## CHAPTER V — That It Would Be Better for Intemperate Clerics to Withdraw from the Sacred Orders

How much better, then, it would be for men of this kind to restrain themselves now from administering their order than to provoke the sword of divine fury against themselves; and how much more modest it would be for them to withdraw from Christ’s altars and not serve than to pollute them by approaching!

It is pious to believe that anyone who now recognizes and abandons his own sins and humbly restrains himself from his ministry will obtain on the day of judgment the very order of which he had voluntarily deprived himself.

This seems to be signified in the book of Ezra, where the genealogy of the priests is described (II Esdr. VII). There the sacred history relates that certain priests sought the record of their genealogy; and because they could not find it, they were expelled from the priesthood.

Those are truly sons of priests who live as priests. They preserve the line of priestly descent who offer their life as a sacrifice to God and, by living religiously, testify that they have sprung from priestly stock. When they imitate the examples of holy priests that they read, they recognize themselves as sons of priests in the sacred writings.

But those who live carnally and, by following the footsteps of the wicked, seem to descend from the generation of worldly people are rightly expelled from the order of priests, since through their disgraceful life they cannot be found to be their sons.

It should also be noted what follows there:

“Athersatha said to them that they should not eat of the holy of holies until there arose a learned and perfect priest of God” (ibid.).

In this prohibition, what else should be understood through the mystery of allegory except that one who is unworthy of the priesthood should restrain himself from receiving the sacraments and from administering the priestly order until Christ, who is truly the learned and perfect priest, rises in judgment?

As the Psalmist says:

“The earth trembled and was still when God arose in judgment” (Ps. LXXV),

so that he whose terror causes any fallen person here voluntarily to deprive himself of his dignity may, restoring him in judgment through a welcome reversal, raise him to the height of the order he lost, saying:

“Friend, go up higher, and then you will have glory in the presence of all who recline with you” (Luke XIV).

But there are some—and this must not be passed over—who, in accordance with the Apostle (Eph. IV), having lost hope, have handed themselves over to uncleanness. For, having utterly despaired of continence, they restrain themselves from administering the order they have received and thus confidently suppose that they can sin with impunity.

It is as though a servant were to say to his master: “Because I cannot fulfill what you command, I defect to the camp of your enemies and surrender myself to them to fight against you,” as though he could please his master by fleeing and could not provoke him by rising in arms against him.

To such men I declare firmly and without any ambiguity that they deceive themselves with an empty and frivolous promise if, by failing to perform their office, they believe that they have been stripped of the office. Although the order or office of anyone may cease from regular attendance or execution, nevertheless the sacrament of the order remains in the ordained person.

Just as a man, even if he ceases from the conjugal act, is in no way released from the bond of marriage, so a cleric, even if he does not perform the duty of his order, is not thereby stripped of the sacrament of that order.

They must therefore beware lest that fearful sentence come upon them, which the Apostle pronounces:

“It is impossible,” he says, “for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to disgrace” (Hebr. VI).

They plainly seem to act as though some Israelite, wishing to fornicate with idols, were to say:

“Because I cannot keep the harsh and rigid law of God, I will pass over to the rite of the Gentiles,”

as though one who withdraws from the law were no longer bound by the law, and as though, although he might not deserve a reward for observing the law, he would nevertheless not be liable to punishment for despising it.

But let us hear what divine severity says to such men in Deuteronomy:

“When anyone hears the words of this oath and blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘There will be peace for me, and I will walk in the depravity of my heart,’ and joins the drunkard to the thirsty, the Lord will not forgive him. Rather, the Lord’s fury and jealousy will burn most fiercely against that man, and all the curses written in this book will rest upon him. The Lord will erase his name from under heaven and consume him for destruction from all the tribes of Israel, according to the curses contained in the book of this law and covenant” (Deut. XXIX).

Let the cleric, then, to whom intercourse with women is forbidden, offer sacrilegious repudiation to the venerable altars, so that, like an unrestrained horse, he may leap forth into the desire for lust. But although he receives freedom from God and departs from him as though absolved, he does not escape the snares of God’s curse and his own destruction.

The Psalmist says:

“Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII).

And the Lord says through Ezekiel:

“Nor shall the thought of your mind ever come to pass, when you say, ‘We shall be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stones.’ As I live, says the Lord God, surely with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and fury poured out I shall reign over you. I shall lead you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I shall subject you to my scepter” (Ezek. X).

## CHAPTER VI — Concerning Two Incontinent Priests

What I am about to relate, it is said, happened in our own time.

In the regions of Gaul, under the administration and authority of a certain religious abbot named Benedict, there lived a priest who, the more abundantly he was endowed with material resources, the more grievously he was oppressed by a lack of religion and decency.

When his concubine died and he was left a widower, he undertook to repeat the marriage. What more is there to say? He joined himself—as though by the law of a marriage contract—to a prostitute, gathered friends and neighbors into a wedding assembly according to custom, and provided a lavish banquet with every kind of abundance.

The abbot, however, while lying on his sickbed and already approaching his blessed end, heard of this. He sent two monks to him and, under threat of strict disciplinary punishment, forbade him to commit so shameless a crime.

But the priest, driven by the impulse of the wickedness he had conceived, could not obey. With punishable recklessness, he carried out everything that the order of the wedding required.

While the whole place resounded with uproar and was given over to wantonness, the priest, like an ox being led to sacrifice, abandoned the banquet and entered a bridal chamber not of pleasure but of destruction. And—O terrifying God in your counsels concerning the sons of men! (Ps. LXV)—he was struck by sudden death. In one and the same moment he discharged his semen and breathed out his life.

Such should have been the reward of one who had resolved to pass from the Lord’s sanctuary to the brothel of a catamite and a swine’s wallow.

Perhaps, because he did not regularly approach the sacred altar, he therefore believed that he could sin with impunity. But he learned by experience what the Apostle had said:

“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebr. X).

At another time, when Pope Stephen—who imitated the fiery zeal of Phinehas (Num. XXV)—had ordered all the clerics of Rome who had remained incontinent after Pope Leo’s prohibition to leave the assembly of the clergy and the church choir, so that, although they had abandoned the women and corrected themselves through the lamentations of repentance, they would nevertheless, because they had disobeyed the holy man, depart from the sanctuary for a time and thereafter expect no permission to celebrate Mass, a priest lived beside the canonical house of blessed Cecilia established across the Tiber.

He was unwilling in any way to abandon the woman, nor could he ever regard these statutes as anything but entirely empty and frivolous.

One day, while he was healthy, vigorous, and strong, he arranged himself in bed during the evening hours to rest. But struck by the sudden judgment of divine vengeance, he was found in the morning as a lifeless corpse.

Immediately the religious assembly of the aforementioned canonical house sent two clerics to consult me about what they should do with the dead man. If we have understood the matter correctly, we advised that, since he had been a priest, they should bury him near the church, but that they should perform no service of hymns or psalmody for him, so that terror might increase among the sexually impure and the glory of chastity might flourish more abundantly.

And certainly it seems fitting that the dead man should possess, in accordance with the prophet, the burial of an ass, since while alive he despised being bound by human law. As it is said through Jeremiah concerning Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah:

“He shall be buried with the burial of an ass; he shall be putrefied and cast outside the gates of Jerusalem” (Jer. XXII).

Indeed, whoever bears the mark of military service, wherever he flees, always carries with him the sign of the service to which he had sworn allegiance; and whenever he sees the scar of the brand impressed upon him, he recognizes himself as a deserter from the army and guilty of defection.

So too, when a cleric is shown to descend into filthy brothels while bearing the seal of the Holy Spirit that he received on the day of his consecration, he cannot erase it from himself by any pretext, even though there he also receives the mark of which John says in the Apocalypse:

“He will make all, small and great, have the mark of the beast on their right hand or on their foreheads” (Apoc. XIII).

But what has the mark of the beast to do with that sign of which it is said:

“These who were upon Mount Zion with the Lamb had his name written on their foreheads” (Apoc. XIV)?

“What fellowship does light have with darkness? Or what partnership does Christ have with Belial? What agreement does the temple of God have with idols?” (II Cor. VI.)

## CHAPTER VII — The Writer Attacks the Concubines of the Clergy
Meanwhile I address you as well, you hares of the clergy, morsels of the devil, exiles from paradise, poisons of minds, swords of souls, aconites for those who drink, toxins of banqueters, material for sinning, occasions of perishing. You, I say, I address, you women’s quarters of the ancient enemy, hoopoes, screech owls, owls, she-wolves, leeches, saying, “Bring, bring,” without ceasing (Prov. XXX). Come, then, listen to me, whores, brothels, kisses, wallows of fattened swine; beds of unclean spirits, nymphs, sirens, lamias, Dianas—and if anything else monstrous or prodigious is found that may suitably be judged to belong to your name. For you are the victims of demons, destined for the destruction of eternal death. From you the devil feeds as though on delicate dishes; he is fattened by the abundance of your lust. “For,” according to Scripture, “he dwells in the secret places of the reed and in moist places. You are vessels of wrath and of the Lord’s fury, stored up for the day of vengeance” (Job XL).

You impious tigresses, whose bloody mouths know no thirst except for human blood. You harpies, who swoop around the Lord’s sacrifice and seize it, cruelly devouring those who had been offered to God. For I may also appropriately call you lionesses, who, after the manner of wild beasts, raise your manes and, with bloody embraces, tear unsuspecting human beings to pieces for their destruction. You sirens and Charybdes, who, while producing the sweet song of deception, construct an inescapable shipwreck, with the sea swallowing all. You raging vipers, who, through the burning impatience of lust, behead Christ—who is the head of the clergy—for the sake of your lovers.

For just as the Midianite women once aroused the hearts of the Israelites to intercourse with them by the adornment of embellished clothing (Num. XXV), so you, by the allurements of elaborate dress or painted faces, drag wretched men away from the ministry of the most holy altar, in which they had been engaged, so that you may suffocate them in the slippery glue of your love. And just as those Midianite women persuaded those whom they had enticed to worship idols, so you too, after the sign of the cross has been impressed upon these men, in a certain way compel them to worship the image of the beast. Those men, surely, unless perhaps they repent, will not escape with you the saying of the Apocalypse:

“If anyone,” it says, “worships the beast and his image, and receives his mark on his forehead or on his hand, he too shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath, which is mixed unmixed in the cup of his anger; and he shall be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments shall rise for ever and ever, and they shall have no rest day or night” (Apoc. XIV).

Moreover, just as Adam, among all the fruits of paradise, desired only that one which God had forbidden, so among the whole multitude of the human race you select only those who have been entirely forbidden every association with womanly affection. Through you the face of Damascus fights against the tower of David, while through you the ancient enemy strives to assault the summit of ecclesiastical chastity. You are rightly, I confess, dipsades or cerastes, who suck the blood of wretched and unsuspecting men in such a way that you pour deadly poison into their inward parts. Hence you belong to the number of those women concerning whom Moses said to the leaders of Israel:

“Why did you spare the women? Are these not the ones who deceived the children of Israel at the suggestion of Balaam and caused you to transgress against the Lord in the matter of Peor?” (Num. XXXI.)

For what boldness of mind would not shudder to touch hands anointed with the most sacred chrism or oil, or hands accustomed to the Gospel or apostolic pages? Scripture says of the malignant enemy that his food is chosen. Through you, therefore, the devil devours his chosen food, when he crushes the holier members of the Church with his teeth, as though by the double weight of suggestion and pleasure; and when he joins those men to you, he turns them, as though transferring them, into his own entrails.

In a full synod, Pope Leo, of holy memory, decreed that any women found within the walls of Rome prostituted to priests should thereafter be assigned as female slaves to the Lateran palace. We too decree that this salutary statute, entirely filled with equity and justice, should be propagated through all the Churches, so that, after first receiving the decree of the apostolic see, each bishop may claim for his Church the female servants whom he finds in his diocese subjected to sacrilegious intercourse with priests. This is in accordance with the law of equity: those who are convicted of having stolen the service of God’s servants from the sacred altars should at least make up to the bishop for this service through the servitude of their diminished civil status.

But why should I go on speaking to you? Rather, listen to what almighty God says to you through Jeremiah:

“Hear, O women, the word of the Lord, and let your ears receive the word of my mouth. Teach your daughters lamentation, and each her neighbor mourning, because death has climbed through your windows; it has entered your houses, to scatter the children outside and the young men from the streets. And the dead body of a man shall fall like dung upon the face of the land, and like hay behind the back of the reaper, and there shall be no one to gather it” (Jer. IX).

Indeed, let each of you hear what the same Lord says individually to her through the same prophet:

“Because you have forgotten me and trusted in falsehood, I have stripped your thighs before your face, and your disgrace has appeared: your adulteries, your neighing, and the crime of your fornication upon the hills. In the field I saw your abominations” (Jer. XIII).

Therefore let her fear and tremble to the depths, lest that curse come upon her which God, the avenger of iniquity, threatens against unclean women through Moses:

“You shall be subject to these curses: May God make you a curse and an example to all his people; may he make your thigh rot and your swollen belly burst. May the accursed waters enter your belly, and, as your womb swells, may your thigh rot” (Num. V).

Let her also consider that this pleasure of the flesh, which she now enjoys, produces for her that bitterness of which John says in the Apocalypse:

“Those who were cast into the lake of burning fire gnawed their tongues because of their pain, and in their pains and wounds they blasphemed the God of heaven and earth” (Apoc. XVI).

But while I avoid the excesses of a longer style, I pour out, as it were, from a great whirlpool of passion only a small spark upon the herds of southern beasts of burden.

Finally, hear me, traps of the clergy. If you wish to recover the kingdom of heaven, which is closed to you, reject as quickly as possible your detestable associations, and restrain yourselves under the discipline of worthy satisfaction and repentance. Let holy discord arise among you, stirring up and kindling in you the fuel of salutary hatred; and let it violate the love that is hateful to God. Do not turn vessels consecrated to God into vessels of dishonor. Do not, after the example of Belshazzar, adapt these vessels to the use of your pleasure (Dan. V), lest God’s zeal suddenly blaze against you in the fury of anger and the sword of his indignation, once drawn, pierce both of you.

I certainly know of a priest who strictly forbade his dying concubine, when she was asking to perform penance, to do so, and absolutely promised that he himself would discharge the penance owed on her behalf. She, trusting easily in the priest and learned man, was deceived and thus plunged herself into Tartarus with the leaden mass of which the prophet Zechariah bears witness (Zech. V). Therefore cast away deceitful deceivers like serpentine poison, and hasten to tear yourselves free as though from the bloody teeth of lions.

Nor should it frighten you that perhaps a ring—let me not say of faith, but of faithlessness—has given you in pledge; that the notary has drawn up the ratified documents and dowry records as though by the law of marriage; or that an oath has been exchanged on both sides to confirm, in a certain way, the bond of marriage. All this—which among others is the foundation of marriage—is judged among you empty and frivolous. For since Scripture says, “A wife is given to a man by God” (Prov. XIX), and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Every tree that my heavenly Father did not plant shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV), nothing that resists the command of almighty God rests upon any foundation of stability.

For upon you falls what the prophet Isaiah declares:

“Because the daughters of Zion have been lifted up, and walked with outstretched necks, and went with glances of their eyes, and clapped their hands, walked with their feet, and advanced with measured step, the Lord shall make the crown of the daughters of Zion bald, and the Lord shall uncover their hair. On that day the Lord shall remove the ornament of their shoes, the little moons, the necklaces, the pendants, the bracelets, the headdresses, the hair-partings, the armlets, the chains, the scent-boxes, the earrings, the rings, the gems hanging upon the forehead, the changing garments, the cloaks, the linen garments, the bodkins, the mirrors, the fine linen, the ribbons, and the light garments. And instead of a sweet odor there shall be stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; and instead of a breast-band, sackcloth. Your handsomest men shall also fall by the sword, and your strong men in battle” (Isa. III).

Therefore, lest you fall together with the men whom you consider most handsome, by the sword of divine fury, lower your outstretched necks, cast away the glances and clapping of your eyes, and humbly subject yourselves to him who is the avenger of crimes. Moreover, if you wish to return to God with unwavering faith, he is ready to grant you full pardon, since through the prophet he says to every fornicating soul:

“If a woman, having departed, takes another husband, will her former husband return to her again? Will not that woman be considered polluted and defiled? But you have been defiled with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. III).

Blessed is such an exchange: when you tear impure clerics away from intercourse with you, you enter the bridal chambers of the heavenly bridegroom to the applause of the angels. “There is joy,” indeed, “among them over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV). And through the prophet: “Return to me, and I shall return to you, says the Lord” (Mal. III).

## CHAPTER VIII — That the person who neglects to correct what he can is culpable

But so that the movement of the running pen may be turned back to him for whom it was begun, since that apostolic sentence says, “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to them, deserve the same punishment” (Rom. I), you must be very much on your guard, venerable father. Although you yourself present yourself conspicuous in the freshness of chastity, you nevertheless permit lust to rule in your clergy like that bloody Jezebel, concerning whom it is said to the angel of the Church of Thyatira:

“I have a few things against you: that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants into fornication” (Apoc. II).

That sentence is certainly authoritative which says: “The person who neglects to correct what he can is guilty of the deed.”

For what did it profit Eli that he himself did not fall into lust, but rebuked his fornicating sons with paternal affection rather than priestly authority? (I Reg. II.) Read, father, the letter that we sent concerning the incontinent conduct of bishops to Pope Nicholas, of pious memory, and understand that whatever of this kind you find written there is likewise addressed to you.

Nevertheless, tell me, please: if you saw a fornicating monk, would you not immediately spit in nauseated disgust, throw heaven and earth into confusion with your shouting, and further cry out that he should be burned by avenging flames? Yet we know plainly that canonical authority prescribes no different measure of repentance for a monk and for a deacon.

Since, then, the measure of sin is one and the same in both, why should there be a difference in the sinner—so that we tolerate this one with composure, indeed even applaud him amicably, while judging the other worthy of hanging? Are we accepting persons and, contrary to the edict of the law, keeping different weights in our purse?

“You shall not have,” says Moses, “different weights in your purse, greater and smaller; nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure” (Deut. XXV).

Or are we also acting against the Gospel, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel? (Matt. XXIII.) Indeed, by as much as a priest is greater than a monk in the privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, by so much is he worse in sin. For while monks have no responsibility for the people, priests have been commanded to bear the sins of the people. As Moses says to Aaron:

“Why did you not eat the sacrifice in the holy place, which is the Holy of Holies, and which was given to you so that you might bear the iniquity of the multitude and pray for it before the Lord?” (Lev. X.)

But how can they now bear the sins of others, when their eyes are always fixed upon swollen bellies and crying children?

Since, however, some of them, while committing these evils, also defend them with this assertion of a viper’s doctrine, let them know that they are entangled in the snares of a damnable heresy. When they fall, they are impure; when they attempt to defend their conduct, they are rightly judged heretics. Hence married clerics are called Nicolaitans, since they derive this name from a certain Nicolas who taught this heresy.

But now it is coming about that, if they prevail, this distinguished new name may receive an addition, so that those who until now have been called Nicolaitans may henceforth also be called Cadaloitans. For they hope that, if Cadalous—who burns with a hellish passion for this—should preside over the universal Church in the place of Antichrist, he will loosen the reins of lust according to their wishes.

On this account his supporters also insult me and slander me, reproaching me that he has not died, in accordance with a certain verse of mine. For among other things I had said:

“I do not deceive you: you will die in the year begun.”

But so that they may prove that I was not lying, let them hear the astonishing outcome of divine providence. Cadalous was indeed elected as pope on the very feast day of the holy apostles Simon and Jude, as though for that office—but with God rejecting and driving him away—and, within that same year, on the vigils of those apostles, he was condemned and deposed by all the German and Italian bishops and metropolitans who were then present with the king.

Therefore, in accordance with the prophet Ezekiel, God in a certain way substituted the dung of oxen for human excrement, when he exchanged the destruction of the flesh for the ruin of honor (Ezek. IV). He died in honor when, by synodal judgment, honor lost its dignity. Now, I do not call him merely twice-dead, but rather a thousand-times dead: throughout the whole world he is mocked, driven out, cursed, and “anathematizatu…” [word truncated in the source].

Let my mockers hear this, then, and, when they have perceived the order of divine providence, let them not accuse me of lying.

But you, man of God, seize the sword, fervent with the zeal of Phinehas, so that you may be able to pierce with a sharp dagger the Israelite coupling with Cozbi the Midianite (Num. XXV). With Samuel also gird yourself steadfastly in the spirit of vengeance, and, to the shame of Saul, cut the exceedingly fat Agag into pieces (I Reg. XV). Let Elijah also hand you the drawn sword from the quiver of the Lord, and let not even one of the priests and prophets of Baal escape when they have been led to the torrent Kishon (III Reg. XVIII).

Moses too, because for love of a certain Israelite he struck down and hid an Egyptian beneath the sand (Exod. II), deserved to obtain leadership over all Israel. And, to recall more especially that victory which pertains to the sacrament of chastity: because David, a fervent warrior, cut off two hundred foreskins of the Philistines, he immediately received Michal, daughter of King Saul, in marriage (I Reg. XVIII). For since Saul had asked for only one hundred but received two hundred when his son-in-law brought them, the man who brings doubled foreskins to the king of Israel is the one who offers to God not only bodily chastity but also purity of heart.

Adonijah, son of Haggith, because he sought an unlawful marriage, cleansed his incest with spilled blood when Bathsheba intervened and Solomon pronounced judgment (III Reg. II).

Remember, then, what that same Solomon says to you:

“My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your soul to a stranger. You have been ensnared by the words of your mouth and captured by your own speech. Do, therefore, what I tell you, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor. Run, hasten, rouse your spirit; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. VI).

You were then ensnared by your own words before your friend when you promised to govern God’s people. Do not forget what is said through Jeremiah:

“Cursed is the person who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII).

That person withholds his sword from blood who neglects to avenge the sins of wrongdoers. But lest you perhaps fear to stand in the camp of chastity and to take up the weapons of chastity against the roaring battle-lines of lust, hear what the divine voice promises you through Ezekiel:

“Behold,” it says, “I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads. I have made your face like adamant and like flint. Do not fear them or dread their presence” (Ezek. III).

Through Solomon also it is said to you:

“Do not fear the sudden terror or the power of the impious when it rushes upon you. For the Lord will be at your side and will guard your foot, lest you be caught” (Prov. III).

And again:

“Every word of God is fire-tested, a shield to those who hope in him” (Prov. XXX).

But if you perhaps raise the objection of impossibility, and, as you said to me face to face, distrust your ability to suffice for this task, hear what true Wisdom answers you through that same Solomon:

“Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction. If you say, ‘Our strength is insufficient,’ he who examines the heart understands, and nothing escapes the guardian of your soul; he will repay each person according to his works” (Prov. XXIV).

Thus, venerable father, gird yourself steadfastly for this contest between chastity and lust. Thus, brandishing the sword of the spirit, inflict a deadly wound upon the lust raging in your Church, so that, as a brave warrior, you may be able to seize the spoils and booty from the hand of the bloody robber, and may deserve to carry back to the author of chastity the insignia of victory won.

# THIRD TREATISE: AGAINST INCONTINENT CLERICS

To Adelaide, Duchess of the Subalpine Peoples

## ARGUMENT

For the reason on account of which he had written to the bishop of Turin, he now writes to Adelaide, a noble woman who, after the death of her husband, governed the peoples of the Subalpine region and the territory of Savoy: namely, so that she might restrain the lust of the clerics living under her authority and by no means allow them to keep concubines. He also strongly commends to her justice and devotion toward the churches, especially toward the monastery of Fruttuaria, whose praises he recounts at length.

To the most excellent Adelaide, duchess: Peter, sinful monk, offers the persistence of his prayers.

Whatever I wrote to the venerable bishop of Turin concerning the injury done to chastity—which is that same queen of virtues—by the clerics, I had previously decided to write to you, had I not feared the slander of those same clerics who would sneer at me. For they would protest and say: “See how impiously, how inhumanely this man prepares to disgrace us, since he does not wish to discuss our affair cautiously and moderately with bishops or ecclesiastical men, but does not hesitate to publish to women what ought to have been dealt with in the sacristy.”

Fearing this, then, I changed the addressee, and sent to him what I had conceived for you. He, however, holds the chair of one Church, whereas in your realm—which extends across the considerable frontier of two kingdoms, Italy and Burgundy—many bishops preside. Therefore it did not seem unfitting that I should write to you above all concerning the incontinence of clerics, since I perceive that you do not lack the virtue suitable for correcting it. Especially since, to the praise of God, I may say that manly strength rules in a woman’s breast, and that you are richer in good will than in earthly power.

Hence, according to the eloquence of a pagan poet [Note: Terence, *Eunuchus*]:

“This man needs a protector, whom I am preparing as his defender.”

I urge and ask you to join yourself to the bishop, your lord, so that, supported by the protection of mutual virtue, you may be able to defeat the battle-line of lust raging against Christ.

## TREATISE III

### CHAPTER I — He urges Adelaide to restrain the lust of incontinent clerics

But while I strive to unite you for battle against the devil, I am reminded of that war which Deborah, the prophetess and wife of Lapidoth, is found to have waged with Barak, son of Abinoam, against Sisera, commander of the army. For it is written of her:

“Because she judged the people, the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment” (Judg. IV).

Following her example, you too bear the burden of the kingdom without the assistance of a male ruler, and people flock to you who desire to have the verdict of a legal sentence imposed upon their disputes. But strive to dwell, like her, beneath the palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah is interpreted as “exalted”; Bethel as “house of God.” Dwell, then, beneath the palm tree, and always contemplate above you the victory of Christ’s cross. Sit also between Ramah and Bethel, so that you may not cling only to what is earthly, but may always live with the apostles in the upper room and with holy Anna the widow in the temple. Of her the evangelist says:

“She did not depart from the temple, serving by fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke II).

And because Deborah is interpreted as “bee,” you too should make honey and continually turn the sweetness of divine praise upon your lips:

“How sweet,” he says, “are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

Certainly, to pass over much else, this drop seemed to me to flow from a kind of honeycomb when these words of true humility happened to come from your mouth: “What wonder is it, father, if almighty God has deigned to grant me, his most worthless servant, however little power among human beings, when he sometimes grants marvelous virtue to even the most contemptible herb?”

You therefore showed yourself to be a bee, distilling the sweetness of a honeycomb from your mouth, as it is written:

“For honey proceeds from the mouth of the prudent; the sweetness of honey is beneath his tongue, and a dripping honeycomb is upon his lips” (Gen. III).

Sisera, however, is interpreted as “exclusion of joy,” a name that most suitably fits the enemy of the human race, who excluded the first man from the joy of paradise in which he had rejoiced. But since this is not the time to linger over unraveling the mysteries of the allegory, Deborah said to Barak:

“The Lord God of Israel has commanded you: Go and lead the army to Mount Tabor, and take with you ten thousand fighting men from the sons of Naphtali and from the sons of Zebulun. I shall lead Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin, his chariots, and all his multitude to you at the torrent Kishon, and I shall deliver them into your hand.”

Barak said to her: “If you come with me, I shall go; if you do not wish to come, I shall not proceed.”

She said to him: “I shall indeed go with you, but in this instance victory shall not be credited to you, because Sisera shall be delivered into the hand of a woman” (Judg. IV).

We pass quickly over these plain words of the historical account, lest, if we linger too long in expounding the figures, we cause boredom for readers. It is enough to say this much: Barak is interpreted as “flash.” A flash does have light, but it does not last long; as soon as it begins, it ends. So there are some rulers of Churches who begin to flash, so to speak, when they kindle themselves with zeal for vengeance in order to correct the evils of their subjects, but they are extinguished at once, because, broken by some adversity or relaxed by the torpor of sloth, they quickly fail. Hence that Barak, representing a sluggish and enervated shepherd, said to Deborah: “If you come with me, I shall go; if you do not wish to come, I shall not proceed.”

Therefore, just as that man and woman—Barak, namely, and Deborah—supporting one another with mutual assistance, undertook battle against Sisera and utterly defeated him with his forces and nine hundred iron chariots, so you and the bishop of Turin should take up arms against Sisera, the commander of lust, and slaughter him with the sword of chastity as he dominates the children of Israel—that is, the clerics of the Church. In this way the bishop, indeed all the bishops who reside within the boundaries of your administration, may restrain the clerics through priestly discipline, while you extend the force of your earthly authority against the women.

God knows only three women; women beyond these have not yet come into his knowledge. He knows virgins with Mary, widows with Anna, and wives with Susanna.

### CHAPTER II — That concubines must be kept away from churches

The women of those clerics who cannot contract marriages by lawful right we may appropriately call not wives but rather concubines or prostitutes. Therefore, since they do not deserve to be recognized by God, they are rightly judged to be excluded from the temple of God.

For if Miriam, the sister of Aaron, who spoke against Moses with a light remark, was immediately covered with leprosy and removed from the tabernacle for seven days (Num. XII), by what right will these women be permitted to enter the Church, when they bring the filth of lust into that same Church, take the vessels of the Lord for their own uses, and, to speak more plainly, compel the ministers of the altar to minister to their own lust?

Come, then, be a womanly champion of the Lord. Like Deborah with Barak—that is, with the bishops joined together—pursue Sisera to complete destruction. And just as Jael, the wife of Heber, placed the tent peg upon Sisera’s skull, struck it with a hammer, and pierced both temples, so pierce the devil’s head with the sign of the cross and crush the author of lust, who excludes clerics from heavenly joys.

Such a victory greatly rejoices God, who sometimes triumphs through women with more glorious praise. Judith, an example of widowly continence, rejected the gold-covered and purple-shining marriage chamber of Holofernes; girded in mind with stronger weapons, she also boldly cut off his drunken head with a thrust of her dagger (Judith XIII). To deserve to receive this strength from the Lord, she had earlier rebuked the hesitant and timid priest, Uzziah, who had set God a limit of five days. She reproached him with the severity he deserved, saying:

“This is not speech that calls forth mercy, but rather speech that provokes anger and kindles fury. You have appointed a time for the Lord’s mercy and set a day for him according to your own will?” (Judith VIII.)

Esther, when she bravely exposed herself to death for the salvation of her people, compelled Haman, who eagerly thirsted for Israelite blood, to die by hanging (Esther VIII). The wise woman who lived in Abel threw the severed head of Sheba son of Bichri to Joab, commander of the army, and thus turned away from the city the danger of the siege that threatened it (II Sam. XX). Another woman at Thebez threw a fragment of a millstone from the fortress tower and crushed both the head and brain of Abimelech, who was violently attacking it (Judg. IX). Abigail, the wife of Nabal, removed the threat of slaughter from her household when, by disregarding her husband’s folly, she offered a gift to the angry David (II Sam. XI; I Sam. XXV).

You too can turn away the sword of divine fury from your household and from the regions over which you preside, if, even while the bishops are negligent, you strive to conquer lust, which is supported in the very citadel of ecclesiastical authority.

For what is now happening in the territories of Christians appears to be what is recorded as having happened in the fields of the Philistines. For, as the ancient History relates:

“Samson caught three hundred foxes, joined tail to tail, and tied torches between them. When he had set them alight, he released them so that they ran here and there. They immediately went into the fields of the Philistines. When these had been set on fire, the crops—already strong and still standing in the stalk—were burned so completely that the flames also consumed the vineyards and olive groves” (Judg. XV).

### CHAPTER III — That heretics and evil priests are like foxes

This history, although it principally signifies heretics, who are contained as though in a number of three hundred because they verbally confess the faith of the Holy Trinity, nevertheless, while they cloak themselves in the covering of orthodox faith at the beginning of their speech, conceal behind them the fire of perverse doctrine, by which the crops of every good work are burned. Although, I say, heretics are represented by these foxes, incontinent clerics with their concubines can nevertheless be fitted to them without impropriety. They walk as though with loosened feet, when they sometimes falsely put forward the appearance of decency.

But when they are joined tail to tail with torches set alight, it is because the impure are glued together by the hidden fire, insofar as they can conceal it, of their shameful love. These little foxes, then, joined together with fire intervening and coupled by the torches of lust, consume all the fields of the Philistines. For they destroy the spiritual fruits of the Church and, insofar as it depends on them, set the good works of the faithful people ablaze with the fire of divine indignation, concerning which fire the Psalmist mystically says:

“He gave their cattle over to hail and their possessions to fire” (Ps. LXXVII).

For just as good priests commend the offerings and vows of all the faithful to God, so those who are unworthy of the sacred altars often burden them horribly. That evil priests are compared with foxes the prophet Ezekiel also testifies, saying:

“Your prophets, Israel, were like foxes in the deserts” (Ezek. XIII).

For the moment, let this suffice concerning the clerics.

Concerning the churches adjacent to you, I would have warned you not to diminish their goods after the manner of any wicked rich person. But while several bishops and heads of monasteries were conversing with us in your presence, none of them complained that any trouble had been inflicted upon him either by you or by your administrators, except only the bishop of Augusta. Yet he did not complain that anything of his had been diminished by you; rather, he complained that nothing had been bestowed upon his Church from your generosity.

Blessed, I say, is the rich man in this age to whom his neighboring fellow citizens are able to bring only this accusation. At the monastery of Fruttuaria, where I was a guest for almost ten days, I clearly recognized how humane and gracious your rule was toward the Churches. There, under the shelter of your protection, the brothers serve God as securely as unfledged chicks are warmed beneath a mother’s wings. And how appropriately the name Fruttuaria was given to that place! We believe that it was provided not by human ingenuity but by divine providence.

For since Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness,” that is unquestionably Mount Ephraim where the true Israelites dwell. As they cultivate the fields of minds with the continuous sentences of sacred Scripture, as with hoes, abundant harvests of spiritual crops spring up there, to be carried by angels into the heavenly granaries.

That, I say, is truly Mount Ephraim: the strength of the army, the mass of valiant warriors. There an unrelenting war is constantly waged against the devil, and the opposing forces come face to face in battle—on one side the army of the Israelites, on the other the army of the Chaldeans. There Agag, the fattest of men, is cut to pieces by the hand of temperance (I Sam. XV); and Eglon, king of Moab, is slaughtered with the sword of chastity after his thigh has been pierced (Judg. III). Eglon is interpreted as “calf of sorrow,” signifying the victim of destruction. There the kings of the Midianites, Zebah and Zalmunna, are slain by the sword of the true Gideon (Judg. VIII); there the head of pride is cut off in Goliath (I Sam. XVII); disobedience is rejected in Saul (I Sam. XV); fraud, with all its sacrilegious duplicity, is hanged in Ahithophel (II Sam. XVII); and in Achan son of Carmi an immense heap of stones is piled upon avarice (Josh. VII).

There Jesus—not that son of Nun—truly conquers the kings of the Amorites and makes his soldiers tread upon their necks (Josh. XI). There Bezalel makes the ark for the God of Israel from acacia wood, which does not decay; constructs the tabernacle; raises the golden lampstand with its seven lamps; and fashions the mystical priestly vestments, shining with gold and jewels (Exod. XXXIII). There Solomon builds a temple for the Lord from precious stones and imposes such silence upon the stonecutters and masons that he permits neither hammer, axe, nor any iron tool to resound there (I Kings VI).

There Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, together with the rest of the multitude, girded with the weapons of virtue, restore the walls of Jerusalem, while nevertheless not ceasing to fight against the enemy forces that wish to hinder the work. Thus they are diligently attentive and ready on both fronts: while one hand is working upon the wall, the other continually holds the drawn sword; while on one side the structure of the building is completed, on the other the barbarity of the attacking enemies is driven back (I Esdr. III; II Esdr. IV).

And what more shall I say? Except that there is that workshop in which the evangelical woman’s drachma (Luke XV) [Col. 0421A] is daily beaten out by the hammers of regular discipline, and thus is restored to the image of her Creator (Gen. I), according to which she had been formed at the beginning. And truly, there is the craftsman of the world’s structure, of whom, as the evangelist Mark testifies, they said: “From where does this man have all these things, and what is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such mighty works that are performed by his hands? Is this not the carpenter’s son and Mary’s, the brother of James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon?” (Mark VI.) He, I say, the carpenter’s son, who is himself likewise a craftsman, there moves the bellows with his own hands—that is, his servants, utterly emptied of the weight of temporal affairs and dried up from every moisture of earthly love. Of this craftsman the divine voice says through Isaiah: “Behold, I have created the craftsman who blows upon the fire of coals and [Col. 0421B] brings forth a vessel for his work” (Isa. LIV). Hence Jeremiah also says: “All these princes,” he says, “have turned aside, walking deceitfully; bronze and iron—they are all corrupt. The bellows have failed; the lead has been consumed in the fire; the smelter has smelted in vain, for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (Jer. VI).

Through these, therefore, he breathes forth the power of the Holy Spirit, so that by their words or examples cold hearts may grow fervent in love of their Creator. There Jesus plainly often enters to his disciples through closed doors (Luke XXIV; John XX); not only does he address them with a greeting of peace, but through his breathing he pours into them the sacrament of the Holy Spirit. In that upper room [Col. 0421C] he celebrates the Passover daily with those same disciples; and while he pours forth the power of mystical speech, he inflames them with the ardor of his love. It is worthwhile to observe how the Lord’s swarm of bees continually runs back and forth through its hive, and, occupied with various tasks, strives eagerly to fulfill what has been assigned to it. For they carry different burdens, pack together honey, and enclose that nectar from which [uncertain: lavi], of wondrous sweetness, and grace are set before the dishes of the supreme King.

There, in the sight of David, king of Israel, the priests and Levites, together with the Nathinaeans, resound with nablas, trumpets, cinyres [cynires], zithers, and every kind of musical instrument (I Chron. XV); and, playing the instruments of mystical song, they alternate the watches of their service, saying: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CV). I pray Almighty God, O Fructuaria, that he may release me from the bond of this flesh before he permits me truly to hear that you have been cast down from the religious state in which I saw you.

For the rest, venerable sister, strive always to climb from good things to better ones; and just as you are forbidden through the Apostle to place your hope in the uncertainty of riches (I Tim. VI), so also do not distrust the mercy of divine clemency. And because I know that you are troubled by the repetition of a second marriage, when the Lord was tested by the Sadducees concerning a woman who had been married to seven brothers, and they asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection, he answered thus: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII; Luke XX). For if women with several husbands in no way belonged to the kingdom of God, Truth would certainly not have answered here, “They will be like the angels in heaven,” but rather would have said, “For they will be like the evil spirits in hell.” From this word of the Savior it is therefore plainly gathered that, provided a genuinely religious life is not lacking, the plurality of successive marriages does not exclude a person from the kingdom of heaven. For Jesus is such a bridegroom that whomever he embraces in the arms of his love, he immediately restores in the purity of flourishing chastity. And I say this not to give audacity to those who may yet marry many times, but so that I may not withdraw the medicine of hope or repentance from those who have already done so.

## CHAPTER IV. That zeal and compassion ought to be moderate in a judge

[Col. 0422B]

Be discriminating toward offenders with a certain balanced skill of judgment, so that you neither burn precipitately for vengeance nor become altogether lax in sparing them; so that neither immoderate zeal for punishment inflames you nor excessive compassion restrains you from exercising discipline. Certainly, because the mind is disturbed as soon as an injury is inflicted, it can scarcely pronounce a right judgment immediately. For just as still water admits the gaze of one looking into it, but when stirred becomes clouded, so the human mind, at the very moment of disturbance, does not perceive the undisturbed rule or straight line of right judgment. It is therefore necessary to postpone the sentence, so that, once the scales of justice have been balanced, a tranquil mind may suspend the judgment [Col. 0422C] that a disturbed mind was unable to form.

In this matter it is especially edifying to observe how calm, how grave, and how discerning King David was in pronouncing judgment. Joab and Shimei had seriously offended him, yet so long as he lived, and anger or fury could have had a place in him, he bore them with equanimity. But when he was already approaching death, and was no longer urged by any goad of anger formerly suppressed, he ordered his son to take vengeance upon them after his death—namely, at the time when, having been removed from human affairs, he could no longer take pleasure in the punishment of those who had offended him.

“You know,” he said, “what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of Israel’s army, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed and shed the blood of war in peace [Col. 0422D]” (III Kings II). And shortly afterward: “You shall therefore act according to your wisdom, and you shall not bring his gray hairs peacefully down to the underworld.” Concerning Shimei he said: “You also have with you Shimei the son of Gera, the son of Jemini, from Bahurim, who cursed me with a terrible curse when I was going to the camp.” And after a few intervening words he added: “You shall bring his gray hairs down with blood to the underworld” (ibid.).

Here one should note how praiseworthy and admirable this man’s discernment was: so long as he could be angry, he did not wish to take vengeance; but when every cause of fury and anger had now disappeared, lest justice be entirely passed over, he exercised the discipline of retribution. For when the avenger has nothing personal at stake, vengeance is drawn forth by sound judgment. Thus David did not feed upon vengeance, because he was not tormented by the injury; zeal did not inflame him to excess, nor did compassion make him disorderly in his leniency. In this way, as a discerning avenger, he both forgave the injury inflicted upon him without laxity and punished it without rage.

You too, venerable sister and lady, imitate the example of this holy king, so that you may never abandon the practice of compassion together with justice. Yet do so in accordance with the apostolic precept, that mercy may exalt itself above judgment (James II); and let every calculation of your judgment tend toward the glory of Almighty God, so that, when you have completed the office of the stewardship entrusted to you, he who now holds your spirit in his hands may raise you from earthly rule to the sovereignty of heavenly glory. [Col. 0424A]

Moreover, I commend the monastery of Fruttuaria more and more to your protection, as truly the bridal chamber of Jesus. I ask you always to maintain such vigilant watches of your guardianship over it that, through you, that heavenly bridegroom of yours may rest there sweetly. May Almighty God bless you and your sons, who are of royal character, and lead them not only to growth in age but also to growth in holiness. And may Lord Adrald, rector of the monastery of Bremetum, a religious and prudent man, be most respectfully greeted by me through you. If he wishes me to write something to him as well, let him instruct me by writing.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0423]

## 421–422. NINETEENTH OPUSCULUM: ON THE ABDICATION OF THE EPISCOPATE. TO NICOLAS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

### Argument

He entreats the supreme pontiff and earnestly begs him to permit him to lay down the burden of the episcopate. He adduces as his principal reasons that he is advanced in age and therefore more suited to rest than to labor; that he undertook this burdensome office not willingly but under compulsion; and finally that, because of his sins, as he himself says, he is unworthy to sit at so lofty a summit of honor and dignity. That it is lawful, if time or reason should so require, to renounce the episcopate, he proves by numerous examples and authorities of holy men. At the end he prays God to give the pontiff a mind by which he may satisfy his petitions.

[Col. 0423B] To his lord Nicholas, universal pope, Peter, a sinful monk, offers servitude.

Your breast, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, recognizes that, unless the necessity of the Apostolic See had then compelled me, and the ancient affection that I had long held for you had invited me, after the death of the lord Stephen of holy memory—your predecessor, indeed, but my persecutor—I would immediately have cut away from myself the episcopate, which had not been canonically conferred but violently thrust upon me. For you remember, my lord, how many complaints I often laid before you, how many groans, and finally how many deep sighs I drew from the innermost parts of my being, and how often I drenched my sorrowful face with abundant tears. Yet at that time I did not obtain release from you, because the welfare of the Roman Church, which seemed to be threatened with ruin [Col. 0423C], did not demand it.

Now, however, with you guiding the helm of Peter’s ship, the whole Church of Christ rejoices in tranquil peace. The storms of the winds restrain themselves; the billowing surges of the tempests grow calm; the seas become gentle; and the entire serenity of heaven appears to have been renewed. Since, therefore, under your holy pontificate the universal Church enjoys joyful peace, I ask that rest not be denied to my white hairs and my already very advanced old age.

Therefore, for the remission of all my sins [Col. 0423D], which I have wickedly committed, I surrender the right of the episcopate; and by this ring—for you have taken the staff—I renounce it, abandoning from now on every hopeless complaint that it be restored to me. I also return to you both monasteries, and I implore that, as rest is permitted to a veteran and discharged soldier, so it may be permitted to me.

## ON THE ABDICATION OF THE EPISCOPATE

### CHAPTER I. It is proved by examples that the episcopate may be relinquished

[Col. 0424B]

Perhaps it will be objected to me here that it is not lawful to relinquish an office once accepted. To this I briefly state what I think: many do not abandon the rights of the pontificate, and they are on the wrong side; but concerning all those whom we read to have relinquished it with right intention, there is certain hope that they rejoice in eternal fellowship with Christ. Nevertheless, we do not say this so that the episcopate may be abandoned indiscriminately, unless necessity or some rational cause should demand that it be done.

Indeed, while providing himself with a successor, Blessed Valerius, bishop, enthroned the great Augustine as bishop of the Church of Hippo.

Lucidus, bishop of Ficocles, realizing that his approaching death was near, hastened to the harbor of the monastic order and exchanged the priestly insignia of his dignity for monastic garments. And, so that you may know what this conversion achieved for him, the authentic history of the register testifies that, at the very moment of his departure from life, the grace of the Holy Spirit shone most joyfully upon his face. Before he died, the blessed apostle Andrew also appeared to him and announced at what hour he would depart from the body.

What shall I say of Blessed Adalbert the martyr? Because he set aside the see of the Church of Bohemia, he put on the monastic habit and merited to find the triumphant crown of martyrdom.

And, to pass over the others deliberately, there was a certain holy penitent whose name for the present escapes me. In Gaul, after he had relinquished the episcopate nearly seven years earlier [Col. 0425A], an angel finally appeared to him and commanded him to return to the episcopate. He refused, until, at the same angel’s admonition, blessed Remigius arrived with all speed. Thus, fearing lest deception might perhaps have crept in, and even fearing what was safe, he yielded to human authority, though previously he had stood firm against the angelic oracle.

There was also that bishop of Sabina who abandoned the episcopal throne and, despising priestly dignity, founded the monastery of Farfa. How noble a man he was in Christ is attested by ancient tradition, which celebrates the marks of his holiness, and by modern devotion, which frequently commemorates his pious memory with blessing. How many, both before and afterward, endured in that same see until the end of their lives [Col. 0425B] and brought God no such laborious fruit!

Nor will I pass over you, fortunate Bonitus, who, taking advantage of this particular circumstance—that it had happened that you received the Church’s charge from the hand of a king, that is, a layman—despised the see and immediately withdrew yourself to the discipline of a more remote life.

The venerable Gaudentius, bishop of Apsara, whose friendship I was privileged to enjoy and through whom God had already performed a by no means insignificant miracle, also relinquished the episcopate. Sailing from the Slavic kingdom, he reached the shores of the city of Ancona, not far from which he happily died two years later.

For Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Nola, in order to assist a widow who was seeking her son, laid down the episcopal office [Col. 0425C] and subjected himself to a certain tyrant like a worthless slave.

Moreover, in the ecclesiastical history written by a certain Roman archivist, I remember reading that Martyrius, bishop of Antioch, relinquished his see because of the disobedience of a divided people. It says as follows:

“Returning,” he says, “to Antioch, and finding the people divided, with Zeno favoring them, he renounced the episcopate before the Church, saying: ‘To a clergy not subject to me, a divided people, and a Church lying in squalor, I renounce, while preserving for myself the dignity of the priesthood.’”

There is also inserted there the account that a certain Appio, a patrician who, under the impious Anastasius, had been forcibly consecrated a presbyter in the city of Nicaea [Col. 0425D], was, because he was prudent, made prefect of the praetorium by decree of the most pious emperor Justin, who had succeeded Anastasius to the throne. Thus, indeed, imperial piety corrected what had been presumed under tyrannical rule.

I have judged it necessary to report this so that, since I too have been drawn in by force, it may be inferred from this what ought rightly to be decreed concerning me also, in imitation of ancient authority. Although it may seem to belong to another question to determine whether the fact that he was made prefect of the praetorium from a presbyter should be counted as support for authority or as a precedent against it.

## 424. CHAPTER II. What Blessed Gregory thought concerning relinquishing the episcopate

Moreover, blessed Pope Gregory in no way prohibited bishops from withdrawing from the dignity entrusted to them if necessity seemed to require it. It will suffice for us merely to note the title of the relevant register, lest we burden the letter with sprawling length. For the person who explained the volume of the register says this (Book IX, Letter 41):

“Gregory in no way denied successors to pontiffs who voluntarily renounced their sees, and he judged that afterward they should be adequately supported from the revenues of the Church they had left,” together with the other matters appended there at greater length.

For this reason the same distinguished prelate, concerning the bishop of First Justiniana who was suffering from an illness of the head, issued the following judgment after presenting the discussion:

“If, however,” he says, “the most reverend John should perhaps ask, because of his affliction, to be free from the honor of the episcopate, then, once he has submitted his request in writing, it should be granted.”

Blessed Jerome, moreover, while treating of an idle ruler of the Church, added:

“Immediately,” he says, “he will be struck by the response of the indignant Lord: ‘Wicked servant, why did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest?’” (Luke XIX.) Explaining this at once, the teacher says: “That is, you should have placed it upon the altar, since you were unable to bear it. For while you, a sluggish merchant, hold the coin, you occupied the place of another who could have doubled the money.”

What should I say of the bishop of Lyon, named Justus, who both governed the pontifical office entrusted to him laudably and relinquished it not without praise? [Col. 0426C] A certain violent madman had burst into such insanity of a frenzied mind that he attacked everyone he encountered violently, battered them with blows, cut off the limbs of many, and finally inflicted death upon some. Once, when many were pursuing him, he broke into the doors of the Church and began to defend himself. Necessity then taught him to return to his senses, when he was already being compelled to depart from life. Behold, the holy priest hastened forth at this, placed himself as defender before the man seeking refuge in the Church, and opposed his pursuers.

But those whose relatives had either been killed or mutilated pressed him vehemently and demanded the accused for punishment with relentless insistence. What more need be said? At last matters reached the point that the merciful pontiff, having accepted a surety so that the accused might not succumb to death, as though in satisfaction for the victory, handed him over to their hands [read: “might hand him over”]. But as soon as he came into their power, he was killed.

Immediately the man of God, terrified as though he himself had been the author of this homicide, trembled with fear, abandoned the Church, and afterward lived an eremitical life in the regions of Egypt. I have committed this to writing just as the servant of God, Lord Stephen, who attends upon your presence, related it.

Peter, archbishop, also relinquished the Church of Ravenna; while he was still alive, Honestus succeeded him, during the reign of Otto I, who was then governing the empire.

## 425. 

That distinguished Gregory Nazianzen, whom historians call “God-speaking,” is also said to have abandoned the Church of Constantinople under the religious and catholic emperor Theodosius. If this should perhaps not be believed by us, let the words of the history itself be set down here:

“The holy synod,” it says, “confirmed Gregory the God-speaker in the episcopate of Constantinople and placed him unwillingly upon the throne, since he was laboring greatly and freeing the city from the wound of heresies. When this most wise and blessed man learned that certain people from Egypt were envious of this matter, he withdrew voluntarily from the throne of the imperial city after delivering a conciliatory speech. When he rejected the throne, the emperor and the synod advanced Nectarius.”

These, moreover, are not our words but the words of the history itself.

## CHAPTER III. That souls handed over to the punishments of Gehenna receive refreshment on the Lord’s days

[Col. 0427B]

Nor do I think that what I learned from the account of Humbert, archbishop and a man of the highest authority, should be consigned to silence. For when he was returning from the borders of Apulia, he asserted that in the regions adjacent to Puteoli a rocky and craggy promontory rises between black and foul-smelling waters. From these waters, as they exhale, the most dreadful little birds are customarily seen suddenly arising; from the evening hour of Saturday until the dawn of Monday they are accustomed to appear to human eyes.

During this allotted period they seem to roam freely here and there across the mountain, as though released from bonds. They extend their wings, comb their feathers with their beaks, and, as far as can be understood, relax in the tranquillity of refreshment granted to them for a time. These birds are never seen to feed, nor can they be caught by any skill of a fowler.

At the dawning of Monday morning, behold, a great raven, resembling a vulture, begins to croak heavily after the birds just mentioned, with its hollow throat. They immediately plunge into the waters and hide themselves, and do not again offer themselves to human eyes until, when Saturday is already growing dark, they emerge once more from the chasm of the sulphurous pool.

Hence some declare that they are the souls of human beings assigned to the avenging punishments of Gehenna. They are tormented throughout the rest of the week, but on the Lord’s day, together with the nights immediately before and after it, they enjoy refreshment for the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. The noble poet Prudentius also bears witness to this assertion in his little works of hymns.

But after I had set down in writing this account of the birds and the raven, which sometimes appeared among the black waters and sometimes hid themselves, Desiderius, the religious abbot of the monastery of Cassino, arrived and categorically denied that the matter was so. When I brought him and Humbert, my informant, into conversation with each other, Humbert said:

“I do not defend the testimony of this allegation; nevertheless, I simply reported what I heard from the inhabitants of that place.”

But since these men—Desiderius and Humbert—are of such authority that faith ought to be denied to neither, I too do not rashly affirm what I have written. Rather, whether it is true or not, I decide that it should be left to the investigation of readers.

To come, then, to the matter for which I prefaced these remarks: a bishop—who, if I remember correctly, was in charge of Capreae—saw the greater Pope Benedict, who had already died, sitting as if bodily upon a black horse. When he saw him begin to travel on his way, he said: “Ho! Are you not Pope Benedict, whom we know clearly to be dead?”

“I am that unfortunate man,” he replied.

And the bishop said: “How is it with you, Father?”

“I am afflicted,” he answered, “with grievous torments. Yet I am not deprived of hope of recovery, if help is provided. But go, I ask you, to my brother John, who now occupies the apostolic see, and, having acted as my envoy, announce to him that he should distribute among the poor, for my salvation, especially that sum which is stored in a certain chest. Let him know that I must thus be redeemed, whenever divine mercy has decreed this.

“For the other things that have been given to the needy on my behalf have profited me nothing at all, because they were acquired through plunder and injustices.”

After hearing this, the bishop hastened to Rome and reported to Pope John the words of his deceased brother. He immediately laid aside the burden of the episcopate, put on the monastic habit, and in this way secured salvation for himself through another’s misfortune.

Humbert also related to me the story of Benedict’s namesake [Note: [Col. 0427D] Of the eleventh of that name] and nephew, who, third after him, succeeded John II in the usurpation of the Roman see. A certain vassal, while traveling, happened to pass near a mill while mounted on a horse. Suddenly he saw an enormous monster; at the sight of it sudden terror seized him, and he trembled in astonishment.

The monster seemed to end only in the ears of an ass and in a tail; in all other respects it was a bear. When the traveler froze in terror at this portent and fearfully attempted a headlong flight, the shapeless apparition formed words in a human voice:

“Do not be afraid, man,” it said. “Believe without doubt that I was once a human being, just as you are now. But because I lived like a beast, after the end of my life I deserved to bear the appearance of a beast.”

When he asked who he had been, it replied:

“I was that Benedict in name alone, who recently and unworthily held the summit of the apostolic see.”

When asked what retribution he was now undergoing, he said:

“Now, until the day of judgment, I am dragged and hauled through thorny and filthy places, through sulphurous regions exhaling foul odors and blazing with fires. But after the final judgment, my body and soul together will be swallowed by unremitting torment and by the irrevocable cauldron of the infernal abyss, so that no hope of recovery will remain for me hereafter.”

After this and similar words, he disappeared.

But when I inquire why he was seen in this form, I discover that there is a meaning in what was seen. Since that wretched man, from the very beginning of his accursed pontificate [Col. 0429A] until the end of his life, wallowed in the mud of lust, it was not inappropriately that he appeared to begin with the ears and to end in the tail of an ass. For the ass is a lustful animal, as the prophet indicates when he says concerning those devoted to the impurity of the flesh: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. XXIII).
