As for the fact that he bore the appearance of a bear in his other limbs, this teaches that he lived carnally in every respect. For, as natural philosophers report, when a she-bear gives birth, she does not produce a cub, according to the custom of beasts, but pours forth a lump of flesh. Immediately she shapes what has been expelled by licking and lapping it repeatedly, and thus, with her tongue forming it into her likeness, brings it forth (Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 36).

Rightly, therefore, one who lived lustfully and carnally appeared in the form both of an ass and of a bear. Who would not see how much better it would have been for him to abandon the episcopate and do penance than, by persevering in it until the end of his life, to have utterly lost true life?

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the monk who was condemned in hell and afterward liberated

But since we have introduced this sorrowful matter, let us append another miracle of divine mercy, which had a joyful outcome, from the same Humbert’s accounts.

“In the monastery,” he says, “of Blessed Sylvester, which is situated in the territory of Urbino, a certain monk died. From the beginning of the nocturnal cockcrow until the second hour of the day, his lifeless corpse, washed and bound according to custom, lay in a bier while the brothers sang psalms all around it.

“When, after most of the solemn Mass rites had already been completed, the Agnus Dei was being said according to the rule, suddenly the one who had been lying dead in the midst of them rose when his soul returned. The brothers were astonished and terrified by this entirely new marvel: the man whom they had carried out while performing the funeral rites they now saw to have received his living spirit again.

“But when they had approached more closely and eagerly waited to hear words from his mouth: “Ah, wickedness!”—he began to pour forth curses and insults against God, impiously blaspheming the blessed name of the Savior, spitting with sacrilegious mouth upon the sign of the life-giving cross offered to him for kissing, and not fearing to tear the undefiled Mother of God with shameful reproaches.

“‘Why,’ he said, ‘are you singing psalms for me, or attempting to offer sacrificial offerings? For I descended into the very depths of flaming Tartarus, and there my master and lord Lucifer irrevocably assigned me. He placed upon my head his own bronze crown, glowing perpetually with inextinguishable heat; with the same metal he clothed me in the cloak that he himself wore. The cloak was so long that it flowed down to my ankles, and so fiercely burning that it seemed to emit drops as it melted.’

“When the brothers unanimously urged him to do penance and to disclose his hidden deeds, he anathematized and blasphemed; and not only the remedy of penance but all the mysteries of our redemption he condemned with a raging and sacrilegious mouth. But the monks, devoutly returning to the ever-victorious weapons of prayer, began, casting off their garments, to strike their bodies with scourges, beat their breasts with their fists, and labor at psalmody and every kind of prayer within their power.

“When all the brothers were thus engaged in mournful prayers and fasting and were suspended in expectation of divine mercy, at last the splendor of heavenly power flashed forth. Behold, the desperate man, who had been swallowed by the gaping chasm of the sea, returned to the surface. He praised the omnipotence of God the Savior, renounced the wicked deceptions of Satan, adored the cross, and begged for penance.

“He confessed that after renouncing the world he had fallen into fornication, which until then he had revealed absolutely to no one by any act of confession. Praising and blessing God, he lived until the following day, and, wonderfully restored to his Creator, departed from this world in a holy confession.

“Thus, indeed, the fruit of threefold prayer blossomed: that prayer seized its prey from the very entrails of Gehenna and placed a living stone, taken from the straw of the flames, in the structure of the heavenly Jerusalem.”

Archbishop Humbert related these things to me; his words appear to be founded upon apostolic truth.

## CHAPTER V. That the episcopate is a difficult office

[Col. 0430C]

If, then, the man who had fallen while a monk and who had to give an account only of his own soul deserved to be condemned by so terrible a sentence, with what frame of mind can any unworthy bishop like me be secure, when he is answerable for as many souls as perish through his negligence or evil examples?

Since it is evident that some have voluntarily stripped themselves of episcopal rule even because of a slight impediment, it is enough to insert one example here. It is readily found in the history that Cassiodorus translated from Greek into Latin. We write here merely the unadorned words of that history, so that we may remove the scruple of doubt from those who hesitate.

“Silvanus,” it says, “was first a rhetorician, a disciple of the sophist Troilus, and, having become a perfect Christian, was devoted to the monastic life. He disdained to wear the teacher’s cloak. After this, Bishop Atticus seized him and ordained him bishop of Philippopolis.

“But after spending three years in Thrace, and being unable to bear the cold, since his body was very weak and delicate, he asked Atticus to appoint him to another place, saying that he avoided those regions for no other reason than the cold. When another had been ordained in his place, Silvanus remained in Constantinople, perfectly observing the monastic life. He was so free from all arrogance that, often, amid the great multitude of the city, he went about despised and wearing sandals.

“After some time had passed, the bishop of the Church of Troy died, and the Trojans came seeking a bishop. While Atticus was considering whom he ought to ordain, it happened suddenly that Silvanus came to greet him. When Atticus saw him, he immediately ceased deliberating.

“Then he said to Silvanus: ‘You no longer have any excuse by which you can escape ecclesiastical cares. Troy does not have cold weather; behold, a place suited by God to your body is ready for you. Prepare yourself, therefore, and depart immediately for Troy.’

“Thus Silvanus departed.”

But if anyone should perhaps accuse him of rashness, condemn him for having despised the office entrusted to him merely because of the cold, and blame him for moving elsewhere for the sake of bodily comfort, let him hear of the notable miracle that later shone forth through him, and let him at least cease to tear the just man with the envious bite of reproach.

For the history continues:

“After this had happened, I shall recount the miracle that occurred through his hands. A very large ship, which had carried enormous columns, had recently been built on the shore of Troy. When they wished to draw it down to the sea, it could not be moved at all, despite the many ropes and the people pulling it. When this had continued for many days, they suspected that the ship was being held back by a demon.

“Then they came to Silvanus the bishop and asked him to offer a prayer at the place, believing that in this way the ship could be drawn along [the text has: ‘it could be drawn there,’ or something similar]. But he said in humble speech that he was a sinner and asserted that this was the work of some just man, not his own.

“When they entreated him, he came to the shore. After praying, he touched one of the ropes and ordered them to continue their labor with effort. Then, when they pushed briefly, the ship moved swiftly into the sea.

“This miracle caused all the provincials to hold that man in reverence. Indeed, if this Silvanus had sinned by abandoning the episcopate and moving to another place, he would have appeared not marvelous through the display of a sign’s power but rather pitiable through guilt. The power of the miracle therefore bore witness to his holiness.

“Moreover, if, as is said, the episcopate may not be abandoned for any reason, what are we to make of the fact that so many holy bishops are found throughout the various volumes of histories to have transferred themselves from their own Churches to others, since they plainly left their own sees before moving to the others? Most of them, when they rejected the rule entrusted to them, did not yet know at all that they would transfer themselves to another.”

Certainly, reason itself teaches that it is a lesser matter to withdraw from the episcopate altogether than to transfer from one see to another. Modern sophistry, therefore, shall not restrain me from doing what the examples of venerable Fathers urge. Indeed, if that blessed Silvanus abandoned the episcopate without reproach merely because of bodily discomfort, why should I be accused of transgression for forsaking pastoral governance, when I am daily entangled in the affairs of secular cares, growing lukewarm in the fervor of divine love and falling into the death-dealing coldness of a sluggish soul? Scripture says: “As a cistern makes water cold, so wickedness makes the soul cold” (Jer. VI). I often remember having been so inflamed by the fire of divine love that I immediately longed to break through the enclosure of the flesh and, released as it were from the mire and the darkness of prison, yearned from the depths of my being for the light of eternity. For at that time I had, as the Lord promises through the prophet, a heart of flesh—or, as it seemed to me, a heart of wax (Ezek. XI). This, melted by the flame of heavenly desire, frequently moistened my tearful face with abundant tears. I dreaded hearing, and even more dreaded uttering, anything that did not summon one to Christ; and I counted all the trifles and babblings—or *naeniae*, “dirges”—of secular speech as the snarling jaws of dogs or the bites of serpents. Often, with the mind’s immediate gaze, I saw Christ fastened with nails and hanging on the cross, and eagerly watched the blood dripping down into the mouth held beneath it.

But if I should try to commit to writing whatever I was permitted to contemplate—whether concerning the most sacred humanity of our Redeemer or concerning that ineffable vision of heavenly glory—the day would pass before the sequence of the matter could be set down. Now, however, hard and stony, continually worn down by external business, I do not dissolve into the tears of inward compunction. Indeed, I often place my hand upon my breast and show it, like a purulent wound, to the physician of souls, crying out and shouting in the deepest supplication: “You who,” I say, “have illumined the Tartarean caverns with the rays of your divinity, drive away the darkness of this heart, and shine upon it serenely with the light of your truth.”

But Jesus sometimes stands beside the blind man crying out by the roadside and restores his sight (Matt. X; [Col. 0432C] Luke XVIII); sometimes he passes by, as though he did not hear the man crying out in idleness, and thus the wretched blind man nevertheless remains in his blindness. I—I, alas!—like another Samson (Judg. XVI), lament that I have lost the gifts of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, as though they were the seven locks of hair; and, with the eyes not of my forehead but of my heart gouged out, I turn the millstone of secular cares. I am that Zedekiah to whom the Babylonian king, first killing his sons, took away the fruits of good works (IV Kings XXV), and afterward tore out his eyes when he deprived him of the inner light of contemplation.

If, then, that holy man Silvanus did not hesitate to leave Thrace because of mere bodily discomfort, why should I not abandon Rome to avoid so many wounds to my soul? Yet it is not entirely harmless even to my body, since it is productive of fevers, and not merely occasional ones. Thus I remember that I once composed this tetrastich:

### VERSES ON ROME

Rome, devourer of men, subdues the lofty necks of men;

Rome, producer of fevers, is exceedingly rich in the harvest of death.

Roman fevers are faithful by an unchanging law.

Whomever they once seize, they scarcely leave alive.

Detained, therefore, by adversity both of soul and of body, let the fugitive return to his lord; let him spurn the pigs and their husks and let the son return to his father’s embrace (Luke XV); let him grow warm again with Samson’s former strength as his hair grows back (Judg. XVI), so that he may put on the first robe that he had lost and, his strength restored, lay low those who had conquered him.

## CHAPTER VI. On a Simoniacal Bishop Who Could Not Name the Holy Spirit

Meanwhile, we judge it worthwhile to insert here also what we learned from the report of Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church. For while he was still performing only the office of subdeacon, Pope Victor sent him as *apocrisarius*—papal representative—to Gaul, and there he convened a synod. At that synod, by the authority of the Apostolic See, he deposed six bishops entangled in various crimes. Among them was a certain bishop who, because he had insinuated himself into the summit of the episcopate through the simoniacal heresy, was unable, however hard he tried, to express the Holy Spirit in words. He pronounced “Father” and “Son” quite readily and easily; but when he reached “Holy Spirit,” his tongue immediately faltered and at last remained rigid. Rightly, then, while he bought the Holy Spirit, he lost him, so that the one excluded from his soul was consequently far from his tongue as well. Overcome by this impediment, he relinquished the episcopal office. But far be it from me to judge this man worthy of the catalogue of holy men who gave up their pontifical insignia for the love of Christ.

Since mention has once been made of that most prudent man, I shall not be silent about another notable matter he reported, even if it does not greatly concern the subject at hand. For while he was preaching in the Aretine Church, venerable pope, in your presence, about estates unjustly possessed by Churches, he appropriately introduced the following example:

“In the regions of the Germans,” he said, “a certain count, rich and exceedingly powerful—but, a marvel to find among men of that rank, of good reputation and innocent life, as far as human judgment could assess him—died nearly ten years ago. After his death, a certain religious man descended in spirit to the regions below and saw the aforesaid count standing at the highest step of a certain ladder. He said that the ladder appeared to be erected amid the hissing and crackling flames of avenging fire, and established to receive all who would descend from that same lineage of counts.

“There was a grim and monstrous abyss, infinitely wide and sunk into the depths, from which the ladder rose upward. A succession of those being burned was thus linked together in order: whenever a new one of them arrived, he occupied the first step of the ladder, while the one found there, together with all the others, descended to the bottom of the steps nearest to them. And when, at intervals of time, more and more men of the same family came to that ladder after the death of the flesh, those already there immediately gave way and, compelled by the unavoidable necessity of judgment, moved down to the lower places.

“While the man who witnessed these things was asking the cause of this dreadful condemnation, and especially why that count of his own time was being punished, since he had lived so justly, so properly, and so honorably, he heard: ‘Because of a certain estate belonging to the Church of Metz, which his great-grandfather had taken from blessed Stephen, and which this man, the tenth heir, inherited from him, all these have been assigned to the same punishment. And just as a common fault of avarice joined them in sinning, so likewise a common punishment has bound them together in enduring the atrocious torments of the fire.’”

Let unjust possessors of ecclesiastical property take heed of this and exercise careful caution, lest, while they gorge themselves on the revenues of others, they later feed the devouring flames with their own marrow. Since we wish to serve not so much the strict rule of writers as the edification of our brothers, we have inserted this matter as something apparently foreign to the intention of the work we had begun, so that, in a certain sense, we might bind some drifting object with the cord of our pen, lest oblivion carry it away entirely.

For when someone goes out fishing, if chance suddenly brings him a wild animal or a bird, he catches it, even though he had planned nothing concerning hunting or fowling. Moreover, so that evangelical authority might not be lacking from our assertions, when our Savior approaches the house of the ruler of the synagogue to raise his daughter, he heals a woman suffering from an issue of blood (Matt. IX), as though apart from the intention with which he had begun. What wonder, then, if we writers sometimes interrupt what we have begun, yet do not abandon it, inserting something which we nevertheless perceive to pertain to edification?

Indeed, this too does not depart from our purpose. If that man perished because of one small possession of the Church, what should be thought of the man who, under the title of bishop, does not relinquish the whole Church, although he presides over it unworthily? Let us now, after this digression, return to our subject.

Nor shall I be silent about what is related in the *Tripartite History* concerning blessed Milesius the martyr. Indeed, so that it may provide fuller assurance to readers, I shall append the very words of the running text:

“Then also,” it says, “the bishop named Milesius was crowned with martyrdom. At first he served as a soldier among the Persians; afterward, having abandoned military service, he zealously adopted the apostolic way of life. For it is said that, when he had been ordained bishop in a Persian city, he often suffered much, was beaten and dragged about, but endured everything with manly courage. Since he could persuade no one there to become a Christian, he took it very grievously, cursed the city, and departed from it.

“After a short time, when the leading men of that same place sinned against the king, an army arrived with three hundred elephants, overthrew the city, and, as though plowing a desolate region, committed it to seed. Bishop Milesius, carrying only a pouch containing the sacred book of the Gospels, went on to Jerusalem to pray, and from there to Egypt, to see the monks living there.

“The Syrians, who wrote down his deeds and life, testify to what kind of saint he was and what a worker of miracles. Behold this man: he set aside the rights of the governance entrusted to him, yet not only incurred no guilt of condemnation, but even obtained the power to perform miraculous works.”

## CHAPTER VII. On Arnulphus, Bishop of Metz

Certainly, as we survey the breadth of histories with a curious gaze, blessed Arnulphus, bishop of the Church of Metz, encounters us like a golden star. By the rays of his example he dispels the darkness of our ignorance, gives unconquerable strength to our arguments, and unties every knot of uncertainty concerning this chapter.

As we have learned from the truthful report of brothers who testify that they have read his written history, he held the office of duke in the kingdom of Lothair, not far from Flanders. He was also the father of Pepin and the grandfather of King Charlemagne. When, kindled by the ardor of the divine Spirit, he set aside his affection for his wife and sons and exchanged the splendors of worldly glory for the glorious poverty of Christ, he hastened toward the desert. It happened that, while traveling, he had to cross the river called the Moselle.

When he had reached nearly the middle of the bridge thrown across it, where the river channel ran deeper, he threw his ring into the stream under this condition of a pact: “When I recover this ring, drawn from the foaming waves, then without doubt I shall trust that I have been released from the bonds of all my sins.” Immediately afterward he sought the desert, where he lived for no short time, dead to himself and to the world.

Meanwhile, after the bishop of the Church of Metz who then held office had died, divine providence raised blessed Arnulphus to the rights of pastoral governance. Although he continued in the Church to abstain from eating meat, as he had become accustomed to doing in the desert, a fish was once brought to him as a gift. When the cook disemboweled it, he found Arnulphus’s ring in its entrails and hastened joyfully to offer it to his master.

When the blessed bishop saw it, he immediately recognized it. He marveled not so much at the vein of the gleaming metal as at the fact that, through divine mercy, he had obtained forgiveness for his guilt. What heightens the wonder is that the journey from the bridge where the ring had been thrown to the place where the fish was presented to the venerable bishop takes two days.

Then the man of God, absolved from his sins, was all the more tightly bound by divine fear. He considered himself more greatly indebted because he saw that the goodness of heavenly mercy toward him was greater. Choosing a successor for himself, he again sought the desert; there, having laid down pastoral care, he lived until his blessed death. Thus that distinguished man taught us by what he did that we too should do likewise.

Moreover, scarcely fifteen days have yet passed since I saw the venerable man Farnulphus voluntarily stripped of the administration of ecclesiastical governance. He had held a see in the Apulian city of Cisternum; he abandoned it, and for nearly seven years has not ceased to afflict himself by fastening two iron bands of considerable weight around his chest and belly. He uses wine either never or rarely, and is worn down by frequent fasts. This great man urged me to renounce the episcopate no less by his words than he challenged me by his example.

Furthermore, the broad West does not fail to know how holy and how remarkable in life Hildulphus, archbishop of Trier, was. As the history of his deeds testifies, he entreated Jacob, bishop of the city of Leuca—now called Toul—to provide him with a suitable solitary place in which to dwell. He first chose a successor for himself; then, building a monastery, he proceeded under the strict rule of monastic discipline. The many miracles performed through him there testify with a clarity brighter than daylight that this man of God, after abandoning the episcopate, not only incurred no stain of guilt but also offered God a sacrifice of sweet fragrance.

What shall I say of Deodatus, a man of supreme holiness, likewise bishop of the Church of Trier? As an authentic history relates, he obtained from Girbaldus, the most holy bishop of that same city of Leuca, a place in the Vosges forest. There he renounced the world, lived commendably, established monasteries, and, after a long campaign in Christ’s service, entered the senate of life crowned with laurels.

What of Gondebertus, the renowned archbishop of Sens? Burning with heavenly desire, he abandoned the Church entrusted to him and built the monastery of Sens in a place called Grandiavum, giving it its name from that Church which he had left. I had resolved not to exceed the number twenty, but I cannot allow what lies before my eyes to remain concealed.

Finally, leaving the others aside, let us turn to an example from our own household. Lambertus of venerable memory, who was the third bishop to preside over the Florentine Church before you, spurned the office of the pontificate and subjected himself to monastic discipline. Your own beatitude’s sublimity knows how glorious a reputation fills the mouths of men concerning him and how sweetly the fragrance of his good name perfumes the nostrils of their minds.

Blessed Nonnus the martyr, also called Hippolytus, must likewise not pass unnoticed by our memory. After he had converted thirty thousand Saracens to the faith of Christ through highly effective preaching; after he had also called blessed Pelagia from the brothels to the chastity of the Church; and finally after he had lucidly explained several books of sacred exposition, he at last abandoned the episcopate. He departed from the region of Antioch, from which he originated, and sought the Roman territories.

When blessed Aurea had completed her martyrdom at the city of Ostia, with a stone fastened to her neck and cast into the sea, blessed Nonnus gathered her holy body with devout reverence and buried it with every care. The same persecutor, named Ulpius, then ordered him to be plunged into a pit full of water beside the channel of the Tiber. After he had completed his triumphant martyrdom, Christian devotion buried his body in the city called Portus. Immediately a voice was heard, like that of infants crying out for nearly an hour: “Thanks be to God.” Since he deserved such an end to his life, it clearly became evident that, when he abandoned the episcopate, he incurred no offense before God.

In our own times also, the bishop of Penne voluntarily abandoned the pontifical see and submitted himself to his successor with the utmost sincere devotion. His successor himself told me that the former bishop was so subject to him in obedience and humility as though he had never remembered having held primacy over anyone.

In our age as well, Liutulphus, bishop of Cales, cast himself down from episcopal dignity and handed the Church over to his successor, who still survives. Thus, if he did not lack courage, he secured for himself the free opportunity to perform penance. Happy, surely, is the man who arranges the condition of his life in this mortality so that he may lament in penitence what he has done wrong. Happy, I say, is the prudent man who casts far from him whatever obstructs his path to truth. For whatever we have committed in this life is either corrected here, in proportion to the sin, through scourges, or is unquestionably reserved for future punishments.

## CHAPTER VIII. On a Convert Who Was Beaten by Saints Andrew and Gregory

Therefore it is not out of place to insert here briefly what we have learned from the trustworthy report of the brothers. In the monastery called Clivus Scauri, which blessed Gregory founded within the walls of the city of Rome, a certain boy was offered by his parents so that thereafter he might serve God.

When he later grew older, he left the monastery and returned to the world, joining a wife to himself in a marriage bond. Then, when he had reached young adulthood, he was suddenly struck in the throat by divine judgment. As the affliction of his illness grew worse, he began to approach death. At last, a wicked fugitive, he asked to be carried back to the monastery; there he received repentance for his evil ways and the monastic habit.

While his wife and several others were attending him as he lay in bed, he began to groan heavily, uttering howls; and as though he were suffering from delirium, he babbled in disordered cries. When they asked why he would not rest, he said: “Do you not see blessed Andrew the apostle and holy Gregory jointly scourging me with the sharpest blows?”

Howling again and emitting mournful cries, he would breathe for a little while and then say: “They have just beaten me because I left the monastery and took a wife.” Again, after weeping and wailing, he would rest for a moment and say: “They have just chastised me because I not only gave nothing to the poor who begged, especially to the Scots, but also, shamefully, frequently mocked them.”

Again repeating his shrieks and groans, he asserted: “I borrowed six coins from a certain poor widow and refused to repay them. As many paces as she labored in coming to me to demand them, so many blows I have now suffered from the hands of the saints while they beat me together. But so that you may know that I am not lying, the day after tomorrow, at the sixth hour, I shall depart from this world.”

It was then Friday. During the night when the Lord’s Day dawned—the day called Palm Sunday—he suddenly sprang from his bed, to everyone’s amazement, seized the scapular and hair shirt that were beside him, and immediately entered the church of blessed Andrew, bewildered and hurrying. There, lying prostrate, he said to the brothers present: “Behold, having been scourged by the blows of the saints, I depart from the body so purified as I came forth clean from the font of baptism.”

During the sacred solemnities of Mass, when the Passion reading had scarcely been completed, he gave his spirit back to God at the hour he had foretold. When, according to custom, his body was stripped for washing, bruises and marks were visible everywhere on his limbs, as though his body had been struck with actual rods.

But what wonder is it if the saints of God, who are to judge the world, pursued the guilt of a rational human being, when, as we learned there, they also demanded vengeance from a brute animal? In the same monastery there is a crypt called that of Blessed Gregory. There, among other things, his spring still overflows with clear, cold water from which he drank, and his stone bed can still be seen, where he rested in summer.

Once, a pregnant little dog entered this crypt by chance, either to drink because it was overheated or, rather, to give birth in that place. Before it reached the water, however, as soon as it came near the aforesaid bed, it collapsed and died.

With what great dread, then, must divine judgments be weighed by human beings, when God exercises such terrible discipline even upon animals without reason? If almighty God did not wish an innocent little dog even to touch the plain water of this holy place, with what displeasure do we suppose he tolerates a perverse person approaching the sacred altars to receive his body and blood? Yet when every wicked person provokes and goads God by his evil acts, divine patience does not immediately inflict vengeance upon him, although it reserves him for everlasting punishment.

## CHAPTER IX. On Pandulphus and John, Princes Condemned in Hell

While I am plowing out this section of my composition with my pen, behold, Desiderius, the devout abbot of the monastery of Cassino, arrives. Just as he is joined by the kinship of his name to blessed Daniel, so the testimony of truth does not separate him from that saint. He tells me something which reason itself persuades me to write down.

“A servant of God,” he said, “lived as a solitary in the region of Naples, on a precipitous rock beside the public road. While he was chanting psalms at night and opened the window of his cell to observe the hours, behold, he saw many black men, like Ethiopians, traveling along the road and driving pack animals laden with hay over a long distance.

“When he inquisitively asked who they were and why they were transporting this fodder for beasts, they replied: ‘We are malignant spirits, and we are preparing not fodder to feed animals but rather fuel with which to burn human beings. For we are awaiting shortly Pandulphus, prince of Capua, who is already lying ill, and John, master of the soldiers of the city of Naples, who is still alive and well.’”

Immediately the man of God went eagerly to the aforesaid John and faithfully related everything he had seen and heard. At that time the Emperor Otto II was hastening toward Calabria to fight the Saracens. After hearing these things, John said: “Now we must respectfully meet the emperor and, together with him, give prudent consideration to the state of this land. After the emperor’s departure, I promise that I shall both abandon the world and assume the habit of the monastic order.”

To test whether what the man had reported was true, he immediately sent a messenger to the walls of Capua. When the messenger arrived, he found Pandulphus already dead. The master of the soldiers, John himself, survived by scarcely fifteen days before the emperor reached those regions.

After his death, Mount Vesuvius—from which Gehenna frequently belches forth—burst into flames, clearly demonstrating that the hay prepared by the demons was nothing other than the fire of a savage conflagration owed to wicked and reprobate men. For whenever a reprobate rich man dies in those regions, fire appears to erupt from that mountain; and such a mass of sulphurous resin immediately flows from Vesuvius that it forms a torrent and, rushing downward, descends into the sea. There one may see bodily what John says in the Apocalypse concerning the reprobate: “Their portion will be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (Apoc. XIX, 20).

Indeed, the grandfather of the Salernitan prince Guaimar—the same Guaimar who, not many years ago, was killed by the swords of his own men on account of his many acts of violence and tyrannical oppressions—once suddenly saw black and sulphurous flames erupting from Mount Vesuvius in the distance. He immediately said: “Without doubt some wicked rich man is about to die and descend to the underworld.”

But, O blind mind of the reprobate man—or rather, O dreadful judgment of the Creator over us!—on the following night, while he was lying securely with a prostitute, he expired. She, unaware of what had happened, as she later reported, endured him for some time and scarcely at last managed to throw from herself not a man but the lifeless corpse of the prostitute’s companion.

## CHAPTER X. On the Priest Who Perished on Mount Vesuvius

Moreover, a certain priest in the Neapolitan region, wishing to learn with certainty what he was not permitted to know, rashly resolved to approach the place where the infernal abyss was belching forth most fiercely. He celebrated the solemnities of Mass and, thus vested and as though armed, set out on his journey. But when he approached more boldly than people ordinarily did, he did not appear again, since afterward he was unable to return.

Another priest had left his mother ill at Benevento. While he was accompanying his master through the Neapolitan territories, he gazed at the flames as they poured forth and heard the cry of someone lamenting, which he recognized without doubt as the voice of his mother. He noted the hour and then discovered most clearly that his mother had died at that time.

To return, then, to what came before: it should now suffice to have enumerated twice twelve holy bishops who, burning with the fire of divine love, resolved to desist from ecclesiastical administration so that, freed from earthly affairs, they might cling to God more closely and more familiarly.

These venerable bishops, like the twenty-four elders in truth, fall down before the One seated upon the throne and adore the One who lives forever and ever (Apoc. IV), casting their crowns before the Lord’s throne. They cast their crowns before the Lord’s throne when, for his love, they lay aside the ornaments of their own dignity. In their likeness, they also hold golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, because, in order to offer prayers to God as a purer fragrance of sweetness, they strive to separate themselves from all the actions of this world.

If I were not avoiding the weariness of a longer composition, I might appropriately add blessed Athanasius to these examples. Under the Arian Emperor Constantius, he withdrew from the Church and concealed himself in the prison-cell of a certain holy woman. There he remained hidden from all mortals, except his hostess, for twice three years.

I could also number among these the most blessed Martin, who in a certain sense abandoned the right of episcopal office, since for nearly three lustrums—fifteen years—before his death he completely absented himself from synodal councils so that he might live more familiarly with God.

I might also fittingly add blessed Gaudiosus, who, while holding the see of the Church of Abitina, which belongs to the African diocese, fled with Saint Quodvultdeus and the other bishops when the Vandals were ravaging Africa, and founded a monastery in the city of Parthenope. If he fled to escape the swords of the Vandals, how much more ought I to flee the snares of eternal death?

Sergius, metropolitan of Damascus, could likewise appropriately be joined to these examples. He abandoned his Church for the love of Christ and came to Rome as a pilgrim. Finding the basilica of the blessed Boniface and Alexius almost deprived of priestly services, he approached Benedict, bishop of the Roman See, and obtained by his prayers permission to establish the monastic rule there. Living religiously in that place for a long time afterward, he ended his life.

Blessed Gregory also, as is found in the history of his register, gave three bishops—namely, the bishop of Justiniana Prima, the bishop of Ariminum, and a third—free permission to abandon their Churches because of a mere illness of the head. He reserved for them the necessary stipend from the Churches they had left and did not refuse to appoint successors in their place. Anyone who has read the letters sent to Anatolius, subdeacon of Constantinople, and to the bishops Marinianus of Ravenna and Aetherius will have no doubt about this.

## CHAPTER XI. On Three Other Bishops Who Likewise Abandoned Their Churches

Behold: to the twenty-four bishops whom we enumerated above we join these three who, by the authority of Blessed Gregory, abandoned their Churches. We add blessed Gaudiosus and Quodvultdeus, and also Sergius, metropolitan of Damascus. Thus we unquestionably find thirty bishops who renounced their sees for the love of God.

Let the investigator of ancient times, let any researcher of histories or annals, tell me: when so many holy Fathers abandoned pastoral custody, did any pontiff of the Apostolic See ever oppose them? Did anyone rebuke any one of them through written letters of legation, or condemn him by synodal judgment? Let him speak, I say—or, since he can find nothing to assert, let him bite his bold tongue with his teeth and not gnaw at me with unjust slanders.

Did not Pope Benedict the Younger [Note: [Col. 0441D] The ninth of that name.], whom we mentioned above, also deprive himself of the administration of the apostolic summit and establish as his successor Gregory [Note: [Col. 0442D] The sixth of that name.], who was called Gratianus, in the Roman See? Later, when a synodal council debated the matter in the presence of Emperor Henry, the one who had accepted the office was deposed because simony had intervened; the one who had relinquished it was not excommunicated.

Furthermore, we can also bring Blessed Benedict forward as an example for imitation, like some great pontiff, since there is no doubt that he abandoned the governance entrusted to him.

Leo, abbot of Nonantula, has also returned to my memory. While he still wore the clerical appearance and had already returned from Jerusalem after fulfilling his devotion, he arranged his life so that he possessed nothing except one single donkey. Each day he traversed the surrounding woods and pastures with it, gathering materials with which he might provide the brothers with *anitergia* [the term is uncertain] for the necessities of nature. When this glorious work of his hands had been completed, and he had finished the Psalter together with that exercise, the holy priest immediately approached to offer the sacred mysteries to God, not without many tears.

Later, when he was forcibly drawn into the governance of the monastery, he used to say—a lament which I too frequently utter in misery: “I held Jesus by the feet, and now, wretched and blind, I turn the millstones of the world.” Scarcely two years had passed when he returned the pastoral staff to Otto, who then held the scepter of the empire. Thereafter, remaining with Saint Boniface within the walls of Rome, he secured for himself nothing from the remainder of his life except the provisions of eternal life. Later, when a blind man came to his burial, he is said to have been restored to his former sight.

But lest, through a lack of bishops, we be thought to have turned to less suitable examples among abbots, let me cite one not bearing a different title: Leo, archbishop of Ravenna. As soon as paralysis seized his mouth, he rejected the episcopal see and, thus deprived of it, survived for nearly four years. Frederick succeeded him while Otto III was reigning prosperously, and Leo assigned him Church properties sufficient for his support.

Supported, therefore, by the authority of these and other Fathers, I irrevocably renounce both the episcopate and the monasteries into your holy hands, and I cut off from myself every right to raise any question or make any demand in the future. Since, on account of my countless sins, I am unworthy to persist in ecclesiastical dignity, may divine mercy grant me, venerable father, through your holy prayers, to remain for whatever life is left to me in mourning and penitence.

For I confess that, being both criminal and vicious, I attained this honor—and not without reproach—and lived in it blameworthily. Therefore it seemed safer to me to depose myself voluntarily than to undergo, before the tribunal of the terrible Judge and in the sight of all angels and human beings, the sentence of deposition under eternal condemnation.

But let these matters now suffice. May almighty God, who by the incomprehensible plan of his providence has both cast me down from the ambition of holding governance and raised you to the summit of ecclesiastical dignity, inspire your holy heart, whose inhabitant he is, to send me through sacred letters such commands as may accord with my vows and my desires.

[Col. 0442D] Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0441]

### 441–442. TWENTIETH OPUSCULUM. APOLOGETIC WORK ON THE RENUNCIATION OF THE EPISCOPATE

#### ARGUMENT

Blessed Peter Damian excuses himself before the pontiff for having, conscious of his own weakness, renounced the episcopate. Since no one should ascribe this to inconstancy—for it is not permitted to lay down an office once undertaken—he gives a brief reply and demonstrates, by the examples of many Fathers who declined to make use of the episcopate when it was conferred upon them, that he adopted the safer counsel of freeing himself from so great a burden. He further declares that presiding over others and carrying out the episcopal office is a difficult and exceedingly laborious task.

[Col. 0441D] To Hildebrand, most beloved elect of the Apostolic See and rod of Assyria: Peter, sinful monk, offers service.

[Col. 0442D] They say that those who have labored in investigating the natures of things report this as naturally implanted in lynxes: when they look back over their shoulders, they immediately forget the one who went before them. At once, plainly, the mind too loses whatever the eye has ceased to see. And although this beast surpasses every other animal in the sharpness of its vision, so that it is even able to penetrate stone walls, it suffers from this defect: whatever it may be from which it has once turned its eyes, it does not afterward recall to memory.

I would say that you bear some likeness to these animals, were I not restrained by reverence for your greatness. It is astonishing that such keen prudence—or, what is far more glorious, such sincere and fervent charity, which receives me warmly when I am present—should never deign to visit me, when absent, either by letter or by word. Moreover, since I do not deserve to receive letters from you, if I were dealing with anyone else I would say that the letter of charity which the Apostle mentions is not written among you on tablets of fleshly hearts (II Cor. III), but has, as they say, been erased from the innermost wax. Yet while I consider what I should say, I must no less consider to whom I am speaking. Therefore, since I do not dare to make use of the freedom of speech, I place my finger upon my mouth. I shall now briefly add what my mind is more strongly inclined toward, bringing this complaint of protest to an end.

# APOLOGETICUS ON THE RESIGNATION OF THE EPISCOPATE

## CHAPTER I. That Peter Damian had charge of two bishoprics

Blessed is the almighty dispensation of the Creator, because, when I recently ascended to you, burdened by the weight of two bishoprics—one to govern, the other to visit—I crossed the precipitous ridges of the Alps; and then, casting off the burden of tribulation, relieved and free, I returned like a fugitive, by right of return, to my beloved solitude.

It pleases me, therefore, with a certain vigor of mind, as though I were moving feet long chafed by fetters and lifting necks subdued by harsh chains, to sing joyfully that prophetic verse: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm CXV, 17).

You plainly know, and you remember, that these burdens were thrust upon me, not undertaken by me; and, so to speak, I did not enter the net—I was violently covered by it. Therefore, when an opportunity arose, I willingly cast off a burden which I had not previously assumed of my own accord.

And because you are the apostolic see, because you are the Roman Church, it seemed right to me, in laying down and returning what I had been unable to carry, not to approach a structure of stones, but rather those in whom the sacrament of that Church itself is alive. During the Jewish persecution, wherever the apostles were, there the primitive Church was said to be. Now too, when that Simon—the old moneychanger—repairs hammers and anvil, when he usurps the city of Rome as though it were his workshop for a pestilential commerce conducted by moneyers, wherever Peter, fleeing with you, draws you, there he plainly shows all that the Roman Church is.

Thus, when I resolved to renounce ecclesiastical government to you, I did not err, because I worthily restored to the Roman Church—which you are—what belonged to it. And, to confess that I have confessed myself to you, for this renunciation a penance of a hundred years has consequently been imposed upon me, namely through those remedies established by monastic rules. If this seems insufficient, add more yourselves; even commit me, if you wish, to imprisonment. After so many excesses of wandering and harmful freedom, what remains except that the discipline of confinement and silence should restrain me?

But perhaps that flattering tyrant who has always pitied me with Neronian mercy, who has caressed me by boxing my ears, who, to put it so, has certainly stroked me with an eagle’s claw, will burst forth into this complaint: “Look, he seeks a hiding place and, under the guise of penance, tries to evade access to Rome; he contrives to gain leisure from disobedience, and while the others rush into battle, he seeks for himself the shadowy shelter of a degenerate life.”

But I answer this holy Satan of mine with what the sons of Reuben and Gad are known to have replied to Moses their leader: “We shall go armed and girded into battle before the sons of Israel until we have brought them into their places. Our little ones, and whatever we may possess, shall be in fortified cities because of the ambushes of the inhabitants. We shall not return to our homes until the sons of Israel possess their inheritance, nor shall we seek anything beyond the Jordan, because we already have our possession on its eastern side” (Numbers XXXI).

Thus, to accompany you, I take up arms; but, with Christ as your leader, once you have gained victory after the battles, I shall immediately withdraw. I shall say to the Lord’s chosen what Barzillai the Gileadite, descending from Rogelim, also said to King David: “Your servant will go forward a little way with you from the Jordan; I beg you, let your servant return, and let me die in my own city” (II Kings XIX).

## CHAPTER II. That an episcopate may sometimes be resigned

Perhaps it will be objected to me here that a government once accepted may not lawfully be abandoned. To this I briefly state what I think: many do not relinquish the rights of the pontificate, and they are on the wrong path; but concerning all whom we read to have resigned with right intention, there is sure hope that they rejoice in eternal fellowship with Christ.

Nor do we say this so that an episcopate may be abandoned indiscriminately, unless, that is, great necessity compels it. Indeed, blessed Valerius, while providing himself with a successor, enthroned the great Augustine as bishop of the Church of Hippo. Lucidus, bishop of Ficoclensis, when he realized that his own death was approaching, hastened to the harbor of the cenobitic order and exchanged the episcopal ornaments of his dignity for monastic garments. And so that you may know what this conversion gained for him, as the authentic history of the Register testifies, at the very moment of his departure the grace of the Holy Spirit shone most joyfully upon his face. Before he died, blessed Andrew the Apostle also appeared to him and announced at what hour he would depart from the body.

What shall I say of the blessed martyr Adalbert, who, having set aside the chair of the Church of Bohemia and putting on the monastic habit, deserved to find the triumphant crown of martyrdom? And, to pass over the others deliberately, there was a certain holy penitent whose name for the moment escapes me. Nearly seven years after resigning his episcopate, he was finally ordered, by an angel who visited him, to return to the episcopate. He refused until, at the urging of that same angel, blessed Remigius arrived with haste. Thus, fearing lest deception should perhaps creep in, he yielded even to human authority, although earlier he had stood firm against an angelic command.

There was also that bishop of Sabina who abandoned the pontifical throne and, scorning priestly dignity, built the monastery of Farfa. An ancient tradition testifies what a noble man in Christ he was, celebrating the marks of his holiness; and modern devotion bears witness as well, frequently commemorating him piously in blessing. How many remained in that same see, both before and afterward, until the end of their lives, yet brought God no fruit so laborious!

Nor will I pass over you, fortunate Bonitus, who, taking advantage of this one circumstance—that it had happened that you received the Church’s charge from the hand of a king, that is, a layman—scorned the chair and immediately devoted yourself to the discipline of a more remote life. What, I ask, would this man have done if he himself had endured the torments by which our bishops are afflicted? If troops of shield-bearers and lancers had gathered behind the back of a mounted man? If armed companies had crowded around him on every side, stationed in battle order like the commander of a gentile army? And if he, who ought reverently to have proceeded with a choir of singers, had been forced to hear on every side the clamor of clashing weapons?

Hence it happens that various orders of clerics do not now accompany the pontiff as is fitting; rather, camps and warriors armed with flashing weapons accompany him. Let us also consider what sort of thing this is: some endure these circumstances unwillingly, yet those whom they tolerate they purchase more dearly, whether they wish it or not, with the estates and resources of the Church. Every day there are royal banquets, every day pageantry, every day a nuptial feast; and those who ought to have refreshed the needy instead revive the bearers of red tablets. And while the bishop ought to be the steward and provider of the poor, strangers belch over their table amid an abundance of delicacies, while those whose entire substance it is are shut out far away and waste away from lack of food.

## CHAPTER III. Against the squanderers of ecclesiastical property

Among all these evils, the following surpasses them and seems almost to equal diabolical wickedness: estates are squandered for military service, every possession of land is disposed of, and even tithes and parish communities are added as benefices for secular persons. This dishonorable generosity deprives the needy of the means by which they live, and also discourages the diocesan clergy and people from paying tithes. One and the same action removes bodily support from the former and prepares danger to the souls of the latter. No one doubts that the whole of this will rebound upon the head of the excessively munificent man—provided that his own vanity, rather than some ancient necessity, draws him to it.

Indeed, many things could be added concerning the manifold sufferings of bishops, were I not prevented by the rule of epistolary brevity.

But, oh, what a crime! The apostolic see alone torments me so greatly that it turns me away from saying all these things. In that see, where we are accustomed to admire a bishop of reverend majesty, we now see Mintio, a contemptible person [Note: He means Cadalus.].

That venerable man, Peter, bishop of Apsara [in the upper work corrected to “Ausara”], had experienced this. He resigned his episcopate and, sailing from the kingdom of the Slavs to Italy, landed on the shores of the city of Ancona. While he was recounting to me the reverence shown him throughout the surrounding kingdom and enumerating the vexations of his burdensome unrest, he related, among other things, one matter which I will not allow you to remain ignorant of.

“A certain man,” he said, “degenerate in morals but distinguished by the titles of his ancestors, joined to himself in a nuptial bond a blood-relative of his own family. What more need be said? Forbidden, he persisted; excommunicated, he remained attached; and he reckoned the entire force of ecclesiastical censure as childish tales and trifles.

“It happened to him, certainly as a sign of divine indignation, that loaves from the wedding tables, thrown into the streets before the mouths of dogs, were not touched. Moreover—oh, dreadful severity of divine vengeance!—while he stood obstinately and did not humble himself before priestly commands, he who had refused to keep watch over himself for his salvation was suddenly struck down by a lightning flash descending from heaven while he slept in his chamber.

“Thus, thus, by dying, he experienced the sentence of divine fury—he who, while he lived, had scorned to apply medicine to his wound.”

We have said this to show how holy in authority that man was who abandoned the episcopate.

But as we pursue these matters, something else also comes to mind, something which you yourself recently told us, venerable Hildebrand. Although it may not seem to belong especially to the matter now in hand, nevertheless, as we commit it in some fashion to writing—lest the abyss of utter oblivion swallow it—we fasten this fleeting matter with little stakes, as it were.

As I remember you reporting, the bishop of the Church of Novara told you the following; to use his own words:

“When I was traveling as the companion of a certain bishop in the regions of the Germans, and the hour of refreshment was already approaching, he began to grow agitated and anxiously to search for some suitable provision to set before me, since he had nothing with which to help me on my journey. As need pressed him on one side and charity enlarged his heart on the other, he was placed in difficulty and did not know at all what he should do.

“Then suddenly cranes—forming, as their letters mutually fit together, the word *grues*—began flying in a troop over our heads. In equal formation, as though from opposite sides, they arranged themselves like two camps under a single commander.

“Then the bishop, standing firm in the fervor of faith, said: ‘Lord, command one of these cranes to be cast down to us, so that your servant may satisfy charity with the gift of your blessing.’

“What a marvelous speed of divine answer! Scarcely had the word left his mouth when a crane of no small size was immediately brought down to the ground before our faces. Thus faith, which worked through love, was fulfilled.”

When you had told me this, I immediately asked: “Was that bishop a spiritual man?” You replied—whether by what means I do not know, but you had learned that the man lived for his own flesh—that it was so. Thus it is plainly evident that this virtue had been obtained not by uprightness of life, but by faith joined to charity.

You added also that, according to the report of blessed Leo, bishop of the apostolic see [Note: Leo IX is meant], you had learned that there had likewise been a bishop of carnal and ill-considered conduct who had obtained such abundant grace from the Lord beyond his merit that he frequently displayed powers and signs; indeed, by the command of his great authority, he even drove demons from possessed bodies.

Among these signs of power, the following also occurred. In the presence of that same Leo of holy memory, a demoniac stood before the bishop. When the aforesaid bishop commanded the spirit of wickedness to depart, the demon resisted with certain perverse words of pride. At last, however, when solemnly adjured by the name of Christ, he could resist no longer.

As he shook the wretched man’s head this way and that, raising his hair stiffly upward in a certain fearful horror and opening his mouth with efforts as though to vomit something out, the bishop immediately intervened: “You shall by no means depart through the mouth, as you are attempting to do. What you are planning will be entirely frustrated. I command you to leave through the rear; I do not permit you access through the mouth. Depart, therefore, through the foul passages, unclean inhabitant, and leave behind you the filthy traces appropriate to you.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when the most wicked spirit was expelled in a flow of diarrhea.

## CHAPTER IV. God rewards by a miracle a certain bishop’s mercy toward a poor man

Another bishop, as you also related, being extremely thirsty, ordered wine to be brought to him. When the cupbearer had completely emptied all that was in the vessel into a cup and brought it to the bishop, behold, a poor man insistently begged that it be given to him, saying that, unless he drank because of his excessive dryness, he would immediately expire.

The servant, on the other hand, asserted both that he had left nothing remaining in the vessel and that no other wine could possibly be found in that place. Thus the strong bishop, caught in these difficulties, unable on the one hand to postpone his thirst, yet judging it impious on the other to drink while another man was in danger, turned away from himself and came to the aid of his suffering brother.

He therefore ordered the wine to be given to the poor man. But the more completely the hope of drinking had now failed, the more fiercely the bishop’s thirst raged. He accordingly instructed the servant to search for the wine vessel, in case he might find even a drop, however small, of consolation. The servant resisted for some time, firmly affirming that he had kept nothing back; at last, compelled more by the command than encouraged by hope, he obeyed. To his astonishment he found the vessel, which he had left empty, full of wine.

A certain abbot, as I was told, driven by a desire for a delicious dish, ordered a *naupreda* to be procured. When the servants said that this kind of fish could scarcely be found in that place, someone declared that he had seen a single *naupreda* displayed for sale, which could not be bought for less than twenty Pavia solidi.

The abbot ordered the money to be counted. After the cooks had done their work diligently and the fish had been prepared lavishly, it was set before the abbot. But before he touched it, behold, a poor man at the door anxiously begged that precisely what had been set before the abbot be given to him.

Immediately, without hesitation, the man of God sent the whole fish, just as it was, to the poor man. At once the poor man, who seemed to be carrying the very platter filled with the fish, rose aloft; and, balancing it in his hand as though carrying a gift, he passed into heaven before the eyes of all.

Thus it is clearly proved that what is given to the needy is sent on to God, and that what we hide in the bosom of the poor we store up in heaven.

The following matter, which we now add, is not a miracle, but it is not foreign to the edification which everything we write serves. A certain bishop had ordered a *naupreda* to be prepared for him. Shortly afterward, while he was devoutly attending the sacred altars amid the solemn rites of Mass, the memory of the *naupreda* tempted him with the alluring desire to taste it.

Because he was a man of distinguished spirit, he was ashamed, before the eyes of the unseen and all-seeing Almighty, that he could suffer such thoughts. After completing the offices, he ordered that the feverish fish of his soul be given to a poor man. Thus the little dog of pleasure, which might somehow have lived beneath the table of the body, had presumptuously burst into the holy of holies; struck down by the club of penance, it deserved to perish.

A certain poor head of a household possessed only one coin in his little chest. He eagerly wished to spend it on buying something to eat with bread. While, deprived of richer foods, he had long revolved this matter in his mind, a poor man meanwhile arrived and asked for mercy.

The man was suspended in thought, as though standing at some midpoint. If he gave the coin, he feared for his afflicted flesh; if he kept it, he feared incurring the guilt of refusing mercy. At last the spirit conquered the flesh, and, imitating the widow of the Gospel, he lent his small sum to God, the good debtor, in the person of the poor man (Mark XII; Luke XXI).

He returned home, and the bread that he usually ate was set before him. The table was poor, but his conscience was rich in good hope. The loss to his flesh was compensated by the profit of piety. Then suddenly an unknown man, whom he had never seen before, hurried up anxiously and placed twenty Pavia solidi, tied in a linen cloth, in his hand. He said that they had been sent to him by his master, as though he had been expected, and departed without delay. When the poor man, astonished, wished to inquire further, the stranger had disappeared.

## CHAPTER V. Damian avoids the labors of the episcopate because of the burden of age

I do not set down the names of the men because the sequence of what happened remains more easily fixed in the mind, whereas the names, with other concerns intervening, have—as I confess—been intercepted by forgetfulness. Nor do we care greatly to appear hunters of names, provided that the sequence and order of events do not escape us. Yet even concerning these events that we write, because we happened to hear them in passing, we do not have complete certainty in every respect that they preserve an unblemished line of credibility.

Therefore, lest a narrative arranged without names wrinkle the noses of fastidious readers, I shall for the moment refrain from such matters. Certainly it is healthier, leaving everything else aside, to return to myself, to lament myself, and continually to set myself before my own eyes.

For now my eyes are growing dim, and the humors of phlegm abound more than usual. Wrinkles are coming upon me, and my gums threaten the ruin of my teeth. Finally, the head that until now was sprinkled with gray hairs is already whitening with swanlike brightness; my voice is hoarse, my strength fails—and, alas, what grief!—the root of my vices alone within me knows nothing at all of old age.

Indeed, every day I keep death before my eyes, and I already stand, in a certain sense, presented before the tribunal of the terrifying Judge. Now, in a certain imagination of the mind, wicked spirits attack me terribly as I tremble in my final breath, with savage faces and dreadful appearance; now holy angels, gentle and white as snow, approach as though to help me.

Not long ago I learned of an event which, whenever it often moves my mind, usually magnifies my fear. A certain penitent was living in our region in exile under the guise of a pilgrim. When he was questioned about the fault that had compelled him into exile, he said:

“I was going with my neighbor to cut wood, and behold, a serpent of beam-like size, raising two scaly necks and heads, crept along in winding coils. When it saw us walking there, it immediately attacked us, its eyes flashing and its mouths sharpening themselves like three-forked tongues.

“My companion immediately swung his axe and cut off one of its heads; then the tool fell from his hands. At once the serpent, violently inflamed with the fury of rage, raised itself aloft. It lifted the only head that remained, seized the author of its wound with a bite, and, as soon as it had attacked him, entangled and wrapped him in its winding coils. Then, claiming the whole man by its strength, it carried him away into the hidden recesses of an underground cavern.

“As he was being dragged away, he did what alone he could: he called upon me and repeated loud cries to me, asking either that I should hurry to him as a ready helper or that I should hasten to hand him the axe which was in my hands. But I, wretched and degenerate, liable to avenging flames and myself deservedly destined to be devoured by serpents—woe to me, a murderer!—trembled. Although the matter required action with my hands, not with my feet, I prepared to flee. For this reason I endure the exile imposed upon me by the priests and am compelled to mourn myself as truly the cause of that man’s death.”

This story of mournful calamity so shakes and agitates my whole heart that I am unable either to commit the immense fear of my heart to writing or to express it in speech. I often meditate upon it: behold, a man and a beast, both together in a cavern. No mediator intervenes; no rescuer approaches. Pity does not soften the beastly heart, especially since violent greed is compounded by this as well: a heavy vengeance is exacted in compensation for the insult inflicted.

I ask: what was the appearance of that event then—or rather, what could the wretched man’s state of mind have been—when he had become prey to an enemy who knew nothing of mercy; when no hope of escape remained, but he had instead been delivered to bloody teeth as food, immediately to satisfy the beast’s ravenous belly?

I therefore often paint the image of this fearful occurrence in my mind. Then, with anxious reflection, I consider that dragon, the author of every cruelty, how he seizes and devours souls, often repeating that verse which the Prophet sang: “Lest at any time,” he says, “he seize my soul like a lion, while there is none to redeem and none to save” (Psalm VII). Does so brief a passage not offer sound minds a long source of fear?

Moreover, it is said that something occurred scarcely a year ago in a village not far from this region. A certain farmer, rising early while dawn was barely breaking, saw a dragon of enormous size. Thinking it was a log, he immediately settled himself upon it as though sitting on a beam. The beast at once stirred and raised its head; it overwhelmed the man with its bloody mouth and, in a moment, swallowed him alive in ravenous greed.

And so that even heavier fear may shake our hearts, and vigilant anxiety may compel us to dread the divine judgments hanging over us, we often see such things happen to men of good character and upright life, while, on the other hand, carnal and undisciplined men appear—as we have mentioned above—to shine even with powers.

To avoid lingering longer, a certain man returning from Jerusalem related that the following happened to him and his companions. Weary from the labor of the journey, they were resting beside the road at night when suddenly a terrifying lion came upon them as they slept.

A presbyter of pious reputation and honorable life, who had already returned four times from visiting the Lord’s tomb, was resting in the middle, with his companions surrounding him on every side. The enormous beast rushed in but touched none of those who first came before it. Leaping over the others and disregarding them like discarded logs, it singled out the presbyter, rushed upon him, and attacked him violently. Then, like a bloodstained hunter, it exposed its prey to other lions that were not far away.

The lions suddenly devoured him as he cried out and roared horribly within the hearing of his companions; and immediately afterward they pursued his fellow travelers as far as the tower into which the latter had climbed, trembling.

This certainly seems sufficiently terrifying to weak minds: that the rod should restrain those who deserve rewards, and that discipline should watch over those who are worthy of heavenly grace.

## CHAPTER VI. That the servant of God foretells a city’s destruction by fire but does not take care of himself

The following also seems worthy of no less fear. I learned of it from the report of a certain religious abbot of the diocese of Pisa (see the scholia at the end of the work).

He said plainly that, within the recent age now past, there was in a certain city of the Germans a servant of God of holy conduct and good reputation who lived in a small cell beside a monastery. It had been revealed to him that, unless the people very soon restrained themselves from their wickedness through penance, their entire city would be subjected to fire within thirty days.

He made the meaning of his vision known not only to the city’s bishop but also took care to spread it without delay throughout the whole population. But they persisted in the wickedness of their ways, judged the man of God to be delirious, and, utterly despising the threats of God, refused to correct their actions. The man of God ordered the monastery’s most valuable possessions to be carried into hidden recesses where they could be preserved unharmed by the fires.

Why linger over the details? At last that mournful day arrived, and avenging fire arose from the city’s seven regions. Behold, the monks anxiously rushed to the servant of God’s cell and urgently begged him to leave in the face of the impending danger.

But he refused entirely, committing everything to divine judgment and calmly awaiting what God might choose concerning him. The fire, raging in globes toward the stars, seized and engulfed everything. It not only set all the other things ablaze, but also—alas, it is painful to say—the monastery itself and the servant of God with his entire cell.

This judgment of God should not so much be investigated as feared. For what human mind can penetrate the abyss of divine judgments, since he is indeed “terrible in his counsels toward the children of men” (Psalm LXV)? Who could have believed that the man who, through revelation, had been granted knowledge of the destruction of a doomed city would not know that he himself was about to be burned by the same terrible flames?

When I consider these and similar things in my mind, when I examine them through subtle meditation, not knowing what still threatens me, I am struck dumb, my whole inward being trembling. Then I return to tears; and if weeping sometimes does not break forth because of the hardness of my heart, my mind nevertheless wastes away under an even heavier grief.

I often ponder what it is to lie beneath insatiable dragons, to be among irreconcilable enemies, to live in death, to dwell in flames. I also consider why this element was chosen above all others to torment the wicked: though a single spark leaping apart cannot be endured in any limb even for a moment, avenging flames absorb miserable people departing this life, and the endlessly gaping, ravenous Gehenna closes over them.

My mind could supply much more to say from these matters, were I not prevented by the brevity appropriate to a letter from lingering longer. Yet on this occasion something else comes to mind which I am not reluctant briefly to record.

Two men from among the leading citizens of Faenza, who had departed this world some time ago, appeared together in a vision to a certain deacon. They seemed to be clothed in iron tunics, extending down to their feet in the manner of priests. The deacon asked them: “Do you who are in that life bless the Lord continually?”

They replied: “We who are tormented in hell by eternal fire never bless the Lord.”

Clearly, what adds weight to my anxiety is that the brother whom we mentioned earlier, as may be inferred, was standing upright when he was granted the foreknowledge of the revelation; at the time when he encountered the danger, he may perhaps have been lying in some fault. For when we stand on slippery ground, we suddenly slip; and even now, in a moment of time, we are stained by the world.

Hence that matter also returns to my memory which I happened to hear had once occurred in the city of Benevento. The prince of that city had a presbyter, a man of holy conduct, unceasingly devoted to the divine offices and especially to the solemnity of the Mass.

As he reverently attended the sacred mysteries each day, an angel of the Lord customarily came and, in the presence of the prince, took the sacrament of the Lord’s body from the hands of the celebrant. But, oh, the slippery and uncertain condition of this ruinous life! The man who had enjoyed the pure service of angels suddenly fell into the abyss of filthy lust.

What more need be said? The time came for performing the sacred mystery. The presbyter, who was accustomed to conduct the rite, was compelled to do so; but inwardly he was cruelly tormented by the accusation of his conscience. He dressed, approached, trembled, and quaked, yet dared to offer the sacrifice.

Behold, the angel came as he had been accustomed to do; and, while the prince watched, he squeezed a sponge soaked with water over the presbyter’s head and cleansed his entire body by wiping it. When the mysteries had been completed, he squeezed the same sponge again and poured over all his limbs every filth and stain that he had previously drawn from the presbyter’s body.

When the prince saw this, he was astonished and bewildered. He took the presbyter aside and privately confronted him. Questioned whether he had recently committed any crime, the presbyter at first, as though horrified by the deed, denied it. Then, conscious of his wrongdoing and compelled by the prince’s authority, he finally confessed that he had fallen the previous night with one of that same prince’s chambermaids.

In the same city I also saw a monk named Madelmus. Living in a cell beside the monastery, he was called an enclosed monk or solitary. He told me that on Holy Saturday of Easter, the day preceding the Lord’s Resurrection, he had adorned approximately fourteen lamps in the church which he was accustomed to attend. After placing water in all but one, he poured oil over them.

When the others had been supplied and one remained because there was no oil, he asked the abbot for some but could not obtain it. At last, unwavering in faith, he filled the lamp with water, applied a flame, and the lamp shone throughout the entire night along with the others. Although it is the natural property of water always to extinguish fire, the water sustained it.

The abbot was then summoned as a witness. Astonished and terrified at the sign of power, he was ashamed and embarrassed that he had not given the oil. That monk was also said to have displayed certain other powers. But woe to him! He walked securely with closed eyes and paid no attention to the traps of the crafty enemy. Later he fell into the abyss of lust; and the man who until then had been held in great reverence by the prince and the citizens was publicly beaten with rods and, amid dishonorable ridicule, shamefully shaved bald.

## CHAPTER VII. That it is an exceedingly difficult thing to rule others

I have said these things so that it may be plainly evident that many snares are laid for those who walk along the road of this mortal life; the hidden enemy conceals various stumbling blocks, sets many traps, and daily places numerous nooses and snares before our steps.

Let those who wish to become bishops say to me: “Set yourself over the peoples to govern them.” But I cannot protect myself amid so many swords and weapons; how, then, can I free others from the deceptive traps of hidden ambushes?

The burden which I cannot carry must therefore be laid down. It is better to cast off the weight than, to the detriment of the Lord whose servant I am, to perish with a broken neck. For now, the sole testimony of blessed Jerome will suffice—one which, less than an hour ago, I remember having before my eyes.

While treating of an idle shepherd of the Church, he added: “Immediately he will be struck by the response of the indignant Lord: ‘Wicked servant, why did you not put the money on the table, so that when I came I might at least have exacted it with interest?’” (Luke XIX.)

That same teacher immediately explains this, saying: “That is, you should have placed upon the altar what you were unable to carry. While you, a sluggish merchant, held the coin, you occupied the place of another who could have doubled the money.”

I confess that I gladly took up this counsel of the holy man, and I cast off the burden beneath which I was being compelled to collapse. Indeed, I, a sluggish merchant, placed upon the altar the money which I could not double.

There was, there was once—but that time has now passed—in which the modesty of shame, the mark of mortification, worthy severity, and the discipline proper to the priestly character could be maintained. For, to rebuke myself alone as I ought, you yourselves see that as soon as I come to you, lo: sallies, jests, charms, urbanities, talkativeness, volumes of questions, [Col. 0454A] and every plague of idle words burst forth shamelessly. These things show us to be no longer priests, but rather orators and rhetoricians—or, what is disgraceful, buffoons.

As soon as we begin exchanging words, certain allurements of mutual conversation gradually creep in. They unbecomingly soften all the mind’s firmness and dissolve the strength of severity into uncontrolled laughter and shameful jokes. Hence the mind, scattered outside itself, becomes confused; the edge of the heart is blunted; the light of divine love is extinguished; fear and priestly reverence toward others are lost; and, more dangerously still, the straight path of virtuous living, which ought to have been set before others as an example, is not maintained.

But if, whether from shame or fear, we refuse to descend to such things, we are immediately judged inhuman and rigid, like those whom Hyrcanian tigresses of stone gave birth to [Col. 0454B] (Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 2). I restrain my pen. For I blush to attach even more disgraceful absurdities: hunting, bird-catching, the madness of dice, and chess. These certainly make a spectacle of the priest as a whole; but they especially turn his eyes, hands, and tongue into a kind of genuine theatrical performance, and thus place upon the demons’ tables foods that are seasoned and made more palatable.

453 Here, if anything concerning the venerable bishop of the see of Florence has come to my attention, I recall it, and I do not believe it alien to edification.

Once, when I was accompanying him on a journey, we eventually entered an inn for the night. I withdrew into the presbyter’s cell, while he remained in a spacious room with a crowd of travelers.
