When morning came, my Agaso informed me that the aforesaid bishop had presided over a game of chess. This report pierced my heart most sharply, like an arrow, and inflicted a wound of indignation.

At an hour that seemed suitable to me, I went to the man and rebuked him sharply. Taking up my opening words, I said: “With balanced hand I draw out the rods; I seek to inflict blows, if there is anyone who will offer his back.” He replied, “Let the fault be brought forward; penance will not be refused.”

“Was it right,” I said, “was it fitting for your office, in the evening, to play together in the vanity of chess and to defile, by the contamination of sacrilegious mockery, the hand that offers the Lord’s Body and the tongue that mediates between God and the people? Especially since canonical authority decrees that bishops who play at dice are to be deposed. And what benefit is it to someone whom authority effectively condemns, even if an external judgment does not follow?”

He, however, made a shield of defense for himself from the difference between the names and said: “Chess is one thing, dice another. That authority therefore prohibited dice, but, by saying nothing, allowed chess.”

To this I replied: “Scripture does not mention chess; rather, it includes both kinds of game under the name of dice.”

Therefore, since dice-playing is prohibited and chess is not mentioned by name, it is beyond doubt that both kinds are included under a single term and condemned by the authority of a single ruling. Then he, being gentle in disposition and perceptive in mind, humbly accepted the reasons once they had been given. He firmly resolved never to repeat the fault, and asked that penance be imposed upon him. I immediately instructed him to go through the Psalter three times in meditation, and to wash the feet of twelve poor persons, distributing twelve coins among them and providing for their refreshment.

The purpose of this arrangement was clear: since the fault is committed chiefly with the hands and speech, by washing the feet of the poor he might rather wash his own hands from the contagion of the fault; and by imprinting his mouth upon the feet of others, he might restore peace with the Lord, whom he had offended through lamentable jokes.

We have related this, 454 so that from the correction of another it may be recognized how dishonorable, how absurd, and finally how shameful such amusement is in a priest.

Moreover, beloved, to return to the matter for which I proposed to write these things, do not henceforth trouble me by urging me to abandon the harbor of quiet into which, with Christ guiding through you, I have fallen back, and to attempt again to plow through the foaming heaps of storms, the jagged whirlpools, and the Scyllaean gulf [Note: [Col. 0455B] He alludes to the office of the cardinal bishop of Ostia].

For although I am wretched and he is holy, nevertheless, since my case is in some way like Samuel’s (1 Samuel VIII, 16), let a not dissimilar sentence be pronounced upon both. He abandoned the dignity of the principate, yet anointed David as ruler. We too, following his example, desire, by God’s authority, to ordain a pontiff of the Apostolic See and immediately withdraw from the citadel of our own pontificate.

[Col. 0456A] Behold, beloved, while I have drawn out the words of a fuller address to you, I have violated the rule of epistolary brevity. If anyone therefore wishes to accuse me of excessive prolixity, let him rather accuse a charity impatient of silence. Let him not fail to understand that there is concise prolixity wherever the writer of a flowing style extends his discourse in such a way that he still does not express the whole desire of his full heart.

We also append Stephen, whom we carry in our hearts among our foremost friends, at the end of the letter, and we beseech him not to be forgetful of one who remembers him. May he rescue wretched Peter from the hands of Hildebrand, at whose command the prison of Herod stood open to the great Peter.

## SCHOLIA

This also seems worthy of no less fear: namely, what the holy cardinal relates in this passage about a certain enclosed servant of God in the diocese of Pisa, who had foreseen the fire in which he was burned in his cell. It seems to me to be the same event that Marianus Scotus expressed in these words (Chronicle, Book III, Sixth Age, under the year 1058):

> “The city of Podelbruna, together with two monasteries, was consumed by fire on the Friday before Palm Sunday.”

In the monastery there was a monk named Paternus, a Scot, who had been enclosed for many years. He also foretold the conflagration and, seeking martyrdom in his cell, was burned. On the Monday after the octave of Easter, departing from Cologne [reading uncertain], I visited that same place for the sake of prayer because of the good things reported about his tomb.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0455]

455–456 **TWENTY-FIRST OPUSCULUM: ON FLEEING ECCLESIASTICAL DIGNITIES**

### ARGUMENT

He strongly commends as prudent a certain monk who had renounced the dignity of abbot. He places before his eyes the grave burdens, cares, anxieties, masses of business, and dangers with which the life of those who preside over monasteries is filled, and concludes most openly and truthfully that such dignities are not merely not to be desired, but to be avoided as far as possible.

He writes, however, that the same monk still has a task no less demanding: he must be able to repel and overcome the temptations that the demon will inflict upon him, since the demon would attempt everything in order to bring him to regret his most excellent deed. He therefore urges him to gird himself bravely to withstand the assaults of the enemy, lest, if he acts otherwise, he necessarily slip back once more into the waves of ambition.

[Col. 0455C] **To Lord B., most religious abbot, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of due servitude.**

Most beloved Father, I give worthy thanks to God, the author of good things, who through his Spirit has taught you, at this perilous time, to cast away the dry branch of empty authority and hasten with unhindered steps to the private guardianship of your soul.

Now you have truly begun to be my abbot, since you have ceased to preside over others. Behold, rescued from the yoke of a many-sided servitude, by God’s mercy you have been restored to free liberty. You had necessarily been the servant of secular people, and also the servant of monks: of the former, lest they harm the monastery; of the latter, lest they produce against you the scandal of a conspiracy.

You feared the former lest they plunder the goods of God’s house; the latter lest they devise against you the engines of domestic sedition. While one head is subjected to so many masters, the unhappy soul is bound, as it were, by a manifold chain, so that it cannot follow the footsteps of its Creator.

Tell me, Father—tell me, I say, as one who has experienced it: who can govern a monastery in this iron age without danger to his own head? Indeed, who can possess an abbot and a monk at the same time? As soon as someone begins to become an abbot, he ceases to be a monk; and whoever eagerly seeks the summit of abbatial office seeks nothing other than to cast off the monk as an unbearable burden and, lest he appear an apostate, to conceal himself beneath the false color of governance.

[Col. 0457A] In order that sin may remain hidden, the pretext of authority is sought; and the diseased skin of pastoral office is laid over the wound of a perverse mind, so that it may be concealed by the foul odors of poisonous pus. To such men the Gospel saying aptly applies:

> “Woe to you,” he says, “for you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to human beings, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity” (Matthew XXIII).

## ON FLEEING ECCLESIASTICAL DIGNITIES

### CHAPTER I. The wretched condition of those who govern souls

A monk is commanded to die to the world. But how does an abbot fulfill this command when he is oppressed by the tumult of so many cares and entangled in so many complications of secular affairs? He continues the day by talking and handling various matters, and divides the night by giving counsel. While he does not take care to complete the office with others and always anticipates sunrise in order to fulfill the office of the first synaxis, when the assembly of the brothers commonly breaks its silence, does he alone among them never bring forth a virgin [i.e. unstained] saliva? Nor is a tongue fit to utter the heavenly word available when it has first been dissolved in such lengthy coils of earthly speech.

Furthermore, since a monk is commanded to desire nothing in this world and to pursue no ambition whatsoever, what does that abbot retain of a monk whom we see, as though belching forth Etnean flames, blazing with the torches of avarice, extending the boundaries of estates, gathering money here and there with such greed, and panting with all his desires to acquire what belongs to others?

For him, whatever he possesses is nothing unless he has also sought out what he lacks. The monastery becomes his lodging, while a horse’s back is his daily dwelling. Gloves, spurs, whip, stirrup straps, and whatever other equipment belongs to riding never wither through idle neglect, while the priestly vestments used in serving the sacred altars are often found eaten by moths.

What marketplaces, what tribunals, can be found empty of abbots? What court, what bedchambers of princes, are not seen dug up by the iron staffs of abbots? The threshold of the palace is constantly worn down by the footsteps of abbots, and their complaints or quarrels are thrust importunately into the ears of kings.

They do not avoid the camps of combatants. Rather, under the pretext of negotiated peace, you may often see hooded monks torn apart and crushed among the very ranks of helmeted soldiers. Whoever wishes to know what has been done in a forensic matter should seek out not the judges’ praetoriums but rather the abbots’ lodgings. Whatever is done in the world is sought from them as though they were masters of secular affairs.

But since the Lord says, “Take care,” he says, “lest your hearts be weighed down by carousing, drunkenness, and the cares of this world” (Luke XXI), and again, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew VI; Luke XVI), the Apostle also cries out in agreement: “No one engaged in warfare for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (1 Timothy II).

Whoever voluntarily seeks the administration of a monastery filled with so many earthly activities—is he believed to be doing anything other than cursing the continued carrying of Christ’s military service, as though already weary? And while he refuses to carry Christ’s yoke, which is indeed easy (Matthew XI), upon a tender neck, he does not aspire to his banquet of refreshment. That refreshment is promised by the very mouth of Truth to those who are not wearied beneath his light burden:

> “Come to me,” he says, “all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (ibid.).

Moreover, whoever wishes to loosen his military belt before his discharge does not deserve to reach the citizenship of the heavenly homeland; and the one for whom the battle is burdensome can never receive the crown of victory.

Especially culpable is the man who, in order to flee the labor of military service, greedily pants after command over that same service. Though he is seen by human eyes as a commander of war, before the sight of the hidden judge he is judged a faithless deserter.

He flees who, in order truly to avoid the danger of fighting, pretends outwardly to carry the standard in the place of the standard-bearer. And he who could not walk among the troops is seen, driven by the desire to command, as the first soldier in the forward wing.

The unhappy man does not recall what the Holy Spirit terrifyingly cries through the mouth of blessed Benedict (Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 2):

> “Whoever undertakes the governance of souls must prepare himself to render an account.”

And again:

> “Let the abbot know that he will have to render an account to God, the most just judge, for all his judgments.”

He also says elsewhere:

> “Let the abbot know that whatever lesser usefulness the master of the household may find in the sheep rests upon the shepherd as guilt. For whoever wishes to become judge of souls does not know how harsh and exacting a judgment he must expect.”

As Scripture says:

> “The severest judgment will be upon those who govern” (Wisdom VI).

### CHAPTER II. The art of presiding is easily learned but difficult to fulfill

In these newly appointed abbots I see one thing that greatly astonishes me. A man who, having been subject to another’s rule for ten years or more, could never attain such knowledge that he appeared to be a perfect monk—on the very day he is placed in authority suddenly assumes the appearance of a superior and expresses the majesty of a ruler, so that you would say he was not recently elected but born an abbot.

He suddenly becomes severe in countenance, imperious in voice, sharp in correction, and prompt in judgment. If he takes offense, wholly ignorant of making satisfaction, he disdains to recline anywhere except on an octagonal chair, prepared as though it were a senator’s curule chair in the senate-house.

At his own pleasure he orders this to be done and forbids that with threats; he binds, releases, brings forward, and removes. In all these matters he does not seek counsel from us juniors [or “seniors”; variant reading], but, sufficient unto himself, arranges the laws of his own antiquity as though he were self-created.

To the devoted and submissive he promises favor; against those who resist he breathes vengeance with the destructive force of a fire-dart, so that he seems to act under prefectural insignia rather than serve the office of ecclesiastical humility.

His throat is nauseated by receiving the common food with us. Cooks must prepare several and varied dishes for one particular belly. For gross food drawn from the common brothers’ cauldron is judged unworthy of a man of delicate and refined constitution.

Recently departed from the dormitory, he cannot rest unless he has a private and separate chamber. Though young, though strong in body, he does not know how to walk if there is no staff upon which he may support himself.

In these matters, and many others too lengthy to pursue, he suddenly becomes a master, so that in the entire rule of presiding he seems to offend at nothing, like some ancient father. How skillfully and imperiously he knows how to command everything with a kind of majestic authority—the man who, for so long as a subordinate, never learned to obey his teachers.

The art of presiding, I would say, is easy to learn: it is learned so readily that anyone, however dull in other matters, is approved as soon as he begins as a highly skilled master in this one. And, to hold it more firmly, he not only displays his knowledge of himself very quickly but also completely forgets, from the memory of his pupil, the art of obedience, which is different from his own.

Very many dangers threaten the rulers of monasteries. Through the license of immunity itself, when it flatters them, they freely fall; or, compelled by the necessity of worldly disturbance, they offend even unwillingly.

But suppose that no secular trouble strikes them and that every storm of worldly turbulence everywhere subsides. Who can endure the evils of internal sedition and bear the weariness of monks alone? Who can satisfy so many and such diverse wills? Who can compose himself amid so many different forms of [human] monstrosity?

They decide that their superior ought to live spiritually, yet they compel him to toil all day in the business of secular lawsuits, lest ecclesiastical goods perish or, God forbid, the house of God decline from its state of security. They more tolerantly endure the collapse of all regular discipline through the abbot’s absence than the suffering of loss to the advantage of ecclesiastical property.

If he corrects the vices of offenders by a judgment of strict punishment, he is impious. If he acts more leniently toward them, he is thought alien to zeal for God. If he occasionally binds himself by the discipline of silence, it is said that when the shepherd falls silent, the wolf attacks the flock.

Let me speak somewhat more freely. With what face can he command others to be silent when his talkative tongue declaims in continuous verbosity? When he fasts, he is said to be seeking human praise; when he eats, he is described as a father to his own belly but a stepfather to another’s.

If covered in finer clothing, he is said to seek empty glory; if content with roughness and poverty, he is said to disgrace the monastery. If the word of preaching is prolonged, it is spat upon and despised, and is said to provoke sleep more than to contribute to edification. But if his speech is brief, they say that what he did not take care to store in his own vessel he cannot pour out for others, and that a spring which dries up in the veins of its hidden channel does not pour abundant streams through its pipes.

[Col. 0460A] There is one thing that monks value highly in their abbot and exalt with the highest praises: namely, whether he has influence among the powerful of the world; whether he possesses unrestricted power to harm and to help; whether he is not ashamed to speak in public and pursue his own cases.

Hence, in our time, monks wish no one to preside over them unless he is tall in bodily stature and distinguished by the renowned titles of his great-grandfathers. Let him be holy, let him shine with the splendor of every virtue; nevertheless, if he lacks those gifts of nature, even if an Antony were brought forward, they unanimously declare him unworthy of election.

Moreover, they tolerate no ruler given to them except one from the number of their own congregation. If an outsider is proposed, then, even if he shines with the virtues of miracles, their opposition prevents him from attaining the office of authority.

They fear that he might someday prefer others to them; they dread that he might presume to correct something in the custom in which they have now grown old; that, God forbid, he might teach mortification; that he might compel them to fast through a vain superstition; that he might love austerity; that he might issue new commands; that, most intolerable of all, he might perhaps restrain them from their own will.

Thus they plainly prefer one of their own swinish flock whom they deem worthy to guard them over an outsider perfect in every completion of religious life and holiness.

That man—he, certainly—is now exalted as abbot; he is judged worthy of the dignity he has received who knows how to extend the estates of fields, construct the turreted roofs of buildings, acquire an abundance of earthly wealth, and provide those entrusted to him not merely with necessities but also with superfluities.

But if, while caring for such things, the care of souls is postponed, it is said that among the many important good works any minor fault is mercifully forgiven. Everyone can attend to the benefit of his own soul; not everyone is given the ability to provide for matters so difficult and necessary. There is easily room for pardon where, with this consideration, we neglect lesser matters in order to devote ourselves more diligently to greater ones.

But if an abbot refrains from external affairs and devotes himself to spiritual pursuits, there is grieving and sighing, and each person complains about the loss of domestic resources. “Behold,” they say, “the holy house is being destroyed, our possession is being diminished, and through the negligence of one man the welfare of so many men is reduced to nothing.

“Let an accounting be made; let us calculate: since he received authority over us, an authority unworthy of him and under an ill-fated omen, how many and what kinds of ornaments has he added to the Church? How many estate-holdings has he acquired? Where, finally, has he enlarged the boundaries of our possession?”

Clearly, if the matter is carefully investigated, this place is seen, in his time, not to have been increased but rather to have been diminished in many respects.

Struck repeatedly by these and similar goads of calamity, and disturbed by the wickedness of their subjects, abbots can neither lead a peaceful life nor labor for the winning of souls as their office commands. But when we speak of the depravity of certain abbots or monks, let no one suppose that we are attacking religious and honorable men along with them.

On the contrary, we humbly kiss the footsteps of such men and adore Christ in them, as is fitting. We do not gnaw even at those very offenders with the tooth of envious detraction; rather, in fraternal compassion, we grieve over the morals that deserve correction. Through the negligence of their dissolute way of life, they generate scandal not only for us but also provide secular people with material for disparaging and detesting the sacred order.

Therefore, dearest one, you have acted most laudably and prudently: you cast off the heaviest burden of unfruitful labor and hastened, with your shoulders lightened, to the leisure of fruitful rest. This counsel was not given to you by flesh or blood, but was inspired from heaven by divine mercy.

For now you have leisure to become concerned with greater care for your own salvation and to be secure, in many respects, from the obligation of rendering an account for so many souls. Nevertheless, since the aged enemy of the human race, who employs a thousand arts of harming, never ceases to assault the minds of God’s servants and does not permit them to rest from the temptations he inflicts, it is necessary for you to watch over your own guardianship all the more anxiously the more you are permitted to withdraw from responsibility for others.

You have changed your place, but not your enemy. Wherever you go, whether you wish it or not, you carry with you the burden of your corruption. From it thorns and thistles must continually emerge, and it is beneficial for you to exercise yourself tirelessly in uprooting them.

Human beings who might contrive to shoot the arrows of their tongues against you are absent; invisible enemies are present, and they never cease to fight fiercely against you. The former could be reconciled with you by an easy settlement once their complaints had fallen silent; the latter do not know how to enter into a peace treaty with a human being.

The former know no weapons against you except external ones; the latter rage impiously within the very walls of your mind and fight in the very city of your breast. And, to make the encounter seem more dangerous, they discover in your own flesh certain treacherous fellow soldiers and enlist them to strengthen their side.

That from which your enemies gain strength lives in your own household; and when the battles of the hostile spirits rise against us, the monsters of vice, joined to them and packed together in their ranks, press upon us savagely.

### CHAPTER III. By what arts the demon attacks those who have renounced positions of authority

[Col. 0461D]

Therefore, dearest one, strive through perseverance in holy conduct to press forward in such a way that your mind does not know how to turn its eyes backward. Let the apostolic saying always remain in your memory:

> “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling” (Philippians III).

Let your feet be, as Ezekiel says of the sacred creatures, “straight feet” (Ezekiel I). That is, let them know how to travel the narrow road once undertaken, so that they disdain to turn back on backward steps toward the breadth they have left behind.

Some, after laying down the office of their priorship, burn amid such great waves of temptation that a violent struggle can scarcely find room in their hearts. The evil spirits set before them how many and how great gains of souls they could have acquired for God if they had patiently wished to remain in the position they had held.

“How many,” they say, “would have hastened from secular dress to Christ’s service at your exhortation! Even those who were left behind would easily have restrained themselves from their wickedness. But this good your wandering has taken away; the vice of instability has excluded it.

“Were you born for yourself alone, so that none of your neighbors should feel any comfort from you, and no fruits should spring from you, as from a barren tree—and therefore one destined for the fires (Matthew XXV)? The servant who placed his master’s talent in a napkin (Luke XIX) did not escape the sentence of strict punishment; through the very thing by which, as though cautious, he thought to provide for himself, he fell unwarily into the danger of condemnation.

“You have given your reward to others; you have cast away from yourself the means of acquiring everlasting recompense.”

Amid these thoughts they also recall the goods of this world with which he had formerly abounded. They magnify the poverty in which he is now seen to have been unhappily placed. And, so that the battering ram of temptation may strike the wall of his mind more sharply, they add:

“Consider, then, how much better it is to abound in all temporal goods with God than, against God, to lack every resource for sustaining necessity. Since you did not fear God, and by casting yourself down and disgracing yourself you showed contempt for him, you ought at least to have secured the temporal stipends of this life for your own use.”

Now the false love of those brothers whose devoted service he had enjoyed is secretly introduced; now considerable envy is stirred against those who opposed him. He grieves for the former because they complain that they remained deceived by the one in whom they had hoped; for the latter because they boast that they have escaped unpunished for their excesses of presumption.

He thinks the former are wasting away from his deposition and the latter are mocking his misfortunes like enemies. He imagines the former are being crushed by their rivals and grieves that the latter are arrogantly raised up on the horns of pride.

These and many other phantoms of thought the most wicked spirits inject into human minds—particularly into those that do not enclose themselves with the strong guard of watchfulness.

Hence we see some who, after leaving the office of superior with great fervor [or “after departing”; variant reading], later hasten back to the same vomit with the importunity of ambition. Hemmed in by the density of manifold temptations, they either reach what they desire or grow lukewarm in the fervor of the holy work with which they had burned.

But you, dearest one, gird yourself, according to your wisdom, as a strong warrior equipped with the armor of the virtues. Always stand ready in the battle line against the ambushes of the crafty enemy. Despise the empty glory of this world; reject the blandishments of earthly happiness; regard whatever smiles in the world as the dream of a deceptive imagination; and let your heart, lifted toward the true blessedness of the heavenly homeland, burn with all its inward being.

When the battle grows, when the uproar of temptations bears down upon you, let your joyful mind immediately flee to this harbor and delightfully rest as though in a fortified stronghold, so that what is said through the Psalmist may be fulfilled:

> “You will hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men; you will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues” (Psalm XXX).

Having set aside the sluggish idleness of torpor, watch wisely in the pursuit of every virtue; persevere immovably in what you have begun. Do not regret having left the monastery. Rather, let your conscience reproach you for having awakened too late, so that you, who now choose to be poor with Christ temporarily, may together with him enjoy immortal riches in the glory of the eternal kingdom; and may he command you to be placed among the elect abbots at the resurrection, for love of whom in this life you removed yourself from the order of abbots.

Behold, dearest Father, prompted by the sweetness of my love for you, while I strove to write more to you, I exceeded the measure of epistolary brevity. But I ask almighty God that these rustic and unlearned words may benefit you, and that your holiness may not cease to pray for your servant in return for them.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0463]

463–464 **TWENTY-SECOND OPUSCULUM: AGAINST COURT CLERICS, THAT THEY MAY BE PROMOTED TO DIGNITIES**

### ARGUMENT

He attacks clerics who, in order to obtain episcopates and ecclesiastical dignities for themselves, devote themselves to the service of secular princes. He teaches that they are not thereby free from the detestable crime of simony merely because they do not use money to carry out those wicked purchases. Rather, they are entangled in that guilt all the more, because they sell themselves—which is worse—in order to obtain priestly offices.

He also says that princes must beware lest, by entrusting the governance of churches to wicked and criminal men, they transfer the sins of others onto themselves. He develops this at length and confirms it with many arguments.

[Col. 0463B] **To Lord Boniface, most reverend bishop, Peter, a sinful monk, offers servitude.**

The Wise Man admonishes us:

> “With a buyer,” he says, “conduct business about a sale; with an envious man, about giving thanks; with an impious man, about piety; with an honorable man, about honor” (Ecclesiasticus XXXVII).

He had also prefaced these words:

> “With a religious man, conduct business about holiness, and with a just man, about justice” (ibid.).

Therefore, no speech is more appropriately directed to a priest than to a priest.

Since, venerable Father, many things about modern bishops displease me, I consider this intolerable: that some, while pursuing ecclesiastical honors with excessive heat, as though in the vapors of Etna, indecently prostrate themselves as surrendered slaves into the clientage of the powerful.

They abandon ecclesiastical life while desiring churches. In order to seize tyranny over their fellow citizens, so to speak, they disdain to be fellow citizens. They flee military service so that they may be placed above soldiers. And while they are not ashamed to exchange the temple of God for a palace, they pass from canonical religion into the order of laymen.

They lay down the weapons of virtue, abandon the battle array of spiritual warfare, desert the camp, and loosen the military belt. They disdain to receive with the others the gift of a soldier’s pay and pant only after the supremacy of dictatorship or imperial power.

Since they do not enter through the door of the Church but through a secular back entrance, they become not shepherds of sheep but thieves and robbers, as the Truth testifies:

> “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door is a thief and a robber” (John X).

Moreover, if a military tribune is chosen from among the soldiers not from another but from the same military service; if someone born of that same realm is more often promoted to the height of royal dignity; if, finally, someone from the inhabitants of the same estate is placed over a rural administration—how can Christ’s Church alone be entrusted to any stranger or unknown person as though it were a worthless stable?

If earthly affairs are arranged through their own household members, how is the holy Church—which is the scepter of the kingdom and the court of heavenly power—transferred to outsiders while its own are disregarded? Nevertheless, whoever he may be, if he is chosen by those over whom he is to be placed, he is not judged an outsider.

## AGAINST COURT CLERICS

### CHAPTER I. Clerics devoted to the service of secular princes

But who can tolerate that ecclesiastical authority be entrusted to a man who, in order to obtain the Church, abandons the Church and disdains to render service to his own Church so that he may arrogate to himself the governance of another’s?

Furthermore, since the prophet testifies of the just man, “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah XXXIII), who can defend from the giving of gifts a man who has both surrendered himself to the command of another’s servitude and is shown to be squandering his resources on the expenses of a lengthy campaign?

That prophetic statement is plainly explained in such a way that three kinds of gifts are identified: a gift from the hand, a gift from service, and a gift from the tongue [Note: [Col. 0463C] On these matters, see also Letter 1 of Book II]. A gift from the hand is money; a gift from service is the obedience of submission; and a gift from the tongue is the favor of flattery.

465 But if these three kinds of gifts are rightly considered, the middle one contains both the first and the third. For in the obedience of submission one recognizes both the gift from the hand, which is money, and the gift from the tongue, which is the favor of flattery.

Who is more plainly shown to provide money in order to obtain honors than the man who spends so much on the use of vehicles and squanders such sums of his resources in preparing the adornments of expensive clothing?

And he surpasses the man who weighs out money once, because he is not content merely to expend his resources but also does not hesitate to subject himself like a slave sold to a master.

Now, who could doubt that, when the opportunity is given, he smears his master with flattering words, so that he may soothe him with ingratiating adulation? And, in order to win his favor, the cunning observer investigates what would please him most. His eyes gleam; by his gestures he gives signals; with his mouth he displays the cheerfulness of a serene heart. He hangs upon his nod, waiting for his lord’s command as though for an oracle proclaimed through the Sibyl’s mouth by Phoebus. He is ordered to go, and he flies out; he is commanded to stand, and he becomes a stone. If his master is hot, this man sweats; if the other suffers the heat, this man complains of the scorching heat. But if the master grows even slightly cold, this man, trembling in his very entrails, must become numb. If the master wishes to sleep, this man becomes drowsy; if he is full, this man is compelled to belch. Thus, no longer his own man, he says nothing except what he suspects will please the other.

As Isaiah says concerning certain men not unlike these:

> “Who say to those who see, ‘Do not see,’ and to those who look, ‘Do not look upon for us the things that are right.’ Speak to us what pleases us; behold for us errors; take the way away from me; turn aside the path from me; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before my face” (Isa. XXX).

In this way, according to the Psalmist, while he heaps up the oil of maliciously flattering adulation, he fattens the mind of the other, which is the head of thought:

> “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. CXL).

And Solomon says:

> “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. I).

For sinners entice when they either introduce evils to be committed through flattery or exalt evils already committed with praise.

These testimonies of Scripture plainly show that whoever flatters, through amplification, specially earns the general name of “sinner.” And when the Psalmist says, “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. IX), and the one who acts wickedly is blessed, both the one who praises and the one who willingly accepts praise are bound by an equal liability of guilt.

## CHAPTER II. That flattery among clerics is simony

This kind of gift is both worse for sinning than the other gifts and more burdensome to repay. For the other two can easily be found without this one, whereas this one can scarcely, or never, be fulfilled without those two. To sellers of churches, if they are greedy, money suffices when it is weighed out; if they are ambitious for glory, the favor of flattery sometimes serves in place of the price. But those who hand themselves over to the princes of this world in order to obtain honors both lavish money of necessity and do not fail to lick their patrons with soothing flatteries. Let them not, therefore, deny that they have given money who, in their ambition for preferment, offer their service to princes. They serve from a desire for domination; and, in order to abound in wealth, they spend both their resources and themselves. They humble themselves so that later they may exalt themselves with impunity; they present themselves as attendants so that they may lead; they are worn down by labors so that they may rejoice; they are afflicted by poverty so that afterward they may swell with continual feasting on wedding banquets. And, as though a table of sale had been set out before them, by lending their service they purchase authority.

For they love the first places at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called “Rabbi” by men (Matt. XXIII).

Let others provide a quantity of lifeless metal, weigh out the amount of foolish money, count the bronze coins, and weigh vessels embossed in relief. Let others, I say, give coins; these men give the price of themselves. Is not diligent submission a price? To turn from spiritual to carnal marriage: surely Jacob, who served for his wives for twenty years, should not be said to have given no price because he did not weigh out money to his father-in-law Laban. But hear, with Scripture as witness, what both his wives complained:

> “Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father’s household?”

And immediately Scripture adds:

> “Has he not regarded us as foreigners, and sold us, and consumed our price?” (Gen. XXXI).

Yet Jacob had given no money for his wives, except that he guarded his father-in-law’s flocks. While he performed the office of shepherd for him, he earned the marriage with both his daughters. Do you wish to hear the price from Jacob’s own mouth?

> “By day and by night,” he says, “I was consumed by heat and frost; sleep fled from my eyes. Thus for twenty years I served you in your house” (ibid.).

David likewise gave Saul no other price for his daughter except that he performed his military service. Hence he says through messengers to his brother-in-law Ish-bosheth:

> “Give back my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines” (2 Sam. III).

He counts the victory of his labor as the dowry, which Saul had also accepted as a kind of money in place of a marriage payment. Thus he says:

> “Speak to David in this way: ‘The king requires no marriage payment, except one hundred foreskins of the Philistines, so that vengeance may be taken on the king’s enemies’” (ibid. XVIII).

Therefore, just as Laban sold his daughters and consumed their price—not because he stored away a profit in money, but because he received the payment of laborious service—and just as Saul sought from the marriage of his daughter not gifts of gold or silver but the labor of war, or the distinction of victory, and accepted it in place of a dowry, so that man must necessarily be proved a seller of the Church who purchases the service of submission in exchange for the largesse he wrongly hopes to receive from her.

And since the one who accepts the price is said to sell the Church, this man is more properly said to keep selling it, because the commercial transaction which the former entered into once, the latter prolongs through a long, so to speak, and sustained business. And the wretched cleric, as many services of feigned humility as he has displayed, has weighed out so many sums of money, as it were. While he hunts through his flatteries for the title of bishop, he puts on the mask of a parasite. And while he breathes ambition for the episcopate, he presents himself as a stage actor. Therefore he must be called not simply a simoniac but a simoniac of every kind, because by a threefold form of sale he has committed whatever it was by which the Church could be sold. Let him not boast that he has not given money of metal who offered himself for sale—the thing he possessed that was more precious; who plunged himself into the shipwreck of such hard labor and squandered no small part of his own resources on the expenses of this enterprise.

Let us suppose, for example, two clerics possessing equal wealth, one hundred pounds of coin each. Let one of them go to the king’s court and gradually spend for his own purposes what lies hidden in his purse; let the other remain with Jacob in his tents and not be compelled to empty a purse swollen with money. Later, on the same day, let a church be assigned to each of them. Let the former, a sinister trafficker, pour out as the price of sacrilege all the bronze that his purse had preserved; let the latter, because he served at court, contribute nothing new, but approach the administration of the Church as a merchant who has paid nothing.

Which of these two, I ask, bought the Church at the higher price? Surely the one who, although he gave nothing to his patron, oppressed by so many hardships and labors, spent everything he had on the expenses of such a difficult and prolonged undertaking; while the other bought it more cheaply, having counted out his money to the seller without labor. For clear reasoning shows that the one who lost all he possessed together with his labors bought the Church for more than the man who, at ease and idle, paid the agreed amount.

Moreover, since the civil laws also decree that every court official must be completely excluded from the clergy, this man migrated from the Church to the court. And, alas, what monstrous madness—that he should be preferred to clerics, when a cleric becomes a court official! He became a servant of the world so that he might usurp the right of the Lord, indeed the seat of pestilence, in the house of God. If he once receives an investiture from the hand of the giver, or rises to the height of governance by any means whatsoever, then, as soon as he has found supporters for himself, he distributes lavish gifts from the resources of the Church.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning a certain bishop of Bologna

In our own times, a certain bishop presided over the Church of Bologna in precisely the manner we have described: he was a court official. After he had sold off the very extensive estates belonging to ecclesiastical law that were situated in the suburb, he subsequently fell silent. Thus, for nearly seven years, until he died, he languished paralyzed and speechless.

It was justly ordained by the dispensation of heavenly judgment that the man who had made his tongue the interpreter of a deadly business should, together with it, completely lose the power of all eloquence. Every courtly bishop draws some men to himself by gifts and grants broader benefits to others; thus he is chosen by those who had not chosen him. And, so that nothing belonging to Simon may be lacking in him, he purchases the election itself by sacrilegious sale.

Nevertheless, he disguises the disgrace of his crime in this respect: under the pretext of ecclesiastical fidelity, he binds the townsmen by the solemnity of an oath. Yet no one harms the Church more grievously than those very treacherous “faithful” men who long to plunder her resources. When he gives gifts to them and compels them to swear allegiance, ostensibly to the Church but chiefly to himself, he does not consult the Church; he opens for himself a way to possess his position securely.

Whether he does this before his consecration or after he has been consecrated, he must greatly fear that, not for the advantage of the Church but rather for his own confirmation, he is wasting the goods of the holy place and plunging himself into the abyss of the Simoniac heresy while trying to exalt himself. Thus he falls disastrously before the divine gaze from the very height at which he arrogantly exalts himself among men. As it is written:

> “You cast them down while they were being raised up” (Ps. LXXI).

Nor should this be passed over: just as the man who reaches the summit of governance unwillingly, if he suffers anything harsh or adverse there, receives an increase of merit and may hope, not in vain, for the reward of eternal joy in return for the tribulation he endures, so the man who voluntarily seeks office or thrusts himself into it importunately will scarcely obtain a reward for the adversity he suffers in governance. Let him therefore attribute what he suffers to himself and ascribe everything that is torn apart to himself. Let him balance the labors he endures against the honors, and place the fruit of his labors in the dignity he has obtained, rather than presume upon a future reward, with the Lord bearing witness concerning such men:

> “For they have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

For he himself brought about the cause by which his mind, shaken by so many disasters, collapses. Indeed, the man who is compelled and drawn into the administration of earthly affairs, when he has endured adversity in its execution, will not lack the reward of his labor. But if the administration is obtained by a price or by entreaties, he is ashamed to demand the benefit of recompense for his labors, since he remembers that by importunate anxieties he extorted for himself the opportunity to labor.

We have said these things so that those who have obtained ecclesiastical dignity by serving princes may not boast that the commerce of simony is absent from them. Let them not applaud themselves for the rule of gratuitous advancement when they do not fail to recognize that they have bought what they possess through hard labors.

## CHAPTER IV. That the sins of a bishop who has not been rightly ordained rebound upon the head of his promoter

Princes and all who ordain churches must be exceedingly careful not to bestow holy places without consideration of divine judgment, according to their own will and pleasure, lest, to their own disgrace, they confuse the order of divine law with the statutes of the sacred canons.

For whoever ordains a Church of God not according to rule but by the exercise of power causes all the evils of the one who has been promoted to rebound upon the head of the promoter. Hence the distinguished preacher, after saying, “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. V), immediately added:

> “Nor share in the sins of others” (Eph. XXXII).

Whoever does not hesitate to advance an unworthy, wicked, and therefore greedy man to governance is plainly shown to share in the sins of others. And when the Church of Christ, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, is defiled by anyone’s improper ordination, all the leprous contagion of that deadly infection is transferred into the soul of the ordainer.

The history of the Romans relates—for Paul the Deacon, *Roman History*, at the beginning of Book II, after Eutropius—that when the Goths asked the emperor Valens to send them bishops from whom they might receive the beginnings of the Christian faith, he sent them teachers who were not orthodox but of the Arian doctrine, and entangled the untutored people in the errors with which those teachers were involved.

But, O equity of divine judgment, worthy to be proclaimed and truly praiseworthy! When the Goths had already been violently driven from their ancient settlements by the armies of the Huns and had been kindly received by Valens on this side of the Danube, within Roman territory, without any treaty of alliance, nevertheless, by divine judgment, they afterward rose up in arms against Valens and overthrew his army in a most savage slaughter.

When Valens learned of this, he departed from Antioch and hastened against the Goths, surrounded by countless forces. Led by belated repentance, he ordered the holy men to be recalled from exile; yet he soon engaged battle and was defeated. At the first attack of the Goths, the ranks of the Roman cavalry were thrown into confusion and abandoned the exposed infantry. The infantry were then surrounded by the enemy’s cavalry and overwhelmed by clouds of arrows. As they fled here and there in panic, scattering like madmen, they were utterly destroyed by hostile swords.

The emperor himself, wounded by an arrow, fell from his horse. Carried by a soldier on a worthless covering, he was burned with terrible flames when the Goths arrived. By the just judgment of God, he was consumed by the fire of vengeance at the hands of those whom he himself had struck with the fire of unbelief. Thus, in accordance with the sentence of Scripture, “fire went out from the thornbush and devoured the cedars of Lebanon” (Judg. IX).

This example from Scripture also appropriately brings to mind what we remember to have been set down in the same Book of Judges. In this iron age, while those who are worthy of governance flee and those who rightly deserve rejection approach irreverently, the effect of their conduct seems to enact what is there expressed through the mystery of allegory.

For it says that “Jotham stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim, and, raising his voice, cried out: ‘Listen to me, men of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.’ The trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and they said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’ It answered them, ‘Can I abandon my richness, which gods and men alike use, and go to be promoted among the trees?’ The trees then said to the fig tree, ‘Come and reign over us.’ It answered them, ‘Can I abandon my sweetness and my very pleasing fruits, and go to be promoted among the other trees?’ The trees also spoke to the vine: ‘Come and reign over us.’ It answered them, ‘Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and men, and be promoted among the other trees?’”

Then Scripture adds:

> “All the trees said to the bramble, ‘Come and reign over us.’ It answered them, ‘If you truly establish me as king over you, come and rest in my shade’” (ibid.).

It would be too long to say that Gideon represents the type of the Savior (Judg. VIII); that through his many wives the various nations are to be understood, joined to one another through faith; that through his seventy sons are signified the peoples of as many languages; that through the concubine the Synagogue is signified; and that through Abimelech the Antichrist is signified, who will be the son of the Synagogue. Hence in the Apocalypse it is said to those who will believe:

> “They say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. II).

And just as he killed the seventy brothers, so this one will persecute all the nations that do not agree with him. Passing over these matters, which seem to require a longer treatment, and insofar as the brevity of a letter permits, we shall briefly touch upon the figure of this lengthy history, insofar as it appears to fit the discussion we have begun.

What, then, should we understand by Jotham, whose name means “finished” or “perfect,” except some holy and learned preacher? He ascends Mount Gerizim and cries out with a loud voice (Deut. XXVII). First he ascends, and afterward he cries out. He rises onto the mountain before raising his voice. For unless a teacher of virtues first ascends to the summit, he cries out in vain. As Isaiah says:

> “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isa. XL).

Gerizim signifies the holy Church, which is the school of all virtues and fertile with the abundance of heavenly harvests. This is the mountain assigned by Moses for the giving of blessings; and the Church is the mountain of blessing, whose children are told through the Apostle:

> “You were called to this, that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance” (1 Pet. III).

We received this inheritance from our widowed mother, for whom her husband deigned to die; concerning her the Psalmist also says:

> “Blessing her widow, I will bless” (Ps. CXXXI).

And appropriately Gerizim, which means “division” or “newcomer,” figures the holy Church, because the Church of the Gentiles, which formerly existed wholly divided from the law of God, became a newcomer at her first calling and, through the growth of grace, has now become entirely of the household. Hence Paul says to those already firmly rooted and settled, as it were, in a city:

> “You are no longer strangers and newcomers, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II).

But, leaving aside many matters, let us rapidly pass over what has been proposed. The trees of the forest are vain and fruitless men, exposed by the justice of their barrenness to avenging flames:

> “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III).

But who are signified by the olive tree, which displays the sign of peace and pours forth the richness of oil, except those who, anointed with the richness of the Holy Spirit, reconcile human beings to their Creator by proclaiming peace?

> “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace!” (Rom. X).

The fig tree bears the image of the sacred law. Hence the Gospel says that “a certain householder planted a vineyard,” in which he also planted a fig tree. “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Matt. XXI; Isa. V). In it the divine hand planted the Decalogue of the law. But this fig tree produced and cast off for the former people its early figs—dry and useless—whereas it brought the new shoot of Christian faith to the maturity of inner richness and sweetness. Concerning these Jeremiah says:

> “I see figs, good figs, very good, and bad figs, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad” (Jer. XXIV).

The fig trees, therefore, may appropriately be understood as those who have been sufficiently instructed in the knowledge of the sacred law. The vine also seems to signify nearly the same thing as the fig tree. For the Lord says:

> “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John XV).

And since vines come from branches, what wonder if holy teachers are also called vines, so that what the Savior of the world possesses by nature, they may glory in possessing by grace? As they do not cease to proclaim the triumph of the Lord’s Passion, through the clusters of their teaching they, as it were, soak our dry hearts with the wine of blessed blood.

Concerning this wine, Jacob speaks allegorically of our Savior:

> “He will wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX).

Christ’s robe was the Synagogue in the Apostles and the other believers; his cloak was the Gentile people. Concerning them the prophet says:

> “As I live, says the Lord, you will clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX).

Christ washed these people in the blood of the grape, which, crushed in the battle of the cross, he pressed from himself. Hence John says:

> “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I).

Since, therefore, the olive, the fig tree, and the vine—that is, spiritual men—refuse to rule over the wild trees, namely earthly and carnal men, the bramble offers itself to them, to be consumed by them and, in turn, to consume them either through the example of an evil way of life or through the fire of erroneous doctrine.

The bramble bristles with thickly growing thorns. It signifies any perverse person who is so thickly covered with the roughness of sins as with a hedge of thorns. Hence it was said to the first man:

> “Your earth will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III),

that is, your body will be subject to the piercing stings of vices. And through the prophet the Lord says:

> “They surrounded me with the thorns of their sins” (Lam. III).

When the trees seek a king—that is, when various perverse people choose a ruler according to the flesh—the bramble comes forward: namely, any reprobate who both increases within himself the fire of condemnation through their perversities and consumes them through the reciprocal burning of an evil way of life or teaching. Hence it is said there:

> “Let fire go out from it and consume the inhabitants of Shechem and the city of Millo; let fire go out from the men of Shechem and from the city of Millo and devour Abimelech” (Judg. IX).

Jotham, standing on the summit of the mountain, speaks these things. Through the holy preachers in the Church, we learn how to resist the perverse and reprobate when they seek vain things.

Behold, venerable brother: you asked for one letter only, but in addition you have received another. In return, I also ask this of you: while one complete letter of our affection is sent to you, let a pair return to us according to the ethical character of our former discussion. If you still take pleasure in hearing more extensively about courtly bishops, do not hesitate to read the letter on the same subject [Note: Col. 0471C, Letter 1 of Book II] that I once sent to your fellow cardinals.

I also add this at the end of the letter: henceforth, just as those who have been promoted by serving the Church are customarily called bishops, so those who become such by serving princes should be called *curiales*, “court officials,” from the court.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0471]

473–474. TWENTY-THIRD OPUSCULE. ON THE SHORTNESS OF THE LIVES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS AND DIVINE PROVIDENCE.

ARGUMENT.

As Alexander, the supreme pontiff, returns from the assembly of fathers at Mantua, he sends this letter to meet him. In it, in answer to Alexander’s inquiry, he explains why the life of Roman pontiffs is for the most part short and narrowly limited. He then pours himself out in admiration of divine providence and goodness, from which so many and such great benefits have proceeded, and daily proceed, to humankind; and he shows that all things were created for the sake of humankind and subjected to human dominion. He therefore urges mortals, when they contemplate that so many things have been made for their sake, to render immortal thanks to God, best and greatest, the inexhaustible fountain of beneficence; and, despising these earthly pleasures, to strive with all the earnestness of their minds toward the true joys prepared in heaven for those who live piously and holily.

[Col. 0471C] To LORD ALEXANDER, bishop of the supreme see, PETER, sinful monk, his service.

[Col. 0472C] Since I hear, venerable father, that as you return from the Mantuan council you are now drawing near the neighbouring regions, I judged it fitting to come to meet you with the present of a letter—the gift, namely, in which you take especial delight. And sweet report at once roused me to set out diligently on my journey to you. For Jacob, of whom Scripture says that he “dwelt simply in tents” (Gen. XXV), thought that his earthly-minded brother must be won over by gifts because he knew that he loved earthly things alone. I too, who have dwelt simply at home with Jacob, because I do not doubt that spiritual things please you more than any carnal ones, strive to win your favour with a spiritual gift.

Yet, when David fled from Absalom, Hushai the Archite, who returned to Jerusalem, benefited him more than Ittai, who did not leave David’s side as his inseparable follower in flight (II Reg. XV). David likewise established a law in Israel that the share of the man who goes down to battle should be equal to that of the man who remains with the baggage (I Reg. XXX). And Moses aided the people of Israel more powerfully at Rephidim while, as it were, remaining idle in prayer, than Joshua did when he met the attacking Amalekites terribly armed. Scripture plainly attests this when it says: “When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered them even a little, Amalek prevailed.” But no gift is more fittingly given to anyone than that which is requested by the very person to whom it is given.

[ON THE SHORTNESS OF THE LIFE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS AND DIVINE PROVIDENCE.]

CHAPTER I. Why the life of Roman pontiffs is short.

Once, certainly, if I remember rightly, you earnestly asked me what cause I thought there was for the fact that the bishop of the apostolic see never lives for a long time, but ends his final day within a brief space of time: so much so that, after the blessed apostle Peter, who presided for about five lustres of years, no Roman pontiff afterward equalled this period of tenure; indeed, in modern times scarcely anyone is raised to the summit of that see who exceeds the limit of four, or at most five, years. Those who consider this are struck, so to speak, by a prodigious astonishment, since, so far as our knowledge extends, this necessity of living briefly is found in no other Church in the whole world.

But insofar as the secret of divine dispensation is revealed to mortals, it seems to us that this order of heavenly judgment is arranged for this purpose: to instil the fear of death into humankind and, in the very primacy of glory, plainly to show how contemptible the glory of temporal life is. Thus, when the foremost of human beings dies within so short a span of time, each person, shaken with fear, may be prompted to watch for his own awaited death; and the tree of humankind, seeing that its crown and summit have fallen so easily, may tremble in all its branches, shaken by the condition of fear.

475 But perhaps someone will object: why does this same brevity of life not befall kings as well? For Octavian Augustus, during whose reign the Saviour of the world deigned to be born of the Virgin, and King David, from whose stock he deigned to spring, flourished on the royal throne, the one for fifty-six and the other for forty years. After them, other rulers, indeed, of each kingdom also reigned for periods that, though shorter, were nevertheless not as exceedingly brief as those of the Roman pontiffs.

The answer to this is easy. Since one pope presides over the whole world, while the boundary of each several kingdom confines the many kings throughout the world, and since every emperor falls at the pope’s feet, the pope, as king of kings and prince of emperors, surpasses in honour and dignity all who live in the flesh. Hence, when any king dies, only the kingdom over which he presided is deprived of his rule; but when the pontiff of the apostolic see dies, the whole world is bereaved, as of a common father. For what does Africa feel concerning the kings of Asia, or Ethiopia concerning the rulers of the West? Whether they die or live, since they are far removed from it, Africa and Ethiopia are alike unaware of either.

There is another reason: the death of any king is not a great terror, since secular rulers who preside over popular multitudes are often killed by the sword. For, to mention a few out of many, Gaius, Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius—all these emperors held the principate one after another in uninterrupted succession; and, except Claudius, all were killed either by their own swords or by those of enemies. Afterwards too, as Roman history relates, Macrinus, Antoninus, Alexander, Maximus, Gordian, Decius, Gallus, and Volusian: all these, succeeding one another in continuous order, were struck down by the slaughtering sword.

Thus the hearts of hearers are not distressed by the death of secular rulers, because they are exposed to the accidents of different kinds of death. But because a pope’s life is ended only by the law of natural death, the report of his passage from this life is not heard without grave fear. Moreover, because earthly rulers, as has been said, are each confined within the boundaries of their own kingdom, there is no reason why news of their death should spread through foreign provinces of the world. But because the pope alone is the universal bishop of all churches, when he is deprived of light, news of his death spreads through the broad realms of the earth.

And just as the sun, because it alone gives light, if it should suffer an eclipse, necessarily causes the whole world everywhere at once to fall into darkness, so, when the pope departs from this life, because he alone is in the world, the report of his death immediately traverses the farthest stretches of kingdoms. Consequently, those whom the fall of so exalted and singular a person disturbs are also frightened in the depths of their being by the end of their own calling. Here it should be noted how greatly Almighty God wills that the life of the Roman pontiff should benefit people for their edification, when he has decreed that even his death should serve the salvation of nations. With what earnestness ought he, while he lives, to devote himself to the gain of souls, when even his death is provided to call human souls back to their Creator, so that, considering himself the father of the world, he may not grow numb through negligence in urging upon so many children their inheritance.

CHAPTER II. The gifts of divine goodness and beneficence are proclaimed.

[Col. 0475A]

Here it pleases me to raise the mind’s gaze for a little while and briefly investigate how great a grace is divinely bestowed upon humankind. For by the ordinance of the divine gift all the elements serve humankind, and not only heaven and earth, air and water, but everything in them concurs in administering human utility. First, the four elements which we have named serve humankind because the human being consists of them; then, because they supply outwardly whatever they possess. In the moisture of the earth the root of herbs and trees grows together; afterward the earth brings them forth for human use to the height fixed by nature. The grass of the field itself is converted into the flesh of animals, and human entrails are nourished by the flesh of animals.

The animals themselves, while they live, are assigned to various services of humankind: some, of course, provide themselves as mounts for their riders; others plough the fields for seeds to be entrusted to them and brought forth; others supply us not only with an abundance of milk but also, as though subject to the teaching of the Gospel, divide two tunics (Luke III), when they cover themselves with hides and us with fleeces. But since the brevity of a letter does not permit us to linger over individual cases which even the prolixity of books could scarcely enumerate, let us be content with that brief conclusion of the Psalmist:

> “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field; the birds of the air and the fishes of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII).

And this among other things is very wonderful: neither birds in flight, nor lions in their strength, nor tigers in their swiftness, nor elephants in their enormous height escape the dominion of human subjection. The lion indeed has such terror in it that, when it gives forth its roar, many animals which could escape its attack by the speed of their running are immediately compelled to fail altogether and, stupefied and astonished, to check their steps. Yet a lion is captured by a human being and shut in cages like a feeble cat. Likewise the tiger, which in the Parthian language is called “arrow,” is said to traverse eight hundred stadia in a single run and, in the course of an entire day, to pass across the whole world from east to west (see the Scholia at the end of the opuscule); nevertheless, though it runs so incredibly, it does not always escape the snares of hunters.

But although all wonderful animals are subject to human powers, even the smallest or unclean creatures are proved useful for human health. What is more worthless than a bedbug? Yet if a leech has stuck in the throat, when its smoke is taken in, it is immediately vomited out; and difficulty in urination is relieved by applying it. What too, according to the Law, is more unclean than a vulture? Yet it contains as many remedies as it has limbs (PLINY, Book XXIX, chapters 4, 6). Consider, certainly, a bishop already of great age, who was said to have converted no small number of thousands of Gentiles to faith in Christ. He reports that while passing through Ethiopia, when hunger had closed his throat, he ate the flesh of a great dragon, so that even according to the letter that saying of the Psalmist might seem fulfilled:

> “You crushed the head of the great dragon and gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians” (Ps. LXXIII).

CHAPTER III. The varieties of the seasons are described.

But since almighty God has subjected all things to man, this too is no less marvelous: that time itself distinguishes itself by so beautiful a variety of qualities. For first the winter cold hides in the newly tilled fields the seeds entrusted to it; then the mildness of spring compels the world to give birth to its manifold offspring of shoots; next the summer heat scorches the crops; finally rainy autumn plucks grapes from the vines and swelling fruits from the trees. Yet the almighty Creator does not heap together the yields of trees and fields into one confused mass, so to speak, but distributes different things to be done or eaten at different times. For if all fruits suitable for eating came together at the same time, their accumulation would produce disgust in those eating them, and their simultaneous consumption would turn abundance into want. But now they have been varied among different seasons in such a way that, while some are being eaten, others ripen; and while some, having been consumed, pass away, others soon ripen and take their place. If the crops, too, were all ready to be gathered at once, they would burden farmers with labors impossible to bear. But because they are distributed among the various stages of the seasons, the abundance of the harvest is not diminished and human labor is lightened.

For that some crops are late Moses himself attests to Pharaoh. After hail had struck Egypt, he says: “The flax and the barley were damaged, because the barley was in ear and the flax was already producing capsules; but the wheat and the spelt were not damaged, because they were late” (Exod. V). Of the early fruits he says shortly afterward: “The vegetation of the land was devoured, and whatever fruit there was on the trees that the hail had left” (Exod. X).

Since the seas and rivers, marshes and pools, with their countless kinds of fish, are compelled to serve man alone; the air, together with birds and rain; and the earth, together with cattle and all its growing things—we nevertheless set these matters aside as small and consider greater ones.

Let us therefore omit the fact that the structure of this world is arranged with such great art of proportion that air and fire, the two elements of masculine gender, preside, while the other two, which are of feminine gender—water and earth together—lie beneath; and that by this sort of double marriage everything observable among us as proceeding from any original material is brought forth.

Let us also be silent about the fact that the entire machinery of heaven serves human purposes so wonderfully that, revolving perpetually, it struggles against the spheres of the seven planets, so that while those seek the rising-place, this continually declines toward the setting-place. Yet by the force of its magnitude it draws them along with it and compels them to complete their own circuits through the zodiac within the period appointed to each.

In this universal contest of the world, a not insignificant mystery of spiritual symbolism is discovered if we consider what conflict exists within man, that is, within the lesser world. For what does the sphere of heaven, which encloses the planets, signify except the human body, which covers the rational soul? That soul is, as it were, contained by the number seven of the planets, since it is imbued with an equal number of gifts of the Holy Spirit.

And what does it mean that the sphere slips toward the setting-place, while the planets strive together toward the rising-place, except what the Apostle says: “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V)? Does he not complain that the sphere is, as it were, fighting against the planets when he laments the conflict between his flesh and his soul, saying: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. VII)? And as though the sphere were dragging the planets behind it, he immediately added: “And taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.”

The seven planets therefore strive toward the rising-place when the rational soul, stirred by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, tries to return to God, who is clearly the beginning of all things. The sphere, however, slips toward the setting-place when the flesh, neglecting higher things, is weighed down into the depths of vices. Hence it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX).

But the brevity appropriate to a letter does not permit us to pursue these matters at greater length. What shall I say about the fact that this same machinery of the heavenly sphere continually rolls back upon itself, and not outward, so that in the revolution of one of its hemispheres it completes the day, and in the revolution of the other it completes the night? In this way, when one revolution of the entire heavenly sphere has been completed, the number of twenty-four hours is fulfilled, by which one day together with its night is completed.

Thus, while heaven serves man, the day is illuminated by the rays of the sun, and the night is adorned by the moon and the varying appearance of the twinkling stars. But because these things are perceived bodily, we pass them over and now come to greater and invisible matters.

## CHAPTER IV. That angels range throughout the whole world to aid human beings

Whoever is occupied with the utterances of the divine Scriptures does not fail to know that a multitude of heavenly powers moves daily throughout this world and extends to us a helping hand in the struggle. Of them Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). For they minister to God for this purpose: that they may protect us from the assaults of wicked spirits. Hence Paul also says: “They are ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebr. I).

Human frailty could not withstand the cunning of so subtle and experienced an enemy unless angelic power drove him back from the temptations of the elect. Hence, from the day of baptism until death, an angel is assigned to each of us, both to guard the one who fights valiantly against temptation and to continue providing assistance in good works. We would give examples, if they were not already widely known through constant experience.

Here we should note how much grace God grants to man, and how great an injury God suffers from man. God assigns angelic powers to human guardianship, while unhappy man, abandoning the cleanliness and purity of the virtues, pollutes himself with filth and the squalor of vices. He wallows in the stench of exhaled, muddy lust; he is defiled by the filth of worm-ridden avarice; and finally his soul is changed, like the rivers of Egypt, into the blood of hatred and murder (Exod. VII). At last, falling as though into a sewer of excrement, he is disgraced, wrapped in the refuse of manifold wickedness. The angel endures this stench and the dishonorable nausea of corruption most unwillingly and grievously, even though, bound by the law of heavenly authority, he does not abandon obedience.

In the sight of angels nothing is foul, nothing reeks of obscenity, except vice and sin. Thus they shudder at our guilt and abhor our filth, just as a person is compelled to spit out the stench of an exhaling latrine. Hence, each day before the tribunal of the eternal Judge the angel complains about the wickedness committed by his charge, and, declaring its obscenities one by one, confesses that he has suffered a grievous injury.

For if a powerful king wished to entrust an underage son to the guardianship of one of his nobles, and the boy afterward, driven mad by insanity, smeared himself with flowing saliva and the mucus of his nostrils, then either threw himself into a fire with frenzied recklessness or, like a filthy swine, rolled himself in the mire of a foul bog, would not that guardian immediately demand that the charge be returned and cast off the service of the ward [printed *papatis*, uncertain]? 

How much more, then, should we believe that the angelic sublimity both glorifies God, the giver of all good things, when it beholds the holy conduct of the saints, and, in his presence, condemns the crimes of perverse human beings by carefully enumerating them?

Moreover, at the day of judgment those who would have become their defenders had they lived rightly will be witnesses against their wickedness. In this way, therefore, what was provided for the salvation of those who live rightly becomes a source of destruction for those who act badly, because the holy angels assigned to assist the just increase the punishment of the reprobate.

Happy, therefore, are those who live justly: while they fight without reconciliation against malignant spirits, they are fortified by the aid of angelic strength. Add also that the wicked spirits themselves are assigned to serve our advancement. For when we are tempted and do not succumb; when we are attacked and prevail; when the violent enemy indeed assails us but does not conquer us, he increases the weight of our future reward; and while he inflicts the labor of combat, he supplies us with the occasion for victory.

## CHAPTER V. That everything serves man, even hell

Behold: while we rapidly and briefly survey all things, we find that everything serves human purposes in harmony—heaven, earth, and hell alike. Someone might perhaps accuse us of presumption if an authoritative statement of Scripture did not come to mind. But Paul says to the Corinthians: “For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come. All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. III).

Yet all things truly belong to man only if man himself is truly man. For there is one who is man in name alone, and there is one who is man in reality and truth.

Hear Solomon: “Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man” (Eccl. XII). But what is the conclusion of the matter except the one of whom the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X)? Christ is the end of the law for righteousness, because whatever either the old or the new law says is without doubt referred to him. “For righteousness” is not said idly, because the word of the divine law justifies and cleanses the soul from filth, as the Truth says to the disciples: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV).
