To fear God is to despise, by cursing and abhorring them, all the things that God forbids. To keep his commandments is to practice in deeds everything that he orders.

He therefore fears God who earnestly takes care to avoid what he forbids. He keeps his commandments who strives to fulfill what he commands. “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man.” It is as though he said plainly: Whoever does not strive to avoid what is forbidden, whoever neglects to fulfill the commands—because he lacks reason—has indeed the name of man, but does not possess the reality of man, since he does not truly exercise the virtue of the name by which he is called.

Let him believe himself truly a man who acknowledges the Author of human beings; otherwise, “the one who does not know will not be known” (1 Cor. XIV). What man is without these things Scripture plainly defines when it says: “The stars are not clean in his sight” (Job XXV); how much less man, who is rottenness, and the son of man, who is a worm? Hence Abraham, when he is raised to the summit of the highest conversation and specially earns the grace of divine intimacy, is humbled by remembering this humility when he says: “Shall I speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes?” (Gen. XVIII).

Among the Greeks, too, the following custom is said to be observed. When an emperor is appointed to office, as soon as he has been crowned with the imperial fillets, adorned with the glory of crown and scepter, surrounded by the service of nobles, and received by the melodious choirs of psalm-singers, someone comes forward and stands before him. With one hand he offers a vessel full of the bones and ashes of the dead; in the other he holds finely combed flax tow, softly loosened from hanging fibers. Fire is then applied to it, and suddenly, in the blink of an eye, it is consumed as the flame devours it. Thus the emperor is to consider in the one what he is, and in the other to see what he possesses.

In the ashes he recognizes himself as ash; in the tow he already gathers an understanding of how suddenly the world will burn on the day of judgment. Thus, while he considers both himself and his possessions to be so vain and so worthless, he will not become arrogant because he has ascended the height of imperial power; and while it is undeniable that both possessor and possession are subject to the common fate of all, he will not be puffed up as though he had been raised to the summit of a unique dignity.

Let man therefore consider the beautiful order of the world’s condition. While he sees that everything has been assigned for his use, let him give thanks not to himself but to his Creator. Let him trample down the world’s alluring glory beneath the judgment of his mind; let him regard the vigor of the flesh as already dry dust; let him always place the day of his calling before his eyes as a mirror; and let him tremble before the strict judgment of the final examination. Thus, while he is now subject to the laws of his Creator, he who appears distinguished among earthly creatures will also be truly exalted in heavenly glory.

## SCHOLIA

“Likewise the tiger, which in the Parthian language is called *sagitta* (‘arrow’), traverses eight hundred stades in a single run, but the whole world in a full day, and so forth.” Unless these statements are understood as hyperbole, they are altogether fabulous. Its speed is indeed so great that Marcus Varro, in Book I of *On the Latin Language*, wrote that up to his own time it had never been captured. Yet Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Malice of Herodotus*, attests that it is sometimes captured. Thus, just as the speed of certain human beings is commonly compared with that of the swiftest animals—for example, 2 Kings II: “Now Asahel was a very swift runner, like one of the gazelles that linger in the woods”—so the speed of those animals that hold the highest rank in swiftness is sometimes expressed hyperbolically. The holy cardinal mentions the tiger and its mystical significance in Letter 18 of Book II.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## TWENTY-FOURTH OPUSCULUM. AGAINST REGULAR CLERICS WHO POSSESS PRIVATE PROPERTY

### ARGUMENT

He first condemns the vice of obstinacy, than which nothing can be more displeasing to God or more destructive to human affairs, since from it, as from a fountain, the seeds of dissension and discord flow into the Church. He then attacks with the utmost severity certain clerics who, although they were supported in common from the revenues of the churches, nevertheless possessed money and other goods separately, and obstinately asserted that they were permitted to do this by law.

He refutes them with the strongest arguments and clearly proves that clerics belonging to the group called canons can possess nothing of their own or privately, but ought, as soon as they are initiated into sacred orders, either to give all their goods to the poor or to place them in common. Therefore he begs the supreme pontiff himself to compel by his own authority and jurisdiction what human and divine laws require clerics to do.

To the most blessed lord Alexander, pope, Peter, a sinful monk, offers service.

As far as the measure of our understanding permits, venerable father, no evil in the human race is a crime more destructive than the defense of wickedness. Hence David says: “Do not incline my heart to evil words, to make excuses for sins” (Ps. CXL). The offense against God deserves anger; the excuse provokes vengeance.

This vice, just as it emerged from the root of the human race, sprouts daily and, like branches bursting forth from a tree, does not cease to produce new growth. When Adam was asked why he had eaten from the forbidden fruit, he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III). When the woman was also asked why she had done this, she said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid.). It is as though each of them indirectly hurled the crime back at the Creator and attacked the one by whom they were reproved, saying: This guilt must surely be attributed not to us but to you, who joined a wife to the man and decreed that the serpent should live among human beings in paradise.

That disciple who answered the Lord when he was questioned about Abel—“Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. IV)—was, as it were, the *primischolus* (“chief pupil”; the precise force is uncertain) of them both. David was carefully guarding against this vice when he said: “May the storm of waters not overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII). For when a person sins, he falls as though into a pit; but when he defends his sins, the mouth of the pit presses over him so that no exit may open. Thus a person falls into the pit when he sins, but closes the mouth of the pit upon himself when he makes excuses.

From this defense or excuse of crime heresy arises. For heresy is interpreted as “choice.” And when someone tries to defend what he chooses, having abandoned the path of truth and being swept through the precipices of perverse doctrine, he must necessarily slip into heresy. The difference between a sinner and a heretic is this: a sinner is one who commits an offense, whereas a heretic is one who defends sin through perverse doctrine.

But because we have as teachers the holy apostles and apostolic men, we ought not choose what seems right to us, nor obstinately and stubbornly defend what has once been chosen. Rather, we must adhere irrevocably to those things defined by approved teachers of the Church.

## AGAINST REGULAR CLERICS WHO POSSESS PRIVATE PROPERTY

### CHAPTER I. He attacks the obstinacy of the clerics with the words of Saint Augustine

We have prefaced this for the following reason: we grieve that certain holy brothers of the canonical order have burst into such unrestrained and audacious liberty that they not only claim for themselves the right to possess money, but also obstinately assert that this right belongs to them by the authority of their rule.

To refute them convincingly, we could indeed gather many examples from the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments, if our predecessors, the Fathers and teachers of the Church, had been entirely silent on this subject. But it is superfluous for us to break up the clods there with inferior hoes where such vigorous cultivators of the soil of the living have already furrowed the fields with the sharpest plow of their tongues.

Let Augustine therefore come forward first as a witness and decide, with the manifest authority of his examination, whether a canon ought to possess private property. For in the sermon entitled *On the Conduct of the Clergy* he says:

“Let your Charity know that I said to my brothers who remain with me that whoever has anything should either sell it and distribute it to the poor, or give it away, or make it common. Let him have the Church, through which God feeds us. And I granted a delay until Epiphany for those who either had not divided their possessions with their brothers or had indeed divided among their brothers what they possessed but had not yet done anything with some of their own property, because the lawful age was awaited. Let them do with it what they wish, provided that they are poor with me; together let us await the mercy of God.

“But if they do not wish this—and perhaps some do not—certainly I am the one who had decided, as you know, not to ordain anyone a cleric unless he wished to remain with me, so that if he wished to depart from the undertaking, I might rightly remove his clerical office from him, because he would be abandoning the promise and settled fellowship of the holy society.

“Behold, in the sight of God and of you, I change my decision. Let those who wish to have something of their own, for whom God and his Church are not sufficient, remain where they wish and where they can. I do not take their clerical office from them, but I do not want to have hypocrites. It is evil to be such a person; it is evil to fall away from one’s undertaking; but it is worse to pretend to undertake it. Behold, I say that the one who abandons the fellowship of the common life already undertaken, which is praised in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts IV), has fallen. He has fallen to his own harm; he has fallen from his holy profession. Let him heed the Judge—but God, not me.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whoever wishes to remain with me, if he is prepared to be fed by God through his Church and to have nothing of his own, but either to distribute it to the poor or to place it in common, let him remain with me. Whoever does not wish this has his freedom; but let him see whether he can possess the eternity of happiness.”

In the second sermon of the same work he likewise says:

“Whoever lives in hypocrisy, whoever is found possessing private property, I do not permit him to make a will concerning it; rather, I will erase him from the register of the clerics. Let a thousand councils appeal against me; let him sail wherever he wishes against me; let him certainly be wherever he can. The Lord will help me, so that where I am bishop he cannot be a cleric.”

Perhaps I have been excessive in prolonging the example of this blessed teacher. Would that at least he himself were granted credibility, since our words are altogether disregarded. In the words of this holy man it is plainly shown that a cleric who possesses money cannot himself be Christ’s possession or inheritance, nor can he possess God as his inheritance.

We do not say this, however, of all clerics, but specifically of those who are designated by the name “canonical” and live in a congregation. To them, because God is offered as their portion, earthly possession is forbidden. Thus the Lord himself says to Aaron in Numbers: “You shall possess nothing in their land, nor shall you have a portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel” (Num. XVIII).

### CHAPTER II. He does the same with the words of Blessed Jerome

But if, for the removal of money from clerics, the authority of so great a teacher alone should perhaps still not suffice for someone, let him attend carefully to what blessed Jerome is found to have decreed on this matter. For he says the following, among other things, to the bishop Heliodorus:

“Consider, brother: you are not permitted to possess anything of your own. ‘Everyone,’ says the Lord, ‘who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple’ (Luke XIV). Why are you a Christian with a timid heart? Look with Peter upon the net that was left behind (Matt. IV); look upon the tax collector rising immediately from the toll booth to become an apostle (Matt. IX). ‘The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head’ (Matt. VIII; Luke IX); and you measure spacious porticoes and immense areas of buildings? Do you expect an inheritance in this age? You cannot be a fellow-heir of Christ.

“And hear the Lord, not far afterward, saying: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that is yours, give to the poor, and come, follow me’ (Matt. XIX). But you have promised that you are perfect. For when, having abandoned the warfare of the world, you castrated yourself for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, what other life did you pursue except the perfect life?

“Now the perfect servant of Christ possesses nothing except Christ. Or if he possesses anything besides Christ, he is not perfect; and if he is not perfect, although he previously promised God that he would be perfect, he has lied. ‘Everyone who lies kills his soul’ (Wis. I).

“Therefore, to conclude: if you are perfect, why do you desire your paternal goods? If you are not perfect, you have deceived God. The Gospel thunders with divine voices: ‘You cannot serve two masters’ (Matt. VI); and does anyone dare to make Christ a liar by serving both Mammon and the Lord? He cries out repeatedly: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Matt. XVI); and I, loaded down with gold, imagine that I am following Christ?”

To the presbyter Nepotianus he adds, after much else:

“Therefore, let the cleric who serves the Church of Christ first interpret his own name; and, having set forth the definition of the name, let him strive to be what he is called. For if *klēros* (κλῆρος) is called *sors* (‘lot’) in Latin, they are called clerics because they are of the Lord’s lot; or because the Lord himself is the lot—that is, the portion—of the clerics. And because either he himself is the Lord’s portion or he has the Lord as his portion, he ought to present himself in such a way that he both possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord.

“He who possesses the Lord, and says with the Prophet, ‘The Lord is my portion’ (Ps. LXXII), can possess nothing apart from the Lord. But if he possesses anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or varied furnishings, the Lord does not deign to become his portion together with these portions.

“But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance, and I do not receive portions among the other tribes, but live like a Levite and priest from tithes, and, serving at the altar, am sustained by the altar’s offering, having food and clothing, I shall be content with these and, naked, follow the naked cross.”

Blessed Prosper, too, when he prohibited clerics from possessing money as private property, expressed the following judgment: “There cannot be unity of wills where there has been diversity of resources.”

Behold, to condemn and utterly abolish the money of canons, we have brought forward as witnesses three teachers—not ordinary ones, but unconquerable—“so that by the testimony of two or three witnesses every word may stand” (Matt. XVIII).

### CHAPTER III. How frivolous the defense of the canons is

But when we bring these things against them, they immediately produce for us the book of their rule and return to the authority of their rule. Since it grants them a private fund of property, they complain that they are suffering prejudice.

We neither reject this rule entirely nor grant it complete authority. We approve it insofar as it agrees with the holy teachers of the Church; but we cast it aside and spit upon it insofar as it does not accord with their authoritative institutions.

Let their rule itself now be brought forward, and let us discern, on at least one little page, whether it should be accepted in its entirety without distinction, or cautiously and suspiciously only in part. The following is plainly found in one of its sections:

“The judgment of the holy Fathers teaches that clerics should not be pursuers of riches, nor should they receive the goods of the Church without due order. For those who serve the Church, yet do not possess what they need, either accept it willingly or demand it; they are thinking too carnally. It is unworthy that the faithful and diligent devotion of clerics should, for the sake of a worldly stipend, disregard eternal rewards, so that they must render an account of what they receive and multiply their own sins through the sins of others.

“Therefore it is necessary, indeed beneficial, for clerics, when receiving ecclesiastical expenses, to avoid endangering themselves. Accordingly, from their own resources as well as from the Church’s resources, they should neither accept nor demand more than is appropriate; that is, they should accept food, drink, and clothing, and be content with these, lest by accepting more they appear to burden the poor—not without great sin—and lest they accept what a poor person would have lived on.”

Behold, in these words this rule agrees with us and with the authority of the whole Church, since it proclaims that clerics ought to be content with food, drink, and clothing. But what follows immediately afterward appears utterly absurd, inept, and frivolous:

“Those, however, who neither abound in their own resources nor possess ecclesiastical estates, and who provide great benefit to the Church, should receive food and clothing in the canonical congregation, together with shares of alms.”

For Prosper’s book says of such men: “Clerics whom either choice or birth has made poor, living in a congregation, should receive the necessities of life.”

First, therefore, it gives food and clothing; then it makes them sharers in alms. The former is for the necessary support of life; the latter for stuffing up a heap of worldly goods: the former so that they may live bodily, the latter so that they may feed the fuel of eternal death.

The very monstrosities of these creeping words and the disgrace of their shameful and confused expression must also be considered. For after stating that clerics should receive, together with food and clothing, shares of alms, it seems to give the reason for this: “because,” it says, “it is said of such men in Prosper’s book: ‘Clerics whom either choice or birth has made poor, living in a congregation, should receive the necessities of life.’”

Speak, reformer of Tullian eloquence; speak, new Demosthenes. Prosper says that clerics should receive the necessities of life—is that why you command that, in addition to food and clothing, shares of alms also be apportioned to each individual? According to your interpretation, does “receiving the necessities of life” mean that, after receiving food and clothing, they should receive shares of alms?

How well the clerics act who proclaim you with praises, who embrace with joyful hearts the grave and unbearable edicts of your law! And truly the things you promulgate are grave and unbearable, since, from the greatest to the least—that is, even if there is a little boy of two or three years in the clergy—you pile up for each one five pounds of wine and four [pounds] of bread, so that he may be filled not merely to vomiting but to the point of having his entrails forced out.

And to make the full force of your discernment apparent, you command that even if he is refreshed only once a day, this measure of bread and wine should in no way be reduced—so that if the reins of the meal are loosened beyond the limit of your sobriety, the belly and flanks are compelled not merely to belch but to burst.

Apart from certain judgments of the holy Fathers found in the same little book, therefore, just as the unpolished style bristles in its wording, so its distorted understanding in many of its judgments needs correction. He did not know how to discover what he should write; and if he did discover any absurdities, he did not know how to write them. These flowers of eloquence love those whose thorny conduct opposes ecclesiastical discipline.

### CHAPTER IV. He proves the case by arguments

Indeed, since the holy Fathers do not differ in condemning clerical private property, but agree with one spirit and one voice in strictly forbidding and utterly removing money from clerics, let us approach the source and seek again the principal origin of the stream from which they drew these things.

Although it is sacrilegious to dispute the judgment of such men, let us nevertheless not fear to approach their teachers—that is, our own teachers’ teachers—so that we too may deserve to be instructed by those who instructed our teachers. When the source from which the stream of purity arises has been exposed, the rashness of defiling and abusive audacity may be refuted.

It is therefore established and clear that the rule of the canons proceeded from the standard of apostolic life; and whenever each spiritual community maintains the proper discipline of its order, it imitates, in a certain sense, the infancy of the nursing Church.

Let us hear, then, what way of life and order of living the Church, newly come to the faith under the apostles, maintained:

“The multitude of believers,” as Luke says, “had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own; but they had everything in common” (Acts IV).

Behold: where there was no diversity of possessions, unity of wills flourished. Clearly, where there is no division of wealth, the affection of many minds is gathered into a union of charity. For mind is divided from mind where the sharing of resources is not maintained; and where ownership of possessions is diverse, the minds of the possessors are not one. But wherever all surrounding things are possessed in common, the minds of different people converge in one will, because they find nothing over which they ought to quarrel with one another.

Therefore, any cleric who tries to possess a private fund of property cannot follow in the footsteps of the apostles, because he will not have one heart and one soul with his brothers. He may have, together with Judas, a money box and money, but he cannot have unanimity and pure harmony with the apostles (John XII).

Of the apostles’ rule it is read in their Acts: “As many as were owners of fields or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts IV). Immediately afterward it is added: “It was distributed to each according to what each had need of” (ibid.).

Come now, cleric, who claim for yourself permission to store away money and usurp the right to possess private property: tell me, I beg you, whose resources are those from which you are permitted to have a private fund. Are they yours, or the Church’s?

But if you are permitted to appropriate your own money, how did you place it at the apostles’ feet? If the goods you store away belong to the Church, why did you despise what was your own? Moreover, if you kept something back from your private possessions, hear the Apostle rebuking you terribly:

“Why,” he says, “has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and defraud the price of the field? While it remained, did it not remain yours, and when it was sold, was it not in your power? Why have you put this matter in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (ibid.).

But if you are trying not to possess private property but to divide the Church’s goods, which are plainly held in common by you and your brothers, then say, Teacher Jesus, say to my brother that he should divide the inheritance with me.

[Col. 0486D] And it should be noted that the evangelist had prefaced this by saying: “Someone from the crowd said to him” (Luke XII). You, therefore, not as a Levite or cleric, but as an ordinary person from the crowd, and a layman, ask Jesus to command that the inheritance be divided between you and your brother. He immediately answers: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (ibid.). And he soon adds: “See and beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke). Do you wish, then, to divide? You will not have Jesus as judge or divider, but rather as the avenger of schismatic division. “The one who is not with me,” he says, “is against me; and the one who does not gather with me scatters” (ibid. XI).

Moreover, if you are permitted to possess money, none is better than your own. But if you possess what had been yours, what, then, did you leave behind when you came to the religious order? Rather, having returned to your vomit (Prov. XXVI; II Pet. II), and abandoning the plough while turning your gaze backward, you will no longer be fit for the kingdom of heaven (Luke IX). But if you are permitted to store ecclesiastical goods, you appear to have increased your riches, not rejected them, so that you seek the profit of money more than the institution of religious life, and wish not so much to ascend to the height of holiness as to pile up heaps of money. Shall clerics be granted what Christ did not permit the apostles? For when he sent them to preach, as Mark says, he commanded them to take nothing on the way except a staff: neither a bag, nor bread, nor copper coins in their belts (Mark VI); [Col. 0487A] but for you, as a receptacle for copper—that is, money—may a chest, rather than merely a belt, suffice.

And since the Apostle calls greed “the service of idols” (Col. III), how do you worship Christ, when you venerate an idol in money? For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement, moreover, between Christ and Belial? Or what share does the faithful have with the unbeliever? (II Cor. VI.) What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols?

Clearly, when, contrary to the institution of your order, you store money in a chest and put your trust in uncertain riches, although you ought to place your hope in God alone—for “where your treasure is, there without doubt is your heart also” (Matt. VI)—you should no longer rightly be called a worshiper of Christ, but a worshiper of coins. And when the Lord says of the Levites, “I am their inheritance” (Num. XVIII; Deut. XVIII), and you answer in song, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. LXXII), behold: if you maintain your order, if you despise the abominable profits of money, you are both God’s inheritance, and God is your inheritance.

But this whole sacrament is turned into adultery when the wretched cleric becomes a servant of money, serving it assiduously as though it were God by carefully guarding it. He himself is possessed by the money he possesses, since, under the rule of greed, he is compelled to fix his heart upon it and serve it with sleepless vigilance. Shall I therefore cast Christ out of the chest of my breast and pack money into his place? Certainly Christ is so noble a treasure that he utterly refuses the company of private property and does not allow himself to be enclosed together with the filth of money. Therefore, for Christ to fill the little chamber of your breast, let the copper coin depart from him; for Christ to impress his image upon your soul, let the worthless didrachma bearing Caesar’s image disappear.

CHAPTER V. What evils arise from private property among canons

The ownership of private property finally causes clerics to disdain the command of their bishop; to abandon the true freedom of discipline and obedience; and, in the disgraceful and most shameful reproach of surrender, to submit their necks to secular persons. When the Lord says to Moses: “Bring forward the tribe of Levi and make it stand before Aaron the priest, so that they may minister to him, keep watch, and observe [Col. 0488A] everything pertaining to the worship of the multitude before the tabernacle of testimony; and let them guard the vessels of the tabernacle, serving in his ministry. You shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons, to whom they have been handed over by the sons of Israel” (Num. III).

Who could doubt that Aaron and his sons possessed the authority of bishops? Who does not know that the tribe of Levi prefigured the order of clerics? The Levites are therefore handed over as a gift to Aaron and his sons by the sons of Israel, when the clerical order is taken from the whole Christian people for the watchfulness of ecclesiastical worship and offered so that its members may attend upon and minister to their bishops. But whoever is a servant of mammon abhors the practices of ecclesiastical discipline.

Nor should what immediately follows there be passed over: “I,” says the Lord, “have taken the Levites from among the sons of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the sons of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine” (ibid.); [Col. 0488B] so that it may clearly be evident that the order of clerics is the private possession of almighty God, just as God himself is the special inheritance of clerics. And how great is the senselessness and madness if the one to whom God is offered rejects him and seeks instead the advantage of earthly possessions? Whoever is not satisfied with God as his inheritance does not know what could satisfy him, because furious desire blinds the eye of his mind.

And certainly whoever is such—because he violates his order for the love of money—is plainly unworthy to hold ecclesiastical dignity. Hence Solomon also says: “As one who throws a stone onto a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool” (Prov. XXVI). Since among the gentiles Mercury was called the god of a shrine [f. profit], or of money, “a heap of Mercury” means a mound and mass of coins. And since a minting rule is impressed upon a coin, what is represented by a heap of coins except the assembly of clerics who follow the rule and display the image of true holiness?

What, moreover, do we understand by the stone except the hard, foolish, and senseless mind of the one who, because he does not believe with unquestioning faith that God exists, places his hope in some earthly possession? Of him the Prophet says: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God” (Ps. XIII). Honor is given to this fool when someone devoted not to God but [Col. 0488D] to money is promoted to the summit of an ecclesiastical rank. But just as a heap of coins is scattered when a stone is thrown upon it, so, through the arrival of an unworthy or stone-like shepherd, the compact order of those who walk according to the rule and of clerics obedient in charity is destroyed. For it is weighed down by the shadow of a wicked shepherd and, like a heap of heavenly coins, is overthrown by the mass of a hellish stone.

Honor must therefore be denied to a fool and senseless person, lest the heap of holy clerics, like spiritual coins, be submerged. Of this same fool Solomon says a little earlier: “Lame in his feet and drinking iniquity is the one who sends words by a foolish messenger” (Prov. XXVI). What else, surely, seems to be expressed by these [Col. 0489A] words except that the office of preaching should not be entrusted to anyone who is carnally wise and therefore foolish?

For of holy preachers it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. LII; Rom. X.) Thus, if any administrator of the Church appoints worthy and capable persons to positions of dignity, he walks as though on straight feet. Through them the word is scattered and travels everywhere; and what he cannot accomplish by himself, he strives to fulfill effectively through them.

But if he presumes to appoint carnal and reprobate men, he walks lame in his feet. He is also said to drink iniquity, because, when he sends the words of holy preaching through a foolish messenger and, contrary to the Apostle, hastily lays hands on him [Col. 0489B] (I Tim. V), he shares in the sins of others. For even if someone speaks prudently, nevertheless, if he himself does not do what he says, he is rightly judged spiritually lame on the journey. Hence it is appropriately added there: “Just as beautiful legs are useless to the lame, so a parable is indecent in the mouth of fools” (Prov. XXVI).

He plainly rests upon beautiful legs who shines with the brilliance of eloquent speech. But when, without good works, he suppresses polished eloquence, he advances straight legs of words as though they had no stride. Thus he has, as it were, beautiful legs for appearance but not useful ones for walking: bound by the gout-like snares of vices, he himself limps shamefully while inviting others to walk nimbly.

In the mouth of such fools, therefore, a parable is indecent, because, while they sound spiritual and live carnally, their life does not agree with their lips. Correct preaching does not free those who speak honorably but live dishonorably; rather, a biting conscience vehemently accuses them. Hence it is fittingly added there: “As when a thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools” (ibid.).

A thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard when the one who is drunk with love of this life generates within his mind the prick of reproach. In the mouth of fools, then, a parable is like a thorn, because, while they say one thing and do another, their mind is sometimes rebuked within itself and pierced by something like the sharp point of a thorn. Indeed, the conscience of one who lives badly but speaks well pricks him: in what he utters outwardly, he is wounded inwardly by a certain spur of shame and fear.

CHAPTER VI. Who are fit for the office of preaching

[Col. 0490A] Let the discussion therefore return to those with whom it began: a cleric who has been captured by love of money is in no way fit to administer the words of doctrine. This is also demonstrated by the apostolic example we proposed above. For when Scripture first says, “The multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul,” and immediately adds, “Nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common,” it then at once says: “And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all.” It then continues: “For there was no needy person among them” (Acts IV).

What is the meaning of the fact that the sacred historian, while speaking of apostolic continence and common life, suddenly interrupts his subject as though introducing new material and, as if changing his style, leaps to recounting the steadfastness of their preaching, saying, “And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection”? Why does he insert one subject into another, when he ought to have pursued and continued what he had begun, unless to show openly that only those are fit for the office of preaching who possess no profit from earthly resources and, possessing nothing individually, possess everything in common? “Having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Cor.).

These men, since they are hindered by no obstacles of earthly things, stand ready for the Lord’s camps on the field of battle. Stripped of possessions and girded only with the weapons of virtue, they fight against the ranks of vices with the sword of the Spirit; they are capable warriors for striking down the necks of resisting enemies. Unequal to this battle and feebly yielding are those who, not content with what is common, seek to be burdened with ownership of private property.

Hence in Deuteronomy it is said to those marching to battle: “Whoever has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that everyone may eat from it, let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man perform his duty” (Deut. XX).

But now, venerable father, let it suffice to have prolonged this unpolished discussion thus far. Nevertheless, so that these words may have an effective force against the rebellion of disobedient clerics—or rather, of coin-worshipers—may the holy [Col. 0490D] vigor of your apostolate impel you.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0491]

495–496 OPUSCULUM TWENTY-FIVE. ON THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD

ARGUMENT

The whole purpose here is to show what the dignity of a priest is, what his office is, how great the innocence required of one who undertakes so sublime a charge must be, and how not only crime but even the suspicion of crime must be avoided. At the beginning, however, something I had forgotten to mention: he gives thanks to the same man because he had sent him many gifts.

[Col. 0491A] To Lord A., venerable archbishop, Peter, sinful monk, sends the devotion of his fullest affection.

When the patriarch Jacob says to his son Joseph, “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers” (Gen. XLIX), I can appropriately say: the blessings of my father—not of his fathers, but of that same father of mine—have been strengthened by blessings. For so many were the blessings that your generosity directed to me that one commended another, and those that followed strengthened those that preceded, as Scripture says.

Moreover, if David deserved thanks when he sent gifts to the elders of Judah from the spoils he had taken from the Amalekites, saying, “Receive a blessing from the spoils of the enemies of the Lord” (I Reg. XXX), how much greater are the thanks I owe, since I have received blessings not bloodied by the hands of the enemies of the Lord, but sanctified and drawn from the sanctuary of the Lord!

But, so that the discourse may turn from the occasion of bodily gifts toward the sacramental meaning of spiritual blessings: since the Apostle places great happiness in what he says—“You have been called for this purpose, that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance” (I Pet. III)—how great is the dignity granted to you, that is, to the highest priests of the Church, so that you may not only possess the blessing presented to you, but may also hand it on to others!

And it is not just any blessing, but even an episcopal one, by which it is your right to ordain a bishop. And since it is a matter of no small terror and dread even to be a priest of a lower order, for he too is commanded by the law to bear the iniquity of the people (Num. XVIII), how fearful and trembling-hearted must it be for those who now surpass all others in ecclesiastical dignity, since they must also answer before all others at the tribunal of the terrifying Judge!

Therefore careful consideration must be given to this: the one whom the exalted dignity of the highest priesthood raises to wear the insignia of ecclesiastical eminence must also be lifted up by the height of a praiseworthy and demanding way of life. Just as he stands above others through the lofty summit of the dignity he has received, so a surpassing life and the splendor of spiritual conduct must adorn him above others.

Hence Moses says: “The high priest—that is, the chief priest among his brothers—upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood, and who has been clothed in holy garments, shall not uncover his head, nor tear his garments; he shall not enter at all upon any dead person. He shall not be defiled even by his father or mother, nor depart from the holy places, lest he pollute the sanctuary of the Lord, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him” (Lev. XXI).

The priest’s head is anointed with oil when his mind is nourished by the richness of the Holy Spirit. The same oil consecrates his hands when the devotion of good will, which the priest carries in his mind, is visibly displayed in his work.

[ON THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD]

CHAPTER ONE. What it means for a priest to depart from the holy places

[Col. 0492B] It is plainly the mark of a holy priest both to think about holy things and to express clearly in his works what he has conceived in his mind. Otherwise, what benefit is there in thinking of something good unless he diligently watches over it and completes that very thing in action?

The priest must therefore labor so that his head may be consecrated through the contemplation of a devout will, and his hands may be anointed with the grace of spiritual oil through the evident sign of holy action. He is also said to be clothed in holy garments, because it is fitting that a priest always be adorned with the clothing of piety and justice, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with justice” (Ps. CXXXI).

He is commanded not to uncover his head—that is, not to open his heart to the desires of this world, but always to keep it hidden in the pursuit of attaining the heavenly kingdom. He is also ordered not to tear his garments, meaning that he should always walk clothed in the garment of honorable and devout conduct, lest, God forbid, he tear it apart through the interpretation of some perverse deed.

He is further forbidden to enter upon a dead person, clearly so that he may carefully withdraw his foot from evils by which the soul dies and guard himself from dead works with vigilant concern. Of these the Apostle says: “Christ rescued us from dead works in order to serve the living God” (Heb. IX).

It is also added that he must not be defiled by father or mother—that is, that he must not be polluted either by the affairs of the world or by the desire for this mortal life. Hence it is rightly added that he shall not depart from the holy places, lest he pollute my sanctuary.

A priest departs from the holy places when, neglecting care for souls, he wanders after earthly desires. He departs from the holy places when, setting ecclesiastical discipline aside, he becomes excessively entangled in the business of passing worldly affairs. There [Col. 0493A] it is immediately and aptly added: “Lest he pollute my sanctuary.”

The sanctuary is polluted when any priest, scattered among earthly desires and weakened by secular concerns, does not hesitate boldly to stand at the most sacred altars; that is, when what the Prophet says comes to pass: “And it shall be: as the people, so the priest” (Isa. XXIV).

Therefore, so that the Church of Christ may flourish in its own purity and not be soiled by the foul contagion of those who minister badly, it is aptly added there: “He shall marry a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated, and he shall not take a defiled woman or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, lest he mingle the stock of his lineage with the common people of his nation; for I am the Lord who sanctifies him” (Lev. XXI).

The priest’s wife may appropriately be understood as his life and conduct. It is commanded that she be a virgin, so that she may remain free and uncorrupted by the worn-out lust of the unclean spirit, which violates souls. Let her not be a widow, but joined in a blessed covenant to the heavenly bridegroom. She is also forbidden to be repudiated, defiled, or a prostitute, lest, if she is polluted by the filth of lust and the contamination of luxuriant vices, she be separated from that same bridegroom of souls by a fatal divorce.

The Apostle had given this defiled wife a bill of divorce when he said: “What things were gain to me, these I considered loss for Christ; for whose sake I have counted everything as loss, and regard it as dung” (Phil. III). It is as if he said: “That defiled and prostituted wife to whom I had been joined in Judaism, I abandon through divorce; and, with the bill of divorce intervening, I cast her away like dung.”

From such a wife of a priest, children are not begotten who offer sacrifice to God, but rather those who incur the severity and vengeance of divine judgment. Hence, when the divine voice says to the prophet Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of fornications, because the land will surely commit fornication away from the Lord,” he, as Scripture testifies, “went and took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to Hosea: Call his name Jezreel” (Hos. I).

Although this name may seem to signify prosperity, since it is interpreted as “seed of God,” here it nevertheless denotes God’s vengeance and wrath, as is immediately added: “For yet a little while, and I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu; and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end, and on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel” (ibid.).

That Jezreel here signifies not salvation or prosperity but rather the wrath of God is also indicated by what immediately follows: “She conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said: Call her name ‘Without Mercy,’ because I will no longer continue to have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will utterly forget them. And when she had borne a third child, he said: Call his name ‘Not My People,’ because you are not my people, and I will not be your God.”

From these names of the sons of the fornicate woman we clearly learn that whoever joins himself as a husband to an unclean life as to a wife and takes pleasure in her deceitfully flattering embraces cannot beget from her children who please God, because a sweet fruit cannot come from a bitter root: “For a bad tree cannot produce good fruits” (Matt. VI).

Therefore the priest must beware of taking a defiled woman or prostitute as his wife, but must always display the honor of chaste and modest conduct. From this wife he may be able to beget not illegitimate but legitimate children, as he strives, by divine grace, to make the noble fruits of good works grow.

It is necessary, then, for a priest to take a priestly wife, from whom he may produce offspring that will answer to their father’s lineage. Hence it is appropriately added there: “He shall not mingle the stock of his lineage with the common people of his nation” (Lev. XXI).

A priest associates the stock of his lineage with the common people of his nation when, living in a common manner, he is not distinguished from the people by the merit of a more illustrious life; when, finally, he walks along the broad and spacious path of worldly conduct and does not separate himself from the common crowds through the honor of spiritual manners.

But for a priest to produce offspring worthy of his lineage, he too must not depart from the footsteps of his fathers—that is, of the holy priests who came before him—lest, if he degenerates from their illustrious ancestry by living ignobly, he lose the right of the priestly office which he had been unworthily exercising.

CHAPTER TWO. That the nobility of priests is a holy life

[Col. 0494C] Hence, in the Book of Ezra, after it has been stated concerning the sons of priests—the sons of Hobaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, and the sons of Barzillai, who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name—it is immediately added: “They sought the record of their genealogy, and did not find it, and they were expelled from the priesthood” (I Esd. II).

Clearly, those who do not find the record of their genealogy are rejected from the priesthood, because those who recognize that, through the ignobility of secular life, they have degenerated from the noble stock of their preceding fathers ought properly to be expelled from the priesthood by the force of canonical judgment.

The priest of the Church must therefore be noble, so that, as the Lord’s minister, he may be ashamed to be a servant of sin. He brought us to this nobility, of whom the Apostle says: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love; and his blood wiped away from us the slavery of sin” (Col. I). Of him John says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Apoc. I).

For a priest to possess this purity in himself above all others, he should strive to display clearly in himself the mark of Christ’s blood, as the Apostle says: “I always carry the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. VI).

Hence the law also commanded that the tip of the right ear of the high priest, and likewise his right hand and foot, be touched with the blood of a sacrificed ram (Lev. II). Thus, to bring the discourse swiftly to its conclusion, the priest carries the blood of the sacrificed ram on his ear when he eagerly delights in hearing the mystery of Christ’s passion.

The same blood is smeared upon his right hand when he effectively performs what he has understood as a diligent hearer. His right foot is marked with the same blood when the priest’s life is fortified against the temptations of the devil by remembrance of Christ’s passion, so that, having received power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, he does not fear their bites or the poisons of their feeble fury.

Or, certainly, because the foot is the extremity of the body, what is signified by this except the completion of good work? Namely, that we should bring every good thing we begin perseveringly to a happy conclusion.

Hence the divine voice says to the Israelite people: “If you listen,” it says, “to the voice of the Lord your God, so as to do and keep his commandments, the Lord your God will make you higher than all the nations” (Deut. XX). In these words what is figured in the limbs is plainly expressed: “If you listen to the voice of the Lord your God”—behold, the blood of the sacrificed ram reddens on the priest’s ear. What follows, “so as to do,” is the working hand. What is added last, “and keep his commandments,” is perseverance in good work. For it benefits no one to begin a good work unless he strives to preserve it until he completes it.

And it should be noted that only the priest’s right ear, hand, and foot are commanded to be smeared with that blood, so that he may always preserve the uprightness of a right-handed way of life and faith in all things and, by straying from the path, not encounter the winding deviation of the left.

Or, certainly, he should always hold the mystery of the Lord’s passion as the right and superior thing, so that he may utterly despise all the allurements of this world as left and worthless.

Indeed, because the priest is the leader and standard-bearer of the Lord’s army, he is commanded to walk adorned with these marks of distinction and to carry before the ranks of ecclesiastical soldiers who follow him the banners of the blood and cross of Christ.

The prophet Zechariah was depicting this when he said: “On that day what is upon the bridle of the horse shall be holy to the Lord” (Zech. XIV). Before the Savior’s coming, what was the human race except like a horse without a bridle, which unrestrained freedom carried everywhere across the fields of its pleasures?

But our Redeemer placed a bridle in its mouth when he set before it the holy Gospel, by which all the vices of wanton licentiousness are restrained. Upon this bridle the holiness of the Lord—that is, the cross—is placed, because all the commandments of the holy Gospel breathe the cross and invite us to carry the cross after Christ.

CHAPTER THREE. That a priest must avoid even the slightest suspicion of crime

[Col. 0495D] The same thing was signified by that golden plate which the high priest wore upon his head for glory and beauty, on which the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, was inscribed (Exod. XXVIII). For just as there were four letters there, so likewise there are four horns of the cross embracing the four parts of the divided world.

The priest carried it for glory and beauty, since the Apostle also says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). Let the priest therefore carry the golden plate on his head, so that he may continually turn the cross of Christ over in his mind. Let him also consequently apply the holiness of the Lord to the bridle of his horse, so that he may crucify his flesh with its vices and desires.

The priest then applies both the golden plate to his head and the holiness of the Lord to the bridle of his horse when he directs the gaze of his mind toward the cross of Christ and restrains his body, like a savage horse, from every freedom of wanton vices.

For this reason the mystery of carrying the cross in two ways is written, since both Elijah (IV Reg. II) and John the Baptist [Col. 0496B] had leather belts around their waists (Matt. III). Of our Savior John says in the Apocalypse: “He had a golden belt around his breasts” (Apoc. I).

It is evident that the human heart is situated between the two breasts. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved will dwell between my breasts” (Cant. I)—that is, “he will continually rest in my heart.”

What, then, does it mean to gird the loins, where lust is especially vigorous, with leather belts, which are made from dead animals, except to restrain on every side through bodily affliction all the unlawful movements and kindling of carnal passions?

And what does it mean to have a golden belt around the breasts except to keep ever watchful with attentive care against the troublesome fantasies of encroaching thoughts?

We gird our loins with a leather belt when we restrain the wantonness of the flesh through abstinence from food. We have a golden belt around our breasts when we fight in an unbroken struggle against the assaults of hostile thoughts.

Then what follows there will come to pass. For immediately after the prophet had foretold that the holiness of the Lord would be upon the bridle of the horse, he added: “And there shall be cauldrons in the house of the Lord like bowls before the altar, and every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be sanctified to the Lord of hosts” (Zech. XIV).

The Lord was commanding that cauldrons be turned into bowls and that a golden belt be worn around the breasts in the Gospel, when he said: “Beware lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness and the cares of this world” (Luke XXI). Understand “cauldrons” in overeating and drunkenness; understand the belt around the breasts in the cares of this world.

The breasts of those who longed for the fish of Egypt, who, nauseated by manna, hungered for melons, and yearned for onions and garlic, were plainly cauldrons. Or were they not cauldrons who cried out fervently, “We sat over pots of meat”? (Num. XI.)

Those hearts are cauldrons in which gluttony reigns, and in which, through the heat of desire, foods and various abundance of dishes are boiled. But these cauldrons are turned into bowls, stand before the altar, and are sanctified to the Lord when the holiness of the Lord is placed upon the bridle of the horses, and finally when the golden belt is applied to the inner breasts.

Then, clearly, cauldrons and pots of meat are changed into golden bowls, full of incense—namely, “the prayers of the saints” (Apoc. V). These bowls are placed before the altar, although previously, while they were cauldrons, they were rather occupied with the smell of the kitchen.

[Col. 0497A] The priest’s mind is then a golden bowl, full of the spiritual spices of incense, when it is vigilantly devoted to prayers and pious works. This bowl is said to be before the altar because he does not cease to offer to God as a sanctuary everything that he thinks.

And then this cauldron is sanctified to the Lord, and therefore, having received within himself the grace of consecration as a gift from the supreme giver, he now rightly pours it into others by the laying on of hands.

But I, as one who is speaking, have forgotten myself: by prolonging the discourse too long, I have gone beyond the bounds of epistolary brevity. Let these words therefore suffice, provided that I, who began with a blessing, also conclude my sentence with a blessing.

May the right hand of God, venerable father, fill you with its blessings and, with the flock entrusted to you accompanying you, lead you into the heavenly kingdoms.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0497]

503–504 OPUSCULUM TWENTY-SIX. AGAINST THE IGNORANCE AND NEGLIGENCE OF CLERICS

ARGUMENT

He gravely condemns the ignorance and extraordinary incompetence of priests, as well as their negligence—or rather, contempt—in sacred matters. He clearly shows how harmful all these things are both to the priests themselves and to the orders of other people whose salvation has been entrusted to them. He also shows how cautious bishops ought to be in promoting such men to ecclesiastical dignities, lest their sins rebound upon the bishops themselves. In the final section he carefully commends this matter to the bishop to whom he is writing.

[Col. 0497B] To Lord V., most reverend bishop, Peter, sinful man and monk.

Because I see you, most reverend sir, holding the summit of the priesthood in the Church, I confidently believe that a priestly spirit is also present in you. I have therefore decided to communicate especially to you the grief of my heart that torments me concerning priests. For, through the sluggish negligence of bishops, priests are now found so lacking in learning that they not only fail to attain an understanding of what they have read, but scarcely even stammer out, syllable by syllable, the very letters of the flowing text. And what does one who himself, like a stranger, does not understand what he says now ask for the people in his prayers? For it is written: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV). And since the Apostle commands that our service be rational [Col. 0497C] (Rom. XII), how will that service be rational where the one who offers it does not grasp the meaning of his offering? Since almighty God, in those who offer, considers the wishes of their minds more than he attends to the sound of their voices, what can he obtain in his prayers who implores what he does not know?

What else, then, should be thought to happen to such men except what happened to those priests whom the king of the Assyrians established in the cities of Samaria after the captivity of the Israelite people, and who were ignorant of the ceremonies of divine worship? For since they did not know how to worship God according to the observance of the legal commandments, the fury of lions killed them. These are the words of Scripture: “And it was reported to the king of the Assyrians: The nations whom you transferred and settled [Col. 0497D] in the cities of Samaria do not know the ordinances of the God of the land; and the Lord sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the rite of the God of the land” (2 Kings XVII). But Peter says: “Because the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Col. 0498B] (1 Pet. V).

Therefore priests who do not know the ordinances of God are exposed to the teeth of lions, because surely the fury of evil spirits devours those who, persisting in the worship of sacrifices with rash presumption, do not know how God is rightly worshiped. Thus they perform the office of priests without knowing the mystery of the priestly office. And just as through their ignorance there came about what Scripture testifies: “Each nation,” it says, “made its own god, and they placed them in the high shrines that the Samaritans had made; each nation in its cities in which they dwelt” (2 Kings XVII)—so now we grieve that through the ignorance of false priests, who do not know how to teach God’s people, the same thing is happening: some, whose god is their belly and who set their minds on earthly things, worship lust [Col. 0498C] (Phil. III); others revere greed, which is the service of idols (Eph. V); others serve robbery, others perjury, others homicide, others poisoning, with sacrilegious devotion; and thus they offer the service of slavery to various crimes as though to images and carved idols.

Everyone is called the servant of the one whose work he performs. Of such people the Apostle says: “For God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves—those who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I). Such people, through the faith they profess, are enclosed within the walls of the Church, but through the merit of their rejected life they are outside. “For they profess to know [Col. 0498D] God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I). They parade the words of faith, but eagerly persist in works of impiety. Hence it is also read there: “So these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless served their idols” (2 Kings XIV). The Truth itself rebukes them when it says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI).

[AGAINST THE IGNORANCE AND NEGLIGENCE OF CLERICS.]

**505 CHAPTER ONE. That the unlearned must not be promoted to the priesthood**

Since, then, through the foolish ignorance of priests the uneducated people perish, it would have been fitting for episcopal gravity to refrain from promoting such men and not, through rash haste, transfer the excesses of others onto itself—especially since the Apostle says to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. V). For whoever promotes to the sacred order a man either disgracefully fallen or ignorant of the divine law entangles himself in the sins of the one to whom he entrusts the opportunity to sin. He binds himself not only to the crimes in which that man is already entangled, [Col. 0499B] but also, in advance, makes himself liable for those he is yet to commit.

There is another matter concerning priests of the secular order that displeases me: just as they mingle with secular people in the common habitation of civic life, so many of them likewise do not differ from their companions in conduct or uncultivated manners. They serve secular concerns indiscriminately and do not restrain themselves from the follies of idle talk. Indeed, through quarrels and disputes they frequently withdraw from charity toward their neighbors; and although they know that the flames of envy or of any earthly desire are burning in their breasts, they nevertheless thrust themselves shamelessly before the venerable altars and do not withdraw from the ministry of offering the sacred oblation.

They do not consider that the sons of Aaron were consumed by the fire of heaven precisely because they presumed to offer strange fire in God’s sacrifice: “Nadab and Abihu,” says Scripture, “the sons of Aaron, took their censers, put fire and incense upon them, and offered before the Lord strange fire, which had not been commanded them” (Lev. X); and immediately it adds: “And fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord” (ibid.).

When we approach to offer to God the oblation of the dread sacrament, we must therefore take great care not to bring strange fire—that is, the flame of lust or the fuel of any vice—among the saving sacrifices. Rather, let that fire burn in the censers of our minds, and let the flame of divine love kindle our hearts, which the Spirit of God administers to our inward parts through invisible grace.

Those who intend to minister at the sacred altars must therefore be admonished not only to guard their hearts from the fire of burning passions, but also to restrain their tongues—which in a certain sense stand between God and us as mediators—from the frivolity of superfluous speech. Peter (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; Luke XXII; John XIII), because he recognized that his tongue, which was guilty, had sinned, refused to have it as a patron between himself and God as a mediator. Instead, while he wept bitterly, he placed the hope of his reconciliation in the intervention of tears and obtained pardon with the eyes by which he had not sinned. Let the saliva of our tongue therefore remain virginal or chaste until the mysteries of the Mass have been completed, so that it may either restrain itself under the discipline of virginal silence or utter sober words under the chastening moderation of decorous speech.

**506** What an insult of profound disgrace it is, moreover, that some are so negligent and so sluggishly careless about the utensils of the sacred altar that they patiently watch cups of tin, or even of some inferior metal, grow rough and repulsive through long neglect; that they offer and wrap the Lord’s body in a filthy linen cloth; and that they do not hesitate to place the Savior’s body in a vessel upon which any powerful person—though he too is a worm—would not deign to set his own lips.

What shall I say about the torn and decaying [*prandeis*—the printed reading is uncertain] of the sacred altars; what about the various vessels necessary for ecclesiastical services; what, finally, shall I say about priestly vestments? And lastly [Col. 0500B], what shall I say about the books in which we cannot even read without difficulty the very things that we still preserve in our tenacious memory? All these things, when placed before the eyes of those who see them, provoke laughter in the frivolous and lamentation in the wise.

Therefore priests of the highest rank must be very cautious and dread greatly lest what is done wrong by those who appear to be subordinate be demanded from those of higher standing, who ought to correct these things. No mortal, as I think, performs anything greater in the divine mysteries than priests who themselves belong to the secular order. Let it be granted that patriarchs, metropolitans, or any bishops consecrate, prepare the divine chrism, and carry out the other functions that specially belong to their privileges [Col. 0500C]. Yet neither a bishop, nor chrism, nor anything else in the ecclesiastical sacraments is greater than the body and blood of the Savior. The things, therefore, that are more important and sublime in the Church are shared by priests together with pontifical dignity. And although each is commanded to remain within his own limits, those who are in some respects subordinate are found equal in matters of greater excellence.

**CHAPTER II. That no one sins more grievously than a wicked or ignorant priest**

No one, then, is convicted of sinning more grievously than a priest who, through ignorance or a rejected way of life, while ministering unworthily, contaminates—as far as it lies with him—the sacraments of the saving sacrifice [Col. 0500D].

If someone speaks against a king or any person of higher rank through the vice of detraction, or even attacks him by plundering or destroying his possessions, he can easily regain favor if he makes worthy satisfaction and corrects the offense. But if he lays hands on him, if he boldly assaults his person, if he rushes upon him like an enemy—because the matter is criminal rather than pecuniary—nothing else is demanded from him but punishment. It is no longer a question between them of restoring a private peace, but only of increasing the interest of vengeance.

In the same way, it is one thing to offend God through the various forms of human weakness, and another to sin in the offering of his most holy body and blood. Just as it is one thing to neglect the edicts of a king’s promulgated law and another to wound the king himself by hurling the weapon of one’s own hand at him. The Israelite people repeatedly involved themselves in many crimes, but never defiled themselves so cruelly as when they crucified the Lord. Certainly, whoever does not fear handling the Lord’s body with polluted hands is convicted of sharing in the guilt of those who crucified Jesus.

Such men should tremble exceedingly at that apostolic sentence which says: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and exposing him to contempt” [Col. 0501B] (Heb. VI).

Almighty God tolerates no greater presumption of injury from anyone; indeed, no one sins more grievously than a priest who, despite the prohibitions of the canons, offers sacrifice unworthily. In every other manner of sinning we offend the Lord, as it were, in his possessions; but when we sacrifice unworthily, we do not fear laying hands, as it were, upon his person, since it is written: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II).

Let priests go now, then, and thrust themselves upon the sacred altars for the profits of this life; let them grow rich from the offerings of the faithful for the sake of their own affection and that of their relatives—not, of course, to provide food for orphans and widows, nor to supply assistance to travelers, but to carry away shameful profits for themselves or their own. Let them go, I say, and refresh themselves and their own solely through their miserable acquisition, so that afterward they may feed the abyss of eternal fire with their own marrow.

What condemnation they incur, surely, if they are forbidden to consume the sins of the people, yet from the things they acquire they purchase neither books nor ornaments nor utensils for their churches, but spend everything on the expenses of necessity or kinship! Especially since these things are given to priests for the very reason that they should devote themselves to prayers and vows on behalf of the people and should bear their sins. Hence Moses says to Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron: “Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place, which is the Holy of Holies, and which was given to you so that you might bear the iniquity of the multitude and pray for it before the Lord?” (Lev. X).

But although the Lord suffered on the cross for the salvation of the world, he is now slain on the altar for the advantage and wealth of one priest. Then he was crucified for the whole multitude of the people; now the saving victim appears to be offered as though for the benefit of one little man.

These indeed are sons of the holy Fathers who, while they flourished in the priestly order, are to be called not legitimate sons but rather bastards, and therefore are not without reason excluded from the number of their heirs. Those men, according to Jeremiah, were nourished in saffron-colored garments; these, alas, have embraced dung (Lam. IV).

**CHAPTER III. Who is truly a priest**

He truly exercises the priesthood who does not oppose the rules of the Fathers and does not violate the paternal institution. Hence Moses says: “Let the priest who has legitimately succeeded his father offer fine flour warm as a most fragrant odor to the Lord” (Lev. VI).

That man legitimately succeeds his father as priest who expresses the nobility of the holy Fathers in conspicuous works; who does not disgrace the lineage of his ancestors through the shame of an illegitimate manner of life. Otherwise, whoever degenerates from the titles of his forefathers and their illustrious nobility, whoever represents himself as not legitimate but adulterine or alien through his morals, plainly shows that he ought to be expelled from the priesthood.

Hence in the book of Ezra it is said of certain men: “They sought the record of their genealogy, but did not find it; therefore they were expelled from the priesthood [Col. 0502B]” (1 Esd. II). They were also immediately forbidden to eat from the holy things of the Holy of Holies.

Therefore, just as those who preserve the nobility of the venerable Fathers through the integrity of holy conduct rightly persevere in the dignity of priestly office, so, conversely, those who degenerate from the merits of their preceding Fathers ought also to be deprived of the office of their paternal dignity. Those who have become unlike the glory of their fathers must not remain priests in their fathers’ office, nor in any way succeed to their rights when they have degenerated from their noble character.

Through the prophet Hosea the Lord condemns all such men as though they were one person, saying: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as my priest; and because you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children. As their number increased, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into disgrace. They eat the sins of my people and lift up their souls toward their iniquity; and it shall be: as the people, so the priest. I will visit his ways upon him and repay him for his thoughts” (Hos. IV).

I do not wish to enumerate all their crimes, which they commit either in the offering of the mystery or even amid the sacraments of human regeneration—in the scrutinies, in the creeds, and in the sacrament of baptismal washing. I omit the bread destined to be changed into saving sacrifices, which sometimes becomes moldy before it is consecrated and offered; and even the mystery itself is not consumed within eight days, but is often kept until the third month, to the injury of almighty God [Col. 0502D]. I pass over the fact that sometimes water is not mixed with wine in the Eucharist, and thus, in a certain way, the people are separated from Christ through the error of a hidden schism.

I am weary of extending these matters further, and of things like them, lest, while pursuing them at greater length, we should seem to be covering over the disgrace of the Christian religion.

**CHAPTER IV. That bishops must be watchful in restraining the crimes of clerics**

Therefore holy bishops must strive to confront these evils, which are advancing toward the destruction of the Christian people; they must not permit the works of the apostles, which are now being destroyed by false priests, to perish, nor allow so arduous a labor of Christ to be lost for the sake of increasing the wealth of a few men through earthly profit [Col. 0503A].

For the moment I wish to suppress what is overflowing from my mind, **509** but I cannot: zeal strikes out a spark while the pain of conscience sets the furnace ablaze. What will become of any bishop facing supreme condemnation who takes away the profit of a fallen priest and restores to him the office of sacrificing? Such a bishop no longer merely shares in another’s sins but becomes their author. Indeed, like Judas Iscariot, he hands the Savior over to impious hands for a sum of worthless money; he sells Christ in a commercial transaction and, for love of money, betrays the author of life. Such a bishop immediately becomes guilty of all the crimes for which that priest ought to have been stripped of his priestly insignia.

To return, then, to the subject from which the writing digressed, it seems to us, if it is agreeable, that bishops should adopt this policy: suspend the unworthy and those who have disgracefully fallen from administration; and over those who remain appoint suitable men from their own side, who should frequently visit and guard them.

The king of the Assyrians did something similar when he sent a priest to instruct the rest in Samaria: “Bring there,” he said, “one of the priests whom you brought away captive, so that he may live with them and teach them the ordinances of the God of the land” (2 Kings XVII). That priest, as Scripture continues, lived in Bethel and taught them how they should worship the Lord.

In Bethel, therefore—that is, in the house of God—it is fitting that a superior man should preside, one who can instruct the others in the rules of the priestly office. For we must greatly fear what is said through Moses: “If a person sins through ignorance and does something contrary to any of all the commandments of the Lord that he has commanded not to be done; if the anointed priest has sinned, causing the people to offend, he shall offer an unblemished calf to the Lord for his sin” (Lev. IV).

From these words we must note with great fear what he says: “If the anointed priest has sinned, causing the people to offend.” For a priest who sins through ignorance of God’s law also entangles the people in his sins, and through his ignorance weighs down with himself those whom, if learned, he could have lifted up.

But you, venerable sir, whom both an illustrious life and distinguished learning—and, more excellent than these, the burning fervor of spiritual zeal—make radiant, should delegate the guardianship of others to younger men in such a way that you yourself do not cease frequently to move here and there [Col. 0504B]. Do what Solomon urges in Proverbs: “Run about, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. VI). Let this also not escape your notice, which he says afterward: “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction” (Prov. XXIV). There he removes every excuse when he adds: “If you say, ‘We do not have the strength,’ the one who examines the heart understands” (ibid.).

Therefore keep watch over the flock entrusted to you as an outstanding shepherd, so that you may remove idle shepherds from its care and yourself, with David, break the jaws of attacking bears and lions (1 Sam. XVII); or, with Abraham, after you have struck down the Amalekites, bring your brother Lot out from the yoke of captivity and return with triumphal glory to Melchizedek, the king of righteousness [Col. 0504C] (Gen. XIV).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0503]

**511–522 THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OPUSCULUM. ON THE COMMON LIFE OF CANONS. TO THE CLERICS OF THE CHURCH OF FANO**

**ARGUMENT**

A disagreement having arisen among the canons of the Church of Fano—some having contributed their goods to the common fund of the Church, while others wished to live separately for themselves—he writes to them and urges them, after laying aside all contention, to follow the practice of the apostles and of the primitive Church; to wish to be canons not in name only but in reality. He endeavors to persuade them of this by many arguments, for there cannot be unity of minds among those between whom there is division of possessions; and he writes many other things in the same vein.

To the holy brothers in Christ, the clerics of the Church of Fano, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings.

It is a long time, beloved, since report has spread in these regions that a considerable disagreement has arisen among you, because some of you had undertaken to live according to canonical regularity, while many others would not consent, wishing instead to live among their own possessions in private. We do not find this surprising, because it is not uncommon; but we grieve over it, because it is dishonorable.

It seems sufficiently absurd that a cleric should display the appearance of an order while maintaining the way of life of secular people; and the one whom the condition of his profession separates from the crowds of laymen ought not to be proved a layman by either domestic conduct or the detestable possession of private property.

For what can satisfy the greed of one for whom God himself cannot suffice as a possession?
