A cleric, just as according to the etymology of the word he is himself God’s lot, is likewise said to have almighty God as his portion. Hence Jeremiah says: “The Lord is my portion, said my soul; therefore I will hope in him” (Lam. III). And elsewhere God says: “You are the work of my hands, my inheritance, Israel” (Isa. XIX).

If, therefore, the cleric is God’s portion and God is his portion, he seems to inflict no slight insult upon his Creator if, over and above this singular talent, he burns to accumulate earthly money. For in the book of Numbers God commands Moses concerning the Levites, saying: “You shall take the Levites for me in place of every firstborn among the children of Israel. I am the Lord. And their cattle in place of every firstborn animal of the children of Israel” (Num. III). And again: “Take the Levites in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites in place of their cattle; and the Levites shall be mine. I am the Lord; let them walk in my commandments” (ibid.).

It is as though he were saying more plainly: Just as I specifically claim them for myself as my own right, so I determine that they must continually serve me without subjection to any earthly way of life. Nor do I permit those devoted to my service, who are adorned with the title of free nobility, to be ignobly subjected like slaves to the yoke of secular business.

[ON THE COMMON LIFE OF CANONS.]

**CHAPTER ONE. That clerics do not possess as private property the things they own**

It must also be noted that the Lord testifies that not only the Levites but even the cattle of the Levites are his, so that he may clearly teach that those who are bound to ecclesiastical service owe God not only the expenditure of their diligence and labor but also the private ownership of the possessions they hold. Let them know that both they and what belongs to them are subject not to their own but to divine ownership.

But nowadays it seems insufficient for certain clerics—though I am speaking only of some—that they withdraw their possessions from God by living carnally, unless they also withdraw from the watchfulness of ecclesiastical administration by living in alleyways and at market stalls. They judge it plainly more pleasant to inhale the smells of taverns than to tread daily the threshold of the divine sanctuary; they take greater delight in gazing upon the women’s weaving rooms than in dwelling over the pages of heavenly discourse.

Poor Samuel (1 Sam. I), after being weaned, does not return home with his parents, but remains continually in the service of the temple. John, so that he might preserve the purity of an innocent life, hastens while still young to the solitude of the desolate wilderness (Matt. III; Mark I; Luke III); there he received the grace of prophetic preaching, which he could not have merited while living amid the crowds of the people.

But now, conversely, those who are dedicated to divine ceremonies despise the Church’s sanctuaries as remote, while they desire to live amid the murmurs of the noise of the marketplace [Col. 0505D].

But let us hear what divine authority commands concerning the encampments of the Levites, and thus we can rightly judge where clerics ought especially to live. “Do not count the tribe of Levi,” it says, “nor include their total among the children of Israel; but appoint them over the tabernacle of the testimony, all its vessels, and everything pertaining to its ceremonies. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its utensils, and shall serve in it; and they shall pitch their tents around the tabernacle” (Num. I).

A little later, after first saying, “The camp of the children of Israel shall pitch, each by its companies, divisions, and army” (ibid.), it immediately adds: “But the Levites shall pitch their tents around the tabernacle” (ibid.).

If, then, by the Lord’s command the Levites pitch their camps beside the tabernacle, and are not permitted to withdraw from the tabernacle or to lodge among the crowds, why should clerics now shrink, in accordance with the decree of the divine constitution, from dwelling beside the Church, so that they may devote themselves to meditation on sacred discourse with greater freedom because of greater quiet? At least let them render to the Church, which is illumined by the splendor of evangelical grace, what those men rendered to the tabernacle, which was veiled beneath the darkness of ignorance by the figure of enigmas.

And certainly it is very much out of order if that reverence which was then offered to the shadowed image is now denied to the truth. The fact that the tabernacle was not the truth itself but rather an image of the truth is testified by the Lord when he commands Moses: “See that you make everything according to what was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV; Heb. VIII).

What Moses saw on the mountain was our truth; what he made for the Israelites as a tabernacle was merely an image of the truth. The ministers of the tabernacle then ate manna, destined without doubt to die; in the Church, however, we receive the sacraments of Christ, destined to live eternally. Concerning this Church Paul says: “For it is the true tabernacle, which God established and not man” (Heb. VIII).

As for the temple of Solomon, and how constant and diligent the watch of its ministers is said to have been—you are not, I believe, ignorant of this, and we judge it superfluous to write about it. Who, especially from the book of Chronicles, does not clearly observe that Solomon, according to the arrangement of his father David, appointed the offices of the priests in their ministries and the Levites in their order, so that they might praise and minister before the priests according to the rite of each day, and appointed gatekeepers in their divisions at each gate? (2 Chron. VIII.)

**514 CHAPTER II. That he cannot be called a canon who is not regular**

If, then, those who by the command of the law were bound by marital unions displayed such diligent watchfulness in their sanctuaries, what must clerics do now, who, endowed with the purity of chastity, have been freed from all bonds of carnal intercourse? Clearly, how can anyone be called a canon unless he is regular? How can he be a monk unless, according to the force of his name, he is also solitary?

They wish to bear the name “canon,” that is, “regular,” but do not wish to live regularly. They seek to divide among themselves the common goods of the Church, but they disdain to live together in common at the Church.

Indeed, this is not the pattern of the primitive Church; it departs greatly from the discipline of apostolic institution. They had one heart and one soul, sold their fields, placed the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, and distributed to each according to his need. No one called any of the things he possessed his own; rather, everything was common among them (Acts II).

By contrast, the prodigal son said to his father: “Give me the portion that falls to me,” and then squandered all his goods with prostitutes.

Here the lines between the elect and the rejected are clearly distinguished: the former rejoice in holding with others in common what is their own; the latter, just as they tear their minds away from the bond of charity, likewise divide their possessions from their brothers.

Where there is division of possessions, there is certainly no unity of minds. Charity creates communion; greed creates division.

Hence Luke says: “Someone from the crowd said to Jesus” (not, of course, someone from the distinguished, but from the crowd, because he was filthy with the foul squalor of greed): “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” And when he replied, “Man, who appointed me judge or divider between you?” [Col. 0507B] he immediately added to those standing nearby: “Take care and beware of all greed, because a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke XII).

By these words the Truth plainly indicates that some desire to divide what is common precisely because they are inflamed by the torches of desire and greed.

Ananias and Sapphira are struck by the sentence of bodily death not because they divide what is common, but because they do not make common what they have retained from their private possessions (Acts V). Judas, because he was not content with sharing the money with the others, fell into the abyss of betrayal and fell away from the fellowship of the apostles (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXVII; John XIII). Lot, abandoning Abraham’s fellowship through the division of their possessions, was compelled to serve under the harsh bonds of barbarians (Gen. XIII, [Col. 0507C] XIV). Esau, roaming through the forest paths in pursuit of hunting, lost his birthright (Gen. V). Jacob, dwelling simply in tents, received the fullness of his father’s blessing (ibid.).

**515 CHAPTER III. That wandering monks must not be called monks but gyrovagues**

In the monastic order, we properly call monks those whom we see remaining regularly in cloisters under the authority of an abbot. But those whom we see possessing private property, wandering indiscriminately here and there, and dissolving into the fluidity of their own will, freed from the laws, we judge worthy to be called not monks but rather gyrovagues or Sarabaites.

There are therefore Sarabaites among monks, and also among clerics. But the Lord says: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII; Luke XI).

These men, because they do not gather with God in brotherly charity, tear apart the purse of their minds through discord and lose whatever fruits of virtue they may have, scattering them as though through a hole. Hence the prophet says of a foolish man: “He gathered wealth and put it into a perforated bag” (Haggai I).

Moreover, not only those who divide the unity of the faith should be called schismatics, but also those who separate themselves from brotherly charity through the vice of pride or greed. For faith is not greater than charity. Since God himself is charity (1 John IV), and whoever remains in charity remains in God (James I), one who has fallen away from charity is no less to be condemned than one who has strayed from the faith.

For if someone observes the whole law but stumbles in one matter—that is, in charity—he has become guilty of all; and consequently he is also shown to be liable to faithlessness.

Certainly, if, according to Peter’s words, the devil goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. V), whoever abandons the folds of brotherly fellowship voluntarily hands himself over to the bites of that bloody beast.

A heifer grazing in the herd does not fear the wolf’s attack; but when it ventures alone to roam through the forest paths, it is compelled to satisfy the appetite of wild beasts. Geese flying in formation make little of the hawk; but the one that falls behind is sometimes pierced by its beak and cannot escape its claws.

Bees gathered in their hives make honey, and as long as they remain together, sweet combs produced by their labor are set before kings. But if they scatter and, abandoning their leader, fly about as wanderers, they must waste away from hunger and want.

If someone surrounded by the ambushes of enemies withdraws from the one beside whom he is pressed together, he exposes himself, as prey, to the enemy’s arrows.

The Church of Christ, as the prophetic oracles testify, is the camp of God (Gen. XXXII). Into it the enemy assault does not break as long as the soldiers of Christ, girded with the armor of virtues, are gathered together in the bond of charity and in unity of spirit.

Whoever, like the wretched Achan, is separated from them by desire for gold or silver is stoned by the true Joshua and by the common judgment of the whole people (Josh. VII).

[Col. 0508C] Therefore I beseech your holiness, dearest brothers: having driven out the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. XVI), leave behind the homes of your birth together with the patriarch Abraham (Gen. XII); gather yourselves with the Apostles in one upper room in the Church (Acts II); and, together with Barnabas and Stephen (Acts IV), those true renouncers of worldly possessions, contribute whatever belongs to each of you to the common fund, so that, living among you in fraternal unanimity, the Holy Spirit may deservedly deign to visit you.

For you are the salt of the earth; but, as the Truth says: “If the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be seasoned?” (Acts II.) A small amount of salt sweetens much, and by a small number of clerics the multitude of the entire Christian people is taught and instructed. For just as bishops are known to hold the primacy of the twelve Apostles, so also the priests of the Church represent the order of the seventy disciples. This is surely represented figuratively by that encampment of the Israelite people at Elim (Num. XXXIII). There twelve apostolic springs flowed, to drench the arid hearts of human beings with the rains of the divine word. There seventy palms flourished: namely, the same number of disciples, who, when the world had been crushed under the slavery of the devil’s tyranny, would bring the palms of Christ’s victory.

Those springs water the palm trees; so the holy pontiffs overflow with words, from which the other priests of the Church continually flourish in the hope of heavenly rewards. These priests, by the number seventy multiplied tenfold, seem to signify that through the Spirit of sevenfold grace the Decalogue of the Law is fulfilled.

When the Lord therefore sent these seventy disciples in pairs before his face, and admonished those who were to teach others that they themselves should live irreproachably, he placed at the very beginning of their teaching, as something supremely necessary and fundamental, the command that they despise monetary gain, cast away the filth of avarice, and possess no private property. “Do not carry,” he says, “a purse, nor a bag, nor shoes” (Luke X). Through Mark also he forbids them to have bread or copper in their belts, or to be clothed in two tunics; but, wearing sandals and carrying only a staff, they were to go on their way (Mark VI).

Why was this done? Was it only for their sake? But let us grant that it was done for their sake; why, then, was it written for us? “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction” [Col. 0509B] (Rom. XV). Why, then, do we read these things in the Church, except so that we may fulfill in our works the very things that are read? Especially those who, through the succession of changing times, perform their office must necessarily conduct themselves according to their example.

Therefore God forbids his preachers to possess anything earthly, so that those who have been appointed to extinguish the heat of desire in the hearts of their hearers may themselves beware of loosening, to the ruin of others, the reins of ambition and avarice. To this is added the fact that often, on the occasion of a journey, when a woman’s form appears before him, the minister of the altar conceives the flame of lust. For while he travels from his own home to the Church and back again, suddenly the evil spirit prepares snares, sets the woman’s birdlime-trap [*viscarium*], and places before the deceived man a seductive face upon which he gazes.

But whoever burns either with the flame of avarice or with the heat of lust, with what face, with what conscience, does he approach the divine altars? This is why the sons of Aaron were consumed by divine fire: they presumed to offer the Lord a strange fire. For it is written:

> “Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took their censers, put fire and incense upon them, and offered before the Lord a strange fire, which he had not commanded them; and fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord” (Lev. X).

The altars of the Lord receive not a strange fire, but only the fire of divine love. Concerning this fire he himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII.)

Whoever, therefore, burns with the flame of earthly or carnal desire in the censer of his breast, and does not fear to stand before the sacred mysteries, is undoubtedly consumed for the time being by that fire of divine vengeance of which Scripture testifies: “And now,” it says, “fire consumes the adversaries” (Hebr. X).

Indeed, it is exceedingly impossible, my brothers, for one who is weighed down by concern for his household affairs, who by living and speaking among the crowds of common people mingles with them daily, to take part with a pure heart in the holy mysteries. In those awe-inspiring sacraments heaven is opened, and the angelic powers dwell together with human beings. How great, then, should be the purity of clerics; how spotless, and finally how removed from all the stench of worldly business! For they enjoy the fellowship of angels as their companions and table-fellows, and exist as God’s co-workers and stewards of the heavenly sacraments.

## CHAPTER IV. How the good are corrupted by the company of the wicked

We are not speaking here only of priests, but of all clerics who, in whatever degree of their ministry, discharge the duties owed to the sacred altars. For even if someone is pure in himself, he is sometimes defiled by the company of the wicked. If this did not happen to some people, the prophet would never have lamented:

> “Woe is me, for I am a man of polluted lips, and I dwell among a people having polluted lips” (Isa. VI).

He declared himself polluted in his lips because he lived among those whose lips were polluted.

Moses too is clearly understood to have suffered this very thing in the land of Midian, if one carefully investigates why the Lord wished to kill him. For it is written:

> “And when he was on the journey, at the lodging-place, the Lord met him and wished to kill him” (Exod. IV).

It is very strange that the Lord is suddenly described as wishing to kill the man whom he had already made his intimate and fellow-worker, to whom he had disclosed the secrets of his counsel and will, and whom he was now directing in the execution of his obedience. But it is undoubtedly meant to indicate that, whatever stain of contamination he had contracted from his long residence among the Midianites, he had to be cleansed by fear and correction of his negligence, since he was approaching as the bearer of heavenly commands for the correction of others.

His wife Zipporah prudently understood this; concerning her Scripture immediately adds:

> “Then Zipporah took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son” (Exod. IV).

For it would have been absurd if one who was an Israelite in himself appeared gentile in his son. Therefore, whoever ought to instruct others in the way of righteousness must take great care that he himself, God forbid, not appear to err in anything.

This is also why the Israelite people were inflamed with zeal for righteousness to avenge the crime of Benjamin, and yet that same people was first struck down by the swords of Benjamin (Judg. XX). Who would not be moved by the fact that the Lord was consulted twice and twice gave his consent to undertake battle against Benjamin, and yet in the first battle twenty-two thousand Israelites fell, while in the second eighteen thousand fell?

What, then, are we to understand and perceive in these events except that those who desire to remove the diseases of another’s wickedness must first be healed of the swelling of their own wound? Thus, once cleansed through punishment of themselves, they may proceed to strike the wrongdoing of others, just as it is said in the Gospel:

> “Let him who is without sin among you first cast a stone at her” (John VIII).

Hence, when they rightly consulted God and said, “Who shall be the leader of our army in the battle against the sons of Benjamin?” he answered, “Let Judah be your leader” (Judg. XX). Since *Judah* is interpreted as “confession,” Judah is rightly appointed leader of that war: so that those who wish to assist others confessing their error may first strive through confession to correct their own faults.

## CHAPTER V. How common life brings about unity of spirit and righteousness

Therefore, dearest brothers, if you wish, among the people of God over whom you have been set as examples, among whom you shine like lights in the world while holding fast the word of life; if, I say, you wish to seek the gain of souls among them, and desire to call the wandering back to the rectitude of religion, first straighten within yourselves whatever is crooked, if anything is found there; and, coming together in the school of Christ, remain harmoniously in a common life and unity of spirit.

Let there be no division of houses among you, no rift of minds, no diversity of possessions. Always remember that God rejects an altar made from split stones:

> “For if you lift your knife over it,” he says, “it will be defiled” (Exod. XX).

The stones are split who reject the fellowship of fraternal society, who do not wish to live with their brothers and associate with them in harmony. Christ does not receive such people into his body, since he judges them cut off from the unity of his members. Rather, the altar is to be built from those stones of which the Apostle Peter says:

> “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II).

He is the foundation of that house, “other than which no one can lay” (I Cor. III); he is its summit, who was made “the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII).

Moreover, does the Lord command this without purpose?

> “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal” (Matt. VI).

Who, I ask, can observe the meaning of this command if the cleric does not observe it? Perhaps married people, who raise children and pay tithes to God by his own authority? “For whoever offers,” as Paul says, “must have something to offer” (Hebr. VIII).

Furthermore, how can someone stationed in the choir of those singing psalms keep his heart fixed in prayer when he is thinking about his little chests and boxes, lest a bold hand steal upon them? When he is worrying about storerooms and barns, lest they serve thieves? When he fears that insufficiently trustworthy locks may not hold back intruders, and is always afraid of the break-in of thieves who may creep in?

Perhaps I am mistaken; but can the Truth lie, when it says: “Where your treasure is, there is your heart also”? (Matt. VI; Luke XII.) It might even be considered more tolerable if they performed the divine offices in their own inner chambers and, without laboring farther afield, sought God there where they kept their possessions; so that when it was said to them, “Where your treasure is, there is your heart,” it could appropriately be added: “There also is your God.”

[Col. 0512A]

But since this matter is not to be laughed at but mourned, I beseech you, my most beloved brothers and lords: do not make light of what we suggest, but gather yourselves in the school of Christ under the discipline of the Holy Spirit, so that he may remain with us now and until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII), as he promised, and afterward lead you to the glory of his Father through a happy reward.

Perhaps I shall displease some, because, while I wish to restrain others within the bounds of regular life, I myself exceed the proper measure of an abbreviated letter. But the writer’s lack of skill is well compensated if the listener advances wisely.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0511]

## OPUSCULUM TWENTY-EIGHT. THE APOLOGY OF THE MONKS AGAINST THE CANONS

### ARGUMENT

The monks complain that they have been excluded by the canons from the assembly of the entire Church, although they themselves derive their origin from the Apostles, indeed from the prophets. They severely rebuke a certain man who dared to say: “The sacraments of the Church must in no way be administered by monks.” Finally, they prove by the example of Saints Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius, and by the decree of Pope Boniface IV, that monks possess the power of binding and loosing.

[Col. 0511D] To all the most loving clerics and canons, all the monks unanimously.

Dearest brothers, if you are worthy to hear it, we greatly wonder how, or for what reason, you attempt to separate us from the fellowship and unity of the universal Church, since it is evident that the universal Church was founded, governed, and sifted free from varied error by monks, not by canons.

The Apostles, founders and rulers of the Churches, lived according to our custom, not yours, as Luke the Evangelist reports in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts I). Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, in the books he composed in praise of our people, calls the primitive Christians monks, not canons; he calls their dwellings monasteries and says that they performed and wrote many praiseworthy things.

Certainly Moses and Elijah belonged to our order, not yours (Exod. III; III Kings XVII); they began their life in the wilderness. Our authors were the companies of prophets with whom the reprobate Saul often sang (III Kings XIX). It would take too long to turn through the pages of the Old Testament; let us come to the New, which we left above.

Certainly, if you perceive the Apostles and their successors with unblinded eyes in the pages of the New Testament, you will find that they lived in the monastic manner, not the canonical manner; and you will undoubtedly find that the Lord granted them the power of binding and loosing (Matt. XVIII).

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—why do you attempt to separate us from this privilege? Do you not know that to those to whom the Apostle said, “For you have died,” namely, to the world (Col. III), he said in another Epistle: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this world?” (I Cor. VI.)

Therefore, if, as you say, we have died to the world—that is, to vices and sins—we are not ashamed, because the same Apostle says: “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also rise with him” (II Tim. II; Rom. VI); likewise: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I); and elsewhere: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

But so that those who had heard themselves called dead so many times would not be disturbed, he said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this world?” (I Cor. VI.) Behold our liberty. Why? Because the same Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (II Cor. III).

Woe, then, to us and to you if we have not died to the world. If, therefore, we have died to the world and live for God, we shall prove that you have lied in every respect, because you say that for this reason—that we have died to the world—we cannot administer ecclesiastical matters. But why do you exalt yourselves? Recall our beginnings and yours; and, on the authority of the Fathers, let him whose claim is more fitting judge with an eye equipped for discerning.

## APOLOGY OF THE MONKS AGAINST THE CANONS

### CHAPTER I. The monks’ complaint against the canons

We complain greatly against you because one of your number dared with reckless speech to say: “Communion must in no way be received from monks.” Moreover, he excommunicated those who received it and, to our disgrace—or rather, to his own condemnation and theirs—ordered them to be readmitted to communion.

But what can we say against him? We know that he is almost entirely uneducated and guilty of many crimes; therefore, following Solomon, we avoid answering a fool according to his folly, lest we become like him (Prov. XXVI). But, so that we may not appear to have been overcome, we wish to answer the fool according to his folly, as the same Solomon advises, lest he seem wise in his own eyes (ibid.). We plainly demonstrate that he has miserably fallen into the sect of the rebaptized.

Nor is it surprising that fraternal hatred has earned him this fate, since the Apostle John thunders:

> “He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II).

But so that the poison of his venom may not spread farther, we plainly show that these sacraments were lawfully received and administered by our predecessors above all clerics, just as it is read in the Life of Blessed Martin: wine consecrated by a certain anchorite was sought as a blessing by the greatest and most venerable men; indeed, bishops and counts often spent the night before his door to obtain a blessing.

Moreover, the apostolic Telesphorus is proved to have been one of the anchorites. Dionysius, Adeodatus, and Stephen, recently deceased, are likewise read to have been monks; yet they governed the apostolic see with the greatest glory. Gregory, taken from a monastery and forcibly invested with the episcopal insignia, not only brought forth his own decisions but also strove to improve the dispositions of others.

Should we also suppose that Martin of Tours is to be omitted, before whom, as he stood at the divine sacrament, a globe of fire appeared? Did any madman forbid anyone to receive the divine sacraments from the hands of these men because they had been monks? God forbid.

Let the insane and arrogant doctrine therefore depart, and let the authority of the holy Fathers prevail. That authority separates from the Church those who disdain to receive the divine sacraments from the hands of any priest—not merely to receive them, but even to accept them reluctantly—provided that the priests are of the true faith. This will suffice for those who contradict us.

### CHAPTER II. How the administration of the sacraments was lawfully permitted to monks above all clerics

[Col. 0514B]

But since it is extremely dangerous to wish to remain silent, we introduce other witnesses as well: Basil, Athanasius, and Augustine, and also Jerome, interpreter of the sacred Law; likewise Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, and Augustine, prelate of the English, all of whom were undoubtedly monks.

Were the Roman prelates whom we mentioned earlier, or those whom we have now listed, considered less praiseworthy because they were monks? Certainly not. Would any madman dare to say that they did not ordain bishops, presbyters, and deacons? Or perhaps that they did not impose penance upon criminals and most graciously add absolution, as was appropriate? They certainly could do so.

Now, then, consult the eight holy councils, especially the Sixth and Seventh Councils; there you will find that it was lawful for monks to dispute, without any scruple, in the presence of the council concerning all who were present. But let this now suffice.

Let us come to the consecration which, through God’s dispensation, we received from bishops. Would any fool dare to say that we are consecrated differently from the canons? No one. For the bishop earnestly asks that the blessing of the Lord be poured out equally upon both.

And when he consecrates them individually, he earnestly asks this for all priests, saying:

> “Let these hands, O Lord, be consecrated, so that whatever they bless may be blessed, and whatever they consecrate may be consecrated.”

Behold the common blessing. Where, then, is the separation? It would take too long to pursue these matters.

Let us examine the form of our clothing and yours. Bring forth both. Did the prophets and Apostles use our attire or yours? Perhaps you will say, “Ours.” And what of what is read concerning Elijah:

> “A hairy man, and girded with a leather belt around his loins” (IV Kings I);

and what Paul says concerning him and those like him:

> “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Hebr. XI);

and what John the Evangelist says concerning John the Baptist:

> “He had a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. III; Mark I);

and what the angel commands Peter:

> “Gird yourself and put on your sandals” (Acts XII);

and what Agabus said concerning Paul’s belt:

> “The man whose belt this is, the Jews will bind in Jerusalem and hand over to the Gentiles” (Acts XXI).

Scripture would not mention the clothing of these Fathers by name unless they had used it personally.

If this seems doubtful to you, at least lend an ear to the testimony of those on your own side. Read the Conferences of the Fathers, which Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, worked to abridge in polished language; and if you do not wish to believe us, at least believe his writing. For under his instruction we wrote this page.

Therefore we follow in the clothing not only the Fathers mentioned above, but also, beyond that, the most exalted court of heaven—something that is difficult for you to hear. Who would doubt that the Seraphim have six wings, since Scripture says: “Six wings to one, and six wings to the other” (Isa. VI)?

Indeed, we too are covered with six wings: two on the head, two on the right and left, and two in front and behind. If this seems incredible to you, investigate what Boniface composed in defense of our cause. And if you still wish to oppose us, declare from the authority of the Fathers the founders of your customs and clothing; prove by testimonies what you bring against us; and, if your life accompanies your claims, expect, with God’s help, that still higher things than those we have said must be spoken.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

## DECREE OF POPE BONIFACE

### How monks honored with the dignity of the presbyterate possess the power of binding and loosing

*(From the authority of Boniface IV, Supreme Pontiff, 16, question 1, in Gratian’s Decree.)*

[Col. 0515C]

> “There are some who, supported by no doctrine, assert with the utmost boldness, inflamed more by the zeal of bitterness than of love, that monks, because they have died to the world and live for God, are unworthy of the power of priestly office; that they are unable, by the divinely imposed power of priestly office, either to grant penance, to bestow Christian initiation, or to absolve. But they are entirely mistaken.
>
> “For if the ancient adversaries were proclaiming the truth on this account, the most blessed Gregory, equal to the apostolic see and distinguished by monastic observance, would never have ascended to the highest dignity; yet this power of binding and loosing was granted to him by God in the highest degree. Likewise Augustine, disciple of that most holy Gregory and illustrious preacher to the English; and the most blessed Martin of Pannonia, whose fame for holiness, spread far and wide, resounds throughout the whole world; and many other most holy men, shining in the most precious monastic habit, would never have been girded with the pontifical ring.
>
> “But are they forbidden to use the powers mentioned above because they were monks? Certainly not. For Blessed Benedict, the gracious teacher of monks, in no way prohibited this; he merely declared that they should be free from secular business (St. Benedict, Rule, chap. 4). This is strongly commanded not only to monks but also to canons by the apostolic writings and the institutions of all the holy Fathers: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (I Tim. II).
>
> “Instructed, then, by the examples of so many Fathers—whose teaching it is extremely dangerous to resist—we believe that the office of binding and loosing is worthily administered, by God’s working, by monastic priests, if they have worthily been raised to this ministry. Whoever clearly considers the status, habit, and power of monks affirms this without hesitation.
>
> “For example, *angel* in Greek, in Latin, means ‘messenger.’ Priests, therefore—monks as well as canons—who daily announce God’s commands to the people are not inappropriately called angels. But each angelic order, the more closely it contemplates the glory of God, is undoubtedly strengthened by clinging to his divinity with greater power. The distinguished order of the Cherubim is proclaimed to be among these; the habit of monks is suitably shown to bear their likeness.
>
> “For just as the Cherubim, monks are covered with six wings: two in the hood by which the head is covered; two others by which the feet are covered, as plausible arguments demonstrate. We say that the part of the cowl displayed by the arms constitutes the other two wings; and thus, finally, we assert that the number of six wings is most certainly fulfilled.
>
> “We therefore command in every way that those who contend that presbyters of the monastic profession should be barred from every exercise of priestly power be restrained from such wicked attempts in the future; for the higher each person is, the more powerful he is in these matters as well.”

The bishop must sing Mass at the ordination of a presbyter, and likewise the abbot at the ordination of a monk, because it is the remission of sins. For this reason the king will leave his kingdom, the high priest his pontificate, the bishop his bishopric, the count his county, and many rich men and women their possessions in the world; and they will come to the monastery to serve God.

Far be it that a monk living under a rule or an abbot should be subjected to other people. It is wicked to say, as some do: “A monk does not have the power of binding and loosing,” because they have died. They truly have died to this world, just as the holy Apostles did. Did the holy Apostles not have the power of binding and loosing? One of them said: “For if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him” (Rom. VI).

Who can better loose or bind a sinner than one who has been loosed by God from sins? Who can better give souls to God than the one who is nearest to him? Those who gnash their teeth in this way against monks are wretched, and their words are empty.

But hear why they say such things. The Law says: If a cleric is caught in adultery or in any crime, whether he has confessed it himself or has been convicted by others, according to the councils of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers he cannot return to his dignity except through worthy penance.

For this reason, inflamed by much anger and envy against monks or against Catholic men, they desire day and night to find snares by which they may unjustly entangle them. For those who are altogether unable to purge their own sins, how can they forgive the sins of others? Can the blind lead the blind?

Therefore, whoever wishes to take away the property or honors of the Church, let him be anathema. What more shall I say? Turn and see that nothing is better than to leave the world [Col. 0518A] and follow God, who says: “Come to me, all of you, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI). [The supplied text is grammatically incomplete here.]

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0517]

## OPUSCULUM TWENTY-NINE. ON THE CHEAP CLOTHING OF ECCLESIASTICS

### ARGUMENT

To Abbot Mainard, who was accustomed to wear more expensive clothing, he shows how unbecoming it is for ecclesiastical men, and especially for monks, to desire the splendor of garments. He also adduces many examples drawn from the sacred writings, from which he clearly proves that such pomp of clothing is hated by God, since all the saints of both the Old and New Testaments, and Christ himself, did not blush to use cheaper clothing.

[Col. 0517B] To Lord Mainard, dearest brother, Peter the sinful monk sends greetings in the Lord.

When all kinds of medicine have been tried and suitably applied, and the sick man dies, the physician’s conscience has no grounds for reproach. For the one who has fulfilled all the arguments of treatment appropriate to the physician Archigenes has done everything he could. Therefore, when the feverish man dies, the one who had discharged the duty of healing is not held guilty. He displayed the diligence proper to his art, and therefore will not be exposed to accusation.

It has been a long time, brother, since the fever of expensive clothing began to burn in you and, so to speak, the heat of ambition, like a deadly fever, scorched your inward parts. I, like a physician, although an inexperienced one, applied to you the oil of gentle and pleasant admonition, and frequently poured in the wine of stern correction. Nor did you lack the medicinal spices of Scripture: as I strove to expound its judgments, I did not cease to spread before you, as it were, aromatic spices.

And since, together with the other brothers, I have always been content before you with cheap garments, by doing first myself what I advised, I had, as it were, first drunk the antidote; and thus I urged you to drink what I had poured out. Finally, I applied the cautery of burning, when I directed against the brightness of your garments the threat of infernal fires.

Did James not impress the iron of cautery upon the rich, when he declared that here their garments were exposed to moths and there their flesh to flames, saying:

> “Come now, rich men, and weep, howling over your miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and will eat your flesh like fire” (James II).

The metal that is now possessed through avarice is then turned into plates; and the flesh that is now adorned with dyed garments is afterward scraped by shrieking flame.

Did the Savior not also apply a medicinal instrument to the ambition for clothing, when he declared that the rich man, adorned in fine linen and purple, burned in infernal flames? (Luke XVI.) According to the testimony of Scripture, nothing else is blamed in this rich man except that, beneath the brilliance of his garments, he is read to have feasted splendidly without mercy.

Yet undoubtedly, even in the adornment of more elegant clothing, the desire for empty glory is detected. No one longs to be dressed in expensive garments where no stranger’s gaze can behold him. Rather, each person desires to shine in more elegant clothing so that his polished appearance may delight the eyes of those who admire him, and so that he may feed the seductive pleasure of strangers’ eyes. But while he charms the eyes of those looking upon him externally, he offends the sight of the inner Judge.

## ON THE CHEAP CLOTHING OF ECCLESIASTICS

### CHAPTER I. The clothing in which Holy Church delights
The powerful of this world plainly delight in the gaudy trappings of their attendants, especially if the markers of their lodging are splendid, and if the various attendants who go before them appear distinguished by the magnificence of their dress. But let us look at John, Christ’s marker; let us consider the illustrious forerunner of the King [Col. 0518C]. He went before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke I), to turn the hearts of fathers toward their children and the disobedient toward the prudence of the righteous. Let us therefore consider, O Emperor of heaven and earth, in what garments He delights His own forerunner to be clothed. But, as the Gospel bears witness, we learn that his garment was bristling with camel’s hair. Concerning him the Savior says: “What did you go out into the desert to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matthew III; Mark II; Luke VII). It is as though He openly declares that those are judged worthy of the service not of a heavenly but of an earthly king who eagerly desire to be adorned with carefully fashioned garments for the splendor of empty glory.

The royal court delights in soft garments; the Church [Col. 0518D] delights in rough and unadorned ones. “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm XLIV). The Church, therefore—or every faithful soul, which is itself a daughter of the holy apostles—rejoices not in shining outwardly but in appearing adorned before the eyes of the hidden Judge. She is not pleased with the painted beauty of garments, but glories in the varied splendor of virtues. Scripture also speaks of this variety: “She is clothed round about with variety in golden fringes” (ibid.).

Do you wish to hear of the variety of garments that delights the heavenly Bridegroom’s gaze? A soul conspicuous in the whiteness of snowy chastity is seen before the eyes of almighty God to be clothed in spiritual linen, or a *colobium*. When it is also kindled by the flame of fervent charity, it is drenched in the redness of *dirotinum* [uncertain term], or twice-dyed saffron. But when it eagerly desires either to be wholly mortified to this world or to be perfected through martyrdom, then it is dyed, as it were, with the blood of shellfish, and thus imitates the appearance of royal purple. Nor should the green of *pisticus* be thought absent for long, since, while the mind firmly hopes for the joys of the ever-green pasture, it continually flourishes unfadingly, as though in the beauty of an emerald. Hence Peter also says: “God has regenerated us unto a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, preserved in heaven” (1 Peter I).

The Lord testifies that He has clothed the soul in these garments when He speaks through Ezekiel, saying: “I clothed you in garments of various colors, I shod you with hyacinth, I girded you with linen, I clothed you with fine cloth, and adorned you with ornaments” (Ezekiel XVI). Peter likewise demands this adornment, this spiritual ornament of clothing, from women, when he cuts away from them the trappings of seductive and brothel-like adornment: “Let their adornment,” he says, “not be outward, in the braiding of the hair, or the wearing of gold or silver, or the elegance of clothing and garments; but let it be the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God” (1 Peter III).

An invisible adornment delights the invisible Bridegroom, and when He sees a holy soul shining with virtues, He immediately hastens into her embrace. To her He said: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and comely, like Jerusalem” [Col. 0519C] (Song of Songs VI). He says, “like Jerusalem,” not like Babylon, which John saw surrounded with purple and scarlet, gilded with gold, precious stones, and pearls, holding in her hand a cup full of abominations and the uncleanness of her fornication (Revelation XVII). The devil inhabits Babylon; Christ inhabits Jerusalem. The former is refreshed by the vanity of luxurious dress; the latter delights in rough and humble garments, provided humility of heart is not lacking.

Moreover, the brilliance of garments often provokes the author of pride, whereas roughness invites Christ to show mercy to anyone who has been humbled. For, as the sacred history of the Kings testifies: “The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were each sitting on his throne, clothed in royal attire, in the open space beside the gate of Samaria, while all the prophets were prophesying falsehood in their presence” (3 Kings XXII). The author of falsehood delighted in the allurements of affected dress, and through the mouths of the prophesying men he had fashioned workshops of deception from the appearance of an obscured beauty.

But when that same Ahab received the harsh words of Elijah’s threats, as he deserved, and terrified, feared the sword of divine wrath hanging over his own neck, Scripture bears witness: “He tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed down. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: ‘Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me? Therefore, because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring the evil in his days’” (3 Kings XXI).

## CHAPTER II. How Wearing Splendid Garments Is Destructive to the Soul and Hateful to God

Behold, Ahab is adorned in imperial purple and is deceived by a deceptive spirit; he puts on sackcloth and turns away the sword of divine wrath. Girded with royal insignia, he is caught in the snare of deception; covered with sackcloth, he earns indulgence from delayed vengeance.

Let the monk devoted to empty glory therefore go forth, conspicuous in a shining robe, and feed the allurements of onlookers’ eyes with the brilliance of his garments. But while he shines in his clothing, he lies exposed to the deceptions of wicked spirits; moreover, he provokes against himself the sentence of divine indignation, since, devoted solely to outward things, he invites human eyes to admire him. The more elegantly he is clothed before the eyes of those who look upon him, the more contemptibly he is despised by God, who condemns pride.

Job, on the other hand, who fell naked upon the ground, who scraped his streaming pus with a potsherd, and who, rotting in a dung heap and teeming with worms, was despised even by his wife, obtained the address of divine consolation (Job I, II, XXXVIII). For God does not recoil in disgust from the filth of bodily contagion when He finds purity of heart.

Moreover, what does the Apostle say? “Having food and coverings, with these let us be content” (1 Timothy XVI). Why, when he says “having food,” did he not immediately add “and clothing,” but, after first saying “having food,” at once adds “and coverings”? Why else, except that he clearly teaches us to be clothed in coverings so contemptible that they are not worthy to be called garments?

Indeed, King David, naked and content with an *ephod* alone, publicly danced and leapt before the ark of the Lord (2 Kings VI). Isaiah, the evangelical prophet, walked naked and barefoot for three years before men and women (Isaiah XX); and does the monk, who has professed the burial of carnal life, still pant after the display of a gleaming garment? Yet Isaiah himself, even before he walked naked, was not softened by some luxurious covering but was clothed in sackcloth. For unless he had gone about covered in sackcloth, the divine voice would never have commanded him: “Loose the sackcloth from your loins” (ibid.).

Esau, plainly, as Scripture reports, kept very fine garments at home for hunting; but another, clothed in them, received the primacy of his father’s blessing [Col. 0520D] (Genesis XXVII). Jacob, who, as though under evangelical teaching, had previously possessed not two tunics (Matthew X), later sought in prayer a simple garment together with food: “If God will be with me, and will guard me on the way by which I walk, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, the Lord shall be my God” (Genesis XXVIII). Thus the man who had two garments for the sake of honor is overwhelmed, while the man content with one is exalted by almsgiving to divine glory.

Herod too, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, was seen conspicuous in royal clothing (Acts XII). While he was addressing the people and they were acclaiming him as possessing the voice of a god and not of a man [Col. 0521A], he was immediately struck by an angel; and because, devoted to empty glory, he had known how to transfer to God the glory attributed to himself to be transferred to himself as God, he died, consumed by worms when sudden judgment came upon him.

Thus, yes, thus is the one worthy of being cast down by divine judgment who arrogantly seeks to be exalted before human eyes because of the brilliance of a more elegant habit. Even the Creator of angels, while He lay crying in a manger (Luke II), is read to have been wrapped not in scarlet or shining robes but in lowly swaddling cloths. Let earthly pride therefore blush, and let the arrogance of redeemed humanity be confounded and stand amazed, when humility, the Redeemer’s humility, suddenly flashes forth with rays breaking out from it.

Moreover, at the very saving moment of His Passion, Herod clothed Him in a white garment and then sent Him back under this mockery to Pilate (Luke XXIII). When the Apostle says, “Let us go out to Him beyond the camp, bearing His reproach” (Hebrews XIII), the man is proved unwilling to bear Christ’s reproach who, swollen with arrogance, disdains to be clothed in coarse garments. Whoever, standing in the discipline of mortification, despises a white or any other humble garment casts away from himself the reproach of the Savior who died for us.

## CHAPTER III. He Discourages the Desire for Costly Garments

You therefore, beloved, now vomit forth, as though it were the filthy discharge of a deadly disease, the desire for costly garments, and expel it from the stomach of your weakened mind. It is no slight sickness of the soul to delight in the superstitious splendor of bodily clothing. Whoever scatters himself through desire for outward adornment has excluded the grace of the Holy Spirit, in which he ought to delight. If he felt its sweetness in his mind, he would by no means desire the empty vanity of bodily elegance. The Wise Man warns that this must be avoided, saying: “Never glory in clothing, and do not exalt yourself on the day of your honor” (Ecclesiasticus XI).

Desire, therefore, the splendor of that garment in which you may always flourish before the eyes of God, not that in which you may pass the moments of this deceptive and frivolous life. Now, therefore, use filthy garments whose squalor you may be able to change into unfailing whiteness.

Concerning this garment of both kinds Zechariah says: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments, and angels stood before his face. And he answered and said to those who stood before him: ‘Take away the filthy garments from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you and clothed you in changing garments’; and he said: ‘Place a clean turban upon his head’” (Zechariah III).

For what should be understood by Jesus, the great priest, except the Mediator between God and human beings? Just as, through Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who had come forth from the royal tribe of Judah, and Jesus son of Jehozadak, who administered the priestly office, the Israelite people escaped the yoke of Babylonian captivity after seventy years and rebuilt Jerusalem’s temple, which had been destroyed, with renewed splendor, so the number of the elect, after the periods of this life—which pass in the sevenfold repetition of days—is rescued from the servitude of mortality through Jesus Christ, who is the true king and priest, and the temple of God, which is the holy Church, is renewed in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Of this servitude the Apostle says: “Creation itself will also be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans VIII). Then Jesus removes the filthy garments from His body, which is the Church; then He assumes the rule of honor and glory, because the entire choir of the elect is freed from the mournful squalor of temporal sorrow and clothed in the robe of immortality amid the splendor of everlasting happiness.

The Church also sings this most openly in the psalm for the dedication of a house: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Psalm XXIX). A clean turban is also placed upon his head, because he is crowned with the glory of eternal happiness.

With this blessed garment in view, beloved brother, despise every seductive allure of corruptible clothing; scorn the frivolous and fluttering strips of a shining habit. Content with what is meanest and cheapest, bind yourself under the law of the holy rule. “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans XII); seek the lowest place at the spiritual wedding feast; dread any affront to humility, and if it should at some time creep in through negligence, correct it through repentance.

Remember, therefore, what is said through Solomon: “If the spirit of one who possesses power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes X). It is as though he openly says: If you perceive the spirit of the tempter gaining power against you in any matter, do not abandon the humility of repentance.

Therefore consider it more glorious to be humbly covered in a white garment with Christ (Luke XXV) than to be irrecoverably buried amid avenging flames with the proud purple-clad rich man (Luke XVI).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0523]

533–534. THIRTIETH TREATISE. ON SACRAMENTS ADMINISTERED BY THE UNWORTHY.

ARGUMENT.

He endeavors to recall the Florentines, who were at odds with their bishop because they suspected him of simony, to concord, clearing himself of the charge that, when he was at Florence, he had communicated with that bishop. For, he says, it would not have been right to condemn a bishop without cause, especially when the crime alleged against him was not proved. He also inveighs severely against certain monks who shunned communion with that bishop and had advanced to such audacity that they maintained that neither baptism nor any other sacrament conferred by him was valid; this he refutes. Finally, he exhorts the Florentines that, if they have anything against their bishop, they should refer it to the Roman pontiff, to whom it belongs to pronounce judgment on such matters; meanwhile, however, they should communicate with him.

[Col. 0523A] To the beloved citizens of Florence in Christ, PETER, a sinner and monk, offers the service of fraternal charity.

When we came to you, beloved brethren, as you recall, we labored earnestly to reconcile you with your bishop; and, renewing the bonds of friendship that had been broken, to breathe into you the spirit of a peace brought about by mediation. But since, with a view to assisting the aforesaid priest among you, we advanced many considerations that can be distorted by hostile interpretation and corrupted by popular crowds, lest we ourselves be branded with an undeserved disgrace and lest they—God forbid!—incur the charge of falsehood, we commit in this written passage what we frequently expressed orally before you, so that what you heard uttered by mouth you may also see written down in letters, and no liar may dare either to put an interpretation upon our words or to depart from them, since in us the writing hand and the speaking tongue agree with one another in undiscordant unity.

We therefore anathematize and irrevocably condemn the Simoniac heresy, the first of all heresies to burst forth from the depths of the devil’s entrails and to raise itself ruinously against the rule of the nascent Church. It still proceeds from the devil’s own gall and is most pestilently conveyed into the children of perdition. To its author Peter says: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of sin” (Acts VIII). But a dove has no gall; and since the Holy Spirit came upon the Lord in the form of a dove (Matthew III), he who swelled with the bitterness of gall could not be capable of the dove-like Spirit. Therefore we unhesitatingly assert that all who are corrupted by the pest of this abominable heresy are heretics, and we judge them condemnable and to be excluded from their offices, in accordance with the judgments of the sacred canons.

[ON SACRAMENTS ADMINISTERED BY THE UNWORTHY.]

CHAPTER I. Whether the sacraments of the Church can be conferred through evil persons.

Nevertheless, we are confident that such fullness of grace is present in the holy Church that in it, beyond all doubt, good things may be conferred through evil persons, clean things through defiled persons, and sacraments through accursed persons. This is truly the body of Christ and, according to the Apostle [Col. 0524A] (1 Timothy III), the pillar and foundation of truth. Nor do we establish this anew through our own rashness, but confirm what has already been established by the authority of the holy Catholic Fathers. This is also proved by many testimonies from the New and Old Testaments in the little book to which we gave the name *Gratissimus* [Note: [Col. 0523C] You have it below, in treatise 6.].

But although, after the Simoniacs had been wholly condemned and unquestionably reckoned among heretics, their sacraments could be defended by the authoritative decree of the canons, as we set out in the aforesaid book, nevertheless, that synodal censure might put them to still greater shame, it was decreed in the Roman council held under Nicholas of holy memory (Decree of Pope Nicholas, in Gratian, I, question I, chapter *De caetero*) that whoever had until then been promoted by them to the rank of any ecclesiastical degree should remain in the ministry of the office received; but that then and thereafter whoever allowed himself to be promoted by a Simoniac should gain absolutely nothing from that promotion and should lay aside the rights of ministry as though he had received them in no way at all. For this reason, therefore, we now disapprove not only the Simoniacs but also the sacraments administered through them.

You frequently heard me declare all these things aloud, if you have not forgotten. For we write nothing other than what we have spoken. If, then, you and I agree in one judgment concerning Simoniacs and the future rejection of their consecrations, why do we still quarrel with one another? There is, plainly, a question concerning your bishop: some of you think that he entered by purchase, while others, with the freedom of a steadfast mind, affirm that he entered freely and through the door. The former allege what they suppose by tumultuous, contentious abuse; the latter, confessing what they know, repel the accusation by refuting the charge brought against him. And who am I, that I should thrust out the signal of my hand amid these opposing ranks and ascribe so dreadful a crime to a man before it is canonically proved? For although error must always and everywhere be avoided, it is still more tolerable if someone justifies a sinner than if he prejudges an innocent person. A synod is imminent every year; the Apostolic See is open to all who approach it. Therefore, whoever hopes to have a just accusation against the bishop should appeal to the Roman Church. For we insignificant little men cannot in the corners of alleyways render void what we do not doubt was instituted at the very supreme pivot of the whole world.

You see, therefore, that I write simply these things alone which you heard me say orally when I was present. Let every fabricator of lies, then, blush: seeing that I did not judge lightly in a matter of unsettled controversy, he nevertheless shamelessly yelps that I am a defender of the Simoniac heresy. Let it suffice that by these few words I have given you my account, lest a longer composition compel you to be wearied by excessive length.

From here I turn my discourse to my fellow monks, from whom I do not fail to know that this cause for contention proceeds. [Col. 0525B] For they say that by priests of this kind neither chrism can be made, nor a church dedicated, nor clerical rights conferred, nor can the solemn rites of Mass ever at any time be celebrated. They allege these things so shamelessly that last year they compelled catechumens in three parishes to be baptized without the application of chrism. But since Christ is doubtless named from chrism, they take away nothing else from baptism than Christ when they remove the sacrament of chrism. And certainly, unless I am mistaken, no heresy ever broke out into such audacity as to presume to divide chrism from the washing of baptism—that is, Christ from a Christian.

But if chrism secretly brought from another Church, with their own Church disregarded, is believed to be used, as one of their supporters indeed invents, then behold: so far as they are concerned, adultery is committed in spiritual things and the sacrament is turned into sacrilege, since the chrism of their own Church is cast aside and chrism from another is substituted by the contrivance of clandestine fraud. Finally, blessed Pope Gregory says in the final clause of his last homily: “But may almighty God, who speaks through me in your ears, himself speak these things in your minds.”

Since, therefore, he concludes his book with this ending, he plainly shows that almighty God himself spoke all that was written in it. This man, through whom such an indweller speaks, in a homily delivered on priests (Homily 17), most plainly confesses that the Holy Spirit is given from heaven through the laying on of the hands of a Simoniac. “For who,” he says, “are those today in the temple of God who sell doves, except those who receive a price in the Church for the laying on of hands?”—a laying on through which the Holy Spirit is given from heaven. There he repeats the same judgment and, as though to slower persons or to those still doubting, impresses it upon them again, saying: “Therefore the dove is sold, because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price.” But since we have written much on these matters in our book, we do not linger longer here over such points; let the reader alone understand.

CHAPTER II. That the Holy Spirit can bestow his gifts through the ministry of an unworthy person.

[Col. 0526A]

Moreover, the Church is greater than Ramah, and Christ is greater than Samuel. If, therefore, the spirit came upon Saul—whom an evil spirit was accustomed to torment—when he came to Ramah, where Samuel prophesied with David, so that he stripped himself of his garments and prophesied naked, singing with the rest, for the whole day and night (1 Kings XVI and XIX; 1 Kings X), what wonder is it if the Holy Spirit comes in the Church upon any reprobate person and pours the gifts of his grace into others, not through that person’s merit but through that person’s ministry?

If, I say, the divine Spirit suddenly seized him and did not depart from him throughout so long a period of time, although he was wholly a vessel of the devil and the spirit of wickedness possessed him openly, not secretly, in body and soul together, what is new if that heavenly splendor shines upon the sewer of any reprobate man, yet is defiled by no contagion of obscene filth? But why do we now pursue these points, when above we have stated that consecration by Simoniacs was recently forbidden? Plainly because these very persons who taught that baptism should be performed without chrism still rage against those who were ordained without payment by Simoniacs before the synod. They pronounce them heretics together with their ordainers; they blaspheme, anathematize, spit upon, reject, and cast out their Masses and all the mysteries performed through them; and they terribly curse their blessings, although the Apostle says: “The cursed shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI).

In their curses they employ the testimony of the prophet Malachi, which says: “I will curse your blessings” (Malachi II), without attending to what the Lord says concerning priests in the book of Numbers: “They shall invoke [Col. 0526C] my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them” (Numbers VI). The priest invokes the Lord over the man in words, but the Lord himself effectively brings the blessing about over him. Thus the effect of the blessing does not rest on the merit of the priest; the invocation of the divine name administers it, so that the power of the Creator fulfills what sounds forth from a human mouth and often truly effects his sacrament through the ministry of an unworthy man.

But foolish and unlearned people, darkened in this word of the prophet, err, not knowing what they say or whereof they affirm. For in the sacred Scriptures “curse” is sometimes used for barrenness, just as “blessing” is used for the abundance of temporal things. Of this blessing it is said in the book of Kings: “The Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his house. And it was reported to King David that the Lord had blessed Obed-edom and all that belonged to him because of the ark of the Lord; and he said: ‘I will go and bring back the ark with blessing into my house’” (2 Kings VI). Hence, when the Psalmist first said, “Blessing I will bless her widow” (Psalm CXXXI), he immediately added, to show of what blessing he spoke: “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm CVI). And elsewhere: “He blessed them, and they were multiplied exceedingly.” Here it is plainly shown that “he blessed” means “he multiplied.” Similar is what the sons of Joseph said to Joshua: “Why have you given me the possession of one lot and one measuring-cord, when I am so great a multitude and the Lord has blessed me?” (Joshua XVII). Blessing, therefore, sometimes signifies multitude and sometimes abundance.

Conversely, to every reprobate person who despises the commandments it is said through Moses: “Cursed be your granary and cursed your remnants; cursed be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land” (Deuteronomy XXXVIII); whence a little later: “The Lord will send upon you famine and hunger” (ibid.). Therefore, in this testimony of Malachi, that we may not understand a weapon of cursing or anathema to be hurled, but rather the punishment of famine and want to be threatened, he begins by saying: “If you will not,” he says, “lay it upon your heart to give glory to my name, I will send want upon you”; and immediately follows: “And I will curse your blessings” (Malachi II). Since he first states want, what he means by “blessings” becomes clearer than light. It is as though he said: If you despise my commandments, setting in your hearts what you chiefly fear, I shall make you groan under the deficiency of want and poverty, so that the barrenness of your own land may strike you while the vice of barrenness accuses you in producing the fruits of good works; and want of bodily provisions may torment you, who neglect the nourishment of souls.

And, to prove this yet more clearly by the words of the same prophet, he says much later: “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, and let there be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord, whether I shall not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out upon you a blessing unto abundance” (Malachi III). Now if the Lord had wished “curse” there to mean the anathema, he would not have said, “I will curse your blessings,” but rather: “I will curse you, who dare to bless though you do not deserve to do so.”

And to prove most plainly from the Gospel as well what we say, the Lord is read to have said nothing else to the fig tree except this alone: “Let no one ever again eat fruit from you” [Col. 0527D] (Matthew XXI). Peter called these words a curse when he afterwards said to him: “Rabbi, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered” (Mark XI). Such also was the curse given to the first man, to whom it was said: “Cursed is the earth in your work, which shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis XXXI). But this curse of barrenness also excludes the blessing of abundance, just as in Pharaoh’s dream the cows devour cows and the ears of grain devour ears of grain (Genesis XLI).

CHAPTER III. That those who attack priests blaspheme the sacraments.

Just as, therefore, here he promises those who keep the commandments no blessing other than one of abundance, so there, on the contrary, he threatens those who do not keep them with the curse of want. Otherwise, how could almighty God curse the priestly blessing which the power of his own name consecrates? For, since, as was said above, the person over whom the name of the Lord is invoked is beyond doubt blessed by the Lord himself, how can it follow that the Lord should curse that blessing through which he himself blesses a man by the invocation of his name? Hence the authority of the canons (Apostolic Canon 46, and distinction 32, chapter *Praeter*, paragraph *Sciendum sententialiter*) forbids even those baptized by the most pestilent heretics to be baptized again, lest the name of God invoked over them seem to be annulled or rendered void.

Moreover, whoever attacks any priests with slander also blasphemes their sacraments. Let him consider, too, what blessed Jude the Apostle says in his Epistle about blasphemers. For after he had spoken of certain people who despise dominion but blaspheme majesty, he immediately added: “But Michael,” he says, “the archangel, when disputing with the devil, contended concerning the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy against him, but said: ‘May the Lord command you’” (Jude I). If, therefore, the highest angel did not presume to bring a judgment of blasphemy against the devil, how does a man not fear to mock sacraments that are full of the power of the Holy Spirit? For, since Truth says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either here or in the future” (Matthew XII), there is great cause for fear lest it be plain that he is offended by them, without whom the offense of sins cannot be remitted.

But why do we complain only of their disparagement of priests or sacraments, when they are said to tear apart almost everything, to spit upon everything, and to mock everything with public derision? “There is no pope,” they say, “no king, no archbishop, nor priest.” Hence it came about, as is said, that about a thousand people, deceived by these trifles and foolish tales, departed this world without the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. For they think that through the priests of this age no reality can be effected in the sacraments; and very many churches are found which they consider not merely unworthy of their entering, but not even fit for the service of a greeting. [Col. 0528D] For they disdain even to greet churches which they suspect were dedicated by certain unworthy bishops.

Indeed, as Luke relates, Paul said: “I appeal to Caesar” (Acts XXV). Festus replied to him: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go” (2 Corinthians XII). Is a pope more wicked than Nero? Do we believe these monks to be holier than Paul? Why then did Paul, who had already ascended to the tribunal of the third heaven, not disdain to stand before Nero’s presence? What monk is there who, through arrogance in his own holiness, ought to reject the judgment of the Apostolic See, where the institution of ecclesiastical dignity is regarded, not a man’s merit? They themselves judge in the corners of lanes and reject synodal law; they pass judgment on monks, gnaw away at all clerical persons, and spare only the laymen, whom indeed they ought to pursue more keenly and sharply. They see a monk walking along: “Look,” they say, “a scapular-wearer!” They observe a priest or bishop going by and declare that they see a shaven-beard. Even if a blessing is sought from them, they make no reply at all; they immediately turn away their eyes, asserting that those to whom a reply would be made are unworthy.

CHAPTER IV. Why the Jews Were Ill-Disposed toward Christ.

Even if we associate and eat together with sinners, we are immediately sprinkled with the salt of detraction, torn apart, and entangled with them in the same sentence of condemnation. Indeed, we—I say, we ourselves—are judged unworthy of their conversation and are deemed undeserving of their companionship. But this is not the rule of monks; it is the superstition of the Pharisees: “The scribes and Pharisees murmured, saying: ‘Because this man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15). This was the root and entire cause from which the savage fury of Jewish rancor against the Lord blazed up; from this the malice of their viper’s gall conspired in his death—namely, because they thought themselves guardians of the ceremonies of the Law, while they accused the Lord of being a friend of tax collectors and of violating the Sabbaths.

I am pleased to endure this calumny with my Lord, and I would rather live bodily with him in the house of Levi than dwell “in the tents of sinners” (Psalm 83)—that is, with those holy men who resist God. These men, despising the rule of Christ in their conduct, follow the doctrine of the Stoics (Cicero, *Paradoxa*), defining all sins as entirely equal. We, however, place Jonathan between the holy David and the rejected Saul. Although Jonathan surpasses Saul in the sincerity of truth and faith, he nevertheless does not equal David in merit and devotion.

Our brothers must therefore be admonished not to be excessively just or excessively wise. Concerning the first, Solomon says: “Do not be excessively just” (Ecclesiastes 7); concerning the second, the Apostle says: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Romans 12). Bad is the wisdom obscured by the darkness of error; good is the simplicity that does not depart from the path of the Catholic faith. Odious is the holiness that slips into heresy; while scorning to walk along the well-worn road, it is compelled to wander through winding paths and ruinous byways.

Excessive impurity certainly plunged the Novatians, who are also called Cathari, into the filth of heretical contagion; excessive holiness cut the Luciferians off from the unity of the ecclesiastical body like destructive branches. While they forbid what is permitted, and thereby boast that they are defenders of justice, they are judged enemies of the Church, so that, shut out from it, they may croak to themselves like frogs in marshes—although, while they were within it, they confused everything by their untimely clamoring.

This kind of people is rightly compared with frogs or locusts. For just as those creatures once afflicted Egypt, so now the Church is ravaged by these men. Scripture says of the locusts: “They covered the whole surface of the earth, laying everything waste”; and immediately it adds: “Thus the grass of the earth was devoured, and whatever fruit there was on the trees” (Exodus 10). Locusts lay waste the entire surface of the earth and devour the grasses together with the fruits of the trees. So every kind of detractor tears apart and gnaws away either our weaknesses, as though they were the grass of the lowly, or, like the fruits of trees, the works of the perfect, consuming them with the envious tooth of malicious jealousy.

Against such people the Apostle says: “Receive us; we have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one” (2 Corinthians 7). And elsewhere, reproaching them, he says: “Do you bite one another? Do you harm one another? Take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5).

But although we, established in the sacred order, ought to be God’s hunters, as it is said through Jeremiah, “I will send my hunters, and they will hunt” (Jeremiah 15), we abandon the prey of worldly people, bare our teeth, and snarl at one another. Like rabid little dogs, we tear one another apart with mutual bites.

Let swollen presumption now be restrained; let burdensome holiness make itself equal to its brothers. Whoever wishes to be holy should be holy before God and should not, through arrogance, place himself above a weak brother. Therefore, let the puppy whose duty was to drive away strangers by no means, after scorning them, turn to tear apart those of the household, lest someone who could have slept peacefully under a roof be driven outside the doors to *naubare* [read *cubare*, “lie down”] in the open air.

[Note: The ending of this letter appears to be incomplete.]

Let the name of the Lord be blessed.

[Column 529]

541–542. THIRTY-FIRST OPUSCULUM: AGAINST AVARICE AND GREED FOR GIFTS

## Argument
