He vehemently detests the vice of avarice, especially in the acceptance of gifts, and urges the cardinal bishops to endeavor, if possible, to uproot and eradicate it from the entire Church and from the minds of priests. The most holy man gives this admonition wisely. For he saw that nearly all the disasters and troubles by which the Christian commonwealth was then burdened and indeed tormented flowed from the source of avarice. If the chief of the Church crushed this most loathsome pest, it plainly appeared that it would then easily be abolished throughout the entire Catholic world.

[Column 529C] Peter, a sinful monk, to the cardinal bishops of the Apostolic See: greetings in the Lord.

Just as words are signs of thoughts for those present, so letters are instruments of souls for those who are absent. As the skill of the art of war is learned in war so that it may afterward be taught in peace, so at times, while something is taught in leisure, it is exercised more cautiously in battle. In the conflict of the Apostolic See, in which you are still laboring unanimously, I too fought as a combatant. But now, behold, since I have been released from the military belt and settled in the peace of the municipality, I am glad to teach what I learned.

## Against avarice and greed for gifts

### Chapter I. That judges cannot accept gifts, not even gratuitously

Among all the battle lines of vices that roar around you, amid the thickest storms of descending darts, like hailstorms, you must keep especially vigilant watch against avarice, and a shield must always be set against its arrows. It hastens headlong to inflict a deadly wound on the wretched; yet its first aim is to extinguish not the sight of the forehead but that of the heart. Hence the Wise Man says: “Gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges, and, like a mute man, turn aside their corrections at the mouth” (Ecclesiasticus 20; Deuteronomy 16).

It arms those who approach with gifts and, through them, conquers and blinds the hearts of those who obtain access to the ears of rulers. Concerning these the Lord complains through Isaiah, saying: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves; they all love gifts and pursue rewards” (Isaiah 1).

Someone may say: “I ask for nothing, but if something is offered freely, I do not refuse to accept it.” Here those who seek gifts are not being censured, but those who merely love them. They are also rightly called companions of thieves, because, while they receive stolen gifts, they fear being detected by their own accomplices and associates as though in the crime of theft.

It must also be noted that he says, “They pursue rewards.” For although they provide their benefactors with the assistance they request, they nevertheless do not escape the stains of guilt: by receiving repayment for their favor, they lose the fruit of eternal reward. Concerning them he says shortly afterward: “Alas! I will be consoled over my enemies, and I will avenge myself on my foes” (ibid.).

The sons of Samuel are plainly recorded as having had no other crime except that they loved gifts and did not follow the example of their father’s purity; thus they irrecoverably lost the leadership of the people of Israel. And it must be noted that when Scripture says of them, “They turned aside after avarice; they accepted gifts,” it immediately adds: “They perverted judgment” (1 Samuel 8). It is close and almost inevitable that, after a gift has been accepted, judgment too should be perverted by a corrupted judge.

Oh, how clean Samuel’s face was from gifts when he said: “I have lived before you from my youth to this day. Behold, here I am; speak against me before the Lord and before his anointed: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or anyone’s donkey, whether I have falsely accused anyone, whether I have oppressed anyone, whether I have taken a gift from anyone’s hand; and I will despise it today and restore it to you” (1 Samuel 13).

Hence it is also commanded in the Law: “You shall not accept gifts, which blind even the prudent and subvert the words of the just” (Exodus 23). Deuteronomy says similarly: “You shall not accept a person’s status, nor gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the just” (Deuteronomy 16).

How averse Abraham was to receiving gifts when he resisted Bara, the king of Sodom, saying: “I lift my hand to the Lord, the Most High God, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of woven cloth to a sandal strap I will accept nothing of all that is yours” (Genesis 14).

How free Moses was from gifts received, when he called the all-knowing Lord as witness: “You know,” he said, “that I have never taken even a donkey from them, nor afflicted any one of them” (Numbers 16). For where gifts are coveted, it follows that just as the judge justifies one who has paid him, so he afflicts the one who has given nothing.

Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who justify the wicked for gifts and deprive the just of his justice!” (Isaiah 5). Immediately he threatens them with the vengeance owed them, adding: “Therefore, just as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root will be like ash, and their shoot will rise like dust” (ibid.).

The same prophet elsewhere complains of them, saying: “All have turned aside to their own way, each one to his own avarice, from the highest to the lowest” (Isaiah 56). Avarice plainly provokes against itself the anger of almighty God, and it torments the heart it possesses with constantly empty thoughts. Hence he complains about the avaricious people, saying: “Because of the iniquity of his avarice I was angry, and I struck him; I hid myself and was indignant, and he went wandering in the way of his heart” (Isaiah 57).

### Chapter II. That fruit is gained from wealth if it is distributed to the poor

No corruption of a wound surely stinks more intolerably in God’s nostrils than the dung of avarice. Every greedy person, while he piles up the profits of filthy money, turns his reception room into a latrine and heaps it up like a mound of dung.

Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Their silver will be thrown outside, and their gold will be as a dunghill; their silver and gold will not be able to rescue them on the day of the Lord’s fury” (Ezekiel 7). And elsewhere it is written: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own—how long?—and burdens himself with thick mud!” (Habakkuk 2). For an avaricious person to burden himself with thick mud against himself means to heap up earthly profits together with the weight of sin.

The prophet Habakkuk also says: “Woe to him who gathers evil avarice for his house, so that he may set his nest on high and think himself safe on the day of evil!” (ibid.). Just as wood does not satisfy fire, so accumulated money does not calm the heat of avarice. Rather, as a flame rises when fuel is added, so avarice increases while profits are amassed.

Hence Ecclesiastes says: “The avaricious person will not be filled with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Ecclesiastes 5). He would gain fruit from them if, without loving them, he wished to distribute them well; but because he loves them by retaining them, he leaves them here without fruit. The text continues: “Where there are many riches, there are many who consume them” (Ecclesiastes 5). And what benefit does their possessor have, except that he sees his riches with his eyes?

Concerning them Solomon also says: “Riches preserved to the harm of their lord. For they perish in grievous affliction; he begets a son who will be in extreme poverty” (ibid.). To show how unfaithful riches are to their possessor, he immediately adds: “As he came naked from his mother’s womb, so he will return, and he will take nothing with him from his labor. A thoroughly miserable infirmity! As he came, so he will return. What benefit, then, does he have from laboring for the wind all the days of his life? And so forth” (ibid.).

Do we perhaps amass profits in order to buy estates and lands? But what benefit is there in extending the boundaries of one’s property, when these cannot enlarge the narrow limits of our life? Hence the Wise Man says: “Do not attend to unjust possessions, and do not say, ‘I have sufficient for life’; for nothing will benefit you at the time of vengeance” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

Isaiah also says: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, even to the limit of the place! Will you alone inhabit the middle of the earth?” (Isaiah 5). As though he plainly said: “How far will you extend yourselves, when you cannot live in the common world without companions? You oppress those adjacent and contiguous to you, but you always find others against whom you can extend yourselves.”

Hence it is written: “Whoever seeks to become rich will not be innocent” (Proverbs 23). And elsewhere it says: “Nothing is more wicked than an avaricious person. Why are you proud, earth and ashes? Nothing is more iniquitous than loving money” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

Certainly this is a harsh and exceedingly fearful sentence. For if nothing is more wicked, nothing more iniquitous, than an avaricious person, then he is not better than parricides, is not preferred to adulterers, is equated with heretics, and is likened to idolaters. Hence the Apostle says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3).

Let someone be chaste, sober, devoted to feeding the needy, committed to hospitality; let him fast, keep vigil, and continue the day into the night by singing psalms. If he is nevertheless avaricious, he loses everything, so that among all the guilty he cannot find anyone worse than himself: “For nothing is,” as it is said, “more wicked than an avaricious person, and nothing more iniquitous than loving money” (Ecclesiasticus 10).

What, then, will it profit you not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not even to swear falsely, and to guard yourself entirely from every crime, provided that, if avarice is not expelled from you, nothing worse, nothing more wicked, than you can be found?

### Chapter III. What avarice is

Let the avaricious person go, build the walls of the Church, devote himself to preaching, reconcile those at variance to peace, strengthen those who waver in the truth of the Catholic faith, attend daily to offering sacrifices, and withdraw from worldly business. Yet until the fire of avarice is extinguished within him, all the bloom of his virtues is burned up, and no one more criminal than he is found.

Indeed, after Scripture has stated that nothing is more wicked than an avaricious person, lest any doubt about the word “avaricious” arise, it vigilantly adds: “Nothing is more iniquitous than loving money.” Therefore, to be avaricious is nothing other than to love money.

Money already acquired is loved, and money still to be acquired is likewise loved. Avarice is like a two-headed serpent: it is accustomed to bite with either mouth and to pour in its deadly poison through either, whether another’s property is sought or property already possessed is enjoyed with delight.

Concerning the person swallowed by both mouths of this serpent it is written: “For a covetous and miserly man, wealth is without reason; and what is gold to an envious man? He gathers unjustly for others, and another will revel in his goods” (Ecclesiasticus 14).

There are also those who burn with every desire to seek what belongs to others, but once they have obtained it, they recklessly squander it. There are those who do not covet acquiring what belongs to others, but preserve what is theirs under a jealous guard, as though it were sacred to Ceres. Most loathsome, however, is the kind that both shamefully seeks what belongs to others and guards what has already become its own with sordid tenacity.

Such people are worse than the dragons of Babylon, who, although they are said to guard an immeasurable heap of gold and silver, nevertheless seize no one’s property; content, as it were, with their own possessions, they do not covet those of others.

But why should I gather wealth which no one brought here on entering, and which cannot accompany anyone departing from the world? Hence the Apostle says: “We brought nothing into this world, and it is beyond doubt that we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 5).

### Chapter IV. How harmful it is to desire wealth

What wonder, then, that we said above that nothing is more wicked than an avaricious person, when greed is said to be the root of all evils? In whoever the root of all evils exists, that person is consequently convicted of being guilty of all evils, because one who has its root in the soil of his heart cannot avoid its poisonous growth.

Nor should we pass over what he says: “By desiring it, some have wandered from the faith” (Matthew 26). This is plainly like the betrayer of the Savior, who, in order to receive a small sum, sold the Creator of all things for money and, for the love of worthless money, handed over the author of life.

So too Balaam son of Beor (Numbers 22), who, while he coveted the profit offered to him, despised faith in God and gave counsel for the downfall of the people of Israel. Some men of no negligible authority report [see the scholia at the end of the opusculum] that this man was Helin the Buzite, descended from Buz, who was the second son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. This Elihu is said in the Book of Blessed Job to have been Job’s friend (Job 32), because he had been a prophet and possessed the power of spiritual grace revealed to him. But after he had gradually turned aside into the vice of avarice, he became a soothsayer instead of a prophet, and from a soothsayer he was transformed into a magician.

Behold what benefit avarice provides: while it takes faith away from people, it turns a prophet into a magician and plunges him from the height of apostolic dignity into Tartarus.

Had Gehazi not also wandered from the faith, when, as he accepted the silver offered by Naaman, he supposed that his master’s spirit was absent? But Elisha said: “Was not my heart present when the man returned from his chariot to meet you?” (2 Kings 5).

Here we must carefully consider that, if the man who took payment for a prophet’s power was punished, how could anyone dare to sell the pope’s judgment? “You accepted,” Elisha said, “silver and garments in order to buy olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, servants and maidservants; but the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and to your descendants forever” (ibid.).

There are plainly two founders of the heresy of simony, one in the Old Testament and the other in the New; and these produced two kinds of simoniacs, namely, sellers and buyers. Gehazi sold the gift of the Holy Spirit (2 Kings 5); Simon Magus attempted to purchase it (Acts 8).

Nor should only the person who gives or receives payment for sacred orders be called a simoniac; so too should one who sells a synod or traffics in priestly judgment. But perhaps someone may say: “Then does the one who gives anything for a synodal sentence incur the crime of simony?” I would not say this, because Naaman did not sin when he offered a gift to the fraudulent servant out of reverence for the one who had cleansed him.

It is one thing to desire justice for one’s case, whatever it may be; it is another to hold for sale the canonical judgment established through the Holy Spirit. With what conscience do we accept payment for issuing a judicial decision when the person to whom we offer venal support is contending either justly or unjustly?

If he is litigating justly, we unquestionably sell the truth; but if unjustly, we fight against the truth—which is Christ—with the reckless audacity of an impudent person. Hence it is commanded in the Law: “You shall execute what is just, what is just” (Deuteronomy 16).

Anyone who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward is said, in a legal sense, to execute what is just unjustly. For he is rightly said to execute what is just unjustly who does not hesitate to sell the justice he professes. But the person is proved to execute what is just justly who, in asserting justice, seeks nothing except justice alone.

### Chapter V. That not only those who make agreements are simoniacs, but also those who demand money without an agreement

Since there are some who, either before they perform the ministry of consecration or before the case has been decided, make no agreement about payment, but afterward demand it as though from debtors and press vigorously for extorted remuneration, let them not doubt that they incur the crime of Gehazi (2 Kings 8). After Naaman had been healed and was already departing, Gehazi dared to demand money for the gift of the Holy Spirit.

And just as Gehazi was struck with no other blow than the plague of leprosy, which removed people from the camp, so this man is not merely lightly stained but is covered with that crime’s defilement, which separates him from the sacraments of the Church.

[Note: Elsewhere we shall discuss the fact that the holy doctor did not actually resign the episcopate, although he wished to do so.]

I plainly saw, while a certain one of our brothers was performing the office of the episcopal dignity—I suppress his name but identify his vice—how he leapt and swelled with excitement as the appointed time of the synodal council drew near, as though the season of threshing or harvesting were approaching. He girded himself to gather gifts, sharpening not an edge of steel but the sickle of eloquence with which to cut them down. He was even said to have pseudo-apostles of this fraud, who scraped together money from here and there and stuffed it into purses already vomiting with coins.

If someone should perhaps be angry with me for reproving my fellow priest so sharply, let him rebuke John and Matthew (John 12, 13, 2, 18; Matthew 26), who, while pursuing the truth of the sacred history, call their fellow apostle, who coveted money, a sacrilegious betrayer.

The ancient enemy often deceives those who hope for profits of this kind, so that he may in no way fulfill what he promised them. Just as bird-catchers entice a hawk by luring it with the bait of meat, but as soon as they have it in their hand withdraw the meat and bind its feet with a thong, so the devil first promises profit, but afterward withdraws it and casts upon the person only the snare of sin.

Thus the one who covets gifts, like a mouse trying to gnaw the bait, is strangled by the trap. The distinguished Fabricius guarded himself most effectively against this. When Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, discovered that Fabricius was poor while waging war against the power of the Roman state, he began to solicit him and promised him a fourth part of his kingdom if he defected to him. Fabricius rejected and abhorred this offer and, more glorious than any king, remained in his poverty.

Let the Christian who is avaricious hear this and blush at his paganism and at the Gospel of the pagan man. Often a gift is accepted with the intention that, if the benefactor should prove guilty, the benefactor may gain an escape from justice. This is easy to promise but difficult to fulfill. Once gifts have been received, if we wish to act against the giver, our words immediately grow soft in our mouth, the sharpness of our speech is blunted, and our tongue is hindered by a certain shamefaced embarrassment.

The mind, conscious of the gift it has received, weakens the vigor of judicial judgment and suppresses the freedom of eloquence. Even if the uprightness of the judgment is not entirely taken away, the authority to judge is nevertheless enfeebled.

Some, however, are found to maintain this precaution regarding themselves: while the business of a judicial case is still pending, they accept nothing even from someone who offers it; once the disputes have been settled, they do not reject what is offered freely. But when cases arise, it often happens that what they thought they had accepted freely they are compelled to repay in other cases. The danger of the river, which they had hoped to leave behind them, they unexpectedly find before them, to be swum across.

This, then, is safe and unimpaired: “Let us shake our hands free from every gift,” as the prophet says, and preserve for ourselves the frank freedom both to harm and to help, so that we may not litigate under the servitude of money but serve in the freedom of justice.

If someone complains of the narrowness of his household means, let him hear attentively what is written: “Because of poverty many have sinned, and whoever seeks to become rich turns away his eye” (Ecclesiasticus 27).

If, then, those who suffer poverty in their household sin—those who see that even what is necessary for their sustenance is lacking to them—if, I say, even these sin while eagerly acquiring not superfluous things but necessities, what judgment awaits those who strive to become rich in order to live in extravagance? Those who store up various kinds of metal and garments vulnerable to moths?

The Apostle James thunders a terrible threat against them: “Come now, you rich, and weep, howling over the miseries that will come upon you” (James 5). After saying this, he immediately gives the reason: “Your riches have rotted; your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and it will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days” (ibid.).

### Chapter VI. That wealth is not desired for need but for luxury

Those of this kind do not complain of poverty in order to support the necessities of nature with the aids of need, but so that their tower-like platters may breathe the fragrance of Indian spices and adulterated wines may shine yellow in crystal vessels with honey.

They desire to become rich for this purpose: wherever they go, a bedchamber may be ready for them, clothed with elaborate and wonderfully woven hangings and ornaments of curtains, so that they may wrap the walls of the house from the eyes of beholders as though covering a corpse to be buried.

Then they spread seats with tapestries displaying prodigious images and hang coverings before the ceilings, lest anything falling from above descend upon them. Afterward the crowd of attendants is divided. Some stand reverently beside their master and watch his slightest nod, should he happen to give an order, with excessive attentiveness, like observers of the stars. Others, devoted to Martha’s service, run restlessly in every direction like swallows.

Amid these insanities of delirious ambition, why do they seek backcloths that do not deserve to be seen by their own masters? Their ornament suffers a serious loss because eyes do not emerge at the back of the head or from the neck. What useful kind of wealth is it that, possessing no use beyond mere beauty, cannot nourish its possessor by its appearance? It serves only the allurements of other people’s eyes, since it is hung behind its possessor, not before his sight.

A similar madness is believed to be present when a little bed is decorated with such elaborate expense that it surpasses the ornament of any most sacred object, or even of the apostolic altar itself. How absurd it seems that the bed on which corruptible flesh is relaxed in the rest of sleep should be cultivated more carefully than the altar of the cross, on which the sacrifice of the Lord’s body is offered!

Thus, whereas sobriety used to commend pontiffs, they have now become gluttons through their lavish expenditure. Royal purple, because it is of a single color, is despised [see the scholia at the end of the opusculum]; cloaks dyed with various brilliant colors are assigned to adorn the elevated bed.

And while domestic purple cloths seem shabby to our eyes, foreign skins delight us because they are bought at great price. The hides of sheep and lambs are despised, while ermine, *gebelline*, marten, and fox skins are sought.

Yet sheep and lambs are honored in the sacred utterances and represent either the Church or the person of the Savior: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10); and, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Of the others, either let there be complete silence, since they are unworthy for Scripture to mention, or, if any remembrance of them is found, they prove to have an unfavorable meaning. Such is the saying: “Foxes have dens, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8; Luke 9).

Behold, Christ is not reclining in little foxes, while the Christian sleeps beneath fox skins. He rejects the animals honored with the name of the world’s Redeemer, but counts as his ornament those that signify the figures of the rejected.

Yet these rich men are struck by no small obstacle: while they cover themselves with decorated and painted blankets—woe, woe to them!—they cannot sleep with their eyes open.

We should therefore envy Regulus, once a Roman consul (Eutropius, *History*, book 2, at the end), whose Carthaginian captors, while he remained steadfast in his love of the republic, cut off his eyelids. And indeed, what use is this beauty of appearance if it is not seen? What use is such splendid variety of objects if the mind of the beholder is not nourished by it?

This is plainly a splendid kind of wealth: while one uses it, it cannot be seen; while it is seen, it cannot provide use. I am weary of adding the remaining vanities—not ridiculous things to be laughed at, but absurdities to be mourned. It is tedious to enumerate all the monsters of ambition and prodigal madness.

The papal miters are studded in various places with glittering gems and golden leaflets. Imperial horses, which, while they gather swift steps with arched necks, exhaust the hands of their riders, linked to the reins, by their untamed ferocity. I omit rings fitted with enormous pearls. I pass over staffs no longer merely conspicuous with gold and gems but buried beneath them.

I do not remember ever seeing episcopal staffs covered with such a continuous radiance of shining metal as those carried by the bishops of Esculanum and Trani. Yet both were cast down: one in the Apulian regions, when Nicholas was presiding; the other in the Lateran Church, before Alexander—that is, before Roman pontiffs.

Nor did it profit them that they used wooden, gilded staffs, since the merit of priesthood is produced not by the brilliance of garments but by the standard of spiritual virtues; and it is not glittering pearls or gems but golden character that befits a priest.

For just as true humility in a priest wins God’s favor and commends all his other good qualities, so the swelling of arrogance and the ambition of vanity provoke against him the anger of divine indignation and fight against whatever good he may perhaps once have accomplished.

Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Will I not be indignant over these things?” (Isaiah 57). A priest ascends a high mountain when he raises himself into the arrogance of pride through certain insolent displays of artificial adornment.

And since the priest’s soul is joined to Christ as a bride by the bond of a spiritual marriage, if he so pursues outward adornment that he neglects inward beauty, he in a way introduces an adulterer into his husband’s bedchamber.

Hence the divine voice immediately adds: “Because beside me you uncovered yourself, and you received an adulterer” (ibid.). O what bitter pain it is if, while the husband is present, an adulterer is introduced, and in the marriage chamber where the bridegroom reclines an incestuous rival is admitted!

Therefore it is immediately added: “You enlarged your bed and made a covenant with them; you loved their bed with an open hand.” And, so as not to remain silent about adornment or luxury, he adds at once: “You adorned yourself with royal perfume and multiplied your spices” (ibid.).

After he has condemned the arrogance of the proud and of those who live luxuriously, he immediately consoles the spirit of the humble and healthily afflicted: “Remove,” he says, “the stumbling blocks from before my people, for thus says the Lord, the exalted and sublime one, who dwells in eternity and in the holy place, and also with the contrite and humbled in spirit, in order to give life to the spirit of the humble and life to the heart of the contrite” (Jeremiah 7).

Finally, the heart of the priest must be the temple of God and the sanctuary of Christ, not—as it is written—a den of thieves (Matthew 21), nor a receptacle of filthy money.

For in the divine judgment every mind is counted as whatever it turns over in thought through desire. If it imagines fornication or adultery, it becomes a brothel of prostitutes. If it meditates the shedding of blood and hatred, it is a field of raging warriors. If someone turns over in thought the delights of foods and pleasant banquets, what else does he appear to be before God than a cauldron or kettle in which food is cooked? If he handles disputes and litigation, what else is seen than the tribunal of a judge or a courtroom?

Hence, when the Lord said to Ezekiel, “Enter and see the exceedingly wicked abominations that these people commit here,” he immediately adds: “I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles and animals, an abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall all around” (Ezekiel 8).

Whatever occupies the mind is seen as though depicted on a wall. The mind itself takes on the images of the things it turns over through diligent meditation; it is painted, as it were, with various images of actions according to whether it meditates on vain or useful things.

If someone now gazed at the glittering stars, then lowered his eyes to a latrine; if he admired the radiance of shining gold and then contemplated the rough rust of iron with contempt, so, so indeed the human mind, while it meditates on earthly and lowly things, plainly appears as earth. But when it handles what belongs to piety, when it thinks about divine and heavenly things, it rightly appears as heaven, the temple of God and his sanctuary.

### Chapter VII. That the Roman Church is the seat of the apostles
Now, moreover, the Roman Church, which is the seat of the apostles [Col. 0540B], ought to imitate the ancient senate of the Romans. For just as at that time that earthly senate communicated every plan for this purpose and directed and diligently applied the united efforts of its industry toward it: that the multitude of all nations might be subjected to Roman rule; so now the attendants of the apostolic see, who are the spiritual senators of the universal Church, ought zealously to devote themselves to this one endeavor: that they may be able to subject the human race to the laws of Christ, the true emperor.

And just as the consuls of the Romans then brought back victories from different parts of the world after the slaughter of their enemies, so these men now ought to free human souls held captive from the hand of the devil. For these titles of victory, for these triumphs, they ought always to yearn—namely, that they may rejoice to seize the spoils of perishing souls from the ancient plunderer and bring back victorious standards to their king Christ [Col. 0540C].

David foreshadowed this conflict when he victoriously captured the city of Rabbah. Rabbah is interpreted as “multitude” or “great,” and is rightly understood to signify the whole of this world. Accordingly, David captured the city of Rabbah (IV Kings XII) when Christ subjected the great and abundant multitude of this world to his laws. David also took the crown from that king’s head and placed it upon his own, as Scripture testifies. The true David, Christ, fulfilled this when he stripped away the world’s wise men, by whom the devil was in a certain manner adorned, and transformed them into the diadem of his own beauty and glory.

The multitude of the faithful is called not only Christ’s crown but also the crown of every teacher by whose preaching it is converted. Thus Paul says to the Philippians: “Therefore, my most beloved brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord” (Philippians IV). He also carried away, according to Scripture, a very great quantity of spoil. Spoil is taken from Rabbah when individual faithful and devoted people are converted from this world to the service of almighty God.

You, I say, holy pontiffs—you above all ought to be plunderers of this kind. Every day you should labor to snatch human souls from the hands of their wicked possessor and bring back triumphal spoils to your king David. Yet it is not enough that, once snatched from the devil, someone is converted to God through holy devotion, unless immediately afterward he is also crushed by the hardness of his former condition, as though by the frequent hammer of holy preaching. Hence Jeremiah says: “Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer shattering a rock?” (Jeremiah XXIII.)

The words of the Lord are like fire because they drive away coldness and kindle warmth in minds; but they are also a hammer because they soften the hardness of obstinacy and stubbornness. Accordingly, sacred history appropriately adds: “And bringing his people, he sawed them, and drove iron chariots over them; he divided them with knives and led them through in the likeness of bricks” (I Kings XII).

For what are we to understand by iron chariots—which are, of course, a kind of wagon—if not the strong and impregnable chariot of the holy evangelists and, consequently, the utterance of all the divine Scriptures [Col. 0541B]? For, as we have already said elsewhere, iron is indeed a base metal, yet it subdues every metal. Just as iron dominates all metals, so evangelical doctrine is known to soften hardened minds.

What, then, does it mean to drive iron chariots over captive people except to thresh the threshing-floor of human minds with the wheels of sacred Scripture? Its purpose is that the divine word may crush within them the clods of resisting vices and strive to smooth and level them for receiving the harvest of heavenly commandments.

And what does it mean to divide them with knives except to open the conscience of sinful people to confession through the preaching of the divine word? Concerning this word the Apostle says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI) [Col. 0541C]. A person is then divided, as it were, by spiritual knives, when he is cut by the sword of the divine word so that the wounds of his soul may be exposed.

But why is it said that he led them through in the likeness of bricks, unless because bricks are both earthly and baked? A sinner is then turned into the likeness of a brick when, at the sound of preaching, he conceives the fire of the Holy Spirit and, truly humbled, recognizes that he is earth and mud.

Thus every converted and penitent person is fashioned into the image of a brick: he is humbled by the mud of his frailty and, as it were, reddens or blazes with divine love, so that, while he considers himself earthly dust, he may kindle his heart to give thanks to God, who has recalled him. Hence Adam is also interpreted as “red earth,” so that from the name of the first parent each person may learn either what he is by origin or what he ought in practice to be.

Toward these triumphs, therefore, priests of the Churches and holy pontiffs ought to have strained—rather than dissolving in sumptuous dishes of food or in the wanton insolence of seductive pleasure. For after the beginning of the newly created world, the human race lived for nearly sixteen hundred years without drinking wine or eating meat; yet no one whom Scripture records wasted away from sickness all the way to death.

## CHAPTER VIII. Epilogue and conclusion of the little work.

But now, to conclude briefly with the ending of an epilogue what has been treated more fully above: having performed the function of a whetstone, while I myself do not cut, but sharpen more and more the edge of the cutting iron, may avarice be uprooted from our hearts, since it is most clearly condemned by the converging testimonies of all the Scriptures—and, together with Achan son of Carmi, be buried beneath as many judgments of the Fathers as beneath stones (Joshua VII).

Let us not delight in accepting gifts, lest, in the examination of the hidden Judge, we be—God forbid!—cast down from the priestly order, as the sons of Samuel, for this reason, lost the dignity of judicial authority. Let us not sell a synod, nor reduce a synodal decree to a price, lest we appear to be trafficking in the Holy Spirit, the author of the sacred council.

Let ambition for worldly pomp depart; let the splendor and extravagance of clothing be restrained; let the excessive consumption of food and drink be moderated [Col. 0542B]. Let our money pass into the hands of the poor; let the purse that had swollen through avarice become full again after being emptied through mercy.

Let our riches and our treasure be the profits of souls, and let precious talents of virtues be stored in the treasury of our breast. On this altar above all let us offer sacrifice, and, after overthrowing what surrounds us, let us finally sacrifice ourselves to God as living victims, so that although we are seen as priests in the eyes of human beings, we may also exercise the rights of true priesthood in the sight of the hidden Judge.

## SCHOLIA.

Since royal purple is of a single color, it is despised; cloaks, however, dyed with various brilliant colors, are assigned to adorn the elevated bed.

From this passage it is easily inferred that purple had been the dress of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church long before the date asserted by some more recent writers—and not merely of those who were raised from the clerical order to such a sublime height, but also of monks taken from the cloisters of Saint Benedict and appointed to that dignity.

For it is established that those to whom Peter Damian writes were monks of Saint Benedict’s family, yet he addresses them as follows: “Although the native purple garments are filthy in our eyes, foreign skins delight us because they are purchased at a great price.”

I believe, as I was saying, that the use of purple among the prelates of the Holy Roman Church was much older than certain modern writers suppose. Indeed, if an argument drawn from paintings has any force in these matters, the author of a book dedicated to the blessed Desiderius, abbot and cardinal, around the year of the Lord 1060, and transferred from the Casinensis library to the Vatican along with many others, also proves that the use of purple among not only clerics but monks was extremely ancient.

On the front of that book, Desiderius himself—I mean Desiderius, monk and abbot of the sacred monastery of Cassino and cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia—is depicted in two garments, one close-fitting and the other reaching to the feet; both are, as it were, consular purple, adorned with a golden band at each extremity [Col. 0542D].

There can be no doubt that the painting was made while Desiderius was alive. Apart from the fact that the verses prefixed to the beginning of the book by that anonymous Cassinese writer address him as present, this is also shown by the square panel that Desiderius wears at the back of his head. The very ancient monuments of the City—which we have observed in great number—demonstrate that this was customarily an indication that the person was living at that time; Cardinal Deacon John also testifies to this in *The Life of Saint Gregory*, book IV, chapter 84.

Furthermore, just as the cardinals succeeded to the place of the ancient senate, so it is very likely that the Roman pontiffs had bestowed purple upon them much earlier than these recent writers believe.

Yet when they say that Innocent IV established in the year of Christ 1244 that cardinals riding publicly on horseback should wear a red hat, and that Paul II in the year of the Lord 1464 ordered by his decree that the cardinals’ hats should be made of scarlet silk, and also wished horses and mules to be covered while being ridden with cloth of the same color, it seems strange that other historians should write that in the time of Clement VI, around the years of Christ 1353 and 1358, cardinals and their horses alike were clothed and richly adorned in purple cloth.

This is recorded concerning Cardinal Aegidius Albornotius by the writer of that age, Matteo Villani, in *Florentine Chronicle*, book III, chapter 54, and book VII, chapter 100. The author of the life of the blessed Peter of Luxembourg, who was created cardinal in the year 1386, although by a pseudopope, also mentions in two places quite openly not only red hats but also red capes.

But, without passing over this point here, it should also be noted that certain abbots of the Benedictine order used violet to display their dignity, although their monks went about dressed in black. This is clear from the ancient register of the monastery of Farfa, from which it plainly appears that approximately thirty-five abbots, up to Suppo, who lived in the year of the Lord 1040, governed the monastery dressed in these garments.

It is easy to believe that this violet color was taken away from abbots—especially those living in Rome, who were accustomed to be present at the sacred consistory of the most illustrious cardinals and at the side of the supreme pontiff—by the injuries of time, wars, and other such circumstances, as well as by human malice [Col. 0544A].

Nor is this surprising, since the professors of the Benedictine order were permitted by the rule of their most holy father to use any color whatsoever. Therefore, when they shone with cardinalatial or any other dignity and wore a purple or violet cloak, they did not need a dispensation from the supreme pontiff, as did followers of another institution whose rule prescribed otherwise.

Although Saint Benedict himself went about with his monks in black clothing, he nevertheless gives this general instruction: “Let monks not complain about the color or coarseness of any of these things, but let them use whatever can be found in the province where they live.”

Accordingly, Paul the Deacon of Cassino aptly explains this passage as follows: “Monks should not complain if their foot-cloths are white and their tunics brown—that is, if the foot-cloths are of one color, the tunic of another, and the cowl of yet another.”

And Ferriolus, reporting the words of Abbot Smaragdus, says: “Let them also avoid a color that is white or excessively red, by which the appearance of the body is often displayed to those who see it, to their own destruction.”

These are the words of Ferriolus, who advised such monks as though by way of counsel. In view of these facts, it is plainly established that if monks living in cloisters could be covered with clothing of every color, who would doubt that ecclesiastical dignitaries, with even greater right, could be distinguished by purple or violet garments without the pontiff’s order and without penalty?

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0543]

# THE THIRTY-SECOND LITTLE WORK. ON LENT AND THE FORTY-TWO STATIONS OF THE HEBREWS

## ARGUMENT.

On the occasion of a certain man who abstained from more sumptuous foods for forty days—not only at the time when this was sanctioned by the Church but also at other seasons of the year—the author gathers from the sacred writings the mysteries and certain special privileges of this number forty.

He then interprets mystically the forty-two places in which the Hebrews stayed for a short time before reaching the fields divinely destined for them, showing with the utmost clarity that the life of the Christian is secretly signified by these places as progressing through certain stages of virtue toward perfection and happiness.

[Col. 0543C] To the most reverend brother Hildebrand, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of intimate love.

What you and I recently discussed in a private conversation, venerable brother, we do not regard as idle or superfluous if it is also arranged in the sequence of a written treatise.

I said, if you have not forgotten, that I knew a servant of God who, besides those Lents established by the Fathers and fixed within their appointed limits throughout the annual cycle, secretly observed other [“Lents” / uncertain reading: *carinas*, manuscript *cartinas*]. Through these, he broke the illicit appetites of carnal passions and crucified the itching desires of burning allurements.

At one time he abstains from fish for forty days; at another he restrains himself from eating either fruits or even vegetables that are especially suitable for him [Col. 0543D]. Sometimes he eats the first cherries of the season, sometimes melons, sometimes figs or grapes, or whatever happens to taste more delicately. But as soon as his appetite is provoked to eat, discipline is immediately applied, so that he does not touch what he has desired.

And because he craves more eagerly what the ardor of eating has already tasted, he immediately places the bridle of abstinence upon his jaws—not condemning the foods that God created for the faithful to receive with thanksgiving, nor ignorant that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving (I Timothy IV).

He begins by eating everything, although that eating is more useful for torment than for the benefits of pleasure. In this abstinence, therefore, the appetite of the stomach is broken and the heat of desire extinguished—not, God forbid, is God’s creation condemned. A richer reward is gained precisely because this abstinence from apparently insignificant things is neither celebrated nor famous, [but] is practiced openly and yet remains unknown as though it were secret.

If, brothers, someone asks why he does not use this or that food, he immediately replies that he knows it to be harmful to his bodily ailments. Yet while this man is speaking of illnesses of the soul, the other understands him to be speaking of bodily discomfort. He has been accustomed to maintain this abstinence from each of those foods for a full cycle of forty days.

## [ON LENT AND THE FORTY-TWO STATIONS OF THE HEBREWS]

### CHAPTER I. Abstinence is more difficult in things that are despised.

[Col. 0545A]

You yourself recently confessed to me that you entirely restrain yourself from eating leeks or onions because you take particular pleasure in these pungent foods. In such despised things, therefore, abstinence is more difficult and glory is less.

For it is easier to abstain from meat than from salt; it is more difficult to reject the fruits of trees than the fragrant spices sprinkled into dishes. Although it was a fruit, not a spice, that expelled our parents from paradise (Genesis III), the fault does not lie in what is more costly to purchase, but in what can be desired more eagerly.

Yet abstinence from superior things is raised up by the applause of approval, whereas contempt for insignificant things does not seem worthy of praise. Consequently, what has less honor in public carries greater weight of glory in secret.

As the outstanding preacher says: “This momentary and light affliction of ours, he says, is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure” (II Corinthians IV).

Indeed, it seems to me that the servant of God whom we mentioned derives this from an infusion of the Holy Spirit: he always wishes to run from one Lent to the next through the various successive changes of abstinence, and never wishes to depart from the line established by this sacred number.

This is the number by which the heavens opened the cataclysm, when, after the filth of iniquities had been washed away, divine mercy renewed the face of the world (Genesis VII). Through the observance of this number Moses obtained the commandments of the law written by the finger of God (Exodus XXIV); through it Elijah also reached the mountain of God, Horeb, with unfailing agility of step (III Kings XIX) [Col. 0545C].

This number acquired far greater glory when the Lord himself fasted for forty days in the desert (Matthew IV) and afterward deigned to lie in the tomb for the same number of hours (Mark I). After the Resurrection, too, he lived with his disciples for forty days (Luke IV), until he ascended victoriously to the seat of his Father’s majesty (Acts I).

The brother, therefore, who is delightfully nourished by the mystery of this sacred number, so that he may always be carried within its boundary through the changes of salutary abstinence, is doubtless being advanced by the impulse of the divine Spirit. As he continually walks within the measure of the number forty, he testifies that he is hastening with the Israelites from Egypt toward his homeland.

For by this number the Israelite people entered the promised land (Numbers XIV; Deuteronomy XXIX; Joshua V). And O, how profound and marvelous is the height of the mystery! For by the same line of the sacrament through which God turned toward human beings, the human being returned to his Creator.

In the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt there are forty-two stations, and the coming of the Lord and Savior into the world is likewise introduced through forty-two generations, which the evangelist Matthew enumerates, saying: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matthew I).

By that same number, therefore, the Lord descended into the depths of this Egypt, while the people of Israel ascended to the promised land. He descended, I say, so that the other might ascend. He assumed the form of a servant (Philippians II), so that the other might go out free from the prison of servitude.

And Moses carefully wrote: “The children of Israel went up with their strength” (Exodus XIII). For what is the strength of the elect except Christ, who is the power of God? (I Corinthians I.) Whoever therefore ascends, ascends with the one who descended to us, not out of necessity but through condescension, so that there may be no doubt that what is said through the Apostle is true: “The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Ephesians IV) [Col. 0546B].

### CHAPTER II. Against those who understand sacred Scripture only literally.

Since, then, on the occasion of the brother mentioned above, we have entered into the subject of this discussion, we do not think it idle to linger over it a little longer. This is especially so because some people, ignorant of divine reasoning, complain that it is frivolous and superfluous for the description of these stations to be read in the Church.

They think that knowing or reading such things contributes absolutely nothing useful. They suppose that the historical account merely narrates something that happened, that it passed away with that ancient time, and that it has no relevance whatever to our present knowledge.

But if we carefully weigh the very words of Scripture, we find with the utmost clarity how extreme a madness it is to say this. The historical account says: “These are the stations of the children of Israel, from the time they went out from the land of Egypt with their strength, under the hand of Moses and Aaron”; and immediately it adds: “And Moses wrote down their departures at the command of the Lord” (Numbers XXXIII).

Have you heard that Moses wrote these things at the command of the Lord? Who would dare say this? Indeed, who would presume with reckless lips to chatter that what is written at the Lord’s command contributes no usefulness and offers no benefit of salvation?

Therefore, my brother, if it is not burdensome to you, I shall undertake to touch briefly and concisely upon the figures of those stations and to record in short words what I have been able to investigate from the statements of the Fathers, so that some complainant may infer from a taste of the crumbs that fall how abundantly the table of the full feast overflows with nectarous dishes.

It must be noted, however, that the whole of this account—whatever is read as having happened there historically—is fulfilled in us through the mystery of spiritual understanding. What was then done visibly corresponds to us through spiritual interpretation; that ancient age served our own time. For, as the Apostle says, “These things happened to them as a figure” (I Corinthians X).

We are leaving the furnace of Egyptian slavery and striving to enter the promised land through the many stations—that is, through the various advances of virtue. But since, with the sole exception of the tribe of Levi, the corpses of nearly all the Fathers were laid low in the desert, while only their children reached that land, it is fitting that our old self should perish and that the new self, created according to God (Ephesians IV), should grow strong to obtain the land of the living.

That the tribe of Levi did not perish in the desert with the others is clearly inferred from the fact that, after the number of all the Israelites from twenty years old and upward had been recorded by Moses, the following was immediately added: “The Levites were not numbered among the tribes of their families with them” (Numbers II).

For the Lord says to Moses: “Do not number the tribe of Levi, nor include their total among the children of Israel” (Numbers I). Later Scripture says: “This is the number of the children of Israel who were recorded by Moses and Eleazar the priest; among them there was no one of those who had previously been numbered by Moses and Aaron on Mount Sinai” (Numbers XXVI).

The Lord had foretold that all would die in the wilderness. These words of the historical account plainly show that, while the others were struck down in the desert, the tribe of Levi reached the promised land safe and unharmed.

Whoever, therefore, is able to establish himself in the order of priests or Levites; whoever does not wish to acquire with the rest of humanity a share in the land as an inherited portion, but is content to possess the Lord alone with the tribe of Levi—such a person certainly does not die in the desert of this world but is deemed worthy to enter the promised land alive and unharmed.

Whoever, therefore, desires to reach the promises made to the Fathers should disdain to possess, with the tribe of Levi, a cord of inheritance in the land. For the one who has cast himself down upon the earth for the sake of earthly things, who trusts that he will enjoy himself longer in the place where Passover must be celebrated with bitterness and passed through swiftly, saying, “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast,” deservedly hears: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”

Such a person is destroyed not by day but by night, like the firstborn of the Egyptians. Indeed, he did not despise Egypt but served the rulers of darkness, who themselves demand his soul by night, because he hated the light and did not attain the truth of righteousness.

But while we advance too freely toward external matters, almost forgetting the promise made at the outset, let us now return, so to speak, by a kind of restoration, to the stations of the Israelites, in which we promised that we would linger for a while.

### CHAPTER III. Christ’s descent to us took place through forty-two stages.

As has been said, the children of Israel reached, through forty-two stations, the beginning of the inheritance they were to take (Numbers XXXIII). The beginning of the inheritance was the place where Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh received the land of Gilead as their possession.

Just as they ascended through forty-two stations, so our Savior descended into the Egypt of this world through the same number of forefathers. If we now understand how much sacramental meaning this number contains—human ascent, namely, and divine descent—let us begin to ascend through the stages by which Christ descended and build for ourselves as our first station the one that he himself had as his last.

If someone comes to us by various places so that, when he returns, he may lead us back through the same places, then where he ends we begin our journey, and where he began we finish. Christ’s first generation began with Abraham, but the final one, like the last station, ended with the Virgin.

And because Abraham is interpreted as “exalted father,” we begin this journey from the Virgin’s childbirth, so that, traversing the successive stations that follow, we may finally reach God, the exalted Father.

The Virgin’s childbirth first meets those of us who wish to leave Egypt: believing that the Word of God, made flesh, has come into this world, we abandon all that is perishable and transitory, rest in him alone, and establish in him the dwelling-place of our rest and hope.

After this, if we strive to advance and ascend to each successive degree of faith and virtue, we ought to remain there until the virtues can be turned into habit. Then we are not judged to be merely passing through the deserts of spiritual life, but to be making a station or even dwelling in those advances of virtue.

For one who begins a good work without intending to persevere passes through the road as though hurrying along it; but one who remains in the holiness he once undertook builds a station there, so to speak.

It should also be noted that although going and remaining—and therefore journey and station—are entirely different from one another and do not correspond, Scripture nevertheless confirms that both occurred in that Israelite expedition: they are said to have had both a journey and stations through the desert.

For we who strive to enter the land of the living must both remain firm through the fixed purpose of our profession and always advance through the evidence of improving our way of life and accumulating progress.

The children of Israel therefore first set out from Ramesses. Ramesses, as some think, is called in our language “turbid agitation” or “the agitation of the moth.” This signifies that all worldly things are established amid agitations and disturbances and are shown to be subject to corruption, which the moth represents. The soul ought not to remain in them but should depart without hesitation.

Others have thought that Ramesses means “agitation” or “thunder.” This can appropriately be applied to us: when we have been stirred by the preaching of the evangelical trumpet, awakened as though by the thunder of heavenly clouds, we leave the Egypt of this world.

They departed in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the moon—at the full moon, that is, and at the beginning of spring. So too, when we are illumined by the rays of the highest light, when flowers of good will break forth in us, when everything is renewed, and when, finally, the meadows of our hearts grow warm through the fuel of the sun above, then we hasten to go out from the darkness of Egypt.

The second station is at Succoth. Succoth is interpreted as “tents.” The first progress of the soul, therefore, is to separate itself from earthly agitations and, recognizing itself as a pilgrim and resident alien, to establish not a permanent dwelling but a tent of exile, mourning with the Prophet: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Psalm CXIX.)

Then they come to Etham, or, as the interpreters of the Septuagint say, Buthan, which lies at the farthest boundaries of the wilderness. Etham signifies “strength.”

Those who now live as pilgrims for God in the world, who acknowledge themselves to be residents and exiles, must be stronger in humility and patience precisely in proportion as they show themselves weaker in earthly actions.

Buthan is interpreted as “valley,” which in no way departs from the same meaning. Whoever hastens toward the land of the living must remain in the valley of humility and patience to endure the darts of temptations.

From there they set out for Pi-hahiroth, which faces Baal-zephon, and encamped before Migdol. Pi-hahiroth is said to mean “mouth of nobles,” by which the tongue of teachers is signified.

When someone is established in the valley of patience and is struck all the more severely by the blows of persecutions or carnal temptations, it is all the more necessary that he be helped by the mouth of nobles—that is, by the exhortations of holy teachers [Col. 0549C].

But if the name should be given not as Pi-hahiroth but as Osiraath, as another edition attests, it must be understood that Iraath means “village.” Thus one comes to the mouth—that is, to the first entrance of this village—which signifies the beginning of a new way of life.

Hence they come not to a city but to a village, because every beginner must for a time restrain himself within the limits of a suburban way of life and must not rashly attempt the height of senatorial perfection.

Accordingly, it is well said that Arioth faces Beelsephon (Numbers XXXIII). Beelsephon is interpreted as “the ascent of a watchtower” or “of a tower.” For one ascends from small things to great.

This station was not at the watchtower itself but faced the watchtower. For every beginner, even if already striving by desire toward the contemplative life, has not yet reached the summit of contemplative perfection.

Therefore the passage appropriately adds: “And they encamped at Migdol” (ibid.). Migdol is said to mean “magnificence.” A person who has newly come to the service of God already holds before his mind, by intention, the ascent of the watchtower and magnificence, but does not yet possess them through the effect of virtue.

Although he is already nourished and sustained by the hope of contemplation and perfection, he does not yet enjoy the radiance of perfected purity or heavenly grace.

If Beelsephon is interpreted as “lord of the north,” as some say, what is signified by this lord of the north except the ancient enemy, who rules over hearts that are cold and alienated from the love of God? We encamp before him—that is, against him—when we fight against him in an unbreakable struggle.

From there they set out through the Red Sea and came to Marah, which is interpreted as “bitterness.” It is the proper order that those who hasten toward a land flowing with milk and honey should drink in the bitterness of labor and temptation in the wilderness of this life and reach the sweetness of inward reward through the harshness of present discipline.

Hence the Apostle says: “Every discipline, he says, does not at present seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews XII).

For those stationed in the expedition of spiritual warfare, bitter things are sometimes mingled with sweet and sweet things with bitter, so that the human condition may learn through them both what weakness it suffers from itself and what strength it ought to hope for from God.

Thus it is said to the same people: “I afflicted you and fed you with manna in the desert, which your fathers did not know, until it might be known what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy VIII).

### CHAPTER IV. The apostles are the leaders of the Christian people.

It follows that, having departed from Marah, they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. You see to what an abundance of sweet fruits and flowing waters they come after the bitterness of temptation [Col. 0550C]. Through the struggle of temptation they are led to palms, and through the scarcity of intolerable thirst they come to the well-watered abundance of living waters.

For almighty God, the physician of souls, so orders all things that, as though spices were mixed with honey, he mingles glad things with sad and sad things with glad, so that a weak mind, sometimes struck, may never become proud in prosperity, and, sometimes refreshed, may not succumb in adversity. Moreover, Elim is interpreted as “rams,” which are indeed the leaders of the flocks that follow. And who are the leaders of the rational flock—that is, of the Christian people—except the holy apostles? These, indeed, are the twelve springs watering the dryness of minds with the streams of heavenly teaching.

But because our Savior chose not those twelve apostles alone, but also appointed another seventy, there are described there not only twelve springs but also seventy palm trees. For they too are called apostles, as is recognized from the words of blessed Paul. For, when he was speaking of the Savior’s Resurrection, he said: “He was seen by Cephas, and after this by the eleven; then he appeared to all the apostles” (I Corinthians XV) [Col. 0550D]. From these words it is plainly inferred that, besides those twelve, other disciples also are not improperly called apostles.

But after leaving Elim, they pitched their tents beside the Red Sea. Note that they do not enter the sea again, but pitch their tent beside the sea, so that they may see the sea and the heaps of its waves only from afar, but in no way fear its motions and assaults. We too, after the waves of temptations and the dreadful shipwrecks of the sounding sea, often set before our eyes the very evils we have endured, so that, now standing as it were on the shore, we may give worthy thanks to God our deliverer [Col. 0551A].

Having departed also from the Red Sea, they arrived in the desert of Sin. Sin is interpreted as “thornbush” or “temptation.” Thus the hope of prosperity begins to dawn upon Christ’s soldier, and words of divine conversation are promised. For from the Bush the Lord appeared and commanded Moses to carry his instructions to the children of Israel (Exod. II). There, therefore, you are given a sign of the mercy to be hoped for, where the beginning of Israel’s visitation took place.

But Sin is not without reason also called “temptation.” Temptation often intervenes even in visions, since sometimes the spirit of wickedness transforms itself into an angel of light (II Cor. VI). Therefore one must act cautiously, so that the kinds of visions may be distinguished. Thus, when Jesus son of Nave saw an angel, and did not at all doubt that temptations could sometimes be present in such visions, he immediately asked the one who appeared, saying: “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” (Josh. V). For through the Apostle, the discernment of spirits is also numbered among the gifts of the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII). Moreover, since Sin is said to be interpreted as “hatred,” this too does not depart from spiritual understanding. Whoever reaches a vision or conversation with God immediately conceives hatred of the world.

## CHAPTER V. That the illnesses of the soul are vices, but the death of the soul consists in grave sins.

[Col. 0551C]

Having advanced from there, they came to Depthca—or, as another translation reports, Raphaca (Exod. III). Depthca, finally, is said to mean “a knocking.” And after we have reached the Church, which that Bush signifies—where a person is deemed worthy of God’s conversation, where the vision of angels is seen—we then begin to ask, seek, and knock at the secrets of the heavenly kingdom, in accordance with the Lord’s command and promise: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. VII; Luke XI).

But if someone prefers to accept Raphaca, which means “health,” this name is suitably applied to the soul that was formerly sick but has now, through the gift of the holy Church, been freed from the bonds of sickness. For this is the soul to which it is said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Ps. CII). Which Lord, I ask? “The one,” he says, “who heals all your illnesses, who redeems your life from destruction.” The illnesses of the soul are, of course, vices; the death of the soul consists in grave sins. “For when sin has been completed, it gives birth to death” (James I).

Then they come to Halus. Halus is interpreted as “labors” or “leaven.” Certainly, labors follow health, because the holy soul ought to desire health for no other reason than that it may be able to endure labors and afflictions for God. This is why Peter’s mother-in-law recovered from her fever: so that she might minister to the Lord through assiduous service (Matt. II; Mark XII). This is why Paul was healed through Ananias (Acts IX), so that afterward he might toil through continual labors. Hence it was said to that same Ananias concerning him: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Matt. XIII).

But since Halus is also said to mean “leaven,” an interpretation of fitting significance is offered to us here. For this is that leaven which the woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Luke XIII), that is, the holy Gospel. In this desert the people murmured, and received both manna and quail. And since not only leaven but also manna signifies the sacred Gospel, these two wonderfully coincide at the tenth station, so that after the Decalogue of the law has been set forth, the bread of the Gospel may appear to follow.

[Col. 0552B]

After this they come to Raphidin. Raphidin is interpreted as “the praise of judgment.” And certainly it is very fitting that labor should precede praise, and that praise should arise after labor. Yet this is not praise of just anything, but “the praise of judgment” [which is added]—that is, praise proceeding from the judgment of reason, not praise arising from the vanity of pride. “For the spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

Other interpretations of these names are also found. But if we embraced everything they suggest to us in this subject, the concise order of a letter would no longer be preserved; instead, the book would swell into burdensome immensity. Therefore we pass briefly over the stations of the Israelites, not to search out their inner chambers of mystery, but simply to display, as it were, the outer surfaces of their walls in their names.

Then they come to the desert of Sinai. Sin, which we mentioned above, and Sinai are undoubtedly one desert; but Sin is said to be the plain itself. Sinai, however, is a mountain rising above that same wilderness, on which the Lord promulgates the ordinances of the law and Moses constructs the tabernacle (Exod. XXIV). This is most appropriately fitting: after the rational soul has begun to possess right—and therefore praiseworthy—judgment, it then constructs within itself a tabernacle for its God and, now worthy of conversation with its Creator, receives the heavenly mysteries of his commandments.

After this they set out for the graves of concupiscence, where a beautiful order is woven together. For when the blessed soul has become a tabernacle for its Creator, and, intent upon the commands of divine law, has begun to contemplate heavenly things, the heat of its seething vices is immediately extinguished and every desire of carnal enticement is buried, so that the flesh no longer moves against the spirit, nor the spirit desires against the flesh (Gal. V).

From there they pass into Aseroth, which is interpreted as “perfect courts” or “blessedness.” O how beautiful the order of the mystery, how lovely the sequence of spiritual growth: after you have buried the desires of the flesh, you immediately arrive at the court of perfection and the reward of blessedness. Blessed is the soul that is no longer oppressed by any vices of the flesh, because it immediately enters into the blessedness of receiving its recompense.

After this they came to Rethma, or Pharam. Rethma, as we think, is interpreted as “completed vision”; Pharam, however, as “visible mouth.” What else is understood in these names except that every holy soul, after the desires of the flesh have been buried, and after it has been brought to the court of perfection, should, secure in the reward of blessedness, soon come to the completed vision of God and behold his visible mouth—that is, God’s present appearance?

For now, as the Apostle says, we see him in a mirror and in an enigma; but then face to face (I Cor. XIII). “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.” Yet because all these things cannot be possessed fully in reality by any of the saints while they remain established in the flesh, they already possess them in hope—the hope, of course, that they hold most firmly, because they possess the Holy Spirit as a pledge, the Spirit who strengthens them in the labors of this journey.

Hence the interpretation according to which Rethma is said to mean “sound” or “juniper” is not judged inappropriate. For they report that this wood preserves fire within itself for a long time (Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 25), so that if its embers are covered with ashes, they remain glowing until the following year. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit, as we read, possesses knowledge of speech (Wis. I), and was sent upon the apostles in the form of fire (Acts II), this interpretation—by which Rethma is called “sound” or “juniper”—seems most suitably to apply to the Holy Spirit.

From there they departed and encamped at Remon Phares, which among us is called “lofty division.” For when the understanding of the soul returning to God increases, it is immediately given perfect knowledge, by which it knows, loftily and sublimely, how to divide earthly things from heavenly things and to separate all that is perishable and transitory from what is everlasting.

But if Remon Phares, as it is found elsewhere, is said to mean “the division of the pomegranate,” this undoubtedly signifies the holy Church, which, like many seeds enclosed within a single rind, gathers the whole multitude of believers into the inseparable unity of the catholic faith.

Then they cross into Lebna, which is interpreted as “whitening.” We are not unaware that whitening is sometimes used of a crime, as when tombs and walls are called whitened (Matt. XXIII; Acts XXIII). But here that whitening should be understood of which Isaiah says: “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow; and though they be red like crimson, they shall become white like wool” (Isa. I). And in the Psalm: “They shall be whitened in Selmon” (Ps. LXVII). And in the Apocalypse, the hairs of Jesus are described as resembling white wool (Apoc. I).

Therefore here “whitening” is appropriately understood as proceeding from the splendor of the true light and descending from the clarity of the highest vision. But if Lebna, as some say, is rendered “brick”—the material in which the Israelite people were compelled to labor in Egypt—this signifies that just as they, after such lofty places, return again to brickmaking, so we, for as long as we wander in the desert of this world, are sometimes compelled by necessity to descend from the heights to the depths and to pass from spiritual things to the works of earthly action.

After this they come to Ressa, which is rendered “bridles,” and not inappropriately. For if, after the summit of perfection, we descend to muddy works, we must be bridled by the bonds of discipline and the reins of repentance, lest we rush headlong through precipices, but quickly return to the purity of our customary cleanliness.

Ressa is also interpreted as “visible” or “praiseworthy temptation.” Although the mind of every just man may already be advancing toward the heights, it is nevertheless still brought down into the depths by temptation, lest it be lifted up by pride because of its virtues. For the stimulus of temptation is applied to guard humility. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given me a stimulus of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Cor. XII). This temptation is therefore visible because it is manifest, and praiseworthy because it is salutary.

## CHAPTER VI. That in temptation the flesh must be subjected to the spirit.

[Col. 0554B]

From there they advance to Ceelatha, which is interpreted as “church,” so that all who are unstable and drive themselves headlong through the precipices of vice may be recalled to the Church by the bridles of sacred Scripture. Or, according to another edition, it is Machebat, which means “the rule of the rod.” Both expressions appear to indicate authority. For it is necessary that the spirit presiding over the tempted flesh should rule it. When the flesh abandons the struggle, the spirit, as though from above, should threaten it with the rod, applying the discipline of rigid fear.

From there they come to Mount Sepher, or Sephar, which is called “trumpeting.” The trumpet is a sign of war. For the horse of God scents battle, and when it hears the trumpet it says, “Ha!” (Job XXXIX). So Christ’s soldier, when he feels himself surrounded by the assault of advancing vices, immediately takes up the weapons of the virtues, proceeds to battle, and engages the enemy at close quarters, lest, released into ignoble torpor, he be easily destroyed by his adversaries. Then he will be able to sound the trumpet more gloriously—that is, to call others also to spiritual combat.

Hence it is said that from there they departed and came to Harada, or, as it is said elsewhere, to Charadath, which in our language means “made capable.” Thus, having now himself become a preacher, he may deservedly say with the Apostle: “Who made us capable ministers of the new covenant” (II Cor. III).

Departing from there, they come to Maceloth, which is interpreted as “from the beginning.” Whoever strives toward the summit of perfection contemplates the beginning of all things, while turning all the desires of his inward being toward God. And while he continually directs his heart toward its Author, he does not depart from the beginning of all things.

Or, if Maceloth, as some think, is said to mean “assembly,” the Church is understood by it, since all the faithful assemble there. Hence it is sung: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

Then they come to Tharath, or, as it is read elsewhere, to Caath, which means “patience” or “confirmation.” Whoever desires to enter the land of the living through the labors of the present life must be strengthened by patience to endure the dangers of the world. Or if Thahath, as some say, is rendered “dread,” let it be said to each person who is striving—or who perhaps has already triumphed through divine grace: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI).

From there they depart and come to Thare, which in Greek is interpreted as “ecstasy” (*ecstasis*), and in our language is called “contemplation.” It follows that whoever has previously been tested through patience should then reach the grace of contemplation; and whoever was formerly pressed down in tribulation should afterward be lifted up to the joy of inward vision.
