But if Thare, as some think, should be understood as “cunning” or “malice,” this may not improperly be referred to the overseers of the Churches, so that they themselves may fear for their hearers who labor amid the tribulation of temptations. For the cunning and malice of the one of whom it is said must be guarded against: “Because our adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V).

Then they proceed to Methca, or, as it is read elsewhere, Maathica, which is interpreted as “new death.” The devil’s cunning is never guarded against so perfectly as when we die with Christ, so that we may be rendered, as it were, insensible to the temptations of the crafty enemy. Contemplation produces this new death: it makes both the world dead to us and us dead to the world.

But if Methca, as some prefer, is rendered “sweetness,” what wonder is it if one comes from contemplation to sweetness, since contemplation itself is nothing other than ineffable and boundless sweetness?

After this they come to Hesmona, which is called “haste.” For after we have reached the sweetness of contemplation, we cannot endure delay or slowness. O how painfully that man endured delay who said: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend, and that the mountains would melt before your face” (Isa. LXIV). How grievously did the man endure this delay who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I)—and much more truly and entirely.

But if it is said to derive from Senna, which signifies “bones,” this pertains to strength of steadfastness. The lover of Christ must possess this, lest excessive love make him impatient.

From here they pass into Mosoroth, which is thought to signify “excluding.” For the soul that has reached perfect love of its bridegroom excludes from itself the temptations of the cunning corrupter. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. IV).

But if Moseroth, according to some, is interpreted as “bonds,” a sound and entirely fitting understanding shines forth. Every holy soul that is joined in love to its heavenly bridegroom must necessarily be inseparably connected to him by continual meditation on the Scriptures, as by certain bonds. Concerning these bonds it is said to Christ through Isaiah: “The lofty men shall pass over to you, and they shall be yours, and they shall walk after you, bound with bonds” (Isa. XLV).

Hence they come, not without reason, to Banaeim, which signifies “fountains” or “cultivations”—that is, the place where the soul drinks from the fountains of divine Scripture and cultivates them, meaning that it examines and ruminates upon them subtly. It cultivates them, I say, while keeping the Gospel command that not even one jot or one tittle of the law should pass away until all things have come to pass (Matt. V).

But if Beneiaacan, as some say, is translated as “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing,” this signifies that whoever has been instructed and abundantly equipped by the divine utterances must afterward draw others along with him and beget sons. When he threateningly sets before them weeping and the gnashing of teeth, he imposes upon them, in a certain sense, the necessity of turning to God. These, then, are the sons of necessity or of gnashing, of whom it is also sung prophetically: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII).

## CHAPTER VII. Why temptation is mingled with virtue.

[Col. 0556B]

After this they ascend Mount Gadgad, which is interpreted as “messenger,” “girding,” or indeed “cutting.” To those to whom we announce the words of God, we must undoubtedly admonish them both to gird themselves with the weapons of the virtues and to cut down the backs of invisible enemies with spiritual swords. While we diligently teach them to do this, we ascend with them into the mountains.

But if Gadgad, as some think, signifies “temptations,” it is understood that temptations cannot be absent from those who are striving toward the heavenly homeland. Often temptation is mingled with virtues so that a richer reward may be acquired by Christ’s laboring soldier.

And because one passes through the evils of temptations to the good things of rewards, it suitably follows that, departing from there, they came to Jetebatha—or, as it is read elsewhere, Jatbatha—which is interpreted as “goodness” or “the good.” Thus, through the trials of temptations one reaches goodness, which is undoubtedly Christ.

From there they departed for Ebrona, which is called “passage.” Everything must be passed through by the mind, and you must fix the gaze of your mind upon him alone with whom you can remain without passing on.

After this they come to Asiongaber, which is interpreted as “the counsels of a man.” For after we have cast ourselves wholly upon Christ, after we have placed all the trust of our heart in him, we must no longer be childish in our understanding, imitating the Apostle who says: “But when I became a man, I put away childish things” (I Cor. XIII). And again: “Do not become children in understanding” (I Cor. XIV).

But because “whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow,” they come again to the desert of Sin, which is Cades. We have already said above that Sin is interpreted as “temptation.” Just as a gold or silver vessel is often struck by a hammer and often surrounded on every side by a file as it is polished, so that it may become brighter (Eccl. X), so repeated temptation cleanses the rust from a steadfast soul that does not yield. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessel, and temptation tests righteous people” (Eccli. XXVII). And because Cades is called “holy fruitfulness,” you see that holy fruitfulness follows the furrows of temptations.

From there also they arrived at Mount Hor, at the extreme borders of Edom. Hor is interpreted as “mountainous.” Whoever, when tested, does not fall but bears fruit through temptation will necessarily ascend as a victor to the mountain that is Christ. For this is that mountain, curdled and fat, of which the Psalm says: “A mountain of God is a fat mountain” (Ps. LXVII), and of which the prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isa. II). This mountain is called “mountainous,” because where Christ is, there undoubtedly also is the Christian. “Where I am,” he says, “there also my servant shall be” (John XII).

Then they come to Salmona, which is interpreted as “the shadow of a portion.” And rightly so: after we have ascended the mountain that is Christ, fleeing the heat of vices, we remain beneath the shelter of his protection. Concerning this shadow Jeremiah says: “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins; of him we said: In your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. IV). And the angel says to Mary: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke I).

Salmona is also called “a little image” in some sources. This certainly fits that place without absurdity, since there the bronze serpent was hung (Num. XXI; John III), representing the image of the crucified Savior.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the passage into Phinon is through restraint of the mouth.

Moreover, they pass into Phinon, which is interpreted as “mouth” or “restraint of the mouth.” It is called “mouth” because as soon as we understand the mysteries of Christ’s passion, we proclaim with our mouth what we believe in our heart, as it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV). And the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

It is called “restraint of the mouth” because, since we cannot penetrate such profound mysteries of human redemption, we place, as it were, a finger upon our mouth, leaving the height of Christ’s divinity to those greater than ourselves and treating only his cross. As the Apostle says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. VIII).

After this they set out for Oboth, which is rendered “magicians” or “python-spirits.” This makes it understood that, after the image of God conceived in the reasoning of the heart, and after the faith received and expressed through confession of the mouth, heretics rise up against us, proclaiming the error of poisoned unbelief, like python-spirits and magicians scattering the wicked songs of their incantations.

From there they pass into Gebarim, which lies in the territory of the Moabites. Gebarim signifies “heaps of stones of those who pass over.” These, however, are living stones—the saints—from whom not only the heavenly Jerusalem is built, but the present Church also is adorned like a display of glittering pearls. They are rightly called “passing,” because in their minds they trample upon all earthly and transitory things and hasten to pass over to heavenly things.

But if it is called not Gebarim but Gai, as another edition attests, this likewise does not depart from the meaning of “those who pass over.” For Gai is interpreted as “chaos.” Abraham says to the rich man: “Between us and you a great chaos has been fixed” (Luke XVI). The saints therefore always desire to pass over to him, so that, like blessed Lazarus, they may happily rest in his bosom.

Hence it follows quite appropriately that after the chaos of python-spirits and magicians—that is, the dark cunning of heretics—they immediately come to Dibongad, which is said to signify “the bee-hive of temptations.” Bees carry honey in their mouths but sting with their barbs; so heretics openly present pleasant words, but conceal behind them the stings of error. At first they distill sweetness from their mouths, but afterward scatter the error of barbed falsehood. Hence the Prophet laments, saying: “They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns” (Ps. CXVII).

From there they departed for Helmondeblathaim, which is rendered “contempt of palates”—that is, of figs—or “contempt of reproach.” The fig is a delightful fruit; by this it is understood that those who are now drawing near to heavenly gifts must despise every enticement of carnal pleasure.

But if “contempt of reproach” is preferred, we are undoubtedly instructed by this that, whenever we are dishonored by the insults of heretics or of any reprobate persons, we should not be disturbed. Through both interpretations we are profitably taught neither to be moved by the mockery of dishonorable contempt nor to be weakened by any pleasures of earthly sweetness, so that we may be able to say of this world with the Prophet: “As is its darkness, so also is its light” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

From there they migrate to the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nabo. Abarim is interpreted as “passage”; Nabo as “departure.” This signifies that when the soul has advanced through all the stations of the journey and through every virtue, because it has now ascended to the summit of perfection, it immediately passes in mind from this age and departs.

Even if it still appears to remain in the world, it has already withdrawn from the world in the flesh, though it does not walk according to the flesh (II Cor. X). As it is said of Enoch: “He was not found, because God transferred him” (Gen. V). So whoever, perfect in holiness and already dead to the world, passes through the world dwells in the region of the virtues.

The final station is in the plains of Moab, above the Jordan, opposite Jericho. For the passage through so long a journey is undertaken for this purpose; for this purpose one sighs amid so many hardships and labors through the vast solitude of this world: that we may arrive at the Jordan—that is, draw near to the inexhaustible fullness of heavenly wisdom.

Building the tabernacle of our pilgrimage beside it, let us hasten to wash ourselves in its streams from all the squalor of Egypt, so that, purified, we may be able to enter the promised land and be as the bride is described in the Song of Songs: “Her eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside the fullest streams” (Song V).

It should also be noted that this journey ends not in the mountains but in the plains, because the loftier the perfection with which the saints are endowed, the more deeply they are founded in humility. They also build their stations opposite Jericho, because they wage irreconcilable war against the world, which is signified by Jericho. To them it is said: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

## CHAPTER IX. Epilogue and conclusion of the little work.

I have therefore passed over for you, venerable brother, the stations of the Israelites in summary and haste. I reserve the deeper mysteries for your leisure, which is more ample. I have supplied an occasion for inquiry and understanding, but not the capacity for complete understanding. I have merely opened, as it were, the doors of those stations; it is for your wisdom to enter them and examine their mysteries like hidden treasures of heavenly wealth.

For myself, let it be enough to have achieved this much: that no foolish person, ignorant of what he says or of what he asserts, should continue to chatter that these things offer no benefit; rather, let him not doubt that everything abounds in the mystical sacraments of spiritual allegories.

Thus, after we have pitched the camps of so many stations and endured the hardships of so long a journey, with Aaron and Moses already dead—that is, with the old priesthood and law set aside—we have entered the land of the evangelical promise under the leadership of Joshua. I mean a land flowing with milk and honey, overflowing with the mysteries of Christ’s humanity and divinity.

Now nothing else remains for us except to build a temple for the Lord in the Jerusalem of our heart, made conspicuous by the beauty of the virtues, like gold, silver, and every variety of precious stone. In the vestibule of this temple, following Solomon’s example, let us raise two columns, one on each side, and place chains upon the capitals of those same columns. For Scripture testifies: “He set up one column on the right and another on the left.” Immediately afterward it says: “He called the one on the right Jachin,” that is, “firmness”; “and the one on the left Booz” (II Chron. III), that is, “in strength.”

For what should be understood by the column on the right, which is called “firmness,” except the love of God? And what by the one on the left, which is called “in strength,” except love of neighbor? “Firmness,” that is, strength itself, is one thing; “in strength” is another, because loving God himself is one thing, while loving one’s neighbor in God is another.

A measure is established in love of neighbor; but we are commanded to love God without any measure whatsoever. Therefore, in the vestibule of the temple we raise the column called “firmness” when, in the present Church—which is the vestibule of that heavenly Church—we love God firmly and steadfastly with all our strength. For love itself, as John the Evangelist testifies, is God (I John IV). And concerning God the Prophet sings: “You are my God and my strength” (Ps. XLII).

We set up the column called “in strength” on the left side of that same vestibule when we love our neighbor in God as ourselves. Here it should be noted that Scripture continues: “And he made, as it were, chains in the inner sanctuary and placed them upon the capitals of the columns” (II Chron. III). In the inner sanctuary of our mind we place chains upon the capitals of the columns, by which we connect the two columns to each other, because we neither love God without our neighbor nor truly love our neighbor without God.

You, venerable brother, can most excellently build this temple, with God lending his hand to you—you who have borrowed from the Egyptians golden and silver vessels together with precious garments (Exod. XI). For the one who reads poets and philosophers, by whom he is strengthened more subtly for penetrating the mysteries of heavenly speech, takes treasure from the Egyptians with which to build a tabernacle for God.

May he himself deign to build this tabernacle in our mind who was able to restore the temple of his body, once destroyed, within the space of three days.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0559]

## 573–574. THE THIRTY-THIRD LITTLE WORK: ON THE GOOD OF SUFFRAGES AND VARIOUS MIRACLES, ESPECIALLY THOSE OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN.

### ARGUMENT.

Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, had threatened Blessed Peter Damian through an intermediary that, unless he came as soon as possible to visit his monastery, he would not receive the benefit of the prayers of the monks of Cassino if he died while Desiderius was still alive. Moved by this threat, he writes to the same man in the present letter, asking him to withdraw it; he pleads the difficulty of the journey and exaggerates the seriousness of the punishment with which he had threatened him. Finally, after praising highly the virtue of obedience, he makes it sufficiently clear that he will comply with him.

[Col. 0559D]

To Desiderius, archangel of the monks, Peter, a sinful monk, offers service.

I cannot allow you to remain unaware, venerable Father, that Guidunculus—that is, our little boy—drove a sharp thorn of grief into my innermost being when he reported to me, in due order, what you had threatened me with. He reported that you had said that unless I visited the monastery of Cassino, which you rule with such distinction, I would not have the prayers of that holy place if I died while you were still alive.

Whenever I call these threats back to mind, they do not prick us like a needle; rather, like a stake or a pointed weapon, they pierce our innermost being. For I am hemmed in on every side by the obstacles of a double necessity. On the one hand, my advanced age makes me suspect that death is near; on the other, to be deprived of the prayers of so many saints is no slight danger.

As I contemplate coming, I am inwardly terrified lest, while seeking the monastery, I die outside the monastery. Although death is uncertain for others, it is undoubtedly near for the aged. For an age that is not succeeded by another threatens the end of life with its nearness.

Yet I am equally afraid not to come, lest, if I remain inseparably attached to the brothers among whom I live, I lose the richer and incomparably greater assistance of the assembly [“of a more holy kind,” or something similar, *f.*]. Thus, placed at the center of both dangers, I cannot clearly discern what I ought rather to do, since whichever of the two I choose, I cannot escape the snare of ambiguous suspicion.

[ON THE GOOD OF INTERCESSIONS AND VARIOUS MIRACLES.]

## CHAPTER I. That dreams should not be believed.

Here one is reminded of what Gellius says: Alexander dreamed that dreams should not be believed. Whatever Alexander may choose, the dispute is brought to this conclusion: the dream he saw should not be believed. For if dreams are rightly believed, that dream which asserts that it should not be believed is lying. But if dreams should by no means be believed, it follows likewise that no faith should be placed in that dream.

Something similar is also found in sacred speech, where it is said: “I said in the excess of my mind, Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV). One may answer it: If everyone is a liar, then you are too; and the statement you, a liar, have uttered will already be false. But if you yourself are not a liar, the statement will no longer be true, because if you are truthful, it is recognized that not every human being is a liar.

Yet lest sacred Scripture also be exposed to accusation in the manner of pagan writings, let it rather defend itself by its own authority. It should be noted that the phrase “I said in the excess of my mind” comes first. Through the excess of his mind, therefore, he passed beyond himself when he made his pronouncement concerning the condition of humanity. It is as though he clearly said: “I uttered a true statement about the falsehood of all human beings from the place where I myself was above humanity.”

He was a liar to the extent that he was human; but he was not a liar at all to the extent that, through the excess of his mind, he ascended above humanity to contemplate the highest things.

But since almost fifteen days’ journey separates us, it would have been fitting for you to experience first what you command an old man to do—you who are strong in age and exceedingly powerful in bodily strength. Add to this that you abound in vehicles and in the services of attendants pressing closely around you.

Phalaris is also said to have offered an example of this law. Although he had turned kingship into tyranny and cruelly mangled every kind of criminal with elaborate punishments, a certain craftsman offered him a bronze bull and constructed it so that condemned people could be thrown into it while it was glowing with fire.

The craftsman believed that Phalaris would especially enjoy cruelty, since he knew him to be always eager to inflict punishments and to be the author of inhuman brutality. In particular, whenever someone cast into the beast uttered cries, the bull seemed in some way to bellow through its nostrils and mouth.

But Phalaris repaid his generous benefactor with the reward he deserved. “Friend,” he said, “I thank you for the gift you have bestowed; but I command you, by my wish and irrevocably, to experience first what you have taught me.” At once the craftsman was thrown into the bull and was himself the first to experience what he had taught should be inflicted on others. He became the author of the punishment, though he had previously been the maker of the instrument of the punitive labyrinth.

So you too should do what you command, and, as a young man, hurry to an old man whom you invite to walk to you.

Nevertheless, I shall now speak seriously: if it were possible for me, after traveling so long a road, to reach the threshold of our blessed Father Benedict, I would count it a reward of no small magnitude. And I firmly believe that if I should happen to die on that pilgrimage, the ruin caused by my own guilt would not weigh upon me so heavily as the dignity of its merits would raise me up.

## CHAPTER II. A wondrous example concerning Bassus of Anici.

This hope of mine is further strengthened by what a religious and prudent man, Stephen, cardinal priest of the Apostolic See, told me about five days ago. For he said that a certain Bassus, a Burgundian by birth, of the diocese of Anicium, devoutly visited the church dedicated under the distinguished title of the Mother of God and ever-virgin, which is called “at the Podium,” for the sake of prayer. After completing his prayers and fulfilling his devotion, he began to return to his own place.

When he had come to a certain village in which a cell belonging to some monastery—whose name escapes me—was inhabited by religious brothers, he was seized by illness, fell, became sick, and died. Then, after the corpse had been washed and wrapped according to custom in linen, it lay lifeless in the midst, while the pious watch of the faithful kept vigil around the bier. When much of the untimely night had passed and dawn was approaching, the man who lay dead suddenly sprang up, and amazement and intolerable terror seized all those standing around him.

Then, crying out in a loud voice, trembling, and dreadfully frightened, he began to beg those present [Col. 0562D] to persist vigorously in psalmody and pious prayers, so that by their holy prayers they might drive away the loathsome spirits of wickedness, who seemed to be visible everywhere in the corners and along the walls of the house. When the demons, after prayers had been poured out to God, vanished like smoke scattered by the wind, he laid aside his terror and, emboldened by the courage of renewed security, publicly recounted before everyone what had happened to him in secret.

“Upon leaving my body,” he said, “two angels of radiant splendor immediately met me, and they began to lead me with them toward the heights. But behold, blackened demonic troops, like battalions of Ethiopians, surround me on every side; they demand me back as their own man with an exceedingly harsh and importunate insistence. ‘This man is ours,’ they say. ‘He lived under our dominion and did not fail to obey our laws. For the law of the flesh was always dominant in him; but the law of the spirit he utterly ignored.’

“But the blessed angels replied: ‘We do not deny that he was yours [*vestrum*, added in the margin], while he lived in his own way. It is not permissible to resist the truth. But since he has died in the service of the heavenly Queen, our Lady, he shall in no way be subjected to your impiety on account of the sins of his life, since he brought his life to an end with a pious conclusion. Nor can he perish from the sight of the eternal Judge, since he secured for himself the aid of His Mother.’

“To this they replied: ‘Since God is without doubt a just judge, He will never take away what belongs to us, nor will He act prejudicially against us, since He utterly ignores injustice.’

“When they attempted to use force against the angels, while the angels, now more gently and calmly resisting because they knew the truth, nevertheless declared that help would immediately come to them and threatened the swift arrival of the Mother of God, behold—a sudden flash like fiery lightning, a radiance of shining brilliance, illuminated the scene. While all marveled, the Queen of heaven arrived, reverently surrounded by angelic attendants.

“Then the condemned spirits, although they were terrified at the first arrival of such glory and their eyes were dazzled by its excessive brilliance, nevertheless complained of the wrong done to them and protested that their property had been taken away by angelic violence, saying: ‘If God is just, He will never take the impious man from our hands.’

“To them the Blessed Virgin replied: ‘Although this man, as you assert, was yours by the depravity of his conduct and lived impiously, or carnally, nevertheless my most merciful and compassionate Son and Lord will never allow him to become subject to your cruelties, since He sees that he died while serving me on his pilgrimage. Especially since this man had confessed his sins to priests and had received judgment through repentance and lamentation, although, overtaken by sudden death, he was unable to complete it.’

“At this they rejoiced as though they had found an opportunity for victory, and, as if taunting her, objected: ‘Since you are the mother of truth and of eternal justice, can you be unaware that he committed this monstrous and bloody crime, which nevertheless was never made known to anyone through a spoken confession?’ By this they were calling out, in name only, a grave crime which I had committed.

“Although the Blessed Virgin truthfully recognized the sin from those who were the authors of the lie, she modestly kept silent for a little while, as though paying reverence to the truth. But then, restoring her speech, she said:

“‘What you allege is indeed true. But because, with my merciful Lord and Son, mercy habitually exalts itself above judgment (James 2), and because He takes less delight in the punishment of sinners than in the remission of sins, He immediately looked upon me and said: “Return at once to the body, man. Confess this crime, which the wicked have rightly brought against you, to the priest in the presence of the monks of this neighboring cell. By the command of my authority, ask them to undertake the measure of penance imposed upon you and to strive to fulfill it for your absolution when you are about to die. When this has been done, return to me immediately, without delay. For I shall not cease waiting here for you until you return.”’

“When he had recounted these events in order, the holy brothers undertook the penance imposed upon him, both out of charity for him and in obedience to the divine Virgin. Soon afterward, joyful and cheerful, he died as though falling asleep. Thus, by dying, he proved the truth of what he had said while alive.

“If I should die while hastening toward you as a traveler on a blessed journey, I trust that the protection of Saint Benedict will in no way fail me.”

### CHAPTER III. The Blessed Virgin commands that a prebend taken from a cleric devoted to her be restored.

Stephen also related another matter to me, though he did not regard it as equally certain with the one recounted above. “I remember hearing,” he said, “that a certain cleric was foolish, worthless, frivolous, and incompetent. Moreover, he seemed to possess no quality of religious character, no seriousness or modesty of canonical discipline. Yet among the ashes of this useless life, already dead and extinguished, there remained in him a tiny spark of a very small fire: every day he approached the most sacred altar of the Blessed Mother of God and, reverently bowing his head, sang this angelic and evangelical verse:

“‘Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women’ (Luke 1).”

When a new bishop had noticed such an extent of foolish incompetence, he considered it unworthy that the usefulness of the Church should be held by a useless person, and he took away from him the prebend that he had received from his recently deceased predecessor. But when poverty in his household oppressed the cleric, and he had nothing else by which he could live, the pious Mother of God appeared to the bishop during the night as he slept. A man preceded her, carrying a burning torch in one hand and a rod in the other.

The Blessed Virgin immediately ordered him to chastise the offending bishop with several blows of the rod he carried. “Why,” she said, “have you taken away from my chaplain, who kept daily vigils for me, the Church’s provision, which you yourself had not bestowed?”

The priest soon awoke in terror, restored the cleric’s prebend, and honored more generously as one dear to God the man whom he had perhaps thought unknown to God.

If, then, that man earned the food by which his body lived merely by singing one little verse of praise, how faithfully will those hope for eternal things who offer daily prayers at every hour to the blessed Queen of the world?

Hence a beautiful custom has also arisen in certain churches: every Saturday, Masses are celebrated specially in her honor, unless a feast or a Lenten weekday prevents it. We too, in the hermitages or monasteries whose ministers we are for the glory of Christ, have assigned three days in each week to the saints, and on those days we celebrate Masses specially in their honor.

And lest we seem to undertake this merely according to our own inclination, but rather at the prompting of reason [*“know, or something similar,” added in the margin], know that, according to the pious opinions and judgments of illustrious men, the souls of the dead rest and are released from punishments on Sundays; but on Monday they return to the prisons of punishment to which they have been assigned. For this reason, the honor of Masses is offered especially on that day to the angels, so that their protective defense may be obtained both for the dead and for those who are dying.

Friday, moreover, is appropriately assigned to the life-giving cross, since that day was reddened by the glorious blood of the Lord hanging upon the cross. On that day all our brothers, whom the monastic order binds together, add this also to the increase of their own salvation: they scourge themselves in the chapterhouse in place of one another, and, in addition, celebrate a fast on bread and water. They assert that in this way we truly share in the cross and undoubtedly die with Christ, if on the very day on which He suffered we too mortify our flesh through the sufferings of the cross.

They also add that, since through the long course of approximately five thousand years the whole human race had been pressed down under the iron yoke of the devil, and on this particular day had been triumphantly freed by the distinguished standard of the cross, it is entirely fitting that on this day—which broke the chain binding all ages—our flesh should pay, as it were, the assessment of a tribute, through which it rejoices, freed from the fetters of its captivity.

They further say that, when the eternal Judge shines forth on the day of the dreadful examination, surrounded everywhere by angelic attendants, and when all the elements are shaken by terror at such majesty, the blessed cross will be carried forward by the angels, held ready in their arms, and will be set before the faces of all mortals—not adorned now with gold or pearls, but more radiant than the sun and all the stars through divine power.

Who, then, will stand before the sublime throne of the fire-spewing tribunal with such a sincere heart and free conscience as the one who recognizes that he has paid his service to the life-giving cross, through which he was freed from being the devil’s servant?

For these and other arguments the holy brothers determine that one must fast on Friday; and thus they show themselves crucified together with the crucified Lord. And what hardship is it if any Christian devotes one day of his soul each week to this, when a medicinal diet also urges him to do so for the preservation of bodily health? For Caesar Augustus, under whom the Savior deigned to be born of the Virgin, as a certain history relates, followed the advice of physicians and always abstained on one day each week, so that, with his body lightened, he might remain vigorous and healthy.

On the same day they also celebrate Masses in honor of the holy cross, so that they may obtain the cross’s protection on the day of necessity.

### CHAPTER IV. Why Saturday is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin.

Saturday, which is interpreted as “rest,” on which day God is read to have rested, is very appropriately dedicated to the most blessed Virgin. Wisdom built herself a house (Proverbs 9), and in it, through the mystery of the humility she assumed, rested as though in a most sacred bed. Worthy honor is certainly offered to her, and those who offer it undoubtedly receive the assistance of assured protection.

Accordingly, I shall faithfully recount what I learned from the account of my brother Damian, at that time archpriest and afterward a monk, unless my forgetful memory deceives me.

Another brother of mine, named Marinus, a layman in his habit but reverent in spirit, eventually reached the point of death as illness of the lungs and chest grew worse. Meanwhile, at the first light of a certain day, he suddenly began, as though rejoicing at the arrival of anyone who came, to smile broadly, laugh happily, and eagerly brighten his face with festive serenity. Then, breaking into speech, he addressed those sitting around him with great urgency:

“Rise, rise,” he said, “and reverently stand up for my Lady.”

Then, directing his words elsewhere in a changed voice, he said: “And what is this, my Lady, Queen of heaven and earth, that you have deigned to visit your poor servant? Bless me, my Lady, and do not allow me to go into darkness, to whom you have brought the light of such a presence.”

When he had filled the room with words of this kind, Damian arrived from the church after completing the nocturnal offices to God. He was related to that man—and to me—as a brother, and he asked what was happening around the sick man.

Marinus declared that he was certain of his approaching death, but he complained bitterly against those sitting nearby:

“Alas, brother,” he said, “how ignorant, how inexperienced, how irreverent our household members are, and how lacking in discipline! And you, vigorous Bonizo”—for there was among them a wealthy man of that name, a merchant—“how could you remain seated when the heavenly Queen arrived? The Queen of the world came, and you neglected to rise? The Mother of the eternal Emperor came, and you considered her presence insignificant?”

Bonizo replied: “You are still delirious, and, driven mad by illness, you are pouring out these empty words. Or perhaps what you say is true? To us these things certainly seem empty and frivolous.”

He answered: “Do you not know that this illness from which I suffer has never been accustomed to alienate the minds of the sick? Know firmly and without the slightest doubt that the blessed Mother of our Redeemer, accompanied by angelic footsteps, visited me. She showed me the cheerfulness of her serene face, blessed me, and immediately departed.”

Soon afterward he died. Then an elderly priest named Severus, who had been his spiritual father, related that long before, while Marinus was still vigorous and flourishing in sound health, he had stripped off his clothes, fastened around his neck the strap with which he had been girded, and offered himself to the altar of the Blessed Mother of God like a slave.

Then, as though he were a bad servant before his mistress, he had himself beaten, saying:

“My glorious Lady, mirror of virginal purity and model of all virtues, whom I, wretched and unhappy, offended through the obscenity of my corrupt flesh, and violated the chastity of my body, of which you are mother and author, I now surrender myself to you as your servant, since this is the only remedy remaining. I submit the neck of my body to the command of your dominion. Bend the rebellious; receive the stubborn; and may your piety not reject the sinner whose undefiled virginity bore the author of true piety.

“Through this little gift of my servitude I offer you a payment, and from now on, for as long as I live, I shall pay an annual tribute as a fixed assessment.”

He therefore placed a certain sum of money at the foot of the altar and departed, trusting in the mercy he had sought.

Perhaps, then, my brother did not tell this particular story about his brother, but one like it. Although I do not retain the words because of forgetfulness, I do not depart from what was reported, so far as I am able, except by a certain resemblance. May this little verse of confession therefore serve me in all that has been related or is to be related, and render me excusable before the heavenly gaze in those matters in which I err unknowingly.

### CHAPTER V. That prayers and intercessions are nourishment for the dead.

To join what is above with what is below, then, do not, do not, pious father, persist in the sentence of threats you have pronounced. Do not withhold the medicine of your prayer from your sick son, whether while he lives or after death.

Moreover, because, while I live, wretched as I am, I sow nothing through the torpor of sloth, after my death, if you survive me, I hope for nourishment from your hands, so that the sacrament of your offering may become food for my soul, and the sacrifice of your prayer may be life-giving nourishment for me.

And what wonder is it if the sacrifice of the sacred offering is believed to be refreshment for the dead, when it sometimes becomes nourishment even for the living who are placed in danger?

For the venerable elderly priest and monk Peter, who lived religiously for almost seventy years under the authority of the monastery of Nonantula and now leads an angelic life in this hermitage, often told me what he himself had learned from the report of brothers who came from the region near Lake Como.

He said that certain stonecutters had carved cauldrons from a vein of stone in the earth near Mount Clavenna. When their work was finished, they had already emerged and were preparing to return. One of them realized that, through forgetfulness, he had left behind a tool. He recalled his loss and entered a hollow cavity in the mountain to retrieve it.

But behold, part of the cave collapsed behind him in a small fall, and a mass of stone rubble enclosed him so completely that he could not return. His companions repeatedly attempted to dig through to him so that they might bring out at least the mangled and crushed corpse of the dead man, but all their labor now proved useless. At last, exhausted and utterly despairing, they returned home.

Afterward, before the circle of the passing year had fully elapsed, his friends and relatives were moved by a certain impulse of intimate affection to search for him more carefully, so that they might perhaps recover from his remains at least some trace of him.

They approached the mountain with various digging tools, examined it here and there, and, moving around more carefully, sought the entrance to the hidden fissure. After removing the rubble with great labor, they continued digging, panting as they worked, and penetrated farther into the excavated interior of the mountain.

Then suddenly they saw alive and unharmed the man whom they had scarcely hoped to find even dead. With hymns and songs of rejoicing they brought him out as though from a tomb.

When he was asked how he could have lived for so long without food, he replied: “From the time I was enclosed in that narrow cavern, a little bird resembling a dove flew to me every day and brought me in its beak a small offering of white bread. This food so sweetened and refreshed my entire being that I thought myself filled with royal—or rather, heavenly—delicacies.

“On only one day, however, because my usual food-bearing attendant did not come to me, I was tormented by unbearable hunger.”

His wife had arranged for the sacrifice of the saving host to be offered daily for his soul. But on one day, when the harshness of winter weather had become dreadful, she postponed going to the threshold of the church. Thus, when they compared their accounts with one another, it became plainly evident that on that day he had been notably weakened by hunger because no sacrifice of praise had been offered for him.

### CHAPTER VI. The example of a woman who tried to redeem her dead husband’s soul by almsgiving.

Nor do I consider the following matter worthy of silence, which Atto, a citizen of Auximum of blessed memory, a prudent and honorable man, related in my presence.

“A certain woman,” he said, “was left a widow when her husband died. She placed great hope in a certain priest for the salvation of the man mentioned above, her husband, and through a household servant she repeatedly sent him gifts of food and drink. Through her servant she always begged him to remember the deceased. He readily promised this, but, being greedy and miserly, he never offered the poor woman even a blessing from the things she herself had brought.

“As a result, she soon became weary of making such frequent journeys and accused the priest’s stinginess within herself.

“Then one day the same matron sent the priest, through the bearer of her pious gifts, a cooked hen, bread baked beneath the ashes, and a small vessel of wine.

“Since the servant happened at that time to be especially hungry, and was inwardly enduring a tumult of complaint and resentment against the priest, she looked all around her, cautiously withdrew into a more secluded corner, sat down by herself, and, both eating and assisting herself, greedily consumed everything she had been carrying.

“After the woman had been refreshed with food and drink, she immediately exulted in the joy of her heart, prostrated her head upon the ground, then raised herself, stretched out her hands toward heaven, and burst into this prayer:

“‘Almighty God,’ she said, ‘who give food to all flesh (Psalm 135), just as my flesh has been refreshed by this bodily food, so by your mercy may the soul of my master today be satisfied in paradise.’”

The woman returned to her mistress, who asked what answer she had received from the priest. The servant reported that he had given thanks and promised to watch over the deceased.

The following night the husband appeared in a vision and thanked his wife for the gifts of the previous day. When she carefully asked what condition he was in—whether punishment constrained him, or whether some prosperity, if only it might be so, smiled upon him—he replied:

“Until yesterday I was in a bad state, and among the other troubles of my misery hunger afflicted me most severely. But yesterday, because you provided a banquet, I was splendidly refreshed; my hunger was utterly consumed, and I abounded in generous courses of food.”

After saying this, he immediately disappeared.

When the woman awoke and began anxiously to consider her husband’s words, she was greatly astonished that he had said he had received a banquet from her only on the previous day, since she had sent a gift to the priest so many times.

After pondering her husband’s words with deeper reflection, she understood that what he had said was not without a hidden meaning. She summoned the servant and began to question her strictly about what she had done with the gift and what the priest had replied.

The servant, shaken with fear, began inventing now one story, now another. Suppressing the truth, she stammered through evasions and unconvincing fabrications. But her mistress did not believe her and threatened her harshly and fiercely.

At last, compelled by necessity, the servant revealed what had actually happened. She confessed that she had eaten what she had brought and had poured out prayers for her master.

### CHAPTER VII. That almsgiving given to the poor is more fruitful than an offering celebrated by a carnal priest.

When this matter had happened, it was quickly repeated by the mouths of the people and spread throughout the regions by widespread report. It was established by the testimony of many that almsgiving to the poor is more useful and fruitful than any offering delivered into the hands of priests living according to the flesh. For the dead man was unaware of what had been given to the priest, whereas he experienced what he received from the poor woman as a solemn banquet.

Almsgiving is sought so that human souls may not go into darkness, and by earthly gifts it purchases the kingdoms of the stars.

Accordingly, certain monasteries in our regions have recently adopted an excellent rule of practice: besides their other works of piety, the abbot should keep three poor men beside him at a private table, and should place before each of them a measure of food like that received by any brother (Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 46). Since the rule prescribes that the abbot’s table should always be shared with guests, this arrangement newly fulfills both purposes: the abbot’s table is attached not to the proud of the world but to holy guests, and he himself does not fail to eat with the brothers.

Indeed, so that more abundant nourishment may benefit the poor, monasteries and hermitages give them tithes of every kind of produce, not only of animals but also of birds and eggs.

For the devotion of the dead they have also newly added this practice: they always celebrate annual octaves for the more beloved deceased, and offer the vows of annual remembrance not merely on the one day of burial but throughout an octave [a week].

I suggest and humbly ask that you yourself adopt this familiar institution of theirs, which I have described, and that you not disdain to borrow an example from humble brothers. It is certainly better for teachers to learn from their pupils than proudly to remain ignorant of what is right. It is more honorable for a superior to learn what he does not know than not to know what ought to be said.

O glorious virtue of humility, through which a person truly becomes a disciple of the Savior! “Learn from me,” He says, “for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). This is the virtue through which the teacher offers God the pleasing sacrifice of earnest labor, and the disciple offers his service.

It happened that I learned from the venerable brothers of the monastery of Cluny two remarkable examples of holy humility. One of them is especially capable of instructing superiors, the other of edifying subjects.

Marcuardus, the rector of that church, appointed Maiolus as his substitute and secured leisure and rest for his own advanced old age. While Maiolus was living privately in the infirmary, he asked one evening for cheese. The cellarer, occupied with many duties, as commonly happens, not only failed to give it to him but also rebuffed his attendant with harsh replies. He complained about the crowd of abbots and said that he could not endure the annoyance of so many masters.

When the old man heard this, he suffered no small scandal. Since he had completely lost the light of his eyes, the pain clung more stubbornly to his heart. For the more a blind man is deprived of outward sight, the more subtly he turns over in his heart whatever he has heard; and because his attention is not dispersed among external things, he is inflamed more fiercely by the inward spur of zeal.

When morning came, he ordered his attendant to lead him by the hand to the chapterhouse. Once brought there, he addressed the abbot in these words:

“Brother Maiolus,” he said, “I did not appoint you over me so that you might persecute me, nor so that you might rule over me like a buyer over a slave. I chose you so that, like a true son, you might share the burdens of your father.”

After adding much of this kind, he said, almost moved to anger: “Are you, I ask, my monk?”

When Maiolus replied, “I am, and I declare that I am no less yours now than I was before,” Marcuardus said:

“If you are my monk, immediately yield your seat and reclaim the place you formerly occupied.”

When Maiolus heard this, he rose at once and went to the humble place, as he had been ordered.

Marcuardus, therefore, returning as though by restoration, occupied the vacant seat. He accused the cellarer against whom he had been angry, and, after the man had immediately prostrated himself on the ground, rebuked him severely. Finally, he imposed upon him the measure of penance that seemed appropriate.

When he had completed the office of so lengthy a tribunal, he promptly stood there dethroned and ordered Maiolus to return to his seat. Maiolus immediately obeyed without hesitation.

### CHAPTER VIII. The great power of obedience.

In this holy man, then, the virtue of true obedience and the mortification of monastic discipline are clearly displayed. In him are truly seen both the dignity of imperial patience and the majesty of apostolic humility reigning.

Ordered to lay aside the office of prior, he did not disdain to do so; ordered to resume it, he obeyed patiently and humbly. In both cases he was dead to himself and bound by the strap of perfect obedience. Since he had wholly subjected himself to the commands of another, he allowed no desire of his own judgment to live within him.

But because such great humility in the blessed man could not be barren, the root that had first conceived through the dew of the Holy Spirit spread forth the shoot of its growing branches.

Once, when the man of God was going to Rome, he ordered a certain brother to travel with him, because, as he had been asked, he had decided to appoint him prior in the monastery of Saint Paul. The brother resisted, raising various obstacles of difficulty. He offered one excuse after another and finally, stubbornly, refused to obey.

Maiolus bore the brother’s disobedience calmly and continued on the journey he had undertaken, leaving him behind. The brother remained in the monastery through his disobedience, while the other brothers vehemently reproached him and unanimously criticized the obstinacy of his hardness.

At last, coming to his senses, he took up arms against his own will and girded himself with the weapons of saving obedience. Soon inflamed by the fervor of heavenly grace, he hastened rapidly after the blessed man’s footsteps.

While Maiolus proceeded unknowingly along the road he had begun, the other hurried anxiously after him, breathing hard in his sudden haste. Soon he reached a river whose ford the man of God had already crossed, and Maiolus was still standing on the opposite bank.

When the monk halted on the nearer bank because he had no boat in which to cross, he saw his master standing at a distance. He did what alone he could: he immediately fell to the ground and humbly prostrated himself. Since, while begging pardon, he might not have been heard through the organ of his mouth [Col. 0572A], he made his whole body into a tongue.

When Maiolus saw this from afar, he immediately understood what it meant, sent a boat, and had the monk ferried across to him. The man of God at once asked why he had come. The monk both begged pardon for his earlier conduct and promised that he would fulfill whatever else Maiolus might order.

Then Maiolus said: “Do you undoubtedly desire penance?”

When the monk replied, “I do,” Maiolus immediately added: “Then kiss this man.”

By chance, a leper with a swollen and diseased skin was standing there. The monk immediately rushed to kiss him, and the leprosy vanished completely from his cleansed body.

Thus holy obedience found the fruit of its humility: the monk not only earned pardon by correcting himself but also displayed a sign of so evident a virtue. The man whom pride had nearly been able to bring to apostate ruin was enabled by humility to display apostolic virtue.

I describe all these matters, venerable Father, not without great fear, lest through my own forgetfulness or the boldness of an unreliable report I deviate even slightly from the line of truth. Therefore I do not assert these things with confidence; but because they were brought to my knowledge, as it were, through this form of report, I offer them as my opinion.

Yet whoever praises obedience must take the greatest care that the mark of rebellious disobedience does not stain him. For when deeds differ from words, the author’s name is disgraced. Whoever attacks by his actions the very thing he establishes with his mouth undoubtedly destroys the law he proclaims.

Therefore I beg the very author of obedience and humility to deign soon to drive away from me the reproach of this disgrace and to permit me to sing this verse of the Prophet at the doors of the monastery of Cassino:

“Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am the one who spoke; behold, I am here” (Isaiah 52:6).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

### WORK THIRTY-FOUR. On various miraculous narratives, with a similar discussion of various apparitions and miracles.

### ARGUMENT.

This entire work is filled with astonishing examples, which are called by the single name “miracles.” It is unquestionably clear that they possess great power to inflame minds toward virtue and to deter them from vices.

To the lord Desiderius, archangel of the monks, and to the other holy brothers, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the service of most devoted obedience.

Since the ardor of your charity burns unquenchably in my heart and does not permit me to grow lukewarm in remembering you, something recently came to my mind that prompted me to send you this communication.

For while I was dwelling attentively in contemplation of you, and was present in the sight of my heart to the angelic and holy assembly of the brothers as though I were bodily present, among many other matters I suddenly remembered the letters you sent under the form of a question. I have not yet replied to them, hindered as I have been by the demands of the synod.

If I remember correctly, the letters contained the following: A jealous woman, who suspected her husband of adultery, asked a neighboring woman how she might claim him for herself and keep him content with his own marriage bed. The latter woman, plainly wicked and evidently liable to avenging flames, instructed her through the poisoned counsel of the ancient serpent to receive the Lord’s body as though she were about to communicate, carefully preserve it, and afterward give it to her husband with certain magical practices.

The particle, having been received from the priest and kept hidden in a small cloth until an opportunity arose, produced a miracle that caused no little astonishment. For this fragment of the Lord’s body was found to have been transformed into flesh as far as its middle, while the other half did not change its appearance as bread.

Thus, if I remember correctly, you proposed this matter and then asked what it signified. Since it is unnecessary to linger longer over the question, I shall briefly explain what seems to me to be the case.

Almighty God transformed that most sacred mystery into the appearance of flesh in order to expose the unbelief of the wicked woman, by displaying the visible reality of the Lord’s body. Thus she, who had previously believed it to be mere bread, as it appeared, might see the appearance of true flesh and, by her own judgment, condemn the sacrilegious boldness of the crime she had begun.

But the fact that one half remained as it was serves as testimony to a still clearer judgment: when you consider that in one and the same substance there is on one side the appearance of bread and on the other the appearance of flesh, you understand in both alike the reality of true flesh and true bread, because He Himself is the bread that descended from heaven (John 6), and He is likewise the flesh that came forth from the substance of the Virgin’s womb.

For that neighboring bishop of Amalfi, of blessed memory, whose name I do not know, repeatedly testified under oath, in the presence of Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, that once, when he was approaching the Lord’s table to celebrate the sacrifice but hesitated in disbelief concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body, during the very breaking of the saving host a wholly red and complete piece of flesh appeared between his hands, so that it even bloodied his fingers and thus removed every scruple of doubt from the priest. Here one must note how immense is the danger of touching so fearful a sacrament with unworthy hands. But why speak of the sacraments themselves, when we sometimes see terrifying judgments visited even upon those who offend through the vessels used for them?

[On Various Miraculous Narratives, with a Similar Discussion of Various Apparitions and Miracles.]

## CHAPTER I. The Terrible Example of Arnaldus, Bishop of Arezzo, Alienating the Lord’s Chalice and Removing It from the Church

You too knew Arnaldus, certainly, the bishop of the see of Arezzo, quite intimately. Martin the hermit, a man of great reputation and celebrated renown, told me about him [589]: he took a golden chalice from a monastery under his jurisdiction and alienated it because of certain pressing necessities. A noble and devout woman, who had offered that chalice to the saints, had prudently caused an anathema to be engraved upon it, so that no one might remove it.

Meanwhile, a certain brother, overcome by sleep, happened to see a lake boiling with the heat of an immense fire and exhaling pitchy and sulfurous stench amid coils of dreadful smoke [Col. 0574A]. Around this lake sat certain exceedingly grim figures, like Ethiopians, likewise black, upon black horses as tall as towers. Within it were countless monsters of cruel torturers, while the condemned appeared to be suffering horrifying and diverse punishments.

Among them, he suddenly happened also to see the bishop Arnaldus. He was immersed up to his neck in those overflowing waters of excessive heat, and two terrifying Ethiopians were restraining him. One of them seemed to hold an iron frying pan, the other a golden chalice. The former filled the chalice with water from the pan, while the latter immediately pressed the same chalice to the bishop’s lips and compelled him to drink it down completely. Thus they never ceased: one plunging the cup into his gaping mouth, the other, forced to do so, drinking without interruption.

Why delay over many details? When the bishop heard of this vision, his friends strongly urged him to return the chalice to the monastery. He promised that he would return it, though perhaps with some hesitation. But while the matter was postponed until the following day—in fact, while he failed to keep watch over his own salvation—the heavenly sentence did not sleep over him. For blessed Peter says of those who traffic in greed through deceitful words: “Their judgment from long ago is not idle, and their destruction does not sleep” (1 Peter 2).

One day, as the third hour was already approaching, he ordered a chair to be brought to the terrace of the castle where he was staying, so that he might receive the warmth of the rising sun and drive away the remnants of the morning chill. While his household servants and companions stood around him as he sat, and while he, secure, cheerful, and merry, exchanged witty and urbane remarks with them, a sudden pain struck the crown of his head like a sword and compelled him to cry out, “I am dying, I am dying!” At once his attendants carried him to his bed. He received the mystery of holy communion and immediately breathed out his spirit.

Let everyone therefore fear who either disperses the utensils of an ecclesiastical mystery or makes light of the inscription of a dreadful anathema, lest, while he walks as though secure, the snare of a hidden judgment seize him.

Alas, how wretched and unhappy is the human condition! Certainly, although the bishop mentioned above had allowed the sluggish torpor of negligence to creep over him in this matter, in other respects he was sharp, ingenious, and cautious, and so eloquent that, since he ran most swiftly through his words, he could not unjustly have been called “circumcised in lips” [Col. 0574D]. But since the Apostle says, “The prudence of the flesh is death; the prudence of the spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8), what does it profit anyone to be skilled in the prudence of this world, to grasp hidden matters with the perception of a lively intellect, or, through crafty cunning, to transform himself like Proteus into monsters of various shapes?

## CHAPTER II. Another Terrible Example: Bishop Tedaldus

Meanwhile, on the occasion of this discourse, there returns to my memory what Bishop Tetaldus, the predecessor of this man, once added to a sermon he was preaching while stationed in the pulpit on the feast of blessed Donatus [Col. 0575A].

“In the regions of Lombardy,” he said, “from which I derive my origin, there was a man of shifting intelligence and exceedingly sharp subtlety: double-minded, charming in speech, trained in devising and fabricating inventions, and extraordinarily crafty in discovering and varying his plans. He never raised his arms against the torrent; rather, from whatever side the breeze of worldly turbulence blew him, he immediately held out a suitable cloak of cunning and deceit.

“It happened that, after his death, a certain brother saw him in a nocturnal vision. There was a fiery lake, steaming with flame-belching fires and striking terror into those who saw it with the crackling globes of its flames. Dragons of monstrous size seemed to besiege the lake, and various kinds of serpents wandered around it in every direction [Col. 0575B].

“The man of whom we spoke, confined in the very chasm of the hissing flames, attempted to escape, but grieved that the beasts blocked the way. Now he prepared flight from this side—but behold, a serpent was there to meet him. He tried to break out by another route, but behold, another beast, hissing with open throat, had again closed the passage. Again he tried other places of escape, but as the beasts rose against him, no route of flight was open at all.

“Since Truth says, ‘With the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you’ (Matthew 7; Mark 4), this happened to him by the just judgment of God. For just as, through the vanity of carnal cunning, he had known how to free himself from whatever snares of this world, so afterward, in the opposite reversal, he could escape by no skill the punishment by which he was tormented. If he had tried to exercise in the divine commandments the prudence in which he was skilled, he would not be burning among the ravenous mouths of serpents; rather, he would be rejoicing among the ranks of the blessed.”

## CHAPTER III. Another Example: A Certain Man Who Failed to Honor a Sacred Place

One event plainly occurred in our region concerning a man wise according to the flesh, and it ought not to pass by in silence. A leading citizen of Fano, named Hugo, entered the church with arms and armed men on the very night that follows Good Friday and precedes the holy Sabbath of the Lord’s burial, while divine offices were being celebrated there. He violently seized a man whom he hated and cruelly bound him [Col. 0575D]. Because he had presumed upon this novel act, almighty God condemned him with a novel punishment.

For although, as far as I can see, he retains an intact power of understanding, everyone regards him as insane, emptied of sense, and demented; they spit upon him, reject him, and reproach him. His wife, according to blessed Job’s complaint, recoils from his breath (Job 19), and his daughter-in-law drives him away as though he were possessed. His son does not admit him to table or conversation. His servants turn their eyes away; his friends, dependents, soldiers, relations, and kinsmen disdain him. Even the bishop of the city—and, to gather everything briefly, virtually all the clergy and people—have for almost twelve years considered him mentally powerless and insane [Col. 0576A], and, as though he were possessed, have not deigned to associate with him.

Although he is wealthy and his household is abundant, his ragged and unwashed clothes hang about him; his unkempt hair is repulsive; his head reeks from the offense of long-accumulated sweat; his whole body is filthy through prolonged neglect.

When this man learned that I was present, he hastened to me, described the evils he suffered, and set forth his complaint against his family in sober speech. So far as I could gather from the tenor of his words, he argued reasonably. I therefore summoned his son, the bishop, and also a great many people from the city, and carefully asked what disorder, delirium, or foolishness they saw in him, on account of which they attributed insanity to him.

From them I could learn nothing else—not even a single word indicating any definite sign—except only this: “He is demented.” All of them unanimously asserted this with one voice. When I said, “How do you know this? By what indications do you infer that he is insane?”—finding nothing else to say, they repeated the same thing again: “He is demented.”

This seems to me to be a profound and marvelous judgment of almighty God: that the man who is known to have knowingly and deliberately become foolish should knowingly and deliberately be punished by the reputation of madness; and that he who voluntarily made himself mad should be judged demented by the whole people against his will. He is rightly adjudged insane against his wish who has attempted to become insane by his own choice.

Indeed, if he were truly mad, he would be less wretched to the extent that he would be unaware of the evils of his disgrace which he suffers. He is therefore not like the dead of this world, who do not feel (Psalm 142), but like the dead of hell, who are continually dying and never cease to feel death itself [Col. 0576C].

Apart from that terrible judgment at the end of the world, almighty God now also punishes as they deserve not only any cruel deeds but also proud or sacrilegious words. He avenged the fact that Belshazzar, drunk, handled the sacred vessels irreverently (Daniel 5); nor did he leave unpunished the boastful words uttered arrogantly by Nebuchadnezzar: “Is this not great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4.) And behold, as the prophet testifies, while the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: “To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has departed from you, and they will drive you away from among men; your dwelling will be with beasts and wild animals” (ibid.).

The Lord also punished Zedekiah, king of Judah, who by his wicked acts had despised God’s command (2 Chronicles 36). He likewise avenged the prophet Hananiah, not because he did evil, but because he spoke a lie. Jeremiah said to him: “The Lord did not send you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall send you from the face of the earth; this year you shall die” (Jeremiah 28).

## CHAPTER IV. The Slaughter of a Quarrelsome, Insolent, and Blasphemous Cleric

In our own times [Nostris f.] it also happened that, in the kingdom of Burgundy, there was a cleric who was exceedingly proud and arrogant—not only devoted to carnal life in a worldly manner, but also dreadfully warlike, contrary to his own order.

He had usurped for his own control the church of blessed Mauritius, renowned for its many estates. A certain powerful man, however, claimed on the contrary that it belonged to his own jurisdiction and contended for it with no small bitterness and hostility. At last, with both sides agreeing, a day of battle was fixed, and many armed bands, roaring on either side, gathered together.

The powerful man mentioned above sent a messenger to the enemy camp to inspect the preparations for battle carefully and report back to him quickly. At that time the cleric was hearing Mass with his supporters, who were about to fight. When the Gospel was reached, these words were read at the end: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23; Luke 14, 18) [Col. 0577B].

Immediately the cleric burst out insolently with this sacrilegious statement: “This judgment is not true. For if I had humbly bowed before my adversaries, I would not today possess such great numbers of estates and dependents.”

The messenger returned and faithfully reported to his master not only what he had seen in the preparation for battle, but also what he had heard from the mouth of the cleric speaking arrogantly. Then the other man rejoiced and became glad in the Lord, and undoubtedly encouraged his soldiers to hope that victory would be theirs.

The armed companies of the different sides were gathered together. Battle was joined on both fronts; strength was opposed to strength; the forest of weapons was brought down, and arms inflicted upon human bodies raged among them.

The cleric had a mare which he had mounted for battle, of such speed and strength that no horse or mule seemed capable of being preferred to it for fighting. By chance—or rather by God’s arrangement—it happened that on the preceding night the animal escaped after being loosed from its stall and, finding a pile of salt, ate a great deal of it.

As the cleric, stationed in the battle line, came to a stream of water and there engaged the weapons of his opponents at close quarters, the animal, thirsty from the quantity of salt it had consumed, violently tore the reins from the rider’s hand and claimed them entirely for itself. Then it immediately plunged its head eagerly into the water to drink.

While the cleric struggled with the animal with the hand that held his shield, he was forced to expose his face to the enemy’s darts. And behold, suddenly a sword pierced his mouth like a bolt of lightning [Col. 0577D], and that wicked man brought his life to an end in such a manner.

How fittingly he suffered vengeance in that part of his body with which he had vomited blasphemy against the Lord from a black gall! Since the Prophet says of such men, “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56), he who brandished his tongue and teeth against God like a sword deserved to pay the penalty of a material sword through those same members.

This man plainly experienced what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Because the tower of Siloam fell upon eighteen men and killed them” (Luke 13). But whom does that tower mystically signify, except the one to whom the Psalmist sings: “You have led me, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy”? (Psalm 60.)

The very name Siloam also suits this interpretation. For Siloam is interpreted as “sent.” Without doubt this is the one who says, “The one who sent me is with me” (John 8). And there the man blind from birth receives light from him who says, “I am the light of the world” (Matthew 21).

Elsewhere, the fall of this tower is spoken of under the figure of a stone: “Everyone who falls upon that stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” A man falls upon this tower or stone and is broken when he sins through some weakness; but its ruin crushes him when he blasphemes proudly. Therefore the tower of Siloam fell upon this cleric and utterly crushed him, as he had deserved through his blasphemy.

## CHAPTER V. That God Leaves No Sin Unpunished

What wonder is it if grave sins consign us to torments, when God’s subtle judgment does not leave even the smallest offenses unpunished? Or what is new in his condemning the sacrilege of wicked speech, when he also despises the praises proclaimed in his honor if they are not uttered worthily?

I learned from the report of Adraldus, a prudent and religious man who presides over the monastery of Bremet, what I am writing; he said that it had also been committed to writing.

“A cleric of the Church of Cologne,” he said, “was crossing a ford in a river. And behold, blessed Severinus, formerly bishop of that same Church, took hold of the reins of his horse and, restraining him, brought him to a halt.

“When the cleric, astonished and greatly amazed, asked why so distinguished a man of such celebrated reputation was lingering there, the bishop said: ‘Give me your hand, and learn what concerns me not by hearing but by touch.’

“When he had placed the cleric’s hand into the waves, such heat consumed it that his flesh melted away and flowed off on every side, leaving the bones bare, scarcely held together by clinging joints.

“The cleric said to him: ‘Since [cum adde: reading uncertain] your name is held among us in such great blessing, and your fame is celebrated by the unanimous praises of the whole Church, why does this pestilential abyss constrain you, and why, alas, are you tormented by so great a fire?’

“The holy bishop answered: ‘Nothing else remains in me to be punished by vengeance except this: when I was established in the royal court, I involved myself too deeply in imperial counsels and did not perform the offices of the canonical assembly at their appointed intervals of the hours. In the morning I heaped them all together, and then spent the entire day freely and unconcernedly on the business pressing upon me. For this negligence concerning the hours I suffer the punishment of this burning.

“‘But you, humbly implore the mercy of almighty God, that he may restore your hand to its former state of health.’

“When this had been done, he said: ‘Go, my son. Entreat our brothers, the clerics of the Church, and the other spiritual men, to pour out prayers for me, to give assistance to those in need, and to persevere in the vows of sacrifices. When these things have been accomplished, I shall undoubtedly soon be released from the bond of this punishment and shall joyfully join the choirs of the blessed citizens who await me.’”

This ought certainly to instill great fear in us: if an intolerable punishment of purgatory bound a holy man who was guilty of only one fault, alas, alas, what sentence must be imposed upon me and those like me, whom the length of so many offenses weighs down? [Col. 0579A]

## CHAPTER VI. That God’s Praises Must Not Be Polluted by Filthy Thoughts

The offices of ecclesiastical observance must therefore be distinguished according to the successive moments of time and performed under the discipline of great fear and reverence toward God, lest, while we sing psalms, we mingle the fruit of the spirit with the sluggishness of the flesh.

What does it profit to offer God a sacrifice of praise and, through the torpor of negligence, to defile oneself with filthy thoughts? This mixture of good and evil is signified by that Gospel passage where it is said that, while the Lord was teaching, certain people came at that very time and reported to him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13).

Since Pilate is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammer,” whom ought we to understand by him except the devil, who is always ready to strike human beings with the blows of offenses? Hence the Prophet also says that he holds a rod over the shoulders of men: “You have overcome the rod of his shoulder, as on the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9).

What is blood except sins? What do sacrifices signify except actions that are upright and acceptable to God? Pilate therefore mingled the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices because the evil spirit either pollutes our prayers with wicked thoughts or corrupts good works by the contamination of some sin, so that blood pollutes the sacrifice, when the guilt of an offense disfigures the victim of a good work offered to God.

Hence it is written that when Abraham devoutly offered God a sacrifice of cattle and birds, birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away (Genesis 15). What do the birds signify except wicked spirits flying through the air? We drive birds away from our sacrifice when we carefully protect the offerings of our works from the malign spirits that attempt to defile them.

The same Adraldus whom I mentioned earlier, while he was traveling with me in the kingdom of Burgundy, said:

“In this place through which we are now passing, something happened which, if we recount it, does not seem pointless. A certain brother of our monastery [certainly the Cluniac monastery], a man of devout mind and upright conduct, was once passing through here. And behold, a certain long-haired man, apparently returning from a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, was carrying a palm in his hand.

“When the pilgrim and the monk met and passed one another in opposite directions, the former said: ‘Compline in bed is neither salvation nor progress.’

“When the brother heard this, he was astonished and frightened; and when he suddenly looked behind him, he could not see the man. For as soon as he had spoken the words, he had completely disappeared.

“The brother immediately returned to his conscience and discovered that on the previous evening he had returned tired from a journey and, throwing his weary limbs onto his bed, had completed the canonical hours while lying down.

“Whether that man was an angel, or truly a human being as he appeared, we leave to God’s judgment.”

In this same hermitage of Fonte Avellana, where I now live, there had previously been a man named John who, weakened by certain lingering illnesses, always appeared thin and emaciated. Trusting in this feebleness of his body, he often recited Compline while lying in bed.

It happened that a certain demoniac was nearby who shamelessly disclosed many secrets and disgraceful acts of human beings. When the aforesaid John ordered the demon to depart and scourged him with certain exorcistic questions, the demon said:
