“So you are the one who whispers Compline beneath your coverlet every day, and who now attempts, as though you were a holy man, to drive me out and release the vessel under my jurisdiction from my power?”

When the brother heard this, he blushed, because through a lie he also recognized the author of the truth [Col. 0580B].

Another hermit, who was called John of Anso, was insistently ordering the demon to depart and repeatedly adjuring him by the divine name. The demon said:

“Have you forgotten what I did to you this night? For, if it has not slipped your memory, you know that when I transformed myself into the shape of a wild boar, you pursued me like a hunter. But although I appeared to be a boar, I suddenly assumed the form of a beautiful woman, rushed to kiss you, and triumphed gloriously when you poured out your seed.”

If the wicked spirit boasted of having triumphed over a sinful brother through the power of sleep, how much more do we think it rejoices over those who fall into adultery or incest? Thus almighty God often displays a terrifying judgment even in this life, yet wretched human beings do not cease to repeat what must be punished.

For Robert, king of the Gauls, the grandfather of this Philip who succeeded to the scepter of his paternal inheritance, took a close relative as his wife and fathered by her a son who had in every respect a goose-like neck and head. Nearly all the bishops of Gaul excommunicated both of them—the husband and the wife—with a common sentence.

Such terror from this priestly decree seized the entire people everywhere that they withdrew from his society, and no one remained to serve his necessary needs except two little servants. Yet even these, after the king had eaten or drunk, judged all the vessels from which the king had eaten or drunk to be abominable and consigned them as fuel to the flames.

At last, compelled by these hardships, the king returned to sound counsel, abandoned the incestuous union, and entered into a lawful marriage.

## CHAPTER VII. That Co-Godmothers Must Not Be Taken as Wives

King Otto of the Teutons, who was later created Roman emperor, also took Adelaide, queen of Italy, who had been his co-godmother (*commater*), as his wife [596].

His son Almificus, who presided as pastor over the Church of Mainz, began steadfastly to rebuke him and publicly condemn the criminal and shameful marriage. The father, however, grew extremely angry, ordered him to be arrested, and immediately committed him to prison. The prison confined him for approximately a year, but the bond of fear did not bind his tongue from correction [Col. 0581A].

When his father decided to release him from custody during the course of the Lenten fast, the son refused to leave before he had completed the psalter, which he was writing in letters of gold. Nevertheless, when he did leave, inflamed by zeal for priestly authority, he did not remain silent but immediately hurled against his father the weapon of public excommunication.

O truly worthy priest of royal birth, who in God’s cause recognized neither imperial grandeur nor paternal affection; rather, while he placed paternal and royal authority in God alone, he judged this man, who resisted God’s laws, to be entirely alien to himself.

He said to his father: “You think that I am acting insolently against you and that you are suffering prejudice. You will soon learn that on the holy day of Pentecost we shall both stand together before God, and there our dispute will be weighed between us on the scales of justice. There it will appear more clearly than daylight which of us holds the line of equity and which contradicts the laws of God.”

And it happened on the very day of the sacred solemnity just mentioned that, while the aforesaid Augustus, crowned with imperial regalia and surrounded by choirs of many bishops and bands of nobles, was attending the solemnities of Mass, a sudden judgment came upon him and he was found dead. The bishop, however, had already fallen asleep in the Lord.

Thus, thus, the man who had refused to be judged among men for an incestuous marriage was compelled to be dragged before the tribunal of the eternal Judge; and he who had disdained to listen to a bishop subject to him could not escape the terrible majesty that came upon him.

I write these things, venerable father, and many others besides, not without the anguish of great fear, lest either my informants have not kept to the path of sheer truth, or I myself, through forgetfulness, have failed in some respect in recounting their reports. Yet with my conscience as witness, I strive to recall and record these things on tablets as best I can, not from a desire to lie but from a concern for edification.

If, however, some forgetfulness has crept into these accounts—or rather, whatever I have done wrong through the weakness of the human condition before I am released from the bonds of this flesh—may divine mercy, through your prayers, restore it to my memory and permit me worthily to mourn it, lest something remain hidden for which I must repent while alive but which will be brought before the eyes of the dying.

When Horno, abbot of Cluny, had brought me to his monastery, an old brother was lying sick in the infirmary, afflicted by increasing swelling throughout his body. When he learned that the abbot was present, he became joyful and began to implore divine mercy:

“Lord,” he said, “from whom no hidden thing is concealed, I ask you: if there is any guilt in me that I have not yet confessed, mercifully recall it to my memory, so that, while my abbot is present, I may confess it purely and be absolved by him, who above all others possesses this authority over me.”

After he had spoken, a voice of this sort sounded in his ears: “Certainly there is something in you—certainly there is something—which you have not yet confessed.”

Although he heard only the voice and did not see from whom it proceeded, he added in prayer: “Make clear, Lord, what this is, so that, after confessing it, I may correct my error.”

Then the same voice explicitly identified a certain sin [as he was asking], which he immediately recognized as having been committed by him. He promptly summoned the abbot, made his confession, and purified himself; a few days later he died in holy peace.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Terrible Example of a Despairing Man Who Killed Himself

The cleric about whom the same Hugo, rector of the monastery of Cluny, gave me a trustworthy account did not meet such an end:

“A certain religious bishop,” he said, “while on a military expedition, came to the bank of a river, stopped there, and, tired, began to refresh his spirit. While he was resting quietly, he heard a voice emerging from the riverbed and clearly uttering these words: ‘The hour has come; the man has not come.’

“On hearing this, the bishop became anxious. Thinking that this could not be without a mystery, he awaited the arrival of the event with vigilant attention. But while he waited as an attentive observer and pondered this and that, behold, a certain cleric was hurrying along very swiftly, spurring his horse and hastening to cross the river as quickly as possible.

“The bishop warned his men to place themselves quickly in the approaching man’s way and restrain him from the force of his course. When the cleric, rushing headlong, attempted to enter the river and cross it without delay, while the bishop’s men violently opposed him and compelled him to stop, he said:

“‘Please, stop! Let me go; withdraw! For the king’s command is pressing upon me. This is not something that can be postponed. The king’s business is urgent; unavoidable necessity commands.’

“What more need be said? The holy bishop, having him forcibly restrained, compelled him to lodge with him when night came. But, oh, the wretched and lamentable condition of humanity, which can more easily bring evil upon itself when evil is absent than avoid it when evil threatens!

“While the bishop and his men were overcome by heavy sleep, the cleric found a vessel of water in the lodging. He plunged his head into it, became his own executioner, and brutally killed himself. But just as this man, though by a hidden yet strict judgment of God, suffered the destruction of his flesh, so another escaped, through God’s merciful kindness, the death of both soul and body.”

## CHAPTER IX. A Vow-Breaker Is Struck by Illness So That He May Repent

What I am now about to relate I have heard frequently, both from the report of the abbot of Cluny already mentioned [598] and from the mouth of the man to whom the event itself happened.

There was a young man in the regions of Aquitaine who began to discuss the salvation of their souls with other young men of his own age. After deliberation, they finally decided and proposed, in a unanimous mutual agreement, both to reject the pomp of worldly dress and to transfer themselves to the way of monastic life.

But while the matter was still being delayed in suspense and the course of events was being shaken by manifold changes, the tender young man’s mind also failed to remain fixed in its purpose [Col. 0583A]. What more need be said? His mind completely changed, and he betrothed a wife.

As time passed, his mind gradually erased from itself the memory of his holy purpose, and under the pretext of marriage he began to seethe more impatiently to satisfy carnal pleasure. While divine mercy kept watch over him, he was suddenly struck by illness and soon reached the point of death.

His household and relatives were therefore discussing the burial of one who seemed already dead. While his lifeless corpse appeared to be laid out in their midst and only a faint movement barely throbbed in his chest, behold, two exceedingly grim Ethiopians with savage faces attacked him—as it seemed to him—like roaring lions. They seized him with rapacious violence and tore him forcibly from his body. Then they bound his feet and arms with hard bonds and began to carry him, one after the other, like a kid hanging from a pole.

It would take too long not only to set down in writing the pains and torments he endured, and the things he saw and heard, but even to hear them recounted in order in the simple words of the one who reported them. Let it suffice to add this much here: while they were carrying him through places of obscure darkness, behold, blessed Peter the Apostle, shining and flashing, came to meet him. He snatched him from the shoulders of his bearers and released him from the bonds by which he was tormented.

They immediately departed, leaving their prey behind, gnashing their teeth and howling, and lamented tearfully that an injustice had been done to them. But the blessed Apostle took the young man with him to the monastery of Cluny and, placing him outside, ordered him to wait there until he returned.

“Entering my monastery,” he said, “I shall visit it and inspect everything around it, observing what is happening; then, after considering all things, I shall return to you.”

But as soon as the young man had been left alone, behold, the same Ethiopians returned, more cruel and fiercer than before. No longer seizing him by the hands and feet, they seized him by the very genitals and suspended him in this way, not without the most grievous pain.

For just as a sparrow is snatched by a hawk’s beak or a featherless dove by an eagle’s talons, so this wretched man was seized by those wicked spirits, dragged through the air, suspended by his private parts, and carried farther away like recovered prey that had been lost. Behold, blessed Peter, appearing with an exceedingly radiant and terrifying splendor, hurled himself like lightning upon them, seized his plunder as though in a violent spiritual assault, and beat the most wicked kidnappers fiercely with the keys he carried in his hand.

He then brought the young man all the way to his own home and, restoring the spirit to the body, restored both substances to health. For the young man immediately recovered [599], made arrangements for his household without delay, and, hastening to the monastery of Cluny, assumed the habit of holy conduct with very fervent devotion.

Thus the deserter from the divine army, while being taught by heavenly discipline through the chastisement of his father, is snatched from the hand of the bloodthirsty robber, and the wandering sheep is recalled to the shelter of its own shepherd.

But now, restraining itself, let the pen hold back its stylus, lest the epistolary summary exceed the rule of brevity.

Write, if you please, this distich in the refectory, beneath the feet of the Apostles:

The apostolic senate kindles with the flame of tongues,  
And a fruitful voice brings forth varied utterances.

## DISCUSSION: ON VARIOUS APPARITIONS AND MIRACLES

### Argument

He informs the archbishop—who, as one greatly delighted to hear such matters, was especially pleased by them—that the canons of the Church of Velitrae, over which he presided, had at last emerged and returned, as the saying goes, to good fruitfulness; and that, according to the discipline prescribed for them, they were now ordering their lives not as formerly under compulsion but freely and willingly. He then relates several examples and marvels that happened to many people, from which no small benefit may be derived.

To the venerable lord archbishop A., Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of the fullest devotion.

Because I know, venerable Father, that your holy mind rejoices especially in the salvation of human beings, so much so that whenever you happen to hear of the progress of souls, you cling to it and delight in it as though to sweet banquets and pleasant food.

I report to you concerning our canons, namely those of the holy Church of Velitrae: those who, despite our many labors and exertions, seemed incorrigible are now, by divine grace, coming to their senses and proceeding along the path of the canonical rule—not compelled now, but rejoicing. Moreover, each of them completes the psalter every day during Lent; on three days each week they all abstain together from wine and cooked food. They seem to possess so ardent a zeal for strict observance that throughout the whole of Lent before Easter, and also during the Lent that customarily precedes the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, each man, on three days a week, strips himself in the chapter house before the brothers, confesses his own sins, and endures the discipline of the harsh scourge of leather thongs. From this sign, plainly, of holy conduct you can clearly gather what you ought to think about their other ways of life and observances. And, O saving discipline—indeed, affliction of the flesh!—in which, while the body is exposed to human sight, it appears before the eyes of God adorned in garments that flash with light. In fact, scarcely a month has passed since the event I am reporting occurred. [Col. 0584C–D; p. 600]

# DISPUTATION ON VARIOUS APPARITIONS AND MIRACLES

## CHAPTER ONE. The Holiness of the Hermit Baruncius

Baruncius was plainly my brother in complete unity of spirit and unique in the sweetness of a very special affection. While he was carrying out necessary work—not in the desert itself, but in a certain village subject to the desert—he fell into the extremity of illness. When he recognized that death was impending, he asked the brothers who were diligently attending him to impose a penance. They judged that three, or at most four, psalms would suffice for a holy and innocent man; but he requested that they assign him ten years of penance and immediately send word to the brothers remaining in the desert that it should be performed as soon as possible.

Accordingly, on the following night, while each of the brothers stationed in his cell, after cockcrow, stripped himself and applied himself to bodily discipline, and while the brothers were hurrying to complete the penance before Baruncius died, Baruncius said to Brother Lambert, who was assiduously assisting him: “Why do you not prepare yourself and, like the other brothers, adorn yourself with ecclesiastical garments? For all the brothers from the desert have visibly attended me up to this moment, clothed, to be sure, in white and shining stoles, and conspicuous in the brilliance of their gleaming garments as though singing in a choir.”

He therefore compelled Lambert to dress in imitation of them. Here it should be noted that, while those brothers were at some distance from him, stripped and engaged in bodily discipline, they appeared to him—so to speak—not with carnal but with spiritual eyes, clothed in beautiful attire. The venerable Father Liutprand, who reported this to me, also subsequently made known to me another matter, which is not without value for the edification of those who hear it.

“At the beginning,” he said, “of that Lent which, by ecclesiastical institution, precedes the Nativity of the Lord, such a severe attack of sudden illness suddenly fell upon me that I could scarcely stand firmly on my feet, much less fulfill the rule of daily observance. As I wavered amid dark and confused thoughts, completely despairing of keeping the fast, and deciding thereafter to allow myself a daily relaxation in food, a gentle sleep suddenly stole over me, and I inclined my head slightly over the book to which I had been attending.

“Then it seemed to me that the entire cell was full of smoke, and that several men were there, shouting at one another in loud and mutually conflicting conversations. Suddenly the holy brother Juventius, who lives honorably in that same desert, burst through the door of the little cell. With the zeal of the strictest correction he drove the men out, violently forcing them outside without delay. ‘Is this desert’s rule not inviolable,’ he said, ‘so that no one dares hold a conversation in his cell, but the censure of silence immediately restrains the lips of those who enter?’

“Then he suddenly seized a towel and threw out all the chaos of smoke and the foul mass by which the cell was filled. When this had been done, I immediately awoke from sleep and recognized, with great joy of heart, that my mind was free from every darkness of smoky thought. Then, once every weariness of temptation and illness had been driven away, I found in myself such strength and power of virtue that throughout that whole Lent until the Lord’s Nativity I scarcely ever felt even lightly hungry; and, unless I am mistaken, on not one day did I require any other food besides bread and water.” [Col. 0585A–D; pp. 600–601]

## CHAPTER TWO. The Intemperance of the Bishop of Paris Is Punished by God

And O that the same thing had happened to Albuinus [or Albericus, son of—] the bishop of the Church of Paris. When he was celebrating, if I remember correctly, the fast of the seventh month, and, the two days of fasting already completed, had reached Saturday, a remarkable wild animal caught in the hunt was brought before him. At once the wretched man was fatally and corruptingly inflamed by desire for the food, and he decided to transfer the fast to the following week; immediately he ordered the cooks to cook the pig more carefully.

That day the miserable man satisfied the appetite of his belly; but on the eighth day, namely the following Saturday, he ended his life. And he certainly deserved this fate, since in the desert he made the sanctuary of the Church, as it were, into “graves of lust” (Num. XI). But what wonder is it if, where the fault was so open, vengeance was visibly inflicted, when we often see a pitiable outcome in a matter and yet, because the cause of the heavenly dispensation remains hidden, do not understand its mystery? [Col. 0586A–B]

Leo, formerly bishop of Pozzuoli but now a noble hermit, recently reported to me and to the brothers that, when a certain demoniac was in the monastery near Parthenope, built in honor of the blessed confessor Agnellus, he suddenly leapt upon a man standing nearby and, striking him in frenzied rage, immediately killed him.

And O, who is capable of penetrating the depth of God’s judgments! As soon as the frenzied man had killed the innocent, he was immediately freed from the demon and restored to his former mind and reason; thereafter he never again suffered the distress of that affliction. When asked why he had committed this deed, he replied: “I did not see a man, but a black dog, which, as it seemed to me, was trying to seize me with its teeth; I killed it.”

In this outcome of a hidden dispensation, therefore, it was not clear why either the one man had deserved to be killed by a sudden wound or the other had deserved to be freed from the demon. The former, as far as human judgment is concerned, was killed innocently; the latter, insofar as outward appearance of guilt is concerned, seems to have deserved punishment. And what wonder is it if the merits of others are not disclosed to us, when we ourselves often do not know, through the dullness of forgetfulness, what we have done? [Col. 0586B–C; p. 602]

## CHAPTER THREE. The Blessed Virgin Mary Frees Countless People from the Punishments of Purgatory at the Assumption, Her Feast

The religious priest John reported to me the following account, which, he said, happened in Rome a few years ago.

On the Assumption of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, while the Roman people, according to custom, were occupied at night with prayers and litanies and were making their way by the light of lamps through the churches of the various districts, a woman in the basilica established in honor of the same blessed Virgin, at the Capitol [or Campitello], saw her godmother, who had been dead for about a year.

Since she could not reach her to speak with her through the crowd flowing together, she tried to wait for her at a certain narrow passage, at a point where there could be no doubt that, once she had left the basilica, she would have to pass by. As the woman was passing, she immediately questioned her: “Are you my godmother, Marozia, who died some time ago?” This had been her name while she was alive.

When the other replied, “I am,” she asked, “And how is it with you now?”

She answered: “Until today I was held by no slight punishment, because, while still at a tender age, I defiled myself through the shameless enticements of wantonness with girls of my own age. Alas, I somehow consigned this very matter to oblivion and, although I confessed it to a priest, I did not receive a judgment or imposed penance.

“But today the Queen of the World poured out prayers for us and freed me, together with many others, from the places of punishment. So great a multitude has today been rescued from torments through her intercession that it exceeds the number of the entire Roman populace. Therefore we visit everywhere the holy places dedicated to that glorious Lady, our mistress, and eagerly offer her acts of thanksgiving for such great benefits of mercy.”

When her goddaughter remained uncertain about this and did not readily believe her words, the other added: “So that you may test and know for certain that what I am saying is true, know that when this year has passed you will undoubtedly die on this same feast. If, however, you live longer—which cannot happen—you will clearly prove that I have spoken falsely.”

After saying this, she vanished from the woman’s sight. The woman immediately put on a hair shirt and, anxious about her death, began to live more cautiously in accordance with what she had heard. What more is there to say? When nearly a year had passed, she began to fall ill during the vigils of the preceding day; on the very day of the feast she ended her life, just as had been foretold to her.

Here it should be noted—and it should not cause slight alarm—that because of the sin she had committed, which the woman mentioned above had consigned to oblivion, she endured punishments until the intervention of the undefiled Mother of God. [Col. 0586D–0587C; p. 603]

## CHAPTER FOUR. A Most Beautiful Apparition of the Saints in the Church of Saint Cecilia at Rome

Bishop Rainaldus of Como also told me this account, which he said he had learned from the venerable Humbert, formerly bishop of Saint Rufina.

“A priest,” he said, “was resting in the silence of night when his godfather, who had died, called to him in a vision, saying: ‘Come and see a spectacle that you will not be able to judge trivial.’ He then led him to the basilica of blessed Cecilia. In its atrium there appeared Agnes, Agatha, and Cecilia herself, together with a choir of many blessed virgins, conspicuous in the marvelous splendor of their dress and appearance.

“These women were preparing a magnificent seat, standing higher than the other benches arranged on either side. Suddenly the blessed Virgin Mary came with Peter, Paul, and David, surrounded by shining throngs of martyrs and other saints, and seated herself upon the prepared seat.

“While silence prevailed in that most holy assembly and all stood there reverently, a certain woman, although poor, yet decently clothed in a sheepskin garment, fell at the feet of the undefiled Virgin and begged her to have mercy on the already deceased patrician John.

“When the woman repeated this request three times in entreaty and could obtain no answer, she added: ‘You know, my lady, Queen of the World, that I am that wretched woman who used to lie naked and trembling in the atrium of your greater basilica. As soon as he saw me, that man pitied me with compassionate mercy and threw over me this skin, which he himself was wearing.’

“Then the blessed Mother of God said: ‘The man for whom you are asking is weighed down by a great mass of crimes. Yet he possessed these two virtues: he was compassionate toward the needy and was devoted to the holy places with great humility. For he frequently carried oil on his own shoulders and supplied fuel for the lamps of my Church.’

“When the other saints also bore witness to this concerning the patrician, asserting at the same time that he had done the same for their churches, the Queen of the World immediately ordered that the patrician be brought forward. Suddenly a multitude of demons dragged the aforementioned John, bound on every side with punitive cords and severely worn down by the roughness of the chains surrounding him.

“Then our Lady ordered him to be released and joined to the assemblies of the saints. But she ordered that the bonds from which he had been freed be placed upon and fastened around another man who was still living in this life.

“Then that assembly of saints was dissolved, and each one, departing in a different direction, vanished from the sight of the one who had witnessed it.

“The blessed Apostle Peter came to his own church, where at once a choir of all his successors, namely the Roman pontiffs, met him, wearing mitres and dressed for festal celebration. The blessed Peter himself, who until then had appeared clothed in Hebrew garments, as he is seen everywhere in paintings, then also received a tiara on his head; and, like the others, he was adorned on his body with episcopal vestments.

“Then they began to intone, with melodies and honey-sweet cries, the responsory called ‘You are the shepherd of the sheep.’ Thus they led him to the place of the priestly choir. When he arrived there, that prince of the apostles began the nocturnal office, saying: ‘O Lord, open my lips.’ Then, according to canonical custom, he recited the three psalms, as many readings, and the responsories appointed for the feasts of the apostles.

“When everything had been properly completed in order, and the morning praises had likewise been finished, the bell of that church sounded. Immediately the priest who had been seeing these things awoke, and the dream came to an end.” [Col. 0587C–0588C; p. 604]

Moreover, the same bishop mentioned above told me that a certain monk, whenever he passed daily before the holy altar of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, used to recite, according to custom, the following antiphon:

“Rejoice, Virgin Mother of God, immaculate; rejoice, you who received joy from the angel; rejoice, you who gave birth to the splendor of eternal light; rejoice, mother; rejoice, holy Virgin, Mother of God. You alone are an unmarried mother. Every creature praises you. Mother of Light, intercede for us.”

One day, as he was passing by and reciting this antiphon, he heard a voice proceeding from the same altar: “You have announced joy to me; joy will come to you.” [Col. 0588D]

## CHAPTER FIVE. By Reciting the Office of the Dead Every Day, a Man Is Introduced into the Heavenly Kingdom

The same bishop also told me that a certain brother did not use the daily office, nor indeed the solemn office of the saints, but only the office of the dead, in which he took delight.

When, having paid the debt of human nature, he stood before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge, a crowd of demons began vehemently to accuse him of this crime: that, neglecting the rule of ecclesiastical institution, he had scorned to render vows to God through the customary offices of the liturgical assembly.

Then the blessed Queen of the World, the ever-virgin Mary, and all the choirs of the saints with her came vigorously to his aid and united in interceding for him. “This man,” they said, “was our chaplain and minister; and because he always willingly took part in the funerals of the dead, he undoubtedly ministered to all of us. Therefore let this man, who while he lived devoted himself to pious services toward us, never fall into the hands of the wicked.”

Thus, through the prayers of the blessed Virgin and the supplication of all the saints, he was found worthy to pass into their company. The bishop who reported this matter did not know, however, whether that brother had returned to us and reported these things, or whether he had related them to others still living in this life. [Col. 0589A–0590A; p. 604]

I write these things to you familiarly, venerable brother, because I delight in your conversation, whatever it may be, as in a sweet banquet. My mind continually rejoices and grows eager whenever something occurs to me that may suitably be written to you.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0589]

605–606. OPUSCULUM THIRTY-FIVE. ON THE PORTRAITS OF THE CHIEF APOSTLES.

ARGUMENT.

He gives the reason why, in paintings, the apostle Paul is depicted on the right and Peter on the left: namely, because Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin, a name interpreted in Latin as “son of the right hand”; and he proves that this name most fittingly belongs to Paul. He also sets forth many prerogatives of that same Paul. Finally, he explains why the Church of Jerusalem, although Christ suffered in it, is not the head of all the Churches.

[Col. 0589B] To Lord DESIDERIUS, abbot of holy conversion [or, “way of life”], and to the religious community, PETER, a sinful monk, service in the Lord.

When I learned that Lord Martin had set out on the journey to you, I immediately ordered the notary to take down my words. But since, venerable father, I lived familiarly with you throughout the whole Lenten season, and we discussed orally whatever seemed to require discussion, and repeatedly made known whatever was to be communicated or considered, I can find nothing new that can be written to you now, since I reflect that everything which could be necessary has been repeatedly covered in our mutual conversation. What, then, shall I do? Having begun to speak, shall I foolishly fall silent because matter fails me?

# ON THE PORTRAITS OF THE CHIEF APOSTLES

## CHAPTER ONE. Why Peter is placed on the left and Paul on the right in paintings

[Col. 0589C]

But as I look upon the writer’s hand, armed with a pen and, as usual, poised for writing, a pleasing subject presents itself to me, upon which my mind is eagerly invited to discourse. For by this right hand of the notary there suddenly occurs to me the question which you yourself have very often put to me: why, in painted images throughout all the provinces adjoining Rome, Peter, who is first, is placed on the left, while Paul, his fellow apostle, is placed on the right, although, according to common understanding, the order of things demands that Peter, the prince of the apostolic senate, should rightfully occupy the Lord’s right side, and Paul, who is younger, the left. But it is altogether hard to suppose that devout and God-fearing antiquity admitted so outstanding and renowned an arrangement of the apostles inconsiderately and without reflection. For it must not be believed that the Emperor Constantine—indeed Pope Sylvester—and after them princes and priests, ever watchful and diligent in the letter of ecclesiastical discipline, would have judged this arrangement of so great princes unworthy of notice if they had considered it in any respect deserving of correction. Therefore, lest the order of this holy history appear disordered, let what seems to us be briefly made known to your holiness.

Who doubts that Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin? Now Benjamin in Hebrew is called in Latin “son of the right hand.” What wonder, then, if he is placed on the right who inherits, by paternal right, the name of the right hand? Indeed, so that the ancient history may plainly seem to suit blessed Paul, Scripture does not without reason say: “For when Rachel’s soul was departing in pain and death was already imminent, she called the name of her son Benoni, that is, ‘son of my sorrow’” (Gen. XXXV). But his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” By Rachel, whose name is said to mean “sheep” or “the beginning of sight,” the Church is not unfittingly signified. For she both lives innocently after the likeness of a sheep and burns in the depths of her being, through the pursuit of contemplation, to behold the form of her Redeemer, who said to the Jews asking him: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII). Thus, as Benjamin is born, his mother Rachel dies: when Saul is drawing near to the light of new rebirth, the Church is cruelly assailed by him through persecutions, as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Saul,” he says, “was ravaging the Church, entering houses and dragging off men and women, delivering them into custody” (Acts VIII).

[Col. 0590C]

Accordingly Rachel fittingly calls him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow,” whom Jacob calls Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand”: for Paul, who was the sorrow of Mother Church and in some manner killed her by attacking her while he himself was being born, was called the son of the right hand by God the Father, when through him divine power fought against the nations as through its mighty right hand, forcefully hurled the darts of words, inflicted saving wounds upon hearts, and, after enemies had been conquered and overthrown through him, triumphed gloriously. Hence Paul himself says to the Galatians: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the nations, immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood” (Gal. II). Therefore Paul is not undeservedly called son of the right hand, through whom the whole multitude of the nations, which is to be placed at God’s right hand, is gathered into the sacraments of faith. Girded with the word of God, which is the sword of the Spirit (Eph. VI), he still fights, even to the end of the age, against the fury of every vice and wicked spirit; and, like Christ’s lightning hand, hews down the stiff necks of those resisting God with the swords of heavenly utterance brandished aloft. Paul therefore rightly holds the dignity of the right side beside the Redeemer, since he is unquestionably exercising the power of the divine right hand. Does he not confess himself in some manner to be God’s right hand fighting against the devil when he says: “Thus I run, not as though toward an uncertainty; thus I fight, not as one beating the air” (I Cor. IX)?

## CHAPTER TWO. Paul’s prerogatives are set forth

Paul was caught up to the third heaven (II Cor. XII), where he also heard secret words which it is not permitted for human beings to utter. Who, moreover, does not know that earthly life signifies the left hand, while heavenly life signifies the right, as the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Cant. II)? The left hand is said to be under the head because the present life is trodden underfoot as despised beneath the mind of every elect person, which mind is undoubtedly the head of thoughts. But God’s right hand is said to embrace the bride because, when a faithful and holy soul is set aflame by the burning fire of her Creator, she is cherished on every side as if by divine embraces. He, therefore, who, still surrounded by the frailty of flesh, is known to have ascended to heavenly life is rightly called son of the right hand.

[Col. 0591D]

Almighty God continually extends this son of the right hand, as though his own right hand, over the whole breadth of the world, and by it gathers peoples of adoption into the unity of faith. The supreme husbandman works this right hand through the threshing floor of his Church and winnows spiritual harvests by it, so that, when the grains of mystical wheat have been cleansed, he may bring them into the heavenly granaries. God extends this right hand far and wide when Paul traverses the whole world in order to gather nations into the sacrament of faith. For the greater the strength of charity with which he burns, the more exceedingly he changes his place by wandering from region to region. He longs to pass from one place to another because the spur of the charity which fills him drives him onward. For, though far from the Romans, he writes: “I make mention of you always in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey, by God’s will, to come to you. For I desire to see you” (Rom. I). Detained at Ephesus, he writes to the Corinthians: “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you” (II Cor. XXII). Again, while remaining at Ephesus, he speaks to the Galatians: “I wish that I were with you now and could change my voice” (Gal. IV). Also, shut up in prison at Rome, because he is not permitted to go himself to the Philippians, he promises to send them his disciple, saying: “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how matters stand with you” (Philip. II).

[Col. 0592B]

Even bound with chains and detained at Ephesus, he writes to the Colossians: “For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit” (Col. II). Behold how the apostolic heart is kindled by the fire of fraternal love, how it is constrained by longing to labor for the salvation of the nations! Here he is held in body; there he is led in spirit. He bestows the affection of paternal love upon those present and extends it to those absent. To those before him he offers deeds; to those who hear him he expresses his wishes. He is effectively present to those with whom he is not; nor is he absent from those with whom he is. We understand his love better if we consider further his words to the Corinthians. For he says: “I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I shall pass through Macedonia, but perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter” (I Cor. XVI). What is it that so anxiously divides him among so many places except that he is bound to all by one charity? For charity, which is accustomed to unite things divided, compels Paul’s one heart to be divided among many. Yet it gathers that heart in God all the more ardently as it scatters it more broadly through holy desires. Thus, by preaching Paul wishes to speak to all at once; by loving he wishes to see all at once. For, while remaining in the flesh, he wishes to live for all, and, by passing from the flesh through the sacrifice of faith, he wishes to benefit all.

Nor is it surprising that the outstanding preacher burns more fervently in fraternal charity, or that an abundance of true love overflows in him above all mortals, since the fountain of life, which calls him a vessel of election (Acts IX), determined to pour itself abundantly into him and deigned incomparably to water him with the streams of its mysteries. Hence he says: “Do you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER THREE. Paul is distinguished above all others by a wondrous privilege

This the Savior of the world bestowed upon blessed Paul by the privilege of singular grace, a privilege which he granted to no mortal after the mystery of his Incarnation. For after that blessed and divine humanity of the Redeemer was raised to sit at the right hand of the Father’s majesty, so that he no longer associated bodily with human beings but rather presided over the powers of heaven, he taught Paul so effectively—not through a teacher but especially by himself—and entrusted to him all the mysteries of his deeds, that Paul not only had no need at all of the teaching of his predecessors, but even surpassed them in the full depth of all heavenly wisdom. Thus Peter himself, first of the apostles, marvels at Paul’s wisdom, saying: “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, as also in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters, among which are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort” (II Pet. III).

[Col. 0593B]

Paul himself testifies that, in learning the mysteries of evangelical teaching, he had not some human being as his teacher but God as his special instructor; in the opening of his letter to the Galatians he says: “Paul, an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. I). For the fountain of eternal life, like an immeasurable torrent, poured its entire self at once into the vessel of its election, whereas into the other apostles it poured out the streams of its wisdom through long intervals of time. And a little later: “For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to human beings; for neither did I receive it from a human being nor learn it, but through revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.). What the Lord taught Peter, while still mortal, through many demonstrations, he bestowed all at once upon blessed Paul when he was already established in the glory of the Father’s majesty. It is as if a teacher, while a private person, teaches disciples, but after he has ascended to possess the scepters of royal rule, chooses out from among many one outstanding person, after setting aside the crowds of retainers, to instruct more nobly.

Therefore, to return to the point from which the discussion began: when blessed Peter is placed on the right, his primacy, which he received among the other apostles, is honored. But when Paul occupies the place of that same right side, the mystical sacrament of the figure of Benjamin, whose son he is, is recalled. Yet it is not without mystery that blessed Peter holds the left side of the Lord. For active life is signified by him. And just as contemplative life is expressed by the right hand, so active life is expressed by the left. That present life—that is, active life—is figured through blessed Peter is shown especially by this: as the Gospel history very frequently testifies, Peter loves the Lord more than all his fellow disciples (John XX), while the Lord bestows upon John, rather than Peter, the prerogative of altogether special love (John XIII).

[Col. 0593D]

For contemplative life is signified by John, but active life by Peter, as has been said. For all the saints in this life, in the likeness of Peter, love God more and are, as it were, loved less, since they endure for his sake the hard troubles of labors but, still surrounded by mortal flesh, do not attain the sweetness of his embrace. But those who are now with God in some sense love him less and are loved more, since they feel no storms of labor for his sake and yet enjoy the delights of his intimate familiarity. It is therefore not surprising if blessed Peter sometimes seems to hold the left side, since by the authority of the Scriptures he also contains the figure of active life.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Why blessed Paul has no chair of his own

One thing concerning blessed Paul appears outstanding: although all the apostles, distributed among the regions of the earth, possess their own chairs, he, because he holds none in particular, seems in some respect to preside over all in common. (See the scholia at the end of the opusculum.) Since he founded the universal Church throughout the whole world, it is fitting that, as he scattered the seed of faith in all places, so he should also hold the right of presidency in all places. For he says to the Corinthians: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV). But to the Romans: “I have,” he says, “glory in Christ Jesus before God, in the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit; so that from Jerusalem, and round about as far as Illyricum, I have filled all places with the Gospel of Christ. But I so preached this Gospel not where Christ had been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation; but as it is written: ‘Those to whom no announcement concerning him was made shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand’” (Rom. XV; Isa. LII).

[Col. 0594C]

This, then, is the reason why Paul holds no chair in particular: because, if we dare compare lesser things with the highest, he seems, after the likeness of Christ and without prejudice to the right of the other apostles, to preside over all the Churches.

But according to common understanding, because the Lord suffered at Jerusalem, the Church of Jerusalem rather than Rome ought to preside over all the Churches. Nevertheless, since by the authority of the canons the Roman Church holds first place, Alexandria second, Antioch third, Constantinople fourth, and Jerusalem now fifth, it is evident that the Lord and Savior does not preside by a special right over any single chair, but that one shepherd presides universally over all. It is therefore clear that the order of the Churches has been established according to Peter’s privilege, not according to the incomparable excellence of the Redeemer. For what all the apostles possess, each according to his measure, through the grace of a bestowed gift, Christ possesses in its entirety through the sovereignty of his natural majesty. Therefore Paul bears a certain likeness to Christ, if it may be said, in that he presides not merely over one Church but over all.

Blessed Paul, then, does not without reason hold the right side in paintings, since this is demanded not only by a more abundant harvest of fruits but also by the sacrament of figurative interpretation. My mind still longs to write more on this theme, but the bearer of this letter, who is hurrying to you and would rather fly than run, does not allow me even the slightest delay for writing. May divine clemency command you, most beloved ones, that your holy fraternity not cease to pray for me.

611. SCHOLIA.

Clearly, because he himself (Paul) founded the universal Church throughout the whole world, it is fitting that, just as he scattered the seed of faith everywhere, so also he should hold everywhere the right of presiding. In this Epistle, blessed Peter Damian seems to attribute rather too much to Paul. For although what he recounts concerning the deeds of that Apostle is true, it must nevertheless be understood with caution, since Peter alone—not Paul—is the shepherd and prince of the whole world. Therefore the praise is indeed true [Col. 0595B] that the Church bestows upon him when it says, “preacher throughout the whole world”; and what he himself asserts is true: “My daily urgency, the concern for all the Churches” (2 Cor. 11). Yet it is absolutely certain that the very honor which, at first sight, Cardinal Damian confers upon Saint Paul belongs more properly to Saint Peter, concerning whom Leo the Great says (Letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica):

> “Among the most blessed Apostles, although there was a likeness of honor, there was a certain distinction of authority; and although the election of all was equal, nevertheless to one was given the precedence over the others. From this pattern, the distinction among bishops also arose.”

Saint John Chrysostom says (Homily 87 on John):

> “Why, leaving the others aside, does he address Peter alone about these matters? He was the mouth, the prince, and the summit of the apostolic assembly. For this reason Paul also went up to see him before the others.”

Thus we shall understand Damian according to the mind of Gregory the Great (Gregory, *Commentary on 1 Kings*, chapter 4): insofar as the apostolic office of preaching the Gospel and absolving sins is concerned, we should consider all the Apostles—not merely Paul—to have been sent throughout the whole world [Col. 0596B], though with a certain subordination to Peter, who has been placed over the universal flock, as Saint Cyprian teaches in *On the Unity of the Church* and in Letter 55 to Pope Cornelius.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0595]

## 613–614. THIRTY-SIXTH OPUSCULUM: ON DIVINE OMNIPOTENCE IN RESTORING WHAT HAS BEEN CORRUPTED AND IN MAKING THINGS DONE UN-DONE

### Argument

He discusses clearly and at length God’s omnipotence, eternity, infinity, providence, and other matters of this kind, exceedingly lofty and obscure, against those who dared to set something like a limit to divine power, asserting that God cannot make things done become undone. He proves this to be false by the most compelling arguments. Finally, he reveals at length to Abbot Desiderius his goodwill and affection toward the monastery of Cassino, setting them before his eyes as though in a painting.

[Col. 0595C] To Lord Desiderius, most reverend rector of the monastery of Cassino, and to the entire holy community, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the kiss of peace in the Holy Spirit.

## ON DIVINE OMNIPOTENCE IN RESTORING WHAT HAS BEEN CORRUPTED AND IN MAKING THINGS DONE UN-DONE

### Chapter I. That God can do many things which he does not will

He who alone is rescued from the storms of the sea, while he sees the net still endangered among the rocks and reefs, amid threatening and swelling heaps of waves, is inhuman if he does not grieve for his companions laboring in danger. I, therefore, having laid aside the episcopate, rejoice that I have been set, as it were, upon the sands; but when I see you battered by winds and tempests, and tossed amid the yawning chasms of the sea, I sigh not without brotherly compassion. He is mistaken, Father—he is mistaken— [Col. 0595D] who trusts that he can at once be both a monk and a servant of the court. Poorly does he trade who presumes to abandon the cloisters of monks so that he may carry the warfare of the world. A fish rescued sound from the waves is sound not so that it may live for itself, but so that it may feed others. We are called and drawn out so that we may live for others and die to ourselves. The hunter loves the stag, but so that he may make it his food; he pursues goats and hunts hares, but so that he himself may prosper and they may cease to exist. People also love us, but not for us: they love us for themselves and desire to turn us into their pleasures. When we pursue them into outward things, what else do we do but reject our monk who was hiding within?

At once the condition of a life striving toward higher things is overturned, the discipline’s rigor is weakened, the restraint of silence is dissolved, and mouths are opened to pour out whatever desire suggests. Hence arose the matter that now comes to mind: whether God can restore a virgin after her fall. For once, as you may remember, when we were both reclining at table and something said by blessed Jerome came up in conversation, he said: “I speak boldly: although God can do all things, he cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. He can indeed free her from punishment, but he cannot crown one who has been corrupted.”

Although I was fearful, since I would hardly have dared to dispute the testimony of so great a man, I nevertheless told you, my like-minded father, plainly what I thought. “I confess,” I said, “that this opinion has never been able to please me. I attend not to who says it, but to what is said. It seems exceedingly dishonorable that impossibility should be so lightly ascribed to him who can do all things, unless this is understood under the sacrament of a higher meaning.”

You, on the other hand, replied that what had been said was established and sufficiently authoritative: namely, that God cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. Then, running through many matters in long and extended arguments, you finally brought the conclusion of your definition to this point [Col. 0597A], saying that God cannot do this for no other reason than that he does not will to do it.

To this I replied: “If God can do nothing that he does not will, while he does nothing except what he wills, then he can do absolutely none of the things that he does not do. It follows, then, that we should freely confess that God does not make it rain today for this reason: that he cannot; that he does not raise up the sick for this reason: that he cannot; that he does not kill the unjust, and does not free the saints from their oppressions, for this reason: that he cannot. God does not do these and many other things because he does not will to do them; and because he does not will to do them, he cannot do them. It follows, therefore, that whatever God does not do, he cannot do at all.”

This seems so absurd and ridiculous that such an assertion cannot suit not only almighty God, but even a frail human being [Col. 0597B]. For there are many things that we do not do and yet can do. If, however, we happen to find something of this kind in mystical and allegorical Scriptures, it should be received cautiously and reverently rather than boldly and freely proclaimed according to the letter.

So it is with what the angel says to Lot as he hurries toward Zoar: “Hasten, therefore, and save yourself there, because I cannot do anything until you have entered there” (Gen. 19). And: “I regret that I made man” (Gen. 6). Likewise, Scripture says that God, foreseeing the future, was touched inwardly by grief, and many things of this kind. If anything like this is found inserted in the divine books, it must not immediately and indiscriminately be spread abroad with the brazen presumption of common speech; rather, it must be expressed under the discipline of modest and sober language. For if it is disseminated among the common people that God is impotent in some respect—something which it is impious to say—the uneducated populace is immediately confused, and the Christian faith is disturbed, not without great danger to souls.

God is said not to be able to do something in precisely the same way in which he is said not to know it: namely, whatever is evil, just as he cannot do it, so he does not know how to do it. He cannot, for example, lie, swear falsely, or do anything unjust, although he says through the prophet: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45).

But when he says in the Gospel, “Concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father” (Matt. 24; Mark 13), this must undoubtedly be understood to mean that the disciple does not know this, while he himself is wholly ignorant of nothing [Col. 0597D]. For since Jesus—the Word of the Father—established all times, and all things were made through him (John 1), what logic would allow him who knows everything to be ignorant of the day of judgment, which is a part of time? Yet concerning the same Savior the Apostle writes: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). Why are they hidden, unless because they are not openly manifest to everyone?

When, after the Resurrection, the disciples again asked him about that day of judgment, he said: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). It is as though he said: “It is not beneficial for you to know this, so that this suspension in uncertainty may exercise you more and more continually in works of piety and restrain you from every vanity, if any should creep in” [Col. 0598A]. Thus he knows for himself what he does not know for the Apostles. He proves this unmistakably here, when he declares that the Father, with whom he is one, knows this: “For I and the Father are one” (John 10).

Thus, according to the sound of the words, he asserts that he somehow does not know what the Father knows, just as he is sometimes signified as somehow not possessing what the Father possesses. Hence the Apostle also says: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15), as though the Father did not possess the kingdom so long as he himself held it, and as though, once he had handed it over to the Father, he himself would no longer hold it. Yet to hand the kingdom over to God the Father means nothing other than to lead believers to contemplate the appearance of God the Father.

The Son hands the kingdom over to God the Father when, through the mediator between God and human beings, the multitude of the faithful is transferred into contemplation of the eternal divinity—that is, when the dispensation of likenesses through angels, principalities, powers, and virtues is no longer necessary. In their person it is not unfittingly understood that the following is said in the Song of Songs to the bride: “We will make for you likenesses of gold with silver ornaments, until the king is in his chamber” (Song 1)—that is, until Christ is in his hidden place. “For our life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, appears, then we also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3).

Before this happens, we now see through a mirror in an enigma—that is, through likenesses—but then face to face (1 Cor. 13). This contemplation is promised to us as the end of all our actions and the eternal perfection of our joys. “For we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

What he said to his servant Moses, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3), and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (John 8), we shall contemplate when we see him eternally. For he says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). This will happen when the Lord comes and brings to light the things hidden in darkness [Col. 0598D], when the darkness of this mortality and corruption has passed away.

Then our morning will come, of which the Psalm says: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see” (Ps. 5). The words “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15) are understood to refer to this contemplation: that is, when he has led the righteous—among whom the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, now reigns through faith—to the contemplation of God the Father (1 Tim. 2).

Many such statements are found, finally, in the sayings of Scripture. If we are content to receive them according to the superficial letter, they will not be able to pour into us the light of truth; rather, they will produce the darkness of obscurity. Therefore, when it is said that God cannot do or know some evil, this must not be referred to ignorance or impossibility, but rather to the perpetual rectitude of his will. Since he does not will evil, he is rightly said neither to know nor to be able to do any evil. But whatever he wills, he unquestionably can do, as Scripture testifies: “But you, master of power, judge with tranquility and dispose of us with great reverence; for power is present with you whenever you will” (Wis. 12).

### Chapter II. That the will of God is the cause of all things’ existence

The will of God is the cause of all things, whether visible or invisible, so that they exist. Indeed, before created things proceeded into the visible forms of their own appearances, they already lived truly and essentially in the will of their maker: “What was made,” John says, “in him was life” (John 1). And in the Apocalypse he likewise testifies that the twenty-four elders said: “You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created” (Rev. 4).

It first says that they existed, and afterward that they were created, because what was expressed outwardly through the work of creation already existed inwardly in the providence and plan of the Creator. Moreover, just as God’s will is the cause that things not yet created come originally into being, so it is likewise an effective cause that things which have been lost return to the order of their former condition: “Surely I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord? Rather, I desire that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18).

To return, then, to the matter previously introduced: what prevents God from being able to raise up a virgin after her fall? Is it that he cannot because he does not will to do so, and that he does not will to do so because it is evil—just as God is said neither to will nor to be able to lie, swear falsely, or do anything unjust? But far be it from us to say that it is evil for a violated woman to become a virgin. Indeed, just as it is evil for a virgin to be violated, so it would undoubtedly be good for one who had been violated to return to virginity, if the order of divine disposition permitted it.

For example, for a human being after the fall to undergo death’s punishment was evil, although it occurred by God’s just judgment. God did not make death (Wis. 1), since he himself is rather the death of death, as he says through the prophet Hosea: “I will be your death, O death” (Hos. 13; 1 Cor. 15). Indeed, at least after the mystery of our redemption, it would certainly be good for a human being to become immortal, if divine mercy were to dissolve the sentence once pronounced.

God should not be said either to refuse or to be unable to do this because it would be evil for a human being to become immortal. Rather, by his just judgment and for the increase of our salvation, he willed that only so much of the punishment of redeemed humanity should remain as he himself knew to be appropriate.

In this way, then, it is evil for a virgin to remain corrupted after violation; but it would be good if God were to restore in her the seal of virginity. Yet even if God does not do this at all—whether to frighten virgins, so that they may fear losing what afterward they cannot recover [Col. 0600A]; or because justice and equity dictate that what she threw away as something worthless through the allurements of the flesh, she should not be able to restore even through the lamentations of repentance; or certainly so that, while she sees the signs of her own ruin remaining in herself, she may devote herself continually to more severe remedies for her affliction—whether, then, the violated virgin does not return to her former integrity for these or for other reasons of heavenly providence, God must nevertheless by no means be said to be unable to do this, but rather unwilling, so that the freedom of the most equitable will may be preserved and impotence—far be such a thought—may not be ascribed to majesty.

God cannot do what is evil because he cannot even will it. Yet this must not be referred to impossibility, but rather to the natural goodness of his singular mercy. What is good he can will and do, even though, through some consideration of his prudence or providence, he may do certain good things rarely or never.

Otherwise, before the Savior’s coming one might have said that God could not create a Son from the Virgin’s womb—something he had never done and was going to do only once. Even if he had never done it, he could both will and do it, because it was good. How, then, could God be unable to raise up a virgin after her fall, when he is undoubtedly almighty and this is good?

### Chapter III. That without doubt God can restore a virgin after her fall

The raising up of a virgin after her fall is understood in two ways [Col. 0600C]: either according to the fullness of merit or according to the integrity of the flesh. Let us therefore see whether God can accomplish both.

According to merit, the Apostle calls the community of the faithful a virgin when he says to the Corinthians: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). For there were not only virgins among that people of God, but also many who were bound by marriage, or who practiced continence after losing their virginity.

And the Lord says through the prophet: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her again? Will she not be called polluted and defiled? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3). This return to the Lord plainly means, insofar as the quality of merits is concerned, that a corrupted woman is made whole and a prostitute is restored as a virgin.

Why else does the same bridegroom say: “I will no longer remember any of your sins” (Jer. 31)? In the carnal embrace of a man’s marriage, the virgin generally gives herself to the bridal chamber, and, after the corruption of the flesh, the bond of love, and the loss of chastity, she departs polluted. By contrast, the one to whom the heavenly bridegroom has joined himself immediately washes away the stains of disgrace and calls her back to the flower of fragrant chastity. From a brothel he restores a virgin; from corruption, he restores integrity.

Hence we know that many men and women, after the abominable enticements of pleasure, have attained such purity of religious life that they not only surpassed in holiness any who were chaste and modest, but also exceeded the merits of many virgins, which are by no means to be despised [Col. 0601A]. To them is repaid not merely the measure of their former merit; rather, together with the remission of guilt, the accumulation of added reward is undoubtedly increased.

Behold, it has been proved, I think, that according to merit God can raise up a virgin after her fall. But according to the flesh, who, even if of deranged mind, would doubt that he who raises up the fallen and releases the bound (Ps. 145), who finally heals every sickness and every disease (Matt. 4), could restore the seal of virginity?

Indeed, he who fashioned the body itself from the most tenuous fluid of seed, distinguished it into the appearance of human form through the varied lines of its limbs, and brought into being a creature that previously did not exist—could he not recover one that already existed but had been damaged? I openly confess it—yes, I confess it—and, fearing no quibble from contentious disputation, I firmly affirm that almighty God can make any woman who has married many times a virgin again, and restore in her very flesh the seal of incorruption, just as it was when she came forth from her mother’s womb.

I have said this not to disparage blessed Jerome, who spoke from pious devotion, but to refute with the invincible reasoning of faith those who, taking occasion from his words, assert that God is impotent.

### Chapter IV. How it can happen that what has been done has not been done

[Col. 0601C]

Finally, concerning the objection made by many in this matter of disputation, I see that I must answer under the judgment of your holiness. They say: “If, as you assert, God is omnipotent in all things, can he bring it about that things which have been done have not been done? He can certainly destroy anything that has been done, so that it no longer exists; but it cannot be seen how he could bring it about that things which have been done had not been done. It can happen that from now onward Rome does not exist; but how could it happen that it was not founded in antiquity? No opinion can grasp this.”

With God inspiring me, I shall answer them as follows. First, I think my challenger should be admonished with Solomon’s words: “Do not seek what is too great for you, and do not investigate what is beyond you” (Sir. 3). Then it must be said that what God does is something, whereas what God does not do is nothing: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1).

Of him it is written elsewhere: “He who made the things that are to be” (Eccl. 3). Likewise: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sir. 18). And the Apostle says: “He who made the things that do not exist” (Rom. 4).

All these testimonies of Scripture plainly attest that God made what did not exist; they do not say that he destroyed what existed, but that he created future things, not that he abolished past things. Although God is also often read to have overthrown something in order to bring about something better—for example, the world through the flood of waters (Gen. 7), and the Pentapolis through the burning of fire (Gen. 19)—he took away their existence and their future existence in such a way that he did not at all take away their having existed.

Yet if you carefully consider the merits of the wicked people who were then destroyed, since they pursued vanities and empty things, tending not toward being but toward nothingness, you may rightly judge that they did not truly exist. Hence Scripture testifies that they complained in the affliction of their spirit:

> “Short and wearisome is the time of our life, and there is no relief at the end of a human being, and no one has been known to return from the underworld. For we were born from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been. We shall be as though we had not been, they say, because even now, when they seemed to exist, they belonged rather to nothingness than to true being” (Wis. 2).

“I am who I am, and this you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3). Whoever departs from him who truly is must cease to be, because he tends toward nothingness.

Hence, again, they are said to groan:

> “Our body will be reduced to ashes, and our spirit will be dispersed like soft air. Our life will pass like the traces of a cloud and will dissolve like a mist driven away by the sun’s ray. Our name will be forgotten, and our time is the passing of a very slight shadow” (Wis. 2).

Therefore the prophet says: “All the nations are before him as though they did not exist, and they are regarded by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40).

## 620

Solomon also says: “Before you the whole world is like a moment on a balance and like a drop of morning dew” (Wis. 11). Countless similar statements are found in Scripture, by which wicked people are compared with exceedingly slight or worthless things, or are said to be nothing even when they seem powerful.

Hence David says: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. 36). For when they swell with riches, when they arrogantly exalt themselves above others, and finally when they oppress their inferiors through the violence of tyranny, then, I say, they are more truly nothing, the farther they are from him who truly and supremely is.

### Chapter V. On future contingents and the use of philosophy in sacred disputation

[Col. 0602D]

But what do those vain people and introducers of sacrilegious doctrine intend, who, while setting traps of their questions for others, fail to notice that they themselves first fall headlong into them? While placing frivolous inquiries as stumbling blocks before those who walk simply, they themselves rather strike against the stone of offense.

“Can God,” they ask, “bring it about that, after something has once been done, it has not been done?”—as though this impossibility seemed to apply only to past things, and were not likewise found in present and future times. For whatever exists now, so long as it exists, cannot not exist. Likewise, what will exist cannot not exist, although some things can equally happen or not happen: for example, my riding today or not riding, seeing a friend or not seeing one, rain falling or the air being clear.

The wise people of this age customarily call such things “contingent either way,” because they can equally happen and not happen. Yet they are called “either way” more according to the variable nature of things than according to the consequence of statements. According to the natural order of changing circumstances, it can happen that it rains today, and it can also happen that it does not rain. But as far as the consequence of reasoning is concerned, if it is going to rain, then it is altogether necessary that it rain; and therefore it is entirely impossible that it not rain.

What is said about past things consequently applies no less to present and future things: just as everything that was must have been, so everything that is, so long as it is, must be; and everything that is going to be must be going to be. Therefore, as far as the order of reasoning is concerned, whatever was cannot not have been; whatever is cannot not be; and whatever is going to be cannot not be going to be.

Let the blind rashness of those who are unskilled among the wise and ask vain questions take note of this. If they perversely refer these matters, which belong to the art of reasoning, to God, then they make him wholly impotent and powerless not only in past things but also in present and future things.

Because they have not yet learned the elements of language [Col. 0603C], through the obscure darkness of their arguments they lose the clear foundation of faith. Still ignorant of what is taught to children in school, they thrust the calumnies of their complaints into the divine mysteries. And because, even among the rudiments of learners and of human arts, they have been unable to acquire any expertise, they disturb the purity of ecclesiastical discipline with the cloud of their curiosity.

The arguments that proceed from dialecticians or rhetoricians are plainly not easily applicable to the mysteries of divine power. May it be far from us that things invented to serve as instruments of syllogisms or as conclusions of statements should stubbornly intrude into sacred laws and oppose the necessities of their conclusions to divine power.

Yet if this expertise in human arts is ever applied to the treatment of sacred writings, it must not arrogantly seize for itself the right of mastery. Rather, like a maidservant serving her mistress, it should submit in a certain obedience of service, lest, if it leads, it go astray and, while following the sequence of external words, lose the light of inward power and the straight path of truth.

For who cannot plainly see that, if faith is granted to these arguments according to the order of the words, divine power would be shown to be impotent at every moment of time? According to the objection of the frivolous question, God is unable to bring it about either that things once done were not done, or conversely that things not done were done; that things which now exist, so long as they exist, do not exist; that things which are going to exist will not exist; or, conversely, that things which are not going to exist will exist.

The ancient investigators of the liberal arts, both pagans and participants in the Christian faith, treated this question at length. Yet none of them dared to rush into such madness as to ascribe to God the mark of impossibility or—if he was a Christian—to doubt his omnipotence. They discussed the consequence of necessity or impossibility according to the remarkable power of the art alone, without making any mention of God in these disputes.

But these people, who introduce an old question in a new form, while striving to know things higher than they can comprehend, rather dull the edge of their minds, because they do not fear to offend the very author of light.

Therefore, since this question is shown to pertain not to an examination of the power of divine majesty but rather to expertise in the dialectical art, and not to the power or substance of things but to the manner and order of reasoning and the consequence of words, it has no place in the mysteries of the Church, though it is debated in schools by immature students.

For it does not concern the rule of faith or moral goodness, but fluency of speech and the polish of words. Therefore let it be enough for us to defend in brief compass the faith that we hold; as for the wise of this age, we yield to them what is theirs (1 Cor. 3). Let those who wish have the letter that kills, provided that, through God’s mercy, the Spirit who gives life does not depart from us.

## 622. Chapter VI. That God encloses all things—both times and places—together within the bosom of his presence

[Col. 0604C]

It is therefore established that almighty God encloses all ages in the treasure of his eternal wisdom in such a way that nothing can approach him or pass away from him through the moments of time. Remaining in that ineffable citadel of his majesty, he contemplates all things established in the sight of his presence with one simple act of perception, so that neither do past things ever wholly pass away from him, nor do future things ever succeed to him.

For him, to exist always and to be the same is one and the same throughout eternity. While he circumscribes everything that passes away, he encloses within himself the courses of all times. And just as he restrains all times within himself without transition, so likewise he contains within himself all places without spatial intervals.

Hence he plainly says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Hence his Wisdom says: “Alone I encompassed the circuit of heaven” (Sir. 24). Concerning this Solomon also says: “For although she is one, she can do all things; and remaining in herself, she renews all things” (Wis. 7).

And again: “If heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built for you!” (2 Chron. 6). Concerning his Spirit it is also written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things” (Wis. 1). Again it is said: “For he is the maker of all things, possessing all power and seeing all things” (Wis. 7).

And the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). Again it is written of him: “He measures heaven with the span of his hand and encloses the whole earth in his fist” (Acts 7; Isa. 40).

The interior and superior position belongs to the throne over which he presides. By measuring heaven with his span and enclosing the earth in his fist, he is shown to be outside, all around, the things he created. For what is enclosed within is contained externally by the one who encloses it.

Thus, through the throne over which he presides, he is understood to be within and above; through the fist by which he contains, he is signified to be outside and beneath.
