For he himself remains within all things, outside all things, above all things, and beneath all things. He is superior through power, inferior through sustaining, exterior through greatness, and interior through subtlety.

Where, then, could anything exist apart from him, who, although nowhere present through bodily bulk, is absent nowhere through his uncircumscribed substance? Of him the Apostle says: “All things hold together in him.” And again: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Col. 1).

He is, so to speak, a placeless place, which contains all places in itself without itself moving through places. Although he fills all things together, he does not occupy parts of a place through parts of himself; rather, he is wholly everywhere—neither more spread out in larger places nor more contracted in smaller ones, neither higher in lofty places nor more humbled in the lowest, neither greater in great things nor smaller in small things. He is one, the same, simple, and equal everywhere. He needs no creature, but every creature needs him.

For even before he created the angelic powers, before anything temporal had existed [Col. 0605C], he possessed the full and perfect riches of immortality and glory. Therefore, in creating what did not exist, he was impelled not by the necessity of solitude or of any lack, but summoned solely by the goodness of his own mercy.

Nor could the condition of created things add anything to his blessedness, since he is so full and perfect in himself and through himself that nothing is added to him when a creature exists, nor does anything depart from him when it perishes. “All the rivers flow into the sea, and the sea is not filled” (Eccl. 1).

### Chapter VII. On God’s simple and single, yet distinct, knowledge and providence of all things
It is plainly as coeternal with God to be able to do all things as to know all things, and likewise to exist always. Thus, dispensing the laws of all natures from that supreme hinge of reality, He embraces all times—past, present, and future—within the secrets of His providence, so that nothing entirely new is added to Him, nor does anything depart from Him through the succession of moments. Nor does He contemplate different things with different looks, as though, when He attends to the past, He were disengaged from the present or the future; or again, when He considers the present or the future, He were to turn His eyes away from the past. Rather, with the single and simple gaze of His most immediate majesty, He comprehends everything simultaneously.

Nor does He discern all this confusedly or indistinctly; He distinguishes everything and separates each thing according to its own proper character. Certainly, one who sits in a theater does not see everything at once: when he directs his gaze before him, he does not see what is behind him. But one who stands not within the theater but above it, elevated over it, comprehends the entire interior circuit of the theater on every side in a single glance. So almighty God, because He incomparably rises above all things that pass through their courses, sees all things simultaneously and in their present reality, subject to His sight.

And so that what we are saying may be grasped not only by a lively intellect but also easily understood by anyone slow of mind: within this very brief instant of time in which we say the word “heaven,” there is greater change for us than there is for God in looking upon all the infinite spans of the ages simultaneously. For when the first syllable of this word is spoken, the second still remains; and when the second sounds, the first has already passed away. But God, in one single and ineffable act of His contemplation, sees everything simultaneously, and by seeing distinguishes it. Encompassing all things, He penetrates them; penetrating them, He encompasses them.

Hence the apostle Peter says: “Let this one thing not escape you, beloved: with God one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (II Peter I). And because the number one thousand is complete, he set a thousand years for the length and duration of all the ages. Hence the Psalmist also says: “A thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday, which has passed away” (Psalm 89:4); for whatever is expected by us as future is already wholly known to God and is reckoned as though it were past.

For He is, as He Himself says of Himself, “the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 1:8). And through the prophet: “Before Me no god was formed, and after Me there shall be none” (Isaiah 43:10).

Indeed, because He rises ineffably above all things at the summit of reality, and embraces, as it were, within a circle of His own depth and eternal counsel not only all the spans of time but also places and all creatures, viewing all these things in one single act of contemplation and always with one simple gaze, He is rightly called alone powerful, alone eternal, and alone immortal.

Hence the Apostle says: “To the King of the ages, immortal and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory” (1 Timothy 1:17). And again: “Blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:15–16). For angelic power, although it is powerful, is so not from itself but from Him. Although it is immortal and its blessed life is enclosed by no end whatever, nevertheless, because it changes places and times, it must not be called coeternal with its Creator, since He Himself is, naturally and essentially, power itself, immortality itself, and eternity itself.

Hence Moses says: “The Lord shall reign forever and beyond” (Exodus 15:18). Angelic blessedness, moreover, according to the measure of its created condition, is not improperly regarded as eternal, since it is shown to be subject to no limit whatever. It is rightly said to live forever, because it never ceases to live blessedly. But He not only reigns forever; He reigns forever and beyond, because He holds all the volumes of the ages within the bosom of His providence. He comprehends them not as past or future but, truly, as present and subject to His sight, with the keenest discernment. By the command of His dominion He governs all things; everything obeys His laws. He arranges all creatures according to the inclination of His will; He regulates and orders the manner of life of all; He distinguishes the forms and species of all things; He grants to each, as He wills, appropriate capacities of power. From Him and through Him is whatever exists; without Him, whatever exists is undoubtedly nothing.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the eternity of God

For almighty God there is no yesterday or tomorrow, but an everlasting today. Nothing flows away from Him, and nothing is added to Him; nothing in Him is changeable or different from Himself. That “today” is unchangeable, unfailing, inaccessible eternity, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be diminished. Everything that among us slips away and runs its course, or changes through the alternation of times, stands with Him in the present day and remains immovably.

In that “today,” that day on which this world took its beginning still remains unmoved; in it also is already present the day on which the world will be judged according to the equity of eternal judgment. Nor does any failure of mutability enter that light which, without approach, illumines what it chooses, and, without withdrawal, abandons what it rejects; for, remaining immutable in itself, it orders all mutable things. Thus He created things that pass away within themselves in such a way that what has been created cannot pass away with respect to Him. Nor does time flow inwardly before His sight, as it runs outwardly among us through external things.

Thus in His eternity everything remains fixed, while externally the unfixed volumes of the ages continually pour forth. For God’s one day is His eternity. The Psalmist sees that day neither closed by an end nor opened by a beginning when he says: “One day in Your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 84:10).

What, then, is there that He cannot do with respect to all things past or future—He who fixes and establishes all things that have been done or are to be done, without any transition, in the presence of His majesty? That time which preceded the things that were made is equally present to Him without passing away, as is that time which encompasses all things that will come afterward.

Hence in the Scriptures, which were spoken by the prophetic Spirit, the past is often found in place of the future, and things to be done long afterward are narrated as though they had already taken place. Thus the Lord, through the prophet, says of what He would suffer: “I gave My body to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn My face away from those who reproached and spat upon Me” (Isaiah 50:6). Of His resurrection He says: “I have risen, and I am still with You” (Psalm LXVII). Of His ascension and the sending of the gifts of the Holy Spirit it is said: “Ascending on high, He led captivity captive; He gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). For in the eyes of that Wisdom from which these words proceeded, all times stand together—future and past—as truly present, fixed, and always immovable.

“ They gave gall for My food” (Psalm 69:21) is therefore equivalent to “they will give,” and “They pierced My hands and My feet” (Psalm 22:16) is the same as “they will pierce.”

Let the advocates of a superfluous question now come forward—or rather, those who strive to be devotees of perverse doctrines—and let them say: “Can God bring it about that things which have happened did not happen?” To them I answer at the outset that this is not so, because it belongs to divine goodness to bring something forth from nothing, not rather to make nothing out of something; for it is written: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

I wish to prove that God makes something from nothing; you strive to show that He makes nothing from something. But now, I ask you, remove all these things together: pour out all the humors of this pestilential disease in one effort, so that one draught of an antidote may suffice to meet a multifaceted illness, and we may not be compelled to require several kinds of remedies for your cure.

Come, then, answer this, I ask: Can God make something past so that what happened did not happen; or make something present that now exists, while it exists, not exist; or make something entirely future not be future; or, conversely, make all these things their opposites? These propositions seem to us to be handed over to execration rather than to writing.

Tell me, proposer of a crafty question: do you also believe that whatever God does is good, and therefore is something, while whatever He does not do is nothing? Hear Scripture: “God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). And again: “Without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

“But because you cannot deny this,” you say, “I agree.” Yet, by asking that one and the same thing both have been and not have been; both exist and not exist; both be future and not be future, you are plainly striving to confuse everything that has been done or is to be done and to display them wavering between being and non-being. Nature does not contain such a thing. Nothing can simultaneously be and not be; but whatever is not in the nature of things is undoubtedly nothing.

Thus, hard exactor, you demand from God that He do what is not His to do—that is, nothing. But behold, the evangelist stands against you, saying that without Him nothing was made. God has not yet learned how to make nothing. Teach Him, then, and command Him to make nothing for you.

Again I ask you to answer: do you believe also what the Prophet sings, to which all the testimonies of Scripture give harmonious assent: “All that the Lord willed, He made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Psalm 135:6)? It is clear that this too cannot be denied by you.

Since God can do all things, why do you doubt that God can make something simultaneously be and not be, if this is good to do? But if it is useless to confuse things between being and non-being, and God made all things not useless but good—or rather, if it is evil, and therefore nothing—God does not do this at all: “Without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

Furthermore, the will of the supreme and omnipotent Maker is so effective a cause of the existence or non-existence of all things that what He wills to exist cannot fail to exist, and what He does not will to exist cannot exist. The power of God has brought it about that what He established as existing can no longer not have existed; what He established as having existed, so long as it exists, can no longer not exist; and what He established as future can no longer fail to be future.

Why, then, should God’s power be judged weak in what it can do by those foolishly wise people precisely where it is recognized as more powerful and more wondrous? Everything that exists is from Him. He has bestowed upon things this force of existence, so that once they have existed, they cannot not have existed.

## CHAPTER IX. That evils should be said rather not to exist than to exist

All evils, such as injustices and crimes, even when they appear to exist, do not exist, because they are not from God; and therefore they are nothing. God plainly did not make them, without whom nothing was made (John 1:3).

Accordingly, if anything good has been done by human beings, it cannot lose its being or its having been, because it is God’s work, even if it has been done through human beings. Hence the prophet says: “For You have accomplished all our works in us” (Isaiah 26:12). All good things are both God’s and ours, because He works in us, granting the power to carry out the work.

Solomon also says: “In His hand are both we and our words, and all wisdom and knowledge of works and discipline” (Wisdom 7:16). In Him also, as the Apostle says, “we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

But if an evil deed has been done, even then it was nothing when it appeared to exist. Hence Scripture testifies that the very authors of wickedness and depravity complain in the underworld:

“All those things,” they say, “passed away like a shadow, and like a messenger who runs ahead, and like a ship passing through water in motion, whose track, once it has passed, cannot be found, nor the path of its keel in the waves” (Wisdom 5:9–10). A path made in the waves immediately disappears.

Again they say: “Or like a bird flying through the air, no sign of its journey is found.” A third image, not unlike these, is added: “Or like an arrow shot toward its appointed target: the divided air immediately closes in upon itself, and its passage is unknown” (ibid.).

The track of a ship, the passage of a bird, and the flight of an arrow quickly come into being and immediately close up again. So every wicked person, as soon as he begins, immediately falls away. Hence they add: “So we also, once born, immediately ceased to be.” Rather, at the very moment when they appear to exist, they do not exist, because they are far from Him who truly is.

In contrast, it is said of the just man: “Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many times, because his works were pleasing to the Lord” (Wisdom IV). Of the wicked it is said: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Psalm 73:18). He does not say, “after they had been lifted up,” but “while they were being lifted up,” because they become empty through the very process by which they swell with pride; they fall from the point at which they become exalted.

It must not therefore be asserted that they become nothing only after they reach their end. Without doubt, they are already nothing when they appear to be something: nothing according to the testimony of truth, something in the shadow of darkness.

Perhaps that rich man was still feasting splendidly (Luke 16:19), supported by ranks of attendants and surrounded by troops of warriors—the one whom the prophet saw exalted and lifted up (Isaiah 36:1). Yet, as he passed at once toward the contemplation of higher things, he recognized that the man whom he had perhaps thought to be something great was nothing.

Hence it is written: “For the hope of the ungodly is like down carried away by the wind, and like thin foam dispersed by a storm, and like smoke scattered by the wind, and like the memory of a one-day guest who passes by” (Wisdom 5:14). By gathering so many examples of momentary things, the author indicated not merely that all the glory of the reprobate is something contemptible, but that it is nothing.

Evils, then, even when they appear to exist, do not exist, and they are far from Him who truly and supremely is. Good things, however—that is, the things created by the good Artisan—which you, whoever you are, ask whether they can simultaneously exist and not exist, cannot do so, because this alternation has no place in the nature of things, which the rational Artisan established as existing.

Since it is evil to confuse being and non-being, and since such confusion is rather nothing, this confusion of alternation was not made by the good Creator, who made all things good. In evils, however, this alternation of confusion may somehow appear: they seem to exist but do not exist, and therefore are, as it were, and are not. They exist indeed on the surface of appearance, but not according to the judgment of truth.

Even to evils themselves, nevertheless, we cannot precisely grant this difference, that they simultaneously exist and do not exist, because they appear to exist but do not exist. Hence they are more truly said always not to exist than to exist and not exist.

## CHAPTER X. That God can do all things, whether He does them or does not do them

It is therefore clear that this alternation about which the question is asked—whether something can simultaneously have been and not have been; exist and not exist; be future and not be future—can in no way belong to the natures of existing things. It belongs only to verbal disputes arising from the consequences of argument and reasoning.

Therefore, it must be believed with unwavering faith that God can do all things, whether He does them or does not do them. For what is evil ought rather to be called nothing than something. Thus it does not prejudice the statement that God can do all things, even though He cannot do all evils, since evils should be reckoned not within all things but rather outside all things.

Hence divine power often arms itself against the syllogisms of dialecticians and destroys their subtleties; it confounds the arguments of all philosophers concerning what they already judge necessary and unavoidable.

Hear the syllogism: “If wood is burning, it is certainly being consumed; but it is burning; therefore it is being consumed.” Yet Moses sees the bush burning and not being consumed (Exodus 3:2).

Again: “If wood has been cut down, it bears no fruit; but it has been cut down; therefore it bears no fruit.” Yet Aaron’s staff in the tabernacle is found, contrary to the order of nature, to have produced almonds (Numbers 17:8).

What, otherwise, are all those great wonders and signs displayed in Egypt before Pharaoh: transferring the multitudes of the children of Israel while the Egyptians perished, through the divided sea (Exodus 7–14); bringing forth abundant streams from the rock of dry stone (Exodus 17; Psalm 78); and destroying the walls of Jericho not with the clash of weapons but with the sound of trumpets (Joshua 6)?

Finally, what is it that, to the astonishment of all ages, caused the sun to stand still in the heavens at Joshua’s command for the space of one day (Joshua 10), and caused it to return ten lines toward the east for Hezekiah (2 Kings 20; Isaiah 38); that extinguished the power of the raging fire around the three youths, and restrained the bloody jaws and savage mouths of the lions around Daniel (Daniel 3, 6)?

What, I ask, are all these things except a confounding of the empty opinions of the wise men of this world and a revelation to mortals of the glory of divine power against the customary order of nature?

Let the dialecticians come—or rather, the heretics, as they are thought to be. Let them see to it themselves. Let them come, I say, weighing words, airing their questions with puffed-out cheeks, proposing, assuming, and drawing conclusions that seem to them unavoidable. Let them say: “If she gave birth, she had intercourse; but she gave birth; therefore she had intercourse.”

Did this not seem, before the mystery of human redemption, to be an argument of impregnable force? Certainly God could both cause a virgin to give birth before the fall and restore a virgin after the fall. Both were good; and although until then He had done neither, He was nevertheless to be believed capable of doing both.

Indeed, it is more wondrous and far more excellent for a virgin to remain undefiled after childbirth than for one who has been defiled to return to virginal honor after her fall. For it is greater for someone to enter through closed doors than for doors that have stood open to be closed again.

If, then, our Redeemer, born of a Virgin (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:31), did what is greater and far more excellent, will He not be able to do what is lesser—to restore any defiled woman? God was able to proceed from a virgin womb while preserving virginity; will He not be able to restore the loss of violated virginity?

How, then, is a murderer restored, so that after worthy repentance he is no longer a murderer? How is a thief restored, or a perjurer, or a robber? How are those guilty of every crime, after they have truly corrected themselves, no longer what they were? Hence it is written: “Turn the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Psalm 37:10).

“But,” you say, “I admit that any defiled woman after repentance is no longer what she was, so that she is no longer branded with the mark of fornication. Nevertheless, she does not return to her former glory according to truth.”

I answer in opposition that He who was able to proceed from His mother’s womb with virginity unharmed is also able, if He wills, to restore the seal of virginity in any woman whose virginity has been violated.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Creator of nature is also the Transformer of nature

Let the objection of this superstitious question be brought forward once more. Let us also see from what root it has grown, so that it may not, in its headlong rush, bury the rich fruits of sincere faith, but that the stream, together with the source itself, may dry up in a chasm worthy of the earth.

To affirm that God cannot restore a virgin after her fall, they add, as though it followed logically: “Can God bring it about that what has happened did not happen?” This is as though, once it is established that a virgin has been defiled, it could no longer be made the case that she is again intact.

As far as nature is concerned, this is true, and the judgment stands: something that happened and something that did not happen cannot be found to be one and the same. They are mutually contrary, so that if one exists, the other cannot exist. What happened cannot truly be said not to have happened; conversely, what did not happen cannot rightly be said to have happened. For things that are contrary cannot belong together in one and the same subject.

This impossibility is rightly asserted if it is referred to the weakness of nature; but far be it from us to apply it to the divine majesty. He who gave nature its origin easily, whenever He wills, removes nature’s necessity. For He who presides over created things is not subject to the laws of the Creator; and He who created nature turns the natural order according to the command of His dominion. Whoever established that created things should be subject to the ruling nature has reserved for His dominion the obedience of obedient nature.

To anyone who considers the matter, it is plainly evident that from the very beginning of the world’s birth the Creator has altered the laws of nature according to His will—or rather, so to speak, has in some way altered nature itself against nature.

Is it not against nature for the world to be made from nothing? Hence philosophers say: “Nothing comes from nothing” (Aristotle, *Physics* I, text 34). Is it not against nature for animals to be created not from animals but from inert elements, by the command alone? For a sleeping man to lose a rib without pain? For woman to be made from a man without a woman, and for all the limbs of a human being to be differentiated from one rib? For the two of them to look upon one another naked and not only not to blush but not even to know shame (Genesis 2:25)? There are many other examples that it would take too long to pursue.

What, then, is surprising if He who gave nature its law and order exercises dominion over that same nature according to His will, so that nature’s necessity does not resist Him but, subjected to His laws, serves as a handmaid?

Nature itself has its own nature—namely, the will of God—so that just as all created things preserve His laws, so nature, when commanded, may reverently obey the divine will, forgetting its own rights.

What is it, indeed, that we see even today: the salamander lives in fires and not only suffers no injury from burning but is even nourished as though by fuel? Certain little worms are both born and live in exceedingly hot waters. What is it that makes straw so cold that it preserves snow buried in it for a very long time, yet so warm that it ripens any unripe fruit?

What is it that causes fire, although it is itself luminous, to blacken whatever has been burned by it; and although it shines itself, to discolor whatever it surrounds and touches, beautiful as it is? Yet stones baked in glowing fire are themselves white; and although the fire is redder, they become white in the flames. White is suited to light, black to darkness.

Although fire burns in wood and cooks stones, it produces contrary effects in non-contrary things. Stones and wood are different, certainly, but they are not contrary, as white and black are; yet in the stones one effect is displayed, and in the wood another. Fire brightens the former and darkens the latter, although it would altogether fail to exist in the former if it did not live in the latter.

Why is there such weakness in coals that they are broken by the lightest blow and crushed by the slightest pressure, yet such durability that they are spoiled by no moisture and overcome by no age? Indeed, they are so durable that those who establish boundary markers customarily place them beneath the ground, so that by displaying them they may refute disputants who, after many long years and the passage of time, claim that a fixed stone is not a boundary marker.

Who could make them last so long without decay, buried in a damp pit where wood would rot, unless that fire which corrupts other things brought this about? Lime also preserves the fire it has received and concealed so secretly that no one perceives it by touch; yet when it is extinguished, it is then kindled and felt. To drive out the force of the hidden fire, water is poured over lime; although it was previously cold, it becomes hot from the very thing by which all hot objects are cooled.

But if oil, which is itself fuel for fire, is applied instead of water, no heat, however slight, is awakened by its infusion.

What, then, is surprising if almighty God shows Himself great in great things, since He also works so wondrously in the smallest and most insignificant things?

What is more worthless than a snake’s skin? Yet if it is boiled in hot oil, earache is wonderfully relieved by it. What is lower than a bedbug? If a leech has stuck in the throat, once the smoke of a bedbug is taken in, it is immediately vomited up; and difficulty in urination is also eased by applying it.

What shall I say of the diamond, which is cut neither by fire nor by iron nor by any other force, except only by the blood of a he-goat? What is it that makes the lodestone wonderfully attract iron? Yet if a diamond is placed beside it, it not only no longer attracts iron at all, but, if it had already attracted it, immediately releases it when the diamond approaches—as though one stone feared another, and, in the presence of a greater power, lost its own strength.

Nor is it unknown why the stone of Arcadia is called asbestos: once kindled, it cannot thereafter be extinguished. Why did the pyrites stone, which is found in Persia, receive its name from fire, except because, if the hand holding it presses too hard, it burns the hand?

Again, in that same Persia a stone is produced called selenite. Its inner whiteness increases as the moon waxes and afterward decreases as the moon tends toward waning.

What is it, moreover, that makes Sicilian salt from Agrigentum flow when it is brought near fire, yet crackle as though in flames when it is thrown into water? What is it that produces among the Garamantes a certain spring so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, yet so hot by night that it cannot be touched?

Who provided in Epirus another spring so marvelous that, although it is cold to those who touch it, torches lit in it are extinguished as in other waters, while extinguished torches, unlike in other waters, are kindled in it?

Who established in Egypt a fig tree of such a kind that, when its wood is thrown into flowing water, it does not float, as wood ordinarily does, but sinks into the depths—and, more marvelous still, after remaining there for some time, rises again to the surface of the water, precisely when, having become waterlogged, it ought to have been weighed down by the burden of moisture?

What is it that causes apples to grow in the fields of Sodom, reaching the appearance of ripeness but, when tested by a bite or pressure, to vanish into smoke or ash as their skin disintegrates?

What is it also that causes mares in the regions of Cappadocia to conceive from the wind, while their offspring live for no more than three years?

Hence the island of Tilos in India has such a property that all the branches of its trees are never stripped of their covering of leaves. Hence also that land in the western regions has acquired the distinction that birds emerge from the branches of its trees, living and winged fruits bursting forth in the likeness of apples.

For, as those who testify that they have seen it report, a small hanging object gradually begins to suspend itself from a branch, then forms itself into the image and shape of a bird. Finally, as it acquires however little plumage, it separates itself from the tree by opening its beak, and thus the new inhabitant of the air almost learns to fly before it learns to live.

Indeed, who could sufficiently enumerate all these great works of divine power that occur contrary to the common order of nature? They must not be examined by human arguments but rather left to the power of the Creator.

What, then, is surprising if He who arranged the natural laws of all things and bends the order of nature itself according to the command of His most effective will should, if He so wills, restore any violated virgin to wholeness—He who preserved His virgin mother by being born from her?

For it was equally possible for God first to keep Enoch and Elijah alive in the flesh, and afterward to raise Lazarus and the widow’s son from their tombs.

## CHAPTER XII. On the palace of Romulus and the philosopher who fell

I do not know whether this is found in written sources, but it is widely circulated by popular report within the walls of Rome that Romulus, who is said to have founded the City, built a palace whose ruined walls, though half-demolished, can still be seen over much of the site. Trusting in the solidity of his work, he is said to have burst forth with these words:

“It is certain and immovably fixed: unless a virgin gives birth, this house will not collapse.”

Thus, if what is reported is true, a prophecy came forth from the mouth of a pagan, as the event itself proved. On the night when the Savior proceeded from a virgin womb for our redemption, the palace, so it is said, collapsed.

To a man ignorant of God, both things seemed impossible: that a virgin should give birth and that a building should fall. But He who was always able to do both, though for a long time He kept both within the secrets of His wisdom, revealed both through the effect of His work at the fitting time.

It is truly astonishing that now human beings within the embrace of the Church—not merely reborn but even born within it—so boldly and shamelessly bring a charge of impossibility against almighty God, and do not fear immediately to be swallowed up by the abyss of the earth’s chasm.

Let the frenzied tongue now blush, and let the tongue that does not know how to be eloquent learn at least to be silent. If it cannot produce words that build up, let it at least know how to remain silent without destroying faith. Otherwise, let it cut off its foreskin with a knife in punishment, rather than merely apply a bridle to itself through the discipline of silence.

Let those who wish ventilate their questions according to the proper method and order of inquiry; but let them not, through their evasions and the childish nonsense of the schools, insult the Creator. Let them know that this impossibility belongs to the very nature of things and to the consequences of words proceeding from a formal argument; it does not belong to divine power, and nothing can escape the power of the divine majesty.

Thus, according solely to the order of nature and the condition of words, if something exists, then, so long as it exists, it cannot not exist; if it existed, it cannot not have existed; and if it is future, it cannot not be future.

Otherwise, contrary to the order of natural property itself and to the material of existence, what is there that God cannot overturn? What is there that God cannot create under a new condition?

Let them therefore examine, according to their limited capacity, merely the elements of letters, which they still need; let them not arrogate to themselves divine mysteries beyond their reach.

A certain philosopher—[Note: Some suppose that this was Thales.]—while investigating the courses of the stars and the paths of the heavenly bodies at night, suddenly fell into a muddy well. Iambe, who was his maidservant, versified his fall, saying:

“My master did not know the vile mud lying beneath his feet, yet he was attempting to investigate the secrets of heaven.”

It was from her name, moreover, that the iambic meter received its name.

Let those who exceed the limits of their capacity take this to heart. In their proud rush to attempt things above them, let them learn—not only that they do not know what they say against God, but also, through the sentence of punishment deservedly inflicted upon them, that they have spoken carelessly and foolishly.

## CHAPTER XIII. On those who, blaspheming against the Lord, were covered with leprosy
From the account of a certain deacon, prudent and honored in worldly estimation, I learned the following, which I now relate:

“In the region of Bologna,” he said, “two men who were bound to one another both by a covenant of friendship and, if I remember correctly, by the relationship of godparenthood, were reclining at a banquet. A cock was brought to their table. One of them seized a knife and, as is customary, cut the dish into pieces; he then poured ground pepper mixed with sauce over it. When he had done this, the other immediately said: ‘Indeed, godfather, you have dismantled the cock so completely that Saint Peter himself could not restore it, even if he wished to.’

“At once the other replied: ‘Certainly not only Blessed Peter; even if Christ himself should command it, this cock will never rise again.’

“At these words the cock suddenly sprang up alive, [Col. 0616A] covered everywhere with feathers. It beat its wings and crowed, shook its feathers, and sprinkled the entire sauce over those who were dining. Immediately the sacrilege of blasphemous rashness was followed by a deserved punishment. For, as the pepper was being sprinkled, they were struck with leprosy. They not only endured this affliction until their death, but also left it to their descendants for all generations as a kind of inheritance.

“Hence it came about that they were reduced to the service of the holy Church of Bologna, which is distinguished by the name of Blessed Peter the Apostle. Their descendants, as the narrator asserted, have remained leprous down to the present day and have been assigned this obligation by the force of the canon: that they must bring to the Church, from the work of their hands, winnowing baskets.

“Thus, indeed, condemned to a double punishment—the torments both of leprosy and of servitude—they teach others not to speak rashly any longer about divine power. And the cock (Matt. XXVI), which formerly rebuked Peter when he denied the Lord on earth, then proved Peter when he was reigning with the One whom he had denied in heaven.

“Perhaps they were punished by the imposition of such a canon not without divine judgment: just as grain is separated from chaff by the winnowing basket, so, through the discipline of discernment, they might learn which words ought to be rejected as chaff and which ought to be uttered as though useful for nourishment. For all kinds of perverse people, while they do whatever their heart suggests and indiscreetly and insolently pour forth whatever their tongue itches to say, suppose, if scourges do not sometimes overtake them, that God either does not exist or does not care about human affairs.

“‘The fool said in his heart: There is no God’ (Ps. XIII). And again: ‘How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?’ (Ps. LXXII.) Therefore some people, at the very moment of a wicked deed or immediately after acting wickedly, incur the movement of divine wrath, so that they themselves may no longer mock heavenly patience and others may restrain themselves from doing similar things by observing their punishment.”

634 **CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the man whom an evil spirit killed after he had committed adultery**

Indeed, while I was living near the town of Parma and applying myself there to the study of the liberal arts, I came to know something which does not seem useless to transmit, by the course of the writing pen, for the knowledge of posterity. [Col. 0616D]

To the west of the aforesaid city there is a basilica outside the walls, adorned with the joint title of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. One night, on the eve of the feast of those same martyrs, a certain man rose early and led his oxen out to more distant pasture. A neighbor of his, inflamed with the most wicked flame of lust, lay in wait for him, intending to violate his wife.

That same night, therefore, the cunning intruder approached the man’s house. When he found the opportunity, not long after the husband had departed with the animals to pasture, he pretended through diabolical deceit that he was suffering from a fever and, disguised as the husband, entered the man’s bed.

While he trembled as though chilled, chattered his teeth, and sobbed repeatedly, the unhappy woman, sympathizing with him as with a sick husband, began to hold him in her arms, cover him with a blanket, and warm him with every care at her disposal. But he conceived pain in his mind and gave birth to wickedness: he violated another man’s marriage bed, brought destruction upon himself, and quickly departed.

But behold, after scarcely a short interval had passed, the husband returned and went back to his bed. His wife immediately reproached him vehemently, saying: “Today you will surely be able to enter the church of the holy martyrs, which is so close to you, and take part with the other Christians in the divine mysteries!”

When the astonished man asked what she meant, and learned the whole course of the affair as it had happened, the two of them, discovering that they had been mocked and deceived by the most shameful trickery, were overwhelmed by unbearable anguish.

Meanwhile, as the people gathered from every direction at the church to hear the office of the nocturnal praises with devotion, the two of them finally recovered their composure and came there as well. Setting aside all shame, they laid their complaint before everyone. The woman in particular tore out her hair, drenched her sorrowful face with abundant tears, and uttered mournful cries toward heaven:

“Lord,” she said, “you know the hearts of human beings; you are witness to my conscience. I swear that on this most holy night I recoiled even from the embraces of my own marriage bed, and I had no knowledge whatever that I was mingling with another man, especially with a stranger. I beg you, Lord, do not look upon my sins, but let it please you to avenge before you the injury done to your saints. Therefore, in the sight of your people, now display your power, and for the glory of your most holy name bring forth the author of my betrayal. Let him be brought into the midst, and let him not gain profit from the refuge of his deceit by escaping the enormity of his most cruel crime.”

While the woman poured out many such words in bitterness of spirit—not quietly but in loud cries—and the people, sympathizing with her grief, likewise implored divine mercy with prayers and petitions, the author of the crime, wherever he was hiding, was suddenly seized by a demonic spirit and driven into extreme fury and madness.

Then he burst newly into the church, while the people stood amazed, and turned everyone’s attention upon himself by tearing and rending his own body. Roaring and growling, he cruelly lacerated himself with his own hands: now he leapt upward as though flying, now hurled himself down with tremendous force, now struck his head against the wall, now threw himself in madness upon the pavement. He pitifully battered all his inward parts.

In this manner the evil spirit did not cease to dash him about until it tore the unhappy soul from his body before the people who were present. Those who witnessed it gave immense glory for justice to God, who neither allowed the sinner to depart unpunished nor failed to console the innocent woman.

When this was later reported to me, it was said that the stones against which he had struck himself could still be seen reddened with his pus and blood. This man too, perhaps, believed either that God did not know what is committed secretly or that he was in no way able to avenge himself upon those who commit crimes, saying in his heart: “The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob understand” (Ps. XCIII).

But whether someone tramples upon God’s commandments or provokes God by insults, it is no slight offense to transgress arrogantly. And in the few cases—whether among those who commit wicked deeds or those who speak proudly—in which divine judgment suddenly strikes, it shows what the others, who appear to be immune, deserve for a time.

Let anyone who puts his mouth in heaven cease—yes, let him cease—so that his tongue may pass over the earth (Ps. LXXII). For a person who tears God apart with derogatory words is plainly doing this in such a way that he also contends against God’s servant concerning God’s inability. [Col. 0618B]

**CHAPTER XV. He concludes that it must be affirmed that God can make what has been done undone**

When, therefore, this question is proposed—“How can God bring it about that what was done should not have been done?”—let the brother of sound faith answer that what has been done, if it was evil, was not something but nothing. For that reason it must be said not to have been, since it had no material basis for existence: the creator of all things did not command it to come into being.

But if what was done was good, then it was certainly done by God. “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII, CXLVIII). “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

Therefore the statement—“How can God make what was done not to have been done?”—is equivalent to saying: “Can God bring it about that what he himself did, he did not do?” That is: “Can God make it so that God did not do what God did?” Whoever asserts this deserves to be spat upon, not to receive an answer, but rather to be consigned to the cautery. Nevertheless, for refuting the wicked and the contentious, what was said above should be committed to memory. We shall merely touch upon it here in brief, lest the length of our writing become tedious to the reader. For we intended to publish not a book but a letter.

Among the other points, however, let this one statement of ours not escape our memory: for the Creator and God of all things, the ability to do all things is coeternal with him, just as is his knowledge of all things. He encloses, fixes, and eternally establishes all times—past, present, and future—in the bosom of his wisdom, so that nothing new can come to him and nothing can pass away from him through being left behind.

But what is that virtue, what is that power by which God can do all things? What is that wisdom by which he knows all things? Let us inquire of the Apostle: “Christ,” he says, “is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

There is true eternity; there is true immortality. There is that eternal today which never passes away; there is an everlasting present, that today which is fixed with such perpetual stability that it knows neither how to pass away nor ever to turn into the past.

Therefore, to overcome the shamelessness of contentious people, for whom the answer previously given to the proposed question is still insufficient, we may appropriately say that in his ever-unchanging and most constant eternity God can bring it about that what had been done, in the course of our passing time, should not have been done. Thus we may say: “God can bring it about that Rome, which was founded long ago, was not founded.”

The word “can,” which belongs to the present tense, is properly used in reference to the immovable eternity of almighty God. But with reference to us, where there is continuous movement and perpetual passing away, we would more suitably say “could,” so that we understand the statement—“God can make Rome not have been founded”—as referring to him in whom “there is no change, nor shadow of alteration” (James I).

Among us, this means: “God could.” For in relation to his eternity, whatever God could do, he also can do, since his present never turns into the past. His today is not changed into tomorrow or into any succession of time; rather, just as he himself always is what he is, so whatever is present to him is always present.

Therefore, just as we may rightly say: “God could have caused Rome not to be founded before it was made,” so likewise we may appropriately say: “God can cause Rome not to have been founded even after it has been founded.” “Could” applies according to us; “can” applies according to him.

For the power that God possessed before Rome came into being remains forever unchangeable and impassable in God’s eternity. And so, concerning any matter whatever, we may say that God could do it and likewise that God can do it, because his power, which is coeternal with him, is always fixed and immovable.

For “God could” belongs among us only; in God himself there is not “could” but an immovable, constant, and unchanging power that always is. Whatever God could do, he undoubtedly can do, since with him there is not being and having been, but eternal being; consequently, there is not having been able and being able, but an immovable and everlasting ability.

For just as he did not say, “I am who both am and was,” but rather, “I am who I am; and he who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III), so it undoubtedly follows that he should say: “I am not he who could and can, but he who can immutably and eternally.”

The power that was with God before the ages is with him today; and the power that is his today was likewise with him before the ages. It remains fixed and immovable through all the ages that are to come, eternally.

Therefore, just as God could, before anything was made, cause it not to be made, so likewise he can now cause what has been made not to have been made. The power he then possessed has neither been changed nor taken away. But just as he himself is always what he is, so God’s power cannot be changed.

For he is the one who says through the Prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. III). And in the Gospel: “Before Abraham was made, I am” (John VIII). He is not changed according to our condition from future being into being or from being into having been; rather, he is always the same and always is what he is.

Thus, just as God is always one and the same, so with him there is always an unfailing and impassable ability to do all things. And just as we truthfully and without any contradiction whatsoever say that God is now and always what he was before the ages, so likewise we truthfully say that God now and always can do what he could do before the ages.

If, therefore, God can do everything that he could do from the beginning, before the creation of things, including causing what now exists never to have come into existence, then he can cause what has been made not to have been made. His power is fixed and eternal: whatever he has ever been able to do, he is always able to do. The variation of times finds no place for change within eternity. Rather, just as he is always the same as he was in the beginning, so he can do everything that he could do before the ages.

The conclusion must therefore be added to the proposed argument:

If the ability to do all things is coeternal with God, then God can cause what has been made not to have been made.

But the ability to do all things is coeternal with God; therefore God can cause what has been made not to have been made.

It must therefore be firmly and faithfully affirmed that, just as God is called almighty, so he truly can do all things without any exception, both those things that have been made and those things that have not been made. Let this saying from Esther be set down as an inviolable seal at the conclusion of this little work:

“Lord, almighty king, all things are placed under your authority, and no one can resist your will. For you made heaven and earth and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven. You are Lord of all, and there is no one who can resist your majesty” (Esther XIII). [Col. 0620C]

**CHAPTER XVI. He bears witness to his affection for the brothers of the monastery of Cassino and commends their manly virtue**

Nevertheless, although this question is foolishly brought forward against God, it has other hiding places and still contains obscure recesses and retreats. For this reason we refrain from examining it more subtly, since we have proposed an epistolary abridgment and wish to avoid an extended volume. We have especially resolved not to touch upon anything else in this subject of debate except to repel, by arguments of truth, the accusation brought against us concerning God’s inability.

But while we set these matters down, we cannot restrain in silence what our heart burns to express, so that at least a spark does not escape. Therefore, to address you all together now, I do not want you to be unaware, venerable brothers, that ever since I crossed the threshold of your glorious monastery, I have continually kept you before my eyes and bound you to me in the deepest affection. Indeed, if I may confess it, after returning from most holy Cassino I experienced what happened to the woman returning from the tabernacle at Shiloh (I Sam. I): my face was no longer turned in different directions. In spirit I live continually with you; I am always present with you. [Col. 0621A]

Otherwise, if I am not with you because I do not see you with bodily eyes, then the eyes themselves would not be in the head, since they cannot see the head; or the eyes would be absent from one another, since neither can see itself, nor can the two see each other through mutual contemplation.

Blessed are those who live with you; blessed are those who die among you and in your holy works. It must surely be believed with devout faith that the ladder which once seemed to rise from Mount Cassino into heaven still lies spread with cloaks and flashes with lamps (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 37). Just as it then received the leader, so now it sends to heavenly things the army that follows. Those who have already died do not stray from its glorious path, for while they lived in this exile they followed its footsteps.

This is that burning of intimate fervor which blazes unquenchably in my heart; this is the perpetual subject that occupies my lips.

Among the other flowers of virtue that I found in that full field which the Lord blessed (Gen. XXVII), I confess that this pleased me greatly: there I found no schools of boys, who often weaken the rigor of holiness, but all were either old men, with whom the noble man sat at the gates of the Church (Prov. XXXI), or men rejoicing in the beauty of youthful conduct.

Like the sons of the prophets, they are capable of seeking Elijah through the deserts (II Kings II); or else they are still blooming in the flower of adolescence, and, according to the Apostle John (I John II), have conquered the evil one.

Behold what now occurs to me to say for the consolation of my divine Peter, who was once a citizen of Capua and is now enrolled in the service of the eternal King.

**CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the boy admitted through closed doors**

A certain little boy, five years old—the son of the most noble man Hubaldus, who lives with me in the wilderness—had become a monk in my monastery.

Once, in the deepest silence of night, while the brothers were sleeping, he either went out or was carried away; I do not know which. But while the baker lay in the bakehouse, his sleep having been interrupted for a moment, he wanted to pull over himself a garment that lay near him, so as to keep out the cold. When he stretched out his arm, he found the boy sleeping beside him.

Suddenly astonished and greatly frightened, he rose quickly, lit a lamp, and went around the whole house with anxious care. He found every entrance closed and bolted. In the morning, no small amazement arose among the brothers: how could the boy—who, beyond all doubt, had rested the previous evening in his own bed in their sight—have entered the bakehouse while the doors were closed?

It is indeed read concerning the apostles, when they were to be led out of the public prison: “An angel of the Lord came by night, opened the doors of the prison, led them out, and said: Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (Acts V).

Again, concerning Peter, it is read: “As the angel went before him from the prison to the iron gate, it opened of its own accord for them” (Acts XII).

And concerning Paul: “Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosed” (Acts XVI).

But since the angels did not lead even the blessed apostles out of prison without first opening the doors, it is exceedingly astonishing how the boy could have entered a house closed on every side, without the doors being opened—whether by human magic or by the tricks of unclean spirits.

The boy himself, when carefully questioned, added that certain men had taken him and led him to a great banquet, where all kinds of delicacies seemed to be present, and where they made him eat. He also reported that, as they carried him as far as the castle overlooking the monastery, they placed him on the very bell that hangs high beside the basilica. [Col. 0622C]

We have decided to record this so that each of us, when he considers that even these children, who do not yet know how to sin, are subject to the snares of the evil enemy, may himself bear patiently whatever he suffers.

For if innocent children sometimes endure the deceptions of the evil enemy, with how much patience ought sinners to bear the troubles inflicted by that enemy? Therefore I urge that brother whom God visits through tribulations to rejoice and confidently believe that the rust of his soul is being cleansed by the hammer of the temptation that strikes it.

For this is not, as the devil pretends when frightening him, a sign of future damnation, but rather an indication of eternal salvation.

May the Holy Spirit, who is eternal light and the remission of sins, enlighten and absolve you all, and command you to keep a diligent remembrance of me in your holy prayers.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0621]

641–642 **THIRTY-SEVENTH LITTLE WORK. CONCERNING VARIOUS SACRED QUESTIONS, WITH ANOTHER TREATISE ON THE SAME SUBJECT FOLLOWING THE EARLIER ONE**

**Argument**

He discusses certain questions proposed to him by Alberic, formerly a monk of Cassino and now a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; then, taking the opportunity, he explains several obscure passages in the sacred Scriptures and in their interpreters.

**To Alberic, his venerable brother, Peter, the sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.** [Col. 0621D]

Ancient history relates that when the sons of Joseph—Ephraim and Manasseh—demanded wider spaces for their possession, they received this answer at the command of Joshua: they were to go up into the hill country, cut down the dense forests, and thus procure larger spaces for themselves by the work of their own hands (Josh. XVII).

A little later he also said to the seven tribes: “How long will you remain sluggish through laziness and not enter to possess the land which the Lord, the God of your fathers, has given you?” (Josh. XVIII).

You too, brother, when you press me with certain little questions and earnestly ask that they be solved for you, must soon be sent to the mountains of the teachers and to the forests of the Scriptures. There, sweating through continual labor, you must cut down the thickets of the woodland, tear out the knots and trunks of doubts, and cultivate new ground for yourself, as though with the hands of your own investigation.

Thus the soil of heavenly speech must be tilled with the mattocks of one’s own subtlety, so that you do not hunger while waiting for nourishment from another’s hands. Rather, gathering by your own labor an abundance of rich produce, you may soon live joyfully amid the fullness of spiritual delights.

Meanwhile, while your own crops are lacking, let our supply assist you—not, I will not say, a granary, nor indeed, what is less, a barrel, but at least a very small measure of a bath—and let your poverty be somewhat moderated by our little fields.

There is something between living splendidly and perishing utterly from famine. You therefore wish me not only to explain what you ask but also to commit it to writing, so that ignorance may perish in such a way that forgetfulness does not afterward creep in.

**[CONCERNING VARIOUS SACRED QUESTIONS]**

**QUESTION I**

Come, then. You ask what is meant by the statement: “Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign; and he reigned two years over Israel” (I Sam. XIII).

Some think it should be understood in this way: that at the beginning of King Saul’s reign he had a son who was one year old and was still crying in the tender infancy of his first year—namely Ish-bosheth—and that this son reigned over Israel for two years after his father’s death.

But since this interpretation is rejected by more learned men, let us seek another from ourselves. Blessed Jerome teaches that it should be understood to mean that Saul was innocent, like a one-year-old child, when he began to reign, and remained in the simplicity of that innocence for two years. But the one who was then a son through humility afterward became a servant through pride.

**DOUBT II**

You also ask who the Cherethites and Pelethites were, who are said to have been David’s warriors (I Sam. XXX; II Sam. VIII).

It is read in the Book of Numbers that the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; and you shall bring them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant and make them stand there with you. I will take of your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear with you the burden of the people and you may not be burdened alone” (Num. XI; II Chron. XVIII).

From the stock of these men, therefore, two kinships arose, one of which was called Cherethite and the other Pelethite. Cherethite is interpreted as “giving judgment,” while Pelethite means “punishing”: those whom the former condemned to death by pronouncing sentence, the latter punished by inflicting vengeance.

**DOUBT III**

You add: Why are David’s sons said to have been priests, when they are known to have had no blood relationship with the sons of Aaron beyond that which they had with the other tribes?

It must be understood that, since venerable priests and teachers are appointed among the people, rulers or teachers are sometimes designated by the name “priests.” Thus elsewhere we find: “Ira the Jairite was David’s priest,” that is, his teacher.

Likewise, when it is said, “David’s sons were priests” (II Sam. VIII), it should be understood as though it said that they were teachers of their brothers, or else leaders among the others, as the ancient translation has it.

For where the newer edition says, “David’s sons were priests,” the old edition reads: “David’s sons were princes of the royal court.” [Col. 0624B]

**DOUBT IV**

You further state that you do not understand what is written: “There was a third battle at Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus, son of Saltus, the Bethlehemitic embroiderer, struck down Goliath the Gittite” (II Sam. XXI).

This can easily be understood. Gob is interpreted as “lake.” And just as the one who is thrown into a lions’ pit is in danger, so David, as though handing himself over to the teeth of a lion, plunged into battle when he entered into conflict with the raging Goliath.

The same David is rightly called Adeodatus, “given by God,” because he was chosen by God for the kingship. He is also called the son of Saltus, “the woodland,” because he is recognized as having been brought out from the pastures of the wooded country where he tended sheep.

Nor is it without reason that the same David is called an embroiderer, for his mother belonged to the family of Bezalel, who built the tabernacle of the covenant in the wilderness and wove into it various embroidered works.

He is also appropriately called a Bethlehemitic, because he originated from Naomi, and they had gone out from Bethlehem in a time of famine and were later brought back to that same Bethlehem when abundance blossomed again.

That this Adeodatus, with all these appellations attached to him, is unquestionably David is made clear by what follows: “These four were born to Rapha in Gath, and they fell into the hand of David and his servants” (II Sam. XXI).

I would also explain what is mystically signified by these things, were I not prevented by the brevity of a letter. According to the mystical interpretation, all these matters refer to Christ.

For he is Adeodatus, “given by God,” of whom Isaiah also says: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. IX).

He is not inappropriately called the Son of the Woodland, because he deigned to be born according to the flesh from the Jews. Since they produced no fruit of spiritual growth, they proved barren like wild trees, not planted in a garden but born in the forest. Hence it is read: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. XL), that is, in the fruitless people of the Jews.

Our Redeemer is also rightly called an embroiderer, because he applies himself to the work of weaving: he clothes himself with his faithful people and weaves from them garments of righteousness. For the Apostle speaks of his garments: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V). And through the Prophet: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX).

Of Christ’s faithful the Psalmist sings: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” And through Ezekiel the Lord reproaches the soul whom he fittingly adorned with spiritual garments but who abandoned him after defiling herself with the filth of adultery:

“I clothed you,” he says, “with garments of various colors, I put sandals of violet upon you, I girded you with fine linen, I clothed you with delicate fabrics, and I adorned you with an ornament.” Shortly afterward: “You were clothed with fine linen, embroidered work, and many colors” (Ezek. XVI).

What wonder, then, if our Redeemer is called an embroiderer, since he clothes the soul whom he takes as his bride with the embroidered beauty of virtue?

For he is the Wisdom of God, of whom Solomon says: “She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands” (Prov. XXXI). Her fingers took hold of the spindle, and all her household were clothed with double garments. His flesh also became a covering in the Passion. But that same fine linen and royal purple became his garment in the Resurrection.

He is also rightly called a Bethlehemitic, because he is recognized as having been born of the Virgin in Bethlehem.

As for the statement that there was a third battle at Gob, this means that the true David, the Savior of Israel, has always had faithful warriors—before the Law, under the Law, and afterward in the grace of the Gospel—through whom he fought against the Philistines, that is, against the evil spirits.

David came to this third battle at Gob, which is interpreted as “lake,” because our Redeemer, when he came as one stronger than the strong man armed (Luke XI), descended by himself even to the depths below.

Therefore the Psalmist says: “They placed me in the lower lake, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII). There he struck Goliath the Gittite, because, when he rescued the souls of the elect from the confines of Gehenna, he inflicted a deadly wound upon the ancient enemy who had exercised tyranny over them.

**DOUBT V**

You also ask why there is this discrepancy in the sacred Scriptures: in the Book of Kings David is said to have purchased the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, together with the oxen that were to be offered as a burnt offering, for only fifty silver shekels (II Sam. XXIV), whereas in Chronicles he is said to have given six hundred gold shekels for the threshing floor alone (II Chron. III).

It must undoubtedly be understood that in the Book of Kings David is said to have bought only the oxen for fifty silver shekels; how much he paid for the threshing floor is not stated there at all.

The Book of Chronicles, on the other hand, says nothing about the oxen but reports that the threshing floor was bought for six hundred gold shekels. This becomes clear if the actual sequence of the words in both books is carefully considered.

For in the Book of Kings the order of the words is as follows: “So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty silver shekels” (ibid.). The passage should be punctuated so that Scripture first says, “David bought the threshing floor,” without stating the price; then it continues, “and the oxen for fifty silver shekels.”

In the Book of Chronicles it reads: “So David gave Ornan six hundred shekels of gold of the most exact weight for the place, and built an altar there to the Lord” (I Chron. XXI).

Thus Scripture has divided the matter between the two accounts: one records the price of the oxen, the other the price of the threshing floor alone. The matters to which the measure of the price is assigned are different, but the sacred Scriptures do not contradict one another.

645 **DOUBT VI**

You further thought it necessary to consult me about what is read: “There was a battle dispersed over the face of the whole country, and many more of the people were consumed by the forest than were devoured by the sword” (II Sam. XVIII).

Concerning this statement, these are the words of Blessed Jerome in his *Book of Hebrew Questions*: “The Jews suppose that this forest, which is said to have consumed more than the sword devoured, contained extremely savage beasts, by which more were consumed than were devoured by the sword.”

But this, as it is said, was the interpretation of the Jews. It seems to us instead that the mad and senseless men who had become rebels with Absalom, blinded because God had abandoned them, struck against the trees that confronted them. For this reason it is said that more fell, killed by the forest’s consuming them, than were slaughtered and devoured by the sword.

There is no doubt that it should be understood in this way if one attends even superficially to the continuation of the text. For after it first says, “Many more were those whom the forest consumed from the people than those whom the sword devoured on that day,” it immediately adds:

“It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants while he was sitting on a mule. And when he had entered beneath a dense and great oak, his head became caught in the oak; and while he was suspended between heaven and earth, the mule on which he had been riding passed on” (II Sam. XVIII).

**DOUBT VII**
What you further inquire—what became of the Lord’s ark and the tabernacle of the covenant, which were fashioned in the wilderness—is something whose ignorance scarcely causes any harm, while knowledge of it is scarcely proved to offer any benefit. Nevertheless, as the authority of Scripture relates, on Mount Abarim, where Moses is known to have been buried (Deut. XXXIV), the tabernacle together with the ark, and also the altar of incense, are found to have been hidden by the hands of the prophet Jeremiah. This is clearly indicated if one carefully considers the beginning of the Second Book of Maccabees: “For it was contained in the writing how the prophet, having received a divine response, commanded that the tabernacle and the ark should accompany him until he went out to the mountain on which Moses ascended and saw the glory of God; and when Jeremiah came there, he found a cave, and brought the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense into it, and blocked the entrance (II Macc. II).” These three sacred objects, then, as has been said, Jeremiah concealed on the aforesaid Mount Abarim. But if anything else was subsequently done with them, or if indeed they remained untouched, since Scripture nowhere records it, let our curiosity also presume not to investigate it.

## DOUBT VIII

That passage of Isaiah which you ask to have explained—“For the transgression of my people I struck him, and he shall give the impious man for his burial, and the rich man for his death” (Isa. LIII)—seems to us to mean the following. The almighty Father struck the Son on account of the sins of his people, because he determined that he should undergo the punishment of the cross in order to erase our sins. For this purpose the Son was handed over by the Father, so that the servant might be set free; as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). For this purpose the innocent one was struck with wounds, so that the sinner might rejoice, healed by the bruise of his wounds. As the same Isaiah says: “But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes, and by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. LIII).

But our Redeemer deigned to suffer for two peoples, namely the Gentile and the Jewish peoples, one of whom was rightly called impious and the other rich. The Gentile people were impious because, serving idols, they were ignorant of the piety of divine worship. This piety is called in Greek θεοσέβεια, “reverence for God.” The Jewish people, however, had been rich, because, when they received the Sabbaths, circumcision, the new moons, and all the ceremonies of the divine law, they abounded as though in the copious riches of a heavenly treasury. Paul rejoiced that the Corinthians, who had already been converted, abounded in these riches when he said: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus; because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, so that you lack no grace at all” (I Cor. I).

Our Savior, therefore, for the death that he assumed upon himself, restored to the Father two peoples raised from death: the Gentile people, who formerly served demons impiously, and the Jewish people, who, although holding the letter that kills and ignorant of the Spirit who gives life, nevertheless possessed the riches of the divine law.

## DOUBT IX

Finally, what you ask concerning the meaning of that passage of the prophet Jeremiah—“From the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good things or evil things” (Lam. III; Apoc. V)—is a famous question known throughout almost the whole Church. Many ask about it, and it is constantly repeated on the lips of many. But, through the generosity of him who opens the book and looses its seals, this question is easily resolved, provided that confidence is drawn not from ourselves but from him.

The almighty Father both delivered the innocent Son into the hands of the impious and nevertheless did not depart from the straight path of justice, since he determined that justice should flower from the very place where he permitted him for a time to be subjected to injustice. As it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “Since you are just, you arrange all things justly” (Wis. XII): you even condemn one who ought not to be punished.

The Father therefore permitted the Son to undergo death, but he did not command those who killed him to put him to death; otherwise they would have been guiltless, since they would have been attributing the ministry of impiety to the author of piety.

God therefore granted power to Christ’s persecutors, but did not command them to kill him while persecuting him. Hence the prophet first says there: “The Lord did not approve of overthrowing a man in his judgment” (Lam. III). The Lord would indeed overthrow a man in his judgment if he commanded that an innocent man be condemned. But to condemn is one thing, and not to rescue someone from the punishment of condemnation is another; to drive people raging into sacrilegious attempts is one thing, and not at all to restrain the madness of a fury that has been accepted is another.

Hence the passage continues, not by ignorance but by rejection: “Who is he who said that something should happen when the Lord did not command it?” (Ibid.) It says that the Lord did not command it, though he did not forbid it. God therefore did not command the persecutors to crucify our Savior, because he found nothing in him that deserved punishment. Yet he did not prevent him from being crucified, because, since he was to suffer for the salvation of the world, he did not at all rescue him from the hands of the impious.

Thus the passage fittingly adds: “From the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good things or evil things” (Ibid.). Good things would have proceeded if he had rescued him from the punishment inflicted upon him; evil things would have proceeded if he had found in him a crime deserving punishment. In Christ’s Passion, therefore, neither good things nor evil things proceed from the mouth of the Most High, because the Father neither frees him by an exercise of power nor condemns him according to the equity of the law. Although he does not find him to be a sinner, nevertheless, because he has been placed in the Passion for the salvation of the world, he does not rescue the innocent one.

He sees him subject to no sins, yet he does not return him acquitted from the hands of the impious, so that while the innocent one undergoes punishment, the one who is a sinner may return to pardon. And while one who does not owe the debt pays the debts of all, all who were held bound under the debt of the oldness of original sin may, once the bond has been canceled, be restored free according to the law.

## DOUBT X

There is also something that you do not ask about but which I have often pondered: why David, while he was alive, mercifully spared Joab and Shimei, against whom he was angry, but, when dying, commanded Solomon—his successor in the royal scepter—that they should be destroyed.

“You know,” he said, “what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of the army of Israel, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether, whom he killed and whose blood of war he shed in peace. And shortly afterward he added: ‘Therefore you shall act according to your wisdom, and you shall not bring his gray hairs peacefully down to the underworld’” (III Reg. II).

Concerning Shimei also he said: “You also have with you Shimei the son of Gera, the son of Gemini, from Bahurim, who cursed me with a terrible curse when I was going to the camp”; then, after inserting certain remarks, he added: “You shall bring down his gray hairs with blood to the underworld” (Ibid.).

For what reason, then, did David, when dying, condemn those whom he had spared during his lifetime, when surely the order of reason demands that while alive he should have pronounced a sentence of vengeance upon rebels or any enemies, but, when dying, should mercifully have spared them?

It must be understood that the kingdom of David—who, worn down by so many persecutions and hardships, and afflicted with his fellow soldiers by so many adversities and privations—signifies this present age, in which Christ is afflicted with his members and the Church is torn by many tribulations. The kingdom of Solomon, however, who surpassed all the rights of royal dignity in riches and glory and rose above every height of princely power, proclaims the glory of the life to come, in which Christ, truly peaceful, enjoys eternal rest with his own and solemnly feasts on the fare of the heavenly banquet.

One and the same Redeemer of ours, therefore, is now David and then will be Solomon, because now, as “strong-handed,” he does not cease to fight against the devil through his members; but then, when every conflict of flesh and spirit has been completely stilled, he will reign with his body, which is the Church, in eternal tranquility as the truly peaceful one.

Now, in his elect, he is pressed down as David beneath the burdens of calamities, driven hard by persecutions and various pressures of adversity, and worn down by tribulations and hardships; afterward, like Solomon, he will possess an overflowing abundance of immortal riches.

Now David, fleeing from the face of Absalom, leaves ten concubines in the house (II Reg. XV), whom Absalom shamefully defiles through incest. This signifies that, when our Redeemer was expelled from the Jewish city and hastened into the desert of the Gentiles, he left the Jews in the house of the law—not walking in a manly manner, but living according to a womanish way of life.
