They are aptly represented by the ten concubines, because, while they weakly observe the ten commandments of the law, they do not deserve to ascend into the chaste marriage chamber; instead, remaining without the ring of faith, they receive concubinage in place of marriage. Absalom pollutes them in his wantonness, because the evil spirit, as though prostituting them, corrupts the reprobate souls of the impious.

Concerning them it is written: “David afterward did not go in to them, but they were shut up until the day of their death, living in widowhood” (II Reg. XX). For they lost the husband of whom Isaiah says: “For seven women have taken hold of one man” (Isa. IV), and concerning whom Solomon says: “For there are seven hundred queens” [Note: III Reg. XI. This was not said by Solomon, but by Scripture concerning Solomon. By Solomon, however, it is said: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines” (Song VI).]

Thus seven received the one whom ten had lost. The holy Church joined to herself the heavenly bridegroom, filled with the sevenfold gift of the Spirit. The synagogue, however, which had received the commandments of the Decalogue, lost that bridegroom and remained a widow, because, while it steadfastly persisted in the house of its customary rite and legal ceremonies, it refused to go out with King David into the desert of the Gentiles.

David, therefore, while alive tolerates those whom he condemns at the end, because Christ, the Judge of the human race whom David prefigured, now mercifully spares those upon whom at the end of the age he will impose the sentence of just condemnation. David thus signifies the granting of mercy; Solomon signifies the execution of justice.

For one and the same Redeemer of ours now, as David, patiently tolerates the perversities of the reprobate, and afterward, coming in his glory as Solomon, slaughters them as if with the flashing edge of his judgment.

This alternation of divine judgment is frequently found in David’s own words, as in the passage: “I shall sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C). And: “God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. LXXXIII). “Mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Thus mercy is placed before truth, as David before Solomon, so that those whom David mercifully sustains, Solomon may justly condemn through judgment.

It should also be noted that Joab, who committed murder with his own hands, represents those who do evil; while Shimei, who merely cursed the king, represents those who speak perversely. For both those who act wickedly and those who persist in wicked and false speech will undoubtedly be condemned in the examination of the final judgment, as the same David says: “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Ps. I).

But lest this already exceed the threshold of an abbreviated letter, we impose silence upon our pen, lest we ourselves also be judged unteachable while striving to teach you these questions.

# ANOTHER ARGUMENT ON VARIOUS SACRED QUESTIONS

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0630C]

The subject of this argument is almost the same as that of the preceding one: blessed Peter Damian, having been asked by the same Alberic, disentangles two further questions.

TO HIS DEAREST BROTHER ALBERIC, PETER, A SINFUL MONK, GREETINGS.

## [ANOTHER ARGUMENT]

### DOUBT I

You are said to wonder, dearest brother, why not only the Scripture of the Old Testament but also many doctors of the Church maintain that a human being develops in the mother’s womb over ten months, and do not admit that he emerges within the space of nine months. To avoid wandering through many examples, it is enough to offer only one. For Solomon says in the Book of Wisdom:

“I too am a mortal man like everyone else, and descended from the earthly one who was formed first. In my mother’s womb I was fashioned as flesh; I was coagulated over a period of ten months in blood, from the seed of man and the pleasure of a fitting sleep; and, once born, I received the common air” (Wis. VII).

Yet blessed John the Baptist and Christ himself, the author and creator of nature, were born within the course of nine months, without even reaching the slightest fraction of the tenth month. John was conceived, as is written, on 24 September, and was born on 24 June. Our Savior, however, was conceived in the virgin’s womb on 25 March and was born for the salvation of the world on 25 December.

In both these conceptions and births—that of the servant and that of the Lord—nine full months are found, while the tenth does not appear to have begun at all. Nevertheless, if the two periods are carefully considered, the Lord is found to have remained in his mother’s womb two days longer than John.

Since, then, most people are born within the course of nine months, without any doubt whatsoever, why do the doctors say that they are coagulated in the womb over ten months?

As far as we are able to understand, the ancients reckoned the months as consisting of only thirty days. The rule now observed—that some months contain thirty days and others thirty-one—derives from the institution of that Romulus who founded the city of Rome.

For Romulus, since he possessed an energetic but rustic character, while organizing the structure of the new empire he had begun, established as the beginning of each month the day on which he observed the rising of the new moon, so that he made that day a Kalends on which the new moon had first appeared. But because the moon sometimes seems to be seen later and sometimes earlier, it happened that when it appeared later the preceding month received more days, and when it appeared earlier it received fewer. Hence some months came to have thirty-one days, while others received only thirty.

This rule in the reckoning of the months, as we conjecture, is now retained among us from his institution.

But because, as it seems to us, the ancient holy men did not follow this rule of a pagan man, they assigned only thirty days to each month. It is enough for us, therefore, to insert the example of one doctor. Blessed Augustine speaks as follows (Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5; and Book LXXXIII of the *Questions*, question 56):

“This temple was built over forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” (John II.)

If this number is multiplied by six, the entire period during which the Lord remained in his mother’s womb is completed. For forty-six times six makes 276 days, and this number of days completes nine months and six days, which are reckoned as ten months for women giving birth.

These words unmistakably show that only thirty days are assigned to each month. For if thirty is multiplied by nine, it makes 270. Thus in 270 the number thirty is found nine times; according to the testimony of this blessed doctor, these constitute nine months. The remaining five days are accepted as the tenth month.

Since among us there are seven months, each of which contains thirty-one days, several days remained beyond nine months according to the ancient reckoning. These they counted as the tenth month, taking the part for the whole. Thus, when the months were shorter in quantity, more were named in the reckoning: what we now call nine, they then called ten, with a part being put for the whole.

Let this explanation of the question proposed for the present suffice for you, until it happens that you hear a better one from the learned.

### DOUBT II. On the Day of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection

There is also uncertainty concerning the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, which this year occur in every respect as they did at the particular time when the Lord was crucified. You ask whether this occurs rarely or frequently. Some affirm that they have never seen it, while others maintain that it has happened several times in their lifetime. You, however, who desire to be a disciple of truth, fear to put faith in such great variation, lest you be led into the error of conflicting opinions.

But know that, insofar as we can gather from the tradition of earlier writers, this coincidence of the Lord’s Passion has never recurred in precisely this way since the time when the Lord was suspended on the cross, except once, and is now repeated for the second time.

For in the 533rd year after the Lord’s Passion, the Paschal solemnity occurred in the same month, on the same day, and under the same lunar phase and concurrent, which was the first and fifth, as had occurred in the first year of the Lord’s Resurrection; and this year the same thing happens, so that everything coincides.

For just as at the time when the Lord suffered the month was March, the day was the eighth before the Kalends of April, it was Friday, and the moon was fourteen days old, so everything likewise occurred in the 533rd year afterward, and occurs similarly in this year, which is the 1065th.

Four learned men composed the Paschal cycle: Hippolytus, Eusebius, Theophilus, and Prosper. After them, Victorius, an Aquitanian by nationality and an exceedingly meticulous calculator, at the request of Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome, revised the matter more carefully and composed the same cycle with highly cautious investigation.

He extended the series of years to 532 years, so that in the 533rd year the Paschal solemnity would begin in the same month, on the same day, the same weekday, under the same lunar phase, and with the same concurrent as those on which the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection had first shone.

In this year in which we now live, we see the Lord’s Passion, which is to be celebrated tomorrow, returning to the same order. Since this year renews that first order of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, it undoubtedly agrees with the calculation of Victorius that we mentioned. Meanwhile, until the matter can be examined more distinctly, let both of us, dearest brother, be content with this explanation.

I do not want you to be unaware, however, that after this present Paschal solemnity has been completed, Easter will likewise occur in the ninety-fifth year, with all these things coinciding: the month, day, weekday, lunar phase, the fifth concurrent—which is nevertheless a leap-year concurrent—the epact, and the position in the nineteen-year cycle.

After the fifth leap-year concurrent, in the 247th year, the Paschal solemnity will likewise occur. Thereafter it will happen three times that Easter, in the ordinary sequence, will recur in the ninety-fifth year in the same manner, with all the things mentioned above coinciding together.

But with this fifth concurrent, which is now present, the Paschal feast has never happened to occur in this way since the first Lord’s Passion, except for that one occasion which Victorius established and which is now repeated for the second time. Nor will it ever again occur that all those things coincide—that is, the month, day, weekday, lunar phase, epact, and the same position in the nineteen-year cycle—unless likewise in the 533rd year.

But since this age is already to be closed by its end, it is superfluous to extend the volumes of the ages through the ephemerides of a lengthy calculation.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

# 653–654 THIRTY-EIGHTH OPUSCULUM. AGAINST THE ERROR OF THE GREEKS CONCERNING THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

## ARGUMENT

Writing to the patriarch . . . . , he argues against the heresy of the Greeks, who impiously affirmed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son. He eloquently refutes this opinion and proves by the firmest arguments and authorities that the contrary is true. He writes to that patriarch on this subject because the patriarch had requested the Roman pontiff to clarify this very question.

TO THE MOST BLESSED LORD L., PATRIARCH, PETER, A SINFUL MONK, OFFERS HIS SERVICE.

The religious bishop of the Church of Popilius reported to me that he had heard from the mouth of the most reverend patriarch of Gradus that you had sent to the apostolic see, in sacred letters, a question of great importance to the Catholic faith, and that, with the vigilance proper to your priestly office, you had requested that it be most clearly resolved by the most holy Pope Alexander through invincible testimonies of Scripture: namely, why among the Latins the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father and the Son, while among the Greeks he is believed to proceed from the Father alone.

With regard to this question, I presume to disclose what I think, with the assistance of the very Holy Spirit concerning whom the matter is being discussed. I do so not because anything concerning this matter has been assigned to me by you or commanded by the authority of the Roman pontiff. For how would he deign to entrust so important a matter to an unskilled man, when he is undoubtedly surrounded by so many holy and highly learned men who constantly live in his company?

But although I am ignorant and an unworthy servant in the house of my Lord Jesus, I take pleasure in thrusting myself even into those services to which no one has considered it worthwhile to summon me.

## [AGAINST THE ERROR OF THE GREEKS CONCERNING THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT]

### CHAPTER I. On the Authority of the Roman Pontiff

Clearly the prudence of your holiness deserves to be praised and raised up by worthy commendations, since, in seeking the resolution of the question concerning the Holy Spirit, you brought it not to someone else but specifically to Peter, whom heaven undoubtedly recognizes as having received the keys of wisdom and power.

Nor was it fitting for a man of such dignity and wisdom to seek the secrets of the heavenly mystery from anyone other than the one whom neither flesh nor blood could instruct, but to whom God himself deigned personally to reveal his secrets.

“Blessed are you,” he says, “Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

The Founder of the world chose him above all other mortals from the whole earth, granting him by a perpetual privilege the principal seat of the teaching office in the Church, so that whoever desires to know something divine and profound may have recourse to the oracle and teaching of this teacher, and may not be ashamed humbly to submit to him what needs to be resolved, even if he himself is not ignorant of the matter in question.

For did the angel coming from heaven not know how to teach Cornelius, whom he sent to Peter so that he might learn what he ought to do?

“Send men,” he says, “to Joppa, and summon Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with a certain Simon the tanner, whose house is beside the sea; he will tell you what you must do” (Acts X).

The holy angel could certainly have taught the Gentile what was appropriate for his salvation, but he did not wish to usurp the office of one whom he knew had been entrusted with teaching.

What, then, is surprising if a priest, distinguished in holiness and thoroughly instructed in divine eloquence, sent to the teaching of the prince of the apostles, to whom even an angel sent Cornelius, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, for the purpose of being taught?

Paul also says the following to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. I).

He, therefore, who had not been made an apostle by men but by Christ himself and God the Father, and who had been sufficiently instructed by the author of wisdom, nevertheless came to Peter’s teaching and remained with him in the heavenly school not merely in passing but for many days.

“I came,” he says, “to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days” (Ibid.). Through the mystical number of the seven and the eight, he learned the mystery of both the Old and the New Testament.

It was therefore fitting that your holy prudence should direct the question for resolution to the see of that man to whom even a man ignorant of the faith was sent by an angel, and from whom even an apostle who had already been instructed by God received fuller teaching.

And through Moses it is said: “You have Aaron and Hur with you; if any question arises, refer it to them” (Exod. XXIV).

Would that Aaron—that is, Christ, the mountain of strength—be present, and that Ur, namely that fire which is the Holy Spirit himself, concerning whom we are writing, also be present, so that through us as well, a very small member of the Roman Church, he may disclose what is hidden from some, and so that Christ, the Key of David, may undo the knot of this question like the seal of a certain mystical book.

### CHAPTER II. What Is the Origin of the Greeks’ Error?

Let us begin by saying where the origin of this ignorance arises, so that nearly all Greeks, and some Latins as well, maintain that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Son but from the Father alone.

They base this on the Lord’s words: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). And again: “Behold, I send to you the promise of my Father” (Luke XXIV). And: “When the Paraclete has come, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

Again he says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV). And elsewhere he says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (Ibid.). And again: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Matt. VII.)

On the basis of these and similar testimonies—not only from the Gospels but also from other Scriptures—they assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds in no way from the Son but only from the Father.

For among the teachers of the Latin language something similar is often found that may appear to agree with this opinion. Blessed Jerome, in the exposition of the faith that he sends to the bishops Alypius and Augustine, says among other things: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit, the true Lord proceeding from the Father, equal in all things to the Father and the Son.”

Augustine, inveighing against the heretic Maximus, also says: “The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father.”

Blessed Pope Leo, too, on the silver tablet that appears to have been erected before the most sacred body of blessed Paul the Apostle, says among the other articles of his faith: “And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be adored and glorified together with the Father and the Son.”

In the creed of the Council of Nicaea it is also said: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds properly from the Father, and is true God just as the Son”; and somewhat later: “And in Scripture we find the Holy Spirit also to be true God, to proceed properly from the Father, and always to be with the Father and the Son.”

And again: “The Son,” it says, “is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds properly and truly from the Father.”

Nevertheless, these and other testimonies of Scripture, or the words of holy teachers, do not prejudice the Catholic faith, by which we believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and likewise affirm that he proceeds from the Son.

For although the Lord himself and the holy teachers of the Church also unanimously assert that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, they nowhere maintain that he does not proceed from the Son. Indeed, when the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, it is necessary to believe that he also proceeds from the Son, because the Father and the Son are undoubtedly of one and the same substance.

For when the Son says, “I and the Father are one” (John X), how can the Holy Spirit both proceed and not proceed from that which is one?

But this ineffable reality, which cannot be grasped by any faculty of human reason and cannot be discerned by any perception or consideration of the mind, must be gathered solely from the statements of the divine words.

For, as the Apostle says: “The Holy Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is in him? So also no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God; and these we speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in the teaching of the Spirit” (I Cor. II).

Indeed, how could human perception reach the manner in which the Father ineffably begets the Son, or how the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father or from both, unless almighty God revealed this to mortals through the instruments of the prophets or through his incarnate Word?

“For faith,” as the Apostle says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Heb. XI).

The statement of John remains firm: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

Therefore, in seeking to comprehend the supreme and ineffable mystery of the true faith, let us not follow the investigation of human opinion, but embrace only the truth of the heavenly word, so that what is believed about God may above all be what has been divinely declared; and in those matters which the supreme and incomprehensible Truth affirms, let the steadfastness of our faith not waver.

### CHAPTER III. That the Holy Spirit Proceeds from the Father and the Son Together

There is no question, whether among the Greeks or among the Latins, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; nor does this matter require testimonies, since this very point and the examples presented above make it evident.

But that he proceeds from the Father and at the same time from the Son—this is where the question arises—and the authority of the Gospel teaches us this when the Lord says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (John XIV). And elsewhere: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father” (John XV).

Since, therefore, the Father sends the Paraclete in the name of the Son, and the Son sends him from the Father, it is perfectly clear that, just as he is sent by both—who are undoubtedly one—so likewise he proceeds from both.

And since he is often called the Spirit of Truth, while Christ is Truth, the Spirit who is the Spirit of Truth is undoubtedly the Spirit of the Son. Hence he says elsewhere: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine” (John XVI). He will receive from what is mine, that is, because he is also in me.

Hence also, in Isaiah, the Father’s voice to the Son: “My Spirit,” he says, “which is in you, and my words which I have placed in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your offspring, forever” (Isa. LIX).

This is that very power which went out from him, as it is written in the Gospel, and healed everyone (Luke VI).

And again, concerning the woman freed from the flow of blood: “I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII).

Hence also the Apostle says to the Galatians: “Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV). And elsewhere: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

Here, when the Apostle says “the Spirit of his Son” or “the Spirit of Christ” (Rom. VIII), does he add “and of the Father,” so as to say, “the Spirit of Christ and of the Father”? Since he omits the name of the Father and calls him the Spirit of the Son, does it rightly follow that the Spirit must be denied to belong to the Father?

The same Apostle also says to the Philippians: “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Phil. I).

For this reason the Wisdom of God, who is undoubtedly Christ, says: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Sir. XXIV).

Therefore, just as when he is called the Spirit of the Son or of Christ it does not immediately follow that we can separate him from the Father, so when he is called the Spirit of the Father we cannot separate him from the Son.

Blessed Peter also says: “Concerning this salvation the prophets sought and searched, who prophesied of the future glory in us, searching into what time or what sort of time the Spirit of Christ who was in them was signifying, foretelling the sufferings that are in Christ and the subsequent glories” (I Pet. I).

That the Son sent this same Spirit upon the disciples is also affirmed by the same Peter in the Acts of the Apostles, when he says: “Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift, which you see and hear” (Acts II).

For this reason, when he had risen from the dead and appeared to the disciples, to show openly that the Spirit proceeds from him, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX).

Nor should it be thought that that bodily breath, which then struck the air, was the Holy Spirit; rather, by this fitting sign it was suitably shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. Isaiah too, when speaking of the Son of God, added: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked” (Isa. XI). In agreement with this statement, Paul says in the Epistle to the Thessalonians: “Then that wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (I Thess. II). This is also mystically indicated in the Book of blessed Job, where it says: “He will hear the sound of his voice in terror, and the noise proceeding from his mouth” (Job XXXVII).

Finally, in this passage the mouth of the Father is understood as the Son, through whom the decree of the divine law is proclaimed to us; while the sound proceeding from his mouth is the Holy Spirit, who, coming from the Son, sounded forth wondrously when he descended upon the apostles with a sudden noise, in the variety of tongues. “Suddenly,” he says, “there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty Spirit” (Acts II). This sound, which came forth from the mouth of Christ, is undoubtedly that two-edged sword which John saw proceeding from the same lips in the Apocalypse (Apoc. I). Of this the Psalmist also says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII). Since, then, as has been said, the mouth of the Father is the Son, the Spirit of the mouth of God must be understood as nothing other than the Spirit of Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. Removes a doubt that might arise.

If it is asked: since the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit likewise is from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son? The answer is not inappropriate: the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father; but the one is begotten, while the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he was begotten; while the other is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both.

Nevertheless, both that generation and this procession are not merely ineffable but altogether incomprehensible. Yet in matters that we cannot penetrate with the acuteness of our mind, we give firm faith to those through whom the Holy Spirit spoke, as though the matter lay before our eyes. Although the hidden mysteries of that profound depth are unknown to us, we do not doubt what the Lord says; nor do we hesitate over what is found in the prophetic utterances.

## CHAPTER V. Removes another doubt.

But someone may perhaps object to me: “You do not understand the Gospel; you do not know what the prophetic oracles mean, since they often present one thing on the surface of the letter while containing something else in the truth of spiritual understanding.”

To this we readily reply that there have been many apostolic and catholic men whose approved piety and holiness, demonstrated by the signs of many virtues, left nothing at all uncertain. These men explained the orthodox faith in simple words and committed it to writing for the memory of posterity. It was plainly their task to examine this matter from apostolic and prophetic statements; for us, nothing remains except to obey their established definitions. The pressure of necessity lay upon them, so that they might inquire into these matters subtly and carefully and define a certain rule of faith; but we must walk only by the path along which our forefathers proceeded.

What they then eagerly drew from the evangelical, prophetic, and even apostolic springs, they faithfully passed on to those who came after them, offering it to us, as the Psalmist says: “Bless God the Lord in the assemblies, from the springs of Israel” (Ps. LXXVII). We now receive securely and without any fear the purity of faith which flows into us through them as through channels of truth, and we rejoice to draw it as though from the very original source of the divine fountain.

Let us therefore hear what blessed Ambrose says concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit in the sixth book of *On the Faith*, which he sent to the emperor Gratian. “For,” he says, “the Spirit is not sent as though from a place, nor does he proceed as though from a place, when he proceeds from the Son.” And shortly afterward: “When the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he goes forth from the Son.” Nor is it without reason that he proceeds from both, since he is equally in both, as the same Ambrose says in the eighth book of the same work: “The Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father; so the Spirit of God is in the Father and in the Son.”

Augustine, although throughout nearly the whole book that he composed on the Holy Trinity he innumerable times asserts that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together, nevertheless we give at least one of his statements, lest we seem to have passed him over altogether through negligence. “In that holy Trinity,” he says, “there is one Father, who alone essentially begot one Son from himself; and one Son, who alone was essentially born from one Father; and one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Jerome too is said to have written this: “The Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, is coeternal with the Father and the Son and in all things equal to them. This is the holy Trinity, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; there is one divinity and power, one essence: the Father, who begot; the Son, who was begotten; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Yet this cannot be found in his exposition of the faith—that is, in the one that we read.

Blessed Pope Gregory also says in the Creed of his confession: “I believe in the unbegotten Father, the begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal and proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

If those who know only Greek and do not know Latin should reply that the Roman teachers of eloquence are not sufficient for them unless Greek-speaking Fathers are also brought forward, let them hear what blessed Athanasius declares in the book he wrote against Arius: “I believe,” he says, “in the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son, and also in the Spirit, the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father and belongs both to the Son and to the Father, because he proceeds from the Son as well, just as it is written in the Gospel that by his breathing he gave the Holy Spirit to the disciples” (John XX).

Blessed Cyril likewise says the following concerning this same procession of the Spirit, against Nestorius: “Although the Spirit is his in substance, and personal distinctiveness is understood insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of Truth, and Christ is the Truth. Hence he proceeds similarly from him, just as he proceeds from God.”

## CHAPTER VI. Removes yet another doubt.

But it may still be asked: since the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, why did the Son himself say that he proceeds from the Father? What was the reason that he did not say, “He proceeds from the Father and from me,” but rather said, “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father”?

Why do we think he did this, unless it is because he habitually refers even what is his own to him from whom he himself is? The Son is from the Father, and from the one from whom he has his being as God he likewise has it that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him also. Hence elsewhere he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John VII).

If, then, it is clearly recognized here that the teaching is his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must it be understood that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him as well, where he says, “He proceeds from the Father,” without at all saying, “He does not proceed from me”?

A similar statement is the one he makes elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me” (John XII). What does he mean by saying, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me”? How does he believe in him, and how does he not believe in him? How are such contrary and mutually conflicting words to be understood? “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me”—unless it is understood in this way: whoever believes in me does not believe in what he sees, so that our hope may not be in the creature but in the one who assumed the creature; in order that he might make it known to mortal beings that he is one with him, and cleanse human hearts so that they might contemplate himself together with him.

Likewise, when he says, “My teaching is not mine,” he creates no small darkness in our minds unless the order of the dispensation distinguishes flesh from spirit. For he did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but, “My teaching is not mine.” What he called his own, he also called not his own. How can this truly be so unless he called it his own in one respect and not his own in another? According to the form of God, it is his; according to the form of a servant, it is not his.

When he says, “It is not mine, but his who sent me,” he directs the gaze of our mind toward the Word himself, who was hidden in the flesh, so that we may recognize him as one with the Father. The Father’s teaching is the Father’s Word, who is the only Son. Therefore the statement, “My teaching is not mine,” must be understood as though he said: “I am not from myself, but from him who sent me.”

## CHAPTER VII. How the Holy Spirit is said to proceed properly from the Father in the Nicene Creed.

Since, then, he declares that his teaching, which he dictates together with the Father, is not his but the Father’s, what wonder is it if he says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father—from whom the same Son had received that he should proceed from him also?

Thus, in the Creed of the Council of Nicaea, which we mentioned above, the Holy Spirit is not simply said to proceed from the Father, but the word “properly” is added: “And in the Holy Spirit,” it says, “who proceeds properly from the Father.” This propriety is not attributed to the Father so that the Holy Spirit may proceed from him alone, but because it was given by him to the Son that the Spirit should proceed from the Son as well.

Hence Augustine says in his book *On the Holy Trinity*: “It is not without reason that in this Trinity the Word of God is said to be no one but the Son, nor the Gift of God anyone but the Holy Spirit, nor the one from whom the Word was begotten and from whom the Spirit proceeds principally anyone but God the Father.” He immediately adds: “I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son; but the Father too gave this to him—not to one who already existed and did not yet possess it, but whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word, he gave by begetting him.”

Therefore faith must not be disturbed when it hears that the Holy Spirit proceeds properly or principally from the Father, since from the Father it is given to the Son that he should proceed from the Son, from whom the Son himself proceeds by an ineffable and incomprehensible generation. Thus the Son himself, who is the wisdom of the Father, says through Solomon: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV). And in the Gospel: “For I came forth from God and came” (John VIII).

Moreover, this must be guarded against with the greatest care: while we assert that the Son has received from the Father that the Paraclete proceeds from him, we must not also believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father for our sanctification. Far be it from us to believe this, lest a diversity of degrees appear to be arranged within the simple and incomprehensible divinity, since Scripture says: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exod. XX).

Without any doubt, then, we must believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both together, although the Father gave this to the Son: that, just as he proceeds from the Father, so likewise he proceeds from the Son. For the Holy Spirit is an ineffable communion of the Father and the Son. Therefore he seems to bear this name because it is indisputably fitting alike to the Father and the Son. For that is properly said of him which is commonly said of them: the Father is Spirit, and the Son is Spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy. And just as his name belongs equally to both, so he proceeds from both together.

We could still gather several examples from Scripture, and it would not be impossible to bring forward, together with their arguments, distinguished defenders of the catholic faith in support of our assertions. But because the law forbids us to plant groves of trees beside the altar (Judg. VI), we do not wish to cover the fruits of the Spirit with the shady leaves of protracted speech.

Therefore, your Holiness, venerable father, although you are fully and abundantly nourished by the food of heavenly eloquence and nevertheless hunger more and more for the truth, do not meanwhile disdain this very meager breakfast of a poor man. Later you will taste from the hands of our lord the pope—as though through the prophet Habakkuk, indeed through an angel—the royal delicacies of a banquet (Dan. XIV).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

---

## 663–664. THIRTY-NINTH LITTLE WORK. AGAINST THOSE WHO SIT DURING THE DIVINE OFFICE.

### SUMMARY

He praises the discipline and order that the archbishop of Besançon maintained in his Church. Above all, he praises the fact that the archbishop had prepared his own tomb while still alive, so that he might always have the final day of life before his eyes. Yet he saw one matter deserving correction while he was staying with him: during the celebration of the sacred rites, both clerics and those who had not been initiated into sacred orders took part while seated. He clearly demonstrates that this was contrary both to prescribed discipline and to their dignity.

To the most reverend lord V., archbishop, Peter, sinful monk, offers service.

## AGAINST THOSE WHO SIT DURING THE DIVINE OFFICE

### CHAPTER I. On the magnificence of the archbishop of Besançon and the avarice of the clergy.

You are not unaware, venerable father, that while I was received as your guest by you, I painted everything as though on a tablet of my mind, so that henceforth nothing could be erased by forgetfulness. I retain, in particular, the cloister behind the apse of the church, dedicated solely to your dwelling, where you can devote yourself so privately and so remotely to prayer and reading that you seem to have no need of an eremitical solitude.

I also remember the other cloister, which occupies the right side of the church, where the white-clad company of your clerics shines like an angelic choir. There, as in the heavenly gymnasium of Athens, they are instructed in the language of the sacred Scriptures; there they diligently devote themselves to the studies of true philosophy and exercise themselves daily under regular disciplines.

Nor does it escape me that, in addition to these, you are now building two other canonical houses at the same time: one, namely, with the church of Saint Mary Magdalene, and the other with the church of Saint Lawrence, if I remember correctly. Since your church is not wealthy, it is remarkable how it can devote itself to such laborious and magnificent structures and daily meet such lavish expenses.

But I confess that I was pleased above all by this: you then showed me your tomb, most carefully prepared by you as though it were to receive you today. There, as a payment for the gravediggers, five solidi in coins are tied into the shroud at each of the four corners, so that during the funeral rites your gravediggers may seem not to lack a reward even in this work of piety.

In this you appear to follow the example of the patriarch Abraham. When he was trying to bury his wife Sarah (Gen. XXIII), and all the sons of Seth were freely offering him their choicest tombs, he rejected what was free and purchased from Ephron, son of Seor, the double cave. For in the number four as well you seem in some way to have imitated his example: just as he redeemed the cave for four hundred shekels of silver, so you too seem in some manner to purchase your burial for four times five solidi.

Here one should note how detestable is the avarice of clerics who hope for profit from the Church’s burials, since even pagans who do not know God shun this. They reject money when it is offered; these men shamelessly demand it even when it is refused. Those pagans, despising Abraham’s price, say: “Bury your dead in our chosen tombs, and no one will be able to prevent you.” These men, the equals of pagans, say: “Weigh out the money and receive the burial” (Gen. XXIII).

But you, venerable father, seem to me to have acted with wise counsel when, while still alive and in good health, you decided that a burial should be made for you. For whenever this deceitful life flatters us, or the mind is perhaps lifted up by the enticing height of some dignity, as soon as one directs one’s eyes toward such a house awaiting him, he recognizes that he is dust and considers himself, as he is, ashes.

Hence Solomon says: “What need is there for a man to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what is useful to him in his life, during the number of the days of his pilgrimage and of the time that passes like a shadow?” (Eccles. VII). Nor do the enticing movements of sensual titillation prevail in dissolving the flesh into the streams of lust, while the mind is compelled to imagine the worms that swarm and the putrefaction flowing from those same bodies.

Thus Solomon also says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (ibid.). In the house of mourning the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what will be.

But those who have planted the root of their heart in the sandy pleasure of this world, when the world smiles upon them and gentle, tranquil delight caresses them, undoubtedly shrink from the memory of death as from gall or wormwood. Hence the wise man says: “O death, how bitter is your memory to a man who has peace in his possessions, to a tranquil man whose ways are directed in all things, and who is still able to receive food!” (Ecclus. XLI).

But if some person is weighed down by the misfortune of grievous calamity, if persistent illness or poverty of household resources constricts him, death becomes sweet to him, and he is entreated to hasten its flying steps. Hence the same man says: “O death, your judgment is good for the needy man and for him whose strength is failing because of weakened age” (ibid.).

Yet a person ought by no means to dread or desire his end according to the variations of this life, but only insofar as death or life is judged beneficial either to his own salvation or to that of his brother. This is declared by the one who says: “I am constrained by both desires: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I).

Blessed Peter also said to his hearers: “I consider it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by way of reminder. For I know that the laying aside of my tabernacle is swift” (I Pet. I). In these words the good shepherd plainly shows that he wished both to live and to die not for himself but for his disciples. For shortly afterward he says: “I shall take pains that, even after my death, you may frequently call these things to mind.”

Your burial therefore pleases me, since you have set it before your eyes as a memorial sign, so that, while it is seen, the green vigor of this present life—wrongly flourishing—may wither for you, and the mind, gathered into itself, may diligently begin to think about what is to come. For when a person reaches that destination, he undoubtedly finds what he can in no way change. Hence Solomon admonishes us, saying: “Always remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccles. VII).

### CHAPTER II. That for clerics to sit while the divine offices are celebrated is a bad custom.

I also saw in your church one sign of torpor and sloth, which I corrected then, as the time and circumstances permitted, and which I do not now consider it superfluous to commit to writing. Many of the clerics there sit while either the canonical offices of the hours are being celebrated or the terrible sacraments of the Mass itself are being offered.

I discovered that this sluggish negligence was also present in some monks throughout the regions of Gaul. This is plainly a fault of bad custom, deserving correction and needing to be completely rooted out from the field of the Church militant, wherever conditions remain sound. Of this Church it is written in the Song of Songs: “What will you see in the Shulammite, except the companies of armies?” (Song VII). And again: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with its battlements; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the strong” (Song IV).

For while an unrelenting war threatens us everywhere against the spirits of wickedness, it presses more fiercely during the singing of psalms. When we pray, we then fight as though in battle array against the assaults of our malignant enemies, so that we must either yield weakly to those who overcome us or, when they fall in the Lord, triumphantly mock them.

When they see our bodies grow dull through enervating sitting, they immediately hope to gain victory through the ruin of the inner person as well. Of them Isaiah says: “I will put him into the hand of those who humbled you and said to your soul: ‘Bow down, that we may pass over you’” (Isa. LI). After the soul’s bowing, he immediately adds concerning the body’s bowing: “And you have laid your body like the ground and like a road for passersby.”

The two substances—soul and body—are so united in us that, when one acts diligently, the other is often strengthened; and while one, relaxed through negligence, yawns, the other too grows numb with the sluggishness of sleep. When Joshua saw an angel holding a drawn sword, he said: “What does my Lord say to his servant?” (Josh. V). The angel gave him no other command and imposed nothing else for him to carry out except this: “Take off,” he said, “the sandal from your feet”; and he added: “For the place on which you stand is holy.”

Since, then, that place was owed the nakedness of bare feet because it was holy, why should the church, which is likewise a holy place, not deserve at least the reverence of clerics standing? Moses too was told: “Do not come near; remove the sandal from your feet. For the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III).

Why do we read these things divinely commanded to the ancient Fathers throughout the sacred pages, unless so that we may believe that we owe reverence to holy places? Is the place in which, through the mystery of Christ’s life-giving Passion, his body is offered less sacred than the place where God spoke through his angel?

In Deuteronomy too it is written that the Lord said to Moses: “Stand here with me, so that I may speak to you all the commandments, ordinances, and judgments” (Deut. V). He did not say, “Sit” or “Recline,” but “Stand with me,” so that by standing he might learn what he would later teach while seated.

Now, while we are on active service, God wishes us who minister to him to stand before him, so that afterward we may deserve to sit with him in the tranquility of the heavenly city. Moreover, if someone had such an abundance of gifts that, so long as the office remained, he did not cease distributing gifts to individuals, even he would plant his foot firmly if the disease of gout bound his joints. Thus he would accept the comfort of standing for a dying body, while by sitting he would despise the adornment of a soul destined to reign forever.

If offices respectfully attend a king or any earthly nobleman in his domain, with what audacity of presumption do we dare to sit when we celebrate praises before the terrible presence of the divine majesty? Daniel says: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). Behold: although some of the innumerable angels are said to minister to God and others to stand before him (Apoc. I), none of them is found here sitting on a bench.

### CHAPTER III. That angels are angered against men sitting in church.

The angelic powers stand trembling before him, and earthly, corruptible men disdain to stand! Since it is rightly believed that angelic presence is always present at those ecclesiastical offices, as Scripture says, “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII), and since they not only carefully observe our vigilance or sloth but also report all things in order to the heavenly Judge, how great, we may suppose, is the zeal that moves them against us when they see us sitting irreverently in the sight of him before whom they themselves stand trembling?

When Zacharias the priest was placing the incense, he saw an angel beside the altar—not seated, but standing. “The angel of the Lord appeared to him,” says the evangelist, “standing at the right side of the altar of incense” (Luke I).

Blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne.” Standing before it, certainly, not sitting. Shortly afterward he says: “All the angels stood around the throne and the elders” (Apoc. VII).

Isaiah, after saying, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and elevated throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple,” immediately added: “The seraphim stood beneath it” (Isa. VI). Behold: where the seraphim do not dare to sit, does a man of clay sit, yellow and unclean like a menstrual cloth? Where the powers of heaven do not claim seats for themselves, does a human being enjoy leisure as though it were ordinary and domestic, although he knows himself to be dust and ashes?

A king enters the wedding feast and finds a man who perhaps not only lacks wedding garments but is also sitting disgracefully against the rule of that feast. What else should he be thought to command except that the man, with hands and feet bound, be immediately cast into the darkness? (Matt. XXII.)

Indeed, concerning Eli the priest, who was sitting, Scripture says: “He fell backward from his seat beside the gate, broke his neck, and died” (I Sam. IV). King Belshazzar of Babylon was also sitting when a finger writing appeared on the surface of the wall of the royal hall and announced that the destruction of him and his people was imminent that very night, with the Medes and Persians approaching (Dan. V).

The kings Zebah and Zalmunna of Midian were resting with their army when Gideon suddenly attacked them as though they were secure and slaughtered them with flashing swords (Judg. VIII). The Amalekites likewise were reclining upon the face of the earth when David suddenly invaded them and did not cease striking them from evening until the evening of the following day (I Sam. XXX).

By contrast, Elijah says: “As the Lord of hosts lives, before whose presence I stand” (I Kings XVII). “I stand,” he says; “I do not sit, I do not yawn, I do not grow slack.” The Lord also says to him: “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord” (I Kings XIX). He does not say, “Sit,” but “Stand before the Lord.”

Did David and the seven choirs with him sit before the ark of the Lord? No; rather, as Scripture testifies: “The king himself played the instruments, danced, and leapt with all his strength before the Lord” (II Sam. VI). Thus they led the ark with rejoicing and the sound of the trumpet.

Note also what the Lord says to Moses: “Bring forward the tribe of Levi and make them stand in the presence of Aaron the priest, so that they may minister to him, keep watch, and observe whatever pertains to the service of the people before the tabernacle of testimony” (II Chron. XV). He does not say, “Let them sit, yawn, and sleep,” but “Make them stand,” so that they may minister, keep watch, and observe.

Moses on the mountain, for forty days and as many nights, never sat even for a moment and took no food or drink, but stood continually before the Lord in fasting (Num. III). And you, who sustain yourself by daily nourishment, are burdened by standing before the presence of your Creator for even a brief period?

For thus it is written in Exodus: “Moses therefore stood there with the Lord for forty days and nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water, and he wrote upon the tablets the ten words of the covenant” (Exod. XXXIV).

Even today some brothers, while devoting themselves to divine praises, are not content with the mere labor of standing, but strive in addition to weary themselves through other exercises of the body.

To say nothing of the others, there is a certain brother named Gezo, who is now separated from our dwelling by no great distance. He is already advanced in age, about sixty years old, and goes through the entire Psalter by bending his knees, in such a way that he completes one verse while prostrating himself on the pavement and another while immediately rising. Thus, throughout the whole course of the Psalter, one *metanoea*—a prostration or act of penitence—is always made for every pair of verses.

Another man was also with us, more advanced in age, who was rightly called Dominicus. He confessed to me that he often performed a thousand *metanoeas* each day, while he was continually wearing an iron coat of mail directly against his flesh. But anyone who wishes to hear more about such things should take care to read through our little works.

### CHAPTER IV. That laypeople too ought not to sit in church during the divine offices.

For now it is enough for me to suggest to your Holiness that you first correct this disgraceful fault of negligence in your own Church, and then extend the sickle of salutary correction through the branches of the others.

It must be strictly prohibited not only to clerics but also to laypeople of either sex that, except as is customary during the readings of the nocturnal office, no one should sit while the divine hymns are being sung, unless bodily illness compels him.

We have seen many men, not only of the sacred order but also of the secular order, who are so content with the strength of their standing throughout every office of the ecclesiastical assembly that they do not deign to lean either on a railing or on any adjacent support whatsoever. The more laboriously they stand in the sight of the heavenly majesty that observes them, the sweeter the delight of inward rest they acquire; and the more difficultly they endure the heaviness of their bodies, the more abundantly their merit lifts them toward God.

Moreover, as the history of Eutropius records, the consul Varro, because he suffered defeat at Cannae while fighting against Hannibal, never afterward, until the end of his life, took food while reclining. If pagans do this to extend the renown of their name, what ought Christians to do in order to acquire seats in heavenly glory?

Indeed, if we possessed a fervor worthy of God, it would have been fitting for us, during the watches of divine praise, not merely not to sit but also to sing psalms without ceasing, with our hands extended upward. The Psalmist urges us to this when he says: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places, and bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII). And the Apostle says to Timothy: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute” (I Tim. II).

The distinguished teacher of the Church, Ambrose, also testifies that he saw the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius always praying with their hands extended. His words imply that the bishop himself was praying in the same way at that time, although he does not say so explicitly, in order to avoid glory. It is certainly plausible that those who pray together with him would not differ from him in the manner of prayer. Otherwise, if Ambrose prayed differently, the manner of prayer displayed by them was shown to him so that he might henceforth be formed according to that rule of prayer.

When blessed Paul spoke to him about the aforementioned martyrs, whose bodies he had found in the same place, he significantly added: “in which you stand and pray.” The distinguished priest stood when he prayed; he did not sit like these men and occupy himself with idle matters.

Furthermore, since the Apostle also says: “Are they not ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. I), where should the blessed company of angels be believed to move about more frequently than in the Church, where it knows that God’s people gather—the people for whose sake it is sent? And if we hastily rise to any person of greater power, with what presumptuous audacity do we not fear to sit before the angelic powers?

But you, beloved, since in the western regions you are distinguished and renowned in reputation among priests, destroy everywhere, insofar as you can, this reproach of disgraceful sitting, and strive not sluggishly to fulfill the other duties that belong to priestly stewardship. Argue, entreat, rebuke, and, as the same Apostle advises, “be watchful in all things, labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry” (II Tim. IV), so that, when it is necessary to stand before the presence of the supreme Shepherd, you may be able to present abundant and worthy fruit from the ministry you have completed.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

---

## 671–672. FORTIETH LITTLE WORK. ON RESTRAINING ANGER AND ROOTING OUT HOSTILITIES.

### SUMMARY

He congratulates Bishop V. on recovering, by God’s grace, from a serious illness. Taking this as his occasion, he urges him to restrain his anger, to uproot completely any seeds of hatred and hostility that may be in his heart, and finally, in accordance with the commandment of the evangelical law, to forgive all injuries and offenses committed by his enemies.

To the most reverend lord V., bishop, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

## ON RESTRAINING ANGER AND ROOTING OUT ENMITIES

### CHAPTER I. Why illnesses are sent by God.

The order of the divine arrangement is truly worthy of praise, because while it cuts, it heals; while it strikes, it instructs; it remedies while it inflicts a wound. For this reason, venerable Father, divine severity surrounded you with the blows of bodily affliction: it restrained you from frivolity as though you were a teachable boy, and therefore struck you with the hammer of discipline, so that it might cleanse you, as a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, from the filth of encrusted dross or overlaid rust. Hence it is said through the prophet concerning the incorrigible and undisciplined: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline [Col. 0649B] (Jer. V).” And again: “The refiner has blown in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed (Jer. VI).” Concerning them, too, the divine voice says elsewhere through the prophet: “The whole house of Israel has become dross to me (Ezek. XXII).” The house of Israel is then turned into dross when a sinner, struck by divine retribution, either falls into the abyss of despair or, through impatience, rises up against the authority of the One who justly rages against him. But, on the contrary, as the metal remains, the dross flies away beneath the divine blows when any penitent, chastised by heavenly punishment, casts off from himself the rust of his bristling vices and shines with the whiteness of virtues blossoming anew and with the radiance of a resplendent life.

We clearly see this accomplished in you through the regard of divine grace, since you have received all your enemies back into favor and, having first recovered from your inward illness, have also become healthy in body and restored joy to the Church. Therefore, with David, you ought to sing to God with a voice that cannot displease him: “The Lord has chastised me severely, but he has not handed me over to death (Ps. CXVII).” And with Jonah: “When my soul was fainting within me, I remembered the Lord, so that my prayer might come to you, to your holy temple (Jon. II).” Thereafter, you ought to conclude your thanksgiving with the same prophet, above all in these words: “But I will sacrifice to you with a voice of praise; whatever I have vowed, I will repay for my salvation to the Lord (ibid.).”

We, too, who by God’s generosity have been deemed worthy to receive you back as though you had been lost, should offer him the sacrifice of the calves of our lips [Col. 0649D]—and say with Sarah, the daughter of Raguel: “Blessed is your name, God of our fathers, who, when you are angry, show mercy, and in the time of tribulation forgive the sins of those who call upon you (Tob. III).”

I had often pressed upon you, acting plainly as a mediator, that you should restore renewed peace with your enemies, and that, as a priest, you should forgive those who hated you and unjustly injured you. But the movements of your spirit, which no human flatterer could soothe, were subdued by divine severity; and, so to speak, your anger was appeased by anger. He wished to rage against you in order to remove your rage: he poured out the spirit of vengeance in order to restore in you the spirit of gentleness.

## CHAPTER II. How wisdom is lost through anger

Your judgment can now clearly demonstrate with what earnestness the vice of anger must be avoided. For those who then seemed hateful to you and wholly unworthy of access to your friendship, you now enjoy with the sweetest affability; throwing yourself upon them without fear, you take delight, as it were, in being bound by the pleasant embraces of friendship. Then you rightly said: “My eye is troubled because of anger (Ps. VI)”; but now you can sing with a joyful voice: “The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes (Ps. XVIII).”

The commandment of the Lord is charity. “This is my commandment,” he says, “that you love one another (John XIII).” This commandment truly enlightens the eyes of the heart, just as jealousy and hatred, by contrast, blind them. “Whoever,” as John says, “hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes [Col. 0650C] (John II).” In contrast, the Lord says: “I have come as light into this world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness (John XII).” Indeed, if everyone who believes in Christ does not remain in darkness, and everyone who hates his brother is, according to John’s statement, in darkness, then the one who is blinded by the darkness of deadly hatred is plainly shown not to believe in Christ.

From the reasoning of this apostolic and evangelical teaching, therefore, it follows that whoever is struck by the blindness of hatred is counted needlessly among Christ’s faithful; and whoever is hateful must necessarily also be an unbeliever, lacking faith in God, since he has lost the charity divinely established toward his neighbor. Only that faith is truly called faith which “works through love” (Gal. V). Let anger, therefore, be excluded from the minds of the elect—anger which generates hatred and, through its poisonous offspring, blinds still more disastrously the eyes of the heart that it has itself disturbed. Every angry person truly destroys himself when he thirsts for injury to his neighbor, or, what is more atrocious, for his death. Hence it is written: “Anger kills the foolish man, and jealousy slays the little one (Job V).”

Moreover, since it is written: “But you, Lord, judge with tranquillity (Wis. II),” whenever we restrain turbulent movements of the spirit through the strength of gentleness, we endeavor to return to the likeness of our Creator. For when anger lashes the mind’s repose, it disturbs it as though torn and divided, so that it no longer agrees with itself, and confuses the form of its inward likeness like agitated water. And when anger moves the fluid heart, it does not correspond to its own origin, like the image of a swelling wave.

Finally, through anger wisdom is lost, so that one does not know what should be done or in what order. Hence it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool (Eccles. VII).” Of it we read elsewhere: “Anger destroys even the prudent,” because a confused mind, even if it is able to understand something subtly, cannot carry it out when weighed down by the mass of a deadly vice. Moreover, anyone accustomed to anger frequently will never be able to practice justice. Someone might say that I am lying, if the Apostle had not written in his epistle: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God (James I).” For when the disturbed mind sharpens the judgment of its reason, it considers right not what God commands but what fury suggests.

How great the plague of anger is becomes evident in the fact that the company of an angry person is forbidden to us; indeed, according to the judgment of ancient Scripture, he is struck, so to speak, with a kind of excommunication when he is separated from the fellowship of his neighbors. Solomon says: “Do not associate continually with an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a scandal to your soul (Prov. XXII).” And again: “It is better,” he says, “to sit in a corner of the roof than with a quarrelsome woman and in a common house (Prov. XXI).” Hence [674] whoever does not restrain himself by human reason must live alone like a beast. Through anger, harmony is broken, and thus the fellowship of those living together is often violated. As it is written: “An impetuous man produces quarrels, and an angry man digs up sins (Prov. XXIX).” The angry man is said to dig up sins because he forces even evil people, whom he provokes to insane fury, to become worse through impatience.

## CHAPTER III. How anger excludes the Holy Spirit

Moreover, through anger the light of truth is lost; it is lost, and the ray of the unsetting sun is hidden from the sight of the darkened mind. Hence the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger (Eph. IV).” For when anger casts the darkness of confusion over the mind, God immediately hides from it the ray of his knowledge.

Through anger, certainly, the splendor of the Holy Spirit is excluded, and an evil mind does not deserve to become his dwelling. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI.) For when he said “humble,” he subsequently added “quiet,” because when anger removes both quietness and humility from the mind, it immediately closes its dwelling to the Holy Spirit; and when the mind exalts itself through insane fury, it condemns itself, as though with doors bolted, so that the Holy Spirit may not enter it.

It must be understood, moreover, that anger often pretends to bear the color of tranquillity and displays an outward appearance of calm, while it does not openly leap forth in indignation. Meanwhile, however, while it burns more fiercely within the mind as in a furnace, although it remains silent outwardly, it forms loud voices within the tribunal of conscience. Hence Solomon says: “The expectation of the wicked is fury (Prov. XI).” And a certain wise man says: “The thoughts of an angry person are generations of vipers; they devour the mother, the mind, that gave them birth.”

The physicians, moreover, teach that the human soul is threefold. It is, they say, rational, irascible, and concupiscible.

It is therefore not restrained without great labor, since it is said to arise not accidentally but to be naturally implanted. Nevertheless, we must not despair of victory over this vice, any more than over concupiscence. Our nature, in which these things are said to be originally implanted, was indeed corrupted by the transgression of our first parent, but through the grace of our Redeemer it has been restored to its former state of health. And although the law of the flesh fights against the law of the spirit, our mind easily overcomes the darkness of its former condition if it perseveres in the power of heavenly grace, which it has conceived through renewal.

Hence the Apostle says: “For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death (Rom. VIII).” Immediately he adds: “For what was impossible to the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh; and, on account of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us (ibid.).”

Moreover, if anger or concupiscence, which are said to be naturally implanted in us, could not be overcome through the power of the spirit, that same outstanding preacher would never have commanded the impossible. For he says: “But now put away all these things from you: anger and indignation (Col. III).” To the Ephesians also he says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice (Eph. IV).” As for concupiscence, it is superfluous to produce examples of it, since the ancient law forbids it and the entire authority of the sacred Scriptures condemns it.

Those things, therefore, which are commanded to be overcome through divine commands can be overcome through divine grace. What, then, is worse than anger, which is vomited forth from the gall of the ancient dragon and truly rages like deadly poison in the heart of some furious person? For “anger,” as it is written, “has a demon (1 Kings XVIII).”

We recognize this also by experience if we carefully consider the history of the angry Saul. Scripture says: “When the Israelite women sang as they played their tambourines and instruments of joy, ‘Saul has struck down his thousand, and David his ten thousand,’ Saul became exceedingly angry, and this saying displeased him.” Then it continues: “On the following day, an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house (1 Kings XVIII).”

Here we plainly see what we read written: namely, that anger has a demon. In Saul, anger came first into his heart, and immediately introduced the spirit of wickedness; then it inflamed his madness into a frenzy of furious jealousy and incited him to kill David, in whom the Holy Spirit dwelt. For Scripture testifies: “Saul held a spear and threw it, thinking that he could pin David to the wall (ibid.).” The spirit that was the author of anger raged in its vessel and inflamed him against the innocent with the torches of deadly envy.

## CHAPTER IV. The example of a presbyter delivered over to the devil because of anger

Something almost similar happened in the territory of Urbino nearly a decade ago. It came to our knowledge not so much through rumor as through the very presence of the event. As day was already turning toward evening, the unsetting sun was setting in the hearts of two presbyters, and the spirit that causes discord inflamed them against one another with mutual insults, quarrels, and reproaches.

When one presbyter was mangling his fellow presbyter with shameful insults and mockery, and each had sprinkled the other with the sharp salt of slanders and reports, one of them, roaring threateningly and gnashing his teeth, seized a spear, set out, and began hastening with furious steps toward his house, which lay some distance away.

But when the darkness of night overtook him and the inner darkness of his heart possessed him still more destructively, behold, five black riders on equally black horses met him. The one who appeared to be the chief among them taunted him, saying: “I have often urged you to submit to me and to come under the patronage of my companions.

“Since you have evaded me so many times, you will no longer be able to escape the yoke of my dominion.”

He appeared to be a certain nobleman named Romanus [676], who had often urged the presbyter to become his subject. The presbyter, struck by the horror of overwhelming terror, immediately brought both hands together at the command of the one who ordered him; then, kissing that man’s hands like a surrendered captive, he entrusted himself to his master’s protection.

This event corresponds to what Solomon says: “The evil man will not be innocent when hand is joined to hand (Prov. XI).”

The other immediately questioned him: “Do you know who I am?” He promptly replied: “Are you not my lord Romanus?” But the other said: “Far from it, far from it! I am the devil, to whom you are now committed and with whom you will henceforth be bound in indivisible companionship.

“Stand firm, then, in your faith, and keep what you have promised.”

After these words and actions, he immediately disappeared.

Then the presbyter, trembling, confused, and terrified, reached his house with no little horror and agitation. A short time later he came to the bishop of holy memory, named Teuzo, seeking penance, with me also present. We immediately deprived him of the office of his priestly dignity. Since the summer heat was then burning and the time for cutting the harvest was approaching, in accordance with the rule of the *carina* [perhaps: “canons”], we imposed confinement in prison custody; we prescribed years of penance with suitable moderation; and we all encouraged him so that he might undoubtedly recover in the hope of certain restoration.

From this event it is plainly understood that an angry person, when inflamed by the zeal of immoderate fury, is possessed by a demon, according to the testimony of Scripture. For is someone not driven by a demon when, in order to punish the innocence of a person who has not harmed him but rather obeyed him, he is sometimes moved—indeed, when he has lost the free judgment of his mind—to exercise vengeful punishment even against insensible things?

This is evidently what Cyrus, king of Persia, did, as Herodotus, the ancient historian, relates. When Cyrus was crossing the river Gyndes, surrounded by troops, one of the royal horsemen, outstanding in whiteness and beauty, entered its violent channel, where whirlpools rose because the ford was dangerous. As the surging waves rushed upon him, he was overwhelmed and drowned.

Then the king, moved by anger, resolved to take vengeance upon the river, declaring that the stream which had swallowed the splendid horseman should be left so passable that it would scarcely reach a woman’s knees. Thus, as is conjectured, he spent an entire year on this ridiculous labor. Opening many ditches on both sides, he wounded the river, as it were, with just as many wounds in its flanks; he divided its waters into four hundred and sixty channels and forced them to flow away as though they were the blood of his enemy. He punished with poverty the rich stream against which the tyrant had raged.

## CHAPTER V. How anger makes a person insane

You see, then, how anger makes a person insane. While it carries out what impatience suggests, it exposes itself as food for the mockery of those who laugh. Through every vice committed by human beings, the poisonous ancient enemy pours his venom into the wretched heart in various ways. In the plague of anger, however, the serpent shakes all his inward parts and pours forth every bitterness of gall, to such a degree that he makes the prudent mind devoid of prudence, the rational person mad, and the intelligent person insane. He alienates the wretched and compels them to rave like those seized by madness.

Although this is entirely forbidden to all Christians, priests must especially beware of it. Since Truth commands all the faithful in common that anyone who is at odds with another should leave his gift before the altar and not presume to offer it until he has been reconciled with his injured brother (Matt. V), how much more diligently must this be done by a priest, who is about to offer not a weight of metal, not a corruptible pearl, not even bundles of grain, but the sacrament of the life-giving Eucharist [Col. 0655A]!

And since that singular offering was offered for enemies in the beginning, as the Apostle testifies: “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son (Rom. V),” with what frame of mind, with what audacity, does a priest presume to approach so terrible a sacrament and the banquet of the heavenly table if, while celebrating the mystery of reconciliation, he scorns to be reconciled with his brother?

An enemy offers the sacrifice that dissolves enmities; unreconciled, he approaches the mystery of peace. Yet to forgive one who has sinned is a greater sacrifice than to offer sacrifices of praise, and the holocaust of good will is more pleasing to God than the sacrament of an outward victim.

Therefore, we do not believe it irrelevant to insert here what is widely reported by some people. A certain man, it is said, killed a person more powerful than himself. From the latter’s son he suffered many troubles of war—not according to the laws of the Gospel, but according to the custom of the world. As the avenger of his father’s death, the son thirsted for the slaughter of men and repeatedly carried off the spoils of plunder.

The murderer, caught amid these difficulties, decided to approach the imperial court, in case he might find some relief from so many calamities. When the son, the avenger of his father’s blood, learned of this, he pursued him, accompanying him eagerly, whether to bind him under the law of the courts or suddenly to overwhelm him with swords. At that time the emperor was staying in the Germanic regions.
