As the murderer proceeded modestly, walking as though secure, while his pursuer hastened after him more rapidly, it finally happened that, as they drew near one another, each came within the other’s sight. But the man guilty of homicide had the support of scarcely four or five companions, whereas the slain man’s son was surrounded by nearly thirty armed retainers. The murderer therefore urged his small company to flee.

Seeing that he could not escape from the hands of his pursuers, he sought the protection of his soul and took refuge beneath the shelter of humility. Throwing down his weapons, he stretched out his arms in the form of a cross, cast himself prostrate on the ground, and awaited either the mercy of those who might pity him or the blows of those who would strike him.

But the victor, already master of the situation, restrained his hand out of reverence for the cross and even prevented anyone else from striking him. Finally, making a complete peace, in honor of the holy life-giving cross [678], he granted him not only his life but also forgiveness for the offense of his father’s murder.

After achieving this distinguished victory—a victory that was not so much over the other man as over himself, and, to speak frankly, not so much over an enemy as over his own heart—he went to the royal court, which was nearby. But as soon as he entered a church to pray, something extraordinary and deeply astonishing occurred: the image of the Savior represented on the cross seemed to greet him three times by inclining its head.

O how glorious and distinguished a commendation, that he should deserve to be reverently received by the author of mercy because, out of reverence for him, he had relinquished vengeance; and that he should receive the honor of salvation from the one for whose sake he had set aside revenge, which is opposed to salvation!

When the emperor immediately heard this, he received him with the honorable and affectionate friendliness that was appropriate and enriched him with abundant generosity in gifts. O, if that man had been performing the office of the priestly order, how confidently he could have approached to offer a gift to God!

By contrast, how dangerously and harmfully does anyone approach the sacred altars who heaps within his heart the confusions of anger or hatred and awaits the time for vengeful recompense! What was provided for the increase of refreshment becomes a conflagration for human beings.

## CHAPTER VI. The portent that occurred to a Salernitan presbyter while celebrating Mass

Perhaps this explains what the venerable Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno, recently reported as having happened to one of his presbyters. That presbyter, in order to accumulate monetary profit, had been eagerly seeking considerable usury from widows and thereafter lived in carnal conduct.

On one occasion, while he was celebrating the office of the Mass, during the very fraction of the Lord’s body, three sparks of fire suddenly sprang forth from the heavenly sacrament and struck the celebrant’s breast with terrifying force. What this may have signified, the judgment of a discerning investigator will determine.

Nor do I think the following should be passed over in silence. The same ruler of the Church of Salerno and the most religious and truthful abbot of the monastery of Cassino, Desiderius, told me—in a manner of speaking, with one mouth—that a certain bishop, whose name presently escapes me, was about to consecrate a church in a certain fortified town. He requested relics of the blessed confessor Barbatus from the man who was then elected to the Church of Benevento.

That man, complying with his brother’s request, brought the sacred relics from the most pure reliquary [*bustia*; reading uncertain], properly sealed them, and on the appointed day sent the hidden gift to the petitioner through a trustworthy monk. But as soon as the little reliquary was opened after the seal had been broken, it was found to be entirely empty.

The bearer was astonished that the relics he believed enclosed were missing; the bishop grieved that he had been deprived of the hope he had placed in them. Nevertheless, as the planned undertaking was already upon him, the church was dedicated. The messenger returned carrying the reliquary, which he believed to be empty.

But behold, as he walked along, he felt that something was moving inside the relic-container. He immediately opened the little vessel and found within it the entire sacrament of the venerable relics, just as he had received it to bring [679]. Shortly afterward, however, the aforementioned church was completely destroyed, as was the entire fortified town in which it had been established. Whether this happened on account of the priest’s deserts or through some other divine judgment could not be made entirely clear to us.

## CHAPTER VII. He who scorns to fulfill a vow perishes miserably

Another event now comes to mind, which the aforementioned archbishop of Salerno reported as having happened to one of his fellow citizens. Caught in a storm at sea, he vowed with an earnest promise that he would become a monk. But after being rescued from the shipwreck, he scorned to fulfill his vow for love of this life.

When a year had passed, on the very day on which he had offered his vow to the Lord for his preservation—namely, the Kalends of January—he was running about here and there, leading dances with children who were playing and laughing, and uttering some frivolous and clownish words [reading uncertain: *noaret*, perhaps *boaret*, “shouted”]. Suddenly a stone fell upon him from a roof and crushed him.

Thus that unhappy man, who had voluntarily scorned to abandon the world, lost it against his will; and he lost the deceptive sweetness of the flesh because, by loving the flesh, he had lied to the truth.

What is written therefore happened to him: “Before destruction the heart is exalted (Prov. XVIII).” And the Apostle’s statement: “It is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. X).”

If the anger of the living God is to be feared by all sinners, then it must certainly be feared more earnestly and terribly by one who labors under the vice of impatience. While he turns the turmoil of an irritable spirit within his breast, through his anger he provokes the movement of divine fury against himself. For what is more just than that anger should deserve anger, and that vengeance should produce, by retaliation, another vengeance?

Hence the wise man says: “He who wishes to take revenge will find vengeance from the Lord, and he will keep his sins in store (Ecclus. XVIII).” In contrast, he salutarily admonishes us, saying: “Forgive your neighbor who wrongs you, so that, when you pray, your sins may be forgiven (ibid.).” Then, as though arguing, he immediately adds: “Does one person preserve anger against another and seek healing from God? He shows no mercy to a person like himself and yet prays concerning his own sins?” (ibid.) He continues, as though in indignation: “Though he is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for reconciliation?” (ibid.) And as though a prayer poured out for an angry person could not be heard so long as he remained in anger, he appropriately adds: “Who will make supplication for his sins?” (ibid.)

And because, when death is recalled as coming swiftly before our eyes, the swelling of anger must immediately be restrained, he fittingly continues: “Remember the last things, and cease from enmity; remember the fear of the Lord, and do not be angry with your neighbor (ibid.).”

Let the fury of anger therefore be restrained in the heart, so that it may never break forth into speech. As it is also said in Ecclesiastes: “Remove anger from your heart, and take away malice from your flesh (Eccles. XI).”

To anger, like a swift and raging river, the Lord has set the restraint of three barriers. Through these he commanded that the rush of fury be held back by the reins of discipline. He fixed the first barrier in the heart, the second in the throat, and the final boundary of resistance in the voice:

“Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment”—here he placed the barrier of the heart.

“But whoever says, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council”—there is the obstacle of the throat.

“But whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna (Matt. V)”—there is the obstacle of the voice.

These, then, are the barriers, as it were, and the obstructions and embankments of the heavenly command, by which the rush of anger and fury is pressed down. So that, like a rapacious river, it may not overturn everything in its path, it is restrained under the judgment of disciplined reason.

Let our mind therefore be not like glass, which breaks impatiently at the first blow of impact, but rather like a vein of precious metal, which is purified beneath the hammer’s blows. Glass would plainly be far more excellent than the brilliance of all metals if it did not yield immediately to the first blows and if, with the natural solidity of its strength, it endured the injury of impact. But because it breaks more quickly, it is judged inferior and contemptible among the other kinds of metal. Glass is made from sand through the ingenuity of human craftsmanship and is therefore compelled to preserve the nature of its innate fragility.

## CHAPTER VIII. The outstanding craftsman of glassmaking and the reward he received from the Emperor Tiberius

Nevertheless, history relates that under Tiberius Caesar a certain craftsman devised a particular tempering process by which glass could become ductile and flexible and, in accordance with the nature of each metal, remain unbroken and solid under the blow of one striking it.

When he had been admitted through the doors of the imperial palace, he presented the emperor with a small vessel tempered by the art he had devised. The enraged emperor immediately threw it onto the pavement. The vessel was not broken at all but was found folded on one side, like a bronze or silver vessel.

The craftsman immediately lifted the small vessel from the pavement, brought a small vessel from his bosom, and corrected the vessel—not one shattered by a fissure, but bent obliquely, in the manner of metal.

Amazed by this, Caesar said to the craftsman: “Is there anyone besides you who knows how to produce this composition of glass?” The craftsman swore that there was no one on earth except himself who understood the ingenuity of this art.

When Caesar heard this, he immediately ordered him to be beheaded. He reasoned that if the exquisite subtlety of this art became known to the common people, gold would be spat upon as though it were mud, and every kind of metal would lose its value. And indeed, if glass lacked such a fragile nature—if, made ductile, it could receive the blow of one striking it—what brilliance of any metal could ever equal the penetrating clarity of glass?

To return, then, to our subject: just as the fragile nature of glass devalues it, while the strength of solidity commends the other metals, so through anger the entire structure of the virtues collapses; and through the majesty of imperial patience, a dwelling for God is constructed within us, gleaming with the splendor of shining gems. For just as anger uproots the virtues, patience causes them to grow together.

## CHAPTER IX. How Blessed Peter Damian, prone to anger, moderates himself

Moreover, I too, who am writing these things as best I can, am goaded by a natural sprinkling of anger, and often the slightest offense, having shaken me, disturbs the secrets of my tranquillity. Thus what is scarcely touched in me by a needle or a thorn often seems to me to have been pierced by a Phalarian weapon. I take a light rod for a bull’s-hide whip, and, when enduring a slap, I sigh as though struck by a lead-weighted scourge.

But inwardly—so far as action is concerned—let anger say what it wishes, let it gnash, roar, grind its teeth: in all that it suggests to me within, insofar as I can refuse it, it will have no outward assistance from me. Let it swell with inflation, blow, rage, rage fiercely, and rise up: I will not give it my limbs, so that through them, as through weapons, it may accomplish what it attempts.

“Do not,” says the Apostle, “present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin (Rom. VI).” I do not give it my hand, so that through it, swollen with fury, it may strike or seize anything. I do not move my tongue or lips, so that through them it may pour out the bitterness of its gall.

When I completely deny these aids to raging anger, it is necessary that soon, like a flame without fuel, it either languish or perish entirely, or pass uselessly like wind through unobstructed air, since there is no obstacle against which it can rush headlong. Broken against itself, it is beaten back, deprived of the material of fuel in which it might exercise itself.

I answer anger in the same way as I answer tickling lust. Sometimes desire inflames me, sets me ablaze, shakes my inward parts, and raises the sexual organs; but in all these things let it do by its own powers whatever it can, for it cannot have the assistance of my cooperation. The fury of anger cries out—I hear it; the heat of lust boils—I feel it. But I extend no helping hand to those cries, nor do I supply fuel to those raging flames. I do not aid the former by taking revenge, nor do I fan the latter through the act of lust.

In this way, then, it is necessary that the fury of anger fly away uselessly and fail, and that the heat of lust extinguish itself when fuel is not supplied to its material. Through reason I can restrain nature, but I cannot wholly destroy it; I can soothe it, but not entirely extinguish it.

Let each person do to me whatever he wishes: I must seek patience within myself, and I must not expect to gain its fruit from another person’s virtue. For where there are no battles to provoke, there is no victory to be crowned. The protection of a shield is opposed in vain when neither the point of a dart nor the edge of a sword is brandished. If the flame of a furnace dies out, the purity of the metal is not tested. Thus it is not another person’s gentleness that will make me patient; within me must be raised the defenses of towers, which drive away and repel from afar the storms of the darts that assail me.

I have dictated these things to you, venerable Father, without skill, not to teach you who, by God’s authorship, are a teacher of the Church, but so that, on the occasion of your address, I might benefit those who are turbulent and like me. Nor do I fear that your holy prudence will take offense if some younger person presumes, with humility, to suggest something to you, since you know that the Lord said to human beings through the prophetic voice: “Come and rebuke me (Isa. I).” And you know that Moses, the Lord’s fellow-worker, patiently heard from Jethro, a gentile: “You are wearing yourself out with foolish labor (Exod. XXXVIII).”

May almighty God, who has restored you to us in health, venerable man, make you avoid the squalor of every vice and, as his vessel baked by fire, fill you with the brightness of spiritual virtues.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0659]

## 683–684 FORTY-FIRST OPUSCULUM. ON THE TIME FOR CELEBRATING MARRIAGES

### Argument

He devotes the whole work to refuting certain people who were not ashamed to assert that marriages contracted during the fast of Lent are valid, provided that intercourse does not take place, and therefore ought not to be dissolved. He consequently demonstrates that marriages are contracted by consent, not by intercourse.

[Col. 0659B] To Lords V. and P., religious clerics of the Church of Faenza, Peter, the sinful monk, the service of fraternal charity [Col. 0659C].

## ON THE TIME FOR CELEBRATING MARRIAGES

### CHAPTER I. The time for celebrating marriages according to the sacred canons
You have complained to me, your brotherhood, that certain men, confusing the order of ecclesiastical discipline and, in the prophet’s words, “placing God behind their bodies” (Ezekiel I), contract marriages during the Lenten fast; but, in order to evade the judgment of the canons, after taking a wife and celebrating the wedding, they maintain that only intercourse was lacking. Your complaint has an additional and more serious point: some who appear spiritual on the surface and claim knowledge of the Scriptures attempt to excuse them. For although the authority of the canons decrees that anyone who celebrates a wedding from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, during the three weeks before the feast of Saint John, or from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany, must be separated, they establish the rights of marriage solely in marital intercourse and assert that those who contract a union during the aforesaid periods, merely postponing carnal relations, ought not to be separated. Anyone who has even slightly crossed the threshold of sacred eloquence easily recognizes how absurd and frivolous this is.

For if marriages are said properly to consist in intercourse, why do the sacred canons prohibit a marriage from ever being joined without a public wedding? Do they want a man to have intercourse with his wife publicly? And since this is so dishonorable and filled with shame that, throughout the long ages of the entire human race, no one is ever recorded to have attempted it except two men—Paris, namely, and a certain philosopher—how can canonical judgment prescribe what even the unrestrained lust of a pagan people judged most disgraceful? Moreover, if the celebration of a wedding consists solely in carnal relations, why is a widowed person permitted to contract a second marriage, but prohibited by canonical authority from a third or fourth? Is it perhaps denied—something entirely ridiculous—that after a man has been joined to a wife for a second time, he may thereafter return to his own bed? Indeed, if intercourse is marriage, then whenever a man has intercourse with a woman, he is plainly convicted of celebrating a marriage.

Therefore, if someone repeats the carnal act a hundred times, he incurs not merely the crime of polygamy, contrary to canonical rule, but of having a hundred wives. Whoever presumes to assert this is unquestionably believed to be insane. Intercourse, which is nevertheless rightly permitted, is not marriage but rather a matter belonging to marriage. “For not every woman,” according to the judgment of Pope Leo, “who is joined to a man is the man’s wife; just as not every son is his father’s heir.” And shortly afterward: “There is no doubt,” he says, “that a woman in whom it is shown that there was no nuptial mystery does not belong to marriage.” From these words, therefore, we can clearly discern that one thing is the nuptial mystery and another the carnal act. What is done canonically is a sacrament; what is usurped contrary to the canons is sacrilege.

The same thing may be judged wholesome or harmful according to the appropriateness of the time. Whoever prunes vines in the chill of winter destroys the vineyard. Whoever sows in summer ruins the grain. The earth becomes suitable for receiving seed only when it has been tilled at the proper time. Whoever hires masons during a snowstorm constructs a ruin. Whoever cuts the sap-filled wood of spring in order to raise the walls of houses or join the ceiling panels wearies himself with the frustration of useless labor. And, to come to the sacraments, whoever ordains clerics outside the appointed times does not advance them, but places an obstacle of offense in the way of their being advanced thereafter. Whoever indiscriminately and at an unsuitable time celebrates the sacraments of chrism or baptism is called not so much a minister of the sacrament as guilty of sacrilege.

## Chapter II. Against Those Who Pervert the Appointed Times

Since the ecclesiastical sacraments themselves require the succession of their appointed times and derive their efficacy from the suitability of the designated time, how can marriages alone have validity if they confuse the established times? As Solomon says: “Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed seasons” (Ecclesiastes III). And shortly afterward: “A time for weeping and a time for laughing, a time for mourning and a time for dancing, a time for embracing and a time to be far from embraces” (ibid.).

Therefore, those who dance and laugh at the time for weeping, and who embrace when they ought to be far from embraces—just as the order of time is perverted among them, so rightly are pleasure changed into bitterness, joy into grief, glory into disgrace, and the bridal chamber into a brothel. Since the laws take care that during the season of harvesting or grape-gathering lawsuits should by no means be argued and legal business should not be settled, and since the nature of the times requires that whatever is then decided in the tribunals of judges be considered invalid, how does the Lenten season not annul marriages that the authority of the canons condemns? Do the sacred canons perhaps contain less force than pragmatic sanctions? It is said that the essence of marriage is intercourse, which, if absent, cannot be called a nuptial mystery.

According to them, then, the blessed Virgin Mary also married a man carnally, since in accordance with the testimony of the Gospel she entered into a nuptial union with her betrothed Joseph: “Before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matthew I). But because the evangelist does not explicitly use the word “wedding,” perhaps the claim that the Blessed Virgin celebrated a wedding will not be believed when I make it. Let one of the commentators be brought forward as a witness, as the occasion requires.

Bede says in his exposition of Matthew:

> “It must first be noted that when he says, ‘Before they came together,’ the words ‘came together’ do not indicate intercourse itself, but the time of the wedding, which ordinarily precedes it—when she who had previously been a betrothed woman begins to be a wife. Therefore, when he says, ‘Before they came together,’ he means: ‘Before they properly celebrated the solemn rites of the wedding, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.’ For afterward they came together in the order just mentioned, when Joseph, at the angel’s command, received his wife.”

Ambrose likewise says:

> “Do not be troubled by the fact that Scripture frequently calls her a wife: it declares not the loss of virginity, but the testimony of marriage and the celebration of the wedding.”

Since it is therefore clearer than daylight that the blessed Virgin Mother of God did not marry, and yet unquestionably celebrated nuptials according to the testimony of Scripture, how can it be said that, where intercourse was absent, nuptials cannot be called nuptials?

We, on the contrary, freely confess both that intercourse can occur without marriage and that a marriage can rightly be called a marriage without intercourse. For there are at times celibate marriages, and there are marriages deserving to be called virginal marriages. In these, a wife is joined to a husband by the bond of a marriage settlement, yet, preferring the desire for the heavenly bridal chamber, she does not unite with him carnally in any way (see the scholia at the end of the treatise). It is said that the blessed John the Evangelist was taken away by the Lord from a marriage of this kind. Although he remained a virgin, the marriage he rejected was nevertheless called a marriage.

The blessed Apostle also appears to invite his hearers to this kind of marriage when he says: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (1 Corinthians VII). First declaring that it is good not to touch a woman, and then prescribing that each person should have a wife because of fornication, the discerning teacher plainly invites us to celibate marriage, so that, if we can merely escape the snare of fornication, we should not seek carnal relations in marriage. It is entirely clear that the institution of marriage was established from the beginning for the begetting of offspring and the propagation of posterity.

## Chapter III. For What Purpose Marriage Was Instituted

As far as the antiquity of the world is concerned, the purpose of marriage is the procreation of children. Yet just as the earth is cut open by the plowshare alone, although, for this to be possible, the other necessary parts are attached to the plow; and just as only the strings of a cithara and similar musical instruments are suited to singing, although the other components of the instruments’ framework are also present, though not struck by the singers—so other elements are added to this purpose, namely the propagation of offspring: partly because of the sacrament of conjugal marriage, and partly for the sake of honorable appearance, including the assembly of the betrothed, the arrangement of the formal banquet, bridal gifts, the documents of the marriage settlement, and whatever else there may be. All these things joined together are called a wedding.

In ancient times, as has been said, these things were directed solely toward the propagation of offspring. Now, however, as the world is already growing old and the teaching of him who is virgin from a virgin shines forth, they are plainly directed toward avoiding fornication. At that time, apart from the higher mystery, it was said: “Cursed is the man who has no offspring in Israel.” Now it is said: “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church” (Ephesians V). And the Apostle says: “The time is short; from now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none.” And again: “I want all of you to be as I am” (Colossians III).

Indeed, as we said above, the one who preaches that a man should take a wife but not touch her appears to seek not the production of offspring but the closing of the abyss of fornication; he desires not a swollen womb and the cries of infants, but an undefiled bed and the celibacy of conjugal continence. When he says, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Corinthians VII), and elsewhere, “Return to one another, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (ibid.), he plainly shows that he desires mutual chastity between spouses; he permits the mingling of the flesh reluctantly.

It is therefore established by what has been set forth above that whoever denies that marriages can take place without intercourse obstinately fights against the Apostle, through whom Christ speaks. He both wishes all people to live continently as he himself does, and nevertheless advises each person to have his own wife lest he fall into fornication.

Let the foolishly wise and wisely senseless be ashamed—those who stubbornly assert that a man who took a woman as his wife during Lent, without intercourse having taken place, ought not to be separated from her. They have sometimes burst into such madness that they even deny that a woman known to have been abducted by a man on Good Friday itself, the holy day on which the Lord was crucified, should be abandoned. While shamelessly asserting a supposedly lawful marriage, they strengthen a sacrilegious concubinage by crafty arguments. For while the Lord was suffering the fastening of the cross, that man was turning over in his mind the pleasure of filthy lust [variant: “filthy pleasure”]. While the whole world was dying with its Redeemer, as members truly die with their head, he was meditating on the foulness of inflamed desire.

I shall briefly touch upon what happened in my time on the day of the Lord’s crucifixion. At Ravenna, many animals were slaughtered in the marketplace by the weighers, and by common decree of the senate, especially through the decision of the venerable hermit Martin, they were all thrown to the dogs. What, then, would those zealous for God have done if they had seen a newly married woman proceeding to the bridal celebration, or had discovered crowds of friends conducting wedding dances while abandoning the adoration of the cross?

## Chapter IV. The Punishment of Those Who Celebrate Weddings During Lent

But tell me, authors of this new assertion: if it should happen that, during the course of Lenten observance, a wife unites carnally with her husband, do you impose penance on them while preserving the marriage, or do you separate them from each other by divorce, with the marriage documents dissolved? Behold, canonical authority decrees that whoever falls with his spouse during that period is restored by only forty days of penance.

How, then, can you say that marriages consist solely in intercourse, and judge that the two are identical, contrary to the entire testimony of sacred eloquence? Canonical judgment, without any hesitation, divides marriages instituted at unlawful times, but strikes intercourse only with the penalty of a small penance. Tell me, I say—and I speak with your permission—if marriages are to be said to consist solely in intercourse, why are marriages contracted contrary to the commands of the laws condemned even to divorce, while only a light measure of penance is imposed for intercourse? For if the two are one and the same, then, just as they are not different in sin, they ought not to be subject to different judgments. Where the cause is the same, the penalty for both ought also to be one.

Moreover, what does it mean that canonical sanction prescribes that virgins who do not preserve themselves, if they take as husbands the very men who violated them, are reconciled after one year’s penance because they have violated only weddings? If marriage is nothing other than intercourse, why are prostituted virgins said to have violated weddings when they certainly did not violate intercourse but rather completed it? Indeed, if marital rights are fulfilled by intercourse alone, then filthy brothels should no longer be condemned; they should instead be crowned as places of merit, and foul dens of prostitution should be bridal houses. Has our philosophers’ argumentation finally brought us to the point where marriage documents and the pleasures of obscene prostitutes possess the same merit? Is the den of a brothel to be regarded as the same as an undefiled bed?

And, to speak with indignation, is furtive intercourse to be considered worth as much as the public—and therefore honorable—celebration of a wedding? Let crafty cleverness therefore be confounded, and let it not trust that what truth separates can be joined by a multiplicity of words. Let presumptuousness, which deserves punishment, also be restrained, lest what it now secretly begins through rash attempts grow afterward everywhere through the vice of illicit unions. Let these disastrous marriages be dissolved, and let ecclesiastical discipline remain in the condition of its proper force.

Let what was contracted contrary to the provisions of the laws be rescinded, lest the cancer now arising, spreading wickedly, grow and extend from one person through the members of the ecclesiastical body. Thus let priestly authority now oppose reckless presumption, so that the Christian religion—God forbid—may not be carried about and tossed by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians IV), but may remain immovably firm in the rule of apostolic tradition.

## Scholia

It is said that the blessed John the Evangelist was taken away by the Lord from a marriage of this kind.

There were therefore not only our holy cardinal, but also others who asserted that the bridegroom at the wedding celebrated in Cana of Galilee was this same John the Evangelist, and that, when called by Christ to follow him, he sent word to the bride that he would not proceed with the marriage. This opinion, received from ancient histories, is expressly confirmed especially by two men renowned for the holiness and learning of the Benedictine order—namely, the venerable Bede and Rupert the abbot.

Bede’s testimony, committed to writing nine hundred years ago, concerns this John (Bede, *Homily on Saint John*):

> “But he loves him above all because, chosen by him as a virgin, he remained a virgin forever. For the histories relate that, when he wished to marry, the Lord called him away from the wedding; and therefore, having withdrawn him from carnal pleasure, he bestowed upon him the greater sweetness of his love.”

Rupert, who lived in the time of Damian, speaks as follows (Rupert, *On John*, Book II, at the end):

> “John the Evangelist, having left his wedding—for it is almost everyone’s opinion that this wedding was his—we believe that he began to follow the Lord. For the histories relate that, when he wished to marry, the Lord called him away from the wedding.”

The same truth is also confirmed by two very ancient prologues prefixed to the Gospel according to John, one attributed to Jerome and the other to Augustine. The text of the former runs as follows:

> “The Lord called John away from the wedding when he wished to marry.”

Sebastian Barradius observes that Saint Thomas, among others, maintained that Jerome was the author of this prologue (Barradius, *Commentary on the Gospels*, vol. II, book III, chapter 1):

> “This opinion,” says Barradius, “is followed by Saint Thomas (2–2, question 186, article 4), and when he explains that prologue attributed to Saint Jerome, he considers it to be the opinion of Saint Jerome.”

The testimony of the other prologue is as follows:

> “This, indeed, is John, whom the Lord called away from the storm-tossed sea of marriage and to whom he entrusted his virgin mother to a virgin.”

Baronius readily admits that this prologue also ought to be attributed to Augustine, leaving other authorities aside for the moment (*Annals*, vol. I, under the year of Christ 31). He says:

> “Augustine, in his preface on John the Evangelist, has the following: ‘This, indeed, is John.’”

And so forth, as quoted above. Yet when Baronius saw this, he nevertheless insisted that the opinion concerning John’s marriage must be entirely rejected, calling it fabricated, recently invented, and ridiculous. Interpreting Augustine’s testimony, he said that Augustine meant that John was called away from a wedding not because he had taken a wife and left her, but because he had never taken one at all. Augustine, he adds, testifies to this at the end of the same work, using these words (*On John*, final treatise, near the end):

> “He was loved more because he neither took a wife nor, from the beginning of his life, ceased to be most chaste.”

Thus Baronius appeals to Augustine. Nevertheless, with respect for so great a man, I would not hesitate to affirm that these words of Augustine favor the most holy Fathers—Bede, Damian, Rupert, Thomas, Bonaventure, and the others—more than they favor Baronius himself. When Augustine, or others as well, say that John the Evangelist did not take a wife, this amounts to saying that he did not live with or cohabit with a wife.

Moreover, many other writers, distinguished both for holiness and for learning, teach that Damian’s opinion conforms to the truth. The Angelic Doctor, Saint Thomas, says (2–2, question 186, article 4, response to objection 1):

> “So that no one would lose hope of attaining perfection, he called to the state of perfection even those whom he found joined in marriage. Yet it could not be done without injury for husbands to abandon their wives, just as it could be done without injury for all to abandon their riches. Therefore he did not separate Peter, whom he found joined in marriage, from his wife; but he recalled John, who wished to marry, from the wedding.”

The Seraphic Doctor, Saint Bonaventure, says (*Life of Christ*, part II, chapter 20):

> “Although it is uncertain whose wedding was celebrated in Cana of Galilee, as the master touches upon in the *Scholastic History*, let us nevertheless consider it to have been the wedding of John the Evangelist, as appears in the prologue to John, where Jerome seems to affirm this.”

Saint Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, says (*Chronicle*, part I, chapter 3, title 5, section 6; and part III of the *Summa*, title 1, chapter 2, at the beginning):

> “After the wedding had been celebrated in Cana of Galilee, which is commonly said to have been the wedding of John the Evangelist,”

and, with certain intervening words:

> “John, however, followed Christ as a virgin, without consummating the marriage.”

To these men of such authority add Nicholas of Lyra, who deserved exceptionally well of sacred letters. Writing about three hundred years ago on the second chapter of John, he not only confirmed in his exposition that the prologue to John was Jerome’s, but also supported the opinion of the earlier Fathers in these words:

> “It is also commonly said that this wedding was the wedding of John the Evangelist, from which Christ called him before the consummation of the marriage through carnal union. From this the Church observes that, before carnal union, one spouse may lawfully enter religious life. This seems to follow from Jerome’s statement in the prologue, where it is said that Christ called him away from the wedding when he wished to marry. From this it appears that the wedding was his, since Christ is not read to have been present at any other wedding. This also appears from the fact that Jesus’ mother was there as though at the wedding of her nephew. For it is not likely that she would have come unless the matter had concerned her greatly, just as she went to her kinswoman Elizabeth, though in haste, as we read in Luke I; for, as Ambrose says, she did not willingly remain in public but rather in the privacy of prayer.”

Many other men of the greatest authority and learning subscribe to the same opinion: Thomas de Vio, Cardinal Cajetan, in the second chapter of John; Dominicus Soto, *Sentences* IV, distinction 17, question 1, article 4. Relying on no authority other than that of Saints Jerome and Augustine, Soto concludes from this action of Christ that one spouse may enter religious life even when the other is unwilling, provided the marriage is ratified but not consummated.

Dionysius the Carthusian writes as follows on the second chapter of John:

> “Jerome holds that the bridegroom was John the Evangelist, the son of the sister of the most blessed Virgin.”

John Major writes in the same place:

> “John, son of Zebedee, is thought to have contracted this marriage; so Jerome and Augustine believe. Unless one is supported by evident reason, it is shameful to contradict their opinion.”

Sylvester Prierias says (*On the Gospel for the First Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany*):

> “It must be understood that it is commonly held that this wedding was the wedding of John the Evangelist,”

which seems to echo Jerome’s statement in the prologue.

Robert Caracciolus, bishop of Aquino, *On the Praises of the Saints*, sermon 35; Hugh of Prato, sermon 18 for the Sunday after the octave of Epiphany; Michael de Palatio, *Commentary I on chapter 2*; John Thomas Turgillus, vol. I, on the same Gospel; John Osorius, vol. I of the *Sermons*, on chapter II of John; and, to omit others, Philip Diez, vol. III of the *Sermons*, for the Second Sunday after Epiphany, also wrote in our own more recent times:

> “It is commonly held,” he says concerning this wedding, “that it was the wedding of Saint John the Evangelist, from which the most holy Savior of the world called him.”

Since, therefore, this opinion concerning John’s marriage rests upon testimonies of such authority and has such patrons—men whom it is reasonable to believe were not persuaded by a frivolous tradition—and since Bede and Rupert affirm that it was drawn from ancient histories, confirmed by accepted and ancient prologues, and commonly held for six hundred years down to our own time, I do not see why it should so easily be considered fabricated, recently invented, and ridiculous.

As for Nicephorus’s testimony (*History*, book VIII, chapter 30), that the bridegroom of this wedding was Simon the Cananaean, his opinion has weak foundations and no ancient adherents apart from himself; it is rightly rejected by learned writers. This is especially so because, although he records such a wedding, he does not assert that Simon was called away from it. “Helena,” he says, “the mother of the emperor Constantine, built a sacred church at Cana of Galilee, where the wedding of Simon the Cananaean was celebrated.”

Hence the opinion of Alexander III (*Decretal*, chapter “Verum,” *On the Conversion of Spouses*), by which the bridegroom is said to have been called away from his wedding, seems rather to be understood of John, whom writers testify to have been called by Christ:

> “After a legitimate present consent, it is lawful for one spouse, even against the opposition of the other, to choose a monastery”

—as certain saints were called away from their weddings—

> “provided that carnal union has not taken place between them.”

Cardinal Baronius, after saying (*Annals*, under the year of Christ 31):

> “In this matter, one ought rather to agree with Nicephorus, who asserts that this was the wedding of Simon the Cananaean,”

immediately adds:

> “Moreover, Nathanael was also from Cana, a town of Galilee,”

as Jerome relates (*On Hebrew Places*), “situated in Galilee of the nations.”

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0667]

## Treatise Forty-Two. On Not Breaking a Pledge Made to God; with an Added Dissertation on the Same Subject

### Argument

While the holy doctor was staying at Milan as legate of the Apostolic See in order to correct the vices of the clergy of that Church, a certain Landulf was his chief assistant, a man distinguished both by nobility of birth and by no ordinary knowledge of letters, who brought considerable zeal and authority to the accomplishment of that undertaking according to plan. When the same clergy stirred up a popular sedition, and both men were demanded for destruction by the raging minds of the populace, he vowed that, as soon as he had escaped so dreadful a tempest, he would bid farewell to human affairs and hasten to the haven of religious life. Yet, after the popular uprising had been calmed by Damian’s skill and eloquence and he had obtained the fulfilment of his vow, he neglected to perform it. Damian therefore writes to him and, recounting the examples of many who had paid severe penalties to God for faith not kept, exhorts him to fear breaking a pledge made not to a man but to God.

[Col. 0667B] PETER THE SINNER, monk, sends greetings to LANDULF, a cleric of senatorial stock, conspicuous for the brilliance of literary learning.

I waited and confidently expected that, as agreed, you would undertake the institution of the sacred order. But because the king of Egypt did not oppress you with the service of mud and brick (Exod. I, V), and because, when the satraps pressed upon you, he did not cast you out from the campaign of his service, but rather, like that Levite from the side of Mount Ephraim, a Bethlehemite father-in-law detained you with blandishments and, binding you by love for his daughter, charmed you with many delights of conversation and refreshment (II Kings XXIX; Judges XVI), you have with human rashness failed to fulfil what you promised not to a man but to God.

### On a Pledge Made to God

## Chapter I. That a vow may not lawfully be left unfulfilled under any excuse

[Col. 0667C]

I ask you, my brother: what excuse can your prudence offer? What argument can it make, that it may be permitted not to fulfil what it promised with Christ as judge and the angels as witnesses, when the Lord says through Moses: “If any man makes a vow to the Lord, or binds himself by an oath, he shall not make his word void; but shall fulfil all that he promised” (Num. XXX)? Or perhaps does this excuse the falsehood and seem an adequate refuge for defence: that the city of Milan, having then turned to sedition, threatened our sudden destruction? And that what necessity imposed, if freedom of will is lacking, does not remain binding? But canonical authority decrees that if a widow, fearing violence for the sake of piety, receives the sacred veil as though she were not going to persevere, she must not withdraw from the purpose she has once undertaken.

[Col. 0667D] [Col. 0668B] [variant: “persevering”]

Far be it, then, that fear should absolve a man when it does not excuse women even in judgment—especially since, when I warned you not to bind yourself by such a vow through fear of death unless you would also subsequently fulfil your promises by the effective reality of a living work, you devoted yourself to divine judgment if ever you should violate the commitment of the pledge you had made. I shall relate what is known recently to have happened among us in a not dissimilar matter.

## Chapter II. Arduin condemned because he had not assumed the monastic habit as he had vowed

A certain man named Arduin, famed for prudence, illustrious in birth, and wealthy in riches, had promised me in earnest devotion that, if he could not do so earlier, at least when ten years had elapsed he would withdraw to the monastery of Saint Vincent, situated in the territory of Urbino, in order to assume the monastic habit. At last, when the term of the agreed compact had expired, I pressed him continually for payment; but he evaded and wheedled, promising every good thing in words while postponing the actual result of his conversion through various evasions. Even the superior of the said monastery favoured his wishes and dissuaded him from converting, since he was supported by that man’s very necessary assistance.

[Col. 0668C] Meanwhile he took to his bed when bodily illness came upon him; after confessing his sins, he was absolved by the judgment of a priest and gave much to the poor and to churches. So completely did he set all his affairs in order that he bound the kinsmen and relatives attending him by this adjuration: “I beseech you,” he said, “by the charity which is God, let no one ask that I be restored to this mortal life, lest—God forbid—unexpected death later find me unprepared” (II John IV).

[Col. 0668D] [Col. 0669A] Some time after his death, the man appeared in a vision during the night’s rest to the aforesaid abbot. It seemed that an emperor, if I remember rightly, or some other exalted power, was staying in a broad plain of open country with the leading men of the whole realm and a numerous army. As the abbot gazed about in astonishment, behold, Arduin was being hurried along by certain persons as if by guards. “Ho!” he said, “stop your step, plant your foot, rest a little. Will you not speak to me, Arduin?”

[Col. 0669B] “Come, brother, what is your condition? Are you joyful or suffering? Is punishment or glory present?” To him, sad and weeping, Arduin replied: “Why do you ask me about glory, when I am afflicted with unceasing punishments and am not even permitted to breathe for a moment?” The abbot said to him: “What of Saint Vincent? Does he not now aid you in your need, when you so diligently strove to assist the stewards of his house?” He immediately added: “Saint Vincent long caused me to hope for an audience with him; but because, long wearied, I did not deserve to obtain it, I have now completely lost that hope, disappointed.”

Here we should carefully observe how straight is the line of divine justice, indeed how artful is God’s measure of vengeance. While still alive, he both promised and delayed that he would convert in the monastery of the blessed martyr; now he both hoped, as though by virtue of his promise, to come into the presence of the same martyr, yet did not obtain it at all. And it was fitting that the abbot who had hindered his conversion should especially see this vision.

[Col. 0669C] Another man, equally well known to me, was prominent as a citizen in the city of Ravenna, vigorous in legal knowledge and adequately trained in the rules of grammar. He made an agreement with me: that if I left the world, he would do so as well. Why say more? When at last I came to conversion, I demanded fulfilment of the promise, but could not obtain it. For he joyfully sent me on ahead while he held back his own steps by artifice. Not many days later, however, when the envy of his furious mind had inflamed him against his brother-in-law, his hand, suddenly struck by a sword, became numb; and thereafter it remained so stunned and rigid that it was more a burden than a strength to its bearer.

[Col. 0669D] Thus rendered useless, he cast off the world, though he had misused it; and no longer a left-handed man, but wholly right-handed with Benjamin (Gen. XXXV), he remained in holy religious life until his death.

## Chapter III. A bishop struck in the throat because he took a poor widow’s pig; he enters religious life

Meanwhile John, bishop of Comacchio, also comes to mind. While he was delaying his conversion through long periods of time, it happened one day that he was staying on an estate he possessed in the woodland territory. There he ordered that a pig belonging to a certain poor widow, which she was raising as the hope of her livelihood, be taken away and promptly prepared for the benefit of his own dishes. She sent entreaties, poured out tears and groans, and demanded that the loss of her care be restored to her. But while the pious bishop provided more for his own stomach and table than for her, he made light of the command of its Author, who says through the prophet: “Assist the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow” (Isa. I).

[Col. 0670A] But he who was thought absent when he established the command showed that he was present when he inflicted judgment. For, while the bishop made the widow’s tears delights for his own gluttony, he was immediately struck in the throat and suffered a wound which he could not escape by any medical treatment while he lived.

[Col. 0670B] Hindered by this affliction, when, according to Scripture, affliction alone at last gave understanding to his hearing (Ps. XXVIII), he yielded to sound counsels, exchanged episcopal insignia for monastic profession, and afterward lived for a long time in the monastery of Pomposa, built in honour of the ever-virgin Saint Mary. Yet until his death he suffered such distress from the injured throat that he could not swallow food except with great difficulty. Thus at meals he always reclined at a double table of brethren succeeding one another, and could scarcely take enough food to restore his stomach.

But while we recall this bishop, we are prompted on this occasion to write also what happened to the bishop of Chiusi. On that very Wednesday which is called the beginning of Lent, he had a feast furnished with costly dishes and a bath prepared; summoning soldiers and crowds of attendants, he spent the day splendidly, joyfully going out to meet Lent with a wedding feast as though a bride were arriving.

[Col. 0670C] The sole discordance with the rule was this: while ashes still darkened their heads, their bellies, gorged with wine and swollen with dishes, were burning hot. But, O divine mercy watching over us! Though the bishop had then been healthy and vigorous, paralysis suddenly seized him, making his face shameful to behold and twisting his mouth; throughout the many years for which he afterward survived, he bore upon himself this mark of divine punishment.

## Chapter IV. Adam, bishop of Sempronium, dies unexpectedly because he had delayed entering religious life

[Col. 0670D]

## Chapter IV. Adam, Bishop of Sempronia, Dies Unexpectedly Because He Had Delayed Entering the Religious Life

Shall I also pass over Adam, bishop of Sempronia, who had often promised that he would become a monk, but always tried to put forward excuses dressed up as plausible reasons? Once, when he was suffering from a mild fever, he summoned me to him. When I pressed him forcefully to become a monk, he declared that he wished to do so; yet, as seemed to emerge through certain gaps in his words, he was trying to postpone the matter. At last, the argument that prevailed most strongly with me was this:

“Indeed, father, I promptly obey whatever you command. Nevertheless, I do not want you to be unaware that as soon as I have become a monk, this Church will unquestionably be exposed to plunder and raids; moreover, wicked men will uproot its possessions and estates from their very foundations.”

Hearing this, I was deceived and, alas, failed to foresee the danger threatening the Church. As I departed, therefore, I instructed him and his attendants that, if his illness should grow at all worse, they should either immediately inform me through the judge or carry him to the nearby monastery.

After I had left, however, his brother sent me this message:

“My lord, as we hope, will recover through divine mercy. Nevertheless, I urge you to return to him, in the following manner: on Sunday, approaching more closely to the monastery of Saint Vincent, which is scarcely five miles from the bishopric, rest there. On Monday, rising early and pleasantly performing the morning praises on horseback, reach us at dawn, before the day has fully broken; and afterward, I ask, do not hesitate to come. For if you come, the labor of your journey will not be deprived of a suitable compensation.”

When I heard this last remark, I immediately felt nauseated and horrified. As though I had been offered the prospect of gifts, I flatly refused to go in pursuit of money; with conscience as my witness, I am not lying when I say that I even rebuked him rather severely, as the author of an unbecoming embassy.

Nevertheless, gathering myself again, I began to fear that, if this man should pass from this life, my conscience might later torture me by accusing me of negligence. Why delay over words? At last I obeyed, and, observing in order everything he had instructed, [Col. 0671C] when dawn had scarcely begun to break, I approached the light of the church [f. I reached the threshold of the church].

But behold: while all around them people were making a din and uttering weeping and wailing, the bishop’s lifeless corpse lay inside the chamber, with scarcely two boys attending it. In this event, surely, and with the greatest care, one must consider how cunningly the scheming enemy lies in wait for the unwary lovers of this life. With precision and guile he had arranged through the mouths of the messengers that I should come at precisely the moment when the bishop’s unexpected death would precede me—so that his departure would forestall me and render my arrival useless.

What benefit, then, is there in our being summoned to the grace of conversion if we always set before ourselves the shield of excuse and, as though God did not see within, construct a fabric of necessities that do not compel us? For if he rigorously judges even the smallest things unjustly taken from us, should one believe that he would calmly endure a person’s being taken away from him—namely, a precious possession?

## Chapter V. Christ’s Providence toward a Thief of Alms

I shall relate what Guarimpotus, an elderly man of the highest integrity, exceptionally well educated in letters and a physician, told me:

“A certain man secretly stole someone else’s pig and concealed it in a pen. Yet this man was devoted to works of mercy and, above all, was assiduous in showing kindness to pilgrims and guests.

“Meanwhile, the rich Jesus appeared in the form of a poor man and, seemingly disfigured by an already luxuriant head of hair, appeared to need a barber’s skill. The man immediately rose respectfully and, among the other services of courteous hospitality, began to cut his hair with shears. But while he trimmed and worked at it, behold, he discovered two eyes hidden at the back of the head beneath the hair.

“The man was terrified; trembling with astonishment, he anxiously asked what the thing he saw might be. The other immediately replied: ‘I am called Jesus, who behold everything everywhere. These are the eyes with which I also saw the pig that you recently shut up in the pen.’ And at once he disappeared.

“The man immediately came to his senses, recognized the divine mercy shown toward him, and cleansed himself by making satisfaction for what he had wickedly presumed to do.”

But since I am joined to you by such complete familiarity in brotherly affection, I ask you not to be reluctant to hear one small thing that I am saying. For the abundance of pure and unsuspecting love is shown in this: that whatever comes to mind, I should express it not so much courteously as simply.

## Chapter VI. The Theft of Pambo the Roman Punished by Divine Theft

Certainly, a certain man named Pambo, distinguished by birth but poor in means, was staying with me in the same lodging when King Henry, of pious memory, received the imperial crown.

During the very vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, when the darkness of the approaching night was already thick, a fairly large herd of pigs was being driven along the long arcade of the market. The aforementioned Pambo rushed into the darkness among the market-stalls, seized one of the pigs, blocked its throat so that it would not grunt, [Col. 0672C] and, rejoicing, carried it away to his companions to be prepared for the following day.

When the sacred solemnity dawned, he enjoyed his crime and exulted, satisfied that his offense had gone unpunished. Perhaps he thought that God had not noticed it. But on the following night he learned that divine retribution had kept watch over him.

For while he was sleeping, having carelessly guarded his horse, a thief cunningly withdrew the rein that he had tied around his hands, took away the horse with its bridle, and carried off the saddle as well. On waking, he realized that he had been punished by a subtle judgment: by the very hand with which he had stolen the pig, he discovered that his horse had been stolen from him with interest.

Although in this man vengeance followed guilt immediately, it is not surprising that punishment is sometimes delayed for certain reprobates and that they enjoy their crimes for a longer time. As Scripture testifies: “They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend into hell” (Job XXI).

## Chapter VII. A Lustful Cleric Perishes in a Fire with His Concubine

I remember clearly that, when I was studying and teaching the liberal arts near the town of Parma—when I was still in the very flower of adolescence, when new manhood was beginning to appear upon my face and the heat of lust was inflaming the flesh—a certain cleric named Zeuzolinus kept his concubine near my lodging. She was, as they say, slippery in appearance and attractive with a beauty sufficiently indecent.

This man, then, glossy and always carefully dressed and conspicuous, went about in such a way that his head was never covered by anything except a Ghibelline-fur cap (*gibellinica pellis*); by a fuller’s art he gave his linen garments a snow-white finish with wheat flour; and finally his shoe unmistakably resembled an eagle’s beak.

Moreover, he had a thin, sweet, ringing voice, so much so that when he sang in church he soothed the hearts of his listeners and turned the faces of the assembled people toward himself. Both of them abounded in pleasures, their flushed faces glowing; every day they applauded one another with laughter and mockery, with glances of the eyes and the festive allurements of buffoonery.

Since I was physically close to these follies and depraved habits, I could not be mentally distant from them. What shall I say? As I watched these things, I endured the torments of aroused lust; even after I came to the desert, the memory of that seduction did not cease to strike me repeatedly. Often, I confess, the malignant enemy set this spectacle before me and tried to persuade me that those who lived so pleasantly were happy and supremely blessed.

But since we have described the beginning of this happiness, let us also add the end at which they arrived. For after they had lived for nearly twenty-five years in this luxurious pleasure, during the previous year, when a fire was raging throughout the city, they were found together in one house and both were consumed by the flames. Thus, truly, the flame of lust deserved the fire of combustion; and what a sweet life had contributed, an outcome bitter, alas, demonstrated.

But to return to those guilty persons who both promise their conversion and deceive others: a certain priest named Maurus devotedly entrusted himself to me a few years ago and assured me that he would become a monk in the desert. Soon, however, his heart changed, and he violated the covenant he had made with God on my behalf.

But so that the blindness of his mind might break out upon the surface of his flesh, and the darkness concealed within might be plainly depicted on his forehead, a wound suddenly arose in his eye. It disfigured him with disgraceful deformity for as long as he lived.

Later, while he was traveling to Rome out of devotion to prayer and was crossing a river with a very shallow current, all the others passed safely across the ford, but his horse alone was suddenly found without its rider. They searched for him, running back and forth through the riverbed, and found him there, submerged by the waters, a lifeless corpse. Thus, by preferring the refuse of his wandering to a holy purpose, he lost, deceived, the reward of both labors.

But as I prolong my discourse, drawn on by the sweetness of your affection, I am not unaware that I am now exceeding the limits of a concise letter. Yet I, an unlearned man, am not instructing you, a learned one; I am not presenting examples from Scripture. Rather, like a rustic, I have related only household matters, so that I might rouse a stomach dulled by daily fare, though fit only to eat cheap pods or green herbs.

I therefore send you back to the storehouse of your own mind, where certainly very many pages of Scripture are kept. There let your wisdom diligently inquire which is better: whether, having paid the debt of your conversion, you should sit in the seats of those who judge; or, having failed to pay it, stand before the tribunal of the most just Judge to render an account (Matthew XIX).

This much I know: if you could be converted from the vanities of the world by any means, you would unquestionably become the mouth of God, the herald of Christ, the trumpet of heavenly eloquence, the destroyer of the devil, and the founder of an eternal building. Finally, you would be the light of the Church and an impregnable wall of the Christian army.

# A Second Treatise: On Keeping the Faith Pledged to God

## Argument

He attempts, by many arguments, to show that Atto, a lawyer by profession, who had formally promised that, once dedicated to God, he would spend the rest of his life in a monastery, wickedly refused to keep his pledge. He tried to defend his perjury with certain quibbles and deceptive argumentative snares, as people of this kind commonly do. Peter endeavors to deter him from so heinous a crime by setting before his eyes both the enormity of the offense and its punishment.

## Peter, a Sinful Monk, to Atto the Advocate: Greetings in the Lord

It is established, illustrious man, that you voluntarily committed yourself into the hands of Abbot Mainard and vowed, out of a heavenly desire, to undertake the monastic way of life. Now, however, with your mind changed, as is said, you not only intend to violate your vow, but also quibble that this can be done through many subtle arguments.

For this reason, you are said to have angrily challenged the same abbot in these words:

“Show me an authoritative judgment of Scripture by which you may either rightly accuse me of having been withdrawn from the world or acknowledge that I am legally bound to the monastic rule.”

To answer a man learned in law first on the matter of civil law: Roman laws provide that what has once been granted by the giver may in no way be revoked.

## On Keeping the Faith Pledged to God

### Chapter I. That It Is Wicked to Violate Vows and Promises Made to God

Since this rule is commanded to be observed among human beings, how much more must it be kept inviolate before God! A person does not lose what he has once received; but is God to be defrauded of the right to his own possession?

Leaders of earthly warfare claim for themselves those who have professed military service. We swear allegiance under the weapons of the divine campaign, imprint upon ourselves the mark of the heavenly soldiery, and do not fear to brand ourselves with the stigma of desertion?

You gave God not gold, not a horse, not, finally, something belonging to another and outside yourself, but yourself—and now you are trying to withdraw yourself? What payment, then, will you exchange with the Lord in place of yourself? “For what exchange will a man give for his soul?” (Matthew XVI).

Although Moses commands in the Law: “A man who makes a vow and promises his soul to God shall give the price according to its valuation” (Leviticus XXVII), one must carefully note what is added a little later: “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a human being, an animal, or a field, shall not be sold or redeemed; for whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to the Lord” (ibid.).

Hear also, my son, how a wise man plainly pronounces a terrifying judgment against you: “The beginning of man’s pride is apostasy from God, for his heart has departed from the one who made him; because pride is the beginning of every sin. Whoever clings to it will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow him in the end” (Ecclesiasticus X).

Therefore, my brother, following the counsel of the same wise man: “Turn to the Lord and abandon your sins; pray before the face of God and lessen your offenses” (ibid.). And he immediately adds: “Return to the Lord and turn away from your injustice; hate exceedingly the abomination, and acknowledge the just laws and judgments of God, and stand in the portion of the proposal and prayer of the Most High God” (ibid.).

Let this saying of the same man not escape you: “Do not be hindered from praying always, and do not fear being justified even unto death, for the reward of the Lord endures forever” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII).

Nor should you forget this: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclesiastes V).

Ecclesiastes also says: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of your affliction comes and the years approach of which you will say: ‘They do not please me’” (Ecclesiastes XII).

### Chapter II. That One Who Does Not Fulfill His Vows Appears to Mock God

You offered yourself to God, and then, becoming a deserter, withdrew yourself? You make God into a child and yourself into an egg. For while you try, as if in play, to withdraw yourself after having first offered yourself to him, you appear to wish to babble at him as though he were a child.

“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians VI).

You deceive the author and offend the truth by lying. Since God is unquestionably Truth, he is offended by no fault more than by lying.

Hear, then, what the Lord says through Moses in Deuteronomy: “When you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay fulfilling it; for the Lord your God will require it of you, and if you delay, it will be counted against you as sin. If you are unwilling to promise, you will be without sin; but what has once gone forth from your lips you shall observe, and you shall do as you promised to the Lord your God, having spoken by your own will and with your own mouth” (Deuteronomy XXIII).

Indeed, consider also how fearful is this sentence which the Lord thunders through the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

You promised, and you do not fear violating your promise? You vowed, and you neglect to fulfill your vow? Yet the Psalmist says: “Come and repay” (Psalm LXXV). Solomon likewise says in Proverbs: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger; you are ensnared by the words of your mouth and captured by your own speech” (Proverbs VI).

If, then, a man who pledges his hand to a stranger and makes himself liable to render an account on his behalf is so bound, how much more do you owe an account to God, since you did not promise on behalf of someone else or a stranger, but specifically offered yourself to God!

You began to grow fervent with the fire of divine love when you resolved to devote yourself to the service of the heavenly soldiery. You began to burn in spirit, but through the degenerate sluggishness of the flesh you grew cold.

Therefore, through the Apocalypse of John, this divine sentence is directed against you, when your sluggish spirit is recalled from its holy purpose: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am beginning to spit you out of my mouth” (Apocalypse III).

Except as food is vomited out, nothing is judged suitable for any use at all. You, however, entered the body of Christ as a sweet meal of refreshment when, through the judicial force of your pledge and commitment, you gave yourself over to keeping watch in his service. Now, alas, you are vomited out as something rejected, as you try to break and violate the vow of your promise, paying no attention to what the Lord says through Moses in the Book of Numbers: “If any man makes a vow to the Lord or binds himself by an oath, he shall not make his word void; but he shall fulfill everything that he has promised” (Numbers XXXII).

In the sight of human beings you are indeed a layman, as your secular clothing and dress show; but in the sight of almighty God you have fallen from being a monk through violating the pledge of your sacred purpose. You appear to stand before human beings, but in the presence of the Lord you have fallen. For what was permitted to you before your commitment will no longer be permitted to you, since you are succumbing after deliberating upon a better purpose.

### Chapter III. The Good Works of Those Who Break Faith with God Please Him Less

But since perhaps you do not believe me and disdain to trust my words, let blessed Pope Gregory at least suffice for you. In the third homily of his exposition on Ezekiel, he explains this through the following words:

“There are some,” he says, “who practice the good things they know and, while practicing them, deliberate upon better things; but when they reconsider those better things, they alter what they had decided. They do the good things they have begun, but they succumb to the better things they had resolved upon.”

Such people appear to stand in their works before human judgment, but before the eyes of almighty God they have fallen in their deliberation. Hence it frequently happens that even their good work pleases God less, because when they are placed inconsistently on a better level through the deliberation of the mind, the very inconstancy of their thought accuses it.

But since all the perfected ones observe themselves with great subtlety of discernment, so that they never slip toward worse things either in action or in thought, and continually weigh how much they advance each day, it is rightly said of them: “They did not turn back as they went; but each one proceeded straight before his face” (Ezekiel XXIII).

You, however, my brother, present yourself as moving backward instead. You do not proceed before your face with the holy living creatures, but ridiculously try to return behind your back. Nor do you notice what the Lord says through Isaiah: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed, criminal children! They have abandoned the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, they have turned away backward” (Isaiah I). Of them Jeremiah says: “They have turned backward and not forward” (Jeremiah VII).

Consider, then, that those who turn backward and away, among an evil seed and criminal children, are placed among those who do not succeed to the rights of the inheritance with those worthy of blessing, to whom it was said: “You were called for this, that you might possess a blessing as your inheritance” (1 Peter III), but rather with those who incur the sentence of everlasting damnation, to whom it is said: “Cursed are those who depart from your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII).

You had begun to free yourself, brother, from the snares of this destructive and deceptive world and to hasten toward the sweetness of God. Now you are planning to depart from God and entangle yourself once more in the snares of the world? Against this Peter says: “For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter state has become worse than the former” (2 Peter II).

For it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn backward from the holy commandment delivered to them. The true proverb has happened to them: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Proverbs XXVI).

Moreover, as it is said through the prophet: “How hard and bitter it is to have abandoned you, the Lord your God” (Jeremiah II). And again, concerning you and those like you: “They have abandoned me,” he says, “the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (ibid.).

Paul warns against them, saying: “Look, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living and true God” (Hebrews III).

One does not depart from God by the steps of one’s feet, but by the perpetration of wicked deeds. And when the heart falls from the height of a loftier purpose, then the unhappy soul is separated from God, who is the summit and hinge of all good things.

It is not enough for you to try, through violated faith, to break the pledge of the sacred order; you also wish to defend that perverse position boldly and spread it among others through certain frivolous arguments. For you argue, as I suppose, that although someone commits himself to an abbot and promises to undertake a sacred purpose, he is not forbidden to violate the promise of such a pledge.

From these assertions, surely, heresy arises, unless your attempt is restrained as quickly as possible. For as soon as someone slips into heresy, he is not immediately marked by right with the name “heretic.” Rather, he alone is rightly called a heretic who upholds error and defends the perversity of abominable faithlessness.

Furthermore, we believe it is not beside the point to offer at least a few examples from the sacred canons, so that from various authorities it may clearly appear how firmly the wall of justice resists your turning away; so that, when the footsteps of your inconstancy wander astray, no escape may lie open at all, but wherever you turn, the reins of authority may restrain you and may unanimously—and therefore forcefully—resist your perverse attempts. And while you strive to wander through winding paths, with obstacles placed all around, you may be compelled against your will to return to the straight line of the right road.

Consider, therefore, what the Council of Chalcedon decreed (Act XV, canon 7):

“Those who have chosen the life of monks, we decree, shall come neither to military service nor to any worldly rank or dignity. But those who attempt this and do not do penance, so that they may return to what they first chose for the Lord, shall be anathematized.”

### Chapter IV. Those Who Abandon the Purpose of Religious Life Are Condemned by the Decrees of the Councils

Hear also the decree of Pope Leo (Pope Leo, letter 90, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, in Gratian, 20, q. 3, *Propositum*):

“A monk’s purpose, undertaken by his own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin.”

What a person has vowed to God, he must repay. Therefore, one who, having abandoned the profession of solitude, has fallen into military service or marriage must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance. For even if military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, to abandon the better choice is nevertheless a transgression.

You undertook the monastic purpose by your own judgment when you promised that you would enter the monastic order.

This is why that eminent man does not say that what someone has put on must not be taken off; rather, he says that what one has vowed to God must be repaid. He thereby clearly teaches that to vow is to undertake, and that to break a vow is unquestionably to violate a sacred purpose.

This is why he does not subsequently say that someone has abandoned the sacred habit; rather, he says: “To abandon the better choice is a transgression.” This is also why it is found in the Council of Toledo (Council of Toledo VI, canon 48):

“Paternal devotion or personal profession makes a monk; whichever of these it may be, it will hold him bound [variant *alligatum*, “bound”]. Therefore, we close access to return to the world for such men, and we forbid all return to the secular life.”

But we should now desist from these matters, lest, while striving to support our proposition with numerous testimonies of Scripture, we seem to be weaving scraps together in a brief letter.

Instructed for the moment by these examples, carefully consider how punishable an offense it is to violate the pledge of a sacred order. Therefore, dearest son, reject the poisonous counsels of those who flatter wickedly; shudder at the laughable pardon urged by those who advise what is harmful, or rather deadly; and close your ears to the hissings of the ancient serpent.

Do not delay entering the sacred purpose, as you promised, so that you may not, God forbid, be overthrown in punishment with those who have apostatized, but may instead, with those who have held to the apostolic teaching, eventually be raised to glory as Christ extends his hand.

[Col. 0679]

# Forty-Third Little Work: On the Praise of Flagellation and, as They Call It, Discipline

## Argument

He attempts, by many arguments, to show that the custom interrupted by the monks of the monastery of Cassino—namely, the practice of chastising the body with blows before everyone on each Friday—ought to be restored.

## Peter, a Sinful Monk, Sends Servitude in the Lord to the Holy Brothers Dwelling in the Heavenly School on Mount Cassino

The observance of Friday, to which your holy devotion has dedicated both the saving fast of abstinence from food and the discipline of apostolic scourging, has attracted what multitudes of people as an example of salvation and, like a young olive tree planted by God, has sprouted into branches multiplying in abundant shoots. Witnesses to this are not only your monasteries—that is, those which rejoice in imitating the footsteps of their teachers—but also the multitudes of cities and villages which, joining together and rejoicing, eagerly take up the same institution.

So great is their zeal that many, fired by the devotion they have conceived, consider themselves to suffer no small loss of their own salvation unless they adopt the rule of this observance as quickly as possible.
