They have no doubt that, while on the day of the cross they mortify themselves through bodily abstinence from food, they truly share in the passion of the Redeemer; and they rightly believe that they will reach the glory of the Lord’s resurrection when, while Christ hangs upon the cross, they too crucify the allurements of their flesh upon the gallows of renounced nourishment.

Hence the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Timothy II). And again: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be together in his resurrection” (Romans VI). And shortly afterward: “But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him” (ibid.).

## On the Praise of Flagellation and Discipline

### Chapter I. How Great Is the Devil’s Cunning

But one must know that the enemy of the human race, when he is unable to snatch the whole sacrifice from the hands of those offering it, tries, in the manner of a harpy, to take away at least some part of it.

Thus, when Abraham had offered God a sacrifice from various animals, it is written: “The birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away” (Genesis XV). Birds descend upon slaughtered carcasses when the aerial powers hurl themselves down to snatch the sacrifice of our afflicted bodies, so that they may either tear the whole thing from the hands of those making the offering or, having seized a part of it beforehand [variant *praereptam*, “snatched beforehand”], applaud themselves as though they had won a triumphant victory from the spoils.

For this reason, the spirit of ancient pride [Col. 0680A] cries out to you through the mouths of certain people, as through the instruments of its vessels:

“It is not entirely wrong to wear down the body by fasting, but it is extremely shameful and dishonorable to uncover one’s limbs before the eyes of so many watching brothers.”

And from whom does this voice proceed, if not from the one who compelled the parents of our race to be ashamed of their nakedness? (Genesis II.) Before the serpent’s voice, Scripture says: “Both of them were naked, Adam namely and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” But after the cunning of the crafty dragon had instilled its poisonous counsels into them, it is immediately written: “When they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths” (Genesis II).

I shall say boldly, my dearest brothers, that whoever is ashamed to be stripped of his clothing in order to suffer with Christ has certainly heard the serpent’s words; and because he is confounded by his nakedness, he is hidden, like the first parent, from the divine sight, so to speak: “I heard your voice,” he says, “in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself” (ibid.).

Indeed, without doubt, the person who scorns bearing the reproach of Christ is concealed from the face of God, since the Apostle says: “Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Hebrews XIII).

The humble brother therefore goes outside the camp together with Paul and does not fear bearing the Savior’s reproach. But every proud and arrogant person seeks a hiding place with the first parent, so as to avoid the sight of God, who sees everything. He is surely among those to whom it is said: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity, because I do not know you” (Luke XIII). “I do not know you,” he says, because, fleeing from me, I did not see you; that is, I rejected the pride of your arrogance.

### Chapter II. Who Are Said to Be Hidden from the Face of God

At the beginning of this saving observance, each of you received discipline while naked and did not fear the disgrace of nakedness. Who subsequently bewitched you and taught you to be ashamed of Christ’s passion, which is the glory of the world and the salvation of humanity?

Far be it from me to presume to apply to you, my lords, what the Apostle says to the Galatians: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh?” (Galatians III).

Yet I shall say boldly what he says in reproaching the Corinthians: “You gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise. For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face” (2 Corinthians XI).

Who could doubt that all these things pertain to the teaching of those who dogmatize perversely? Moreover, just as God said to Adam: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” (Genesis III), so it is not undeservedly that this may be addressed to you with a rebuke of severity:

“Who led you to fear bearing the insult of Christ’s cross, unless you heard the words of someone giving wicked counsel?”

This is also why, when I carefully investigated what was at issue, you answered me plainly that Stephen, the cardinal of pious memory, had mocked this practice with taunts and, spitting upon it as though it were an unworthy thing and looking upon it with abhorrence, had absolutely forbidden it to be done again.

This is not surprising, since the Apostle says: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Corinthians I).

I believe that the lord Stephen flourished in certain virtues through the grace of Christ; nevertheless, he was said to have suffered from the disease of pride, as the fervor of youth urged him onward. And perhaps, by the just judgment of almighty God, it happened that he suffered a sudden death because of the offense of this statement.

For only a short time after he had spoken these words to you, he received an antidote. On the feast of Blessed Scholastica the Virgin, he rose for the nocturnal office as though vigorous and already recovered; yet on that same day he himself first died suddenly, and then his younger brother, his full brother, also died. They were buried together on the following day.

It may perhaps rightly be believed that divine moderation arranged this so that the venerable brother would incur the judgment of an unexpected death especially on the day of that virgin against whose monastery he had uttered the arrogance of an incautious statement. Thus, because of this fault, no injury might come upon his soul, for which his flesh, collapsing so suddenly, had paid the punishment of momentary death.

For often the mercy of divine justice is mingled in such a way that in this life the sinner receives a fitting repayment for the crime he has committed, so that there he may escape the vengeance of eternal damnation; and here the punishment of a torment that comes to an end may strike him, so that there he may escape the vengeance that never ends.

### Chapter III. A Fitting Punishment for a Smith Established by Divine Judgment

[Col. 0681D]

This plainly brings to mind what Peter of Burgos, a most distinguished man, recently reported to me:

“There is,” he said, “in the region called Pilonicum, a smith exceptionally skilled in the art of hammering, and widely renowned everywhere for making spears and arrows. Rejecting the iron tools and implements suited to human needs, he took pleasure in sharpening those fit for inflicting wounds and slaughtering warriors, so that no small number had already fallen in battle by means of his [Col. 0682A] inescapable swords.

“Once, when he had fallen after receiving a not particularly serious wound in the chest, since he was far from his own people, he was received into someone else’s house and lay there. He carefully treated the little wound with medical skill until, having recovered a little strength, he grew better and regained his health. When his wife sent a conveyance so that he might return home, he rose promptly, apparently in good health. But—an astonishing miracle!—he left his entire arm, with the shoulder, behind on the bed. And, to hear something unheard-of, he felt no pain or discomfort at that time; instead, he marveled at it as though it belonged to someone else, suddenly discovered himself disabled, and saw the arm, torn away from him, lying at a distance. It happened, plainly, by the just judgment of God that he suddenly lost the arm with which he had so confidently fashioned weapons serving sudden death; and where he had not suffered a wound, there he found himself wounded—the man who, through the skill of his deadly craft, had often inflicted unforeseen wounds on very many people.”

## CHAPTER IV. The threat of a terrible judgment

To return, then, to the subject with which the discourse began: whoever is ashamed to submit to discipline because of the nakedness of his body undoubtedly, like Adam, fled from the sight of God walking in paradise, and is convicted of laughing [reading: mocking] at the suffering of the crucified Christ. He does not follow the one who, in order to free us from the curse, himself became a curse (Gal. III); rather, he imitates the one who sees everyone from on high and is himself prince over all the sons of pride (Job XLI). That one was clothed in glory, of whom the prophet says: “Every precious stone was your clothing” (Ezek. XXIV); yet, because of the arrogance of his swelling pride, he fell into everlasting shame.

But this is the one whose persecutors and followers alike unanimously confess his disgrace. Those who plotted against him say: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. II); but those who repent cry out: “We considered him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. LIII). In these words the prophet had already said above: “He had neither appearance nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no aspect to him; and we desired him despised, the least of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; and as though his face were hidden, he was despised, and therefore we did not esteem him” (ibid.).

Tell me, then, whoever you are who arrogantly mock Christ’s passion: when you disdain to be stripped and scourged with him, and ridicule his nakedness and all his sufferings as mere jokes, nursery songs, and delirious dreams, what will you do when you see him—who was publicly stripped and hung upon the cross—conspicuous in the splendor of his majesty, surrounded on every side by angelic hosts, enclosed in the immensity of incomparable radiance, and ineffably glorious above all things visible and invisible?

What, I ask, will you do when you see him whose disgrace you now despise seated upon the fiery and exalted tribunal, and terrifyingly judging the whole human race with the strict examination of justice? Then the sun will be darkened, the moon will be wrapped in darkness, the stars will fall from heaven, the foundations of the mountains will tremble, the heavens will flash with mournful rays, earth and air alike will be consumed by flames raging upward, and all the elements will be thrown into confusion (Matt. XXIV). And you, elegantly, softly, and becomingly dressed—what will you do amid all this? With what face, with what presumptuous boldness, will you hope to share in the glory of the one whose dishonor and shame you scorned to bear?

## CHAPTER V. Christ’s wounds are medicines for our senses

[Col. 0683B] Who will gather you, delicate and tender as you are, into the company of the martyrs, on whose bodies there will be seen in glory not only the marks of blows but also the scars of countless wounds? Christ was not ashamed of the shame of the cross, while you are embarrassed by the nakedness of your foul flesh, destined to be devoured by worms.

He is stripped, beaten, bound with chains, smeared with spittle; his flesh is pierced by a fivefold wound, so that we may be healed from the assault of vices that enter us through our five senses. But you—wanton, perfumed, insolent, delicate, and tender—do not wish the treasure of your flesh to be exposed to human beings, lest, God forbid, it should be considered mortal or earthly rather than something great!

The apostle Paul is beaten publicly with rods three times, and is not ashamed; he receives forty lashes less one five times in court, and rejoices; moreover, he says that he rejoices in cold and nakedness (II Cor. V). Peter, together with all his fellow apostles, is scourged and battered before the council of the Pharisees; and they all glorify God and exult because Jesus deemed them worthy to suffer insults for his name (Acts V).

David, stripped of his own garments and girded with a linen ephod, dances with all his strength before the ark of the Lord. Seeking not his own glory but God’s, and turning away from the dignity of royal character, he rejoices with song in honor of God Almighty. Michal says to him: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants! He was naked, as one of the buffoons might be naked” (II Sam. VI). The proud king’s daughter could not endure the man’s humility and therefore did not recognize the glory of the nakedness by which he served the Lord.

Such a woman, then, those deserve to have as their teacher who declare that their flesh must not be stripped before their brothers. And because these people, withering at the root of pride, never bring forth spiritual fruit, what Scripture also testifies concerning her aptly applies to them: “Therefore Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child to the day of her death” (ibid.).

They, too, deservedly ought to be driven away from you with severity, just as David broke her down by his reply: “As the Lord lives,” he said, “I will play before the Lord, and I will become even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (ibid.). To Michal, together with her disciples living in luxury, the Lord says in a certain sense through Isaiah: “Now hear this, delicate woman, dwelling confidently, who say in your heart: ‘I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know childlessness.’ These two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day: childlessness and widowhood” (Isa. XLVII).

The holy Spirit who was in David plainly impelled him to walk naked; but Michal was incited by that paternal possessor to rebuke him insolently. Of that possessor it is said: “Because an evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (I Sam. XVI). Therefore it must be believed without any doubt that the divine Spirit impels the person who humbly strips himself for the honor of Christ’s cross, while that proud man, raised up by Saul’s spirit into an arrogant swelling, is the one who disdains to strip himself in order to share in the crucified Christ. This pride so separated him from the author of humility himself that not even Samuel could obtain pardon for him.

The Lord commands Isaiah, that outstanding prophet, to walk naked publicly before all the people, while a monk who, so to speak, is not worth a single *stater* is ashamed to be stripped before a few brothers: “Go,” he says, “untie the sackcloth from your loins and remove your sandals from your feet”; and immediately it follows: “And he did so, walking naked and barefoot” (Isa. XX).

It should be noted that he does not say “soft linen” or “delicate cloth,” but: “Untie the sackcloth from your loins.” From the softness of the garment you may infer how delicately and softly all those whom the Spirit of truth filled, even under the old law, lived.

Kings and prophets, therefore—indeed, the Savior and the apostles as well—were not at all afraid to be stripped when the order of persecution demanded it. But you, like a delicate servant of the Lord, fear being seen naked, lest you be struck by the evil eye of those who see you!

And truly, your brothers are young ravens who glory in bearing the disgrace of their Lord; but you, as it is said, are the son of a white hen, rejoicing to appear adorned and smart. Yet while, in your pride, you scorn the blackness of the ravens, you incur the whiteness of the leprosy denounced by the ancient law.

## CHAPTER VI. The baseness and stench of our body

Come now, brother: what is this flesh, which you cover with such diligent care with clothing and nourish softly as though it were royal offspring? Is it not a mass of rottenness? Is it not a worm, dust, and ashes? The flesh as it now is is not what the wise man attends to; rather, one ought to consider the pus, poison, stench, and filthy corruption that it will become hereafter.

What thanks, then, will the worms give you, which are going to devour the flesh you have nourished so softly and pleasantly? Come, I ask: why did Christ suffer? Was it to wash away his own guilt and erase the offenses he had committed? But hear Peter speaking of him: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (II Pet. II).

Why, then, did he suffer? Peter himself answers again: “Christ,” he says, “suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (II Pet. II). Christ, therefore, suffered first; the apostles immediately followed him, and we too are commanded to imitate their footsteps, as one of them says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI). Why, then, do we read that Christ suffered, unless so that we might follow his example step by step?

I beseech you, therefore, beloved, close your ears to the serpentlike hisses of those who speak perversely, and guard them in the simplicity of the poor and crucified Christ Jesus as virgins. Drive from your mouth the golden cup of Babylon and the cup of God’s wrath, which is offered to you with flattering sweetness. Avoid the pestilential poisons of the proud who adulterate the word of God.

Concerning them the Apostle says to Timothy: “Avoid profane and empty talk, for they advance greatly toward impiety; and their speech spreads like a cancer” (II Tim. II). May a twofold fear not, God forbid, befall you and me—the fear which the Apostle expresses in different places: “I fear for you, lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds should be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus”; but “for myself I fear lest I have labored among you without cause” (Gen. III; II Cor. XI).

Of them he also says: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ; their end will be according to their works” (II Cor. XI).

Let the holy mind, therefore, not fear sharing in Christ’s cross through blows; let it not be ashamed of his disgrace through bodily nakedness, since he himself says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke IX).

The person who contemplates with the clear vision of his mind the rewards of the future recompense is never confused by the nakedness of his body; nor does one who looks ahead and considers the sweetness of eternal blessedness that will be repaid to him shrink from the brief harshness of blows that flies past in a moment.

O how delightful! O what a remarkable spectacle, when the heavenly Judge looks down from heaven and a man sends himself below for his sins! There the guilty man himself, presiding in the tribunals of his breast, performs a threefold office: in his heart he appoints himself judge, in his body the accused, and in his hands he gladly presents himself as torturer.

It is as though the holy penitent were saying to God: “It is not necessary, Lord, for you to command that I be punished by your office; it is not fitting that you yourself strike me with the vengeance of a just examination. I lay hands upon myself; I take vengeance upon myself; I repay my sins their due.”

This is precisely what the apostle Peter urges when he says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a reviler, or a coveter of what belongs to others; but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed” (I Pet. IV).

Indeed, where this takes place, the demons flee, and they shudder to behold what is done to Christ’s glory and to their own disgrace. In contrast, angels attend this spectacle, rejoicing over the sinner who has been converted (Luke XV); and joyfully announce this to God, while the invisible Judge himself already takes delight in seeing it.

This is the victim that is slain while alive and carried through the angels as an offering to God. Thus the sacrifice of the human body is invisibly mingled with that one sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross; and thus the whole sacrifice is stored in one treasure—both what each member offered and what the head of all the elect offered.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0685]

## OPUSCULUM FORTY-FOUR. ON THE TEN PLAGUES OF EGYPT AND THE DECALOGUE

### ARGUMENT

It teaches that certain pernicious and most dreadful vices, which must be avoided by everyone, and especially by those who have undertaken a stricter way of life, are indicated by the plagues of Egypt; and that, as antidotes, the individual commandments contained in the Decalogue are set diametrically opposite to the individual plagues.

[Col. 0685D] To his most beloved brother JOHN, no longer of Laon and therefore a praiseworthy man, PETER the sinful monk sends the affection of paternal love.

You recently despised Pharaoh, my son, and at the same time abominated the slavery of the proud king and oppressor of Egypt. Therefore it is now necessary for you, as you proceed through the desert, to undergo many kinds of temptation, to endure the privations of thirst and hunger, and thus, through arduous dangers and the straits of various afflictions, to reach the promised land.

You must therefore hasten with the Hebrew people to Mount Sinai and there receive the commands of the divine law, so that, armed with them as with weapons and a breastplate, you may repel the darts of hostile forces rising against you and not succumb to whatever circumstances of adversity may assail you.

But this law was given to the people on the fiftieth day after they had gone out of Egypt. The number fifty is dedicated to repentance, as may be gathered from many passages of Scripture. This is signified both by the year of Jubilee and by the fiftieth psalm, which David composed in repentance. And just as in the Gospel one debtor owed five hundred denarii and another fifty (Luke VII), so also the man who owed one hundred measures of oil was ordered to write fifty instead (Luke XVI). All these things emit the salutary fragrances of repentance, provided that the nostrils of understanding are not lacking to draw in the fragrance of the mystery with discernment.

Therefore, to be worthy to receive the decrees of the divine law, correct yourself through repentance and confess the wickedness of your past guilt. Thus, running within the number of repentance, you will reach God’s mountain through confession of sin.

This also corresponds most fittingly to the fact that the mountain is called Sinai, which is interpreted as “bush.” For through the bush, which is surrounded everywhere by thorns, the harshness of our sins, which pierce the Lord, is signified. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of their sins” (Lam. III). And in the Apocalypse it is read: “Every eye will see him, and those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him” (Rev. I).

This mountain, therefore, prefigures the holy Church, in which both confession and remission of sins take place. For Moses saw the Lord in the bush, and that bush represented the Church, in which the Lord is seen. Hence Moses himself, when he asked, saying, “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII), received the answer that he should stand upon the rock and from there see the Lord’s back. That rock, plainly, is faith, upon which the catholic Church is built, and through which the Lord is seen.

## [ON THE TEN PLAGUES OF EGYPT AND THE DECALOGUE]

### CHAPTER I. The divine law is the medicine for the plagues

From this mountain, therefore, it is necessary to receive medicines capable of healing you from the sickness that you contracted in Egypt. For what were the plagues that occurred in Egypt except wounds? And what was that heavenly law except the medicine of those same wounds?

The sinner must vomit out the filth of his guilt through confession and then drink the cup of repentance from the vessel of the divine law. Here the antidote is swallowed, so that the illness of the sick soul may be healed.

Moreover, souls dissolved in carnal enticements run through the fields and meadows of their pleasures and, like unbridled horses, revel amid the blandishments of seductive wantonness. For they encourage one another, as the Book of Wisdom testifies, and say: “Come, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as in our youth with speed; let us fill ourselves with precious wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of time pass us by; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through; let none of us be deprived of our luxury; everywhere let us leave signs of joy” (Wis. II).

These wanton and neighing horses, the stronger they are in the force of rich fatness, the more inwardly are they known to be dissolved by the sickness of a worse disease. And when the bridle of the divine law is applied to them, what else is being placed upon their rotting limbs than a bond and restraint, so that what had begun entirely to gape open and flow away might be tightened by the fastenings of heavenly commandments?

Hence that evangelical Samaritan, approaching the man who had been wounded by robbers, bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine (Luke X). Hence God promises through Ezekiel, saying: “I will seek what was lost, bring back what had been cast away, bind up what had been broken, and strengthen what had been weak” (Ezek. XIV).

The plagues, therefore, were inflicted in Egypt because wounds are inflicted upon human souls in the world. It is necessary, then, for all who are wounded to come to Mount Sinai, that is, to the Church, so that the bonds of the heavenly commandments may bind their wounds. For as many plagues as there were, so many commandments were divinely proclaimed, so that as many wounds as there are in the sick heart, there may be just as many medicines capable of being applied to them.

### CHAPTER II. The promulgation of the divine law

[Col. 0688B]

But before we discuss the concordant number of the plagues and the legal commandments, it must be said that, just as the Hebrew people are read to have received the Decalogue on the fiftieth day after the paschal lamb was slain (Exod. XII, XIX, XX), so likewise, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, the Holy Spirit appeared upon the apostles in a diversity of languages (Acts II).

There the law is said to have been written by the finger of God, and the Holy Spirit, who was given to the disciples on the day of Pentecost, is called the finger of God, just as the Lord himself says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke XI).

There the people hear voices, thunder, and the resounding blast of a trumpet; they see torches and flashes of lightning and the mountain smoking. In the voices, thunder, and loud blasts of the trumpet there is the vehement cry of those preaching; in the torches and flashes of lightning, the brightness of miracles.

All these things were completed through the power of the Holy Spirit: the apostles, burning with zeal, thundered in the variety of languages and shone with the radiance of virtues. But the fact that the Lord descended in both fire and smoke teaches mystically that, just as he illuminates the faithful with the ray of his knowledge, so he darkens the eyes of unbelievers, as though with the smoking darkness of error.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came into this world so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). And through Isaiah it is said: “Impiety has been kindled like a fire; it will devour thorn and brier; it will burn in the thickness of the forest, and the pride of smoke will be rolled up” (Isa. IX).

But since these mysteries, which can scarcely be explained even in lengthy volumes, do not suit the brevity of a letter, let us return to the plagues of Egypt and the commandments of the law. Let us see that our wounds and the heavenly medicines are contained here and there under the same number, so that as many diseases as there are, just so many antidotes may be applied; and, when the balm of salvation is applied to each wound, the rational soul may immediately be restored in every respect to its former state of health.

Moreover, when the soul is loosened through the flow of wantonness, it needs the binding of the divine law. And when it is bound by the bonds of the heavenly commandments, it is brought back to the strength of the desired salvation through the remedies placed upon its wounds.

### CHAPTER III. The first plague

Come, then: the first plague occurs when the waters are turned into blood (Exod. VII). These plagues, moreover, occur only in Egypt, that is, in the darkened heart oppressed by the gloom of blindness.

The waters are turned into blood when the blind mind, so far as it is concerned, confounds and violates the purity of right faith. For just as through water all crops emerge from the womb of the earth, so spiritual nourishment and virtues come forth from faith.

Water is therefore turned into blood when the foolish heart is darkened by the blindness of unbelief. As the Apostle says of certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I).

To this first plague, that is, to this most pestilent wound, the medicine of the first commandment is immediately applied: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). This is the medicinal bond by which the wound of unbelief must be bound, so that, hearing it, you may worship one God alone and not pour out the rottenness of decaying unbelief into many gods.

And, by the just judgment of God, it literally happened that the Egyptians were made to drink the blood of that river in which the Hebrew infants had first been killed.

### CHAPTER IV. The second plague

[Col. 0689C] The second plague is an abundance of frogs (Exod. VIII). The frog is a noisy animal and habitually croaks in muddy marshes. Heretics and philosophers are judged similar to it: like frogs upon muddy marshes—that is, amid crowds soiled by the filth of unbelief—they make empty outcries against Christ with futile objections.

While, through fallacious arguments, they do not cease chattering with importunate cries, they bring weariness to the ears but no nourishment for life to the mind.

To this disease, which rages lethally in the soul, the second commandment comes as a cup of salvation. The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX).

For one takes Christ’s name in vain who believes him to be not the Creator but merely a creature. Creation is subject to vanity. Such people are therefore certainly vain, because, exchanging God’s truth for a lie, they place their faith in vanity.

### CHAPTER V. The third plague

The third plague is gnats (Exod. VIII). This creature is so tiny and minute that, while it balances itself in the air and flies unstably in wandering twists here and there, it eludes the sight of anyone trying to see it.

Yet when it settles upon our body, it stings, so that although you cannot see it while it flies, you are compelled to feel it when it pricks. As they fly around and intrude themselves more persistently, they do not cease to trouble our faces and prevent those who wish to rest from doing so.

Thus this plague clearly signifies the vice of wandering and restlessness. Some who suffer from this disease run uselessly here and there and, as though subject to evil changes of fortune, do not rest because of impatience.

But because these gnats are very small and harmful, seeming to have not so much weight as a bite, those who serve the vice of wandering consider what is signified by the gnats to be a light sin; yet they are pierced by the sting of guilt, which is not light.

The bite does not increase the weight, but penetrates: the lighter they judge this vice to be, the more deeply the sting of sin must pierce the lower parts of the languishing soul.

The medicine of the third commandment therefore meets this sickness when it is said: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX; Deut. V). Sabbath means rest. Where there is sanctification of the Sabbath, there certainly is the Spirit of God. Hence it is written: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

The words must be weighed carefully: if the Holy Spirit rests only upon the quiet person, then he abandons the restless one.

Indeed, just as the second commandment is referred to the Son, so this third commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit, who is likewise the third person in the Holy Trinity. The magicians also attribute that third plague to the Holy Spirit, since they themselves cannot produce gnats, saying to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. II).

The Apostle urged his disciple to observe this Sabbath when he said: “Attend to reading and teaching” (I Tim. IV). Elsewhere: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V). Through the Prophet the Lord urges us to the observance of this Sabbath when he says: “Be still, and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV).

It is as though he said: Observe the spiritual Sabbath; avoid the restlessness of wandering, so that, fixed through the grace of the Holy Spirit, you may not be troubled by gnats, but may be sanctified by the observance of the spiritual Sabbath.

It should further be noted that only these three commandments were written on one tablet, while the other seven were contained on another. The former pertain to love of God, the latter to love of neighbor. Therefore there are no more than two tablets, because there are two distinct impressions of love.

[Col. 0690D] That three commandments were written on one tablet and seven on the other is gathered especially from what the blessed Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just” (Eph. VI). “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise—“so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

Why is this commandment called the first, unless because it was placed at the beginning of the second tablet? It is also said to carry a promise because, unlike the other commandments, this commandment is followed by the promise of longevity: “Honor your father and mother, so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

This commandment, therefore, which is fourth in the general number of the commandments, is placed first on the second tablet.

### CHAPTER VI. The fourth plague

Opposed to this is the fourth plague, namely the *cynomya*, which is called the dog-fly (Exod. VIII). Nothing is more doglike than to ignore one’s parents and fail to show reverence to those who gave us birth.

Doglike behaviors also harass them like flies circling around: those who do not know how to honor their parents withdraw from natural dignity through the inconstancy of frivolity and tear at their parents like dog-flies when, snarling and barking against their begetters, they torment them through impatience.

For this plague to be cured, fitting reverence must be shown to parents.

### CHAPTER VII. The fifth plague

The fifth plague is the death of livestock (Exod. IX). All who, scorning the marriage bed, pollute themselves with the foulness of other women and dissolve themselves indiscriminately in the excesses of obscene lust—what else should they be called than brute animals, utterly alien to the reasoning of spiritual understanding?

They have become “like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI). And through Jeremiah it is said: “I satisfied them, and they committed adultery, and they luxuriated in the house of a prostitute; they became lustful stallions, each neighing for his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V).

These animals must necessarily perish, utterly destroyed, unless the medicine of the divine law comes to their aid. It is therefore said: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX).

This fifth commandment is set against the fifth plague like a medicinal bond, so that, while each person is compelled to be content with his own marriage bed, the immoderation of unbridled lust may in no way extend toward the embraces of another’s flesh.

### CHAPTER VIII. The sixth plague

The sixth plague consists of wounds, and swollen, inflamed boils (Exod. IX). In the wounds the deceitful and purulent malice of those who hate is exposed; in the boils, swollen and inflated pride; in the inflammation, seething anger and the madness of inflamed fury.

There are souls that are murderous, in which these plagues arise and rage most fiercely; unless they shed human blood, they do not allow them to rest.

To this furious and savagely raging disease the sixth commandment comes as heavenly medicine: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). Whoever hears this is to suppress within himself the destruction arising from evil will, so that the poison conceived in a malicious conscience does not burst forth externally into the act of shedding blood.

### CHAPTER IX. The seventh plague

After this comes the plague of hail, where hail and fire were carried together (Exod. IX). These two things are opposites: cold in the hail, heat in the fire. So those who steal what belongs to others are cold toward brotherly love but inflamed by the heat of desire.

Lightning and thunder are also said to have been mixed with the hail. What is signified by lightning and thunder except intolerable terror? It is characteristic of thieves first to fear capture and then punishment, trembling in their innermost parts, yet still not cease carrying out the wickedness once conceived.

These plagues—hail, fire, lightning, and thunder together—devastate like fields the hearts of those who secretly seize what belongs to others; and, if any crops or shoots of good will are present, they scatter them all.

The medicine of the seventh commandment therefore comes to the aid of this worst wound: “You shall not steal” (Exod. XX). Each person, recognizing this, should not destroy the crops of his heart through this manifold plague, but should fill the storehouse of his soul with the fruits of good works, fulfilling the Apostle’s saying: “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer; rather, let him labor with his hands, so that he may have something to give to those in need” (Eph. IV).

### CHAPTER X. The eighth plague

The eighth plague is locusts (Exod. X). By these creatures, which destroy the shoots of crops and gnaw the harvests with their pestilential mouths, who can be better signified than those who slander their brothers and set false accusations against them [reading: impose false charges upon them]?

For they devour the shoots of another’s field when they not only suppress the good qualities of their brothers, which they ought to proclaim, but also go further and brand them with the mark of a false offense.

They gnaw because, out of envy, they conceal not only their true virtues but also stamp upon them the stigma of a fabricated depravity. Do they not gnaw like locusts, of whom the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another”? (Gal. V.)

The commandment appropriately set against this plague is: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exod. XX). Thus every false witness, who will not go unpunished, must restrain himself from biting another’s life, cast away his locust-like teeth, and not strip away the green shoots of another’s field.

### CHAPTER XI. The ninth plague

The ninth plague is now the density of darkness (Exod. X). No one falls into deeper inner darkness than the person who violates the fidelity of the marriage chamber and seeks to invade another man’s wife.

But the splendor of the divine law illuminates these darknesses, which a heart devoted to lust must endure, when it says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. XX).

Here it should be noted [lacuna] that he does not say “you shall not take” or “you shall not defile,” [lacuna] which is more: “you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” [lacuna].

Above it was certainly said, “You shall not commit adultery”; here it is said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” Thus two commandments appear to concern one matter.

There the deed of adultery, by which one violates another’s marriage bed, is forbidden; here even the desire of one who wishes to violate it is prohibited. There the foul and unlawful intercourse of adultery is condemned; here the appetite for adulterous desire is also restrained.

Indeed, the very desire to violate another’s marriage is adultery, as the Lord says: “Whoever looks at another man’s wife in order to covet her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

Therefore let no one covet another’s wife, lest he suffer the palpable darkness of gloom in his heart. And if perhaps he already suffers it, let him admit the flashing ray of the legal commandment and thus cast away the darkness of a blinded conscience.

### CHAPTER XII. The tenth plague

[The supplied source ends here.]

Finally, the tenth plague is the death of the firstborn (Exod. XI). A human being has two sons, so to speak: one when he performs an action belonging to this present life, and another when he undertakes something spiritual that tends toward eternal life. [Col. 0693B] But the spiritual fruit, as our firstborn, ought to hold first place in our works. Hence the Lord also says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI; Luke XII). As though he were saying: “Bring forth spiritual fruit, which is truly your firstborn; but let whatever belongs to the necessities of this life be second in the inheritance.”

For this firstborn, together with Jacob, the blessing is due (Gen. XXIV); but concerning Esau and those like him, Scripture says: “An inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX). Concerning these two children it is figuratively said in Deuteronomy:

“If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and they bear him children, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn; and if he wishes to divide his possessions among his sons, he may not make the son of the beloved wife firstborn and set him before the son of the hated wife. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn, and shall give him a double portion of all that he possesses; for he is the beginning of his sons, and the rights of the firstborn belong to him” (Deut. XXI).

Of all these matters we here undertake to explain only that statement: the beloved wife is the soft, pleasurable, carnal life; the hated wife, however, is the spiritual life, since it is rigid, strict, and altogether hostile to the allurements of carnal pleasures. The rights of the firstborn therefore belong to her son, because the fruit of the spiritual life deserves to have as its reward him who, according to John, is “the Firstborn of the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I). [Col. 0693D]

But this firstborn—that is, the spiritual fruit—undoubtedly dies for the person who, not content with his own possessions, turns his attention to those of others; who covets what belongs by fraternal right and, with the torches of avarice kindled, desires the goods of his neighbor. But the tenth commandment of the law is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX). Let that person therefore hear this commandment attentively, lest he lose his firstborn, so that he may rejoice in his own firstborn and in no way covet what belongs to another.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Benefits and Praises of the Divine Commandments

These, dearest son, are the decrees of the divine law. From them all the instruments of Holy Scripture proceed, and upon them the entire discipline of holy religion rests. These are truly the bonds of flowing wounds; these are the health-giving medicine of sick souls. All those plagues that we endured in Egypt—and indeed all the diseases within that we conceived on the plain of worldly life—we ought to cure at Mount Sinai (Exod. XIX), that is, on the height of the sacred vocation.

Remain always in these things, therefore, and meditate diligently upon them; and, so to speak, continually grind these pigments or spices in the apothecary of your mind. Do not leave this chamber of fragrances, but examine here more carefully all the hiding places of your soul; scrutinize all the secrets of your inward parts; apply to each wound the medicines you recognize as suitable; and, once you have obtained health, strive with vigilant care to preserve it. For relapse is worse than fever; and, as physicians testify, diet must be observed no less than treatment: namely, you must avoid foods that are harmful, and despise as deadly poison whatever proves injurious or opposed to the antidotes you have received.

This is that ten-stringed psalter, which we are commanded to strike by the frequent stroke of the plectrum—that is, to tighten and sound through holy works as many strings as there are commandments. Having these things well ordered, ascend the mountain heights with Moses; grasp the summit of a stricter life, so that together with him you may deserve to hear:

“Go and say to them: ‘Return to your tents; but you, stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments, statutes, and judgments’” (Deut. V).

You too, having rejected the world, remain continually with the Lord and stand ready in his presence. For he does not say, “Sit here,” or “Recline with me,” but, “Stand here with me,” so that you may understand that spiritual leisure is established in the exercise of labor.

Stand, therefore, on the mountain with the Lord, so that you may wage unremitting war against the spirits of wickedness and vigorously break the wanton impulses of carnal passions. Fight, then, against the barbarism of the vices that assail you, so that, victorious with Joshua, you may subdue the rebellious kings (Josh. X), and he himself may command you to trample their necks beneath your victorious feet. Thus, enriched by the spoils of your enemies and adorned with the titles of victory, may you as a triumphant conqueror reach the promised land—or rather, may you continually possess the land of the living as an hereditary gift together with the true Israelites.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0695]

## OPUSCULUM FORTY-FIFTH. ON HOLY SIMPLICITY, WHICH OUGHT TO BE PREFERRED TO PUFFED-UP KNOWLEDGE

### Argument

He consoles the monk Ariprand, who had not cultivated his intellect through the liberal disciplines in the world. He shows that the desire for knowledge is the origin of all evils; that knowledge itself, especially when separated from Christian virtues, is harmful to its professors and useless to others; but that holy simplicity is secure and highly beneficial. Accordingly, he urges him, if he wishes to know something profitably, to approach God through contemplation of divine things.

[Col. 0695A]

To Ariprand, son of holy hope, Peter, a sinful monk: the affection of paternal love.

A servant is exceedingly ungrateful if, after receiving spears or swords through his master’s generosity, he immediately girds himself with those same weapons and rises against his lord in battle. A soldier is guilty of treason if, enriched by imperial gifts, he claims that a crown suits him better than the service of submission or obedience.

You confess, my son, that you are frequently attacked and endure the darkness of harassing thoughts, because, although you have a teachable heart and are very ready to learn, you sought the entrance to the true light before learning the blind wisdom of the philosophers. You flew to the desert first, following the footsteps of fishermen, before sweating over—not merely the studies, but even the follies—of the liberal arts.

## ON HOLY SIMPLICITY, WHICH OUGHT TO BE PREFERRED TO KNOWLEDGE THAT PUFFS UP

### CHAPTER I. How Harmful the Desire for Knowledge Is

Divine mercy has therefore earned this complaint from you, for it also granted you the gifts of a subtler intellect. Surely, if at the very beginnings of your military service the ancient enemy attacked you with the same kind of combat by which he overcame the first parents of the human race at the beginning of the world’s creation, this is no wonder.

These were the serpent’s first words to the woman; with these hisses the most dreadful dragon dripped his poisons into her heart:

“God knows,” he said, “that on whatever day you eat from it”—plainly, from the apple—“your eyes will be opened,” and “you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III).

Look, brother: do you wish to learn grammar? Learn to decline God in the plural. For the skillful teacher, while newly establishing the art of obedience, introduced into the world an unheard-of rule of declension for worshiping several gods.

Moreover, he who was plotting to bring in the entire host of vices set the desire for knowledge as commander of the army, and thereafter brought all the troops of iniquity into the unhappy world. What wonder, then, if he still hurls against the son of Eve the very dart that the ancient enemy once hurled against that same Eve? An experienced opponent cannot despair of success when he launches against his children the same battle by which he remembers that he formerly gained victory over our parents.

But since our Redeemer is a shepherd—not indeed of dogs, wolves, or growling wild beasts, but of sheep, and not only of sheep but also of lambs—is it not permitted, I ask, for a shepherd to hold a disciplinary rod over his flock and assign it at will either to the table or to pasture? For in the legal ceremonies the Lord commands that at one time oxen, at another calves, at another rams, and at another yearling lambs be sacrificed.

### CHAPTER II. Why God Calls Some Young Men and Others Old

If, then, each owner may do as he wishes with his own flock, how could it not be permitted for your Creator to place you, like a very tender lamb, upon the table of refreshment, while reserving the rest of the flock for the pastures of outward life? Thus he might already draw you within his own entrails in a special intimacy, while in the meantime he waits, through the governance of a loving dispensation, for others to be converted at their appointed times.

Samuel, still a little boy like a tender lamb, is placed, so to speak, upon the Lord’s table with three measures of flour and a jug of wine, when his parents dedicate him to Eli the priest and to the temple of God that was at Shiloh (1 Sam. I).

John the Baptist, not only himself a lamb but one who would proclaim the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, is chosen from the flock of a priestly household and goes into the desert (Luke III; John I, etc.), so that the Lord might be delightfully nourished by him, as by a feast of sweet food.

For people are not enlisted for the battle line of spiritual warfare solely according to their own choice. Rather, he who inspires them to turn to himself apportions over them the several stages of their ages and times: drawing some to himself when already ripe in advanced old age, strengthening others with the vigor of youthful growth; taking these while they bloom in the beauty of early adolescence, and bringing in those, like unfledged nestlings, from the very beginning of nursing infancy.

Ahijah is already nearly blind from excessive old age, yet he sees with the clarity of prophetic eyes Jeroboam’s wife approaching from a distance:

“Enter,” he says, “wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else? I have been sent to you with a harsh message” (1 Kings XIV).

Ezekiel is vigorous at the age of thirty, when, stationed beside the river Chebar, he is advanced to the office of administering prophetic grace (Ezek. I).

David, scarcely yet bearded in the first bloom of adolescence, is chosen from behind the nursing flocks of his father’s subjection and is advanced both to sound the psalter of spiritual allegory and to attain the height of the royal scepter (1 Sam. XVI). [Col. 0697A]

To Jeremiah it was said:

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. I).

And why should I enumerate more? He who kindled Eleazar, already chilled by the frost of old age, with the ardor of triumphant martyrdom (2 Macc. VI), himself strengthened the still tender sons of blessed Felicity with the steadfastness of unconquered faith.

### CHAPTER III. Why God Established the World Through Uneducated and Simple Men

“But perhaps,” you will say, “I would win many people if the grace of preaching flowed through me, if I possessed an abundance of literary knowledge.”

And I reply that Eleazar too could have recalled many from idolatry if he had lived (2 Macc. VII); the Maccabees and countless martyrs of Christ could have strengthened very many for the contest of faith if they had decided to postpone the punishments inflicted by persecution. But because they built up others more effectively by enduring the torments of punishment through martyrdom than by preaching, they set the word aside and left to those who followed an example for imitation.

You too provoke those who see you more powerfully by hastening after Christ than you could have advanced those who heard you through any complexity of words. For almighty God does not need our grammar to draw people after him. At the very beginning of human redemption, when it would certainly have seemed most necessary to scatter the seeds of the new faith, he sent not philosophers and orators, but rather simple men and fishermen.

Hence we read that Samson seized the jawbone of a donkey that was lying there and killed a thousand Philistines with it (Judg. XV). What does killing a thousand men with the lying jawbone of a donkey mean except casting down, through the tongues of humble and simple people, the complete number of unbelievers from the position of their perversity and inclining them toward the humility of Christ through the ministry of holy preaching?

For since Samson is interpreted as “sun,” after this sun shone upon the world, after he scattered the rays of his miracles and signs throughout the earth, he immediately subdued the necks of all who resisted him and struck them down from the rigidity of their proud life.

### CHAPTER IV. What Is Required in a Preacher

You too, my son, if you are to receive the office of preaching, imitate either the example of the donkey of which it was said, or that of the sheep. The latter, while alive, makes an ugly sound—“baa,” but when dead sings sweetly in musical instruments. So also those who live carnally can bleat inanely with the sheep, but cannot diligently fulfill the office of a preacher.

The Prophet also says: “Praise the Lord with the tambourine and the choir” (Ps. CL). Leather makes no sound unless, once left dry, its moisture has departed. If, therefore, you wish your tambourine or your string to produce a clear sound in the hearts of your hearers, let all the moisture of carnal life evaporate from you; let your mind dry up from every flow of itching lust.

Cold congealed in the chest also commonly interrupts the voice. If you wish, therefore, to thunder forth the word of God with a clear voice, take care that the flame of divine love in you does not grow lukewarm, lest the cold of the prince who sits in the north (Isa. XIV) creep upon you.

That man had already conceived this cold when, as the Lord walked in the garden at the afternoon breeze, he answered him in a kind of hoarse voice:

“I heard your voice,” he said, “and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Gen. III).

Since the midday heat had already departed from him, the breeze too is the offspring of cold. Moreover, the removal of innocence had already stripped him naked. What else do all these things suggest except that the cold of extinguished love had constricted his inward parts, and therefore his voice sounded hoarse in the Lord’s ears?

The priest Eli had also already been bound and numbed by this cold. He said to his sons:

“This is not a good report, my sons, that I hear—that you are causing the people of the Lord to transgress” (1 Sam. II).

Because the cold of love for the Lord had closed this preacher’s throat, his voice, sounding hoarse, so to speak, did not effectively resound in the hearts of his sons.

If, therefore, you wish to have a voice that thunders in preaching or is effective in prayer, always strive to let divine fervor inflame you, lest the torpor of cold interrupt your voice. For the prayer or preaching of a cold mind is not accepted and, like a hoarse voice, is not heard.

Abraham had plainly remained a stranger to this cold. Scripture declares of him:

“The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the very heat of the day” (Gen. XVIII).

And that heavenly Bridegroom, as it is said in the Song of Songs, feeds and reclines at midday (Song I).

Indeed, when the sharpness of your heart moves you to complaint, what are you doing except fighting against God with the very weapons God has bestowed? And since it is no small crime to be ungrateful to God, you must fear greatly lest you spring into tyranny against God from the very source from which you ought to have offered him thanksgiving; and, while you demand immoderately the knowledge that puffs up, foolishly offend against the charity that builds up (1 Cor. VIII).

For what do you know? Perhaps almighty God, the dispenser of merits, bestowed upon you the insight and agility of a subtler intellect for this purpose: that he might already show you, in a certain sense, a sign of future recompense, compensating with the sharpness of a living mind for that deadly knowledge which you rejected for love of him.

Since letters arise from understanding, and understanding does not proceed from letters, a person whose understanding is sound has no need of letters. In the literary school, where boys first receive the elements of articulated speech, some are called alphabet-learners, others syllable-learners, some name-learners, and others calculators; and when we hear these names, we immediately recognize from them what progress each boy has made.

### CHAPTER V. How the Holy Spirit Teaches Us

But when understanding is opened to someone through the gift of the Holy Spirit, because by the implanted power of a lively intellect he comprehends everything easily, he will have little need of these stages of learning.

As it is said of those three boys:

“He gave them knowledge and discipline in every book and wisdom; but to Daniel he gave understanding of every vision and dream, so that the wise men of Babylon could not equal their prudence, nor could the magicians, soothsayers, or diviners match them in revelations of heavenly mysteries” (Dan. I).

But, leaving aside the ancients, let us return again to modern examples. Blessed Benedict is sent to the study of letters, but soon recalled to the wise folly of Christ. Because he exchanged the school for holy rusticity, he left this written on a woman’s sieve—something that the wise men of the world cannot express upon the table of geometric or astronomical learning.

Martin too is ignorant of letters; yet this fool and unlearned man recalls the lost souls of three dead men from the underworld. Antony does not practice rhetoric, but, conspicuous throughout the whole world, is read, so to speak, in living letters.

Hilarion casts aside Plato and Pythagoras and, content with the Gospel alone, shuts himself within a sepulchral cave. Yet behold: he commands demons, though the studies of philosophers do not adorn him.

If you too had learned these things in the world, as you earnestly desire, perhaps the Lord would not have you today within the boundary of his allotted portion.

For there is a wisdom of which it is written:

“For by wisdom all who have pleased you, Lord, from the beginning were healed” (Wis. IX).

And there is a wisdom of which it is said:

“This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, animal, demonic” (James III).

And, oh, how many people this same earthly and animal wisdom did not allow to make a prosperous journey, so that they fell into mortal danger before they could enjoy what they desired!

## CHAPTER VI. That Human Wisdom Is Subject to Many Dangers

Gualterus was, plainly, a companion of my teacher, Ivo. For nearly thirty years he pursued wisdom through the western regions in such a way that he traveled from kingdom to kingdom. He penetrated not only the cities, towns, and provinces of the Teutons and Gauls, but also those of the Saracens of Spain.

But as soon as, after gathering studies from nearly the whole world, he exchanged exile for a settled dwelling and, as though established in peace, began to teach boys, certain rivals of his—followers or supporters, evidently, of another wise man—killed him from ambush as he was walking unsuspectingly.

Pierced by swords, he did not, as I believe from what was reported to me, ask for priests; he made no confession or act of repentance concerning what had happened. Rather, until his final breath he did not cease crying out only this: “Alas, what a loss!” If anything was said either about making confession or about some other matter, he, already deranged, repeated only this: “Alas, what a loss!”

Thus he wove, like a spider, the inextricable threads of a web, as it seemed to him; but as soon as the wind of final necessity struck them, everything was immediately scattered into nothing. For, as the Prophet testifies, “our years shall be meditated like a spider” (Ps. LXXXIX).

I do not enumerate how many useful gifts Hugo, a cleric of the Church of Parma, possessed, because I avoid the tedium of a ragged style. He was so ambitious in the study of the arts that he had an astrolabe made for himself out of the brightest silver. While aspiring to the height of the episcopate, he made himself chaplain to the emperor Conrad.

When he returned from him, laden with royal promises and almost certain of attaining the dignity he desired, he fell among robbers. A certain presbyter in the Teutonic regions, who had a layman as his associate, attempted to attack Hugo’s grazing horses. When Hugo promptly opposed him, the presbyter pierced him with a lance and killed him. Then he clearly discovered that nothing he had learned had been of any use, when at once he lost both the sweetness of his derisive life and the dignity of the position he had coveted.

### CHAPTER VII. The Effects of Worldly Wisdom

Moreover, it often happens that some who are carnally wise both live for a long time and are never able to find what they desire. Trusting in the vanity of their wisdom, while they hope that everything will easily be available to them, they suppose that they have no need of the testimony of religion. While they boast of empty wisdom, they do not fear to live foolishly.

Therefore, those who observe them reject their conduct, spit upon their life, mock their way of living, defile their reputation, and condemn their testimony. Consequently, those who had resolved to live according to the desire of the flesh are often compelled, when the judgment is turned in the opposite direction, to suffer want, while simple and peaceful people, by contrast, abound in the necessities of life.

Hence the Lord says through Isaiah:

“Because I called and you did not answer; I spoke and you did not hear; and you did evil in my sight, and chose what I did not wish: therefore, behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst; behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall praise because of the exultation of their heart, and you shall cry out because of the pain, and howl because of the contrition of spirit” (Isa. LXV).

Even today, certainly, a brother lives in the city of Rome, born from the highest nobles of Gaul. I conceal his name because I shudder to expose a brother’s disgrace. I do not know whether he lacks anything useful. He shines with so many flowers of outward goods: noble as an emperor; handsome in appearance, as Cicero would put it; as Virgil might sing; a powerful trumpet in the Church; perceptive and acute in divine law. When disputing scholastically, he runs through the words of a book as though they had been written out before him; when speaking in the vernacular, he does not offend against the rules of Roman refinement.

What should I say about monastic order? What about mastery of regular discipline? In knowledge of these matters he has grown so strong that he cannot even teach them diligently. But, alas, his life is such that no one envies him to another, and no one asks to bring him into his own company. To put the matter briefly: the monastic door is closed to this foolish wise man as a resident, though access is not denied to rustic, unlearned, and disorderly people.

Hence the wise man rightly says:

“Better is the man who lacks wisdom and is deficient in understanding but fears God, than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High” (Ecclus. XIX).

This is also demonstrated in my lord Leo, who is enclosed. We have placed a learned fool; let us also introduce a wisely unlearned man.

This Leo, although he has learned no letters apart from the Psalms—or some very slight and elementary matter—surpasses all grammarians and philosophers of the world in knowledge of the Scriptures and in the depths of spiritual counsels. Whenever any of us comes to him for advice about some matter of the soul, we receive a word from him with such confidence as though we were carrying away an oracle of the prophetic Spirit.

But since he is also thoroughly known to you and frequently included in our little works, let it suffice to present here one saying that recently fell almost casually from his mouth, yet could not be heard casually by me.

While I was carefully inquiring among other principles of spiritual living whether, after completing the office of the nocturnal synaxis, he could sleep if he wished, he declared that he did not know this at all. When I repeated the question several times and asked whether he slept around dawn, he replied that he was wholly ignorant of this, because he had never experienced it.

He added that he was accustomed to answer his own thoughts:

“The heart may become agitated,” he said, “the eyes may flutter, the mouth may not cease muttering through frequent yawns, and the head may nod and sink downward; but since none of these things can kill me, they will in no way prevail upon me to consent to sleep at this time.”

We had also composed a distich about this matter, which we do not think it pointless to insert here:

> He does not break the rule who, singing psalms at night, sleeps again—

> Yet let him not place his head down everywhere before the synaxis.

But alas for me, wretched man! The difference between me and Lord Leo is the difference that occurred between mighty David and a foolish actor. David had performed mighty deeds by his strength; the actor merely sings of his triumphal achievements with his voice.

He knew how to mortify himself in conflict for God; we compose little verses like children. And what, I ask, is more remarkable than that a man exhausted in strength and of extremely frail body should have spent nearly seventy years in the monastic habit and still not know whether he is able to sleep when the dawn of daylight breaks?

This man, therefore, is prudent; this man is truly to be called wise: while he casts the world beneath his feet, he mocks the very prince of the world through philosophy.

### CHAPTER VIII. That Those Who Approach God Have No Need of Human Disciplines

Therefore, dearest son, do not seek the kind of wisdom that could belong to you together with the reprobate and the pagans. Who lights a lamp in order to see the sun? Who uses [an uncertain word: “scolacibus”] in order to see the brightness of shining stars? Thus, whoever seeks God or his saints with a sincere gaze has no need of an alien light in order to behold the true light.

For true wisdom itself reveals itself to those who seek it, and without the aid of adulterated light it displays its unfailing radiance. Hence it is written:

“Wisdom is radiant and never fades; she is easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her. She anticipates those who desire her, so that she may first show herself to them” (Wis. VI).

Seek that wisdom, therefore; embrace it ardently with all your inward parts. Through it may you not only be able to know, but also to live, and through it to rejoice without end. Establish in God, who is true wisdom, the end of your seeking and understanding. Meditate upon him continually; rest in him always.

To him it is said in the same Book of Wisdom:

“To know you is perfect righteousness, and to know your justice and power is the root of immortality” (Wis. XIII).

Fix the entire gaze of your mind upon him. From that fountain of wisdom take a draught for your thirsty heart, so that, having conceived within your inward parts the strength of that life-giving drink, you may continually flourish through the moisture of heavenly grace and pour into others the streams of a well-watered fountain dripping from you.

And I ask that almighty God may one day display through you to your brothers what he promised through Isaiah to his poor:

“The needy and the poor seek water, and there is none; their tongue has dried up with thirst. I, the Lord, will hear them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them” (Isa. XLI).

And immediately afterward it continues:

“I will open rivers on the bare hills and springs in the midst of the plains; I will make the desert a pool of waters and the impassable land into streams of waters” (ibid.).

Since, therefore, dearest son, you have offered yourself like a very tender lamb, the demons flying through the air attack this offering, either to snatch it from your hands or to corrupt it by casting upon it the filth of evil thought.

You, like Abraham, drive away the birds rushing upon their attack, so that you may preserve your sacrifice undefiled and whole (Gen. XI). For from their quiver, beyond doubt, this poisoned arrow of thought is drawn: that you may envy your contemporaries who remain in the world for studying letters, and believe them cautious and prudent while considering yourself deceived and foolish—as though, if you too had done this, you would then have offered God a more acceptable sacrifice of your conversion.

But you truly offered to God everything that, hastening toward a better and lasting possession, you refused to acquire for love of him. It is better to offer everything at once than to distribute it piecemeal. For just as it is better to give a sheep than the sheep’s fruit, so it is more praiseworthy to offer the whole art to God at once than the fruits of the art.

Julian Caesar and the martyr Donatus learned at the same time. The former remained devoted to his studies; the latter followed the footsteps of truth. Yet Julian flourished so successfully in his wisdom that he wrote eight books against the Galileans—for that is what he calls Christians or the apostles—and against the Gospel. Donatus, however, became foolish, so that he entered the heavenly height with the glory of triumphant martyrdom.

The evangelist John learned almost nothing in the world. Rejecting the subtleties of orators and dialecticians, he moved as a little child to the simple folly of Jesus. Yet, when at the beginning of his book he thunders terribly about the mystery of the highest light, the blind subtlety of the philosophers immediately grows dim in the darkness of their studies.

Moreover, blessed Pope Gregory praises the discipline of grammatical art so far in his letters that he denies it to be suitable for Christians (Greg. the Great, *Reg.* IX, Ep. 45).

Jerome is dragged before terrifying tribunals and beaten with savage blows. Yet the only charge brought against him is that of the name of Cicero. He binds himself under a curse to suffer this punishment if he should read secular books any longer, as though he were denying Christ through the sacrilege of apostate treachery.

For they said to him: “You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian.”

And he replied: “If I read secular books any longer, I have denied you” (Jerome, *Epistle 22, On the Care of Virgins*).

A sufficiently honorable and useful wisdom, surely—one that is compared with the denial of Christ and likened to heretical treachery, so that reading it is equivalent to denying God! If, then, the man who had learned that earthly doctrine is restrained from using it, how much more must the one who has not yet experienced it be prevented from approaching it? If the former is held back from what he knows, how much more cautiously must the latter be restrained from learning it?

You sit down, brother, at the table of God. Let the banquets of heavenly eloquence suffice for you. Cast away the darnel that intoxicates the minds of those who eat it into madness; receive the grain that strengthens the souls of the hungry with sober nourishment.

Let the throat of your soul not disdain the food of life-giving nourishment, but cast far away the follies of falsehood and the refuse of vanities.

May almighty God, dearest son, instruct you with the teaching of his law, so that he may flood your heart with the light of true wisdom; may he receive from your hands the holocaust of a living sacrifice and advance you toward the growth of spiritual virtues; may he grant that you always remain in him, and may he himself delightfully rest in your inward parts, so that, as he promised, like a branch on the vine, you may never cease to put forth the shoots of devout works. Amen.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0703]

## OPUSCULUM FORTY-SIXTH. ON BEARING CORRECTION WITH EQUANIMITY

### Argument

He praises Ariprand, a recruit in spiritual warfare, because as a young man he withdrew to the desert, and urges him, following the example of Christ the Lord, not to abandon regular discipline. Accordingly, he should bear with an even temper the corrections not only of elders but also of younger men, which are highly beneficial for washing away stains of the soul and for the progress of both the one who corrects and the one corrected. On this occasion he says much about the goodness of correction, why it is given, and whether Saint Paul rebuked Saint Peter without fault.

[Col. 0703C]

To Ariprand, dearest brother, Peter, a sinful monk: the affection of paternal love.

You require, most beloved son, that I write something to you, and you implore that something also be written to you who, at my dictation, frequently write to others. But from what could I begin writing more suitably for a writer than from the mystical dignity of writing itself? In you, who write, there are three fingers and one hand; in the one to whom you write, there are three persons and one God. Therefore, when you draw a continuous line from diverse strokes, let your intention always be directed toward that One whose mystery you discern in yourself through a certain likeness.

And because, while you were still engaged among adolescents in the school’s training-ground, when no down—or scarcely the slightest—of puberty yet covered the flower of the boyish face, [Col. 0703D] the fervor of the Holy Spirit urged you to undertake not the monastic way but rather the discipline of the desert, beware lest, under the pretext of still-weak age, you violate the rule of the holy place; lest you weaken the rigor and severity of blessed conduct; lest you wish to alter the customary practice of severity; lest you presume to impose upon it some novelty of foreign invention.

For even he who is the teacher of the angels in heaven kept on earth the custom he found; [Col. 0704C] nor did he disdain to preserve an earthly practice, although he had come to display a heavenly one. To pass over countless examples, why did he permit his head and feet to be sprinkled with ointment by a woman’s ministry, unless because it was the custom of the Palestinian and Jewish region for its inhabitants to be anointed more frequently? Hence he says: “But you, when you fast, anoint your head” (Matt. VI; Luke VII). And what wonder is it if the Lord preserved the custom of his homeland in life, when he also did not disdain to observe it in the sacred rites of his burial? For John reports: “Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jews’ custom to bury” (John XIX; Matt. XXVII).

Therefore, when he who is Wisdom itself, through whom all things were created, does not refuse to preserve human tradition even in matters that seem almost entirely insignificant, how presumptuous is it for anyone to break a rule of discipline that he knows was handed down by the holy Fathers?

## On Bearing Correction Equably

### Chapter I. The benefits received by those who bear corrections with equanimity

Among the other distinctions of holy conduct—which you observe flourishing in others and which you yourself, by the support of divine mercy, already preserve irreproachably—take particular care never to bear corrections heavily, and never to be ashamed of being reproved on any occasion even by your juniors. This practice is so familiar and native to this place that whoever is corrected flees and cannot live with us.

For this purpose a person from the world is subjected to the instruction of regular discipline: so that the rust he contracted through the world’s seductions may be removed by the file of harsh correction. Hence Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: “Turn back to my correction; behold, I shall pour out my spirit upon you” (Prov. I). It does not say, “to my flatteries,” but: “Turn back,” it says, “to my correction.”

Therefore, to some who disdain being corrected it says: “They will rise early, and will not find me, because they hated discipline, and did not receive the fear of the Lord, nor consent to my counsel, and disparaged all my correction” (ibid.). Again it admonishes, saying: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor grow faint when you are corrected by him: for whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and, like a father in his son, he takes pleasure in him” (Prov. III).

Correction is rightly called not human correction but the Lord’s correction when, in the love of Christ, any severity is imposed by one neighbor upon another; and he deviates far from wisdom who does not bend his proud heart beneath divine reproofs. Hence the same Solomon says: “He who loves discipline loves wisdom; but he who hates reproofs is foolish” (Prov. XII).
