For this reason the same fool complains in the Book of Proverbs, saying: “Why did I hate discipline, and my heart did not consent to reproofs, nor did I hear the voice of those teaching me, nor incline my ear to my teachers?” (Prov. V.) But whoever accepts reproofs with equanimity does not depart from the company of the wise. Hence it is written: “The ear that hears the reproof of life will dwell in the midst of the wise; but he who rejects discipline despises his own soul” (Prov. XV).

Stepmothers, finally, indulge their stepchildren; fathers often apply harsh blows to their own offspring. The former, plainly, nourish those who hate them; the latter educate and afflict those whom they love. Hence it is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son; but he who loves him diligently instructs him” (Prov. XIII). And elsewhere: “Open reproof is better than hidden love. The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Prov. XXVII). Again it is written: “Instruct your son, and do not despair; do not set your hand [or, according to the variant, ‘your soul’] to his killing” (Prov. XIX).

A father’s hand is set to the killing of his son when, seeing him act wickedly, he not only does not rebuke him but even takes pleasure in punishing his deeds, and is not ashamed to exalt with flattering words one whom he ought [to correct] with harsh blows.

### Chapter II. That it is characteristic of the wise to love correction, and of the foolish to hate it

[Col. 0706A]

Whoever, then, is wise regards the harshness of the severity imposed as medicine for the wounds of his soul. Hence it is written: “If you correct a wise man, he will understand discipline” (Prov. XIX); and again: “Correction benefits the prudent more than a blow benefits a fool” (Prov. XVII). Of this prudent person it is also said: “He who is patient is governed by much prudence; but he who is impatient exalts his own folly” (Prov. XIV).

The impatient person exalts his own folly because, the more he is wounded by anyone on account of his impatience, the more fiercely he rages against them in daily quarrels. Hence it is written: “The wicked man always seeks quarrels; but a cruel angel is sent against him” (Prov. XVII). A cruel angel is sent against one who seeks quarrels because it is fitting that a cruel possessor invade the mind in which cruelty dwells; for, as the Apostle says, “Anger has a demon.”

Therefore, immediately after teaching that a cruel one is sent against the impatient, Scripture adds: “It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool trusting in his own folly” (ibid.). Of this foolish and impatient man it is written: “Do not befriend an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. XXII).

Moreover, just as a sick person who cannot take an antidote dies, so one who cannot be corrected cannot be relieved of the illnesses of his soul. Hence Solomon again says: “Do not withhold discipline from a child; for if you strike him with the rod, he will not die; you will strike him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Prov. XXIII).

Do you wish to hear what threatens those who reject correction, who disdain being rebuked by their elders? “Sudden destruction,” he says, “will come upon the man who, stiff-necked, despises the one correcting him, and healing will not follow him” (Prov. XXIX). A little later it adds: “Instruct your son, and he will refresh you and give delights to your soul” (ibid.).

Indeed, a still-untamed horse is struck on the hoof with a slipper, so that later it may endure the iron spur being fastened to its underside. A rough bull likewise has a ring of pliant vine fastened to it, so that, becoming accustomed to this, it may surely learn not to dare resist the yoke later. Thus every younger brother should be rebuked even when he is not sinning, so that afterward he may bear the discipline of true correction with equanimity.

In contrast, concerning one who has not been corrected it is written: “He who delicately nourishes his servant from childhood will afterward find him rebellious” (Prov. XIX). Concerning this servant the wise man says: “Food, a rod, and a burden for the ass; bread, discipline, and work for the servant” (Ecclus. XXXIII).

### Chapter III. That corrections are like swords to the impatient

Nor do I heap up so many testimonies of Scripture for you, dearest son, as though I judged them necessary for the conduct of your holy character; rather, I do so in order that through your example I may counsel those of your own age. For you have not brought us a vessel filled with the waters of Jericho, which I might sprinkle, like Elisha (IV Kings II), with the salt of heavenly wisdom and thereby cleanse of their bitterness.

Nor have you offered yourself to us as a pot filled with colocynths, whose exceedingly bitter taste the ground flour of the divine word might turn into sweetness and thus make edible for the sons of the prophets. You have not appeared as a reed shaken by the wind in the desert (Matt. XI), but rather as that which produced honey, on which John, the Lord’s forerunner, lived.

You have brought, brother, a hive full of dripping honeycombs; you have offered yourself to us as a field needing not to be hoed with mattocks but already ready to be cut down by full sickles—not bristling with buckthorn and thorns, but yellow with the beauty of abundant harvests.

[Col. 0707B] In contrast, concerning the negligent and foolish man the wise man says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a fool, and behold, nettles had filled everything” (Prov. XXIV).

To the impatient, corrections are indeed like swords; but if they wish these swords to be changed into sickles, they must exchange the bristling thickets of their vices, by which they are made rough, for fields of grain. Hence, after the prophet had said concerning our Savior, “He will judge the nations and rebuke many peoples,” he immediately adds: “And they will beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles” (Isa. II).

The order is plainly appropriate: first the sinner is rebuked; then swords are beaten into ploughshares and spears into sickles. For when an impatient person has been made gentler through discipline and, like a level field, is cut open by the knife of reproof, he is then sprinkled with the sweet seed of holy preaching and at last clothed with the fruitful harvest of good works. For him, swords have become ploughshares and spears are turned into sickles.

The one who previously avoided being pierced as though by a sword when reproved now willingly endures the ploughshare of sacred teaching, so that he may bear fruit, and awaits the sickle of the heavenly harvest, so that he may fill the storehouse of the celestial granary.

### Chapter IV. That correction is necessary for regular discipline in religious communities

Every spiritual community plainly suffers from the mystical poverty of the Israelite people if it does not employ frequent correction motivated by fraternal zeal. This was the condition of that people when Saul’s royal rule began: it had no ironsmith. Scripture says: “For no ironsmith was found throughout all the land of Israel” (II Kings XIII).

Now, just as iron powerfully subdues the other metals, so the hammer of correction represses the vices of wrongdoers and, as though by forging, breaks the hardness of a rigid mind. Hence it is said through Isaiah concerning the very chief of spiritual smiths: “Behold, I have created the smith who blows upon the fire of coals and brings forth a vessel for his work” (Isa. LIV).

Ecclesiastes also speaks of iron: “If the iron has been blunted, and it is not as before but has become dull, it will be sharpened with much labor; after diligence comes wisdom” (Eccles. X).

But the Philistines remove the ironsmiths from the land of Israel when evil spirits, under the pretext of false piety, take away the zeal for correction from the lips of the brothers. Hence it is added there: “For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make a sword or a spear” (I Kings XIII). A little later: “Thus the edges of ploughshares, mattocks, tridents, and axes were blunted, even as far as the goad used for correction” (ibid.).

While the Philistines fear swords, they remove the smiths, so that, when the manufacture of weapons is restrained, there is no one left to manufacture the other implements needed for labor. For, as the Apostle testifies: “The sword of the Spirit is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

Because perverse spirits fear this sword, they remove the smiths from the land of Israel, restraining those who ought to rebuke the errors of wrongdoers from maintaining the discipline of correction. Through this dissolution of negligence it happens that in the various communities of God’s servants not only does the word of sacred preaching cease to be heard, but the practice of honorable crafts also ceases.

For, since the strict discipline of instruction does not restrain them, devoted to their own wills they do not know how to write, and they learn none of the practices of honorable crafts or manual labor, although the Apostle says: “He who does not work, let him not eat” (II Thess. III).

Since these things are necessary to them, they approach secular men, or even reprobates, because they cannot find them among themselves. Hence it is said there: “So all Israel went down to the Philistines, to sharpen each one his ploughshare, his mattock, his axe, and his hoe” (I Kings XIII).

Israel therefore goes up to the Philistines but goes down in order to sharpen the implements required for its needs, when men of the holy order descend to the lowliness of secular people in order to obtain from them some useful benefit.

You see, then, that if the authority of correction is removed from a sacred community, the vigor of discipline is utterly weakened and the whole religious life is destroyed; for, while each person follows the judgment of his own will, he returns to secular things and violates the institution of spiritual observance.

Therefore, whoever burns with zeal for regular life gladly embraces corrections and takes pleasure in being reproved even when he is innocent—not because his conscience accuses him of having sinned, but because he hopes that this will benefit the other hearers, so that, while he himself, innocent and clean, is reproved, others who have fallen or are about to fall may perhaps be corrected.

### Chapter V. Why blessed Paul rebuked blessed Peter

[Col. 0708D]

This brings back to memory what Paul writes to the Galatians: he rebuked blessed Peter, his fellow apostle, yet inwardly agreed in his desires with the one whom he outwardly reproved as though in disagreement:

“When Peter had come to Antioch,” he says, “I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they had come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Gal. II).

Immediately it is added: “And the other Jews consented to his dissimulation, so that even Barnabas was led by them into that dissimulation” (ibid.).

O how harsh these words appear on the surface, and, if they are considered only syllable by syllable, how utterly alien they seem from the dignity of the apostolic summit! Peter is blameworthy, to whom all the kingdoms of the earth were entrusted for rebuke and correction (Matt. XVI). He is opposed to his face, at whose command the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened to Christ’s faithful. He is declared the author of dissimulation, although he is first among the preachers of truth.

And, so that the injury may be made still more emphatic, attend carefully to what follows: “But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. II.)

What is this, blessed Paul? Why do you tear apart your superior with reproofs and exasperate him with reproaches? How are you not afraid to confound before the faces of men the one who by special right has been granted authority over the universal Church of the whole world?

Or perhaps you have forgotten what your common Teacher instructed both of you? “If your brother sins against you,” he says, “correct him between yourself and him alone; but if he does not hear you, take with you two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII).

Yet you do not summon him to a private meeting, nor address him secretly before witnesses; you rebuke him publicly before everyone and, what is more serious, you write that you did this for the knowledge of future generations.

Have you also forgotten what you yourself commanded Timothy? “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father” (I Tim. V).

But in the fact that Paul openly rebuked blessed Peter before everyone, he appeared outwardly to contradict him, yet fulfilled the desires of his heart. Peter did not dare to receive the Gentiles who were coming to the faith into fellowship at table in the presence of those who had believed from the circumcision, lest they suffer scandal and soon withdraw from the faith, still tender, on that account.

And therefore, although he had been accustomed to eat with the Gentiles, when certain men came from James he withdrew from their company, fearing for those who had believed from the circumcision, lest, if they saw him eating with Gentiles, they should suffer the danger of unbelief.

For anyone who reads the Acts of the Apostles cannot doubt that Peter thought in every respect as Paul did: namely, that the Gentiles ought not to observe Jewish rites. Indeed, Peter is unquestionably found among the apostles as the first author of this opinion, although Paul now accuses him as though he were a transgressor.

For he says: “Now therefore why do you tempt God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are” (Acts XV).

Peter therefore wanted to be rebuked most emphatically before everyone; he rejoiced to be confounded by the rebuke of the one reproving him, so that, once corrected, he might abandon what he was doing unwillingly, and might find a companion in what he alone had feared to attempt.

Thus, when Paul opposed Peter, he undoubtedly agreed with him inwardly, although he reproved him outwardly. Otherwise, how could Paul condemn in another what he himself had done under a similar necessity?

For the sake of the Jews, who maintained that observance of the Law and the ancient rites had to be retained, he circumcised Timothy, the son of a Gentile; and he himself, fulfilling a vow, shaved his head and offered a sacrifice according to the ceremonies of the ancient Law (Acts XVI, XXI). [Col. 0710B]

### Chapter VI. Whether blessed Paul sinned when he rebuked blessed Peter

In appearing to correct Peter, Paul therefore assisted him rather than opposed him; and he did not, as Porphyry thinks, fight arrogantly against him, but served him humbly. This correction by Paul was a ministry of obedience, not a disciplinary rebuke; not rashness in reproach, but unanimous harmony of will.

You, therefore, dearest son, whenever you are corrected for any reason—even if your conscience in no way reproaches you for having sinned—gladly embrace what has been laid against you, and humbly confess yourself guilty before your brothers.

This will be an example for them to imitate, and it will bring you an increase of virtues. Remember what is said through Solomon: “It is better to be corrected by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools” (Eccles. VII).

Let your will, then, be such that even the one who perhaps rebukes you more harshly may agree with the intention of your heart; and, when he attacks you harshly, let him comply rather than resist.

Let your conduct shine before those present, and let your reputation breathe the fragrance of blessing among those absent. Be, as we said above, a field and an abundant mass of grain, breathing the fragrance of spices, so that almighty God may also take delight in you and say: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which God has blessed” (Gen. XXV).

Since you are called Ariprandus, and *aretē* (ἀρετή) means “virtue,” may you, like a most fertile field, bear a hundredfold heap of fruits and merit offering God a banquet of virtues.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0709]

## 741–742. Forty-Seventh Opusculum: On Chastity and the Means of Guarding It

### Argument

Among the other virtues he especially commends chastity to his nephew Damian. To make it easier for him to preserve it, he urges him to receive the Lord’s body daily. Then he instructs him against the devil’s snares. Finally, he asks Damian to commend him to the prior, reminding the prior to maintain hospitality.

[Col. 0709D] To Damian, his dearest son: Peter, a sinful monk, sends the affection of a father’s love.

[Col. 0710D] Because the bearer of the letter is anxiously preparing to depart, I cannot compose what must be sent with a polished arrangement of style; and I want you rather to consider the meaning of the truth than to hunt after the ornamented allurements of words.

Meanwhile, since I am unable to write back at length, let this simple message suffice for you, which the Apostle commands Timothy, as though his equal in age: “Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching” (I Tim. IV). He had already prefaced this with: “Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity” (ibid.).

## On Chastity and the Means of Guarding It

### Chapter I. That the virtue of chastity is more difficult for the young

To say nothing for the moment of the other virtues that have now been enumerated in the letter, strive not merely to preserve chastity in the bodily members, which I placed last, but to ensure that this same virtue reigns and flourishes most powerfully in the depths of your heart.

No virtue, indeed, endures more severe struggles in the flower of adolescence than chastity, which is attacked by the innate heat of enticing pleasure, rising like a fire in a furnace.

But since I cannot discuss this subject more fully, because excessive haste leaves no time, I shall not hesitate briefly and quickly to record here what the empress Agnes—formerly crowned with a golden diadem, but now placed far more happily and incomparably more exaltedly in the bridal chamber of the eternal King—reported to me yesterday as the twilight of evening was already passing away. I do this so that in your mind not so much the sprawling length of speech as the dignity of a remarkable example may prevail.

While the aforesaid bride of Christ and daughter of blessed Peter was delightfully nourished by the ordering of every virtue, she lingered especially upon the purity of chastity and modesty. Thus, while we were exchanging words about the salvation of souls and were especially, as it were, turning over in our hands certain fresh blossoms of chastity, she brought forward the following account:

“After the emperor Otto,” she said, “had victoriously taken the kingdom of Italy from Berengar [Note: In the year of Christ 95], he immediately transferred two of Berengar’s daughters, whom he had captured, into exile in the German lands.

“These girls, who by the beauty of their lovely faces and the exceptional attractiveness of their bodies displayed the dignity of their royal lineage, soon had many nobles of the kingdom earnestly pressing Empress Adelaide to allow them to unite themselves to the honor of so elegant a beauty through marriage.

“But when the girls utterly scorned all their suitors with equal disdain and rejected mortal marriage with the proud disdain of holy arrogance, one of them placed two young chickens beneath her breasts and concealed them between her clothing and her flesh until they had completely putrefied.

“Whenever she saw people coming to converse with her, she would secretly loosen her clothing and delighted to exhale the stench upon the nostrils of those speaking with her. When those conversing with her suffered this daily injury to their noses, the deceived concern of the suitors finally ceased; and the virgin of Christ, through the feigned putrefaction of another creature’s flesh, preserved the inviolability of her own body.

“Thus it happened that afterward both sisters chose the religious life and irreproachably maintained the monastic discipline until the end of their lives.”

### Chapter II. That frequent reception of the Eucharist is a defense of chastity

Therefore, O son, be ashamed either to be weakened by the vice of lust or to succumb in thought, when you see the weaker and more fragile sex triumphing with such glory. And, so that you may—as I may put it—drive the roaring beast from the field under your authority, strive, brother, to arm yourself already every day by receiving the Lord’s body and blood.

Let the hidden enemy see your lips reddened with Christ’s blood, and let him shudder in terror at them and immediately flee in fear into the hiding places of his darkness. For what you receive under the visible appearance of bread and wine, he, whether he wishes it or not, recognizes as the truth of the Lord’s body and blood.

Moreover, the same venerable queen then told me that recently in the church at Worms, when the Eucharist had through negligence been kept for a longer period in a little box, only flesh was subsequently found there. Thus, when many people looked at it with great curiosity, they undoubtedly judged that it was nothing other than real and solid flesh.

Rainaldus, also the venerable bishop of the Church of Como, was present and truthfully related what had happened to him shortly before:

“There is,” he said, “in the church which, by God’s help, I serve—and who, unless I am mistaken, is still alive today—a priest with so little knowledge of letters that he can scarcely even read a written passage syllable by syllable in public. Yet, constrained by extreme poverty, he is compelled somehow to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass.

“Once, when he had carried the Eucharist of the sacred offering to a sick person, a little of the Lord’s blood remained in the chalice, since he was, as usual, sluggish and negligent. When he discovered this upon returning to the church, he did not wish to consume it, being hindered by disgust; instead he immediately washed the chalice and threw it into a marble basin containing consecrated water.

“And, O great sign of divine power! The part of the basin touched by what had been poured from the chalice suddenly turned blood-red. There, plainly, two larger drops of blood appeared; and neither they nor other smaller ones visible nearby could be washed away or rubbed off by any means that might in any way erase the redness impressed by the blood.

“Since that purple blood clung so tenaciously to a stone vessel, how much power do we think that heavenly virtue claims for itself in a Christian breast?”

Therefore, dearest son, do not delay to fortify yourself more frequently with these heavenly sacraments, by which you may repel the devices of diabolical cunning and deceitful plotting. Gird yourself, rise up, stand constantly and firmly in the battle line, and do not be unaware that an indefatigable adversary is tirelessly fighting against you.

### Chapter III. The devil transforms himself into an angel of light in order to deceive a monk

While I am saying these things, another matter now returns to my memory: the archdeacon Hildebrand of the Roman Church related the following in the presence of the bishop and the others mentioned above:

“I saw two holy monks and enjoyed no small degree of intimacy with them. They lived separately in cells at the monastery built in a place called Aachen. One of them, who appeared to possess the greater simplicity, was called Marinus; the other was called Romanus by his proper name.

“Marinus scarcely passed a day on which he did not either see the devil in some form or hear him in a dream—so much so that the ancient enemy often sang responsorially with him and celebrated the offices of divine praise together with him.

“On one occasion the author of darkness transformed himself into an angel of light and, as though dictating a law to him, commanded him: ‘Beware: since you have been worthy both to see and to address an angel of God, it is unworthy that you speak with human beings thereafter.’

“Immediately, as though he had received a command from God, Marinus withdrew entirely from conversation with the brothers and bound himself under the strict censorship of silence.

“When his brother Romanus first, and afterward the abbot of the monastery, earnestly insisted that he speak to them, and he offered no response [the source is defective: supply ‘a response’ or something similar] with his closed lips, the abbot violently broke into his cell, chastised the indiscreet brother with blows appropriate to the offense, and compelled him to resume the duty of speech.

“Then he added this admonition: ‘For this reason the ancient adversary, always the enemy of good works, attempted to impose silence upon you: so that you would lose the fruit of fraternal edification and those who ought to be raised up by you would have no help from your consolation.’

“Thus the brother, because he had sinned not through malice but through simplicity, quickly returned to his right mind; and, rejecting the devil’s suggestion, he humbly consented to the admonitions of his devout father.”

But while I urge you, my son, to thwart the snares of the ancient enemy, I shall not omit what the aforesaid queen said she had heard from the mouth of blessed Leo IX, pontiff of the Roman Church.

The aforesaid pope said:

“My aunt, having become a nun, was established in a certain monastery of men. There, living in her own cell with a certain dwarf—that is, a woman of short stature—she patiently and humbly performed the offices of daily praise.”

### Chapter IV. That the devil is recognized by the sign of the cross

One night, when she had risen earlier than usual before the office of the nocturnal assembly [source text is defective: “the passage,” “the hour,” or something similar], she repeatedly called for her companion in the customary manner. But when the latter, weighed down by deep sleep, did not answer at all, the woman finally became angry and, without considering what she was saying, exclaimed: “Devil, get up!”

At this word the devil immediately approached, reproducing the likeness of the woman who was sleeping. Returning the verses responsorially, he began to sing psalms together with her. When, continuing their melody, they reached the passage of the Psalter that says:

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from his face; as smoke vanishes, so let them vanish” (Ps. LXVII),

and what follows, the evil spirit immediately stopped and did not dare to utter these verses.

When the holy woman wondered about this inwardly, she became afraid; and, rightly suspecting what had happened, she made the sign of the holy cross upon herself. At once the evil enemy vanished, revealing by his fraudulent concealment who he was—the one who had joined the holy woman as her companion in singing psalms.

This wicked spirit also brought the venerable matron, during the night hours, the corpse of a certain man who had been hanged for his crimes; and, in order to frighten her, he procured for her this sort of gift, so to speak. She immediately informed the abbot of the place and the assembly of the brothers what the most wicked enemy had done to her; and she obtained through urgent prayers that all the brothers should pour out prayers together for the wretched man.

Afterward it was divinely revealed to someone that, through the prayers of the brothers, the man had obtained mercy. Thus the ancient enemy was deceived: while he contrived to mock the living man, he was compelled to suffer loss on account of the dead.

### Chapter V. An example of Christian charity
Therefore examples of this and similar demonic temptation are set before you, so that you too may vigilantly awaken against the snares of the cunning deceiver, and, while it delights you to hear of the victories of others who wrestle with the enemy, may not yourself grow lax through the sluggishness of an enfeebled body.

But let this suffice. Commend me to the brothers, and humbly suggest on my behalf to the lord prior that he not grow lukewarm in his customary fervor of piety and mercy, but, insofar as the household resources permit, not cease attending to the reception of guests and the assistance of the needy.

I also offer him an example appropriate to this matter, which I trust will be of no little benefit to the purpose I am striving to commend to him. For the same Queen Agnes mentioned above also says that a certain man in the regions of Alemannia used to traverse the hidden valleys of the forests, the rugged mountain passes, and the dark woods in pursuit of hunting [Col. 0714D]. While he was anxiously hurrying here and there, carefully searching out the lairs of wild animals, he found two women—a mother and her daughter—wandering miserably through the winter heaps of frost and the deep, rough snow.

Immediately moved by compassion, he said to his companion, who alone was following him: “Let us lift these women onto our horses, each of us taking one, and carry them to human habitations. Otherwise they may perhaps be exposed to the bites of wandering wolves, or they will certainly die from the violence of the excessive cold.”

His companion utterly refused and was indignant that he should be asked to endure such an affront. The lord replied: “If you disdain it, I alone will carry both, and I will gladly endure this affront you describe.” When he had placed one behind himself and the other before him, sitting between them [746], his companion at last, moved and ashamed, yielded one to his lord and took the other himself to carry.

Thus they transported them through extremely difficult places and along long, winding paths, not without great danger, until they happened upon a mill. There they set the women down. The lord also added that he should give one of them a garment with which she might somewhat mitigate the force of the cold.

Some time afterward this man became a monk. Later, when his illness grew worse and he was brought to the point of death, he began to cry out to the brothers standing around him with great alarm, saying: “Do you see the innumerable crowd of demons that surrounds me on every side, and that does not cease to look upon me with terrifying eyes [Col. 0715B] and attack me?”

Although the brothers devoted themselves to continual prayers and psalmody, he nevertheless remained terrified and trembled inwardly. At last the man who, as has been said, had accompanied him on the hunt came nearer and cried out: “Do you not see that the woman whom I transported with you to the watermill, holding in her hands the garment I then gave her, is waving it and violently driving all the demons from this house?”

A short while later, behold, thanks be to God, they were expelled, and, driven away by this woman, they completely vanished from my sight. Thus that man died in the security of a good hope, and, when he was dying, he found offered to him the fruits of mercy that he had displayed while alive. For it often happens that, amid the many darknesses of bodily actions [Col. 0715C], one light of a good work breaks forth and carries a person to a good end and safe harbor.

## CHAPTER VI. How, through one good work, God’s mercy saves sinners

I therefore do not think it irrelevant to append what Stephen, chaplain of the same queen, an upright and prudent man, related. He said that Stedelandus, emperor of Gaul, reported the following, which later came to the knowledge of one man through another informant:

“There were three prostitutes, devoted to the obscene filth of brothels and, so to speak, shamefully prostituted to every passerby [Col. 0716A]. But since that region was inhabited indiscriminately by Saracens and Christians, they shamefully offered themselves to Christians, while utterly rejecting the company of Saracens.

“When the latter complained that they were despised in this shameful business and that an injury was being inflicted upon their people, they finally dragged the women before the governor’s tribunal and pressed them vehemently to consent to sexual relations with their own people as they did with Christians.

“But when they could not obtain this crime from the women, whether by threats or by flatteries, the governor pronounced sentence and condemned them to death. What more is there to say? At once the executioners approached and struck their naked necks with drawn daggers; but although they repeatedly struck, they could not even cut the outermost skin [Col. 0716B].

“Meanwhile, since the women willingly desired to die while the executioners were unable to kill them, they were committed to prison custody. During the night the Savior appeared to one of them, who seemed to be the foremost among the others, and said to her: ‘Do not be afraid. Today I shall bring your contest to an end, and I shall receive you, crowned with martyrdom, into the loveliness of my glory.’

“On the following day they were led to the judge’s tribunal. After an inquiry, the same sentence nevertheless remained in force. Their spirit was what it had been before, and as previously they detested in every way the embraces of the Hagarenes.

“Therefore the executioners, having proved that they could accomplish nothing against their necks, cut their throats with a sword [defaecant; perhaps *desecant*] [748], and thus made martyrs of prostitutes.

“But since this writing has now been carried farther than I had decided when I began [Col. 0716C], the pen must be restrained and a limit set to this abbreviated letter.”

At last I implore the clemency of divine mercy, that, among the other distinctions of the virtues and of the whole of holy religion, he may pour into you an inviolable strength for preserving chastity, and keep the vessel of your body in sanctification and honor; so that he who says in the Song of Songs, “I am the flower of the field, I am the lily of the valleys” (Song II), just as he deigned to become for you the Son of the Virgin, may also cause you to blossom with the flowers of chastity.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0715]

# 749–750. THE FORTY-EIGHTH LITTLE WORK: ON SPIRITUAL DELIGHTS

## Argument

He strives to lead an upright monk, excessively devoted to eating and to the selection of foods, toward contempt for earthly banquets and toward meditation upon and love of heavenly delights, by placing before his eyes the sweetness of spiritual feasts.

[Col. 0715D] Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord to his upright brother.

[ON SPIRITUAL DELIGHTS]

## CHAPTER I. On the Jubilee and its mysteries

A man who is compelled to go into battle nevertheless fights vigorously under compulsion, and, when he wins a triumph through courage, corrects the disgrace of his shameful trembling. But if he begins unwillingly and, as soon as adversaries appear, turns his back with a fearful heart, then, even if while fleeing he has disregarded the enemy’s weapons, he will still not escape the mark of disgraceful degeneracy.

You too, brother, insofar as can be understood, did not willingly swear yourself to the arms of spiritual warfare [Col. 0717A]. After giving your name and professing the vows of your probation, you have done nothing distinguished, nothing brave, nothing worthy of praise. Instead, after departing from Egypt, you began to complain about the scarcity of food and drink and to sigh for all the delights of Egypt (Exod. XVI), lamenting with that carnal Israelite: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in Egypt, when we sat beside pots of meat and ate bread to satiety!” (Dan. III.)

Therefore the king of Babylon sent you into a burning furnace, but he could not see the Son of God walking with you amid the glowing masses of flame. The persecutor brought in a pile of straw, naphtha, pitch, and tow; but divine power did not extinguish the force of this fire against you (ibid.). Of that flame it is said: “It burst forth and rose forty-nine cubits above the furnace” [Col. 0717B]. For it could not reach the number fifty—that is, the mystery of the mystical Jubilee.

The year of Jubilee is a year of rest. Therefore that carnal fire of concupiscence does not belong to rest; rather, it generates scandals, harassing and disturbing the reprobate mind as it burns with seductive enticements.

It does not belong to the fire of the fiftieth day, of which it is said: “The whole of Mount Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire, and its smoke ascended as though from a furnace” (Exod. XIX). Nor does it correspond to the fire which, likewise on the fiftieth day, descended upon the apostles in a variety of tongues after the glory of the Lord’s resurrection (Acts II). Each of these fires descended, since both certainly came from heaven. But that other fire is said not to have descended but to have ascended, so that it appears to proceed from the wantonness of carnal concupiscence.

## CHAPTER II. What the manna was and what it signifies

Do not, brother—do not serve the lust of gluttony or of the flesh, since you have pledged yourself as a soldier to the author of sobriety. Be ashamed to be the servant of carnal pleasures; do not subject to barbarian chains your neck, already submitted beneath the noble yoke of Christ.

Let not King Eglon of Moab possess you under his dominion (Judg. III), but let Ehud, together with you, pierce him through with an unexpected dagger. And when King Agag of Amalek oppresses earthly Israel under his rule (I Sam. XV), do not let him oppress you, but let Samuel, in your presence, cut him limb by limb into pieces [Col. 0717D].

Do not delight in that destroyer of Jerusalem (II Kings XXV), who, because he suggests the pleasures of seduction, is said to hold dominion over the cooks of the flesh.

If you delight in eating something sweet, let that divine and mystical manna taste upon the palate of your heart, of which it is said: “Its taste was like semolina with honey” (Exod. XVI). This semolina is made from a grain of wheat which, falling into the earth and dying, bore much fruit (John XII). But this semolina is sprinkled with honey because the humanity of the Redeemer is full of the sweetness of divinity. For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (II Cor. V).

Or certainly, the honey in the semolina is spiritual sweetness in the letter [Col. 0718A]. Hence the Hebrew people are described as having prepared for themselves little cakes from the same manna: “The people,” it says, “ground it in a mill or pounded it in a mortar, cooked it in a pot, and made from it little cakes of taste, like bread dressed with oil” (Num. XI).

A little cake cannot be tasted unless it is first opened; otherwise what is stored within its enclosure cannot be savored. The oracles of the prophets are like certain little cakes, which, beneath a kind of bodily casing of words, conceal the mystery of spiritual understanding.

He could not open this little cake to whom it was said through Isaiah: “Read this book.” And he replied: “I cannot, for it is sealed” (Isa. XXIX). The eunuch asked that this little cake be opened for him when Philip said to him: “Do you think you understand what you are reading?” He replied [Col. 0718B]: “And how can I, unless someone shows me?” (Acts VIII.)

It is as though he were saying: “I am indeed holding this little cake in my hands, but I cannot eat from it unless a learned hand opens it for me and explains to me the marrow of the Spirit that lies hidden in the straw of the letter.” Those of whom Jeremiah spoke could not open it by themselves: “The little children asked for bread, but there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV).

Therefore, beloved, grind this manna—the food of life-giving nourishment—finely in the mortar of your meditation. Boil it continually in the pot of fervent love, so that from it you may be able to fatten the inward parts of your soul as though with heavenly richness. This food of inner refreshment sweetens the throat of your heart; this summons your spirit to that heavenly banquet. Finally, let this food taste delightfully upon the palate of your mind; let it kindle you to hunger for the nourishment of heavenly refreshment.

## CHAPTER III. That the hope and rest of the saints are in God alone

Therefore, restrain your appetite for various foods; let one alone be hungered for, let one alone be sought with every desire: “One thing,” he says, “I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI).

This is that unity which the flame rising forty-nine cubits lacked (Dan. II), because carnal appetite, being dragged and wandering through many things, does not possess that one thing—the cause and end of rejoicing—in which it may delightfully rest.

The Jubilee is completed by this unity, because in the love of the Creator alone the whole hope and purpose of the saints is placed, and in him their entire rest is established [Col. 0718D]. In everything they do, they strive toward him, and in him, as in a Jubilee, they rest from all the vanities of the world.

Indeed, just as the seventh day, celebrated throughout every week, or the seventh year of rest, likewise celebrated throughout every seven-year period, signifies the rest of this present time, in which the saints love God alone and rest in him from all the disturbances of the world, so the Jubilee—that is, the fiftieth year—signifies that final rest in which all the elect forever enjoy secure and unending repose.

In this life, the soul of each holy man rests upon God alone through the force of firm hope and pure love, for the flesh is troubled by many calamities of adversity [Col. 0719A].

Every week had a Sabbath of days, and every period of seven years had a Sabbath of years; but the Jubilee was the Sabbath of Sabbaths. Seven times seven produces the sum forty-nine; when one is added to it, the number fifty, which is the Jubilee, is completed.

In this number, just as we speak of seven times seven, so in our understanding we double the rest of souls and bodies. In the Jubilee of our rest—that is, in the life of eternal happiness—each of the elect enjoys unchanging rest not only in soul but also in body, so that neither substance is ever troubled by any disturbance or affliction.

In the Jubilee, trumpets are sounded (Lev. XXV), and each person returns to his possessions. For, as the Apostle says, “the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise” (I Thess. IV).

What is it to descend with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God except, in a certain manner, to resound amid the harmonious blasts of trumpets? And what is it for the dead who are in Christ to rise except for each one to return to his possessions?

Then Abraham, then Moses, then Pilate, then Herod, then every just person or sinner returns to the rights of his possessions, when he is reclothed with the flesh that he had laid aside for a time, so that each person may receive, together with his own body, what he deserves.

The reprobate now possess, in a certain manner, rest of both substances, since they complete the pleasure of their souls and bodies. Thus the flame of concupiscence, which proceeds as though from a Chaldean furnace, from their heated minds, seems to rise to seven times seven (Dan. III), that is, to forty-nine. But because in the intention of their minds they do not strive toward the unity that is God, they will not reach the fullness of the blessed Jubilee.

## CHAPTER IV. How God rests in us

But since we seek the Jubilee—that is, rest—in God, we too must offer a Jubilee to God within ourselves. For to the one whose heart does not permit God to rest in this life, he will not afterward grant the rest of heavenly life.

Does he not, in a certain way, seek the rest of the Jubilee in us when it is said through Isaiah: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI.)

Did not that dove, which then foreshadowed the same Spirit, also seek rest? Of it we read: “Because it did not find a place where its foot might rest, it returned to Noah in the ark” (Gen. VIII).

The dove did not find rest in the water of the endangered world, because the Holy Spirit in those who perish with the world does not rest at all. But the dove returns to the ark, in which there were eight souls, because the Holy Spirit deigns to dwell in those in whom, through the washing of baptism, there is firm hope of blessed resurrection.

Hence it is written: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I) [Col. 0720A].

Does the Lord not promise that he will have rest among us when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV)?

He complains that he has not found this rest with anyone, saying: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head” (Luke IX).

Therefore whoever has conceived the poisons of any wickedness in his heart must hasten to drive the foxes out of the den of his breast, so that the Son of God may rightly recline his head there.

O whoever you are, turn your heart—the cave of foxes—into the mortar of chaste meditation; in it, do not cease to grind finely the manna of heavenly speech, so that from it there may arise for you bread dressed with oil [Col. 0720B]. For bread dressed with oil is the understanding of sacred Scripture, seasoned with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

May the Spirit pour these things into you, dearest brother; may he cast off from you, with Samson, the bond of sluggishness and idleness, and kindle you fervently to fight bravely against the enemy (Judg. XVI).

In desperate circumstances it is glorious to act bravely; it is a mark of outstanding renown to win an unexpected victory for one who had fallen into ruin.

Marcellus, consul of the Romans, once fell heedlessly into the hands of the Gauls. With armed enemies surrounding him on every side and no means of escape at all available, he rushed upon their king, Virdomarus [Vitromarus], like a most blazing thunderbolt. After killing him, he also slaughtered, together with his colleague Marcus Scipio [Col. 0720C], very large forces of the enemy.

What wonder, then, if what is known to have been accomplished against a human being through human courage is now accomplished against the devil through the power of the Holy Spirit?

Therefore, dearest brother, let the ignoble idleness of this long-standing sluggishness be shaken off from you. Let a manly hand seize the weapons, and let it set the shield of inward vigilance against the twisted spears of those who attack [754].

Let marauders not find you, like Ish-bosheth, sleeping in bed while they strike you in the groin (II Sam. IV); rather, let the ranks of the Philistines find you, like David, resisting them invincibly (II Sam. II).

Therefore, if by God’s help you wish to deserve this victory, do not continue murmuring with that carnal Israelite: “Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna” (Num. XI) [Col. 0720D]. Instead, joyful and vigorous, sing with the Prophet: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII.)

Let the appetite for carnal delight not cease to invigorate the stomach of our mind. Those carnal feasts nourish nothing but the worm; these spiritual feasts do not permit a person to die, but preserve him in the loveliness of eternal freshness.

The former compel those who crave them to thirst for a drop of water in the fire with the rich man (Luke XVI); the latter disclose to us, with Daniel, the secrets of the heavenly mystery (Dan. X).

Of the former it is said: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI). Of the latter it is said: “Your lips drip honey, bride; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV). And again: “A garden spring, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon” (ibid.).

I do not write about the vanity of costly clothing, a disease with which you are said to suffer, because, as you yourself understand, I cannot extend the pen farther, since the paper is running out. I therefore direct your prudence to the letter I wrote on this subject to your venerable abbot Mainardus, asking that you not hurry through it carelessly but attend vigilantly to what matters.

May almighty God drain from you the strength of carnal sense and confirm your mind in the solidity of spiritual desire.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0721]

# 755–756. THE FORTY-NINTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE COMPLETE FORMATION OF A MONK

## Argument

The holy teacher sends greetings to his young kinsman, the monk Classensis, and arms him against the snares of the devil with salutary admonitions. First of all, he urges that bodily purity, moderation in food, devotion to prayer, humility of spirit, and the virtue of obedience should shine in him. Then he asks him to avoid the company of women and to use no verbal embellishments in conversation. Again he urges him to restrain love of relatives, not to seek any gift, not to detract from the reputation of others, and not to desire that people take account of him through feigning illness. Finally, he advises him not to admit criticisms to his ears, to acknowledge his falls, and to imitate the few among the many—those of proven virtue.

[Col. 0721B] Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord to the boy Marinus.

[ON THE COMPLETE FORMATION OF A MONK]

## CHAPTER I. What care must be taken to preserve chastity

An inexperienced recruit is easily struck down in the first encounter of battle unless, after the trainer’s instruction has first been supplied, he is carefully trained.

But you, who have recently sworn yourself to the vows of divine warfare, who enrolled your name among the youthful ranks in the profession of a holy purpose, are recognized as needing salutary admonitions all the more eagerly because you have undertaken to bear, not an earthly but rather a divine military service.

Of this the Apostle says: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful before God” (II Cor. X).

Moreover, because you are joined to me by the bond of blood—for you are my kinsman—I think I must take care of your salvation with greater concern, since your tender age, still in need of another’s help, seems both to require this and to demand it from me by the duty of kinship.

For since the Apostle judges that the man promoted to the rank of bishop must have children subject to him with all chastity (I Tim. III), and counts the chastity and obedience of children among the virtues of a priest, you, although you are not my son, are nevertheless rightly not considered a stranger to my care, since you appear close to me by genuine kinship. Especially since I myself gave you the monastic habit, I cannot, without cause, declare myself released from responding to your consultations.

First of all, dearest son, strive with vigilant skill to preserve chastity [Col. 0721D], and exclude every crime of deadly pollution, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, you may know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honor (II Thess. IV).

This is holiness, without which no one will see God. Let the tunic of your body be kept clean, and at the wedding of so great a king let it not be found stained by any filth of wanton luxury.

## CHAPTER II. That sobriety is the safeguard of chastity

[Col. 0722B]

Therefore let chastity always be in your body and always in your mind, so that the lilies of undisciplined flesh may shine like cultivated flowers in plowed soil, while the root also remains unshaken in the grace of its own freshness.

When the enticement of the flesh tickles you and the incentives of lust arise, spring forward at once to the apostolic weapons (II Cor. XII); seize also the evangelical sword as a fervent warrior, and, with Christ as your leader, you will easily cut down the roaring battle-lines and barbarity of the enemy.

Let sobriety be your daily and inseparable companion, never at any time torn from your company when gluttony pricks you. For when the pores of the inward parts are filled with food, there is no doubt that the flame of lust claims its own strength there.

This plague is driven away by dryness; when the moisture of the savage body fails, lust also withers as it dries up. Just as fire is opposed to water, so luxury is hostile to cold; therefore, when the nourishment of food deprives the natural heat of the flesh of its fuel, the heat of lust must also be extinguished.

I do not want you to hanker after more luxurious foods; I do not want you to indulge abundantly in wine, or even presume at times to argue about distinctions of color or taste.

“This thin wine of the Lagaean [grape] is harsh; that one weakens through the strength of the Venacian; this one is red like Porrothasia; that one shines golden with the beauty of Mareotis. This is forbidden to be read; that is nauseating dregs; baptism has crept in; I expected wine, but very little wine seems to have been mixed with this water; this wine indeed owes much to the Aminean vine, but it almost strives to surpass the Raetian.”

Do not therefore make yourself an expert on the taste of Arigis or Rhodia, or on what intensity of sweetness they possess when compared with the purple Pretians and Psythians. All these things are the arguments of a philosophizing palate and the material of detestable gluttony.

In taking food, let frugality mitigate harshness, and let restrained tasting commend even common fare. Nor is it enough to restrain gluttony with more sumptuous foods unless a person also knows how to keep measure with the coarser ones.

The fault of a gluttonous throat is sometimes committed through any ordinary food, just as the pleasure of intercourse is fulfilled with a deformed prostitute. But one who has grown accustomed to fill his stomach with a small measure of dry bread does not readily know how to judge of rich foods.

One who fears drinking water to satiety does not seek to gorge himself on drinks made with honey. If you wish, therefore, to live among delicacies under the laws of sobriety, take care also not to loosen the reins of gluttony among the simplest foods.

Why should we seek tasty food? However much expense is lavished in preparing it, it does not taste to us before it enters the mouth; and after it has been carried through the stream of swallowing, the stomach into which it has slipped does not distinguish it.

The entire route of our pleasure, to which we devote ourselves with such ambition, is enclosed within the very short measure of a single palm. For one who desires Christ and feeds upon Christ himself—who descended from heaven (John VI)—does not greatly distinguish from what precious foods dung is produced.

Whatever is not perceived after the throat should therefore be the same to you as bread and vegetables. For if the palate does not store up food for itself but for the stomach, why does it choose as though something more refined what the stomach admits indifferently?

## CHAPTER III. That the thought of death drives away shameful impulses

Therefore, so that chastity may not suffer shipwreck after being endangered, let sobriety, the teacher of your body, hold the helm amid the dangers of this tossing life.

Always remain watchful and attentive to driving away thoughts [Col. 0723C], because it is no less necessary to restrain the flesh from seductive titillation than to guard the mind from the phantom of shameful thoughts.

I know a brother in Christ who preserves this strict rule of his mind with constant and vigilant attention. Whenever a suggestion of lust slips in, he immediately says to his thought, as though ready to depart: “Let us go to the cemetery.”

At once, imagining all the cemeteries and graves, he carefully examines the corruption and putrefaction of decaying corpses, as well as the swarming worms and the stinking broth of flesh. When he considers that those bodies, once blooming in the freshness of their living flesh, were subjected to such sufferings, he does not doubt that his own body also will shortly become what he now sees in them.

He provides a remedy for luxury who offers his eyes the sight of corruption; there is no lodging-place for lust in a mind in which a grave is present.

How often did that brother impress upon his genitals a glowing knife and plowshare, as though a cautery, so that, as though a fire had been kindled in the flesh fixed there, smoke seemed visibly to exhale all the way to his nostrils!

When necessity occasionally requires that you cannot refuse a woman’s conversation, always present the appearance of being absent: let your eyes be sidelong and directed elsewhere. Speak to her from a distance, refrain from chatting, and with your gaze fixed upon the ground do not allow yourself to judge whether her face is pale or flushed.

It is said that blessed Romuald, returning from a conversation with the countess Sibylla [Col. 0724A], cunningly said to the disciple accompanying him: “What an elegant and beautiful face that woman has—unless, alas, she were afflicted by the loss of one eye!”

The disciple replied: “God forbid, master! Just as her face is certainly beautiful, so also her eyes, as I cleverly observed, are sound and vigorous.”

The master immediately rebuked him with the sharpest severity: “And who taught you to look into women’s faces?”

Then, recognizing that he had been caught, the disciple blushed, moved to repentance, and pledged with the most determined promise that thereafter he would be more cautious.

For the crafty adversary is a painter, but one who can easily bring things seen back to memory, while he can scarcely form upon the walls of our minds the outlines of unfamiliar images.

If you wish to rise to the summit of perfection, it is now necessary to exercise yourself in every pursuit of virtue—especially while your age is wax, while your tender habits can still be led without resistance in any direction.

Let exercises in virtue therefore grow alongside your bodily development, so that habit may make easy what the weakness of human frailty recoils from. Let the small capacity of your inward parts now be fitted to an equally small quantity of food, so that, as the cavity of the vessel is contracted by its own freshness, a modest measure of grain may afterward fill it easily.

## CHAPTER IV. That silence is the teacher of speech

Let the tongue grow accustomed to restraining itself under the discipline of silence, and let it learn through silence what it may afterward utter gravely in speech. Otherwise, if it now neglects to guard strict silence, it will later be unable to restrain the itch of speaking.

Now let the knees become supple through frequent acts of repentance; indeed, let the other limbs also be softened by various exercises, so that afterward you may not appear hard and rigid, like certain people, and, as they say, “clean-handed,” as though about to offer something to sacred Ceres.

Be attentive to performing the duty of diligence, and always ready to refuse no service that is brought to you; strive yourself to serve everyone. If you are ordered to prepare or bring something, rise at once and hurry quickly, so that the voice of the one giving orders may appear to have been directed especially to you [759].

But I warn you above all, and with the strictest insistence, not to be offended by the private fasts of any of the brothers.

I know the vices of certain people like myself. Some are tormented by such a bitter gall of jealousy and envy when others are fasting that they turn the salvation of those others into their own destruction and, so to speak, fall headlong by the ladder of another’s progress.

They say: “It is not permitted to do anything except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of our elders encourage.”

They can easily be answered that, if *rule* derives from *ruling*, it seems to pertain more to the strictness of fasting than to the loosening of the belly or to gluttonous excess. Therefore those among them should rightly be judged the greater, and their examples should be followed, who, entering through the narrow gate, are known to live under the laws of sobriety and the stricter discipline of the cross of Christ [Col. 0725A].

Accordingly, when a dispute arises over the word “rule,” those men ought rather to be urged toward fasting than these others restrained from the strictness of the purpose they have undertaken.

Do not shrink from corrections, however harsh or numerous; embrace them willingly. Just as gold or silver is brought to a polished appearance by the file, so our soul, scraped by corrections, is cleansed of its sins or of a certain rusty filth.

Take care also that, following the example of some, while you refuse to obey, you do not, God forbid, turn against a negligent superior with the biting complaint of accusation.

Let Samuel therefore return to your memory. He honored a slothful and inert master so patiently and humbly that, summoned three times in the silence of the deep night, he came running and did not resent the watches that repeatedly interrupted his sleep [Col. 0725B].

He could have objected as though reproaching him: “Why are you not afraid to command a stranger with such authority, when you are sluggish in commanding your own sons?” Yet, as Scripture testifies, he did not grow arrogant or attack him with complaints. Rather, hurrying swiftly at the command of the one giving orders, he simply said: “Here I am, for you called me” (I Sam. VIII).

## CHAPTER V. That confession is the remedy for sin
Have you ever sinned? For there is no human being who does not sin; and perhaps it has become known that, after a shipwreck, the first plank is simply to confess one’s fault. Prompt confession readily brings forgiveness; for if a defense of falsehood is added, what may perhaps have been a slight puncture by a needle may appear to have been pierced through by a broad spear-point. Hence, when David is accused of the guilt he had committed, as soon as he burst forth in the voice of confession, saying, “I have sinned against the Lord” (I Kings 12), he immediately heard from the prophet’s mouth: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die.” And since the opportunity has presented itself, I will not allow you to be deprived of this further consideration: some who have been placed in the religious order from childhood perish through disobedience alone, mingled with pride, while many in the world, after perpetrating the crimes of monstrous offenses, earn pardon through their zeal for humility.

For David committed adultery and murder (I Kings 11), whereas Saul proved disobedient to Samuel (I Kings 13). But what of the fact that the former, without any intermediary, earned pardon in an instant, while the latter was reconciled neither by his own confession nor by the prophet’s exceedingly mournful, bitter, and prolonged entreaty? Clearly, if the sequence of Scripture is examined in both cases, Saul is found to have been more abundant than David in words of repentance. David said only what has already been mentioned: “I have sinned against the Lord”; Saul, however, said: “I have sinned, for I have transgressed the Lord’s words and your commands, fearing the people and obeying their voice” (I Kings 15). Later repeating the same confession, he said: “I have sinned” (ibid.). Samuel’s exceedingly patient prayer was also added; of him it is said: “And Samuel was grieved, and cried out to the Lord throughout that whole night.” But the divine voice replied: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him, so that he may not reign over Israel?” (I Kings 16).

[Col. 0725C–D; 0726A]

## CHAPTER VI. Why David’s confession earned pardon, but Saul’s did not

What, then, is the reason that the repentance of one was mercifully received, while that of the other was rejected under the scrutiny of strict severity? Surely it is that the former, making light of the crime of disobedience in a spirit of pride, did not repent with a whole heart; whereas the latter indeed spoke few words, but the bitterness of genuine grief filled his inmost parts, pierced through by the sword of divine fear.

I ask that those who obey disobedience, yet insolently boast of being exempt from graver crimes, not neglect to consider this. We often see some of them frequenting the tribunal of confession, devoutly prostrating themselves alone, accusing themselves in tinkling and carefully composed words more cleverly than humbly; and for that reason their conduct never advances toward the benefit of suitable correction, because, like Saul, they repent with their mouths while swelling with pride in their hearts.

When you are healthy and strong, do not make yourself ill voluntarily. Do you understand what I am saying? For there is something that displeases me greatly in most monasteries: some men who are vigorous in body and plainly have no need of medical skill today offer a vein to be heated for Nemitor; tomorrow they apply leeches to themselves; the day after, they devise various contrivances of medicines. Meanwhile, fine flour is ground, carefully fashioned cakes are baked only over still-warm ashes; they explore the inlets of rivers and even of the seas; nor is the market allowed to be idle, because a fish has sought the depths of the sea. Indeed, it is considered an unfortunate calamity if a fish-bearing field is found barren—where, plainly, necessity produces abundance and abundance produces poverty.

Meanwhile, whatever animal of land or sea is led to the sacrifice, an expert cook must be sought, one who can regulate the fires with such a measured balance of discretion that, by his artful and masterly tempering, the heat reaches the bones without burning the surface of the flesh—as though by some sort of magic the heat both passed over and did not touch the exterior, yet penetrated into the interior. What more need be said? At last they sit down—or rather, lie down—and, with nauseated stomachs, nibble greedily; with their voracious disgust they can scarcely compel themselves to taste whether the things they have fashioned are genuine.

[Col. 0726B–D; 0727A]

Do not ambitiously aspire to a position of governance, when, about to depart shortly, you do not know the day of your own calling. In that very monastery at Classe which you now inhabit, in our time a certain monk held the office of prior. He ardently desired to become abbot as well; but while he strove for this, while he convened little councils, while he contrived his schemes and tirelessly wielded the hammers of cunning, he fell ill and was brought to his final extremity. Then, suddenly turning to madness, he let flow from his mouth, without knowing it, what he had conceived knowingly in his mind. “Soon,” he said, “I shall seize it; the monastery will be given to me; the staff is at hand. I shall receive it and prevail.” In the midst of these words, therefore, he died, leaving the brothers a sinister expectation concerning him.

[Col. 0726D–0727A]

## CHAPTER VII. The example of Zeuxis in painting Venus

Look inattentively, then, upon the negligent; but observe attentively those who are earnest and watchful concerning their souls. The former example is given so that you may not inquisitively judge the faults of others; the latter so that, through holy imitation, you may shape yourself by emulation of the good.

Set before yourself, therefore, certain outstanding brothers from the whole community of the monastery, whose upright footsteps you can safely imitate. And so that you may more easily aspire toward the goal to which I am leading you, I shall give you an example from antiquity.

Zeuxis of Heraclea (Cicero, *On Invention*, book II) was hired by the people of Croton at a great price to paint a remarkable image of Diana and to fashion her likeness with incomparable mastery in his art. He asked that all the virgins of the city be gathered together in one place, so that he might borrow from their appearance the elegance of the work he was about to make. But since it was not permitted for modest and honorable maidens to appear in public, their brothers were brought to the gymnasium, so that from their beauty the painter might infer what he should judge concerning the still greater loveliness of their sisters.

Since nature, however, does not assign all the qualities of beauty to one person—so that what it grants to one limb it often takes away from another—it happens that one and the same human body excels in beauty in one respect but suffers deformity in another. From the whole group of boys, therefore, the painter chose only five, whom he kept before his eyes in order to assemble the elegance of each one’s beauty.

But why have I extended this narrative at such length? Surely so that you too may choose a few from among many, according to whose standard you may strive to portray the beauty of the inner person. For example, just as he borrowed shining eyes from one, well-shaped ears from another, and from yet another milk-white cheeks flushed with red, so you likewise should learn from one a ready obedience, from another the most fervent charity, from this one watchfulness through the night, and from that one the discipline of prolonged silence. Thus, just as he transferred the forms of different bodies into the appearance of a single image, so you may restore within yourself, from the various virtues of holy men, the one true image of God, and afterward return happily to know that same Creator.

[Col. 0727A–D]

## CHAPTER VIII. That duplicity of heart must be avoided

Beware of duplicity; be simple (I Corinthians 5), so that what is spoken by the tongue may be present in the mind. Unleavened bread is established in solidity, whereas leaven is corrupted in fermenting cavities. In the unleavened bread there are truth and sincerity; in leaven there are malice and wickedness. Whoever walks simply is unleavened, and has put on the new person; whoever, through duplicity, is leaven, has remained in the error of the old self and therefore has not attained the grace of newness. For what does it profit to profess oneself a Christian in words while being, in reality, an antichristian?

[Col. 0728A–B]

Be wholly immersed always in the Prophets, wholly in the Gospels; occupy your heart on every side with the various sayings of sacred Scripture, so that no part of it may lie empty for admitting the fantasies of vain thoughts. If perhaps an unpolished discourse is repellent and the honey of God has no taste in the throat of your heart—“How sweet are your utterances to my palate, O Lord,” says the Prophet, “more than honey and the honeycomb!” (Psalm 118)—pray, fast, and cut away from yourself every enticement of earthly pleasure, so that what seems tasteless not in itself but because of you may become sweet in your mouth. For those boys who had resolved to abstain from the king’s banquets deserved in return to receive the wisdom and knowledge of all books. Daniel also, because he had been the author of this discipline, received in addition the knowledge of every vision and dream (Daniel 1). It was a fitting exchange of divine recompense: those who restrained themselves from the pleasure of bodily food opened the mouths of their minds to the banquets of spiritual understanding. Let the flesh therefore grow dry, so that the well-fed mind may grow fat.

## CHAPTER IX. Saint Romuald’s advice that we preserve sobriety and flee hypocrisy

Let the more edible foods be excluded, so that the hidden judge may inspect the inward battles and, instead of the food of dung, set before us the sweetnesses of heavenly nourishment. Nor should you unwisely apply what the man of God Romuald often said to his disciples:

“Brothers,” he said, “when you are dining in any gathering, while the others are intent upon the food, abstain at the very beginning of the meal; and when they have already been satisfied to some extent, begin yourselves, so that you may both escape the charge of hypocrisy and preserve the rule of sobriety without causing offense.”

I once saw at Pomposa a monk who was exceptionally learned in divine law and the disciplines of the rule. As was reported, he had made this mutual agreement with the brother who sat beside him: when the customary personal cup of wine had been set before each of them, each would be content daily with the measure belonging to either of them. Thus, from what would have suited one, the two sustained themselves under the moderation of sobriety. When his companion was absent, however, even in the heat of summer—which is notably more intense in that place—he allowed the wine in his own cup to sour to such a degree that he often found worms swarming in it.

Martin, therefore, surnamed “the Bald”—for that was his name—when he reached his final days and his entire body had swollen terribly with dropsical fluid, asked all of us who appeared to be standing around his bed to deem him worthy of being beaten individually with brooms. After he had died in perfect faith and holy confession, he later appeared in a vision to a certain brother. He was in a flourishing and flower-filled grove belonging to a most splendid region, adorned with a white robe and radiant in appearance. He was reclining on a little bed decorated with distinguished and marvelous coverings. But let this suffice here, lest, while we weave the story, we exceed the limits of an epistolary summary.

[Col. 0728B–D; 0729A]

## CHAPTER X. That it is unbecoming for monks to speak about secular matters

I had indeed already decided to command silence with my pen; but when we see someone drying up from prolonged thirst, it is exceedingly miserly to offer him only a cup. Take care, therefore, dearest son, that, while you are within the monastery’s enclosure, you do not mingle conversation about secular affairs with secular people; and just as you disdain to report such matters, disdain likewise to hear them.

At once let holy indignation reply, and let the fervor of pious zeal erupt and break the foolishness of disordered speech: “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (I Corinthians 6.) And indeed, what has a monk to do with secular nonsense? Why should I drag into the monastery’s boundaries the noisy law courts, the tribunals of judges, and the halls of kings? Why should I, a dead man, tell stories about battles, about marriage contracts rescinded after divorce, about exalting some people by the titles of their birth and disgracing others through the novelty of cobblers?

To be pointlessly occupied with these and similar trifles—what is it, I ask, except to turn one’s throat away from the clear fountain of divine praise and roll around in one’s mouth the filth of muddy clay? Hence the Lord not unjustly complains through Jeremiah, saying: “My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2).

Look, indeed, at the very structure of your cloister: it is four-sided, so that the layout of the place itself may clearly teach that you ought to be separated on every side from the noise of worldly intercourse. It is wholly indecent and dishonorable, and in every respect absurd, that what someone is accustomed to belch forth in taverns among innkeepers, what is commonly circulated among the women’s quarters of weavers, should be able to find a place in the holy choir of monks.

When I see the Prophets and Apostles wishing to speak to me, when I behold Christ revealing his Gospel to me, should I abandon them and inquire whether ships that have recently crossed the Adriatic have yet put in, how much salt is selling for, or whether the tax-collector sells a measure of grain at a higher price? Let every foolishness of empty rumor therefore depart from the mouth of Christ’s soldier; and let the tongue that blushes with the blood of the immaculate Lamb—or rather, of the supreme Word—disdain to soil itself with the filth of idle speech.

Do not slander anyone, but do not even deem it worthy to lend your ear to slanderers. “Do not associate with slanderers,” says Solomon, “for their destruction will come suddenly, and who knows the ruin of both?”—that is, of both the one who slanders and the one who lends an ear to the slanderer.

Rather, if reason demands it, accuse someone of a crime committed; rebuke him sternly, not fearing to reprimand him more severely in his presence. But do not tear apart someone who is absent, nor gnaw at him with a spiteful tooth before others. Often, I do not know why, we calmly endure one who rebukes us more severely, while we cannot tolerate even the slightest accusation from another.

Require of yourself that your mind always depend upon the mind of the abbot, and that you humbly follow not the judgment of your own heart, but always his command. Pray, therefore, that through him—as through an instrument of his truth—God may disclose to you what he determines you should do according to the disposition of his good pleasure.

[Col. 0729A–D; 0730A]

## CHAPTER XI. That Christian nobility is to be sought from Christ, not from ancestors

Do not at any time weave an ornate lineage of great-grandfathers, wishing to boast of the empty nobility of another person’s name. Clearly, whoever is an heir of God and a fellow-heir of Christ surpasses every pedigree of earthly descent.

Nevertheless, it is a great thing to be a Christian, not merely to appear or to be called one; and the person who displeases God often pleases the world more. Some people, with crafty cleverness, as though by disparaging them, magnify the names of their ancestors; and, to make them seem powerful and magnificent, they accuse them of pride or cruelty.

Do you grasp what I mean? I accuse Achilles of being guilty of much bloodshed, so that you may understand that he was vigorous in the pursuit of war. I indict Hannibal for invading Italy, so that you may recognize him as bold and strong.

Remember that you should often pray so that, with your body prostrate upon the earth, your mind may be raised to heaven. Sleep more often with an empty stomach; let sleep relieve the thirst that accompanies you to your bed. Moderate wakefulness is the cause of pure prayer, but indiscriminate wakefulness often becomes an occasion for idle talking; for someone whose eyes are fluttering and whose lips are yawning cannot read or pray, and so sometimes wishes to spend the time in chatter.
