Therefore, seek your bed late and rise more moderately for the vigils. Let sleep precede your lying down, not lying down precede sleep, so that, the more reluctantly necessity grants rest when it has been postponed, the more eagerly it may be seized by weary limbs.

Meanwhile, avoid little rumors, petty boasts, and flattering sycophants as the poisons of a serpent’s bite; and let them at once hear, as though an antidote had been brought forth: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be immediately turned back and put to shame!” (Psalm 69.)

I am not content with anything moderate in you, my son; what I desire to perceive in you is wholly supreme, wholly perfect. Having therefore laid aside every sluggishness of idleness and torpor, engage yourself against yourself; contend with yourself, fight with yourself. Seize the sword of evangelical discipline and cut off all the necks of the vices that roar around you. Endure everything hard and harsh always for the love of Christ, and regard it as the exercise of virtue.

Whatever appears pleasurable and soothing to the flesh, shudder at it as truly the devil’s bait. For whoever hopes to find the caresses of the flesh in the monastic rule is like someone trying to squeeze sap from dry wood. Circumcise from your lips every kind of buffoonery, clever pleasantry, wit, joking, and verbal humor as though it were a sort of foreskin of paganism. For we are disciples of fishermen, not of orators, so that from the mouth of a Christian it may be Christ’s simplicity that resounds, not Cicero’s Latin eloquence.

Break all your own wills; gird yourself on every side, with the Apostle, in Christ’s mortification. Show on every side the marks of the cross impressed upon you, so that the more closely you now follow the footsteps of the judged one, the more exaltedly you may afterward enjoy the fellowship of the judge.

Greet all the holy brothers of your monastery in my name. If you ever see my dearest brothers Boninus and Peter singing somewhat more loudly than usual, place this distich in their hands in my name:

> You who draw forth instruments from Philomela’s strings,  
> May the inmost voice of the heart sing well in the melodies of the mouth.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0730B–D; 0731A–A; 0732A]

# OPUSCULUM FIFTY. INSTRUCTION OF A NUN. TO BLANCA, COUNTESS, NOW A RELIGIOUS WOMAN.

## ARGUMENT

He instructs the most noble woman Blanca, who, having abandoned wealth, children, and every other beloved possession, had withdrawn into a monastery to serve God, with exceedingly prudent precepts and salutary admonitions, pointing out almost with his finger what she should flee and what she should seek. First, while she is still an inexperienced and untested combatant in spiritual warfare, he fortifies her as with a very sharp weapon, exhorting her bravely to accept poverty, hardship, and tribulations, which must be endured by those who serve God. He urges her to convince herself that those beloved by God are buffeted for a time by various storms in this world, until, having entered the harbor of their most blessed homeland, they may enjoy eternal tranquility.

Then, desiring to lead her to a more perfect state, he invites her with the full force of her mind to love God. Next, to guard against the devil’s ambushes, he shows her the shield of contemplation of death. He clothes her in still stronger arms by placing before her eyes an image of the final judgment drawn from the inner sanctuaries of sacred Scripture, and he kindles her to meditate upon it continually. Finally, judging her to be sufficiently and abundantly fortified by the protection of fear, he leads her back once more through the way of love to her homeland, to the happiness of that everlasting contemplation which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart.

[Col. 0731A–B]

To Blanca, formerly countess, now joined to the heavenly Bridegroom, Peter, a sinful monk, offers the joy of his heart in the Holy Spirit.

## INSTRUCTION OF A NUN

### CHAPTER I. He exhorts Blanca to receive hardship and poverty bravely

I approach to feast at a royal wedding; I desire to see bridal chambers adorned with gold and shining jewels; I eagerly long to be nourished by wedding banquets. Let mystical gifts therefore be brought from every side; let both prophetic and apostolic adornments not be lacking at so excellent a wedding.

Let our evangelical Isaiah now come forward and generously display what he has prepared: the adornment of shoes, crescents, necklaces and pendants, bracelets and headdresses, hair ornaments and anklets, chains and scent-boxes, earrings and rings and gems hanging upon the forehead, changes of clothing, cloaks and linen garments, needles and mirrors and fine linen, ribbons and summer coverings. All these things must be bestowed upon a spiritual wedding and carefully fitted to the new bride, so that she may be able to please the gaze of the true Bridegroom.

Thus adorned with these ornaments and arranged in this variety of jewels was that queen whom the Psalmist contemplated and described:

> “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety” (Psalm 44).

A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and, as the Evangelist testifies, Jesus was invited to the wedding with his disciples (John 2); but he was there as the friend of the bridegroom, not as the bridegroom, as one who would dine, not as one who would marry. This wedding, however, surpasses that one by so great a privilege that here Jesus may rightly be believed to be not a friend but the Bridegroom.

And because “whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Corinthians 6), this Bridegroom is joined not merely to the bride but united with her; and from this union there is born not corruption, but rather the restoration of integrity.

There Jesus turned water into wine; here that same Jesus made both wine and food of himself. Food, because he is himself the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6); wine, the wine that gladdens the human heart (Psalm 103), and which is his Spirit, of whom he says again: “How splendid is your intoxicating cup!” (Psalm 22.)

For the Spirit of God intoxicates the mountains of human beings, so that, as though alienated from their senses, they reject the wealth, honors, and glory of this world, while they burn with flaming desires to undertake every hard and harsh thing for God. Those whom the Jews, truly foolish and mad, addressed by saying, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2), had been intoxicated by this must.

This must also filled the man from among the sons of the prophets whom Elisha had sent to anoint Jehu as king. Concerning him, the frenzied wise men said to Jehu: “Why has this madman come to you?” (II Kings 9.) What wonder, then, if those who are merely human, when they are filled with the divine Spirit, are judged insane by the wise men of this world—and therefore by those who are truly without wisdom—when even the one who is the teacher of angels was said to have a demon (John 8)? Indeed, as the Evangelist Mark testifies, he was even thought to be deranged:

> “He came home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread. When his own people heard this, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, ‘He has lost his mind’” (Mark 3).

You too, venerable lady, had conceived this drunkenness of the Holy Spirit with a sound mind when you resolved to leave the world. Shaking out the wings of a simple dove, you flew to the little nest of the innocent and simple, saying then:

> “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly and rest?” (Psalm 54.)

Now, too, you sing securely:

> “Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude, waiting for him who will save me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm” (Psalm 54).

This drunkenness impelled you to despise extensive and exceedingly fertile estates, to avoid the fortified defenses of towers and castles, to cast away the dear bonds of relatives and the affection of household dependents; and, greatest of all these things, to renounce your only son—still a youth and not yet of age—without the consolation of a marital union. You who had been accustomed to walk surrounded by tightly gathered ranks of retainers have now learned humbly to sit in a corner of the monastery with the poor women of the Holy Spirit.

This sober—as I may call it—drunkenness taught you to choose wool instead of linen, and dark and contemptible garments instead of purple and brightly colored ones. This drunkenness persuaded you to set aside fine wheat rolls and dishes laden with rich foods, and to confine yourself to the measured ration of bread. This skilled and modest drunkenness clearly urged you, while you were still enjoying the first flower of adolescence, after being widowed by your husband’s death, not to consent to suitors so illustrious and so magnificent, not to renew your marriage—as everything seemed to urge you to do—but to show yourself dead to the world, determined to live now for Christ alone.

Indeed, like a skilled merchant intent upon a profitable market, you cast away the world in order to acquire heaven; you anticipated death in order to escape the sentence of death; you chose poverty in order to possess an abundance of riches that do not perish.

770

## CHAPTER II. Why the just are sometimes permitted to be afflicted by the unjust: so that they may be moved, even by necessity, to turn to God

[Col. 0733C]

Yet, so that your conversion might appear all the more remarkable, the world did not drive you away from itself; the sole ardor of the divine Spirit impelled you. Indeed, just as divine providence arranged matters for bringing the Israelite people out of Egypt (Exodus 3), Moses was sent at the very time when Pharaoh had already been stirred up to oppress them with harsh labor. Thus, while one called the minds of the Israelites, which clung deformingly to Egypt, as though drawing them, and another, by raging, seemed to drive them forward, the people—fixed shamefully in servitude—might be moved either by evils impelling them or by goods inviting them.

This also happens frequently among the people of God: when heavenly rewards have been proclaimed, the wicked are permitted to rage against the elect, so that, if we neglect to leave when called to the promised land, we may at least be driven onward by the pressures that rage against us. Thus Egypt—that is, the present life, which oppressed us while flattering us—may help us by pressing upon us; so that the very thing which, while cherishing us, had crushed us under the yoke of servitude may, while afflicting us, show us the way of freedom.

This, then, is why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of the future good things they love, they may also suffer the present evils they dread, and, while love summons them, suffering may drive them toward an easier departure.

But when prosperity in this life smiled upon you from every side, it was not the flattering world that impelled you. Rather, Christ—“more beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Psalm 44)—summoned you through the breath of the Holy Spirit to the abundance of his dowry:

> “Rise,” he said, “my beloved, my bride, and come: my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (Song of Songs 2).

A holy soul is rightly called Christ’s beloved and bride, because it is joined to him through faith and love. But this bride lies, as it were, still prostrate while she is entangled in worldly activities; she rises when she is raised up for the service of God. It is as though he were saying: “You who lie in the softness of secular life, rise now, and raise yourself to the intimate companionship of my contemplation.”

> “My dove, in the clefts of the rock.”

If, according to the Apostle, the rock is Christ (I Corinthians 10), the clefts of the rock are the wounds of the Redeemer. These are not five by chance—the wounds of the spear and the nails—but because we had been wounded by the five senses, through these five wounds we have been restored to perpetual salvation.

These were the gates through which, on the Sabbath, the Prophet forbade heavy burdens to be carried. In these clefts, therefore, God’s dove dwells, because every holy soul places the whole hope of its salvation in the passion of its Redeemer. There it is defended as though from the attack of a hawk, because there it is guarded from all the snares of evil spirits. There it plainly builds its nest, because there it heaps up the offspring of good works.

Of this rock the Psalmist says:

> “The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Psalm 103).

What are “mountains” in this passage except the lofty depths of Scripture that must be understood? Those who already know how to make the leaps of contemplation ascend the high summits of divine sayings as though they were mountain peaks. Since the weak cannot reach these heights, it is rightly added there: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” For the weak are not exercised by sublime understanding; humble faith in Christ alone holds them secure.

As for what is added there—“in the hollow of the wall”—walls are commonly made of stones for guarding vineyards, as Isaiah says:

> “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill; he surrounded it with a wall and dug it around” (Isaiah 5).

What, then, are we to understand by a wall of stones except the protection and watchfulness of angels? When the soul is placed in combat, enclosed and surrounded by them, it is guarded from all the temptations of hostile spirits.

As for what follows—“Show me your face”—the soul is said to show its face to the heavenly Bridegroom when, as though with an unveiled face, it contemplates his appearance with its inner eyes.

> “Let your voice sound,” he says, “in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.”

O what a gracious exchange—or rather, what unspeakable sweetness arises in human hearts, when Creator and creature delight in one another through reciprocal affections, as the Prophet says:

> “May my praise be pleasing to him; but I shall rejoice in the Lord” (Psalm 103).

[Col. 0734A–D; 0735A]

## CHAPTER III. That everyone who despises the world ought always to strive to attain the love of God

This is the highest aim of every holy soul released from the bonds of the world, and all its attention here must be directed toward striving for the love of God through the growth of all its works, and toward finally resting in the delightful embraces of the true Bridegroom.

Just as someone is initiated into the ecclesiastical ranks in order to reach the summit of the priesthood—or, to speak more appropriately in your case, as a virgin is betrothed with a dowry in order to marry—so all who leave the world ought always to strive to be joined more closely in love to their Creator.

Otherwise, what benefit would it have been to break the yoke of Egyptian servitude and cross the Red Sea if one were never granted entry into the land irrigated with milk and honey? Milk is the fruit of the flesh; honey flows down from above. And because our Redeemer came from heaven and assumed flesh from a virgin, this is the land of the living, toward which we must always hasten with steps intent upon love.

Embrace this Bridegroom, venerable sister, in the arms of true charity; delight continually in him—“delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 36). Receive his body and blood frequently even with the mouth of the flesh, so that you may deservedly hear this saying of his:

> “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4).

The adversary is terrified when he sees the lips of Christians reddened with Christ’s blood. For he recognizes there the sign of his own destruction and cannot endure the instrument of the divine victory by which he was taken captive and overwhelmed.

Let Christ therefore appear to you in your mouth through his mystery, and let Christ live for you always in your heart through the fire of his love, so that what the bride says in the Song of Songs may also apply to you:

> “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts” (Song of Songs 1).

What else is signified by myrrh, that exceedingly bitter kind of aromatic substance with which the corpses of the dead are also embalmed, except Christ’s passion? What else is recognized by “between the breasts” except the place of the heart?

Whoever, therefore, embraces Christ continually in the secret place of his heart; whoever constantly meditates upon the mystery of the Passion for the sake of imitation—for such a person Christ becomes a bundle of myrrh and, according to the saying of sacred Scripture, dwells between his breasts.

Hence the same Bridegroom says to the bride:

> “Place me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song of Songs 8).

We often tie some sign upon our finger or arm to preserve the memory of something we do not wish to consign to oblivion, so that, when the sign is frequently observed, the matter that forgetfulness might have interrupted may be kept continually in memory.

Whoever seems to love Christ but avoids doing good works has, in a certain sense, placed the bridegroom as a seal upon his heart, but has not placed him at all upon his arm. Whoever, however, appears devoted to good works but is cold and sluggish in the fire of divine love has placed an image of holiness upon his arm, but has not yet impressed Christ’s seal upon his heart.

Therefore, so that the holy soul may be marked with Christ’s character in both places, let it place him as a seal upon its heart, so that it may burn to its very marrow with the flames of his love. Let it also place him upon its arm, so that it may persist vigorously in works of piety.

Paul had placed Jesus as a seal upon his body, as upon his arm, when he said:

> “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Galatians 6).

He had placed Jesus as a seal upon his heart when elsewhere he joyfully said:

> “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world!” (ibid.)

He bore in his body the marks that had been impressed, and he gloried in having that one's seal in his mind.

The heavenly Bridegroom himself, moreover, places each of his elect as a seal upon himself and, in a pleasing reciprocal act, keeps him in view, as though lest he be erased from memory. In accordance with this, he promises Zerubbabel, the leader of Judah:

> “On that day I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant, and I will place you like a seal in my presence” (Haggai 2).

Conversely, concerning a certain rejected king the Lord says:

> “Though Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring upon my right hand, from there I would tear him away” (Jeremiah 22).

[Col. 0735A–D; 0736A–B]

## CHAPTER IV. An exhortation that she may always rest in the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom
Therefore, venerable sister, strive continually toward this reciprocal relationship [Col. 0736C], so that the heavenly Bridegroom may always receive you through the grace of his love, and so that you may not—God forbid!—turn your eyes away from him through love of any temporal thing; thus, gazing upon you with subtle attention and finding no stain of offense, he may say: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs IV); and you, burning indescribably with love for him, may utter from the depths of your heart: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands; his head is the finest gold, his throat most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (Song of Songs V).

The Beloved is white through virginity and ruddy through his Passion. He is white because he says: “I am the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs I). He is ruddy, of whom John says: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” [Col. 0736D] (Apocalypse I). “Chosen out of thousands”: concerning him Solomon says, “I found one man among a thousand” (Ecclesiastes VII). The number one thousand is to be understood as the perfection of the whole human race, among which the Savior is solitary like a sparrow in a building (Psalm CI).

“His head is the finest gold,” because “the head of Christ is God” (I Corinthians XI); and just as gold surpasses other metals, so he—though incomparably so—surpasses all creatures. His throat is called most sweet because the minds of his hearers are sweetened by the honeyed sweetness of his words. “How sweet are your words to my palate,” he says, “more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm CXVIII).

He is also altogether desirable because, as Peter testifies, the angels long to look upon him [Col. 0737A] (I Peter I); or because the mystery of his humanity kindles every desire in the minds of the elect, so that they are moved not only by the glory of the resurrection, but also invited to imitate him by the very disgrace of his Passion.

Therefore, venerable sister, take continual delight in this Bridegroom of yours; place all the desires of your heart in him; and, lulled to rest in his embraces, find repose there from every storm of the world.

## CHAPTER V. An exhortation to remain always girded against the ambushes of temptation

Meanwhile, while you embrace the Bridegroom, beware diligently of the adversary; for you are still on the open sea and have not yet enjoyed the security of a harbor. This military encampment is not a dwelling of repose; this is a road, not a homeland. We walk; we do not dwell.

“For the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job VII). Therefore, if the battles of temptations are absent, rejoice indeed, but do not place excessive confidence in your security; instead, arm yourself vigilantly against the sudden and unexpected attacks of lurking enemies. For often some who have turned from the world to God experience, at the very entrance of their conversion, an utterly peaceful tranquility of body and mind; but as time goes on, they are wearied by harsh trials of temptation.

This is recognized as occurring by divine dispensation, lest they be broken by the severity of temptations at the very beginning of their new life. For if the bitterness of temptation met them while they were still tender and inexperienced in inward conflict, they would easily return to the things from which they had not yet gone far. Hence it is written: “When Pharaoh had sent out the people, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is near, thinking that perhaps they might repent when they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt” (Exodus XIII).

Thus, for those departing from Egypt, battle is removed from their immediate path; because those who abandon the world are granted a certain tranquility of peace, lest, disturbed and terrified in the very novelty of their weakness, they return to the things they had despised. First they are soothed by the sweetness of security; first they are nourished by the quiet of peace. But once they have known that sweetness, they endure the struggles of temptation all the more tolerably, inasmuch as they have come to recognize more deeply in God the one whom they love.

Therefore, rejoice in whatever prosperity perhaps attends you now in such a way that you do not sleep through what threatens later. Be cautious, then, and watchful on every side; make yourself so vigilant that your enemies may never find you drowsing. For against you are to be joined the lineage of your birth and the flower of your age, the beauty of your appearance and the memory of the wealth you have cast away. To avoid the arrows of these battles, no shield seems to me stronger than meditation on death and the terror of the final judgment.

## CHAPTER VI. The soul, when it departs, is constricted by what anxieties of pain

One must consider how, when the sinful soul has begun to be released from the bonds of the flesh, it is shaken by bitter terror and torn by how many gnawing goads of conscience. It recalls the forbidden things it committed; it sees the commandments that it negligently scorned to fulfill. It grieves that it received the time granted for repentance in vain; it mourns that the fixed moment of strict retribution is inevitably approaching.

It strives to remain but is compelled to depart; it wants to recover what it has lost, but is not heard. Looking behind itself, it counts the course of its entire past life as though it were one very brief stage of a journey; it directs its eyes before itself and discovers the expanses of endless perpetuity.

It mourns, therefore, because within so brief a span it could have acquired the joy of all ages; it also laments that, for the pleasure of so brief an enticement, it lost the indescribable sweetness of everlasting delight. It is ashamed because, for the sake of that substance which was subject to worms, it neglected the one that was destined to be joined to angelic choirs.

Now it raises the rays of its mind, and, contemplating the glory of immortal riches, is confounded that it lost them because of the poverty of this life. When it turns its eyes downward toward the dark valley and dreadful gloom of this world, and marvels at the splendor of eternal light above, it clearly understands that the thing it loved was night and darkness.

If only it could have earned renewed time for repentance—what a difficult way of life it would undertake! What promises, great and many, it would make! With how many bonds of devotion it would bind itself!

Meanwhile, as its dimming eyes waste away, its breast palpitates, its hoarse throat gasps, and its teeth gradually blacken and contract something like rust; as its face grows pale [Col. 0738C] and all its limbs stiffen—while these and similar services that precede nearby death are being performed, all its deeds and words are present together. Its thoughts themselves are not absent, and all these things bear bitter testimony against their author.

Everything is heaped before the eyes of the one who looks back, and what he refuses to see he is forced, unwillingly and under compulsion, to attend to. Moreover, on one side there is a dreadful host of demons; on the other, angelic power. In the one who stands between them, it is clearly discerned to which side the right of possession belongs.

For if signs of devotion appear in him, he is coated with the allurements of angelic invitation and summoned to depart by the sweetness of harmonious melody. But if the darkness of his merits and the squalor of his foulness assign him to the left-hand side, he is immediately shaken by intolerable terror, thrown into confusion by the violence of a sudden attack, invaded precipitately, and violently torn from the prison of his wretched flesh, so that he is already dragged in bitterness toward eternal punishments.

After his departure from the body, who could explain how many armed ranks of wicked spirits lie hidden in ambush, how many snarling wedges equipped with deadly weapons block the way, and how, like legions massed in military formation, they attack so that the soul may not pass through freely?

To turn these things and others like them frequently over in one’s heart—what else is this than to reject the seductive flatteries of this life, renounce the world, suppress the enticing impulses of the flesh, and steadfastly preserve the single purpose of attaining perfection?

## CHAPTER VII. Statements of Scripture concerning the day of judgment

[Col. 0739A]

The terror of the final judgment must also be added, so that by its bitterness the false sweetness of this world may be despised. We rise courageously to avoid the troubles of the devil’s warfare if we thoughtfully consider the danger of the final necessity.

For if that sudden and terrible coming of Christ is properly weighed, what will there be in the world in which the human mind, even when foolish, may take delight? That is the day toward which all the purpose and culmination of the preceding ages are gathered, and to which all the volumes of Sacred Scripture minister. Concerning it blessed Peter says, to shake the hearts of his hearers with fitting terror: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat” (II Peter III).

And he immediately adds: “Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and devotion, awaiting and hastening toward the coming of the day of the Lord, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?” (Ibid.)

The apostle Jude also says concerning it: “Behold, the Lord will come with his holy thousands to execute judgment against all, to convict all the ungodly of all the works of their ungodliness by which they acted ungodly, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him” (Jude I).

John says of it in the Apocalypse: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves” (Apocalypse I).

Malachi also says: “Behold, the Lord of hosts comes, and who will be able to consider the day of his coming, and who will stand to see him?” (Malachi III). And shortly afterward: “Behold, the day will come, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who commit ungodliness will be like stubble; and the coming day will set them ablaze, leaving them neither root nor branch” (Malachi IV).

And through another prophet it is said: “Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations will come” (Haggai VIII).

Again, another says: “The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift; the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the strong man will be afflicted. It is a day of wrath, that day, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah I).

Here the prophet is considering how near and how swiftly the terrible day of judgment is approaching. To emphasize its swiftness more clearly, he heaps together so many words denoting haste: he repeats “near” twice, then adds “swift” and “exceedingly,” so that he plainly teaches that what unbelievers and blind-hearted people think to be far away is already seen by the eyes of faith at the threshold. These people already stand, as it were, trembling before the judge’s tribunal, whom those others hold in contempt because of his supposed absence over a long duration.

Isaiah proclaims this day of final and irremediable necessity, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, and full of indignation and wrath and fury, to lay the earth waste in solitude and to destroy its sinners from it; because the stars and their brightness will not spread their light, the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light; and I will visit evils upon the world and their iniquities upon the ungodly” (Isaiah XIII).

And again he says: “Behold,” he says, “the Lord is strong and mighty, like a storm of hail, a crushing whirlwind, like the rush of many waters overflowing and poured out upon the earth” (Isaiah XXVIII).

The same prophet says elsewhere: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar; his fury burns, and it is grievous to bear; his lips are filled with indignation, and his tongue is like devouring fire, and his spirit is like an overflowing torrent, to destroy the nations utterly” (Isaiah XXX).

Again he says: “And suddenly, at once, the Lord of hosts will visit it with thunder and the shaking of the earth, with a loud voice of whirlwind and storm, and with a flame of devouring fire” (Isaiah XXIX).

Concerning this fire Peter says: “But the heavens and the earth that now exist have been reserved by the same word, kept for fire on the day of judgment and the perdition of ungodly men” (II Peter III).

The prophet also says concerning it: “The Lord will make the glory of his voice heard and will display the terror of his arm in the threat of fury and the flame of devouring fire” (Isaiah XXX).

Of this dreadful vengeance the Lord says through Moses: “My sword will devour flesh” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

Jeremiah says: “The sword of the Lord will devour from one end of the earth to the other; there is no peace for any flesh” (Jeremiah XII).

For the earth is said to be devoured by the sword, and peace is declared absent from all flesh, because whoever now lives carnally, or is convicted of pursuing earthly things immoderately, must necessarily be slain by the sword of final strictness.

Concerning this sword the Lord says through Ezekiel: “My sword will go out from its sheath against all flesh, from the south even to the north, so that all flesh may know that I, the Lord, have drawn my sword from its sheath, never to return” (Ezekiel XXI).

The prophet Amos also speaks of this sword: “All the sinners of my people will die by the sword, those who say, ‘Evil will not approach and will not come upon us’” (Amos IX).

This terror of divine judgment had disturbed the inner ears of the prophet Nahum when he said: “The sound of the whip, and the sound of the rushing wheel, and of the neighing horse, and of the boiling chariot, and of the mounted rider, and of the flashing sword, and of the glittering spear, and of the multitude of the slain, and of the heavy fall; and there is no end of corpses” (Nahum III).

Daniel plainly describes what he saw concerning divine judgment, saying: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat; his clothing was white like snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire; a fiery and rushing river came forth from before him” (Daniel VII).

And shortly afterward: “The judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Ibid.).

These books are to be understood as the saints themselves, whose merit is now hidden from them by the guardianship of humility and wrapped up like the volume of a book so that it may not be read. Then, however, for their glory, it is opened to the eyes of all, so that in them transgressors may read, as though in the lines of a written text, the commandments of the divine law that they had refused to keep while they lived.

There they are compelled to read who here, through the arrogance of pride, disdained to hear the words of God. There they recognize that the Lord’s yoke was easy and his burden light for the gentle and patient (Matthew XI), although here they had judged it intolerable for the necks of their pride.

There every proud person is confounded, and whatever had been exalted is bent beneath the indignation of such great majesty. Hence Isaiah says:

“The haughty eyes of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men will be bowed down. The Lord alone will be exalted on that day; for the day of the Lord is upon every proud and lofty person and upon every arrogant one, and he will be humbled; and upon all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, and upon all the oaks of Bashan, and upon all the high mountains, and upon all the elevated hills, and upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall, and upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon everything beautiful in appearance. The sublimity of men will be bowed down, and the loftiness of men will be humbled; the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and idols will be utterly crushed. They will enter the caves of rocks and the pits of the earth, away from the face of the Lord’s fear and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isaiah II).

I might perhaps explain these words in sequence, were I not avoiding exceeding the limits of an epistolary abridgment. I will merely touch on this point in passing: the day of divine judgment is said to threaten insensible things, but through figures drawn from things without reason, the stupidity of condemned human beings is understood.

The lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon are the powerful of this age, raised high by the excellence of earthly prominence but barren of the fruits of good works. Oaks, however, do produce fruit, but not fruit by which human beings are refreshed; rather, fruit by which swine are fed. The swine are to be understood as unclean spirits, which are fattened by the filthy works of sordid people.

The lofty mountains and elevated hills (Psalm LXIV) are the proud, stretched upward as though by the accumulation of swollen thoughts, but strangers to the grain with which the valleys abound and to all the fruits of spiritual pursuits.

The lofty tower and fortified wall signify those who, although they are sinners, establish themselves as though in a citadel of innocence and, covering themselves with a shield of defense, do not allow the arrows of their reprovers to reach them.

Tarshish is said to mean “the exploration of joy.” Whoever in this world seeks out whatever may give him joy—when the day of the Lord comes upon him, it waters him with the troubles of grief and sadness, through which his joys will become bitter forever.

The day of the Lord comes not upon everything that is beautiful, but upon everything beautiful in appearance, because the weight of divine judgment presses upon the person who is inwardly confounded by the deformity of secretly advancing vices, while outwardly he is cloaked in a certain beauty of pretended virtue, or rather of respectability.

Although much more could be supplied, we postpone a more detailed exposition of these matters because we are avoiding the excesses of a longer style. We also refrain from inserting further examples of the terror of divine judgment, because, since the whole purpose of heavenly speech serves this fearful examination, it is not necessary for us to labor longer in magnifying it.

For fully conveying this truth, even if everything else were lacking, those words of Truth alone would suffice: “Those days will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of creation, which God created, until now, nor will be” (Mark XV).

## CHAPTER VIII. A warning not to return to the world under the appearance of piety

But you, my lady—my lady, I say, and indeed my queen—betrothed to my Lord, the heavenly King, by the ring of living faith and the pledge of the Holy Spirit: read these things, and others like them, which are written concerning the bitterness of divine fury and indignation threatening lovers of the world, again and again; meditate upon them attentively, so that by this antidote, as it were, of a bitter preparation you may escape the hiss of the ancient serpent and his deadly poison.

For I have often experienced in myself that, when the bitterness of this thought is spread through my innermost being, the stomach of my mind, so to speak, is dried up against all the fluids of the world that flatter it evilly. Often the malignant spirit is placed upon the tongue of a flatterer like a bird on a branch, and, as through the channel of a vessel, poison flows into another vessel and pours itself lethally into the inner parts of the hearer.

But stop your ears to the persuasive songs of the Sirens, and prudently escape shipwreck in Scylla’s whirlpool. Let the terror of the Judge fix your heart in its holy purpose, so that the wind of flattering favor may never tear it away.

For that ancient seducer who once vomited the poison of his cunning upon Eve through the serpent (Genesis III), perhaps still behaves toward you as toward a daughter and will hiss through another of his vessels:

“Return home,” he will say, “under the very habit of your sacred profession; govern your household; set forth the form of a pious life; maintain discipline of gravity and moderation toward your son and his contemporaries; prudently provide a wife suitable to one who is about to fall; and do not permit the retinue of those who obey you to withdraw from their allegiance.”

In constructing these schemes, the spirit of wickedness does not care by what garment he draws you back to the world, provided that he is confident that through worldly acts he will rule your mind.

## CHAPTER IX. The monk who, returning from the desert to a monastery, fell through impurity and died

Since many examples are available, we judge it especially fitting to relate what happened to us a few days ago.

A certain monk of simple character and humble modesty joined us, intending to live with us for a time; and for nearly eight years he lived with us in the desert not only chastely but, according to the testimony of all the brothers, commendably. Since he was skilled in writing, he also copied for us not a few volumes of books with exemplary care.

Recently, however, when he appeared vigorous, with a well-nourished body and stronger than usual, he began obstinately demanding permission to return to his own monastery. The adversary had put this into his heart, as the outcome of the matter later made perfectly clear.

For as soon as, in accordance with his request, he returned to his monastery, he fell through the discharge of his thighs with another monk, an old man of evil days, equally skilled in letters and in book production; and thus, by the sudden contagion of a most wicked crime, he defiled all the purity in which he had lived for so long. And lest so punishable a fault pass without vengeance, he soon fell ill, took to his bed, and after a few days departed from this life, confessed and confounded.

Thus, thus, let the one who stands take heed lest he fall (I Corinthians X). And whoever, following only a command, does not hesitate with Lot’s wife to look behind him, let him at least be terrified by the sight of that little pillar of salt (Genesis XIX) and by God, the avenger from above.

## CHAPTER X. The burial of Sophia, margravine, and her intolerable stench

But perhaps it is said in reply that your little body is exceedingly thin and delicate, having been tenderly nourished from the earliest beginnings of nursing infancy on the most sumptuous and almost royal banquets; that you cannot now be content with the tables of the sisters, since formerly you were accustomed to magnificent dishes; and that you cannot even tolerate their smell or share their common foods, since you had been accustomed to season marine delicacies and other exquisite dishes with Indian spices.

Against these wickedly flattering persuasions—or rather, arrows manifestly shot with the honey of contention from the devil’s quiver—you, a disciple of the Crucified One, should wisely advance and drive them away from you by diligent reflection upon your condition.

Consider, then, that the flesh now nourished by carefully prepared dishes will shortly be forced to swarm with worms; and that it then becomes food for things that gnaw, although now it is delightfully fattened by the pleasure of food. The more pleasant a softness it secured for itself through such upbringing, the more grievous the stench it exhales when putrefied.

Behold, while we are writing these things, Sophia returns to our memory: the sister of Uguzo and daughter of Rainerius, both margraves. Nearly six years ago, while she was still healthy and unharmed, she asked the abbot of the monastery of Saint Christopher the Martyr to construct a burial place for her. When he resisted and declared that she was delirious, she obtained it only with difficulty.

As soon as she entered the enclosure of the monks and saw the tomb that had been made, she collapsed into illness for reasons known to whatever judgment; shortly afterward she miscarried and died.

Her tomb was made of plaster and secured on every side by the skillful work of masons. For approximately a continuous year it emitted such a flood of stench [Col. 0744A] that it could scarcely be endured and did not allow the brothers to rest in the whole half of that enclosure. Although many tombs around it had collapsed and had incurred much lower expense, none except this one caused distress to the nostrils. Thus it became clearer than daylight that the more tenderly and softly human flesh is raised, the more terribly it is transformed into putrefaction and nausea.

When the brothers asked me why this had happened, I explained what seemed to be the case:

“This,” I said, “is, as I think, being divinely done for your salvation, so that in that one body which you saw as so beautiful and attractive, you may clearly understand what ought also to be thought concerning other women when tempted by lust. For that flesh was truly already putrefaction when it invited the slippery eyes of those who looked upon it; what it was then, it now plainly reveals. And every human flesh that is now seen to live does not then generate putrefaction in itself after death; rather, it merely makes manifest at that time the putrefaction that it had always been.”

## CHAPTER XI. The wife of the duke of Venice, who, after excessive delicacy, rotted throughout her body

To strengthen what we assert, it is fitting to produce an example from living flesh as well. I learned and relate what follows from the report of a truthful and honorable man.

The duke of Venice had as his wife a citizen of the city of Constantinople. She lived so tenderly and delicately and indulged herself in pleasure so extravagantly—indeed, not merely superstitiously but, so to speak, elaborately—that she disdained even to wash with ordinary water. Her servants therefore took pains to collect dew from the sky from every direction, from which they prepared a sufficiently laborious bath for her.

She did not touch her food with her hands either. Her eunuchs cut every item of nourishment into the smallest pieces, which she then placed in her mouth with little golden forks and two-pronged utensils, nibbling at them.

Her chamber, moreover, was fragrant with so many kinds of incense and aromatics that it is unpleasant even for us to recount such disgrace, and perhaps a hearer may not believe it.

But how hateful the pride of this woman was to almighty God was made clear by the punishment he inflicted. For when the blade of divine judgment had been brandished over her, her entire body rotted, so that all the limbs of her body decayed on every side and the whole chamber was filled with an utterly intolerable stench.

No one could endure such an assault upon the nostrils—not the perfumer, not the little servant; scarcely one maidservant remained in diligent attendance, and she could do so only with the aid of some fragrant substance. Even she approached hurriedly and immediately fled away again.

After being consumed for a long time by this illness and miserably tortured, she ended her life, while even her friends rejoiced.

Let the flesh itself teach what flesh is; and what dead flesh declares, let living flesh also testify.

## CHAPTER XII. The punishments of the condemned

But would that those who are such were afflicted by temporal punishment in a way that the pit of Tartarus would not also await them!

There, according to the measure of joy, the measure of torment is repaid; and the more deeply a person is raised here by the swelling of boastfulness, the more deeply he is swallowed there in the abyss of devouring fire.

Hence it is said concerning the perverse soul under the figure of Babylon: “As much as she exalted herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Apocalypse XVIII). And elsewhere: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments, and the stronger the person, the more severe will be the torture” (Wisdom VI).

For the very carnal enticements and the other vices that inflamed wicked people here are there changed into pitch and resin and lend strength to avenging flames.

As Scripture says (Job X), there is the shadow of death. This is nothing other than the darkness of the division [probably “deprivation”] of vision, because each condemned person, when kindled by eternal fire, is darkened away from inner light.

The nature of fire is to display both light and heat from itself; but that avenging flame of past vices has heat but absolutely no light. Hence Truth says concerning the one whom it rejects: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew XII).

If, then, the fire that torments the reprobate could have light, the one who is rejected would not be said to be cast into darkness. The Psalmist also says: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” [Col. 0745C] (Psalm LVII).

Fire falls upon the ungodly; but when the fire falls, the sun is not seen, because the flame of Gehenna blinds those whom it devours to the vision of true light. Thus the pain of burning torments them outwardly, while the punishment of blindness darkens them inwardly, so that those who sinned against their Creator in body and heart may be punished in body and heart together; and so that those who, while living here, served their evil pleasures with both may feel punishment in both.

Hence the prophet aptly says: “They descended into hell with their weapons” (Ezekiel XXXI). The weapons of sinners are the members of the body, by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive. Hence Paul rightly says: “Do not present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity” (Romans VI).

To descend into hell with one’s weapons means to endure the torments of eternal judgment with those very members by which one fulfilled the desires of pleasure, so that pain may then absorb them on every side—those who now, subjected to their pleasures, fight on every side against the justice of the just Judge.

Yet these punishments torment those immersed in them beyond their strength, while also preserving them by extinguishing the support of life: thus the end brings life to an end in such a way that the one tormented lives forever without end. For through torments he hastens toward an end, yet, continually failing, endures without end.

Thus for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, failure without failure: death lives, the end is always beginning, and failure does not know how to fail.

Therefore, let those who are now devoted to lust live according to the will of their own flesh, so that afterward soul and flesh may perish together. Let them now suck out the marrow of worldly sweetness, so that then, filled with the wormwood of perpetual torment, they may grow bitter in all their inward parts (Job XXI).

It is necessary that those gnash their teeth there who here rejoiced in eating; that those weep there without remedy by whom laughter was enjoyed here in pleasure; and that those who here breathe in the scents of aromatics and pant after the sharpness of spices be tortured there by sulfurous stench and surrounded by the darkness of pitchy smoke.

“For they spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend to the realms below” (Numbers XIV).

## CHAPTER XIII. The cold monk is worthless seaweed; the fervent monk is a fruitful vine

[Col. 0746B]

These things, however, must be impressed upon minds that seek to return to the Egypt they have left behind, minds that ignobly desire to sit beside pots of meat (Exodus XVI), so that through these waves of thought and storms of terror the Red Sea may in some manner be made for them—a sea that stands in their way and prevents them from returning.

But you, venerable sister, who follow the living creatures of the evangelical chariot and of the heavenly wheels, whose feet are straight (Ezekiel I), and who, when they walk, do not turn back—surely, as we confidently trust, you will not follow Lot’s wife (Genesis IX), but rather imitate Anna’s steadfast virtue, whose face was no longer turned in different directions (I Samuel I).

And since what is praised by a flatterer is despised by ecclesiastical authority, consider both of these judgments:

“The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts wickedly is blessed” (Psalm IX): this is the flatterer’s voice.

“Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII): this is the voice of the Church.

That the measure of the curse is also equal to the measure of the crime in the case of the reprobate is attested by the prophet David, who pronounced thirty curses against Judas Iscariot, just as Judas sold the Lord through sacrilegious commerce for thirty pieces of silver.

The first of these is: “Set a sinner over him”; the last is: “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double cloak” (Psalm CVIII). If anyone seeks them carefully through the sequence of the psalm, it is certain that he will not find them scattered here and there.

Learn also the order of things from the sequence of Scripture. First the law is written; then the history of the Judges is woven; finally the book of Kings is set down. For here we fulfill the commandments of the divine law; afterward we come to judgment; at the end, if our case is not found wanting, we reign without end with Christ.

These are the yields that must be brought forth from the fields, to be carried into the heavenly granaries.

If a vine is rich in grapes, it surpasses all the trees and shrubs of the forests; but if it is barren, it is judged more rejected and worthless than the other shrubs. Hence the divine voice says to the prophet:

“Son of man, what will be made of the wood of the vine among all the woods of the forest that are among the trees of the woodland? Will wood be taken from it to make a work, or will a peg be made from it to hang any vessel upon?” (Ezekiel XV).

Thus, certainly, if a monk is intent and fervent in producing the fruits of good works, nothing among human beings can be more excellent than he. Otherwise, if he grows cold and barren, withers, and snores in sleep, he is rightly despised as worthless seaweed and is not even equal to secular people.

If someone burns with zeal for the pursuits by which perfection is attained but still, through weakness, retains inwardly something of the vices of his former life, a secular person—even if demonstrably religious and devout—is nevertheless not wholly comparable to him.

For flawed gold is better than pure bronze; a dull pearl is more precious than Parian marble; and a pale carbuncle is more pleasing than a blue hyacinth.

You too, if, standing as it were in the dawn’s first light, you still sense within yourself something of the darkness of your former life, do not despair of reaching the fullness of light quickly. Take care only not to rest in the softness of the flesh, but exercise yourself vigilantly in the labors of holy discipline.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Dominicus sang twelve psalters together with discipline and began a thirteenth one
Would that you might now be granted to see my master Dominicus, who would teach and form you by the example of his most effective and radiant life in what we, with our unskilled tongue, endeavor to accomplish by words. For nearly fifteen years now he has worn an iron breastplate next to his flesh; he is also girded around the body by two iron rings and constricted by two more around the upper arms. But since we have already set forth more about him in other little works of ours, let us now report what he related to us when he came barely six days ago.

He said: “I happened to learn that you had written that I had recited nine psalters in a single day, together with bodily disciplines. When I heard this, I was shaken and terrified, and, with conscience reproaching me, I groaned: ‘Woe is me! Behold, this has been written about me without my knowing it; yet I do not know whether this could have been done by me.’ Therefore I will try again, and I shall recognize with certainty whether I have been able to accomplish it.”

Accordingly, on Wednesday I stripped off my clothes and, armed with scourges in both hands, remained awake throughout the whole night, not ceasing to sing psalms and beat myself, until, on the following day, after completing the customary twelve psalters, I struggled through a thirteenth as far as the psalm, “Blessed are they” (Psalm 31).

Moreover, to show by one example what often seems hard and harsh to us, and how childlike and contemptible he considers it: a certain brother was extremely reluctant to wear himself out under the blows of scourges, and judged it most burdensome both to inflict the wounds upon himself and to endure them. Nevertheless, at length, yielding to the frequent exhortations of Lord Dominicus as he pressed him insistently, he did not cease to discipline himself with his own hands through the chanting of the entire psalter and, in addition, fifty psalms.

That night preceded the Lord’s Day and the feast of Blessed Michael. When morning came, that brother went to the aforementioned old man and, fearing that he might be rebuked for his lack of discretion, related in order what he had done. The old man replied:

“Do not, brother, be fainthearted, nor despair because of the weakness that is yours at present. God is able to raise you from the lowest depths to higher things and, like the infancy of your milk-white way of life, strengthen you toward the growth of youthful vigor.”

He added: “We too began at first by gradual steps, and little by little, although weak and fragile, we were led to the place where divine mercy wished to bring us.”

Thus it came about that he did not rebuke him for immoderate fervor, as the brother had feared; rather, lest he succumb to despair, he restored his courage as though he had done scarcely anything.

By the example of this holy old man, the practice of performing the discipline became so deeply established in our regions that not only men but also noble women eagerly undertook this form of purification. For the widow of Tethbald, a woman certainly of exalted birth and no low rank, once related to me that, according to the prescribed rule of this discipline, she had completed a penance of one hundred years.

## CHAPTER XV. On the everlasting blessedness of the heavenly Jerusalem

Therefore willingly and always listen to the deeds of the good: either so that, if you can imitate them, you may acquire the fullness of their reward, or so that, if they are impossible, they may preserve you more abundantly in humility. Let your spirit be raised toward those things promised in the homeland, so that, rejoicing, it may despise whatever hardship it fears along the way. When the weight of shining gold is considered, the labor of the journey is lightened. When a crown is set forth as the prize, the race across the stadium is completed with alacrity.

Consider, then, how blessed is the one who, when so great a multitude of the rejected is turned away, is judged worthy to enter the wedding feast with the splendid company of the elect; how great is the dignity of always standing before the sight of the Creator and contemplating the appearance of the Truth in its immediate presence; of seeing God face to face and taking part in the angelic choirs. There each person is so filled with present joys that none is anxious about future adversity. There, while the tranquil mind delights in the beauty of unbounded light, it also rejoices ineffably in the rewards of its fellow citizens.

There they both drink from the fountain of life when thirsty and thirst even while drinking, because there neither the eagerness of desire can produce craving nor satiety grow weary. From the fact that they always stand before the author of life, they draw the whole power of blessedness. From this comes the eternal freshness of flowering youth, from this the loveliness of beauty, and unfailing vigor and wholeness.

From that fountain of eternity they receive the ability to live eternally and rejoice ineffably; and, far more excellent still, they grow strong in the likeness of that same Creator. As the evangelist John testifies: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Then death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15), and every corruption of human nature collapses utterly.

Concerning this city, that holy man Tobias said: “The gates of Jerusalem shall be built of sapphire and emerald, and the whole circuit of its walls of precious stone; all its streets shall be paved with white and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through its lanes” (Tobit 13). Concerning it John also says: “Its gates were each made from a single pearl, and the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass” (Revelation 21). He immediately adds concerning it: “It has no need of the sun or the moon, for the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (ibid.).

There, moreover, human nature, which had been corrupted, rejoices, cleansed of every squalor of suffering; made unleavened, it remains in the purity and sincerity of its own cleanliness. The flesh, made spiritual, agrees with the spirit, and the whole human being is in no way discordant with the will of its Creator.

Then what the bridegroom says to the bride is fulfilled: “Come, my bride; the time of pruning has arrived” (Song of Songs 2). When a shoot is pruned, what is superfluous is cut away while what is useful remains. Thus, from human nature everything that the Creator made remains, but what the devil added is removed.

There the hidden things of each person are open to the eyes of all. There the minds of all, fused together in the unity of mutual love, do not disagree with one another in any diversity; rather, all are bound together unanimously in the common pursuit of the will. Among us, when one festival is celebrated, another is not observed; there, however, the joy of all solemnities is always heaped together, because those who are unquestionably the cause of the solemnities are present.

There ignorance is absent, and impossibility is absent, because in the Wisdom to which they are united they know all things, and in the Omnipotent they can do all things. There, with unveiled face, we shall contemplate how the Father ineffably begets the Son and how the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. There we shall see how he who is absent nowhere is everywhere not in parts but wholly; how he can attend to each person as though free from all, and attend to all as though free from each; how he who surpasses the heavenly realms supports the foundations of the abyss; and how he who penetrates the innermost parts of the world also surrounds all its outward regions.

There the sweetness of fragrance surpasses the power of all spices and exceeds every perfume. There the ears of the blessed are caressed by the melody of harmonious sweetness. There, in meadows blooming with very pleasing beauty, shining lilies never fall, and purple roses with saffron-colored flowers do not wither.

Certainly, of the everlasting blessedness of that heavenly Jerusalem, there is incomparably more in reality than the human mind can conceive; more is conceived by the mind than can be explained in any words. Why, then, should I say more about the joys of those blessed citizens, since all the elements entirely serve their most fortunate will, and all things are turned at their nod and transformed according to their judgment?

For true is that saying: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Psalm 134). And what is said of the head ought rightly to be believed also of his members.

May almighty God introduce you, venerable sister, into these joys; and may he himself be your reward when he takes you to himself—he who became the price when he redeemed you. Commend me to Moses and Aaron, your leaders, namely the holy priests Vitalis and Rodulphus [Note: Concerning Vitalis and Rodulphus, see Letter 14 of Book V]. They know, of course, that we inserted headings contrary to the custom of a letter for this reason: to relieve the double tedium of an unpolished and overextended style.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0749]

## 787–788 THE FIFTY-FIRST LITTLE WORK: ON THE EREMITIC LIFE AND APPROVED HERMITS

### ARGUMENT

He attempts to lead the monk Teuzon—soon distinguished for holiness, who had left the monastery after disagreeing with his abbot, and who, after many insults, finally expelled the holy teacher himself when he had come to him together with that abbot in order to reconcile them—toward gentleness and moderation, by setting forth the causes and sources of such great arrogance. These were, plainly, that he had followed the institution of monastic life under no one’s discipline, as though he were his own teacher; and that, although he professed to be an hermit, he nevertheless spent his life in the middle of a city and among crowds of secular people.

Accordingly, he warns him not to adopt an individualistic manner of life, demonstrating how dangerous this is by the sad end of certain monks. He also shows that the actions of monks must be restrained by the bridle of discretion. Finally, lest he, thinking so highly of himself, despise others, he sets before his eyes the virtues of certain men who were nevertheless extremely modest and did not exalt themselves as he did. At last, in order to offer him an example of humility, he asks his pardon if anything perhaps seems to have been spoken too harshly by him.

[Col. 0749D] To Lord Teuzon, hermit: Peter, a sinful monk, sends the goad of renewed charity.

He is shown to love his neighbor less who pretends to disregard the injury of an inflicted wound so completely that he binds himself entirely under the censure of silence. For while he supposedly looks after himself by the virtue of patience, he thinks little of extending the hand of salutary correction to his fallen brother; and while he serves immoderate patience, he does not escape the sentence of diminished charity.

For the Lord does not say, “If anyone sins against you, endure it and remain silent”; rather, he says, “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him,” so that the one rebuked may return to his senses and, correcting what he did wrong, recover again the height of charity from which he had fallen.

There are, in fact, two persons: the one who has fallen and the one who has been injured. Charity, therefore, which judges between the two, ought so to balance the scales of justice and so to preserve the rights of equity between them by an unshaken examination that it should strive no less earnestly to prevent the injured party—God forbid—from falling through impatience than to raise, through the recompense of worthy satisfaction, the one who has fallen.

## [ON THE EREMITIC LIFE AND APPROVED HERMITS]

### CHAPTER I. With what difficulty Albizo and Blessed Peter Damian were admitted within the threshold

[Col. 0751B] Through distant regions unknown to us, across precipitous mountains and the rocky crags of the Alps, we sought you. At last, after reaching your door, following many volumes of our prayers and of your arguments, when the spirit had almost failed from its exhausting descent, we were finally admitted, like importunate headstrong men—Lord Albizo was accompanying me at the time.

Eager and not moderately desirous to receive instruction for our edification, we were immediately compelled, at the very beginning of our mutual conversation, to devote ourselves to certain quarrelsome disputes. We had been longing to examine subtle and hidden matters of spiritual warfare, yet could scarcely manage to ward off the tangled and useless questions arrogantly thrown at us, plainly the material of a foolish quarrel.

For we had come to see Elijah or Paul humbly hiding in the wilderness, but contrary to our expectation we found, in a sense, Xenocrates declaiming grandiloquently in the gymnasium; indeed, while intending to behold a gentle lamb for the sake of imitation, we encountered instead a savage bull violently brandishing its horns.

Amid the thickest hailstorm of questions and disputes, that gentle preacher returned, as far as possible, to our memory, saying: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels; but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all” (2 Timothy 2). And again: “Do not contend in words, for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (ibid.). This also had not entirely escaped us: “But avoid profane and empty speech, for it contributes greatly to impiety” (ibid.).

As we silently communicated these and similar thoughts to one another, our conscience also responded with that same Apostle, in a kind of loud silence: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Corinthians 11).

What more is there to say? At last, when we had been placed in a narrow pass and hemmed in by the straits of manifold objections, where the opportunity for reasoning ceased to be available, we immediately fled to the examples of the saints, so that at least those might be believed whose authority is unquestionably admitted as proof in every matter.

When Saint Romuald was brought forward as a witness concerning a certain point of dispute, the question was at once raised whether Romuald had ever been a saint or whether he was now received in paradise. Although this question concerning the holy man was raised against the faith of all the churches of our provinces, nevertheless, in support of our party’s position, we summoned as witnesses those saints whose celebrated and ancient reputation could not waver even among ordinary and ignorant people: namely, Leo and Gregory, once most illustrious bishops of the Roman see. One of them promulgates authoritative canonical decrees; the other irrigates the Church with the clear and profound fountains of heavenly eloquence.

But once these names had been mentioned, the same amount remained to be done. For the question was doubled concerning them as well: how can anyone be certain that these men too were such as deserved to be believed without hesitation, or even that they were worthy to be counted in the catalogue of the saints?

### CHAPTER II. How both were again shamefully expelled

As these and many other things flowed shamelessly through the course of our conversation—things that not only failed to produce the edification whose growth we desired but rather generated the useless darkness of interminable questions—we finally recalled the saying, “The Lord will make a brief word” (Isaiah 10). As though emerging from the stormy whirlwinds of a foaming sea, we tried to make for the safety of a harbor, and began with charity, about which there seemed to be no question.

There was, in fact, an intolerable and deep-rooted hostility between you and the abbot of your monastery. He, being a gentle man and simple of spirit, surpassed all the rights of worthy satisfaction and humility by his pledges, and appointed us executors of a pact of mediation between you and him.

But while we imprudently sought to arrange the friendships of others, we fell into irreconcilable hatred directed against our own heads. Rather, we fell upon the side of the barking Charybdis, although we thought we had escaped the shipwreck of Scylla’s whirlpool. Then, after a few irrationally offered explanations, poured forth impatiently amid quarrels and fear, so as to establish more firmly—not uproot—the hatred as massive as a beam, we were finally seized by our girdles and violently cast out; and, as though condemned, we were no longer deemed worthy of familiar conversation at the door.

We were punished with fitting vengeance, so that, having fallen into the crime of commending charity, we might be judged worthy of perpetual hatred—a harsh fate in the case of homicides. Nevertheless, lest we seem lightly to laugh at matters that pious minds should read with fraternal compassion, let it suffice to have woven the history of this shameful confusion up to this point.

### CHAPTER III. That arrogance’s swelling overtakes monks who dwell in the city

Now, if it is possible for you to listen patiently, I will not hesitate to explain merely where the origin of this diseased corruption has crept upon you.

You were worn down by no discipline of monastic training, chastened under the custody of no elders; still hard and rigid in the very recruit-training of your new conversion, you began to undertake the path of this purpose. You began to teach before learning, to expound before observing the commands of the rules.

To this is added the fact that you decided to lead the eremitic life not in the wilderness but within the walls of a populous city, where whatever is commanded by the author of so magnificent a name is seized upon as though an oracle of prophecy had been brought back from a Sibylline shrine.

But, I ask you, if you are a monk, what have you to do with cities? If you are an hermit, what have you to do with crowds of citizens? What do cells, noisy marketplaces, or towered fortifications contribute to you? Indeed, when people seek solitude in cities as though the forests had failed, what else should be believed except that they are pursuing not the perfection of the solitary life but rather favor and glory?

There, therefore, surrounded by the favor of the crowd that you have sought, whatever your mind, even when unprepared, dictates is held as law by your own judgment; whatever your headlong tongue lets flow is treated as a verdict. You do not measure yourself according to the testimony of your own conscience but rather according to the opinion of the flattering crowd, before which a saleable pallor in the face and the heard name of fasting produce astonishment in people’s minds.

Not to know wine in the city is a prodigy; to drink it in the wilderness is sufficiently ignoble. Oil in the wilderness is a great luxury; among the people, however, whoever does not even eat lard is awarded the palm of abstinence. Haircloth is clothing in the wilderness, but a spectacle in the city. To walk with one’s legs and feet uncovered is a rule in the wilderness, but in the marketplace it is regarded as indiscriminate affliction. In the wilderness a soft bed is rushes or papyrus; among citizens, being content with a coarse blanket earns applause.

What makes a rare way of life marvelous there is common here through brotherly society. Consequently, what is raised there by the trumpet of praise does not deserve glory here, where it has been generally adopted.

### CHAPTER IV. On the abstinence of certain brothers

But would that you were present and could judge with your own eyes what is done in these woods by men unknown and despised! Nevertheless, if there is perhaps some swelling of arrogance in you, may it not displease you to learn briefly something about their way of life.

To say nothing of their continual frugality, their shortage of clothing, the rigor of silence, and their constant withdrawal, there are some among us who, among the other costs of strictness, restrain themselves from drinking wine with such severity that for almost a decade they have tasted none of that liquor, not even at the Easter feasts. Some of them are still blooming in the flower of youth; others are already advancing toward the more mature age of venerable old age; others also deprive themselves of grapes and vinegar; but many abstain from rich foods, eggs, and cheese as though from meat.

### CHAPTER V. On Martin Storax

We have in a cell a rustic and uneducated man who can barely stammer through fifty psalms, yet repeats those same psalms seven times every day, always with litanies appended. For nearly fifteen years he has not gone out; he has neither cut his hair nor shaved his beard. His hair itself clearly bears witness to this, for it now perhaps flows down longer than he is tall. We by no means approve this kind of strictness.

His life follows this continuous pattern: for three days each week he eats absolutely nothing; for three other days he takes a certain measure of bread with water; on Sundays and the principal feast days he prepares for himself not a stew or any sort of broth, but a certain fried preparation as food. Merely to have seen it and not touched it we regard as almost a meal; to have tasted or even smelled it we count as part of the penance.

Furthermore, two snakes, as is said, have wandered familiarly in his cell for several years. He himself also admits that, while he lies prostrate and persists in the petitions of the litanies, they run about his head here and there in gentle, mild play; forgetting their poisonous bites, they offer him devoted service like retainers to the master of a household.

Behold: even poisonous beasts agree among themselves in serving monks, while the monks themselves, alas, recoil from one another with viper-like savagery.

It is astonishing that he tolerates such a great stench there without ever complaining; astonishing that for so many days he keeps muddy water in a jar like a cesspool for drinking; that he never washes his change of clothing and never changes his garments except when he is about to receive the Eucharist. Yet he immediately removes those garments and safely stores them for that purpose, for the sake of cleanliness.

He never receives food before sunset, except that on Sundays, preserving the reverence due to those days, he takes around the sixth hour one of the small offerings made for the sacraments, and thus, according to the rule, breaks his fast (Saint Benedict, Rule, chapters 38 and 41).

What should I say about his unexpected vigils? He himself once told me: “During the day, at no time do I grant rest to my limbs. In the evening, singing psalms and praying, I finally surrender my wearied entrails to sleep when I recognize that the hour of the nocturnal assembly is already approaching, so that as soon as invading sleep seizes the body with all its force, it may suddenly drive it away from the assault of daring violence, as though striking a bell.”

Often, when I was asked to go out for the needs of the churches or to establish peace, although I recognized that it would be harmful to me even if it benefited others, I consulted this brother in faith that divine grace might deign to instill in him what he should judge expedient for me.

At once holy simplicity fixed a concise conclusion to the proposed matter: “What use is a candle if it gives light to others while its devouring flame consumes it meanwhile?”

I gladly embraced this answer and resolved to observe it as divinely given, provided only that charity and obedience were preserved.

### CHAPTER VI. On Leo of Sitria and three other monks

But while I linger too long in enumerating the virtues of one man, I am delayed from touching even briefly upon the others. I shall therefore come to my lord Leo—truly a Leo—who continually challenges the ancient dragon, namely the head and author of wickedness, to battle; and from the very training of his unformed youth into mature old age he has fought against him tirelessly, as though armed face to face.

Truly a Leo, who, ever watchful, sleeps to the world and is in a sense absorbed in contemplation of divine things. What more should be said about this man than that we see him dead to the world and crucified with Christ? Here is the standard of perfect mortification; here is the rule of the solitary life; here is a discipline worthy of imitation by those hastening toward the summit of perfection.
