Whatever strictness and whatever continence have been mentioned above, understand them as present correspondingly in this man; above all, however, venerate in him charity, humility, and gentleness. His speech, sweet as honey, comforts the sorrowful, teaches the ignorant, and reconciles the angry. Who, frightened by the austerity of his correction, has not resolved to return? Or who, oppressed by however dense a darkness of approaching temptations, has departed without consolation?

He shows himself gentle to those who run well and stern toward those who offend. Yet he does so in such a way that austerity raises gentleness into authority, while gentle meekness in turn restrains that same austerity.

The rigor of abstinence in him is so great that in his face one sees more an image than the body of a living man. Once, when I asked him what consolation I might find, since even during fasts a small measure of bread seemed to me insufficient, he immediately gave me this advice:

“On other days put half of that measure before you; but on the day when you wish to relax something of the severity of your customary rule, allow yourself the whole amount of the prescribed quantity. Then the rare allowance will be sufficient, whereas what now seems small is offered without discrimination.”

As a remedy in such great need, this advice was in some fashion pleasing because of the merit of the one giving it; but my curious attention to eating, I confess, heard not what it had been expecting.

Recently also, during the familiar exchange of our conversation, he said to me: “My brother, let others do great things, according as divine grace has granted them; but I am not ashamed to be content with my weakness if, day by day, it can fulfill two years of penance.”

Once, while prudently instructing me to resist temptations, he related that something had happened to another man, as was appropriate to his subject. “I knew a brother,” he said, “who, while the spirit of fornication was grievously troubling him and he was devoting himself intensely to frequent prayers, was finally resting one night upon his bed when an angel of God stood beside him, seized a sword, and cut off his testicles.

“Although he thought he was awake, he did not dare to ask what was happening, being held down by the authority of the divine power. Yet he suffered such force of pain in his genitals as though a physical blade had actually cut away part of his body. From that time onward, the brother not only was no longer subject to such passions, but, as though the flesh had already died, felt no further sting of lust in himself.”

When I asked which brother it had been, he replied: “It makes no difference to me.” Much later, when forgetfulness might already have crept in, I encountered the man among others and said: “My father, did you not admit that something of this kind had happened to you?” Then, unexpectedly confronted, he did not think he ought to deny what he believed he had said.

But why do I linger over individual cases, when I see such a dense company of distinguished men looming before me? I shall therefore pass over my lord Lupus, the lamb of true gentleness. Before he shut himself permanently into the prison that he now inhabits for eternal freedom, he refrained from wine for approximately three continuous years and allowed himself no broth or sauce.

I pass over Peter, who permits no trace of a bed to remain in his cell but continually wears down the bare floor, whether in winter or summer. Nor do I count Leo, who always girds his loins with an iron chain over his naked body, lest he exceed the limit of sobriety by passing beyond the moderation of nourishment.

### CHAPTER VII. On Leo, the hermit of Praezensis

But behold, another Leo appears, who, having almost forgotten that he has completed the course of old age, has long borne the burden of aged years; and although a veteran soldier of the divine campaign, he still guards the camp with, so to speak, the fervor of a recruit.

Among his other gifts of virtue, he so excels in devotion to vigils that throughout the whole year, not even on the shortest night, the brothers gather for the nocturnal office before he has slowly completed the psalter with his litanies. Afterwards, according to the custom of the wilderness, he performs the psalter for the dead.

Moreover, although, as is commonly believed, he has already surpassed one hundred and forty years of age, after he had resolutely enclosed himself he bound himself by this rule as well: every day he should wear himself down with heavier scourges. On no day does he break his custom of eating, except on the more solemn feast days, when he eats only around evening.

Throughout his entire life he has never reduced his blood and has never taken an antidote. This too must not be passed over: divine grace has so anointed him with the oil of gladness that neither the gravity of old age has been able to draw a sorrowful expression across his face nor his more secluded life produce anything rigid or harsh in his countenance. Rather, he always appears cheerful, always joyful, always festive with a certain courteous serenity.

### CHAPTER VIII. On Dominicus Loricatus

But why, while commemorating holy men, do I wander through various places, when I hold within the threshold and before my hands the man whose praises I cannot adequately proclaim, unequal as I am to the task?

Since our cells are situated opposite one another, separated only by the intervening space of the basilica, he and I are neighbors. If I devote myself to enumerating his virtues, the days would pass before the material for writing appeared capable of running out.

I mean Dominicus, my teacher and my lord. His tongue is rustic, but his life is sufficiently skillful and graceful; and that life preaches far more usefully for edification through living deeds than the sterile tongue of certain people, which carefully weighs empty words adorned with polished urbanity.

For a long cycle of years he has been girded with an iron breastplate next to his flesh and wages unceasing war against wicked spirits. Always ready for battle, fortified not only in heart but also in body, he advances as a fervent warrior against the enemy ranks.

His continuous way of life is this: scarcely a day passes in which, singing two psalters and wielding scourges in both hands, he does not strike his naked body—and this during the less severe period. For during the periods of Lent, or whenever he has to perform penance—for he often undertakes a penance of one hundred years—then, each day, while striking himself with the blows of the scourges, he completes at least three psalters in meditation.

As we learned from him personally, a penance of one hundred years is completed in the following way. Since, according to our rule, three thousand strokes of the scourge regularly complete one year of penance, and since the chanting of ten psalms, as has often been demonstrated, allows for one thousand strokes, while it is beyond doubt that a psalter consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, those who calculate correctly find five years of penance in the discipline of this psalter.

Whether you count five twenty times or twenty five times, the result is one hundred. It follows, therefore, that whoever sings twenty psalters with the discipline may be confident that he has completed a penance of one hundred years.

Yet our Dominicus surpasses most people even in this, because while some exercise one hand in performing the discipline, he, truly a son of Benjamin [“son of Gera, son of Jemini”], fights tirelessly with both hands against the rebellious enticements of the flesh (Judges 3). As he himself told me, he easily completes this penance of one hundred years in six days, according to the customary practice.

### CHAPTER IX. On the rationale of the discipline
I also remember that, at the beginning of an approaching Lent, he asked us to impose a thousand years of penance upon him; and he completed almost all of them before the season of fasting had ended. But if this kind of penitential discipline should seem harsh to someone, and perhaps even superfluous, so that he does not himself undertake it and does not wish it to be undertaken by others, I shall briefly explain what I, a sinner, think about the matter [Note: Compare Letter 8 of Book V and Letter 1 of Book VI]. When the holy devotion of the faithful scourges itself in remembrance of its sins, it believes that it shares in the sufferings of its Redeemer. For our Savior himself, as the Gospel bears witness, was beaten with whips (Mark I; John XIX); and the apostles were beaten in the presence of the council (Acts I); and Paul received forty lashes less one, five times (II Cor. I). Innumerable martyrs likewise endured harsh beatings; anyone who has the leisure to read their histories cannot be unaware of this. We therefore rejoice that we have received this form of penance from those from whom, plainly, we learned the instruments of every spiritual discipline.

Moreover, if we establish fasts, vigils, nakedness, hair shirts, kneeling, and other practices of this kind as remedies of penance in order that through them we may suppress the allurements of vice and apply some bitterness to the pleasures of the flesh, what could more appropriately be called penance than when the sinner presents himself naked before the sight of his Judge and, in the manner of convicted thieves, chastises by scourging the very flesh that had sinned? It also adds weight to the matter that we read of certain people who, after their guilt, were carried away in ecstasy to judgment and there paid this penalty (Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium). Should we then believe that God himself, who exacts this form of penance from the unwilling, would disdain to receive it from the devout who offer it of their own accord? We have said these things by way of excess, in order to commend the discipline and remove from tender and delicate monks the boldness to disparage it.

Now let the narrative return to Dominic, with whom it had begun. Indeed, although curved old age already weighs him down and he is further wasting away through frequent illnesses, it is astonishing where such fervor burns in him, so that in spiritual exercises he always shows himself unconquered and tireless. For, as I learned from his own account, he often continues through two psalters while standing and carrying out the discipline, so that in the meantime he neither sits nor rests from the blows even for a moment, with an incredible fervor of mind.

Once, when I asked him whether he could spend some time kneeling under the weight of the iron garment, he gave me this answer beneath his obscurity:

796 “When my health answers my desire, I sometimes customarily bend my knees a hundred times for each group of fifteen psalms throughout the whole psalter.” At the time I did not attend carefully to this; but afterward, turning over in my mind what he had said, I was astonished and terrified that a thousand prostrations were performed by a weakened man in a single psalter.

One day, after Vespers, he entered my cell and said: “Master” (for out of humility he addresses me by this unworthy title), “today I did what I do not remember ever having done before: I completed eight psalters melodiously between day and night.” His whole face then appeared so rubbed by the scourges and so bruised by certain furrowed welts that he seemed to have been beaten like a ball, in the manner of pounded porridge.

His psalmody came so easily to him for this reason: as he himself asserts, he did not so much repeat the words with a tongue that loudly articulated them as pass through their meaning with the liveliness of his mind.

On one occasion he lived apart from me. When I had entered to see him and asked under what rule of life he was then living, he replied that he was living carnally, and that every Thursday, as well as on Sundays, he relaxed his customary severity of abstinence. When asked whether he ate any kind of stew, eggs, or cheese, he denied it. Again, when asked whether he ate fish or fruit, he said: “I give fish and fruit, if any are available, to the sick, of whom I sadly see no small multitude lying in our region.”

When I confined him with the questions of a strict interrogator, saying, “How, then, do you live more leniently on those days, if you eat nothing that must either be cooked by fire or found on trees?” he replied: “I gladly eat fennel with bread.” At once I clearly understood how carnally the man lived who had placed his delicacies in fennel.

He plainly possesses an abundant gift of tears, but one that alternates. When he restrains himself in confinement under strict silence, he soon weeps abundantly whenever he wishes; but if he is frequently engaged in conversation, he complains that he has lost the power to weep. I too often reproach him for the poverty caused by my slowness, saying: “Alas, my father, these tears of yours are unfruitful, since they cannot give birth to other tears through prayer. For I would wish—something that follows naturally—that just as you are my father, so your tears might likewise become the mothers of my tears.”

## CHAPTER X. A necessary admonition concerning the discipline of discernment

I could still write much to you, and other things no less worthy, about the brothers known to us, if I were not especially anxious to avoid the weariness of an over-elaborate style. I also fear that this page may fall into the hands of those about whom it speaks and offend the minds of those who rightly detest being praised in this life.

I have set these examples before you so that, while you consider perhaps the greater virtues of others, you may judge your own; and, putting aside the swelling of singularity, may recognize that you are running with many others in the stadium of sacred service. As soon as the things said to Job exceed his own strength, he immediately hastens to the refuge of penance (Job XXXIII), 797 so that he even places his finger upon his mouth, saying: “I have spoken lightly” (I Reg. X). After Elijah had learned that seven thousand men had not bent the knee to Baal, he learned not to swell with thoughts of his singularity, since he had many companions in his innocence.

Those whom I mentioned above were neither distinguished nor famous, nor certainly notable in the opinion of the crowd; rather, despised and clothed in rags, they judge themselves so inferior to all good people that they do not place themselves above us or people like us by any sign of conversion. Yet they do not disdain to eat with us at the common table; indeed, as though we were their equals, they familiarly offer us every service of charity.

You too, if you wish to walk rightly, discerningly, and fruitfully along the path of true religion, should be so stern and severe toward yourself that you appear cheerful and easygoing to others. Strive so to excel within yourself in the stronghold of uprightness that you nevertheless know how to bend mercifully toward weaker brothers. Arrange the reins of justice in the tribunal of your mind so that you do not become harsh toward those who offend, but forgive them leniently. Let there be sorrow in your heart and joy in your face. When a brother arrives, let your flesh feel relief, and do not be excessively troubled if you fail to complete the task of your customary service. When a brother knocks at your cell, let the sad wrinkles immediately disappear, let the contracted face relax, let a serene countenance meet him, and let your hastening brow display joy.

Count sin in yourself as a danger of death; in others, call it the frailty of their condition. Decide that another is worthy of the rod, while you consider yourself liable to scorpions. Do not be more righteous than the righteous; and although you fear committing sins, do not hesitate to grant pardon to those who sin. That is not true justice which drags other minds into the pit of despair. That is not praiseworthy medicine which cuts away what is rotten in such a way that it also corrupts what is sound. It is a harmful fire which tries to burn the thorns in such a way that, with raging flames, it also leaps upon houses and sets them ablaze.

Indeed, one who customarily and readily tears apart the vices of others will not escape the stain of sin; for although he may burn with zeal for justice, at some point he must stumble into the snares of detraction. Clearly, unless our own life shone brightly in our eyes, the conduct of others would not displease us so greatly. If we were strict with ourselves, as judges ought to be, another’s fault would not find such rigid censors; our discipline extends itself toward others, while, regarding our own excesses, only the claims of compassion and gentleness are preserved.

But why say these things? Because you are said to judge all your brothers with so harsh and supercilious a verdict that throughout the whole year you receive the divine sacraments only once—and then not from the priests of your own monastery, but from priests sought elsewhere. I repeat what you say: “Who ordained this priest?” The answer is: “That bishop.” And you ask: “How, or by whom, was he promoted to the office of bishop?” “By the pope, of course.” “But how that happened,” you add, “let them look to it themselves.” Then you continue: “Suppose at last that the pope freely consecrated him bishop; did the pope himself also freely ascend to the summit of the apostolic see?”

With this destructive darkness of astonishing questions, so far as you are able, you throw the whole world into confusion; and, like the sea, generating a storm from within yourself, you neither rest yourself nor allow others to live in peace. For from such foolish hesitations and others like them, heresies and schisms often emerge disastrously, cutting unwary human souls off from Catholic unity.

To address you in the apostolic words: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV). Not everyone who is in the governor’s residence is assigned the office of issuing judicial decisions; nor has everyone who is within the Church received the keys of the Church. When someone arrogantly stretches himself out to judge what belongs to another, he is found all the less capable of considering what belongs to himself.

The order of communal life is properly arranged when each person is content within the boundary of his own jurisdiction. But when one person oversteps another’s limit, every line of right living must necessarily be thrown into confusion. Let it therefore be enough for us to consider what belongs to us, lest, while we pursue what belongs to others without moderation, we be deprived of the fruit of our labor and its worthy reward.

“For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James II). And Paul says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (II Cor. V).

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the monk drowned in a river

I once saw a monk living the eremitical life with considerable strictness and severity. Pale in face, greatly afflicted in body, and with his eyes fixed upon the ground, he seemed dead to the world. He had not tasted wine for eleven years. But, O terrible judgment of God, and profound abyss of supreme strictness! It is painful to speak of it.

At one point this man fell into madness and, becoming savagely inflamed with the rage of a beast, suddenly tore himself from the hands of those struggling to hold him in different directions and from the bonds with which he was tied. Where a great whirlpool was spinning, he plunged into the chasm of the foaming river and perished.

Although no one’s merit can be lost through any form of death, we have nevertheless prefaced this account so that we may never place obstinate confidence in any of our good works, but may always fear what judgment heaven may pronounce concerning us. Let our minds not rashly presume to judge those who are with us; for although we see the path on which we are presently walking, we do not know where our course will end. The road that is being traveled is visible, but where it leads is hidden.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the monk who sought the devil’s protection

[Col. 0761C]

Since the opportunity has presented itself, we do not think that the terrible fate of another monk should be passed over either, even though we do not see that it particularly belongs to this little work.

In the monastery at Perugia, namely that of Saint Saviour, over which I myself recently presided, there had shortly before been a certain monk named Guinizo, exceedingly crafty and shrewd, intensely devoted to worldly arguments and contentious disputes. Since he did not cease to rage both against changing abbots and against disturbing the brothers, he went so far as to seek the devil’s protection for overcoming his rivals and even to surrender himself bodily to the devil’s command. The seductive spirit nevertheless promised him, at his request, that three days before he died it would announce his death to him.

The wretched man believed this and, living for a long time afterward, remained under this deceptive security. At last, when he had fallen ill, the wicked guarantor appeared and, as it had promised, announced that he would die the day after tomorrow. He immediately summoned the brothers and told them in order everything he had agreed upon with the most wicked spirit.

When they urged him, saying, “Confess; do penance,” he suddenly fell asleep and could not be awakened, whether they knocked or shouted. If they stopped speaking to him or wished to say anything other than “penance,” he soon awoke and spoke with them; but as soon as he again heard the word “penance,” he stiffened in his senses, overcome by sleep, until, delivered over to his horrifying death, he was unhappily handed over to the one to whom he had surrendered himself.

Afterward, for many nights, a black pack of dogs did not cease to stand by his grave and guard it as though it were a deposit, so that those who saw them were shaken with no small horror.

Alas, how harmful a thing a stubborn and contentious spirit is in a monk! Because this man refused to have temporal peace with his brothers, he lost the joy of eternal peace, plunged into Tartarus. Although this does not altogether fit the present style of writing, we have nevertheless taken care to commit it to these pages, so that a memorable event might not be removed by forgetfulness, but might be fastened here as though with a cord to a stake; and so that anyone who is restless may learn to what end an angry quarrel leads.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the patience of the monk who was blinded

Among all the things commanded to us by divine law, there is nothing toward which a monk should strive more earnestly than to have patience in all things, by which he may bear the injury of another’s perversity with equanimity. This virtue plainly carries a monk to the summit of perfection and gives him a courageous spirit when he fights against the enemies of God. It grants victory over all vices and makes the human mind unconquerable against the raging, headlong assaults of the world.

And what more can I say? Whatever has been said above, or could have been said, about the strictness of abstinence or any kind of bodily affliction is almost nothing if patience itself, the nurse of the virtues, is lacking. The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “Bodily exercise is useful for a little; but patience is useful for all things” (I Tim. IV).

When I was a young man residing in the city of Faenza for the sake of literary studies, I happened to hear the story I am about to tell. A quarrel had arisen between two men living near one another, and one of them gouged out the other’s eyes. After the blinded man saw that he had become of little use to the world, he sought admission to a monastery.

Later, when the man who had inflicted the injury himself fell ill and anxiously sought the monastic habit, he judged it inappropriate to be carried to the same monastery because of the man on whom he had recklessly laid hands. While the monks were secretly discussing the matter, news of it finally reached the more acute hearing of the blind man.

When he learned fully what was impending, he immediately began to beg earnestly and to implore with every prayer he could command that the brothers receive that man with complete charity and, in addition, order him—the blinded man—to labor in service as that man’s guardian and minister. Persisting in his importunate prayers, he finally obtained his request. He served with the clear eye of charity the man whom he could not see with the light of the flesh.

He diligently attended the bedridden man, warmed him with coverings, brought him whatever he needed, and gently encouraged him to take nourishment. He even gladly carried and brought back the sick man, as was said, to the private place of digestion.

Thus—yes, thus—the man who had lost the two lights of his bodily eyes shone with charity and patience as though with two eyes in the face of his soul.

## CHAPTER XIV. Where the writer concludes what has been said with humble satisfaction

I have set before you, Father Teuzo, the preceding material from a letter so that you may cease swelling with thoughts of singularity; I have included this final matter so that you may learn to endure with equanimity even the offenses of younger brothers, should any occur. Since I judged this especially necessary for your character, I have consequently preserved it as the final part of this disputational narrative.

Now, therefore, restrain that excessively rigid and stubborn disposition of your mind, and compose yourself toward your brothers with patience and gentle charity. Whoever does not live in harmony with his friends and fellow-dwellers because of his savagery must necessarily live alone and like a beast, after the manner of wild animals. Whoever, then, does not disdain to be a disciple of his Redeemer should learn to show himself gentle and humble toward his neighbors: “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

Finally, whoever desires to be a temple of the Holy Spirit, to repeat the same point, should not depart from humility and the quietness of gentleness. For he says: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet?” (Isa. LXVI).

Therefore do not strike at their minds with contentious questions; do not toss them about with your horns like a bull of grim neck, lest, while they flee from you, what was once said about a horned ox be hurled against you as a reproach:

> It has hay on its horn  
> [Note: Horace pretends that this is said of poets, *Satires* I.4.]

Show yourself, then, tranquil and quiet in the sight of everyone. Above all, submit yourself with complete obedience and humility to those who are from God, so that those who seek Christ in you may consequently find Christ, and so that, in the gentleness they see outwardly, they may discover the author of gentleness presiding more deeply upon the throne of your mind.

Clearly, if your breast is the ark of God, as is fitting for one under protection, let it contain not only the rod that strikes, but also the manna that grows sweet upon the palate of a brother’s mind. Let it contain not the zeal of bitterness that terrifies, but rather the zeal of charity that corrects beneficially. Let the thorn of correction prick the wound of those who offend in such a way that the oil of gentleness may also soothe it with a gentler kind of treatment.

But while we have ardently pursued the edification of our brother, we have gone beyond the proper length of a letter. For that reason, contrary to the custom of letters, we have also suitably attached headings to each section, lest the fullness of a fragmented style should seem to produce weariness in the reader’s mind.

Now, therefore, my dearest father and lord, I immediately throw myself at your feet [folio reading: *prostratus*] and humbly ask pardon with tears poured forth: namely, that you graciously forgive my mouth and not drive me, who have rashly presumed to rebuke you, away from the sweetness of your charity—provided, of course, that what has been set forth above is beneficially accepted.

For the sake of satisfaction, I do not refuse either to place my bare shoulders beneath your rod or henceforth to obey reverently the paternal laws of your holiness. I hope, however, that this correction of mine will not be without benefit to you. For while what has been rebuked by the boldness of a younger man may perhaps taste bitter to your mind, which is so weighty, so mature, and certainly so holy, you can plainly learn in your own person what you ought to feel in the hearts of others when you speak harshly to them.

I ask you, venerable father, always to deign to pray for me, a sinner. Since I do not hope to see your face again in this life, I ask the divine mercy that, when the belt of our service has been laid aside, it may bring us again before one another’s eyes in such a way that one citizenship of the heavenly Jerusalem may be assigned to us who have earned it, and that a mutual recompense of merits may extend to us both.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0763]

# 803–804. THE FIFTY-SECOND LITTLE WORK: ON THE GOOD OF THE RELIGIOUS STATE AND THE MORAL INTERPRETATION OF VARIOUS ANIMALS

## Argument

In this letter, after lamenting at the very outset the corrupted morals of humanity and the calamity of his own times, he extols the happiness of those who, fleeing the storms of the world, take refuge in the safest harbor of religion. In this regard he particularly admires the monks of Cassino, not hesitating to compare Mount Cassino itself with Noah’s ark, which during the Flood had been a refuge for every kind of living creature. Taking this as his opportunity, he digresses into descriptions of the natures and properties of animals, which, as Epiphanius does among the Greeks, he remarkably transfers and adapts to human conduct and usefulness.

To Lord Desiderius, archangel of the monks, and to the holy community, Peter, a sinful monk, sends his service.

Whoever carefully considers the crimes of the raging world understands what thanks you who have abandoned the world owe to your Redeemer, God. Shame and decency have perished; and while the discipline of ecclesiastical vigor gradually collapses, the plague of every vice and depravity increases day by day as it floods over everything. It seems especially in our own time that the prophetic word is being fulfilled:

> “There is no truth, there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed” (Hosea IV).

And because the ruling authority not only fails to restrain these things but allows them to occur with the joyful approval of its favor—and laughter is provoked where lamentation, indeed rage and impatience, were deserved—it is rightly said later by the same prophet:

> “They have made the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies; all are adulterers, burning like an oven heated by the baker” (Hosea VII).

And because the heat of greed or lust first seizes the princes, as though they were the roof-beams and rafters of a house, and then spreads through their subjects as through level ground, he added shortly afterward:

> “They are all hot as an oven, and they have devoured their judges; all their kings have fallen, and there is none among them who calls upon me” (ibid.).

And because a good people do not deserve good rulers, and therefore the whole world, like a single body, is drenched in the contamination of continuous crimes, the divine voice reproaches it through the prophet, saying:

> “Where is your king, Israel, who should save you now in all your cities? And your judges, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and princes’?” (Hosea XIII).

And immediately it adds:

> “I will give you a king in my wrath, and I will take him away in my indignation” (ibid.).

Thus it happens that, while the rulers of the world preserve not laws but profits, no judgment of legal sanctions restrains their subjects, who are also inclined toward evil. This is what the world suffers in our time, as is said through Isaiah:

> “Every head is sick and every heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I).

## ON THE GOOD OF THE RELIGIOUS STATE AND THE MORAL INTERPRETATION OF VARIOUS ANIMALS

## CHAPTER I. That religious people are like sheep snatched from the jaws of a wolf

For this reason, beloved, you must take the greatest care to give perpetual thanks to God, who has chosen you out of the world at a time when it is evident that anyone can be saved in it only with difficulty. You have fulfilled what is commanded through Zechariah, with the Lord crying out:

> “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north” (Zech. II).

And again:

> “O Zion, flee, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon” (ibid.).

To these words Truth says:

> “I have chosen you out of the world; and because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

For just as, if a fierce beast were to seize a weak sheep in its jaws, while a shepherd pulled even one of its limbs from the jaws of the beast greedily swallowing it, so Christ rescued you from the mouth of the bloodthirsty predator when, as the world perished, he chose you for the service of his obedience.

Hence it is said through the prophet Amos:

> “As if a shepherd rescues two legs or the tip of an ear from the mouth of a lion, so shall the children of Israel be rescued, those who dwell in Samaria” (Amos III).

Thus there is no doubt that, through the gift of more abundant grace, what is said elsewhere by the same prophet has been granted to you:

> “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. One part was watered, and the part upon which I did not rain dried up” (Amos IV).

For earthly and carnal hearts, parched as though by burning heat, wither under prolonged drought when they do not receive the streams of heavenly grace through showers of compunction. Concerning this land the divine voice says:

> “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V).

But concerning that mind which truly thirsts for the Lord and longs for the fountain of wisdom with unfailing desire, Isaiah says:

> “For I will pour out water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry ground. I will pour out my spirit upon your offspring and my blessing upon your descendants, and they shall sprout among you like grasses, like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLIV).

## CHAPTER II. That monasteries are fishponds of souls

When almighty God therefore removed you from the world and established you in his service under monastic discipline, what else is he seen to have done than, as once in the cataclysm, to choose you few from among the many perishing and bring you into the hiding place of a pitch-covered ark (Gen. VII), so that you might live?

The enclosure of a monastery is a fishpond of souls. In it live the fish that, according to the command of the Law, have little fins; and, so that they may be transferred into the body of Christ, they provide delicacies for the tables of the Israelites. Fish that have fin-like scales also leap above the waters.

What, then, are represented by the finned fish except chosen souls? They alone pass into the body of the heavenly Church, because now, supported by the little fins of the virtues, they long to leap through heavenly desire and seek what is above through contemplation, although they fall back again upon themselves because of mortal flesh.

Can the enclosure of a monastery therefore, in spiritual understanding, be more rightly called either merely a little pool or fishpond, as has been said, or also a catching-place for heavenly cattle, or indeed an aviary for birds? The Psalmist places these three kinds of animals when he says:

> “The cattle of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea” (Ps. VIII).

The prophet Hosea also mentions them when he says:

> “They shall be gathered into the beasts of the field, and into the birds of the sky, and also into the fish of the sea” (Hosea IV).

By which of these three names, then, would a coenobium be more properly expressed? But, as is clearly seen, all three names undoubtedly suit the monastery enclosure, since within it a diversity of spiritual animals is held together, fused in the fire of unanimous and undivided charity.

There live, as has been said, the spiritual fish, constantly swimming through the streams of sacred Scripture. For if there were not a spiritual fishpond in which heavenly rather than earthly fish lived spiritually, the Lord would never have said to blessed Job concerning the typical skin of Behemoth:

> “Will you fill a net with its skin, and a fishpond with its head?” (Job XLVIII).

There also are the cattle of that field of which Jacob says:

> “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. XXVII).

Concerning the cattle—that is, the elect living in the unity of holy charity—Isaiah says:

> “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together” (Isa. XI).

For through the inner organs of holy charity the wolf dwells with the lamb, because those who were robbers in the world rest in peace with the gentle and mild. The leopard lies down with the kid, because the one who was marked with the varied stains of his sins consents to humble himself with the one who despises himself and confesses himself a sinner. The calf, the lion, and the sheep dwell together, because the one who prepares himself through a contrite heart for a daily sacrifice to God, the other who raged like a lion in cruelty, and the third who persists like a sheep in the simplicity of innocence have come together in the folds of holy Church.

There also are the birds of heaven: those who raise themselves aloft on the feathers of the virtues and, from the citadel of their minds, look down upon all earthly things as they pass beneath them. Disdaining to creep along the earth under the yoke of carnal desire, they seek the freedom of the air and lift themselves toward heavenly things through the balanced contemplation of the mind.

The Lord speaks of these birds in the Gospel when he testifies that the mustard seed has grown into a tree:

> “When it has grown,” he says, “it is greater than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and dwell in its branches” (Matt. XIII).

Nor is it surprising that, through the figure of spiritual understanding, a human being is compared with the cattle of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea, since humanity itself, for whose sake all other things were created, is called every creature:

> “Go into the whole world,” he says, “and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI).

The natural actions of cattle are also found, through spiritual understanding, in human conduct, just as something is found in human beings that pertains to the duties of angels. The all-powerful God, creator of all things, just as he created earthly things for human use, so also through the very powers of their natures and the necessary movements that he implanted in brute animals took care to instruct human beings beneficially.

Thus, by means of the animals themselves, human beings can learn what they ought to imitate, what to avoid, what they may beneficially borrow from them, and what they should rightly despise. In this way, while the rational human being is instructed even by things lacking reason, he may always walk carefully and along an unobstructed path toward his creator by the way of wisdom.

But so that what we are saying may shine forth more clearly, let us not hesitate to set down here some animal natures and briefly indicate how they correspond to human conduct, as briefly and concisely as the brevity of a letter allows. We do not claim for ourselves expertise in such matters as though we had tested them personally; but whatever has been handed down to us by those who have labored to investigate the natures of things, we judge without dispute or retraction to be inserted into our little works.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the nature of the lion

807 Since the lion is the strongest of beasts and, as Scripture bears witness, fears the encounter with no one (Prov. XXXI), it also seems to possess, in a certain natural way, a subtle intelligence. When it is sought by hunters, it immediately catches their scent and, in order to deceive the pursuit of those tracking it, devises a new and crafty fraud. Dragging its tail along the ground, it covers its tracks as it walks; and thus it escapes the hunters’ snares and avoids being captured.

The wicked spirits are the hunters of human beings. In the manner of hunters, they seek flesh when they savagely pursue people of every kind in order to make them live carnally. But whoever belongs to that lion of whom Jacob says:

> “A lion’s cub is Judah,”

catches the scent of the hunter because he detects the ambushes of the crafty enemy (Gen. XLIX). He had cleverly caught that enemy’s scent who said:

> “We are not ignorant of his designs” (II Cor. II).

This is in contrast to those of whom John says:

> “They have not known the depths of Satan” (Rev. II).

The lion also covers its tracks with its tail, which is the hindmost part of its body, because it conceals the perversity of its former life under the covering of a new way of life, as it is said:

> “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI).

And elsewhere:

> “You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Thus the lion’s tail covers its impressed tracks when the covering of subsequent uprightness overlays its former life (Prov. XXVIII).

This also belongs to the matter: the same lion rejects yesterday’s food and turns away from the remnants of its own meal. And you, human being, utterly recoil from the sin by which you were satiated, lest you appear, like a dog, to return to your vomit (II Peter II).

Add also that the lion sleeps with open eyes. So you too, so rest while asleep to the world that you persevere in keeping your eyes ever wakeful in the Lord. Thus it is said:

> “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V).

The lioness gives birth to a dead cub. The cub remains dead for three days, until its father comes on the third day and breathes upon its face, thereby quickly bringing it to life.

May the contemplative life also give birth to you dead to this world, and may the almighty Father send you the spirit of his enlivening power. May he who on the third day raised up the lion’s cub from the tribe of Judah likewise make you, through the three-day span of faith, hope, and charity, live not for the world but for himself, so that with the Apostle you may sing aloud:

> “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the authalopus

[Col. 0768D]

The authalopus [antaplon or aptalon] is also an exceedingly fierce and violent animal, so much so that neither a hunter dares approach it nor any pursuer venture near it. It has long horns shaped like a saw, with which it can cut down very large trees and bring them to the ground. When it becomes thirsty, it comes to the Euphrates and drinks from it; near this river there grows a certain shrub called *Gericina*, with slender and projecting branches. When the authalopus comes to the *Gericina* and, in playful wantonness, attempts to sport among it, it entangles its horns in the thickly growing branches. When, after struggling for a long time, it is utterly unable to free itself, it begins to cry out in a loud voice. Roused by these cries, the hunter rushes up and kills it while it is held fast in its own bonds. [Col. 0769A]

You, servant of God, who have been instructed by the two Testaments and are invincibly fortified as though by two horns—by which you can both protect yourself with unconquerable defense and most vigorously drive back hostile spirits—after you have laudably begun to thirst for God, the living fountain, and after you have drunk from the streams of the great Euphrates, that is, of heavenly discourse, do not now occupy yourself with the business of secular affairs. Do not, like a wanton animal, entangle yourself in the branches of carnal pleasures, lest, while these bind you in their bonds, the utterly wicked adversary suddenly attack and, like an evil hunter, inflict a mortal wound upon you. The hunter is roused by the sound of the cry when the flame of lust sets you ablaze. [Col. 0769B]

For no cry of sins rises more loudly into heaven than that concerning which it is said to Abraham: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous; I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me” (Gen. XVIII). But if the incentives of lust are to lose their strength, the company of women must unquestionably be avoided from afar.

## CHAPTER V. That the sight of women must be avoided

On a certain mountain in the East there are fiery stones, called male and female, and known as *pyroboli*. When they are far apart from one another, they do not ignite; but if the female approaches the male, fire immediately comes forth from them, so that everything around the mountain is consumed by the vaporous flames. From these stones, therefore, we are taught that, if we do not wish to be consumed in the fire of lust, we should avoid the sight of women, lest from the appearance we behold a flame spring forth which may spread within us not through the thickets of a mountain but through the thickets of the mind. [Col. 0769C]

To extinguish the incentive of lust, it is also worthwhile for us to imitate the example of the beaver. Its testicles are especially necessary for medicinal remedies. When the beaver sees that a hunter is pursuing it because of its genitals, it bites them off and throws them before the hunter’s face. The hunter immediately withdraws, since he has seized the thing for which he was pursuing it. But if it should happen that another hunter finds it again and, pursuing it more fiercely and urgently, compels it to despair entirely of any escape, then, finding itself in desperate straits, it rises up into the hunter’s face and shows that it lacks the male organs for which it is being pressed. Thus it is freed from the weapon of its pursuer by showing that it lacks what is being sought.

You too, if you wish to elude the innermost hunter’s snares, diligently strive to cut away from yourself the kindling touches of seductive lust. Cut away from your breast every intention of indulging in excess, and so, as though driving back the root of wantonness, repel the shameful parts when you lay aside the act of lust together with the will itself. And when the evil spirit, like a wicked hunter, wages war against you with the weapons of wantonness, rise up immediately in your strength and show that you lack the material for indulgence [the wording *testones ostende* is uncertain in the transmitted text], saying to it: “Why do you pursue me? Why do you try to entangle me because of something that is no longer in me? Behold, I have no shameful parts, since, having cut away the seedbed of wantonness, I preserve inviolate my purpose of chastity.”

For my Lord says to me through Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree,’ for thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose the things that I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters’” (Isa. LVI). I am indeed one of those of whom he himself says in the Gospel: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX). [Col. 0770A]

In this way, therefore, we must carefully beware lest the crafty enemy pierce our hearts with the barbs of his temptations and, by the art of cunning deceit, tear away the fruit of chastity or of any good work. [Col. 0770B]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the hedgehog

The hedgehog also represents this figure. Covered all over with spines, it enters a vineyard at the time of the vintage and seizes whichever grape it sees to be the best. It immediately shakes it so violently that all its grapes are scattered upon the ground. Then, descending, it rolls over those same grapes until they are all pierced by the points of its spines. Thus it returns laden on every side and carries this food to its young. [Col. 0770C]

The vineyard of good works must therefore be guarded, lest the ancient enemy climb upon it and cast down the swelling and therefore ripe grapes of spiritual virtues; then pierce them with the points of his temptations and offer them as food to the beasts of the earth, that is, to hostile powers. Thus shaken and cheated of his labors, a man may cry out with a groan what is read in the Song of Songs: “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I did not keep” (Song II).

For just as the hedgehog strips a cluster of its grapes, so the devil strips any careless person of good works. The spirit of wickedness is crafty in a thousand forms; it is always devising new tricks of illusion so that it may not only strip those whom it deceives but also utterly devour them.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the little fox

The little fox also presents an image of this. Pretending to be dead, it truly brings death upon birds. When it is hungry and nothing presents itself to its anxious search as food, it looks for red earth; and when it finds it, it rolls its whole body in it so that it appears to be bare and bloody flesh. Then it throws itself upon the ground as though dead and holds its breath so that it does not breathe. Since it thus appears bloody and swollen, careless birds do not doubt that it has perished. They descend to eat it; but it suddenly springs up, seizes them, and truly devours those whom it had deceitfully invited to devour it. [Col. 0771A]

The ancient deceiver represents this fox: to those seeking carnal gain he pretends to be dead and exposes his works to them as though they were his limbs, for them to feed upon: “The works of the flesh are manifest, as the Apostle says: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, greed, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries” (Gal. V). These are plainly the entrails of the wicked spirit; these are the daily food of the reprobate and of those who live according to the flesh. While the lost gape at these as though hungry, the malignant spirit, like the deceitful fox among birds, swallows them down and transfers them into the entrails of its own body. Of such it is said through the Prophet: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII). [Col. 0771B]

Herod was a portion of this fox, designated by the name of his head when the Lord said: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII). This fox lay hidden in that scribe as in the pit of its own den, when he heard from the mouth of Truth: “Foxes have holes” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). The offspring of this fox are likewise the heretics, of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II).

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the polyp

And why should it seem strange if the kingdoms of the devil are seen to excel in the deceitful cleverness of the little fox, when among fish also there is found no lesser ingenuity of artful fraud? Since man has been placed above all living creatures, he is warned through those creatures over which he rules to beware of dangers. [Col. 0771C]

The polyp finds a rock in shallow waters along the shore. It clings to it by an astonishing means and assumes its color and appearance. Thus, covering its back in the likeness of a stone, it catches many fish that slide toward it without any suspicion of fraud; and while they simply suppose it to be a cliff, it shuts them in through the accidents of its hidden craft. By such devices, therefore, prey that comes of its own accord is deceived; and while it does not fear fraud, it does not know how to avoid the abyss of ultimate shipwreck.

But what is the rock except Christ? What is the polyp except a deceitful and perverse man, and therefore a heretic? He clings to the rock and falsely assumes the appearance and color of stone, because, like his master, he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. XI). He clings to the rock because, although not through his conduct, at least through his profession he is joined to the holy Church; and, seizing and devouring unsuspecting fish, he entangles the dull-witted and simple in the errors of his faithlessness. Hence the Apostle also says: “For you endure it if anyone devours you, if anyone takes you captive” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, in such tricks and frauds of animals the mystery of a salutary allegory is sometimes discerned.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the hydrus and the crocodile

The hydrus is an animal that lives in the depths of rivers and is savagely hostile to crocodiles. When it sees a crocodile sleeping with its mouth open on the riverbank, it rolls in the mud, so that with its slippery body it may more easily slide into its jaws. Then it swiftly leaps into the mouth of the sleeping crocodile, which, suddenly roused, swallows it. But the hydrus tears apart all its entrails until, when the crocodile has been utterly destroyed, the hydrus emerges alive and victorious from its carcass. [Col. 0772A]

What does this crocodile represent except death and hell? What does the hydrus signify except the victory of the Savior? The hydrus is therefore covered with mud when our Redeemer clothes himself with the mud of human flesh. It enters the crocodile’s belly because the Lord penetrated the bars of hell. It destroys the innermost parts, and the Lord overturns the dominion of death. The hydrus returns in victory after gnawing through and penetrating the corpse, because our Savior, after biting hell by dying, rose from the tomb in triumphal glory. Hence, through the Prophet [and Apostle], the victor taunts death: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV). And again: “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, I shall be your bite” (Hos. XIII).

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the charadrius

We do not doubt that the charadrius also expresses a figure of our Savior, if we consider his wondrous nature with due amazement. This bird is entirely white, and no spot of blackness is found in its feathers. Anyone who is ill can determine without doubt, by the presence of this bird, whether he is shortly to recover or must die as death approaches. For if the illness is mortal, as soon as the bird sees the sick person it immediately turns its eyes away and looks at him no further. Thus an indication is given that the sick man will die from the malady he has contracted. But if that sick person is going to live, the charadrius at once fixes its gaze upon his face, draws all his sickness into itself, and then flies eagerly toward the heat of the sun; by exposing itself to the sun it burns away the sick man’s illness and scatters it through the air. A wondrous sight! Immediately the sick man rises and, cleansed of all the heaviness of his afflictions, recovers. [Col. 0772C]

Reason clearly shows that the figure of this bird suits our Redeemer. Christ is white like the charadrius, because no stain of sin appeared to darken him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II; Isa. LIII). Of him the bride also says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song V)—white in virginity and innocence, ruddy with the blood of martyrdom.

He came as a merciful visitor to the sick people of Israel, but he turned his face away from them, since they were dying of the disease of faithlessness and unbelief. When he looked upon the Gentile people, who were likewise sick, he mercifully fixed upon them the eyes of his compassion, transferred their sickness to himself, and restored them to their former health. [Col. 0773A]

“For truly,” as it is said through Isaiah, “he himself took our infirmities and bore our sins. And we thought him to be like a leper, struck by God and humbled; but he was wounded for our iniquities and crushed for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruising we were healed” (Isa. XIII).

He scattered the sickness through the air by flying about, because he defeated the aerial powers by his strength. He ascended into the heat of the sun and burned away the force of the illness, because, returning to the Father, who is the sun of justice, and swallowing up death, he ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men (Ps. LXVII; Eph. IV).

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the phoenix

The phoenix, a bird that dwells in the regions of India or Arabia, likewise signifies our Redeemer in both his death and resurrection. He himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X).

When this bird has completed five hundred years of life, it enters the woods of Mount Lebanon and loads both wings with various fragrant spices. The priest of the city of Heliopolis detects this by certain signs, and immediately, having gathered together branches and twigs, builds a heap. Upon this heap the phoenix, laden with spices, descends and burns itself with the fire placed beneath the branches. [Col. 0773C]

On the following day the priest comes and finds the wood he had arranged burned up. Carefully examining its ashes, he finds a very tiny worm, yet blazing with the sweetness of an extraordinary fragrance. Returning on the second day, he finds it taking the form of a little bird through feathers and the flight feathers of its wings. Finally, on the third day, the priest comes and sees a fully formed phoenix standing in complete condition.

The phoenix therefore laid down wings filled with the sweetness of spices because our Redeemer descended to us from heaven with the double fragrance of both Testaments, saying: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. XIII).

At first he is found to be a worm—that one indeed who says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI). I mean the one signified by that worm which rose in the morning, struck with its tooth the ivy placed over Jonah’s head, and made it wither (Jonah, final chapter). For, preceded as though by the morning sun, the Lord of evangelical grace cut off the synagogue, truly a barren ivy, with the tooth of his severe judgment and made it wholly withered and dry.

Then the phoenix becomes feathered and is lifted into the air, equipped with the oar-like feathers of its wings, because the Lord, victor over death, is raised to the Father’s seat [*consessum*, OCR uncertain], while the heavenly powers everywhere rejoice together. Of him the Psalmist says: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII). [Col. 0774A]

Indeed, wings are implanted in us also, according to our measure—namely, spiritual virtues. If we use them manfully, we are lifted to heavenly things; but if through the sluggishness of indolence we lay them down, we must be plunged into the depths of the vices that steal upon us.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the *sarra* or *serra*

The *sarra* [*serra*], a sea-monster with very long fins, represents this matter. As soon as it sees a ship under sail, it too girds itself with the oars of its wings and strives to sail after the ship. But after scarcely lasting through forty stadia of this contest, it fails, and, exhausted, lowers its wings amid the perils of the sea. It is therefore forced, while the waves devour it, to slide back again to the place from which it began to row. [Col. 0774B]

The ship that sails signifies the holy Church or any faithful soul. Raised upon the wood of the cross, it avoids the foaming storms of the wave-tossed world and hastens by the rowing of virtues toward the harbor of perpetual rest.

But the *sarra*, while pursuing it, gives out, because any soft and dissolute soul begins fervently enough but, growing weary in labor, does not reach the shore of perfection which it had resolved to enter. There are some who, when they see others proceeding along the path of an honorable life, take up the journey after them, stirred by devout desire. But when they are overwhelmed either by excessive labor or by the flooding waves of some adversity, they immediately fail in their work; and thus, in the likeness of the *sarra*, they slide back to the place from which they had begun to sail. Of such it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. II). And the wise man says: “There is a friend who is a companion at table, but he does not remain in the day of necessity” (Ecclus. VI).

The rulers of the Churches ought therefore to come to the aid of such people with tireless exhortation and, amid the very dangers of the raging storm, strengthen those who are tossed about with the powerful arm of preaching, so that they may prevent them from being swallowed by the sea’s shipwreck while confirming them in the strength of perseverance upon the unshaken root of steadfastness.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the sea-urchin

The sea-urchin, a very small fish, also indicates this. It brings immense ships running under full sail to a complete stop. It is certainly remarkable how a fish so tiny in body can hold back so enormous a vessel, so that it seems to cling as though fixed by roots. [Col. 0774D]

The sea-urchin therefore fixes a ship in the waves. Should not the ruler of the Church likewise strengthen souls tossing amid the floods of temptations? To him who, not long before, had begun to sink while his feet tottered upon the sea, but deserved to be sustained by the hand of his rescuer, it was said: “And you, when you have once turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII).

Let the bishops, therefore, diligently watch over the souls entrusted to them, lest the ravager attack again those whom they have once rescued from the disasters of the world and compel them once more to return to their vomit.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the tiger, and what is mystically understood through it

The tiger gives an indication of this matter through a certain likeness. As the story goes, whenever it finds the empty den from which its offspring has been carried away, it immediately and swiftly follows the tracks of the abductor. Although he may outstrip it with the agility of a swift horse, he does not doubt that he can be overtaken by the more agile beast, as though by flight. When he sees that no refuge is open to him, he contrives the following trick by deceitful cunning: when he discovers the beast close behind him, he throws a round glass sphere before its eyes. Looking at it, the tiger is deceived as though by the reflection of its own body in a mirror and supposes that it is seeing its young. [Col. 0775B]

It therefore holds back its course, wishing to embrace its offspring. But when it discovers that it has been cheated by an empty image, it pours forth all its strength to catch the horseman. As it presses upon the fugitive with greater speed, he throws another sphere before the pursuer’s eyes. Yet the mother’s memory of the deception does not exclude her persistence. The tiger, as though about to suckle its young, turns the false image over in its mind. In this way the tiger is deprived of its young, and no vengeance is taken upon the hunter.

To apply this appropriately to ecclesiastical purposes, what is the hunter except a preacher? Hence it is said through the Prophet: “I will send many hunters against them, and they shall hunt them from every mountain and from every hill” (Jer. XVI). And what should be understood by this tiger except the devil?

We seize a cub from the tiger when we call any person converted from the world—which is the devil’s den—to the way of holiness. When, therefore, we feel the spiritual tiger running after us through the devices of its temptations, we throw a glass sphere before it when we show it fragile human beings in whom it may see its own image. To show it its own people means to hide our own people from its destructive sight. The ancient enemy sees his own image in his people, in whom he finds the perversity of his own wickedness. [Col. 0775C]

Concerning these glass-like people, reflecting his image, it is said in the Apocalypse: “If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark upon his forehead and upon his hand” (Apoc. XIV), and so forth.

Let us therefore strive to guard the cubs we have taken from the tiger, so that, having been snatched from the bloody breasts of the savage beast, we may not cease to refresh them daily with the milk of heavenly discourse. Otherwise, God forbid, what was said to the Pharisees may be applied to us: “Woe to you, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has become one, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matt. XXIII). Let rather that be applied to us which Truth says to the Father concerning himself: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John XVIII). Of him John also says: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John XIII).

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the pelican, and what it signifies

Finally, how greatly he loved his own, the pelican also shows through the power of its nature. This bird, as those who have devoted themselves to investigating the natures of animals report, loves its young beyond comparison, but its ungrateful offspring does not repay it with a fitting return. As soon as its young begin to grow, they all together attack and assail both parents. The parents strike them back, and because they do not know how to observe moderation in discipline, they turn the rod of instruction, so to speak, into swords, killing their children with excessive blows. On the third day, however, the mother bends over the dead, opens her side by striking it with her beak, and from it maternal blood drips upon the lifeless young; immediately it restores them unharmed to life. [Col. 0776A]

This event seems not so much a figure as an evangelical history. Through Isaiah the Creator of human beings openly complains: “I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have despised me” (Isa. I). He was also struck by those same reprobate sons, as the pelican is by its young, as another Scripture says: “Wicked men rose up against me without mercy; they sought to kill me, and they did not spare spitting in my face and wounding me with their spears.” [Col. 0776B]

The pelican kills its young by striking them back, because God struck the perverse people with the grievous calamity of captivities and wars. As it is said to them through the Prophet: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. V).

But good is repaid to the ungrateful children in place of evil when they are recalled to life by their mother’s blood. The Wisdom of God, the mother of all living things, hanging upon the cross, opened his side and thus recalled the slain to life through the outpouring of his most holy blood.

But just as the young of this bird, as we have said, express the hardness of ungrateful offspring, so, conversely, the hoopoe presents a figure of piety. Thus, just as a discerning mind finds in one something to reject, so Christian piety may learn from the other what to imitate.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the hoopoe, the eagle, and the coot

When these birds are weighed down by old age, so that they can neither fly nor see, their children, moved by dutiful compassion, pluck out their parents’ old feathers, warm their eyes with their own wings, and soothe their entire bodies on every side as though by rubbing and stroking them. Until, renewed throughout their bodies, they grow young again, with feathers flowering everywhere, they recover both sight and flight through the devoted service of their offspring, as though returning to the first bloom of youth.

But why should we marvel at the hoopoe displaying the entrails of mercy toward its parents, when we see the coot extending maternal compassion even toward the offspring of another kind? For, as investigators of nature report, the eagle, which is called the queen of birds, exposes its young to the flashing rays of the sun and holds them suspended in the vastness of the air with a loving talon. Whoever preserves the fearless sharpness of his eyes with undisturbed strength of sight, the mother judges fit to perpetuate the glory of the royal race. But if any one of them turns away his eyes, dazzled by the sun’s ray, he is cast out as degenerate and unworthy of such outstanding nobility and is not counted among the offspring, like one disinherited and illegitimate. [Col. 0777A]

Whoever through weakness of sight is deprived of his natural nobility does not in some sense receive the inheritance of his race among the freeborn offspring.

But when this eaglet has been cast down from the eminence of its native lineage, a certain common bird—the coot, called in Greek *phēnē* (φήνη)—receives it as an adopted child and kindly nourishes it among its own young as though it were natural to them. Thus the one whom the eagle cruelly made deprived of his paternal inheritance, the coot adopted as a co-heir to its own children, as though moved by maternal compassion.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning vultures and the weasel

So that, being engaged in spiritual combat, we may also borrow the weapons of virtue from birds: just as we are astonished at human—or rather Christian—compassion in the coot, so let us admire even more deeply the fruitful virginity of vultures. They are said, unlike other birds, never to indulge in intercourse, but to conceive entirely without any mingling with the male sex. Thus, if human examples do not move us to preserve the purity of chastity, at least the modesty arising from the virginity of vultures should impel us. Nor does a short span of life confine those born from this astonishing singularity, since their long-lived existence extends to as many as one hundred years.

Bees likewise are free from intercourse, and in giving birth they are not corrupted in any way. Just as one sex is not mingled with the other in conception, so virgin integrity is not violated in producing offspring. For it is not a womb but, so to speak, a mouth that gives birth to their young; they remain wholly undefiled and intact, free from every contagion of corruption. With their mouths they gather their young from leaves and thus send forth the swarm of their posterity.

But why should we proclaim the miracle of fruitful virginity only in flying creatures, when even in lowly creeping things we can admire conception and birth no less? The weasel, as physicians report, conceives through its mouth but gives birth through its ear. If we consider it suitable to compare human beings with filthy and insignificant creatures, we may perhaps appropriately apply this to certain brothers who fast less but obey humbly.

By conception through the mouth we understand food, as Truth says: “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled into the sewer” (Matt. XV). By birth through the ear obedience is signified, as it is written: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). [Col. 0777D]

There are some brothers who, either because of bodily illness or because of mental weakness, can scarcely fast, but they eagerly gird themselves for the execution of obedience and undertake whatever is enjoined upon them. The more strength they receive from food, the heavier labors of obedience they bear. Through the mouth, therefore, they conceive food as seed by eating it with pleasure; and they bring forth the fruit of that food through labor in obedience, as through the ear. The seed that enters through the mouth emerges through the ear, because, so to speak, the conception of food gives birth to the fruit of obedience; and what delights them when they eat it as though conceiving, the labor of obedience exhausts them as though in childbirth.

The asp, on the other hand, because it blocks its ears against enchantments, signifies the disobedience of an obstinate mind. When the magician Marsus charms it at the mouth of its cave so that it may come out, it immediately presses one ear firmly against the earth and places its tail against the other like an impenetrable barrier. Thus, while the sorcerer’s voice does not penetrate the interior of its ears, it remains motionless in its den. The depravity of many people imitates the example of this serpent: while they love earthly things here, they do not trust in the lastingness of the life to come there. They place earth and tail against their ears, as it were, so that the voice of preaching may not enter.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the ascida and the halcyon

Just as the asp expresses those who fix their hearts upon earthly and temporal things, so the ascida [*asida*] represents those who place their hope in heavenly things. It is indeed a winged animal, but unable to fly; it is also naturally forgetful and devoid of the powers of memory. Therefore it never gives birth except when, looking toward the stars, it recognizes that the Pleiades (*vergiliae*) have already begun to rise toward the upper regions.

It gives birth in summer, around the month of June, trusting in the heat of the sun. It hides its eggs in dust or sand so that, while the mother forgets her young and complete forgetfulness conceals the place where she deposited them, the warmth of the sun and the mildness of the air together may cherish the eggs, and the young may emerge as though from the mother’s attentive brooding. With the sun acting as midwife, the young of the ascida are born, warmed as though the mother herself were brooding over them from above.

This bird, conscious of its own forgetfulness and despairing of giving birth by itself, first raises its eyes to heaven, so that the mildness of the air may supply its young with what the mother’s dullness denies them. So we too, in order that the germ of good work may spring forth from us, should not hesitate to implore the favor of the divine Spirit from heaven, so that he himself may pour strength into our hearts, which our own foolishness weakens, for the production of offspring that brings salvation.

The bird called the halcyon is also said to be wondrous in producing its young. Just as the bird we have mentioned seeks summer warmth in giving birth, so this one chooses winter, amid the cold of the seashore. In winter it lays its eggs in the sand of the seashore, precisely when the force of storms rises more violently into heaps and the stronger waves strike the shores. But, O exceedingly astonishing miracle of heavenly ordering! As soon as the halcyon has laid its eggs upon the shore’s sands, no matter how rough the waves or how violently the storm has shaken the sea, the ocean becomes calm with peaceful tranquility. The swelling waves subside, all the whirlwinds of the raging winds grow still, and as long as this bird broods over its eggs, the sea lies calm and quiet. [Col. 0778D]

For seven days it sits upon the eggs, and for seven days after they are hatched it nourishes its young. In this very brief span of time they grow up and, becoming fledged, begin to fly away on the oar-like feathers of their wings. During these fourteen days the weather is clear, the sea calm, and no storm of blowing winds hisses at all.

The holy Church holds the type of this bird, since through the number seven it both broods and nourishes. Those whom, through the sevenfold Spirit of grace, it gives birth to faith in baptism, it brings through the gifts of that same Spirit to the growth of holy action. But in explaining the birth of this bird we have postponed lingering over the matter, lest we too seem to produce weariness for our readers. We have therefore passed over this without explaining it, so that it may be merely a wonder to readers but become a sacrament of spiritual understanding to those who consider it more deeply.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the doves, the ibis, and the hyena

Nature also offers no ordinary marvel in the case of doves. In the regions of India there is a tree called in Greek *peredixion* [*peridexion*], whose fruit is exceedingly sweet and very pleasant. The doves take great delight in the favor of this tree, for its fruit refreshes them and its shade protects them.

A most terrible dragon pursues them with savage ferocity and attempts to swallow them, opening the abyss of its bloody throat. But just as the doves fear the dragon, so the dragon likewise fears the tree we have mentioned. It fears especially the tree’s shadow, so that if the shadow lies on the right side of the tree, it flees far away to the left; but if the shadow is seen on the left, it turns to the right. [Col. 0779C]

As long as the doves remain beneath the shelter of that tree, the cruel beast cannot harm them by any ambush. But if it finds them far from it, it suddenly attacks them without any obstacle to prevent it.

We, to whom dove-like simplicity is commanded, must plainly flee to the tree of the sacred Scriptures if we wish to avoid the bloody rage of the inward dragon.

But the one whom the dragon signifies is likewise indicated by the ibis. For it is a dusky and unclean bird, polluted by the foul squalor of obscene excrement. It always feeds on dead carcasses and continually dwells near the shores of the sea, ponds, or rivers. It searches out whatever putrid or decayed corpse is cast out by the waters [Col. 0779D], so that it may feed upon it, since it fears to entrust itself to the waves; and because it cannot swim and dares not plunge into the currents, it is content to satisfy the frenzy of its appetite with whatever filth the waves spew forth.

But whom does this bird represent, as it prowls around the margins of the waves in the frenzy of hunger, except the one of whom Peter says: “For our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Peter V)? What else do the corpses of fish cast out upon the waters signify but the rotten and decaying hearts of those who live carnally and are rejected? Of them the Apostle says that they “are rejected men, shipwrecked with regard to the faith” (II Timothy III).

The sea retains living bodies but casts out corpses; so also, in the streams [Col. 0780A] of Scripture, those can remain who live for God. Whoever dies to faith or to right conduct, however, must necessarily be vomited out—corrupt and foul—from the body of Christ, which is the Church, as Scripture says: “Because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation III).
