Indeed, because she grows lukewarm from the warmth of what she had previously conceived, as though from the man she had been she turns herself into a woman; and for this reason she is aptly compared with the hyena, which sometimes changes from male to female and at other times from female to male. Therefore it is called an unclean animal and, for that reason, is forbidden as human food. Concerning it Jeremiah says: “The den of the hyena has become my inheritance” (Jeremiah XII).

## CHAPTER XX. On the panther

[Col. 0780B]

The panther appears wholly contrary to the dragon by the diversity of its nature. This animal is indeed variegated in color, but beautiful in appearance and gentle by reason of its simplicity; it is proved to be hostile only to the dragon. After the panther has refreshed itself with various kinds of hunting, it withdraws into its lair and sleeps. After three days, restored by sleep, it rises and emits a great roar with a cry; together with that roar there issues so marvelous a fragrance of sweetness and intensity that it seems to surpass every kind of perfume or spice.

All the beasts of the forests to which that scent reaches immediately gather around it and delight in the breath of such sweetness. The dragon alone, when it hears the panther’s voice, [Col. 0780C] contracts in extreme terror and at once hides itself in underground caves. There, unable in any way to endure the power of so great a fragrance, it stiffens in stupor and, exhausted of strength and utterly helpless, collapses as though dead. The other animals, however, because they are nourished by the scent of that delightful sweetness, never leave the fragrant panther’s footsteps wherever it goes.

Anyone devoted to sacred eloquence knows with how many flowers of interpretation this subject might abound. But we wish to extricate ourselves from it as quickly as possible, since we are hastening on to other matters.

The panther is plainly interpreted as “the one who receives all things,” and we do not doubt that this suits the one who says: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII). It is variegated, and Christ is clothed in the variety of all nations. Since the panther is beautiful, it is not unlike him of whom it is written: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm XLIV). And the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely” (Song of Songs I).

As for the fact that it is a gentle animal, this too is said of Christ through Isaiah: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem, for your king comes to you, gentle and saving” (Isaiah LXII).

When he says, “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John IV), he is, as it were, satisfied by certain hunts—the first fruits of the elect. He himself, having slept in death for three days, afterward emitted the roar of apostolic preaching and spread through the forests of all nations the fragrance of spiritual perfume. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII). He also says: “Thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord, and who through us manifests the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing—an odor of death unto death to some, but an odor of life unto life to others” (II Corinthians II).

This, then, is the fragrance of spiritual grace, this is the perfume of human salvation which the heavenly panther breathes forth, so that it may draw to itself the wild beasts of the forests—that is, the multitude of the nations. The dragon alone is plunged into the abyss of an underground pit, because the ancient enemy, who according to John is called the devil and Satan, was cast down from heaven and is bound in the abyss by the chain of the heavenly sentence (Revelation XXI).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the salamander, the doe, and the lynx

[Col. 0781B]

The salamander too, although small, is said to possess a remarkable nature, to such an extent that if it should happen to fall into fire, all the fire’s power is immediately extinguished, as though by a flood of overflowing water. To make clear what is signified by this, humility in patience restrains the fire-breathing man from the heat of vengeance.

The doe, which in Latin is called *caprea*, also offers a useful example for our way of life. Living on the peaks of mountains, it possesses not merely the ability to see with remarkable acuity but also to distinguish with extraordinary discernment, so that it can see people in distant and far-removed regions and shrewdly determine whether hunters or travelers are approaching.

So we too, if we abandon earthly things and strive upward to the lofty citadel of the mind, are raised by the divinely bestowed grace of discernment to distinguish spirits, whether they are from God: whether they direct us toward our homeland like travelers, or drive us like hunters toward the snares of their temptations and the traps of their ambushes laid below.

The lynx likewise has such incomparable sharpness of sight that it can penetrate not only any solid body but even walls of stone. This is demonstrated in the following way: if a lynx stands on one side of a wall and meat is placed on the other, it immediately longs for it and pants for it to be given to it, as though nothing at all stood between them.

If, then, a dumb animal possesses such lively keenness of vision, how much more deeply does almighty God see into the innermost parts of the human mind? “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews IV).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the nature of serpents

But in serpents too there are found certain indications of natural cunning, which may not unprofitably be drawn into examples for our way of life. When a serpent [lacuna] grows old and its eyes begin to grow dim, for a period of forty days and as many nights it takes no food at all but is worn down by continual abstinence.

The more its body is compressed by the dryness of emaciation, the more its scaly skin is loosened; and as the flesh diminishes from its former bulk, the exhausted skin becomes distended. Then it seeks either a fissure in hard earth or a crack in a stone, and, forcing itself through the narrow opening, it passes across it, thus completely shedding its skin together with its old age. It immediately becomes new, and with this its strength and sight are restored.

We too, if at some time we grow lukewarm from the youthful fervor of holy desire and become dim-sighted through the old age of a dissolute life, should pass through the narrow straits of strict repentance, so that, while we shed the old skin of outward desire, we may return to the former newness of the inner person.

There is another characteristic of the serpent: when it desires to drink, it first vomits out its venom; but after it has drunk enough water, it returns to the place where it vomited and takes back its vomit.

A certain presbyter reported that, in his presence, a serpent vomited upon a stone and then hurried off to a spring to drink. While it was making for the spring, the presbyter turned over the stone. When the serpent returned and did not find the venom it was to reclaim, it searched here and there and immediately expired.

We too, when we desire to drink in the streams of heavenly eloquence, must by the effort of pure confession vomit out all the poisons of our vices and falls. But let us beware of returning to our vomit, since we are commanded not to crawl upon the earth with serpents but to hasten toward the things that are above (Colossians III).

There is moreover something noble and highly distinguished in the serpent: it is said to flee a naked man but to attack and bite a clothed one. It is as though a strong warrior were to attack an armed man but fear one without weapons.

Do you not wish to fear the devil? Strip yourself of the garments of earthly things. Are you clothed? Then dread the encircling serpent. Do you wish, after the example of the serpent, to become new and to make the old age of your languishing soul bloom again with the beauty of youthful adolescence? Fast with the serpent throughout the cycle of forty days—that is, restrain yourself from carnal desires throughout the whole course of this life.

For this same serpent also shows how great is the power of fasting: as soon as it tastes the spittle of a fasting man, it immediately dies and expires. Therefore, servant of God, do not begrudge yourself fasting, so that the one who tries to swallow and devour you when you are swollen with food may die.

Furthermore, the serpent exposes its whole body to the blows of its attacker but hides only its head. So you too, when placed amid persecutions, conceal Christ within the hidden places of your mind; but, if circumstances require it, hand your body over to the hands of your persecutors.

It is also believed that there is a kind of viper which, if it bites a person, turns his entire body into poison. Another viper species is said to possess such fierce venom that if any bird happens to fly over it, it immediately falls dead through the power of the stench it exhales.

These creatures have been granted the natural power to mate or give birth according to the following custom: the male thrusts his head into the female’s mouth, and she, unable to restrain herself because of excessive passion, bites it off and promptly swallows it. From the eyes of this severed head two young are born. At the time of birth they gnaw through their mother’s flanks on both sides, and thus they burst forth, at once killing their mother and being born.

They are therefore parricides before they are sons; and for this reason nothing beyond two offspring is ever found to exceed the number produced by this species.

There is also, as they say, another species called the *jaculum*, which suddenly penetrates a person while flying and passes straight through him as though nothing at all opposed it.

The merciful Creator has bestowed diverse powers and cunning upon brute animals for the instruction of human nature, so that from the investigation of animal cleverness too we may transfer examples of no little value to our own conduct.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the wild ass, elephant, unicorn, eagle, and ant

[Col. 0783B]

Who taught the wild ass to emit a bray for twelve hours of the day and the same number of hours of the night at the equinoctial point of the month of March, and, as though by the mechanism of a natural clock, to distinguish the moments of the hours? For it brays once during each hour, whether of day or night, and by this shows that the time of the equinoctial balance has arrived.

Who taught the elephant to love perpetual chastity? Yet when compelled by the law of nature, it turns its head backward and mates as though unwilling and nauseated; and once the female has conceived, she does not return to intercourse.

While she trembles with fear of the dragon that savagely lies in wait for her, she gives birth not elsewhere but in water reaching as high as her breasts. For if she gives birth outside the water, the dragon attacks and suddenly devours her young.

Who granted the unicorn this nobility, that although it disdains to be conquered by strength, it allows itself easily to be overcome by the art of humility? It is never captured by hunters unless it first reclines in the lap of a virgin.

Who taught the eagle this kind of medical treatment? When it grows old, its wings begin to grow heavy and its eyes dim; then it seeks a spring of water and flies opposite it up to the circuit of the sun. There, poised in the clearer expanse of the upper air, it burns its wings in the sun’s heat and completely scorches away the dimness of its eyes. Then, descending, it plunges three times into the spring, and thus the vigor of its wings and the sharpness of its eyes are renewed far better than youth had provided them.

Who, I ask, trained the ant in this manner of threshing, so that it distinguishes the grains of crops and, rejecting the inferior, chooses the grain of the finer kind? It carefully examines a heap of grain and, disdaining barley in a certain sense as fodder for beasts of burden, rejects it. But when it finds a grain of wheat, it gladly takes it.

It also detects the approach of clear weather by certain signs. When it sees its storerooms becoming damp with atmospheric moisture, it carries out on its own shoulders the grain stored for its food; and, taking precautions against domestic loss, it dries it in the scorching rays of the sun. And, as though this were not enough, it bites off the grains with its own mouth, lest they swell again in the severity of winter rains and, deprived of the hope of food, sprout into plants.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the viper, hawk, serpent, and bear

Who also taught the viper that, when the desire for intercourse excites it, it should immediately hurry to the shore and seek union with the sea-moray? When the viper signals its presence by hissing, the moray immediately comes forth and joins itself to the venomous beast of another element.

Who established such laws for hawks that, wherever they nest, they do not pursue any prey within a broad circuit on either side, and, although they live nowhere except by warfare, peace is preserved there where they bring the spoils of their conquered enemies?

But when they discover that their young are already feathered and able to fly, they drive them from the nests with their feet and beaks. As though emancipated by law, they expel them far from their own dwelling, so that from an early age they may be trained to seize prey and may not sink into laziness, relying on their parents for food; instead, from the very beginning of their first flight, they become accustomed to the frequent violence of plunder.

Furthermore, where did the bear learn, when it gives birth to shapeless offspring, to distinguish its young by licking them with its tongue along the various outlines of their limbs, and to form them, like a potter, into the natural shape and image of their species?

Indeed, who thoroughly taught it the instruments of medical art, and who prescribed for it the powers of herbs and the applications of healing? For whenever it is struck by the blows of a very grave attack or wounded by arrows, it applies to its wounds the herb called in Greek *phlomos* (φλόμος), and thus, by mere contact, removes all the pain of the wounds and recovers its former health.

The serpent too—an observation that had escaped us earlier—if it suffers blindness, is restored to its former sight by eating fennel. As soon as it feels its eyes becoming clouded, it seeks the familiar remedy without delay and is not disappointed in the result it hopes for.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the tortoise and the various medicines of animals

The tortoise, after feeding on the entrails of a serpent, when it senses the venom spreading through its own entrails as well, does not neglect to apply oregano to itself immediately as a remedy.

The crafty fox too, when it senses death threatening, cures itself with resin from a sweating pine and by such a remedy extends its life over a longer span. For those animals themselves which apply medicine to themselves from external things are also shown to possess within their own bodies the material for healing.

From the flesh of the viper called the *tyrus*, not only is theriac prepared, but various remedies for healing are also provided. Slices of ivory are employed in different medicines. Hyena bile restores clarity to the eyes, and its dung is likewise known to heal the wounds of dogs. Every sick wild beast recovers its health if it drinks a dog's blood. Galen recounts how useful human excrement is for many kinds of medical treatment.

[Col. 0785A]

The ostrich, camel, frogs, chameleons, cranes, storks, eagle bile, hawk’s blood, and the dung and flesh of the swallow—what diseases they remedy can be stated by one whose purpose is to discuss bodily cures.

Physicians report that if the skin of a serpent, which it sheds, is boiled in hot oil, it wonderfully alleviates earache. To those who do not know their uses, bedbugs appear to be of no value; but if a leech has lodged in the throat, fumigation with them causes it to be vomited out immediately. Moreover, difficulty in urination is relieved by applying bedbugs.

Physicians also know how many medicines are contained in the fats of pigs, geese, hens, and pheasants. Peacock dung is known to lessen the inflammation of gout. If a sick lion devours a monkey, it immediately recovers from its illness. [Col. 0785B] If a leopard drinks the blood of a wild doe, it escapes the power of disease. A sick bear devours ants. A languishing stag begs for little branches of an olive tree so that it may be healed.

Why, however, did the powerful Creator of all things place all these properties in the natures of animals, unless because through them he provided human beings with various benefits for this life? Thus, while creatures subject to humanity support one another, everything may be directed toward the benefit of the one who has been set over all.

And while a person marvels at the goodness of the Maker in his works, let him not cling to created things but desire to behold the Creator.

If anyone diligently examines all the natures of animals that we have touched upon above, he will be able profitably to transfer them into examples for human conduct, so that from the very nature of beasts, which lack reason, a human being may learn how to live.

For, as the Apostle says, “God does not care for oxen” (I Corinthians IX); but when something remarkable is observed in brute animals, the human being is immediately admonished to turn whatever it may be toward consideration of himself.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the wolf and the sheep

What is it that makes a wolf unable to escape if it is seen by you first, but, if it sees you first, is proved to take away your voice? And, to make the matter still more astonishing, if you become speechless, you loosen your garment and immediately recover your speech.

If the wolf should suddenly rise against you, seize a stone and it immediately flees. What is the stone except Christ? (I Corinthians X.) If you seize him, as is fitting, you will certainly escape the wolf of spiritual wickedness that pursues you.

And, to dispose of this point without delay, loosen your garment through confession, so that you may possess the freedom not of a mute but of an eloquent person for proclaiming the preaching that must be sown, as Scripture bears witness: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah XLIII).

Who, I ask, taught the sheep to fear the scarcity of winter and therefore, in autumn, to crop the grasses like an insatiable creature without limit? For then it seizes its food more eagerly than usual and, knowing that the grass will soon be lacking, fills itself more abundantly while it may, so that it may prepare itself, as it were, for the coming scarcity and store up provisions for its sustenance before the green grass fails.

Nor is it without reason that the elephant, formidable to bulls, fears a mouse. The lion, king of beasts, is afraid of the tiny scorpion; that same lion is killed both by the serpent’s venom and by the scorpion’s sting.

Who would not marvel that the lion, which shakes bulls with flowing manes from its neck and, raising its chest, proudly lifts its terrible face above the beasts, fears the sting of a very small scorpion?

Who would consider it unworthy of astonishment that the elephant, which carries turreted fortifications filled with so many armored soldiers, should be brought down and die from the blow of a single tree? For it does not yield when bearing thirty-two armed men, or more, together with towers rising above them like cities; yet it falls at the collapse of one tree.

Against this tree it often leans or stands firmly, or relaxes itself in repose and sleep. Some people also set traps for it because of its ivory: they cut almost halfway through the tree which the elephant habitually leans against, on the opposite side, so that the tree collapses upon the body of such enormous mass.

But while, my brothers, we pursue by careful enumeration certain animal natures for your edification, we must by no means forget that we have undertaken not a book but a letter. Therefore the freedom of our running discourse must be restrained and our will curbed, so that charity may serve edification while the sober brevity proper to a letter does not exceed its measure.

Your monastery, then, beloved ones, is a kind of paradise in which the almighty Creator, having placed diverse human dispositions, created, as it were, three kinds of animals: terrestrial, aquatic, and flying.

This is that ancient ark of mystical significance in which the species of all animals are enclosed. This, finally, is that vessel which Peter saw being lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners, containing all quadrupeds, reptiles of the earth, and birds of the sky.

But when the command is given there, “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X), we believe, through the mercy of Christ, that these animals which you are have been cut away from this world by the sword of the divine word and fused into the body of their Redeemer by the fire of perfect charity.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On restraining the rashness of empty talk

It must be guarded against with the greatest care, because you are not yet resting in a harbor station but are still laboring amid the whirlwinds of storms, lest a breath of vain spirit issue from your mouth and extinguish the flames of this fire.

For breath sometimes kindles flames and sometimes extinguishes them [Col. 0786D], and, so to speak, blows upon them. When a person proclaims the mysteries of sacred teaching, he blows; and when he devotes himself to idle tales, he also blows. Just as he inflames the heart of the listener with love of God through words of edification, so he causes it to grow cold toward heavenly desires through idle words.

But this breath of which we have spoken might perhaps be considered ridiculous unless it were confirmed by testimonies of sacred Scripture. Hear, then, what the Lord says through Isaiah about a salutary breath: “I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry to the end; for the spirit shall go forth from my presence, and I will create breath” (Isaiah LVII).

Hear under different words what Paul says about an evil spirit: “Avoid profane and empty words, for they make great progress toward impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer” (II Timothy II).

Hear again, through Isaiah, about one who blows well: “Behold,” he says, “I created the smith who blows upon the fire of coals and brings forth a vessel for its work” (Isaiah LIV). And immediately concerning mutilated vessels—those, that is, which are fashioned for dishonor through idle words—he adds: “And I created the destroyer to lay waste; every vessel that has been fashioned against you shall not prosper” (ibid.).

What this vessel is that is destroyed by the destroyer is made perfectly clear when the following words are immediately added: “And you shall judge every tongue that resists you in judgment” (ibid.).

What does Isaiah mean here by saying, “You shall judge every tongue that resists you in judgment,” except what the Truth says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew XII)?

I confess, my brothers, that scarcely anything is done in monasteries from which my mind more fearfully suspects God’s judgment to hang over monks. For their tongue runs on through a continuous impulse, like a torrent flowing down a steep slope; and when the bell sounds, it is for them as though a sudden blow had immediately crushed their head.

This, however, concerns certain people; God forbid that I should say it of all.

Since the Rule commands that from Easter until the Kalends of October they should go out in the morning and work from the first hour until nearly the fourth hour, doing whatever is necessary, and from the fourth hour until the sixth should devote themselves to reading, certain men, postponing their zeal for all these hours of work and reading, abuse them in storytelling and give entirely to empty talk whatever they owe to labor and reading.

The holy man who established the Rule would never have changed the hour except because of the necessity of continuing the work (St. Benedict, Rule, chapter 48), nor would he have substituted the fourth hour for the third unless he had provided for the necessary labor.

Yet those too are workers of iniquity who exercise the hands of their tongues in idle conversations. Does not the tongue have a hand, since Scripture declares: “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue” (Proverbs XVIII)?

And how dishonorable it is that, in this office by which the human being is set above all creatures, the Giver himself should so frequently be offended by humanity! Since the human being presides over the other natures and subjects them to the laws of his dominion, how shameful it is that he cannot tame the thin piece of flesh enclosed between his jaws?

Hence James also says: “Every nature of beasts and birds is tameable, but no human being can tame the tongue” (James II).

No restraints imposed by any teacher can control the tongue of one who refuses to restrain it; otherwise, if it strikes and strives, it will undoubtedly attain what it desires.

Moreover, that all animals are subjected to human dominion is attested by the divine voice speaking to Noah: “Let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth and upon all the birds of heaven, with everything that moves upon the earth; all the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand” (Genesis IX).

And so that we may marvel all the more at serpents being tamed even by human beings, Pliny testifies that in Egypt a very savage asp was tamed by a certain head of a household and used to come out of its cave daily to his table to receive food.

Marcellinus the Count also writes that a tiger was tamed and sent from India to the emperor Anastasius.

With this example in view, the Apostle appropriately says: “All kinds of beasts are found in the tongue” (James III). For there is the lightness of birds, the ferocity of beasts, and the poisonous deceit of serpents. Those who set their mouths against heaven and whose mouth has spoken vanity (Psalm CXLIII) are birds, as it were, in their lightness. Fierce beasts are those who have sharpened their tongues like a sword (Psalm LXIII). Finally, serpents are those of whom it is said: “The venom of asps is under their lips” (Psalm XIII).

Therefore, wherever people devote themselves to superfluous foolishness and, as it were, pile up tokens in idle words, the one listening inwardly perceives not human speech but, as it were, a many-species outcry of beasts.

He is the one of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “My beloved looks through the window; he looks through the lattice” (Song of Songs II). And he says through the prophet: “I attended and listened; no one speaks what is good” (Jeremiah VIII).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the crab and the oyster

But so that our discourse may not depart from the subject it once began, let us pursue the vices of speaking people through examples drawn from animals that do not speak.

The *hydrus* never enters the crocodile’s jaws unless the crocodile is found yawning. For if it keeps its mouth closed, it does not fear the attack of the ambusher.

When the *authalopus* cries out, unaware of its own destruction, it invites the hunter’s sword; but so long as it remains silent, the speed of its flight deceives the skill of its pursuer.

To bring forward what the devil generally does to a monk, as the crab does to the oyster: since the crab eagerly desires food and is shrewdly watchful of danger, its hunting is both difficult and dangerous. It is difficult because the inner flesh that serves as food is enclosed in stronger shells; dangerous because, if the crab inserts its claws, it is immediately and inescapably trapped when the two shells close again.

What, then, can it do to obtain what it seeks? How can it fulfill the desire of its longing unless it turns to the devices of an elaborate deception?

It therefore carefully watches to see whether an oyster opens itself to the rays of the sun in places protected from every wind. Then the stealthy attacker throws in a pebble and prevents the oyster from closing by placing an obstruction between its shells. Thus, finding the open shells blocked, it safely inserts its claws and tears out the oyster’s inner flesh.

What, then, could the oyster more suitably signify than a monk? He lives while he is enclosed under the discipline of silence; but he perishes when he opens himself too immoderately to speech. He is like the oyster which, when it does not gape, preserves its life intact; but when it speaks without restraint, is emptied of the vitals of life.

What does the pebble signify, which is inserted so that the oyster may not close, except the hardness of habit by which a person becomes hardened lest he soften himself toward repentance? Like a stone, the evil habit obstructs the person who devotes himself to the foolishness of stories, preventing him from opening himself from his vanity.

What does the crab signify figuratively, since it naturally walks backward, except the apostate spirit, which, after once withdrawing from the Creator, never ceases to slip backward?

Hence the devil is interpreted as “flowing downward.” Just as it is said of the holy animals that their feet were straight (Ezekiel I), so the feet of the devil and his followers are always turned backward.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the monkey, and how a monkey may be captured

[Col. 0789B]

Since the discourse has introduced the subject of feet, just as a hunter traps a monkey, so a cunning ambusher often ensnares the soul.

I have not found this written down, but I heard it from the mouth of one who reported it: a person who wishes to capture a monkey alive first sews himself shoes of crimson color and attaches leaden soles beneath them. When he sees the monkey at a distance, he ties the shoes to his own feet with red thongs in full view of the animal, and by this action teaches it, as it were, what it should later do. Then he secretly removes the shoes, leaves them there, and cunningly hides himself near the place as an observer.

After the hunter has, as it thinks, departed, the monkey, an imitator of human actions, puts the abandoned shoes on its own feet and fastens them tightly with their straps. But behold, the hunter immediately leaps out from his hiding place and captures his pupil entangled in its own bonds.

So the malignant spirit often teaches some person—an evil and insolent vessel—to entangle innocent people in the bonds of sins. By the evil that he displays before their eyes, he himself invites them as a guide and teacher; and while the imitator follows what is wicked, he is himself caught in his own snares.

The following incident also now comes to mind, which my lord Pope Alexander related to me recently, before a month had fully elapsed, so to speak.

He said that not long ago Count William, who lived in the region of Liguria, possessed a male monkey, commonly called a *maimo*. His wife, being utterly shameless and wanton, used to play with it in an excessively lascivious manner.

I myself saw two sons of hers whom that punishable she-wolf had borne by a certain bishop. We omit naming the bishop, because we do not delight in marking anyone with infamy.

Since the woman often played with the wanton beast, clasped it in her arms, and caressed it with embraces, while it likewise displayed certain signs of lust and by various gestures strained to reach her naked flesh, her chambermaid said to her: “Allow it, if you please, to do whatever it wishes, so that it may become clear what it is trying to attempt.”

What more is there to say? She allowed it, and—shameful to relate—the beast had intercourse with the woman. Then the habit took hold, and an unheard-of criminal relationship grew established.

One day, while the count was uniting with his wife in the customary manner of marriage, the *maimo*, stirred as though by a jealous spirit, suddenly leapt upon them both. It seized the man, as though he were a rival, with its arms and sharp claws, caught him in its teeth, and tore him irreparably. Thus the count was killed.

The innocent man, while preserving the fidelity of the marriage bed toward his wife and feeding his animal at daily expense, suspected no harm from either, since he was showing the clemency of a benefactor. But, oh crime! The woman shamefully violated the right of marriage, and the beast brandished a sword against its master’s throat.

Indeed, a rather large boy was recently brought both to the aforementioned pope and to us. Although, as they say, he was already twenty years old, he was completely without speech and very similar in appearance to a *maimo*, so that he was also called by the same name.

From this a sinister suspicion could arise if such a creature—not merely beastlike but monstrous—were then being raised in his father’s house.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the whale
But while we are speaking of the woman’s shameful faithlessness, that sea creature also comes to mind which, as we are told, carries an enormous mass of sand upon its body and raises its back above the waves, so that, like an island, it rises above the sea. Believing this without hesitation to be an island, sailors bring their vessels alongside it, drive in stakes, moor the ship, and prepare fires. But as soon as the beast feels the heat of the fire, it immediately plunges into the depths and swallows both the ship and the sailors in a deadly shipwreck. Indeed, Gerard—our monk, of course—reported that he had seen a whale caught on the shores of Normandy, from whose tongue’s flesh fourteen pack animals were heavily laden. But to return to the point from which I digressed: what wonder if a sailor found no faith in a beast when a husband found none in his own wife? What wonder if the dumb beast, pretending to be an island, is submerged by the storms, when a woman, having violated marital fidelity, is exposed to bestial embraces? For what in this world is so truly ours, so completely our own, that suspicion of various misfortunes could be absent from it?

In our own times, I heard that the event I am about to relate took place. A certain fisherman placed his little son in the prow of his small boat, and, proceeding into the current, caught a large eel. Delighted, he threw his catch into the boat, so that its head was turned toward the boy, while the boy sat opposite it. But while the fisherman, intent upon rowing, was trying to return and, cheerful because of his good fortune, felt no anxiety, the terrified boy cried out mournfully at the sight of the fish: “It is looking at me; now the beast is going to devour me!” His father, joking with him, replied: “You will devour it; it will not devour you.” When the boy repeated the same thing a second time, but his father dismissed his words as childish nonsense, the fish suddenly leapt into the air, violently attacked the boy, seized him at once, and, with its prey, plunged back into the water; neither the fish nor the boy was ever seen again.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A brief conclusion to the little work

[Col. 0791A]

Behold, my brothers: what possession in this world is so secure that we may safely cast ourselves upon it? What belongs to us that we ought not to regard as a turning wheel? Solomon teaches that this wheel must be feared and that the memory of the Creator must always be present. For when he said, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of your affliction comes,” he added shortly afterward: “and the wheel be broken above the cistern, and the dust return to its earth, from which it came” (Eccli. XV). Let us therefore beware of trusting in any unstable possession, or of bringing ourselves alongside the sand of a deceptive island like inexperienced sailors. Let us therefore approach Christ, the safest harbor for those at sea; and, delivered from maritime danger, let our tongues speak only of him as the refuge of faith and certain rest—him who establishes and orders the natural laws of mute creatures, so that in all creatures the virtue and power of the Creator alone may be proclaimed.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0791]

831–832  
## THE FIFTY-THIRD LITTLE WORK: ON PATIENCE UNDER THE ATTACKS OF THE WICKED

### Argument

He urges Dominic the Lenten-wearer, admirable in the mortification of his body, not to depart with his companions because of the troubles inflicted by wicked men, but, instructed by the precepts of Sacred Scripture and strengthened by the examples of the saints, to endure with an even temper the adversities into which God permits his servants to fall, so that, exercising himself in good works and enduring evils, he may be recognized as a true member of Christ.

[Col. 0791B]

To Lord Dominic and the other brothers who dwell in the hermitage on their neighboring mountain, Peter, a sinful monk, offers his final service in the Lord.

### ON PATIENCE UNDER THE ATTACKS OF THE WICKED

## CHAPTER I. That patience is the queen of virtues

You wrote to me, most beloved, that the envy of so many perverse and violent men harasses you, and that unless I hastily and quickly come to your aid, you will give up the place and provide yourselves with someone else who will not be subjected to these robberies and troubles. I confess that this message, when I heard it, struck me heavily, and your faintheartedness saddened me more than the hostile adversity itself. For since you appear constantly to devote yourselves to the divine writings, it is astonishing that patience, the queen of virtues, should still be unknown to you, when all the volumes of Scripture serve it. “For whatever things,” as the Apostle says, “were written were written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4).

Why for our instruction? Was it so that we might learn to construct the snares of syllogisms, to adorn thunderous and polished words with the colors of rhetorical eloquence, and to distinguish the melody of musical sweetness? Was it so that we might learn, as they say, to mark out the signs of the stars with a mathematical rod? We are certainly not instructed by Sacred Scripture to investigate such things; rather, through it we are summoned to examples of patience. Hence it immediately continues: “so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (ibid.). For the same Scripture that teaches us to hold fast to patience also lifts us up through the hope of consolation, because, when it tells how many punishments and afflictions God’s elect have endured, it also shows what rewards they have obtained through them.

A physician plainly applies leeches to the swollen limbs of a sick person and permits them to draw poison together with blood from the innermost organs; yet the intention of the physician and that of the leech are different. The leech desires nothing except to drink blood; the physician aims at the sick person’s recovery. The leech is satisfied and dies, while the sick person, as he loses blood, regains health. Finally, the leech feeds and exults in its own death, while the sick person, as he is wounded, is raised up to a condition of health. What wonder, then, if almighty God, who is the physician of souls, disposes us by the hidden art of his governance so that he makes medicines for us from the wounds of others, in order that, while a hostile wound is inflicted upon us, the antidote of salvation may be prepared from it above all?

The *tyrus* is a species of serpent whose blood is used to make theriac, which destroys the raging plague in those who have been poisoned.

## CHAPTER II. That medicine is prepared for us from tribulations

If, then, a human being knows how to drive out poison with poison, how much more can God, in his wondrous power, provide useful things for us from the afflictions of others? For what else do all the deeds of the saints recount except the pressures and struggles they endured from the assaults of every kind of wicked person? Our Redeemer himself, having assumed the form of a servant from the undefiled Virgin, did not bring it into the heavenly kingdoms before he had passed through all the torments of mockery and punishment attested by Scripture.

What is new, then, if a sinful human being suffers the loss of things outside himself, when he who could never sin endured the cross in his own body? (1 Peter 2:21.) Indeed, according to the Apostle, you have not yet resisted to the point of blood (Hebrews 12:4). But would that at least this could be said of you, which he said to certain patient people: “You accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions” (Hebrews 10:34). Hence another apostle also says: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James 1:2).

There are plainly two things which, if we attend to them vigilantly, enable us easily to overcome the insolence and injurious troubles of any violent people: namely, precepts and examples. For the holy Scriptures exhort us to repentance, and every one of the elect has endured with an even temper whatever could be inflicted by the raging members of the devil.

That we are rescued from the depth of the tribulation inflicted upon us with the help of divine admonitions and the examples of those who came before us is rightly represented in the prophet Jeremiah by the man emerging from the well. For, as Scripture testifies (Jeremiah 38), they had thrown him into a pit in which there was no water, but mud; afterward, to lift him out, they lowered ropes and old rags to him. What else are the ropes than the Lord’s precepts? Since they both convict us when we are placed in evil action and rescue us, they are like things that bind and draw, constrain and lift. But lest the person bound by these ropes be injured while he is being pulled, old rags are lowered at the same time; for, so that the divine precepts may not terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers strengthen us, enabling us, by comparing ourselves with them, to dare to do what we fear because of our weakness.

## CHAPTER III. That we should rejoice in adversity and fear in prosperity

If, then, we hasten to be lifted from this depth of an afflicted life, let us be bound with ropes—that is, let us be constrained by the Lord’s precepts. Let the old rags also be present, by which the ropes may be held more securely—that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who came before us, lest the subtle precepts wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while they lift us.

The Apostle Paul appended certain old rags when, in order to raise up his disciples, he commended to them the examples of the ancients alongside his spiritual precepts, saying: “The righteous experienced mockeries and scourges; moreover, chains and prisons. They were stoned, they were cut in pieces, they were tempted; they died by the sword” (Hebrews 11:36–37). And shortly afterward: “Therefore, having so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience the race set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). And again: “Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you; looking to the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebr. I).

Earlier, when he spoke spiritual precepts, he had, as it were, lowered ropes; afterward, when recalling the examples of the great, he supplied, as it were, old rags. Indeed, a servant of God ought then to fear when he receives something temporal, and then to rejoice when he loses it; for one whose purpose is to climb to heavenly things will unquestionably proceed more easily empty than burdened.

834  
## CHAPTER IV. That friendship among religious men should be acquired without gifts

I shall tell you what recently happened to me. I went to the city of Milan on the mission of Lord Pope Nicholas. While I was there, the abbot of Saint Simplicianus sent me a small silver vessel as a gift. When I suddenly saw what had been offered, I initially rejected it with aversion and carefully investigated why he was offering me a present. I suspected that he might perhaps have some business and that, by anticipating and forestalling me, he was trying to occupy me with gifts.

Among us—the ministers, that is, of the Apostolic See—it is customary to accept absolutely nothing from those whose business is still pending, but not to refuse it from those who are entirely free of business if they wish to give. This rule applies to all of us, though only to those who guard themselves somewhat better against greed. What more need be said? We meet for a common conversation; it is asked why he has given the gift; he is questioned whether he has some case. He is found secure and free from every side, so that in reality he seemed to answer: “I dwell in the midst of my people.” Nevertheless, I also investigated whether, when he had risen through the ecclesiastical ranks or assumed the governance of the monastery, he knew of any intrusion of a commercial exchange in return for advancement.

When he had utterly denied all this and maintained that he had given the gift not for such reasons but only in order to find an entrance into our friendship, I replied that he should take back what was his and should not redeem our friendship for a price in the manner of worldly people, but should possess freely what is legitimate among brothers.

Yet, to speak confidentially, my mind was in such a state that, even after examining him strictly, I found nothing blameworthy in him; and if he had pressed me to accept the gift, I would not have been displeased in the least by his forcefulness. I wanted to be compelled, as it were, and driven unwillingly to comply. When he entirely refused to take back what he had once given and did not even incline his ear to my requests, I, now more secure and bolder, pressed him more harshly to recover his property.

Meanwhile, the day passed. While I was engaged in nightly meditation upon the appointed psalms, my conscience began to reproach me more sharply and, as if bringing a case before me, to argue: “If this man is good, as he appears to be, you wished to take the money of an innocent man, since no case prevents him from expecting your help. But if he has business, it is unworthy of you to make your tongue, which ought to serve both parties freely—as it serves you—a source of profit against a holy brother.”

As this struggle against me continued to press in, and I could no longer endure the outcry of my reproaching thoughts, at twilight I hurried to the man, [manicavi: perhaps, “took him by the hand”], and opened to him the wound of my wasting conscience. When the two of us were arguing with each other, he that he would not take back what he had once given, and I that I could not keep it, I finally brought our friendly dispute to this conclusion:

“I have two new monasteries, one of which, with God’s help, has already been brought to completion, while the other has not yet been secured by episcopal dedication. If you please, accept a share in these holy places and, as you wish, send as a gift for a blessing whatever may benefit your soul.”

By this argument I concealed the shamefulness of my greed and, as though not accepting, cunningly accepted. Later, when I returned to the hermitage, I entered my cell hastily, but could scarcely enter it as myself; and I, who had poured myself disorderly outside myself, afterward entered myself, so to speak, only with great difficulty, by the just judgment of God.

Among other things, the darkness of that gift so confused my mind, and, like a teeming worm, did not cease to gnaw at my entrails, that, as my conscience bore witness, I would rather have been struck with leprosy than wounded by that gift. On the one hand I considered the brother’s great generosity: he owed me nothing, yet he offered it. On the other hand I considered my own avarice, which had accepted what it had not earned through its office.

I was then ashamed that I had forgotten what is said by the Wise Man: “Let your hand not be stretched out to receive, and let it be gathered together for giving” (Ecclesiasticus 4:31). And since, according to the Apostle, it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), I judged him blessed and myself wretched.

“Woe is me,” I said, “when Scripture commands the hand to be shaken free of gifts received” (Isaiah 33:15). How do you shake your hand so as to reject what is offered, when you rather thrust it forward to receive, clench it to seize, and draw it back to store away what you possess?

In truth, avarice is glue in the hand of the receiver: whatever is placed in it, it does not permit to be shaken off, but compels it to cling like a fish.

What, then? No longer able to endure the quarrel within my mind, I set about returning his gift to the holy brother. Then, with God’s help, for the rest of my life I shall keep watch more carefully against the filth of gifts.

Behold what I said above: a servant of God ought then to fear when he receives something temporal, and then to rejoice when he loses it. From now on, therefore, neither under the pretext of constructing a monastery nor for the supposed needs of the servants of God will I hold as material for righteousness anything in which I can exercise the strength of greed.

Just as a man who longs to loosen the belt of chastity, in order to provide heirs for himself, enters into the bonds of marriage and, under the name of producing offspring, serves the allurements of pleasure, so some people, since they cannot be Christ’s or be content with the nakedness of the apostles, rejoice in becoming involved in governance or in various activities, so that, while satisfying their own avarice, they may appear to be serving a charitable necessity.

But let us, beloved, always rejoice, endure with an even temper the injuries inflicted upon us, and moreover provide useful things to those who harm us. Let our hand be cautious and suspicious in receiving, but generous in distributing according to our ability. Let the mind be fearful in prosperity and secure in adversity. And when it does good and endures, let it confidently reckon itself among the members of Christ. For whoever lives rightly and is worn down by scourges now follows Christ’s footprints in both respects and will afterward not be deprived of fellowship with him.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0795]

837–838  
## THE FIFTY-FOURTH LITTLE WORK: ON THE FAST OF SATURDAY

### Argument

He exhorts the monks to fast on Saturday, in honor of Christ’s burial, cheerfully and devoutly, as they customarily did on three other days of the week, setting before their eyes the benefits and merit of this fast.

[Col. 0795C]

To the holy brothers established in the hermitage at Gamugni, Peter, a sinful monk, sends the kiss of peace in the Holy Spirit.

### ON THE FAST OF SATURDAY

## CHAPTER I. That everything in this world serves human use

Tenants of houses or stewards of fields, while eagerly striving to please their masters, do not allow the customary levies to be reduced during the period of their stewardship. We too, to whom not the care of just any possessions but the guardianship of your souls has been entrusted, are greatly afraid if, under our care, the return of your crops that was being carried into the Lord’s granaries is diminished; if the obligation of your holy service is not fulfilled through our watchfulness—God forbid.

For whatever is worked at in this world benefits human use; only the fruit of souls serves the use of its author. We are therefore compelled to await the divine judgment with all the more fear because we must render an account not of crops soon to be carried through the channels of privies, but rather of souls that display the image of their Creator. We are not brought to account concerning fallow lands subject to ploughshares and knives, but concerning rational lands that must be cultivated to receive the seeds of heavenly speech.

Just as we must therefore be fearful, since we are commanded to watch over your guardianship, so you also, with great joy of heart, ought to hasten toward the crown set before your holy labors, not diminishing what you have begun but lightening its burden by looking toward your destination.

Among the other flowers of your holy way of life and exercises of piety, I suggest to your charity that the customary rule of fasting be maintained on four days each week, and especially on Saturday, which is already wavering in the minds of some, unless it is relaxed by the weak.

I know well that the fasts of three days pass without struggle or disagreement. But on Saturday the weak and lukewarm mind gradually begins to waver at a certain midpoint between abstaining and eating, and, as though standing at a crossroads, hesitates which way it should turn. Soon it is loosened from its firmness and begins thinking about tables, dishes, cups, and everything belonging to food. It pretends that the body is weak, while turning the pleasure of eating over and over in its thoughts; and it despairs that it will be able to endure the coming night’s activities.

Meanwhile that old, drowsy instigator of the itching appetite kindles the desire for refreshment and pours in the poison of destructive pleasure. It teaches the golden path of moderation and insists that the ruin of excess must be avoided above all; that it is better to eat with sobriety than to nourish the frenzy of eating with doubled hunger.

For the ancient deceiver skillfully casts this hook of his cunning into his children, just as once he baited it to catch the parents of the human race (Genesis 3). He had drawn our parents, pierced by the goad of appetite, and the crafty scout still watches for an entrance through appetite by which to catch us. He also brings forward every kind of flatterer and sycophant, so that they may say outwardly what he sows inwardly, in order that the wretched human being may easily fall amid so many crossbows and engines, amid so many whirlwinds of weapons and storms of missiles; against him, the siege of tongues and the rebellion of thoughts join forces and fight with one accord.

Moreover, we must not omit that the same struggle arises in weak minds on Wednesday during both periods of Lent, when there is fasting five days each week. It arises from the Saturdays at other times of the year, when the whole observance of fasting is confined within four days. For since the malignant enemy is not sufficiently able to violate the Saturday of Lent among God’s servants, he tries at least to violate Wednesday. But when the rigor of that day is lost, it is immediately transferred to the assault of Saturday, so that the ancient adversary may never cease bringing on the battle and the servant of God may never lose an occasion for victory.

## CHAPTER II. Why it was instituted that monks should fast three days each week

You, beloved, must not abandon without cause the rule handed down by the Fathers and already kept by you for so long. Join the fast to the most salutary observance of the life-giving burial of the Lord.

Indeed, these three days mystically contain three different periods of time: Friday, Saturday, and the Lord’s Day. Therefore, among the other days, we ought especially to observe these—two in the chastisement of the flesh, and the third in the joy of spiritual gladness. On Friday the Lord hung upon the cross; on Saturday he rested in the tomb; and on the Lord’s Day he rose again.

For this whole life is, as it were, Friday: in it we live as dying people, and in it we are commanded daily to carry the cross after Jesus. Saturday, which certainly means “rest,” signifies the interval from the day on which we die until the day of resurrection, when we are presented, with our bodies restored, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. The Lord’s Day will be that eternity after the judgment which will have no end of light and glory.

In this Saturday of passing time, therefore, let each of us afflict his body so that he may afterward rest sweetly in that other Saturday. Here, let the fervent spirit mortify the blandishments of its flesh so that there it may rejoice, happily destined to feast. Here, let him mourn at the Lord’s burial with the holy women so that there he may behold the glory of him who rose from death.

Let mournful eyes, pale faces, lowered expressions, and unkempt hair be signs that we are disciples of the one crucified or lying in the tomb, so that, now mourning and fasting with the apostles, we may afterward join them at the banquet of honey and roasted fish (Luke 24).

But so that the fruit and benefit of fasting on the seventh day may become clear not so much through words as through events, we think it worthwhile to borrow briefly from one of our own little works for your edification.

## CHAPTER III. The miracle by which the fast of Saturday was approved

I remember having already written what I am about to say where I once discussed eight fasts. As soon as I had written those things, I shall not conceal what happened for me to learn, whether by chance or rather by divine prompting.

An elderly brother, who had already spent nearly thirty years in a hermit’s cell, came to me and disclosed privately a vision that had happened to him.

“Master,” he said, “I often felt the goad of resentment and anger toward you because you insisted so strongly that people should fast on Saturday. Meanwhile I desired to go to Jerusalem; and as I burned more fervently each day with this desire, one Sunday night, while I was asleep, a certain splendid cleric appeared to me in a vision and said: ‘Brother John’—for that was his name—‘do you wish to come to Jerusalem?’

“When I replied that I did, he immediately led me there in a dream. He showed me many of the holy tombs as he went around them, designating specifically whose each one was. At last, with the same guide, I reached the Lord’s tomb. And behold, behind the tomb stood a cleric with a serene face and handsome appearance, decently adorned down to the neck with a white stole. He said to me:

“‘Three days ago you truly adored the life-giving cross, and yesterday, while fasting, you likewise truly adored the Lord’s burial. From this, with every doubt removed, recognize that you most truly celebrate and adore both the cross on Friday and Christ’s tomb on Saturday, if you fast on those days in prayer and psalmody.’

“Instructed by this oracle, I lost the scandal I had held against you, Father, and thereafter, whenever circumstances permitted, I fasted on Saturday with no less devotion than on Friday [‘I shall fast,’ in the manuscript].”

The holy brother reported this to me, although at that time he knew nothing whatever of what we are writing and still knows nothing of it. I have not been reluctant to write it down so that, if that earlier little work does not happen to come into your hands, at least this may not escape the knowledge of your brotherhood.

## CHAPTER IV. The negligence of our elders harms posterity even by example

Therefore, beloved, we must beware lest this holy way of life grow lukewarm in our time and, gradually diminishing, perish altogether—God forbid. We know that only scanty remains now survive of what was once great and arduous. And just as what was neglected by our elders is not restored by us, so what is lost among us through negligence will by no means be restored by the posterity of our successors.

Thus that saying of Horace is proved true (Book III of the *Odes*, ode 6):

> The age of our parents, worse than that of their ancestors,  
> Brought forth us, more degenerate,  
> Soon to produce  
> An offspring more vicious still.

Thus we shall be guilty not only of our own negligence but also of others’ way of life: while we ourselves fail by inducing them to slacken, we generate for posterity the cause of failure. For when their slothful life is censured, they will at once run back to us and set us before themselves as a shield of defense, so that we who were predecessors in life may consequently become authors of guilt.

“For we are no better,” they will say, “than our fathers. We seized what we found; we hold what we learned.” And so we shall be apostles of another’s sluggishness, and teachers not of instruction but of forgetfulness; not leaders to victory but predecessors into flight.

Remember what is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclesiasticus 2:14). And: “I appoint to you,” he says, “just as my Father appointed a kingdom to me” (Luke 22:29). Why? Certainly not because you began, but because, he says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (ibid.).

Therefore, beloved, let us cut this reproach away from our age; and let us faithfully transmit to our children, undefiled and whole, the emblem of virtue that we received from our fathers. If the eremitical life is to be diminished, let its diminution begin through others; let us not be found first in the sacrilege of this fraud. Otherwise, when our fathers—the founders of this way of life—reach the crown, we may be compelled, while they accuse us and press us severely, to undergo the sentence of vengeance.

For they imitated the struggles of the blessed martyrs with much sweat, while we discuss only the solemn celebrations of the martyrs; and, although we did not take part in the battles, we are eager to rejoice over victories already won.

## CHAPTER V. That our life is the Saturday of the final resurrection

[Col. 0800A]

This whole life is, in a certain sense, the Saturday of that final resurrection. Now, as it were, we celebrate its eve and keep vigil for the eternal solemnity to which we sigh.

But one who is hurrying to a wedding, or awaiting the banquet of some great festival, does not long to anticipate the breakfast of the preceding hour. We, invited to that nuptial banquet of eternal refreshment, have already begun to hasten, yet, while still living softly and luxuriously, we anticipate, as it were, the proper hour for eating.

What has a meal to do with a tomb? What have feasts to do with a grave? If, with the disciples rather than with the soldiers, we are guarding the Lord’s burial, let us bring a mixture of myrrh and aloes (John 19), not cauldrons and kettles. In the former are the bitterness of the mind; in the latter are the allurements of pleasures.

At a burial we ought to beat our breasts, not inflate our bellies with food; we ought to bathe mournful faces in tears, not indulge in emptying cups; we ought not to gorge ourselves with unmixed wine, but temper our drink with weeping (Psalm 101:10).

Yet we do not establish these practices rashly or without discernment, as though we were to deny humanity to the weak or health to those who are sick. Nevertheless, let the sick person indulge himself in discretion in such a way that, when he recovers, he does not abandon the salutary rule of custom. Let him live more leniently, but let the one who is well remain nonetheless in the rigor of his continence.

Therefore, beloved, let us not find it burdensome to observe the fast of Saturday, so that, while now, under the chastisement of our bodies, we are buried with our Redeemer into death, we too may afterward rise with him and feast with him in the radiance of heavenly glory (Romans 6:4–5).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0799]

843–844  
## THE FIFTY-FIFTH LITTLE WORK: ON CELEBRATING VIGILS

### Argument

In this letter he exhorts his monks to celebrate the vigils of eight festivals, which, through lack of devotion and abuse, he complains are neglected by many of his contemporaries. He easily dispels the arguments brought forward by people of little piety that seemed to speak against them.

[Col. 0799D]

To the holy brothers established in the hermitage, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greetings.

Human weakness naturally suffers from this illness: it easily falls from the rigor of continence, but rises with difficulty to the condition of virtue and disciplined living. Hence, when we attempt to undertake something strict for God, we necessarily travel the road of labor alone, scarcely accompanied by anyone; but if we relax ourselves even slightly toward the streams of pleasure, we immediately find many willing companions to imitate us.

We lament this, beloved brothers, because many venerable fasts throughout the yearly cycle—which until now we have honored in the ancient tradition of our forebears—are now, with certain people introducing what seem to be new sects, being neglected indiscriminately and changed into banquets of midday meals. We do not consider it pointless to enumerate them here and to offer, insofar as the brevity of a letter permits, the reasons why each should not be omitted.

### ON CELEBRATING VIGILS

## CHAPTER I. Why we fast on the vigils of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin and the nativity of Blessed John the Baptist

Come, then: why should not the vigils of the Assumption of blessed Mary, ever-Virgin, be celebrated with fasts? We certainly know that this custom was held from antiquity down to us, indeed down to the present day. Is it because the Mother of God did not pass from this life through martyrdom? But if this is the reason why one should not fast, then the nativity of blessed John the Forerunner of Christ is anticipated by a fast without cause, since he is known to have come into this world through the womb, not to have departed from it by the sword as a boy-prophet.

But if the dignity of the matter is examined attentively, both festivals are rightly preceded by fasts, because the Blessed Virgin suffered the distress of the flesh when she died, while Blessed John, by the condition of his birth, emerged from his mother’s womb crying and weeping. We rightly suffer with them through the fasts of the preceding day, so that, when their solemnities dawn, we may enjoy shared joy with them; so that, afflicted together with them in sorrow, we may likewise feast together with them when the festival brings joy.

But perhaps someone will say that the Blessed Virgin, who gave birth to the Author of life without pain, felt no pain in dying. Yet by what authority can anyone declare that she did not suffer bodily when she died, when a sword pierced her soul while she still remained in the flesh? (Luke 2:35.) Especially since the mediator himself between God and human beings, when about to die, said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). Of him Peter also says: “God raised him from the dead, having loosed the pains of hell” (Mark 14:62; Acts 2:24).

But whether, when dying, she felt no pain—which God could certainly have granted—or whether she felt it—which he permitted—where, I ask, does this preacher of feasting and enemy of salutary abstinence come from, except from the number of those of whom the Apostle complains, saying: “For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians 3:18–19)?

When Moses and Aaron paid the debt of death, each was mourned individually by the Israelite people for a month-long period of days [MS *mensurno*; perhaps *menstruo*] (Numbers 20:29; Deuteronomy 34:8). When Jacob died, all Egypt followed him with the mournful lamentation of seventy days (Genesis 50:3). Yet you refuse to sympathize with the dying Mother of God for even a single day, so that you may rightly boast amid her solemnities?

Moreover, concerning the Nativity of the Savior, something no less dishonorable and indecent is done when, on the eve of it, some people, although they eat only one meal, nevertheless indulge in wine and various preparations of food. Indeed, that bread descended from heaven for this purpose, that it might now be common food even for human beings, whereas until then it had belonged exclusively to angels (John 6); it is sufficiently absurd if, when divine nourishment bursts forth from heaven, earthly foods do not make room for it. And then the swallowing of foul wine dulls the nostrils of the mind, when already the heavenly fragrance breathes forth with the honeyed sweetness of grace. For everyone awaits a friend whom he ardently desires to see, arriving from far away, not occupied with feasting, but eagerly fasting.

Although that singular birth knew nothing at all of the weariness of labor, labor is nevertheless familiarly joined to childbirth, as the Truth testifies when it says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers her distress because of her joy, since a human being has been born into the world” (John 16). Hence, not without reason, just as the whole holy Church dies with the dying Christ, rises with him when he rises, and ascends with him when he ascends to heaven, so in a certain manner it shares the labor of childbirth with his blessed Mother in her suffering; and, as though herself in labor, she mourns during the vigils, so that, when the childbirth of salvation has been brought forth, she may rejoice with her in the holy Nativity. Thus, for the glory of so great a solemnity, not only may the mind swell with spiritual exultation, but the flesh itself, which had been afflicted, may rejoice in anticipation of relief, according to the Prophet’s saying: “My soul thirsted for you, and how greatly my flesh also did?” (Psalm 62).

## CHAPTER II. The abuse by some of soothing the voice so that they may sing better.

Some brothers of the spiritual militia, plainly—and this must not be passed over—sustain themselves during the aforementioned vigils under this pretext: that they may grow stronger and more vigorous for rendering the melodies of the ecclesiastical office. But if we desire to soothe divine ears rather than merely human ones with whatever careful sweetness our voices possess, the drum of our body will sound more loudly when dry than when smeared with wine’s liquid or the richness of oil. It is better that, in return for the labor of fasting, the song be moderated under the sober guidance of discretion than that, for the superstition of singing, a worldly example of dissolution be offered to the spiritual order.

Clearly, when it is recognized that the long period of Lent established by the Fathers serves the Nativity of the Lord, it is astonishing how so distinguished a festival should be deprived of the sole honor of its vigils. Moreover, how are we not ashamed that, as has already been said, by drinking water we anticipate the birth of a servant—namely, blessed John the Baptist—while at the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity we stink of wine without restraint? Especially since that day is hotter from the summer heat and longer in duration than all the days of the year, whereas this one is both short and damp. And certainly, if the earnestness of the vigils is pleasing, we keep watch more freely as abstainers than when weighed down by the drunkenness that induces sleep.

[Col. 0802D] It is also fitting to fast at the vigils of Epiphany, because of the greatness of the solemnity in which so many sacraments, as it were, converge into one; nevertheless, those who can be persuaded otherwise are not forbidden to partake of sauces and wine. Here, I imagine, the advocate of a softer life will become angry; here the disputant over smoking food will wrinkle his brow, shouting that I am introducing novel fasts from abroad which I cannot support by any authority of the Fathers.

But, so that I may not continue to wallow in the mud with him, and may quickly free myself from this point, let him tell me why blessed Gregory, in the arrangement of the Masses, appointed a special Mass for this day and entitled it the Mass of the Epiphany vigil. Why, then, does he call them vigils in which the freedom to eat is not chastised by the discipline of fasting? And since, according to ecclesiastical custom, Masses of the vigils are always celebrated at the ninth hour, so that they evidently seem to belong to the solemnities of the following day, why is this called a vigil Mass when it is celebrated at the third hour, before the meal, and plainly does not serve the following day?

Let our gluttons therefore search through the individual days of the whole annual cycle; and when they nowhere find vigils being named at which Masses ought to be celebrated without fasting, they must necessarily confess that at the vigils of Epiphany, along with the celebration of the Masses, fasting too must be observed, with all doubt removed.

## CHAPTER III. Why one ought to fast on Saturday according to the judgment of blessed Silvester.

Furthermore, concerning Holy Saturday, which precedes the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, the reason is also clear why it must be strictly observed as a fast. For if we truly share in the suffering of the author of life, dead and buried; if, established in the company of the disciples, we mourn together with the apostles, it is shameful if we belch from a full dish while he whom we have wept over still lies in the tomb.

According to the testimony of Scripture, the apostles share the Lord’s mourning in grief until, after rising on the third day, he gladdens them with his new appearance (Matthew 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20). But, so that we may be spared the annoyance of this controversy, we send the advocate of the belly to the decisive testimony of blessed Silvester; if his words are believed, all quarrels among us immediately cease.

The words of Silvester are these: “If every Sunday is held and celebrated on account of the Lord’s resurrection, it is right that every Saturday should be undertaken with the rigor of fasting on account of his burial, so that, mourning with the apostles over the Lord’s death, we may deserve to rejoice with them over his resurrection.” And again: “If every Sunday is believed to be adorned with the glory of the resurrection, every Saturday preceding it must be devoted to the fast of the burial, so that he may rightly rejoice in the resurrection who has wept over the death.”

After such words, so plain and repeated in various ways for the sake of the slow-witted, I see nothing else that ought to be added by me, except this: if that holy man judges that all the Saturdays of the entire year should be dedicated to fasting because of that one Saturday of the Lord’s burial, while that one Saturday—which is primary and pre-eminent—is dissolved in feasting, how can the model or pattern of abstinence be transferred from it to the remaining Saturdays?

It must therefore be constantly asserted that, just as Good Friday precedes all the Fridays of the year under the strict judgment of discipline, and just as the day of the Resurrection surpasses the other Sundays in the glory of its solemnity, so also Saturday, which lies between the two, must necessarily be observed with greater rigor of abstinence than the other Saturdays. For just as Good Friday is recognized as the day of the cross and of sorrow, so Saturday is recognized as the day of burial and mourning.

If, however, because of the labor of those who come from far away to the waters of baptism, or because of the weakness of various frail persons, the practice has become established among some of living somewhat more indulgently on that day, this ought to be borne by spiritual persons, not demanded. Otherwise, if they devote themselves to eating food while all the apostles are still weeping, they would show themselves—God forbid—excluded from their company.

## CHAPTER IV. Why “Glory to God in the highest” is sung at the vigil of the Lord’s resurrection.

Nor should anyone object to us that at that time “Glory to God in the highest” is sung during the solemn celebrations of the Masses. This is done for the sake of those who are to be baptized, so that, when the glory of the resurrection has already begun to dawn, they may be seen to be baptized into the Lord’s death (Romans 6). Therefore the Mass, which is forbidden during the day itself, is commanded to be celebrated at night, so that, at a certain midpoint between Christ’s death on the one side and his resurrection on the other, the saving mystery of universal baptism may be established.

In the sacrament of baptism, in imitation of Christ, we both die and rise again. We die when we are immersed in the water; we rise when we are washed. Hence the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6). We are plainly immersed in the saving bath for this purpose: that we may die to all sins; and for this purpose we are raised up: that, rising with Christ, we may henceforth live for righteousness alone, as the same Apostle says: “Jesus Christ died for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (ibid.).

Hence that same Mass appears in a certain manner to be both Lenten and Paschal: after the Alleluia is sung, the Tract, which belongs properly to Lent, is immediately added. But if, with the adversary obstinately insisting, it is maintained that Easter is altogether completed after the Mass, we are not drawn further into the dispute; only on this condition, that the eating of meat be immediately undertaken by the laity. For there is no reason why the freedom of Paschal food should be postponed until the following day, since, as is said, Easter is entirely completed.

But if this plainly seems contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, the adversary must necessarily confess that the day of the Lord’s burial is not Easter, but rather the vigil of Easter, and therefore, at least by the rule of vigils, must be devoted to fasting.

## CHAPTER V. That the Saturday fast was celebrated by a heavenly vision.

[Col. 0804D]

As soon as I had written these things, I will not conceal what I came to know by chance—or rather, by divine prompting. An elderly brother, who had lived in an eremitical cell for nearly thirty years, came to me and disclosed to me alone a vision that had happened to him.

“O master,” he said, “I have often endured the goad of hostility and anger against you because you insisted so strongly that Saturday should be observed as a fast. Meanwhile, I desired to travel to Jerusalem; and as I burned more fervently each day with this desire, on Sunday night, while I was asleep, a certain splendid cleric appeared to me in a vision and said: ‘Brother John’—for that was his name—‘do you wish to come to Jerusalem?’ When I answered him that I did, he immediately led me there in a dream. As he went around many tombs of the saints, he specifically identified whose each one was. At last, with the same guide, I reached the Lord’s tomb.
