And behold, behind the tomb stood a certain cleric with a serene face and handsome appearance, decently adorned down to the neck with a white stole. He said to me:

“‘The day before yesterday you truly adored the life-giving cross, and yesterday too, while fasting, you truly adored the Lord’s burial. From this, with every scruple of doubt removed, recognize that you most truly celebrate and adore both the cross on Friday and Christ’s tomb on Saturday, if you fast on those days while praying and singing psalms.’

“Instructed by this oracle, I lost both the scandal I had held against you, Father, and from then on, whenever circumstances permitted, I fasted [I shall fast] on Saturday with no less devotion than on Friday.”

This the holy brother reported to me, although at that time he knew nothing at all of what we are writing, and even now remains entirely unaware of it.

Indeed, concerning the Greater Litany, some act disgracefully and quite openly against the decision of the canons, because on that occasion it is not observed on account of blessed Mark, whose feast falls on the same day. But since our assertion is called a joke by the conspirators of the belly, let the canonical authority itself be introduced plainly, so that there may be no escape.

The Council of Mainz says (chapter 3): “It has pleased us that the Greater Litany be observed by all Christians on one day, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, just as we have found it established in the Roman Church and as our holy Fathers established it: not riding on horseback and not dressed in costly clothing, but let us fast, sprinkled with ashes and clothed in sackcloth, unless illness prevents it.”

But if this authority should still perhaps be insufficient for anyone, let the Apostolic See suffice; let broad Rome also suffice, which confirms this fast not only by promulgating it in a decretal document, but also preserves it by living observance each year. Here it should be noted that the holy Fathers decreed fasting to prevail over the twofold solemnity—namely, that of Saint Mark and that of Pentecost, within whose period this day often falls—while nevertheless solemnly fulfilling the ecclesiastical office.

Hence we also bear this heavily: many brothers, while shrinking from fasting at the vigils of the blessed apostles Philip and James, put the solemnity of Pentecost forward as an excuse for their dissolution, saying that no one ought then to be constrained under the judgment of fasting, since the season commands feasting rather in Paschal rejoicing.

To these I answer briefly and concisely: if the festivals of the Church and the ecclesiastical discipline of fasting are so mutually opposed that they cannot be celebrated together, then neither can the Greater Litany mentioned above, nor those three days of Rogation before the Lord’s Ascension, nor the vigil of Pentecost be devoted to fasting. And, lest this seem insufficient, that fast too must be abolished which, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the holy Fathers unanimously established should be held in the same week.

And since, as is said, fasting cannot coexist with solemnity, and according to the judgment of some fasting has no force in the presence of a festival, but the festival always prevails, let the vigils of the apostles Peter and Paul therefore be removed from the octave of blessed John the Baptist; let the vigils of blessed Mary the Virgin also be erased from the octave of the martyr Lawrence; and during Lent let a second meal be added to every major festival.

But if ecclesiastical rule does not permit these things, and the world—which has already grown old under the institution of apostolic tradition—has in no way assented to novel doctrines, then it must be admitted that festivals, unless they are pre-eminent, do not prejudice fasts. Thus, while each retains its proper right, the ecclesiastical office may be performed for the sake of the solemnity, and bodily discipline may not abandon its established purpose.

Hence it is clear that whoever refuses to fast at the vigils of these two most venerable apostles, James and Philip, is not moved to do so by love of the festival; rather, according to the counsel of his eloquent gluttony, he is being caressed by the sweetness of living softly.

## CHAPTER VI. How blessed James the Apostle died.

Furthermore, many people think little of the vigils of blessed James, who is the brother of the evangelist John, and irreverently and thoughtlessly pass them over. This is perhaps presumed because the same festival is not celebrated at its proper time. For, as we learn from Luke’s testimony in the Acts of the Apostles, blessed James was killed around the time of Easter.

After first saying, “Herod killed James, the brother of John, with the sword,” Luke shortly afterward added: “It was then the days of Unleavened Bread” (Acts 12). Around that same time blessed Peter was released from his chains, while this James had shortly before been beheaded by Herod’s sword.

Because the two festivals could not be celebrated freely and without restriction within the Paschal feasts, they were necessarily transferred to another time by the discernment of the ancient Fathers. But if that solemn day is to be deprived of the honor of its vigils for this reason, then the festival itself ought not to be celebrated either. And if this apostolic festival is rightly transferred to another time because of the necessity of Easter, it is surely fitting that its vigils should also accompany it inseparably.

The authority of the canons is absolute: it generally commands that all the vigils of the apostles be celebrated. But if the adversary is still found obstinate in pressing his argument, I will add this also: if that festival is deprived of its rightful honor because its time is changed, then the great Paschal solemnity itself will no longer deserve honor, since it follows not a fixed certainty of time but rather the calculation of the full moon.

Ecclesiastical faith holds that our Redeemer was crucified on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day he had also previously been conceived in the Virgin’s womb. If we wish to follow this calculation of time, we must celebrate the Lord’s resurrection every year on the sixth day before the Kalends of the same month. This is plainly not done because it is fitting first to pass through the fourteenth moon with the Passover of the Unleavened, so that we may reach the new Passover, as from the shadow of the Law to the grace of truth.

## CHAPTER VII. Why the Beheading of blessed John the Baptist has no vigil.

Let the enemies of holy vigils and the destroyers of venerable fasts therefore go and declare that reverence ought not to be shown to the Paschal solemnity, so that, because its time varies, it should lack the dignity of the faithful’s devotion and customary worship. And since they have thought wrongly about Easter, let them consequently admit the same necessarily about the Ascension and Pentecost.

But if they object to us that the Beheading of Saint John does not have a vigil because it is transferred from the season of the Lord’s Passion—the time in which the holy Baptist was killed—to the month of August according to custom, we reply that this does not happen because the festival has been moved, but because, since we have received his holy Nativity with vigils, we are content at his beheading with the solemnity of a single day, so that the weakness of the people may not be burdened.

Finally, concerning the vigils of blessed Bartholomew, which some people have already begun gradually to violate, the judgment is no different. On one occasion an abbot, accompanied by men of no low standing, came from distant regions to us living in the desert, having eaten lunch and intending to eat supper. On the following day, the day of the apostolic festival, he was asked, as he was about to depart, to take breakfast, but he refused and yielded to no entreaties.

But, O divine judgment worthy of restoring what was due! Whether in the convent of nuns, which he then visited, or among some laypeople to whom he went, he was unable to find even a trace of wine throughout that entire day. Thus, compelled by divine providence, he was forced to pay the debt of fasting on the very festival whose vigil he had not feared to violate against the rule of ecclesiastical institution; and, so to speak, he paid on the feast for what he had done wrong on the eve.

These things, therefore, beloved ones, concerning the eight vigils to be celebrated meticulously at their proper times, we have written and sent to your holiness with an unblemished pen. We exhort you to gird yourselves manfully to correct the abuses that are now insolently emerging, as true soldiers of Christ.

Let the spirit of ecclesiastical discipline therefore be maintained through you; let the standard of the paternal tradition remain; let the order of religion not fall from its dignity; let ecclesiastical vigor not grow soft. Indeed, I do not doubt that, if this writing falls into the hands of those who hate fasts, it will be shamefully spat upon. These are the people whose oiled and shining skin swells with pride, who, while waging irreconcilable battles against sobriety, grow fat and blaze with red, flaming faces.

For my part, out of love or hatred for no one, I may not conceal what I rightly think. And since I know that Julian Caesar wrote eight books against the Gospel of Christ, I am in no way ashamed to have my little work torn apart with biting words by those who oppose evangelical discipline.

Let them say with their ancient caterers: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22). And let us answer with the servants of Christ: “Let us fast and celebrate the holy vigils, so that in the heavenly festival we may happily feast, destined to live without end” (1 Corinthians 15).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0807]

# FIFTY-SIXTH LITTLE WORK. ON THE FLEETING GLORY OF THE WORLD AND CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD.

## ARGUMENT.

He compares the empress Agnes, entering Rome not with proud display but with attire reduced below the appearance of a private woman, in order to visit the manger of Christ the Lord, with the Queen of Sheba, who entered Solomon’s royal court with magnificent splendor. He also praises her because she wonderfully despised royal pomp. Then he clearly demonstrates, by the example of Roman kings and foreign rulers, that the dignities of this world are fleeting and subject to many disasters. He sharply reproves those who glory in nobility and wealth, since all mortals have the same beginning and the same end.

[Col. 0807D] To Agnes, empress crowned with the shield of God’s good will: Peter, a sinful monk, offers his service.

## ON THE FLEETING GLORY OF THE WORLD AND CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD

### CHAPTER I. A comparison of the empress Agnes with the Queen of Sheba.

The Queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10; 2 Chronicles 9); the empress Agnes went to Rome to learn the Fisherman’s folly. For, as Paul says: “Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save believers through the folly of preaching” (1 Corinthians 1).

The former, as sacred History testifies, entered with a large retinue and riches, with camels also carrying spices, an immeasurable quantity of gold, and precious gems. The latter, together with her kinswoman Hermisinde, inflamed with no lesser fervor of the Holy Spirit, came like Mary Magdalene with the other Mary to the tomb (Matthew 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20), not to anoint Jesus’ body with aromatic ointments, but to water his feet with streams of tears. For they no longer seek the living among the dead, but, adoring him, they hold the feet of the risen one.

The earthly Solomon unlocked for the Queen of Sheba the knots of her questions and the mysteries of riddles. Our queen, however, proposed to have nothing unfastened for her except the bonds of her sins. For Solomon, who was a figure of Christ and, as it were, an image or prophecy, represented the person of our Savior. Of him it is said: “He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand.” Immediately it is added that “he also discoursed about trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, and he discussed animals, birds, reptiles, and fish” (1 Kings 4).

There is no doubt that all these things correspond to our Redeemer, to whom it belongs to treat them with careful consideration. He spoke three thousand proverbs because, while discussing almost everything under a veil—through the mystical deeds of the earlier Fathers, through the allegorical oracles of the prophets, and through the teachings of the radiant Gospel—he counted, as it were, three thousand proverbs in his words.

Hence Matthew says in the Gospel: “Jesus said all these things to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them” (Matthew 15). His songs also number five thousand, because the choir of virgins, who are described under the number five, continually sings a new song before his throne, as John says in the Apocalypse (Revelation 11); or because there are five wounds of the Lord’s body, by which his triumphant victory is proclaimed throughout the whole world. His songs are counted under the same number under which his wounds are held, through which his singular victory earns the glory of eternal praise.

Hence, when it is said in the Song of Songs, “Arise, my beloved, my bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow of the wall,” it is immediately added: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet” (Song of Songs 2).

Since we are not treating these matters exhaustively, but are passing over them quickly and briefly, it is enough to say that, since the rock is Christ, the clefts of the rock are without doubt the scars of the Lord’s body. But when, after the clefts of this rock, the sweet voice of the bride is commanded to sound in the bridegroom’s ears, what else is every devout soul, or the holy universal Church, taught than to return songs of praise according to the same number of five wounds? It is taught to return as many songs as the wounds received for its sake which it recognizes, and to dedicate all the senses of its body to him whom it sees wounded by just as many wounds for its sake.

The five wounds of our senses were healed by the five scars of the Lord’s body.

As for the statement that Solomon discoursed about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing out of the wall, this must necessarily be referred here to a spiritual meaning, since the surface meaning of the words cannot stand at all. Hyssop is not seen growing out of walls, but germinating from rocky mountains. Our wall, therefore, is the very condition of our mortality, which separates us from contemplation of the Creator like an obstacle formed by a hidden house and compels us to incline downward toward the depths.

“For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9). From this wall, then, hyssop grows out, because from the fragility of our mortality emerges what must always be cut away by the iron of repentance. The inner parts are purified by hyssop, which not inappropriately signifies the confession of sins.

### CHAPTER II. The wisdom of Christ and Solomon compared.

Our Solomon therefore discoursed about trees—that is, about human beings rooted within the groves of the growing Church—from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing out of the wall: that is, from the eminent saints made white by the radiance of righteousness to sinners and the fallen, and finally to those converted to the lamentation of repentance.

Hence what follows: “He also discussed animals,” namely, the helpers of the saints, Catholic men; “and birds,” namely, human beings lifted toward heavenly things by holy desires; “and reptiles and fish,” that is, those who drag the breast of desire along the earth and those who wander through the currents of worldly affairs.

It is also said that Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the Easterners and Egyptians, because our Redeemer surpasses the understanding both of angels and of human beings. Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen. What is represented by the number four, except the quadriga of the evangelists? And what by the number twelve, except the senate of the apostles? Through evangelical and apostolic doctrine, the Lord is carried throughout the whole breadth of the earth.

“For God’s chariot is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, on Sinai, in the holy place” (Psalm 67). Since Sinai is interpreted as “commandment,” it is clear that the Lord is carried among those alone in whom the observance of heavenly commandments takes place.

It should be noted that, just as the kingdom of David—who, worn down by so many hardships, signifies the Lord laboring still in the course of mortal life—so the incomparable glory of this Solomon prefigures the same Lord reigning after the end of the world in the majesty of the Father’s summit.

Hence it is said there that there was no silver and that it was considered of no value in Solomon’s days. How can this stand according to the literal sense, so that it may be believed that in Solomon’s time silver either did not exist at all, and had therefore been completely removed from the earth, or was worth not even the slightest amount?

For if it was of no value, as is said, then surely a thousand talents of silver could not be appraised at even the value of a single egg. The text itself and the order of the words refute how frivolous and absurd this would appear to believe. After saying, “There was no silver, and it was considered of no value in Solomon’s days,” it immediately adds: “For the king’s fleet went with the fleet of Hiram by sea once every three years, bringing from there gold and silver” (1 Kings 10).

Why would that fleet carry this metal through so many dangers at sea if it had no value at all? Shortly afterward it is said that “gold and silver vessels were offered to him” (ibid.). Then it adds that “a chariot came up from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred and fifty” (1 Kings 10).

Silver therefore was not without value, since vehicles were purchased with it. But silver signifies the brightness of ecclesiastical preaching, of which it is said: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver” (Psalm 11). We shall regard this silver of holy preaching as being of no value, so to speak, and shall have no need of it in any way after we have been transferred from this calamity to the kingdom of the true Solomon.

For then we shall not need the word of preaching, where we are granted to see face to face, in his beauty, the King of glory whom we have been accustomed to hear from the mouth of the preacher. As the Lord promises through the prophet, saying: “No one shall say, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all shall know me, from the greatest to the least, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 11).

### CHAPTER III. He removes an objection.

[Col. 0811B]

But perhaps someone will assert that we are violently bending the words of Scripture toward our own understanding, and will claim that what Solomon appears to assert about himself applies in every respect specifically to the Savior. Let the advocate of this objection therefore say by what reasoning it can properly belong to Solomon that he says, as though about himself:

“For God gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, consummation, and midpoint of times, the changes and alterations of seasons, the changes of human beings, the courses of the year and the arrangements of the stars, the natures of animals and the rages of beasts, the force of winds and the thoughts of human beings; and I learned whatever things are hidden and unforeseen” (Wisdom 1).

To pass over the other points for the moment, how could he have known the thoughts of human beings, when elsewhere he himself says to God: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings”? (1 Kings 2.) But who learned all hidden and unforeseen things, except our Redeemer, in whose breast all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden? (Colossians 2.) He certainly learned through his humanity what he naturally knows through his divinity.

To this Solomon, then, you recently came, O queen—not like that woman of Sheba, in chariots, on horseback, and with elephants, but rather in tears, groans, and laments. You are therefore truly the Queen of Sheba. For Sheba is interpreted as “humble” or “of the plain.” And rightly “of the plain.” You descended into the field of battle to join hands in combat; and, standing in the camp of Christ, you fight the enemy without weakness.

You came, I say, not so that he might painstakingly unravel the mysteries of riddles for you, but so that, through the ministry of his simple key-bearer, he might unlock for you the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. You came humble to the humble, poor to the poor; and, as though together with the richly adorned and unadorned shepherds of the flocks, you came to adore the child crying in the manger (Luke 2).

To see you then—and the things around you—was a spectacle greatly to be wondered at and an edifying example of the Savior to be imitated. Your clothing was dark and woolen. The animal on which you sat—not to call it a horse, but rather a burdo (mule; printed *burno*) or a burricus (little donkey)—barely exceeded the size of a sluggish ass.

You had exchanged your crown for a veil, purple for sackcloth, and the hand that had been accustomed to carry a scepter in the manner of a dove [or a column] was now worn down by carrying a psalter. Truly, because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44), that flourishing beauty of gems and the adornment of garments glittering with gold had now migrated inward, and the inner appearance of the bride shone in the sight of the hidden observer.

To her the bridegroom says: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4). And again: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely” (Song of Songs 6).

That delicate neck, from which a necklace (*murena*) once hung with golden ornaments and gleaming pearls, is now roughened by the edge of a woolen garment. Hence the ministers of that heavenly bridegroom flatter you and say: “We shall make golden ornaments for you, studded with silver” (Song of Songs 1). And the bridegroom continues: “You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Song of Songs 4).

Amana is said to be a mountain of Cilicia, which many also call Taurus. Sanir and Hermon are mountains of the land of Judah, where lions and leopards are believed to dwell.

### CHAPTER IV. How the crown of glory is increased for us through good examples.

These mountains, therefore, are to be understood as the kings, princes, and various powers of this world, which raise themselves like mountains to the summit of pride and provide a dwelling for evil spirits as though for leopards and lions.

You will therefore be crowned from these mountains, because as many princes and powerful people of the world as are converted to God through your example, for all of them the reward of eternal glory will be increased for you. You will be not only crowned but yourself a crown, as the prophet testifies when he says: “You shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God” (Isaiah 61).

You have lost, O queen, the husband after whom you disdained to enter another marriage-bed or to accept the bond of any suitor, unless he surpassed your former husband in the distinction of a more excellent glory. What, then, could you do? That husband of yours was an emperor; he held the summit of royal dignity and, what is singular among human beings, administered the monarchy of the Roman Empire. Since, therefore, he excelled in so lofty a citadel of eminence, no one superior to him could be found among humankind. Since you could not find on earth a husband suitable and pleasing to your eyes, you rushed headlong into the embrace of the heavenly Bridegroom. Headlong, I say: “For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI).

O blessed pride, O blessed elevation of mind, worthy of every proclamation of praise, which, while it despised the rights of a carnal marriage-bed, passed gloriously into the *dotalia*—the bridal endowments—of the eternal King! A carnal husband plainly corrupts the mysteries of virginity; but that heavenly Bridegroom immediately and without difficulty restores to virginal honor even those whom he joins to himself after they have been violated, so that they may cast off the stains of their contracted defilement and, like little trees that were previously dry, bloom again with foliage and return to the grace of their former beauty.

Moreover, when a woman about to marry a carnal husband is adorned, money gathered from relatives and acquaintances everywhere is quickly collected, and whatever can be obtained is immediately crammed into purses or sealed chests, so that the more heavily laden the woman hastens toward her husband, the more splendidly she may appear, and the more ardently he may burn with devoted love for her. You, by contrast, in order to enter into marital covenant with the heavenly Bridegroom, squander the accumulation of the royal treasury; you scatter every radiant object, together with gold and silver, and pearls; your purple hangings—or rather, your gilded ones—are hung from the ceilings of churches; royal ornaments serve the sacred altars. To put it plainly, nothing is spared, and nothing is withheld from the needy or from the churches except what is found outside your own property. You cast everything away, you dissipate everything, so that, wholly unburdened—indeed, naked—you may arrive at the embrace of the heavenly Bridegroom.

## CHAPTER V. How much the good examples of great men and women are worth

I do not explain these matters on your account, venerable empress—for I fear that by these words I may rather offend you—but rather so that, while the distinction of your virtue is brought forth in some measure, no small edification may be provided for those who read. For when so great an eminence is cast down to the pavement for love of its Creator, what neck of pride, immediately erect from the stiffening tension of its own rigidity, would not be bent? What inflation of any haughty mind would not at once subside when it sees the possessor of such glory now like a contemptible slave? Moreover, who would fear poverty in passing things when he sees voluntary poverty in a woman whom, only a short time before, he had seen ruling so many kingdoms? Or who would shudder at the indignity of an unkempt appearance when he considers that a vile thread has been preferred by royal majesty to golden embroidery and royal splendors?

I shall come to the table and, so to speak, to the hungry abundance of lavish banquets. What, I ask, is it like to send around the tables, one after another, the piled-up mass of dishes before you and the feasts of gleaming meats, yet not taste even a little of the meats’ fat? To handle delicacies with your hands, yet not savor them in your mouth? Indeed, to nibble only cautiously at bread itself or at any food of less elaborate preparation? You often complained to me that you were unable to restrain your appetite for eating to the extent that, from what you saw set before you, you could not at some time indulge yourself somewhat excessively. Hence the frequent tears, hence groans, hence deep sighs. You mourned because, however carefully you observed discipline and however earnestly you pursued strictness, you could not completely overcome nature.

But, as I perhaps did not keep silent even then, your fast, O queen, is manifold. We sometimes fast from food, but you fast from purple; you fast from the crown and from so many and such magnificent displays of imperial glory. Abstaining from these things is rightly called a fast, since every carnal mind is delightfully nourished by them. For if simple water poured out by David is turned into a sacrifice, as Scripture testifies (II Kings XXI), how much glory before God is earned by contempt for so many possessions and honors?

O how weighty, how praiseworthy is the abstinence by which a young woman accustomed to it fasts from a man’s embrace! Is it not also a serious fast that you, who once were accustomed to raise these people to the summit of honors and insolently to deprive others of their dignity, now content with humble household possessions, avoid human sight and persist diligently in prayer and the chanting of psalms? Since formerly you were Susanna with a husband (Dan. XIII), you have rightly now become Anna after a husband (I Kings I); and because then you had preserved conjugal chastity undefiled, you now remain continually in the church with the daughter of Phanuel—whose name is said to mean “temple of God” (Luke II).

This is why you asked me, through the venerable Rainald, bishop of Como, whether it was permissible for a person, while discharging the bodily necessity itself [editorial correction: “the discharge itself”], to repeat some psalms. To this I explained what occurred to me at the time: that almighty God also visited holy Job when he was seated upon a dungheap (Job XVIII and following), and that blessed Agnes the martyr, whose namesake you also are, found both an angel and angelic clothing in the worn and filthy places of a brothel. The Apostle likewise commands us to pray everywhere when he says: “I wish, therefore, that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute” (I Tim. II). Yet these matters ought rather to be pondered in the heart than explained in speech.

I have said this, although it would have been worthy of silence and should by no means have been spread through many mouths, so that it might plainly become known to readers how intensely the ardor of divine love burns in your holy breast, so that you do not consent to be silent from divine praises even for a brief moment. What will those say who make the church not a place of prayer but a place of talking, and not a sanctuary but a meeting-place, and therefore mix secular speech within that house which is clearly constructed for the sole purpose that one may be entirely free there from the business of worldly activity?

But so that those who stream to the threshold of the apostles may profitably imitate the example of your holy devotion, you also made me sit beneath the hidden confession of blessed Peter before the sacred altar; and, through mournful groans and bitter sighs, you began with the tender frivolities of your five-year-old infancy, only recently weaned. As though blessed Peter himself were bodily presiding there, whatever subtle or minute thing had been able to tickle the inward parts of your humanity, whatever was vain in your thoughts, and whatever superfluous matter might have crept into your speech, was unfolded in faithful narration.

For this reason it seemed to me that I should impose no other burden of penance upon you as you confessed than that I should repeat the saying of the divine commission: “Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out.” Or that which is sent through the angel to those who were in Thyatira: “I will not lay any other burden upon you; only hold fast what you have” (Rev. II). For, God as my witness, I imposed upon you not even a single day of fasting or any other affliction; I merely commanded you to persevere in the holy works you had begun.

## CHAPTER VI. With what purity of mind the relics of the saints should be venerated

Would that such groans and tears burst forth in confession from certain murderers and those guilty of various crimes; would that the spirit of a mind wasting away and pierced by the sharpest pain groaned thus, and guilty breasts sobbed thus, as there were lamented either the phantoms of empty thoughts or the foolish frivolities of childish levities. Let those who hasten with pious devotion to venerate the bodies of the saints be stirred by this example. There let them vomit up the diseases of their own guilt, as though they were harmful humors and illnesses; let them, through the efforts of pure confession, receive more urgently the saving antidote of penance. There let them establish the baptism of penance, into which they have been immersed through the judgment of priestly office, so that they may lay aside the garments of the old person and henceforth live, having passed from the old into the new.

But you, my lady—for since I do not doubt that you are the bride of my Redeemer, I am not at all ashamed to call you my lady—my lady, I say, plant your foot in the root of perseverance and burn inwardly with love for him to whom, through the hands of priests and the poor, you daily send everything, so that what is prescribed in the Law may rightly happen to you: namely, that if someone should happen to love a woman captured in war and wish to take her as his wife, he must first shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured (Deut. XXI); thus, when she had emerged according to custom into the freedom of an Israelite woman, he might lawfully join her to himself in marriage.

Your nails, therefore, together with your hair, have already begun to be cut; the garment with which you were clothed has already begun to be removed, because whatever is seen to surround or adorn you outwardly in the beauty of your personal ornaments or in the preciousness of your possessions is daily expended in works of piety. It remains for you to reach the innermost sweetness of your Bridegroom and that most pleasant unity of the joined spirit: “For whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him” (I Cor. VI). That is, let the flavor of divine love flow into your inward being; let that flame of intimate sweetness kindle the hidden recesses of your breast, a flame unknown both to the wretched world and to every carnal mind, so that you may fervently exclaim what is found in the Song of Songs: “The throat of my beloved is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (Song V); and so that he may in grateful exchange answer you: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song IV).

Do not be troubled if some adversity should perhaps strike you; for this happens so that the inward disposer may draw you toward this sweetness. When a mother wishes to wean her child, she sometimes applies gall to her breasts, so that, while he rejects what he finds abhorrent, he may be compelled to turn to nourishment that will strengthen him. For this reason also the king of Egypt is permitted to strike and tear apart the Israelite people (Exod. V), so that they may be urged to hasten toward the fields of promise.

## CHAPTER VII. Examples of kings and commanders who lost the happiness of the world through a most unhappy end

But, to say nothing of you, who, by reciprocal requital, have both hated the world and are now, being hated, cast out by it, does not the same happiness quickly turn into bitterness even for those kings by whom this world is loved and to whom it flatters through deceptive trickery? Thus a man who today carries home the signs of victory from his enemies and advances in triumph with a display of glory may tomorrow be pierced ignobly by an enemy’s sword as he turns his back in flight.

Indeed, on the very day when Belshazzar, already drunk, dared to defile the vessels of the Lord’s temple with the lips of his concubines, he fell beneath the swords of the Medes, while Darius was obtaining the victory (Dan. V). Galba, the Roman emperor, ruled for only four months and died after being struck by a sword in the Roman Forum. I say nothing of Nero; I pass over Otho, whom the histories of the Roman state testify to have been killed by their own hands. Was Vitellius not killed by the commanders of Vespasian? Was Pertinax not killed by the praetorian soldiers? Macrinus, Antoninus, Alexander, Philip, Gallienus—did not all these emperors suffer the swords of military violence? Domitian, moreover, was stabbed through the conspiracy of his own men. Probus [Charus], while he had his camp above the Tigris, was suddenly killed by a heavenly thunderbolt.

But whoever wishes to know more fully should run through the histories of Roman antiquity in sequence; there he will plainly see how few rulers of the state died a natural death. For Gordian, Philip, Decius, Gallus, Volusianus, Gallienus, Quintillus, Aurelian, Numerian, Licinius, Constans, Constantine the Younger, Julian the Apostate, Valens, Gratian, Valentinian the Younger, John, Valentinian III, Majorian, Anthemius, Nepos—all these governors of the Roman Empire—were they not either killed in repose by the seditious treachery of their own men or, while under arms, destroyed by hostile swords?

And what did it profit certain men that their long life endured for many years more in this world? To pass over countless examples, the emperor Valerian engaged in battle with Shapur, king of the Persians, in Mesopotamia and lost. Shapur immediately captured him and consigned him to the bonds of unremitting imprisonment. As history relates, he grew old in ignoble servitude among the Parthians; and for as long as he lived he was subjected to this disgraceful punishment, so that the king of that province, with Valerian bent down, would place his foot upon his neck and thus mount his horse, swollen with arrogance.

Who is there, then, upon whom fortune does not shift, turning now from adversity to prosperity and now from prosperity to adversity with theatrical variability? What great glory and favor from his own people smiled upon Hannibal when at Cannae he laid low Paulus Aemilius together with so many ranks of Roman soldiers? And when, finally, he sent to Carthage three bushels of gold rings, which he had stripped from the hands of Roman knights, senators, and soldiers? He also subjected very many cities of Italy to himself, to such an extent that the Roman citizens had already decided to abandon Italy and despaired utterly of the condition of their collapsing empire.

But how contrary was the turn of this success when his brother Mago was captured by Scipio near Carthage in Spain, when the head of his other brother Hasdrubal, severed by the sword, was thrown before Hannibal’s own camp, and when Hannibal himself, after the inescapable danger of flight, was finally compelled by pressing necessity to kill himself with poison?

How contrary was the turn of fortune for that outstanding Pompey, who, after so many triumphs and famous victories achieved throughout various regions of the world, after overcoming twenty-two kings in the eastern climate alone, died with his head severed by the sword of the contemptible Achillas! Caesar too, whom the whole western world, greedy for victory, could not satisfy, and whom the Ocean—with its shores ablaze with the slaughter of countless nations—opposed as an inconvenient and arrogant obstacle, so to speak, endured the swords of senators within the curia; pierced by twenty-two wounds, he died beneath them.

## CHAPTER VIII. Examples of women whose joys were seized by death

Are women also found to be immune from the wheel-like whirling of this world’s deception? Cleopatra, indeed, ruled magnificently over all Egypt; that kingdom is said to contain one hundred thousand villages. To this was added the fact that Antony, who ruled both the East and Asia, rejected Octavian Augustus’s sister by divorce and joined this woman to himself in marriage under ill-fated auspices.

But to what end did such glorious and magnificent spouses come? Antony, defeated by Augustus in a naval battle at Actium, fled to Egypt; there, when his affairs were desperate, he deliberately took his own life. Cleopatra too, afterward compelled by a similar necessity, willingly threw herself into her husband’s costly tomb; applying an asp to her own breasts, she died while the snake sucked her blood and she drew its poison into herself.

Semiramis too—how many massacres she carried out after her husband’s death, how many kingdoms she subjected to herself, and by what end she finally perished—the ancient annals plainly attest.

Since, therefore, the deceptive happiness of this world is exposed to so many calamities of the world, since temporal power is subject to variation through so many disasters, and since the order of events confounds itself through an alternation like theatrical whirling, what person of sound mind would not turn his thoughts away from things so frivolous and fleeting?

And, so as not to pass over matters that are especially well known to you, with what glory Pope Victor and your husband, the emperor Henry—both men of holy memory—were then flourishing in age and distinguished in dignity, when the moon, pouring its serene radiance over the earth, suffered an eclipse and suddenly withered, changing the mirror of its ruddy splendor into something ignoble—not merely pallor, but darkness. This, as soon became clear, signified nothing other than the approaching death of both rulers. For both died in that same year.

But when, afterward, approximately two years ago, the moon was turned to blood—since blood signifies sins, as David says, “Deliver me from bloodshed, O God” (Ps. X)—it signified, as far as I can see, nothing other than that the holy Church was to be stained with the blood of the crime of Cadalus. For Cadalus, anathematized a thousand times, while scattering limitless sums of money among peoples in order to purchase the Roman Church, turns human hearts through greed into the appearance of bronze, as though into blood. Thus, while pestilential people do not cease to possess the redness of this metal, the splendor of the Church is in a certain manner turned into gore. For the heart that desires something assumes its appearance before the eyes of God. But these matters belong elsewhere.

## CHAPTER IX. That the beginning and end of all mortals are the same

To return, then, to the point from which I digressed: all human beings, whether powerful or poor, receive the same origin and will have no different end. Between these two boundaries there is a certain diversity of life, so that some boast of being distinguished while others grieve that they are needy. But this variety of human life is enclosed within the momentary brevity of time, so that those who are exalted do not long rejoice in their prosperity, and those without glory quickly escape the disadvantage of their abasement.

What, then, is our beginning, and what is our end—things which, as has been said, we cannot vary, but which all mortals possess equally in common? Listen, however, to the wise man speaking in the Book of Wisdom:

“I too am a mortal human being, like all others, and descended from the earthly one who was first made. I was formed as flesh in my mother’s womb; for ten months I was coagulated in blood from the seed of a man, through the pleasure of a fitting dream. And when I was born, I received the common air, and fell upon earth, formed in the same manner, and I uttered my first voice like everyone else, weeping. I was nurtured in swaddling clothes and with great cares” (Wis. VII).

No king, indeed, had any other beginning of birth. And immediately it is added: “One entrance into life is the same for all, and the exit is similar” (ibid.).

If one carefully considers the one entrance into life and the similar exit of which this passage speaks, that variety which occurs in between must necessarily be despised as the vanity of a fleeting dream. This too, which was stated above—“For ten months I was coagulated in blood from the seed of a man, through the pleasure of a fitting dream”—if one does not shrink from considering it attentively and vigilantly, what mind, hearing this, could be proud in the arrogance of its conceit? Who would not immediately be compelled to recognize himself as corruption when he considers the foulness of his origin, so obscene? Let him say within himself: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Eccli. X). After your departure, moreover, what awaits you is first a worm, then dust.

Let the pride of an elated heart therefore blush, and let the person who sees that between birth and death he is bound together with the rest by the common law of nature cease to boast of the distinction of a higher glory.

## CHAPTER X. He concludes by exhorting her to perseverance

But you, venerable lady, who have climbed from the filth of earthly pride to the sublime height of true humility, persist firmly in its citadel. Having once entered through hope into the land of the living, fix the foot of perseverance there immovably, so that you may no longer desire to turn aside onto the slippery road of secular life.

You who once were the wife of an earthly emperor have now, through the dowry of holy profession, become the bride of the Redeemer. Thus prostrate yourself before him in true humility of heart; unite yourself to him with the bond of ardent charity, so that you may be able to sing with fitting voice together with that mystical bride: “I have found him whom my soul loves; I held him and will not let him go” (Song I); and: “My beloved will dwell among my breasts” (ibid.). Since the human heart lies hidden between the breasts, let the continual love of your Bridegroom not depart from the inward parts of your heart; and let the holy soul, now joined to him in your love, never again be torn from the embraces of his sweetness, so that Isaiah’s prophecy may be solemnly fulfilled in you: “As a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isa. LXII).

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0819]

# 865–866. THE FIFTY-SEVENTH OPUSCULUM. ON THE DUTY OF A PRINCE IN RESTRAINING THE WICKED, WITH AN ADDITIONAL DISCUSSION ON THE SAME SUBJECT

## Argument

He reproves the leniency of the same Duke Gothifred in punishing crimes and shows how much harm to peoples results from the excessive kindness of princes. The boldness of the wicked is certainly increased, not suppressed; and human affairs are thrown into confusion unless sins are restrained by corresponding punishments.

[Col. 0819B] To Gothifred, most excellent duke, Peter, a sinful monk, sends greeting in the Lord.

Someone who drinks flavored wine every day, sweetened with honey, eventually finds that the prolonged sweetness offends his taste and takes greater pleasure in the sourness of cheap, flat wine. Indeed, Solomon says: “Whoever eats much honey, it is not good for him.” Among rich and fatty dishes, too, fresh herbs suppress disgust and settle the inner disturbance of a breast nauseated to the point of vomiting.

You, most eminent man, likewise receive many things every day, in a certain manner sprinkled with nectar, since everyone speaks to you according to your wishes and strives to suggest nothing except what flatters your ears. Whatever must plainly be said to you is first carefully arranged, and is beaten and polished, as though by the labor of a smith’s craft: that is, whatever it may be, a humility laid beneath it suggests it, rather than the free authority of the speaker expressing it.

O unhappy summit of worldly dignity, always exposed to deception! For while people say to others what they think, they compose arguments in disguised speech for the powerful; and those who present themselves as pure to others are compelled always to regard the rich with suspicion. Since, then, all sorts of worldly people offer your excellence only honeyed cups—for they suggest only what they judge pleasing to you—the bitterness of my words ought not to be unpleasant amid the sweet allurements of daily flattery, just as amid pleasant banquets the greenness of country herbs is sometimes pleasing.

## ON THE DUTY OF A PRINCE IN RESTRAINING THE WICKED

## CHAPTER I. That the rigor of justice preserves kingdoms

What I have often said to you in living speech, I now repeat through a letter. I freely confess that I am greatly displeased because you neglect this monarchy, in which nearly one hundred thousand people dwell, as though it were some rustic little village, and do not entrust it to a governor by whom it ought to be ruled and administered. For you owe a strict account to the Judge for all those over whom you now preside through the office of government; and the more glorious the eminence of the dignity you hold, the harsher the judgment will be when you render your account. Therefore transfer the burden to another, so that what you cannot carry on your own shoulders you may be able to bear through another, with the labor shared.

I am also not a little displeased because in punishing crimes and restraining the reckless acts of wicked men you are seen to be more lenient than you should be; and while you spare sinners, you are shown to increase their sins. For when the rigor of justice is weakened, the structure of discipline is overturned; and when the judgment of avenging severity is suppressed, reckless license to offend is released.

Disordered compassion truly nourishes impiety; and the timid hand of a physician enlarges the wound of a sick person. It makes the corruption overflow when, instead of cutting, it daily applies a superficial scar to the little wound by merely touching it. Finally, an apothecary who does not mix sharpness into soft ointments can apply no effective power to dry up swellings.

Not all members of the Church perform the same office. One function belongs to a priest, another to a judge. The former ought to overflow with compassionate inward feeling and, in the lap of maternal mercy, continually nourish his children at the overflowing breasts of doctrine. The latter’s duty is to punish the guilty and rescue the innocent from their hands; to maintain the vigor of uprightness and justice and not grow lukewarm in zeal for legal sanctions; not to deviate from the line of equity; and not to weaken the character of legitimate rigor.

He should also always remember what is said through the Apostle: “Do you not wish to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it. For it is God’s minister to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword without cause” (Rom. XI).

In these words, then, it is to be understood [the text reads: “datur, vel aliquid simile,” “it is given, or something similar”] that the sword of the prince is one thing and the priest’s mitre another. You are not girded with a sword for this purpose, that you should stroke or anoint the wrongdoing of violent men, but that you should strive to cut it down with the blows of a flashing blade. Hence what follows: “For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER II. That a judge who does not punish wrongdoers is the devil’s minister

If, then, he is God’s minister who avenges wrongdoing by punishing those who do evil, he is without doubt the devil’s minister who gently strokes criminals and reprobates. Just as the one who avenges the wicked serves God, so the one who flatters those committing iniquity is a minister of the adversary.

A sword must contract rust if it is always stored in its sheath and never exercises vengeance. A sword becomes rough and dull when, always restrained from wounding, it is not sharpened. In contrast, it is said through Ezekiel: “The sword is sharpened and polished; it is sharpened to slaughter victims; it is polished so that it may shine” (Ezek. XXII).

The judge’s tribunal is plainly different from the priest’s chair. The former carries a sword for the purpose of drawing it in punishment of those who live unjustly; the latter is content with the staff of innocence, holding it quietly and peacefully as the guardian of discipline.

Yet if a priest is weakened by immoderate compassion toward those subject to him, he too is rightly condemned by the sentence of divine wrath. For Heli was a priest, concerning whom it was said to Samuel: “Because he knew that his sons were acting disgracefully and did not rebuke them, therefore I have sworn to the house of Heli that the iniquity of his house shall not be expiated by sacrifices and offerings forever” (I Kings I).

Let him be a judge who neglects to settle the cases and disputes of litigants and spends the greater part of the day attending to the solemn rites of Masses and to prayers. But there it is said that even the iniquity of that priest himself could not be expiated by sacrifices and offerings forever, because Heli had not restrained the vices of his sons.

## CHAPTER III. That chastising the wicked is a sacrifice to God

Consider, moreover, what it means that sacrifices and offerings—which chiefly cleanse sins—cannot expiate the negligence shown toward those subject to one’s authority. Many people, deceived by the error of false compassion, foolishly claim that they please God by the very thing through which they cruelly fight against him; they earn wrath through the very thing by which they thought they would obtain favor; and while they grant others forgiveness out of false compassion, they themselves incur the movement of divine indignation.

A man from among the sons of the prophets said to his companion that he should strike him. Because the other refused to strike him, he was immediately attacked by a lion and died (III Kings XXVII). Ahab thought that he pleased God through his compassion when he not only called Ben-hadad, king of Syria, his brother, but also graciously made him his companion in his own chariot. But listen to what indiscriminate compassion deserved to hear: “Because you have let go from your hand a man worthy of death, says the Lord, your life shall answer for his life, and your people for his people” (ibid.).

Saul did not kill Agag, king of Amalek, but preserved him alive after victory had been completed; for this mercy he rightly heard: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you may not be king” (I Kings XIII).

The people showed compassion toward the women of Midian, but Moses said to them: “Why have you spared the women? Therefore kill all the males, even the little ones; and slaughter the women who have known men in sexual intercourse” (Num. XXXI). The same Moses, after the calf had been made at Horeb, said to the sons of Levi: “Let each one kill his brother, friend, and neighbor” (Exod. XXXII). And after twenty-three thousand men had been killed, he said: “Today you have consecrated your hands to the Lord, each one in his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (ibid.).

That Amalekite who boasted that he had killed Saul, pretending that he had taken not a helmet but a diadem from the head of the fighting king, was struck down by David’s sword and died (II Kings I). The killers of Ish-bosheth likewise, when they offered his head to David as though it were a gift, did not escape the sword (II Kings IV); and the man whom they had hoped would thank them for their gift proved instead to be the avenger of the murder they had committed.

Peter too did not permit the lie of Ananias and Sapphira to go unpunished (Acts V); striking them with the sword of his mouth, he terrified the hearts of others lest they presume to attempt anything similar. Paul likewise, when he sought to restrain his disciples from excesses, threatened wrongdoers with the rod (I Cor. IV).

Our Savior too, who appeared like a gentle lamb, as soon as he entrusted Peter with authority over heaven and earth, immediately rebuked him with a harsh reprimand: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a scandal to me, because you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings” (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII).

Why, then, are holy men so often found attacking those who do wrong, whether by verbal correction or by the punishments they carry out, except so that it may plainly become clear that one does not live rightly in this mortal condition if harshness is not mixed with gentle and mild treatment? For where discipline is entirely set aside, where the strict judgment of legitimate rigor is suppressed, human weakness—which is always inclined toward evil—must be released toward unlawful acts.

And the whole guilt of those subject to authority undoubtedly falls upon the one who ought to have restrained them with the reins of discipline, lest they rush headlong into wrongdoing. For what else is the ruler’s disordered compassion than confusion among the people? While he is restrained from governing with a steady rein, all his subjects, like horses without bridles, are dragged over precipices.

They are plainly permitted to do whatever they please, and now it is clearly seen what is often said in the Book of Judges: “In those days there was no king in Israel, but each person did what seemed right to him” (Judg. XVII). And what was said through Micaiah in the time of the most impious king Ahab: “These people have no lord; let each one return to his house in peace” (III Kings XXII).

Of Saul’s time too it is said: “The edges of the plowshares, hoes, forks, and axes were blunted, even to the point of repairing the goad” (I Kings XXIII). The edges of tools are blunted when the zeal and fervor of teachers are extinguished; and there is no goad to prick when no one is present to rebuke the sins of wrongdoers.

Paul had begun to feel this goad pricking him when the divine voice said to him: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts IX).

## CHAPTER IV. That the counselors of kings should be not only compassionate but also prudent
Indeed, what I am about to relate was not handed down to me by the historian’s pen, but was narrated to me in plain speech by Count Ubald, a notably eloquent and prudent man.

“The emperor Theodosius,” he said, “was accustomed to converse with a certain devout hermit. The emperor obeyed his commands and revealed to him the hidden secrets of his conscience. The servant of God, being simple, pure, and almost entirely unfamiliar with worldly perversity, earnestly admonished Augustus to be merciful toward offenders, to refrain from punishing the guilty, and, since he himself asked pardon from the heavenly Judge, not to demand vengeance from his brother—especially since the Judge himself says: ‘With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you’ (Matt. VII).

“Accordingly, the emperor, placing faith in the holy man’s admonitions, began to remit with impunity the offenses of the depraved and of all who caused harm; to pardon sacrilegious persons and those liable to punishment under the law as though their offenses were venial; and also to release from their obligations all who recklessly invaded the rights of others.

“At this the leading men of the kingdom complained. Those responsible for administering the royal mystery [ministry] protested that the world, already in peril, was falling into ruin, and declared that everything was being thrown into confusion by right and wrong alike unless equity and justice speedily came to the aid of human affairs. Finally, they lamented that, through the sluggishness of this superstitious and frivolous mercy, robberies and acts of violence were being committed everywhere; the statutes of the laws were being dissolved; and, through the audacity granted by this freedom, the wickedness of perverse men was being stirred up to attempt every punishable and harmful deed.

“Moved by this complaining report, the emperor sent a messenger to the man of God. He asked his advice, explained what the murmurers were charging against him, and inquired what above all he himself ought to do.

“The man of God carefully examined the matter and recognized that the judgment of his counsel had to be changed. He remained silent in words, but replied through a certain symbolic action. In the presence of the officer carrying the official embassy, he combed his head all around and immediately threw into the fire whatever had been removed or shed into his lap. Then, taking up a hoe, he entered his little garden, demolished all the harmful growth, uprooted the sterile weeds, hoeing all around, and cultivated and protected the green vegetables. He eradicated the former so that, once pulled up by the roots, they would wither; but he tended and cultivated the latter so that they might prosper through the growth of their mature shoots.

“After performing these symbolic actions, he remained in the same disciplined silence and indicated to the messenger that he should return to his lord and report to him in order everything he had seen.

“The messenger returned, not without a certain irritated indignation, and began to grumble and complain that he had not been sent to a sound-minded man but rather to a madman and a lunatic.

“‘I had hoped,’ he said, ‘that he would instruct me with flowing words and, in accordance with the sequence of my inquiry, inform me about everything through an open verbal response. But he, like a man out of his mind and raving, began now to comb his unkempt head of hair, now to hoe his garden after seizing the tool—as though I cared greatly about his nits and lice, or were asking to be taught rural husbandry.’

“Then the emperor, listening carefully to what was being said and pondering the deed with deeper understanding, declared that it was not ridiculous but a mystery, and that what he had asked had been unmistakably expressed to him through evident signs.

“‘The servant of God,’ he said, ‘answered us better by acting than by speaking, and by the genuine oracle of his deed he untied the knot of one of our questions.’”

## CHAPTER V. What is the duty of a ruler?

[Col. 0824C]

What could be clearer than the fact that he combed his head and immediately threw what he had removed into the fire? It was as though he were saying: “By the comb of manifold division—that is, by the examination and discernment of lawful judgment—let every harmful thing perish, and let what is good remain, purified after the evil has been cast away.”

Moreover, he wished to repeat the same meaning through the cultivation of the garden: just as he pulled up the harmful weeds with their clods, but cultivated the good vegetable so that it might sprout more abundantly, so must we, as though with the hoe of balanced justice and discernment, labor both to uproot the wicked from their roots and to arrange the good in tranquil peace, so that they may bear fruit for God.

Those who were present heard this. What they had previously regarded as ridiculous, like old women’s nonsense, they began to venerate as a true sacrament of spiritual and profound wisdom.

Then the emperor, as though confirmed by this prophetic oracle, began to punish the violence of those who lived unjustly; to strike guilt and crimes with the stern correction of his jurisdiction; to restrain the wicked from their impious undertakings; and, by the authority of imperial power, to terrify the hearts of the perverse and restore everything to peace.

Thus the world, which had begun to perish through negligence, blossomed again under the discipline of equity and justice.

I have related this not to assert firmly that it was certainly true, but because I have sampled what was reported to me in a hasty account, insofar as forgetfulness did not interrupt it. Yet antiquity would never have transmitted this story down to us through the spreading of fame if it had not believed that it would benefit posterity as an example for edification.

Within scarcely five years before my birth, Otto III was taken from human affairs. He had flourished magnificently in the dignity of the imperial rank and had vigorously governed the Roman commonwealth. While he had scarcely passed beyond the age of twenty, among the many distinguished and splendid deeds he performed, he put out the eyes of three leading men and counts of the kingdom: namely, Rodulf, Raymond, and Arimund.

By this conspicuous act of justice, he so made the entrails of all who seized the possessions of others tremble, and so established the whole kingdom in the tranquility of security and peace, that almost everyone kept himself fearfully within the limits of his own short measure and did not insolently overstep the boundaries of his lawful property.

Hence this proverbial praise had spread through the mouths of the people: “By the extraction of six eyes, one kingdom was pacified. Three men became blind, and the light of desired tranquility shone upon the entire people.”

You too, magnificent man, set before yourself the examples of holy rulers and of those who preserve legal rights. Keep far from yourself the image of harmful mercy, and always strive to preserve justice toward the people entrusted to you. For it is written: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. CV). And Solomon says: “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I).

Therefore, always inflamed with zeal for uprightness, proceed now along the path of justice, so that one day you may return to the author of justice not to be judged, but to be rewarded.

## ANOTHER TREATISE. ON THE SAME DUTY OF A RULER IN RESTRAINING THE WICKED

### ARGUMENT

He impresses upon the same Gothifred the need to avoid excessive gentleness and leniency, warning him to take great care lest, while sparing a few criminals, he destroy all good people. To persuade him of this more easily, he adduces the example of Duke Hugh, who before him had administered the government of almost the whole of Italy, and praises his severity.

## To the most excellent Marquis Gothifred, Peter, sinful monk, sends greetings.

[Col. 0825D]

Often one messenger is sent after another, so that a matter of great necessity may at least be obtained through persistent petitions. Even that evangelical judge, living outside the Gospel [i.e. contrary to its spirit] (Luke XVIII), who feared neither God nor man, is acknowledged finally to have been overcome by weariness and by the woman’s unremitting persistence.

But you, whom the modesty of an honorable life makes distinguished among human beings and whom reverent fear makes notable before God, ought not to reject my petitions, since you see that I am not complaining as an adversary, but rather suggesting what is useful to you.

I recently wrote you a letter about preserving the rigor of justice, which I now double in length, although I do not depart from the subject once proposed.

## [ON THE SAME DUTY OF A RULER IN RESTRAINING THE WICKED]

### CHAPTER I. The rigor of justice is useful to the good and to the wicked

[Col. 0826A]

Therefore, most eminent man, hold the scales of equitable balance; keep the examination within the balance; always place before your eyes the equal pans of the legal sections.

But perhaps you will bring forward that saying of Solomon: “Do not be excessively just” (Eccl. VII). I, on the contrary, reply to you: “Do not be excessively merciful.”

For just as excessive justice breaks the spirit through timidity, so under excessive mercy a badly freed mind is recklessly unbridled into insolence.

Is not indiscriminate mercy forbidden there: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Prov. XXIII)? And again: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. XIII). And elsewhere: “He who loves his son applies the scourges to him repeatedly” (Ecclus. XXXI). And again: “An untamed horse turns out hard, and an indulged son turns out headlong. Nurse your son, and he will make you afraid; play with him, and he will grieve you. Do not laugh at him, lest you grieve, and in the end your teeth be set on edge” (ibid.).

If, then, a father owes discipline and the rod to his only son, how much more does a ruler owe them to the people, lest a multitude perish through the great audacity of unbridled freedom?

Hence it is written: “An unwise king will destroy his people, and cities will be inhabited through the prudence of the wise” (Ecclus. X).

Therefore, so that the people subject to you may be saved through the observance of just government, it is necessary that you, established in the tribunal of judgment, decide what is just, and that you also instruct those whom you send through the provinces to enforce the edicts of the law strictly.

Thus the wise man, after first saying, “A wise judge will judge his people, and a sensible principate will be stable,” immediately adds: “According to the judge of the people, so are his ministers; and as is the ruler of the city, so are its inhabitants” (ibid.).

What, truly, is holier? What is dearer to God? What is more excellent in the Christian religion than to judge with justice and to confront unlawful undertakings with the discipline of legitimate rigor?

In this way, both the guilty and those who suffer are benefited: the guilty, so that they do not incur the guilt of violence; those who suffer, so that they may escape the danger of impending calamity.

The guilty benefit, so that, content with what belongs to them, they do not seize what belongs to others; those who suffer, so that, defended under the shelter of pure protection, they do not lose their own possessions.

The guilty benefit, lest by harming their neighbors they provoke upon themselves the glory of divine wrath; those who suffer, so that, freed from the wickedness of the impious, they may always give thanks and rejoice in the jubilation of divine praise.

What sacrifice can be offered to God more sweetly than to rescue orphans from the hands of violent men, defend widows, raise up the oppressed, and restore the despoiled and rejected to the titles of their lost rights?

Hence it is written: “In judging, be merciful to orphans as a father, and act for their mother as a husband; then you will be like an obedient son of the Most High, and he will have mercy on you more than a mother” (Ecclus. IV).

What, then, is greater? What is more excellent among human works than that by which a mortal man becomes a son of God, and God bestows upon him not paternal compassion but, what is greater, the entrails of maternal mercy?

Thus the man who stands up for orphans and widows and fights against the wickedness of the impious may rest, like a tender nursling, at the breasts of divine mercy as they cherish him.

### CHAPTER II. The harmonious judgment of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers concerning the punishment of the wicked

In avenging and legally punishing the excesses of the wicked with severity, all agree unanimously and converge upon the decree of a single judgment: both the fathers of the ancient Law and the holy doctors of the Church.

For it is written in the Law: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live” (Exod. XXII). And the Apostle says, among other things: “Whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (I Pet. II).

Blessed Augustine says: “What vanity it is to spare one and bring everyone into danger? For all are polluted when one sins.”

And Jerome says: “He who strikes the wicked insofar as they are wicked, and has a cause for killing in order to strike the worst criminals, is God’s minister.” Again, elsewhere: “To punish murderers and sacrilegious persons is not the shedding of blood.”

And blessed Ambrose says: “To strike an enemy is victory; a guilty man, justice; an innocent man, homicide.”

The saints would certainly not say this about inflicting vengeance upon the wicked unless they believed that bodily punishment could in some measure benefit their souls.

Concerning this, setting aside other matters for the moment, let us briefly insert what Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, thought:

“Death,” he says, “which is inflicted as punishment for sin, is the purification of the sin itself for which it is commanded to be inflicted.”

Sin is therefore absolved through the punishment of death, and nothing remains for the day of judgment or the punishment of eternal fire to find concerning that crime.

When someone receives sin and keeps it with him, and it is not washed away by some punishment or penalty, he passes beyond death with it; and because he did not pay it here in temporal punishment, he will pay eternal penalties.

You see, therefore, how much more serious it is to retain sin than to be punished by death. Here death is given as vengeance, and before the just Judge no one is judged twice for the same thing. But where sin has not been discharged by vengeance, it remains to be extinguished in eternal fires.

By these words of the holy man it is asserted beyond doubt that through temporal punishment the guilty person is absolved and, through immunity from eternal punishment, is spared its torments.

### CHAPTER III. The prudence of Duke Hugh of Tuscany in resigning the duchy

To offer you a domestic—or, so to speak, native—example, no one presents himself more suitably than Hugh, duke and marquis of glorious memory, who held the principate now exercised by you.

He held, I say, both marches [reading possibly “monarchies”]: the one washed by the Tyrrhenian Sea and the one washed by the Adriatic. But when he considered that, because of the wickedness of those who lived unjustly, he could not govern both vigorously, he voluntarily resigned to the emperor the march of Camerino together with the Duchy of Spoleto, while retaining Tuscany under his own rightful authority.

In his time, if I remember correctly, the prince of Capua, while wishing to put gloves on his hands, was approached by those who had conspired against him, as though they were serving him. They immediately clapped both his hands together and then, drawing their swords, stabbed and killed him.

As soon as this became plainly known to Hugh, the incomparable man of virtue and the aforementioned marquis, he lost no time in surrounding the city of Capua with numerous legions of armies. He did not cease attacking it with armed military forces until he captured it in victory and slaughtered the killers of their lord with the fitting punishment of death.

Many other distinguished signs of his virtues are also related about him, so that the splendid fame of his name cannot in any way be erased by the passage of time, but lives solemnly and ever fresh and flourishing on the lips of men.

Among these we could also write several things that would benefit the edification of the great. But because, when they were told to us, we neglected to record each word of the deeds, lest—God forbid—we be mistaken in some detail, we entrust these matters to others to write.

I will not, however, remain silent about a brief story I heard concerning his childhood.

His father, Marquis Obertus [Ubertus, also Albertus], was the natural son of King Hugh. He had married Guilla [Willa], daughter of Marquis Boniface the Elder.

Not long afterward he incurred the indignation of the first Emperor Otto and then, abandoning his wife, fled into exile in Pannonia.

When, after a long time, he was recalled and restored to favor, he found the mother with offspring already grown somewhat large, and was astonished and terrified. The man denied that he had fathered the child he saw; moved by jealous suspicion, he charged the woman who had borne the child with an obscene crime. He declared that he knew nothing of such an unexpected event and denied knowing the mystery of this conception. He claimed that he could not be the father of a child whose pregnant mother he had not left behind.

### CHAPTER IV. The innocence of Guilla, Hugh’s mother, is revealed by a joyful miracle

At last, after the matter had been debated for a long time, it was decided that so grave an accusation could be settled only through evidence of an accomplished purification.

Both sides therefore agreed that an assembly of religious persons should be held in the broad and spacious courtyard of a certain large house. While they sat all around on their benches, the boy alone would be placed in the middle; and if he approached and sought the father whom he had never before seen, he would unquestionably clear his mother of every suspicion.

What more need be said? Bishops assembled; priests of the lower orders, together with monks and abbots, were present. There was weeping, groaning, and sighing. They raised their eyes to heaven, beat their sorrowful breasts with their fists, and drenched their sad faces with flowing tears.

The boy was released into the middle without a nurse or attendant and began to walk. His father sat among the crowd and was not distinguished from the others by any difference in his bench. Ignoring everyone else, the boy approached him deliberately and clung to him with the affection of one who knew him very well.

Thus he freed his mother when, moved by divine prompting, he sought his father. In this way the mother’s disgrace was removed, the son was restored to his father, and the affection of both parents for one another was renewed in their common child.

All who were present, astonished by so great a miracle, rejoiced with the exultation of their hearts, offering worthy thanks to God its author.

Moreover, whenever he rode, he often used to leave the groups of his companions behind and go farther ahead either alone or with a single attendant. At such times he would address farmers or shepherds as follows:

“What do you think,” he would say, “of this marquis they speak about? Is he not cruel and impious? Does he not oppress the poor, ravage the land, and squander all the goods under his authority?”

They would reply: “God forbid! God forbid! What you say, man, is utterly false. There is no power on earth that so restrains violence and robbery, that governs the people subject to it with such peace and security. May that power live, we pray, as a refuge for the poor; may it flourish prosperously for the protection of all its subjects.”

When he heard this, he rejoiced in the Lord. Hence he often used to say:

“I always wish to live toward my subjects, and especially toward the peasants, with such gentleness that the grain which falls from the mouth of my chewing horse may immediately be gathered up by the peasants’ piglets.”

Moreover, when he inquired what was being said about him, what else was he imitating than the example of our Redeemer? Although he certainly knew everything, he asked his disciples as though he did not know: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI).

When they expressed various opinions held by the people, he added: “But who do you say that I am?”

Clearly, this was so that the King of angels might give rulers of human beings an example: they should not pay attention to what is said to their faces in flattery, but should inquire what testimony is given about them in their absence.

In this way, they should correct whatever they discover to be blameworthy in themselves from the reports of others, and grow more eager in carrying out the good things they learn are being said about them.

### CHAPTER V. The death of Duke Hugh

[Col. 0829D]
