To touch briefly upon the end of the aforementioned marquis: when he lay weakened by the illness of his final sickness, and a considerable multitude of people from different orders mourned that the light of the whole kingdom was being extinguished, a certain venerable bishop—whose name escapes me at present—noticed in the wood that was then burning in the fire a sign formed by certain traces of letters.

“Hugh the marquis lived fifty years.”

Those present considered this a favorable omen and supposed that it was a sign of recovered health, their hearts lifted in hope. But shortly afterward he himself died.

He also built six [seven] monasteries on lands under his authority. He enriched them with abundant generosity not only with estates and serfs, but also with gold and silver vessels and various ecclesiastical ornaments.

In one of them—a venerable and religious monastery built in the city of Florence in honor of the Mother of God—his body lies buried.

When Augustus, Otto III, who at that time governed the reins of the Roman Empire, learned of his death, he immediately burst out in congratulation:

“The snare is broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. CXXIII).

He had once been stung by envy against him. But shortly afterward, in that same year, he too died.

Thus the reckless man suffered his own fate, since he wickedly rejoiced at another’s death, failing to heed what the wise man says: “Do not rejoice over a dead enemy, knowing that we all die” (Ecclus. VIII).

We also think it worthwhile to add another matter, which we have often heard repeated among the monks of that same monastery as a memory fragrant with renown.

They say that the aforementioned marquis appeared in a nocturnal vision to Abbot Marino, who then governed the monastery, and warned him to turn his body onto its back in accordance with custom, since it was lying face downward with its mouth toward the ground.

Trusting this vision, the abbot wished to verify the matter. Finding the honorable man’s body lying prone and face down, just as it had been revealed to him, he reverently turned it onto the other side, onto its back, as was fitting.

There is certainly nothing surprising if this man requested the customary form of burial, since the head of all the chosen himself wished it to be observed in his own case.

For the evangelist John says: “Joseph and Nicodemus took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the burial custom among the Jews” (John XIX).

Set this predecessor of yours before yourself, most eminent man, as a mirror, and set before yourself the examples of others who have restrained human wickedness through the rigor of justice.

Rescue the innocent from the hands of violent men. Break the raised necks of the proud and of those who live contrary to the statutes.

Let the reprobate experience you as a ruler; let them not mock you as a priest.

Uproot the roots of harmful plants, so that fruitful plantations may lift up their crowns.

Therefore, exercise the hoe of legitimate vigor in the Lord’s field entrusted to you for cultivation, so that you may bring the yield of a hundredfold harvest into the heavenly granaries and may deserve to receive from the one who hired you the coin of a worthy reward.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0831]

## 877–878. THE FIFTY-EIGHTH LITTLE WORK. ON TRUE HAPPINESS AND WISDOM

### ARGUMENT

He shows how far true and counterfeit happiness are separated from one another, and likewise how greatly those captivated by the sweetness of divine Wisdom abhor the vanities of human learning.

Accordingly, he urges the person to whom he writes that, if he cannot entirely send away profane literature, riches, and the other things that mortals falsely call good, he should at least use them as servants and attendants in attaining true wisdom and happiness.

[Col. 0831A]

## To the most prudent man Boniface, Peter, sinful monk, sends an unbreakable circle of charity.

I am not unaware, brother, that when my letter is placed in the hands of secular men, they immediately investigate the splendor of its eloquence with curiosity. They discuss how orderly its arrangement may be; they ask whether the color of rhetorical skill shines forth, or whether dialectical arguments of subtle refinement envelop its propositions. They also inquire whether what has been set forth is established by categorical or rather hypothetical syllogisms through unavoidable arguments.

## [ON TRUE HAPPINESS AND WISDOM]

### CHAPTER I. How little human eloquence is valued by holy men

But those who live by the Spirit of God despise these and similar ornamented trifles as truly frivolous and vain; and, as the Apostle says, they regard them as refuse (Phil. III).

He also declares that he spoke to the disciples not in words of human wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power (I Cor. I).

What a beautiful, useful, and honorable manner of speech it is when, while arrogantly inflating its author with the wind of empty glory, it empties the cross of Christ, which is the salvation of the world.

Therefore, beloved, do not expect in my writings the itching saltiness of biting eloquence; do not seek the elegance of carefully polished urbanity. Let the simplicity of the sheep please you, for it leads toward God, not the serpent’s cunning, which injects deadly venom.

“The serpent,” he says, “was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. III).

For the Lord, who placed irreconcilable enmity between the seed of the woman and the serpent, called himself not the shepherd of serpents but the shepherd of sheep. He did not say, “My serpents,” but: “My sheep hear my voice; I know them, and I give them eternal life” (John XVI).

The wise men of the world, moreover, regard the simplicity of God’s servants as contemptible. Hence Moses says: “It is unlawful for the Egyptians to eat with the Hebrews, and they consider such a meal profane” (Gen. XLI).

But why is this? He explains elsewhere when he says: “The Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep” (Gen. XLVI).

For, as the Truth says: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI).

Therefore serpentine cunning pleases them, while they recoil from the purity of sheep-like simplicity.

But the Lord says to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John XXI).

Does he say, “Feed my little foxes; feed my dragons”? I have said this, beloved, so that you too may beware of the serpent’s horrible cunning, and so that your holy prudence may be tempered midway between foolishness and cunning.

Hence James, excluding serpentine wisdom, says: “This wisdom does not descend from above, but is earthly, animal, devilish” (James III). Shortly afterward he adds what sort of wisdom we ought to possess:

“But the wisdom that is from above,” he says, “is first pure, then peaceable, modest, persuadable, consenting to the good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy” (ibid.).

Hence Paul also says: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII).

Of immoderate wisdom it is said through Isaiah: “The wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden. Woe to those who are deep of heart, so that they hide their counsel from the Lord, whose deeds are in darkness, and who say: ‘Who sees us? Who knows us?’” (Isa. XXIX).

Through the same prophet such wisdom is also mocked:

“Where is the learned man?” he asks. “Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of children? You will not see the imprudent people, the people of lofty speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of their language, in which there is no wisdom” (Isa. XXXIII).

### CHAPTER II. The distinction between spiritual wisdom and earthly prudence

Elsewhere he distinguishes what separates spiritual wisdom from earthly prudence when he says: “Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching” (I Cor. I).

And again: “The prudence of this world is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. VIII).

Hence, as is said in the book of Genesis, the five kings who refused to be subject to Chedorlaomer were defeated by four kings (Gen. XIV).

And where? In the Valley of the Forest, which is now the Salt Sea.

Who are the four kings except the four virtues that Sacred Scripture calls principal? And what are represented by the five kings except the five bodily senses, and through them external knowledge?

Just as those four virtues proceed, as it were, from the original source of their mother, namely reason, so these five remain in the vanity of earthly wisdom as in a salt-filled valley, and there they are struck down by their enemies.

For it is fitting that in the soul all spiritual wisdom should conquer and the cunning of carnal prudence perish.

Hence it is also read of David: “He made himself a name when he returned from the capture of Syria in the Valley of Salt, having struck down twelve thousand” (II Sam. VIII).

For the true David, Christ—strong in power and beautiful in appearance—struck down twelve thousand men in the Valley of Salt, because through his apostles he triumphed over the salty, or rather false, wisdom of this world.

Since he had twelve warriors of spiritual warfare, he slaughtered through them, as it were, that many thousands of men, when he turned those reputed wise in a foolish way away from the vanity of frivolous wisdom.

One of these warriors says to the Corinthians:

“Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying bodily counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (II Cor. X).

### CHAPTER III. The effects of heavenly wisdom and earthly prudence

Moreover, just as heavenly wisdom makes people heavenly and legitimate sons of the Church, so earthly prudence makes them earthly and illegitimate.

Of them it is said through Baruch:

“The sons also of Hagar, who sought the prudence that is from the earth—the merchants of the earth, and Teman, and the storytellers, and the seekers of prudence—did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember her paths” (Baruch III).

Those who desire to attain worldly prudence and despise spiritual wisdom are therefore sons of Hagar, not of Sarah; and, having become bastards, they are rightly judged Ishmaelites, not Israelites.

And because Hagar is interpreted as “foreigner,” they are not sons of wisdom but foreigners and strangers.

They are not among those to whom the Apostle said: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II).

But you, beloved, to address you in the words of that same prophet, learn where prudence is. For it has been established essentially in God and must unquestionably be sought from him.

But because you do not occupy an insignificant place in the world, and cannot entirely avoid either exchanging words of secular eloquence with those who converse with you or occasionally touching upon the studies of literary discipline, you must use this discernment: in secular matters, make yourself appear as though dull-witted; but in spiritual studies exercise every sinew of your mind. In the former, present yourself as negligent; in the latter, entirely alert.

Since, therefore, you cannot obtain from yourself the condition of being wholly free from the serpent’s cunning in carrying out worldly business, at least strive for this: let spiritual wisdom absorb your earthly prudence and transform it, as it were, into the inner chambers of its own body.

As Scripture says concerning Pharaoh’s magicians: “Each of them threw down his staff, and they were turned into dragons; but Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs” (Exod. VII).

Aaron’s staff devoured the staffs of the magicians because the wisdom of Christ, which that staff signified, nullified all the wisdoms of this world and joined the wise men of the world to the inner organs of his body, which is the Church.

Furthermore, it is absurd and exceedingly dishonorable that the same prudence and subtlety should be applied to human affairs which is devoted to spiritual and divine matters.

Hence the Lord says to Moses:

“Take for yourself spices: stacte, onycha, galbanum of good fragrance, and the clearest frankincense; and you shall make incense compounded by the art of the perfumer, carefully mixed and pure” (Exod. XXX).

We make incense compounded from spices when we give off the fragrance of a multiplicity of virtues upon the altar of good works.

It is mixed and pure because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good works is offered.

Here he appropriately adds:

“When you have pounded all of them into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the testimony of the tabernacle” (ibid.).

We pound all the spices into the finest powder when we examine our good deeds secretly in the mortar of the heart and, if they are truly good, reconsider them with subtle care.

To reduce spices to powder, therefore, is to wear down the virtues through reflection and recall them for examination down to the finest point of hidden scrutiny.

### CHAPTER IV. Our studies should be directed toward pleasing God alone
It should also be noted that it is said of the same powder: “You shall place some of it before the testimony of the tabernacle”; for our good deeds truly please the sight of the heavenly Judge when the mind, by more subtle reflection, crushes them and, as it were, reduces the spices to powder. Let the good that is done not be coarse and hard, lest, if the hand of strict examination does not break it into pieces, it fail to scatter its fragrance more finely.

This care, and such diligent subtlety, must not be applied to earthly matters, but must be cultivated solely so that we may be able to please the gaze of the Creator—not so that we may appear distinguished in this world, but so that before God we may be prudent in our own examination. Hence it is added there: “You shall not make such a composition for your own uses, because it is holy to the Lord”; and immediately afterward: “Whoever makes anything similar, so as to enjoy its fragrance, shall perish from among his people” (Exod. [Col. 0834D] III).

Whoever, therefore, whether in the disciplines of secular letters or in any earthly affairs, displays the care that is principally owed to the deepest examination by which one pleases God, deservedly perishes, because he devotes to temporal and perishable matters the incense that was owed to God alone.

Indeed, what we say about knowledge we must also confess concerning the enjoyment of this life. It would have been fitting for earthly prudence to wither completely in us, and for spiritual wisdom alone to blossom again in us, as the Apostle admonishes, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth” (Coloss. III). It would likewise have been fitting for this life not to live in our heart, but, being wholly dead to us, not to delight us who are dead, as the same Apostle says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

But since these things are impossible for some people, especially secular persons, and they cannot fully attain the summit of both forms of perfection, they must be admonished to strive at least to keep in second place whatever they cannot completely despise.

## CHAPTER V. How secular men ought to conduct themselves in their love of earthly and spiritual things

Since this life delights most secular people like a wife who has been taken away [Col. 0835B], we must strive so that, although through weakness of mind they cannot hate it as they ought, they nevertheless do not undertake to love it immoderately. If they are not yet strong enough to give it a writ of divorce, they should at least be ashamed to grant it priority of love in comparison with eternal life.

Hence it is also prescribed in the Law: “If,” it says, “a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and they bear him children, and the son of the hated one is the firstborn, and he wishes to divide his property among his sons, he may not make the son of the beloved one firstborn and prefer him to the son of the hated one; instead, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated one as firstborn and give him a double portion of all that he possesses. For he is the beginning of his sons, and the rights of the firstborn belong to him” (Deut. XXI).

The two wives of a man are virtue and pleasure, differing from one another in jealousy, as though through a kind of rivalry of resentment and hatred. Pleasure belongs to this life, while virtue belongs to eternal glory. The former is clearly beloved, because with its ill-advised delight it soothes its husband—that is, the fragile spirit of each person—whereas the latter is called hated because it compels people to travel by the narrow and difficult way and continually sets before them harsh and demanding things.

But the son of the hated wife is our firstborn, because our Creator implanted virtue in us from the beginning, whereas pleasure and every carnal enticement arose from the vice of our perversity.

Since, however, this is not the time to explain the figure contained in each word of this commandment with precision, it is enough to say briefly that, if we cannot drive the beloved wife—which is undoubtedly harmful to us—from the fellowship of our bedchamber, we should at least strive to prefer the hated wife, who is sober and honorable, in the dignity of the firstborn. Thus, if it is difficult for us not to experience even a little sweetness from this life, the palm of authority should nevertheless be granted to virtue, while servitude is left to pleasure. The son of the former should excel in the dignity of the firstborn; the son of the latter should remain in the subordinate order, always held under the restraint of discipline.

Would you perhaps like to learn who the sons of the beloved wife are? Let the Apostle Paul be consulted: “The works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, strife, dissensions, [Col. 0836A] factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I warn you of, as I warned you before, because those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. V).

Would you in turn hear what the offspring of the hated wife are? Listen to what he added: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Ibid.).

This son, therefore, as the firstborn, ought to possess a double portion of the substance: namely, he ought to rule both body and soul as the fruit of the Spirit, and possess the rights of both substances—that is, of the inner and the outer person.

## CHAPTER VI. That the love of virtue ought to hold primacy in the heart

If, then, it is difficult for you to be content with one wife, and you are not strong enough to give a writ of divorce to the beloved wife, who ought to be hated, at least ensure that the hated wife, whom you ought to embrace with all your strength, holds the place of honor in the house of your heart.

Let the one who is now wrongly loved occupy the lowest place until, by the very ugliness of her character, she gradually becomes a source of disgust, and from disgust is completely transformed into hatred. Let the son of the hated wife be your firstborn, and let the multitude of the other children render him service.

For this reason Joshua, after Jericho had been destroyed, pronounced a curse, saying: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up and rebuilds the city of Jericho: in his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and in the youngest of his children shall he set up its gates” (Josh. VI).

Because Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” signifies this present life, the man who raises up the city of Jericho in his firstborn is the one who principally loves the goods of the present life. And because the Truth commands in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI), whoever is shown to depart from this command is deservedly condemned by a curse, as the prophet testifies, saying: “Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII).

On the other hand, the man who sets the gates of Jericho in the youngest of his children is the one who uses temporal goods in such a way that he does not possess them with love, but burns inwardly with desire for the reward of heavenly glory. He places earthly things beneath heavenly things in his love and regards transient matters as worthless.

By doing this, he makes the son of the hated wife firstborn, in accordance with the commands of the Law, and, according to Joshua’s sentence, raises up the gates of Jericho in the youngest of his children. In contrast, Cain founded a city in his firstborn, Enoch (Gen. IV), because he did not hope for a future inheritance; and because he hastily devoted himself, as it were, to the Jericho of this world, he incurred the pronouncement of perpetual condemnation. Hence it is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. X).

You, therefore, beloved, if you are not yet able to be content with spiritual life alone, as with the bedchamber of a single wife, but are still held fast by the enticement of earthly conduct that falsely flatters you, let the love of eternal life excel in the house of your heart as the firstborn; [Col. 0837A] and let the care of temporal things, as its inferior and restrained subordinate, serve it. As it is read in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II).

The present life is said to be beneath the head when it is despised and trampled underfoot by the mind, which is the head of thoughts. He is held fast in the embraces of the right hand who is delighted on every side by desires for eternal life alone.

Since Solomon also says, “Give a portion to seven, and likewise to eight” (Eccles. XI), pass through the present life—which is signified by the number seven—in such a way that you already strive with all your inward being to dwell in love of the future life, which is signified by the number eight, representing the glory of the resurrection.

To the former give only passing and fleeting care; in the latter fix a persistent and perpetual resolve of unfailing love, just as it is eternal. Moreover, what we say about transient life we also consequently apply to external prudence: in your mind, both temporal life and secular knowledge should sink down as though pressed beneath the foot of the mind. But the love of eternal life and the pursuit of spiritual wisdom, established as though upon the highest citadel of your heart, should excel, so that, while you despise this fragile life together with its wisdom, you may deserve, in a blessed exchange, to be filled with the divine Spirit, who summons you to eternal glory.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0837]

## OPUSCULUM FIFTY-NINE. ON THE LAST THINGS AND THE ANTICHRIST

### ARGUMENT

He shows first that it is difficult to speak about the last things; then that meditation upon them is useful for despising human affairs; third, he discusses the reign and death of the Antichrist; finally, he discusses the fifteen signs that, according to Saint Jerome, will precede the day of judgment.

[Col. 0837B]

To his beloved brother Adam, Peter, a humble sinful monk, sends greetings in the Lord.

## ON THE LAST THINGS AND THE ANTICHRIST

### CHAPTER I. It is difficult to speak about the last things

When you ask me, dearest brother, to examine what existed before the creation of the world, what will happen to the world after the judgment, and you also diligently inquire about the judgment itself, you act religiously and wisely; yet you drag me toward things unknown and compel me to teach what I have not yet learned. You ask what I do not know; you demand what I am ignorant of.

For Isaiah also says: “Declare to me the former things, and the last things that are to come, and I shall say that you are gods” (Isa. LXI), plainly wishing to express that no one can relate what existed before the world or what will happen after it.

Nevertheless, it is fruitful to inquire, even though the matter cannot be explained completely. The human mind is of such a nature that it cannot remain without thought: either it exercises itself in serious matters or delights in empty ones. And as long as it meditates on useful things, it is protected from the assault of intrusive thoughts. Wickedness finds no place for whispering where the mind, intent upon useful matters, holds firm counsel with sober reflection.

It is therefore worthwhile, and quite useful, to consider how brief the span of transient time is in comparison with that which endures forever. For if we wish to compare with this tiny period—the time from the beginning of the world to the end of the world—the immense expanse of time during which God existed before the origin of this world, and likewise that which will remain after the end of the same world, the comparison is less adequate than if you were to throw a handful of water into the sea or attempt to compare a measure of one cubit with the whole expanse of the earth.

The immensity of the sea and the extent of the earth are finite, as are a handful of water and a measure of one cubit, although the former are larger and the latter incomparably smaller. It is therefore easier to compare finite things with finite things than things that have an end with things that cannot be enclosed by any end.

Since God is the alpha and the omega, the beginning and the end (Rev. XXII), just as he has always existed without a beginning, so he cannot have an end. But this world, from the beginning of its creation, is known not yet to have completed seven thousand years. And who knows how brief the span of time will be until God judges the world?

How, then, can seven thousand, or even ten thousand, years be compared with the interminable essence of the Godhead, which could have neither origin nor end?

### CHAPTER II. How useful it is to meditate upon the last things

[Col. 0838C]

When we examine these and similar matters through vigilant meditation, and humbly turn them over in thought, no small progress is gained by our mind. For while it meditates upon eternal things, it clearly sees how much temporal things ought to be despised.

While the rational mind thinks upon these matters, it also comes to understand that it will not pass away with time, but will live without end. It therefore considers itself to be of such a nature that it must necessarily possess either everlasting rewards or be tormented by eternal punishments.

To examine these things through careful meditation, and also anxiously to guard against the day of judgment, yields no small fruit. On that day, whoever has once fared well will fall no more; and whoever's lot has turned to the left will not rise again thereafter.

Since you ask about the day of judgment and the Antichrist, read the blessed Augustine’s book *The City of God*, and Saint Jerome’s *Commentary on the Prophet Daniel*, as well as the *Apocalypse* with its commentaries. In these works you will be able to find sufficient knowledge of this subject.

For, as the authoritative Scripture first indicates and the later writings of commentators clarify, the Antichrist will reign for three and a half years. After Enoch and Elijah have been killed by him, the archangel Michael will kill the Antichrist himself and the greater part of his members.

This is not contrary to what the Apostle says: “The Lord Jesus Christ will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (II Thess. II). For whether Christ destroys him directly or through angelic ministry, the wicked plague is destroyed above all by him whose power and might overcome it.

Indeed, as the teachers relate, the Lord will kill him on the Mount of Olives, in his tent and upon his throne—namely, at the place opposite which, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended victoriously into heaven.

Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord has cast down upon the holy mountain the face of the ruler of darkness and him who rules all peoples” (Isa. XV).

Of him Daniel says: “He will speak words against the Most High, and will wear down the saints of the Most High; and he will think that he can change times and laws; and they will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time” (Dan. VII).

From this it is gathered that the Antichrist will reign for three and a half years. A “time” is one year; “times” are two years. Thus, after reigning for three and a half years, he will be killed by the sword of divine wrath, so that the tyrant may utterly perish and the whole creation may bow before the true King.

Hence the same Daniel says: “The judgment will sit, so that his power may be taken away, crushed, and destroyed to the end. But the kingdom, the power, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is everlasting; and all nations will serve and obey him.”

### CHAPTER III. How many days will intervene between the death of the Antichrist and the coming of Christ the Lord

After the death of the Antichrist, forty-five days will remain until the coming of Christ. During them persecution will cease, and there will be great peace and tranquility, so that within this period the righteous, if they have faltered in the moment of persecution, may do penance, while the ministers of the devil are dissolved in the security of lethargy and idleness.

As in the days of Noah, they will plant and build; they will hold banquets and contract marriages; and while they are intent upon frivolous vanity, destruction will suddenly overtake them (Matt. XXIV; Luke XVII).

As to your question whether this world will first burn and the judgment then take place, the matter has been settled by the clear opinion of our predecessors: the judgment will come first, and the conflagration of the world will follow.

After the judgment has been completed, fire will suddenly burst forth and occupy as much space in the air as the waters rose when the Flood invaded the earth. This fire will burn the earth and the thickness of the air, and will thus purify the elect.

But since in the letter that we wrote to the countess Blanca concerning the day of judgment we assembled several testimonies from Scripture [Note: [Col. 0839D] The final letter of Book VII], and since the same subject is treated so abundantly by the interpreters of sacred eloquence that it cannot be confined within the brief compass of a letter, we direct you to their overflowing streams and urge you, leaving aside the dry little rivulets, to drink from the fountains of Israel.

## CHAPTER IV. The signs preceding the day of judgment, according to the account of Saint Jerome

We have learned that the blessed Jerome reported fifteen signs, corresponding to fifteen days, that will precede the day of judgment. We do not think it superfluous to insert them here in his very words. By these words, certainly, we neither attribute the force of authority to them nor wholly deny them credibility.

Let the matter, therefore, as it has reached us, be simply incorporated in this work in its own style, so that it may also become known from the pages of the ancient Hebrew peoples what terror of the divine judgment has increased among them.

He says:

**The sign of the first day:** All the seas will be raised upward to a height of fifteen cubits above the high mountains of the world; they will not flow outward, but will stand like walls.

**The sign of the second day:** All the waters will be cast down into the lowest depths, so that they will scarcely be visible to human eyes.

**The sign of the third day:** All the seas will be restored to their former condition, as they had been created in the beginning.

**The sign of the fourth day:** All beasts and everything that moves in the waters of the sea will gather upon the open sea, bellowing and roaring against one another as though in conflict. Human beings will not know what they are singing or what they are thinking, but only God knows, to whom all things live, the function they are performing.

These four signs concern the sea; the three following signs concern the air and the ether.

**The sign of the fifth day:** All the birds of heaven will gather in assemblies upon the fields, each kind in its own order. The same birds will speak and mourn among themselves; they will neither taste food nor drink, fearing the coming of the Judge.

**The sign of the sixth day:** Fiery rivers will rise from the setting of the sun and run toward the face of the firmament as far as the sunrise.

**The sign of the seventh day:** The wandering and stationary stars will scatter fiery hair from themselves over the world and its inhabitants, as appears in comets.

**The sign of the eighth day:** There will be a great earthquake, so that no human being will be able to stand, nor any animal; everything will be thrown to the ground.

**The sign of the ninth day:** All stones, small and large alike, will split into four parts, and each part will strike another part. No human being will know that sound, except God alone.

**The sign of the tenth day:** All the trees of the forests and the plants of the herbs will flow with bloody dew.

**The sign of the eleventh day:** All mountains and hills, and all buildings constructed by human art, will be reduced to dust.

**The sign of the twelfth day:** All the animals of the earth will come from forests and mountains into the fields, roaring and bellowing, neither tasting food nor drinking.

**The sign of the thirteenth day:** All tombs, from the rising of the sun to its setting, will be opened, and the corpses will rise until the hour of judgment.

**The sign of the fourteenth day:** The entire human race that is found will quickly depart from its dwellings and from the places where they are; they will neither understand nor speak, but will run about like madmen.

**The sign of the fifteenth day:** Living human beings will die, so that they may rise again with the dead who died long ago [Note: [Col. 0841A] The ending of this work appears to be incomplete].

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

[Col. 0841]

## OPUSCULUM SIXTY. A MYSTICAL EXPOSITION OF THE HISTORIES OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS

### CHAPTER I. God said: “LET THERE BE LIGHT,” on the first day

[Col. 0841B]

How a human being can be perfected and how he ought to be brought to completion, this book touches upon briefly, insofar as it can be discovered from the order of the world’s creation.

Since the human being is said to be a microcosm—that is, a smaller world—it is necessary that, striving toward the growth of his fullness, he imitate the form of the world’s creation. Just as this visible and corporeal world was brought to completion through the mass and greatness of its parts, so our inner human being should gradually attain fullness through the increase of virtues.

Of this spiritual fullness the Apostle says: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

Light is said to be made in a human being when illumination is granted to him, so that the radiance of faith shines upon him. For the first light of the mind is faith.

Hence the Apostle rightly says to the faithful Ephesians: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” And this is the first commandment in the Law: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one.”

The first day is made in a human being when someone new comes to faith.

### CHAPTER II. Concerning the firmament and the division of the waters

On the second day God made the firmament and divided the waters, so that some flowed down to the lower regions while others remained above.

What, then, is the firmament except the strength of the Scriptures? Hence we read that on the day of judgment heaven will be folded up like a book.

What are the lower waters except the multitudes of human beings, according to the statement in the Apocalypse: “Many waters, many peoples”?

What, then, are the waters above except the choirs of angels? Of them it is said in the psalm: “And all the waters that are above the heavens, bless the name of the Lord.”

The angels do not have the heaven of the Scriptures above them, but beneath them, because they do not need to hear the word of God by reading it: they clearly behold God himself present and are always aflame with his love.

When, therefore, a human being begins, through the firmament—that is, through the teaching of heavenly speech—to divide the lower waters from the upper, separating carnal things from spiritual things and earthly things from heavenly things, then the second day comes to be in him, because he begins to possess not only the light of faith but also discernment concerning things.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning the gathering of the waters into one place beneath heaven

[Col. 0842B]

After the division of the waters—that is, between earthly and heavenly things—it is necessary for the human mind to divide these same earthly things more minutely, and thus distinguish wicked people, itching with the saltiness of earthly wisdom, from the righteous, who thirst for the fountain of faith, as dry land is distinguished from the sea.

For unbelievers and all carnal people are shaken by the waves of the sea of temptations, and swell like storms of desires and arrogance. But all the saints and righteous thirst for God like dry land, and strive to produce green fruits of good works like fertile earth.

Therefore, when God had said, “Let the dry land appear,” on the same day he likewise commanded: “Let the earth bring forth green grass producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit.”

Whoever diligently carries this out, whoever meditates upon it attentively, unquestionably sees the third day dawn already for him. Let each person, therefore, separate himself from the bitter saltiness of those who think carnally; having become dry land, let him thirst inwardly for the Lord, the fountain of life, and for the fountain of divine grace; and let him bring forth the shoots of good fruits, so that the third day may dawn upon him.

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning the luminaries made on the fourth day in the firmament of heaven

When these things have been established and ordered beneficially, the soul of a human being, as though the darkness of vices had been removed, begins to shine with the radiance of virtues.

What does it mean that the earth first puts forth shoots and immediately afterward the luminaries are created, except that, when the shoot of good work emerges, a more abundant light rises in the soul, enabling it to imitate the footsteps of its Redeemer?

Let the human mind therefore hasten to make the harvest of spiritual things germinate, so that it may be illuminated by the gleaming rays of divine light and, while enjoying the light of the fourth day, be lifted up to contemplate heavenly things in the manner of spiritual birds.

### CHAPTER V. That the fish and birds were created on the fifth day

On the fifth day the fish were created. They signify those who receive the sacrament of baptism, just as the birds signify those who lift themselves on the wings of virtues to contemplate heavenly things.

Whoever, having despised the love of the world, disdains, as it were, to tread upon earthly mud and through the grace of contemplation raises himself toward desire for heavenly glory, possesses the fifth day together with the birds.

Such a person no longer walks upon the earth but flies through the air, because, despising all earthly things, he breathes out his thirst for heavenly things, according to the psalm: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.”

Such a person, therefore, is deservedly formed, as a perfect man, in the image of his Creator, since he possesses such dignity of spiritual gifts that he is commanded not merely to observe the pattern of any saints whatsoever, but also, insofar as is permitted, to attempt to imitate the very example of God, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved you.”

There was, of course, a great difference between Paul, who imitated Christ, and those whom he urged to imitate himself when he said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

### CHAPTER VI. Concerning the sixth day

On the sixth day the human being was created in the image and likeness of the Creator. Just as this happened then, at the beginning of human creation, so it now takes place through the sacrament of inner restoration.

Moreover, among all living creatures—that is, among those of both water and earth—he receives a kind of monarchy and a certain primacy of higher excellence, because every perfect person, consummated in virtues, knows how to pronounce a right judgment concerning each thing, as the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.”

Almighty God establishes such a perfect person—dead to the world and living for himself—as his throne, and often proclaims through him the edict of his justice.

Hence that order of angels through which almighty God most frequently decrees his judgments is also called “thrones,” because the supreme Judge sits among them when he exercises judgments through them.

God therefore establishes the perfect man as his throne, so that he may rest sweetly in him. Hence the prophet also says: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, except upon the humble and gentle person who trembles at my words?”

It should also be noted that for each day it is said: “There was evening and morning, the [such-and-such] day.” Evening is the perfection of the good work itself; morning is the light of the mind.

For when a good work reaches perfection, then the light of spiritual grace rises in the mind of the one who performs it, so that, while he carries out a luminous work outwardly, the grace of the Spirit itself illuminates him inwardly.

### CHAPTER VII. That God rested on the Sabbath after all things had been completed

Thus one arrives at the Sabbath, on which God himself, after completing all things, rests and commands the human being to rest.

In this way the human being also becomes God’s Sabbath, and God becomes the human being’s Sabbath, because the human being rests in God, and God in him. “Remain in me, and I in you,” says the Lord. For he himself is timeless time and spaceless place for us.

He is spaceless because he is not confined by place; he is timeless because he never ends.

God is therefore time for us when he says in the Gospel of John: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” By “day” he means himself, and by the twelve hours he means the twelve apostles.

Place, however, is expressed unmistakably where the prophet David, after saying, “But you are the same, and your years will not fail,” immediately adds: “The children of your servants will dwell there”—clearly, in you.

God therefore made heaven and earth, yet he is not said to have rested. He made the plants of the earth and the luminaries of heaven, and he is not said to have rested. He made all that feeds upon the earth and all that moves in the waters, yet nowhere is he ever read to have rested in any of these things.

But once the human being had been fashioned in his image, the Sabbath of rest immediately dawned, and thus the Creator of humanity rested.

And although he himself says through the prophet Isaiah, “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet,” what is not said concerning the creation of those things is asserted concerning the creation of the human being alone: that he rested.

And so that you may marvel still more at the splendid dignity of this seventh day, Scripture says that God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he ceased from all his work. No such thing is found to have been done on the other days.

For what is it for God to sanctify the Sabbath except to build for himself a temple in the mind of a holy and perfect man? As the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you.”

Moreover, just as we have spoken about the Sabbath, reason also requires us to speak about the temple, because God is the temple of the human being and the human being is the temple of God, as John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb.”

God is therefore called the temple of the human being, and the human being the temple of God. This temple of the human being is the spiritual paradise: the holy mind, the perfect mind, the pure mind, distinctly marked in the image of its Creator.

This mind, or rational soul, is rightly called paradise. It is watered by streams of heavenly gifts and adorned with the green shoots of holy virtues, like fertile trees or grasses in spring.

For that fountain or river which is said to go forth there from the place of delight to water paradise, and which is divided into four heads, is the reasoning power of the mind. From it, as from an original fountain, four virtues flow forth like four life-giving currents: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. They make the soil of our heart fertile.

The tree of life is wisdom itself, the mother of all good things, concerning which Solomon also says: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds her.”

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the transgression of the law that was imposed and the experience of misery. But since it is not our purpose to explain everything in order, let these brief observations, appropriate to the subject, suffice.

### CHAPTER VIII. The Lord cast Adam into a deep sleep

[Col. 0845A]

For this purpose the power of God was emptied of itself, so that it might strengthen our weakness; for this purpose the sublimity of God was humbled, so that it might raise up the fallen; for this purpose Life deigned to die, so that, destroying the dominion of death, it might recall the dead to life. This is clearly revealed at the very beginning of the human race. For it is written:

> “The Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs, and filled up flesh in its place; and the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman.”

When the Apostle was speaking about this, saying, “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” he immediately added:

> “This is a great sacrament [Col. 0845B]; but I speak of Christ and of the Church.”

And truly, this sacrament is a sign of great power and of wondrous depth. Adam signifies Christ, and Eve signifies the Church. What does it mean that God first caused Adam to sleep, and then took a rib from his side, from which the woman was to be formed, except that the Redeemer first slept in death, and then blood and water flowed from his side as the sacrament of the Church? Eve was taken from the side of the sleeping man; the Church likewise came forth from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross.

But why did the almighty Creator, when he intended woman to be derived from man—that is, the weaker sex from the stronger—not wish to provide the man’s flesh, but rather a bone, as the material from which the woman would be made? God could have removed flesh from the man from which the woman might be formed, and this would certainly seem more fitting: the weaker sex would then have proceeded from the weakness of flesh rather than from the strength of bone. And, to make the sacrament of the divine work still more astonishing, he did not return bone for bone; instead, he filled with flesh what was lacking in the man’s body. Thus, when Scripture says, “He took one of his ribs,” it immediately adds, “And he filled up flesh in its place.” He could have taken flesh from the man to fashion the woman; he could have restored the loss of bone with bone while leaving the body unimpaired. But he took bone and returned flesh. 894 Thus he formed the fragile from strength: Adam the man was weakened so that Eve might become strong.

Christ was weakened so that the Church might be strengthened; for his weakness is our strength. He bore our weakness for this purpose: that he might establish us in his strength. “For the weakness of God,” as the Apostle says, “is stronger than men”; and elsewhere: “For though Christ was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God.” For even if we are weak in him, we live with him by the power of God.

Indeed, the men of this age who desire to become renowned through the valor of war, and who wish their victories to be celebrated by the mouths of the crowd, when they are about to enter battle place upon their bodies what is weak and soft, and cover it with what is hard and difficult to pierce. They put on iron breastplates and strive to protect the flesh, which readily yields to a blow, so that what is hard and strong on the outside may defend what is soft within [Col. 0846A].

When our Redeemer enters the battlefield of this world to wage war, he arms himself as a strong combatant to overthrow the powers of the air. Because he had to begin a new battle, he assumed a new kind of armor: namely, he placed what was weak on the outside and concealed what was strong. He put on the frail breastplate of flesh and concealed the unconquerable strength of his divinity. Thus, through the flesh, the devil was defeated by the second man—the same flesh through which he had once overcome the first man, and which now became the cause of the devil’s ruin, though it had been the instrument of victory over our first parent.

## CHAPTER IX. How, while the Lord was walking in paradise, Adam hid himself because he was naked.

[Col. 0846B]

A congealed cold customarily interrupts the voice of the heart. This cold had already seized the one who, while the Lord was walking in the breeze of paradise after midday, answered in a kind of hoarse voice:

> “I heard your voice, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.”

Since the midday warmth had already departed from him, the breeze, which is the nursling of cold, came upon him, because the loss of innocence had already left him naked. What else do all these things suggest except that the chill of extinguished love had closed around his inward parts, and that therefore his voice sounded hoarse in the ears of the Lord?

Abraham was entirely free from this cold. Of him Scripture declares:

> “The Lord appeared to him in the heat of the day” [Col. 0846C];

and that heavenly Bridegroom, as it is read in the Song of Songs:

> “He feeds and lies down at midday.”

## CHAPTER X. Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech.

To show that blessed Luke presents us as cleansed from our crimes through the coming of our Savior, he begins the account of Christ’s lineage not from the beginning of the Gospel narrative, but only from Christ’s baptism and genealogy. He describes it by ascending through seventy-seven degrees of descent, as is also clearly shown in the Book of Genesis, where Lamech is said to have spoken to his wives:

> “Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

Vengeance is said to be exacted seventy-sevenfold for Lamech because seventy-seven men are said to have descended from his loins and are subsequently reported to have been swallowed up when the Flood devoured them. But when Lamech is represented as striking or being struck, whom does he signify by this except the first parent of the human race? He not only carried the weapon of sin by which he himself was first struck and perished, but also inflicted a wound upon the whole posterity that was to follow.

Thus seventy-sevenfold vengeance was exacted for this Lamech, because the sin contracted by the first man remained active in the human race through seventy-seven generations, until Christ. Original sin remained, and Christ wiped it away through the sacrament of baptism, where it is said of him:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

## CHAPTER XI. “Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood, and coat it with pitch inside and out.”

[Col. 0847A]

The divine voice commanded that the ark which preserved eight souls amid the waters of the Flood be coated with pitch inside and out. This signifies the holy Church, which advances toward the glory of the resurrection. It is coated with pitch both within and without, so that outwardly it may be gracious in brotherly love, and inwardly remain united in the truth of mutual sweetness.

Whoever loves inwardly but outwardly disagrees with his brothers through the harshness of discordant conduct has pitch within but not without. Whoever, on the other hand, presents himself as affable in appearance and pretends friendship, but does not preserve the truth of friendship in the secrecy of his heart, gapes open damnably within while outwardly he clings through the appearance of applied pitch [Col. 0847B].

Neither of these is rescued from the shipwreck of the Flood, because neither is adequately fortified with the twofold pitch of charity, as God commanded. But whoever shows himself lovable outwardly and preserves a loving heart inwardly outwardly displays the fruit of kindness with the branches of speech, and inwardly fixes a deep root, because he loves from the marrow of his being. This person is coated with pitch both inside and out, because he is joined to his neighbors by the twofold bond of charity.

Moreover, because the ark is first commanded to be made from smoothed wood and afterward to be coated with pitch, this plainly signifies to us that our wood—that is, our hard, uncultivated, and harsh conduct—must first be polished through the discipline of spiritual practice, so that pitch may afterward be applied to the structure once joined together. For as long as people’s conduct is harsh and uncultivated, the glue of charity is applied to them in vain, because they quickly spring apart from one another, since a united bond of polished morality is not maintained among them.

896 ## CHAPTER XII. On the dimensions of the ark of the Flood.

That ark contained the mystery of the cross. Scripture specifies that its length was three hundred cubits. This number is contained in the letter *tau*, which expresses the form of the cross. Just as Noah and his household were saved through water and wood, so Christ’s household is saved through water and wood: it is washed in the water of salvation and marked with the impression of the life-giving cross.

That ark is said to have measured three hundred cubits in length and thirty in height, so that its dimensions might appear to correspond, in the sacrament, to the human body of Christ [Col. 0847D]. For three hundred contains the number fifty six times, and thirty ten times; and the length of the human body, from the crown of the head to the feet, is six times the breadth, which extends from right to left, and ten times the height, which extends from front to back. Thus the ark, in the three-hundredfold number of its length, bears the appearance of the cross, and in the height of its entire structure preserves the figure of the Lord’s body.

And just as seven souls were given to Noah so that they might be saved through the wood amid the waters of the Flood, so the seven Churches, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, are saved in Christ through the wood of the cross and the water of baptism [Col. 0848A]. Through wood, the prince of pride subjected us to his slavery; through wood, Christ the Lord, the author of humility, recalled us to the title of freedom.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the water of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains.

The number fifteen, because it consists of seven and eight, contains within itself the mystery of blessed rest and future resurrection. For God rested on the seventh day, at the beginning of the created world, and on the eighth day, when he redeemed the world, he rose again.

The sacramental meaning of both numbers is contained especially in baptism: there we rise renewed from our old condition, and afterward we are commanded to rest from the disturbance of worldly clamor. Those who swell with the boastfulness of worldly glory or with the vanities of earthly wisdom do not understand this mystery of the seventh day’s rest and the eighth day’s resurrection [Col. 0848B].

Hence it is appropriately said here:

> “The water was fifteen cubits higher than all the mountains which it had covered.”

The mountains signify the proud and exalted. The lofty and profound mystery of resurrection and inward rest therefore transcends all the understanding of the proud wise.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the Flood began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days.

> “The waters returned from the earth, going and returning, and began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days.”

Since, in the mystery of our regeneration, the rest of the seventh day is joined to the resurrection of the eighth, the Book of Genesis rightly says:

> “The waters returned from the earth, and began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days” [Col. 0848C];

for seventy, counted from seven, and eighty, counted from eight, together make one hundred and fifty.

## CHAPTER XV. How the ark rested in the seventh month.

The ark rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia. This rest of the seventieth is fittingly commended in baptism, which that Flood is understood to have symbolized: having risen anew from the oldness of Adam, we are afterward commanded to rest from the disturbance of worldly clamor.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the raven and the dove sent out from the ark.

[Col. 0848D]

In the sea of this world the righteous labor, while the reprobate possess their rest. The raven and the dove sent out from the ark aptly signify this difference. The raven, settling upon corpses, did not return to the enclosure of the ark; but the dove returned, because it found no place where its foot might rest.

Here, where the wicked satisfy themselves with carnal pleasures, holy men cannot find a place where they may set down the foot of their desire in rest.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Noah sent the dove out from the ark a second time.

When the crimes of the world were being cleansed by a kind of outpoured Flood, the dove brought forth an image of the future gift when, by means of an olive branch, it announced that peace had been restored to the earth. Scripture says:

> “After waiting another seven days, Noah again sent the dove out from the ark. It came to him carrying in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves.”

The number seven is assigned to the sending forth and return of the dove because the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning of the world was borne over the waters, filled the holy Church when the age was already growing old and evening was approaching.

## CHAPTER XVIII. “Come, let us build a city.”

> “As they journeyed from the east toward the west, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there.”

Since Christ is the East, as the prophet Zechariah testifies when he says:

> “Behold the man; East is his name” [Col. 0849B],

those come from the east who withdraw from fellowship with Christ by living wickedly or tearing their neighbors apart.

Shinar is interpreted as “shaking of teeth” or “their stench.” They dwell in the plain of Shinar who, not established in the ark of the virtues but rather in the valley of vices, shake their teeth so as to bite and gnaw their neighbors through detraction, and emit stenches while rotting in the filth of a muddy way of life.

But God shakes their teeth when he confounds both the deeds and the words of the wicked. Hence it is said there:

> “Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the speech of the whole earth was confused, and the Lord scattered them over the face of all the regions.”

It is therefore rightly said that those men, grasping after empty glory and saying to one another, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower,” and so forth, dwelt in the plain of Shinar, which among us, as has been said, signifies “shaking of teeth” or “their stench.” For the wicked, when they grow proud against the commands of the divine law, arrogantly raise the neck of their hearts against God, and damnably slander their neighbors; thus they roll all the more readily in the dungheap of an obscene life.

Of the shaking of teeth it is said in the Psalm:

> “You have broken the teeth of sinners.”

Again:

> “God will break their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will shatter the molars of lions.”

Of their stench we also read:

> “The cattle have rotted in their dung.”

Again, in the Lamentations [Col. 0849D]:

> “Those who were nourished in scarlet have embraced dung.”

Again, in Isaiah 3:

> “There shall be stench instead of a sweet odor.”

Whoever wishes to lay a foundation for a building that will not easily be exposed to ruin must not use bricks and pitch, which suddenly come apart, but rather stones and rocks to join the walls, together with mortar of lime and sand, which firmly and securely binds the walls themselves in an unbroken structure of stones.

Thus, because the Babylonians mentioned above used bricks in place of stones and pitch in place of mortar, the building of a carnal life is signified—a building destined to be quickly overwhelmed by the force of winds or the rush of floods.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the five kings of Sodom and Gomorrah who were killed by four kings.

[Col. 0850A]

The wisdom of this world is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Hence, just as in the Book of Genesis the five kings who refused to submit to Chedorlaomer were defeated by four kings, so it happened. And where? In the wooded valley, which is now called the Salt Sea.

Who are the four kings except the four virtues that Sacred Scripture calls principal? What are the five kings except the five bodily senses, and, through them, external knowledge? Just as those four virtues proceed as though from the original maternal source—that is, from reason—so these five remain in the vanity of earthly wisdom as though in a salt-filled valley [Col. 0850B]. There they are struck down by their enemies, because it is fitting that spiritual wisdom should prevail in the human soul and that the cunning of carnal prudence should perish.

Hence it is also read of David:

> “He made himself a name when he returned after striking down Syria in the Valley of Salt, killing twelve thousand.”

899 ## CHAPTER XX. How Abraham sacrificed with God, dividing the animals but not the birds.

> “Taking all these,” Scripture says, “he divided them down the middle and placed each half opposite the other, but he did not divide the birds.”

Earthly animals are set against one another and placed opposite one another because all earthly people rage against their neighbors through quarrels and contentions, or at least burn inwardly against them with hidden kindling of hatred. But those who raise themselves aloft on the wings of heavenly desire, when they offer themselves to God as a sacrifice, do not withdraw from the bond of mutual love.

## CHAPTER XXI. Abraham drove away the birds descending upon the sacrifices.

Evil spirits try to corrupt either our prayers with wicked thoughts or our good works with the contamination of some sin. Hence it is written that, when Abraham devoutly offered sacrifice to God from cattle and birds, birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away.

What do the birds signify except reprobate spirits flying through the air [Col. 0850D]? We drive birds away from our sacrifice when we carefully guard the offerings of our prayers or works against the evil spirits that try to defile them.

## CHAPTER XXII. When the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abraham, and great terror seized him.

When the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abraham, and great, dark terror seized him. The setting of the sun signifies the setting of the world; the great and dark terror represents the gloom of vices and crimes, which daily grow pestilently dreadful through the burning wickedness of reprobate men.

Hence it is added shortly afterward:

> “When the sun had set, a dark mist came to be, and a smoking furnace appeared” [Col. 0851A].

For just as smoke rises from the fire of a furnace that is giving off heat, so the gloom of all vices and crimes is generated from the furnace of burning greed, as the Apostle says:

> “The root of all evils is greed.”

And this occurs near the end of the day—that is, near the end of the world. The smoking furnace therefore produces a dark mist, because the furnace of greed, which burns in the breasts of wicked men, pestilently darkens the world with many different shadows.

Does it not blind the minds of the wretched? It takes away faith and extinguishes the light of every virtue in their hearts. Hence, after the Apostle had said this, he immediately added:

> “Some, desiring it—that is, greed—have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” [Col. 0851B].

They pierce themselves with many sorrows when, for the sake of temporal profit, they spring apart from one another in irreconcilable hostility, and often, when they rush to arms over bodily possessions, strip souls from bodies.

But those who burn with heavenly suns receive pleasures in place of sorrows, because they live together in harmony in the sweetness of brotherly charity. Hence, in that evening sacrifice which Abraham then offered, he arranged the earthly animals separated from one another, but did not divide the birds. Thus Scripture says:

> “Taking all these,” he says, “he divided them down the middle and placed each half opposite the other, but he did not divide the birds.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. “I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me.”

[Col. 0851C]

If we attentively consider the deeds of our Creator, we ought not readily to give credence to every evil report. He whose eyes see all things naked and open did not disdain, when speaking to Abraham about the outcry concerning Sodom that had come to him, to say:

> “I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me. Or is it not so, that I may know?”

This appears to have been said for no other reason than to teach human ignorance not to believe what it hears without examination, not to judge what is unknown lightly, and not to pronounce a sentence before establishing a doubtful matter by testimony.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the Sodomites, while trying to break violently into the angels’ presence, were struck with blindness.

[Col. 0851D]

> “And behold,” Scripture says, “the men stretched out their hand and brought Lot inside to themselves, and shut the door. But they struck with blindness those who were outside, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.”

The Sodomites attempt to break violently into the angels’ presence when impure men try to approach God through the offices of sacred order. There they are struck with blindness because, by God’s just judgment, they fall into inner darkness, so that they are unable to find the door, since, having separated themselves from God by sinning, they do not know by what way they might return to him.

Those who desire to approach God not by the path of humility but through the winding ways of arrogance and pride plainly do not recognize where the entrance might be opened. But since Christ is the door, as he himself says, “I am the door,” those who lose Christ through sins demanding punishment do not find the door by which they might enter the dwelling of the heavenly citizens.

They were handed over to a reprobate mind because, when they do not weigh the burden of their guilt on the delicate scales of proper reflection, they consider a massive weight of lead to be the lightness of empty feathers. What is said there—“They struck those who were outside with blindness”—the Apostle clearly explains when he says:

> “God handed them over to a reprobate mind.”

And what is added there—“so that they could not find the door”—this writer plainly expounds when he says:

> “So that they might do things which are not fitting” [Col. 0852B];

as if he were saying: so that they might attempt to enter where they ought not.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Abraham offered his only son to God as a sacrifice.

When Abraham wished to sacrifice his son to God, he signified, almost point by point, all the mysteries of Christ’s Passion. Just as Abraham—whose name is interpreted “exalted father”—did not hesitate to offer his only and beloved son to God, so the supreme Father handed over his only-begotten Son for us all.

And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, so Christ also carried upon his shoulders the wood of his cross’s Passion, upon which he was to suffer for our salvation.

The two servants who were sent on ahead and left at a distance signify the Jews. Living slavishly and thinking carnally, they did not understand the highest humility of Christ, and therefore did not ascend the mountain—that is, the place of sacrifice. Why two servants? Because, when Solomon sinned, one Israelite people became two peoples. To them the prophet often says:

> “Israel the adversary and Judah the transgressor.”

That ass which Abraham then used signified the senseless folly of the Jews. That brutish folly carried all the mysteries, yet, like an irrational animal, did not know what it carried.

But what does it mean that he said to them:

> “Wait here with the ass; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you”?

Hear the Apostle:

> “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved.”

What is meant by “Blindness in part has happened to Israel”? It means:

> “Wait here with the ass, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter”—that is, “after we have worshiped”—

when the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion has been fulfilled and proclaimed among all the nations. What follows—“And thus all Israel might be saved”—means: “We shall return to you.”

But what does it mean that a ram caught by its horns among the brambles is found and offered in sacrifice in Isaac’s place? The cross has horns: two pieces of wood are joined together, and thus form the appearance of a cross. Hence it is written of Christ:

> “Horns are in his hands” [Col. 0853A].

The ram caught by its horns is therefore Christ, crucified amid the sharp and wounding iniquities of the Jews. Thus he himself complains through Jeremiah:

> “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.”

After the sacrifice had been completed, it was said to Abraham:

> “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed.”

And after the Lord had said, “They pierced my hands and my feet,” he added shortly afterward in the same Psalm:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations.”

After Abraham had offered his son and sacrificed the ram in his place, he called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” because after our Lord had been offered upon the altar of the cross and paid the debt of our death, he thereafter presented himself to the gaze of his faithful, so that all the redeemed might now find him through faith, though until then they had not possessed the eyes of faith.

902 ## CHAPTER XXVI. On Leah and Rachel, the wives of Jacob.

It is not obscure that Laban had two daughters, of whom Jacob joined the younger in marriage. Yet he could not reach her embrace until, unknowingly and therefore unwillingly, he had taken the elder. But because I am speaking to those who know the matter, I need not labor over it with many words.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Who turns to God except in order that, having laid aside the blackness of sins, he may be made white through the grace of forgiveness? Thus God himself promises, saying:

> “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” [Col. 0853C].

That blessed sinner sought this when he said:

> “I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

Leah is interpreted as “laboring”; Rachel as “word” or “beginning.” But if we attend carefully to Scripture, we do not find that Jacob served even one day because of his desire for Leah; rather, he remained in servitude through all those weeks of years for Rachel alone. Moreover, he endured Leah herself for the sake of seeing Rachel.

Who turns to God for the sake of suffering labors, hardships, and the struggles of temptations? Everyone who seeks God hopes and aims at this: that he may eventually reach rest and, in the joy of supreme contemplation, rest as though in the embrace of beautiful Rachel—namely, that through the word he hears he may ascend to behold the beginning he has sought.

But this person must first be exercised by struggles of various kinds before he can attain the sweetness of the inward rest he desires. He is first pressed down by servitude, so that afterward he may rightly be raised to the dignity of perfect freedom.

He serves for seven years under the grace of whitening when he keeps the seven commandments of the Decalogue that concern love of neighbor: bound first by fear and therefore oppressed by the yoke of servitude, he begins at least with the institutions of the old law—honoring parents, not committing adultery, not killing, not stealing, not bearing false witness, and not coveting another’s wife or property [Col. 0854A].

When these have been rightly observed, he is not immediately led, as he hoped, to the delights of contemplation, so that he may enjoy the long-awaited beauty of Rachel. Instead, Leah is unexpectedly substituted for him during the night, because amid the darkness of human ignorance he is assigned the endurance of labor. Yet from this labor he receives abundant offspring, because through it he acquires rich fruits of spiritual gain.

He endures Leah, therefore, so that he may eventually reach the one whom he loves with perseverance. He is urged to strive to serve for another seven years because he must still observe seven other commandments—but now somewhat more freely, not as a servant observing legal commandments, but as a son-in-law observing evangelical ones: that he be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for justice, merciful, pure in heart, and finally a peacemaker.

903 Indeed, if it were possible, a man would wish to undergo none of the hardships of labor, but to reach immediately, at the very beginnings of his apprenticeship, the delights of beautiful contemplation. Yet this does not happen in the land of those who die, but in the land of the living.

This appears to be signified by what Laban says to Jacob:

> “It is not customary in our place,” Laban says, “to give the younger in marriage before the elder.”

The elder is not improperly called elder because she is first in time. In the Lord’s teaching, the labor of good works comes before the rest of contemplation.

When the two periods have been completed—one belonging to the ancient law, the other to evangelical grace—he immediately reaches the embrace of the long-desired Rachel. For whoever desires to attain the delights of divine contemplation must first strive to fulfill the commandments of both Testaments.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Bilhah and Zilpah.

Because every elect person, not content with the limit of his own perfection, also desires to beget children for God through a special fruitfulness, after Jacob entered into the marriage bond with the two sisters, he did not refuse to take the maidservants as well for the purpose of begetting, in order to propagate a more abundant offspring. And, so that everything might be understood as overflowing with spiritual mysteries, the very names of the maidservants were also foreshadowed in mystical figures.

Bilhah is interpreted as “grown old.” Indeed, because the human tongue cannot express the understanding of spiritual substance in naked words, the teaching of wisdom sometimes endeavors to instruct its hearer through certain bodily likenesses. Images drawn from the old life and from carnal senses are conceived bodily; they are adopted for teaching when something is heard about the incomprehensible and immutable essence of divinity.

Rachel therefore preferred to receive children from a maidservant, in whatever manner, rather than remain entirely barren. For the teaching of wisdom, or the grace of contemplation, through external knowledge and the forms of visible things makes known to its hearers whatever it conceals of visible things within its secret depths. Thus it receives children, in a certain sense, through the maidservant, when through the knowledge that is subordinate to it, it gives birth to spiritual children for God.

Zilpah, however, is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” This maidservant therefore represents those whose mouths gape in preaching the evangelical faith, but whose hearts do not gape. Of them it is written:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” [Col. 0854D];

and of them the Apostle says:

> “You who preach that one must not steal—do you steal?”

Yet from this maidservant Leah received other sons who would become fellow heirs, because active life has often adopted many sons of the kingdom through such preachers. Concerning them the Truth says:

> “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do”;

and the Apostle says:

> “Whether Christ is proclaimed from pretense or from truth, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice.”

We understand that this must be considered in them: just as Jacob took all those women from whom he begot sons for the sake of Rachel alone, so whoever, established under the grace of whitening, desires to bear spiritual fruit for God must always direct everything he does toward the grace of contemplation.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How Rachel called her son Benjamin by name.

As her soul was departing, Rachel, overcome by grief and already facing death, called the name of her son Ben-oni—that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father called him Benjamin—that is, “son of the right hand.”

Rachel fittingly signifies the Church. She lives innocently, like a sheep, and through the practice of contemplation burns inwardly with longing to behold the appearance of her Redeemer. To the Jews who questioned him, he said of himself:

> “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” [Col. 0855C].
