Benjamin, at whose birth his mother Rachel dies, signifies Paul; no one doubts that he arose from this stock. And Rachel is said to die as Benjamin is born because, as Saul approaches the light of a new regeneration, the Church is grievously attacked by persecutions through him.

Thus Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Saul was ravaging the Church, entering house after house, dragging off men and women, and handing them over to imprisonment.”

Rachel therefore appropriately calls Benjamin Ben-oni, “the son of our sorrow,” while Jacob calls him Benjamin, “the son of the right hand.” Paul, who had been the sorrow of the mother Church and who, in a certain sense, killed her while he was being born by persecuting her, was called by God the Father “son of the right hand,” because through him divine power fought against the nations as through its strong right hand, hurled the darts of words with force, inflicted saving wounds upon hearts, and, after conquering and overthrowing the enemies, triumphed gloriously through him.

Hence the same Paul says to the Galatians:

> “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, I immediately did not consult flesh and blood.”

Paul is therefore not improperly called “son of the right hand,” since through him the whole multitude of the Gentiles, which is to be placed at God’s right hand, is gathered into the sacraments of faith.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How Onan found hot waters in the wilderness while he was tending the asses of his father.

[Col. 0856A]

This is Onan, who found hot springs in the wilderness while he was tending the asses of Sebeon, his father. This plainly seems frivolous as far as the literal sense is concerned. For what relevance to sacred Scripture is there in reporting that a keeper of asses discovered water in the desert? But where no usefulness appears in the sacred writings, the mind must necessarily turn to spiritual understanding. What, then, does it mean figuratively for Onan to pasture his father’s asses in the wilderness, except that some spiritual man, whose father is God, keeps simple brothers under the discipline of a more secluded way of life? And what does finding hot springs mean except that he breaks forth into tears of compunction, which are drawn from the fervor of the Holy Spirit?

For the very interpretation of the names does not resist this meaning. Onan is interpreted as “the pain of their sorrow,” or “muttering” or “murmuring.” Whoever grieves with the sorrow of true compunction is compelled, as though in a kind of plaintive muttering, to murmur against the wickedness of his life. For he stands principally in righteousness who, compelled by no necessity, strays from the straight path of justice. Thus Onan found hot springs while he was tending the asses of his father Sebeon, because whoever presents himself to God as a son through the rectitude of his life, and grieves from the depths of his heart over his sins, receives, while making himself solicitous in the vigilant care of his brothers, the grace of tears as a divine gift.

For that blessed woman who was a sinner first anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment, and afterward poured the alabaster vessel of precious ointment over the head of him who was reclining. God is the head of Christ; the servants of God are Christ’s feet. Just as she, while rendering service to Christ’s humanity, deserved to attain an understanding of his divinity, so the teacher of the Church, while guarding his members, receives the grace of contemplating the divinity.

## CHAPTER XXX. Judas went down to Thamna to shear the sheep.

Judas went down to Thamna to shear the sheep with Hira the Odolamite, the shepherd of his flock. Thamna is interpreted as “failing”; through it the synagogue is signified, in which kings and prophets had failed, and likewise the anointing, until he should come to whom it had been reserved. Hence it is also said through the Prophet: “When the Holy of Holies has come, the anointing will cease.”

What, then, is meant by Judas, who came to Thamna to shear the sheep, except our Redeemer, who is understood to have come to the synagogue in order to relieve from sins the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel? Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.”

Judas therefore came to shear the sheep, not alone, but with his shepherd, the Odolamite, whose name was Hiras. What are we to understand by the Odolamite except John? Odolamite is interpreted as “testimony in water.” With this testimony the Lord plainly came to the waters of baptism. He indeed possessed testimony greater than John’s, but for the sake of the weak sheep he deigned to use this testimony in the water. Thus, when John saw him approaching the streams of the Jordan, he immediately cried out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” And the Evangelist says: “John bore witness, saying: ‘For I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven and remaining upon him. And I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”’”

The name of that shepherd also corresponds most aptly to this vision. Hiras is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” The Lord was John’s brother, not only according to the seed of Abraham, but also according to the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth. John therefore saw his brother while he was still enclosed in the womb; he saw him in baptism; he saw in the eye of the flesh a human being; he saw majesty in the spirit. Hence John himself comprehended the interpretation of both these names—Hiras, which means “the vision of my brother,” and Odolamite, which means “testimony in water”—in the verse of a single statement, saying: “I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

When Judas came to shear the sheep, Tamar changed her clothing, because she changed her spiritual name. Tamar is interpreted as “changing”; for the synagogue becomes the Church.

Blessed be the name of the Lord.

# DIPLOMA OF ALEXANDER II CONCERNING THE LEGATION OF SAINT PETER DAMIAN IN GAUL

[Note: If you wish to learn more about this same legation of the most holy cardinal in Gaul, read his Works, volume I, book VI, letters 2, 4, and 5. Moreover, we thought it should not be omitted that an anonymous Cluniac monk, a contemporary of Blessed Peter Damian, relates the matter in his treatise on the Miracles of Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, near the end. CAJETAN—You will find the account of the legation itself below, together with other short works of Saint Peter Damian, recently published for the first time by the eminent Cardinal Mai. EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGY.]

**907–908** Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to G., archbishop of Reims; R., archbishop of Sens; B., archbishop of Tours; M., archbishop of Bourges; and T., archbishop of Bordeaux: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0857B]

Your holy fraternity, most beloved, is not unaware that, by the authority of the apostolic see, to which divine mercy has appointed us, responsibility for governing and ordering the condition of the entire universal Church rests upon us. Since, therefore, being occupied with many affairs of the Churches, we ourselves cannot come to you, we have taken care to send you such a man that, after us, no greater authority is held in the Roman Church—namely, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who is both our eye and the immovable support of the apostolic see.

To him, therefore, we have entrusted our office with full authority, so that whatever, with God’s help, he determines in those regions is to be held as valid and firm, as though it had been promulgated by a judgment of our own personal examination. Accordingly, we admonish your venerable holiness with fraternal charity, and furthermore command you by apostolic authority to strive to receive such a great man, as though he were our own person, with worthy devotion, and humbly obey his decisions and judgments out of reverence for Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

For whoever, inflated by the arrogance of pride—God forbid!—should become his contradictor or adversary in judgment will not possess our favor or that of the Roman Church until he has rendered due satisfaction. But since, when we sent Girelmus to you, we still had no hope whatsoever that we could obtain the arrival of the aforesaid Lord Peter, we wish that, if Girelmus began anything among you, it should come before Lord Peter’s direction, and that whatever must be done should be carried out through his hand.

# Concerning the arrival of Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, at the church of Cluny, and how Blessed Hugh answered his indiscreet reproach with an appropriate and sufficient response

**909–910**

[Col. 0857D]

At a certain time the holy man found it necessary, in order to defend his sons, to have recourse to the mother Church and to seek the protection of the Roman see. Accordingly, seeking refuge in that city, he obtained, with great labor and difficulty, Lord Peter—namely, the bishop of Ostia, surnamed Damian—whom he had drawn away from the pope’s side so that he might be given to him as a great Peter, to fight and overthrow his adversaries by his marvelous prudence and eloquence.

For that man was accustomed to singular abstinence and was so worn on every side by the bonds of iron chains that it was scarcely possible to find a way to nourish the weakness of his body sufficiently for him somehow to bear the heavy burden of riding. And because he could often be offended by the slightest scandal, it was necessary frequently to appease him with an apology. Venerable Hugh so inclined himself to this task that he restored his spirit to tranquility, as though he were another Martin, who considered nothing unworthy that humility advised one to do.

When another Gregory came to Cluny—another in the abundance of his eloquence, though not in equality of apostolic life—and had seen the hospitality and discipline, and had observed the rod and the staff, he began to hesitate and marvel at how those who abounded in such goods could be saints or have holy founders, and again, how those could fail to be saints—or perish—who so devoutly endured so heavy a burden of labor and guarded monastic discipline.

At one time he judged the abundance of food; at another he wondered that those who fasted lacked the grace which he saw them possess. Nevertheless, as he himself said, if it could be achieved that both virtues—obedience and abstinence—were joined in them, then certainly nothing would be lacking for apostolic perfection. For this reason he approached and begged the lord abbot that those who were so perfect in other respects that they owed nothing to anchorites should abstain from fat for at least two weekdays.

To him venerable Hugh, an outstanding guardian of discretion, replied: “If, dearest Father, you wish to increase our crown of reward by adding fasting, first try with us the burden of labor, at least for a period of eight days; afterward you will judge what you ought to consider should be added. For as long as you have not tasted the stew, you cannot know what seasoning of salt it requires; and if you have not at least applied your little finger, you will by no means be able to judge the burden of your brother with discretion and worthiness.”

When he heard this, and perceived that the weight of such burdens was unbearable for his own strength, he ceased asking that the burden be increased and began to strike himself with the weapon by which he had wished to strike others, since he could not direct an arrow against them without wounding himself. He understood that the burden was a great one and that what he himself could not undertake ought to be sufficient, since he appeared to stand at such a height of virtue. Thus the prelate, now much more learned, returned more learned than he had come, and carried away with him a great treasure: the avoidance of empty glory and the pursuit of true humility.

# ACTS OF THE SYNOD HELD IN GAUL BY BLESSED PETER DAMIAN, CARDINAL BISHOP OF OSTIA AND LEGATE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, BY ORDER OF ALEXANDER II

**911–912**

Synodal decision between Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Lord Droco, bishop of Mâcon.

[Col. 0859C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

In the time of Lord Alexander, universal and supreme pontiff, and while Henry, son of the emperor Henry, reigned, with Philip as king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1063, something new happened to the monastery of Cluny, which we have decided to record in this little document for the memory of posterity.

Droco, namely, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Mâcon, persuaded by the urging of his household, and especially of his clerics, who—as I may put it—continually fanned him with the fire of evil kindling, attempted to seize a right of power over that monastery and to claim for himself some measure of domination contrary to the privileges of the apostolic see.

Surrounded by wedges of soldiers and accompanied by ranks of armed men, whether under the pretext of preaching or even on the authority of a synodal judgment, he reached the basilica of Blessed Maiolus, confessor of Christ; but, broken by the obstacle of those who resisted him, he could not enter.

He attempted this in order to impose upon the monastery the yoke of a new usurpation and afterward to litigate, as it were, on the basis of a custom that had been imposed. Then venerable Hugh, abbot of that same monastery—clearly not only religious but also cautious and prudent—like a freeborn possessor, recoiled from this yoke of degraded servitude. Like a medicine against the evil of a newly creeping bad custom, he met it with contradiction, and crushed with the foot of a lively intelligence the head that it was attempting to introduce.

He therefore hastened to the Roman synod, faithfully presented his complaint before the holy council, and prayed that it might avert the new danger that beyond doubt threatened the ruin of the holy place. When the sinister report struck the hearts especially of those who judged more soundly, and when they feared, out of pious compassion, lest a place of such religious excellence and such renowned fame should fall even slightly from its state of freedom, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, immediately offered himself among the others. He undertook to come to the aid of the monastery through the dangers of such a long, harsh, and arduous journey.

Accordingly, at the city of Chalon he convened a synod by the authority of the apostolic see. Whatever seemed to have been wrongly exhausted, he corrected by the force of canonical sanction; whatever he could, he established as to be observed according to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline; and, with divine mercy assisting, he concluded the case of the monastery of Cluny—the case especially for the settlement of which he had come—with the best possible judicial decision.

For in the presence of the entire holy council, the document was read that Count William, the first founder and benefactor of the place, had established, in which—except [Mai corrects *propter* to *praeter*] for the Roman pontiff—he left no right and no dominion over it to any mortal or to any Church whatsoever. The privileges of the apostolic see concerning the protection, fortification, and perpetual freedom of the aforesaid monastery, established through the succession of the Roman pontiffs, were likewise read aloud.

All the bishops were questioned whether they considered the privileges they had heard to be valid. With one voice and in agreement they all praised them and decreed by common judgment that they should remain forever to be observed and unharmed. And, as though this judgment were not sufficient under the proclamation of common acclamation, each man was consulted individually; the bishop of Mâcon himself was also questioned. He freely professed before all who were listening that the privileges were valid and were to be preserved with inviolable and perpetual right, no less than did all the other bishops.

Since, among other provisions, those same privileges had decreed under threat of anathema that no bishop should be permitted to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against the monks of the aforesaid monastery, the bishop did not cast the dart of excommunication absolutely—this is how he completely excused himself—but, as he claimed, having been moved by anger, said: “If there are any in that monastery who fall under my jurisdiction, whom I am permitted to excommunicate, I excommunicate them.”

Since it was thus shown that the aforesaid bishop, even if unknowingly, had in some way acted against the privileges of the Roman Church in this excommunication, while he most firmly denied that he had read or recognized the tenor and contents of the privileges, the case was finally brought by the holy council to this decision: the aforesaid bishop was to place his own hand upon the holy Gospels and swear, thereby satisfying the legate of the apostolic see and the holy council.

## Text of the oath

“Let Lord Peter, bishop of Ostia, and the entire holy synod hear,” he said—that is, the bishop of Mâcon—“that on the day when I came to Cluny in anger, I did what I did neither in contempt nor in disdain of the apostolic see or of Lord Alexander, the Roman pontiff; and that at that time I did not fully know the tenor and contents of the privileges that have just now been read in our hearing. So may God and these holy Gospels help me.”

After him, four clerics of his own Church also came forward in the presence of everyone and confirmed by oath upon the same Gospels what he had sworn. Two of the number of seven whom the holy council had appointed to swear remained behind—not at the request of the bishop of Mâcon, but by the concession of the lord bishop of Ostia.

Immediately the aforesaid bishop of Mâcon prostrated himself on the pavement, asked forgiveness, and confessed that he had sinned. He accepted a seven-day penance, during which he would fast on bread and water.

On the following day, while the same holy council was seated, the same bishop, urged by his clerics with madness and insolence, requested that the privilege of his own Church, which had formerly been established by Pope Agapetus, should also be read. In it, practically nothing seemed to have been specially inserted beyond the right and custom of every Church, but only what is recognized as having been granted by common right to all holy places: namely, that no violent person should invade either the things that were already or would thereafter be under their jurisdiction, but that the ruler of the Church should possess all his own property in peace and tranquility.

All the bishops therefore said that this privilege had been read without cause in so great a council and unanimously decreed that it in no way prejudiced the privileges of the monastery that had been read before everyone on the previous day, nor diminished anything of what those privileges declared had been granted through the generosity of the apostolic see.

Thus, by synodal council, the perpetual freedom of the monastery was confirmed, and by the common decision of the holy bishops it was decreed that the holy place should be subject to the Roman Church alone. Immediately every complaint of controversy between the bishop and the abbot was quieted, every division of hostility and disagreement was reconciled, and firm peace was restored between the two spiritual men by the bond of charity.

We have therefore arranged these matters briefly and in order, so that we may pass on to posterity, through the channel of truth and in a faithful cup, the stream of the purest account that we have drawn in our own times.

---

# HYMN ON THE GLORY OF PARADISE

By Peter Damian, cardinal bishop of Ostia, from the sayings of blessed Augustine.

**[1.]**

At the fountain of perpetual life  
the thirsty mind has thirsted;

The soul seeks at once to break  
the closed gates of the flesh.

Exiled, it burns, strives, and struggles  
to enjoy its homeland,

While it laments that it is subject  
to pressures and troubles;

It contemplates the glory  
that it lost when it sinned.

Present evil increases  
the memory of lost good.

**[2.]**

For who could tell how great  
is the joy of supreme peace?

There buildings rise  
from living pearls.

High roofs glitter with gold,  
and banquet halls shine;

This structure is joined together  
with precious gems like the sun.

The city’s road is paved  
with pure gold as with glass:

No mud is present, no filth remains,  
and no plague is seen.

Terrifying winter and scorching summer  
never rage there.

Everlasting roses bloom;  
there is an everlasting spring.

**[3.]**

Lilies gleam white,  
saffron blushes, and balsam drips.

Meadows are green, fields are always in spring,  
and streams of honey flow.

The fragrance of spices breathes forth,  
together with the liquid of aromatics;

The fruits of flowering groves hang there,  
never to fall.

The moon does not change its phases,  
nor the sun or the courses of the stars:

The Lamb is the unfailing light  
of the blessed city.

Night and time are absent from it;  
it bears continual day.

For the saints also shine  
like the brilliant sun.

**[4.]**

Crowned after their triumph,  
they rejoice together in mutual jubilation,

And, now secure, they count  
the battles of the enemy who has been overthrown.

Purified from every stain,  
they know nothing of the battles of the flesh.

The flesh, made spiritual,  
and the mind perceive one thing.

Enjoying profound peace,  
they endure no scandals;

Freed from mutable things,  
they return to their origin,

And contemplate the present  
form of truth.

**[5.]**

From here they drink  
the life-giving sweetness of the living fountain.

From there, always departing,  
they attain the same unchanging state;

Bright, vigorous, joyful,  
they are subject to no vicissitude.

Diseases are absent from the ever-healthy,  
old age from the young.

From here they possess perpetual being,  
for passing away has passed away;

From there they are green, strong, and flourishing;  
corruption collapses.

**917–918**

The vigor of immortality  
has swallowed up the right of death.

They know all things that can be known,  
and cannot be ignorant;

For they also penetrate  
one another’s secrets of heart.

**[6.]**

They will one thing and reject one thing;  
there is unity of minds.

Although each person has a different reward  
according to his labor,

Charity makes what one loves in another  
belong to oneself;

Thus what belongs to each individually  
becomes common to all.

Where the body is,  
there the eagles are rightly gathered,

So that souls may be refreshed there  
with angels and saints.

The citizens of both homelands  
live by one bread.

Ever hungry and always full,  
they desire what they possess.

Neither fullness produces disgust  
nor hunger torments:

Always longing, they eat;  
and while eating, they long.

**[7.]**

A melodious voice continually resounds  
with new harmonies,

And organs, raised into jubilation,  
soothe the ears;

They offer proclamations worthy of the king  
through whom they are victors.

Happy is the soul of heaven  
that sees the king who is present,

And from beneath the high seat  
beholds the mechanism of the world revolving,

The sun, the moon, and the spherical stars  
together with the planets.

Christ, palm of warriors,  
introduce me into this commonwealth

After my military belt has been laid aside;

Make me a sharer in the reward  
of the blessed citizens.

Grant strength to one laboring  
in an unexhausted battle,

So that after being girded  
you may owe rest to one who has earned it;

And may I deserve to possess you  
as my reward without end. Amen.

---

End of the third volume of the Works of Blessed Peter Damian.

# ADDITION TO VOLUME III OF THE WORKS OF SAINT PETER DAMIAN

## MAI’S NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SHORT WORKS

*(New Collection of Ancient Writers, volume VI, preface, p. XXXIII, and pp. 193–244.)*

The collected edition of the Works of Saint Peter Damian—whom Leo XII, the Supreme Pontiff, recently enrolled among the doctors of the holy Church by his decree—is that very complete edition which the monk Constantine Cajetan formerly arranged in four volumes, and which we have more recently had reprinted at Venice in the year 1743.

When I compared this edition with the Vatican manuscripts, however, I discovered several works, partly short works of the holy doctor and partly writings about him, that had escaped Cajetan’s great diligence. They are as follows:

1. Saint Peter Damian’s *Gallic Journey*, written in an almost contemporary manuscript by one of his companions and fellow travelers. I would readily suspect that he was John, a monk and inseparable companion of Saint Peter during the last years of his life. But since, in the Life that he wrote of the holy man, he made no mention at all of the Gallic journey, I scarcely think he could have been so forgetful as not to remember at least his own literary work.

   Moreover, besides the fact that this journey is remembered in the edition of Saint Peter’s Works, there is a contemporary account of the action undertaken by the abbot of Cluny against the monastery of Limoges in the year 1063—the same year in which Peter went to Gaul and dealt with that matter—in Baluze, *Miscellanies*, new edition, volume I, p. 123. There the Cluniacs seem to have acted somewhat unfairly; hence Peter Damian’s equity becomes clear: he prohibited the adversaries from inflicting violence and causing scandals, but deferred pronouncing judgment on the right at issue in the controversy itself (p. 296).

2. An exposition of the canon of the Mass preserved in the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. This commentary, apart from the author’s name being written in it twice, proves itself genuine by its own dignity.

3. Collections from the New Testament, extracted from the writings of Saint Peter by one of his disciples. An old inscription showed that these had existed, but Cajetan did not find them despite a long search, although they were contained in two manuscripts of the Vatican Library.

4. Finally, in the same manuscripts are several letters, or fragments of letters.

I thought that all these works should no longer be deprived of the light of publication.

Trithemius, in chapter 335, also counts a book of our Peter’s *On Meditation on Death*, considering its beginning, among the series of his Works. But Vatican manuscript 373 taught me that Trithemius was deceived when he thought it a separate writing: although it is likewise written separately there, it is in reality nothing other than chapter six of the fiftieth published short work, addressed to the countess Blanca.

The Vatican Urbinas manuscript 165 likewise ascribes to Peter Damian a sermon *On Absalom*, which certainly is not found in Peter’s editions and may be believed to be his genuine offspring. Nevertheless, it has long been published under the names of other authors, and the Ballerinii include it among the additional sermons in volume I of the Works of Saint Leo.

For the rest, as to what Casimirus Oudinus, in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume II, where he discusses our author, says—namely, that he suspects the reliability of the editor Cajetan, as though Cajetan had attributed far more writings to Saint Peter Damian than the truth permits, and had assigned various works of others to him—the opposite is true in every respect. For the Vatican manuscripts, of which there are many, agree completely with Cajetan’s edition. Oudinus therefore unjustly accuses a most religious man and an exceptionally trustworthy editor.

---

# ON THE GALLIC DEPARTURE OF LORD PETER DAMIAN AND HIS JOURNEY BEYOND THE ALPS

[Note: This short work is published from ancient Vatican manuscript 4920; I also saw a recent copy of it in Ottobonian manuscript 944. It is certain that the author was the holy man’s companion on the expedition. Peter Damian himself speaks of this journey in his letter to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, book VI, letter 1, and likewise in letter 4. Furthermore, in Cajetan’s edition of the holy man’s Works, volume IV, pp. 459 ff., are found the documents of his legation: namely, the letters of Pope Alexander II, the decree of the synod of Chalon, and a brief account of what occurred at Cluny. It is clear from the acts of the synod that this legation was carried out in the year 1063. From this short work we learn that Peter was an old man in that year, which confirms the opinion that Peter was born before the beginning of the Christian year 1000. He survived until the year 1072, in which year he died on February 22.]

## PROLOGUE

**1.** Rustic speech, strengthened while stammering upon the foundation of the Catholic faith, shares in some way in the rewards of eloquent refinement; and a written composition in uncultivated language claims for itself a share in the recompense of lucid writing. For one whose learning cannot climb the lofty mountains of Scripture with the stags can prepare for himself a safe refuge with the hedgehogs on a lowly rock.

Let our rustic speech therefore stammer, since eloquent refinement is not present in me; and if I cannot deliver my discourse in polished language, let me dare at least to mutter in whatever manner I can.

*The prologue ends.*

**2.** We believe that it will benefit the edification of many if it is entrusted to the faithful marks of writing how the most reverend man Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, set himself aside for the sake of the peace of the monastery of Cluny and voluntarily delivered himself over to death for the tranquility of that holy congregation.

From the very beginning of its foundation, the monastery of Cluny has been established as completely free in its native and secure liberty, so that, apart from the Roman pontiff, it ought to be subject to no ecclesiastical or secular person. Divine mercy has so ordered this that, to the degree that it is lightened from the burden of earthly subjection, it may be more fully devoted to divine service; and to the degree that it is found subject to no worldly faction, it may be able to fulfill intact the obligation of monastic profession.

Truly noble and freeborn is the service of Christ, which suffers no companionship with earthly servitude! For as long as the people of Israel were oppressed under Pharaoh by the forced labor of mud and straw, they are not read to have offered any sacrifice to God. Moses cried out with divine words: “Let my people go,” says the Lord, “so that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness.”

Let it therefore go out from Egypt, so that it may be able to render the service of divine worship; for there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, no fellowship between light and darkness.

Pharaoh, chastised with blows, agreed to let the people depart; but when it came to separating them from the dominion of his power for a full three days, he refused, swollen with savage pride. For that enemy who is understood through Pharaoh does not want us to be separated from him for a full three days.

Either by action, speech, or even thought, he continually orders us to build structures of mud, even if they are not exposed to fire. But the liberator of Israel, having laid aside the servitude of Egypt and abandoned Pharaoh’s authority, wishes us to be separated from him for three days and to sacrifice to him in that wilderness in which that outstanding prophet, who was placed in the royal court and stripped of Pharaoh’s power, said while remaining there: “Behold, I have fled far away; I have remained in the wilderness.”

**3.** That venerable congregation of Cluny, therefore, in which Egypt claims no servitude for itself and Pharaoh retains no day of the three, lives devoutly in proportion to its freedom from the yoke of earthly domination. But that ancient enemy of all holiness, jealous of the holy freedom of this place, stirred up a certain bishop against it through his goading.

### Note

[Note: Alluding as though to his name, Peter said to the Cluniacs in book VI, letter 5: “You who have been freed through me from draconic bonds.” Moreover, it is sufficiently clear from the following account, which we publish from another recent Vatican manuscript, that Cluny was contained within the diocese of Mâcon.]

## DESCRIPTION OF CLUNY

Cluny is a town in the Aedui region of Celtic Gaul—that is, in Burgundy—six miles from the city of Mâcon, twenty from Chalon, and twenty-four from Lyon. The town itself belongs indeed to the diocese of Mâcon, but by exemption it is subject to the abbot of Cluny in both temporal and spiritual matters.

In this town William, surnamed the Pious, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, having no male offspring, began the monastery called Cluny and appointed Bruno, distinguished in character and learning, as its abbot in the year of the Lord 894.

This monastery, afterward enlarged and enriched, produced many great men, among them Odo, Odilo, Maiolus, and Hugh, enrolled among the saints. It also produced Otho the monk, the disciple of the aforesaid Hugh, soon afterward bishop of Ostia and finally Urban II, supreme pontiff of that name. At approximately the same time in which the Cistercian order began, he reformed many monasteries and priories of his profession and of Saint Benedict into a better form of life, attached them to the monastery of Cluny, and wished the order to be called Cluniac.

He adorned the abbot of Cluny with many marvelous ornaments and with privileges surpassing those of a bishop. For he consecrates chrism and confers baptism and the sacred orders upon all who are established within his jurisdiction and order. He has a royal ensign borne before him, like a pontiff, surrounded on every side by many episcopal mitres; he also wears a pallium in the manner of metropolitans and places upon his insignia a cap like that used by cardinals. He describes himself in letters as a cardinal priest by birth, of the title of Saint Cecilia, asserting that this privilege was granted to him and his successors by Pope Gelasius II and likewise approved by Callistus II, along with many other matters that it would take too long to recount.

For when the abbot is consecrated, a ducal scepter and the emblem of the sword of justice are displayed to him; when he celebrates, a scepter is carried before him, a gift formerly bestowed by Pope Callistus, previously count of Burgundy. A red cap, like that worn by cardinals, is not only carried before him but also placed upon the altar.

They assert that four pontiffs came from his monks: Gregory VII, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II, who was also buried in that monastery. The same monastery produced other men distinguished both in learning and in holiness of life, among them the abbots Peter and Renerius, whose outstanding theological writings survive and whose bodies shine with many miracles.

The abbot of Cluny has in temporal matters very many and extremely wealthy towns subject to him, and countless barons as vassals, who obey his commands. He is count and baron of the city of Mâcon. In spiritual matters he has sixteen monasteries whose abbots wear the mitre, and an incredible number of priories in various regions of the Christian world. He succeeds as heir to deceased abbots, priors, and other monks of his order, and receives the first year’s revenues of all benefices.”

These matters belong to the history of former times, for now there is no monastery at Cluny. **Ed.**

Droco, bishop of the Church of Mâcon, was attempting in the aforesaid venerable monastery to seize for himself a certain right of illicit power and to wield over the monks of that place the rod of an unmerited jurisdiction.

The bishop proceeded to such audacious madness that, surrounded by an armed force of soldiers, he reached the monastery like a rash invader, trampling the ancient freedom of the place beneath his arrogant foot, treating the privileges of the apostolic see as worthless, and burdening with an unconsidered anathema the church of Saint Maiolus, which adjoins the monastery, as well as many monks of the monastery itself.

4. Then the venerable Hugh, father of that monastery [Note: [Col. 0868D] Letters of Saint Peter the Deacon to this man are extant. Peter relates that he wrote the Life of Saint Odilo at his urging.], could not help grieving at the novelty of this presumption. For, viewing the matter with pastoral foresight, he perceived that the place had declined considerably from the state befitting its nobility and that the spirits of the entire congregation were disturbed by an unprecedented sorrow. But lest the leprosy of this depravity, as though by custom, [Col. 0867B] should spread like an intrusive cancer, and lest a place of such holiness should thereafter suffer the disgrace of a degenerate custom, he fortified himself with the counsel of monastic discipline. In this way he both nobly defended the monastery against the novelty of this affliction, and the vengeance of secular power did not obscure its holiness.

That man, who advances strongly fortified not only by religion but also by pastoral prudence, whose angelic face likewise reveals the holiness of his inner person, found himself amid the turmoil of the aforesaid storm. He resolved to approach the council of the Apostolic See. In order to reach safety from the whirlpool of this disturbance into the harbor of a tranquil anchorage, he hastened to enter the single little boat of Saint Peter. Then, before the holy council, as a fluent orator, he presented his complaint about his distress in a faithful and honorable appeal [Col. 0867C] and pleaded the case of this affair as it had occurred, moving the hearts of his hearers to mercy and assistance.

All who had learned of the holiness of this place either by their own sight or through report were disturbed by so sinister a rumor and publicly detested the bishop’s novel faction. And, lest a place of such holiness and such liberty should deviate even slightly from the path of its liberty, each of them, moved by pious compassion, began to consider by what means and in what manner the holy place might be helped [Col. 0868A] and this evil of a bad custom be resisted. Yet none of those whom justice commended by reason of their authority, and to whom the canonical resolution of this case belonged, declared himself willing to undertake the labor of so long a journey and so arduous an expedition.

5. Then the venerable Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, whom, out of reverence for his holiness, because of the weakness of his afflicted body, and because of the venerable maturity of his years, neither the pope nor any bishop or cardinal dared—not merely to command, but even to suggest anything to—immediately offered himself among the others. On the day of battle he set himself against the enemy, ready to fight for the house of Israel.

We believe that this was arranged by divine providence. For, as the outcome of the matter later showed, no one except the bishop of the supreme see could have brought the case to a competent conclusion, unless the prudence of that holiness and his eloquence—fluent and incomparable—had intervened. Indeed, all Gaul revered him not so much on account of the dignity of the Apostolic See as because of the reverend presence of his holiness.

This remarkable and exemplary man then willingly undertook the heavy burden of obedience, though once he had unwillingly accepted the office of distinguished obedience. When called to the dignity of the episcopal summit, he put forward many excuses, loudly declaring that he was unworthy, unadorned in character, empty of virtues, and unequal to the office. But for the hardship of the journey to Gaul, he came without offering any excuse, though he had not been summoned.

These are indeed salutary examples of true obedience: that someone should unwillingly undertake obedience involving dignity, yet willingly accept the burden of humble obedience. For this man’s discerning obedience undoubtedly imitates two soldiers of the heavenly court. Moses was commanded by the Lord to preside over the Israelite people, whereas Paul was divinely instructed to go to Jerusalem. The one was ordered to accept the honor of dignity; the other was admonished to take up the burden of adversity.

But the one upon whom dignity was imposed, after first invoking the opportunity afforded by eloquent speech and then pleading the impediment of his tongue, shrank in fear from the glory of so great a government and fled it. The other, to whom the burden of so great a labor was commanded, not only did not reject it, but, learning through the prophet Agabus what would happen to him in Jerusalem, trusted in purity of heart and said joyfully: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of Christ; for I do not hold my life more precious than myself.” Thus this man, by fleeing the summit of the episcopate, is shown to us as a new Moses; but in the voluntary labor of a long journey, another Paul, the teacher of the nations, is represented to the Church.

## ON THE BEGINNING OF THE JOURNEY

6. Meanwhile the labor of the holy pilgrimage began, [Col. 0869B] and the road of the arduous journey was hastened. Since charity seeks not what is its own but what belongs to Jesus Christ, he entrusted to Christ the Irrigator the monasteries newly planted by him, abandoned all the hermitages that he had either founded or governed under his protection, and left behind the bands of monks whom he himself had brought to the free service of Christ. He quickly undertook the journey beyond the Alps with only three disciples accompanying him.

And because love is strong as death, neither the Jovian Alps, nor the dangers of the Jovian Alps, nor trackless regions, nor the many deadly precipices, nor even the sight of the swan’s head, nor his weak and emaciated body, nor the burden of advanced age could deter him from the journey. He also made light of the fury of Cadalo, who, like a bereaved tigress, thirsted anxiously for his blood. Against this Cadalo—namely, the bishop of Parma, who was then adulterously usurping the name and insignia of the pope—this prelate had written a book in which he condemned, by testimonies from Scripture, his madness, worthy of ridicule, and his abominable apostasy.

He also expressed the interpretation of that perverse name, and what lay hidden at the end of this presumption, in a prophetic encomium [Note: [Col. 0869D] In the work entitled *Synodal Debate*, vol. III, p. 34, Peter says: “Cadalus is called from *cadere* (‘to fall’); it signifies the ruin of the people. Pressius, book I, letter 20: ‘The first part of this name plainly announces a fall, the second a people; for *laos* means ‘people.’”], which we believe he composed by divine inspiration, since we later saw that what he had written came to pass [Note: [Col. 0869D] You may consult Peter’s work 18, vol. III, p. 206; also book I, letter 20. Peter’s most bitter attacks on Cadalo are found throughout his writings.]. Among the other things he had eloquently written about that man’s canine rage, he also composed verses of extraordinary depth and remarkable beauty. We wished to set them down here for the praise of the one and the disgrace of the other [Note: [Col. 0870D] These poems are extant among the other works of Peter Damian, published in vol. IV, p. 46. We therefore omit them here.].

[Col. 0869D] 7. Wounded by these weapons of words—or rather, buried alive beneath the ramparts of Scripture—that man watched the crossroads, byways, and every passable route of the journey through his agents, so that they might either kill him or bring him alive into his presence. But the prudent man, like a confident lion, trod underfoot the various dangers of the journey and the other man’s secret ambushes, making light of them with the step of holy pride.

Indeed, he was supported by the help of the one who promised his faithful servant: “I shall go before you, and I shall humble the glorious ones of the earth.” The dangers of the already-mentioned and often-to-be-mentioned Jovian Alps—routes scarcely ever known to have been passable, and which always threaten travelers with deadly collapse—he traversed, as is said, borne by the aid of no *Marron* [Note: [Col. 0870D] *Marrones* were certain inhabitants of the Alps, as Cangius explains in his *Glossary*]; nor did he proceed on foot step by step, as is customary on that journey, but rather, we saw him run.

It would have been most useful, if it could have been done with his permission, to write something about his self-restraint and conduct on so difficult a journey, at least for the edification of those who, taking the occasion of some journey, break the established laws of silence, abandon the rule of their customary fast, and freely disrupt the discipline of psalmody and almost the whole of monastic observance. But because I fear offending his holiness, it is better to keep the light of his lamp covered in silence than to place it upon a lampstand at the cost of his displeasure.

Yet one must obey God rather than human beings, and it is more fitting to dread offending him than offending any mortal. For the mouth of Truth commands as follows: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Let us therefore write briefly about certain aspects of his conduct, as though they were common matters that ought by no means to be hidden, so that his holiness may not be darkened by any blemish of rumor or stain of praise, the pious devotion of those who hear may be improved, and Christ may be glorified through him.

## HOW LORD PETER CONDUCTED HIMSELF ON THE JOURNEY THROUGH GAUL

[Col. 0870C] 8. During that very summer season, when the days are prolonged beyond their usual length and seem to gluttonous monks to be almost without end, he maintained the order of his practice in such a way that he neither omitted the custom of psalmody or vigils nor postponed the discipline of fasting or silence.

I cannot—and ought not—keep silent about how he deceived us, who constantly clung to his side, in the matter of his fasting, as it was thought. Among the Gauls there is a universal custom of first coating wine vessels internally with pitch and then storing the wines to be preserved in them. The natives of that land say that the wines are seasoned by this as though by some kind of spice, but most newcomers reject them with nausea as though they had been spoiled by pitch. The itch of our appetite quickly commended such wine to us; [Col. 0870D] but he abhorred it so greatly—though, as we thought, through a faithful deception—that he did not even wish to attend the banquet at which it was present.

Thus throughout Gaul he maintained the discipline of a strict fast, since we could not by any prayers persuade him to take even a small sip of this wine. The water of that region, however, is scarcely found anywhere suitable for drinking. He also entirely rejected fish and carefully prepared foods on every occasion. In this way [Col. 0871A] he endured the heat of summer by day and did not abandon the labor of vigils by night.

Yet I cannot look upon it without admiration: when this man was hastening to fight in the synodal battle and had gone forth alone to fight for the deliverance of many, how he deprived himself of strength; and, in order to grant himself the opportunity for preaching, how he continually weakened his body by starvation. So that he might not be marked by any stain of reproach, he had first read in the page of his own conduct what he preached to others more effectively because he practiced it twice over. Like the Apostle, he chastised his body, subjecting it to service, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should prove disqualified.

9. Let this man’s holy warfare now be compared with the battle and victory described as having taken place under Gideon. Gideon is read to have fought against the Midianites, but he immediately removed from military service the soldiers whom he saw drinking water from the river on bent knees. Those whom he saw drinking water with an upright knee he took with him into battle, equipping them with unusual weapons.

For, as it is said there, he did not arm them with the customary defenses of military art. They held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left against the multitude of their enemies; and thus, by the disposition of almighty God, the enemies were terrified by these kinds of weapons and immediately turned to the protection of flight.

So this warlike man, trained under an ecclesiastical drillmaster, proceeded to battle under his commander Jesus. He did not drink the river water with bent knee, because his upright conduct ennobled the teaching of wisdom that he had wondrously drunk with a thirsty heart from the river of Scripture. This soldier had already rejected the company of those soldiers to whom Paul said: “Strengthen the slackened hands and the weakened knees.” For he never drank the streams of spiritual doctrine while weakened in his works.

He armed his right hand with a trumpet and his left with a jar, because he fervently exercised the office of preaching, signified by the trumpet, while he made light of the fragility of the body, signified by the jar. He carried a trumpet in his right hand and a jar in his left because, rejecting the prosperity of the left-hand life, he yearned from the depths of his being for the joys of the right-hand life.

Hence the saying of the elect is rightly seen to apply to him: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.” For he trampled underfoot, by the intention of his mind, the prosperity of the left hand, which belongs to the present life, and placed his whole self in the lap of eternal blessedness, which is received through the right hand.

Thus, as Solomon says: “Length of days is in his right hand, but in his left are riches and glory.” This soldier therefore proceeded armed in such a manner: in his right hand, as it is said, was the fiery law; there was the melodious and terrifying sound of the trumpet; he made light of the body, strengthened the spirit, weakened the flesh, fattened the mind, chastised the outer person, and strengthened the inner one. Neither fear nor love of anyone caused him to extinguish the lamp of his preaching, because, as the Lord says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand.” The light of preaching must not be abandoned for temporal advantage; rather, it must be placed upon a lampstand, so that the grace of preaching may always prevail over concern for the body.

10. Fortified by these weapons of virtue, whenever an opportunity presented itself he scattered the seed of the divine word and planted trees of virtue in the soil of the human heart, watering them afterward with fruitful exhortations. Whenever a bishop, an abbot, or a person of any rank came to him out of due reverence, he always sent him away seasoned with the salt of his wisdom, refreshed by the medicine of holy preaching, soothed by fraternal admonition, and improved in every respect, so that he bitterly regretted not having come earlier.

Thus, amid the fruitful labor of the journey, while he fervently hastened toward the salvation of a single monastery, he also provided incidentally for the infirmities of many. In this the noble disciple imitated the supreme Teacher. For the Savior of the world was traveling to raise the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, but on the journey he freed a certain woman from an issue of blood through the healing power of his garment. And although he deigned to raise the former by the presence of his body, he first wished to free the latter through the mere fringe of his garment.

## LORD ADRALD, ABBOT OF BREMET

11. A venerable abbot named Adrald also accompanied our company [Note: [Col. 0871D] Concerning this man Peter Damian himself writes in *Opusculum* XXXIV, 5: “I learned by report of the prudent and religious man Adrald, who presides over the monastery of Bremet.”]. He had once received the habit of the holy vestment from the monastery of Cluny [Col. 0872C] and had governed for some time the priory of one of that monastery’s houses, called Paternacum.

A man highly learned in literary studies and adorned with expertise in the liberal arts, religious in action and wonderfully eloquent in speech, he then governed with pastoral foresight the celebrated and royal abbey of Bremet. At the threshold of first acquaintance he is judged almost austere and unsuitable; but once you begin to remain in the court of his intimacy, he is suddenly found to have changed, becoming kind, prudent, and approachable.

Among this man’s many gifts of virtue there is one that commends him greatly to people and establishes him more firmly in the devoted affection of many. He is always regarded as generous and liberal, not after the manner of Cluniac generosity or that of any man of his own country, but almost as though nature had made him Italian. The mouths of our servants testify to this: he clothed them not in goatskins or sheepskins but in foxskins. Although, as the saying goes, my fortune prevented him from doing so, he preserved in my case alone the parsimonious custom of Gaul. Nevertheless, I ought not to be silent about this man’s praises, even though he bestowed no rewards upon me.

After this man became a participant in our journey and began to share fully in our common fellowship, everything that had to be done was entrusted to his counsel, and all matters were handed over to his direction [Col. 0873A]. The abbot of Cluny himself placed such confidence in this man’s prudence that he resolved to undertake no business without his advice.

At last, after the summer’s sweat, after very great and numerous labors, after many and varied dangers, after the immense precipices of the mountains and Alps, we came to Cluny, which was awaiting us. It is unnecessary to write about the preparation of the procession and the great devotion of our reception, since they were already receiving him with devoted hands when he arrived—the man whose coming they had long implored with many prayers for the liberty of that monastery.

Then, by common counsel, we began to consider what ought to be decided concerning the summoning of bishops to the synod. For that bishop whose reckless audacity had occasioned this case, once he learned of our arrival through the report of rumor, hid himself by hastening farther away among his own people. Since he was not a native of that land, he could not avoid the future council on that pretext.

Yet he could not evade attendance at the council of Chalon by the protection of flight. The synodal date was arranged with such foresight that distant and more remote prelates could attend promptly. Then, by the authority of the Apostolic See, letters of summons were sent to the bishops, commanding the obedience due to the Roman pontiff and canonically threatening punishment for disobedience. They also announced the place and day of the future council.

## PRAISE OF THE CLUNIAC CONGREGATION AND ITS ABBOT

[Col. 0873C]

12. Meanwhile we remained at Cluny for eight days. There I truly found many Pauls and saw very many Antonys who, although they do not dwell in the habitation of solitude, do not lose the reward of anchorites through imitation in their works.

When I began carefully to observe the order of that congregation, and saw that mutual affection and goodwill remained among them and that monastic harmony prevailed in all matters, my mind immediately returned to the household of the primitive Church, concerning whose praise Luke speaks in this way: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and everything was held in common among them.”

After the pattern of that primitive household—or rather, I should say, of the heavenly homeland—there is no fear of anyone’s want, no burden of anyone’s misery. Charity reigns there; spiritual joy dances; peace binds everyone together; patience bears with all; forbearance moderates them; hope raises them up; faith makes them firm; chastity cleanses them inwardly and outwardly; devoted obedience purifies them; the order of holy and monastic custom is observed without violation; and lively mortification and regular strictness are always maintained.

Why is it necessary to describe the discipline of guarding the cloister or of silence, when no one even dares to walk within the cloister except for some necessary matter, nor in any way to open his mouth to speak without being questioned? In the cheapness of their clothing and the plainness of their beds they in no way transgress the command of Father Benedict.

The offices of divine service are so carefully distinguished among them and so piously extended by deliberate design that no portion of even the longest day can be free from the divine office. They are so worn down by ecclesiastical offices that scarcely can one communicate anything to another in cloistered and proper speech except by signs. These practices are found to have been made so cautious and necessary in every place that they cannot be marked by any stain of frivolity or reproach.

I pass over writing about the equality of food and clothing, the pious compassion shown to the sick, and the appropriate distribution of all affairs, since the abbot himself, whether enjoying good health or weighed down by illness, is not accustomed to claim for himself any private room or anything else exceptional.

13. O noble and Israelite family of Christ, which, abandoning the degenerate slavery of Egypt, crossed the Red Sea safely after its enemies had been drowned, and defeated proud Jericho while bearing the ark of the Lord! It also overthrew the troublesome Nabuzardan—namely, the internal enemy—by the discipline of moderation, and, like a new Judith, slaughtered the wanton Holofernes completely.

Now, with all kings overcome, it makes use of its enemies as though of a kind of promised land, from which it hastens by its works to run toward the true land flowing with milk and honey. That place also possesses abundant almsgiving for the poor and the utmost care for guests and visitors. No poor person leaves from there hungry or unrelieved; no newcomer is received without greeting or permitted to depart without honor.

But the river of this holy activity flows from that fountain which the grace of the Holy Spirit has supplied in the abbot’s sacred heart. From that purest fountain they draw what flows so abundantly, and in the library of his conduct and exhortation they read how to live as monks and how to preserve the order of divine service.

He is lovable in his humility, approachable by all in his character, and remarkable to everyone for the serene dignity of his countenance. Almighty God wished him to be so subject to the fear of God, so fervent in love, and so conspicuous for the flowers of his virtues that he entrusted to him the pastoral office of that church.

I would also speak further about the abundance at this place of external and worldly goods, without which the present life scarcely permits anyone to pass through: how all the stone workshops are arranged according to monastic order; how the great vaulted church, equipped with many altars and richly endowed with the relics of the saints, is exceedingly wealthy in a great and varied treasure; how the enormous cloister, by its very beauty, seems almost to invite monks to inhabit it; how the dormitory is sufficient, and how the continual light of three lamps seems to forbid anything harmful ever taking place there; how the refectory, painted with no superstition but constructed in holy simplicity, provides ample seating for the brothers who take their meals; and how, throughout all the workshops, wherever water is needed, it immediately and wondrously flows of its own accord through hidden channels.

I would speak of these and other things concerning the aforesaid monastery, but because the style of this description is hastening to set down the labor at Limoges [Col. 0875A], it avoids writing such matters out of consideration for the labor involved.

## THE LABOR AT LIMOGES

14. In the city of Limoges there was a celebrated, most devout, and exceedingly wealthy monastery dedicated to Saint Martial, which the abbot of Cluny had recently acquired. But because the monks of that place did not obey him, the greatest discord prevailed there at that time.

Because of this acquisition and out of hatred for the same abbot, they withdrew from the monastery, as secular monks, and began to lodge in its various cells; they attacked the monastery like enemies and thirsted for the blood of the monks whom he had placed there from Cluny.

The monks themselves had burst into such audacity of deranged mind [Col. 0875B] that they burned the town in which the monastery stands, destroyed by fire everything around the monastery, and, unless Roman authority intervened and a person worthy of reverence from the Apostolic See came to their aid, the place seemed destined to ruin.

The abbot did not know what to do about this affair, nor did he know where to turn. He was ashamed and afraid to suggest to us the burden of this journey, and had no hope that the matter could be brought to completion by any other means. At last he gave voice to what filled his mind and prayed that the pain he had suffered might be healed. The abbot himself asked this; the entire congregation demanded it with prayers.

15. Then our bishop of Ostia hesitated for a while to take this labor upon himself and believed that he could scarcely complete it. But because he had come for the salvation of that [Col. 0875C] monastery, he quickly consented and resolved to assist it with the members of his company who were stationed around him.

Before beginning his departure, however, he sat in the chapter house with all the brothers. After delivering a sermon, he prostrated himself completely upon the ground and asked them with many prayers to assist him. He called himself a gyrovague, a Sarabait [Note: [Col. 0875D] A Sarabait is a wandering and lawless monk. See Cangius’s *Glossary*], and, as was his custom, proclaimed himself a wretched monk.

During this, such an abundance of tears was granted to him from heaven that all drew long sighs from the depths of their hearts. Each, displeased with himself, cried out: “O good Jesus, if this man, whom we believe to be more than human, fears while weeping so abundantly, what shall we dry ones do, who in comparison with him are strangers to virtue?”

For, as the abbot later reported in my presence, these tears greatly benefited everyone: they improved the minds of those who heard and strengthened the hearts of those who watched.

Then, by common counsel of the brothers, the abbot decreed that from that time onward one poor person should always be fed and clothed for his sake, and that one psalm should always be sung in common for him. Upon being informed of his death, they were always to celebrate a solemn conventual Mass on his anniversary, prepare a festive meal for the brothers, and distribute whatever remained from the table to the poor for the salvation of his soul [Note: [Col. 0876D] Peter himself mentions this matter in letter VI, 2 and 4.].

Thus fortified by the fellowship of all the brothers and confirmed by the kiss of peace, we came to Saint Martial. Meanwhile, the rumor of our arrival had shaken the hearts of the monks who were harassing the monastery and had caused them to hide in every direction and along the byways [Col. 0876A].

But as soon as we arrived, letters were sent to them ordering them to present themselves before the legate of the Roman See. If they believed their case just, they were to defend their argument by due process of justice, without any suspicion of partiality; otherwise, they were henceforth to live under the authority of the abbot. But because the worm of their former faction gnawed at their vitals and they entirely refused to accept the Cluniac order, they scorned to come to the appointed hearing and utterly forbade him to preside over them as abbot.

Then, after consulting the bishop and count of that city, the matter was brought to the decision of this judgment. In the church of that bishopric, which a devout crowd of people had filled, the prelate recounted before everyone their stubborn absence and how they refused reverence to the legate of the Apostolic See and the obedience due to the abbot [Col. 0876B].

Then, with the people applauding, he commanded by apostolic authority that, unless that hostile audacity ceased injuring the monastery and the monks, they would unquestionably be subject to excommunication. But concerning their refusal to obey the abbot, he deferred issuing a definitive sentence.

When this affair had thus been settled and the monastery had already been restored to peace, we returned to Silvaniacum, lest any part of our journey should be free from the service of God.

## ON THE CONSECRATION OF THE CHURCH AND THE TRANSFER OF THE BODY OF SAINT ODILO

[Col. 0876C] 16. Silvaniacum is a place rich in the frequent commerce of merchants and most renowned, but it is especially devoted to the bodies of the saints. A monastery had been built there in which the bodies of the blessed confessors of Christ—Maiolus and Odilo—rest.

That monastery, however, had not yet been fully confirmed by episcopal blessing. Meanwhile, the date of the synod was approaching. Then, with many bishops present and an innumerable crowd of people attending, the church was consecrated with great reverence. After the body of blessed Odilo had been transferred and the altar dedicated to his name, the bishop of the Church of Chalon received us with the greatest devotion and honor.

## ON THE ASSEMBLED SYNOD

[Col. 0876D] 17. Meanwhile the synod was assembled; the summoned prelates arrived, and a considerable crowd of people hastened there devoutly. The bishop of Mâcon also appeared without hesitation or delay. Trusting in his own prudence—for he was powerful in learning and speech—and in what seemed to be a conspiracy of certain bishops, he rejected an amicable settlement of the case and came eagerly to the synodal conflict as a vigorous warrior intending to triumph.

Almost all the bishops who were present at that time, except the venerable and most eloquent archbishop of Besançon, envied the monastery of Cluny and, as cautiously as they could, trampled upon its cause [Col. 0877A]. They worked by hidden machinations so that the abbot might suffer misfortune rather than triumph in this affair.

For each one believed that his own case was being tried when the Roman discussion examined the business of his fellow bishop. If the abbot gained victory in this matter, none of the bishops would dare resist him any longer. Thus, gathered together with this cautious purpose, they urged him on, intending to help him resist.

But our Roman warrior, forewarned of these machinations and of a conspiracy that was by no means to be disregarded, later pleaded the case in such a way that those whom the other man had already secured as secret supporters became open opponents of his cause.

When the entire council was seated in the church of Chalon, after he had finished the word of preaching, as the custom of the Roman synod requires [Col. 0877B], he began with such an introduction in rhetorical language that it made his hearers attentive and well disposed.

## INTRODUCTION IN RHETORICAL LANGUAGE

18. “The authority of Rome,” he said, “has delegated us to the aid of your fraternity, and our common mother, the Church, has sent us as to her dearest sons. Trusting in your holy fidelity, which is owed to her and which she has also experienced as useful in certain of her affairs, she desires, with your provident assistance, that whatever injury she suffers in these regions may be remedied.

“Through us, the Roman Church laments before your holiness that, because of the insolence of many people, she daily suffers many insults among you. Yet among the other things that she observes to have happened to her, one new and unexpected matter has greatly disturbed her.

“When the report of this sinister rumor recently shook the ears of the entire Roman council, all were at once turned to grief and amazement. After a long deliberation about whom, what sort of person, and how great a man they ought to send in response to so great a presumption, they finally decided to send us.

“You may judge from this how deeply the Roman Church grieves over this matter, my brothers: she did not arrange to send a subdeacon, a deacon, or any cardinal [Note: [Col. 0877D] The holy man alludes to Pope Alexander’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, in which he said: ‘We have taken care to send you such a man that, after us, no greater authority is found in the Roman Church—namely, Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, who is both our eye and the immovable support of the Apostolic See.’ [Col. 0878D]]

[The supplied source ends here, in the middle of the sentence.]

19. Then all the bishops, rendered very favorably disposed by the sweetness of the words already spoken, and not a little attentive because of the gravity of the case, awaited the explanation of the matter for which so great and distinguished a man had come from the Lateran curia. As soon as he saw that they were listening benevolently to his words, he began to explain his purpose as follows:

“None of you, brothers, is unaware that the monastery of Cluny is subject to the Roman curia; and no one doubts that no person other than the Roman pontiff has any jurisdiction over that monastery, which he loves above all the monasteries belonging to him. It is also known to be protected by many privileges of the apostolic see. Yet the lord bishop of Mâcon, disregarding all these things, rashly endeavors, like an invader, to subjugate it and bring it under his authority.”

Then the bishop, because he had already felt the head of his wickedness crushed and the firmness of his mind almost extinguished, rose to recount the case before the entire council. Immediately the matter was presented from both sides, and the arguments of each party were examined. The privileges of the Roman Church, against which the bishop was accused of having acted, were read; the case was defended, blame was assigned, and the controversy was investigated according to the merits of the parties.

At last, after many disputes and various objections from both sides, since the bishop could not clear himself of having acted against the privileges, the matter was brought to the point of this decision. The bishops were asked whether they judged the privileges of the apostolic see to be valid and to remain intact in the form in which they had been read, without injury to them. By a definitive judgment they all decreed that they should remain valid and unshaken.

Then the bishop of Mâcon himself, together with five clerics of that Church, swore with his own hand [Note: The formula of this oath is extant in the edition of the Works of Saint Peter Damian, vol. III, p. 911] that whatever he remembered having done against the monastery, he had done neither to the injury of the apostolic see nor of the pope himself, and that he had not yet known the full substance of the privileges in detail.

In this way the business of the case between the lord bishop and the abbot was brought to an end and committed to a complete settlement. The bonds of peace were established between them, and the quarrels of hostility were driven away. In the same synod some matters were corrected by ecclesiastical censure, others were established by the force of canonical sanction; and although the synod was judged to have been convened with a single case in view, it is clear that afterward it proved beneficial in many cases.

## ON THE RETURN JOURNEY

20. Meanwhile the desire to return arose, and the labor of undertaking the journey again became pressing. Permission was requested, but permission was delayed. For the abbot himself began, together with his companions, to consider how the burden of so arduous a journey might be lightened by compensation in the form of some gift. He knew that this man did not love money and despised presents, and that he had undertaken so great a labor solely out of regard for piety.

He therefore resolved to offer gifts which he would transmit through him not to the man himself but to God, so that, although he did not wish to accept them for himself, he might at least give them to God. He offered a silver-gilt chapel, together with sacred vessels and vestments, pallia, and furnishings.

“Accept,” he said, “master, this sacred vestment and these holy vessels, which we assign to Almighty God [Col. 0878D] and send through you to your holy places, to be devoted to divine worship.”

At first, deceived by the apparently veiled wording of the offer, he did not reject the gifts, since they were said to be given through him to God. Meanwhile the day passed; when the necessary matters had been completed, we gave our limbs over to rest.

In the meantime, a conflict of diverse thoughts seized his mind. He wondered whether some fault might be concealed beneath the appearance of this reception; whether what he had undertaken through regard for a future reward might be destroyed by an earthly gift; and whether he might himself consume, with teeth grown numb, the fruits which he ought to have eaten when ripe, finding them bitter. He considered that it is more blessed to give than to receive, and that blessed is the one who withdraws his hands from every gift. Weighing these and other considerations in the holy examination of his mind, he balanced them against one another.

When morning came, he ordered me to be the first to appear before him. Then, as he often used to do, he began to recall his beloved Baruntius.

“Oh,” he said, “if that dearest brother of ours, Baruntius, were here [Note: Saint Peter Damian, in his discussion *On Various Apparitions and Miracles*, chapter 1, says: ‘Baruncius was plainly my brother in complete harmony, and singular in the sweetness of a very special love,’ etc.], he might pour for us the cup of saving counsel! For he never persuaded me to accept anything; rather, he always urged me to despise earthly things. I reflect that these gifts, brought to us under such a disguise, ought not to be accepted. I fear selling God’s justice on any pretext; I ought not to be a merchant in earthly things. Tell me what you think about this.”

After he had granted me the courage to offer this counsel, I not only praised him for wishing to do so, but repeatedly begged him to carry it out. I impressed upon his holy ears that, since Christ was poor, we who are poor ought to follow the poor Christ.

As a result of this counsel, love for his fatherhood began to arise in me—or rather, as I think, began to increase—although that love itself has not yet come to the knowledge either of me or of anyone else. It was still, as it were, confined by frost within the bud, and had not burst forth either into the ripeness of fruit, the tenderness of blossom, or even the greenness of leaves.

At last, lest the fruit of eternal recompense be lost to us through some gift, and a temporal offering consume an eternal reward, we left the aforesaid gifts with the abbot, despite his refusal and protestations, and utterly declined to burden ourselves with such a weight. I remember that we accepted nothing from him except what was necessary for us and what the length of the journey required.

Thus, after the duties of greeting had been performed on both sides, relieved and cheerful, we returned to the solitude of the beloved fountain of Avellana [Note: In the year 1063, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. Compare Peter Damian, *Letters*, book VI, letter 5].

[Col. 0879]

# EXPOSITION OF THE CANON OF THE MASS

[Note: This excellent little work is absent from the edition of the Works of Saint Peter Damian prepared by Constantine Cajetan, and neither Trithemius nor any other bibliographer, ancient or modern, appears to have known it. Nevertheless, it exists in the Vatican royal manuscript 524, with the title given by us, which is written both at the beginning and at the end of the work. Only Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, pp. 16 and 68, mentions this writing of Saint Peter Damian, on the basis of the catalogue of the manuscripts of Senator Pétau, most of which, as we know, passed into the library of the Queen of Sweden, now the Vatican Library. I therefore believe that our manuscript 524 is itself the Pétau manuscript, with only the numerical designation altered. The work certainly needs no recommendation from me, both because of the author’s glorious name and because of its profound theology and its outstanding expressions of religious devotion.]

## ACCORDING TO PETER DAMIAN

[Note: The manuscript has *Damiani*, not *Damianum*; and indeed we know that Peter was called “Damiani” out of gratitude toward his benevolent brother. Nevertheless, Peter’s companion in the account of the Gallic journey, no. 2, and other authors write *Damianus*.] (G)

[Col. 0879C]

### 1. “Who, on the day before he suffered”

Behold: as we now approach the power of the supreme sacrament, the tongue fails, speech disappears, genius is overcome, and understanding is overwhelmed. For who has known the order of heaven and set out its arrangement upon the earth? Yet let us knock at the door, if perhaps the key may deign to open it and lend us three loaves, which will be especially necessary for us at this banquet.

Faith asks and receives; hope seeks and finds; charity knocks and opens. Faith asks for and receives life; hope seeks and finds the way; charity knocks and opens the truth. For he is the way, the truth, and the life.

“Who, on the day before he suffered”—on the fifteenth day of the moon of the first month, which was then Friday—the Lord suffered. On the preceding night, namely, on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, at evening, in order to fulfill the figures of the Law, after the typical Passover he instituted the sacrament of his body and blood and handed over the chalice to be used continually.

For this had been prefigured in Exodus:

“On the tenth day of the first month, each person shall take a lamb for his household and family, and shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening. And they shall take some of its blood and put it on both doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they shall eat it. And they shall eat its flesh roasted by fire that night, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces.”

And shortly afterward:

“For it is the *Phase*, that is, the passing of the Lord.”

John defines this passage when he says:

“Before the day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.”

And when the supper had taken place, he completed the things that had been prefigured.
