Egypt is the world; the destroyer is the devil; the lamb is Christ; the blood of the lamb is the passion of Christ; the houses of souls are bodies; the families of the houses are the thoughts of the heart. We are stained with this blood through faith in the passion, and with that blood through imitation of the passion, setting the sign of the cross within and without against the hostile powers.

Finally, we eat the flesh of the lamb when we receive the body of Christ in the sacrifice; and we eat unleavened bread—that is, sincere works—with wild lettuces—that is, with bitterness.

[Col. 0881A]

### 2. “He took bread”

For this reason Christ instituted bread and wine in the sacrifice of his body and blood: just as bread and wine refresh the body more than other bodily foods, so the body and blood of Christ refresh and nourish the inner person more than other spiritual foods and drinks. Hence: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

Because Christ took bread and the chalice into his holy and venerable hands, the priest, following Christ’s example, takes the flesh and blood into his hands and blesses each of them personally with the sign of the cross.

Fermented bread ought not to be offered in the sacrifice, both on account of the historical event and on account of the mystery. Thus it is read in Exodus. Leaven also signifies corruption, as the Apostle testifies: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.” [Col. 0881B] Nevertheless, the Greeks, stubborn in their error, prepare the sacrament with leaven.

“He raised his eyes to heaven.” No evangelist records these words. Who, then, was so presumptuous or audacious as to set them forth as spoken by Christ? Certainly the apostles received this form from Christ himself, and the Church received it from the apostles. The evangelists omitted many things, both words and deeds, which the apostles nevertheless supplied. These words can also be confirmed from other passages of the Gospel.

For John, describing the raising of Lazarus, testifies that Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me.” Likewise elsewhere: “And raising his eyes to heaven, he said: Father, glorify your Son.”

But if he raised his eyes to heaven toward the Father when he recalled Lazarus’s soul to his body, how much more should we believe that he then raised his eyes to the Father in heaven when he changed bread and wine into his own body.

“Giving thanks.” From this too it is gathered whence the sacrifice of praise comes. He gave thanks not for himself, but for the redemption of human beings that was to take place in this way.

### 3. “He blessed”

Some have said that Christ effected the sacrament when he blessed, construing the wording in this order: “He took bread and blessed”; one must understand, “saying: This is my body.” Thus he first uttered those words in order to give them the power of effecting the sacrament; afterward he uttered the same words in order to teach the apostles the form for effecting it.

It may rightly be said that Christ effected the body by divine power under the form expressed according to which those who came after him would bless. He himself blessed by his own power; we, however, do so by the power that he manifested to us.

Therefore, when the priest pronounces Christ’s words—“This is my body; this is my blood”—the bread and wine are changed into flesh and blood by that power of the Word by which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; by which he spoke and they were made; by which he changed a woman into a statue; by which he changed a staff into a serpent; by which he changed springs into blood; by which he changed water into wine.

For if Elijah’s word was able to bring down fire from heaven, will Christ’s word not be able to change bread into flesh? Who would dare think this of him for whom no word is impossible, through whom all things were made, without whom nothing was made? Certainly it is greater to create what does not exist than to change what does exist; and it is far greater to create what does not exist from nothing than to transform what exists into something else.

If someone says, “I am entirely certain that he is able to do it, but I am not certain that he wills it,” then, if he doubts that, when Christ took bread and blessed it, saying “This is my body,” the Truth says this, it is entirely true.

And elsewhere: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” And, to express the truth more fully, he added: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

### 4.

I, however, who desire to possess eternal life, truly eat Christ’s flesh and truly drink his blood: that flesh which he took from the Virgin, and that blood which he poured out on the cross.

Just as the widow of Zarephath ate every day, and the flour in the jar and the oil in the vessel did not diminish, so the whole Church receives the flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ every day and never consumes it.

But whether part passes into part, or the whole into the whole, he knows who accomplishes it. I burn what remains with fire, for we are commanded to believe and forbidden to distinguish.

But because the persistence of the questioner presses us, without endangering faith we shall grant that such bread is changed into such a body, and not that one part passes into another. Nevertheless, without diminishing the majesty of faith, I think that, wherever the bread has been consecrated, Christ is wholly present in the whole appearance of bread, wholly under each part, wholly in the large portion, wholly in the small, wholly in what is intact, and wholly in what is broken.

I know, however, that some say: “As long as the appearance remains intact, the whole body exists under the whole appearance; but when it is divided, the whole begins to exist in each of the divisions. It is like a mirror: while it is intact, only one image of the person looking appears; but once it is broken, as many images appear as there are fragments.”

It is asked whether the Lord’s body is local, whether it produces local distance, and whether it should be said to lie, sit, or stand. Many other questions could also be investigated concerning the present subject, but I prefer to leave them untouched rather than define them rashly. For “the beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned.”

In such matters it is safer to remain this side of reason than to go beyond reason, lest, God forbid, the bones of the king of Edom be reduced to ashes.

### 5. “He broke it”

Many people habitually ask, but few understand, what is broken there, what is gnawed by the mouse, and what is burned when the sacrament is burned.

**Answer.** Just as the substance is miraculously changed into the Lord’s body and begins to exist under the sacrament, so in a certain manner it miraculously returns when that body itself ceases to be there.

The argument from place is not valid in this matter: here there are heat, taste, quality, and quantity, although nothing is colored or flavored by the other. What and how great a miracle is this? Nature is conquered, and dispensation withdraws from the law. You should neither seek nature in grace nor ordinary practice in a miracle.

Certainly the nature of God is the Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In the hypostasis of the Son there is also a trinity of substances, namely, divinity, body, and soul. In the sacrament of Christ’s body there is a trinity of appearances, namely, bread, wine, and water.

In the nature of God there is neither accident in substance nor substance under accident. In the hypostasis of the Son there is accident in substance and substance under accident.

Let us therefore answer the first question by saying that the form of bread is broken and crushed, but Christ’s body is taken and eaten. Whatever indicates corruption is referred to the form of bread; whatever indicates taking is referred to Christ’s body.

### 6. “He gave it”

It is asked whether he gave his body at the supper mortal or immortal, capable of suffering or incapable of suffering. I think it sufficient to say: he gave it as he wished.

Nevertheless, without endangering faith, it may be granted that he gave it as he then possessed it, namely, mortal and capable of suffering—not in the sense that it could suffer under the sacrament, but because it could suffer under the sacrament it was believed to be capable of suffering, although it was not harmed.

**“To the disciples.”** It is commonly doubted whether Judas received it. This seems likely when he says: “Drink from this, all of you.” But it is asked why the healing physician gave the sick man a medicine which he knew would be deadly to him.

He gave it for this reason: to teach by his example that a priest ought not to deny communion to anyone whose crime, even if known to him, is not known to the Church, lest he prove not a corrector but a betrayer.

**“Take and eat.”** This should not be understood to mean that the disciples themselves administered to one another the body received from the Lord’s hand. Rather, the one who consecrated also administered it.

Perhaps a further thought still troubles the mind, asking what becomes of Christ’s body after it has been taken and eaten. Christ passes from the mouth to the heart; it is better that he proceed into the mind than descend into the belly. This food comes to be eaten not by the flesh but by the soul; to be tasted, not consumed; to be received by the mouth, but not digested in the stomach. It refreshes the spirit and does not pass into the privy.

If, perhaps, evacuation or vomiting should occur after the Eucharist alone has been eaten, in this respect the appearance serves the senses according to its properties: insofar as it concerns us, it preserves in every way the likeness of corruptible food, but insofar as it concerns itself, it does not lose the truth of the inviolable body. The appearance may be gnawed and stained, but the truth is never corrupted or defiled.

If you should ever see such a thing, fear nothing for it; rather, be concerned for yourself, lest you be harmed if you believe wrongly.

### 7. “This is my body”

It is asked what the priest demonstrates by the pronoun *this*. If he demonstrates bread, it is never appropriate for bread to be Christ’s body, but he demonstrates Christ’s body. Yet when the pronoun itself is uttered, transubstantiation has not yet occurred.

The answer is that the priest is not demonstrating something at that moment, because he is not using those words declaratively but recitatively, just as when he says: “I am the true vine,” “I am the light of the world,” and many other such things. The same applies here.

Under both appearances—namely, of bread and wine—both things, that is, body and blood, are consecrated. Neither appearance is superfluous, however, so that it may be shown that Christ assumed the whole of human nature in order to redeem the whole of it. Bread refers to the body, and wine to the soul.

**“After the supper had taken place.”** He gave this sacrament after the supper in order to commend the final commandment of a testator more firmly to memory.

This does not mean, however, that the Church should be criticized because it is received by those who are fasting. It pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, it should first enter the mouth of a Christian.

**“Taking also this glorious chalice.”** The container is used metonymically for what it contains.

**“This is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal covenant.”** That is, the confirmation of the new and eternal promise.

It is asked whether the water is changed into blood together with the wine. It is said that water signifies the people and is mixed with wine so that the people joined to Christ may be signified.

I say that the water passes into the wine when a small amount of water is poured into a much larger quantity of wine.

It is asked whether what is done is void if the water should be omitted. I say that if someone omits the water through ignorance or forgetfulness, he should be severely punished; nevertheless, the sacrament should not thereby be invalid.

He instituted that the sacrament of his body and blood should be received under another appearance for three reasons: to increase merit, to support the senses, and to avoid ridicule.

To increase merit: because one thing is seen there and another is believed.

To support the senses: lest the mind recoil from what the eye would see.

To avoid ridicule: lest a pagan mock a Christian if he performed such an act.

**“The mystery of faith.”** It is called a mystery because one thing is seen and another is believed.

**“Which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”** It was poured out for the predestined with respect to efficacy, and for all with respect to sufficiency.

### 8. “Whenever you do these things”

We cannot leave Egypt except by celebrating the Passover; therefore, so that we may be protected when the angel lays waste, let us eat the lamb.

But how often? [Col. 0884C] Augustine says: “I neither praise nor blame receiving it daily.”

Of Zacchaeus and the centurion we read: the one joyfully received Christ into his house; the other said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Neither placed himself above the other.

Let each person do what he believes should be done in a devout manner. Nevertheless, I urge that it be received on every Sunday, provided that the mind is not disposed toward sinning.

**“You shall do this in memory of me.”** If someone going abroad leaves some pledge with the person he loves, so that whenever he sees it he may remember that person’s friendship, he certainly cannot look upon it without tears and longing.

Hence also the words: “Being mindful.” Because the Lord himself commanded us to do this in memory of him, the Church proposes three things to be remembered: the passion, the resurrection, and the ascension. The first makes charity spring forth, the second strengthens faith, and the third gladdens hope.

What could kindle charity in us more than that God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all? What could confirm faith in us more than that Christ rose from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep and the resurrection of the dead? “As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ.”

What could enlarge hope in us more than that Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings, so that where he is, his servant might also be?

Because he says that he is remembering the Lord’s passion, he immediately recalls the harsher part of that passion [Col. 0885A], remembering the five wounds in the five crosses. He then proceeds through the three parts of the Lord’s passion, as will subsequently be explained from the text itself.

From this point, therefore, until the corporal is removed from above the chalice, the Lord’s passion is commemorated. For when the priest says, “the pure victim, the holy victim, the spotless victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” one sign of the cross is impressed upon the offering, signifying those openings in the living rock in which the spotless dove dwells, nesting fruitfully.

He makes three crosses together over the offering and the chalice, because in the first three words both appearances are understood. The bread is never separated from the chalice in the sign of the cross except when it is named separately.

[Col. 0885B]

### 9.

Here arises a question that must not be passed over in silence: why is the sign of blessing still made over the blessed and fully consecrated host? Indeed, certain clauses are added in the canon which seem to suggest that the consecration has not yet been completed.

In the canon, words signify one thing and signs indicate another [Note: Manuscript: “other words signify; other words set forth.”]. The words principally concern the consecration of the Eucharist, whereas the signs principally concern the recollection of the history.

The clause “Who, on the day before he suffered” ought to have been placed at the end of the canon, since the consecration is completed in it. But because this would have interrupted the order of the history, he placed the clause, as though compelled by a certain necessity, in the middle, as the heart of the canon, so that what follows might be understood to precede it, according to the figure by which things that follow in sequence may often precede in understanding.

Or rather, so that the order both of the text and of the history may be preserved, let it be said that the signs belong to the recollection of the history, while the words belong to the consecrated elements in this manner: “We, your servants first”—namely, the priests—“but also your holy people”—that is, the Christian people. For the people act through their vow, while the priests accomplish the mystery.

### 10. “We offer to your glorious majesty”

That is, to the majesty glorious above all others. For if the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father, how much more brightly does the divine majesty shine forth!

**“From your gifts.”** That is, from the fruits of the fields, with respect to the bread that is consecrated into flesh.

**“And from what you have given.”** That is, from the fruits of the trees, with respect to the wine that is consecrated into blood.

From these, I say, and from those, we offer a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim; that is, the Eucharist free from every original, venial, and criminal fault.

Or “pure” with respect to thought, “holy” with respect to speech, and “immaculate” with respect to action, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.”

**“This is the holy bread.”** That is, the bread that sanctifies and gives eternal life, with respect to the garment of the flesh.

**“And the chalice of everlasting salvation.”** With respect to the garment of the soul.

**“Upon which may you deign to look with a gracious and serene countenance.”** That is, with a favorable regard. This does not mean that his countenance ever changes, but that God illuminates and makes his countenance serene over us when he displays and reveals his mercy toward us [Note: Here Saint Peter undoubtedly refers to the exposition of the canon by Florus the deacon. See the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon, vol. XV, p. 77. G. Conversely, the anonymous interpreter of the canon of the Mass, printed in the fifteenth century and found by me in manuscript Palatinus 607, appears to have imitated Peter at this point. The exposition of the Canon by Odo of Cambrai, printed in the aforementioned library, vol. XXI, differs throughout], according to the Psalm: “May he illuminate his countenance over us and have mercy on us.”

**“As you were pleased to accept the gifts of Abel,”** and so forth.

The adverb “as” indicates likeness, not equality of quantity. This sacrifice is much more acceptable than that offered by Abel, Abraham, or Melchizedek. Reality is worth more than shadow, and truth more than figure.

Let us therefore offer like Abel, who offered his heart and subjected himself entirely to God. Hence it says: “God looked upon Abel and his gifts”; but he looked first upon Abel and then upon his gifts.

Let us offer sacrifice by slaughtering arrogance like a ram, bull-like ferocity, and goat-like lust, according to the Psalm: “I shall offer you fattened holocausts with the incense of rams; I shall offer you oxen with goats.”

**“A holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.”** Pope Leo added this in the canon.

### 11. “We humbly beseech you”

After the supper Jesus went out to the Mount of Olives and, advancing a little, fell on his face and prayed. Therefore the priest prays while bowing.

Then the betrayer approached and kissed him; the priest represents this by kissing the altar.

And because Jesus, being in agony, prayed at greater length, saying the same words three times, the priest makes three crosses. He makes the first and second separately over the offering and the chalice, saying: “We have received the sacrifice of your Son, his body and blood.” He makes the third by signing himself on the face when he says: “May we be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.”

Because his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the earth, perhaps he impresses a cross over the body because of the sweat of the body, and a cross over the blood because of the drops of blood. Because he fell upon his face, he impresses a cross upon his face.

Or, by the two crosses that the priest makes over the body and blood, the bonds and scourges by which blood was drawn forth are signified—“by whose bruising we have been healed.” By the cross that he makes upon his own face, that is recalled which they spat upon his face, struck him on the face with their hands, and covered his face with a veil.

### 12. “Command these things to be carried”

These words are of such depth that the human intellect can scarcely penetrate them. Blessed Gregory too, interpreter of so great a secret, speaking ineffably about the hour of sacrifice [Note: Here too Peter imitates Florus, as he does occasionally elsewhere], says:

“Who among the faithful could doubt that at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, the choirs of angels are present in that mystery, the highest and the lowest are joined, earthly things are united with heavenly things, and one and the same reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

Elsewhere he says:

“At one and the same time and moment, the consecrated body of Christ is carried into heaven by the ministry of angels and is seen upon the altar before the eyes of the priest, while the hidden sacrament of the heavenly decree nevertheless remains secure.”

The words may be understood here in a simpler, yet safer, manner:

“Command these things”—that is, the vows of the faithful, namely their supplications and prayers—“to be carried by the hands of your holy angel,” that is, through the ministry of angels, according to what the angel said to Tobias: “When you were praying with tears, I offered your prayer to the Lord.”

**“To your sublime altar.”** That is, into the presence of your divine majesty.

Moreover, as blessed Augustine explains, the angel is not said to offer our prayers to the Lord because God learns only then what we wish—for God knows all things before they happen—but because rational creatures must refer temporal causes to eternity, either by asking for what is graciously to be done or by seeking counsel about what they should do, so that what they know must be fulfilled at God’s command they may report either openly or secretly.

From this it also clearly appears that angels are always present at the sacrifice.

### 13. “Remember, O Lord”

The devout mother, the Church, prays not only for the living but also for the dead, and commends them to the saints through the intercession of the sacred offering. This is either because that precious blood, which was poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, is effective not only for the salvation of the living but also for the absolution [Col. 0887C] of the dead.

**“Who sleep with the sign of faith.”** This does not mean that faith itself is there, since faith and hope will be abolished; rather, the sign of faith is understood as the mark of Christianity by which the faithful are distinguished from unbelievers.

**“And sleep in the sleep of peace.”** According to the words: “In peace I shall sleep and rest together.”

Holy Scripture calls them “sleepers,” as the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps.”

**“Be gracious, O Lord, to all who rest in Christ.”** At this point the priest ought to make a particular commemoration of whichever persons he wishes.

**“The place of refreshment.”** Where there is no burning heat of sins.

**“Of light.”** Where there is no darkness of shadows.

**“And of peace.”** Where there is no conflict of punishments.

**“To us also, sinners.”** For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

**“With John, Stephen, Matthias, and Barnabas.”** In this second commemoration of the saints, what was commanded concerning the saints mentioned earlier is supplied in large part.

But it is asked why John is repeated, why Stephen is joined to John, and why Matthias and Barnabas are placed after them.

John is certainly included in the first commemoration with the others because of his apostleship. In this commemoration he is repeated and joined to Stephen because of the privilege of celibacy, for they are virgins.

For this reason virginity is placed before the others and especially commended, because on the cross Christ entrusted his virgin Mother to a virgin.

Stephen’s virginity is especially inferred from the fact that he was appointed by the apostles to minister to widows. Therefore, in that he was placed over women, he deserved to be a witness to the purest chastity.

Nevertheless, John may be understood not as the Evangelist but as the Baptist. Nor is it an objection that he is placed before both the apostles and the martyrs, since the Baptist may rightly be counted among the martyrs.

**“Not considering merit.”** He does not repay according to the measure of merits, but punishes below what is deserved and rewards above what is deserved.

### 14. “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things”

For “all things were made through him,” and “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.”

You therefore create by establishing nature; you sanctify by consecrating nature; you give life by transubstantiating the creature; and you bless by accumulating grace.

This is a simple exposition of providence. “All these things”—that is, bread, wine, and water—you always create as good according to their primordial causes; you sanctify them according to their sacramental causes; you give them life so that they may pass into flesh and blood; and you bless them so that they may confer unity and charity.

You do this “through him,” as through a mediator; “with him,” as with one equal; and “in him,” as with one consubstantial. In the Father authority is signified; in the Son equality; in the Holy Spirit coeternity.

Authority is in the Father because he is the beginning; equality is in the Son because he is the mean; coeternity is in the Holy Spirit because of their fellowship.

On the sixth day the Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, as Mark relates; at the sixth hour by the hands of the Gentiles, as John relates; and around the ninth hour, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

Therefore, to recall the crucifixion that took place at the third hour through the tongues of the Jews, who cried out three times, “Crucify him!” and again, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!”, the priest makes three crosses over the offering and the chalice when he says: “You sanctify, you give life, you bless.”

To recall the crucifixion that took place after an interval of three hours through the hands of the Gentiles, he likewise makes three crosses with the host, saying over the chalice: “Through him, and with him, and in him.”

Afterward, to signify the separation of the Lord’s flesh and soul at his death, he makes two crosses at the mouth of the chalice when he says: “To you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God.”

For although in Christ there are three substances joined together—divinity with the body, divinity with the soul, and the soul with the body—because the soul was separated from the body, the Lord’s death is signified not by three crosses but by two.

15. The priest also extends his hands over the altar table, because Christ stretched out his hands upon the altar of the cross. Yet we can represent these things more subtly and profoundly: for the three crosses signify the three sufferings that Christ endured on the cross, namely passion, propassion, and compassion—passion in the body, propassion in the mind, and compassion in the heart.

Of the passion the prophet says: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is…” He also says: “They pierced my hands and my feet.” Of the propassion of the mind the Lord says: “My soul is sorrowful”; and again: “Jesus began to be fearful and troubled.” Of the compassion of the heart, he prayed for his crucifiers: “Father, forgive them.”

The priest therefore makes these crosses with the Host over the chalice because Christ endured such sufferings in his body upon the cross. For the chalice signifies the passion, according to the saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this chalice pass from me.” [Note: [Col. 0889D] The Codex reads: “above.”]

The two crosses that he makes on the side of the chalice signify the two sacraments that flowed from the Lord’s side, namely the water of regeneration and the blood of redemption.

The corporal is removed from above the chalice because the veil of the Temple was torn, in accordance with what had been written concerning it: “Until now it was closed, and the wood was cast into the waters of Marah, and they were sweetened.” Then the priest himself and the deacon lower the sacrament, which has been raised a little from the altar, because Joseph of Arimathea came, and Nicodemus also came, and, having obtained permission from Pilate, they buried Jesus’ body.

And because he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb, the deacon places the corporal over the mouth of the chalice. Because “his place has now been made in peace,” the deacon kisses the altar table. Because “the principate has been made upon his shoulder,” the deacon kisses the bishop’s hand.

16. The Sacrifice, therefore, is marked with the sign of the cross seven times in the Canon. The first time, three times, where it says, “these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices,” on account of Christ’s threefold betrayal, which was carried out against him by Judas and the Jews.

The second time, five times, where it says: “Which offering, O God, may you deign to make blessed, approved, and ratified, so that it may become the body and blood”; this is on account of the five parties involved in the seller, the thing sold, and the buyers, namely the priests, the scribes, and the Pharisees.

The third time, twice, where it says: “Taking bread, he blessed and broke it. Likewise, taking this glorious chalice, giving thanks, he blessed it”; this is on account of the blessing of the bread, which is transubstantiated into flesh, and of the wine, which is transubstantiated into blood.

The fourth time, five times, where it says: “a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of everlasting salvation”; this is on account of the Lord’s five wounds.

The fifth time, twice, where it says: “the most holy body and blood”; this is on account of the bonds with which the body was bound and the scourges by which the blood was shed.

The sixth time, three times, where it says: “you sanctify, you enliven, you bless,” on account of the crucifixion, which took place at the third hour through the tongues of the Jews, who cried out three times: “Crucify him!”

The seventh time, five times, where it says: “through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” Three times this is done over the chalice, on account of the three sufferings that Christ endured—passion, propassion, and compassion—and twice at the side of the chalice, on account of the water and blood that flowed from Christ’s side.

Among these seven instances, the Sacrifice is marked twice with two signs, three times with five signs, and twice with three signs; altogether, five times five, which makes twenty-five. This number, multiplied by itself, always returns into itself: five times five is twenty-five; five times twenty-five is 125; five times 125 is 625. Thus the number five continually increases and returns into itself, if it is multiplied into infinity, however many times one multiplies it. The sacrament of the Eucharist is always the same Sacrifice.

17. Not only does the impression of the cross, but also the utterance of the voice, indicate what took place near the cross. For the priest, raising his voice slightly and striking his breast, interrupts the silence, representing the contrition and confession of the thief. Alternatively, by raising his voice and striking his breast, he expresses what the centurion and those who were with him did: when they saw what was happening, they were greatly afraid and said, “Truly this was the Son of God”; and, striking their breasts, they returned.

Because Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, gave up his spirit, the priest raises his voice, saying: “For ever and ever.” Since the women were lamenting and weeping for the Lord, the choir responds as though lamenting: “Amen.”

Jesus cried out with a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and therefore the priest, raising his voice, pronounces: “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

Blessed Gregory judged that this prayer should be recited over the Host after the Canon. For this prayer surpasses all others in many respects: in the authority of its teacher, the excellence of its wording, the sufficiency of its petitions, and the fecundity of its mysteries.

Here there are seven petitions, corresponding to the seven gifts, the seven virtues, and the seven beatitudes, against the seven capital vices. Man is sick, the Lord is the physician; the vices are illnesses, the petitions are laments, the gifts are antidotes, the virtues are healings, and the beatitudes are the joys of happiness.

The silence that follows, during the secret prayer, signifies the quiet of the Lord’s burial. On Saturday Christ rested in the tomb according to the flesh; according to the soul, he descended into hell, so that, coming as the stronger one, he might despoil the strong man who was armed.

“Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.” This prayer is called the embolism [Note: [Col. 0889D] So also the Palatine anonymous author, who adds: “that is, an excrescence,” because nothing is requested in it that was not requested in the preceding Lord’s Prayer; yet it is not superfluous, because it is an exposition and repetition of the seventh petition.]. It is an exposition of the final petition of the Lord’s Prayer.

After the sadness of the Passion, one comes to the joy of the Resurrection, according to the saying: “In the evening weeping will remain; in the morning, joy.”

18. The deacon and subdeacon carry the paten, which the priest receives and kisses; with it he makes the sign of the cross over his face. These men, both in their number and in their service, signify those women—namely Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome—who, carrying the paten, that is, a heart opened wide by the breadth of charity, bought spices for the service of the burial.

The priest therefore receives this paten, that is, the heart made broad by the breadth of charity; in other words, Christ accepts it.

Because the crucified One was sought with ardent desire, as the angel said to the women, “I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified,” the cross is impressed upon the face with the paten. Immediately afterward the priest kisses the paten, showing that Christ promptly fulfilled the women’s desire, for he soon came to meet them, saying: “Hail.”

Then the priest breaks the Host into three parts. Reserving two of them outside the chalice, he makes the sign of the cross with the other over the chalice and, saying in a loud voice, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” places the particle of the Host into the chalice.

The priest therefore breaks the Host so that, in the breaking of the bread, we may recognize God, as those disciples did at Emmaus. The joining of the bread and wine signifies the union of the flesh and soul occurring again in Christ’s Resurrection.

The sign is therefore made three times with the Host over the chalice because the power of the Trinity restored the soul of the crucified One to the flesh.

Three crosses are also made over the mouth of the chalice because three women sought the Crucified One at the entrance of the tomb. The deacon removes the corporal from it, signifying that the angel of the Lord rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb.

As for what those parts signify, Pope Sergius determines it, saying:

> “The body of Christ is threefold. The part of the offering placed into the chalice indicates the body of Christ, which has already risen; the part eaten, the body still walking upon the earth; the part remaining on the altar until the end of the Mass, the body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the world the bodies of the saints will remain in their tombs.”

“The peace of the Lord be always with you.” This signifies that Jesus stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: “Peace be with you.”

Because he immediately gave them the power to forgive sins—“Whose sins you forgive…”—the choir therefore cries out to him: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

And lest we speak of peace without possessing it in our hearts, Innocent decreed that the kiss of peace should be given, and it is given to all, so that it may be evident that the people have given their consent to everything that is enacted in the mystery and celebrated in the Church.

[Col. 0891] Here ends the Exposition of the Canon of the Mass according to Blessed Peter Damian.

[Col. 0891]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE NEW TESTAMENT WHICH A CERTAIN DISCIPLE OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN EXCERPTED FROM HIS SHORT WORKS

[Note: [Col. 0891D] In the edition of the Works of the holy teacher Peter Damian prepared by Constantine Cajetan, there are indeed collections of testimonies from the Old Testament, although they are incomplete; but collections from the New Testament are lacking. Concerning this matter the aforesaid editor says in volume IV, page 138:

“We think that you, excellent reader, should be informed that we searched for collections of this kind, excerpted from the works of Saint Peter Damian, with great diligence. Yet only those concerning the Old Testament—and those, as is evident, incomplete—which we now publish were found. For the expositions of the New Testament, which the same author, the disciple of the holy teacher, also compiled, as the old title indicates, could not be found at all.”

But Cajetan certainly displayed his diligence in investigating this work outside the Vatican Library; for its old codex 4930, of which Ottobonianus 962 is a recent copy, contains both collections, from the Old as well as from the New Testament. It is therefore pleasing to enrich the edition of the works of so great a teacher with this writing as well.]

# TESTIMONIES FROM THE GOSPELS

## FROM MATTHEW

### CHAPTERS ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

1. Why only blameworthy women are inserted into the genealogy of the Lord, and why Matthew enumerates forty generations by descending, while Luke describes seventy-seven by ascending.—2. “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be seasoned?”—3. “A bad tree cannot produce good fruit.”—4. “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist.”—5. “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned.”

## I. IN THE EXPOSITION OF THE SAME GOSPEL, OR IN THE SERMON ON SAINT LUKE

[Note: [Col. 0892D] A Sermon on Saint Luke, in which the following passage is partly read, exists in the edition, volume II, page 279. But no published exposition by Saint Peter Damian, whether on Matthew or on Luke, is known, if indeed one ever existed.]

Some people may reasonably be troubled by the question of why the holy evangelist took care to insert only blameworthy women into Christ’s genealogy, while passing over in silence women who were holy and unquestionably praiseworthy.

This was done so that, when our Redeemer is described as having been born from sinners, he may be believed to have descended from heaven to punishment for sinners. He descended in order to bear our sins himself; he ascended in order to make us partakers of his divinity, as the Apostle says: “He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification.”

Hence Matthew, descending through Solomon, whose mother David sinned by desiring, enumerates forty generations; whereas Luke, ascending through Nathan, through whose prophet David expiated his sin, describes seventy-seven generations.

Matthew signifies that the Son of God descended to us sinners in order to become a partaker of our mortality. Luke, on the other hand, indicates that after the Resurrection he ascended to the Father in order to make us sharers in his divinity. As the outstanding preacher says: “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.”

Through the number that Matthew arranges, the assumption of laborious mortality is expressed; through the number that Luke sets forth, the abolition of human wickedness is expressed.

Through the number forty, labor is expressed, by which Christ in his body, which is the Church, is wearied throughout the various periods of this life. Hence Moses and Elijah continued their fasts for forty days; and the Lord himself likewise abstained from taking food for the same number of days.

[Col. 0893B] Through Moses, therefore, the Law; through Elijah, prophecy; and through Christ, the grace of the New Testament are plainly understood.

Through the affliction of the Law, prophecy, and grace alike, then, the labor of the universal Church, wearied throughout all the ages of this mortal life, is indicated.

Hence the children of Israel, worn down by the hardships and labors of their prolonged pilgrimage, entered the promised land after forty years; for all the elect, when they have completed the course of this pilgrimage, will immediately possess the land of the living by hereditary right.

Through the number seventy-seven, which Luke sets forth, the remission of sins is expressed, as the Lord himself testifies in the Gospel. When Peter asked, “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” he replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

The remission of sins is fittingly signified by the number seventy-seven because it arises from eleven and seven: for when eleven is multiplied by seven, it produces the number seventy-seven.

The number ten is recognized as perfect, and by it the Decalogue is signified. But if ten is perfect, it necessarily follows that eleven is imperfect.

What is sin except transgression of the Law? If, therefore, the Law is understood through the number ten, transgression of the Law is rightly represented through eleven. Through the number seven, the whole extent of this world is contained, because the entire course of the present life unfolds over seven days.

Through eleven multiplied by seven, therefore, all our sins are brought to the number seventy-seven, in which the true remission of all sins takes place.

Thus this series according to Luke elegantly begins with Christ’s baptism and ends with the person of God the Father. In Christ’s baptism the remission of all our sins comes to us through the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove.

Thus, redeemed through Christ and cleansed through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are reconciled to God the Father.

The blessed Paul comprehends the meaning of both evangelists in one sentence when he says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and through sin condemned sin in the flesh.”

When he says, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he clearly declares the assumption of our sins, which Matthew displays when he enumerates forty generations by descending.

When he continues, “and through sin condemned sin in the flesh,” he indicates the expiation of all our crimes, which Luke expresses when he describes seventy-seven generations by ascending.

## II. IN THE THIRD SYNODAL SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0893] In the edition, volume II, page 398, nothing is found except a fragment of the first synodal sermon.]

“You are the salt of the earth.”

A very large quantity of food is plainly heaped together in one mass, yet it is seasoned with a small amount of salt. So too the Christian people are numerous, in comparison with whom the number of priests is very small. But when the multitude of the people is sprinkled with the salt of priestly speech, the taste of heavenly wisdom is produced in their hearts, and the palate of the human mind is sweetly seasoned with delight in heavenly things.

In this connection we must be very careful about what is said: “If the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be seasoned?” For when the priest’s heart loses the love of heavenly sweetness, it immediately grows bitter through the saltiness of earthly desire, and therefore can no longer season the hearts of others.

## III. IN THE LETTER TO GEBIZO

*(Edition, volume I, page 192.)*

“A bad tree cannot produce good fruit.”

The tree should properly be understood as the will, not the person. For the same human person can do both good and evil, just as from the same earth both a fig tree and a thorn are produced.

But just as a bad tree never produces good fruit, so from a proud will, which is undoubtedly bad, humility never proceeds pure or undefiled. And just as, when the root is damaged, the branches of the whole tree consequently wither, so from a proud mind, even if some good work is seen to grow green for a time, it dries up like moisture drained from a valley in the aridity of a precipitous rock.

## IV. IN THE SERMON ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

*(Edition, volume II, pages 116 ff.)*

“Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist.”

He excluded one who was greater; he did not deny one who was equal. Hence the angel says to Zechariah: “He himself will go before him in the wisdom and power of Elijah.”

John therefore appears to be the equal of Elijah, in whose wisdom and power he is asserted to come—especially since elsewhere Truth itself says: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished”; and, “If you wish to know, he himself is Elijah.”

But, on the other hand, we encounter the fact that Elisha received a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, in accordance with the manner of his request. “I ask,” he said, “that your spirit be made double in me.”

If Elisha surpasses Elijah twofold, how does John, who is equal to Elijah, surpass him, when no one born of women has arisen greater than John?

Nevertheless, in order to resolve the question, the meaning must be weighed, so that a sober understanding may recognize that what sounds harsh in the outward words proceeds from a devout intention.

It sounded harsh that Elisha asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit, since “the disciple is not above his master.” But this request proceeded from a pure mind, because he asked for nothing earthly but spiritual grace.

Thus Elijah, as though somewhat offended, rebuked his disciple’s careless words when he said: “You have asked for a difficult thing.” Yet, looking upon the simplicity of his pious intention, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it will be granted to you”—not the doubleness expressed by the careless speech, but the gift of the Spirit, which a humble and sincere mind sought with good intention.

In this way Elisha in no respect surpasses John, just as he is not greater than Elijah.

Nevertheless, if we examine carefully the course of sacred history, we find Elisha more abundant or more illustrious than Elijah in the power of miracles.

Elijah, while still alive, restored a dead boy to life; Elisha, already dead, raised a dead man. While Elijah was prophesying, the jar of flour and the jug of oil did not fail; Elisha immediately supplied a besieged and afflicted city, on the following day, with the incredible resources of the enemy camp.

To summarize everything briefly: Elijah shone with twelve miraculous signs, while Elisha, as the truth of Scripture relates, shone with twenty-three. Since we avoid tedium, however, we postpone enumerating them here.

How, then, can I escape the knot of this question, so that the statement of truth concerning John’s greatness may not waver—the statement that among those born of women there is no one greater than John the Baptist?

For if Elisha is greater than Elijah, then he is also greater than John, which is impossible.

But it must be noted that doing something great through miraculous signs is one thing, and being great through excellence of merits is another.

If miracles are under discussion, John is found nowhere in the pages of Scripture to have performed any miracle. But will he therefore be the least of all the saints because he is recorded as having performed no signs of power?

Elisha, then, is greater than Elijah in the display of signs, yet he in no way surpasses him in the abundance of merits.

So too John is indeed the equal of Elijah, because just as Elijah was to be the herald of the Judge, so John became the forerunner of the Redeemer. But he is greater than Elijah because he both pointed out and baptized the one whom he indicated.

John, therefore, is the boundary of human merits. However great the authority of the apostolic senate may be; however far the faith of the patriarchs may advance in the knowledge of God; however strongly the miracles of the prophets may prevail in disclosing hidden mysteries; however greatly the glory of the triumphant martyrs may be heaped up; however luxuriantly the flowering chastity of virgins may bloom; or however much the tongues of teachers may exercise themselves in the word of life—everything is restrained this side of John’s boundary. Nothing of human virtue, nothing of religion, nothing of perfection advances beyond it.

## V. IN THE SERMON ON SAINT STEPHEN THE POPE

*(Edition, volume II, page 184.)*

“Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned.”

The words of Truth must be carefully and fearfully weighed when it says: “Bind the weeds into bundles to be burned.”

The bundles are bound because, in that fire of perpetual damnation, murderers are bound together with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, perjurers with perjurers, and incestuous persons with incestuous persons, without being separated into different kinds of punitive torments.

There the open abyss of Gehenna devours them with infinite punishment—those who here arrogantly exalted themselves upon the horns of pride. There the crackling flame will consume their flesh and marrow, drenched in fatness, who here burned with pleasures and indulged the allurements of heated desire.

They are rightly said to be bound into bundles, because the diversity of retribution will not then separate those whom similarity of wickedness joined here. Those who are now subject to the same crimes will afterward be held bound under the punishment of the same judgment.

Concerning all of them it is said elsewhere, under the figure of one person: “Having bound his hands and feet, cast him into the outer darkness.”

There the limbs are bound for punishment, though here they were carried loose and free toward guilt. Or those limbs are then deservedly restrained in torments which are now wrongly bound away from performing works of compassion.

There the souls of the reprobate are tormented together with their bodies in an unquenchable fire, just as here they were joined in the execution of evil deeds.

Hence it is also said through the prophet: “They descended into hell with their weapons.” The weapons of sinners are their bodily members, with which reprobate people serve the devil and, by living perversely, minister to his authority.

Thus bodies are condemned together with souls in eternal death—bodies that lived together with them in the perpetration of evil deeds. Concerning them the prophet says: “There is Assyria and its graves.”

# FROM MARK

## I. IN THE SERMON ON SAINT MARK

Whoever considers the Gospel of blessed Mark with subtle meditation and examines it with the deep investigation it deserves will find that, although it is written in plain and unpolished words, it overflows with the richest mysteries of heavenly understanding.

It is certainly concise in the brevity of its style, yet expansive in the profound abundance of its spiritual mystery.

For when we scrutinize nearly all the pages of Scripture, we can scarcely find that the Spirit of truth has spoken through the mouth of anyone else with greater caution or circumspection than through the mouth of blessed Mark, so much so that the very sequence of his account and the order of his words contain a great sacrament.

To make this more evident, let us briefly point it out at the beginning of his book.

First he places the miracle by which the Lord commanded a demon crying out through a man’s mouth to be silent, and immediately drove it out. “Be silent,” he said, “and come out of the man.”

The second miracle is that by which he healed Peter’s feverish mother-in-law by driving away the heat of the fever.

The third is that by which he touched and cleansed a leper.

The fourth is that by which he commanded a paralytic to take up his bed and depart.

If this order is weighed with diligent care, it clearly teaches with what great skill of teaching the Holy Spirit held the writer’s pen and, in order to declare the mystery of human redemption, arranged everything along a certain line, so to speak.

At the beginning of the fall of the first man, the devil spoke and persuaded him to eat the forbidden fruit.

Then the woman, because she fell into the desire of pleasure, incurred something like the burning heat of a fever.

After Adam consented wrongly and tasted the fruit of the tree, he was immediately covered with the leprosy of all vices and, finally, like a paralytic, was bound by the sickness of the inner man, unable to perform any good works.

Therefore, because the Son of God came, as the Apostle John says, to destroy the works of the devil, he pursued death along the same path by which it had entered the world.

Where the poison of our destruction had been poured out, the physician of souls placed the antidote of salvation. And from the route by which the cunning enemy introduced death, our Redeemer restored the beginnings of returning life.

Thus he compelled the devil, who had spoken for our ruin, to become silent; freed Eve from the fevers of burning desire; cleansed the man not only from the leprosy of vices and crimes, but also released him, previously a paralytic, strong and free to undertake works of compassion.

Just as the whole human race perished in those persons, so in these people healed by the Savior it was restored to its former salvation through the mystery of the preceding figure.

In the chapter of this Gospel, therefore, the diligent reader should learn how profound and mystical are the sacramental mysteries of the gifts contained in the continuation of the writing.

Nor is this surprising, since that book is attributed no more to Mark than to the apostle Peter. Whatever Mark wrote, he heard from the mouth of the blessed teacher, as a cunning investigator, so to speak.

## II. IN THE SAME SERMON

*(Edition, volume II, page 66.)*

### On the fact that Mark differs from the others in certain words but agrees with them in spiritual understanding

Some matters are found to have been arranged by blessed Mark in such a way that they seem contrary to the other evangelists.

Yet, if they are examined more keenly, they are found both to agree with the others and to rest upon the truth of the most sincere faith.

One example is that the others assert that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, while Mark says that it occurred at the third hour.

This difference is certainly resolved as follows: because at the third hour they raised the tumultuous cry, “Crucify him, crucify him,” the Jews crucified the Lord with their tongues at that same hour, while at the sixth hour the Gentiles physically fastened him to the cross with nails.

The others speak according to the bodily, so to speak, historical account of what happened; Mark offered a spiritual interpretation of the furious cruelty of the Jews.

The others also report that Peter denied the Lord three times before the cockcrow. Mark, however, having heard this from the mouth of the denier himself, wrote that the denial occurred not before the cock crowed, but before it crowed twice.

This unquestionably occurred according to the truth of the event, as Mark asserts.

What the other evangelists say should be understood in this way: that the threefold denial began before the cockcrow but was completed after the cock had crowed once.

Since Scripture commonly places a part for the whole, what Matthew says—“Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”—should be understood as though he were saying: “You will begin to deny me three times before the cock crows, but after it has crowed once, you will complete that same denial before it begins to crow twice.”

Thus both what Mark says, “Before the cock crows twice,” and what the others say, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” although they seem outwardly to differ in wording, are found to agree in the most harmonious intention.

# FROM LUKE

### CHAPTERS ACCORDING TO LUKE

1. Why Luke alone among the other evangelists describes three canticles.—2. “For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.”—3. “The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.’”—4. Concerning the report that, while the Lord was teaching, Pilate had mingled the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices.

## I. IN THE LETTER TO THE MONK HONESTUS

[Note: [Col. 0897D] A letter or short work addressed to the monk Honestus exists in the edition, volume III, page 377, but this passage of Peter is not found there, although its subject is not inconsistent with the purpose of that work.]

Blessed Luke, who represents the form of the calf, because a calf is customarily slaughtered as a sacrifice, is found to be the only one among the other evangelists to describe three canticles: the first of Zechariah, the second of Mary, and the third of Simeon.

Although none of the other evangelists inserted a canticle in his own style, this evangelist alone, who expresses in himself the form of the legal victim, describes different canticles: first that of a priest, then that of a Virgin, and finally that of a righteous old man.

This shows that the office of singing belongs above all to the one who has already truly offered himself to God as a burnt offering.

Let the singer therefore be dry and arid, not one who flows moist and wet with pleasures.

A living sheep bleats; a dead one sings. A dry string produces a clear sound, while a wet one produces a dull sound.

Those who come from the world must therefore be cautious and fear greatly lest, while fleeing the snares of worldly conduct, they become more grievously entangled in the bonds of a soft and dissolute life.

Even if they offer something good to God, the offering of the sacrificer is not accepted unless the one who offers is himself also offered, so to speak, by the hands of his devotion.

Hence Cain offered in vain, because he neglected to offer himself first.

## II. IN THE SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

*(Edition, volume II, page 334.)*

“Behold,” Elizabeth said, “when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.”

For the Holy Spirit, who gave him life before he drew the breath of life, also filled the dwelling of his mother’s modesty in which he lived. Thus, although he could not yet bring forth words for human beings, by leaping for joy he was able to announce to his mother’s womb the King of heaven, hidden within the virgin’s womb.

Here it must be asked how the Holy Spirit could pour out his gifts upon him, since, according to the order of human generation, he still existed conceived in iniquities and had not yet been released from the bond of original sin by receiving the circumcision prescribed by the Law.

For the divine voice says through Moses: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

But it must be noted that the grace of the Holy Spirit is not constrained by the Law and is not held by the bond of necessity. Rather, just as he breathes where he wills, so he freely distributes his gifts to whom he wills.

For he inspired the centurion Cornelius before he received the washing of baptism; and upon some who were still Gentiles, while Peter was speaking, he not only fell, as Scripture testifies, but also instructed them to speak in tongues.

What wonder, then, if the Holy Spirit filled blessed John before any remedy of the legal commandment, when divine providence established him as the boundary, and, so to speak, an impassable limit, of the Law itself, of the prophets, and of the whole Old Testament witness?

“For the Law and the prophets,” as Truth says, “were until John.”

This John did not need circumcision together with the Lord; rather, divine election raised him above the Law and above the order of human generation.

He was also granted glory of such great honor that the very Mother of God was present at his birth, and that the Creator of the world consecrated the beginning of his hidden life in the womb by his presence.

The evangelist Luke testifies to this when he says: “Mary remained with her”—that is, with Elizabeth—“about three months, and returned to her own house.”

For from the conception of the Lord until the birth of blessed John there are three months.

Mary therefore did not wish to depart until she had diligently ministered to the aged woman in childbirth and had seen the herald whom she carried in the royal chamber of her body go before her King.

## III. IN THE LETTER TO GEBIZO

*(Edition, volume II, page 192.)*

“The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.’”

What did the one who attends to the secrets of the heart reply to this? “I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning.”

It is as though he were saying: “Take care lest, while the spirits of wickedness are subjected to your commands, your minds are pressed beneath the yoke of pride. For if Satan lost the heaven he possessed through pride, a proud human being can by no means find what he hopes for.”

## IV. IN THE LETTER TO ABBOT DESIDERIUS, ENTITLED “CONCERNING CERTAIN MIRACLES”

*(Edition, volume III, page 587.)*
What does it profit to offer God a sacrifice of praise and, through the sluggishness of negligence, pollute it with foul thoughts? This mixture of good and evil is signified by that Gospel passage where it is said that, while the Lord was teaching, some people were present at that very time reporting to him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.

Since *Pilate* is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammerer,” whom should we understand by him except the devil, who is always ready to beat human beings with the blows of offenses? Hence the prophet is also said to place a rod upon the shoulders of human beings: “You have overcome the rod of his shoulder, as on the day of Midian.” What, moreover, does blood signify except sins? What do sacrifices signify except actions that are upright and acceptable to God? Pilate therefore mingled the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices, because the evil spirit either pollutes our prayers with wicked thoughts or corrupts good works by the contamination of some sin, so that blood pollutes the sacrifice, while the guilt of an offense defiles the victim of a good work offered to God.

Hence it is written that, when Abraham was devoutly offering God a sacrifice from cattle and birds, birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. What do the birds signify except evil spirits flying about through the air? We therefore drive birds away from our sacrifice when we carefully guard the victims of our works from the evil spirits attempting to defile them.

## FROM JOHN

### I. In a Sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

*(Ed. vol. I, p. 243.)*

“This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you rebuild it in three days?”

For six days the almighty God created all his works, and on the sixth day formed the human being in his own image and likeness. Likewise, in the sixth age of the world, the Son of God became the son of man in order to restore us to the image of God. Moreover, on the sixth day of the week the Lord himself suffered, so that on that day the human being might be redeemed by his death—the human being who had previously been fashioned by his work.

On that same day Eve was formed from the man’s rib, on which day the Church came forth from Christ’s side through water and blood. Let us therefore see how, through this same number six, the temple of the Lord’s body was constructed by the art of divine providence.

That temple in Jerusalem had been built over a period of forty-six years; hence the Jews said to the Lord: “This temple was built in forty-six years,” and so forth. This number, when multiplied by six, completes the entire period during which the Lord remained in his mother’s womb. For forty-six times six makes 276 days; this number of days completes nine months and six days, which are reckoned, as it were, as ten months for women giving birth—not because all women reach the sixth day after the ninth month before giving birth, but because the perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth after so many days, as the elders have handed down and the firm authority of the Church preserves.

He is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day he also suffered. On that very day he was buried in a new tomb, in which no dead person had been placed either before or afterward; and on that day he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, where it is established that no mortal seed had been sown. He is traditionally said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

From the day of his conception, therefore, to the day of his birth, 276 days are found—days that contain the number six forty-six times. Thus, by the number through which that ancient stone temple was built, the temple of the Lord’s body was also completed through six. The only distinction is that, in the construction of the temple, the number of years is given, whereas in the building of the Lord’s body the count is made in days.

When, therefore, the number of years of that ancient temple is multiplied by six, all the days during which the Lord remained in the Virgin’s womb are completed. By joining the number through which God made his works with the number through which the temple was constructed, the Lord’s body is produced, so that we may understand that through the temple of divinity constructed in the Virgin’s womb all God’s works were restored, just as the Apostle says: “God purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him.”

But this temple of the body, which divine providence willed to be made through the number six, was destroyed in three hours by Jewish impiety and rebuilt in three days, as he himself says: “Destroy this temple, and after three days I will rebuild it.” The evangelist says: “He was speaking about the temple of his body.”

Nor is it surprising that what was made through six should be destroyed through three and again rebuilt through three, since the number six itself, just as it grows from three, is likewise resolved into three. One, two, and three make six; conversely, half of six is three, its third part is two, and its sixth part is one. This number is called perfect because it consists of its own parts.

The Lord lay in the tomb for one complete day and two nights, because by the single death of his body he freed us from two deaths, namely, of soul and body. And rightly the Lord’s death is signified by the day, by which we are led back to the light; while both our deaths are signified by night, since they are owed to us because of sin.

The entire three-day period most clearly expends itself in the mystery of human salvation: he suffered on the sixth day, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose on the Lord’s Day. This whole life is for us a sixth day, since we are commanded to carry the cross after the Lord.

From the day of our departure until the judgment, a kind of Sabbath is observed, because meanwhile souls enjoy blessed rest. In the resurrection of our bodies, the paschal day rises for us—a day enclosed by no end, but celebrated in the everlasting joy of perpetual gladness.

Therefore, if we are to reach that Lord’s Day fittingly through the Sabbath, we must now, carrying the cross after Jesus, continually celebrate our sixth day. Otherwise, if we now live under the law of the flesh in an inverted order and observe, as it were, the Lord’s Day, unquestionably afterward we shall exchange joy not for joy but for tribulation.

For this reason the Lord, just as he lived forty days in the desert and remained with his disciples for an equal number of days after the resurrection, also spent forty hours from the moment of his death until the dawn of the resurrection. Thus, just as the number of those days, so also the number of hours mentioned expresses the whole period of our life: just as he remained dead for forty hours, so we, having died with him, must live throughout the time we remain here in the continual mortification of the flesh.

### II. In a Sermon on Virgins

*(Ed. vol. II, p. 364.)*

“God does not give the Spirit by measure.”

It may be asked why John the Baptist declares that God does not give the Spirit by measure, when Paul, conversely, says: “To each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” How, then, is it “not by measure,” and how is it “according to measure”?

What John asserts—that the Spirit is given without measure—must unquestionably be understood of our Redeemer, in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” This is plainly recognized if the sequence of the Gospel text itself is considered. For after saying, “God does not give the Spirit by measure,” he immediately adds: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.” Hence elsewhere he says: “We have received from his fullness.”

John therefore agrees with the Psalmist, because John removes the measure from the one whom the Psalmist asserts to have been anointed beyond his companions. But when the Apostle speaks of measure, he wishes this to be understood of individual believers. According to the measure of the Spirit present in each person there is a corresponding measure of virtue and steadfastness, so that one may either resist peacefully the vices that assail him or, placed in combat, endure unconquerable torments.

Samson, indeed, was invincible so long as he had seven locks of hair; and whoever possesses the sevenfold Spirit of grace shows himself unconquered when any storm of battles breaks upon him.

## FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

### In a Letter to Pope Alexander on Removing the Money of Canons

*(Ed. vol. III, p. 483.)*

Whoever is captivated by love of money is in no way fit to administer the words of teaching. This is well made clear by the apostolic example proposed above.

For when Scripture first says, “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul,” and immediately adds, “No one claimed that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them,” it then promptly adds: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all.” It continues: “For there was no needy person among them.”

What, then, does the writer of this sacred history intend when, while speaking about apostolic continence and common life, he suddenly interrupts the subject as though introducing a different matter and, as if changing his style, leaps to recount the steadfastness of their preaching, saying: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection”?

Why does he insert one subject into another, when he ought to have pursued and continued what he had begun, unless to show plainly that only those are fit for the office of preaching who possess no profit from earthly wealth and, having nothing privately, possess everything in common—having nothing, that is, and possessing all things?

These men, while impeded by no obstacles of earthly things, stand unencumbered in the field of battle for the Lord’s camp. Stripped of possessions and armed only with the weapons of virtue, they fight with the sword of the Spirit against the ranks of vices; they are fit warriors to sever the necks of hostile enemies. Unequal to this warfare and feebly yielding are those who, not content with common goods, desire to be burdened by ownership of private property.

Hence in Deuteronomy it is said to those marching into battle: “Whoever is a man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that everyone may eat from it, let him go and return to his house, lest he perhaps die in battle and another man perform his duty.”

## FROM THE LETTERS OF JOHN

### In a Letter to Pope Alexander, in Which He Complains about the Insolence of Wicked Men

*(Ed. vol. I, p. 33.)*

“Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.”

The desire of the flesh pertains to bodily pleasure; the desire of the eyes pertains to the beauty of visible things; but the pride of life expresses the exaltation of earthly honor and rank.

The first human being is recognized as having been tempted through these things, as Scripture testifies: “The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food”—behold, the desire of the flesh. It then continues: “and beautiful to the eyes and pleasing to behold”—behold, the pride of the eyes. Whoever takes delight in what God forbids is convicted of becoming proud through his eyes.

The pride of life was present when that same woman willingly heard from the serpent’s mouth: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

## FROM THE APOCALYPSE

### I. In a Sermon on the Nativity of Holy Mary

*(Ed. vol. II, p. 219.)*

Virgin modesty alone is not sufficient for anyone to attain rewards unless it is also enriched with other virtues. For John is told in the Apocalypse by an angel: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Our Lamb—the one who takes away the sins of the world—possessed charity, because he poured out his own blood for the salvation of human beings. He excelled in the grace of humility, because “he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross.” He preserved patience, because “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.” He despised the height of worldly dignity, because, as John says, when they wanted to make him king, he sought refuge on the mountain.

He loved his enemies, and for them, even while hanging on the cross, he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

That person follows the Lamb wherever he goes who imitates his footsteps not by virginity alone, but also, insofar as he is able, along every path of virtue. He follows the Lamb into the rest of arrival who strives to imitate him amid the adversity of the journey.

That virginity is perfect which is surrounded by the other virtues, founded upon true humility of mind, which preserves itself undefiled not only in the flesh but also guards chastity in speech.

Thus the blessed Virgin Mary, after hearing the mystery of the angelic message, maintained the accustomed restraint of modest silence. Although she could examine within herself what that greeting might be, she judged it superfluous to question the word. By remaining silent, she immediately merited hearing what she had not presumed to seek by questioning.

The angel said to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Jesus.”

### II. In the Same Sermon

*(Ibid.)*

“He had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Christ’s garment is nothing other than the body he assumed from the Virgin. By the thigh, however, the propagation of the flesh is signified. He who came into this world from the Virgin through the propagation of the human race, and who through the mystery of his incarnation revealed to all nations that he was King and Lord, therefore had written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” For at the place where he became known to the world, he inscribed the knowledge of his majesty.

### III. In a Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

*(Ed. vol. II, p. 206.)*

“Each gate was made from a single pearl.”

Those precious pearls which blessed John declares that he saw, and from which he says that the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem were constructed, are the holy apostles. They themselves are gates, and they are likewise pearls, because, while sending out through signs and wonders certain rays of divine splendor, they open an entrance to the glory of the heavenly Jerusalem for the nations converted to the faith. Whoever is saved enters the wayfarer’s life through them, as through gates.

Those stones also held a mystical representation of them—the stones that, at God’s command to Moses, are read as having been set into the breastpiece of the high priest. The priest carried this breastpiece on his chest when he entered the Holy of Holies.

It was therefore commanded that twelve stones be placed upon it, three at each of the four corners, [lacuna] in gold, because the holy apostles proclaimed the truth of the catholic faith concerning the Trinity, which is God, throughout the four-part world.

## FROM THE LETTERS OF PAUL

### From the First Letter to the Corinthians

### I. In a Sermon on Saint Barbatianus

*(Ed. vol. II, p. 351.)*

“Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers.”

But as we say this, we see that a question arises for us, and not without some difficulty. For if signs are said to have been given for unbelievers, what is meant by the statement that our Redeemer is reported to have been scarcely able to perform any miracles in his own homeland because of the people’s unbelief?

As the evangelist Mark testifies: “Many who heard him were astonished at his teaching, saying: ‘Where did this man get all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such mighty works performed by his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon?
