who, equal to the Father and to the holy Spirit,

reigns for ever. Amen.

## XLVIII. In honor of Holy Mary the Virgin. Daily office. At Vespers. Hymn

Star, radiant Mary,

every age praises you;

from you, at the world’s evening,

the Sun of justice rose.

Grant that the heart may be snatched from darkness;

grant that it may enjoy the true light,

which may illuminate the night of the former life

with new merits.

Through you may we be cleansed from vices;

may we be released from the bonds of guilt;

may the mind, freed from torn-out thorns,

bear the shoots of virtues.

Praise be to you, Most High,

who were born from the Virgin;

[Col. 0935C] honor be to the ineffable Father

and to the holy Spirit. Amen.

## XLIX. Readings at Matins. First reading

Blessed Mother of God, Virgin Mary, temple of the living God, palace of the eternal King, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. You are the rod from the root of Jesse. You are the cedar of Lebanon. You are the purple rose of Jericho. You are the cypress on Mount Zion; by the singular privilege of your merits, just as you know no equal among human beings, so likewise you surpass angelic dignity.

To you, by a new and unheard-of miracle, it was granted that the Word whom God begot before the ages should become your son, and that the human being whom you bore at the end of the age should be the true and perfect Son of God.

## L. Second reading

[Col. 0935D]

O glorious mother, in whom alone fruitful virginity is found, you brought forth the Son from an undefiled womb in such a way that the integrity of inviolate chastity increased, and lust did not violate the seal of the virginal enclosure.

The Holy Spirit overshadowed you when you conceived—not so that he himself, God forbid, might become the seed of offspring in your most sacred womb, but rather he made use of the Creator’s virtue and power.

From you our supreme priest took the victim of his body, which he offered as a sacrifice upon the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world.

You are the rising light of Nazareth, the glory of Jerusalem, the joy of Israel, the honor of the world, the nobility of the Christian people.

## LI. Third reading

O Queen of the world, ladder of heaven, throne of God, gate [Col. 0936A] of paradise, hear the prayers of the poor; do not despise the groans of the wretched. Through you may our vows and sighs be brought before the sight of the Redeemer, so that what is excluded by our merits may through you obtain a place at the ears of divine mercy.

Wipe away sins, release crimes, raise up the fallen, free the shackled. Through you let the brambles and shoots of vices be cut down; let the flowers and ornaments of virtues be supplied.

Appease by your prayers the Judge whom you bore as Savior in a singular childbirth, so that he who through you became a participant in our humanity may through you also make us participants in his divinity. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## LII. Hymn at Prime

Blessed Mother of God,

[Col. 0936B] splendor of the human race,

through whom from slaves we have become free

and children of the light.

By your pious prayer,

make your Son favorable to us;

him whom we have gravely offended,

make gentle toward us, we beseech you.

Praise be to you, Most High,

who were born from the Virgin;

honor be to the ineffable Father

and to the holy Spirit. Amen.

## LIII. Hymn at Terce

Mary, honor of humankind,

throne of the eternal King,

house built with seven columns

by Wisdom.

Commend us to the Judge who is to come

with humble prayer;

may he see us intent upon your praises

as gentle and kindly.

Praise be to you, Most High,

who were born from the Virgin;

honor be to the ineffable Father

and to the holy Spirit. Amen.

## LIV. Hymn at Sext

Mary, temple of the Lord,

mother of God and of humankind,

then truly Virgin of virgins,

when you gave birth to the Son.

Grant us to carry him

in the fervent lap of our mind;

born from your flesh,

may he reign in our senses.

Praise be to you, Most High,

who were born from the Virgin;

honor be to the ineffable

Father and to the holy Spirit. Amen.

Father and Holy Spirit. Amen.

**LV. Hymn at None**

O singular woman,

Virgin who alone gives birth,

Splendid gateway of life,

Through which heaven’s halls stand open.

By your sacred prayers,

Release us from the bonds of our sins;

Presenting your merits,

Transfer us to heaven’s rewards.

Praise be to you, Most High,

Who were born of the Virgin;

Honor be to the ineffable Father

And to the Holy Spirit. Amen.

**LVI. Hymn at Compline**

Mary, royal Virgin,

Descended from David’s line,

Noble not so much through your father

As through the dignity of your offspring.

You who have been torn away from the old stock,

Graft us onto the new shoot;

Through you may the human race become

A royal priesthood.

[Col. 0937B]

Praise be to you, Most High,

Who were born of the Virgin;

Honor be to the ineffable Father

And to the Holy Spirit. Amen.

**LVII. These prayers are to be said at the hours of the day**

O God, who deigned to send your Son to us through the Virgin, grant that, with the prayers of that blessed Mary interceding for us, we may continually hasten toward you. Through the same Lord.

**LVIII. Another**

O God, who assumed the truth of human substance from the material of a virginal womb, grant that, through the prayers of your blessed Mother, we may so cast off our degenerate oldness that we may put on you, the Author of the new generation. Who, with the Father—

**LIX. Another**

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may be lifted up through the prayers of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, through whose ineffable childbirth you provided the remedy of human salvation. Through the Lord.

**LX. Another**

O God, who restore the origin of a corrupted stock through the dignity of the virginal womb, mercifully grant that those weighed down by the burden of their own guilt may be raised up by the intercession of the blessed Mother of God. Through the Lord.

**LXI. Rhythm concerning Saint Mary the Virgin**

O Mother of the Eternal,

Virgin Mary, of the Word—

What voice, what tongue of flesh

Could equal your praise?

[Col. 0937D]

You, new star of the sea,

Lofty window of heaven,

Ladder that joins heaven to earth,

Joining the depths to the heights.

You conceived the Immense One

And gave birth to the Parent;

The Maker and what was made

Become one: Creator and creature.

The One whom the world cannot contain

Was wholly contained in the womb;

The One by whom the ether is encircled,

A maiden’s womb enclosed.

Clothed in the form of a servant,

Yet not divested of divinity,

He truly assumed what was yours,

But did not lose what was his.

[Col. 0938A]

The Origin of all things arises;

He becomes the Ancient of Days;

The beginning of the universe begins,

Made from the things he made.

Conception made fruitful;

Birth did not violate you;

He entered and came forth,

Yet left you closed.

You are Aaron’s rod,

Fruitful though dry,

Which brought forth a shoot,

Yet remained a virgin.

The bush shone before you,

Which burned without being consumed:

You, without the heat of passion,

Gave the fruit of your womb.

A virgin before childbirth,

And a virgin after childbirth;

With the birth of offspring

The integrity of modesty increased.

He is the angels’ food,

Nourished by your milk;

He who supplies waters to the sea

Sucks drops from your breast.

You carry in your lap the Offspring

Who balances the mass of the earth;

You cherish the One by whom you are cherished,

You preserve the One by whom you are protected.

[Col. 0938C]

Caress, Mother, your dear Son,

Who created you;

Press grateful kisses upon him,

Bind his limbs with swaddling bands.

Embrace the heavenly King

Whom you brought forth,

Whom the sun and moon serve,

And every creature.

The choirs of the Powers tremble

Before the One whom lowly cloths cover;

Heaven and earth are afraid

Of the One whom a maiden carries.

He whimpers in his mother’s lap,

He reigns on his Father’s throne;

He observes his mother’s law,

He governs the laws of the world.

[Col. 0938D]

You are the fountain of the living spring,

The dawn of the Dawn;

The sealed book,

Given to the victorious man.

You are the closed gate of the temple,

The hall of the heavenly King;

The treasury of the talent,

Through which we have been redeemed.

Garden of delights,

Fragrance of sweetness;

You are that full field

Which God blessed.

From you came forth the cluster of grapes,

Which, pressed in the winepress of the cross,

Waters the parched minds

Of the Holy Spirit.

You are also heavenly earth,

Fruitful in milk and honey;

From you Truth arose,

Removing the doctrine of errors.

You draw the stronghold of nobility

From the stock of your offspring.

Indeed, daughter of kings,

But Mother of the King of kings.

[Col. 0939A]

Hail now, Virgin who has borne a child;

Hail, full of grace:

Deign to hail our own race,

With that greeting of Gabriel.

When he greeted you,

He changed Eve’s name;

Restore us, holy Virgin,

From where that wicked woman fell.

Release what we owe;

Avert what we fear;

Obtain what we desire;

Bring to completion what we hope for.

Praise be to the Trinity;

Honor be to the Unity,

To whom the law and order of all things

Are manifest throughout every age. Amen.

**LXI. Rhythm concerning the same most holy Virgin**

Who is this knocking at the door,

Breaking the sleep of night?

[Col. 0939C]

“It is I who call you, O most beautiful of virgins,

Sister, spouse, most splendid jewel!

Rise quickly and open, sweetest one.

I am the Son of the Most High King,

The First and the Last,

Who came from heaven into these shadows

To free the souls of captives,

Having suffered death and many injuries.”

At once I left my bed,

I ran to the bolt,

So that the whole house might lie open to my Beloved,

And my mind might see fully

The One whom it most greatly desired to see.

But by then he had passed on;

He had left the door.

[Col. 0939D]

What then, wretched woman, what could I do?

Weeping, I followed the young man,

Whose hands fashioned humankind.

The watchmen of the city found me;

They stripped me,

Took away my cloak and gave me a mantle,

They sang to me a new song,

By which I might be brought into the King’s palace. Amen.

**LXIII. Rhythm on the Angelic Salutation**

Hail, daughter of David, born holy for the world,

Prudent, sober Virgin, betrothed to Joseph,

Given as an example for the salvation of all,

Already proved a companion of the heavenly citizens.

Mary, through you misery comes to an end,

And through you mercy is recalled;

Through you the star of the sea is given to voyagers,

The light of the way is opened, the harbor is shown.

Grace made you gracious to all;

It clothed you in the lily and scattered the rose upon you;

It made you beautiful with the flowers of the virtues,

Radiant both within and without.

Full of healing medicine, rich in ointments,

Cleanse the filth of sins, heal the wound of the mind

Of this suppliant of yours who trusts in you,

Who sings these sacred rhythms before you.

The Lord, King of all, made for himself from you

A perfumery, which he set over all others;

In it the Savior prepared wondrous spices,

By which he sweetly refreshed all the elect.

[Col. 0940B]

The whole Trinity makes its dwelling with you:

The Father, the Word, and the Spirit took their seats there;

For this reason you now offer yourself more generously

As a reading for the faithful’s devotion.

Blessed one, bless those who bless you;

Make them prosper in your praises;

Fix sweetness in the minds of your servants,

That they may always burn with good works.

You are the finest form among women,

You who are Mother of the King of glory, pure Virgin;

By this you are proved more worthy than every creature,

Through the Lord’s singular care.

And blessed is God, who created all things,

Who sanctified you in your mother’s womb;

Blessed is the Son whom your virginal womb bore,

Whom he himself formed.

[Col. 0940C]

Your fruit, Lady, is the fruit of heaven,

By which the angels and the assembly of the saints are fed;

The contemplation of Christ is their food—

They who walk along the path of his commandments.

The King of kings entered the dwelling of your womb,

And dedicated that tabernacle to himself;

There he fashioned the sword by which he struck down the enemy,

And the sweetest manna by which he fed the faithful.

The savor of your offspring is our consolation;

Through you we have received a draught of eternal life—

May the Lord grant it to us through your aid,

He who lives forever and ever. Amen.

**LXIV. To the same most holy Virgin. Verses against stormy weather**

O merciful woman, O sovereign woman, command with your word

That we not be devastated, that we not be stoned by the blow of hail.

You possess the broad side of pontifical authority, Mother from of old;

Therefore we pray that we not perish in the savage whirlwind.

Calm the storm, and grant us the use of serene weather;

Restore the clear, lovely star hidden behind the cloud.

Virgin, we ask that we not perish through plague or wrath;

May the grim days grow dark, and may the dreadful lightning cease.

**LXV. Paracteric poem concerning the same most holy Virgin**

Ladder and throne of God, splendor of the world, gate of heaven;

Hail, Mother of Christ, ladder and throne of God.

You are the new star of the sea, through whom light was restored to the earth;

You are also the rising of the sun, the new star of the sea.

[Col. 0941A]

You conceive without a man, you alone, Virgin who gives birth,

You who conceive the Word through the Word, without a man.

The underworld fears what the earth dreads and the stars revere;

They bear within the caves of their breasts what the underworld fears.

Through the Virgin, life returns to the human being whom the virgin destroyed;

Death, conquered by death, perishes; through the Virgin, life returns.

Lift above the stars, we ask, what Eve cast down;

That woman weighs us down with guilt; you, lift us above the stars.

Highest glory to the Father, glory to the begotten Son,

With the equal Spirit, highest glory to the Father. Amen.

**LXVI. Mass of Saint Daniel the Prophet. Prayer**

O God, who revealed the mystery of the new grace to the ancient fathers, grant, we beseech you, that your Church may be sustained by the aid of Daniel, whose prophetic teachings founded it. Through the Lord.

**LXVII. Another prayer**

O God, who through the fathers of both Testaments established the foundations of your one Church, grant that we may be protected by the patronage of blessed Daniel, whose mystical revelations have profitably instructed us. Through the Lord.

**LXVIII. Secret**

O God, who freed Susanna through the judgment of blessed Daniel, mercifully regard these gifts and, through his venerable prayers, defend us from every adversity. Through the Lord.

**LXIX. Postcommunion**

O God, who through the prophet Habakkuk sent a meal to blessed Daniel, grant, through Daniel’s intercession, that we may preserve with sincere minds, undefiled, what we have received from the heavenly table. Through the Lord.

**LXX. Of Saint John the Baptist**

The voice preceding the Word senses him in his mother’s womb.

**LXXI. Of Saint Peter the Apostle**

Peter, abandon the ship of the sea and receive the key of heaven;

Having spurned the waves, restore to me the harbor of peace.

**LXXII. Hymn of Saint Peter the Apostle**

Prince and herald of the apostolic senate,

First shepherd of the faithful,

Guard the flock entrusted to you.

Restore us with the nourishment of the Word;

As their guide, lead the refreshed sheep

Into the heavenly pastures.

[Col. 0941D]

The keys of the gate of heaven above

Have been entrusted to you, Peter,

And by your laws both earthly things

And heavenly things lie open.

You lay the rock of true faith,

You lay the foundation of the building

Upon which the Catholic Church,

Firmly established, rises.

Your shadow, as you walk,

Becomes medicine for the sick;

Tabitha’s bier rejected

The woven garments she had used.

The angelic power releases

The one bound in a double chain;

Once his sandals and clothing are taken up,

The prison doors open.

[Col. 0942A]

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXIII. Of Saint Paul the Apostle**

Paul waters the whole world

With honey-flowing rains.

**LXXIV. Of Saint Paul the Apostle. Hymn**

Paul, excellent teacher,

Trumpet sounding for the Church,

Flying cloud and thunder,

Across the broad circle of the world—

Thunder powerfully for us

And irrigate the fields of our hearts;

By the heavenly rain of grace

May our dry minds grow green.

[Col. 0942B]

O great merit of Paul:

He ascended to the third heaven;

He heard the words of the mystery,

Which he dares not utter to anyone.

While he scatters the seeds of the Word,

A most abundant harvest rises;

Thus the granary of heaven is filled

With the fruits of good works.

Like a shining lamp,

He floods the world with rays;

He drives away the darkness of errors,

So that truth alone may reign.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

[Col. 0942C]

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXV. Of Saint Andrew the Apostle. Hymn**

Once a catcher of fish,

Now a fisher of human beings,

Andrew, tear us from the waves

Of the world with your nets.

Peter’s brother in the flesh,

Not unlike him in the order of death:

Those whom one flesh brought forth,

The cross made brothers for heaven.

O truly noble offspring!

O pair sharing a crown of glory!

The devout fathers of the Church

Are equally sons of the cross.

Going before your brother to Jesus,

And a vigorous guide who points to life;

Be also for us wretched people

The blessed guide of the journey.

[Col. 0942D]

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXVI. Division**

Andrew’s feast is celebrated;

A clear light rises for the faithful.

Through him they abandon the darkness

And return to the true light.

[Col. 0943A]

Aegeas rages against the apostle

With a threatening spirit;

Through him he sees the people of Achaea

Go after the Lord.

He does not know how to fear threats;

He cannot yield to torments;

The burning ardor of faith

Feels no force of punishment.

Bound to the cross’s gallows,

He hung joyfully for two days;

From the one placed in death itself

The eloquence of life flows.

A light descending from heaven

Suddenly surrounds him;

He who deserved to die in this way

Sought the Author of light.

[Col. 0943B]

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXVII. Of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist. Hymn at Vespers**

Venerable guardian of the Virgin,

Great treasurer of the eternal Word,

Wipe away the crime of your servants,

Holy John.

You suddenly leave your father in the flesh,

And thus follow your heavenly Parent;

Having rejected the fish, you are commanded

To enclose the crowd of human beings.

[Col. 0943C]

A river bursting forth from an everlasting spring,

You run as the world’s thirsty places’ satisfier;

The breast drank from the full breast

What it now pours forth.

You, the world’s glory and the heaven’s radiance,

Obtain pardon for our ruins;

Grant us to penetrate the supreme sacrament

That you taught.

By contemplating the Father’s hidden Word,

You remove error from faith throughout the world;

Transfer us, good guide,

To enjoy the eternal vision.

[Col. 0943D]

Let praise be offered to the Father and to the equal Son;

One majesty, the same power,

With whom the Holy Spirit likewise fills

The whole world. Amen.

**LXXVIII. At Matins**

Let the faithful people rejoice with the angels

And the crowd applaud with festive joys;

At the Lord’s Nativity

Let the apostle’s praise come forth.

Beloved above the others,

He held the privilege of love

With the Master

Because of his virginal merit.

He drew streams of wisdom

From Christ’s breast;

From here he irrigates the fields of the heart

And resounds with the Father’s Word.

[Col. 0944A]

When he was placed upon the cross,

The Lord entrusted his Mother to him;

The Virgin became mother to the virgin,

And he cherished her in place of a son.

With bowed hearts we ask you,

Senator of heaven, gracious one:

Grant us to see the face of the Word,

By which you teach us to believe the Word.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXIX. At Lauds**

Let the holy Church proclaim

The great merits of John,

By which he empties the darkness

And illumines it with the words of life.

[Col. 0944B]

The Spirit suspended his heart

Among the heavenly saints,

So that it might behold

The profound, hidden mysteries.

And that blessed eagle

Flies eagerly toward its food,

Which nourishes the citizens of heaven

And refreshes us on the way.

Here, in the choir of so many thousands,

He holds the first place among the virgins;

Thus he becomes the Lamb’s attendant,

As one inseparable from the Mother.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

[Col. 0944C]

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**LXXX. Mass on the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle. Prayer**

O God, who willed your Church to stand upon apostolic foundations, grant, we beseech you, that through the prayers of blessed Bartholomew we may both persist in the right faith and always abound in devout works. Through the Lord.

**LXXXI.**

Through the prayers of blessed Bartholomew, your apostle, O Lord, we beseech you: make this offering presented to you a life-giving sacrament for us. Through.

**LXXXII.**

We beseech you, almighty God, that the heavenly gift which we have received, through the intercession of your apostle blessed Bartholomew, may come to us not for judgment but for the increase of eternal salvation. Through.

**LXXXIII.**

Grant, merciful God, to your Church that, having been built by the teachings of your apostle blessed Bartholomew, it may also be protected by his continual aid. Through the Lord.

**LXXXIV.**

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that your Church may rejoice, supported by the defenses of the apostle blessed Bartholomew, whose magnificent examples also instruct it. Through.

**LXXXV.**

We beseech you, almighty God, that the help of your apostle blessed Bartholomew may never be lacking to us, whose venerable triumph we do not cease to honor daily. Through.

**LXXXVI. Mass on the translation of Saint Matthew the Apostle. Prayer**

O God, at whose command even the bodies of the saints are distributed among different places of the earth, grant, we beseech you, that we who celebrate the translation of your apostle blessed Matthew may ourselves also be transferred from our perversity to the uprightness of devout living. Through.

**LXXXVII.**

May this sacrificial victim, we beseech you, O Lord, release the bonds of our guilt and, through the intercession of your apostle blessed Matthew, obtain for us the gift of heavenly grace. Through.

**LXXXVIII.**

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who have received heavenly gifts, through the intercession of your apostle blessed Matthew, may through them be stirred to hunger for eternal refreshment. Through.

**LXXXIX. Mass of Saint Barnabas the Apostle. Prayer**

O God, who joined blessed Barnabas to your apostles in preaching, grant, we beseech you, that we may attain fellowship with him, whose glorious triumph we rejoice to celebrate. Through.

**XC.**

Sanctify with your blessing, we beseech you, O Lord, the gifts offered; through your granting it, may they kindle in us the flame of your love, by which blessed Barnabas conquered all the torments of his body. Through.

**XCI. Postcommunion**

Refreshed by the nourishment of the heavenly table, we beseech you, almighty God, that, through the intercession of your apostle Barnabas, we may preserve with a sincere mind what we have received with our mouth. Through.

**XCII. Prayer at Vespers**

O God, who after the burning of his scorched flesh granted your apostle blessed Barnabas the refreshment of heavenly glory, restrain in us, we beseech you, the heat of carnal passions and drench our hearts with the dew of your grace. Through.

**XCIII. Verses on the deeds of the Apostles**

This book contains those whom the lights of Christ reveal

To be at once the consecrated salt of God and of the world.

All the fabrications of false gods lie utterly destroyed,

Through whom the Church shines.

The Lord chose for the world those whom the Creator,

Foreknowing before the ages, knew to be the offspring of God.

The loving Spirit filled their breasts,

Giving them power to thunder forth the heights of God in various tongues.

In his goodness he granted them power to move mountains,

And the right to loose and bind on earth and in heaven.

At their command savage demons flee;

The bodies of the dead become alive again.

Giving these holy minds the ability to see the heart’s inner things,

God from heaven works wonders through them.

They are called heavens, prophets, and flying clouds—

They water hearts made dry by holy doctrine.

They drive away various bodily illnesses by a mere utterance,

And illnesses of the soul through the aid of devotion.

[Col. 0946A]

Prudent reader, read through the apostolic victories carefully,

Which blessed faith holds, so that you may not hesitate to believe.

He who neglects them does not know their boundaries,

Or how they possess the blessed heavenly realms.

The apostolic assembly, following the Lord’s commands,

Shines brightly in the world, renowned for the doctrine of faith.

This book preserves blessed Peter and Paul,

The two Jameses, Bartholomew and Thomas,

Saint Andrew, Simon, Thaddeus and Philip,

The four Evangelists and the leaders,

Matthias, and likewise Barnabas, royal vessels.

[Manuscript lacuna]

These shining stones glitter in Christ’s lineage,

Whom it is permitted to venerate throughout the regions of the world.

[Col. 0946B]

One faith held those whom the blessed crown now holds;

One glory indeed always possesses them in Christ.

From these begin the glory of martyrs,

The blessedness of confessors, and virginal modesty.

All worshipers of Christ, celebrate these patrons always

At the solemn season, with your voice singing to God.

When the Judge comes with them at the threshold of the age,

May the almighty Lord properly repay good things to the good and sad things to the wicked,

And grant us all fellowship with the saints,

To enjoy everlasting light.

**XCIV. From the preceding**

O gracious Spirit, come; breathe upon our double [nature?],

Come according to our prayer, O gracious Spirit.

May I be able worthily to exalt the temples dedicated to you;

May I exalt with praises the temples dedicated to you.

They possess forever the lofty joys of heaven,

And with their merits possess glory without end.

The prophets duly proclaim through the mouth of God

The Offspring of God; the apostolic voice proclaims through the mouth of God the Offspring.

Born here of the Virgin, he cleansed the sins of the world;

Born of the Virgin, he crushed the underworld.

The Lord wondrously restores the losses of heaven that were destroyed;

The Lord restores the losses of heaven through blood.

The merciful King himself commanded the devout to plunge into the waters;

The merciful King himself carried the devout to heaven’s heights.

The Sower filled the small seeds with abundant fruits;

The Sower granted the small seeds to bear a hundredfold.

The savage hearts shine through the breath (*flamine*) of these saints [reading uncertain],

Through various flowers the savage hearts shine.

Lilies mixed with roses and violets [lacuna] give fragrance;

The holy lilies shine again, mixed with roses.

Christ distributes the golden realms of heaven everywhere;

He grants the golden realms of heaven to his disciples.

At first the blessed faith shines more brightly through Peter;

By his fragrance the blessed faith shines at first.

Blessed Rome, you shine through the body of holy Peter,

And also through his doctrine; blessed Rome, you shine.

He bore broad trophies of the cross for Christ;

With his head turned downward, he departs bearing the broad trophies of the cross.

Mighty Paul, wondrous in action, shines everywhere;

Beheaded, the mighty one shines everywhere.

O Romulus’ city, greatly venerable in the glory of Peter and Paul,

Whom you retain—O greatly venerable city!

[Col. 0947A]

James accomplishes deeds of salvation and is slain everywhere;

Lying in Galicia, he accomplishes deeds of salvation.

Armenia, worshiping blind idols [lacuna],

Is turned toward Christ, worshiping blind idols.

Bartholomew, flayed, you shine in the world;

Beheaded, flayed, you shine.

Macedonia rightly sings your excellent deeds, Matthew—

You who suffered in Persia and sang excellent deeds.

On the cross, Peter, your brother preaches throughout the world;

Saving Achaea on the cross, Peter, your brother.

That Simon, crucified, rescues the Salens by his utterance (*famine*);

That Simon also drives away Egypt.

The burning Thaddeus brought countless men [to Christ];

Pontus and Armenia, countless men.

Pierced through, Thomas brought many doctrines to the world;

He brought many doctrines to Persia and Media.

[Col. 0947B]

Raising himself above the stars, John cleansed the schism;

The Ephesian holds him who raises himself above the stars.

Touched by the love of God, Philip is stoned,

When he converts the Gauls, touched by the love of God.

James, behold, you shine, most holy brother of the Lord;

Hurled down, you depart; James, behold, you shine.

Matthias, you are numbered by lot among the Apostles;

Saving Judaea, you are numbered among the Apostles.

Barnabas burns with the fire of God and condemns false doctrines;

And, as he dies consumed, burns with the fire of God.

How beautifully you glitter, Alexandria, with the blood of Mark;

Constantina likewise—how beautifully you glitter!

You shine by resisting, radiant Bithynia, through Luke;

The royal city also shines by resisting through you.

[Col. 0947C]

The suppliant servant offered these little poems as a gift;

Small, powerless, insignificant, he offered these little poems.

O divine Power, graciously accept the apostolic gift,

Vows and devout prayers, O divine Power.

**XCV. Rhythm concerning Saint Vincent the Martyr**

May heaven, earth, sea, and air,

The elements together,

All proclaim the triumphal glory

Of the Most High King.

He trampled the fury

Of the roaring lion

Through the strong warrior,

Soon to be the victor, Vincent.

He indeed scorned the anger

Of the judge Dacian,

His savage threats and fury,

As though they were the buzzing of a gnat:

Chains, scourges, prison

Darkness—even the wounds themselves are wounded;

Deaths are added to deaths;

But a house founded upon a firm rock

Cannot be overthrown by the force of winds or blasts.

His body, worn down by hunger,

Is seen as though nourished

By sumptuous feasts

And royal foods;

For the angels’ food

Refreshes the mind’s belly

Of the one who seeks God

And thirsts and hungers for nothing else.

[Col. 0948A]

The bloody beast rages,

Roars, and grows savage;

It burns, snarls, and sets in motion

Every kind of torment:

Iron, fires, potsherds, the rack—

It twists, scorches, and divides

The joints of his limbs;

Blind fury brands the severed members

With the cautery of glowing plates.

The soldier of Christ presses down force with

The strength of his heart, and, full of the Holy Spirit,

Extinguishes the fires of the flesh

With fire.

Struck with scourges and pierced with wounds,

He rejoices; he dreads the sluggish

Torturers and fears only

The executioners’ slackness.

Battles roar, enemies strike:

This is the law of victory;

The fight rises, the palm grows,

And the glory of the crown.

The glorious victor of Christ,

[Col. 0948B]

Clad in purple, entered the court

Of the highest heaven,

Accompanied by a white-robed

Assembly of shining angels,

Singing a sweet song.

Soon his body is thrown

Into the broad fields unburied;

The dogs are afraid, the birds tremble

To approach more closely.

Citizens, the field bears a noble treasure:

Neither predators nor thieves,

To conceal it,

Are able to dig it up.

For the mad Dacian

Sewed him into a sack,

As though he were an accused man

In a murderous cloak,

And ordered him to be sunk in the sea’s waves.

The sea cannot contain the sacred weight,

But it is carried to the shore by heavenly guidance

And, swift, overtakes the hastening rowers.

Now, serene Victor,

O blessed crowned one,

After your triumph,

Most unconquered martyr,

[Col. 0948D]

In the light of the eternal kingdom,

A living stone radiating,

A bright star among the fiery

Ranks of angels.

After sweat and labor,

After completing the course,

With the just King granting it,

He bears the promised prize.

Clad in a robe of purest white,

The sun’s heat and the moon’s brightness

Yield to your splendor;

All things are surpassed

That offer their wondrous spectacle

In this world.

Ruler of heaven, Son of God, we ask:

Raise up those sunk down; release those bound,

Through the merits of the great saint Vincent.

Raise up those whom many sins oppress;

Fix our hearts above,

So that they may love nothing but heavenly things.

Grant those redeemed in mercy

By your precious blood

To ascend heaven’s heights

At the end of their earthly lives—

You who order the laws of all things forever.

Immense and eternal King,

At whose command all created things tremble,

You who reign with the Father

And the Holy Spirit

Forever and ever. Amen.

**XCVI. Of Saint Vitalis the Martyr. Hymn at Lauds**

Distinguished glory of the martyrs,

The golden star of Vitalis,

Through the glory of his combat,

Floods the city with rays.

Girded with the sword of faith,

He comes to the aid of Christ’s soldier;

While he stretches out his hand to the fallen,

He teaches him to trample the enemy.

He is suspended on the rack,

But regards the punishment as nothing;

The ardor of his deepest love

Feels no force of torment.

[Col. 0949C]

Buried beneath the earth,

He is raised above the stars;

Covered with rubble,

He shines in heavenly places.

For us, unconquered martyr,

Grant that after our fall we may conquer,

And after victory

Be transferred worthily to heaven’s glory.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**XCVII. On the feast of Saint Anthimus. Hymn**

Let our praise proclaim Anthimus,

Distinguished glory of the martyrs,

Whose victory all the elements

Bear witness to.

He tramples the fury of rulers,

Laughs at the executioners’ hands;

The strength of his founded faith

Is not shaken by the force of punishment.

After the guards of prisons,

After the triumphs of blows,

He is suspended, bound to a stone,

And thus sunk into the waves.

But O happy shipwrecked man!

He soon sees a glorious angel,

Immediately lays down his bond,

And returns free to his lodging.

[Col. 0950A]

His head cut off, he dies,

But victorious he seeks the stars;

While he bears the cruelty of death,

He purchases the glory of life.

The martyr Anthimus is worthy

Of great praises and vows,

For he shone forth through signs

And so many wondrous miracles.

By sacred prayers he freed

The weakened flesh and soul

Of Pinianus

From every bond of disease.

A mad demon’s fury torments someone

With wounds;

The enemy of peace is driven out,

And thus the mind is restored to peace.

[Col. 0950B]

We ask you, gracious martyr,

With the voices of heart and mouth,

To commend us

To the fearsome Judge

With humble prayer.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**XCVIII. On the solemnity of Saint Ursicinus. Hymn**

The excellent sweet martyr Ursicinus

Offers a delightful feast,

In which the conquered man became victor

And, glorious, sought the stars.

For after horrific punishments

The weakness of the flesh is afraid,

But soon he returns to his heart,

And is joyfully struck down:

The worthy plunderer blushed

When he succumbed to his plunder,

And, with the enemy fallen, he destroyed

The one who inflicted the wound upon the standing man.

[Col. 0950D]

And aid us amid our struggles,

Distinguished martyr;

Grant those in conflict confidence,

And, once defeated, to conquer again.

Thus, physician of souls,

Bring help to those who languish;

By a draught of heavenly grace

Sick souls are healed.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father;

Honor to the Only-Begotten Son;

Highest majesty to the equal Spirit

Of both. Amen.

**XCIX. Mass of the Seven Holy Sleepers. Prayer**

O God, who in your blessed martyrs Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine raised up the first fruits of the future resurrection, grant that we may so rest from the world’s disturbance that we may deserve to awaken from the dust of the earth to heavenly life. Through.

**C.**

Sanctify, we beseech you, O Lord, the gifts of your people through the intercession of your blessed martyrs, and mercifully cleanse us through them also from the stains of sins. Through.

**CI.**

Refreshed by the nourishment of the heavenly table, we beseech you, almighty God, not to permit us to be deceived by any errors, since through the glorious seven martyrs you have confirmed us in the glory of the blessed resurrection. Through.

**CII. Of Saint Apollinaris, Bishop and Martyr. Responsory at Vespers**

Blessed Peter the Apostle said to his disciple Apollinaris: “Come.”  
Verse: “Rise.”  
Verse: “For behold, you have been instructed in everything that Jesus did.”  
“And go forth.”  
Verse: “For a multitude of people is dwelling there.”  
“Preach.”  
Verse: “For it is clear to you that he is truly the Son of God.”  
“And do not be afraid.”  
Verse: “Today the radiant martyr Apollinaris has entered heaven victorious; rejoicing companions, sing: Come.”

**CIII. Hymn at Vespers**

O consul clad in the insignia

Of the eternal kingdom,

With devoted mind we ask you:

Labor to open heaven’s court

To the people, Apollinaris.

May the pious gatekeeper of this highest Olympus

Look favorably upon the servants of so great a fosterling,

Who rejoice to resound your praises

With sweet hymns.

When Ravenna lay pressed in deepest darkness

And gaped after the empty rites of demons,

You, a famous Lucifer entering from the eastern shores,

Came shining.

[Col. 0951C]

The blind boy of bereaved Irenaeus

Proves that you shine as a beneficent star,

You who open the eyes of the father’s heart

And those of the son’s brow.

No medicine can help the sick Thecla,

Nor the multitude of profane gods;

You make the heart turn toward heaven

And raise its joyful face.

The joyful citizen of Classis admonishes the shore:

With the power of its sacred tongue now opened,

Its words confess the eternal Word of the Father,

Which has been opened.

You restore a girl who had died

By a double death to both kinds of merciful life;

Breath immediately fills the flesh on the one hand,

God the mind on the other.

[Col. 0951D]

Let us return glory to that Father

Who grants such things to worthy ministers;

Let honor be to the Son and to the Holy Spirit

Throughout every age. Amen.

**CIV. At Matins**

Let the choir of heavenly beings rejoice;

Let the crowd of the faithful applaud;

Let the passion of Apollinaris

Be the world’s rejoicing.

When he dies the death of the flesh,

Stripped of his holy body,

He is clothed in the robe of glory;

He casts off the prison of the flesh

And ascends to heaven’s palace.

[Col. 0952A]

Rejoice now, noble metropolis,

Ravenna truly illustrious:

What Rome possesses in the keeper of the keys,

You possess in his disciple.

We ask you, supreme bishop,

With the voices of heart and mouth,

To commend us

To the coming Judge

With humble prayer.

Glory be to the unbegotten Father

And to the Only-Begotten Son,

And likewise to the Holy Spirit,

The undivided God. Amen.

**CV. On the birthday of Saint Apollinaris. Mass. Introit**

“Rise, receive the Holy Spirit and likewise the pontificate, and go to the city called Ravenna; preach the name of Jesus there, and do not be afraid.”

Psalm: “May the Lord Jesus Christ send his angel, who will prepare your way, and may he grant you what you ask.”

**CVI–CVII. Prayer**

O God, who willed us to be instructed in apostolic teachings through your blessed martyr and bishop Apollinaris, grant, we beseech you, that we may both preserve what he taught and attain what he promised. Through.

**CVIII.**

O God, who received blessed Apollinaris, placed upon burning coals for confessing your name, as an offering of sweetness, grant, we beseech you, that we may always offer you the incense of devout dedication and sacrifice offerings of a contrite heart. Through.

**CIX.**

May our Lord send his angel, who will prepare your way, and may he grant what you ask.

[Col. 0952C]

Verse: “Peter, placing his hand upon the head of blessed Apollinaris, said to him: Alleluia.”

**CX.**

We humbly beseech you, Christ, glory of the Father, true light of the world: extend your right hand to fallen servants, that, with your mercy favoring us, they may be able to stand against the struggles of the crafty enemy.

Verse: “O God, who work with Peter, my teacher, work also with me, so that your name may be glorified.”

**CXI.**

Let the heavenly ranks proclaim in joyful voices

The clear and noble praises of Apollinaris the martyr.

Let all the fourfold regions of the world

Resound with the sweet melody of this drama.

Let Antioch, foster-mother of so distinguished a citizen,

Rejoice exceedingly, as is its due.

Above all, let happy Ravenna applaud,

Purpled by his sacred blood.

O new strength, incapable of being conquered;

O most unconquered tower of David,

Regarding every kind of torment as nothing!

Laughing at the deep wounds of his entrails,

Scorning the harsh marks of blows,

He cools with water his limbs burning hot with flames.

Then he endured prison darkness,

Long exiles, and the deprivation of food;

He endured suspension upon the rack.

[Col. 0953A]

Soon the sacred bonds of chains bind his arms;

Raging executioners’ madness does not fear

To crush his mouth with a stone.

Opening the prison-bars of hell,

He raised up the lifeless daughter of the patrician.

Who could recount how many blind people’s eyes,

How many weakened bodies,

He divinely restored?

We ask you, radiant star of the Church,

Bright lamp of bishops and gem of martyrs:

Cleanse our hearts from vices through assiduous prayer,

Strengthen them with virtues, raise our heart to the stars,

And make us behold Christ forever. Amen.

**CXII.**

Blessed Apollinaris said to the vicar: “Be confident, because I shall not place incense with my hands before demons, but I shall offer to my Lord Jesus Christ the incense of praise and sweetness.”

Verse: “I offer myself as a sacrifice for the salvation of my sons, whom [lacuna].”

**CXIII.**
Sanctify us, O Lord, by this venerable mystery, most renowned of all, us whom in your mercy you redeemed by your own blood; rescue and protect us from the crafty enemy by your strong arm, you who, together with the Father, the most high Lord of all things, rule all that has been created. I have acquired it. Therefore I am secure. Versicle: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.” And his own …

## CXIV.

Eternal God, who appointed substitutes for your apostles throughout the whole breadth of the world in the defense of truth, and from among them bestowed such great grace upon blessed Apollinaris, the disciple of your key-bearer, that he built your Church upon the foundation of the new faith and directed the brutish hearts of the gentiles toward the institution of your law; and to whom, by your granting it, was also given this: that, enriched alike with patience and glory, he should disregard the dreadful tortures of punishment and shine forth with the wondrous powers of signs—therefore, adorned by right of the priesthood and together with the triumph of martyrdom, he offered himself to you as a sacrifice of sweetness and brought into your granaries the abundant fruits of souls, sprung from the seed of his preaching. Through Christ our Lord.

## CXV.

“I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.”

## CXVI.

[Col. 0953D]

God, who have deigned to bestow upon us the pledge of eternal salvation, grant us, we ask, through the intercession of blessed Apollinaris, your martyr, to attain the fullness of that same truth. Through him.

## CXVII. On Saint Ruffinus the Martyr. Hymn.

Let the throng of the faithful sing the great merit of Ruffinus, by which he became victor over the world and, set free, sought the stars.

The unconquered warrior offers his face to stones; but the hail of stones did not impose silence upon his words.

[Col. 0954A] Then he is beaten with leaden weights; he is believed already to have died. But he who is thought dead rises more eagerly to arms.

He is thrust into a furnace raging with fiery flames; but the furnace of the conflagration becomes a grove of refreshment.

For a glorious angel plunged into it amid crackling flames, and at his command the fire immediately lost its strength.

## CXVIII.

The outstanding martyr struggles like a lion that knows not how to be conquered; with fearless mind he tramples every kind of punishment.

A stone is hung around his neck, and thus he is plunged into the waves; he whom water gave birth to for Christ reaches Christ through the water.

Now freed from the burden of the flesh, he is clothed in a red weight, with a crown woven upon his head from precious stone.

We ask you, blessed martyr, from the depths of our humble hearts: may your merits set free us, whom our own debts weigh down.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXIX. On Saints Donatus and Hilarianus. Hymn.

We sing the glory of the renowned triumph by which Donatus, victorious, sought heaven—Hilarianus being his companion alike in punishment and in the crown.

These two, like twin lamps, shine and remove the darkness from the world and the earth, while they thunder in words and flash forth in signs and prodigies.

They strip demons of their captives and spoil, tormenting them with the harsh whips of prayers; they restore strength to the sick and light to the blind, both alike.

After a woman had been shut in a tomb for three months, she came forth from the grave—“a talent” [the corrupt text is uncertain]; thus, having died, she was restored to her living husband, lest she should remain dead.

A fragment of a shattered chalice rises again into its former shape; although a small part has perished, not a drop of liquid falls from it—a new thing for the world.

We ask you, lofty princes of Olympus, that the right hand of Christ, through your fatherly prayers, may raise us when fallen and strengthen us when broken.

[Col. 0955A] Praise and honor to the Father and to the equal Son; one majesty and the same power, with whom the Holy Spirit likewise fills the whole world. Amen.

## CXX.

Donatus, golden star, martyr and offspring of martyrs: in martyrdom you are preceded by those whom you anticipate in faith.

For us, outstanding bishop, glory and light of the Church, aid by your holy prayers those who celebrate your feasts.

You who grant a dead woman to utter living words after three months, resurrect through the Spirit those buried beneath the weight of sins.

By life, light, and conduct, the monk Hilarianus, having rightly fulfilled the duty of hospitality, becomes a judge and a martyr.

You, bright lamps of the world and living stones of heaven, admit us unhappy ones, through your merits, to your rewards.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXI. On Saint Donatus, Bishop and Martyr. Sequence.

With the Lord’s golden lyres, let noble Tuscany, Italy, a monarchy, praise him on cymbals—the dwelling-place of the saints, which Arretium makes holy.

In it Donatus the martyr, the lamp of bishops, the way, model, and mirror, possesses a renowned basilica and preserves Januarius, the golden star of heaven.

[Col. 0955D] No human efforts, no eloquence of speech, can worthily exalt him according to the merit of his glory.

For what he was able to endure, who will be able to recount?

For three continuous days he is exposed to the vapor of a furnace, so that the longer he is burned, the more quickly it may burn afterward; but when the martyr enters it, not even a hair is harmed.

Soon, comforted by angelic companionship, he rejoices; while fiery globes hiss, the ardor of faith increases. Thus the flame of desire destroys the power of the fire.

[Col. 0956A] The victor is dragged away from the fire and carried before the tribunal. He is questioned, accused, and the same answer is given, for the house stands firm upon a stable rock.

When the flesh is surrounded by punishments, the mind is fixed among the stars; the torments are made light by the rewards seen there.

Thus he considers a thousand deaths a sweet rest.

The savage hands of the executioners tear the sinews of his entrails; the loosened structure is dissolved after the bonds are removed: a divided exit, a manifold death.

Then he is handed over to the fierce bites of beasts; but the beasts, laying aside their untamable rage, bend their necks, released from above, to holy prayers.

O Lucifer of Hesperia, O glory of the Church, who could bring forth all your praises?

We do not strive to accomplish this, but are overcome with joy.

Therefore, with bowed minds, we beseech you: through your merits release us from the debts of our guilt, and join us to the assemblies of the elect through your holy prayers.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; all honor, equal for both, to the Spirit, whose one power rules all ages. Amen.

## CXXII. On Saint Fidelis the Martyr. Hymn.

The holy Church proclaims the great merits of Fidelis, who by death destroyed death and, victorious, sought the stars.

Having cast off the burden of the flesh, he is clothed in the robe of glory; with tears wiped from his face, he possesses true joys.

When he dies, struck down by the sword, a savage storm arises; thus vengeance from the just Judge is threatened against the wicked.

An evil spirit attacks one of the executioners; immediately the dreadful pest is driven away when he is joined to the sacred soil.

With the prayers of heart and mouth we ask you, blessed martyr: lead us, through your footsteps, to the rewards of life.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXIII. On Saint Gregory the Pope. Hymn.

Now the apostle of the English, now the companion of angels, Gregory, as you once aided the nations, now aid those who believe.

You despise the abundant riches and all the glory of the world, so that, poor, you may follow Jesus, the Prince of the poor.

An angel appears as a needy shipwrecked man while asking for alms; you then offer both a gift and a silver vessel.

From that time Christ sets you over his Church; thus you receive the rank of Peter, whose rule you also follow.

O outstanding pontiff, light and glory of the Church, do not abandon in dangers those whom you instruct with so many commands.

Honey that sweetens the heart drips from your lips; your eloquence surpasses the power of fragrant spices.

You wonderfully unravel the mystical riddles of sacred Scripture; Truth itself teaches you its theoretical mysteries.

Having received the apostolic office and glory, release us from the bonds of guilt and restore us to the seats of heaven.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXIV. On Saint Benedict the Abbot. Hymn, for Vespers.

Precious jewel of the heavenly King, rule of the righteous, path of monks, Benedict, withdraw us from the filth of the unclean world.

Despising the earth and fixing your heart upon the stars, you compel parents to become heirs; you deserved to restore the broken vessel, filled with God.

A great hermit in a small body, you surpass your age and overcome labor; fervent, you fulfill the strict beginnings of a disciplined life.

When a boy had been buried beneath a mass of stones, as soon as you prayed, you raised him by your prayer; thereafter sensation was restored to the flesh, and the flesh alike to health.

By right, under the appearance of a gentle dove, you behold the sister’s soul, ignorant of gall, entering the highest summits of the starry heaven.

Afterward, bearing a glorious triumph, you seek the lofty stars after conquering the world; coverings spread over the cell aflame with radiant light.

Praise and honor to the Father and to the equal Son; one majesty and the same power, with whom the Holy Spirit likewise fills the whole world. Amen.

## CXXV. For Matins.

Most unconquered standard-bearer and leader of the sacred army, Benedict, defend us with the strong arm of prayers.

With these arms conquer the detestable fury of the lion, with which you once drove the most dreadful blackbird from your mouth.

Nettles joined to brambles heal a wound with wounds; the mind set aflame by God extinguishes fires with fires.

Sending the cross like a stone, you break the cup of poison; the vessel of death cannot bear the sign of life.

The brother whom the most wicked spirit then dragged about as a wanderer is restored to stability when your staff strikes him.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXVI. For Lauds.

Golden dawn rises, restoring the yearly feast, when Benedict climbs the lofty palace of heaven.

How great a reward he receives in the heights, who shone so brightly in the depths, whose miracles glitter throughout the wide regions of the world.

The earth disgorges the corpses of those deprived of his grace; thus the flowing wave licks the dry footprints of the devout.

Through the sun’s ray he sees the circuit of the whole world, his mind fixed upon the Creator; he sees all things subject to him.

[Col. 0959A] We ask you, blessed Father, from the depths of a humble mind, to grant that those whom you teach to despise the earth may ascend to heaven.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXVII. Epitaph of Lodoicus, the Holy Priest.

The man of God, Lodoicus, lies closed within this cave; for him martyrdom occurs without the killing of executioners.

He had refused wine and did not altogether eat bread; once a week, he thus gave himself food twice.

In a different order he was both painter and priest; he offered each service equally to God.

A rising light for the city, he shone as a light for the whole world; he burned and kindled, he went and enabled others to go.

Mirror of the Church, living stone, sacrifice, and temple, raise us by your prayers, us whom our evils weigh down.

## CXXVIII. On the Birthday of Confessing Pontiffs. Hymn.

The year of the sacred pontiff’s birthday shines forth; let the devoted people rejoice in celebration, and let songs resound with joyful heart to Christ, who rules all things.

Despising the joys of his own body, he endured a long martyrdom of the cross; he suffered a torment more grievous than a wound, becoming his own executioner.

A renowned standard-bearer of the sacred army, he had been a model of virtues for those who followed, kindling their hearts with powerful words and also with excellent conduct.

He bore twelve stones upon his breast and shone beneath the covering of a double-dyed tunic; bells rang sweetly against it, and pomegranates hung down.

By his prayers, Creator of all, raise up those overwhelmed by the weight of sins. To him be praise, dominion, and supreme glory throughout all ages. Amen.

## CXXIX. For Lauds.

Christ, glory of the saints and victory of those who struggle, release us from the bonds of our sins through the prayers of the confessor.

Make us follow his footsteps, worthy of imitation; be yourself the common reward, you who became both the price and the ransom.

For although placed in the depths, he excelled in lofty conduct; humble in rank, he was exalted by his illustrious work.

His mind intent upon heavenly things shudders at worldly disturbances; nothing now delights the anxious soul that does not lead to the homeland.

[Col. 0960A] His spirit, set aflame for that place, yearns with every effort; already in a riddle it sees the inaccessible light.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father; honor to the Only-begotten; supreme majesty, equal for both, to the Spirit. Amen.

## CXXX. On All the Saints. Verses

[Note: [Col. 0959] These verses suffer throughout from wholly incurable corruption. Nevertheless, they are presented in this form by the editio princeps, the Paris edition, and its reprint issued by Bassano.]

He published the names of those who had received their lot in the world, whom he had imbued individually for periods of two and three years; secular learning had likewise provided them with healing, and divine grace freely had done so as well.

So that they might cast out the rotting diseases of fever and apply health-bringing care to illnesses, driving dreadful diseases from their limbs and bodies;

and those found mute, lame, deaf, one-eyed, and cross-eyed, who corrupt words as they speak with harsh utterances, and whatever else is called infirm, he restores from heaven, Christ granting salvation;

and thus, by medicine, they thrust forth the light of the flesh from foulness.

Yet they are not enriched by the exceptional gift of virtues; they carry purses stuffed with deceptive gold and trample bags of money, like deadly poisons, while giving everything freely for the sake of the heavenly offspring.

Meanwhile the prince of the world, who held the scepters, cruelly punished the martyrs by savage edicts.

Then he plunged the holy brothers into the depths of the sea, into the open waters, trusting in the power of the Thunderer; and the cold waters, softened by glassy fragments, carried the saints to the shores more quickly than a word could be spoken.

Thus, by the sacred power that restrained the salt sea, the swollen blue waters were quieted across their wave-tossed fields, while the Father’s right hand opened a harbor for them.

The impious man, seeing the banners of this triumph, devised another harm with Gorgon-like poisons: for the savage man prepared fierce fuel for the flames and filled the furnace of the sacraments with kindling.

He ordered the holy men to be thrust into it, fragrant, so that the pyre might roast the innocent limbs in its embers—limbs that the swollen sea, surging with dark waves, had earlier been unable to drown.

Thus the flame of the furnace, fed by kindling, grew cold, so that the soldier of Christ, disregarding the storm of the fire, might return immense thanks for his safe life;

as a salamander is accustomed to mock the pyres of hearths, even when heaps of pyres have perhaps been piled up.

Then they are compelled to climb upon the open wood of the cross and to endure the dense arrows of quivers.

Soon the eternal Sower, who triumphs by holy right, shattered the dreadful darts of the guilty executioners.

Afterward they received the bloodstained wreaths of martyrdom, migrating to the lofty summits beneath the vault of heaven.

## CXXXI. On the Annunciation of the Virgin.

Behold, the herald prepares the enclosed chamber for the King.

## CXXXII. On the Nativity of the Lord.

He who was born from eternity comes forth from the Virgin’s womb.

## CXXXIII. On the Supper of the Lord.

[Col. 0961A] He who is head of the righteous wipes the feet of his fosterlings.

What he forbade to one [or: willed for one], Peter wishes to release for all.

## CXXXIV. On the Baptism of the Lord.

Behold the river, the fountain; the wave washes the one who washes the world.

Be washed, O Jordan, by him by whom you yourself are the more fully washed.

## CXXXV. On Saint John the Baptist.

The voice that precedes the Word perceives him in the maternal womb.

## CXXXVI. On the Offering of the Lord.

Now the one whom heaven receives is held in Simeon’s arms.

## CXXXVII. Where the Children Say, “Hosanna.”

The stars, heaven, and earth fear him whom the she-ass carries; the assembly proclaims “Hosanna” to God with a great voice.

## CXXXVIII. The Transfiguration of the Lord.

Here God displays what he concealed beneath the covering of flesh.

## CXXXIX. The Lord Says to His Disciples, “Watch.”

[Col. 0961B] The King of the watchers commanded those whom sleep had overcome to rise.

## CXL. Where Judas Betrays the Lord.

The fierce false wolf extends flattering kisses to the Lamb.

## CXLI. On the Paten.

These dishes bring forth food for perpetual life.

## CXLII. Where Christ Prays to the Father.

You pray to the Father, Christ, with whom you likewise bestow all things.

## CXLIII. On the Ascension of the Lord.

God sought the depths, but did not abandon the heights: he is there where he is going; he remains from where he came.

## CXLIV. Where the Holy Spirit Descends upon the Apostles.

The flame of tongues sets the apostolic senate on fire, and a fruitful voice gives birth to various kinds of speech.

## CXLV. On Saint Peter.

Peter, abandon the ship of the sea; receive the key of heaven; and, despising the waves, restore to me the harbor of rest.

## CXLVI. On Saint Paul.

Paul waters the whole world with honey-flowing showers.

## CXLVII. On One Who Remains in Hatred.

He who remains in darkness does not know the footsteps of peace; may the collyrium relieve you when glaucoma burns you.

He creates a gentle sharpness and uncovers what is badly covered; night restores light, and pain often takes away pain.

## CXLVIII. On One Who Pleases Two Enemies.

While he pleases both, Metecus loses both.

## CXLIX. On Hildebrand.

If you wish to live in Rome, proclaim in a clear voice: “I obey the Pope, my lord, more than I obey the lord pope.”

## CL. On the Same Hildebrand.

May he who tames the fury of tigers and the bloody mouths of lions now turn you, the wolf, into a gentle lamb for me.

## CLI. On One Who Fears Everything or Fears Nothing.

Fearing nothing and fearing everything, each is ridiculous: the one swells with pride, the other lies prostrate; the middle course prevails amid danger.

## CLII. On the Rod of Moses.

The rod, to be transformed into itself, devours the magic water-serpents.

## CLIII. On Noah’s Ark.

The ark signifies the Church; the water of baptism signifies its figure.

It is better for you to be written as a king in iron than as a servant in gold.

Choose, O king, to be written in iron rather than as a servant in gold; a king in a chasuble is more illustrious than a servant in a hall.

## CLIV. On One Who First Gives and Later Reclaims.

He violates the bond of friendship by reclaiming his gifts; his hooked hand withdraws what his generous hand previously gave.

He who reclaims a gift soon rightly loses his friend.

From your gift I carry away worthy joys.

How empty are the goods of this world!

When we see the ashes of kings and the bones of our ancestors lying piled in sour, dust-filled tombs, what vigor of body or possession of mind can delight the flesh?

## CLV. The Lord Pope Began a Matter without Me and Wanted to Complete It with Me; Thus He Said with Me, “As It Was in the Beginning,” Though He Had Not Said with Me, “Glory Be to the Father.”

“As it was”—to my loss, since I never sing “Glory”; he who shaved off the head rightly devoured the tail as well.

May he who previously swallowed the marrow grind his mouth upon the bones.

## CLVI. This Is Said to Those Who Make a False Peace.

So that they may prosper, let mouths and hearts be joined in kisses; peace dissolves strife when quarrels come to an end.

## CLVII. That a Friend Often Seems to Be Angry, and an Enemy to Flatter Deceitfully.

The love of the just man rages; the envy of the wicked man flatters.

There is love that is harsh, sweet fury, faithful anger; there are also tyrants who flatter beneath a sheep’s fleece.

Thus even friendly criticism makes fathers fierce.

## CLVIII. Admonition to Pope Alexander.

Whoever wishes to retain the vigor of the apostolic see should weigh the equal scales of strict justice.

For he does not know how to suspend the balanced scales of law whom favor bends or greedy hope draws away.

For the man whose purse, full of gifts, loosens his mouth, justice—destitute—destroys his empty soul.

Rome holds the bars of heaven and governs the reins of the world; whoever seeks more cannot become richer.

## CLIX. What the Servant of God Ought to Do.

I indeed take away much, but I give everything to the brothers; I take from the rich and provide for the poor.

## CLX. At the Meal We Say, “The Poor Shall Eat.” When Breaking Silence We Say, “Precious in the Sight of the Lord.”

“As they shall eat” gives the tables; “Precious” gives back the words.

“The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’”

## CLXI. On Hatred.

As a missile smeared with deadly poison destroys what it strikes, so devouring hatred destroys human souls.

## CLXII. He Who Has Been Castrated Ought Not to Become a Bishop.

He who cannot be cut off ought not to obtain the honor.

## CLXIII. On Roman Fevers.

Rome, devourer of men, subdues the lofty necks of men; Rome, fertile in fevers, is exceedingly rich in the harvest of death; Roman fevers are faithful by established right.

## CLXIV. That One Who Is Ignorant of the Law of Vices Cannot Avoid Ruin.

He who does not know the law labors under the plague of vices; he considers virtue a vice and what is permitted unlawful.

[Col. 0962D] Let no one be secure who has been acquitted by the mouth of the judge; the laws of heaven and the rights of the court are discordant.

The inward judge binds the man whom the outward judge releases; God neither flees from what exists nor fails to see what has been done.

## CLXV. On the Three-Day Fast.

[Col. 0963A] The inexperienced man does not know how severely the three-day fast is accustomed to strike the heel—he who diligently inflates his stomach and restrains the belly breathing out through frequent blasts, just as the breath empties both chambers of a blacksmith’s bellows.

## CLXVI. To Cadalus, Not a Shepherd but an Ancient Dragon.

He ceases to be guilty who punishes his guilt by weeping.

Repeated pride makes the sacrilege of an initiated crime worse; by slaughtering Rome, you now destroy the world with gold.

Alas! the sword of gold is more savage than the sword of iron; the former penetrates the soul, while the latter makes the flesh bloody from without—*fons* [“spring”] in the text; *foris* [“outside”] in the Vatican codex, according to Mai—and the vein of shining metal possesses the force of a dart.

It makes no difference whether someone is killed by iron or by gold.

What does it matter whether someone is killed by bright or dark weapons?

You brandish both against these wretched men, and slaughter both alike.

You had fallen from heaven, but still, slippery dragon, you hiss; vomiting rage from your mouth, you spread a foul stench.

Still broken, you crawl and breathe flames from your nostrils; you swell your scaly neck and gnash your teeth at slaughter and battles.

May you cease to raise your dreadful neck upon your scales, so that the people may live and the evil beast may lose its life.

May the grim viper now restrain its draconic crests—“chelas” [claws] in the Vatican codex, according to Mai.

May a heap of stones piled upon you bury you.

Let the united judgment of the Fathers be a ruin of stones.

May this black pit—“antra” [caves] in the Vatican codex, according to Mai—not be a plague from which you puff with swollen throat.

May the insatiable monster that devours a thousand men crackle.

May the caves of hell close their mouths above you, so that no return may lie open and the wars of the world may cease.

A smoky life flies away; sudden death draws near.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] The Vatican Codex lacks the three final verses, which our author perhaps deliberately omitted [Col. 0964D] because of a prophecy not literally fulfilled; Peter himself discusses this in volume III, p. 206. MAI.]

[Col. 0963C] The swift end of your completed life threatens you.

I do not deceive you: you will die in the year you have begun.

## CLXVII. To a Certain Brother Who Had Grown Sick of Fasting and Vigils.

Sicilian salt is produced on the shores of Agrigentum; what flows amid flames crackles if it is plunged into waves.

He who drags natural laws into opposites agrees with the Creator as much as he disagrees with himself alone.

## CLXVIII. That Some Are Offended by Good Deeds and Pacified by an Offense.

A service spurs some people on; a blow pacifies them.

“Nabal puts the mouth in his heart and the heart in his mouth.”

## CLXIX. On the Tooth and the Lentil.

Change the letter, and what he was eating will be eaten again.

## CLXX. That Flesh without Preaching Bursts into a Forest of Vices.

[Col. 0963D] Flesh, free from the word, grows wild with vices; sterile new fields grow green beneath knives and the mattock.

We know that Hannibal was one-eyed, and Nero likewise; a hernia too afflicted him while he wielded the scepters.

## CLXXI. On the Ruler’s Staff.

Receive a staff of varied governance according to the art of discipline; those whom the bier has wounded, piety restores.

## CLXXII. Lament on the Roman Church, Invaded by an Antipope.

Alas! apostolic see, once the glory of the world:

[Col. 0964A] now, alas, you have become Simon’s workshop.

Hammers beat upon the anvil; coins are infernal.

By the just judgment of God, this condition has come about.

Whoever once purchases the apostolic see does not cease buying it back until he perishes miserably.

You occupy the seat of pestilence, pressed beneath an anathema, together with priests who have slain Christ.

The earth becomes iron for you; [Col. 0964B] the seat of heaven, bronze.

Therefore attend carefully to what I say.

## CLXXIII. On the Misery of the Human Condition.

Alas! unhappy origin of the human race, which through the transmission of flesh still becomes subject to death and gives birth to wretches whom it confines within the boundary of life.

He who touches no wife except through love of offspring, though admirable, is not to be imitated by everyone.

Refreshment cannot exist for limbs without little limbs.

Often a mother’s mind becomes stepmotherly toward orphans, and by a perverse law a stepmother is burdensome as a mother.

## CLXXIV. On One Who Preaches the Just Man and Dismisses the Wicked.

The foolish man pours water from streams upon thirsty gardens.

## CLXXV. Praise of Almsgiving.

He lends to God who provides an expenditure for the needy; he has promised to repay, he who knows no lies.

The completed debt is discharged with heavier interest; for a little, much is returned; for mud, gold.

Thus a half-measure gains a jar, a drachma a talent; thus an obol purchases a kingdom, a cup buys heaven.

Heavenly things are returned for earthly things, lasting things for perishable ones.

Water kills fires; almsgiving cleanses sins.

Water is the death of flame, and almsgiving is the death of guilt; nor does it fill hearts with flowing streams of tears.

It empties these of vices and adorns them with flowers of virtues.

These deeds redeem Christ himself through the bowels of mercy.

## CLXXVI. To a Rich Miser.

He who knows how to join cedars with solid cypresses builds foundations subject to no winds.

You are richer in mud than you are, Pactolus, in flowing water; the wave raises the heap, the sand turns metal yellow, the mud bears crops, and the steep rock bears its summit.

By these things we govern life, and we see this standing far away: God is rich in the widow and poor in the rich man.

## CLXXVII. To a Proud Man.

The mind teems, with cause bearing witness in true words; though it may truly blush, the beautiful rose never lasts forever.

He who stands ready falls, as flesh, once fallen like a flower, rots.

The flying life of man runs on like flowing water.

[Col. 0965A] Remember that you hang like an open leaf before the wind; wicked death subdues your swollen necks beneath its feet.

He who endures living will enjoy a happy death; he who enjoys life will suffer a bitter death.

Brief life prevents you from hoping to live long.

Live mindful of death, so that you may always be able to live.

Live wholly for God; be wholly dead to yourself.

Life produces death; death produces a small, everlasting life.

He who now lives for himself will perish forever by dying.

He who dies to himself will be followed by blessed life.

Thus life is restored to the weary dead as rest.

## CLXXVIII. To a Jealous Slanderer.

It would be better to be bread than to gnaw one’s brother: one is food for the body, the other poison for the soul.

The one who is gnawed does not die; the one who gnaws is held to be a murderer.

Do not look upon others with a roe-deer’s sight while you look upon yourself with a mole’s.

Do not show me your face while you are ready to turn your back on me, making me a mirror while you have become a satchel to yourself.

An octopus does not smell foul to the creature that clings to it.

Lyncean light drives sharp rays into the entrails; although it does not see itself, it penetrates everything that stands far away.

Blunt whetstones sharpen; they cannot withdraw, nor do they obey their own laws, but those of different metals.

The rough file knows how to polish, but not to be polished itself; the crooked slag remains foul while it smooths gold—

for a faithful person becomes worthy of the designation “scabrous flesh” if, with rabid jaws, he attacks a household servant even under colour of law.

He who says what he wants often hears what he does not want.

The tongue has no mouth, but it itself causes bones to be broken, and alone produces shapeless things from different limbs.

Lay aside the evil of the tongue, which you brandish like an arrow, lest stones be returned by a sword’s spear.

## CLXXIX. To Two Enemies, That They May Return to Peace.

Love joins together diverse people; discord tears apart those who are joined.

There is no light of peace where division of heart occurs.

Peace teaches the ignorant; discord blinds the clever.

Nothing remains fixed in human affairs; the order of fortune turns.

Sudden death threatens the rigid neck.

Fiery fever subdues swollen necks beneath its feet and, by divine right, tames those who have been released from their stubbornness.

Those who swelled with pride are compelled to yield to disease; what they give to weakness they had forbidden to true health.

A sling twisted around a tiny stone often lays low one who is savage in face, as though vomiting flames from his mouth, and who thunders terrifying words with gnashing jaws.

## CLXXX. When the Same Letter Is Sent Twice.

He is rightly censured who repeatedly writes to the same person; nevertheless it is not absurd when the matter itself recurs, since the duplication of matters requires words.

He accuses you of not returning a reciprocal response in verse.

He sent as many couplets as there are rivers of paradise, but from your fountain not even a drop flows for me.

Now, therefore, unless you return as many writings as I have written, a blunted pen will fill the empty case.

## CLXXXI. On Certain Antidotes.

Death makes aloe equal to itself; one flavor joins the two together.

You too, sluggish Serapio, obtain an equal bitterness from these; I confess that they are not superior to all poisons.

## CLXXXII. That He Who Receives a Gift Ought to Return the Favor.

A gift from each side joins dear friends, if the bearer returns it and the giver receives it.

## CLXXXIII. To Those to Whom a Blessing Is Sent in the Form of Spoons.

Let others give yellow metal, weighed out on the balance.

But the world lives because Life hung upon wood; thus a small piece of wood is more precious than great gold.

## CLXXXIV. Spoons Sent by the Pontifical Right Hand.

Receive a great gift, a tiny golden piece of wood.

I do not want you to weigh the gift, but to measure the heart of the giver.

I dare to presume upon the whole what does not belong to the part.

As many poems as I have written, so many pieces of wood I have polished for you.

The little sheet is for sale; the rest is given freely.

## CLXXXV. To Those to Whom a Blessing Is Sent in the Form of Spoons.

[Col. 0966B] Stonecutters and craftsmen give signs in marbles and metals; gravediggers put together poor biers.

Nor do we carry the signs of leaders, but the signs of peasants.

## CLXXXVI. He Terrifies a Friend.

As many poems as I write with my fingers, so many I send to you.

The harsh voice says, “Go”; the exceedingly pleasing one, “Come.”

The former gathers lambs; the other scatters kids.

Measured words will be able to compose characters.

## CLXXXVII. To an Enemy.

If we desire the peace of the kingdom, let us also fear the fire.

Amid wars the laws are silent; in peace they speak.

The time of war is here; the times of law will come.

Let strife prevail in such a way that peace does not lose after the wars.

May you not be defeated in court, you who try to conquer in the field.

## CLXXXVIII. Distinction between the Light and the Serious.

Do not, bristling, hurl yourself headlong like a snail.

With gravity, be light; with lightness, be serious.

If your step is serious, do not now move as though bound by a fetter.

It is not beneficial for one fault to yield to another.

## CLXXXIX. That the Laboring Farmer Is Better Off than the Warring Master.

The master stirs up wars; the farmer plows the fields.

The former lies exposed to arrows; the latter rejoices in heaps of crops.

## CXC. On Those Who Do Not Censure Themselves but Others.

An octopus does not smell foul to the creature that clings to it.

There are people who caress their own faults while condemning those of others.

## CXCI. That the Hungry and Thirsty Gladly Take Whatever Is Cheap.

Black hunger commends country herbs to the throat; fiery thirst makes stale wine easy to drink.

The hungry man eats; born with an empty mouth, he greedily licks.

## CXCII. On One Who Glories in the Height of His Voice.

The vocal she-ass brays with a sufficiently lofty voice; the swan’s voice forms sweet melody with gentle humming.

## CXCIII. On Monks Who Put on Chain Mail against the Flesh.

Chain-linked garments provide an unpleasant covering.

Chain-linked clothes are hated as a double plague; weight presses the bones, and cold constricts the entrails.

## CXCIV. On Hildebrand, Who Was Small in Stature but Appeared to Be Great in Prudence.

The little Tigris equals arrows sent forth by hurrying along.

It is indeed worthless iron, yet it subdues every metal; but a powerful magnet draws it after its own tracks.
