The mind that conquers all things confines him within the measure of Sisyphus; and the man whom many fear, unwillingly, submits to me alone.

## CXCV. On the Pope and Hildebrand.

I duly honor the pope, but prostrate I adore you.

You make him lord; he makes you god.

## CXCVI. On the Roman Archdeacon, Who Sent Me Half a Fish.

It is no wonder that Peter is always needy for me, since rivers produce little fish in halves.

## CXCVII. He Congratulates Urban, Who Became a Poor Bishop at Rome.

What Bethsaida was to Peter, Rome now is to me.

When he holds the scepters, he is what he was when he mended nets.

He is always washing nets; for me he plows the blue sea.

He oppresses me on land, though he was utterly needy upon the waves.

He restores me with pods, though a small fish used to feed him.

## CXCVIII. On One Who Has a Son.

When offspring survive, parents live on from death, and the branch grows green at the root like a single flesh.

## CXCIX. That Those Who Preach to One Another Should Not Disagree.

Let neither a wise man be joined to a fool nor an ox to a donkey.

Those who teach divine things should not wholly depart from one another.

## CC. Mistletoe Is Made from the Droppings of a Thrush, by Which the Thrush Itself Is Caught.

It is digested in the backside, by whose foot the little thrush is caught.

## CCI. To One to Whom I Sent a Long Letter and Who Sent Me a Short One.

An obol does not equal a solidus; a pound does not equal a talent.

Plainly, the smaller yields to the larger measure, and this one to the chorus.

A little letter cannot compensate for a book.

The balanced scale holds equal pans opposite one another.

## CCII. On Florence, Where Pope Stephen Died and from Which Pope Nicholas Came.

Small Florence owes a great man to Rome.

She who holds the dead one must be compelled to return the living one.

Thus a new light shone upon the world from the shores of Bethlehem.

## CCIII. On One Who Subdues Himself in Order to Receive the Guilty.

He buys nothing for himself who sells himself under interest.

## CCIV. That Rome Ruled the World So Long as It Obeyed the Laws.

The City ruled the world while it was subject to law.

When it despised justice’s reins, it contracted its kingdom.

## CCV. That Most Chaste Men Are Stingy.

You will scarcely see someone generous with wealth and chaste in body.

## CCVI. On One Who, Brought Up at Arretium, Became Abbot of Pomposa.

He who is accustomed to fill his belly with tasteless lupins now belches up sea feasts from his swollen throat.

## CCVII. On Lord Humbert, Archbishop, Who Sat at the Pope’s Right, While I Sat at His Left.

You, stronger than a kid, raise the sheep’s seat.

The left-hand man has the right hand; the right-hand man sometimes has the left.

## CCVIII. Elegy on Worldly People.

I mourn you, wretched people, whose minds are devoted to the flesh.

You look down upon heaven and consider profit the highest good.

What shall I urge you to do? What shall I advise you to desire?

Now greedily swallow the world’s falsely pleasant marrow.

Fill your entrails with food and load your limbs with fat, lest the worms perish from always eating you in your emaciation.

Extend villas watered by cold springs.

Let there be no number for coins and no measure for metals.

[Col. 0968A] Later your possession will be the narrow tomb.

But you who are enriched by a hope more precious than gold, whose true riches are the rewards of life—those which no thief troubles and no devouring creature furrows—despise empty profits subject to sudden ruin.

Let their gifts yield to the world destined to fall.

Let the heavenly inheritance suffice for Christ’s servants.

Let the ark of the heart conceal the excellent talent of faith.

Let it be your endeavor to store up shining gems of virtues,

and to pluck out the thorns of vices that grow evilly.

Avoid the troubled business of the wandering world;

let a mind set free abide continually upon sacred utterances;

let it now taste the honey sparingly, so that afterward it may overflow with fullness;

thus may our form return to its own beginnings.

Let these be the riches that are heaped up; let these be the honors that are sought;

[Col. 0968B] by these a man is rightly powerful, by these he becomes rich through the ages.

### CCIX. Against the abbot of Cluny, who brought him into Gaul

My death, Cluny, you bring upon my long old age;

you make it so that I do not exist, while you seek that I may exist well;

so that honey may flow for you, banquets blush with spices,

and a spacious pot may offer richly seasoned foods.

Our tables become rough because even Cantabrian fare is lacking,

while I preserve delicacies for you, and black hunger awaits me.

### CCX. Verses of a poor man

Here comes Lazarus, empty of ulcers but filled with poverty,

who seeks to live on crumbs.

The mouths of dogs are absent, but the snouts of foot-soldiers are not;

the former lick his skin, the latter gnaw his seething limbs.

### CCXI. On the three-day fast

How heavily you are accustomed to strike the heel of the three-day fast,

the disciplined mind knows, having often experienced it in battles.

### CCXII. He who says what he wishes hears what he does not wish

He who says what he wishes often hears what he does not wish;

he who speaks what he loves deserves to endure what he hates.

### CCXIII. Epitaph of Peter Damian

What you now are, we were; what we are, you yourself will be.

Trust none of these things that you see destined to perish.

Frivolous dreams run ahead of the clear springs;

ages succeed brief spans of time.

Live mindful of death, so that you may always be able to live.

Whatever is present passes; behold, what remains is coming.

How wisely he provided who left you, wicked world,

to die in mind to the flesh before dying in flesh to you.

Prefer heavenly things to earthly, things that will remain to things that perish.

[Col. 0968D] Let your liberated mind return to its own origin.

Spirit, seek the heights, and return to the fountain from which you emerged;

look down upon whatever weighs heavily in the depths.

I beg you, remember me; piously regard the ashes of Peter.

With prayer and with a groan say: “Spare him, O God.”

### CCXIV. Epitaph of Benno

Rimini, mourn; pour out rivers of tears.

Benno was your glory—alas, behold, it has fallen.

Benno, the ornament of the kingdom, the glory of the Roman people,

himself the father of his country, was the light of Italy.

The wretched felt this harsh companion of the proud;

he restored the fallen and subdued swollen hearts.

He became a roaring lion against the fighter, a gentle lamb toward the unarmed;

thus he always remained just, and in the other respect devout.

[Col. 0969A] Here, while he observed the laws of faith, while he refused to yield,

firmly holding the weight of stern justice.

The throat of the upright suffered the blows of the wicked;

through him peace flourished, and the fortune of war perished.

I beg you, wise men, mourn so grievous a ruin,

and pour out devout prayers to God for your companion.

### CCXV. That you will be a worm and will be devoured by a worm

Man, you have been given to be devoured by the mouth of that which you will be;

why, though you are ashes and a worm, do you swell with a proud neck?

### CCXVI. He summons to repentance

When blood accumulates, the vein requires an incision;

a wound also makes the healthy person well, and a blow brings healing.

The mind generates a fluid that devout confession cleanses;

thus the soul’s blood flows out through the vein of the mouth.

What deadly corruption violates in the entrails requires evacuation—

[Col. 0969B] make yourself vomit forth your own disease by a health-giving effort,

so that the stomach of the mind may be relieved of the burden of guilt.

### CCXVII. Verses on the Simoniacs

By overturning the pestilential seats of authority, God condemns

Simon’s smithy-anvil and the caverns of money;

for afterward the thief creeps through back passages,

and the shepherd approaches accessible doors by a free step.

But when the wicked business of traffickers is absent,

and the heavy money-box does not swell with a saleable talent,

no dealer causes harm, because no sordid commerce is taking place;

for what can moneyed men do where coins cannot cause harm?

Indeed, how can a filthy hand harm woody plants?

Often a sick physician has given health-giving rice;

slaveholders have begotten a fighter, and the blind have begotten one who sees;

a foul bedchamber has produced a handsome man—

[Col. 0969C] nor should offspring be burdened with their fathers’ faults.

Each person is weighed down by his own fault, and is not held by the stain of his companion.

### CCXVIII. A rhythm against the Simoniacs

The turbulent crowd of the world,

error and division,

Simon’s heresy,

zeal and ambition,

compel us to lament

under the duty of the pen.

Let everything therefore be written down

briefly from the beginning,

from the time when the bishop of the highest see,

taught by the Holy Spirit,

began clearly

to correct the crimes of the wicked.

[Col. 0969D] His voice was like that of a father

correcting his sons;

his voice was like that of the Apostle,

gentle toward the Corinthians:

[53] thus he showed himself gentle

toward his fellow bishops.

You know, brothers, that you have undertaken

the governance of shepherds;

therefore it is fitting for you, as teachers,

first to live rightly,

to entreat, to rebuke,

and afterward to admonish.

Not haughty, not puffed up,

not swollen with wine.

[Col. 0970A] Not in costly clothing,

but radiant in virtue;

not injuring the chaste

and sober without cause.

Let the deeds of the Fathers be at hand,

and let the holy canons be at hand;

let the weak and poor

be refreshed by your food;

let no weeping mother of orphans

cry out before you.

Let caparisoned horses give way,

let blind chatterers give way,

let hunting dogs

and the performances of mimes give way,

and let the rapacious hawks

[Col. 0970B] and likewise the chattering birds give way.

In addition, detest

Simon’s leprous heresy,

as well as the crime of adultery

among priests;

let the domination of laymen

withdraw from the churches.

Behold the instructions of the glorious pope,

Gregory;

behold the words of the bishop

of the highest see, the Catholic prelate,

against whom the Babylonian citizens

rush.

From this the wrath of Caesar

was kindled against the Church;

from that the arrogance of the bishops

swelled against him;

the priest of the peoples is furiously assailed by the Church.

[Col. 0970C] From the time when Simon, against Peter,

built a tower of magic,

from that time he fell, struck

by the cornerstone,

against whose blow plainly

nothing is durable.

Of these, one is Christ, their king;

the other is Leviathan;

the former reigns over the hosts of life,

the latter over those of death:

therefore no sane person doubts

which of them is the victor.

Let all who gnaw and tear

the priest of the peoples

repent then and return to their hearts—

those who do not do so purely or sincerely,

but with a malevolent mind.

But let those whom apostolic faith has nourished

be strengthened and founded

upon the solid rock of Peter,

so that after the battle they may obtain

complete victory. Amen.

### CCXIX. An exhortation to Damian that he become a monk

[Col. 0971A]

Almighty One, teach us to act, that we may do what he did.

The rights of the marriage bed fall away when the path of Christ is trodden.

Now you are a father; grant room to the offspring that follows,

so that your footprints may lie open to neighboring feet,

and the crop may spring forth, while what it has produced does not hinder

the young shoots lying beneath their mother’s branches.

The old leaves readily flow toward the beginnings of flowers,

and the grass, once its seed has sprung up, calls for the cutting sickle.

Therefore, beginning to be torn from the earthly turf,

transplant it to heaven, so that hope, once animated, may flourish:

thus let the root of the heart transfer itself from the fields to heaven,

and let fruit break forth upon the tree that will not fall.

### CCXX. Rhythm of a penitent monk

Who will give water for weeping to my unhappy head?

Who will give a fountain of tears to my eyes?

By weeping, cover the pupils with darkness.

Woe to me, fallen!

Not the drops of the sea, nor the sand of the shore,

are equal in number to my crimes;

they surpass the stars and the rains,

and the mountains in weight.

For to what vices am I not liable,

I who have always served evil ways?

Released from God, I lived according to the laws of the flesh,

flowing downward into the depths.

I despised the commandments; I dared what was forbidden;

through wicked judgments I overthrew many.

Guilty toward myself, useless to others,

I am hemmed in on both sides.

[Col. 0971C] I am not worthy to look upon heaven with my eyes,

nor to utter God’s name with my lips;

the guilt that gnaws at me forbids me

to wear away the threshold of the sacred house.

Even now, devoted to sacred services,

I am goaded by the enticements of my former life,

as the laws of a tyrant pursue

a fugitive servant.

I strive in weeping, but my stony heart is rigid;

I persist in prayers, but my wandering spirit departs;

I seek the light, but immediately

the darkness of phantasms appears.

The savage anger, the swollen pride,

the devouring gluttony, the vain self-glory,

the barbarism of all crimes, gnashing its teeth,

attempts to subdue me.

[Col. 0971D] Often I resist and seize my weapons;

I engage in combat with myself, I fight with myself;

but while the law of the spirit yields to the law of the flesh,

I become the enemy’s prey.

Often the heart is kindled by divine fire,

and the mind, transcending itself, is carried into the heights,

but it slips, pressed down

by its native corruption.

The inaccessible light shines, as through narrow cracks,

toward which the attentive mind gazes thirstily;

but behold, the shadow of the flesh,

meeting its gaze, blunts it.

Wounded by a thousand weapons

of the ancient enemy,

I mourn the soul slain in sins:

you who, by dying, emptied the laws of death,

raise it up through yourself.

[Col. 0972A] Palm of the righteous and hope of the penitent,

give your hand, O Christ, and release me,

drawn out from the depths,

from my sins; rescue me from the evils

that threaten from here.

[55] You do not reject the tears of the sinful woman;

you receive the penitent tax collector;

you promise to give life to the thief

already placed in death.

By these entrails of mercy, I beg you,

free me from the chains of so many faults.

I deserve anger; pour out compassion,

fountain of mercy.

[Col. 0972B] Grant that I may always obey your commands;

and thus make me worthy of heavenly rewards,

you who, equal to the Father and to the Holy Spirit,

govern all things. Amen.

### CCXXI. A rhythm on the misery of abbots

The holy Church now mourns,

weeps, and laments,

when it sees such misery

among its abbots

and contemplates

their various dangers.

Almost no abbot today

is able to be a monk,

while he endures

a diverse and harmful business;

and what he wishes to endure,

he suffers as though he were unjust.

Within, like a servant,

he bears the arrogance of monks,

and outside he endures

the trouble of many affairs;

the abbot’s neck bears

this double servitude.

The brothers want the abbot

to live spiritually,

and through secular causes

they compel him to travel.

Who can walk

through such diverse matters?

For while he rides, he is immediately said

to be wandering;

his remaining in the cloister, however,

is called sluggishness;

whatever the wretched man does

is always disparaged.

While he corrects delinquents,

everyone calls him impious;

if at some time he spares them,

they say he is lukewarm.

Who, I ask, can bear

such an ambiguous crowd?

If he imitates Phinehas,

he flees or is expelled;

if he imitates Eli, he is mocked

[Col. 0973A] and held in contempt.

He is hated if fervent,

and worthless if lukewarm.

Perhaps he can correct actions

if they are minor,

and those that require only

two or one pardons;

but the graver offenses the abbot

suppresses, lest he perish.

For if he wishes to speak

about some unclean vice,

an internal sedition

of the monks arises,

and at once his destruction

is secretly plotted.

[Col. 0973B] If at some time he fasts

or keeps silence,

they immediately say that the abbot

is devoted to empty praise;

and if he speaks or gives orders,

he is reproved like a thief.

If the abbot delivers a sermon,

he is branded a chatterer;

and if, remaining silent, he explains nothing,

he is branded a fool.

Whichever way he turns or goes,

he will always be anxious.

Within or without, if any adversity

should occur,

the brothers all attribute this

to the abbot’s negligence;

they gnaw and gnaw him through

and call him a beast.

If the holy house does not grow,

they attack the abbot;

if it grows, they immediately seek

the abbot like enemies.

All strike the abbot together,

as though he were an anvil.

[Col. 0973C] O blessed such a head,

which is gnawed by its members!

A good shepherd whom

the savage teeth of the sheep devour!

A fortunate father who fears

the bite of all his children!

The abbot endures this evil

of the monks within,

and likewise bears outside

the burdens of secular people;

he is anxious and sorrowful,

because everything presses upon him.

For, burdened by cares,

he cuts the night in half with words,

and anticipates the dawn

so that he may speak more often;

then he continues the whole day

in speaking.

These and very many other things

the prelate endures:

secular people prick him from outside,

the brothers wound him within;

the former pursue his body,

the latter gnaw his entrails.

[Col. 0974A] Tell me, dear prelate, I beg you,

what kind of dignity is this?

Within, pain; outside, labor;

on either side, calamity.

By these evils, I confess,

both body and soul are destroyed.

Who among the abbots, I ask, is now able,

in an age of iron,

amid so many calamities,

to bear fruitful rods?

Certainly the honors of prelates today

are barren.

Venerable abbots,

yield these honors;

cast off voluntarily now

the heavy and empty burden,

and henceforth live

in quiet and security.

### CCXXII. Rubric on all orders of all people living in this world

[Col. 0974B] Bishops, attend;

discern the words of God:

the Lord commanded you

to die for your sheep.

If you have made the good things

that you speak

into deeds,

you will give good examples

to your sons entrusted to you.

Priests and deacons,

you who carry the vessels of the Lord,

always be clean

in the sight of the Most High.

Whoever wishes to be a canon

must be good and suitable,

and must obey the bishop

as an illustrious elder.

Let him come to Matins

when the signal of the hour sounds;

setting laziness aside,

let him hurry to the offices.

Parish priests should rightly hear

what the holy Fathers cry out:

that they should leave

the estates they have acquired

to the Church.

[Col. 0974C] A teacher learned in letters

should give the disciples the rod,

so that, taught from childhood,

they may rightly understand doctrine.

Scribes, in straight lines,

should write truthful letters,

and complete their proper distinctions

to the very end.

An unlettered cleric,

devoted to arrogance,

despising the mysteries,

lies like a foolish beast.

[Col. 0975A] He runs through the basilica

out of excessive vanity;

if he remains in one place,

he looks back with twisted neck.

He does not proclaim the words of God,

but always mutters privately,

and recites parables

empty and vain.

Let abbots always keep watch,

and because of every crime

let them not abandon

the sacred studies for worldly cunning.

He cannot be a monk

who is wandering and improvident;

if he lives without a rule,

he will perish by a most evil death.

Devoted monks of God,

keep the law perfectly;

living with chaste bodies,

despise all earthly things.

Authority is among the people,

given by the highest Lord,

and with faith [lacuna]

those who had performed the sacraments.

For no ill-gotten advantage,

or agreed price,

or any friendship,

let him turn aside true judgments.

Let a judge sitting in court

[Col. 0975B] [58] not hope for profit,

but rightly fear God,

and quickly bring the law to completion.

Witnesses, presume not to speak falsely

for any gift,

but speak truthful words

in the presence of the true Prince.

Let notaries be truthful,

keeping faith in their hearts;

nor should they ever write falsehoods

on little documents for money.

Stewards of the people

and all deputies,

let them not twist justice,

nor consume service-payments.

[Col. 0975C] Those holding offices,

let them not agree with the wicked,

but serve rightly,

lest they lose good merits.

Advocates in court proceedings,

let them not defraud by any artifice;

let them loosen the vices of the heart,

and seek judgments.

Let no counselor

or confidential adviser,

because of worldly prosperity,

trust himself in glory.

Let an envoy prudently know

how to recount his missions,

[Col. 0976A] lest, publicly bewildered,

he speak an unprofitable word.

Nourished and wise,

truly fearing God,

he is to be loved by the Lord

and praised by the people.

A receiver who conceals vices,

singing falsehood like a pipe,

by laughing at words just spoken

sows evil in his heart.

A hypocrite pretending to be something else

conceals many vices;

he displays a calm face,

but carries a sword in his heart.

The most wretched drunkards

[Col. 0976B] roar like madmen;

they lose the memory of their minds

and devise nothing good.

Hear also, laymen,

you who serve Christ:

do not despise pastors

for any crime;

put it into effect by your deeds,

and inscribe it in your hearts.

Before death comes,

give your tithes to God;

you will depart from here secure,

and will possess heaven.

Love your wives,

and correct your children;

but govern your maidservants,

and provide work for them.

Whoever fears the God of all

should not swear in business,

nor, out of desire,

defraud anyone of his price.

[Col. 0976C] Let leaders agree with one another

together with their benefices,

and serve God with faith.

A soldier traveling to battle

should keep God in mind.

Let gossips always beware

lest they say more than they have heard;

those who please through lying

commit the greatest sin.

They appear vile to the world,

and are held in disgrace.

Let authority cleanse away vices,

thefts, and robberies,

so that the others, terrified,

may fear to incur punishment.

Married women,

keep faith prudently;

arrange your households,

and run to the temple of God.

[Col. 0976D] Widows, change your clothing;

live in chastity.

Flee those who live luxuriously,

lest they be able to deceive you.

Let girls guard themselves

from all empty glory,

lest in the heat of youth

they fall into adultery.

Prostitutes, turn back;

seek pardon for yourselves.

He who is always accustomed to spare

awaits you every day.

Slaves, serve your master

with an upright mind;

let maidservants likewise

serve usefully.

In prosperity, let no faithful soul

have joy,

or in adversity sorrow,

beyond measure.

[Col. 0977A] You who live in the world,

all serve the Lord,

so that, aided by his right hand,

you may reign above the heavens.

### CCXXIII. A rhythm on the day of death

You strike me with grave terror,

last day of life;

the heart mourns, the loins are loosened,

the wounded entrails tremble,

while the anxious mind

paints your image before itself.

For who could explain that fearful spectacle,

when, the course of life measured out,

the soul struggles to be released

from the bonds of sick flesh,

drawing near to its end?

The senses perish, the tongue grows stiff,

the eyes dissolve;

the chest palpitates, the hoarse

human throat pants;

the limbs grow numb, the face pales,

the body’s beauty departs.

Behold, the forces of different spirits

converge:

on one side angelic powers,

on the other a crowd of demons.

They draw nearer,

as merit invites them.

[Col. 0977B] Thoughts, words, and deeds

are also present,

and against the will of the one who sees,

everything is heaped before his eyes;

wherever he turns,

he sees them placed before him.

Conscience itself, biting,

torments its guilty subject;

it mourns that the times for correcting deeds

have flowed away.

Full of grief and lacking fruit,

late repentance remains.

Then the false sweetness of the flesh

is turned into bitterness,

[Col. 0978A] when perpetual punishment

follows brief pleasure;

what was believed to be great

is now seen to have been nothing.

And the mind is lifted up

to the glory of the highest light;

it despises the filth of the flesh

in which it was sunk and rolled,

and, rejoicing, is released

from its prison-bond.

But once it has left, the soul experiences

a difficult road,

where the furious armies

of dreadful pestilence rush upon it,

and in their various places

array their battles.

For here are the instigators of gluttony,

there of avarice,

elsewhere the supporters of anger,

elsewhere of pride;

each mass of vice

prepares its own battle lines.

[Col. 0978B] If one troop gives way,

another immediately rises up;

every art of war is attempted,

every engine of battle,

lest the soul thus escape the disgrace

of its enemies.

O what grim monsters

the savage warriors are!

Black, fierce, and ferocious,

they breathe flames from their nostrils;

their dragon-like necks swell,

and they drip poison from their throats.

They arm hands skilled in battle

with serpentine coils;

with these iron-like weapons

they attack those who approach;

those whom they draw toward themselves

they enslave to eternal fires.

[Col. 0978C] I beg you, unconquered King Christ,

come to the aid of the wretched one,

at the final hour of death,

when I depart at your command.

Let no authority over me

be granted to the impious tyrant.

Let the prince of darkness fall;

let the Tartarean faction fall.

Then lead the sheep already redeemed

back to its homeland,

where I may enjoy seeing you

through the ages. Amen.

### CCXXIV. A rhythm against those who are secure from the king’s vengeance but cannot escape Christ

[Col. 0978D] All the reprobate rejoice

and are glad together,

those who had previously awaited

the king’s coming in terror.

They rage, yield, swell up,

and insult the wretched.

Those who ought to be mourned

with every fountain of tears

are lifted high

on the horns of pride;

thinking madness strength,

they laugh at those who are sane and weep.

But what does it profit you, perverse ones,

you sons of Gehenna?

Not to avoid, but merely to change

the tribunal of judgment?

Safe under a mortal king,

you will not escape Christ.

Behold, he will come like lightning,

threatening and terrible;

the sun’s heat and the moon’s brightness

will be wrapped in darkness;

the stars will seek the depths of earth,

torn from the axis of heaven.

[Col. 0979A] The earth will burn utterly,

the regions of heaven will tremble;

the elements will be thrown into confusion,

the thunder will roar,

fiery flashes will gleam,

and frequent lightning bolts will fall.

In the fury of the one who comes

a mighty storm arises;

the whole mechanism of the world,

shaken, is shattered;

a mass of seething flame

breathes through the vast air.

Then all the impious who pierced him

will behold him,

resting upon a fiery throne

in a terrifying form.

They will ask the mountains

and beg the hills,

pleading to be buried.

Soon the hidden things of every heart

will lie open to all;

words, deeds, and the mind will be seen

as though they were a solid body,

and they will give bitter testimony

against their authors.

The wicked spirits themselves,

the crimes they had suggested,

[Col. 0979B] recorded in lengthy volumes,

will read out and explain,

enumerating the places,

times, and manner of the deeds.

All the hosts of angels

will rage against the wicked;

the elements will oppose them,

heaven, earth, and lifeless things;

every creature of the universe

will threaten them in opposition.

Behold the head of the wicked,

that savage beast,

dragged naked before

the presence of all:

[Col. 0980A] its arts, thefts, deceits,

frauds, and schemes are exposed.

### CCXXV. Thus far on the coming; from here, on the punishments of hell

O how dreadful, how horrifyingly

the Judge thunders,

when he orders the accursed

to be plunged into prepared flames;

soon the pot of Styx,

swallowing the living,

devours them.

The wretched are vaporized

within and without;

the crackling flames hiss

like a burning furnace;

from mouth, nostrils,

and even eyes they flow.

[Col. 0980B] Immortal death kills,

but does not utterly destroy;

fire burns but does not consume,

nor does it admit an end.

Life dies, death lives;

the end always begins.

The seven renewed plagues

renew the punishments:

smoke, stench, cold, heat,

hunger, and fiery thirst;

worms are never satisfied,

though they gnaw the entrails.

There are pain, torment,

weeping, and gnashing of teeth;

there are the roars of lions

[Col. 0980C] and the hissing of serpents,

mixed with which

are the howls of those who weep.

Dragons of enormous bulk

open their relaxed jaws wide;

their eyes shoot fiery arrows;

their tails produce scorpions’ claws,

and their feet vipers.

They strive to cease to exist,

but do not cease to exist;

they live for death and wish to die,

but cannot in any way.

Those who lived wickedly

endure life as torment.

[Col. 0980D] Keep these things before your eyes,

madmen, fearing them;

turn them over with careful attention,

examining them closely,

and loosen the necks of your minds

from the bonds of wicked habits.

For he is prepared to grant pardon

to those who turn back,

while he still presses upon the perverse

the sentence of vengeance.

Salvation and honor to the pious King

through eternal ages. Amen.

### CCXXVI. A rhythm on the glory of paradise

[Col. 0981A] The thirsty mind has thirsted

for the fountain of everlasting life;

the soul, seeking to have

the gates of the flesh broken at once,

burns, longs, and struggles

to enjoy its homeland in exile.

[63] While it groans that it is subject

to pressures and distress,

it contemplates the glory it lost

when it sinned.

The memory of lost good

increases present evil.

For who could express

how great the joy of highest peace is,

where buildings rise

from living pearls,

[Col. 0981B] roofs shine lofty with gold,

and dining halls radiate?

This structure is joined

with precious gems like the sun;

the city’s street is paved

with pure gold as with glass.

Mud is absent, filth is lacking;

no plague is seen.

Horrifying winter and scorching summer

never rage there;

the purple flower of roses

brings perpetual spring;

lilies gleam white, saffron reddens,

and balsam exudes fragrance.

The meadows are green, the crops blossom;

streams of honey flow;

the scent of spices breathes,

and a flowing abundance of aromatics.

The fruits of flowering groves hang there,

never destined to fall.

The moon does not change its phases,

nor the sun or the course of the stars;

the Lamb is the unfailing light

of the blessed City.

Night and time are absent from it;

it bears unending day.

For all the saints likewise shine

like the radiant sun.

Crowned after their triumph,

they rejoice together in mutual jubilation,

[Col. 0981C] and, now secure,

count the battles of the prostrate enemy.

Purified from every stain,

they know nothing of the battles of the flesh;

flesh made spiritual and mind

feel as one.

Enjoying abundant peace,

they endure no scandals.

Stripped of changeable things,

they return to their origin,

and contemplate

the present form of truth.

From this they drink

the life-giving sweetness of the living fountain.

[Col. 0982A] Thereafter they receive

a condition of existence that is always the same:

bright, living, and joyful,

[64] exposed to no accidents.

Diseases are absent; always healthy,

the old are young.

Hence they possess perpetual being,

for passing away has passed away;

there they are green, vigorous, and flourishing;

corruption has collapsed,

and the strength of immortality

has swallowed the power of death.

Knowing the One who knows all things, they know all things;

they cannot be ignorant.

[Col. 0982B] For they also penetrate

one another’s secrets of heart:

they will and refuse one thing;

there is unity of minds.

Although each person’s reward

may be different according to labor,

this love makes each one’s

what he loves in another;

thus what belongs to individuals

becomes common to all.

Where the body is, there rightly

the eagles gather;

there souls are refreshed

with angels and saints.

The citizens of both homelands

live by one bread.

Hungry and always full,

they desire what they possess;

satiety does not grow weary,

nor does hunger torment them:

always longing, they eat,

and eating, they long.

A melodious voice continually

resounds new harmonies,

and instruments, raised in jubilation,

soothe the ears.

They offer praises to the King

through whom they are victors.

[Col. 0982C] Happy is the soul that sees

heaven’s present King,

and beneath his lofty seat observes

the mechanism of the world revolve,

the sun, the moon,

and the spherical stars with the planets.

Christ, palm of warriors,

introduce me into this commonwealth

after my military belt has been removed;

make me a sharer in the gift

of the blessed citizens.

Grant inexhaustible strength

to me laboring in battle,

so that, after I have laid aside my military belt,

you may grant rest to one who has earned it,

and so that I may deserve to possess you

as an endless reward. Amen.

### CCXXVII. A rhythm on the death of Wido

[Note: [Col. 0983C] Amaduzzi published this in *Anecdota litteraria*, volume IV, p. 434; he introduced it there as follows, on p. 421: “I judge that a certain rhythm belongs to the eleventh century. Twelve years ago I copied it from a parchment manuscript codex in quarto, which is kept in the sacristy of St. [Col. 0983D] Fortunatus at Todi. Although this codex contains sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus, the rhythm must certainly be disassociated from him, both because I have never known verses composed by him and because it plainly appears entirely foreign to the character of the fifth century, around whose middle Chrysologus lived. Therefore we do not hesitate greatly to attribute this rhythm to Peter Damian, and indeed three principal reasons support this attribution. The first is that perhaps the copyist believed that, since Peter Damian was a citizen of Ravenna, the rhythm had the same author as the sermons of Peter of Ravenna—so they are entitled in the codex—that is, St. Peter Chrysologus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, and therefore did not hesitate to append it to them. The second is that I find this kind of rhythm familiar to Damian and entirely suited to his age. The third, finally, is that in [Col. 0984C] the rhythm I see a certain Wido or Guido mentioned, an illustrious man, for whose faults he implores God’s favor, and whom I do not think different from the man who was count of Forocornelium, and whose name is mentioned in two of Damian’s letters. In the first [Col. 0984D] (*Epistle* 7, Book IV), the vision of the priest Rainer is related: in accordance with the simplicity of those times, Count Guido seemed to be awaiting him after Wednesday in that place of punishment where Count Hildebrand of Tuscany and the other Count Lothar were being detained. In the second (*Epistle* 19, Book VI), fish are identified as having been given to him by Guido and brought from the city of Faenza, so that he would not lack food from them for many days. But whether this Guido, count of the Cornelians, is the same as the contemporary Guido who is called ‘the most illustrious count’ in the charter of the Faenzan concord—see this at the end of volume or part I of the works of St. Peter Damian—where Ermellina, his most serene wife, is also mentioned, and who is also remembered elsewhere, I myself, amid such obscurity of affairs, would not dare to determine anything, although this nevertheless seems very probable to me.”]

You have heard something newly

and swiftly come to pass:

the most illustrious Wido

has paid the debt of death.

Surrounded by ambushes

of his own soldier,

while the enemy held him captive,

he fell, executed by beheading.

As he began to fall from his horse,

pierced by a second wound,

[Col. 0983B] so that two wounds might cleanse

the faults of mind and flesh.

Lest he be given to demons

to be tormented longer,

he was delivered into the hands of his own men,

so that he might die more quickly.

Christ, who neither judge now

nor condemn for ever,

let what Wido suffered here

be a remedy for him.

May it benefit him, most merciful one,

that he strove to visit

places most sacred,

worthy of your presence.

To see your manger—

what is that but to believe

that you were born there

of the Virgin, true Light from Light?

To look upon your glorious tomb,

O Lord—

what is that but truly to believe

that you rose from it?

When the Mount of Olives is climbed,

you are believed to have returned to heaven;

spare Wido, O Lord,

when you return as judge.

[Col. 0984A] Here, once and again,

he sought your tomb;

a third time he was intending it,

when a span of time

was granted to him.

He held this desire,

though he could not accomplish it;

repay it with an equal gift,

O generous giver of grace.

The place of the blessed Virgin,

most renowned throughout the world,

he frequently approached as a suppliant

and honored as he was able.

Often seeking the great assistance

of the Apostles,

as I hope, more than twenty times

and five times he came to Rome.

Those whom he sought as helpers,

he made his advocates;

and, while he outlived them,

he devoted himself and his resources to them.

Someone may say of him:

“He was excessively weak.”

And I say:

“God is exceedingly favorable.”

I cannot say anything sinister

about anyone,

so I have written of his journeys,

which are on the right side.

[Col. 0984B] If anyone is pleased to read

and wishes to judge rightly,

they do not look toward Tartarus,

but toward the joys of the saints.

Whoever wishes to learn fully

the knowledge of so great an evil

must first come to know

the Aubertine wickedness.

He attempted falsely to destroy

at one time two elders

whom he had;

[Col. 0985A] as was clearly shown in truth.

One of them, who did not survive,

was grieved when he heard

that his companion,

close to him by nature,

had died.

The perpetrator of so great a crime,

under the guise of a false soldier,

promised them at some time,

by hand and by oath,

[Col. 0986A] that he would keep fitting faith with them,

and preserve continual peace

at all times,

as long as he lived in the body.

If these agreements stand firm,

may God, who knows all things,
himself judge,

and avenge it as pleases him.

[Col. 0985] “And my tongue shall exult in your righteousness, O God.”

End of the fourth and final volume of the works of Blessed Peter Damian, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Bishop of Ostia, of the Order of St. Benedict, a most eloquent and holy teacher.

[Col. 0985]

### COLLECTED EXCERPTS ON THE OLD TESTAMENT FROM THE SHORT WORKS OF BLESSED PETER DAMIAN, EXCERPTED BY AN ANONYMOUS DISCIPLE OF HIS, THROUGH THE CARE AND LABOR OF DOM CONSTANTINE CAJETAN

First published from a manuscript codex of his Anician Library.

### 65–70. CAJETAN’S PREFACE
[Col. 0985B] Excellent reader, the writings of the Catholic Fathers possess this special quality: in them, as in most pleasant gardens, the flowers of the sacred Scriptures exhale their fragrance everywhere. In gathering these flowers afterward and arranging them in order, the talents of later generations exercise themselves not without praise. Thus our Bede, a man distinguished no less for religious devotion than for learning and renowned for holiness, interpreted the Epistles of Paul by collecting into one volume, in marvelous order, what that most weighty and holy teacher had said in scattered places. Likewise Saint Paterius, bishop of Brescia, and Alulphus, also a monk—both Benedictines—published, for the benefit of posterity, what they had selected from the writings of Gregory the Great that pertained to the explanation of sacred letters. I pass over the others who, with equal care and no different industry, accomplished the same thing from the works of other authors. [Col. 0985C]

Following their example, a disciple of Saint Peter Damian, who had evidently spent much time in his writings, composed and elaborated from them a kind of patchwork collection of passages from sacred Scripture. As the title makes clear, he addressed this work to Damian, abbot and nephew through the sister of that most holy cardinal and bishop Damian, to whom two letters of the same [Col. 0986B] blessed uncle are extant.

This is that abbot Damian whom, as I believe, Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni and formerly abbot of the monastery of Cassino, honorably remembers at the beginning of his Commentary on the Apocalypse. I know that I saw this work some years ago in a most ancient manuscript written in Lombard letters, in the possession of Horace della Valle, a jurist who has deserved well of me and of Roman antiquity. Bruno recalls that, at Damian’s request, he wrote a Commentary on the prophet Isaiah. Yet Damian must have presided over a monastery other than Fonte Avellana, since the one who stood at its head and, so to speak, was its monastic ruler, was called not abbot but prior. The writings of Saint Peter Damian show that this custom was observed not only during his lifetime but also continued among later generations. The author of the Life of Saint Ubald, bishop of Gubbio, Theobald, his successor and prior of that same monastery, clearly demonstrates this. [Col. 0986C]

Moreover, from the written records of the monastery of Nonantola, built in the territory of Modena, we have observed that this Damian of ours was abbot of that monastery and also a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; [71–72] so Rangerius, author of the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and his spiritual [Col. 0987A] son, testifies when describing the funeral rites of his death:

“There was,” he says, “the bishop of Maguelonne, named Godefredus, and Benedict, bishop of Modena, and Aribert, bishop of Reggio, and the bishop of that same city, namely Mantua, named Ubald; and also Damian, cardinal of the Roman Church, who was likewise abbot of the monastery of Nonantola. All these men had come to hear his wisdom and to receive his counsel, as he and the other Catholics often used to do.”

Thus Rangerius. Since he testifies that this occurred in the year of Christ 1080, nine months after the blessed passing of Pope Gregory VII, there can be no doubt that this abbot Damian was created cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by that same supreme pontiff, Gregory—especially because of the exceptional affection with which he revered his most holy uncle, the grateful remembrance he inspired, his apostolic virtues, and his immense [Col. 0987B] services to the Roman Church. I have wished to say this briefly, so that it might in some measure become known who this abbot Damian was. [Col. 0988A]

But although the name of the writer who drew this work from the books of Saint Peter Damian is not given by the manuscripts, it is nevertheless evident that his labor has the greatest usefulness. In particular, while he brings forward testimonies from each of the most holy cardinal’s individual little works, he discloses to us with the steadfast fidelity of a disciple and eyewitness that those very works—which one might perhaps otherwise doubt—were written by so great a teacher. We hope, moreover, that this work, which we now bring to light, and the others that, with God’s favor, we are preparing for publication, will prove neither useless nor unwelcome to your studies, reader. [Col. 0988B] Farewell, and commend me to Christ the Lord in your prayers.

IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY AND UNDIVIDED TRINITY. HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF TESTIMONIES FROM THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT, WHICH ONE OF HIS DISCIPLES CAREFULLY EXCERPTED FROM THE MIRRORS OF THE REVEREND PETER DAMIAN.

[Col. 0987]

70–74 HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0987C] To his lord and father, Lord Damian, reverend abbot, the last servant among the monks offers the service of sincere devotion.

Recently, while your diligence, delighted as though by certain nectarous feasts, repeatedly reviewed the deeds of your uncle, our father Peter the bishop of blessed memory, I found in them something remarkable, which I perceived to overflow with the greatest usefulness. For when that illustrious man judged the arrogant eloquence of those people contemptible who, seeking the reputation of genius in every matter they undertake, strive to thicken whatever they invent with a manifold obscurity—laboring with tangled constructions of thought and unusual expressions to block it up, so that no one may grasp what they say or penetrate the inner substance of their discourse without an effort of shameful labor—he, on the contrary, earnestly desired to open and clarify the way for all readers, smoothing whatever was lofty and illuminating whatever was obscure, not only by reasoning but also by examples from the Scriptures.

Furthermore, if he had advanced something that might perhaps seem uncertain to those less skilled, he firmly surrounded it with testimonies from those same Scriptures, as though with anchors cast out, fastening it with immovable stability so that no one could continue to toss upon the waves. By fortifying it against all the attacks of its opponents, he blocked every entrance for ambush, so that no approach might lie open to any arrow. [Col. 0987D]

Indeed, he was accustomed to hold this support of the Scriptures so firmly in his writings that he sometimes decided to apply it even to words which, once the arguments had been presented, already stood closed on every side and unshaken. Thus, just as any city, after the circuit of its ditches and the impregnable defense of its strong walls, is still distinguished by lofty constructions of fortifications—not so much for the necessary strength of its defenses as for the beauty of the desired ornament—so he too seems often to have inserted many passages of Scripture into his writings for ornament alone. Or perhaps, as may reasonably be judged, he did so so that, by allowing an occasion for discussing them in this way, his discourse might make clear that what appeared outwardly empty possessed inwardly a fruitful substance. [Col. 0988C]

No one who frequents the thresholds of Scripture can be permitted to doubt that the passages so frequently introduced into his writings often concealed a wealth of mystical and sacred meaning. If they had not been unlocked, they would have been more likely to overwhelm than to illuminate. Penetrating and examining their inner parts with the hand of lucid exposition, and drawing every hidden thing completely out from its recesses, he made them, once their light had been revealed, appear clearer.

Whenever the words of reason alone seemed unable to satisfy, other testimonies were brought forward, which themselves often concealed their meaning beneath the veil of allegory or within the secret of some mystery, and thus compelled him to labor once more toward their explanation. In this way, by divine providence, it came about that many hidden things in sacred Scripture, most clearly unlocked through his works, shine for us with the brightness of evident understanding. [Col. 0988D]

When that diligent man had therefore considered how elegantly the testimonies of sacred Scripture mentioned above had been explained, I judged it worthy and exceedingly useful that excerpts from those books should be gathered into the single body of a separate volume, lest they lie hidden and unknown amid so many bulky compilations, to their detriment. By this consideration he clearly rendered no small service to all into whose hands these works would one day come; yet he appears to have provided especially for those who are not permitted to read many books. Since such people cannot rise to grasp the fullness of the entire work, at least, by applying themselves to these small portions, they need not remain completely hungry and fasting in the presence of the teaching of so great a man.

Those who are less able to draw a fertile catch from the channel of a vast torrent with a capacious net should not disdain to suspend an easy catch on the thread of a slender hook from this small inlet, drawn aside as though into its own channel, so that they may fill the measure of their refreshment with sufficient nourishment. [Col. 0989A]

Your holiness therefore deigned to entrust this undertaking to me—not, certainly, because the poverty of my understanding concealed it from me, but perhaps rather because you hoped that I would faithfully carry out what I thought I could accomplish according to my own capacity. Nor was this without reason, since you had long ago recognized that I had been favored, solely through his graciousness, by a certain privilege of affection from that same Father.

Therefore I myself, although not unaware of my own barrenness and not at all regarding myself as suitable for this task, nevertheless tried, without offering any excuse, not to withdraw my shoulder from this burden of obedience. I did not do so because I rashly trusted in the strength of my own abilities, but because I hoped that I could earnestly assist both the obedience with which I longed to comply with your command and the merits of the oft-mentioned Father, whose praise could not fail to support whatever result might come from my work. [Col. 0989B]

To this must be added that the difficulty of the work itself was not yet clear, since the initial instruction merely advised me to excerpt the testimonies in the order in which they happened to be found in his notebooks. But after I had proceeded through part of the work and deliberately observed that, under the method begun, the order of the work was becoming more confused than clear, and that the result might lead the reader more toward sleep than meditation, I judged it much better and more fruitful to undertake a labor of whatever difficulty than to pursue that unproductive ease.

I therefore abandoned the continuation of the original arrangement, in which the Old was mixed with the New, the Hagiographa, or the acts of kings, with the prophets, and began to organize everything afresh. I arranged and distinguished each testimony according to its own book, so that anyone who wished to seek them out more diligently might find each one in the same order in which it is situated in its respective book. [Col. 0989C]

Nor did I deny this careful treatment even to the preliminary incidental passages mentioned above. I inserted only their simple text among the others, so that, if I had placed them there together with their explanations, I would have doubled my own labor and caused the reader annoyance by repeating what he would recognize as already read earlier.

Moreover, I tried to give these passages titles in such a way that I expressly named the individual locations occupied by each in its own notebook. Nevertheless, let the reader beware: if he reads in a title “in the letter to such-and-such a person” or “in the sermon of that saint,” and does not find in that one letter or that one sermon everything he was perhaps seeking, let him not conclude that I should nearly be accused of falsehood. There are several letters addressed to one person, and in the praise of a single saint there are likewise several polished sermons. [Col. 0990A]

Accordingly, let him not doubt that what is found in these passages may be found in others as well, although the titles themselves will often be able to teach him this. He should also attend to the following point: when I found certain matters situated in different places, explained more fully in one place and more briefly in another, or even somewhat differently in style or order though under the same meaning, I sometimes selected from either side what seemed appropriate and composed it into the form of a single statement. At other times, when the matter required it, I placed both explanations here separately and in full, just as I found them there.

Nor should this point be passed over: in some cases I found passages proposed there that fit the statements so well that they ought not to be altered in their prefaces here. In other cases, I had to take what was suitable not only from passages set out somewhat farther away but also from those that followed; in still others, I was compelled to adapt material newly issued on its own. [Col. 0990B]

No one should find this surprising, since the statements preceding these passages did not everywhere refer directly to them as though they necessarily had to follow, even if they supplied the reason for introducing them. Hence it is clear that it was not necessary for every statement capable of being adapted to the introductory passages here to adhere to them everywhere.

But now, as I approach the end, I turn my words to you, Father, so that, to whom the beginnings are devoted, the conclusion may also rightly serve. First, I humbly beseech pardon before the greatness of your holiness for the errors by which I may perhaps seem to have failed in this undertaking. I also ask you to grant me, together with this favor, that you leave nothing uncorrected that ought to be corrected, lest afterward another hand find something outside this work to tear away while attacking me. [Col. 0990C]

For I do not suppose that I have run in such a way that I shall be found entirely and everywhere irreproachable. Whenever I appear deserving of rebuke, I prefer, confessing it myself, to attribute the fault to my own ignorance rather than defend it insolently.

If, however, I have accomplished anything that may perhaps please you, I attribute it, after God—to whom principally all the gifts that he distributes must be returned—to the obedience I have shown to your holiness and to the merits of that same Father, so often to be remembered. [Col. 0990D] I ask that your piety deign to commend me to the mercy of His majesty by your worthy prayers. I humbly request the same reward from all those whom this labor of mine may one day have benefited. [Col. 0991A]

[Col. 0991] The Prologue ends.

77–78 HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS.

1. God said: “Let there be light,” on the first day. 2. On the second day he made the firmament and the divisions of the waters. 3. “Let the waters that are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear.” 4. On the fourth day the luminaries were made in the firmament of heaven. 5. On the fifth day the fish and birds were created. 6. On the sixth day man was created. 7. On the Sabbath the Lord, having completed everything, rested and commanded man to rest. 8. The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs, and so forth. 9. When the Lord was walking in paradise, Adam hid himself because he was naked. 10. Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech. 11. “Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood, and coat it with pitch inside and out.” 12. Concerning the dimensions of the ark of the flood. 13. The water was fifteen cubits higher than all the mountains it had covered. 14. The flood began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days. 15. The ark came to rest in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia. 16. Concerning the raven and the dove sent out from the ark. 17. After waiting another seven days, Noah again sent the dove out from the ark. 18. “Come, let us make ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven.” 19. Concerning the five kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, and the other overthrown cities, who were defeated by four kings. 20. When Abraham was offering sacrifice to the Lord, he divided the cattle in half but did not divide the birds. 21. Abraham drove away the birds that descended upon the sacrifice. 22. When the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great and dark horror seized him. 23. “I shall go down and see whether they have actually done according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” 24. When the Sodomites attempted to break violently in upon the angels, they were struck with blindness. 25. Abraham offered his only son to God to be sacrificed. 26. Concerning Leah and Rachel, the wives of Jacob. 27. Concerning Bilhah and Zilpah, the maidservants. 28. Rachel called her son Ben-oni, but his father called him Benjamin. 29. This is Anah, who found hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of his father Zibeon. 30. Judah went down to Timnah to shear the sheep, with Hira the Adullamite, the shepherd of his flock. 31. Joseph ordered his servants to fill his brothers’ sacks with grain and to put each man’s money back into his sack; but in Benjamin’s sack they were also to enclose the cup together with the money.

The chapters end.

HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS.

CHAPTER ONE. In the letter to Hildebrand and Stephen, cardinals, in which he teaches how the rational soul reaches perfection.

[Col. 0991B]

I would like to touch briefly on how a human being can be brought to completion and how he ought to be perfected, insofar as this may be found in the order itself of the world’s creation. Since man is said to be a microcosm—that is, a smaller world—it is necessary that, striving toward the increase of his own fullness, he imitate the form of the world’s creation. Just as this visible and corporeal world was brought to completion through the mass and multitude of its parts, so our inner human being should gradually come to fullness through the growth of virtues.

Of this fullness the Apostle says in particular: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4). “And God said,” therefore, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1). In a human being, light is said to be made when illumination is granted so that the light of faith may shine upon him. [Col. 0992B]

The first light of the mind is faith. Hence the Apostle already says to the faithful: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). This is also the first commandment in the Law: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6). The first day therefore takes place in a human being when one who is new comes to faith.

CHAPTER TWO. In the same letter.

On the second day God made the firmament, which is heaven, and he made divisions among the waters, so that some might flow downward through the lower regions while others remained above. What is the firmament except the strength of the Scriptures? Hence we read: “For heaven shall be folded up like a book on the day of judgment” (Isaiah 34). What are the lower waters except the multitudes of human beings? And what are the upper waters except the choirs of angels?

For the angels do not have heaven above them but beneath them, because they do not need to hear the word of God by reading it: they behold the Lord himself openly present and continually burn with love for him. When a human being therefore begins, through the firmament—that is, through the teaching of heavenly speech—to see the lower and upper waters, separating carnal things from spiritual things and earthly things from heavenly things, then the second day comes to be in him. For he begins to possess not only the light of faith but also discernment concerning things. [Col. 0992C]

CHAPTER THREE. In the same letter.

Then God said: “Let the waters that are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear” (Genesis 1). Once the division has been made, as was said, between earthly and heavenly things, the human mind must still divide these same earthly things more minutely among themselves. Thus it must distinguish wicked people, itching with the saltiness of this earthly wisdom, from the righteous who thirst for the fountain of faith, as dry land is distinguished from the sea. [Col. 0993A]

For unbelievers, or carnal people, are shaken by the bitter waves of temptations and swell as though in the storms of desire or arrogance. But all the saints and righteous, like dry land, thirst for the Lord and, like fruitful soil, strive to bring forth green fruits of good works.

Therefore God commanded that on the same day the earth should bring forth green grass producing seed, and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit (Genesis 1). Whoever diligently carries this out, whoever meditates upon it subtly, without doubt already sees the third day dawn. Let each person therefore divide himself from the saltiness of those who think carnally and bitterly; having become dry land, let him thirst from the depths for the Lord, the fountain of life; let him bring forth the shoots of good fruits, so that the third day may shine upon him. [Col. 0993B]

CHAPTER FOUR. In the same letter.

When these things have been arranged and salutarily ordered, the human soul, as though the darkness of vices had been removed and quieted, begins to shine with the radiance of virtues. Hence it is said that on the fourth day the luminaries were made in the firmament of heaven (Genesis 1). For what does it mean that the earth first brings forth shoots and immediately afterward the luminaries are created, except that, when the shoot of a good work appears, a more abundant light rises in the soul, enabling it to imitate the footsteps of its Redeemer?

Let the earth of the human mind therefore hasten to bring forth the growth of spiritual harvests, so that it may be illuminated by the gleaming rays of inner light and, while enjoying the light of the fourth day, may also be carried away, in the manner of spiritual birds, to contemplate heavenly things. [Col. 0993C]

80 CHAPTER FIVE. In the same letter.

Hence it is that on the fifth day the fish were created, signifying those who receive the sacraments of baptism; and also birds, signifying those who, on the wings of virtues, raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things. Whoever, having despised the love of this world, as though disdaining to tread earthly mud, advances through the grace of contemplation toward the desire for heavenly glory, possesses the fifth day together with the birds.

Such a person no longer walks upon the earth but flies through the air, because, scorning all earthly things, he thirstingly longs for heavenly things: “My soul has thirsted,” he says, “for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41). [Col. 0994A]

Such a person is already formed, as a perfect man, according to the image of the Creator; for he possesses such dignity of spiritual gifts that he is now commanded not merely to observe the rule of any of the saints, but also to strive, insofar as is permitted, to imitate the example of God himself, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us” (Ephesians 5).

There was indeed a difference between Paul, who imitated Christ, and those whom he called to imitate himself: “Be imitators of me,” he says, “as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). [Col. 0994B]

CHAPTER SIX. In the same letter.

Hence man was created on the sixth day in the likeness of his Creator. Just as this was then accomplished at the beginning of the human condition, so now it is accomplished through the mystery of inner restoration.

Moreover, among all the living creatures of earth, water, and air, man receives, as it were, a monarchy and a certain principality of superior excellence, because every perfect man, perfected in virtues, knows how to pronounce right judgment concerning each of them, as the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2).

Almighty God makes such a perfect man—dead to the world and living to him—his throne, and through him he often proclaims the decree of his justice. Hence that angelic order through which almighty God more frequently issues his judgments is called the Thrones, because the supreme judge presides among them when he exercises judgments of equity through them.

God therefore makes the perfect man his seat, so that he may rest sweetly in him. Hence through the Prophet: “Upon whom,” he says, “does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and gentle person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

It should also be noted that concerning each day it is said: “There was evening, and there was morning.” Evening is the perfection of the good work; morning is the light of the mind. For when a good work reaches perfection, then the light of spiritual grace rises in the mind of the one who acts, so that, while he carries out a luminous work outwardly, the grace of the Spirit itself may illumine him inwardly. [Col. 0994C]

CHAPTER SEVEN. In the same letter.

Thus one arrives at the Sabbath, on which God himself, having completed everything, rests and commands man to rest. In this way man becomes God’s Sabbath, and God becomes man’s Sabbath, since man rests in God and God rests in him. “Remain in me,” he says, “and I in you” (John 14).

He himself is for us both timeless time and spaceless place: spaceless because he is not circumscribed, timeless because he never ends. He is time for us when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11). By the day he means himself, and by the twelve hours he means the same number of apostles.

A place is unmistakably expressed there where the Prophet, after saying, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail,” immediately adds: “The sons of your servants shall dwell” (Psalm 101)—there, beyond doubt, meaning “in you.”

God therefore made heaven and earth, and he is not said to have rested. He made all that feeds upon the earth and all that moves in the waters, and nowhere in all these things is he ever read to have rested. But once man had been fashioned in his image, the Sabbath of rest immediately dawned, and thus the Creator of the universe rested.

Although he himself says through the Prophet, “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 49), he is said to have rested in the creation of man alone, though this is not said in the creation of those other things.

And, to make you marvel more and more at the dignity of this day, Scripture says: “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work” (Genesis 2). No such action is found to have been performed on any of the other days. [Col. 0995A]

For what is it for God to sanctify the Sabbath except to build for himself a temple in the mind of a holy and perfect man? As the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3).

Moreover, just as we have spoken of the Sabbath, reason also requires us to speak of the temple, because God is the temple of man and man is the temple of God. Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw no temple in it, for the almighty God and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21). [Col. 0995B]

God is therefore the temple of man; man becomes the temple of God. This temple of man is the spiritual paradise: namely, a holy mind, a perfect mind, a pure mind, distinctly formed according to the image of its Creator.

This mind, I say—or rational soul—is rightly called paradise. It is watered by streams of heavenly gifts and adorned with green shoots of holy virtues, like fertile trees and grasses blossoming in spring. For that fountain or river which is said there to go forth from the place of delight to water paradise, and which is divided into four heads, is the reasoning of the mind. From it, as from an original fountain, four virtues flow like four health-giving streams: namely justice, courage, prudence, and temperance, which make the soil of our heart fertile. [Col. 0995C]

The tree of life is wisdom itself, the mother of good things. Concerning it Solomon also says: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds fast to her” (Proverbs 1). The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the transgression of the law that was imposed, and the experience of misery.

But since it is not our purpose to explain everything in order, let it suffice here to have briefly touched upon what pertains to this undertaking. [Col. 0995D]

CHAPTER EIGHT. In the sermon on Saint Columba.

For this reason the power of God was emptied, so that it might strengthen our weakness; for this reason sublimity was brought low, so that it might raise up the fallen; for this reason life deigned to die, so that, destroying the dominion of death, it might recall the dead to life.

This is also made clear at the very beginning of the human race. For it is written: “The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled in flesh in its place; and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Genesis 2).

When the Apostle was speaking about this and said, “A man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” he immediately added: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

And truly it is a sacrament indicating great power and marvelous profundity. Adam signifies Christ, and Eve signifies the Church. [Col. 0996A]

What does it mean that the Lord first put Adam to sleep and then drew a rib from his side, from which the woman was to be formed, except that our Redeemer first slept in death, and then blood and water flowed from his side as the sacrament of the Church?

Eve was taken from the side of the sleeping man; the Church came forth from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross.

But what does it mean that the almighty Creator, when he intended to bring forth a woman from a man—that is, the weaker sex from the stronger—did not wish to use the man’s flesh as material for making the woman, but rather chose a bone? God could have taken flesh from the man from which the woman might be formed, and that would certainly seem more fitting. For the weaker sex was being made, and it would seem more consistent for it to proceed from the weakness of flesh than from the strength of bone. [Col. 0996B]

Yet, to make you marvel still more at the mystery of the divine work, bone is not returned for bone; rather, he filled with flesh the place that had been empty in the man’s body. Hence, when Scripture says, “He took one of his ribs,” it immediately adds, “and filled in flesh in its place” (Genesis 2).

He could have taken flesh from the man to fashion the woman; he could have restored the loss of bone with bone while leaving the body unmaimed. But he took bone and returned flesh, and thus formed the fragile from strength.

Adam therefore became weak so that Eve might become strong; Christ was weakened so that the Church might be strengthened. His weakness is our strength, and for this reason he bore our weakness, so that he might establish us in his strength.

“What is weak in God,” the Apostle says, “is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1). And elsewhere: “For if Christ was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For we too are weak in him, but we live with him by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13). [Col. 0996C]

Indeed, the men of this world who seek to become renowned through the valor of war and desire their victories to be celebrated by the mouths of the people, when they are about to enter battle, place underneath whatever in their bodies is weak and soft, and put over it whatever is hard and difficult to penetrate. They clothe themselves in iron cuirasses and strive to protect the flesh, which readily yields to a blow, so that the hard and strong thing outside may defend the soft thing within. [Col. 0996D]

But when our Redeemer enters such a field of battle, when, as a strong warrior, he arms himself to defeat the wickedness of the air, he puts on a new kind of armor because he was about to institute a new battle: namely, he placed above what is weak and concealed what is strong.

He put on the cuirass of weak flesh and concealed the unconquerable strength of his divinity. Thus, thus, through flesh the devil was defeated by the second man, just as through flesh he had formerly overcome the first man; and the very thing that had been the means of victory over our first parent became the cause of his own ruin. [Col. 0997A]

CHAPTER NINE. In the letter to Ariprandus, in which he urges him, as a servant of God, not to devote himself to secular literature.

Cold conceived in the breast is accustomed to interrupt the voice. This cold had already been conceived by the man who, when the Lord was walking in the paradise breeze after midday, answered him in somewhat hoarse tones: “I heard your voice,” he said, “and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Genesis 3).

Moreover, since the midday heat had already departed from him, the breeze, which is the child of cold, approached him; for the loss of innocence had already stripped him naked. What else do all these things suggest except that the chill of extinguished love had constricted his inward parts, and that for this reason his voice sounded hoarse in the ears of the Lord?

Abraham, however, had remained wholly free from this cold; concerning him Scripture declares: “The Lord appeared to him in the heat of the day” (Genesis 18). And that heavenly Bridegroom, as we read in the Song of Songs, “feeds and lies down at noon” (Song of Songs 1). [Col. 0997B]

CHAPTER TEN. In the sermon of Saint Luke.

Blessed Luke, to show that we are cleansed from our sins through the coming of our Savior, begins the genealogy not from the beginning of the evangelical narrative but only from Christ’s baptism. Ascending through seventy-seven degrees of ancestry, he describes the succession of generations.

This is also clearly shown in the book of Genesis, where Lamech is reported to have said to his wives: “Sevenfold vengeance shall be exacted for Cain” (Genesis 4); but for Lamech it is said that vengeance shall be exacted seventy-sevenfold, because seventy-seven generations of human beings are said to have proceeded from his loins and afterward to have been swallowed up when the flood devoured them. [Col. 0997C]

But since Lamech is represented as striking or as having been struck, what else is signified by this except the first parent of the human race? He inflicted upon the whole race of succeeding descendants the weapon of sin by which he himself, having first been struck, perished.

Seventy-sevenfold vengeance was therefore exacted for this Lamech, because the sin contracted by the first man remained active in the human race through seventy-seven generations, until Christ. Original sin indeed remained, and he himself erased it through the sacrament of his baptism, from which Luke begins, where it is said of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). [Col. 0997D]

CHAPTER ELEVEN. In the book On the Perfection of Monks.

[Col. 0998A]

The divine voice commanded that the ark, which preserved eight souls amid the waves of the cataclysm, be coated with pitch inside and out. The holy Church, which advances toward the glory of the resurrection, is likewise coated within and without with pitch, so that outwardly it may be gracious in fraternal sweetness, and inwardly remain united in the truth of mutual love. For whoever loves inwardly but outwardly disagrees with his brothers through an abrasive harshness of conduct has pitch within but not without. Whoever, however, presents himself as agreeable merely in appearance and feigns friendship, but does not preserve the truth of friendship in the hidden recess of his heart, gapes open ruinously within while outwardly he appears joined by the simulation of the pitch spread over him [Col. 0998B]. Neither of these is rescued from the shipwreck of the flood, because neither is fortified by the twofold pitch of charity, as divinely commanded.

But whoever presents himself as lovable outwardly and preserves love inwardly, outwardly displaying the fruit of good works with the branches of the word, and inwardly fixing a deep root because he loves from the marrow of his being—this person is certainly coated with pitch both inside and out, because he is bound to his neighbors by the twofold bond of charity. Moreover, since the ark is first commanded to be made from smoothed wood and afterward to be coated with pitch, this clearly indicates to us that our timbers—that is, our hard and uncultivated ways—must first be polished through the discipline of spiritual practice, so that pitch may then be applied to the structure once it has been fitted together. Indeed, as long as human conduct is harsh and uncultivated, the glue of charity is applied to no purpose, since people quickly fly apart from one another when an even and polished union of mortal life is not maintained among them [Col. 0998C].

## CHAPTER XII. In a sermon on the exaltation of the holy cross

The mystery of the cross was contained in that ark of the flood, whose length Scripture defines as having been three hundred cubits. This number is contained in the letter *Tau*, which expresses the shape of the cross. Moreover, just as Noah and his companions are saved through water and wood, so the household of Christ is saved through water and wood, being washed in the baptism of salvation and marked with the impression of the life-giving cross. That ark, so that it might appear to correspond in its dimensions to the sacrament of Christ’s human body, is said to have had three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. For three hundred contains the number fifty six times and thirty ten times; and the length of the human body—from the top of the head to the feet—is six times its width, which extends from the right side to the left, and ten times its height, which extends from front to back.

Thus the ark, both in the number three hundred that expresses its length and in the character of its total dimensions, bears the form of the cross and the figure of the Lord’s body. And just as seven souls were granted to Noah so that they might be saved through the wood amid the waters, so seven Churches, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, are saved in Christ through the wood of the cross and the water of baptism [Col. 0999A]. Through wood, the prince of pride subjected us to slavery; through this wood, the Author of humility restored us to the rank of freedom.

## CHAPTER XIII. In a sermon on Saint P.

“Fifteen cubits higher did the water rise above all the mountains that it had covered” (Gen. VII). The number fifteen, plainly, because it consists of seven and eight, contains within itself the mystery of blessed rest and the future resurrection: for almighty God both rested on the eighth day when he created the world and rose on the eighth when he redeemed it.
