The power of this number also contains a special sacrament in baptism, where we rise anew from our former state and afterward are commanded to rest from the disturbance of worldly commotion [Col. 0999B].

Those who swell with the ostentation of worldly glory or with the vanities of earthly wisdom do not understand this mystery of the rest of the seventh day and the resurrection of the eighth. Hence it is plainly said here that “fifteen cubits higher did the water rise above all the mountains that it had covered”: the mountains signify the proud and haughty. Thus the lofty and profound mystery of resurrection and inward rest surpasses the entire understanding of the proud wise.

## CHAPTER XIV. In the same sermon

“The waters returned over the earth, going and returning, and began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days” (Gen. VIII). Since, in the mystery of our regeneration, the rest of the seventh is joined to the resurrection of the eighth, it is rightly said in the Book of Genesis that the waters returned from the earth and began to diminish after one hundred and fifty days. For seventy, counted from seven, and eighty, counted from eight, joined together make one hundred and fifty.

## 86 CHAPTER XV. In the same sermon

“The ark came to rest, in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia” (Gen. VIII), because the rest of the seventh is appropriately commended in baptism. This is recognized as having been prefigured through that flood, in which, rising anew from our former state, we are afterward commanded to rest from the disturbance of worldly commotion [Col. 0999D].

## CHAPTER XVI. In the book *On the Perfection of Monks*

In the sea of this world the righteous labor, while the wicked possess their rest. The raven sent out from the ark and the dove signify this difference well. “The raven, sitting upon corpses, did not return to the bars of the ark; but the dove returned, because it found no place where its foot might rest” (Gen. VIII). Here, where the wicked satisfy themselves with carnal pleasures, holy men cannot find where to place the foot of their desire for rest.

## CHAPTER XVII. In a sermon on the Lord’s Supper

While the crimes of the world were once being purged by the outpoured flood, the dove prefigured the likeness of the future gift when, through an olive branch, it announced that peace had been restored to the earth. Scripture says: “After waiting another seven days, Noah again sent the dove out of the ark; and it came to him toward evening, carrying in its mouth a branch of an olive tree with green leaves” (Gen. VIII). The number seven is placed in the sending out and return of the dove, because there are undoubtedly known to be seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The dove returns to the ark in the evening hour because the Holy Spirit, who at the beginning of the world was borne over the waters, filled the holy Church as the age was already growing old [Col. 1000B].

## CHAPTER XVIII. In a letter to the nun Hirmisind, in which it is said that the structure of human pride is quickly destroyed

“When they set out from the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and settled there. And one said to his neighbor, ‘Come, let us make bricks and burn them with fire.’ And they had bricks for stone and bitumen for mortar” (Gen. XI).

Since Christ is truly the East, as the prophet bears witness when he says, “Behold the man whose name is East” (Zech. VI), those come from the East who withdraw from fellowship with Christ by living badly or by rending their neighbors. Shinar is interpreted as “shaking of teeth,” or “their stench.” Therefore those dwell in the plain of Shinar who, established not in the citadel of virtues but rather in the valley of vices, both shake their teeth—that is, gnaw their neighbors with slanders as though with their teeth—and emit stenches, rotting amid the filth of a muddy way of life. But almighty God shakes out their teeth when he confounds both the deeds and the words of the perverse.

Hence it is also said there: “Therefore its name was called Babel” (Gen. XI), because there the language of the whole earth was confused, and therefore the Lord scattered them over the face of the other regions. It is rightly said, then, that those proud men and seekers of empty glory, saying to one another, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven, and let us make our name famous before we are scattered over all the lands,” dwelt in the plain of Shinar—which, as has been said, signifies for us “shaking of teeth” or “their stench.”

For all the perverse, when they grow proud against the commands of divine law, when they arrogantly raise the neck of their hearts against the Lord, and sometimes damnably slander their neighbors, are themselves more readily rolled about in the dungheap of an obscene life. Of the shaking of teeth David says: “You have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners” (Ps. III). And elsewhere: “God will break their teeth in their mouths; the Lord will shatter the molars of lions” (Ps. LVII). Another prophet also speaks of their stench: “The beasts have rotted in their own dung” (Joel I). And Isaiah says: “There will be stench instead of sweet fragrance” (Isa. III).

Indeed, whoever wishes to build a structure that will not easily collapse into ruin must not use bricks and bitumen, which quickly fall apart, but rather stones and rocks to raise the walls, together with mortar of lime and sand to bind those walls in an unbroken joining of stones. The fact, therefore, that the Babylonians mentioned above had bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar signifies a structure of carnal life, soon to be overwhelmed by the force of winds or the violence of floods.

## CHAPTER XIX. In a letter to Boniface the Advocate, where it is said that spiritual wisdom should be preferred to outward prudence

[Col. 1001B]

“The prudence of this world is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. VIII). Hence it is that, as the Book of Genesis says, the five kings who refused to submit to Chedorlaomer were defeated by four kings—and where? In the Valley of the Forest, which is now the Salt Sea (Gen. XIV).

Who are the four kings, then, except the four virtues that sacred Scripture names as principal? What else are signified by the five kings except the same number of bodily senses, and through them external knowledge? Just as those four virtues proceed, as it were, from the original source of their mother—namely, the fountain of reason—so these five senses linger in the vanity of earthly wisdom, as though in a salt valley, and there are overthrown by their enemies [Col. 1001C]. For it is fitting that spiritual wisdom should conquer in the human soul and that the cunning of carnal prudence should perish.

Hence it is also read concerning David that he made a name for himself when he returned after Syria had been captured and twelve thousand had been slain in the Valley of Salt (2 Sam. I).

## CHAPTER XX. In a letter to Pope Alexander

“Having taken all these,” Scripture says, “he divided them down the middle and placed the two parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds” (Gen. XV). Earthly animals are set opposite one another and face each other because all who are earthly rage against their neighbors through quarrels and disputes, or at least burn secretly against them with the kindling of hatred. But those who raise themselves aloft on the wing of heavenly desire, when they offer themselves to God as a sacrifice, do not withdraw from the bond of mutual love [Col. 1001D].

## CHAPTER XXI. In a letter to Desiderius, abbot of Cusin

Evil spirits strive either to pollute our prayers with wicked thoughts or to corrupt good works by the contamination of some sin. Hence it is written that “when Abraham devoutly offered a sacrifice of cattle and birds to God, birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away” (Gen. XV). What do the birds express except reprobate spirits flying about through the air? We therefore drive the birds away from our sacrifice when we carefully guard the prayer—or the offerings of our works—from the evil spirits that attempt to defile them [Col. 1002A].

## CHAPTER XXII. To Pope Alexander, where he complains of the insolence of wicked men

“When the sun was setting, sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great and dark terror seized him” (Gen. XV). The setting of the sun signifies the fall of the world; the great and dark terror represents the gloom of vices and crimes, which daily grow dreadfully through the feverish depravity of reprobate men. Hence a little later it is added there: “When the sun had set, a dark fog was made, and a smoking furnace appeared.”

For just as smoke issues from the fire of a furnace that is steaming, so the darkness of all vices and crimes is generated from the furnace of burning greed. As the Apostle said: “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). This occurs near the end of the day, that is, near the end of the world. The smoking furnace therefore generates a dark fog, because the furnace of greed, which burns in the breasts of wicked men, darkens the world with the pestilential darkness of many perversions.

Does it not blind the minds of the wretched [luxury, desire, or something similar, or greed is missing], since it both removes faith and extinguishes the light of all virtues in their hearts? Hence, after the Apostle had said this, he immediately added: “Some, desiring this greed, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Tim. VI) [Col. 1002C]. They pierce themselves with many sorrows when, for the sake of temporal profits, they fly apart from one another in irreconcilable hostility; and often, when they rush into arms over bodily possessions, they strip their souls from their bodies.

Those who burn only for heavenly things, however, receive pleasures instead of sorrows, because they live together in harmony in the sweetness of fraternal charity. Hence, in that evening sacrifice which Abraham then offered, he placed the earthly animals separated from one another but did not divide the birds. Thus Scripture says: “Having taken all these, he divided them down the middle and placed the two parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds” (Gen. XV).

## CHAPTER XXIII. In a letter to Pope Leo, where he complains that he has been accused

[Col. 1002D]

If we attentively consider the deeds of our Creator, we ought not readily to lend credence to accusations of anyone’s wrongdoing. For he whose eyes see all things naked and open did not disdain, when speaking to Abraham about the outcry concerning Sodom that had come to him, to say: “I will go down and see whether they have actually done according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XI). This appears to have been said for no other purpose than to teach human ignorance not to believe what is heard without examination, not to judge the unknown lightly, and not to pronounce a sentence before approving a doubtful matter by evidence.

## CHAPTER XXIV. In the book *Gomorrhianus*

“And behold,” Scripture says, “the men reached out their hand, brought Lot in to themselves, and shut the door; and they struck with blindness those who were outside, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Gen. XIX).

The Sodomites attempt to break violently in upon the angels when unclean men try to approach the Lord through the offices of the sacred order. But such men are struck with blindness, because by God’s just judgment they fall into inner darkness, so that they cannot find the door, since, having been separated from God by sinning, they do not know by what way they might return to him.

For those who desire to approach the Lord not by the path of humility but through the winding ways of arrogance and swelling pride plainly do not recognize where the entrance lies. Or, since Christ is the door, as he himself says, “I am the door” (John X), those who lose Christ through sins that demand punishment do not find the door [*ostium*], as though they might enter the dwelling of the heavenly citizens. They have therefore been handed over to a reprobate mind, because, while they do not weigh the burden of their guilt with careful consideration on the scales of their own mind, they regard a very heavy mass of lead as the lightness of empty feathers.

What is said there—“They struck with blindness those who were outside”—the Apostle openly explains when he says: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind.” And what follows there—“so that they could not find the door”—this same Apostle clearly interprets when he says: “to do what is not fitting” (Rom. I), as if he were saying, “to attempt to enter where they ought not” [Col. 1003C].

## CHAPTER XXV. In a sermon on the finding of the holy cross

When Abraham wished to sacrifice his son to God, he signified nearly all the mysteries of Christ’s Passion in their order. For just as Abraham—whose name is interpreted as “exalted father”—did not hesitate to offer his only and beloved son to God, so the supreme Father handed over his only-begotten Son for us all.

And just as Isaac himself carried the wood on which he was to be laid (Gen. XXII), so Christ also carried on his shoulders the wood of his cross, on which he was to suffer for our salvation. The two servants left behind at a distance signify the Jews. Living slavishly and thinking carnally, they did not understand the supreme humility of Christ; and therefore they ascended the mountain, that is, the place of sacrifice [Col. 1003D].

Why two servants, unless because, when Solomon sinned, one Israelite people became two peoples? (1 Kings XI.) To these the prophet often says: “Israel the adversary and Judah the transgressor” (Jer. III). The donkey that Abraham then used was the senseless folly of the Jews: that brutish folly carried all the mysteries, yet, like an irrational animal, did not know what it was carrying.

Now what does it mean that they were told: “Wait here with the donkey; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you” (Gen. XXII)? Hear the Apostle: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). What is meant by “A partial hardening has come upon Israel”? It means, clearly, “Wait here with the donkey, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters”—that is, “After we have worshiped,” when the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been accomplished and has been proclaimed among all the nations. What follows—“and thus all Israel will be saved”—means, “We shall return to you.”

What, moreover, is the ram found caught by its horns among the thorns, which is offered in sacrifice in place of Isaac? The cross has horns: two pieces of wood are joined to one another, and thus produce the form of a cross. Hence it is written concerning Christ: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. III). The ram caught by its horns is therefore Christ crucified amid the sharp and wounding iniquities of the Jews. As he himself complains through Jeremiah, saying: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.”

After the sacrifice had been completed, Abraham was told: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). And after the Lord says, “They pierced my hands and my feet,” he adds a little later in the same psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. XXI).

After Abraham had offered his son and sacrificed the ram in his place, he called the name of that place “The Lord sees.” For our Redeemer, after being offered upon the altar of the cross [Col. 1004C] and paying the debt of our death, thereafter presented himself to the sight of his faithful, so that all the redeemed might now see through faith the one for whom until then they had no eyes of faith.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Leah and Rachel, in the book *On the Perfection of Monks*

It is not obscure that Laban had two daughters, of whom Jacob desired the younger in marriage; yet he could not attain her embrace until, unknowingly and indeed unwillingly, he had taken the elder (Gen. XXIX). But since I am speaking to those who understand the matter, I need not labor over it with many words.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Who, then, is converted to the Lord except in order that, having laid aside the blackness of sins, he may be whitened through the grace of remission? As he himself promises, saying: “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow” (Isa. I). That blessed sinner sought this when she said: “I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L).

Leah is interpreted as “laboring”; Rachel as “word,” or “beginning of sight.” But if we attend carefully to Scripture, we do not find that Jacob served even one day because of his desire for Leah; rather, he submitted to servitude through all those weeks of years for Rachel alone, and in addition endured Leah herself for the sake of Rachel’s appearance.

Who turns to the Lord for the purpose of suffering labors, hardships, and the contests of temptations? Every intention of one who seeks the Lord hopes and strives for this: that one day he may reach rest and rest in the joy of the highest contemplation, as though in the embrace of beautiful Rachel—that is, that through the word he hears he may ascend to see the beginning he has sought.

Yet it is necessary that the labor of various struggles exercise him before he reaches the inner sweetness of rest that he desires. He is first weighed down by servitude so that afterward he may rightly be advanced to the rank of perfect freedom. He serves seven years under the grace of whitening when he keeps the seven commandments of the Decalogue that concern love of neighbor: namely, when first constrained by fear and therefore pressed down under the yoke of servitude, he begins at least with the ordinances of the old law—honoring parents, not committing adultery, not killing, not stealing, not giving false testimony, not coveting another’s wife, and not coveting his neighbor’s property (Exod. XX) [Col. 1005B].

When these duties have been properly observed, he is not immediately led, as he had hoped, to the delights of contemplation, so as to enjoy the long-awaited beauty of Rachel; rather, Leah is unexpectedly substituted for her during the night. For amid the darkness of human ignorance, the endurance of labor is imposed upon him, yet from it he now receives a numerous offspring, because through this labor he acquires abundant fruits of spiritual profit. By enduring her, he will eventually reach the one whom he loves perseveringly.

He is therefore advised to labor earnestly in serving another seven years, because it is plainly necessary that he preserve seven further commandments, now somewhat freer—not the legal commandments as a slave, but the evangelical commandments as a son-in-law: that he be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungry and thirsty for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and finally a peacemaker (Matt. V).

Indeed, if it were possible, a person would wish to undergo no hardships of labor either by doing or by suffering, but immediately, at the very beginnings of his training, to reach the delights of beautiful contemplation. Yet this does not take place in the land of the dying, but in the land of the living. This seems to be signified by what Laban says to Jacob: “It is not customary in our place to give the younger in marriage first” (Gen. XXIX). The elder is not improperly called the one who comes first in time. For in the instruction of a human being, the labor of good works comes before the rest of contemplation.

When the two weeks have been completed—one of the ancient law, the other of evangelical grace—the long-desired embrace of Rachel is immediately attained, because whoever desires to reach the delights of divine contemplation must first strive to fulfill the commands of both Testaments [Col. 1005D].

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Bilhah and Zilpah, in the same book

Since every elect person, not content with the limit of his own perfection, also desires to beget children for God through spiritual fruitfulness, after Jacob had entered into the marriage bond with the two sisters, he did not refuse to take the maidservants as well for the purpose of begetting, so as to propagate a more abundant offspring (Gen. XXX). And so that everything might be understood as overflowing with spiritual mysteries, even the names of the maidservants themselves have been pronounced under mystical figures [Col. 1006A].

For Bilhah is interpreted as “grown old.” Since the human tongue cannot express the understanding of spiritual substance in bare words, the teaching of wisdom sometimes tries to instruct its hearer through certain bodily likenesses. Images belonging to an old life devoted to carnal perceptions are therefore conceived; their use is assumed for teaching whenever something is heard concerning the incomprehensible and unchanging essence of divinity.

Rachel therefore preferred to receive children from a maidservant in some fashion rather than remain wholly barren. For the teaching of wisdom, or the grace of contemplation, makes known to its hearers through external knowledge or the forms of visible things whatever it conceals within the secret places of the mind concerning visible things; and thus, in a certain sense, it receives children through a maidservant, when through the knowledge subordinate to it she bears spiritual children for God.

Zilpah, however, is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” This maidservant therefore signifies those whose mouth gapes in the preaching of the evangelical faith, but whose heart does not gape; concerning them it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV), and concerning them the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal—do you steal?” (Rom. II) [Col. 1006B].

Nevertheless, Leah received from this maidservant other sons who would become heirs, because active life has often adopted many sons of the kingdom through such preachers. Concerning them the Truth says: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). And the Apostle says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice” (Phil. I).

We must consider this in them: just as Jacob took all those women and fathered children by them solely for Rachel’s sake, so whoever is established under the grace of whitening and desires to bear fruit for God through spiritual fecundity must direct everything he does toward the grace of contemplation.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. In a letter to Desiderius, abbot, where it is said why Paul is placed on the right and Peter on the left in a painting

“As Rachel’s soul was departing because of her pain, and death was already near, she called the name of her son Ben-oni, that is, ‘son of my pain’; but his father called him Benjamin, that is, ‘son of the right hand’” (Gen. XXXV).

Rachel, whose name is interpreted as “sheep” or “beginning of sight,” appropriately signifies the Church. She lives innocently like a sheep and burns inwardly with the desire, through the pursuit of contemplation, to see the appearance of her Redeemer. To the Jews who questioned him, he said of himself: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII).

Benjamin, at whose birth Rachel the mother dies, signifies Paul, whom no one doubts to have arisen from her stock. It is fitting that the mother is said to die when Benjamin is born, because, as Saul approaches the light of a new birth, the Church is grievously attacked by persecutions through him. Thus Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Saul was ravaging the Church, entering house after house, dragging off men and women, and handing them over to custody” (Acts VIII) [Col. 1007A].

Rachel therefore appropriately calls him Ben-oni, that is, “son of my pain,” while Jacob names him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” For Paul, who had been the pain of Mother Church and who, in a certain sense, killed her by attacking her as he was being born, was called by God the Father “son of the right hand.” Through him divine power fought against the nations as though through its strong right hand; through him it vigorously hurled the darts of words, inflicted salutary wounds upon hearts, and, after conquering and overthrowing the enemies through him, triumphed with glory.

Hence the same Paul says to the Galatians: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might preach him among the nations, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. I) [Col. 1007B]. Paul is therefore not improperly called the son of the right hand, since through him the whole multitude of the nations, which is to be placed at God’s right hand, is gathered into the mysteries of the faith.

## 94 CHAPTER XXIX. To Desiderius, abbot, that he should devote himself to the study of contemplation

“This is Ana, who found hot waters in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of Sebeon his father” (Gen. XXXVI).

As far as the literal sense is concerned, this plainly appears pointless and frivolous. What relevance does it have to sacred Scripture to report that a keeper of asses found water in the desert? But where no usefulness appears in the written account, the mind must necessarily turn to spiritual understanding.

What is figuratively meant by Ana pasturing the asses of his father in the wilderness except that a spiritual man, whose father is God, guards simple brothers under the discipline of a more remote way of life? And what does finding hot waters mean except to break forth into tears of compunction, which are drawn from the fervor of the Holy Spirit?

The interpretation of the names themselves does not resist this understanding. For Onan is interpreted as “their pain,” or “sorrow,” and also as “muttering” or “murmuring.” Whoever is truly saddened by the pain of compunction is compelled, as though in a kind of plaintive muttering, to murmur against the perversity of his own life. Sebeon, however, is interpreted as “standing in equity,” which everyone knows to be fitting for God. For he principally stands in equity who, compelled by no necessity, deviates from the straightness of justice.

Thus Onan, while pasturing his father Sebeon’s asses in the wilderness, finds hot waters, because whoever shows himself to be a son of God through uprightness of life and grieves from the marrow of his being over his sins, while making himself solicitous in the unceasing care of his brothers, receives the grace of tears as a divine gift.

That blessed sinner first anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment, and afterward poured an alabaster flask of precious ointment over his reclining head (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV; John XII). The head of Christ is God; the feet of Christ are the servants of God. For just as she, while devoting herself to the service of Christ’s humanity, was found worthy to attain an understanding of his divinity, so, certainly so, the teacher of the Church, while guarding Christ’s members, receives the grace of contemplating divinity [Col. 1008A].

## CHAPTER XXX. In a sermon on Saint John the Baptist

“Judah went down to Thamnas to shear the sheep, with Hira the shepherd of his flock, the Odollamite” (Gen. XXXVIII).

Thamnas is interpreted as “failing.” Through it the Synagogue is signified, in which kings and prophets had failed; and likewise the anointing, until the one to whom it had been reserved should come, was shown to have failed. Hence the prophet says: “When the Holy of Holies comes, the anointing will cease” (Dan. IX).

What, then, is understood by Judah, who comes to Thamnas to shear the sheep, except our Redeemer, who is recognized as having come to the Synagogue in order to relieve of their sins the lost sheep of the house of Israel? Hence the Bridegroom says to the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song IV).

Judah therefore came to shear the sheep, not alone, but with his shepherd, the Odollamite, whose name was Hira. Whom do we understand by the Odollamite except John? Odollamite is interpreted as “testimony in water.” The Lord came to the water of baptism with precisely this testimony: he had a testimony greater than John’s, but for the sake of weak sheep he deigned to use this testimony in the water.

Thus, when John saw him approaching the waters of the Jordan, he immediately cried out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). And the Evangelist says: “John bore witness, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven and remaining upon him; and I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”’” (ibid.) [Col. 1008C].

The name of that shepherd also corresponds most fittingly to this vision. For Hira is interpreted as “vision of my brother.” The Lord was John’s brother not only according to the seed of Abraham but also according to the kinship of Mary and Elizabeth. John therefore saw his brother while still enclosed in the womb; he saw him in baptism; he saw the man with the eyes of the flesh; he saw majesty in the spirit.

Thus the same John comprehended the interpretation of both names—Hira, namely, “vision of my brother,” and Odollamite, which means “testimony in water”—in the single statement: “And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (ibid.) [Col. 1008D].

When Judah had gone to shear the sheep, Tamar changes her clothing, because she changes her spiritual designation. For Tamar is interpreted as “changing,” for from the Synagogue she becomes the Church. But according to the literal sense, the same name retains the meaning of bitterness—not that bitterness in which a soldier offered gall to the Lord to drink (Matt. XXVII), but rather that in which Peter, after his fall, wept bitterly (ibid.). Judah, however, is called “confession.” Thus Tamar, sleeping with Judah, immediately conceives, because when bitterness is mingled with confession for the production of the fruits of repentance, the holy Church is at once made fruitful. Hence John also says: “Produce, he says, fruits worthy of repentance” (John III). The fruit of repentance first burst forth in Jerusalem, and afterward sprouted throughout the whole breadth of the world. Therefore the Truth says: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV).

For that harlot’s clothing also signifies confession of sins, either because Tamar is composed of two corrupted words—namely, *thamna*, which is said to mean “failing,” and *mara*, which means “bitterness.” In her, bitterness rightly failed when, made fruitful from barrenness, she produced the sweet offspring of a new shoot. Tamar, therefore, is impregnated by one who does not know her, because, with respect to the Gentiles, the holy Church at the beginning, while receiving the seed of the new faith, is not recognized. Hence it is sung: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. XVII). And Isaiah says: “Behold, you will call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you will run to you” (Isa. LV).

Moreover, what does it signify that the kid is sent to her through the same Odollamite, except the reproach of sins made through John? The messenger was, as it were, carrying a kid to the harlot when he said by way of reproof to the crowd hastening to the washing of baptism: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III).

Hiras the Odollamite, however, asked Tamar for a ring, a bracelet, and a staff. The ring signifies the seal of faith; the bracelet, the labor of works; and the staff, the rest of hope. He was, as it were, asking for the ring of faith when he said: “Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but whoever is unbelieving toward Christ the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III). Did the ring not also belong here when he said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom”? (ibid.)

He demanded the bracelet of labor when he said: “Repent” (Matt. III). He also demanded the rest of the staff when he immediately added: “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). It was as though he were speaking plainly: “Do not grow weary under the labor of the repentance imposed upon you, but rather strengthen your spirit with firm hope in the nearness of the heavenly kingdom.”

Judah sought her at the crossroads but could not find her, because she who, according to the Prophet, had been prostituted publicly and beneath every leafy tree (Jer. III) had now restrained herself in her father’s house, that is, under the discipline of Christ. The reproach of sin did not find her, since bitterness had changed her into confession.

She clothed herself in the garments of widowhood, because, apart from the heavenly Bridegroom who died for her, she admits no other. That twins appeared in the womb signifies the two peoples generated in the bosom of the Church through the grace of the Holy Spirit. In the very act of their being brought forth, one extended his hand and, after a scarlet thread had been tied around it, immediately withdrew it; thus he opened the way for the other to be born before him.

For the Jewish people, which had first begun to be born to the light of the Spirit, displayed its own deeds, stained with the blood of the prophets who went before and of the Lord himself. Hence Zara is interpreted as “rising,” because that Hebrew people arose first for the letter of the law, but became later in receiving the grace of the Gospel. In this way the people of the Jews, which had already begun to be born through the Spirit, withdrew its hand; and immediately the people of the Gentiles burst forth and became the firstborn, so that, according to the saying of the Truth, those who were first might be last, and those who were last might become first.

Phares therefore rightly received the name of division. Hence the midwife cried out at his birth: “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” (Gen. XXXVIII). The entire human race, like crooked thickets of the forest, had made a wall against the Lord coming in the flesh, and unanimously resisted him lest he enter to accomplish the mystery of redemption. Hence Paul says: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. I).

But the Gentile people divided this wall, as it were, by being born, when through the centurion Cornelius and others (Acts X), receiving the first fruits of faith and the washing of baptism, it flocked beneath Christ’s standard. Blessed John was considering this alternation in birth when, with crowds of Jews streaming together from every side, he said: “Do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Mark III). It was as though he were saying openly: “The Gentile peoples, who are stones because they worship stones, will become firstborn for the sacrament of regeneration and of the new grace, though by the legal ceremonies you appeared to have held primacy over them.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. In a Sermon on Saint Luke the Evangelist

“Joseph ordered the servants to fill the sacks with grain and to put each man’s money back in his sack” (Gen. XLIV). What are the crops that Joseph bestowed upon his brothers except evangelical and apostolic doctrine, by which the hungry people may live and the flock of Christ may gather the living nourishment of salvation? This is plainly the money that he ordered to be placed in the mouth of the sack; this money is now set before us on the table of the Church, so that interest may afterward be demanded from the traders.

But Benjamin is also given this additional distinction above the others: a cup is placed in his sack together with the money (ibid.). Whom does Joseph indicate mystically except our Redeemer, whom he was already prefiguring through that mystery of his? For Scripture says: “Pharaoh changed his name and called him, in the Egyptian language, ‘Savior of the world’” (Gen. XLI). Whom do the brothers signify except the holy apostles? Whom does Benjamin signify except Paul, who derived his origin from the tribe of Benjamin?

All the brothers therefore receive the fruits of preaching, which they are to sow throughout the world, and the money that they are to place on the table of faith for the profit of interest. To Benjamin alone, however, a cup is also added, so that through Paul, whom Benjamin represented, not the cup of the tabernacle but a broad and open vessel of the word might be offered to the Gentiles.

Hence he says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged; you are not cramped within us” (2 Cor. VI). It is as though he were saying: “Since you see the drink of the word flowing abundantly to you through a generous cup, open wide your mouths, with hearts thirsting to drink, so that the flowing stream may not run uselessly but may find capacious vessels into which it can be poured.”

Of this drink the Lord says through Isaiah: “The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches, because I have given waters in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen one” (Isa. XLIII). The cup of evangelical preaching was therefore given in Benjamin to Paul, so that he might especially cultivate the wilderness of the Gentiles and water its dryness with the abundant rain of holy preaching. Of this rain it is written: “He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth” (Ps. CXLVI).

## CHAPTER XXXII. In a Sermon on Saint Vitale

“If I have found favor in your sight,” Jacob said, “put your hand under my thigh and show me mercy and truth, so that you do not bury me in Egypt, but I may sleep with my fathers, etc.” (Gen. XLVII). What is this, my brothers? What does such anxious concern for the burial of his body by so great a man mean? If we measure this by human custom, we certainly find nothing worthy of such excellence of prophetic mind. Wherever a human body is buried, it is undoubtedly believed that its resurrection will be neither less perfect nor less glorious. But if the depth of the mystical sacrament is sought in the darkness of this question, a clear light of understanding will arise for whoever discovers it.

The corpses of the dead signify the sins of those who live unjustly. Just as the law commands people to be purified after contact with dead bodies (Num. XIX), so after the commission of offenses we are commanded to be washed through repentance. Hence that saying was uttered: “He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit?” (Sir. XXXIV). He is baptized by a dead person who is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person who returns to his fault after his tears.

The burial of the dead, however, signifies the forgiveness of sins. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI). Where, then, were the corpses of the patriarchs to be buried except in that land where the one whose blood brought about the forgiveness of sins was to be crucified?

## CHAPTER XXXIII. In a Sermon on the Discovery of the Holy Cross

“He will wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX). The garment and cloak of Christ are the multitude of the Gentiles, whom the Lord clothed when he joined them to himself through the grace of redemption, as he promises through the Prophet, saying: “As I live, says the Lord, I will clothe myself with them all as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX). The Lord therefore washed his garment in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape when, like a cluster of grapes, he hung upon the wood of the cross. Then blood and water flowed from his side; but the water washed us and the blood redeemed us, so that he might present to himself a bride without stain or wrinkle (Eph. V).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. In a Sermon on Saint Eleucadius

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine,” Jacob said to his son concerning Christ, “and his teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX). The eyes of Christ are the Apostles and Evangelists, who have supplied the light of wisdom to the entire body of the holy Church. Their beauty surpasses, in a certain sense, the austerity of old wine, because their doctrine softens the strictness and hardness of the ancient law. The commandments of the Gospel are far clearer than the precepts of the Old Testament.

The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut converted people away from the company of the wicked and, receiving them into Christ’s body as his members, as it were chew them and transfer them into it. By the name “milk,” however, the doctrine of the law is indicated, which seemed to nourish the carnal people like infants with a cup of milk. The teachers of the Church are whiter than their milk, because they themselves consume solid and substantial food of the word and hand it on to others. Of them the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Heb. II).

The teachers of the Church are rightly said to be white because they are free from the stain of wickedness and appear bright in their works of conspicuous conduct. Therefore, my brothers, we must beware lest the blackness of vices disgrace us, since we have white leaders in Christ’s service. The appearance of affairs is surely perilous when the insignia of the army that follows do not correspond with those of its leaders.

Our blessed fathers willingly offered themselves to endure punishments; we, however, when injured by our neighbor, restrain at least our spirits from revenge. Moses, descending from the mountain as a sign of vengeance, appeared horned (Exod. XXXIV); but upon the Lord, in the Spirit of gentleness, a dove descended (Matt. III). They resolved to despise everything of their own for Christ; let us at least learn not to covet what belongs to others.

*The testimonies of the Book of Genesis end.*

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF EXODUS BEGIN

1. Concerning the store-cities Pithom and Rameses, which Pharaoh built with mud and straw.  
2. Concerning Moses’ staff being changed into a serpent.  
3. As above.  
4. Concerning Moses’ hand, which, when brought out from his bosom, appeared leprous.  
5. When Moses was on the journey, the Lord met him and wanted to kill him.  
6. Pharaoh’s magicians threw their staffs upon the ground; they were changed into dragons, but Aaron’s staff devoured them.  
7. Concerning the ten plagues of Egypt: 1, the waters changed into blood; 2, the plague of frogs; 3, the gnats; 4, the flies; 5, the death of the animals; 6, the sores and blisters; 7, the hail, thunder, and fire; 8, the plague of locusts; 9, the darkness; 10, the slaughter of the firstborn.  
8. Let a man ask his friend, and a woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold and clothing.  
9. They shall take some of the blood of the lamb and put it on both doorposts.  
10. When Pharaoh had sent the people out, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, lest, if wars arose on the journey, they should regret it and return to Egypt.  
11. Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand.  
12. Concerning the bitter waters, which were changed into sweetness by the addition of the wood that the Lord showed Moses.  
13. Concerning the twelve springs of water and the seventy palms at Elim.  
14. That on the sixth day a double measure of manna was commanded to be gathered.  
15. That when the children of Israel saw the manna, they said, “Manhu,” that is, “What is this?”  
16. That the manna kept until the next day became rotten.  
17. That when Israel fought against Amalek, Moses, holding the staff in his hand, stretched out his arms.  
18. That the Lord gave his people the law through Moses on Mount Sinai.  
19. “You shall make an altar of earth for me.”  
20. “You shall not build an altar for me of hewn stones.”  
21. “You shall make silver bases and erect gilded boards upon them.”  
22. “You shall make four columns and their bases covered with silver.”  
23. That twelve precious stones were to be placed in the breastpiece worn by the priest on his chest, three enclosed in gold at each of its four corners.  
24. Moses seized the golden calf, burned it with fire, and crushed it to powder; scattering it into water, he gave it to the people to drink.  
25. That Moses caused twenty-three thousand men to be killed because of the guilt of the cast calf.  
26. “Behold, there is a place beside me; you shall stand upon the rock, and when my glory has passed by, you shall see my back.”  
27. Moses made seven lamps in the tabernacle, with their snuffers and vessels.

*The chapters end.*

# THE TESTIMONIES OF THE BOOK OF EXODUS BEGIN

## CHAPTER I. In a Letter to the Nun Hermisinde, Where It Is Said That the Structure of Human Pride Is Quickly Destroyed

Those store-cities that Pharaoh built with mud and straw—mud, which defiles, and straw, which is destined for the flames—are not without mystical significance called Pithom and Rameses. Pithom is interpreted as “mouth of the abyss,” or “suddenly.” For whoever, according to Paul’s teaching, now builds wood, hay, or straw upon the foundation that is Christ Jesus—the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is (1 Cor. III)—the higher this structure of carnal life is raised, the more readily it is suddenly destroyed, as though submerged in the gulf of the abyss.

Hence it is written: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI). It is therefore rightly said both “mouth of the abyss” and “suddenly,” because from the height of carnal life, which it signifies, one falls not sluggishly but quickly; and that is the mouth of the abyss which appeared to be the summit of ascent, as the Prophet testifies: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII).

Rameses, however, is said to mean “pasture” or “moth.” All the reprobate are pasture for the devil, for he feeds upon them like a wolf upon sheep and fattens himself on their destruction as upon banquets. Of them David also says: “Like sheep they are placed in the underworld; death will feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII).

## CHAPTER II. In a Letter to Hermisinde, Where It Is Said That the Structure of Human Pride Quickly Collapses

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘Throw the staff that you carry in your hand upon the ground’; and he threw it, and it became a serpent. Moses immediately was terrified and fled. And the Lord said to him: ‘Take hold of its tail’; and he took hold of it, and it became a staff again” (Exod. IV).

We all clearly know that the serpent persuaded humanity to death; therefore death comes from the serpent. But what is the staff except Christ, of whom the Prophet says: “A staff will go forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. II)? The staff therefore became a serpent: Christ became death.

Moses was terrified and fled because, when the Lord was suspended upon the cross or dying, the whole number of the apostles trembled in fear and withdrew from the solidity of certain hope and firm faith. Since the tail is the extremity of the body, what does it signify except the end of the Lord’s Passion? Moses therefore seized the tail, and nothing further of the serpent appeared in the staff, because, once the mystery of the Lord’s Passion and cross had been completed, every believer returned to faith, and Christ, having destroyed death, restored in himself through the glory of the resurrection the very thing that he had been.

## CHAPTER III. In a Sermon on Saint Columba

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘What is that which you hold in your hand?’ He answered: ‘A staff.’ He said: ‘Throw it upon the ground,’ etc.” (Exod. IV). Who is signified by Moses except the Jewish people? What by the staff except the power of divinity? And what by the serpent except the mortality of our Redeemer?

Since death is signified by the serpent, mortality is rightly represented in the serpent; or certainly, since it is written, “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. X), because the highest wisdom itself, that is, the Wisdom of God, graciously consented to become incarnate, his mortality is rightly figured in the serpent. Hence in the Gospel, speaking of his Passion, he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so it is necessary for the Son of Man to be lifted up” (John III).

Moses therefore held the staff because the Jewish people, before the Redeemer’s coming, trusted in divine power. But he threw the staff upon the ground because that same people, through the patriarchs and prophets, announced that the Lord would become incarnate. The staff therefore turns into a serpent because our Redeemer, remaining God in himself, became mortal among human beings.

But Moses was terrified and fled when he saw the serpent, because the Jewish people, seeing the Lord who was the Redeemer of the human race in such a condition, was frightened and trembled as though fearful, and did not believe. He is commanded to seize the serpent by the tail because that faithless people, which now refuses to believe, gathers itself back to faith in the final part of the Lord’s body—that is, at a later time in the holy Church, at the end of the world. It seizes the serpent by the tail because, at the final stage of the Church, it confesses as its Redeemer the one whom it had previously despised as mortal.

But immediately the serpent returns to a staff because, as soon as the Jewish people believes in our Redeemer, that same Redeemer will appear for judgment in the power of his divinity. Thus the serpent becomes a staff for it, because the one who was despised on earth as a human being will be seen, coming from heaven, as God above the angels.

Thus the Lord is mystically called both a leper without leprosy and a serpent without venom; likewise he is called foolish without foolishness and weak without weakness, because he so adapts and accommodates himself to our weakness that he both struggles with those who struggle and similarly endures punishments with those who suffer.

## CHAPTER IV. In the Same Sermon

“‘Put your hand,’ the Lord said, ‘into your bosom.’ When he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous, like snow. ‘Put your hand back into your bosom,’ he said. He put it back and brought it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh” (Exod. IV).

What is signified here by Moses’ hand except the Son of God? Hence it is said in the psalm: “Let your hand be made, so that it may save me” (Ps. CXVIII)—as though he were saying: “Let him through whom all things were made be made, so that, while he is created, creation may be freed from the contagion of its guilt.”

This hand is in the bosom of the Father, as John the Baptist says: “The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself declared him” (John I). But when this hand was brought out from the bosom—that is, when it appeared through the mystery of the incarnation—the people from whom he had proceeded judged him to be a sinner, as though covered with the leprosy of crime. Hence Isaiah says: “And we considered him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. LIII).

But when this hand returned to the bosom, it entirely lost its leprosy, because our Redeemer, after returning to the Father and trampling down the power of death, will at the end of the age appear to all the Jews not as a sinful human being but truly as God and human being.

## CHAPTER V. In a Letter to the Canons of Faenza

“When he was on the journey at the lodging place, the Lord met Moses and wanted to kill him” (Exod. IV). It is very astonishing that the Lord is suddenly described as wanting to kill the man whom he had already made his intimate and fellow initiate, with whom he had familiarly shared the secrets of his counsel and will, and whom he was now directing in the execution of his obedience.

But it is undoubtedly understood that, whatever stain of contagion he had contracted from prolonged residence among the Midianites, he therefore had to be purified by terror and by the correction of negligence, since he was approaching as the bearer of heavenly commands in order to correct others. His wife Zipporah prudently understood this; concerning her Scripture immediately adds: “Zipporah at once took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son” (ibid.).

It would have been absurd if someone who was a Gentile in his son were seen to be an Israelite in himself. One who must instruct others in the way of righteousness must take great care lest, God forbid, he himself appear to err in anything. Hence the Israelite people is inflamed with zeal for righteousness to avenge the crime of Benjamin, and yet that same people is first struck down by the swords of Benjamin (Judg. XX).

## CHAPTER VI. In a Letter to Boniface, Where It Is Said That Spiritual Wisdom Should Be Preferred to External Prudence

“Pharaoh’s magicians threw their staffs upon the ground, and they became dragons; but Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs” (Exod. VII). Aaron’s staff swallowed the magicians’ staffs because the wisdom of Christ, which it signified, nullified all the wisdoms of this world and gathered the wise of the world into the inmost parts of his body, which is the Church.

Therefore let spiritual wisdom swallow up our earthly wisdom and transform it, as it were, into the innermost reality of its body. For it is absurd and thoroughly dishonorable to apply to human affairs the same prudence and subtlety that are devoted to spiritual and divine matters.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Ten Plagues of Egypt, in a Letter to the Disciple John

The plagues inflicted in Egypt signify the wounds inflicted upon the human soul in the world. Hence, just as there were many plagues, so many commandments were divinely promulgated, so that as many as are the wounds of the sick heart, so many remedies might be available to be applied to it.

Let us proceed, then. The first plague is when the waters are changed into blood (Exod. VII). These plagues, moreover, occur only in Egypt—that is, in the darkened heart oppressed by the blindness of obscurity. Its waters are changed into blood when the blind mind, so far as it is concerned, confounds and violates the purity of right faith. For just as all crops emerge from the depths of the earth through water, so spiritual nourishment is brought forth from faith.

Water is therefore changed into blood when the foolish heart is darkened by the blindness of faithlessness. Of some such people the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I).

The medicine of the first commandment is immediately applied to the first plague, that is, to this most pestilential wound: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). This is the medicinal bond by which the wound of faithlessness must be bound: when you hear this, worship one God alone and do not pour out the rottenness of your decaying faithlessness into many gods.

And by God’s just judgment, according to the literal account, it happened that the Egyptians drank the blood of that river in which the Hebrew infants had first been killed.

The second plague is an abundance of frogs (Exod. VIII). The frog is a noisy animal and customarily croaks in muddy marshes. Heretics and philosophers are judged to be like it: as though upon muddy marshes—that is, amid crowds filthy with the squalor of faithlessness—they shout against Christ with empty insults. While they persist in chattering with importunate cries through arguments of deceit, they bring weariness to the ears but no nourishment for life to the mind.

The second commandment comes to this disease, which rages lethally in the soul, like a cup of salvation: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX). He takes the name of Christ in vain who believes him not to be Creator but merely a creature: “Creation has been subjected to vanity” (Rom. VIII). Such people are therefore undoubtedly vain, because, exchanging the truth of God for a lie, they place their faith in vanity.

The third plague is gnats (Exod. VIII). This creature is so tiny and minute that, while it balances itself in the air and flies unstably in wandering twists here and there, it eludes the sight of those who wish to see it. Yet when it settles upon our body, it stings, so that although you cannot see it while it flies, you are compelled to feel it while it pricks. As they fly around and thrust themselves upon us more insistently, they do not cease to trouble our faces and do not allow those who wish to rest to do so.

This plague therefore clearly signifies the vice of wandering and restlessness. Those who suffer from this disease run uselessly here and there, and, as though subject to evil changes, do not rest because of impatience. But since these gnats are very small and harmful, seeming to have not so much weight as a bite, those who serve the vice of wandering consider it a light sin; yet they are pierced by the sting of no light guilt. It does not weigh heavily, but it penetrates by its bite, because the lighter they judge this vice to be, the more necessarily the stimulus of sin pierces the inner parts of the weakened soul.

The medicine of the third commandment counters this weakness when it says: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX and XXXI; Deut. I)—the Sabbath, that is, rest. Where there is sanctification of the Sabbath, there undoubtedly is the Spirit of God. Hence it is written: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

The words must be weighed: if the Holy Spirit rests only upon the quiet person, then he abandons the restless person. Indeed, just as the second commandment is referred to the Son, so this third belongs to the Holy Spirit, who is likewise the third person in the holy Trinity.

The magicians also ascribe that third plague to the Holy Spirit when, unable themselves to produce gnats, they say to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII). The Apostle urged his disciple to observe this Sabbath when he said: “Attend to reading and doctrine” (1 Tim. I). Elsewhere he says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. V). The Lord urges us through the Prophet to observe this Sabbath when he says: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV).

It is as though he were saying: “Observe the spiritual Sabbath; avoid the restlessness of wandering, so that, fixed through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the gnats may not trouble you, but the observance of the spiritual Sabbath may sanctify you.”

Moreover, it should be noted that only these three commandments were written on one tablet; the other seven were contained on the other. These three pertain to love of God, while those pertain to love of neighbor. There are therefore no more than two tablets because they are distinguished by the imprint of a twofold love.

That three commandments were written on one tablet and seven on the other is especially inferred from what the blessed Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honor your father and mother”—which is “the first commandment with a promise”—“so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth” (Eph. VI).

Why is this called the first commandment except because it is placed at the beginning of the second tablet? It is said to have a promise because, whereas no such promise is found in the other commandments, this commandment is followed by the promise of longevity. The promise is added to the commandment: “Honor your father and mother, so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth.” This commandment, therefore, which is fourth in the general numbering, is placed first on the second tablet.

Opposed to it is the fourth plague, namely the *cynomyia*, which is called the dog-fly (Exod. VIII). Nothing is so doglike as to disregard one’s parents and fail to show reverence to those who gave us birth. Doglike behavior also assails them like flies: those who do not know how to honor their parents withdraw from natural dignity through fickle levity and tear them apart like dog-flies, harassing their parents in impatience as though growling and barking against them. Thus, in order that this plague may be cured, due reverence must be shown to parents.

The fifth plague is the death of sinners (Exod. IX). All who, having rejected the marriage bed, pollute themselves with the foulness of other women and dissolve themselves indiscriminately in the excesses of obscene lust—what else should they be called but brute beasts, wholly alien to the reason of spiritual understanding? “They have become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI).

And Jeremiah says: “I fed them to satiety, and they committed adultery; they luxuriated in the house of the prostitute. They became lustful stallions, each neighing after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V). These beasts must necessarily waste away in utter destruction unless the medicine of divine law comes to their aid. Therefore it is said: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX). This fifth commandment is set against the fifth plague like a medicinal bond, so that, while everyone is compelled to be content with his own marriage bed, the intemperance of unbridled lust may not extend into the embrace of another’s flesh.

The sixth plague consists of wounds and swollen, inflamed blisters (Exod. IX). In the wounds, the deceitful and festering malice of those who hate is reproved; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the inflammation, the madness of raging and inflamed fury.

There are certain murderous souls in which these plagues arise and rage most fiercely. Unless they shed human blood, they do not permit themselves to rest. To this furious and savagely raging disease the sixth commandment comes as heavenly medicine: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). Thus, when anyone hears this, let him restrain within himself the destruction arising from evil will, so that the venom of a malicious conscience, once conceived, may not burst forth externally into the act of shedding blood.

After this comes the plague of hail, where hail and fire were carried together (Exod. IX). These two are opposites: cold in the hail and heat in the fire. Thus those who steal what belongs to others are cold toward brotherly love and inflamed by the heat of greed.

Lightning flashes and thunder are also said to have been mixed with the hail. What is signified by thunder and lightning except intolerable fear? It is characteristic of thieves to tremble inwardly with fear at being caught first and then punished, yet not to cease carrying out the wickedness once conceived.

These plagues—hail, fire, lightning, and thunder together—devastate the hearts of those who secretly seize what belongs to others, like fields laid waste; and, if any crops or shoots of good will are present, they scatter them all. The medicine of the seventh commandment therefore comes to this worst wound: “You shall not steal” (Exod. XX). Thus, when each person understands this, let him not destroy the crops of his heart with this manifold plague, but fill the storehouse of his soul with the fruits of good works, fulfilling the apostolic saying: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but labor with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need” (Eph. IV).

The eighth plague is locusts (Exod. 10). By these creatures, which destroy the shoots of crops and gnaw the fruits with their pestilential mouths, whom can be represented more aptly than those who slander their brothers and bring a false accusation against them? For they devour, as it were, the shoot of another’s field when they not only suppress the good qualities of their brothers which they ought to proclaim, but finally also brand them with the stigma of a false charge. They gnaw, therefore, because they not only conceal through envy their good words, but also brand them with the mark of a fabricated depravity. Do such people not gnaw like locusts, of whom the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5)? To this plague, therefore, the commandment aptly corresponds which says: “You shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20). Thus every false witness, who will not go unpunished, may restrain himself from biting another’s life, cast away his locust-like teeth, and not gnaw off the green shoots of another’s field.

The ninth plague is now the thick darkness (Exod. 10). No one slips into deeper inner darkness than the person who violates the fidelity of the marriage-bed and seeks to invade another man’s wife. But the splendor of divine law illumines this darkness, which a lust-devoted heart endures, when it says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20). Here it must be noted that it does not say, “You shall not take her,” or “You shall not defile her,” but, which is more, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” Earlier it was said: “You shall not commit adultery”; here it says: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” Thus, concerning one matter, there appear to be two commandments. For there the act of adultery, by which someone violates another’s bed, is condemned; here even the desire of one who wishes to violate it is prohibited. There the impure and illicit intercourse of adultery is condemned; here even the appetite for adulterous desire is restrained. Indeed, the very desire to violate another’s marriage is adultery, as the Lord says: “Whoever looks at another man’s wife in order to covet her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Therefore, let no one covet another’s wife, lest he suffer in his heart the darkness of palpable shadows. But if he perhaps already suffers it, let him admit the flashing ray of the legal commandment and thus cast away the darkness of his blinded conscience.

Finally, the tenth plague is the death of the firstborn (Exod. 12). A man has two sons, so to speak: one when he performs a work belonging to this present life, and another when he accomplishes something spiritual that tends toward eternal life. But the spiritual fruit, as our firstborn, ought to hold first place in our works. Hence the Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6). It is as though he said: Produce spiritual fruit, which is truly your firstborn; but what belongs to the necessities of this life should be second in the inheritance. For the blessing is owed to this firstborn, together with Jacob (Gen. 27). Of Esau, however, and those like him, Scripture says: “The inheritance for which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. 20).

Concerning these two children, Deuteronomy figuratively says: “If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and they bear him children, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, and he wishes to divide his possessions among his sons, he cannot make the son of the beloved woman the firstborn and prefer him to the son of the hated woman; rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated woman as the firstborn and give him a double portion of everything he possesses. For he is the beginning of his children, and the rights of the firstborn belong to him” (Deut. 21).

Concerning all these matters, we need only explain here that the beloved wife is the soft, delightful, carnal life, while the hated wife is the spiritual life, since it is austere, strict, and hostile to all the enticements of carnal pleasure. The firstborn rights therefore belong to her son, because the fruit of spiritual life deserves to have him as its reward who is, according to John, “the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

But this firstborn—that is, the spiritual fruit—undoubtedly dies for the person who, not content with what is his own, attends to the possessions of others, seeks what belongs by right to his brother, and covets his neighbor’s goods, inflamed by the torches of avarice. But the tenth commandment of the Law is: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor” (Exod. 20). Let him therefore listen carefully to this commandment, lest he lose his firstborn; so that he may rejoice in his own firstborn, let him by no means covet what belongs to another.

## CHAPTER VIII. In a Sermon of Saint Eleuchadius

“Let a man ask his friend, and a woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold and garments; and the Lord will give grace to his people in the sight of the Egyptians” (Exod. 12). To say nothing of lingering longer on this point, mystically we ask for gold and silver together with garments, from which we may construct a tabernacle for the Lord, when we read worldly poets and philosophers so that we may make more brilliant progress in the divine utterances. Or, in a more perceptive interpretation, the gold and silver are precious souls, who join themselves to the people of God together with their garments—that is, their bodies—so that they may leave this dark world, as though it were Egypt, and acquire the promised land of perpetual happiness.

## CHAPTER IX. In a Sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“They shall take some of the blood of the lamb and put it on both doorposts” (Exod. 12). What does it mean that the Israelite people are commanded to place the lamb’s blood on the doorposts of their houses, except that it prefigures us carrying on our forehead the cross of Christ, who is the true Lamb? The lamb was sacrificed in the evening; and at the evening of the world Christ suffered. The doorposts are smeared so that the destroying angel may not dare to inflict destruction; and we carry the banner of the cross in our heart and on our forehead, so that the sudden arrival of the enemy may not be able to take away our salvation. Hence we sing with confidence: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4).

## CHAPTER X. In a Letter to the Countess Blanca

“When Pharaoh had sent out the people, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is nearby, thinking that perhaps they might repent if they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt” (Exod. 13). Thus, for those departing from Egypt, nearby battle is withheld, because those who abandon the world are granted a certain tranquility of peace, lest, troubled and terrified in the very newness of their tenderness, they return to what they had rejected. First, therefore, they are soothed by the sweetness of security; first, they are nourished by the quiet of peace. But after they have come to know this sweetness, they endure the struggles of temptations all the more tolerably, since they have learned more deeply in God what they should love.

## CHAPTER XI. In a Sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand” (Exod. 15). We too, having now crossed the Red Sea and drowned the enemy, must carry a tambourine with Mary. What does it mean to carry a tambourine? Hear the Lord saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 8). Whoever crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires, whoever mortifies by abstinence his members that are upon the earth (Gal. 5), truly carries a tambourine with Mary, because he keeps himself dry and free from the harmful fluids of earthly pleasure.

## CHAPTER XII. In the Same Sermon

Moreover, the following point also arises quite appropriately. The Israelite people murmured against Moses at Marah, crying out that they could not find anything to drink (Exod. 15). Then the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood; when he cast it into the very bitter waters, they were immediately changed into sweetness. For what do those bitter waters represent except the letter that kills and the form of a harsh and tasteless law? For it is written: “The Lord established for his people law and judgments, and tested him” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I gave them commandments that were not good and judgments by which they would not live” (Ezek. 20). Yet if the confession of the cross and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion are joined to this law, what was bitter is immediately turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER XIII. In the Same Sermon

It must be noted, in accordance with the truth of the historical account, that after the water had been changed into sweetness, the people came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. For what are the twelve springs except the twelve apostles (Matt. 10), whom the Lord appointed to irrigate the dry and barren breasts of the human race with the flood of their preaching? And what are the seventy palm trees except the same number of disciples whom he sent before his face (Luke 10), so that through them the world might recognize the palms of his victory?

Certainly, the order of the subsequent events appears to have been arranged quite fittingly: first the people were led to the letter of the Law, from which, while it was bitter, they could not pass. But after it had been made sweet through the tree of life and began to be understood spiritually, the people of God immediately passed from the Old Testament to the apostolic springs and palm trees—that is, to the grace of the Gospel.

And it is fitting that after the Decalogue has been received, a sevenfold number of preachers is established, because every commandment of the divine Law is fulfilled through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it without reason that the preachers of the cross appear to be designated by the name of palms, since the cross itself may rightly be called a palm: for upon it victory was achieved over the prostrate enemy of the world. Thus the Bridegroom says of the cross to the bride: “I said, I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruits, etc.” (Song 7).

## CHAPTER XIV. In a Sermon of Saint Eleuchadius

“On the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather on each day” (Exod. 16). On the sixth day a double measure was commanded to be gathered, so that half of it might be kept for the Sabbath. The sixth day, moreover, signifies the sixth age of the world, in which we now are. On this day, therefore, the person who, with a view to heavenly glory, where there is perpetual Sabbath and true rest, both hears and performs the word of God gathers a double portion for the coming Sabbath. He stores up a double portion who both lives well and displays to others an example of salvation. Or, more simply, he gathers a double measure who labors so greatly in good works that his soul is pleasing to its Creator here and may afterward live perpetually with him. What was stored up for the Sabbath could not decay, because good works performed out of desire for heavenly rest will remain forever.

## CHAPTER XV. In a Letter to the Brothers of Cluny

“When the children of Israel saw that manna had been given, they said to one another: ‘Manhu?’—which means, ‘What is this?’ Moses said to them: ‘This is the bread which the Lord has given you for food’” (Exod. 16). Those truly eat manna—that is, “What is this?”—who, when they read or hear, diligently seek out the mystery of the divine word. Within the husk of the literal straw, they seek to uncover the sweet kernel of spiritual understanding. Certainly, the person truly feeds on “What is this?” who is engaged in constant and diligent inquiry into Sacred Scripture. For we eat, as it were, some question—“What is this?”—with the eager mouth of the heart when we apply ourselves vigilantly to penetrating the mysteries of the Scriptures and carefully ruminate the feasts of heavenly speech.

## CHAPTER XVI. In a Sermon of Saint Eleuchadius (Sermon 6)

[Col. 1023D]

Let today’s care be sufficient for the present necessity, and let the rancor of anxiety not anticipate tomorrow’s day. As sacred history testifies, when the Israelite people gathered manna, it produced worms and rotted if anyone, acting faithlessly, kept some of it for the following day (Exod. 16). Thus, whoever, inflamed by the heat of greed, stores up earthly substance for himself as though providing nourishment for his body, causes that worm to boil forth which pierces the conscience and gnaws the hidden places of the heart.

Indeed, the worms of anxieties that avarice generates prepare those other worms of which it is written: “Their fire will not be quenched, and the worm will not die” (Isa. 16), so that fire may kindle fire through the fire of greed, and worm may proceed from worm.

It can also, however, be understood not inappropriately in this way: just as Christ himself, who says, “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21), becomes for some a cause of ruin and for others of resurrection, so likewise his word becomes manna and the sweetness of honey for the faithful; but for the unfaithful and those who live wickedly it becomes a worm—not one that nourishes by refreshing the soul, but one that gnaws the conscience by wearing it down and threatening it.

## CHAPTER XVII. In a Sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

With a staff in his hand, Moses raised his arms in the form of a cross (Exod. 17). Thus it came about that he overcame the ranks of his adversaries by the wood and the sign—that is, by the full mystery of the cross. Sacred history testifies to this when it says: “When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed” (ibid.).

This event conveys to us not only the sacrament of spiritual understanding but also a most salutary example of virtue. For when we take up the cross after the Lord, when we raise our hearts together with our hands to the Lord, the rulers of darkness immediately fall and, thrown down into the depths, are crushed with their strength broken. But if we lower our hands, forget heavenly things, and pursue earthly matters, the victorious enemy immediately pursues us, and, having lost the victory, we are cut down by the swords of our pursuers.

In every spiritual struggle we must carry before us the banner of the cross. If we raise it through visible action, we are undoubtedly victorious; but if, by living sluggishly, we lay it down, we must fall enfeebled at the first assault of our pursuers. Hence that distinguished instructor in spiritual warfare, Paul, says: “Raise your drooping hands and your weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray” (Heb. 12).
