## CHAPTER XVIII. In the First Synodal Sermon

Just as on Mount Sinai the Lord, through Moses, set forth the decrees of the Law to the Israelite people, so in the holy Church the same Lawgiver and Judge, through the ministry of priests, sets forth to the Christian people the commandments for living. Sinai, in fact, is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” For the Lord appeared from the bush, as Scripture testifies, and commanded Moses to bring the commandments to the children of Israel (Exod. 3).

And without doubt God is seen in the Church, just as he promises Moses when Moses asks him to show himself, saying: “Behold, there is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock, and when my glory has passed by, then you shall see my back” (Exod. 33).

But since Sinai is also called “temptation,” what else should this mean except that in the Church, where the Law is given, the temptation of the evil spirit sometimes arises perniciously? It may be that the hope of profit secretly intrudes, leading one to violate the rule of right judgment; or that praise or human favor softens the rigor of justice; or that the malice of anger or hatred drives one to inflict harm; or that fear restrains the heart from judging rightly with freedom; or that cruelty exceeds the measure of deserved punishment.

## CHAPTER XIX. G. G.

“The Lord said to the children of Israel: ‘You shall make an altar of earth for me’” (Exod. 20). To make an altar of earth for the Lord is to hope in the incarnation of our Redeemer. A gift is then received from our God when our humility places upon this altar—that is, upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation—whatever it accomplishes. We place a gift offered upon an altar of earth if we strengthen our actions with faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

Of this altar Isaiah says: “On that day there shall be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar beside its boundary, belonging to his dominion; and it shall be for a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19).

## CHAPTER XX. In a Letter to the Canons of Fano

“But if you make a stone altar for me, you shall not build it of cut stones; for if you raise your knife over it, it will be defiled” (Exod. 20). The cut stones are those who reject participation in brotherly fellowship, who do not wish to live with their brothers or associate with them in harmony. Christ does not receive such people into his body, because he judges them cut off from the unity of his members.

An altar ought rather to be built from those stones of which the Apostle Peter says: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2). He is the foundation of that house, besides whom no other foundation can be laid; he is the summit who was made the cornerstone.

## CHAPTER XXI. In a Sermon on Saint Andrew the Apostle

“You shall make silver bases, says the Lord, and raise gilded boards above them” (Exod. 26). What else are the silver bases understood to signify except the order of the prophets? Since they were the first to speak of the mystery of the Church, we see them rising like bases from the foundation and supporting the weights of the structure placed upon them.

What else are the boards understood to represent except the holy apostles, who were extended most widely throughout the world by their preaching? The apostles’ teaching rests, as it were, upon the bases of prophetic preaching, and by their authority it is firmly strengthened for the stability of its condition. Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board: when the holy prophets agree among themselves in their words concerning the mystery of the future Church, they build up the apostles who follow them and, since they disagree with one another in nothing, fix them more firmly upon themselves.

Nor is it without reason that the bases signifying the prophets are commanded to be cast from silver. The brightness of silver is preserved through use, but without use it turns black. Likewise, before they were illumined by apostolic preaching, the sayings of the prophets, since they were not yet employed in spiritual understanding, remained as though black: they could not be seen because of their obscurity. But after the hand of apostolic preaching wiped away the darkness from the prophecies, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and their mystical meanings were put to use, because apostolic preaching clearly announced that the words had already been explained by events.

Rightly, therefore, both silver bases and gilded boards are commanded to be made, because the apostolic commands are far clearer than the prophetic oracles.

## CHAPTER XXII. In a Sermon on Saint Matthew the Evangelist

“You shall make four columns and their bases covered with silver” (Exod. 27). For what else is understood by silver than the splendor of divine speech? As it is written: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, refined upon the earth” (Ps. 12).

The bases covered with silver support the four columns of the tabernacle, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with divine speech and offering themselves as an example in all things, carry the sayings of the four evangelists both in word and in deed.

Matthew therefore occupies the first place, John the last. They were established at the summit of the apostolic order and, from what they wrote, were formed not merely by hearing but rather by sight and touch, as one of them says: “What we have heard, what we have seen, what our eyes have looked upon, what our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1).

Mark and Luke, who occupy the middle of the catalogue of the Gospels, were not apostles; nevertheless, they were instructed through the accounts of the principal apostles, one through Peter and the other through Paul.

All the holy evangelists, however, possess one authority and one faith. They differ in nothing as they weave the wholly truthful lines of their accounts, and throughout every part of their writing they likewise raise an impregnable bulwark fortified against all the arrows of every heresy.

## CHAPTER XXIII. In a Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

It was commanded that twelve stones be placed in the breastpiece, which the priest wore on his chest when he entered the Holy of Holies: three stones at each of the four corners, enclosed in gold. For the holy apostles preached the truth of the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity, which is God, throughout the four-part world.

These stones are also carried enclosed in gold, because the blessed apostles remain inviolably confirmed in the secret of heavenly wisdom. It is therefore proper that, when the priest enters the sanctuary, he should carry twelve precious stones in the breastpiece of his chest, so that whoever approaches the sacred altars may set before himself examples of apostolic uprightness. Let him imitate, insofar as he is able, the life of those whose ministry he exercises, and fix his gaze upon the pursuits of holy emulation in those whose office he bears.

## CHAPTER XXIV. In a Sermon of Saint Eleuchadius

“Moses took the golden calf which they had made, burned it with fire, ground it to powder, scattered it upon the water, and gave it to the Israelite people to drink” (Exod. 32).

What does that cast image of the calf signify figuratively except the body of the devil—that is, human beings deceived in every kind of unbelief and idolatrous error, joined beneath their pestilential head, as different members, in sacrilegious conspiracy? Over them the spirit of wickedness presides as author, insolently raising itself up and, like a head, tyrannically ruling its own body.

The calf is described as golden because the rite of idolatry appears to have been established as though by wise men. For gold signifies wisdom, as Solomon says: “A desirable treasure is in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21). The calf was therefore golden because the wise men of the world are shown to have been authors of the worship of demons before the grace of the new faith.

Of them the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents” (Rom. 1).

Through this vanity of mad wisdom, poets, philosophers, magicians, those who investigated the stars, and those trained in the knowledge of every liberal discipline used to worship monstrous fabrications of demons. The calf therefore signifies the whole body—that is, the entire society of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry.

Moses therefore burned the calf with fire because our Redeemer, whom Moses prefigured, kindled with the flame of his love the wrongly conspiring hearts of the Gentiles. Hence he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12). And the Prophet says: “There is no one who can hide from its heat” (Ps. 19).

The divine fire is therefore suddenly kindled in the minds of the Gentiles, so that the irrational form of idolatry may be dissolved in them. The whole body of this calf is then ground into powder because that Gentile society, fused into one by the art of diabolical conspiracy, was, at Christ’s coming, beaten out as though by a hammer of saving correction and crushed from the hardness of its rigidity by the power of the divine word. It is beneficially ground down by the word of truth, although, while wickedly whole, it appeared senselessly to stand in the form of its pride.

Then it is scattered into water, so that the Israelite people may drink from it. The crushed calf is therefore put into water because the humbled Gentile people must be washed in the bath of the fountain of salvation. The Israelites immediately drink it, because the holy preachers of the Gospel, who are truly Israelites, receive them into their own members—into the Lord’s body, which is the Church—and, as though by drinking, convert them.

To these Israelites it was first said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10), which means just as much as if it had been said: “Grind and drink.” Thus that calf was absorbed by those whom it had tried to absorb, through the fire of zeal, the edge of the word, and the water of baptism; it was poured into those whom it had attempted to transfer into its own—that is, diabolical—members.

## CHAPTER XXV. In the Same Sermon

Nevertheless, because Moses did not set the limit of vengeance at merely smashing the idol, but went on to slaughter twenty-three thousand men, he taught mystically that it is by no means enough for someone to turn away from the worship of idols or from a wicked way of life unless he also attempts to mortify his own vices with the sword of the Spirit.

Hence the outstanding preacher says: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the worship of idols” (Col. 2; Gal. 5).

It must also be noted that, just as vices are here called our members, so there those who were killed were joined to their murderers by the bond of kinship, as Moses said: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exod. 32).

If anyone delights in rising to arms, if anyone longs to fight against the battalions of enemies, let him turn his hands against himself; there he will find more adversaries to cut down. Thus, after victory, he will not incur the shameful name of homicide, but will appear rather as a glorious victor. Thus he will not deserve to be excluded from the thresholds of the sanctuary, but, consecrating himself to the Lord, will be increased by the blessings of divine grace.

To those men it was likewise said: “You have consecrated your hands to the Lord, each man in his son and his brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (ibid.).

That those who were slain are reported to have numbered twenty-three thousand indicates, through the number of three thousand slain, the threefold form of sins. For we commit every sin either by deed, by word, or by thought. But because the number ten is also doubled there, it is understood that, just as we have refused to keep the Decalogue of commandments with both flesh and soul, so we must also wear down and mortify the vices of both with the weapons of the virtues.

## CHAPTER XXVI. In the First Synodal Sermon

“Behold, there is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock, and then you shall see my back” (Exod. 33). What is this place where the Lord is immediately seen standing upon the rock, except that it should be understood as the holy Church, where, while we steadfastly lean upon the rock of faith, we gaze together with the Apostle upon the glory of the Lord? For this is the Church of which it is said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16).

## CHAPTER XXVII. In a Letter to Damian on Avoiding Buffoonery

“Moses made seven lamps in the tabernacle, with their snuffers, and vessels in which the snuffings were extinguished, from purest gold” (Exod. 37).

We make seven lamps in the tabernacle if we assemble in our minds the gifts of the Holy Spirit received from God. But because, in those holy works to which we devote ourselves while burning through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, certain superfluous things belonging to earthly corruption become interwoven, snuffers are necessarily made together with the lamps.

For what do the snuffers signify except the strictness of repentance? With a snuffer, what is superfluous is removed from a lamp; and through the strictness of repentance the guilt of human depravity is erased. Hence Peter says to those committing superfluous offenses: “Repent, therefore, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 2). It is as though he were saying openly: “Grip the snuffer and cut away the excesses of wicked action.”

It is therefore rightly said that snuffers are made together with the lamps, because even if through the grace of the Holy Spirit we strive to shine with the light of good works, nevertheless, whenever human corruption generates superfluity, we need the remedies of repentance.

But because these very superfluities, which the discipline of repentance cuts away, must be extinguished by the weeping of a contrite heart, it is not without reason that Moses is said to have made, besides the lamps and the snuffers, vessels in which the things removed by the snuffers might be extinguished.

Our vessels are hearts, which ought always to be filled with the flood of tears and weeping. In these vessels, moreover, that oil is stored of which the Gospel says: “The wise virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps” (Matt. 25).

If, then, even those who shine with distinguished works still need tears, what must be thought of wretched me and those like me, who have committed many dark deeds and possess no good works that shine? With how abundant streams of tears must we continually overflow; how constantly must we labor without ceasing in sorrow?

[Col. 1029] Here end the testimonies of the Book of Exodus.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS BEGIN

1. He shall offer before the door of the tabernacle of testimony a male calf from the herd, without blemish.  
2. Salt is to be mixed into every sacrifice; but never leaven or honey.  
3. The priest shall take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil and all the frankincense placed upon the fine flour, and shall burn it.  
4. In the altar, Moses frequently entered and departed from the tabernacle of the covenant.  
5. Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, offered strange fire before the Lord and were consumed by divine fire.  
6. With what garments Aaron must be clothed when he enters the tabernacle.  
7. The high priest shall offer a living goat, and, placing both hands upon its head, shall confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel.  
8. You shall not offer to the Lord any animal whose testicles are crushed, bruised, or cut.  
9. The seven lamps shall burn continually in the tabernacle of the covenant before the Lord.  
10. You shall eat the oldest of the old things and the old; when new things come upon them, you shall cast them away.

Here end the chapters.

# THE TESTIMONIES OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS BEGIN

## CHAPTER I. In a Sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

[Col. 1029C]

“You shall offer a male calf from the herd, without blemish, before the door of the tabernacle of testimony” (Lev. 1). The calf that is commanded to be offered from the herd represents our Redeemer, who descended from the lineage of the patriarchs. With the plow of his cross he subdued the soil of our flesh and enriched us with the fruit of virtues from the seed of the Holy Spirit (Isa. 53).

This calf, without blemish, was offered by the sons of Aaron not in the tabernacle but before its door, because the Lord, who is without sin, was crucified outside the gate under Annas and Caiaphas. He is the Lamb who wiped away the sins of the world (John 1). He is the Kid who slew the author of sin, the devil, with the sword of the cross (Ps. 3). He is the dove, in whose likeness the Holy Spirit descended upon him at the waters of the Jordan. He is also the turtledove, because he is the author of perpetual chastity, as the bride says to him: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove” (Song 1).

## CHAPTER II. In a Sermon to Virgins

“Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven, and nothing of leaven or honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Lev. 2). Whoever either attempts to spend stolen goods on a work of piety or appears to perform some good deed for the sake of empty glory is trying to offer not the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, but the leaven of malice and wickedness.

The Lord likewise does not approve a sacrifice of honey, because he condemns the pleasure of lust and every sweetness of carnal enticement. But salt is commanded to be applied to every offering, so that whatever we offer to the Lord upon the altar of a devoted heart, we may strive always to season with the savor of reason and understanding.

For he says: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt, and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice” (Lev. 2). And, to impress more forcefully what he was saying, lest our mind should at some time become tasteless and foolish, he repeats: “In every offering of yours you shall offer salt” (ibid.).

This is precisely the salt of which the Apostle says: “Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the time; let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4). Of this salt the Lord also says: “If salt has become tasteless, with what will it be seasoned?” (Matt. 5). And, speaking to the disciples about it: “You are,” he says, “the salt of the earth” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER III. In a Sermon of Saint Donatus

[Col. 1031A]

“Let the priest take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the fine flour, and burn it upon the altar as a memorial, a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord (Lev. VI).” For what else is signified by the fine flour than the holy Church of the elect? When it is gathered from the mutually joined members of believers, it is like fine flour mixed from many grains of wheat. And just as fine flour is crushed between both millstones so that the bran may be separated from the flour of wheat, so the holy Church is pressed, as it were, between the two millstones of the Law and the Gospel, so that the surface of the letter may be distinguished from the marrow of the spirit. This Church, truly spiritual fine flour, is united through the water of Baptism and mixed with the oil of chrism; it is also solidified by the fire of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the Apostle: “An offering well pleasing and perfect to God” (Rom. XIII). The frankincense said to have been placed upon the fine flour signifies the prayer of that same Church, as is shown in the Apocalypse of John, where he says that “the bowls full of spices are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. V).

## CHAPTER IV. To Desiderius the abbot

“Moses frequently entered and departed from the tabernacle of the covenant (Exod. XXXIII).” What does his frequent entrance into and departure from the tabernacle mean except that he provides an example: the one who is carried away within into contemplation is frequently pressed without by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; without, he bears the burdens of the carnal. He also always returns to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant, plainly providing a model for rulers: when they are uncertain outside about what they should arrange, they should always enter inwardly into their mind as into a tabernacle and, as though before the ark of the covenant, consult the Lord, if within themselves they search the pages of sacred Scripture concerning the matters about which they are uncertain.

Hence the Truth itself, shown to us through the assumption of our humility, spends the nights in prayer on the mountain (Luke VI), but by day shines forth in the cities through signs of miracles; thereby laying before good rulers the path of imitation, so that, if they already desire to contemplate the highest things, they may nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak by compassion. For charity rises wonderfully to the heights when it mercifully draws itself down to the lowly; and the more kindly it descends to the lowest things, the more vigorously it returns to the highest.

## CHAPTER V. In the letter to Cunibert, bishop of Turin, concerning the continence of clerics

“Having taken their censers, Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, put fire and incense upon them, offering before the Lord strange fire, which had not been commanded them. And fire went out from the Lord and consumed them, and they died before the Lord (Lev. X).” What is it for priests to offer strange fire to the Lord except to approach the holy altars inflamed by the heat of lust? And when Scripture says, “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. V), these men, so far as lies in them, extinguish the Holy Spirit, who ought to burn within them, and offer strange fire when they approach the altar of the Lord burning with the flame of lust. But suddenly the fire of divine fury is kindled against them, and they are terribly consumed by it, as Scripture testifies: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Heb. X).

Certainly it is right that those who approach the sacred altars in filth should perish by the sword of divine vengeance, since the Lord says to Moses: “You shall teach the children of Israel to beware of uncleanness, so that they do not die in their filth when they defile my tabernacle, which is among them” (Lev. XV).

## CHAPTER VI. In a sermon of Saint George

[Col. 1032B]

“The linen tunic,” says the Lord, “shall be worn; linen undergarments shall cover the nakedness; he shall gird himself with a linen belt and place a linen turban upon his head. These are the holy garments with which he shall clothe himself after he has been washed (Lev. XVI).”

Whoever strives to sacrifice himself to God in the tabernacle of Christ, which is the Church, must, after being cleansed in the bath of the sacred font, also clothe himself in various garments of virtue, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI). Thus the one who is reborn in Christ through Baptism as a new human being must no longer wear tunics of skins, signs of mortality, but, having put off the old human being, must put on the new and live renewed in him through devotion to a pure way of life.

It should also be noted that all those garments are described as linen. Linen is brought to whiteness through labor, and a life of virtue is not acquired in the torpor of idleness, but rather through the exercise of arduous discipline.

## CHAPTER VII. In a sermon of Saint Boniface

The law commands the high priest to offer the living goat in this manner: placing both hands upon its head, he is to confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their transgressions and sins, and, having invoked them upon its head, send it into the desert (Lev. XVI). What does it mean for the goat to be placed under both hands of the high priest except that the Son of Man, coming in the likeness of sinful flesh through the will of God (Rom. VIII), was burdened by the persecution of both peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile? He plainly wished to submit himself to the hands of both, since he had come to free both peoples from the yoke of the devil.

What does it mean that, after the confession and invocation of all the iniquities of the children of Israel upon its head, the goat is sent into the desert, except that the one who bore our sins and endured the curses of the Law immediately went into the desert, where he had left the ninety-nine sheep, and brought back the hundredth? (Matt. XVIII.) Hence the Apostle says: “To free us from the curse, he himself became a curse” (Gal. III).

## CHAPTER VIII. To Cunibert, bishop of Turin, concerning the continence of clerics

[Col. 1033A]

“You shall not offer to the Lord any animal that is crushed, maimed, mutilated, or has had its testicles removed (Lev. XXII).” If God so greatly hates sterility in brute animals that are offered to him through the priestly ministry, how much more does he reject it in priests who offer sacrifice to him—so that, just as offspring of the flesh is required in those animals, so priests may produce shoots of chastity in others.

## CHAPTER IX. In a sermon on the Lord’s Supper

“Command the children of Israel,” the Lord said to Moses, “to bring you pure and bright oil of olives for the continual preparation of lamps outside the veil of the testimony in the tabernacle of the covenant. Aaron shall set them from evening until morning before the Lord in perpetual observance throughout your generations; they shall always be placed upon the purest lampstand in the sight of the Lord (Lev. XXIV).”

What else is signified by the seven lamps in the tabernacle than the seven Churches in the one Christian people? In them the oil is commanded to burn unceasingly, because sincere charity, which is given through the Holy Spirit, ought to burn with the fire of a twofold love and always shine forth in clear and conspicuous works.

But since the Catholic and universal Church is undoubtedly one, as Solomon says, “My dove is one, the only one of her mother” (Song VI), why are seven Churches reported in the sacred writings except because she is one through the unity of faith, but sevenfold through the corresponding gifts of the Holy Spirit? These are the seven women who, according to the prophet’s prophecy, took hold of one man (Isa. IV). The man of the Church is Christ.

By this oil of the Holy Spirit all the nourishment of the sacred Scriptures is seasoned, so that the inner parts of our souls may be fattened. When this oil is poured into the life-giving food of heavenly speech, it gives flavor in the throat of the soul; it refreshes its stomach and sweetens the taste of the one who receives it. For it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. III). Hence it must be understood that all the pages of the sacred books are seasoned with the oil of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER X. In the letter to Hildebrand and Stephen

“You shall eat the oldest of the old, and you shall cast away the old when the new has arrived (Lev. XXVI).” The oldest of the old for us is to behold the first human beings of the Lord in paradise; the old is for the Israelite people to observe circumcision, sacrifices, and the commands of various ceremonies.

We therefore eat the oldest of the old with the mouth of the mind when, after the likeness of our first parent, we contemplate the appearance of God. But we cast away the old, far from us, when the new has arrived, while, with the grace of the Gospel shining forth, we pay no attention to observance of the Mosaic Law.

[Col. 1033] Here end the testimonies from the Book of Leviticus.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

1. Bring forward the tribe of Levi and make it stand before Aaron; you shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons.

2. How the people, gathering manna, broke it with a millstone or ground it in a mortar and made little cakes from it.

3. Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people.

4. The spies, proceeding as far as the Valley of the Cluster, cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole.

5. Likewise, concerning the preceding matter.

6. Aaron, taking a censer, ran through the midst of the multitude, which the plague was devastating.

7. Command the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer, perfect in age, without blemish, which has not borne a yoke.

8. Open your treasury, the fountain of living water, so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease.

9. Hear, you rebels and unbelievers. Can we bring water out of this rock for you?

10. How the Lord sent serpents among the people because of their murmuring.

11. How Israel sent messengers to Sihon, saying: “Please let me pass through your land.”

12. How the principal city of Sihon’s kingdom is called Heshbon.

13. “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on a gallows before the sun, so that my anger may be turned away from Israel.”

14. How the tribe of Levi reached the land of promise, while the other tribes lay slain in the desert.

15. How Zelophehad, when he died, left not sons but only five daughters.

16. Concerning the eight festivals that the Lord commanded to be observed throughout each cycle of the year.

17. Arm men from among yourselves for battle, who may exact the Lord’s vengeance upon the Midianites.

18. How the children of Israel, coming to the Spring of Judgment, which is Kadesh, killed all the leaders of the Amalekites and Amorites.

19. How Israel reached the beginning of its inheritance after forty-two encampments.

Here end the chapters.

123–124 HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

## CHAPTER I. In the letter to Pope Alexander, that he take property away from the canons

[Col. 1033C]

“Bring forward,” says the Lord to Moses, “the tribe of Levi and make it stand before Aaron the priest, so that they may minister to him.” And below: “You shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons, to whom they have been handed over by the children of Israel (Num. III).”

Who could doubt that Aaron and his sons possessed the right of high priests? Who does not know that the tribe of Levi prefigured the order of clerics? The Levites are therefore handed over as a gift to Aaron and his sons by the children of Israel when the clerical order is taken from the whole Christian people for the watches of ecclesiastical service and is offered to its bishops so that its members may assist and minister.

But whoever is a servant of Mammon rejects the discipline of the Church. Nor should we pass over what is immediately added there: “I,” says the Lord, “have taken the Levites from the children of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine (Num. III).” Thus it is clearly shown that the order of clerics is the property of God Almighty, just as God himself is the special inheritance of clerics.

But for one to whom God is not sufficient as an inheritance, what could satisfy him he does not know, because a raging greed blinds the eye of his mind.

## CHAPTER II. In a sermon on the Lord’s Supper

“The people went about, and, gathering manna, broke it with a millstone or ground it in a mortar, cooking it in a pot and making from it little cakes, tasting like bread mixed with oil (Num. XI).”

We have, as it were, passed through many jars in the Lord’s storeroom in order to arrive at the single oil-mixed substance, like a little vessel of oil. The manna by which the Israelite people lived signified the sacred word, by which the Christian religion is nourished and grows. It is truly mixed with oil, because it is infused with the mystical anointing of the Holy Spirit.

It should be noted, however, that this same manna, which in the Book of Numbers is said to be mixed with oil, is read in Exodus to have had not the taste of oil but rather that of honey: “Its taste,” he says, “was like fine flour with honey” (Exod. XVI).

What does it mean that this angelic food is first said to have offered the sweetness of honey and afterward to have provided not the sweetness of honey but that of oil, except that our Redeemer, the author and creator of all the sacred Scriptures—whom that manna principally prefigured—before his Passion displayed sweetness like honey through miracles, and after his Ascension poured out the Holy Spirit upon his disciples like oil? (Acts II.)

For he seems to have offered the sweetness of honey when he shone forth through signs and virtues; but he gave the sweetness of oil when he poured out upon his apostles the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Moses fittingly observed this order when, in Deuteronomy, he sang mystically of the rock—which was also manna: “They sucked,” he says, “honey from the rock and oil from the solid rock” (Deut. XXXII).

Of this oil of mystical anointing the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song I). The bridegroom’s name is called oil poured out because, just as Christ is named from chrism, so consequently a Christian is named from Christ.

## CHAPTER III. In the Book *Gratissimus*

“Gather for me,” says the Lord, “seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers and leaders of the people, and bring them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant; make them stand there with you, so that I may descend and speak to you, and take from your spirit and give to them (Num. XI).”

Here it should be noted that he does not say, “You shall take from your spirit and give to them,” but rather, “I will take and give,” clearly showing that one human being does not hand over the Holy Spirit to another, but that he alone distributes the gifts of his grace as he wills.

Hence it is added shortly afterward: “And the Lord descended in a cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men (ibid.).” The Lord is said to have given the men from Moses’ spirit so that it might be clearly taught that those who appoint and those who are appointed ought to have one spirit. Thus the rulers of the Church should by no means think differently among themselves, lest—God forbid!—schisms or destructive heresies arise, but all should teach one thing harmoniously and live together in unity of spirit.

Moreover, just as those seventy whom the Lord appointed after the apostles (Luke X), and approximately as many others whom he wished to help Moses bear the burden of the people, prefigured presbyters, so Moses first, and afterward the apostles, appear to have held the dignity of high priests. And just as neither those men could receive the Holy Spirit from the apostles nor these from Moses, so without doubt this must also be understood of bishops and the other orders of ecclesiastical dignity: namely, that one almighty God, who distinguished them through different degrees of order by the administration of his governance, alone also poured out the grace of his Spirit upon each, as he himself knew.

For in that giving of the Spirit Moses could claim no privilege for himself beyond what the divine voice commanded him: namely, that he should choose the men and, bringing them to the door of the tabernacle, stand there with them. This is the sum of Moses’ task.

What, then, could Moses recognize as belonging to his own power in this gift of God, when, as Scripture testifies, two of those who had been listed were placed in the camp and did not come to the tabernacle, yet received the spirit just as the others, without Moses’ knowledge?

In the statement that the spirit of Moses was taken away and given to others, Moses should certainly not be thought to have suffered any loss of his spirit. It is like any material receiving light from a burning lamp: the lamp is not diminished in its own radiance because of this.

## CHAPTER IV. In a second sermon on Saint Matthew

“The Israelite spies, proceeding as far as the torrent of the cluster, cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole (Num. XIII).”

The two men are, of course, the two peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile. They placed the cluster upon a pole because they suspended the Savior upon the cross. But the one who went first did not look at what he was carrying; the one who followed looked at it.

The Jewish people, which preceded us in time, carried the Lord in the Prophets and the Law, but, because it continually turned away the face of obedience, could not see him. The Gentile people, however, which follows, continually contemplates him as though he had been placed before its eyes.

## CHAPTER V. In a sermon on the Nativity of Saint Mary

This mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who himself testifies in the Gospel, saying, “I am the true vine” (John XV), was plainly signified by that cluster which the spies carried from the land of promise to the children of Israel on a carrying pole (Num. XIII).

With two bearers placed beneath it on either side, one preceding and the other following, the cluster was carried in the middle. For our Redeemer, while the Fathers of the Old Testament proclaimed that he was to come and the preachers of the New announced that he had already come, was carried like a cluster on the pole, so that the minds of believers might be kindled to take possession of the land of the heavenly promise.

The carrying pole borne upon the shoulders of the bearers is the divine Law imposed upon the necks of human beings, and the cluster in the middle joined its parts together; for our Savior, “who made both one” (Eph. II), united the commands of the Law and the Prophets with evangelical teaching.

But the one who went ahead did not see with his eyes what he carried upon his shoulders; the one who followed always looked upon his burden. The one who went ahead therefore suitably signifies the Jewish people; the one who followed signifies the multitude of the Gentiles.

The former carried Christ, as it were, upon its shoulders through the pages of sacred Scripture, but, because it did not recognize him present in the flesh, impeded by the darkness of its unbelief, it turned its back, so to speak, toward his face. The latter looks upon him because the Gentile people openly recognize their Redeemer, in whom they faithfully believe.

The land of promise may also suitably be understood as the body of the most blessed Mother of God, from which our Redeemer wished to spring in human form like a unique cluster, according to what is written: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV).

The most blessed Virgin’s flesh is rightly called the land of promise, since the prophets had promised in many ways, long beforehand, that she would bear the Savior of the world. It truly poured forth milk and honey when, in inviolate virginity, she brought forth God and human being.

Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. VII).

## CHAPTER VI. In the letter to Hermisindis, a religious woman

“Aaron took the censer and ran through the midst of the multitude, which the plague was devastating; and, standing between the dead and the living, he offered incense, and the raging plague ceased (Num. XVI).”

Whom did that Aaron signify except our Redeemer? Since he leapt to run his course like a giant (Ps. XVIII), he seized the censer of his Passion, ran between the dead and the living, and, by the intervention of his cross—on which the incense of his sacred body was burned and that heavenly Lamb was roasted—separated the living from the dead. Like an intervening wall, he shut out from them the destructive fire, so that the devouring flame might swallow all the unbelievers, of whom it is written: “Now fire consumes the adversaries, while the righteous, who live by faith, escape the fire of condemnation” (Heb. X).

The two robbers are already known to have been the first examples of those dead and living, among whom the Lord was crucified: one chosen, the other rejected on account of his faithlessness.

This incense of a saving and singular sacrifice, offered to God the Father upon the altar of the cross, was carried by that mountain of strength between the dead and the living, when he poured forth the fragrance of his knowledge among believers and unbelievers. Hence the words in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song I).

And the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us everywhere the fragrance of his knowledge, because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, an odor of death unto death; to others, an odor of life unto life” (2 Cor. II).

## CHAPTER VII. In a sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“Command the children of Israel to bring a red heifer, perfect in age, without blemish, which has never borne a yoke (Num. XIX).”

The red heifer is plainly the flesh of the Savior, rose-colored through the blood of his Passion. The Lord came to his Passion at the fullness of his age, but the yoke of any sin did not wear down his neck.

Those who offer the heifer are unclean; those who crucify Christ, through whom the world is cleansed, are themselves damnably defiled. But whoever gathers the ashes and casts them outside the camp is clean, because all who proclaim the mystery of the Lord’s cross and Passion throughout the breadth of the world cleanse themselves from the contagion of sins through the ministry of edifying their brothers.

## CHAPTER VIII. In a sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

“Open, Lord, your treasury, the fountain of living water, so that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease (Num. XX).”

For he would not have described an element in such magnificent and divine words—water flowing from the hollows of the earth and afterward being conveyed through channels into recesses. Was it really fitting to call worthless water the treasury of God?

But he undoubtedly calls that the treasury of God of which the Apostle says: “In the breast of Jesus are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II). He also calls it the fountain of living water of which it is said: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV).

Otherwise, by what reasonable connection could he say, “So that, when they are satisfied, their murmuring may cease,” when afterward that same people murmured, saying: “Why did you bring us out of Egypt, so that we might die in the wilderness? There is no bread; there is no water” (Exod. XIV)—along with many other things that, in monstrous madness, it spewed forth amid its tumult?

But Moses, wearied by the disposition of such a harsh and seditious multitude, anxiously calls for the Savior’s coming, just as he had asked at that earlier time when he said: “I beg you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exod. IV).

## CHAPTER IX. In the same sermon

“The multitude having gathered before the rock, Moses said: Hear, you rebels and unbelievers; do you wish us to bring water out of this rock for you?” (Num. XX.)

It was as though he were saying: “We cannot do what lies beyond human powers, because you are unwilling to fulfill what is human. Nor can we display a sign through the power of divinity, because you never cease opposing God through the insolence of rebellion.”

Because of the sins of the people—and he himself had already done this when, at Kadesh, he produced abundant waters by striking the rock—he again lost confidence that he could do so. Therefore, with the Lord forbidding it, he did not bring that people into the land of promise.

“But that rock, according to the Apostle, was Christ” (2 Cor. I). The rod therefore approaches the rock, and water is brought forth for the people to draw. The cross is applied to Christ, and all the hearts of believers are watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

This is the stone of which Zechariah says: “Upon the one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III). But the fact that he struck the rock through unbelief, and therefore did not enter the promised land with the people, signifies the Jewish people, who, not believing Christ to be the power of God, hanged him upon the wood and therefore did not deserve to enter the land of the living.

## CHAPTER X. In the same sermon

“When the people once murmured against Moses, saying, ‘There is no bread; there is no water; our soul is already nauseated by this very light food,’ the Lord then sent fiery serpents among them. When, moved by repentance, they asked for forgiveness, Moses, at the Lord’s command, made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and whoever had been bitten looked at it and was immediately healed (Num. XXI).”

Indeed, through the serpent’s counsel the human being fell into death; bronze, however, is found to be more durable than the other metals. The bronze serpent therefore prefigured the Lord, who drove away the poison of the devil’s suggestion infused into us. The serpent was appropriately made of bronze, so that the one who died through the serpent and the eternal Lord through the bronze might be signified.

For he endured the punishment of the cross in his humanity, but in his divinity he lives perpetual and incapable of suffering. Moreover, the bronze serpent has the likeness of a serpent but does not have the serpent’s poison. Likewise, our Redeemer appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh, but the poison of sin could have no place in him, since he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II).

Nor should it be overlooked that the place where these things happened is suitably called Salmona, which is interpreted as “little image,” because there, plainly, in the form of this bronze serpent, the image of our Savior was represented.

Hence the same Savior says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III).

The bronze serpent is therefore rightly set up as a sign, and the people who look upon it are freed from the bite of the serpents, because all who look with a desire for imitation toward the Savior who was suspended upon the cross immediately escape every poison and the deadly bites of the aged serpent.

It should be noted that the serpent is said to have been set up as a sign. For that righteous Simeon, when the Lord had been brought to the Temple, also prophesied, saying: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II).

Our Redeemer was set up as a sign of contradiction because he was to suffer upon the cross for the salvation of the human race. All the wisdom of the world opposed that cross, but at last, defeated, it yielded to the King of glory triumphing through it, as it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Concerning this sect, we know that it is opposed everywhere” (Acts XXVIII).

## CHAPTER XI. In a sermon of Saint Christopher

“Israel sent messengers to Sihon, saying: ‘Please let me pass through your land; we shall not turn aside into the fields or vineyards; we shall not drink water from the wells; we shall travel by the royal road until we pass beyond your boundaries’ (Num. XXI).”

He did not permit Israel to pass through his territory. Rather, as the same sacred history testifies, after gathering an army, Sihon came out to meet them in the desert, came to Jasa, fought against Israel, was struck by the edge of the sword, and his land was taken by Israel.

But what was historically done then under Moses occurs daily under Christ through the mystery of spiritual warfare. That people then prefigured this battle, because now the holy Church continually fights against the devil.

Sihon has a twofold interpretation. He is called “a fruitless tree,” and he is also called “the exalted one.” Who is this exalted one, who is this proud one, except that reprobate spirit who says: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I shall be like the Most High”? (Isa. XIV.)

Who, I ask, is this exalted one except the one of whom Scripture says: “For he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI), so that, according to the Apostle, he may at some time “sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. II)?

That he is also a fruitless tree needs no explanation, since, like dry wood, he has been assigned to eternal fires.

This Sihon, then, is king of the Amorites, who themselves are interpreted as “speakers” or “those bringing into bitterness.” For all who are subject to the evil spirit through a reprobate life and obey the laws of his dominion are indeed speakers, but not wise.

Many lovers of the world, while empty of heavenly wisdom, are eloquent through the charm of outward speech. Of them Solomon says: “All the labor of a human being is in his mouth, but his soul will not be filled” (Eccl. VI).

The kingdom of the saints, however, is not in speech but in power. But those who are eloquent are also those who bring into bitterness, because, just as the saints distill the honey of heavenly speech, so every reprobate person offers his hearers the poison and bitterness of earthly cunning.

To these, in the person of the holy Church, it is said: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb” (Song IV). They also sing in the figure of that same Church: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII.) Concerning their teacher the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His throat is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable” (Song V).

But of the others, conversely, it is said: “They acted deceitfully with their tongues; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. XIII). Immediately it follows: “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (ibid.).

Hence the Lord complains through the prophet that the vineyard had been changed into bitterness (Isa. V; Jer. II). Although it had formerly received from him the land of milk and honey, it afterward offered him the bitterness of both vinegar and gall (Deut. XI).

The king of these speakers, or of those who bring into bitterness, is Sihon, who is said to be exalted because the devil, the author of pride, rules over the empty talkers and bitter lovers of this world. Hence he himself is also called the prince of this world (John XII, XIV)—that world of which John says: “The world is placed in the evil one” (1 John V).

And the Lord promises his disciples that he will send the Spirit whom this world cannot receive (John XIV).

Israel therefore says to Sihon: “Let us pass through your land; we shall not turn aside into the fields or vineyards” (Num. XXI). We—plainly, we—are those who desire to pass through this world to the land of the living. We, I say, wish to proceed humbly through the boundaries of the proud king toward the homeland of divine promise.

Since “Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who is passing through,” we who are disciples of the one “who did not dwell, but passed through doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him” (Acts X), promise that we shall never dwell with King Sihon, but shall proceed only by the royal road.

But when did we make these promises to King Sihon? When did we reject dwelling with him? When did we make a pact with him concerning eternal separation?

Let us recall the day of holy Baptism; let us bring back to memory the beginning of our new birth. There, without doubt, we find that we renounced the devil and all his pomps and works.

Let each believer remember when he first approached the font of saving washing and received the first seals of faith. Did he not, through the catechetical instruction of the priestly office, use words by which he signified that he rejected the deadly desires of this world and professed that he utterly renounced fellowship with the devil?

This is what is prefigured in the words of the historical account: Israel would not turn aside into the field or vineyard of King Sihon, nor promise to drink in any way from his well.

The field signifies the exercise of works; the vineyard and the well signify the drink of vain arts—astrology, magic, necromancy, and whatever teaches anything vain or sacrilegious against the piety of the Catholic faith.

Concerning these pestilential drinks the Lord complains through Jeremiah against the perverse people, saying: “My people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. II).

Of these it is also said through Solomon: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX). But Israel has its own fountains: “Bless God the Lord in the assemblies, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. LXVII).

Let proud Israel therefore reject Sihon’s waters, despise the streams of heretical doctrines, and “draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. XII).

The one who broke up the fountains and torrents (Ps. LXXIII) says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I give will have rivers of living water flowing from his belly” (John VII).

Let Israel also walk by the royal road, as it promised: “We shall walk by the royal road.” What is the royal road except the one who says, “I am the way”? (John XIV.) At the very moment of his Passion he also declares himself to be a king when he says: “You say that I am a king” (John XVIII).

We have therefore promised the proud king Sihon that we will not drink of his streams, turn aside into fields or vineyards, or deviate from the royal road, that is, hastening to Christ by that road itself, to abstain from all the pomp and works of the devil. But that arrogant Sihon gathers an army and does not permit Israel to pass through his territory.

Who, then, is that people whom Sihon gathers against Israel, except all the reprobate who persecute the Church? Among these are the tyrants, commanders, and rulers of the world, who either oppose Catholic men with the obstacles of contradiction through heretical perversity, or attempt to inflict torments upon the holy martyrs.

But what does Israel do in response to this? Let us consult the historical account: “He came to Jasa [Issar] and fought against him” (Num. XXI). Sihon was struck down by the edge of the sword, and his land was possessed from Arnon to Jabbok [Laboch]. Behold the proud man; behold the arrogant one: he entered the contest, but was crushed and destroyed; he rushed into battle and fell. He who was unwilling to give passage lost his life, and while he disdained to grant passage along the public road, he lost his own royal dominion. Israel, however, who did not obtain passage, reached the rights of hereditary possession; and he to whom passage was not granted made a homeland out of the road.

But where, I ask, my brothers, where was this victory accomplished? Blessed indeed is the place that deserved to witness the triumph of such glory! Where, I say, did Israel overcome the proud king? At Issar. Issar is interpreted as “fulfillment of the commandment.” And if, with God as our guide, we reach this place, we undoubtedly overcome the devil, [Col. 1043A] who is the head and origin of pride. For we conquer the devil when we fulfill the commandments of our Redeemer, although to conquer the devil is itself nothing other than to fulfill the divine commandments.

For when we break the enticements of the flesh, when we resist the perverse passions of our inward parts, when we submit ourselves to the command of the divine injunction and observe not our own wishes but his commands, then without doubt we defeat the ruler of this world and the author of all wickedness. Then that apostolic prayer is fulfilled in us: “But may the God of peace crush Satan beneath your feet” (Rom. XVI). And the Lord grants us what he promised: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke X).

But since Sihon represents the ancient enemy, and his people all the reprobate or the persecutors of the Church, who were struck down by Israel—that is, by the holy preachers—with what weapon were they pierced, and by what sword were they finally killed? Listen to the Apostle, the commander of spiritual warfare and an energetic combatant in the inward battle: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. IV).

The commander and author of those battles, the Lord of warriors, drew this sword of division when he said: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). You have heard of the sword that divides; now hear the division itself: “I have come,” he says, “to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (ibid.).

By this sword, then, Sihon was killed, and his whole army was struck down in a common slaughter, because by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI), the devil fell, and the people subjected to him ceased from the life of their unbelief.

Since Scripture testifies that they were killed by the edge of the sword, it may appropriately be said of these people that they were killed by the sword of the mouth. And when the Lord says, “The ruler of this world will be cast out” [Col. 1043D] (John XII), as soon as Sihon is cast out, Israel—that is, the holy Church—immediately spreads throughout the breadth of the whole world. For as soon as unbelief collapses, extinguished together with its ruler, the faith of the triumphant Church expands; and those who had previously been exiles become possessors after the victory.

Hence it is said to that same Church through Isaiah: “Your people—all of them righteous—will possess the land forever” (Isa. XLVII). Concerning this people he later says: “They will dwell there, plant vineyards, and eat their fruits” (Isa. LXV). The same prophet also clearly declares that the holy Church must be extended through the territories of the nations: “Enlarge,” he says, “the place of your tent, and extend the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes” [Col. 1044A] (Isa. LIV). He explains why this must be done when he adds: “For you will spread out to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations” (ibid.).

Thus the whole land of Sihon fell as an inheritance to Israel. While the ruler of this world is driven out, pierced by the sword of the divine word, the holy universal Church is extended throughout the bounds of that same world.

Nor, I think, should we pass over the statement that his land was possessed from Arnon to Jabbok [Laboch]. Arnon, which is the beginning of Sihon’s kingdom, is interpreted as “their curses.” For the whole world, which before the Savior’s coming was oppressed under the devil’s rule, had its origin in a curse, because it did not know the author of blessing. Concerning him the Prophet says: “He who gave the law will give blessing” (Ps. LXXXIII). Hence the Apostle says: “For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (Gal. III).

Were we not originally under a curse, of whom it is said: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II)?

The end of that kingdom is Jabbok [Laboch], which is interpreted as “struggle.” For all who wish to leave the devil’s kingdom and escape its boundaries must endure the conflicts of assaults by temptation. But if someone fights lawfully, struggles courageously, and prevails, Jabbok will no longer be a city of Sihon but a city of Israel—not, of course, Israel according to the flesh, nor the Jew outwardly, but Israel in Christ, circumcised in heart and not in [Col. 1044C] flesh.

## CHAPTER XII  
### In the letter to Bishop V. and his canons, concerning the restraint of the five bodily senses

The principal city of Sihon’s kingdom is called Heshbon [Esebon], which is interpreted as “thoughts.” This indicates that the greater part of the devil’s power reigns in thoughts. Through Sihon, indeed, the spirit of wickedness is represented; but Heshbon is transferred from Sihon’s dominion into the possession of the Israelites when our thought, which had swollen with the plague of pride, is inclined by the grace of severe humility toward the judgment of its own correction, so that what once arrogantly exalted itself now judges and carefully examines itself and humbly rebukes itself.

At Kadesh, therefore, which is the “fountain of judgment,” we overthrow the Amalekites and Amorites with the devouring sword, because then we lay low the barbarism of all vices and most decisively wage war against the aerial powers, if we live innocently while nevertheless judging ourselves guilty and liable to sins, saying with the Apostle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

Then Heshbon, which we have said is interpreted as “thoughts,” is compelled to pass into Israelite dominion, when our mind is transferred from pride and every earthly desire into love of the heavenly kingdom. The struggle of thoughts can never be absent from Christ’s soldiers, because the uprightness of our conduct does not free us if the mind, armed with virtues, does not resist its own perverse thoughts.

It was enough for the worshipers of the ancient law to do only what was outwardly right. But for us, while the Gospel thunders terribly, it is commanded that, as we strip away wicked deeds, we must also vigilantly struggle against our thoughts: “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

This is why John the Baptist, through whom the old law is represented, is said to have worn a leather belt around his waist (Matt. III). Our Savior, who is the author of the Gospel, was seen by John among seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe and girded at the breasts with a golden belt (Rev. I).

What, then, is the leather belt around the waist except what was said to the ancients: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX)? And what is the golden belt at the breasts except what is said to those who practice the Christian faith: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V)?

Hence also the divine voice commands through the prophet: “Lift up your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem. How long will harmful thoughts remain within you?” (Jer. IV). And elsewhere: “I paid attention and listened; no one speaks what is good” (Jer. VIII). Solomon says: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee the pretender, and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I).

Let us therefore seize the sword of the Spirit and fight without truce against the ranks of thoughts that assail us.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### In the same letter

When that Israelite people had devoted themselves to Baal-peor in the desert and had shamefully fallen into the prostitution of Moab, the Lord, enraged in fury against Israel, said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gallows before the sun, so that my anger may be turned away from Israel” (Num. XXV).

What does it mean that the people plunge into the abyss of lust, while vengeance is exacted upon their leaders? The subjects offend, and the leaders are hung on gallows? Clearly, one person sins and another is punished. Why is this, except that the guilt of subjects redounds to the disgrace of their superiors, and what goes astray among the sheep is attributed to the shepherd’s negligence?

Consider how fearful is the condition of those who preside, since they are punished not only for their own offenses but also for those of their subjects. Moses rebukes them because the law of God accuses them of negligence and sluggishness. He hangs them before the sun because they are brought out for examination and reproved by the light: “Everyone who does evil,” as the Lord says, “hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light” (John III). The one who opens his hidden deeds through the entrance of pure confession comes to the light.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### In the letter to Albert, in which he writes about the Israelites’ stages

[Col. 1046A]

“This is the number of the sons who were recorded by Moses and Eleazar the priest; among them there was none of those who had previously been counted by Moses and Aaron on Mount Sinai. For the Lord had foretold that they would all die in the wilderness” (Num. XXVI).

These words of the historical account plainly show that, while the others were struck down in the desert, the tribe of Levi reached the land of promise safe and uncorrupted. Therefore, whoever is able to place himself among the order of priests or Levites, whoever does not wish to acquire a hereditary share in the land with the rest of humanity but is content to possess the Lord alone with the tribe of Levi, certainly does not die in the desert of this world; rather, he is deemed worthy to enter the promised land alive and unharmed.

Whoever therefore desires to reach the promises made to the Fathers should disdain to possess, with the tribe of Levi, a cord of inheritance in the earth. For whoever casts himself down upon the earth for the sake of earthly things, whoever trusts that he may enjoy himself for a long time where Passover must be celebrated with bitterness and passed through quickly, saying, “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke XII), deservedly hears: “Fool, this night your soul will be demanded from you; and whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (ibid.).

Such a person is killed not by day but by night, like the firstborn of the Egyptians. He did not reject Egypt but rendered service to the rulers of darkness, who themselves demand his soul at night, because he hated the light and did not attain the truth of righteousness.

## CHAPTER XV  
### In the letter to Bishop V. and his canons, concerning the restraint of the five bodily senses

Whoever, through the duty of preaching entrusted to him, urges others to fight but does not fight himself is like one who drowns out the blast of the trumpet but does not dare to engage in close combat. Such a man does not beget a masculine offspring, since he is himself a cowardly father. Salphaad [Zelophehad] prefigured him: when he died, he left not a son but five daughters (Num. XXVII).

Salphaad is interpreted as “shadow in his mouth.” For whoever preaches courageous things but lives weakly, lest he appear shameful, hides himself, as it were, beneath the leaves of honorable speech; he conceals himself under the shadow of his own words, since through the cowardice of his sluggishness he does not advance into the field of battle.

Such a man, insofar as he is concerned, begets not a masculine but a feminine offspring, and this under the number five, since he educates his followers not toward the strength of spiritual courage but toward the idleness of an ignoble life. Because he does not take care to train them in the exertion of spiritual warfare, he compels them to serve external affairs, as though they were the five bodily senses.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### In the letter to Bishop V. and his canons, concerning the eight festivals of the Old Testament

[Col. 1047A]

It is recorded that in the old law the Lord established eight principal solemnities throughout the cycle of each year. These festivals are, in some respect, common to us and to them, though according to the difference of the times. They are theirs through the observance of the flesh; they are also ours through the sacrament of spiritual understanding.

Their first festival is the continual sacrifice, which is commanded to be offered on successive days at the morning and evening hours (Num. XXVIII). He celebrates the solemnity of the continual sacrifice to the Lord who constantly perseveres in meditation upon the heavenly word.

For the morning of our light is the Law and the Prophets, while the evening of this light, according to the order of the times, is the Gospel, as the Apostle says: “We, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X); and David himself says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

He always offers the morning and evening sacrifice to the Lord who, slaughtering himself with respect to worldly affairs, is continually occupied in meditation upon the new and ancient Scriptures. Or we continually offer a morning and evening sacrifice to the Lord when we render worthy thanks to him for our redemption and, fearing his terrible judgment, stand trembling as though before him who presides over the tribunal.

[Col. 1047C]

After the continual sacrifice comes the Sabbath, namely, so that one may rest from every performance of servile work. For a Christian, keeping the spiritual Sabbath means resting from the laborious desire for temporal things, devoting oneself solely to prayer and reading, throwing off the burden of worldly affairs from the neck of the mind, giving oneself with the whole intention of the heart to the contemplation of heavenly things, despising the pleasures of the flesh, and rejoicing in spiritual delight from the hope of heavenly things alone.

Concerning this the Apostle says: “Therefore a sabbatism remains for the people of God” (Heb. IV). He truly celebrates the Lord’s Sabbath who refrains from the works that belong to the world in such a way that he nevertheless does not cease from spiritual activities. Hence the Truth says: “Have you not read that the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are without guilt?” (Matt. XII).

Whoever therefore ceases from the labors of worldly actions and devotes himself to the works of divine service celebrates the Sabbath of the Christian religion. He does not perform servile work because he guards himself from committing sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII).

He does not kindle a fire in his house because he extinguishes from the dwelling of his mind every fuel of vice and every spark of anger and hostility, guarding himself against that fire of which it is written: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isa. L).

Finally, he does not carry a burden on the road, because through repentance he lightens the heart that has been bent beneath the rubble of iniquities. Concerning these things the Prophet says: “For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. XXXVII). And shortly afterward: “I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly” (ibid.).

Furthermore, sitting in his own place, he does not proceed farther, because he makes Christ his foundation and constructs in him the firmest dwelling-place of his rest. He himself is the place of which it is written: “The children of your servants will dwell there” (Ps. CI). He is the foundation concerning which it is said: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. III).

The third festival is the Neomenia, that is, the new moon. The moon is said to be renewed when it is joined to the sun, so that from it, in order to conceive brightness, it may be restored as though from the loss of its light. “Christ is the sun of righteousness.” The moon is first the holy universal Church, and then every faithful soul, illumined by the rays of him who is “the radiance of glory and the figure of substance” (Heb. I).

When any holy soul is truly joined to its Redeemer in love, when it is united to him, as in a bridal chamber, through the inward bond of delight, then undoubtedly it celebrates the solemnity of the Neomenia, presenting itself, renewed by the heavenly light, to the gaze of its brothers, as the Apostle says: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. VI).

For if in all these matters only the external rite of the solemnities is accepted, it seems that no benefit can now be conveyed to us through them; rather, they must be judged superstitious and frivolous. Hence the Apostle says: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of a Sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. II).

What was then a shadow of things to come for the Jew is now the manifestation of present realities for the Christian; and what was given to them under external ceremonies has become for us an instrument of spiritual understanding. For we celebrate the rising of the Neomenia, that is, of the new moon, when we put off the old person and put on the newness of holy conduct.

The fourth place is occupied by the Passover festival among them, in which among us now “that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world” (John I) is sacrificed for the salvation of the whole world. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V).

Connected with this is the festival called Unleavened Bread, during which it is commanded that all leaven be removed from every house. We truly celebrate this festival—which must be understood as one with Passover—if we cast out the leaven of malice and wickedness from the tabernacle of our heart and preserve the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (ibid.).

We must therefore beware lest there be in our minds a counterfeit appearance, the corruption of leaven, or a hiding-place of falsehood. Rather, in the house of our breast, let the integrity of purity and the firmness of truth flourish.

After this comes the festival called that of the New Produce, when firstfruits are offered from the new crops. When the grain reaches maturity, then a festival is celebrated to God, the author of good things, in the perfection of good fruits.

We too celebrate the solemnity of the New Produce if, first breaking up the field of our heart with the ploughshare of discipline, we scatter the seeds of virtues, so that afterward we may reap the grain of good works. Hence the prophet says: “Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow ears of grain” (Jer. IV).

Of the good farmer Solomon says: “He who cultivates his land will raise up a heap of crops, and he who practices righteousness will himself be exalted” (Ecclus. XX). Concerning the negligent laborer he likewise says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, it was wholly overgrown with nettles; thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. XXIV). And again: “Prepare your work outside and carefully cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house” (ibid.).

But whoever renews his inward person from day to day, according to the Apostle’s teaching, whoever furrows his heart with the mattocks of divine fear, sows not among thorns but upon new ground, so that he may reap a harvest yielding a hundredfold. Hence the Apostle says: “He who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. VI).

The same Apostle carefully enumerates elsewhere the fruits gathered from the Spirit even in this life, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. V). Whoever therefore gathers these fruits into the storehouse of his mind undoubtedly celebrates the solemnity of the New Produce profitably.

Next follows the festival of the seventh month, which is called the Festival of the Blast, or of Trumpets. Just as every seventh day is called a Sabbath, so likewise the seventh month is called the Sabbath of the months, and even the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

What is that blast of the trumpets to which we should render annual festivals except the evangelical and apostolic teaching, which, like heavenly thunder and a terrifying trumpet, summons us to the readiness of spiritual warfare and urges us to fight without truce against the spirits of wickedness on behalf of the camp of the eternal Commander?

Who, then, legitimately celebrates the feast of trumpets or of the blast except one who strives to enclose the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments in the treasury of his mind and to entrust the heavenly commandments always to a tenacious memory? To those who celebrate these feasts properly the Prophet says: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Ps. LXXX).

After this comes the festival celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month, during which the Jews are commanded to afflict their souls. We too properly celebrate this solemnity when we chastise our flesh through fasting, restrain ourselves under the strict custody of discipline, crucify the wanton enticements of carnal passions, wear down our body through labors and hardships for the Lord, and slaughter the inward person through the lamentation of compunction and tears.

When we celebrate this festival in this manner, he whom God appointed as an expiation through faith in his blood is reconciled to us.

The eighth, which is also the final solemnity, is called the Feast of Booths, that is, of Tabernacles. It begins to be celebrated on the fifteenth day of that same seventh month. God rejoices in you when he sees you as a pilgrim and exile, and observes you dwelling not in the houses of your homeland but in the tabernacles of exile. “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. XIII).

When we are seen here through the mass of the body, we dwell in heaven through the intentness of our purpose. When, like travelers and resident foreigners, we pass swiftly through all present things by the contempt of the mind, while we hasten toward our heavenly homeland with anxious steps of desire, then the Feast of Booths is celebrated spiritually by us—the feast that was formerly observed among them carnally through the ceremonies of the prescribed rite.

This festival begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and, because it is celebrated for eight days, undoubtedly ends on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.
