For it is said in the book of Numbers: “On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, which shall be holy and venerable for you, you shall do no servile work on it, but you shall celebrate a solemnity to the Lord for seven days” (Num. XXIX). A little later it adds: “On the eighth day, which is the most celebrated, you shall do no servile work on it” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### In the letter to Bishop V. and his canons, concerning the five bodily senses

[Col. 1050C]

“Moses said: ‘Arm yourselves with men from among you for battle, who may exact the vengeance of the Lord upon the Midianites.’ When they had fought against the Midianites, as the sacred history relates, and had conquered, they killed all the males and their kings—Evi, Rekem, Sur, Bur, and Reba—the five princes of the nation” (Num. XXXI).

Evi is clearly interpreted as “beastlike” or “wild.” We therefore pierce this king within ourselves with the spiritual sword when we cut away from ourselves beastlike habits and sever from our breast the rage of bestial anger. For when the Lord says, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V), how can you obtain the blessedness of the meek unless you restrain within yourself the ferocity of the beastlike spirit?

Rekem [Col. 1050D], or, as it is said in the old translation, Rocon, is interpreted as “emptiness.” And what else is everything that is done in the world for the sake of worldly desire except what Scripture says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I)?

Vanity produces vanities, and the vanities themselves produce vanity: the world, which is passing away, makes vain the people whom it deceives, while people turn the world, which they love foolishly, into vanity. The soldier of God, the true Israelite, kills and cuts down this king if he does nothing superfluous, nothing empty, and nothing irrelevant, but strives seriously and rationally to fulfill the commandments of the divine law.

The third king of the Midianites is called Sur, which is interpreted as “wall,” “strong,” or “distress.” What should be understood by a wall or by strength except the obstinacy or stubbornness of a hard mind? But since it is also said to be interpreted as “distress,” this too is not far removed from the vice of hardness, because whoever is hard and stubborn about forgiving his neighbor’s debts is constricted by distress of mind, since he is not enlarged by the breadth of charity.

Concerning this charity the Prophet says: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. XI). Or this may also be understood to mean that the distress of condemnation follows hardness of mind. Hence Solomon says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Prov. XXVIII).

The fourth king of the Midianites is called Bur [Col. 1051B], which is interpreted as “provocation.” You see, therefore, that the names of the kings are shadows and images of vices. For those who bring heavy burdens in through their gates pour into the hidden places of their hearts, through the entrances of their senses, what clamors outside; they undoubtedly provoke God, whom they thereby incite to pronounce a sentence of vengeance.

Hence it is written: “Hypocrites and the crafty provoke the anger of God” (Job XXXVI). And concerning such people it is often said to Ezekiel: “For it is a provoking house” (Ezek. II). The Psalmist likewise says: “Why, O God, has the enemy insulted? Does the adversary provoke your name forever?” (Ps. LXXIII).

Reba, which is said to mean “ordered,” is presented here only if the expression is understood as irony or antiphrasis, so that the one who is called ordered is, on the contrary, disordered and confused. For every vicious person, even if outwardly he presents the appearance of an orderly life, nevertheless turns over in his heart the darkness of confused and disordered thought.

By the five kings of the Midianites, therefore, the five bodily senses are signified, because every vice that reigns in the body depends upon these five senses. They must then be extinguished and cut down by the sword, when they rise up against us in battle and do not cease to cause us to stumble.

Does the Lord not command these kings to be extinguished and killed by the sword of the Spirit when he orders the offending eye to be torn out and the hand or foot to be cut off? “It is better,” he says, “to enter life with one eye or maimed than, possessing two eyes, feet, and hands, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V).

These are plainly the kings of the Midianites. Midian is interpreted as “from judgment.” For all kings who are not governed by the Spirit but obey the senses of the flesh show that they belong not to mercy but to judgment, as it is said of every unbeliever: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III).

By contrast, it is said of the one who hears the Savior’s word: “He does not come into judgment, but passes from death into life” (John V). Rather, each person should strive to exercise himself in holy works and endeavor to purify and sanctify himself in all things. He should never cease to reproach and judge himself.

For whoever judges himself perfectly does not await judgment. To judge oneself perfectly means both not to do what deserves reproach and cautiously to reconsider even what has been done irreproachably. Whoever does this truly kills the kings of the Midianites, lays low the princes of the Amalekites, and excludes from himself every plague of vice.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### In the same letter

Hence the same sacred history testifies: “The sons of Israel departed and came to the Fountain of Judgment, that is, Kadesh; and they killed all the princes of Amalek and the Amorites who dwelt in Tharansem.”

Kadesh is interpreted as “sanctification.” At Kadesh, therefore, which is the Fountain of Judgment, we spiritually kill the Amalekites and Amorites when we strive to sanctify our life through pious works and yet judge ourselves as guilty and deserving of reproach. While we labor always to live irreproachably, nevertheless, through the vigilance of strict examination, we do not cease to accuse our works.

It should be noted that the Fountain of Judgment and Kadesh, which is called “sanctification,” are one and the same place, because every righteous person, while living holily, accuses himself and sanctifies himself more and more by judging and accusing himself. In this way, therefore, the life of the saints is reproved in their own thoughts and yet is found irreproachable in its works.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### In the letter to Hildebrand

[Col. 1052C]

“Through forty-two stages the sons of Israel reached the beginning of the taking of their inheritance” (Num. XXXIII). The beginning of the taking of the inheritance was the place where Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh received the land of Gilead as a possession.

Now, just as they ascended through forty-two stages, so our Savior descended into the Egypt of this world through the same number of ancestors. If we now understand how much sacramental meaning this number contains—namely, human ascent and divine descent—let us begin to ascend by the stages through which Christ descended, and let us build for ourselves as the first stage the one that he had as his last.

For if someone comes to us from some place so that, when he returns, he may lead us through the same places where he left off, we begin the journey where he ended, and where he began we finish. Christ’s first generation began with Abraham; the final one, like the last stage, ended with the Virgin.

Since Abraham is interpreted as “exalted father,” we begin this journey from the Virgin’s childbirth, so that, traversing the successive places of the stages, we may finally arrive at God, the exalted Father.

The Virgin’s childbirth first meets us as we wish to depart from Egypt, when, believing that the Word of God came into this world made flesh, we leave behind all perishable and transitory things, rest in that place, and establish in him the dwelling-place of our rest and hope.

After this, if we strive to advance and ascend to each successive degree of faith and virtue, we must remain there until the virtues are able to become habitual. Then we are judged not to be merely passing through the deserts of spiritual life, but to be making stages, or even dwelling in the very attainments of virtue.

For whoever begins a good work without persevering in it passes rapidly along the road, as it were; but whoever remains in the holiness he has once undertaken builds a stage there, in a certain sense.

It should be noted that although going and remaining—and therefore journey and stage—are wholly opposed to one another and do not naturally correspond, Scripture nevertheless confirms that both were present in the Israelite march, so that the Israelites are said to have had both a journey and stages through the desert. For we who strive to enter the land of the living must both remain through the fixed purpose of our profession and always advance through the growth of a better way of life and the accumulation of progress.

Therefore the sons of Israel first set out from Ramesses. Ramesses, as some think, is called in our language “turbulent agitation” or “the agitation of the moth.” This signifies that all worldly things are established in agitation and disturbance and are shown to be subject to corruption, which the moth represents. The soul ought not to remain among them, but should depart from them without hesitation. Others have thought that Ramesses should be interpreted as “agitation” or “thunder.” This can fittingly be applied to us, since, when we have been stirred by the preaching of the evangelical trumpet, awakened as though by the thunder of heavenly clouds, we leave the Egypt of this world. They departed in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the moon—that is, at the full moon and the beginning of spring. And we, when we are illumined by the rays of the highest light, when flowers of good will burst forth within us, when all things are renewed, when at last the meadows of our hearts grow warm under the influence of the heavenly sun, then hasten to go forth from the darkness of Egypt.

The second encampment is at Succoth. Succoth is interpreted as “tents.” The first progress of the soul, therefore, is to separate itself from earthly agitations and, recognizing itself as a stranger and sojourner, to establish for itself not a dwelling but a tent of exile, mourning with the prophet: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Psalm 11).

[Col. 1053D] Next they come to Etham, or, as the Seventy translators say, Buthan, which is at the farthest boundaries of the wilderness. Etham signifies “strength.” Those who now journey as pilgrims for God in the world, who recognize themselves as sojourners and exiles, must be stronger in humility and patience precisely to the extent that they show themselves weaker in earthly actions. Buthan, however, is interpreted as “valley,” which by no means differs from the same sense. Whoever hastens toward the land of the living must remain in the valley of humility and patience in order to endure the arrows of temptations.

From there they set out for Pi-hahiroth, which faces Baal-peor, and encamp before Migdol. [Col. 1054A] Pi-hahiroth is said to mean “the mouth of nobles,” by which the tongue of teachers is signified. Established in the valley of patience, the more severely one is battered by the blows either of persecutions or of carnal temptations, the more necessary it is that help should come to him from the mouth of nobles—that is, from the exhortations of holy teachers. But if not Pi-hahiroth, but Osirath, is to be read, as another edition bears witness, it should be known that Irath is interpreted as “village.” One therefore comes to the mouth, that is, to the first entrance of this village; and this signifies the beginning of a new way of life. Hence they do not come to a city but to a village, because every novice must meanwhile restrain himself within the limits of a suburban life and must not yet rashly dare to attempt the height of senatorial perfection. Hence it is appropriately said that Airoth faces Beelsephon. Beelsephon is interpreted as “the ascent of a lookout” or “tower.” For one ascends from small things to great. This encampment was not itself at the lookout, but faced the lookout, because every novice, although already tending toward the contemplative life through desire, does not yet aspire to the summit of contemplative perfection. Therefore it is suitably added there: “And they encamped before Migdol” (Numbers 33). Migdol is said to mean “magnificence.” For one newly coming to the service of God already holds before his mind, through intention, the ascent of the lookout and magnificence, but does not yet possess them in the actual accomplishment of virtue. Although he is already nourished and sustained by the hope of contemplation and perfection, he does not yet enjoy the radiance of completed purity or heavenly grace. If Beelsephor is interpreted as “lord of the north,” as some say, what is expressed by this lord of the north except the ancient enemy, who rules over hearts that are cold and alienated from the love of God? Before him—that is, against him—we encamp when we engage him in unremitting combat.

From there they set out across the Red Sea and came to Marah, which is interpreted as “bitterness.” It is the proper order that those who hasten toward the land flowing with milk and honey should drink in the bitterness of labor and temptation in the wilderness of this life and reach the sweetness of inward recompense through the harshness of present discipline. Hence the Apostle says: “All discipline,” he says, “for the present seems not to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12). In the ranks of spiritual warfare, bitter things are mingled with sweet and sweet things with bitter, so that through these the human condition may experience both what weakness it suffers from itself and what strength it ought to hope for from God. Thus it is said to the same people: “He afflicted you and fed you with manna in the wilderness, which your fathers did not know, so that it might be recognized what was in your heart” (Deuteronomy 8).

Hence it follows that, having set out from Marah, they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. You see how, after the bitterness of temptation, they arrive at such a pleasant place of sweet fruits and flowing waters. Through the battle of temptation they are brought to the palms, and through the intolerable scarcity of thirst they come to the abundant irrigation of living waters. For almighty God, the physician of souls, orders everything so wisely that, like honey infused with spices, he mixes joyful things with sorrowful and sorrowful things with joyful, so that the weak mind, when sometimes struck, may never grow proud in prosperity, and when sometimes refreshed may not collapse in adversity. Elim, moreover, is interpreted as “rams,” which are naturally the leaders of following flocks. Who are the leaders of the rational flock—that is, of the Christian people—if not the holy apostles? These are the twelve springs, watering the dryness of minds with streams of heavenly teaching. Yet because our Savior chose not only those twelve apostles but also appointed seventy others, therefore not only twelve springs but also seventy palm trees are described as having been there. For they too are called apostles, as is recognized in the words of blessed Paul. When he was speaking of the Savior’s resurrection, he said: “He was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven; then he appeared to all the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15). From these words it is clearly gathered that, besides those twelve, other disciples may also appropriately be called apostles.

But after leaving Elim, they pitched their tents beside the Red Sea. Note that they do not enter the sea again, but pitch their tent beside the sea, so that they may look from afar upon the sea and the heaps of its waves, while no longer fearing its motion or force. We too, after the waves of temptations and after the fearful shipwrecks of the resounding sea, often place before our eyes the very evils we have endured, so that, now standing as though on the shore, we may render worthy thanks to our God, who has rescued us.

They also set out from the Red Sea and came to the wilderness of Sin. Sin is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” The Christian soldier therefore begins to see the hope of prosperity smile upon him and to receive the words of divine converse. For the Lord appeared from the bush and commanded Moses to carry his commands to the sons of Israel (Exodus 3). There, therefore, the sign of hoped-for mercy is given to you, where the beginning of Israel’s visitation took place. But it is not without purpose that Sin is also called “temptation.” Temptation often intervenes even in visions, since at times the spirit of iniquity transforms itself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11). Therefore one must act subtly, so that the kinds of visions may be distinguished. Thus Joshua son of Nun, when he saw an angel and had no doubt that temptations could sometimes be present in visions of this kind, immediately asked the one who appeared, saying: “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” (Joshua 5). The discernment of spirits is also enumerated among the gifts of the Holy Spirit by the Apostle (1 Corinthians 12). That Sin is also said to be interpreted as “hatred” does not depart from a spiritual understanding. Whoever reaches a vision or conversation with God immediately conceives hatred for the world.

[Col. 1056A] From there they proceeded and came to Dophkah, or, as another translation reports, Raphaca. Dophkah is ultimately said to mean “a knocking.” And we, after we reach the Church—which that bush signifies—where a person is deemed worthy of conversation with God and where the vision of angels is perceived, then begin to ask, seek, and knock at the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, at the Lord’s command and promise: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7; Luke 11). But if one prefers to accept Raphaca, which means “health,” this name is fittingly applied to the soul that was long sick but has now, through the gift of the holy Church, been freed from the bonds of sickness. For this is the soul to which it is said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Psalm 102). Which Lord, I ask? “He who heals all your diseases,” it says, “who redeems your life from destruction” (ibid.). The sickness of the soul is vices; the death of the soul is mortal sins. “For sin, when it is completed, gives birth to death” (James 1).

Next they come to Halus. Halus is interpreted as “labors” or “leaven.” Certainly labors follow health, since the holy soul ought to desire health for no other reason than that it may be able to endure labors and hardships for God. This is why Peter’s mother-in-law recovered from her fever: so that she might minister to the Lord through diligent service (Matthew 8). This is why Paul was healed through Ananias: so that afterward he might toil continually. Hence it was said to Ananias concerning him: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9). But because Elus is also said to be interpreted as “leaven,” an appropriate meaning is thereby offered to us. This is the leaven that the woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Matthew 13)—that is, the holy Gospel. In this wilderness the people murmured and received both manna and quail. And since not only leaven but also manna signifies the sacred Gospel, these come together wonderfully in the tenth encampment, so that the bread of the Gospel appears to follow the Decalogue of the law already set forth.

After this they come to Rephidim. Rephidim is interpreted as “praise of judgment.” It is certainly fitting that labor should precede praise and that praise should come after labor. Yet it is not the praise of just anything, but the praise of judgment—that is, praise proceeding from the judgment of reason—not praise arising from the vanity of pride. “For the spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2). Other interpretations of these names are also found. But if we embraced everything suggested to us on this subject, the concise order of a letter would no longer be preserved; instead, the book would rise into burdensome enormity. We therefore pass briefly over the encampments of the Israelites, not to scrutinize their inner chambers, but simply to display, in their names, what may be regarded as the exterior surfaces of their walls.

Next they come to the wilderness of Sinai. Sin, which we said above, and Sinai are without doubt one wilderness; but Sin is the plain itself, whereas Sinai is the mountain rising above that same wilderness. On it the Lord promulgates the decrees of the law, and Moses constructs the tabernacle (Exodus 20, 25, and 26). This most aptly corresponds to the pattern: after the rational soul has begun to possess a right and therefore praiseworthy judgment, it then constructs within itself a tabernacle for its God and, now worthy of conversation with the Creator, receives the heavenly mysteries of his commandments.

After this they proceed to the Graves of Lust, where a beautiful order is woven together. For when the blessed soul becomes a tabernacle for its Creator, when, intent upon the commands of the divine law, it begins to contemplate heavenly things, the heat of raging vices is immediately extinguished, and every desire of carnal allurements is buried, so that the flesh no longer rises against the spirit, nor the spirit lusts against the flesh.

From there they pass to Hazeroth, which is interpreted as “perfect courts” or “blessedness.” O how beautiful the order of the mystery, how graceful the sequence of spiritual growth: after you have buried the desires of the flesh, you immediately arrive at the court of perfection and the reward of blessedness! Blessed is the soul that is no longer oppressed by any vices of the flesh, because it immediately enters into the blessedness of the reward it is to receive!

After this they came to Rithmah, or Pharan. Rithmah, as we think, is interpreted as “completed vision”; Pharan, however, as “visible mouth.” What else is understood in these names except that every holy soul, after the desires of the flesh have been buried, after it has been brought to the court of perfection and is secure concerning the reward of blessedness, should then come to the completed vision of God and behold his visible mouth—that is, the present appearance of God? “For now,” says the Apostle, “we see him in a mirror and in a riddle; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know just as I also am known” (1 Corinthians 13). Yet because holy persons established in the flesh cannot fully possess all these things in actuality, they already possess them in hope. They hold this hope most firmly because they have the Holy Spirit as a pledge, the Spirit who strengthens them in the labors of this life. Hence that interpretation by which Rithmah is said to mean “sound” or “juniper” is not judged inappropriate. For they say that this wood preserves fire within itself for a long time, so that, if its embers are covered with ashes, they remain glowing until the following year. Since, as it is written, the Holy Spirit possesses knowledge of speech (Wisdom 1), and was sent upon the apostles in the form of fire (Acts 2), this interpretation by which Rithmah is called “sound” or “juniper” seems most aptly to fit the Holy Spirit.

From there they withdrew and encamped at Rimmon-perez, which among us is called “lofty division.” When the understanding of the soul returning to God is increased, perfect knowledge is immediately given to it, by which it knows, loftily and sublimely, how to divide earthly things from heavenly and separate all that is perishable and transient from what is everlasting. But if Rimmon-perez, as it is found elsewhere, is called “the division of the pomegranate,” this undoubtedly designates the holy Church, which, like many seeds enclosed by a single rind, gathers the whole multitude of believers into the inseparable unity of the catholic faith.

Next they cross over to Libnah, which is interpreted as “whitening.” We are not unaware that whitening is sometimes used of a crime, as when tombs and walls are called whitened; but here that whitening should be understood which is spoken of through Isaiah: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow; and though they be red like crimson, they shall be white like wool” (Isaiah 1); and in the Psalm: “They shall be whitened with snow in Zalmon” (Psalm 67). And in the Apocalypse: “The hairs of Jesus are described as white like wool” (Revelation 1). Accordingly, this whitening is suitably understood as proceeding from the splendor of the true light and descending from the brightness of the highest vision. But if Libnah, as some say, is rendered “brick,” the material in which the Israelite people were forced to labor in Egypt, this signifies that, just as they return to brick after such lofty places, so we, as long as we are pilgrims in the wilderness of this world, are sometimes compelled by necessity to descend from the highest things to the lowest and to pass from spiritual matters to works of earthly action.

After this they come to Rissah, which is rendered “bridles,” and not incongruously. For if, after the summit of perfection, we descend to muddy works, we must be restrained by the bonds of discipline and the reins of penitence, lest we rush headlong through precipices, but may quickly return to the purity of our accustomed cleanliness. Rissah is also interpreted as “visible” or “praiseworthy temptation.” Although the mind of any just man may already be advancing toward high things, it is still brought low by temptation, lest it be lifted up by the swelling of pride because of its virtues. For the sting of temptation is applied as a safeguard of humility. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Corinthians 12). This temptation, therefore, is visible because it is manifest, and praiseworthy because it is salutary.

From there they proceed and come to Kehelathah, which is interpreted as “Church,” so that all who are unstable and drive themselves headlong through the precipices of vices may be drawn back into the Church by the bridle of sacred Scripture; or, according to another edition, to Makkheloth, which means “the rule of the rod.” Both seem to express authority. For the flesh of one who is tempted must be ruled by the presiding spirit, so that, when the flesh gives up the struggle, the spirit, as though from above, may threateningly wield the rod by applying the discipline of stern fear.

From there they come to Mount Sepher, or Sephar, which is called “the sounding of the trumpet.” The trumpet is a sign of war. For the horse of God “scenteth the battle, and when he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Ha!’”; and the soldier of Christ, when he feels himself surrounded by the temptation of advancing vices, immediately takes up the weapons of virtue and proceeds to war, engaging the enemy at close quarters, lest, released into degenerate sluggishness, he be easily slain by his adversaries. Then he will be able to sound the trumpet more gloriously—that is, summon others also to spiritual combat.

Hence it is said there that, setting out from there, they came to Haradah, or, as it is said elsewhere, to Charadath, which in our language sounds as “made capable,” so that he who has now become a preacher may rightly say with the Apostle: “He made us capable ministers of the New Testament” (2 Corinthians 3).

Also setting out from there, they come to Makheloth, which is interpreted as “from the beginning.” Whoever strives toward the summit of perfection contemplates the beginning of all things, directing all the desires of his inmost being toward God. And while he continually turns his heart toward its Creator, he does not depart from the beginning of all things. Or, if Makheloth, as some think, is said to mean “assembly,” the Church is understood by this, in which all the faithful assemble. Hence it is sung: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Psalm 132).

Next they come to Tahath, or, as it is read elsewhere, to Caath, which means “patience” or “confirmation.” Whoever desires to enter the land of the living through the labors of the present life must be confirmed by patience for enduring the dangers of the world. Or if Tahath, as some say, is rendered “terror,” let this be said to every person who is struggling, or perhaps who is already triumphing through divine grace: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11).

But, setting out from there, they come to Tarah, which in Greek is interpreted as “ecstasy” (*ekstasis*), while in our language it is called “contemplation.” It follows that whoever has previously been tested through patience should consequently attain the grace of contemplation; and whoever was earlier brought low in tribulation should afterward be lifted up to the joy of inward vision. But if Tarah, as some think, is to be understood as “cunning” or “malice,” this seems not improperly capable of being referred to the overseers of the Churches, so that they may fear for their hearers who labor in the tribulation of temptations. For one must beware of the cunning and malice of him of whom it is said: “Our adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5).

Next they proceed to Methca, or, as it is read elsewhere, Maathica, which is interpreted as “new death.” Diabolical cunning is never guarded against so perfectly as when we die with Christ, so that, like those who are insensible, we may become insensible to the enticements of the crafty enemy. Contemplation produces this new death, which makes both the world dead to us and us dead to the world. But if Methca, as some prefer, is rendered “sweetness,” what is surprising if one comes from contemplation to sweetness, since contemplation itself is nothing other than ineffable and immeasurable sweetness?

After this they come to Heshmonah, which is called “haste.” For after we reach the sweetness of contemplation, we cannot bear the delay of slowness. O how painfully did the one who said endure this delay: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down, and the mountains would melt before your face!” (Isaiah 64). How grievously did the one who said, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1), endure it—indeed, far more so! But if it is said to derive from Senna, which signifies “bones,” this pertains to strength of constancy, which the lover of Christ must possess lest he become impatient through excessive love.

From there they now pass to Moseroth, which is thought to signify “excluding.” For the soul that reaches perfect love of its Bridegroom excludes from itself the temptations of the crafty corrupter. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4). But if Moseroth, according to some, is interpreted as “bonds,” a sound and wholly fitting understanding shines forth: every holy soul that is joined in love to its heavenly Bridegroom must be inseparably connected to him by continual meditation on the Scriptures, as though by certain bonds. Concerning these bonds it is said to Christ through Isaiah: “The exalted men shall pass over to you, and they shall be yours, and they shall walk after you, bound with bonds” (Isaiah 45).

Hence they rightly come to Banacim, which signifies “springs” or “cultivations”—that is, a place where the soul drinks from the springs of the divine Scriptures and cultivates them, meaning that it handles and ruminates upon them subtly. It cultivates them, I say, when it observes the Gospel saying: “Not one jot or one tittle shall pass from the law until all things are accomplished” (Matthew 5). But if Jaakan is correctly rendered, as some say, as “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing,” this signifies that whoever has been instructed and richly equipped by divine utterances must draw others after him and beget children, while, by threateningly setting before them weeping and the gnashing of teeth, he imposes upon them, in a certain sense, the necessity of turning to God. These, then, are the sons of necessity or of gnashing, concerning whom it is prophetically sung: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28).

After this they ascend Mount Gudgod, which is interpreted as “messenger,” or “girding,” or indeed “cutting.” To those to whom we announce the words of God we must undoubtedly give warning that they gird themselves with the weapons of virtue and cut down the backs of invisible enemies with spiritual swords. When we teach them diligently to do this, we ascend the mountains together with them. But if Gudgod, as some think, signifies “assaults,” it is understood that those who strive toward the heavenly homeland cannot be without temptations. Temptation is often mingled with virtues so that a more abundant reward may be gained by the laboring soldier of Christ.

And because one passes through the evils of temptations to the good things of rewards, it fittingly follows that, setting out from there, they came to Jotbathah, or, as it is read elsewhere, Jatbathah, which is interpreted as “goodness” or “the good.” Thus through the experiences of temptations one reaches goodness, which is undoubtedly Christ.

[Col. 1061A] From there they set out for Ebronah, which is called “crossing.” Everything must be crossed in spirit, and you must fix the gaze of your mind upon him alone with whom you can remain without crossing over.

After this they come to Ezion-geber, which is interpreted as “the counsels of a man.” For after we have cast ourselves wholly upon Christ, after we have placed all the confidence of our heart in him, we ought no longer to be children in our understanding, imitating the Apostle, who says: “When I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (2 Corinthians 13); and again: “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Corinthians 14).

But since “whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow,” they again come to the wilderness of Sin, which is Kadesh. We have already said above that Sin is interpreted as “temptation.” For just as a golden or silver vessel is often struck by a hammer and often surrounded by a file, which polishes it here and there so that it may become brighter, so repeated temptation cleanses the rust from a steadfast soul that does not yield. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessel, and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27). And because Kadesh is called “holy fruitfulness,” you see that holy fruitfulness follows the furrows of temptations.

From there they also encamped at Mount Hor, at the farthest boundaries of Edom. Hor is interpreted as “mountainous.” Whoever, when tempted, does not fall but bears fruit from temptation must consequently ascend in victory to the mountain that is Christ. For this is that “mountain made fertile, a mountain rich in fatness” (Psalm 67), of which the Prophet says: “It shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isaiah 2). This mountain is called “mountainous” because wherever Christ is, there undoubtedly also is the Christian: “Where I am,” he says, “there also my servant shall be” (John 12).

Next they come to Zalmonah, which is interpreted as “the shadow of a portion.” And rightly so: after we ascend the mountain that is Christ, fleeing the heat of vices, we sit beneath the shelter of his protection. Concerning this shadow Jeremiah says: “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, has been captured in our sins; to him we said: In your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations 4). And the angel said to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). Zalmonah is also called “a little image” in some sources, which certainly suits that place appropriately, since the bronze serpent was hung there and represents the image of the crucified Savior.

There is also a passage to Phunon, which is interpreted as “mouth,” or “the frugality of the mouth.” It is called “mouth” because, as soon as we understand the mysteries of Christ’s passion, we proclaim with our mouth what we believe in our heart, as it is written: “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115). And the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10). It is called “the frugality of the mouth” because, since we cannot penetrate such profound mysteries of human redemption, we place a finger, as it were, upon our mouth, leaving the height of Christ’s divinity to those greater than us and treating only his cross, as the Apostle says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2).

After this they set out for Oboth, which is rendered as “magicians” or “pythons.” This signifies that, after the image of God conceived in the reasoning of the heart and after the faith received and expressed in the confession of the mouth, heretics arise against us, teaching the error of poisonous unbelief, like pythons and magicians scattering wicked incantations.

From there they pass to Iye-abarim, which is at the borders of the Moabites. [Col. 1062B] Iye-abarim signifies “heaps of stones of those who cross over.” These are the living stones, namely the saints, from whom not only the heavenly Jerusalem is built, but the present Church also is adorned like a structure glittering with radiant jewels. They are rightly called “those who cross over,” because they trample every earthly and transient thing in mind and hasten to cross over to heavenly things. But if not Iye-abarim, but Iye, is to be read, as another edition bears witness, this too does not depart from the meaning of “those who cross over.” For Iye is interpreted as “chaos.” Abraham says to the rich man: “Because a great chaos has been fixed between us and you” (Luke 16). The saints therefore always desire to cross over to him, so that, like blessed Lazarus, they may happily rest in his bosom.

Hence it very suitably follows that, after the chaos of pythons and magicians—which is the dark cunning of heretics—they immediately come to Dibon-gad, which is said to signify “the apiary of temptations.” Bees carry honey in their mouths but sting with their barbs; so heretics openly display blandishments in their words, but conceal behind them, as it were, the barbs of error. At first they distill sweetness from their mouths, but afterward scatter the error of barbed falsehood. Hence the Prophet complains, saying: “They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns” (Psalm 117).

From there they set out for Helmondeblathaim, which is rendered “contempt of palatae”—that is, figs—or “contempt of reproach.” The fig is a delicious fruit; by this it is understood to be necessary that those who now draw near to heavenly gifts should despise all the blandishments of carnal allurements. But if “contempt of reproach” is preferred, we are thereby instructed, though tentatively, that, whenever we are dishonored by the insults of heretics or of any reprobate persons, we should not be disturbed. Through both meanings we are salutarily taught neither to be moved by the mockery of disgraceful contempt nor to be weakened by any delights of earthly sweetness, so that we may be able to say of this world with the Prophet: “As its darkness is, so also is its light” (Psalm 138).

From there they migrate to the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo. Abarim is interpreted as “crossings,” Nebo as “departure.” Here, when the soul has advanced through all the virtues just as it has passed through all the encampments of the journey, because it has now ascended to the summit of perfection, it immediately crosses over in mind from this age and departs. Although it may still appear to remain in the world, since it walks in the flesh but not according to the flesh, it has already withdrawn from the world. As it is said of Enoch: “He was not found, because God took him away” (Genesis 5). Thus whoever is perfect in holiness and already dead to the world has crossed through the world and dwells in the region of virtues.

The final encampment is in the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan opposite Jericho. The crossing of so long a journey is undertaken for this purpose; for this, amid all the hardships and labors, one sighs through the vast wilderness of this world: that we may come to the Jordan—that is, approach the inexhaustible fullness of heavenly wisdom. Building the tent of our pilgrimage beside it, let us hasten to wash ourselves in its streams from all the squalor of Egypt, so that, purified, we may be able to enter the promised land and become as it is said of the bride in the Song of Songs: “Her eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and sitting beside the fullest flowing waters” (Song of Songs 5). It should also be noted that this journey ends not in the mountains but in the plains, because the more exalted the perfection with which the saints are endowed, the more deeply they are grounded in humility. They also build their encampments opposite Jericho, because they fight without truce against the world, which is signified by Jericho. To them it is said: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15).

[Col. 1063] Here end the testimonies of the Book of Numbers.

151–152 BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS OF THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY.

1. That the law was given on Mount Horeb.  
2. The Lord says to Moses: “Go and say to the people: Return to your tents; but you, stand here with me.”  
3. Moses says to the people: “The Lord gave you food, manna, which neither you nor your fathers knew.”  
4. Moses says: “The land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you came out, but awaits rain from heaven.”  
5. That the Lord commands that, when battle is already approaching, the priest should stand before the battle line and exhort the people.  
6. That a fearful man, fainthearted, should not go out to war, but should return to his land, lest he make others afraid.  
7. That, for a woman captured in war and chosen for marriage by the victor, the superfluity of her body should be cut away.  
8. That if the firstborn is the son of a hated wife, the son of the beloved wife may not be preferred to him so as to take the place of the firstborn.  
9. That if a man takes a wife and she does not find favor in his eyes, he should write her a bill of divorce and send her away from his house.  
10. That if judges consider the one who has sinned worthy of blows, they should throw him down and have him beaten in their presence.  
11. Concerning maintaining a just weight and an equal measure.  
12. Moses concerning Asher: “Iron and bronze shall be his footwear.”

Here end the chapter headings.

BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES OF THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY.

CHAPTER ONE. In the letter to Pope Alexander, concerning the insolence of the wicked.

[Col. 1063B]

The human mind, darkened by earthly concerns, strives in vain to raise itself to the summit of contemplation, while it is weighed down, as it were, by heaps of stones and rubble accumulated through the demands of worldly activity. For just as leather, after passing through muddy streams of mire, does not take in grease, so the human mind, unless it has been dried of the moisture of worldly care, does not perceive the grace of heavenly richness. Dry skin absorbs grease; moistened skin repels it. And the human heart, so long as it swells with the dampness of worldly cares, does not admit the nourishment of inward grace.

Hence we read that the law was given on Mount Horeb (Exod. XX), which is interpreted as “dryness” [Col. 1063C]. That mind, finally, which is raised aloft through love of the Spirit is a mountain upon which the Lord’s unimpeachable law—which is unquestionably charity—is divinely promulgated. And this mountain is truly Horeb, which is called “dryness,” where the moisture of all vices is burned away and every flow of lust and carnal enticement is dried by the rays of the sun of justice.

Hence it is that Hiram, at Solomon’s command, made the vessels of the Temple in clayey ground, which eagerly absorbs water (III Kings VII) [Col. 1064B]. Among these vessels is also that which longs to be filled by heavenly rain, saying: “My soul is before you like land without water” (Ps. CXLII); and, thirsting for this, it cries aloud: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI).

## CHAPTER II. In the Letter to the Brothers of Cluny

Let those beware who perhaps still desire to go out into public life, lest, while they gaze eagerly with unrestrained eyes upon empty things, they extinguish their right eye—that is, the power of inward contemplation. Nor should their appetite itch for the leeks, onions, and garlic of that carnal Israel (Num. XI) [Col. 1064C], whose plants’ violent pungency troubles the eyes and provokes tears; for worldly activity, while surrounded by many straits of affliction and harassed by the frequent disturbance of mounting labors, often compels those to weep for whom it promised joy.

Certainly, if the exercise of labor is pleasing, holy rest has its own labor. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Go and say to them: Return to your tents; but you, stand here with me, and I shall speak to you all the commandments, statutes, and judgments” (Deut. V) [Col. 1065A]. While the others rest pleasurably in the tent of their flesh, the servant of God is not ordered to sit down, but to stand with the Lord, so that, the farther he withdraws from the labors of the world, the more vigilantly he may exercise himself in divine service through the fervor of holy rest.

## CHAPTER III. In the Same Letter

“The Lord gave you food, manna, which neither you nor your fathers knew, to show you that man lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord” (Deut. VIII; Matt. IV; Luke IV). Immediately thereafter he adds:

“Your garment, with which you were covered, did not wear out through age, and your foot was not worn down; behold, this is the fortieth year. Reflect in your heart that, just as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord your God disciplined you, so that you might keep the commandments of the Lord your God, walk in his ways, and fear him” (Deut. VIII) [Col. 1065B].

Among these words, special attention must be paid to what he says: “He gave you manna, to show that man lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Here it is perfectly clear that the manna by which they were nourished carnally signified the food of the divine word by which we are now restored in soul.

It should also be noted that concerning this manna the Book of Exodus says: “When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: Manhu?—which means, ‘What is this?’” (Exod. XVI) [Col. 1065C]. Those truly eat manna—that is, “What is this?”—who, when they read or hear, diligently seek out the mystery of the divine word. Within the sheath of the literal straw, they strive to uncover the sweet kernel of spiritual understanding. He truly feeds on “What is this?” who constantly applies himself to Sacred Scripture through careful meditation.

## CHAPTER IV. In a Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

Moses speaks mystically of the holy Church: “The land which you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you came, where, after seed has been sown, waters are led in the manner of gardens to irrigate it; rather, it awaits rains from heaven, and its God visits it continually” (Deut. XI) [Col. 1065D].

For worldly prudence creeps along the ground like a serpent and turns this way and that in slippery variation, whereas divine wisdom thunders from the heavens. “Garden” also has a sinister meaning here. It appears to designate the wantonness of carnal knowledge, as in the passage where Ahab asked for Naboth’s vineyard: “Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it into a garden of vegetables” (III Kings XXI). He tries to turn a vineyard into a garden who wishes to exchange the rigor of virtue for the pleasant beauty of carnal enticement.

The Psalmist likewise compares the wicked to vegetables, saying: “Like grass they shall quickly wither, and like the vegetables of the field they shall swiftly fall” (Ps. XXXVI).

## CHAPTER V. In a Sermon on Saint Anastasius

[Col. 1066A]

“When battle is now approaching,” says the Lord, “the priest shall stand before the battle line and speak to the people as follows: Hear, O Israel: today you are entering battle against your enemies. Let not your heart be afraid; do not fear, do not retreat, and do not dread them, because the Lord your God is in your midst and will fight for you against your adversaries, to rescue you from danger” (Deut. XX).

It should be noted that the priest who preaches when war is already imminent is commanded to stand not elsewhere but before the battle line, so that he himself may lead those whom he urges to battle by his exhortations. He must not, while trying to drive others into battle, be relaxed through negligence in the ignoble leisure of torpor [Col. 1066B], as the Prophet says of certain men who preached great things but lived sluggishly: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII).

## CHAPTER VI. In a Sermon on Saint George

“A fearful man and one fainthearted must not go out to battle, but he shall go and return to his own land, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, as he himself is terrified” (Deut. XX).

By these words we are plainly taught that those who still fear being stripped of earthly possessions cannot fight bravely and suitably for the defense of the faith. For it is more tolerable that, returning in a certain sense to their own house, they should live ignobly [Col. 1066C] and without courage than that, by examples of degenerate fear, they should turn both themselves and others away from the glory of triumph.

## CHAPTER VII. In the Book on the Perfection of Monks

Through Moses the law decrees that bodily superfluity be cut away from a woman captured in war and chosen for the victor’s marriage:

“She shall shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured. Sitting in her house, she shall mourn her father and mother for one month; afterward you shall go in to her and sleep with her, and she shall be your wife” (Deut. XXI).

We shave the woman’s hair when we cut away superfluous senses through rational discipline. We also cut her nails when we sever from her every dead work of superstition. She is likewise commanded to remove the garment in which she was captured so that she may strip off the surface imposed by stories and every sort of fiction and display the solid truth of true reason.

She mourns her father and mother because our mind considers the authors of the liberal arts dead and, in compassion, laments that they perished in error. It is the custom of women to be cleansed each month through the discharge of their blood. Thus, after one month, we are commanded to enter this woman, so that we may take into marriage, as it were, an art belonging to any discipline once cleansed of every pollution of superstition, so that what has now become Israelite may consequently enter into an Israelite marriage and produce a richly fruitful offspring of spiritual works.

## CHAPTER VIII. In the Letter to Boniface, Concerning the Fact that Spiritual Wisdom Should Be Preferred to External Prudence

[Col. 1067A]

“If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and they bear him children, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, and he wishes to divide his property among his sons, he cannot make the son of the beloved wife firstborn and prefer him to the son of the hated wife. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn and give him double of all that he possesses; for he is the beginning of his children, and the rights of the firstborn belong to him” (Deut. XXI).

The two wives of a man are virtue and pleasure, divided from one another by a kind of jealousy born of envy and hatred [Col. 1067B]. Pleasure belongs to this life, while virtue belongs to eternal glory. Pleasure is certainly called beloved because it soothes its husband—that is, the fragile spirit of each person—with its destructive sweetness. Virtue, however, is called hated because it obliges people to travel along the narrow and difficult way and always sets before them harsh and arduous things.

But the son of the hated wife is our firstborn, because our Creator implanted virtue in us from the beginning, whereas pleasure and every carnal enticement arose from the fault of our perversity. But since this is not the time to unfold the figure of this command word by word, it is enough to say briefly that, if we cannot drive away the beloved wife, who is unquestionably harmful to us, from the company of our marriage bed, we should at least strive to place the sober [Col. 1067C] and honorable wife in the dignity of the firstborn. Thus, if it is difficult for us not to experience some small sweetness of this life, nevertheless the palm of mastery should be granted to virtue, while servitude is left to pleasure. Her son should excel in the dignity of the firstborn, while the son of the other should remain behind in the succession of rank and always under the restraint of discipline.

Perhaps you wish to learn who the sons of the beloved wife are. Let the Apostle Paul be consulted:

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V) [Col. 1067D].

Do you wish, in turn, to hear what the offspring of the hated wife is? Listen to what follows:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (ibid.).

This son, therefore, as the firstborn, ought to possess a double portion of the substance, namely, so that the fruit of the Spirit may govern both body and soul and possess the rights of both substances—that is, of the inner and outer person.

## CHAPTER IX. In the Letter to Cincius the Prefect

“If a man takes a wife, possesses her, and she does not find favor in his eyes because of some disgrace, he shall write a bill of divorce, place it in her hand, and send her away from his house” (Deut. XXIV) [Col. 1068A].

Would that this wife of ours—that is, carnal life—might never find favor in our eyes at all, but that her abominable foulness might always offend the nostrils of our minds, as it deserves. Once she has received the bill of divorce through the law of repentance, let her be excluded from the threshold of our marriage in such a way that she does not return again to our embraces.

Hence the wise man says: “Turn your face away from an adorned woman, and do not look upon another’s beauty” (Ecclus. IX). Since she is called “another’s,” she is rightly understood with Hagar as not a wife but a concubine. For Hagar is interpreted as “foreign woman” or “resident alien.”

And because this same shameless woman says through Solomon, “I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon” (Prov. VII) [Col. 1068B], she may rightly be compared with Abraham’s other concubine. For Keturah is called “fragrant.” Carnal life indeed breathes the perfumes of falsehood.

Hence Proverbs says: “Guard yourself from an evil woman and from the smooth tongue of a stranger; let not your heart desire her beauty” (Prov. VI). For this smooth tongue—that is, of carnal life—persuades wretched people to say: “Come, let us enjoy the good things that exist and make swift use of creation as in youth; let us fill ourselves with precious wine and perfume, and let not the flower of time pass us by,” and so forth (Wis. II).

By contrast, concerning the woman who signifies religious life, it is written: “Blessed is the husband of a good woman, for the number of her years is doubled; a strong woman delights her husband and fills the years of his life with peace” (Ecclus. XXVI) [Col. 1068C]. How is the number of a man’s years doubled, except because he lives here in holy conduct and is destined to live there in glory?

These two lives—spiritual and carnal—are plainly divided from one another by a kind of mutual jealousy and draw human hearts toward different ends of living. The one restrains the itch of the appetite, lest it exceed the measure of sober nourishment; the other stuffs the belly and loosens it through excessive pleasures of food. The one feeds on sighs and groans; the other delights in laughter and foolish games. The one raises the spirit upward and suspends it upon the summit of heavenly desire; the other devotes itself to worldly cares and the accumulation of riches. The one endures calmly whatever injuries and whatever adversity are inflicted; the other rather accepts more grievous violence and brings upon itself judgments that must be endured [Col. 1068D].

## CHAPTER X. In the Letter to Peter the Monk

“If the judges consider the one who has sinned worthy of blows, they shall throw him down and have him beaten in their presence.” Immediately thereafter it is added:

“The measure of the blows shall correspond to the measure of the sin, so that they do not exceed the number forty, lest your brother, disgracefully lacerated, be before your eyes” (Deut. XXV).

What was a legal command for that people is for us a mystery of allegory. The number forty signifies the course of human life. Hence Israel travels through the desert for forty years (Num. XIV, XXXII) [Col. 1069A]. Hence Moses (Exod. XXIV), Elijah (III Kings XIX), and the Lord himself (Matt. IV) prolonged their fasts for that many days.

Just as he lay dead in the tomb for forty hours, so likewise after his resurrection he remained with his disciples for the same number of days, so that the gracious Teacher might instruct us, his members, to follow the footsteps of our Head: dead to the world and dwelling as pilgrims in the world.

Mystically, therefore, when the sinner in the law is commanded to be beaten, the number of blows is forbidden to exceed forty, because whoever has performed perfect repentance in this life will afterward feel no punishment for his offenses.

## CHAPTER XI. In a Sermon on Saint Anastasius

[Col. 1069B]

“You shall not have different weights in your bag, a larger and a smaller, nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight, and a measure that is equal and true shall be yours” (Deut. XXV).

Indeed, we do not have different weights in our bag if, within the secret place of our conscience, judging ourselves and others by the same standard, we weigh out the same measures of the legal commandments. We must not impose upon others the rule of strict severity while striving to treat ourselves according to the law of more lenient indulgence.

Concerning this fraud Solomon also says: “A double weight and a deceitful balance are an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. XI) [Col. 1069C].

It is therefore necessary to measure the fruits of the word not with different weights but with the same ones [Col. 1070A], so that what we command others to do, we ourselves may also effectively fulfill in living deeds.

## CHAPTER XII. In a Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

[Col. 1069]

Bronze is sometimes found to be appropriate to the holy apostles, concerning whom Moses says in Deuteronomy under the figure of Asher: “Iron and bronze shall be his footwear” (Deut. XXXIII).

Footwear in Sacred Scripture is understood as the protection of preaching, as it is written: “With your feet shod in the preaching of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). Therefore, since strength is expressed by iron and the perseverance of patience by bronze, iron and bronze are said to be the footwear of the apostles and likewise of any holy preachers.

Through iron they patiently endure evils that oppose them; through bronze they preserve with long-suffering the good things set before them. Concerning these apostles—or apostolic men, that is, holy preachers—after saying to the same Asher, “The rider of heaven is your helper,” Moses immediately adds: “His magnificence makes the clouds race across the sky” (Deut. XXXIII) [Col. 1070B].

For who is the rider of heaven except our Savior, who, after destroying the dominion of death by dying, entered heaven with the angels accompanying him and the disciples looking on? Through his magnificence the clouds race across the sky, because by his authority holy teachers pour the rain of saving preaching throughout the world.

Concerning them the prophet also says: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX). These clouds dissolve into water when they drench the soil of our hearts with the streams of their teaching, making it fertile for producing the shoots of devout works [Col. 1070C].

*The testimonies of the Book of Deuteronomy end here.*

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA BEGIN

1. That the waters of the Jordan were divided while Israel crossed under the leadership of Joshua.  
2. That the Lord commanded twelve stones to be taken from the middle of the Jordan, where the priests had stood, and placed in the middle of the camp.  
3. That the Lord commanded Joshua to cross over to Gilgal with the people and circumcise them there with stone knives.  
4. That the Lord commanded that armed fighting men precede the Ark of the Covenant, that the priests sound seven trumpets, and that they circle Jericho for seven days.  
5. That the Ark contained three things: a golden urn with manna, the tablet of the covenant, and Aaron’s staff.  
6. Joshua said to the people: “But take care that you do not touch anything from the possessions of Jericho.”  
7. That, when Jericho was overthrown, the house of Rahab the prostitute, from which a scarlet cord hung, escaped.  
8. After Jericho was overthrown, Joshua pronounced a curse, saying: “Cursed before the Lord is the man who rises up and rebuilds Jericho in his firstborn.”  
9. That the Gibeonites fraudulently extorted a treaty of peace from the Israelites in the land of the Perizzites and Rephaim.  
10. Joshua said to the sons of Joseph: “If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut out space for yourselves to inhabit.”

*The chapters end here.*

# THE TESTIMONIES OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA BEGIN

## CHAPTER I. In the Second Sermon on Saint John the Evangelist

[Col. 1069D]

“When the people entered the Jordan at Joshua’s command, the upper waters swelled up like a mountain, while the lower waters flowed down into the Dead Sea” (Josh. III).

For among those who are baptized, some persevere in the sweetness of the heavenly grace they have received, while others, living wickedly, do not cease to flow down into the bitterness of sins and fall, as it were, into the saltiness of the Dead Sea, tending toward death through the downward slopes of a wicked life while setting their minds on earthly things.

But let us not be so, beloved, let us not be so. Rather, transferring our mind to true wisdom, let us strive by God’s mercy to advance into the heights of the virtues, so that we may be ashamed to descend into the gulf of vices. Let us always persevere in hastening toward the heights to which we are moving, so that we may continually preserve the sweetness of divine love in our minds [Col. 1070D].

## CHAPTER II. In the Same Sermon

The Lord says to Joshua: “Choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the channel of the Jordan, where the priests fixed their feet, twelve exceedingly hard stones, and place them in the camp where you pitch your tents tonight” (Josh. IV) [Col. 1071A].

Without examining every word, though all are full of mysteries, what is suggested to us by this event except that, after we have crossed the streams of the mystical Jordan and risen from the font of saving baptism, we should strive to set before ourselves for imitation twelve exceedingly hard stones—that is, the firmest examples of the apostles?

We place the stones where the priests fixed their feet in the place of the camp if, stationed in the ranks of spiritual warfare, we hold firmly and steadfastly to the footsteps of the apostles. For according to Solomon’s judgment: “He who is soft and negligent in his work is a brother to one who dissipates his own work” (Prov. XVIII) [Col. 1071B].

Those who are soft and fluid in their conduct rush downward like water; those who are steadfast and firm grow daily into the stronghold of virtue.

## CHAPTER III. In the First Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

“After these things Joshua is immediately commanded to cross over with the people to Gilgal and circumcise them there with stone knives” (Josh. V). “The rock,” as the Apostle says, “was Christ” (I Cor. X).

Therefore, we are circumcised with stone knives when through Christ we cut away from ourselves every enticement of flesh and spirit. Through this circumcision, as the text says there, we drive away the reproach of the Egyptians, because we crush the insolence of the vices that mock us.

“Today,” says the Lord to Joshua, “I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt” (Josh. V) [Col. 1071C].

Nor should it be passed over that Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation.” Carnal life blinds the eyes of the mind, while spiritual life enlightens them: “Reveal my eyes,” he says, “and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII).

For when a person is circumcised from his vices, the sharpness of his mind is revealed for contemplating the mysteries of the divine law. In that place the Israelite people celebrate Passover, and in a type eat that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John I).

Consider the order of events and weigh the mystery of human salvation. After we come out of baptism as from the whirlpool of the Jordan, we establish the stones of apostolic virtue and steadfastness as a testimony of example. Gazing upon them in the zeal of imitation, we are circumcised from the foreskin of our perversity. Thus, with the darkness of vices driven far away and wiped clean, and with our spiritual face revealed, we celebrate the Passover of joy in the light of virtues.

There the people first ate unleavened bread from the produce of the land, and the manna on which they had until then been accustomed to feed no longer appeared. For after that living bread which came down from heaven (John VI) came forth from the field of the Virgin’s womb, and after the grain of wheat fell into the earth, died, and bore abundant fruit (John XII), the manna of the figurative law immediately ceased.

The land of promise is the Virgin’s womb. Concerning this land Isaiah says: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. XLV).

When one reaches this bread, the manna of the old law is no longer sought [Col. 1072A].

## CHAPTER IV. In a Sermon on Saint Andrew

“The Lord commanded Joshua that armed fighting men should precede the Ark of the Covenant, while the priests sounded seven trumpets, and that they should likewise circle the walls of Jericho for seven days. On the seventh day, when the people’s shouting mingled with the sound of the trumpets, Jericho immediately collapsed and was destroyed from its foundations” (Josh. VI).

What is the meaning of the fact that, for capturing the city, no sword is drawn, no weapons are brandished, no spear is hurled, and no military line of troops is massed for an assault, but only priestly trumpets are sounded [Col. 1072B]—and thus victory is obtained over the conquered enemies not by the right of war but rather by the power of a sacrament?

It would surely seem the folly of madness if an evident victory had not followed. But Jericho, which is called “moon,” not inappropriately signifies the world, which comes to an end through the passing moments of time as through monthly wanings.

The holy Ark was the Church; the trumpets are the apostles or any holy teachers of the Church. By their admonitions, as we strive always to fight against the enticements of the flesh and the snares of the ancient enemy, we are summoned by the sound of trumpets to the battle line and to wage war.

These trumpets are reported to have been seven because holy preachers are filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit [Col. 1072C]. The whole period of our mortality likewise unfolds through the succession of seven days.

Therefore the priests carrying the Ark and sounding the trumpets circle the city of Jericho for seven days, and its walls fall through the presence of the Ark and the sound of the trumpets. For throughout the course of this mortal life, while the holy Church is moved and enlarged throughout the whole world, all the pride of the exalted world is broken and every obstacle of unbelief is overthrown through the persistence of holy preaching.

It should also be noted that armed soldiers are commanded to go with the priests, so that those who have not been assigned the duty of producing the sound of preaching should by no means think themselves removed from the conflicts of war. Thus, those who do not preach must nevertheless always walk armed and watchful [Col. 1072D].

The leaders and commanders of this war are therefore the holy apostles, who carry the Ark of the Covenant around the walls of Jericho with the sound of trumpets, because throughout the whole circuit of the world they spread the mysteries of the Church through the ministry of holy preaching.

“For their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

When six days have passed, on the seventh day at last the king of Jericho and all the people are consumed by the devouring sword, because on the last day the devil, who is the king of pride, together with all his followers, will be condemned to everlasting death by something like the sword of divine judgment.

Then what the Apostle says will come to pass: “When he has abolished every principality, every power, and every virtue, last of all the enemy death shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XV) [Col. 1073A].

## CHAPTER V. In a Sermon on Saint Bartholomew

That Ark had been mystically fashioned from incorruptible wood of acacia; it also shone with the purest gold, gilded within and without. It contained a golden urn in which manna was kept, the tablets of the Covenant, and Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed.

What is the golden urn except the pure, bright, sincere flesh of Christ, utterly clean and free from every taint of guilt, containing hidden manna—that is, the angelic bread, the sweetness of eternal divinity?

The two stone tablets signify the inviolable firmness of both Testaments. What [Col. 1073B] does Aaron’s staff express except the saving standard of our great and true High Priest and the mystery of the life-giving cross? In that it is said to have blossomed, it also prefigured the holy cross, flourishing with the verdure of immortal memory.

These are the mysteries of the universal Church; this is also the saving instruction of every faithful Christian soul. What the Ark presented through a shadowy image, the Church now possesses in an exceedingly effective and open truth, as does every mind of the just.

The blessed apostles carried these foods of mystical nourishment, and, explaining them as bread for little ones, broke them open. For after that Gospel saying burst forth—“He opened their minds, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV)—the prophetic lament ceased [Col. 1073C], in which it is said: “The children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV).

This is that daily bread, my brothers, which the Truth taught us eagerly to seek; this is the food of heavenly wisdom, for which we ought continually to hunger.

## CHAPTER VI. In a Sermon on Saint Andrew

“Joshua said to the people: Take care that you do not touch anything from the possessions of Jericho” (Josh. VI) [Col. 1073D].

Our Jesus, the true Savior, likewise forbids anyone to love the things of the world: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matt. VI); and through his apostle: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (I John II).

Therefore, following the example of the unhappy Achan (Josh. VII), let us not steal anything from the anathema of Jericho, so that we bring nothing from the dissolute customs of worldly conduct into ecclesiastical discipline.

Let us not take the cloak, so that after the garment of faith we do not put on the dress of worldly conduct. Let us not take the shekels of silver, so that, although we store up an eternal treasure in heaven, we do not through ambition place any temporal money in a napkin. Finally, let us not take the golden bar, so that we do not introduce into the Church of Christ the carefully wrought doctrines of heretics, nor the weighed-out studies of sharply disputing philosophers, nor the elaborated fictions of poets.

For this is that golden bar, fashioned with polished and refined speech and clothed, as it were, in the golden brilliance of splendid eloquence. Arius, Marcion, Apelles, and other plagues of perverse men stole this bar [Col. 1074A]. In trying to introduce the sects of philosophers into the Church, they seemed in a certain sense to provoke God’s anger against the camp of Israel.

But they were buried with Achan beneath a heap of stones, because they were crushed under the monstrous weight of their sins. We, however, beloved brothers, because our philosophy is Christ—and him crucified—and therefore our teachers are not orators but fishermen, not crafty and eloquent but gentle and simple, should despise the wisdom that blinds and desire the foolishness that enlightens those who are learning.

“For,” as the Apostle says, “because the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (I Cor. I).

## CHAPTER VII. In the Same Sermon

[Col. 1074B]

“All the inhabitants of Jericho are consumed by the slaughtering sword; only the house of Rahab the prostitute escaped, distinguished by the scarlet cord in its window” (Josh. VI).

That house prefigures the one Church, which is cleansed from the disgrace of prostitution through the window of confession in the remission of sins. It is plainly delivered from the common destruction of the perishing world because it ties a scarlet cord in the window of its house, while it does not cease to carry in the mouth of its body the mystery of the Lord’s Passion:

“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

That cord was tied to the house but was visible on the outside [Col. 1074C], because faith in the Lord’s cross is held in the heart and brought forth through confession of the mouth.

While the others perished, all who were found in that house escaped the danger of death. For just as all the elect are saved within the Church, so no one can be found saved outside the Church.

But perhaps someone may ask how both the Ark, which encircled and besieged the city, and Rahab’s house, which clung to the city’s walls, can each signify one Church, since the Ark evidently besieges and attacks, while the house seems to be itself besieged.

This question is easily solved if one carefully attends to the diversity that exists among the members of the Church. For the Church attacks the Church when preachers, teachers and disciples, those presiding and those obeying, appear to proceed from one source of divine regeneration and, finally, to complete the one body of the Church as its diverse members [Col. 1074D].

To this Church the Psalmist says: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV). The apostles themselves, who hurled such powerful and mighty lightning bolts of their preaching to capture the Jericho of human pride, appear in a certain sense to be both fathers and sons of the one and same Church: sons of the patriarchs and prophets, but fathers of all the elect who followed thereafter.

Hence Moses is commanded by the divine voice: “To cast silver bases and raise gilded boards upon them” (Exod. XXVI). What are signified by the silver bases except the order of the prophets? Since they were the first to speak about the mystery of the Church, we regard them as bases rising from the foundation and supporting the weights of the structure placed upon them [Col. 1075A].

What, then, are signified by the boards except the holy apostles, who have been spread most widely through their preaching extended throughout the world? The apostles’ teaching rests, as it were, upon the bases of prophetic preaching, and through their authority it is firmly strengthened for the stability of its condition.

Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board. When the holy prophets agree with one another in their words concerning the mystery of the future Church, they build up the apostles who follow after them as builders; and since they disagree with one another in nothing, they fix them more firmly within themselves.

Nor is it without reason that the bases signifying the prophets are commanded to be cast from silver. The brilliance of silver is preserved through use; without use it turns black. Before they were made bright by apostolic preaching, the sayings of the prophets, because they were not in use for spiritual understanding and could not be seen on account of their obscurity, remained as though black [Col. 1075B]. But after the hand of apostolic preaching wiped away the obscurity of the prophecies, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and it brought their mystical meanings into use, clearly announcing that the words had already been explained by the realities.

Rightly, therefore, both silver bases and gilded boards are commanded to be made, because the apostolic commandments are far clearer than the prophetic oracles.

To return to what was said above, it is not inappropriate if both the ark and the prostitute’s house, which is besieged [Col. 1075C], seem to represent one and the same Church, since, as has been said, the members of that same Church are diverse: some, namely, besieging through the scope of holy preaching; others to be overwhelmed by the darts of saving doctrine, as they shelter behind the defenses of their unbelief or wickedness; 164 some already belonging to the household, others still estranged through their turning away to evil conduct.
