Isaiah had already perceived this conflict as a testimony to spiritual warfare when, after clearly describing the Savior’s coming, he immediately added: “And the heart of Egypt will wither within her, and I will set Egyptians against Egyptians; and man will fight against his brother, and man against his friend, and city against city, kingdom against kingdom; and the spirit of Egypt will be broken within her (Isa. XIX).” Since [Col. 1075D], therefore, dearest brothers, through the siege of apostolic preaching we have been rescued from the slaughter of perishing Jericho—or rather, divinely delivered from the destruction of overturned paganism—let us not find it burdensome to follow our leaders wherever they go before us; let nothing seem onerous that they command for our salvation.

## CHAPTER VIII. In the Letter to the Blessed Causidicus, That Spiritual Wisdom Is to Be Preferred to External Prudence

“When Jericho had been destroyed, Joshua pronounced a curse, saying: ‘Cursed before the Lord be the man who rises up and rebuilds the city of Jericho; in his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and in his youngest child let him set up its gates (Josh. VI).’” Since Jericho, whose name is rendered “moon,” signifies this present life [Col. 1076A], he rebuilds the city of Jericho in his firstborn who loves the goods of the present life above all else. And because Truth commands in the Gospel, “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. VI),” whoever is shown to turn aside from this command is rightly condemned by a curse, as the Prophet bears witness when he says: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments (Ps. CXVIII).”

Conversely, he sets up the gates of Jericho in his youngest child who uses temporal goods in such a way that he does not possess them with affection, but burns inwardly with desire for the reward of heavenly glory. He who places earthly things beneath heavenly things in his love regards transitory matters as worthless. By doing this, he makes the son of the hated wife his firstborn, according to the commands of the Law, and [Col. 1076B], in accordance with Joshua’s sentence, sets up the gates of Jericho in his youngest child. By contrast, Cain built a city in his firstborn, Enoch (Gen. IV), because he had no hope of a future inheritance; and because he prematurely devoted himself, as it were, to the Jericho of this world, he incurred the sentence of everlasting curse. Hence it is written: “The inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end (Prov. XXVI).”

## CHAPTER IX. In the Book on the Perfection of Monks

For some people—and I cannot say this without a groan—enter the order of the new religious life in such a way that they nevertheless never abandon the oldness of their former life. These are clearly Gibeonites, not Israelites. It is well known that the Gibeonites, terrified by fear of death, came to the people of Israel [Col. 1076C] through fraud and cunning, dressing themselves in old garments, 165 and carrying along dry loaves, wineskins, sacks, sandals, and everything else similarly worn out. After their lives had been spared through the treaty they obtained, their fraud was consequently exposed and recognized. When Joshua discovered their deceit, he condemned them under a curse and permanently appointed them as carriers of water and cutters of wood (Josh. IX).

Who, then, are the Gibeonites who, out of fear of death, pass over to the Israelites, except those who flee to the service of the divine army not out of love for perfection, but shaken by the enormity of their sins? Yet some of them, changed in clothing but not in mind, carry dry loaves for food, because they still do not know the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth [Col. 1076D] (1 Cor. V). They are covered with old garments because, still established in the old person, they do not know how to put on the new person, who was created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. IV). Finally, everything they carry appears worn out because they persevere in the vices of their former life, not obeying the Apostle who commands: “Be renewed, he says, in the spirit of your mind (ibid.).” Nor does that sentence apply to them which says: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new (2 Cor. V).” Coming superficially to newness, they persist in reality in oldness, because they do not display amendment and a new way of life in their conduct.

Such people, therefore, are punished by a curse and are in no way admitted [Col. 1077A] to receive an inheritance with the Israelites. For they are not among those to whom it is said: “You were called for this purpose, that you might possess a blessing as your inheritance (1 Pet. III).” Water, however, is tasteless and wood is hard. They are therefore commanded to cut wood and carry water because, ignorant of the taste of spiritual understanding, they are occupied with the hard and insensitive business of external activity. Thus they do indeed seem to confer some usefulness upon the Church by serving it in external matters; but because they live as slaves, they cannot possess an inheritance among the Israelites.

## CHAPTER X. In the Letter to the Brothers of Camugni

“Joshua said to the sons of Joseph: ‘If you are a numerous people [Col. 1077B], go up into the forest and cut out spaces for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you.’ When they complained there and said, ‘We cannot go up into the mountain country, since the Canaanites who dwell in the level land use iron chariots,’ Joshua replied: ‘You are a numerous people and possess great strength. You shall not have one lot only, but you shall pass over to the mountain country and cut down and clear spaces for yourselves to dwell in; and you will be able to go farther when you have overthrown the Canaanite, whom you say has iron chariots and is exceedingly strong (Josh. XVII).’”

I would perhaps explain these matters of great difficulty at greater length if the limit of brevity imposed by a letter did not stand in my way. 166 For now, it is enough to touch on them only superficially: when Joshua [Col. 1077C] commands the people to cut down the dense growth of the forests, this indicates that our Jesus—of course, bearing the same name—commands those who follow him to root out the badly growing shrubs of wooded vices. He urges them to wage war, not make treaties, against the Canaanites, so that they may climb the mountains, striving both to defeat the barbarism of vices and to hasten to attain the lofty summit of virtues.

Moreover, the fact that they timidly complain that they cannot rise up against those who use iron chariots signifies that we, weak and fragile, often despair, as though we could not withstand the assaults of evil spirits [Col. 1078A], which oppose us like iron chariots. When the insolence of gluttony, the gaping maw of lust, and the plagues of every vice mass themselves against us in compacted ranks, like the battle lines of roaring Canaanites, what else is happening but that the Canaanites attack us with iron chariots and block our access, preventing us from climbing from the plains of carnal life to the heights of virtue? But the good commander of our warfare raises our weakness to steadfastness in courageous action and drives us forward against the assaults of our enemies, so that we may advance to higher things.

But how can we triumph over our enemies if we always wish to lie at banquets and continually stuff ourselves with an abundance of cups? Of such people Solomon says: “He who loves [Col. 1078B] banquets will be in poverty; he who loves wine and rich foods will not grow wealthy (Prov. XXI).” And again: “Wine is a wanton thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise (Prov. XX).” To accustom the belly to wine and food: what else is this than to open an entrance for the enemies of the soul, so that they may enter? Hence the same Solomon says: “He who has pampered a servant from childhood will later find him rebellious (Prov. XXIX).”

He kept this servant under control with the reins of abstinence when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection (1 Cor. IX).” He argued against this servant when he said: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both it and them (1 Cor. VI).” He signified that this servant must be restrained beneath the heels when he said: “For many walk—of whom [Col. 1078C] I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame (Phil. III).”

Here, too, we should note that two terrible things are being said, and that the same Apostle pronounces a dreadful sentence against the enemies of the cross of Christ: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha (1 Cor. XVI).” Whoever venerates the belly in place of God is convicted of denying God in some fashion; and therefore these two things, full of terror, appear to be one and the same—namely, God forbid, to be both an enemy of Christ and a worshiper of another god.

*Here end the testimonies from the Book of Joshua.*

## 167–168. The Chapters of the Book of Judges Begin

[Col. 1077]

1. That the tips of Adonibezech’s hands and feet were cut off when he was captured.  
2. Deborah was a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who judged the people at that time.  
3. That Gideon was commanded to go to war against the Midianites with only the three hundred who had lapped up water with their hands.  
4. Concerning the man in the camp of Midian who reported to his companion that he had seen in a dream a barley loaf baked under ashes.  
5. That the cluster of Ephraim is better than the vintage of Abiezer.  
6. Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal, killed his seventy brothers upon one stone.  
7. Jotham stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim and, raising his voice, cried: “Hear me, men of Shechem, so that God may hear you.”  
8. Abimelech, hearing that the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together, went up Mount Zalmon with all the people.  
9. That when Abimelech attempted to set fire to the tower in the midst of Thebez by bringing fire to its doors, a woman threw down a fragment of a millstone and struck it against his head.  
10. That certain men of the people of Ephraim, once coming to the fords of the Jordan, were killed by the swords of the Gileadites because they did not know how to pronounce “Shibboleth.”  
11. Samson caught three hundred foxes, tied their tails together, attached torches to the tails, and set the torches tied in the middle on fire.  
12. That Samson seized the jawbone of a donkey and killed a thousand Philistines with it.  
13. That when the Lord was twice consulted about undertaking battle against Benjamin, he gave assent, and finally Benjamin was struck down by the swords of Israel.

*Here end the chapters.*

# The Testimonies of the Book of Judges Begin

[Col. 1079]

## CHAPTER I. In the Letter to V., Abbot

[Col. 1079A]

“While Adonibezech was fleeing before the sons of Israel, those pursuing him captured him and cut off the tips of his hands and feet (Judg. I).” Adonibezech’s hands and feet are indeed cut off at their extremities when the evil spirit is deprived, among holy men, of the power both of walking and of working. While suffering these wounds himself, he boasts that he had inflicted the same upon others: “Seventy kings,” he says, “with the tips of their hands and feet cut off, gathered the scraps of food beneath my table; as I did, so the Lord has repaid me (ibid.).”

The seventy kings are the seventy nations of differing languages, from whom the ancient enemy had completely taken away, until the Savior’s coming [Col. 1079B], the ability both to walk uprightly and to do good. The physician of souls, Paul, heals both of these twin wounds when he says: “Raise up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed (Heb. XII).”

Adonibezech is interpreted as “lord of lightning” or “lord satisfied with vanity.” As soon as lightning begins to flash, it suddenly disappears. By this the Jewish people may be understood: they flash, as it were, with a certain brilliance when they say, “All that the Lord has commanded we will both hear and do (Exod. XXIV),” but this light soon fades and falls when they bow their necks to dark demons. By the expression “satisfied with vanity,” the Gentiles are signified [Col. 1079C]: content with visible idols, they did not care to return to the mercy of the Creator, and, while ignorant of the worship of truth, they devoted themselves to the vain ceremonies of idols. Of them the Apostle says: “Because they did not glorify God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts (Rom. I).”

Adonibezech, that is, the spirit of wickedness, therefore held dominion over the greater part of these two peoples: the one began to flash like lightning and ceased, while the other, remaining content with the vanity of demons, did not seek the help of its own Creator.

## CHAPTER II. In a Sermon on Saint Cassian

“Deborah was a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who judged the people at that time. She sat beneath [Col. 1079D] the palm tree that was called by her name, between Ramah and Bethel, on Mount Ephraim, and the sons of Israel went up to her for every judgment (Judg. IV).”

The conclusion is reached more quickly if, while the historical narrative is being woven together, it is explained piece by piece along the way. Deborah, whose name is interpreted as “word” or “bee,” may appropriately be understood as prophecy. A bee makes honey, and of prophecy the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII.)

Meanwhile, dearest ones, I do not want you to be unaware that this history, which we have undertaken to discuss on the present occasion [Col. 1080A], requires many words, 169 because it is filled with many mysteries; but for this reason we compress it into a brief treatment, so that we do not burden your affection with the weariness of excessive length.

Let us therefore consider where prophecy is described as having its seat: beneath a palm tree. For those whom prophetic teaching instructs by its precepts, it leads to the palm of the heavenly calling; and as people learn from it the order of living, they become victors over rebellious vices. Nor should it be passed over that she is said to have sat between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah means “exalted”; Bethel, “house of God,” as we have already said. Prophecy is therefore rightly described as dwelling between Ramah and Bethel, because whoever strives to devote himself to prophetic teachings, whoever sincerely gives himself to the words of the sacred Scriptures [Col. 1080B], dwells in the house of God through the desire of his mind in such a way that he always seeks not lowly and fleeting things, but rather exalted and heavenly ones.

She called Barak to herself. Barak is interpreted as “flashing.” A flash does indeed possess light, but it does not last long; as soon as it begins to shine, it immediately fades. This Barak, therefore, represents the people of Israel: first of all instructed by prophetic oracles, it shone for a little while in the Law it had received, but flashed only briefly. In the Law, of which it is said, “Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths (Ps. CXVIII),” that ancient people began to shine, but ceased. It produced a flash resembling a bright life [Col. 1080C], but did not remain in works of light. For when they said, “All that the Lord has commanded us we will both hear and do,” behold, the light of a flash had arisen; but when they suddenly bent their knees before Baal, behold, the flash appeared extinguished.

Deborah therefore said to Barak: “The Lord, the God of Israel, has commanded you: ‘Take with you ten thousand fighting men and go up to Mount Tabor. I will bring Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, to you at the place of the torrent Kishon, together with his chariots and all his multitude, and I will deliver them into your hand (Judg. IV).’” It is as though Almighty God were saying to the former people through prophetic teaching: “Take up the ten commandments of the Law and climb to the summit of virtues; and, with me supplying you strength, overthrow the prince of the wicked and author of all iniquity.”

Nor should it be passed over that Sisera, that commander of the army who was liable to imminent destruction, was previously promised to be led to the torrent Kishon. For what should be understood [Col. 1080D] by the torrent Kishon except baptism? When a catechumen is plunged into the washing of the sacred font, then, like Sisera with his army, the most wicked spirit, together with all the vices that serve him, must necessarily be destroyed.

Barak replied to Deborah: “If you come with me, I will go; if you do not wish to come, I will not proceed (ibid.).” It is as though that carnal Israel were replying to prophecy: “Unless I always have you with me according to the letters, and as though according to a womanly understanding [Col. 1081A], I do not dare undertake spiritual warfare.”

Deborah said to him: “I will indeed go with you, but the victory will not be credited to you, because Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman (ibid.).” It is as though that ancient people were hearing: “Prophecy will indeed be with you externally, as you request; but the spiritual triumph over the ancient enemy will be won not by you, but rather by the holy Church.”

The victory will rightly belong to that Church which, while seeking the marrow of spiritual understanding in the mysteries of Scripture, pays no great attention to the chaff of the killing letter. When the battle had been joined, Sisera at last fled into the house of Jael, a foreign woman. She opened a skin of milk for him in his thirst and gave him drink; then she drove a nail through both his temples into his brain [Col. 1081B], and thus, in human form, killed the devil, the head of perverse men. 170

For what does Jael, whose name is interpreted as “ascent,” signify except the holy Church, through which alone heavenly blessedness is reached? Hence the Synagogue says of this same Church in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII.)

This woman was a foreigner because the holy Church arose from the Gentiles. She first gave the enemy of the Israelites milk to drink and afterward drove the peg into his head, because the holy Church first nourished the enemy of the human race [Col. 1081C] with a carnal way of life, but afterward, by living spiritually, destroyed him with a certain sharpness and the power of the cross.

If the insatiable murderer had not thirsted for the destruction of the human race with utterly unappeasable greed, Scripture certainly would not say of him: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished; he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth (Job XL).”

Milk is the fruit of the flesh and signifies the allurements of carnal pleasure. Therefore, for as long as the Gentile people lived voluptuously according to the law of the flesh, they offered the softness of their life, like milk, to the devil thirsting for our death. But after they had bound themselves under the discipline of the spirit, they immediately took up the weapons of the unconquered cross and pierced with wood the enemy of human salvation whom they had formerly given milk of pleasure to drink, now fortified by the protection of repentance.

Thus the foreign woman—that is, the Gentile Church—overthrew by the sign of the cross alone the one whom the Israelite people had been unable to overcome.

## CHAPTER III. In a Sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

[Col. 1081D]

Gideon, too, figuratively displayed this standard of the cross for himself and his fellow soldiers. He abandoned weapons against weapons, attacked the armed while himself unarmed, and came to fight the multitude of the Midianites after dismissing the larger host and retaining only a few.

By divine instruction he was commanded (Judg. VII), when he came to the river, to remove from the battle every man whom he saw drinking water on his knees. And so it happened that only three hundred men remained, those who had drawn water with their hands while standing.

What does it mean that Gideon advances to war content with three hundred soldiers, except that this number is contained in the letter Tau [Col. 1082A], which expresses the appearance of the cross? If what projects above the cross were added to this letter above its transverse line, it would no longer be merely the appearance of a cross but the cross itself.

Since, therefore, the number three hundred is contained in the letter Tau, which displays the figure of the cross, it is not without reason that in those three hundred who followed Gideon all those are represented to whom it is said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me (Luke IX).”

Those who follow the Lord truly take up the cross to the degree that they themselves are afflicted more severely and are kindled by the fire of devoted compassion toward neighbors who are delinquent or in need. Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Mark a Tau upon the foreheads [Col. 1082B] of the living who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in the midst of Jerusalem (Ezek. IX).” Or certainly, in these three hundred, who are contained in the letter Tau, this is expressed: that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

## CHAPTER IV. In a Sermon on the Holy Virgins

“When Gideon, at the Lord’s command, was sent to the camp of Midian to listen, one of the Midianites confessed to another that he had seen a dream. ‘Behold,’ he said, ‘I seemed to see a barley loaf baked under ashes rolling down into the camp of Midian. When it reached the tent, it struck it, overturned it, and leveled it completely with the ground.’ His listener replied: ‘This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon, son of Joash, an Israelite man; God has delivered Midian and all his camp into his hands [Col. 1082C] (Judg. VII).’”

By Gideon, whose name is said to mean not “one who goes around” but “one who goes around within the womb,” the one is rightly signified who, while enclosed in a virgin’s womb, encompassed and governed the entire structure of the world by his authority.

By Midian, which is interpreted as “judgment,” the unbelieving people are understood, of whom the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged (John III).”

Until the Savior’s coming, both the precepts of the Law and the oracles of the prophets were hidden, like barley beneath its chaff of letters. But after he came, broke the barley loaves, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowds, he also fulfilled the meaning of that action. The Evangelist says that he “opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV).” He deemed it fitting to make bread for souls from what, as barley [Col. 1082D], seemed suited to brute animals.

Just as barley is crushed between two millstones so that the chaff may be separated from the mass of flour, so the teaching of the holy Church is ground, as it were, between two stones—the Law and the Gospel—so that the surface of the letter may be distinguished from the marrow of the spirit.

But, to avoid lingering over these words any longer, this barley flour, sprinkled or mixed with the water of holy baptism and baked by the fire of the Holy Spirit, becomes bread. That bread overturns the camp of Midian because it destroys all the schemes of unbelievers.

This bread, according to the conjecture of that true interpreter, is Gideon’s sword, because, as the Apostle says: “The word of God is the sword of the Spirit (Eph. VI).” With this sword of the Holy Spirit Christ [Col. 1083A], the king of armies, arms his soldiers; with it he also girds and strengthens his women warriors. For he forms the ranks and arrays of his army from both sexes, admitting men and women alike to the reward of blessed combat.

## CHAPTER V. In a Sermon on Saint Matthew

“Is not,” Gideon said, “the cluster of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?” (Judg. VIII.)

Since Ephraim, whose name denotes fruitfulness, represents the Church, what is meant by the cluster of Ephraim except Christ? What by the vintage of Abiezer except the multitude of Jewish priests? Or again, by the cluster may be understood the small number of the faithful in the primitive Church [Col. 1083B], and by the vintage the multitude of the Synagogue.

The cluster of Ephraim is therefore better than the vintage of Abiezer, because more blessed was the primitive Church, which is made fruitful until the end of the age by the offspring of those being reborn, than the Synagogue, which gradually diminishes and daily tends toward decline. Hence it is said through Isaiah:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break into praise and sing, you who did not give birth, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband. Enlarge the place of your tent and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. For you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations (Isa. LIV).”

This woman whose offspring inherit the nations is the Church, which daily calls the human race through her children to the unity [Col. 1083C] of faith. She is the one of whom it is said in the Psalms: “For her who receives the inheritance (in the title of Ps. V).”

She is the vineyard that is commanded to sing praise, as is also found elsewhere in the same prophet: “On that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him: ‘I am the Lord who guard it’ (Isa. XXVII).”

Of this vineyard blessed Matthew also recalls that the Lord said: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to tenants, and went away to a distant land (Matt. XXI).”

This vineyard came forth from that cluster which was trodden under the feet of Jews and Gentiles in the winepress of the cross; from it flowed a stream of precious blood, which healthfully intoxicated minds poorly sober with the wine of spiritual grace.

When the apostles were speaking of this wine in various languages through the Holy Spirit, it was said: “These men are full of new wine (Acts II).”

## CHAPTER VI. In the Letter to Peter, Archpriest, on the Incontinence of Clerics

[Col. 1083D]

“Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal,” whom Scripture reports to have been born of the concubine whom he had in Shechem, “killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, upon one stone (Judg. VIII, IX).”

What is signified by the seventy men except the number of the Church’s preachers, [Col. 1084A] of whom the evangelist Luke says: “The Lord appointed seventy and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come”? (Luke X.)

This same order of preachers was already represented in those of whom the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers and leaders of the people, and bring them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant (Num. XI).”

What, then, are we to understand by Abimelech, who was their brother but illegitimate, except luxurious and carnal clerics? Through the ecclesiastical order they have received, they are indeed brothers of catholic and holy bishops, yet through the depravity of a degenerate life and ignoble works they are judged illegitimate.

They kill their brothers when they destroy the judgments of the holy Fathers and, by living perversely, corrupt their sanctions and decrees. This killing takes place upon one stone [Col. 1084B].

That stone is the Church of the Savior, of whom it is said through Zechariah: “Behold, I will bring my servant Orient, for behold, the stone that I have placed before Jesus; upon the one stone are seven eyes (Zech. III).”

The stone is most appropriately called one in both places, so that the unity of the Church may be commended. Of it the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, she is the only one of her mother (Song VI).”

What are the seven eyes upon the one stone—without prejudice, however, to any higher mystery, if there is one—except those seventy men, that is, holy teachers joined together in the unity of ecclesiastical peace and illumined by the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit? Through these eyes, the holy Church sees where to place the foot of right action and, walking along the way of God’s commandments, not to stumble against the rule of uprightness.

Abimelech, therefore, the bastard and illegitimate one, kills seventy legitimate brothers upon one stone when a portion of the clerics, degenerating from the nobility of ecclesiastical chastity, subjects itself to the laws of obscene lust [Col. 1084C]; and when, judging the sacred canons worthy of rejection, it slays with a kind of impious cruelty their authors—holy men and therefore noble sons of Gideon, that is, sons of the Savior and of the Church.

Yet we do not fail to recognize that it can reasonably be signified by Jerubbaal Christ and by Abimelech Antichrist: just as the former was the son of a concubine, so the latter will be the son of the rejected Synagogue. By the seventy brothers whom Abimelech is said to have killed may be understood the nations of the seventy languages, which Antichrist will persecute at the end of the world.

## CHAPTER VII. In the Letter to Boniface, Bishop, on Bishops Who Hold Public Office

[Col. 1084D]

“Jotham stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim and, raising his voice, cried: ‘Hear me, men of Shechem; so may God hear you. The trees went to anoint a king over themselves and said to the olive tree: “Rule over us.” It answered: “Can I abandon my richness, which both gods and human beings use, and go to be promoted among the trees?” The trees said to the fig tree: “Come and accept kingship over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my sweetness and my exceedingly pleasant fruit, and go to be promoted among the other trees?” The trees also spoke [Col. 1085A] to the vine: “Come and rule over us.” 174 It answered: “Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and human beings, and be promoted among the other trees?”’”

Then Scripture adds: “All the trees said to the bramble: ‘Come and rule over us.’ It answered them: ‘If you truly appoint me as king over you, come and rest beneath my shade (Judg. IX).’”

It would be lengthy to say that Gideon represents the Savior; that through his many wives various nations should be understood, joined to him through faith; that through his seventy sons the peoples of as many languages should be understood; that through the concubine the Synagogue should be understood; and that through Abimelech Antichrist should be understood, who will be the son of the Synagogue. Hence in the Apocalypse it is said to those who are going to believe: “They say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan (Rev. II).” And just as Abimelech killed the seventy brothers, so Antichrist will persecute all the nations [Col. 1085B] that do not agree with him.

Passing over these matters, which seem to require a more extended treatment, let us, insofar as the brevity of a letter permits, touch briefly on the figure of this lengthy history, so far as it appears to correspond to the discussion begun.

What, then, should we understand by Jotham, whose name is interpreted as “completed” or “perfect,” except some holy and learned preacher? He ascends Mount Gerizim and cries out in a loud voice. He ascends first and afterward cries out. He first rises onto the mountain and then raises his voice, because unless a teacher of virtues first climbs to the summit, he cries out in vain. As it is said through Isaiah: “Climb onto a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem (Isa. XL).”

By Gerizim [Col. 1085C] the holy Church is signified, which is the school of every virtue and fertile with the abundance of heavenly harvests. For this is the mountain appointed by Moses for the giving of blessings. The Church is the mountain of blessing, whose children are told through the Apostle: “You were called for this, that you might possess a blessing as your inheritance (1 Pet. III).”

We have received this inheritance from a widowed mother, for whose sake her husband deigned to die; of her the Psalmist says: “Blessing, I will bless her widow (Ps. CXXXI).”

Gerizim, which is interpreted as “division” or “newcomer,” appropriately represents the holy Church, because the Church of the Gentiles [Col. 1085D], which previously existed entirely separated from the Law of God, became a newcomer at its first calling and, through the increase of grace, has now become wholly a member of the household. Hence Paul says to those already firmly rooted and established, as it were, in a city: “You are no longer strangers and newcomers, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. II).”

But, leaving aside many matters and hastening quickly through what has been proposed, let us say briefly: the trees of the forest are vain and fruitless people, deservedly subject to the avenging flames because of their barrenness. “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matt. III).”

What, then, is signified by the olive tree, which displays the sign of peace and pours forth the richness of oil, except those who, anointed with the richness of the Holy Spirit, reconcile human beings to their Creator [Col. 1086A] by proclaiming peace? “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace (Rom. X).”

The fig tree represents the sacred Law. Hence it is said in the Gospel that “a certain householder planted a vineyard,” in which, of course, he also planted a fig tree (Matt. XXI). “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa. V),” in which the divine hand planted the Decalogue of the Law.

But this fig tree produced and cast away its former people as its first figs—that is, dry and useless ones—175 while it brought the new shoot of Christian faith to the maturity of inward richness and sweetness. Of these Jeremiah says: “I see good figs, very good; and bad figs, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad (Jer. XXIV).”

The fig trees, therefore, may appropriately be understood as those who are sufficiently instructed in the teaching of the sacred Law.

The vine also [Col. 1086B] seems to signify nearly the same thing as the fig tree. For the Lord says: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches (John XV).” And since vines arise from branches, why should it be surprising if holy teachers are also called vines, so that what the Savior of the world possesses by nature, they may boast of possessing by grace?

As they do not cease to proclaim the triumph of the Lord’s Passion, they intoxicate our parched hearts with the wine of blessed blood, as though with clusters produced by their teaching.

Of this wine Jacob speaks allegorically concerning our Savior: “He shall wash his garment in wine and his cloak in the blood” (Gen. 49). Christ’s garment was the Synagogue in the apostles and the other believers; its cloak, moreover, is the Gentile people. Concerning them he says through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49). Christ washed these in the blood of the grape, which he pressed from himself, crushed in the winepress of the cross. Hence John also says: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

Since, therefore, the olive, the fig, and the vine—that is, spiritual men—refuse absolutely to rule over the wild trees, namely, earthly and carnal men, the bramble presents itself, both to be consumed by them and, by the example of an equally depraved way of life or by the fire of erroneous doctrine, to consume them in turn. For the bramble bristles with thickly growing thorns; by it is signified every perverse person who is so thickly covered with the roughness of sins as with a thicket. Hence it was said to the first man: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3)—that is, your body shall be subjected to the sharp stings of vices. And the Lord says through the prophet: “They surrounded me with the thorns of their sins” (Lam. 3).

When the trees therefore seek a king—that is, when various wicked men, choosing according to the flesh, seek a ruler—the bramble comes forward: namely, any reprobate who increases within himself the fire of condemnation because of their wickedness and, by living or teaching perversely, consumes them in reciprocal burning. Hence it is said there: “Let fire come out from it and consume the inhabitants of Shechem and the city of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the city of Millo and devour Abimelech” (Judg. 9). Jotham speaks these words while standing on the summit of a mountain, because through the holy preachers in the Church we learn how to resist the various perverse and reprobate people who seek vanities.

## CHAPTER VIII  
*In the letter to Peter, archpresbyter, concerning the incontinence of clerics.*

“Abimelech, hearing that the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together, went up Mount Zalmon with all his people; and, taking an axe, he cut off a branch from a tree, carried it on his shoulder, and said to his companions: ‘What you see me doing, do quickly.’” Then it continues: “Therefore, cutting branches from the trees in rivalry with one another, they followed their leader. Surrounding the stronghold with them, they set it on fire; and so it happened that, by smoke and fire, a thousand people, men and women alike, inhabitants of the tower of Shechem, were killed” (Judg. 9).

It is not the place here carefully to expound the sacred figures contained in this historical account; it is enough for us, so far as our purpose is concerned, to touch briefly upon the matter. The branches of the trees are brief sayings of Scripture. When various unchaste people forcibly twist them to strengthen their own argument, they extinguish numerous crowds of people with smoke and fire together: with the smoke, that is, of error, and with the fire of lust, so that the minds deceived by bad instruction are both kindled by the flame of luxury and bewildered by the darkness of corrupt doctrine.

These are indeed the wages that seemed to come forth from Sodom and Gomorrah after their destruction. “Abraham,” says Scripture, “rising early in the morning, where he had previously stood with the Lord, looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and over the whole land of that region; and he saw ashes rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace” (Gen. 19).

## CHAPTER IX  
*In the same letter.*

Moreover, while Abimelech was besieging the city of Thebez with his forces, he seems likewise to have represented the conflict against chastity. “There was,” as Scripture testifies, “a lofty tower in the middle of the city, to which men and women alike had fled, together with all the rulers of the city. Its door was shut most securely, and they stood upon the roof of the tower behind the battlements” (Judg. 9). The city is the universal Church; the tower is the eminence of chastity. To it men and women alike had fled—that is, the strong and the weak—and also the rulers of the city, namely, the order of clerics, who holds authority in the Church.

“Then Abimelech, approaching the tower, began to fight more vigorously; and, drawing near the entrance, he attempted to set it on fire” (ibid.). In this way, reckless and shameless clerics attempt to set fire to the tower of chastity when they urge many to follow the example of their lust and burning madness. Armed with fires, they attack the tower of chastity when they inflame the chaste with the destructive flame of incestuous persuasion.

But what end is imposed upon this struggle? What titles of victory does this battle win? “Behold,” it says, “a woman, throwing a fragment of a millstone from above, struck Abimelech on the head and crushed his skull. He immediately called his armor-bearer and said to him: ‘Draw your sword and kill me, lest it be said that I was killed by a woman.’ And he fulfilled his command and killed him” (Judg. 9).

To avoid dwelling too long on these words, this fragment of a millstone that crushed Abimelech’s skull is nothing other than that stone which Daniel saw cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. 2)—namely, the Lord himself, who says of himself in the Gospel: “Whoever falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matt. 21). The woman from whose hands it was thrown is the sacred Law, which threatens sudden judgment by Christ against those who commit crimes and despise chastity. Concerning this the Lord says through Jeremiah: “Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer crushing rock?” (Jer. 23).

Abimelech’s armor-bearer is the devil, who supplies all those who attack the tower of chastity with the weapons of lust and the sharp darts of sexual immorality. Concerning these darts the Apostle says: “In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Eph. 6). And the prophet says: “There is Assyria with all its weapons” (Ezek. 32).

The woman therefore struck him with the fragment of the millstone, and the armor-bearer killed him with the sword, because the devil slaughters with eternal death those adversaries of chastity against whom sacred Scripture directs the judgment of divine retribution. Thus, having been their assistant in the struggle, he afterward becomes their torturer in punishment; and the very weapons he had supplied to them against purity he then, in accordance with their deserts, turns against their throats.

## CHAPTER X  
*In a sermon on Saint Antimus.*

Clearly, the faith of certain people is empty and flaccid: it presents on the surface a likeness, but does not possess the truth within. Those who once came from the people of Ephraim to the fords of the Jordan prefigured them. Since they did not know how to pronounce **sebboleth** [shibboleth], but instead said **jebboleth** [sibboleth], uttering it as though with a foreign tongue, they were struck down by the swords of the Gileadites (Judg. 12).

What else should be understood by the Jordan, in which our Savior deigned to be baptized, than baptism? And what else by *sebboleth*, which is interpreted as “ear of grain,” than faith? Just as an ear of grain provides food for human beings, so it is said of faith: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2; Rom. 1). And just as an ear of grain stores many kernels in its awns, so the symbol of our confession gathers within itself many seeds of faith.

When the Ephraimites therefore came to the Jordan, the Gileadites asked them how they pronounced “ear of grain”; likewise, when catechumens come to the washing of baptism, they are questioned by the priests about how they believe. Since Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” the priests of the Church are rightly understood by the Gileadites, for by their preaching they bear witness to God’s works. By Ephraim, which signifies “fruitfulness,” are designated those who come to the ear of faith for this reason: that they may bring forth the harvest of fruitfulness through a crop of good works.

Just as those who come to the Jordan understand “ear of grain” but die because they do not know how to pronounce it, so those who seek the fountain of baptism fall completely away from life unless they strive also to express by the proclamation of good works the faith they have been taught to believe. One thing depends upon the other, so that the seed of faith must rise into the ear of works.

Our Savior plainly demonstrated this. For when he commanded his disciples, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28). It is as though he openly said: “Sow the seed of faith in human hearts, and then teach them how they must express, by the language of works, the ear of the commandments that are springing up, lest those who testify that they are from Mount Ephraim—that is, from the height of ecclesial fruitfulness—commit a solecism in the ear of their works.”

Therefore, beloved, let us beware lest our faith deceive us by the superimposed color of profession alone and, like an empty ear of grain with hollow stalks, swell without the marrow of love. Let us imitate the faith of the martyrs, through which, conquering earthly kingdoms, they attained the promised rewards of heaven (Heb. 11). Let our faith therefore be solid, true, and strong, so that by walking now through faith we may arrive at sight, seeing through a mirror in an enigma, and may one day be brought to the vision of supreme truth itself (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XI  
*In a letter to Adelaide, countess, by which he reconciles her with a bishop because of the incontinence of clerics.*

As the ancient history relates: “Samson caught three hundred foxes, joined their tails together tail to tail, and fastened torches between them. Having set them on fire, he released them to run here and there; and they immediately went into the fields of the Philistines. When these had been set alight, both the gathered grain and what was still standing in the stubble were burned, so thoroughly that the flames also consumed the vineyards and olive groves” (Judg. 15).

Although this history principally designates heretics, who are represented as numbering three hundred because they verbally confess faith in the Holy Trinity, yet, while they cloak themselves at the beginning of their speech under the appearance of orthodox faith, they conceal behind it the fire of corrupt doctrine by which the harvest of all good works is burned up, nevertheless, I say, the incontinent clerics together with their mistresses can also aptly be represented by these foxes. They walk as though their feet were unbound when they sometimes pretend to display the appearance of decency; but when they are joined together at the tails with burning torches, they are, as it were, secretly glued together by the fire of immodest love, having set decency aside as far as they can.

These little foxes, joined together through the intervention of fire and fastened by the torches of lust, consume all the fields of the Philistines, because they destroy the spiritual fruits of the Church and, so far as they are able, set the good works of the faithful people ablaze with the fire of divine indignation. Concerning this fire the Psalmist mystically says: “He gave their cattle over to hail and their possessions to fire” (Ps. 77). For just as good priests commend to God the offerings and vows of all the faithful, so those who are unworthy of the sacred altars often burden them terribly. That evil priests are compared with foxes is also attested by the prophet Ezekiel, who says: “Your prophets, Israel, were like foxes in the deserts” (Ezek. 13).

## CHAPTER XII  
*In a sermon on the holy virgins.*

When our Savior came to the battlefield of this world to conquer the powers of the air, he did not choose rhetoricians and philosophers, but simple people entirely ignorant of literary training, because, as the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise, and the weak things to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

That victory of Samson aptly prefigured this, when he seized a heated donkey’s jawbone and killed a thousand Philistine men. For what is signified by the jawbone of a donkey, which is certainly a simple animal, except the unlearned mouths of simple people? Samson therefore killed a thousand men not with weapons or with various kinds of missiles, but with a donkey’s jawbone, because our Redeemer, whom Samson signified, extinguished the perfect number of unbelievers from the life of their former error through unlearned and rudimentary people.

What wonder is it, moreover, if sacred eloquence designates holy preachers through the donkey’s jawbone, when it sometimes also declares the word of preaching through barley, which is certainly fodder for animals? This is recognized not only through the five Gospel loaves (John 6), but also through the account of the man who reported to his companion what he claimed to have dreamed in the camp of Midian: “Behold,” he said, “I saw a barley loaf, as though baked under ashes, rolling down into the camp of Midian; and when it reached the tent, it struck it and overturned it” (Judg. 7).

## CHAPTER XIII  
*In a letter to the canons of Fano.*

Anyone who ought to instruct others in the way of uprightness must take great care lest he himself, God forbid, appear to err in anything. Hence the Israelite people, inflamed with zeal for righteousness, rises to avenge the crime of Benjamin [Belamin], and yet that same people is first struck down by the swords of Benjamin (Judg. 20).

Who would not be moved by the fact that, when the Lord was twice consulted, he twice gave assent to undertaking battle against Benjamin, and yet in the first combat twenty-two thousand Israelites fell, and in the second eighteen thousand? What, then, is to be understood and discerned in this, except that those who are eager to strike the diseases of another’s wickedness must first be cured of the swelling of their own wound, so that those who hasten to strike the wickedness of others may themselves come purified for the punishment of their own? As it is said in the Gospel: “Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John 8).

Therefore, when they rightly consult the Lord and say, “Who shall be the leader of our army in the battle against the sons of Benjamin?” he replies: “Let Judah be your leader” (Judg. 20). Since *Judah* is interpreted as “confession,” Judah is rightly appointed leader of that battle, so that those who wish to help others confessing their error may first strive to correct their own faults through confession.

*The testimonies of the Book of Judges end here.*

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

[Col. 1091]

1. Concerning Eli, who did not properly rebuke the sins of his sons.  
2. How, when the citizens of Jabesh-gilead sought a covenant from Nahash the Ammonite, who was besieging it, Nahash replied that he would make a covenant with them on the condition that he gouge out the right eyes of them all.  
3. Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign; and he reigned over Israel for two years.  
4. How, when Saul began to reign, no blacksmith was found throughout the whole land of Israel.  
5. Concerning Merab and Michal, the daughters of Saul, whom he promised to David as wives; but when one was taken away, David joined the other to himself as his wife.  
6. How David, fleeing from the presence of King Saul, pretended to be insane before Achish, king of Gath.  
7. Concerning the witch who, repaying good for evil to King Saul, cooked a calf and prepared food.

*The chapters end here.*

# THE TESTIMONIES OF THE FIRST BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

## CHAPTER I  
*In a letter to Pope Nicholas, concerning the incontinence of bishops.*

[Col. 1091B]

Eli knew the sins of his sons, but did not rebuke them with the sharpest denunciation they deserved. When those same sons were killed by the Philistines in battle, he too fell backward from his chair, broke his neck, and died. Moreover, the ark of the Lord was captured by the enemies, and first four thousand, then thirty thousand men were struck down and overthrown by the Philistines.

He did indeed reproach them, and he did indeed rebuke them, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity or authority of a high priest: “Why do you do things of this kind, the very wicked things that I hear from all the people? Do not, my sons; for the report that I hear is not good” (1 Sam. 2). For Scripture testifies that they slept with the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle.

Although he saw them as enemies of God, he still acknowledged them as sons, to his own destruction; and those whom he ought to have struck with a hostile sword he caressed with the gentleness of paternal flattery. The faithful servant in the house of the Lord, Moses, was not like this—Moses, the teacher of the noble Phinehas. Standing at the gate of the camp, he said: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him. He said to them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his neighbor, and his friend.” When twenty-three thousand men had been killed, Moses said: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one in his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. 32).

Clearly, just as those who correct faults are worthy of blessing, so those who flatter sinners are likewise liable to a curse. As the prophet says: “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). A person withholds his sword from blood when he restrains himself from imposing upon the reprobate the punishment of judgment they deserve. For he is guilty of the deed who neglects to correct what he is able to correct (St. Gregory).

Hence the man of God, who is also thought to have been Phinehas, said to the aforementioned Eli: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you kick away my sacrifice and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honor your sons more than me?” (1 Sam. 2).

If Eli, because of only two sons whom he did not rebuke with the denunciation they deserved, perished together with them and with so great a multitude of people, what sentence do we suppose those deserve who sit in the ecclesiastical court and on the seats of judgment yet remain silent about the notorious crimes of wicked people? While they fear disgracing men publicly, they confuse the commandments of divine law to the insult of the heavenly Judge; and while they preserve the office of honor for men who are lost, they cruelly dishonor the Author of ecclesiastical dignity himself.

Therefore the divine voice says to that same Eli, who had despised God by honoring his sons: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held of no account.” Immediately afterward it adds: “Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house” (1 Sam. 2), as though it openly said: “Because through the dignity of pastoral office I bestowed upon you the arm of strength against my enemies, but you were unwilling to exercise it for their punishment, now I will cut off the arm from you—that is, I will take away from you the strength of the priestly dignity—so that you who had been equipped to fight for me will no longer even have a hand with which to defend yourself.”

## CHAPTER II  
*In a letter to the brothers of Cluny.*

The world, which gives birth to darkness, must be fled; withdrawal must be sought, where true light breaks forth as in a desert. Anyone who inserts the darkness in which he always remains into those who consent and obey him must be driven completely from our friendship; indeed, we ought always to wage irreconcilable war against one who blinds the eyes of his friends.

Hence we have learned from the sacred history of the Kings, which relates: “When Nahash the Ammonite came up to attack Jabesh-gilead with his forces, all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash with one voice: ‘Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.’ He replied: ‘On this condition I will make a covenant with you: that I gouge out the right eyes of all of you and make you a reproach to all Israel.’ The elders of Jabesh said to him: ‘Grant us seven days, so that we may send messengers throughout all the borders of Israel; if there is no one to defend us, we will come out to you.’ When Saul heard this, he gathered a great army, took up arms, and, after inflicting a very great slaughter upon the Ammonites, triumphed gloriously” (1 Sam. 11).

What, then, are we to understand by Nahash the Ammonite, that proud king, except either the world rebelling against its Creator or the devil, its prince? Of him it is said: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41). And because *Nahash* is interpreted as “serpent,” the venomous and slippery serpent is rightly represented by him.

What else is signified by Jabesh, which was an Israelite city, except the Christian soul intent upon seeing God through the practice of contemplation? And because *Jabesh* is interpreted as “dried” or “parched,” that soul is aptly understood by Jabesh which abandons the richness of heavenly grace and withers in the heat of carnal desire. For when it ceases to thirst for the dew of the divine gift, it becomes dry, although previously, when it received that dew, it flourished healthily through being watered, as the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will pour water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry ground” (Isa. 44).

But Nahash refuses to enter into a covenant with Jabesh except on the condition that it surrender its right eye. For whoever submits either to the ancient enemy through a perverse suggestion or becomes entangled in the restless activities of this world, when he shamefully makes a covenant with it as with a proud king, must lose his right eye—that is, the light of contemplation. Thus he is made a reproach in Israel, because when he descends from the height of contemplation to carry out earthly or filthy things, it follows that he is bitten in the Church by the slanders of disgraceful mockery.

They ask for seven days’ respite. Since God is read to have rested from all his works on the seventh day (Gen. 2), what is signified by the number seven except rest? The disobedient Saul did not understand this number when Samuel commanded him to wait for him: “You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you must do” (1 Sam. 10). But because the reprobate man despised spiritual rest, an evil spirit seized him and began to torment him (1 Sam. 16).

Through the number of seven days, therefore, the city of Jabesh is delivered from the wicked king, because any soul whom the world, at the devil’s persuasion, attempts to draw to itself and blind with the darkness of secular affairs preserves the eye of contemplation unharmed if, resisting altogether, it perseveres in its purpose of quiet. Our Redeemer delivers it from the temptation it suffers when he finds it resting in the discipline of its withdrawal.

Hence it is written there: “When the next day had come,” he said, “Saul divided the people into three groups, entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch, and struck down Ammon until the day grew hot” (1 Sam. 11).

What is signified by Saul, who was called the Lord’s anointed, except the one who is the true King of Israel, the mediator of God and human beings? What does his dividing the people into three groups signify except that there are three principal virtues of the soul: faith, hope, and charity? Victory in the battle is therefore obtained in the three divisions of the warriors, because every temptation of the devil is conquered by these three virtues under Christ as leader.

Nor is the number of the fighters that Scripture reports devoid of mystery. “There were,” it says, “three hundred thousand of the sons of Israel, and thirty thousand men of Judah” (ibid.). Since the thousand and the ten are perfect numbers, they signify the perfection of the saints; but three hundred and thirty, because they arise from three, signify the divine Trinity.

What, then, are signified by the three hundred thousand or thirty thousand warriors except the holy teachers of the Church, who are orthodox in faith and perfected in religious works? With these Saul overcomes the hostile forces of King Nahash, because Christ, together with the teachers of his Church, triumphs over the crafty plotting of the ancient serpent. For when their teachings or examples are carefully considered, immediately the sluggish hearts that harmful torpor had already invaded grow warm again, and the spirit is inflamed like a sharpened sword to cut down the ranks of the attacking vices.

Hence those same warriors of Israel and Judah say to the messengers who had come to them: “Thus shall you say to the men who are in Jabesh-gilead: Tomorrow you shall have deliverance when the sun grows hot.” For when the mind, initially weakened by sloth, returns to itself and grows warm again with desire for its Creator; when it abandons the torpor of negligence and the flame of holy love kindles the former coldness of insensibility, then, as though the sun were growing hot, victory is gained over the enemies and the besieged city is freed from the hands of the proud king.

Hence it is written of Abraham that “the Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre in the very heat of the day” (Gen. 18). Hence Lot says: “The sun has risen over the earth, and Lot entered Zoar” (Gen. 19).

Rightly, therefore, we reject friendship with either the world or its prince and refuse to enter into a pact of association with them, lest, when we join ourselves to darkness, we be deprived of light.

It should also be noted that the wicked king does not demand that both eyes of his enemies be gouged out, but only one, so as to make them a reproach in Israel. For the evil enemy often takes away from any reprobate person who consents to him the better part of holiness and luminous work, but leaves the lesser part through a certain contrivance of his cunning. Thus, in what is taken away, there is an occasion for condemnation, so that the person may perish; but in what remains, he presumes upon the hope of confidence, so that the sinner does not return to repentance but leans, as upon a staff, upon the remnants of the holiness he has lost. He is torn by infamy by those who know that he has fallen, and thus the loss of pious work becomes a fitting reproach of derision.

## CHAPTER III  
*In a letter to Alberic, in which he answers him concerning ten questions.*

“Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign; and he reigned over Israel for two years” (1 Sam. 13).

Some think this should be understood to mean that, at the beginning of King Saul’s reign, he had a son who was one year old and was still crying in tender infancy—namely, Ish-bosheth—and that this son reigned over Israel for two years after his father’s death. But since this interpretation is rejected by more learned men, let us inquire into another.

The blessed Jerome teaches that it should be understood in this way: “He was innocent, like a child of one year, when he began to reign, and he remained for two years in the simplicity of that same innocence. But he who was then a son through humility afterward became a slave through pride.”

## CHAPTER IV  
*In a letter to Aliprandus, concerning correction and how useful it is in the discipline of the holy order.*

[Col. 1095B]

Every spiritual community plainly suffers from the mystical poverty of the Israelite people if it does not make frequent use of fraternal zeal in correction. This was represented when, at the beginning of Saul’s reign, Israel had no blacksmith. Scripture says: “No blacksmith was found throughout the whole land of Israel” (1 Sam. 13).

Just as iron forcefully subdues the other metals, so the hammer of correction restrains the vices of wrongdoers and, as though by hammering, breaks the hardness of the rigid mind. Hence it is said through Isaiah concerning the very prince of spiritual smiths: “Behold, I created the smith who blows upon the coal in the fire and brings forth a vessel for his work” (Isa. 54).

Ecclesiastes also says of iron: “If the iron has been blunted, and it is not as before but has become dull, it will be sharpened with much labor; and wisdom follows after diligence” (Eccles. 10).

But the Philistines remove the blacksmiths from the land of Israel when evil spirits, under the pretext of false piety, take away the zeal for correction from the lips of the brethren. Hence it is added there: “For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make a sword or a spear” (1 Sam. 13). A little later it says: “The edges of the plowshares, mattocks, tridents, and axes had therefore become blunt, and even the goad had to be repaired” (ibid.).

While the Philistines fear swords, they remove the smiths, so that when the manufacture of weapons is suppressed, there is no one to manufacture the other implements needed for labor. For, as the Apostle testifies: “The sword of the Spirit is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

Because perverse spirits fear this sword, they remove the smiths from the land of Israel when they restrain those who ought to rebuke the errors of wrongdoers from maintaining the discipline of correction. Through this dissolution of negligence it happens that, in the various communities of God’s servants, not only does the word of sacred preaching cease to be heard, but the practice of honorable skills also ceases to be pursued.

For because the strict discipline of instruction does not restrain them, they devote themselves to their own wills and do not know how to write; they learn none of the manual exercises of an honorable craft, although the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). Since such things are necessary to them, they approach secular people, or even reprobates, because they cannot find them among themselves.

Hence it is said there: “Therefore all Israel descended to the Philistines, so that each might sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, and his hoe.” Israel did not ascend to the Philistines but descended, in order to sharpen the implements necessary for its needs, when men of the holy order descend to the low things of secular people to obtain from them some useful advantage.

You see, therefore, that if the discipline of correction is removed from a sacred community, the strength of discipline is utterly weakened and the whole religious life is destroyed. For when each person follows the judgment of his own will, returning to secular things, he violates the institution of spiritual observance.

Therefore anyone in whom the fervor of regular life burns gladly embraces corrections and, even when innocent, takes pleasure in being reproved—not because conscience reproaches him for having sinned, but because he hopes this will benefit the other hearers, so that while he himself is shown to be innocent and clean, others who have fallen or perhaps are about to fall may be corrected.

## CHAPTER V  
*In a letter to Hermisinda, concerning how quickly a structure of human pride is destroyed.*

“Saul had indeed promised to give his elder daughter Merab to David as a wife; but when the time came when she ought to have been given to him, she was not given to him but was joined to another man. Saul’s other daughter Michal loved David, and he joined her to himself as his wife” (1 Sam. 18).

*Merab* is interpreted as “from multitude”; *Michal* as “from whom” or “from all.” What else, then, is signified by Merab except that multitude of unbelievers which is “from the multitude” and is rejected? “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20).

What else is signified by Michal except the holy Church, from whom all the elect arise, or which consists of all the elect? Although she did not bear a son, her barrenness does not obstruct this interpretation. It is one mystery that she was joined in marriage to King David; another that she remained barren; another that she obtained the marriage of Christ the Lord; and another that she did not receive the gift of fertility but bore in Israel the reproach of barrenness.

David, the strong-handed and desirable Jesus, joined this Michal to himself, when he took her away from the service of the proud prince of this world and united her to himself by the bond of intimate association. That proud Saul—namely, the evil spirit—cannot take this Michal, who is the holy Church of the elect, away from him, because her faithful guardian has irrevocably bound her in the embrace of his love. In the Gospel he cries: “My sheep hear my voice, and they will not perish forever, and no one will snatch them from my hand” (John 10).

## CHAPTER VI  
*In a sermon on Saint Columba.*

When our Redeemer enters the battlefield of this world to fight, he arms himself as a strong warrior to conquer the wickedness of the air. Because he had to begin a new battle, he put on a new kind of armor: namely, he placed upon himself what is weak and concealed what is strong. He put on the breastplate of weak flesh and concealed the invincible strength of his divinity.

Thus, through the flesh, the devil is defeated by the second man—the same devil who had earlier overcome the first man through the flesh—and the very thing that had been the means of victory over our first parent now became the cause of his ruin.

This was foreshadowed through the mystery of allegory by the event in which David, fleeing from King Saul, pretended to be insane in the presence of Achish, king of Gath. Scripture says: “His saliva ran down upon his beard” (1 Sam. 21).

Since a beard is a man’s distinctive feature, what does it signify in mystical interpretation except an indication of strength? What, then, is signified by the saliva—which is fluid and flowing—except the weakness of the flesh? And what by the beard except the strength of divinity? The beard is therefore covered by flowing saliva because the power of divinity is clothed with the fragile covering of flesh.

But what David did through the skill of his dispensation was regarded by the ignorant as madness. Hence Achish said to his servants: “You have seen a madman. Why have you brought him to me? Do we lack madmen that you have brought this one to play the madman in my presence?” (ibid.)

Is it not true that something similar also happened to David, our Redeemer, so that he was thought insane by the insane and was said by the demon-possessed to perform miracles through demons? Hence the evangelist Mark says: “When his own people had seen this, they went out to seize him; for they were saying that he had become deranged” (Mark 3). [Col. 1097C] Immediately he added these words: “The scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying: ‘He has Beelzebub,’ and, ‘By the prince of demons he casts out demons’” (ibid.).

Moreover, since saliva frequently runs from the mouths of infants, did his words not seem childish when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6)? Hearing this, the disciples said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” And, as the evangelist reports, “from that time they no longer walked with him” (ibid.). Yet these drops of saliva covered David’s beard, because divine power lay hidden beneath these childish words.

Our Redeemer therefore became weak in order to make us strong; he appeared foolish in order to call us back to true wisdom. Hence the Apostle says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings.” And a little earlier: “Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1). Nor is it unfitting that weakness or foolishness should be spoken of concerning the Lord our Savior, since he did not disdain to be mystically represented even by a leper and even by a serpent.

## CHAPTER VII. In the letter to Abbot Desiderius, in which it is said that the person who casts aside dignity is worthy of greater honor than the person who persists in it

Who would not be edified and aroused to the perfection of charity by this example? Who, I ask, would not be provoked not only to undertake the dutiful practice of loving kindness, but also to return good for evil, by what is read concerning that Pythoness, a woman certainly worthy of the proclamation of great praise? In imitation of God, she treated Saul so well, although he had already been given up as regards his royal eminence and was destined on the following day to be killed by the swords of the Philistines (1 Samuel 27). Like a prudent serpent, therefore, in accordance with the Gospel (Matthew 10), she bestowed a benefit upon one from whom she hoped to receive no advantage.

Moreover, as she herself complains, he had exterminated all the diviners and magicians from the land of Israel, and thereby deprived this same little woman of all the income she had customarily obtained from divination. She cooked the paschal calf that had barely remained for her from her exhausted poverty, and, mixing unleavened bread from a very small quantity of flour, placed it before him so that he might eat. When he, mourning and terrified by the imminence of death, rejected this and absolutely refused to take food, she, on the contrary, pressed him unceasingly with earnest entreaties and with arguments, so to speak, urging him to return the favor to her who was entreating him.

Just as she had obeyed his command, so he should consent to the petitions of the woman supplicating him:

“Behold,” she said, “your maidservant has obeyed your voice; I have placed my life in your hand and have listened to your words, which you spoke to me. Now therefore listen also to the voice of your maidservant, and I will set a morsel of bread before you, so that, when you have eaten, you may recover your strength and be able to undertake your journey” (1 Samuel 28).

Who could have done this once the Gospel was shining forth, when this woman is described as having acted under the shadow of the Law—especially since the Old Testament offers the command: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy,” whereas the Gospel trumpet thunders terribly: “Your Father will not forgive you your sins if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matthew 6; Mark 11)?

Saul was so hostile to diviners and fortune-tellers that he killed them all indiscriminately, and scarcely any of them remained except this poor woman alone. Even she, who survived, was so constrained by the savagery of the royal persecution that, since she did not dare to practice divination at all, she had entirely lost the customary income of her profession. Nevertheless, giving back the very thing that had remained to her, she gladly offered good for evil and fed her enemy, as though the Apostle had already commanded this (Romans 1).

This praiseworthy woman did so at a time when she knew that he would immediately die, and therefore neither hoped that he would now be peaceful nor feared him when angry. People employ arguments in order to drive away those who wish to lodge in their houses and send them to neighboring inns or shops. One place, they say, is run-down, another is preferable; here, because of the severity of last year’s weather, the weakened crop is said to deny the farmers their food, while there the yield of fertile grain is said to have overflowed. Sometimes the shortness of the journey is praised; sometimes the sun is said to occupy the higher regions of the sky. By such carefully arranged words, nothing else is accomplished than compelling the newcomers to provide themselves with another lodging.

This prudent and noble woman, however, argues rhetorically, if I may put it that way, and employs the speeches of orators so that her enemy, while resisting and recoiling, is nevertheless induced to eat.

The testimonies of the First Book of Kings end here.

## 189–190. THE CHAPTERS OF THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

[Col. 1099]

1. Concerning David’s imprecation that from Joab’s house there should not fail a man suffering from a discharge of semen and a leper holding a distaff.  
2. “This is the law of Adam,” David says, “Lord God.”  
3. “David made a name for himself when, after conquering Syria, he returned and struck down twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt.”  
4. Who the Cherethites and Pelethites were.  
5. Concerning the statement that David’s sons are said to have been priests.  
6. How Hanun, son of Nahash, when David sent messengers to console him over his father’s death, tore their garments and shaved half their beards.  
7. Concerning David’s repentance, which was accepted, whereas Saul’s was rejected.  
8. How David victoriously captured Rabbah, the city that Joab was besieging.  
9. How David, fleeing from Absalom, left ten concubines behind to guard the house.  
10. How Absalom, pursuing his father, violated the concubines whom his father had left in the house, following Ahithophel’s counsel.  
11. How Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai the Gileadite brought David, in the camp of Madian, beds, carpets, vessels, and everything necessary for food.  
12. How it is said that more of the people were consumed by the forest than were devoured by the sword.  
13. How Barzillai the Gileadite came with King David as far as the Jordan and refused to proceed with him to Jerusalem.  
14. How David, on his return, committed the ten concubines whom he had left at home to custody and did not enter them again thereafter.  
15. Hence the preceding matter.  
16. Concerning the statement that a third battle occurred at Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus, son of the Forest, a maker of many-threaded fabric, a Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite.  
17. David, seated in the chair, the wisest prince among the three; he himself, like a tender worm of wood, killed eight hundred at one assault.  
18. How David bought the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite and the oxen for a fixed price, offering them as a burnt offering.

The chapters end here.

## THE TESTIMONIES OF THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

[Col. 1099]

## CHAPTER I. In the Gomorrhian book

[Col. 1099A]

“May there not fail,” David says, “from the house of Joab a Gomorrhian sustaining” (2 Samuel 3). The second translation has instead: “one sustaining a discharge of semen and a leper holding a distaff, one falling by the sword and one lacking bread.”

A person is covered with leprosy when he is defiled by the stain of serious sin. To hold a distaff means to abandon the courageous deeds of a manly life and display the seductive softness of a womanly way of living. He falls by the sword who incurs the fury of divine indignation. He lacks bread whom the punishment of his own guilt restrains from receiving Christ’s body. “For he is the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6).

If, therefore, after the discharge of semen you have become a leper and are compelled by the command of the Law to remain outside the camp, why do you still contend to retain the first place of honor in that same camp? Did not King Uzziah, when he had arrogantly wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense, after recognizing that he had been struck from heaven by the plague of leprosy, patiently endure not only being expelled from the temple by the priests, but himself hasten quickly to go out?
