For it is written: “When Azariah the high priest and all the remaining priests had looked at him, they saw leprosy on his forehead, and they hurriedly expelled him.” Then it immediately adds: “But he himself, terrified, hastened to leave, because he had suddenly perceived the Lord’s plague” (2 Chronicles 26).

If a king struck with bodily leprosy did not disdain to be expelled from the temple by the priests, why do you, a leper in soul, refuse to be removed from the sacred altars by the judgment of so many holy Fathers? If he, laying aside the command of royal dignity, was not ashamed to live in a private house until his death, why are you ashamed to descend from the height of priestly office, so that, shut up in the burial place of repentance, you may strive to count yourself among the living as though dead?

And, to return to that mystical history of Joab: if you yourself have fallen by the sword, how will you raise another through priestly grace? If, as your merits demand, you lack bread—that is, if you have been separated from Christ’s body—how will you be able to satisfy another with the food of the heavenly table? If you have been struck on the forehead with Uzziah’s leprosy, that is, if you are dishonored in the face by the mark of disgrace, how will you be able to cleanse another by covering over the memory of the crime committed?

Let swollen pride therefore blush, and let it not vainly desire to exalt itself above itself, when the burden of its own guilt weighs upon it quite heavily below.

## 191. CHAPTER II. In a sermon on Saint Matthew

[Col. 1100B]

When divine mercy promised through the prophet Nathan that one would be born from David’s seed who would build a temple for God’s holy name, and, clearly announcing Christ, added: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son” (2 Samuel 7), he then described what the Church, which is Christ’s body, would be, saying: “Your house shall be faithful, and your kingdom shall endure forever before my face, and your throne shall be established forever.”

Giving thanks, David said among the other words of his prayer: “Yet this seemed a small thing in your sight, Lord God, since you have loved me, unless you also spoke concerning the house of your servant for a distant future.” Then he added: “For this is the law of Adam, Lord God” (ibid.).

It is as though he plainly said: “Just as at the beginning of this earthly world you established Adam as the father of the posterity that would follow and decreed that the offspring of the whole human race should sprout from this root, so now, when you intend to renew the world, you make me like a new Adam, promising that Christ, who is the author and head of the Church, will be born from my seed. ‘This is the law of Adam,’ he says, because just as Adam was destined to possess this visible world in his children, so I too am made the father of a spiritual people, destined to reign forever with him who is in heaven.”

For just as Eve, the mother of the living, was formed from Adam’s rib (Genesis 2), so from the side of Christ, who is to be born from me, the Church emerges to live forever.

Concerning this new and spiritual world it is written: “The foundations of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them” (1 Samuel 2). The world is set upon the foundations of the earth when the holy Church is established as upon foundations by evangelical teachings.

## CHAPTER III. In the letter to B., in which spiritual prudence is preferred to outward prudence

“David made a name for himself when, after conquering Syria, he returned and struck down twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt” (2 Samuel 8).

The true David is Christ, strong in power and beautiful in appearance. In the Valley of Salt he struck down twelve thousand people, because through his apostles he triumphed over the salty—or rather, false—wisdom of this world. Since he had twelve warriors of spiritual combat, he killed, as it were, as many thousands of people through them, converting those who were foolishly wise from the vanity of frivolous wisdom.

One of these warriors says to the Corinthians: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying bodily arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (2 Corinthians 10).

## 192. CHAPTER IV. In the letter to Alberic, in which he answers ten questions

You ask who the Cherethites and Pelethites were, who are said to have been David’s warriors (2 Samuel 8:20). In the Book of Numbers the Lord is read to have said to Moses:

“Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers, and bring them to the entrance of the tent of meeting and make them stand there with you. I will take from your spirit and give to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you and you may not bear it alone” (Numbers 11).

From the stock of these, therefore, two kin-groups arose, one of which was called the Cherethites and the other the Pelethites. “Cherethites” is interpreted as “giving judgment,” while “Pelethites” is interpreted as “punishing,” so that those whom the former condemned to death by pronouncing judgment, the latter punished by inflicting the penalty.

## CHAPTER V. In the same letter

“David’s sons were priests” (2 Samuel 18).

Why are David’s sons said to have been priests, when they are known to have had no blood relationship with Aaron’s sons except as did the other tribes? We must understand that when venerable priests and teachers are appointed among the people, princes or teachers are sometimes designated by the name “priests,” as is found elsewhere: “Ira the Jarite [Ira the Jairite] was David’s priest” (2 Samuel 20), that is, his teacher.

Thus, when it is said, “David’s sons were priests,” it should be understood as though it said: “They were teachers of their brothers,” or certainly “princes among the others,” as the ancient translation has it. For where the newer edition says, “David’s sons were priests,” the old edition reads: “David’s sons were princes of the royal court.”

## CHAPTER VI. In the letter to the brothers at Cluny

[Col. 1102B]

“I will show kindness,” David says, “to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent servants to console him over his father’s death. To summarize the history briefly: “Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut their garments in half up to their buttocks, and sent them away” (2 Samuel 10).

What is signified by Hanun except the spirit of wickedness? What by the beard, which is characteristic of men, except the strength of holy virtues? What also by garments except the clothing of holiness, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131)?

Hanun therefore shaves off half the beard of those who seek the renewal of friendship, because the ancient enemy sometimes diminishes the strength of one who is working courageously. But after shaving the beard, he also cuts the garments, because as soon as the evil spirit takes away inner strength, he consequently strips away the outward honor of an exemplary life.

For what does it mean to cut men’s garments as far as their buttocks except to strip them of the covering of righteousness down to the shamefulness of an obscene and shameless deed?

## 193. CHAPTER VII. In the letter to Marinus

When David is accused of the crime he had committed, as soon as he broke out into a confession, saying, “I have sinned against the Lord,” he immediately heard from the prophet’s mouth: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12).

And since the occasion has presented itself, I will not allow you to be deprived of this point either: some who have been placed in the religious order from childhood perish through disobedience alone mixed with pride, while many in the world, after committing the enormity of grave crimes, obtain pardon through the practice of humility.

For behold, David committed adultery and murder (2 Samuel 11), whereas Saul was disobedient to Samuel (1 Samuel 13, 15). But what of the fact that one obtained pardon without any intervening delay, while the other was reconciled neither by his own confession nor by the prophet’s very sorrowful, bitter, and prolonged supplication?

If the sequence of Scripture is examined in both cases, Saul is found to be more abundant than David in words of repentance. David said only what has already been mentioned: “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Samuel 13). Saul, however, said: “I have sinned, because I have transgressed the Lord’s words and your commandment, fearing the people and obeying their voice” (1 Samuel 15). Later, repeating the same thing, he said: “I have sinned.”

Samuel’s very patient prayer was also added; concerning him it is said: “Samuel was grieved, and he cried out to the Lord all that night” (ibid.). But the divine voice replied: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from reigning over Israel?” (1 Samuel 16).

What, then, is the reason that the repentance of one was mercifully accepted, while that of the other was rejected under the strict examination of truth? It is that the one, making light of the crime of disobedience in the spirit of pride, did not repent with his whole heart, whereas the other uttered few words, but the bitterness of true sorrow filled his inmost being, pierced through by the sword of divine fear.

Let those who obey disobedience while brazenly boasting about the enormity of their graver crimes not neglect to consider this. We often see some of them frequenting the tribunal of confession, devoutly prostrating themselves alone, accusing themselves with tinkling and carefully polished words more cleverly than humbly, and therefore never advancing in their conduct toward the benefits of suitable correction. For, like Saul, they repent with their mouths but swell with pride in their hearts.

## CHAPTER VIII. In the letter to cardinal bishops

[Col. 1103C]

Just as once the Roman consuls brought back victories from different parts of the world after slaughtering the enemy, so these men must now free human souls captive from the hand of the devil. They must always yearn for these titles of victory and these triumphs: namely, to snatch spoils from the ancient robber, the souls that are perishing, and rejoice to bring victorious standards back to their King Christ.

David prefigured this conflict when he victoriously captured the city of Rabbah (2 Samuel 12). Rabbah is interpreted as “multitude” or “great,” and is rightly understood to signify the totality of this world. David therefore captured the city of Rabbah when Christ subjected the great and abundant multitude of this world to his laws.

David took the crown from that king’s head and placed it upon himself, as Scripture testifies. The true David, Christ, fulfilled this when he wrested away the wise men of the world, by whom the devil was in some manner adorned, and transformed them into a diadem of his own beauty and glory.

The multitude of the faithful is called the crown not only of Christ but also of every teacher through whose preaching it is converted, as Paul says to the Philippians: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm in the Lord” (Philippians 4).

He also carried away, according to Scripture, a very great quantity of spoil. Spoil is taken from Rabbah when individual faithful and devoted people from this world are converted to the service of almighty God.

You, I say, holy pontiffs, ought above all to be robbers of this kind: daily to sweat in tearing human souls from the hands of their wicked possessor and bringing spoils of triumph to your King David.

Yet it is not enough that, once snatched from the devil, someone should be converted to God through pious devotion, unless immediately afterward he is also crushed, as it were by the repeated hammer of holy preaching, from the hardness of his former condition. Hence Jeremiah says: “Are my words not like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer shattering rock?” (Jeremiah 23).

The Lord’s words are like fire because they drive out coldness and kindle warmth in minds; they are a hammer because they soften the hardness of obstinacy and perversity.

The sacred history therefore appropriately adds: “He also brought out its people, sawed them, drove them over iron chariots, divided them with knives, and led them through in the form of bricks” (3 Kings 12).

What are we to understand by iron chariots—which are, of course, a kind of vehicle—except the sure and unconquerable chariot of the holy evangelists and therefore the utterance of all the divine Scriptures? For, as we have already said elsewhere: Iron is a base material, yet it subdues every metal. Just as iron rules over all metals, so evangelical teaching is known to soften hard minds.

What does it mean to drive iron chariots over captured people except to thresh the threshing floor of human minds with the dew of sacred Scripture, so that the divine word may crush within them the clods of resisting vices and strive to level and smooth them for receiving the crops of heavenly commandments?

And what does it mean to divide them with knives except to open the conscience of sinful people to confession through the preaching of the divine word? Concerning this word the Apostle says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). A person is divided, as it were, by spiritual knives when he is cut by the sword of the divine word so that the wounds of his soul may be exposed.

Why is it said that he led them through in the form of bricks except because bricks are both earthly and baked? A sinner is turned into the form of a brick when, at the voice of preaching, he receives the ardor of the Holy Spirit and, truly humbled, recognizes that he is earth and clay.

Thus each convert and penitent is fashioned in the image of a brick: he is humbled by the clay of his weakness and, as it were, becomes red or bursts into flame in divine love, so that, while he considers himself earthly dust, he may kindle his heart to offer thanks to God who recalled him.

Hence Adam is interpreted as “red earth,” so that from the name of the first parent each person may learn either what he is originally or what he ought to be in his actual condition.

To such priests of the churches, to such holy pontiffs, these victories ought to have been the object of their desire—not expensive courses at banquets, nor dissolving into the wanton excess of pleasure. For after the beginning of the world’s birth, the human race lived for nearly sixteen hundred years without wine to drink or meat to eat; yet no one whom Scripture mentions wasted away from sickness until death.

## CHAPTER IX. In the letter to Alberic, in which he also answers ten questions

“King David went out from Jerusalem, fleeing from Absalom, and left ten concubines to guard the house” (2 Samuel 15 and 16).

As David fled from Absalom, he left ten concubines in the house, whom Absalom shamefully defiled through incest. This signifies that our Redeemer, when expelled from the Jewish city and hastening into the desert of the Gentiles, leaves in the house of the Law Jews who do not walk in a manly manner but live according to a womanly way of life.

They are appropriately represented by the ten concubines, because, while they weakly observe the precepts of the Law, they do not deserve to enter the chaste bridal chamber of marriage; instead, without being joined by the ring of faith, they obtain concubinage in place of marriage.

Absalom, in his wantonness, defiles them, because the evil spirit corrupts the reprobate souls of the impious as though by prostituting them. He fornicates with such people through the excesses of various crimes and, as an incestuous violator, embraces brothels laid beneath him, so to speak, when he delights in their adulterous deeds.

## CHAPTER X. In the letter to Abbot Desiderius, that the person who casts aside dignity is worthy of greater honor than the person who persists in it

Absalom is interpreted as “the father’s peace” (2 Samuel 13). Through him the Jewish people are signified, the people that persecuted Christ even to death. Concerning this people Isaiah says: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isaiah 1).

It is rightly called “the father’s peace,” because among that people in particular, through the Law that was given, through the sacrifices of victims, and finally through the tabernacle or temple, God appears to have rested. Thus David says: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75). And so that this people may appear to be the father’s peace, hear what follows: “His place has been established in peace” (ibid.).

Alternatively, Judas the betrayer is represented by Absalom; he too is not improperly called “the father’s peace,” as Christ himself complains of him in the psalm, saying: “Indeed, the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm 40).

Christ is also appropriately called the father, as the Prophet testifies: “He shall be called,” he says, “Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9). Thus Christ is called the Prince of Peace, and Judas the father’s peace. To Judas, moreover, Christ did not deny the kiss of peace at the very moment of his persecution (Matthew 26).

Nor is it surprising that Absalom bore the likeness of Judas the betrayer, whom he expressed not only in David’s persecution but also in the very manner of his death (2 Samuel 18). Absalom became caught in an oak as he attempted to pass beneath it; Judas, as Scripture testifies, hanged himself. Since each was overflowing with the gall of viperous wickedness and was unworthy both of earth and heaven, suspended between the two, he lost the earth and could in no way aspire to heaven.

Ahithophel, who likewise wished to pursue David, also chose this same kind of death, as his merits demanded (2 Samuel 17). This man gave Absalom, as he pursued David, the advice that he should defile his father’s concubines, whom he had left to guard the house, and should shamefully commit incest with his stepmothers in order to dishonor his father (1 Samuel 16).

What do David’s ten concubines signify except that part of the Jewish people which does not follow Christ, the true David, as he flees into the deserts of the Gentiles, because it boasts of possessing the Decalogue of the Law? Through the number of the concubines the number of the commandments is expressed. The concubines, therefore, who do not follow David but guard the house, are those who persevere in the guardianship of the Old Law.

Absalom enters in to these concubines of David because the devil, who was in Absalom, fornicates with such people through the excesses of various crimes. It is well said that David had left them to guard the house, because by the provident dispensation of our Redeemer it has been divinely arranged that the remnants of the Jews should be preserved, as it were, to guard the house of the Law.

Those who are now our scribes carry the books of heavenly speech throughout the world in the same language in which they were written, so that, if a doubt should ever arise, those who are our enemies may remove every ambiguity for us. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, show me good things among my enemies; do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law” (Psalm 58).

The Hebrew language, dispersed throughout the whole world, greatly assists the authority of the Christian faith. Hence it is openly added there: “Scatter them in your strength, and bring them down, O Lord, our protector” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XI. In the same letter

“David had come to the camp at Madian, and Shobi son of Nahash, Machir son of Ammiel, and Barzillai the Gileadite brought him beds, carpets, earthen vessels, and so forth” (2 Samuel 17).

The Madianites who supplied King David with bedding and carpets signify nothing other than Gentiles converted to the faith. By devoting themselves unceasingly to pious deeds, they prepare, as it were, linens woven on a loom, in which the Lord may rest sweetly.

These are the evangelical garments that the apostles place upon the donkey and make Jesus sit upon them (Matthew 21). What follows—“They also gave David earthen vessels, wheat and barley, flour, beans and lentils, roasted chickpeas, honey and butter, and sheep and fattened calves” (2 Samuel 17)—signifies the many kinds of food, which are the various dispositions of holy people. David is nourished with his fellow soldiers by these, because our Redeemer, together with his saints, feasts as though hungry upon the righteous works of the just.

## CHAPTER XII. In the letter to Alberic, in which he answers ten questions

[Col. 1107A]

“There was a battle scattered over the face of the land, and many more of the people were consumed by the forest than were devoured by the sword” (2 Samuel 18).

Concerning this statement, these are the words of Blessed Jerome in the Book of Hebrew Questions: “The Jews suppose that this forest, which is said to have consumed more people than the sword devoured, contained extremely savage beasts, by which more were consumed than were devoured by the sword.”

That, however, was the interpretation of the Hebrews. We think instead that the mad and senseless men who had rebelled with Absalom, blinded when God abandoned them, collided with the bushes they encountered. Hence it is said that more fell, killed by the consuming forest, than were devoured by the slaughtering sword.

That this must be understood in this way is clear if one attends even superficially to the continuation of the text. For after stating: “Many more were consumed by the forest than were devoured by the sword on that day,” it immediately adds: “It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants, sitting on a mule; and when the mule had entered beneath a dense and great oak, his head caught in the oak, and, while he was hanging between heaven and earth, the mule on which he had been riding passed on” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIII. In the letter to Abbot D., mentioned somewhat earlier

[Col. 1107C]

“Barzillai the Gileadite, a very old man—that is, eighty years old, as the sacred history testifies—came down from Rogelim and escorted King David across the Jordan. The king said to him: ‘Come, so that you may rest with me in Jerusalem.’ But he refused, pleading his old age as an excuse, and, leaving the king, soon returned to his own home” (2 Samuel 19).

There are some who, following King David—that is, our Savior—cross the waters of the Jordan. This means either that they receive the sacrament of baptism or, which is the second washing, undertake a spiritual vocation. Since Christ, the author of baptism, was baptized in the Jordan (Matthew 3), baptism is rightly understood through it.

But these people return to their former ways and resume worldly activities with changed clothing but not minds, changing their appearance but not their spirit. Since they are unable to rest from the turmoil of worldly affairs, they do not wish to dwell with the king in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace. They are old and aged, and therefore cannot be changed from an old way of life into a new one.

They cross the Jordan and are eighty years old because they have been baptized and believe in the future resurrection, which is signified by the number eight. Yet although they speak humbly and pleasantly to the King, they abandon him and return to the habits of their accustomed way of life.

What does it mean to offer pleasant words to the King except, as the Gospel says, to excuse oneself craftily rather than humbly? “I ask you,” he says, “to consider me excused” (Luke 14).

Barzillai said to the king: “Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king? I shall go forward a little way with you from the Jordan, your servant that I am, but I have no need of this exchange.”

Those who present themselves in this way hold the figure of Barzillai. To any spiritual man who urges them toward higher things, they chant, as though humbly: “We are indeed sinners and obey you, father, but we cannot keep the rule of a stricter way of life. We are weak and fragile, and therefore we judge it better to live somehow without glory beneath a light burden than to die like strong men under the weight of a heavy burden.”

What the same Barzillai had said earlier also agrees with the old age of these people’s inner man: “How many are the days of the years of my life,” he says, “that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?” And he added: “Are my senses still vigorous enough to distinguish what is sweet and bitter? Can food and drink delight your servant? Or can I hear the voice of singers and female singers?” (2 Samuel 19.)

Truly, the inward senses of such people are dull, because they do not discern the spiritual food of the mind or the instruments of inward rejoicing. That heavenly food does not taste good to them, the food to which the Prophet invites spiritual guests: “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33).

Nor do their throats discern those honeys concerning which he said: “How sweet are your words to my palate, Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Psalm 118).

They have not yet reclined at that banquet of Wisdom of which it is said in the Book of Proverbs: “Wisdom has sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table.” There it also follows: “She has sent her maidservants to call from the citadel and the walls of the city: ‘Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you’” (Proverbs 9).

They do not hear the voices of male and female singers either, because they have no comprehension whatsoever of the melody with which the holy martyrs and holy virgins exult before God. Since, living according to the flesh, they do not raise the hearts of their contemplation toward the Lord, they are ignorant of the melodies of heavenly harmony and the honey-sweet delights of angelic song.

Therefore, not undeservedly that old man is said to have been Barzillai of Rogelim, which is interpreted as “feet.” For such people walk on foot, and because they do not know how to lift themselves away from the journey of earthly conduct, they do not rise to grasp the songs of heavenly melody. They wish always to proceed only on foot, and therefore cannot penetrate the lofty joys of inward jubilation. And because earthly actions, in which they are scattered, make them hard and insensible, they cannot contemplate the subtle things of spiritual gladness.

Hence also that Barzillai is said to have been a Gileadite, which is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Since that heap of testimony, called Gilead, is known to have been made by Laban and Jacob from stones (Gen. XXXI), hard and stony people are rightly signified by this Gileadite: because, by not softening their hearts toward the love of spiritual life, they become like stones, hardening in the stubborn strength of worldly affairs. To this hardness belongs the fact that the same Barzillai is also said to mean “my iron.” What is harder than iron, and what more obstinate than a perverse heart? “Wisdom will never enter into a malicious soul” (Wis. I). And appropriately “my iron,” as though any hard and obstinate person were speaking of himself, since, when he resolves to persevere in his own hardness, he never throws himself upon the counsels of another. And because, rigid and unyielding, he does not journey with King David toward the heavenly Jerusalem, from the road he had begun with Barzillai he is recalled to the land of Midian—that is, to the beginnings of his former life.

## CHAPTER XIV. In the same letter.

[Col. 1109B]

“When King David had come to Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines whom he had left to guard the house and placed them under guard. He did not go in to them, but they were shut up until the day of their death, living in widowhood” (II Reg. XX).

The concubines who remain guarding the house without following David are those who persevere in the custody of the Old Law. Of these concubines it is certainly said: “For David did not thereafter go in to them; but they were shut up until the day of their death, living in widowhood.” The Jews are plainly now shut up and live in widowhood, because they do not approach the husband, the holy Church; nor does that heavenly Bridegroom enter in to them, since He disdains to share His dwelling with them as with little women prostituted by the devil. And because they have been polluted by adultery, He gives them a bill of divorce. These women, moreover, who do not follow their husband, are rightly called concubines and are not called wives, because, wholly unworthy of the dowry covenant and marriage bond, they do not bear offspring destined to possess the inheritance of the father’s blessing. To us, on the contrary, it is said: “To this you were called, that you may possess a blessing as your inheritance” (I Pet. III). The Apostle likewise says: “Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. But whoever are of the works of the law are under a curse” (Gal. III).

## 200 CHAPTER XV. In the letter to Alberic, in which he answers him concerning ten questions.

“David did not afterward go in to them, but they were shut up until the day of their death, living in widowhood” (II Reg. XX).

For they had lost the husband of whom it is said through Isaiah: “For seven women shall take hold of one man” (Isa. IV). And concerning them Solomon says: “For there are seven hundred queens” (III Reg. XI). Thus they took seven, who had lost ten. For the holy Church united to herself the heavenly Bridegroom, filled with the sevenfold gift of the Spirit. The Synagogue, however, which had received the commandments of the Decalogue, lost that Bridegroom and remained a widow, because, while it stood immovably in the house of its accustomed rite and legal ceremonies, it refused to go out with King David into the wilderness of the nations.

## CHAPTER XVI. In the same letter.

[Col. 1110A]

“There was also a third battle at Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus, son of the forest, the embroiderer, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite” (II Reg. XXI).

This is easily understood. For Gob is interpreted as “lake.” And just as one who is thrown into a lake of lions is endangered, so David, as it were, handed himself over to the teeth of a lion when he plunged into battle against raging Goliath. The same David is rightly called Adeodatus, since he was chosen by God for kingship. He is also called “son of the forest,” because he is recognized as having been brought out from the pastures of the forests where he fed sheep. Nor is it without cause that the same David is called “the embroiderer,” because his mother was descended from Bezaleel, who constructed the tabernacle of the covenant in the wilderness and there produced various embroidered works.

He is also appropriately called a Bethlehemite, because he traced his origin from Naomi, and they had come out from Bethlehem in a time of famine and were afterward brought back to that same Bethlehem when abundance blossomed again. That Adeodatus, together with all these descriptive names, is undoubtedly David himself is made clear by what follows: “These four were born of Rapha in Gath, and they fell into the hand of David and his servants” (ibid.).

I would explain what is also mystically signified by these things, were I not prevented by the brevity of the letter. According to the mystical understanding, all these things refer to Christ. For He is Adeodatus, of whom it is said through Isaiah: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX). He is not inappropriately called “son of the forest,” because He deigned to be born according to the flesh from the Jews, who, since they produced no fruit of spiritual growth, were sterile like wild trees, planted not in a garden but born in a forest. Hence it is written: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. XL)—that is, among the fruitless people of the Jews.

Our Redeemer is also rightly called “the embroiderer,” because He occupies Himself, as it were, with the labor of a weaving workshop: He clothes Himself with His faithful and weaves garments of righteousness from them. Concerning His own garments the Apostle says: “That He might present to Himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V). And through the prophet: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX). Of Christ’s faithful the Psalmist sings: “Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI).

And through Ezekiel the Lord reproaches the soul that He had fittingly adorned with spiritual garments, but that abandoned Him after polluting itself with the filth of adultery: “I clothed you,” He says, “with garments of various colors, and I shod you with violet, and girded you with fine linen, and clothed you with delicate fabrics and adorned you with ornaments.” And shortly afterward: “You were clothed with fine linen, embroidered work, and many colors” (Ezek. XVI).

What wonder, then, if our Redeemer is called “the embroiderer,” who clothes with the beauty of virtue the soul that He takes as His bride by nuptial right? For He is the Wisdom of God, of whom Solomon says: “She sought wool and flax, and worked with the counsel of her hands” (Prov. XXXI). Her fingers took hold of the spindle; all her household were clothed with double garments; and His flesh also became a covering garment in His Passion. But that same fine linen and royal purple became His garment in the Resurrection.

He is also rightly called a Bethlehemite, because He is recognized as having been born at Bethlehem from the Virgin. As for the statement, “There was a third battle at Gob,” this is understood to mean that the true David, the Savior of Israel, has always had faithful warriors—before the Law, under the Law, and afterward in the grace of the Gospel—through whom He fought against the Philistines, that is, against evil spirits.

David therefore came to this third battle at Gob, which is interpreted as “lake,” because our Redeemer, coming upon the strong man as one stronger than he (Luke XI), Himself also descended as far as the underworld. Hence He says through the Psalmist: “They placed me in the lowest lake, in darkness and the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII). There He struck down Goliath the Gittite, because, while He rescued the souls of the elect from the prisons of Gehenna, He wounded with a deadly blow the ancient enemy who had exercised tyranny over them.

## CHAPTER XVII. In a sermon on virgins.

“David, seated on his throne, the wisest prince among three. He is like the tenderest worm of wood, who killed eight hundred at one assault” (II Reg. XXIII).

What does it mean that David is raised up by so new and unheard-of a proclamation of praise? Who is this figure so humble and yet so exalted? Who, I ask, is this David, so weak and despised that he takes on the appearance of a worm, yet so strong and powerful that at one assault he kills eight hundred men?

In the straw of the letter this may indeed seem ridiculous, unless a mystery lies hidden in the marrow of the spirit. Who, then, is this worm, except the one who sings through that same David in the Psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI)? For just as a worm is produced solely from the material of wood, so the Catholic faith confesses that Christ was born from the virginal womb alone, without the seed of a man.

Although the worm is tender and weak, while the hardness of wood is strong and solid, the worm nevertheless turns the wood into decay and makes it hollow and full of cavities. So our Redeemer, truly strong of hand and desirable, who emptied Himself, who appeared without form or beauty, weak and despised, gradually softened the human race from which He arose and prepared for Himself a great dwelling-place in His elect.

This David, then, sits on a throne because, established in the glory of the Father’s majesty, He judges all things. To Him the Father says: “Sit at My right hand” (Ps. CIX). He is the wisest because He is Himself the Wisdom of the Father.

But how is David called “prince among three,” when He held not merely a principality among others but rather the dominion of a royal scepter over all? This praise diminishes rather than exalts; it lowers rather than raises, since He was not merely among three but above all. Yet although this statement concerning David appears to disagree with Him, there is one to whom it can most fittingly apply.

That blessed and unique man, mystically called a worm, is immediately upon being received by the Word in the unity of person made ruler without inequality in the Holy Trinity. He is therefore “prince among three,” because He is united to the Word, who is one Person in the Holy Trinity.

He killed eight hundred at one assault. The number eight pertains to resurrection, while the number one hundred pertains to perfection. David therefore killed eight hundred at one assault because our Savior killed with the sword of His Spirit all who either seek the perfection of faith or desire the glory of resurrection. Through the mystery of His Incarnation and Cross He made them dead to the love of this world, and He accomplished this in one assault—that is, in the single advent of His Incarnation. “For He died once for our sins, and dies no more” (Rom. VI).

Is His advent not rightly called an assault, of which Solomon says: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song II)? And David says: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII). One who runs undoubtedly makes an assault. The Word of God also comes like a stream of living waters with force, and like a torrent overturns all the defilements of burning doctrines. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon” (Song IV).

Let us therefore give thanks to this King, so humble and yet so exalted, so weak and yet so exceedingly strong, who deigned to become a worm in the wood in order to make us citizens in heaven. For this reason He permitted the ancient enemy of the human race to rise against Him, so that afterward He might triumph over him not only through men but also through women.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In the letter to Alberic, in which he answers him concerning ten questions.

You ask why there is this difference in the sacred Scriptures: in the Book of Kings (II Reg. XXIV) it is read that David bought the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, together with the oxen that were to be offered as a burnt offering, for only fifty shekels of silver; whereas in Chronicles he is said to have given six hundred shekels of gold for the threshing floor alone (I Chron. XXI).

But it must undoubtedly be understood that in the Book of Kings David is read to have bought only the oxen for fifty shekels of silver; how much he paid for the threshing floor is entirely passed over there. The Book of Chronicles, on the other hand, says nothing about the oxen but reports that the threshing floor was bought for six hundred shekels of gold. This is easily seen if the actual sequence of words in both books is carefully considered.

For in the Book of Kings the order of the words is this: “So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.” It must be punctuated in such a way that Scripture first says, “David bought the threshing floor,” without stating the price; then follows, “and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.”

In the Book of Chronicles it is read thus: “So David gave Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold of the most exact weight, and built an altar there to the Lord.” Thus each Scripture divides the matter between them: one counts the price of the oxen, the other that of the threshing floor alone. The things whose price is specified therefore differ, but the holy Scriptures do not contradict one another.

The testimonies of the Second Book of Kings end here.

# BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES OF THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS.

[Col. 1113]

1. Concerning Abishag the Shunammite, who ministered to King David and, sleeping with him, warmed his aged limbs, yet remained undefiled.  
2. That David spared Joab and Shimei while he lived, but when dying ordered that they be destroyed.  
3. That Solomon is said to have had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand cavalry horses.  
4. That it is said of him that he spoke three thousand proverbs and that his songs numbered five thousand; and that he also discoursed about trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish.  
5. That Solomon set two columns, one on the right and one on the left, in the vestibule of the temple, calling one Jachin and the other Boaz.  
6. That the vessels of the Lord’s temple were cast in the plain region of the Jordan, in clayey ground, between Sochol and Sarthan.  
7. Concerning the fact that, when the priests had gone out of the sanctuary, the house of God was filled with a cloud, so that the priests could not stand nearby because of the cloud.  
8. That silver was said not to exist, nor to be considered of any value, in Solomon’s time.  
9. That Solomon had approximately seven hundred wives who were queens and three hundred concubines.  
10. Concerning the woman of Zarephath, to whom Elijah was sent and whom he found gathering two pieces of wood in order to prepare bread for herself and her son.  
11. Concerning the fact that, when Elijah prayed, a small cloud appeared, rising from the sea like a man’s footprint.

The chapters end here.

# BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES OF THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS.

[Col. 1113]

## CHAPTER I. To C., the prefect, where he challenges him to battle.

[Col. 1113B]

“The servants of King David sought throughout all the borders of Israel a beautiful young woman, and they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. She slept with the king and ministered to him, but the king did not know her” (III Reg. I).

Who is this girl, then, who is chosen from all the borders of Israel as though unique, and joined to King David so that she may sleep with him and warm his cooling limbs? Ask Solomon, and he himself will reveal to you the mystery of this girl: “Acquire wisdom,” he says, “acquire understanding” (Prov. IV).

Do you also wish to hear of the embraces of this virgin? He says: “Do not abandon her, and she will hold you fast; love her, and she will exalt you; surround her, and she will glorify you; honor her, and she will embrace you” (ibid.).

Embrace wisdom, therefore—that is, holy life—as a wife, so that we may produce offspring noble and worthy of an inheritance. For from this wife there will succeed to us not a posterity destined to die, but one destined to live forever. Whatever is born from corruption must be corrupted; but what virginity brings forth does not know how to perish. Nor is that which has been begotten from incorruption subject to the defect of corruption.

But let us examine the interpretation of these names, so that we may be able to grasp the mystery. Abishag is interpreted as “my father is superfluous,” or “my father’s roar.” “Superfluous” signifies not superfluity as something unnecessary, but the more abundant grace of God the Father. “Roar,” however, indicates the vehement sound of holy preaching, so that whoever lies in the embraces of Abishag—that is, of religious life—may make the Lion from the tribe of Judah resound through the thundering sound of holy preaching.

Shunammite, in our language, is called “scarlet.” As the holy soul is reddened by the mystery of the Lord’s blood, so likewise it burns with the fire of the Holy Spirit. Hence a scarlet thread is tied to the hand of Pharez, who divided the wall under the mystical separation of the two peoples. Rahab the harlot also, as a type of the Church, hung a scarlet cord so that her house might be saved while Jericho perished.

For this reason, and elsewhere, Scripture recalls concerning holy men: “These are they who came from the heat of Rahab’s house.” And Truth itself says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). This fire, burning in the hearts of the disciples, compelled them to say: “Was not our heart burning within us while He spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

This mystical and spiritual marriage therefore conceives the fervor of grace in the Shunammite and gives birth to the offspring of holy preaching in Abishag: so that what each person carries in the inner chambers of the heart may not fail to bring forth through the service of the mouth, and what is conceived in the heart through scarlet may be brought forth in the mouth through the roar of holy preaching.

Let us therefore conceive the fervor of divine love in the Shunammite, so that we may give birth to the roar of preaching as to the offspring of Abishag.

## CHAPTER II. In the letter to Alberic, where he discusses ten questions.

I confess that I have often wondered why David mercifully spared Joab and Shimei, with whom he was angry while he was still alive, but when dying ordered Solomon, who was succeeding him in the royal scepter, to destroy them.

“You know,” he says, “what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of Israel’s army, Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed and shed the blood of war in peace.” Shortly afterward he added: “You shall act according to your wisdom, and you shall not bring his gray head down peacefully to the underworld” (III Reg. II).

Concerning Shimei he also says: “You have with you Shimei the son of Gera, the son of Gemini, from Bahurim, who cursed me with a terrible curse when I was going to the camp.” Finally, after inserting some intervening words, he added: “You shall bring down his gray hairs with blood to the underworld” (III Reg. II).

What does it mean that David, when dying, condemns those whom he had spared during his life, when the order of reason plainly requires that, while living, he should exercise a sentence of vengeance against rebels or any enemies, but, when dying, should mercifully pardon them?

But it must be understood that through the kingdom of David—who, worn down by so many persecutions and hardships and afflicted with his companions by so many adversities and privations—the present age is signified. In this age Christ is afflicted with His members, and the Church is torn by many tribulations.

The kingdom of Solomon, however—who in riches and glory surpassed all the rights of royal dignity and rose above every height of princely power—announces the glory of the future life, in which Christ, truly peace-bringing, enjoys eternal rest with His own and solemnly feasts upon the food of the heavenly banquet.

Our one and the same Redeemer is therefore David now and will then be Solomon, because now He does not cease to fight against the devil through His members as one strong of hand, while then, when every conflict of flesh and spirit has been wholly stilled, He will reign with His body, which is the Church, in eternal tranquility as the truly peace-bringing King.

Now, in His elect, He is oppressed as David under the burden of calamities, harried by the pressures of persecutions and various adversities, and worn down by tribulations and hardships. Later, as Solomon, He will possess the overflowing abundance of immortal riches.

David, therefore, while living, tolerates those whom He condemns at the end, because Christ, the Judge of the human race whom David prefigured, now mercifully spares those upon whom at the end of the age He justly imposes the sentence of condemnation. David thus postpones mercy; Solomon judges with justice. For our one and the same Redeemer now, as David, patiently tolerates the iniquities of the reprobate, and afterward, coming in His glory as Solomon, cuts them down as with the flashing edge of His judgment.

This alternation of divine judgment is frequently found in the same words, as in the passage: “I will sing mercy and judgment to You, O Lord” (Ps. C). And: “God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. LXXXIII); “Mercy and truth have met together” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Thus mercy is placed before truth, as David before Solomon, so that those whom David mercifully sustains, Solomon may justly condemn through judgment.

It should also be noted that Joab, who committed murder with his own hands, signifies those who do evil; while Shimei, who merely cursed the king, signifies those who speak wickedly. For both those who act wickedly and those who persist in corrupt and false speech will undoubtedly be condemned in the examination of the final judgment, as the same David says: “You hate all who work iniquity; You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. V).

## CHAPTER III. In a letter to Queen Agnes.

[Col. 1116A]

“And Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand cavalry horses” (III Reg. IV).

What is prefigured by the number four, if not the quadriga of the evangelists? And what is expressed by the number twelve, if not the senate of the apostles? Through evangelical and apostolic teaching the Lord is carried throughout the entire breadth of the world.

“For the chariot of God is multiplied by ten thousand; thousands of rejoicing; the Lord is among them, at Sinai, in the holy place” (Ps. LXVII). Since Sinai is interpreted as “commandment,” it is clear that the Lord is carried only among those in whom the heavenly commandments are observed.

It should also be noted that, just as David’s kingdom—worn down by so many pressures—designates the Lord laboring in the course of mortal life, so Solomon’s incomparable glory prefigures that same Lord reigning after the end of the world in the majesty of the Father’s heights. Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the peoples of the East and of Egypt because, obviously, our Redeemer surpasses the understanding of both angels and human beings.

## 207 CHAPTER IV. In the same letter.

Concerning Him it is also said: “For He spoke three thousand proverbs, and His songs numbered five thousand.” It is immediately added: “For He also discoursed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, and He spoke about beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish” (III Reg. IV).

There is no doubt that all these things apply to our Redeemer, who occupies Himself with their careful consideration. He plainly spoke three thousand proverbs: through the mystical events of the figures that preceded Him, through the allegorical utterances of the prophets, and also through the teachings of the radiant Gospel, in which He explained nearly everything beneath the veil of figures, as though He had counted three thousand proverbs in His words.

Hence Matthew says in the Gospel: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables He did not speak to them” (Matt. XIII).

His songs also number five thousand, because the chorus of virgins, who are described under the number five before His throne, continually sings a new song, as John says in the Apocalypse: “It continually sings a new song” (Apoc. XIV).

Or else, because there are five wounds of the Lord’s body through which His triumphant glory is proclaimed throughout the whole world, His songs are counted under the same number under which His wounds are held—the wounds through which His singular victory earns the glory of eternal praise.

Hence, when it is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, my beloved, my bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow places of the wall,” it is immediately added: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet” (Song II).

Since we are not treating these matters exhaustively but passing over them briefly and rapidly, it is enough to say that, since Christ is the rock, the clefts of the rock are undoubtedly the scars of the Lord’s body.

But when, after the clefts of this rock, the sweet voice of the bride is commanded to sound in the bridegroom’s ears, what else is every devout soul, or the holy universal Church, encouraged to do than to return songs of praise according to the same number as the five wounds? It is encouraged, as it were, to render songs corresponding to the number of the wounds it knows He received for its sake, and to dedicate all the senses of its body to Him whom it sees wounded by as many wounds on its behalf.

The five wounds of our senses were healed by the five scars of the Lord’s body.

As for the statement that Solomon discoursed about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, this must necessarily be referred to a spiritual meaning, since the surface meaning of the words cannot possibly stand. Hyssop is not seen to grow out of walls, but to sprout from rocky mountains.

Our wall, therefore, is the very condition of our mortality, which divides us from contemplation of the Creator like the barrier of a hidden house and compels us to incline more readily downward. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX).

From this wall, then, hyssop grows, because from the frailty of our mortality there bursts forth what must always be cut back by the iron of repentance. The inner organs are purified with hyssop, by which confession of sins is not inappropriately signified.

Our Solomon therefore discoursed about trees—that is, about human beings rooted within the members of the growing Church—from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall: from the eminent saints made bright by the splendor of righteousness to sinners and the fallen, who at last have been turned toward the lamentation of repentance.

Hence it follows: “He also spoke about beasts”—namely, Catholic men who assist the saints; “and about birds”—that is, human beings lifted toward heavenly things by holy desires; “and about reptiles and fish”—that is, those who drag the breast of their desire along the earth and those who wander through the currents of worldly affairs.

## CHAPTER V. In the letter to Alberic, where the dwellings of the Israelites are discussed.

[Col. 1117D]

“Solomon set two columns in the vestibule of the Lord’s temple, one on the right and the other on the left. He called the one that was on the right Jachin, that is, ‘firmness’; and the one on the left Boaz, that is, ‘in strength’” (III Reg. VII; II Chron. III).

What is signified by the column that is on the right and is called “firmness,” if not the love of God? And what by the one that is on the left and is called “in strength,” if not the love of neighbor?

For “firmness,” that is, strength itself, is one thing; “in strength” is another, because loving the Lord Himself is one thing, while loving one’s neighbor in God is another. A measure is established in the love of neighbor; but we are commanded to love the Lord without any measure whatsoever.

We erect in the vestibule of the temple the column called “firmness” when, in this present Church—which is the vestibule of that heavenly Church—we love the Lord firmly and steadfastly with all our strength. That love itself, as the evangelist John testifies, is God (I John IV). And of God the Prophet sings: “My God and my strength” (Ps. XLII).

We set up the column called “in strength” on the left side of the same vestibule when we love our neighbor in God as ourselves. Here it should be noted that Scripture continues: “He also made chains, as in the oracle, and placed them upon the capitals of the columns” (II Chron. III).

In the oracle of our mind, therefore, we place chains upon the capitals of the columns, by which we connect the two columns to one another, because we neither love God without our neighbor nor truly love our neighbor without God.

## CHAPTER VI. In a letter to A. P. P., where he complains about the insolence of wicked people.

Concerning the vessels that Hiram made at King Solomon’s command in the house of the Lord, it is written: “For the king cast them in the plain region of the Jordan, in clayey ground, between Sochot and Sartan” (III Reg. VII).

[Col. 1118B]

Sochot is translated as “tents,” while Sartan is interpreted as “their tribulation,” or “those who demolish” or “those who constrain.”

What, then, is signified by Sochot, which we have said is interpreted as “tents,” except holy men, who say: “We have no permanent city here, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. XIII)? And Peter says: “I know that the laying aside of my tent is swift” (II Pet. I).

What, then, is signified by Sartan, which is called “their tribulation,” except the persecution of reprobates who trouble us? These are both demolishers and constrainers, because, while they attempt to demolish and destroy the building of our faith or good work, they constrain us with harsh calamities of insults and pressures.

The vessels of the temple—that is, all the elect—are therefore cast in the plain region of the Jordan, that is, in the humility of baptism, between Sochot and Sartan, that is, between the righteous and the wicked. Thus the example of upright conduct is set before the wicked for imitation, while the persecution of the wicked contributes to the increase of the righteous’ merits.

“The furnace proves the vessels of the potter, and temptation by tribulation proves righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

The vessels of the temple are therefore cast in dry ground because the human mind is not suited to receive the gift of heavenly grace unless it has first been dried of all moisture of carnal allurements. Dry hearts produce a clear sound of harmony; moist hearts produce a dull one. A drum also sounds dully if any liquid dampens it. Thus the human mind must be dry of carnal pleasure, so that its prayer may be sharp in the ears of almighty God.

Indeed, just as the eye, when it exposes itself to the sun’s rays, tries in vain to see and attempts to open its hollow sockets and empty eyelids, yet cannot look upon the brilliance with which it is flooded, so one who has lost the vision of the heart through the merit of worldly life raises himself vainly to desire the light of contemplation.

For if some stranger bursts into the king’s chamber and stands before him as though he were a familiar, he nevertheless does not enjoy the king’s address, because he is not held dear by the grace of prior acquaintance. So we, unhappy and wretched—for I speak of those like myself—often stand alone in the isolation of a narrow cell, trembling before the sole gaze of the divine majesty; yet, because sins stand in the way, we do not merit either the spark of inward brightness or the grace of compunction.

Thus we seem to stand before the king’s presence, but because we are not known to Him through the uprightness of our lives, we do not taste the sweetness of inward conversation. But O honey-sweet delight, when the Lord delights in the servant and the servant delights in the Lord! Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my praise be sweet to Him; but I shall delight in the Lord” (Ps. CIII).

## CHAPTER VII. In a sermon on the Nativity of Saint Mary.

“Then it happened, when the priests had come out of the sanctuary, that a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand nearby because of the cloud; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord (III Kings 8).” “All these things,” as the distinguished preacher says, “were happening to them as a figure (I Corinthians 10).” The glory of the Lord is, of course, understood as Christ, whose faith has filled the world. Concerning this glory, when Moses pleaded with the Lord to spare the sinful people who had worshipped the calf, the Lord replied: “I will be merciful to him; nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory (Numbers 24).”  

But the fact that a cloud filled the house of God, and that the priests could not minister because of the cloud, signifies the proud priests and teachers of the Jews. While they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation, they lose the ministry owed to their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, deserving this on account of their own merits, they did not recognize the worship of faith. Therefore the Lord descended in a cloud upon that temple, to signify the blind darkness of Jewish unbelief. Concerning this it is written: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun (Psalm 18),” so that he might illuminate “those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke 1).”  

To that temple, then, almighty God granted the glory of his coming, but he assumed nothing from it in his own nature. Into the womb of the most blessed Virgin, however, he not only deigned to descend, but from it he also united to himself the perfect substance of our mortality. Therefore, the greater the dignity of our temple, the more glorious ought its solemnity to be. For that body of Christ which the most blessed Virgin bore, which she cherished in her lap, which she wrapped in swaddling clothes, and which she nourished with maternal care—that body, I say, without any doubt is what we now receive from the sacred altar, and we drink his blood as the sacrament of our redemption. This is what the catholic faith holds; this is what the holy Church faithfully teaches.

## CHAPTER VIII. In a letter to Queen Agnes

[Col. 1120A]

“Silver was not valued, nor was it considered to be worth anything in the days of Solomon (III Kings 10).” How, indeed, can this stand according to the literal sense, so that it may be believed either that in Solomon’s time silver did not exist at all and had therefore been completely removed from the earth, or that it was worth nothing—or at least very little? For if it was worth nothing, as the text says, then a thousand talents of silver could not have been reckoned as the weight of even a single sheep. The text and sequence of the words themselves refute how frivolous and absurd such a belief would be. After stating, “Silver was not valued, nor was it considered to be worth anything in the days of Solomon,” it immediately adds: “Because the king’s fleet went with the fleet of Hiram to Tarshish by sea once every three years, bringing gold and silver from there.” Why would that fleet carry this metal through so many dangers of the sea if it had no value at all? A little later it says: “Because gold and silver vessels were offered to him”; and then it adds: “A chariot came out of Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and horses for one hundred and fifty (ibid.).”

Silver, therefore, was not without value, since vehicles were bought with it. Rather, silver signifies the brightness of ecclesiastical preaching, of which it is said: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver (Psalm 11).” We shall regard it as worthless, so to speak, and shall have no need of it in any respect once we have been transferred from this misery to the kingdom of the true Solomon. For then we shall not need the word of preaching, where it is granted to behold face to face, in his glory, the King of glory whom we have been accustomed everywhere to hear from the mouth of the preacher. Thus the Lord promises through the prophet, saying: “No one shall say, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the greatest to the least, says the Lord (Jeremiah 3; 31).”

But perhaps someone may assert that we are violently bending the words of Scripture toward our own understanding, and that what Solomon appears to assert about himself applies in every respect specifically to the Savior. Let the defender of this objection say in what way what Solomon says as though about himself can apply to him: “The Lord gave me true knowledge of these things, so that I might know the arrangement of the world and the powers of the elements, the beginning, consummation, and middle of times, the changes of seasons, the transformations of human beings, and whatever is hidden and unforeseen (Proverbs 7).” To say nothing for the moment of the rest, how could Solomon have known the thoughts of human beings, when elsewhere he himself says to God: “You alone know the hearts of all the children of men?” (II Chronicles 6.) And who has learned all hidden and unforeseen things except our Redeemer, in whose breast are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2), who certainly learned through his humanity what he naturally knows through his divinity?

## CHAPTER IX. In a sermon on Saint Antimus

It is written that “Solomon had seven hundred wives who were like queens, and three hundred concubines (III Kings 11).” But what have I to do with Solomon’s harem? Once the chaff of the words has been shaken away, the mystery is found in the kernel.

What, then, are signified by the seven hundred who are mentioned both as wives and as queens, except those souls who possess the Spirit of the sevenfold grace and exercise, as it were, royal authority over the movements of their vices that surge against them? And what are signified by the three hundred who are likewise called concubines, except those souls who, through faith in the Holy Trinity alone, have entered the king’s chamber, but, lacking the purity of chaste conduct and, in a certain sense, of matronly modesty, are not deemed worthy of the marriage contracts belonging to wives?

These souls, certainly, have been joined to Solomon through a relationship, because they receive the mysteries of our Savior, the true peacemaker; yet, through the degraded torpor of a pandering life, and because they do not possess the affection of modesty toward one husband, they do not rise to the bridal dowry of the marriage covenant. Those souls, however, are worthy of the name of wife and queen who rest solely in desire for the heavenly Bridegroom and fight without truce against the temptations of evil spirits.

Thus Scripture also testifies concerning this same Solomon that “he made foreigners tributary; but from the children of Israel he did not appoint anyone to serve; rather, they were warriors, his ministers, commanders, leaders, and overseers of chariots and horses (III Kings 9).” Here it is plainly shown what distinction exists between concubines and queens, and what difference there is between those who, as slaves of sin, pay the tribute of harsh exaction, and those who, through the leadership of battles brought to peace, receive the insignia of command.

## CHAPTER X. In a sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“The woman of Zarephath said to Elijah, to whom she had been sent by the Lord to provide food: ‘Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood, so that I may go in and prepare for myself and my son a little of the flour and oil that I have, so that we may eat and die (III Kings 17).’” This woman was gathering two pieces of wood with which she might provide a meager meal for herself and her son. But the flour and oil of this widow were blessed for an increase of abundance, so that even then the fruit of charity and cheerfulness might be commended in the mystery of the Church: “For God loves a cheerful giver (II Corinthians 3).”

This holy widow was the Church, of whom it is said: “Blessing her widowhood, I will bless her (Psalm 131).” She was permitted to be joined to any man she wished after the death of her husband, because, when the law had come to an end, the Church immediately merited union with Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10). She longed for food cooked with two pieces of wood, and the holy Church hungers for the living bread from heaven, which was roasted on the altar of the cross.

## CHAPTER XI. In a sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s footprint, was rising from the sea (III Kings 18).” Since it is said not “like a man,” but “like a man’s footprint,” the cross is rightly signified by this, because it is fitted to the Lord’s limbs. And the cross is appropriately called a man’s footprint, because through it God made his passage as man when he returned to the Father. As it is said through John: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father (John 13).” Passover is indeed called a passage. This passage was made through the cross, as the Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (I Corinthians 5).”

Therefore, just as through the Virgin he descended to what is ours, so through the cross he returned to what was his own. The miracle that occurred under Elisha expressed this fittingly. For when wood was being cut beside the Jordan, suddenly the axe-head of a certain man who was cutting timber fell into the water (IV Kings 6).

The testimonies from the Third Book of Kings end here.

# THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

[Col. 1121]

1. How Elisha healed the waters of Jericho by mixing in salt.  
2. Concerning the boys who mocked Elisha as he was ascending to Bethel, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.”  
3. “I beg you,” Naaman said to Elisha, “grant your servant permission to take away a load of two mule-loads of earth.”  
4. Concerning how, when Elisha had put a piece of wood into the water, the axe, which had fallen, returned to its handle.  
5. Concerning how Hezekiah requested that the shadow return ten lines along the steps of the sundial, so that it might be a sign of the recovery of his health.

The chapters end here.

# THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS BEGIN

[Col. 1121]

## CHAPTER I. In a sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross

[Col. 1121D]

When the men of Jericho complained to Elisha that the waters were bad and the land barren, he said: “Bring me a new vessel and put salt in it.” Then he immersed the salt in the spring of water and thus healed the waters of all death and barrenness (IV Kings 2). To sum the matter up briefly, this signifies nothing other than: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1).”

For what are the waters except the peoples of the world? What is the new vessel except the Lord’s body, stained by no defilement of sinful transgression and worn down by no abuse of the old man? What, moreover, is the salt except heavenly wisdom? The Wisdom of the Father therefore descended into a human body and thus turned the minds of all the faithful toward fruitfulness and the sweetness of living understanding.

This sweetness remained hidden until the salt was submerged in the water—that is, until he who says, “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul (Psalm 68),” hung upon the cross. From that time onward, humanity learned what it ought to desire and what it ought to avoid.

## CHAPTER II. In a sermon on Saint Cassian

As Elisha was going up the road that leads to Bethel, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” When he looked back, he saw them and cursed them in the name of the Lord. Then Scripture immediately added: “And two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys apart (IV Kings 2).”

What, certainly, should be understood by Elisha except the Mediator between God and human beings? And what is expressed by Bethel, which is interpreted as “the house of God,” except heavenly blessedness? Our Redeemer was ascending by the road that leads to Bethel when he was approaching his Passion, just as at the sacred and mystical supper he says to his disciples: “I am going to him who sent me (John 16).”

But while he was ascending to Bethel—that is, while through the mystery of his most holy Passion he was striving to return to the Father—little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” The Jews, empty of every weight of seriousness and wisdom, possessed of that childishness of which it is said, “Cursed is the child who is a hundred years old (Isaiah 65),” drag him to the place called Calvary and burn against him with the viperous fury of mockery and insults.

That place was called Calvary from the shaved heads of those who were condemned, because condemned persons were customarily beheaded there. It should be noted that the boys are said to have come out of the city because, as the Apostle says: “That he might sanctify the people through his own blood, the Lord suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13).”

What follows—“For two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys apart”—signifies, through the number of the boys, a number of years. For, as the histories relate, in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, Titus and Vespasian, two kings, came from the forests of the nations like two savage bears from a wild forest and tore the boys apart, because, coming to destroy Jerusalem, they conquered the Jews in fury.

## CHAPTER III. In a letter to Hildebrand and Stephen, where it is explained how the rational soul comes to perfection

[Col. 1123D]

“I beg you,” Naaman said, “grant your servant permission to take away a load of two mule-loads of earth (IV Kings 5).”

What, allegorically, does Naaman the Syrian signify except the human race? For just as Naaman, formerly a leper, was cleansed from all the filth of leprosy as soon as he was washed seven times in the water of the Jordan, so the people of the world, receiving the seven gifts of that dove which descended upon the Lord in the Jordan (Matthew 3; Mark 1; Luke 3; John 1), laid aside the contagion of sins through the washing of holy baptism.

But what does the earth that Naaman requests signify except the incarnation of the Redeemer? This is, in mystery, that promised land said to flow with milk and honey. Milk flows from the flesh; honey comes from above. Since, therefore, in the one Mediator between God and human beings the milk of humanity and the honey of divinity are known to exist, the earth flowing with milk and honey rightly figures the mystery of his incarnation.

But what else does his request to take from this earth a load of two mule-loads signify except that he asks for the teaching of the two Apostles, namely Peter and Paul? Hence one of them says: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked through me among the nations (Galatians 2).”

And because not only the apostles but all preachers must possess knowledge and works, the Lord sent two disciples into the village that lay opposite them; and, as Luke testifies, he sent pairs into every city and place where he himself was about to come (Luke 10). Therefore, when Naaman requests in the holy land the burden of two mule-loads, the human race seems to be asking for apostolic teaching concerning the Lord’s incarnation, so that these bearers may carry into the world the earth from which an altar can be made before the Creator for offering sacrifices. Hence he commands the children of Israel, saying: “You shall make an altar of earth for me (Exodus 20).”

That Naaman had asked the prophet for earth for no other reason than to build an altar to the Lord from it, he himself shows in his words, when he immediately adds: “For your servant will no longer offer holocaust or sacrifice to foreign gods, but only to the Lord (IV Kings 5).”

## CHAPTER IV. In a sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

[Col. 1124C]

“When the sons of the prophets were cutting wood beside the Jordan, suddenly the axe-head of a certain man who was cutting timber fell into the water. Then the prophet threw a piece of wood into the water, and immediately the iron floated and returned to the handle (IV Kings 6).”

What is the axe except the wisdom of God working through the body? What is the iron except divinity? What is the wood except humanity? And the body of Christ is rightly called wood, because it hung upon wood.

The axe was therefore cutting down trees beside the Jordan, because the wisdom of God, beside the flowing course of our mortality, deigned to rebuke the ungodly Jews with the severity of its preaching and, like fruitless trees, to cut them away from the condition of rigid pride. Hence John also says: “Now the axe has been placed at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3; Luke 3).”

Therefore, while the wood was being cut, the iron fell from the handle into the water, because, while Truth rebukes the wild minds of the Jews, divinity, without abandoning the flesh, descended with the accompanying spirit into the depths of hell.

But the wood is thrown into the water and the iron returns, because the Lord’s body, which had hung upon the wood, is placed in the tomb and then rose from the depths of hell when the spirit returned. Hence it should be observed and most carefully considered that our Redeemer first passed through the cross and thus raised his humanity into the glory of the Father’s right hand. He offered us an example, so that by the same way by which the Head is known to have gone before, the members who follow might also walk.

## CHAPTER V. In a sermon on Saint Boniface

“King Hezekiah asked that the shadow return ten lines along the steps by which it had already descended on the sundial (IV Kings 20).”

What do these steps of the sundial, on which King Hezekiah asked the shadow to return by ten lines, mystically indicate except that our Savior descended by the same number of steps to the depths of our mortality when he came to redeem the human race?

He displayed a kind of sequence of steps when he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to circumcision, from circumcision to the Temple, from the Temple to baptism, from baptism to the cross, from the cross to death, from death to the tomb; finally, he descended to hell, so that from there he might rescue the saints and, having crushed the power of death, call them back to heavenly glory.

Plainly, so that he might make us run after him, Truth revealed in the flesh arranged these steps for us by descending to us. In a certain sense, the Sun of Justice, Christ, marked out these moments of a mystical sundial by bending himself toward us. “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18),” so that we might say to him from the heart: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments (Song of Songs 1).”

The sun had descended after traversing the ten steps of the sundial, but it returned again by those same steps. This was evidently a sign by which King Hezekiah might be confident that he would be restored to his former health. The human race, however, did not recover its lost health by the expenditure of its own weakness, when Christ, who is called the true light, humbled himself and traversed those ten steps of the mystical sundial toward our setting. Nevertheless, through the shadow of the ten steps we may also understand the mystery of the heavenly dispensation in another way.

The differences of the ages are like certain divisions of lines on a sundial. For the Sun of Justice, Christ, the first step of descent toward us was from God into an angel. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “The Angel of great counsel (Isaiah 9).” And the God who spoke with Jacob is called an angel.
