Thus through that same Jacob it is said: “The angel of the Lord said to me in a dream: ‘I am the Lord of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and made a vow to me (Genesis 31).’” This was so that the very one who speaks might be shown to be both God and angel.

The second step of descent was in the patriarchs, through whom the Lord himself established the worship of the one God and the foundations of true faith. The third was in the promulgation of the law, which he himself first proclaimed while the people listened and afterward wrote on tablets of stone with his own finger. The fourth was in Joshua son of Nun, in whom, dwelling both in name and in deed, he led the people into the promised land.

The fifth step was in the judges, through whom he himself governed the Israelite people. The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, because he himself principally reigned in them. The seventh was in the prophets, because through them he was both announced and spoke. The eighth was in the priests, in whom he, who is the High Priest, prefigured the mystery of his true and eternal priesthood. The ninth step was signified in humanity. The tenth was in the Passion.

Through these ten steps, as through the shadow of the Old Testament, Christ, the Sun of Justice, descended into the setting of our mortality. Through the same steps, after his resurrection, he ascended victoriously into heaven and illuminated all the shadow of the ancient law with the rays of his truth and new grace, revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and laying bare all things that lay rightly beneath the veil of the letter.

And just as the sun had then proceeded line by line and slowly, but suddenly returned to the origin of its rising, so—indeed, so—our Redeemer had signified those things which, concerning the mystery of his incarnation, he suddenly revealed through the long intervals of time in the glory of his resurrection and ascension alone.

The testimonies from the Fourth Book of Kings end here.

# FROM THE BOOK OF EZRA

[Col. 1125]

[Col. 1125D] In a letter to Cunibert, bishop of Turin

“Certain priests sought the record of their genealogy. Since they did not find it, they were expelled from the priesthood.”

It is pious to believe that whoever now recognizes and abandons his own sins and humbly withdraws from his ministry will receive on the day of judgment the same order from which he had voluntarily deprived himself. This seems to be signified in the Book of Ezra, where the genealogy of the priests is described. There sacred history relates that “certain priests sought the record of their genealogy, and because they could not find it, they were expelled from the priesthood (II Ezra 2).”

Those, plainly, are truly priests who live as priests. They preserve the line of priestly descent who offer their life to the Lord as a sacrifice and, by living religiously, show that they have come from a priestly lineage, while they imitate the examples of the holy priests whom they read about. Then, in the sacred writings, they recognize themselves as the sons of priests.

But those who live carnally and, by following the footsteps of the wicked, descend as though from the generation of worldly people, are rightly expelled from the order of priests, since through their evil life they cannot find themselves to be their sons.

It should also be noted that the passage continues there: “Athersatha said to them that they should not eat of the holy of holies until a learned and perfect priest of God should arise (ibid.).” What else, through the mystery of allegory, should be understood by this prohibition except that the one who is worthy of the priesthood should restrain himself from receiving the sacraments and from exercising the priestly order until Christ, who is truly the learned and perfect Priest, arises in judgment?

As the Psalmist says: “The earth trembled and was still when God arose in judgment (Psalm 75),” so that the one who, through the impulse of fear of him, had voluntarily deprived himself here of his dignity after falling might restore him in judgment, in a welcome reversal, and raise him to the summit of the order he had lost, saying: “Friend, go up higher, and then you shall have glory before those reclining together (Luke 14).”

But there are some—this must not be passed over—who, as the Apostle says, “having lost all hope, gave themselves over to impurity (Ephesians 4).” For, having utterly despaired of continence, they withdraw themselves from the administration of the order they have received. Thus they confidently behave as though they were sinning with impunity, as if a servant were to say to his master: “Because I cannot fulfill what you command, I defect to the camp of your enemies and surrender myself to them to fight against you.” It is as though he could please his master by fleeing, and could not provoke him by rising against him in arms.

To such people I firmly and without any ambiguity declare that they deceive themselves with an empty and foolish promise if, while not carrying out their office, they trust that they have been stripped of the office. For although the order of anyone, or the office within one who has been ordained, may cease from regular practice or execution, nevertheless the sacrament of the order remains. Just as a man, even if he ceases from marital intercourse, is in no way released from the bond of marriage, so a cleric, even if he does not exercise the office of his order, is nevertheless not stripped of the sacrament of that order.

They must therefore beware lest that frightening sentence come upon them, of which the Apostle says: “It is impossible, he says, for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt (Hebrews 6).”

They plainly seem to act as though some Israelite, wishing to fornicate with idols, were to say: “Because I cannot observe the harsh and rigid law of God, I will pass over to the rite of the Gentiles. By withdrawing from the law, I will not be indebted to the law; and thus, although I may not be worthy of a reward for observing the law, I will not be liable to punishment for despising it.”

But let us hear what divine severity says to such people in Deuteronomy: “When anyone hears the words of this oath and blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘There will be peace for me, and I will walk in the wickedness of my heart,’ and joins the drunkard to the thirsty, the Lord will not pardon him. Rather, then the Lord’s anger and zeal against that man will burn most fiercely; all the curses written in this book will rest upon him, and he will blot out his name from under heaven. He will destroy him for perdition from all the tribes of Israel, according to the curses contained in the book of this law and covenant (Deuteronomy 29).”

The Psalmist also says: “Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments (Psalm 118).” And through Ezekiel the Lord says: “Nor shall the thought of your mind be fulfilled, when you say: ‘We shall be like the nations and like the families of the earth, to worship wood and stones.’ As I live, says the Lord God, surely with a strong hand and an outstretched arm and poured-out fury I shall reign over you. I shall bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands in which you have been scattered, and I shall subject you to my scepter (Ezekiel 20).”

# FROM THE BOOK OF TOBIT

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127C] Recall what Scripture testifies concerning Tobit, a righteous man: “It happened,” it says, “that one day, worn out from burying the dead, he came home, threw himself down beside the wall, and fell asleep. Then warm dung from swallows’ nests fell upon his sleeping eyes, and he became blind (Tobit 2).”

Worn out from burying the dead, when he cast himself down as though his strength had been shattered, he lost his sight. Whoever perseveres tirelessly in good works preserves the eye of the heart unharmed; but when he is broken by faintheartedness, he is not unjustly deprived of light. Hence it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance (Sirach 2).” Hence Paul says: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully (I Corinthians 16).”

But what do the lightly flying swallows signify except the light-minded habits of flatterers and smooth speakers? While they soothe with the sweetness of their flattering speech, while they fatten the head of the listener with the oil of flattery, they blind the inner eyes so that they cannot enjoy their accustomed light. “Let the righteous rebuke me in mercy and reprove me,” he says; “but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head (Psalm 140).”

It is as though dung were thrown into the eyes when the words of the flatterer smear someone with their flattering verbosity. Such people often say: “Live while you live; refresh your body with food, lest, if it wear itself down too severely, the fragile flesh, oppressed by so many labors, soon succumb. Adorn your person with more distinguished garments, so that the dignity you possess may be preserved. Let a crowd of clients gather at your sides, so that while the multitude of those who come and go decorates you, the office of honor may then become worthless.”

But if the bitterness of this diabolical wickedness is exposed to us, the darkness brought on by temptation completely vanishes. Hence it is also said there: “Then Tobit took some of the fish’s gall and smeared his father’s eyes; immediately the whiteness began to come out of his eyes like the membrane of an egg, and at once he recovered his sight (Tobit 11).”

The gall of the fish is the wickedness of Behemoth, who is the head and beginning of every iniquity. The blind man is therefore smeared with the fish’s gall, and immediately blindness is driven away, because when the bitterness of diabolical cunning is set before our eyes and exposed, the darkness of shadows is immediately expelled and the inner light, which had suffered something like an eclipse, is restored.

It should also be noted that it is said first that the whiteness came out of his eyes, and only then was the light immediately restored. The person who carries whiteness in his eyes is the one who possesses an opinion of holiness about himself. Therefore, whoever wishes to recover the light should first cut away from himself the whiteness of pretended esteem, so that he does not deny himself to be a sinner if he wishes to escape the blindness of sin.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5).” These are the eyes of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within (Song of Songs 4).”

# FROM THE BOOK OF JOB

[Col. 1129]

[Col. 1129A] From a sermon on Saint George

“Who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” And shortly afterward: “I surrounded it with my boundaries, and I placed a bar and doors, and I said: ‘Thus far shall you come and go no farther, and here you shall break your swelling waves (Job 38).’”

The heart of a wicked person is rightly signified by the sea, which is turbulent with fury, bitter with quarrels, swollen with the pride of arrogance, and darkened by the gloom of malicious deceit.

God therefore separated the sea at that time and restrained its threatening waves from flooding the earth, so that the earth might bring forth green herbs and fruit-bearing trees and afterward produce the harvests’ fruits. Even now he separates from his elect the storms of the wicked who persecute them, and restrains, as though raging, the assaults of the tempests. Although he permits them to rage even to the point of inflicting torments upon bodies, nevertheless, lest they harm souls, he guards his own with the unconquered and ever-watchful protection of his arm, in a certain sense saying to the sea: “Thus far shall you come and go no farther, and here you shall break your swelling waves.”

It is as though he plainly said: “I release you to inflict torments upon bodies; but lest you pour forth upon the soul with swelling billows, I set the shore of my law against you, so that, while a shore is placed before the fury of your waves, the earth of the heart may remain free to bring forth the shoots of its fruits.”

# THE CHAPTERS FROM THE BOOK OF PSALMS BEGIN

[Col. 1129]

1. Concerning the wicked man exalted and brought low.  
2. Concerning the wicked placed like sheep in hell.  
3. “My God, show me good things against my enemies; do not kill them, lest they forget your law.”  
4. Concerning marrow-filled holocausts.  
5. “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me,” and so forth.  
6. Concerning the exaltation of the reprobate.  
7. “The children of Ephraim, bending the bow.”  
8. “The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.”  
9. Concerning what is said: “I said in the excess of my mind: Every human being is a liar.”  
10. Concerning what is said: “Let your hand be present, that it may save me.”  
11. “Like ointment on the head that descends,” and so forth.  
12. “Do not incline my heart toward an evil word.”

The chapters end here.

# THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE BOOK OF PSALMS BEGIN

[Col. 1129]

## CHAPTER I. In a letter to Desiderius, abbot, where the omnipotence of God is discussed

[Col. 1129C]

“I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was no more (Psalm 36).”

Perhaps he was still dining sumptuously, supported by throngs of attendants, surrounded by ranks of warriors—the man whom the Prophet saw exalted above measure and raised up. But then, passing onward to contemplate higher things, he recognized that the one whom he had perhaps believed to be something great was in fact nothing.

For when they swell with riches, when they arrogantly exalt themselves above others, and finally when they oppress their inferiors through the violence of tyranny, then—yes, then—they are more truly nothing, the farther they are from him who truly and supremely is.

## CHAPTER II. In a letter to Hermisindus

“They have been placed like sheep in hell, and death shall feed upon them (Psalm 48).”

Christ has sheep whom he may lead into pleasant and verdant pastures in the heavenly sheepfolds. That roaring lion also has sheep whom he may devour with his insatiably bloodthirsty mouth. He is rightly called Death, because, although he is the author of death, he rages cruelly to inflict destruction upon us. Hence John says: “And behold, a pale horse, and the one sitting upon it; his name was Death (Revelation 6).”

## CHAPTER III. In a letter to Desiderius, abbot, where he says that the one who casts away dignity is worthy of greater honor than the one who remains in it

“My God, my God, show me good things against my enemies; do not kill them, lest they forget your law (Psalm 58).”

By the provident dispensation of our Redeemer, it is divinely arranged that the remnant of the Jews should be preserved, as it were, to guard the house of the law. Thus they are, in a certain sense, our archivists, carrying the books of heavenly eloquence throughout the world in the very language in which they were composed, so that they themselves, who are our enemies, may remove every uncertainty for us whenever some scruple of doubt arises.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, show me good things among my enemies; do not kill them, lest they forget your law.” The authority of the Christian faith is greatly assisted by the Hebrew language, which is scattered throughout the whole world. For unless that testimony which is written among us were added, it could in a certain sense be thought to be a fiction. But when that testimony is brought forward, doubt is immediately removed.

Hence it is appropriately added there: “Scatter them (Psalm 58)”; disseminate throughout the whole world those who have survived from the Jewish people, so that they themselves may bear witness from the ancient books to the truth of the new faith.

## CHAPTER IV. In the book On Contempt for the World
“ I will offer you holocausts rich in marrow, together with incense and rams” (Psalm 65). David promises that, as a great offering, he will sacrifice to God offerings rich in marrow, saying: “I will offer you holocausts rich in marrow, together with incense and rams.” First, therefore, one must know that God by no means commands the hides of victims to be offered to him in sacrifice, but rather the inner parts of the entrails, together with the marrow itself. Hence, in describing the very rite of sacrifice, Moses commands, saying: “After removing the hide of the victim, let him cut the limbs into pieces” (Leviticus 1).

Whoever continually and eagerly pours himself into the activities of worldly affairs removes the marrow and entrails of his holocaust and strives to burn for God only the victim’s hide, which he is forbidden to offer. But whoever desires to offer God a pleasing sacrifice should seek seclusion, pursue the inward parts, and preserve his soul whole and undefiled in its proper virginity, lest, running through the brothels of the world, he lay himself down, like a prostitute, beneath filthy seducers. Therefore, in order to please the sight of the inner Bridegroom, let him not cover himself with the cosmetics of worldly pomp, but anoint all the senses of his mind with the immortal oil of chastity, lest, falling into death through incontinence, he rot in the stench of lust. Let the chaste soul, therefore, enclose itself within the chamber of holy Church and thus rest continually in the bridal chamber of the eternal King.

## CHAPTER V. To Pope Alexander, on the canons.

“Let not the tempest of water overwhelm me, nor let the pit swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Psalm 68). When a person sins, he falls, as it were, into a pit; but when he defends his sins, the mouth of the pit is pressed down over him so that no exit may be open. A person therefore falls into a pit when he sins; but he closes the mouth of the pit upon himself when he makes excuses. From this defense, or excuse, the crime of heresy arises. For heresy means “choice”; and when someone tries to defend what he has chosen, abandoning the path of truth and being swept through the precipices of perverse doctrine, he must necessarily slip into heresy. The difference between a sinner and a heretic is this: a sinner is one who commits a fault, whereas a heretic is one who defends sin through perverse doctrine.

## CHAPTER VI. To Abbot Desiderius, where God’s omnipotence is discussed.

“You cast them down while they were being exalted” (Psalm 72). When the Prophet was speaking of the downfall of the wicked who exalt themselves, he did not say, “After they had been exalted, you cast them down, Lord,” but “while they were being exalted,” because they become empty through the very thing by which they swell; they fall from the place where they become lofty.

## CHAPTER VII. In a sermon on Saint Anastasius.

[Col. 1132A]

Of those who preach great things but live negligently, the Prophet says: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77). Those who summon others to combat against the temptations of vices, but themselves refuse to fight under the ignoble weariness of sloth, certainly aim their arrows, but, having turned their backs, do not deserve the honors of completed victory. Nor does it benefit them that they began well, because they do not persevere courageously to the end. Hence it immediately continues concerning them: “They did not keep God’s covenant, and they refused to walk in his law” (ibid.). It is as though he said: “They did indeed receive the covenant, but they did not keep it; they set foot upon the law at the beginning, but they did not maintain the onward course of perseverance.”

Therefore, whoever summons others to spiritual combat, whoever urges the minds of his neighbors to act bravely, must certainly make his life agree with his speech, lest, while he sets lofty things before others, he himself be pressed down by inertia, content with what is low. Hence the law commands: “You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, a larger and a smaller; nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just weight, and your measure shall be equal and true for you” (Deuteronomy 25).

## CHAPTER VIII. In a letter to Countess Blanca.

“High mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Psalm 103). What are meant here by the mountains, if not the lofty depths of Scripture? Those who have already learned to make the leaps of contemplation ascend the high summits of divine meanings like mountain peaks. Since the weak cannot reach those heights, it is rightly added there: “The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs,” because the frail are not exercised by sublime understanding but are humbly held secure by faith alone in Christ.

## CHAPTER IX. To Abbot Desiderius, where he excuses his ecstasy.

“I said in the ecstasy of my mind: Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115). One may rightly answer him: “If everyone, then you also; and the statement you, yourself a liar, have uttered will already be false. But if you yourself are not a liar, the statement will no longer be true, because, if you are truthful, not every human being is shown to be a liar.”

But lest sacred Scripture, like the writings of the pagans, be exposed to slander, and lest it fail to defend itself by its own authority, we must note what precedes: “I said in the ecstasy of my mind.” Through the ecstasy of his mind, therefore, he passed beyond himself when he defined the condition of humanity, as though he clearly said: “I uttered a true judgment concerning the falsehood of all human beings from the place where I myself was above humanity.” He was a liar insofar as he was human, but was in no way a liar insofar as, in the ecstasy of his mind, he ascended beyond humanity to contemplate the highest things.

## CHAPTER X. In a sermon on Saint Columba.

“Let your hand come to be, that it may save me” (Psalm 118), as though he said: “Let the One through whom all things were made come to be, so that, when he is created, the creature may be freed from the contagion of its guilt.”

## CHAPTER XI. In a sermon on Saint Christopher.

“Like ointment on the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and descended to the hem of his garment” (Psalm 132). The ointment on the head is plainly the Holy Spirit in the Savior, who is mystically represented by Aaron, whose name is said to mean “mountain of strength.” Since Aaron is therefore a mountain of strength, the beard is also a sign of manliness. The beard of this Aaron, then, is the holy apostles, who, through the strength of their manliness—which they had received from the anointing of the Holy Spirit—overcame all the battles of raging persecutors and gloriously triumphed over the ruler of the world, roaring savagely like a lion against Christ’s sheep.

Hence Peter says: “Resist him, he says, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5). Paul also says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications, destroying the counsels of the flesh and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive into obedience to Christ” (2 Corinthians 10).

From this beard of the supreme priest Aaron, therefore, the ointment drips down to the hem of his garment, because through the blessed apostles, and thereafter through the holy martyrs and then the whole Church together, the stream of the Holy Spirit irrigates everything.

## CHAPTER XII. In a letter to Pope Alexander, on removing private property from the canons.

As far as the measure of our understanding reaches, no evil among the human race is a more pernicious crime than the defense of wickedness. Hence David says: “Do not incline my heart toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins” (Psalm 140). An offense against God deserves anger; an excuse provokes punishment. This vice, just as it emerged from the root of the human race, sprouts daily and does not cease to grow like branches bursting forth from a tree.

When Adam was asked why he had eaten from the forbidden fruit, he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3). When the woman, too, was questioned why she had done this, she said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid.). It is as though each of them indirectly hurled the guilt back upon the Creator and reproached the One by whom they were convicted, saying: “This guilt must doubtless be attributed not to us but to you, who joined the wife to the man and decreed that the serpent should live among human beings in paradise.”

That disciple was, as it were, the schoolmaster of both of them, who, when the Lord asked him about Abel, replied: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4).

[Col. 1133] Here end the testimonies from the Psalter.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS FROM THE BOOK OF PROVERBS

[Col. 1133]

1. Concerning the woman called “foreign.”  
2. Concerning the good woman.  
3. Wisdom sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set out her table.  
4. Concerning the difference between the two women.  
5. Cultivate your field diligently, so that afterward you may build your house.  
6. Concerning evil preachers.  
7. As one who throws a stone onto a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool.  
8. The leech has two daughters, saying: “Bring, bring.”

Here end the chapter headings.

# HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM PROVERBS

## CHAPTER I. In a letter to Cincus the prefect.

[Col. 1133C]

“Prudence will preserve you, so that you may be delivered from the foreign woman and from the stranger who makes her words seductive.” And shortly afterward: “All who enter to her will not return, nor will they grasp the paths of life” (Proverbs 2).

What is the prostitute, or the foreign woman whose approach is forbidden to us, if not worldly life, carnal and earthly life, into whose pleasures wretched people cast themselves, dissolving themselves in its deceitful delight and plunging, so to speak, into adulterous embraces with it?

## CHAPTER II. In the same letter.

But hear what the same Solomon says concerning the good woman: “Let your vein be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5). The wife of our youth is unquestionably holy life, to which we were joined from that time onward, as if by pledge and promise, when in baptism we promised that we would renounce the devil and all his pomps.

There he immediately adds: “A most beloved doe and a most gracious fawn: let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, and delight continually in her love” (ibid.). What is signified by the doe, which climbs the heights of the mountains, if not holy Church, which raises herself in love of the heavenly homeland? What do the breasts of this doe signify, if not the two Testaments? We are intoxicated by these breasts when we are filled from the streams of sacred Scripture and, thirsting for the drink of spiritual wisdom, draw it in.

[Col. 1135A] We are therefore commanded to delight in this woman, so that we may be nourished by the richness of heavenly words. It continues: “Why are you seduced, my son, by a foreign woman and warmed in the bosom of another?” (Proverbs 5.) He is seduced by a foreign woman who delights in the enticements of carnal life. She is rightly called “foreign,” because divine law has forbidden her to us.

Again he speaks concerning both women, saying: “Say to Wisdom: ‘You are my sister,’ and call Prudence your friend, and preserve yourself from the strange woman and from the foreign woman who has made her words sweet.” Then he adds: “From the window of my house, through the lattice, I looked out, and I saw the little ones. I observed a foolish young man passing through the streets near the corner and walking close to the way of her house” (Proverbs 7).

Here it must be noted that carnal life, which is called a prostitute, is said to be able to deceive none but the little and foolish. Hence the same Solomon says elsewhere: “The foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing nothing at all, sat at the doorway of her house upon a seat in a high place of the city, and called to those passing by on the way and walking along their path: ‘Whoever is little, let him turn aside to me’; and she spoke to the foolish” (Proverbs 9).

For one who is a mature man and sound in mind can in no way be deceived by the enticement of carnal seduction, or overcome by however fierce a struggle of passions may arise. This woman overcomes only those whom the intention of a wicked will and the foul smoke of earthly desire blind; carnal and earthly life triumphs over them.

Hence it is appropriately added there: “In the darkness, at dusk, in the gloom and darkness of night, behold, a woman meets him in a prostitute’s attire, prepared to capture souls” (Proverbs 7). Carnal life intoxicates the heart devoted to lust and makes it dark like nighttime gloom, since it does not raise the inner eyes toward heaven but fixes them upon earth.

Then it adds: “Talkative, wandering, and unable to remain quiet, unable to keep her feet inside her house; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners” (ibid.). Here it expresses the instability of carnal people, subject to the vice of fickleness and shamefully alien to seriousness.

What is added—“I have woven cords; I have spread my bed with embroidered coverings from Egypt” (ibid.)—suggests nothing other than that the pleasure of the flesh, upon which every lustful person willingly casts himself as upon a couch, is bound by tangled bonds of sins. The fact that the bed is spread with embroidered coverings from Egypt means nothing other than that the life of the lustful is not founded upon the solid foundation of truth, but is colored by the cosmetics of falsehood and shadowy images.

When this prostitute says: “Come, let us intoxicate ourselves with breasts and enjoy mutual embraces until daybreak; for my husband is not at home; he has gone on a very long journey” (ibid.), the meaning is this: The husband of every faithful soul is Christ. He is not at home but has gone on a very long journey when he sees the conscience of someone polluted, and therefore immediately withdraws far from him.

Then she adds: “He took a bag of money with him; he will return on the day of the full moon” (ibid.). Our Redeemer took a bag of money with him when, ascending into heaven, he carried with him the gains of our faith. He will return on the day of the full moon, that is, at the consummation of the universal Church; for the Lord will come to judgment when the number of the elect has been completed.

After saying many things about the extremely destructive cunning of this woman, by which she hunts the souls of the lost—things that, because of their length, we do not consider necessary to insert—he added this at the end: “She has cast down many wounded, and the strongest have been killed by her; her house is the way to hell, penetrating to the depths of death” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER III. In a sermon on Saint Bartholomew.

[Col. 1136B]

Let us therefore hear Wisdom, through Solomon’s mouth, inviting us in clear words to the table of spiritual nourishment: “Wisdom,” he says, “has sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set out her table; she has sent her maidservants to call from the citadel and the walls of the city: ‘Whoever is little, let him come to me. Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you’” (Proverbs 9).

Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father, sacrificed victims when, for the example of our imitation, he allowed the blessed martyrs to be killed. He mixed wine because he offered the Holy Spirit to believers. He set out a table because he prepared heavenly glory for human beings. He sent his maidservants—that is, the holy ministers of the word—who confess that they are weak and fragile.

What therefore remains, except that, abandoning the hunger of the world, we hasten to God’s table? But we cannot find access for entering it except through the holy apostles, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted (Matthew 16). Hence it is written: “Wisdom preaches outside; she gives her voice in the streets; at the head of the crowds she cries out at the gates of the city” (Proverbs 1).

They themselves are also the head of the crowds and the gates of the city, because they are the leaders of the peoples and, by the privilege of their surpassing excellence, the gatekeepers of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER IV. In a letter to Cincus the prefect, concerning exhortation to chastity.

Hear again, under the appearance of women, what difference there is between spiritual and carnal life: “A woman who loves is a crown to her husband, but she is rottenness in his bones when she does things deserving of shame” (Proverbs 12).

The bones of this woman therefore contain rottenness, because when someone joined to carnal life strives to surpass others, when he perhaps boasts of doing something—“bones” being what this signifies—a foul reputation spreads through the people and exhales like the stench of fetid decay.

Concerning such women another Wise Man also says: “If you have a wife according to your soul, do not cast her away, and do not entrust yourself with your whole heart to a hateful woman” (Sirach 7). A woman according to the soul is the life of virtues, a holy manner of life; but the hateful woman is carnal life, which must certainly be hated. If we entrust ourselves to her with all our heart, it will necessarily happen that, like Samson through Delilah (Judges 16), we too fall into the hands of our enemies through her.

Concerning this hateful woman, it is written in Deuteronomy: “If a man takes a wife and possesses her, but she does not find favor in his eyes because of some uncleanness, let him write a bill of divorce, place it in her hand, and send her away from his house” (Deuteronomy 24).

## CHAPTER V. In a letter to the brothers of Gamugnium, where he discusses the transgression of his commandments.

Whoever hastens to build a lofty hall with the stones of the virtues must first clear away the bristling thickets of carnal pleasures. Hence Solomon rightly says: “Cultivate your field diligently, so that afterward you may build your house” (Proverbs 24).

He builds the house of his mind well who first clears the field of his body of the thorns of vices. Otherwise, if the thistles of carnal desires and passions are allowed to sprout in the field of the flesh, as hunger for goodness increases, the whole structure of the virtues within collapses.

Again he says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, they were entirely filled with nettles; thorns covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (ibid.).

What is the field or vineyard of the lazy man except the flesh of anyone unwilling to labor in the efforts of spiritual cultivation? What are the nettles except the itches of gluttony and carnal enticements? What are the thorns, finally, except the stings of carnal passions? What, at last, is the stone wall except the structure of virtues joined together by charity as their central bond?

The field of the lazy and foolish man is therefore filled with nettles and thorns when the flesh of someone living idly is not cultivated through the discipline of continuous labor, but is softened and nourished by the desire for pleasure and wantonness. The material of the stones also becomes unstable and collapses, because the entire structure of the virtues is scattered as though battered by the rams of incontinence.

“For the captain of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 25). The belly is rightly called the captain of the cooks, since the cooks serve it with laborious work. Whoever therefore desires to grow rich in the abundance of spiritual crops should now sweat over the field of his body, furrowing it with the plow of discipline and continence through continuous labor; and, like the clods of his fallow land, he should break them with a wise hoe. Whatever hard or barren thing he discovers in himself, let him wear it down through continual blows of repentance. Let him not cease to uproot from the roots the nettles of itching gluttony and the bristling brambles of carnal desires, so that the fields of his heart may be able to produce abundant harvests of spiritual crops.

Hence the same Solomon says: “He who works his land will be filled with bread; he who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty” (Proverbs 12).

## CHAPTER VI. In a letter to Pope Alexander, on the canons.

“Lame in the feet and drinking iniquity is the one who sends words through a foolish messenger” (Proverbs 26). What else seems to be expressed by these words than that the office of preaching should not be entrusted to anyone who is carnal in his understanding and therefore foolish?

For it is said of holy preachers: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” (Isaiah 52; Romans 10.) Therefore, any ordainer of the Church who appoints worthy and suitable men to positions of dignity walks as if on straight feet. Through them the word is scattered and travels everywhere, and what he is unable to accomplish by himself he endeavors effectively to fulfill through them.

But if he presumes to appoint carnal and reprobate men, he walks lame in his feet. He is also said to drink iniquity, because, while sending the words of holy preaching through a foolish messenger and, contrary to the Apostle, laying hands on someone hastily (1 Timothy 5), he shares in the sins of others.

Even if someone speaks wisely, nevertheless, if he himself does not do what he says, he is rightly judged lame on the spiritual journey. Hence it is appropriately added there: “As beautiful legs are useless to a lame man, so an unseemly proverb is in the mouth of fools” (Proverbs 20).

He plainly rests upon beautiful legs who shines with the brightness of eloquent speech. But when, without good works, he brings forth carefully composed eloquence, he moves straight legs of words as though without the ability to walk. He therefore has beautiful legs to look upon, but not useful ones for walking, who, bound by the gout-like snares of vices, himself limps shamefully while inviting others to walk nimbly.

In the mouth of such fools, therefore, the proverb is unseemly, because, while they sound spiritual and live carnally, their life does not agree with their lips. Their preaching, though they speak honorably while living dishonorably, does not free them; rather, their biting conscience accuses them vehemently.

Hence it is not inappropriately added there: “As when a thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard, so is a proverb in the mouth of fools” (ibid.). A thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard when the sting of reproach is generated in the mind of one who is drunk with love of this life. In the mouth of fools, therefore, a proverb is like a thorn, because, while they say one thing and do another, their mind is sometimes reproved within itself and pierced by something like the prick of a stabbing thorn. Thus the conscience of one who lives badly but speaks well pricks him, when, in the very thing he says outwardly, he is wounded inwardly by a kind of stimulus of shame and fear.

## CHAPTER VII. In the same letter.

“As one who throws a stone onto a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool” (Proverbs 26). Among the pagans Mercury was said to be the god of the shrine [reading uncertain: *sacelli*, perhaps *lucelli*], that is, of money; a heap of Mercury is a pile and mass of coins.

Since a coin bears the mark of the monetary standard, what is represented by a heap of coins except the assembly of clerics who display the image of regular discipline and true holiness? What, however, is represented by the stone except the hard, dull, and senseless mind of one who, because he does not believe with unwavering faith that God exists, places his hope in some earthly possession?

Concerning him the Prophet says: “The fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13). Honor is given to this fool when someone devoted not to God but to money is promoted to the summit of an ecclesiastical rank.

But just as a heap of coins is scattered when a stone is thrown upon it, so, through the arrival of an unworthy—or stony—pastor, the ordered ranks of clerics who walk according to discipline and obey in charity are destroyed as though they had been tightly packed together. They are weighed down by the shadow of a bad pastor and, like a heap of heavenly coins, are ruined by the mass of a hellish stone.

Honor in the Church must therefore be denied to the foolish and senseless, lest the heap of holy clerics, like spiritual coins, be overwhelmed. Concerning this fool the same Solomon said a little earlier: “Lame in the feet and drinking iniquity is the one who sends words through a foolish messenger” (Proverbs 26).

## CHAPTER VIII. In a letter to Pope Alexander, concerning the insolence of evil people.

[Col. 1140A]

“The leech has two daughters, saying: ‘Bring, bring’” (Proverbs 30). The more excessively someone eats, the more necessarily he is inflamed with thirst for drinking. While the mass he has accumulated is cooked in the boiling cauldron of the stomach, it must necessarily be irrigated with frequent draughts.

But when the belly swells with food and drink, it follows that, through the two passages on either side, it expels feces through the anus into the passages and pours fluid from the genital receptacle through the private parts. For just as wine is separated from wine in winepresses, so in the intestines dung is separated from [wine?; printed *viru*, uncertain].

The leech, therefore, which is gluttony, has two daughters: drunkenness and lust. When one disease delightfully conceives, it necessarily gives birth to twin offspring. They say, “Bring, bring,” because, being insatiable, they are also violent exactors.

[Col. 1139] Here end the testimonies from the Book of Proverbs.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS FROM ECCLESIASTES

[Col. 1139]

1. That all the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled.  
2. Dying flies ruin the sweetness of the ointment.  
3. Concerning the spirit possessing power.  
4. Concerning what is said: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.”  
5. Let us all hear the end of the discourse together.

Here end the chapter headings.

# HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM ECCLESIASTES

## CHAPTER I. In the book *Most Beloved*.

[Col. 1139C]

“All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1). The evangelist Luke mystically describes this flowing forth and returning of spiritual rivers when he says: “Jesus called together the twelve apostles, gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases; and he sent them to preach the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

Behold the rivers’ going forth. Afterward he adds: “And the apostles returned and told him everything they had done” (ibid.). Behold the rivers’ return. They return to the place from which the rivers flow because all the elect acknowledge without doubt that they are indebted to the One from whom they had drawn everything that flows spiritually.

Hence Paul says: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Lord; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; there are divisions of works, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12). By mentioning the Spirit first, then adding the Lord, and finally God, he clearly reveals the Holy Trinity, namely, that the one God is unquestionably the author of all graces. He himself distributes his gifts, discerning by hidden providence the merits of individuals and the diversity of their works.

## CHAPTER II. G. G.

[Col. 1140C]

“Dying flies ruin the sweetness of the ointment” (Ecclesiastes 10), because superfluous thoughts, which continually arise and perish in the mind occupied with carnal things, destroy that sweetness with which each person has been inwardly anointed by the Spirit.

Hence, when Truth comes to the heart through a wondrous work of mercy, he first drives out from it the heat of carnal thoughts and afterward arranges within it the gifts of the virtues. This is well indicated to us where, in the Gospel, it is said of the Lord being led to raise the ruler’s daughter: “After the crowd had been put outside, he entered, took her by the hand, and the girl rose” (Matthew 9).

The crowd is therefore driven outside so that the girl may be raised, because unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s inner chambers, the soul, which lies dead within, does not rise again. For while it disperses itself through innumerable thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot gather itself in any way for self-reflection. No one fully grasps Wisdom, who is God, unless he strives to withdraw himself from all the fluctuation of carnal actions.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Write wisdom during a time of leisure, and he who is less occupied with activity will perceive it” (Ecclesiastes 38).

## CHAPTER III. To Abbot Mainard.

“If the spirit of one possessing power rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10). It is as though he clearly said: If you perceive the tempter’s spirit gaining power over you in some respect, do not abandon the humility of repentance. And elsewhere it is written: “Do not be high-minded, but fear,” and seek the last place at the spiritual wedding feast (Romans 11).

## CHAPTER IV. In a letter to Boniface the Advocate, that spiritual wisdom should be preferred to outward prudence.

“Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11). So pass through the present life, which is represented by the number seven, that you may already strive with all your heart to dwell in love of the future life, which is represented by the number eight and expresses the glory of the resurrection. Give the former only a superficial and fleeting concern; in the latter fix a persevering and perpetual resolve, as unceasing as it is eternal.

## CHAPTER V. In a letter to Pope Alexander, against the pope’s judging.

“Let us all hear the end of the discourse together: Fear God and observe his commandments; for this is the whole human being” (Ecclesiastes 12). What is the end of the discourse except the One of whom the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10)?

Christ is the end of the law for righteousness because whatever either the old or the new law says refers without doubt to him. The phrase “for righteousness” is not idle, because the word of divine law justifies and cleanses the soul from defilements. As Truth says to the disciples: “Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15).

To fear God is to despise with execration and abhorrence everything that God forbids. To observe his commandments is to carry out in deeds everything he commands. Therefore, the one who strives to avoid what God forbids fears God; the one who strives to fulfill what he commands observes his commandments.

“Fear God, therefore, and observe his commandments; for this is the whole human being.” It is as though he clearly said: Whoever does not strive to avoid what is forbidden, whoever neglects to fulfill the commandments, because he lacks reason, has indeed the name of a human being but does not possess the reality of being human, because he does not truly use the virtue of the name by which he is reckoned.

Let the one who recognizes the Author of human beings believe that he is truly human; otherwise, “the one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14). What a human being is without these things, Scripture clearly defines when it says: “The stars are not clean in his sight; how much less a human being, who is decay, and a son of man, who is a worm?” (Job 25.)

Hence Abraham too, when he is raised to the summit of the highest conversation and specially earns the grace of divine intimacy, is brought low by remembrance of this humility when he says: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18).

Among the Greeks, too, this custom is reported to be observed: when an emperor is created in office, as soon as he has been crowned with imperial insignia and adorned with the glory of crown and scepter, and when he is surrounded by the service of nobles and received by choirs of singing psalmists, someone comes before him carrying in one hand a vessel full of the bones and ashes of the dead, while in the other he carries flax finely combed and softly teased into hanging fibers. Fire is immediately applied to the flax, and suddenly, in the blink of an eye, it is consumed by the devouring flame. Thus he must consider in the one what he is and see in the other what he has.

In the ashes he recognizes that he is ash; in the flax he already gathers how suddenly the world will burn on the day of judgment. Thus, while he considers himself and his possessions together to be so vain and so contemptible, he does not become arrogant because he has ascended to the summit of imperial power. And since it is beyond doubt that both possessor and possession are subject to the common fate of all, let him who has been advanced to the heights not be puffed up as though he possessed a unique dignity.

Let a human being therefore contemplate the beautiful order of worldly existence. While he sees that everything has been assigned for his use, let him give thanks not to himself but to his Creator. Let him crush the seductive glory of the world beneath the feet of his judgment. Let him consider the vigor of the flesh to be already dry dust; let him keep the day of his calling always before his eyes as a mirror; let him tremble before the strict judgment of the final examination. Thus, while he now submits to the laws of his Creator, he who appears distinguished among earthly creatures will also truly be exalted in heavenly glory.

[Col. 1141] Here end the testimonies from Ecclesiastes.
