# HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 1143]

## CHAPTER I. From a sermon on the feast of virgins.

[Col. 1143A]

“Your name is poured-out oil” (Song of Songs 1). In Greek, *chrisma*; in Latin, *unctio*, “anointing.” From *chrisma*, therefore, comes *Christus*, “Christ,” and from *Christus* comes *Christianus*, “Christian.” Oil is to be understood as the Holy Spirit, just as the Psalmist says to our Savior: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). The name of Christ is therefore poured-out oil, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is spread among as many as there are who truly bear the name of Christ.

## CHAPTER II.

“Black am I, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Cedar, like Solomon’s skin” (Song 1). *Cedar* is interpreted as “darkness”; these are the unbelievers who do not possess the light of faith. “Black am I,” she says, “because of the heat of persecution and because of the adversities I suffer from the sons of darkness; but inwardly I am beautiful, because the king desired my beauty, and all my glory is within.” “I am beautiful,” she says, “like a skin”—that is, like Solomon’s tent. For just as a tent is made from the skins of dead animals, so only those are God’s dwelling place (Eph. 2) who have died with Christ and have also been put to death with respect to the vices and desires of the flesh (Eph. 2).

It continues: “Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1). The same applies to faithful souls who, through desire, are already established in that heavenly glory: “Do not look at me because I am dark”—that is, do not despair or be excessively terrified because tribulations oppress me, persecutions afflict me, and, in this shipwreck amid storms and tempests, swelling waves strike me; “because the sun has discolored me,” since the heat of persecution has burned fiercely over me and obscured the grace and beauty of my loveliness.

It is as though she said: “Do not attend so much to the things by which I am afflicted inwardly as to contemplate the flourishing beauty of my inner loveliness.” The Apostle says something similar: “Do not lose heart over my tribulations for your sake, which are your glory. For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

Jeremiah briefly comprehended this inward beauty and outward blackness when he said: “Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphires” (Lam. 4). Behold the beauty; but hear the blackness, for immediately he continues: “Their appearance was blacker than coal, and they were not recognized in the streets; their skin clung to their bones; it dried up and became like wood” (ibid.).

But let us consider the outward blackness; let it itself reveal the source of the inward beauty: “Tell me,” she says, “you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday” (Song 1). It is as though she said: “O heavenly bridegroom, whom my soul loves indescribably, in whom it continually rests through desire, whom it embraces in the arms of its inmost love, in whom it delights with all its inward being—tell me where you pasture,” that is, “You who are the good shepherd, where do you cause your sheep to pasture? And where do you lie down”—that is, where do you rest amid the heat of persecution and the fervor of our temptation? Where, unless among those who do not know how to yield to raging madness and do not weakly succumb to the assaults of rampant wickedness? Therefore this bride did not call herself beautiful without reason, because in the very crisis of persecution he delightfully rested in her, he who illumines all things by the serenity of his countenance.

## CHAPTER III. From a sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla

“My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will dwell between my breasts” (Song 1). Myrrh is plainly an aromatic substance of extreme bitterness, with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed so that they may not quickly decay. Hence the body of the Bridegroom himself, taken down from the cross by Nicodemus and Joseph, was embalmed with myrrh and aloe, wrapped in linen cloths, and committed to burial (John 19).

What, then, is signified by a bundle of myrrh, if not manifold mortification? For she does not say, “A sprig of myrrh,” but, “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” It is as though she said: “Because I mortify myself in all my conduct and now live by none of the works of my own will, my beloved has not become for me a single branch, but a bundle of myrrh.”

Hence the outstanding preacher also says: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6). He urges us to this manifold mortification as well, saying: “Always carrying in our body the mortification of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh” (2 Cor. 4). For, from the fact that we carry it in our body, we leave no part of the body empty. He, therefore, carries the mortification of Jesus in his body who leaves nothing of himself for himself, who lives not for himself but for Christ in all things, and who crucifies himself everywhere to his own desires.

This beloved, then, becomes a bundle of myrrh, because, presenting himself as though extinguished in all his actions, he gathers, in a certain sense, a manifold sheaf of Christ’s mortification. And aptly it is added: “He will dwell between my breasts.” No one doubts that the place of the heart is between the breasts. The beloved, therefore, will dwell between the bride’s breasts because his unfailing love and desire are not erased from her memory.

“He will dwell between my breasts,” as though she were saying: “He who became a bundle of myrrh to me through the bitterness of his passion will dwell continually between my breasts through the sweetness of my heart; and he who outwardly sharpens me through the example of the death he accepted sweetens me inwardly through the grace poured into me.”

## CHAPTER IV. From a sermon on the Nativity of Virgins

“I am the lily of the valleys” (Song 2). The Bridegroom plainly calls himself a lily on account of the snowy whiteness of his most pure chastity. He is the lily not of the mountains but of the valleys, because he chooses the devout minds of the humble and does not inhabit the crags of the proud.

## CHAPTER V

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered love in me” (Song 2). He does not say, “He gave what he did not find,” but “he ordered” what he found disordered. For some people place wives, children, estates, or honors in the chief place of their hearts; in a certain sense they put God second by loving him less. Such people certainly seem to possess love, but disordered love; nor do they preserve the order of love that Truth itself established when it said: “You shall love God with your whole heart”—that is, the greatest and first commandment—“and the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor” (Matt. 22).

Let no one, therefore, boast of possessing love if it is not ordered, just as neither should anyone boast of possessing faith if it is without works and therefore idle.

## CHAPTER VI

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2). The left is said to be under the head when the present life is despised and trampled underfoot by the mind, which is the head of our thoughts. She is held fast by the embraces of the right hand because she delights on every side in the desires of eternal life alone.

## CHAPTER VII

“Arise, my friend, my bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow of the wall; show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (Song 2).

The holy soul is rightly called Christ’s beloved and bride, because it is joined to him through faith and love. But this bride still lies, as it were, while she is entangled in worldly affairs; she rises when she is lifted up for the service of God. It is as though he said: “You who lie in the softness of secular life, arise now and raise yourself to the familiar fellowship of my contemplation.”

“My dove, in the clefts of the rock.” If, according to the Apostle, “the rock is Christ” (1 Cor. 10), the clefts of the rock are the wounds of the Redeemer. These are not five by chance—namely, the wound of the lance and those of the nails—but because we had been wounded by the five senses, through these five wounds we were restored to perpetual salvation.

These were the gates through which, on the Sabbath, the prophet forbade heavy burdens to be brought in. In these clefts, therefore, God’s dove abides, because every holy soul places the whole hope of its salvation in the passion of its Redeemer. There it is defended, as from the attack of a hawk, because it is guarded from all the snares of wicked spirits. There it plainly builds its nest, because there it heaps up the offspring of good works.

Of this rock the Psalmist says: “The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Ps. 103).

What is added—“in the hollow of the wall”—also deserves attention. Walls are usually made of stones for the protection of vineyards, as Isaiah says: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill; he surrounded it with a wall and dug it around” (Isa. 5). What, then, should we understand by a wall of stones, if not the protection and watchfulness of angels, by which the soul, placed in combat and enclosed and surrounded, is guarded from all the temptations of hostile spirits?

Moreover, when it follows, “Show me your face,” the soul is said to show its face to the heavenly Bridegroom when it contemplates his appearance with its inward eyes, as though with an unveiled face: “Let your voice sound,” he says, “in my ears; for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.” O what a delightful exchange—or rather, what indescribable sweetness arises in human hearts when Creator and creature delight in one another through mutual affections, as the prophet says: “May my praise be pleasing to him; but I will delight in the Lord!” (Ps. 103.)

## CHAPTER VIII

“Behold, Solomon’s couch: sixty strong men surround it, among the strongest of Israel” (Song 3). Strong men surround Solomon’s couch when all the saints, with unwearied perseverance of desire, guard the intimate and peaceful rest of our Redeemer.

## CHAPTER IX

“Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song 4). These are the eyes of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

“Apart from what lies hidden within.” Although the holy doctors now behold their Creator through the grace of contemplation, something great nevertheless still lies hidden—something toward which the vision of the human mind, in this corruptible flesh, cannot aspire.

Then it immediately follows: “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Gilead” (Song 4). Just as the eyes signify the teachers of the Church, who are appointed to see higher and particular things in the lower members, so the hair and flocks of goats signify the simple and subordinate members. Although, because of their simplicity, they do not penetrate certain mystical and exalted matters, they nevertheless adorn the holy Church by their multitude and comparison, like hair adorning the head; for often the figure of sin is removed because of sin.

Gilead means “heap of testimony.” Through Gilead, therefore, we understand Christ, to whom the multitude of all the saints bears witness. Through the hair, or the flocks of goats, we understand the multitude of the subordinate members. The flocks of goats therefore ascend from Mount Gilead because the multitude of all the saints strives to ascend to the heights of virtue from Christ, whom they make their foundation.

From this we can gather that just as there is a distance between the eyes and the hair, so there should be almost the same difference, in the pursuit of contemplation, between those who preside and those who are subordinate: the former should devote themselves to the spiritual pursuits of those entrusted to them and should see not only for themselves but also for them.

## CHAPTER X

“Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song 4). The teeth of the Church are recognized as her holy teachers, to whom it was first said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 2). It is as though he said: “Kill them with what you are—the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of preaching—and transfer them into the body of the Church.”

The teeth of the bride, therefore, are the holy teachers who, because they are simple through innocence, have left everything and been stripped of the fleeces of their possessions, and have been cleansed by the waters of sacred baptism. They are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.

## CHAPTER XI

“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle” (Song 4). Just as the two breasts are the two Testaments, so the two fawns are the two peoples, the children of the Church—namely, the Jewish people and the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XII. From a sermon on the Nativity of Virgins

“You are altogether beautiful, my beloved; altogether beautiful” (Song 4)—inwardly, that is, and outwardly: outwardly in the perfection of conspicuous action, inwardly in the purity of the most chaste thought.

## CHAPTER XIII. In a sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla

“You will be crowned from the summit of Sanir, from the peak of Amana and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4). Amana is a mountain of Cilicia, which many also call Taurus. Sanir and Hermon are mountains of the Jewish land, in which lions and leopards are believed to dwell.

Through these mountains, therefore, we are to understand the kings and princes and the various powers of this world, which raise themselves like mountains to the summit of pride and provide a dwelling place for wicked spirits as though for leopards and lions. Wicked spirits are called lions because of their cruelty; leopards because this animal is of varied color, and thus because of the manifold variety of deception and fraud.

From these mountains every faithful soul, or the holy Church, is crowned when it converts the rulers of the world to the faith or directs them toward the uprightness of holy conduct. It is crowned either because Christ rewards it for the gain brought by them, or because it is honored in the world by those by whom it had previously been oppressed.

It is crowned, I say, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards when it converts the proud and deceitful from their perversity and receives eternal rewards for their reformed conduct.

## CHAPTER XIV. From a sermon on the Nativity of Virgins

“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4). What is signified by the north wind, which is cold, if not the harshness of persecution? What by the seasons of the south wind, if not the relaxation of those who flatter wickedly?

But amid both kinds of persecution, amid both strategies of the evil spirit, the spices of the ecclesiastical garden are commanded to flow, because a brave spirit, caught in these struggles, reveals whatever strength, whatever faith, and whatever unconquered courage it had hitherto concealed. They flow outward like spices when virtues emerge into human knowledge and the fragrances of a good reputation spread far and wide.

## CHAPTER XV

“I sleep, but my heart is awake. The voice of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled, for my head is full of dew and my locks with drops of the night’” (Song 5).

The Church says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake,” because the more the holy mind withdraws itself from the noise of temporal desire, the more truly it perceives inward things; and the more vigilantly it watches over what is within, the more carefully it hides itself from outward disturbance.

The bride therefore sleeps with respect to the affairs and desires of the world, but keeps her eyes open and fully awake in the heat of the love of God. Yet because this is not a time of complete rest but rather of labor and struggle, the beloved suddenly knocks at the door and awakens her by his exhortations for the deployment of battle: “The voice,” he says, “of my beloved knocking.”

The beloved knocks when Christ urges his faithful either to increase their virtues or, certainly, to win the souls of their neighbors.

“Open to me, my sister.” She is a sister because she has become my co-heir in my kingdom and has been admitted into the relationship of my fraternal adoption.

“My beloved,” because, having been freed from the yoke of slavery, you have come to know the secrets of my truth.

“My dove,” because you are free from the bitterness of gall and enriched by the gift of my Spirit, who descended in the form of a dove.

“My undefiled,” because by the outpouring of my blood you have been cleansed from every stain of your sins.

Open, therefore, to me—that is, leave the rest and leisure of the contemplation you love, and devote yourself with the utmost fervor and steadfastness to bearing witness to my truth.

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” Christ’s head is God, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 11); his locks are the inmost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loosely and dissolved but are bound by the bond of the fear and love of God.

What, indeed, should we understand by dew and drops of the night, if not the dark and cold minds of certain reprobates? The bridegroom’s head is full of dew among the reprobates when worldly people grow numb toward the love of God and run down through the wantonness of their pleasures, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24).

When such people persecute and hate the saints of God, in their hearts they are like the bridegroom’s locks, full of drops of the night. And when such people multiply and burden the Church with persecutions, the Bridegroom exhorts the bride to rise and devote herself courageously to the work of preaching.

And the bride says to him: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5.) It is as though she said: “I have stripped myself of the cares and occupations of the world and confined myself solely within the love of contemplating you. How shall I now undertake the journey of wandering about? How shall I endure the noise and struggle of those who revile me?”

That the tunic signifies cares and anxieties is shown by the Lord when he says: “Let the one who is on the roof not descend to take up his tunic” (Matt. 24). This plainly means: “Let the one who stands upon the lofty height of contemplation not descend, so as to become entangled again in the occupations of worldly business.”

“I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5.) That is: “I have washed the steps of my conduct from the splashing of earthly dust with the worthy tears of repentance. How will I now be able to do anything except what I am accustomed to do—to meditate on heavenly things?”

Nevertheless, she postpones the rest of contemplation and, kindled inwardly with the fervor of obedience, immediately bears witness, saying: “My beloved sent his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (ibid.).

The beloved plainly puts his hand through the opening and touches the belly when the Creator visits the heart with a hidden inspiration and kindles it for the struggle of combat and holy labor. That the belly signifies the heart is shown by the prophet when he says: “I am in pain in my belly” (Jer. 4); and he reveals what this means when he adds: “The thoughts of my heart are scattered.”

“I rose to open to my beloved” (Song 5). She rises in order to open because, obedient with a most willing spirit, the holy mind tramples upon its own will so that it may fulfill the divine will with all its strength.

## CHAPTER XVI. In the letter to Blanca and in a sermon on Saints Flora and Lucilla

“My beloved is white and red, chosen from among thousands; his head is finest gold” (Song 5). The beloved is white through virginity and red through his passion. He is white because he says: “I am the lily of the valleys” (Song 2); red because John says of him: “He washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1).

“Chosen from among thousands,” because from the multitude of all the saints he alone was worthy to hear: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3, 12, 17). Concerning him Solomon also says: “I found one man among a thousand” (Eccl. 7).

The number one thousand is to be understood as the perfection of the whole human race, in which the Savior is like a single sparrow in a building: “His head is finest gold,” because “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). Just as gold surpasses other metals, so he, although incomparably so, surpasses all creatures.

## CHAPTER XVII

“His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, sitting beside overflowing streams” (Song 5). The holy teachers of the Church dwell beside the fullest streams of the Scriptures. From them they draw an overflowing flood of true wisdom and pour the secrets of heavenly mystery into their hearers.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In a sermon on Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist

“His belly is ivory, studded with sapphires” (Song 5). Among the members of the human body, scarcely anything is more fragile or tender than the belly. Therefore, by the belly, the fragility of the humanity assumed by Christ is rightly understood.

Ivory is the bone of an elephant, and this animal is said to be exceptionally chaste and of an extremely cold nature. The bridegroom’s belly, therefore, is ivory because the humanity assumed by the Redeemer remained entirely chaste and inviolate, untouched by every contagion of sin. For “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

Sapphire is a stone possessing the color of a clear sky. Hence it is said in the vision of the Lord: “Under his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24). Through sapphires, therefore, the works of divinity are understood, which the Lord displayed in the flesh.

The bridegroom’s belly was therefore studded with sapphires because Christ’s humanity shone with divine virtues. It is not said to be full of sapphires but studded with them, so that the whiteness of ivory might appear among the sapphires. Thus the Lord performed human acts in his assumed humanity, while at times nevertheless displaying divine acts by virtue of his deity.

For hunger, weeping, and finally crucifixion and death were works of his humanity; but performing miracles and raising not only others but even himself from the dead were unmistakable signs of his divinity.

## CHAPTER XIX

“His throat is most sweet” (Song 5), because the minds of his hearers are sweetened by the honeyed sweetness of his words. “How sweet are your sayings to my palate,” he says, “more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118.)

He is also altogether desirable, because, as Peter testifies, the angels desire to look into him (1 Pet. 1); or because the whole mystery of his humanity kindles desire in the minds of the elect, so that they are moved not only by the glory of his resurrection but also invited to imitate him by the very shame of his passion.

He is desirable because he is splendid and conspicuous in his unique birth, his life-giving death, his glorious resurrection, and his triumphal ascension. He is desirable when he speaks and when he performs wonders.

## CHAPTER XX. In a homily on the Nativity of Blessed Mary the Virgin

“I went down to the garden of nut trees to see the fruits of the valleys and to look whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had blossomed” (Song 6). The pomegranate is covered by a bitter rind, but sweetness is hidden in its grains.

There are some people who, while continually suffering the cross of Christ in their bodies through the bitterness of affliction, are refreshed in their minds by the sweetness of inward contemplation. The bridegroom’s pomegranates therefore blossom in the vine because the holy Church never ceases to produce such people.

Of this same vine the bride speaks to the bridegroom in the same Song, saying: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyard; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the blossoms are producing fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed” (Song 7).

He was the vintner of this vineyard who, pressed in the winepress of his passion, opened for us the mystical meanings of divine speech and offered us the wine of evangelical grace. Concerning this wine the bride again says to the bridegroom: “Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy of my beloved to drink” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXI. In a sermon on Saint Mark the Evangelist

“I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6). This is the voice of the Synagogue, which, seeing that such grace had been bestowed upon the holy Church, grieves that it received the faith so late, because it did not recognize the truth of the Gospel.

Aminadab is known to have been a great-grandson of Judah and is counted among the fathers in the genealogy of the Lord. *Aminadab* is interpreted as “spontaneous one of my people”; therefore it not unfittingly signifies Christ, who was spontaneous for his people, because, although he was God, he freely became human. For he who created us not from necessity but solely from goodness also redeemed us by his own will.

Hence James says: “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth” (Jas. 1). He became spontaneous for his people because the human perversity that rejected him was restored by the sole will of divine grace.

The chariot of Aminadab is the Gospel of Christ, constructed from the harmonious diversity of the four evangelists. Christ the charioteer directs this chariot and traverses the fourfold structure of the world with the swiftest speed of preaching, as the Psalmist says: “He sends his word to the earth; his word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147).

Seeing, therefore, the grace of evangelical preaching suddenly burst forth and swiftly pass through all the provinces of the world, the Synagogue, suddenly troubled, complains that it alone is being abandoned in its unbelief while the Gentiles are converted to the faith: “I did not know,” she says; “my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.”

## CHAPTER XXII

“Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups” (Song 7). The navel is the most fragile part of the body. What, then, is signified by the navel of the Church if not the assembly of the weak and infirm? And what should we understand by the bowl if not the order of preachers? They offer the wines of heavenly teaching to the minds of their hearers and intoxicate them with the cups of holy preaching.

The navel of the Church is therefore rightly compared to a bowl, because often some weak and infirm person becomes a vessel of heavenly doctrine. He does not lack wine because he does not cease to be watered by the streams of heavenly speech.

Hence this bowl is rightly called “turned.” A person works more easily with a lathe. Those who have received the grace of preaching not through their own efforts but from God often move through holy preaching more readily and without stumbling.

That this grace of preaching is to be granted to simple men or holy women was prefigured by the victory of Samson: when, inflamed with fury, he seized the jawbone of a donkey, he killed a thousand Philistine men.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Your locks are like royal purple joined to channels” (Song 7). Just as by the head we understand the mind, so by the locks of the head we appropriately understand thoughts. For just as hairs emerge from the crown of the head, so thoughts proceed from the mind.

The color purple, because it resembles blood, indicates by its mystery the Lord’s passion. What, then, do the channels signify if not the minds of the saints? Just as the blood of shellfish is poured into channels so that wool may be changed into a purple color, so the blood of the Lord’s passion is recalled through constant meditation in the minds of the saints. Thus every devout soul is, in a certain sense, dyed with blood so that it may imitate the purple of the eternal King.

In this way we become conformed to our Savior, so that afterward we may also be his co-heirs by merit.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“How beautiful and fair you are, most beloved, in delights; your stature is like a palm tree” (Song 7). The holy mind is called “most beloved in delights” because, while it is afflicted outwardly, worn down by persecutions, it is inwardly aflame with devout desires and refreshed by the sweetness of inward delight.

Its stature is said to resemble a palm tree because it is bent neither by the breezes of enticing vices nor by the terrors of any persecutions. When the rage of its persecutors strikes it as though with battering rams of threats, it remains firmly supported upon the foundation of unconquered faith and, truly standing and rising above them, perseveres unconquered.

It is by no means like the one to whom the prophet speaks concerning wicked spirits: “They humbled you and said to your soul: ‘Bend down, so that I may pass over you’” (Isa. 51). Rather, it preserves what the Lord said to the children of Israel: “I am the Lord God, who rescued you from the prison of the Egyptians, so that you might walk upright.”

And because a palm commonly adorns the hand of a victor, the holy and unconquered soul is rightly said to resemble a palm tree, because throughout the course of its struggle it contemplates the reward of the victory it has accomplished. For this reason it counts as nothing all that it endures among the weak, because, raised upright like a palm, it firmly hopes for what it beholds in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXV. In a sermon on the Finding of the Holy Cross

“I said,” the bridegroom says to the bride, “I will ascend the palm tree and seize its fruits; and your breasts will be like clusters of the vine, your fragrance like apples, and your throat like the finest wine” (Song 7).

The fruits of the cross are all the elect. The Lord therefore ascended the palm tree and seized its fruits because, as soon as he hung upon the cross for our salvation, he drew all the elect to himself through the desire of love.

Then the holy Church began, through the breasts of the two Testaments, to pour forth the wines of spiritual joy and to breathe the fragrance of heavenly desire into human minds, so that, stirred to follow, our mind might rejoice and say: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

## CHAPTER XXVI

“Under the apple tree I awakened you” (Song 8). After the bridegroom had said to his beloved bride, “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” he added: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (ibid.). It is as though he said: “Because I loved you so greatly that through the death of the cross I awakened you when you were dead, you too must love me in return and set me inwardly—not only in your thoughts but also in your works—as the seal of complete and perfect love.”

We should understand the apple tree as the Lord’s cross. Elsewhere he compares Christ himself to this tree, saying: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song 2).

The apple tree, therefore, is Christ’s cross, through which the soul was awakened, released from the bonds of eternal death.

“Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8). What is meant by the heart if not thought? What by the arm if not the strength of action?

We should therefore imprint Christ as a seal upon our heart, so that no hostile attack may be able to violate it. We should also engrave Christ upon our works, so that in everything we do we may show ourselves to be disciples of the crucified teacher.

## CHAPTER XXVII. In the letter to Blanca and in a sermon on Saint Cassian

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8). Often, to preserve the memory of something that we do not wish to consign to oblivion, we tie some sign around our finger or arm, so that, whenever the sign is noticed, the matter that might have been lost through forgetfulness may remain continually in our memory.

Whoever seems to love Christ but neglects to do good has, in a certain sense, already placed the bridegroom as a seal upon his heart. Whoever, however, appears devoted to good works but is cold and sluggish, lacking the fire of divine love, has placed an image of holiness upon his arm but has not yet impressed Christ’s seal upon his heart.

Therefore, so that the holy soul may be marked everywhere with Christ’s character, let it place him as a seal upon its heart, so that it may burn to the marrow with the flames of his love. Let it also place him upon its arm, so that it may devote itself courageously to good works.

Paul had placed Jesus as a seal upon his body, as upon his arm, when he said: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6). He had placed the seal upon his heart when elsewhere he joyfully said: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (ibid.).

He bore the marks of the one whose seal he gloried in possessing in his mind, and those marks were impressed upon his body.

Moreover, the heavenly Bridegroom himself places every one of his elect as a seal upon himself and, in gracious reciprocity, attends to him so that he may not be erased from his memory. This accords with what he promises Zerubbabel, ruler of Judah, saying: “On that day I will take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, and I will set you like a seal before me” (Hag. 2).

Conversely, concerning a certain reprobate king the Lord says: “Even if Jeconiah were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there” (Jer. 22).

The testimonies from the Song of Songs end here.

# BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF WISDOM

[Col. 1153]

1. That the spirit of wisdom is kind. 2. While all things kept profound silence.

The chapters end here.

247 # BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

[Col. 1153]

## CHAPTER ONE. In the book *Gratissimus* (“Most Gracious”)

[Col. 1153D]

“For the Spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and he will not release the accursed from his lips” (Wisdom 1). The Holy Spirit is rightly called benevolent, because he repays those deserving evil with good and bestows the gift of his grace upon those deserving punishment. But who should be understood here by the name “accursed” except our Redeemer, who, in order to free us from the bond of the curse, himself did not refuse to submit to curses? Hence Paul also says: “Christ,” he says, “redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’ (Galatians 3), so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith” (Deuteronomy 21).

The benevolent Holy Spirit, therefore, did not release the accursed from his lips, because he effectively fulfilled, at the appointed time through the performance of deeds, all the punishments of the Lord’s passion and death that he had previously foretold concerning Christ through the mouths of the prophets. For he would in some sense have released him from his own lips if he had not fulfilled in the order of events whatever he had proclaimed about him through prophetic oracles.

Here one should observe how profoundly and mystically, and at the same time how fittingly, the statements of the two teachers agree. For what one said—that the Spirit would not release the accursed from his lips—is the same as what the other asserted: that we receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. And to show of what curse the Wise Man was speaking, he immediately added: “For God is witness to his kidneys, and the true examiner of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue” (Wisdom 1).

Because the unity of the Father and the Son is inseparable and consubstantial, the Father is rightly asserted to be witness of the Son’s kidneys and examiner of his heart. The Son himself is truly the Father’s power and wisdom, believed to differ from him by no inequality and shown to be separated from him by no addition. He is also the hearer of his tongue, as he himself testifies: “Father,” he says, “I give you thanks because you have heard me; I knew, however, that you always hear me” (John 11).

Therefore the Spirit did not release the accursed from his lips because God is witness and examiner of his heart and the hearer of his tongue. It is as though he were saying plainly: The Son of God endured the punishments of the Passion because the Son himself, whose will and providence are one with those of the Father and of the same Holy Spirit, decreed that this should happen for the salvation of the human race. Concerning him the Apostle says: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Galatians 2).

## CHAPTER II. In the second sermon on Saint Bartholomew the Apostle

“While all things held the middle silence, and night was halfway through its course, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from heaven, from the royal seats” (Wisdom 18).

At the Lord’s coming, all things held the middle silence because the prophets had already ceased, while the apostles had not yet come to preach the grace of the new faith. The world was plainly standing at a kind of midpoint, since the oracles of the prophets no longer remained and apostolic preaching had not yet shone forth.

What is understood here by “night” except the devil, who is the author of darkness? He walks, so to speak, when he cannot easily accomplish what he desires; but he runs when he fulfills the wishes of his malice without any obstacle of contradiction and occupies not the edge of the road but its middle, when he sees nothing confronting him that might delay the force of his course.

When, therefore, the world was silent under such a deadly silence, and this opportunity for destroying human beings summoned the devil, he not only occupied the middle of the road but also ran, because he effectively accomplished whatever his wickedness had conceived in his mind. For he already occupied the whole Roman Empire, and it was necessary that those who had hitherto at least in some fashion held to the law of God should now be subject to the laws of the pagans.

Thus, amid this silence of the perishing world, the Lord’s Word came from the royal seats, because the word of evangelical preaching burst forth from the apostles’ breasts, which are truly the seats of the eternal King. They are indeed royal seats, those whom God inhabits; they are kings and Fathers of the Church, as it is said: “All her glory is within, the daughter of kings” (Psalm 44).

These kings, armed with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6), defeated the prince of the world. Concerning this sword of the apostles it is written: “A harsh warrior leapt into the midst of the land of destruction, a sharp sword bearing your unfeigned command; standing, he filled everything with death, and, standing on earth, he reached even to heaven” (Wisdom 18).

[Column 1155] The testimonies from the Book of Wisdom end here.

# THE CHAPTER FROM THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICUS BEGINS

[Column 1155]

## A SINGLE CHAPTER. In the second sermon on Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist

[Column 1155C]

“Moses gave the law in commandments of righteousness, and an inheritance to the house of Jacob, and promises to Israel” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

To avoid dwelling longer on these words, this law, which is called the inheritance of promise, is the holy Gospel. It was promised to the ancient Fathers, but, when Christ came, it was bestowed upon us by hereditary right. Immediately afterward it says: “He appointed David, his servant, to raise up from himself a most mighty king, seated forever on the throne of honor. He fills wisdom like the Pishon, and like the Tigris in the days of new growth; he fills understanding like the Euphrates; he multiplies it like the Jordan at harvest time; he sends instruction like light, and, standing by, like the Gihon in the day of vintage” (ibid.).

These things, then, my brothers, are said so clearly and openly about Christ and the holy evangelists that they do not need exposition to make this known. But when, in these holy and mystical words, you hear the name “vintage,” you who, because of the season, have earthly vintages before your eyes ought to pass from what is outward to what is inward and consider in your wisdom the spiritual vintage.

For at the end of the statement he says: “He sends instruction like light, and, standing by, like the Gihon in the day of vintage” (ibid.). Who is he who sends instruction like light except the one who, after Moses’ face had been veiled, casts the radiance of his Gospel upon a world possessed by darkness?

He therefore stands by like the Gihon, concerning which the Prophet also says: “The Lord our God is a river leaping forth more gloriously onto thirsty ground” (ibid.). And what is the vineyard beside which he stands like the Gihon, and which he never ceases to irrigate with the moisture of his preaching, except that vineyard of which the Prophet says: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5)?

The Lord transferred this vineyard from Egypt, the realm of the old law, and brought it into the land of the Gospel, which flows with milk and honey.

[Column 1155] The testimonies from the Book of Ecclesiasticus end here.

[Column 1157]

1. Concerning what is said: “And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles.”  
2. That the day of the Lord is against every proud person.  
3. That the Seraphim, having six wings each, flew before the face of God.  
4. “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones.”  
5. “I will set a lion over those who were of Moab. Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”  
6. That the vision of all will be like the words of a sealed book.  
7. “The beast of the field, dragons, and ostriches will glorify me, because I have given waters in the desert.”  
8. “Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he will give the wicked one for his burial and the rich man for his death.”  
9. “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?”  
10. “Shall I, who make others give birth, myself not give birth?” says the Lord.

The chapters end here.

# THE TESTIMONIES BEGIN

[Column 1157]

## CHAPTER I

[Column 1157A]

“And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isaiah 2).

For those who resist, admonitions are like swords; but if they wish these swords to be turned into sickles, the bristling thickets of their vices, which make them rough and wild, must be changed into harvests. Hence, after the prophet had first said concerning our Savior, “He shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples,” he immediately added: “And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (ibid.).

The order is surely appropriate: first the sinner is rebuked, and then the swords are beaten into ploughshares and the spears into sickles. For when someone who is impatient has been made gentler through discipline, like a level field cut open by the knife of reproof, he is then sprinkled with the sweet seed of holy preaching, and finally clothed with the fruitful harvest of good works. Thus, for him, swords have been made into ploughshares and spears have been changed into sickles: the one who previously considered being rebuked as though struck by a sword now willingly endures the ploughshare of sacred teaching so that he may produce crops, and awaits the sickle of the heavenly harvest so that he may fill the storehouse of the celestial granary.

## CHAPTER II. In the letter to Blanca

“The day of the Lord is against every proud and lofty person, against every arrogant person, and he shall be humbled; and against all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, and against all the oaks of Bashan, and against all the high mountains, and against all the raised hills, and against every lofty tower, and against every fortified wall, and against all the ships of Tarshish, and against everything beautiful to behold” (Isaiah 2).

The day of divine judgment is said to threaten things without sensation, but through figures drawn from things lacking reason, the stupidity of reprobate human beings is understood. The lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon are the powerful of this age: exalted by the excellence of earthly eminence, but barren of the fruits of good works.

Oaks do indeed produce fruit, but not fruit by which human beings are refreshed; rather, fruit by which swine are fed. The swine are understood as unclean spirits, which are fattened on the filth of sordid human beings.

The high mountains and raised hills are every proud person, stretched upward as though by the accumulation of swollen thought, but alien to the grain with which the valleys abound (Psalm 64) and to all the fruits of spiritual pursuits.

The lofty tower and fortified wall represent those who, although they are sinners, establish themselves as if in a citadel of innocence and, covering themselves with the shield of defense, do not allow the arrows of their critics to reach them.

“Tarshish” means “investigation of joy.” For whoever searches in this age for something from which he may rejoice, when the day of the Lord comes upon him it inflicts the troubles of sorrow and sadness, by which he will be made perpetually bitter.

The day of the Lord also comes not upon everything that is beautiful, but upon everything that is beautiful to behold, because on the day of divine judgment the person is weighed down who inwardly is disfigured by the hidden ugliness of vices that have stealthily invaded him, while outwardly he is covered by a certain shadowy beauty of virtue—or rather, of propriety.

## CHAPTER III. To Olderic, Bishop of Firmin

Whatever human mind, supported by sound counsel, possesses vigor, if it examines itself subtly and diligently, scarcely finds within its own resources anything from which it can reasonably hope for praise. Mortal existence is hemmed in and constrained on every side: what does it know from which it might be exalted?

Who, indeed, knows what will have existed in eternity before God created this world? Yet, although it does not know what existed before the beginning of the world, it perhaps knows what will happen after its end—namely, whether the stars will continue to serve in the ministry of their course, and whether, after the elements that now exist, other elements will in turn succeed them.

Therefore the prophet Isaiah describes those Seraphim whom he saw standing in the presence of the Lord as having six wings: “With two,” he says, “they covered the face, with two they covered the feet, and with two they flew” (Isaiah 6).

They covered the face and the feet, not their own, but certainly God’s. And what should be understood by the face of God except the beginning of the world? What by his feet except the end of that same world?

The Seraphim’s wings are therefore more numerous in those that cover than in those that fly, because, although a very small number of divine works are permitted to fly into our knowledge from the height of God’s works, very many are kept hidden in the treasuries of heavenly secrets.

For Isaiah also testifies that we are utterly ignorant of what existed before the beginning of the world and of what will be after its completion: “Declare to me,” he says, “the former things and the last things that are to come, and I will say that you are gods” (Isaiah 41).

Of the intermediate matters we know something, however imperfectly, insofar as they are disclosed to us by the testimony of the Scriptures. But even in these matters, how great an insufficiency of knowledge we suffer was not denied by the wisest of human beings. Solomon says: “There are righteous and wise people whose works are in the hand of God; yet a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything is kept uncertain for the future” (Ecclesiasticus 9).

Here one should note that, although he speaks of the righteous and the wise—who surely ought to know more subtly—he nevertheless declares that even they are ignorant of what is to come.

## CHAPTER IV. In the letter to Hermisind, that the structure of human pride is quickly destroyed

[Column 1159B]

Those who, having despised the structure of earthly conduct and desire, build the fabric of a spiritual building turn bricks into stone; and they establish halls that will never fall, not on the sand of worldly hope but on the rock of faith, which is Christ.

Hence Isaiah says: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones; they have cut down sycamores, but we shall change them into cedars” (Isaiah 9).

Whoever chastises the wantonness of vices and pleasures with the rigor of a stricter life builds with glowing bricks and squared stones. He overcomes the law of the flesh by the law of the spirit; he transforms bodily strength through the strength of the soul.

Hence Isaiah says again: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” (Isaiah 40). For by saying not “they will assume” but “they will change,” he clearly made known that there is one strength which is laid aside and another which is newly begun.

To the elect the Psalmist says: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 30). Solomon says: “Behold, Solomon’s bed is surrounded by sixty strong men, among the strongest of Israel” (Song of Songs 3).

## CHAPTER V. In the book Against the Jews

Isaiah, bearing witness concerning Christ, says: “I will set a lion over those who were of Moab and over the remnant of the earth. Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 15–16).

For from this nation of the Moabites the immaculate Lamb went forth, the one who takes away the sins of the world and rules over the whole earth. For the one who is called a lion because of his strength is also described as a lamb because of his gentleness.

The rock of the desert is understood as Ruth, who, left desolate by the death of her former husband, bore Obed from Boaz (Matthew 1); from their lineage Christ descended.

## CHAPTER VI. In the sermon on Saint Luke the Evangelist

“And the vision of all will be for you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isaiah 29).

For what is that sealed book except the holy Gospel, wrapped in mystical meanings and removed far from the understanding of the human mind by a certain hidden profundity?

This is certainly the book of which John says: “I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” (Revelation 5).

And what are the seals with which the Gospel book is said to be sealed except those seven sacraments by which the whole order of the Lord’s dispensation is fulfilled: namely, the Lord’s incarnation, birth, Passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, then judgment, and finally kingdom?

The Gospel book is sealed with these seals in such a way that, unless Christ had opened it, it could not be accessible to anyone at all. Hence it continues: “Behold, the lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered so as to open the book and loose its seven seals” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VII. In the same letter

“The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches, because I have given waters in the desert, rivers in the trackless place, to give drink to my people, my chosen one” (Isaiah 43).

For what does the beast of the field signify except the Gentiles, certainly devoid of reason? What do the dragons signify except the malicious? And what are represented by the ostriches, which have wings but cannot fly, except hypocrites?

These beasts therefore glorify God when Christ offers the words of the overflowing Gospel to the Gentile people, which had been deserted and was without a path.

The cup of evangelical preaching was therefore given to Paul in Benjamin, so that he might cultivate the desert of the Gentiles in a particular way and drench its dryness with the abundant rain of holy preaching. Concerning this rain it is written: “He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth” (Psalm 146).

## CHAPTER VIII. In the letter to Alberic, Cardinal, concerning ten questions

That passage of Isaiah which you ask me to explain—“Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he will give the wicked one for his burial and the rich man for his death” (Isaiah 52)—seems to us to have this meaning:

The almighty Father struck the Son because of the sins of his people, since he ordained that, in order to erase our sins, he should undergo the gallows of the cross. For this purpose the Son was handed over by the Father, so that the servant might become liberated, as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8).

For this purpose the innocent one was struck with wounds, so that the sinner might rejoice, healed from the bruising of his own wounds. As it is said through the same Isaiah: “He was wounded for our iniquities, he was crushed for our crimes, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53).

But our Redeemer deigned to suffer for two peoples, namely the Gentile and the Jewish peoples, one of whom was rightly called wicked and the other rich.

The Gentile people were indeed wicked because, serving idols, they did not know the piety of divine worship. This piety is called in Greek *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια), “reverence for God.”

The Jewish people, however, had been rich because, having received the Sabbaths, circumcision, new moons, and all the ceremonies of the divine law, they abounded as though in the plentiful riches of a heavenly treasury.

Paul, already converted, rejoiced that the Corinthians overflowed with these riches when he said: “I always give thanks to my God for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (1 Corinthians 1).

Our Savior therefore, for the death that he took upon himself, returned to the Father two peoples raised from death: the Gentile people, who had formerly served demons impiously, and the Jewish people, who, although holding the letter that kills and not knowing the Spirit that gives life, nevertheless possessed the riches of the divine law.

## CHAPTER IX. In the homily on the birth of the holy Virgin Mary

“Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” And shortly afterward: “Why, then, is your clothing red, and your garment like that of those who tread in the winepress?” (Isaiah 63).

The clothing of Christ is nothing other than the body that he assumed from the Lady and Virgin Mary. Yet his garment is not one thing and he himself another. For our clothing too is called flesh, yet we ourselves are flesh—the flesh with which we are clothed.

Concerning this garment John says: “He had written on his garment and on his thigh: ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’” (Revelation 19). For propagation of flesh takes place through the thigh.

Therefore he who now came into the world through the propagation of the human race from the Virgin, and who through the mystery of his incarnation made known to all the nations that he was King and Lord, had written on his garment and thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” Where he became known to the world, there he inscribed the knowledge of his majesty.

This garment appeared red to the prophet because our Redeemer poured out his own blood for our redemption. To him he himself replied: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and no man from the nations was with me” (Isaiah 63).

He alone trod the winepress in which he was trampled, because by his own power he conquered the Passion that he endured. For although he bore the gallows of the cross even unto death, he rose again from death itself in glory.

It is rightly said: “And no man from the nations was with me” (ibid.), because those for whom he had come to suffer ought to have shared in his Passion. On account of the fact that they had not yet believed, he complains about those whose life was being sought in his death.

## CHAPTER X. In the letter to Cunibert, Bishop of Turin, concerning the continence of clerics

Among pastors, chastity is rightly judged useless when it presents itself as barren, producing no other chastity—especially since the almighty God himself says through Isaiah: “Shall I, who make others give birth, myself not give birth?” says the Lord (Isaiah 66).

Here one should note that, since he says “I make others,” not “other women,” give birth, he is looking particularly for offspring from men and pastors of the Church.

But the evil pastor can lamentingly sing with the same prophet: “I have not labored in childbirth, I have not given birth, I have not nourished young men, nor brought virgins to maturity” (Isaiah 23).

[Column 1161] The testimonies from Isaiah end here.
