3. Concerning what is said: “The partridge brooded over what it did not hatch; it acquired riches, and not in judgment; in the middle of its days it will leave them, and at its end it will be a fool.”  
4. That the Lord says through Jeremiah: “Are my words not like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer crushing a rock?”  
5. That the Lord threatens the inhabitants of Jerusalem with sword, famine, and pestilence because they did not listen to the prophets whom he had sent to them.  
6. That, when Jeremiah is lifted from the well into which he had been thrown, ropes and old rags are lowered to him.  
7. “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood.”  
8. “He has made me drunk with wormwood.”  
9. “From the mouth of the Most High neither good nor evil has gone forth.”  
10. “The sons of Hagar, who sought wisdom, which is of the earth, the way of wisdom.”

The chapters of Jeremiah end here.

# THE TESTIMONIES BEGIN

[Column 1161]

## CHAPTER I. In the letter to P., archpriest, where he speaks of the soul’s departure from the body

[Column 1161D]

“Behold, I will summon all the clans of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord; and they will come, and each will set up his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its surrounding walls, and upon all the cities of Judah; and I will speak my judgments with them concerning all the wickedness of those who abandoned me” (Jeremiah 1).

These words would certainly not resound today in the holy Church if they referred to no one except the earthly citizens of Jerusalem.

What, then, are those clans of the kingdoms of the north except the multitudes of evil spirits, reigning arrogantly in minds so cold? Each of these sets up its throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem when, surrounding the unhappy soul as it departs from the body with a siege so that it may not go forth free, they hold it captive in order to drag it with them now to the punishment of fire—into the cold mind in which they had previously reigned.

Oh, how sorrowful, how mournful is that late and fruitless repentance, when the sinful soul, already beginning to be released from the prison of the flesh in which it was confined, looks behind itself and directs its eyes before itself!

Behind itself it sees, as it were, the extremely narrow and very brief course of mortal life that it has traversed; before itself it sees the length of the endless ages. It weighs how the briefest moment of time, in which it lived, flew past swiftly, and contemplates the infinite expanse of time that is approaching and that it is beginning.

What is brief passes like a point; but no end at all meets the road that it now enters.

## CHAPTER II. In the letter to P., archpriest, concerning the continence of clerics

“Go,” the Lord said to Jeremiah, “and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth, and place it upon your loins” (Jeremiah 13). Concerning it, shortly afterward: “Rise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole in the rock.”

When he had done this and hidden it in the Euphrates, as he had been commanded, after many days the Lord said to him: “Rise and go to the Euphrates, and take the loincloth from there. And I went,” he says, “to the Euphrates and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it; and behold, it had rotted, so that it was fit for no use.” And the Lord said: “Thus I will cause the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem to rot: this very evil people, who do not wish to hear my words, who walk in the perversity of their heart. They will be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use” (ibid.).

What does Jeremiah’s person signify here except the Lord? What does the loincloth signify except the order of clerics?

The whole Church is Christ’s garment, concerning whose members the Prophet says: “You will clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49). But just as the loincloth is intimate to the human body and clings more closely to it than the other garments, so the clerical order is joined more familiarly to divine service than other people are.

Thus the divine voice says there concerning the people of Israel: “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I joined to myself the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, so that it might be my people, my name, my praise, and my glory; but they did not listen” (Jeremiah 13).

To whom, I ask, can these words correspond so aptly and explicitly as to clerics, who have been specially appointed to preach the name, praise, and glory of God?

Just as Israel and Judah were God’s particular people among all the nations of the earth, so now clerics cling specially to Christ before all the members of the Church. These are the linen loincloth joined to the divine body by a closer familiarity.

Linen reaches whiteness only through labor. Likewise, clerics, sometimes laboring at literary studies and sometimes ascending through certain grades over intervals of time, are promoted with difficulty to the dignity of the sacred order.

Otherwise, if someone insists too contentiously that this happened only historically, according to the sequence of Scripture, and is not to be understood spiritually, how could Jeremiah have gone out, girded with a loincloth, among the countless nations of the Assyrians and Chaldeans that were besieging Jerusalem with massed forces, and hidden it in the Euphrates, which flows so far away?

Later, after such a long passage of time had been exhausted, how could he have returned with relative safety and found it rotten, as Scripture testifies, when Jerusalem was surrounded on every side by a ditch, a rampart, fortresses, and such frequent fortifications?

For when that same prophet once attempted to leave for his own village of Anathoth, situated three miles from the city, he was immediately seized at the gate, dragged before the officials, severely beaten, and thrown into prison as a deserter or traitor to his country (Jeremiah 32).

Therefore, since it does not follow that the event should be understood historically, there is no doubt that the mystery of a typical figure is present. The choir of clerics is therefore well represented by the linen loincloth, in accordance with what has been said above.

But what is signified by the command that this loincloth be placed in the Euphrates—that is, in a watery place—and in a hole in the rock, that is, in darkness and shadow, except that part of the clerics which remains under the shadow of pleasure and in the flow of lust?

Concerning their leader the Lord says in the Book of Job: “He sleeps beneath the shadow, in the secrecy of reeds and in damp places. The shadows protect his shadow; the willows of the torrent surround him” (Job 40). And to show how much he delights, together with his companions, in dwelling by the river, he immediately added: “Behold, he will swallow the river and will not marvel; for he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”

As for the statement that it was placed in a hole in the rock, this can suitably be understood as within the enclosures of the Church. For clerics are shut up, as it were, in a hole in the rock when they are commanded to keep watch over their ministries within the thresholds of the Church through diligent attendance.

The loincloth placed in a damp place therefore rotted, because concerning those who remain in the flows of lust the prophet testifies: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1). Beasts rot in their dung when carnal and filthy people enclose their lives in the stench of lust.

It was found fit for no use because the Lord also says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

It is as though he were saying plainly: Whoever, according to the rule dictated by his order, once takes up the ploughshare of chastity, if afterward, inflamed by lust, he turns his eyes back toward Sodom, because he has now despaired of the mountains, shows that he has been made entirely useless for the kingdom of God.

Thus clerics rot like a loincloth placed in a damp place when they fill their damp bellies with gluttony and drunkenness, when they flood themselves with the filth of lust and the muddy streams of debauchery, and so become useless for every purpose. For the more they seem to flourish in the flesh, the more deplorably they wither and grow old in the foulness of their squalid soul.

Concerning them the Psalm says: “They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their pleasures” (Psalm 13).

## CHAPTER III. In the letter to P., abbot

“The partridge brooded over what it did not hatch; it acquired riches, and not in judgment; in the middle of its days it will leave them, and at its end it will be a fool” (Jeremiah 17).

Apart from the fact that this may be understood of those who steal the foster-children of others, it nevertheless appears to be said principally of the author of all wickedness.

For the devil, like a teacher in the chair of pestilence, usurped mastery over human beings whom he himself did not create; and by teaching them error he fostered them, as it were, though he did not give them birth by creating them.

He therefore acquired riches, and not in judgment, because, wishing to grow rich through things belonging to another’s right, he violated the judgment of equity. But in the middle of his days he will leave them.

For the devil is, as it were, still alive, since the sword of the last judgment has not yet pierced him. Though not yet dead, he already leaves his riches, because the human race has now returned in large part to its Creator.

At his end he will be a fool, whom, as the Apostle says, “the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 1). And the prophet says: “With the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked one” (Isaiah 11).

A human being therefore abandons the deceptive teacher and returns to the rightful one when he condemns the new error and returns to the origin of his own creation.

Hence the passage aptly continues: “The throne of glory on high from the beginning, the place of our sanctification, the hope of Israel” (Jeremiah 17).

God, then, who is the beginning of glory, is himself the hope of Israel, because the human race returns through the mystery of its creation to the one from whom it came forth.

The one who sat from the beginning on the throne of glory on high and taught humanity is himself the hope of Israel, so that in the place of our sanctification—that is, in the holy Church—he may teach that same humanity again.

Hence the Psalmist says: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence” (Psalm 21).

Whoever, therefore, by violating faith takes away another’s disciple undoubtedly imitates the example of the Antichrist. And just as the devil, like the partridge, loses what belongs to another, so this person, when judgment intervenes, will not retain what he has usurped.

## CHAPTER IV. In the letter to cardinal bishops

It is not enough for someone, after being snatched away by the devil, to turn to God with pious devotion, unless he is immediately also crushed in the hardness of his former condition, as though by the frequent hammer of holy preaching.

Hence Jeremiah says: “Are my words not like fire, says the Lord, and like a hammer crushing a rock?” (Jeremiah 23).

The Lord’s words are like fire because they drive out coldness and introduce warmth into minds; they are a hammer because they soften the hardness of obstinacy and stubbornness.

## CHAPTER V. In the letter to P., archpriest, concerning the soul’s departure from the body

[Column 1166A]

“Behold,” says the Lord, “I will send against them”—that is, against the inhabitants of Jerusalem—“the sword, famine, and pestilence, and they shall become a curse, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach.” He explains why this happened when he adds: “Because they did not listen,” he says, “to my words, which I sent to them through my servants the prophets, rising early and sending” (Jer. XXIX). By saying “rising early,” he indicates the solicitude and speed of the one who sends, so that the sluggishness of negligence may be found not in the preachers of the word but rather in their hearers.

Since almighty God, speaking to human beings in human fashion, complains that he rose early and thereby, as it were, interrupted his sleep, what reproach might he bring against us if, placed in the final peril of necessity, he were deservedly to answer us as follows: “For your sake, although I was the Creator, I became a creature; for your sake I endured mockery and reproaches; I underwent the cross and passed through all the torments that were owed to you. Yet you did not listen to me, and you despised the ceremonies and commandments of my law.” If he reproached them for despising servants sent by him, how much more terribly will he reproach us for despising himself? If he reproached them for interrupted sleep, how much more can he reproach us with having died and been buried for our sake?

God does not free the Jews, shut up under the siege of surrounding enemies, because they despised the servants sent by him to them: [Col. 1166C] how, then, will he hear Christians who have despised the evangelical commandments sent through his Son? For whoever does not listen to God is not heard by God.

There is one matter that every faithful mind ought constantly and diligently to consider and investigate within itself with anxious inquiry: namely, whether what it has done pleases God, and whether God takes delight in its life or works. For what benefit is there in whatever a person does if it does not please God? Thus it is said of David: “God sought for himself a man according to his heart” (II Kings III; Acts XIII). For if the Creator now takes no delight in a human being, that person will afterward be unable to take delight in the Creator.

Hence we read in the *Life of the Fathers* that when a certain false, celebrated solitary of great reputation was approaching death, a hellish spirit came to him carrying a fiery trident in its hands. And behold, a voice came to it, saying: “Just as this soul did not permit me to rest in it even for one hour, so neither should you show it mercy by tearing it out.” Then the wicked spirit drove the fiery trident into the dying man’s heart and, as it had been commanded, tore out his soul.

### CHAPTER VI. In the letter to the brothers of Sanvicinus, in which he exhorts them to patience

There are two things which, if we watchfully consider them, enable us easily to overcome the insolence and vexing injuries of any violent persons: namely, precepts and examples. For the holy Scriptures exhort us to repentance, and all the elect have patiently endured whatever could be inflicted by the enraged members of the devil.

That we are rescued from the depth of the tribulation inflicted upon us with the help of divine admonitions and the examples of those who came before us is rightly signified by the prophet Jeremiah’s emerging from the pit: “For,” as Scripture testifies, “they had thrown him into a cistern in which there was no water, but mud; afterward, when he was to be lifted out, ropes and old rags were lowered to him” (Jer. XXXVIII).

What are signified by the ropes, if not the Lord’s commandments? Since they both convict and rescue us when we are placed in evil conduct, they as it were bind and draw us, constrain and lift us. But lest someone bound by these ropes be cut as he is being pulled up, old rags are lowered along with them: for, so that the divine commandments may not terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers strengthen us, [Col. 1167B] so that by comparing ourselves with them we may dare to do what, because of our weakness, we fear to do.

If, then, we hasten to be lifted from this depth of a life afflicted by tribulation, let us be bound by ropes—that is, let us be restrained by the Lord’s commandments. Let old rags also be present, by which the ropes may be held more securely: that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who came before us, lest subtle commandments wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while they lift us up.

The apostle Paul added certain old rags when, in order to raise up his disciples, he commended to them the examples of the ancients together with his spiritual commandments, saying: “The righteous experienced mockeries and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested; they died by the sword” (Heb. XI). And shortly afterward: “Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every burden and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with patience toward the contest set before us” (Heb. XII). And again: “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; contemplating the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Heb. XIII).

Earlier, when he spoke of spiritual commandments, he had, as it were, sent down ropes; afterward, when he recalled the examples of the elders, he supplied old rags.

Indeed, a servant of God ought to fear when he receives something temporal, and rejoice when he loses it; for one whose purpose is to ascend to heaven will undoubtedly proceed more easily empty than burdened.

### CHAPTER VII. In the letter to Pope N., concerning the incontinent clergy

[Col. 1167D]

Just as those who correct faults are worthy of blessing, so likewise those who flatter sinners are subject to a curse, as the prophet says: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII). He restrains his sword from blood who restrains himself from inflicting upon the wicked the punishment of a deserved sentence.

A person indeed bears the guilt of a deed when he neglects to correct what he can. Hence the man of God said to the aforementioned Eli, who is also thought to have been Phinehas: “Thus says the Lord: Why have you spurned my sacrifice with your heel, and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and have honored your sons more than me?” (I Kings II).

If Eli perished, together with his two sons and with so great a multitude of people, because he did not rebuke those sons with the severity they deserved, what sentence do we suppose those deserve who sit in the ecclesiastical court and on judges’ thrones, yet remain silent concerning the notorious crimes of wicked people? While they fear publicly to dishonor human beings, they bring the commandments of divine law into disrepute, to the insult of the heavenly Judge.

### CHAPTER VIII. In the letter to Hermisindus

“He has intoxicated me with wormwood” (Lam. III). An intoxicated person scarcely knows what he endures, as though possessed or almost out of his mind. Thus, when any perverse person frenziedly desires the profits of the world, though he is oppressed by so many labors, he does not feel the evils he suffers, because he is led with pleasure toward all the things by which he is wearied in punishment.

### CHAPTER IX. In the letter to Alberic, cardinal, concerning ten questions

Finally, what you ask about the meaning of the prophet Jeremiah’s statement—“From the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good things or evil things” (Lam. VIII)—is a famous question, almost the question of the whole Church. Many ask it, and it is widely repeated on the lips of many. But through the generosity of him “who opens the book and loosens its seals” (Rev. V), this question is easily resolved, if confidence is placed not in ourselves but in him.

The almighty Father both handed over his innocent Son to the hands of the impious and yet did not depart from the straight path of justice; for he determined that justice should flourish from the very place where he permitted him for a time to be subjected to injustice. As it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “Since you are just,” it says, “you order all things; you even condemn one who ought not to be punished” (Wis. XII).

The Father therefore permitted the Son to undergo death, but he did not command his killers to destroy him. Otherwise they would have been guiltless, since they would have ascribed the ministry of wickedness to the author of piety. God therefore granted power to Christ’s persecutors, but he did not command them to kill him by persecuting him.

Hence the prophet first says there: “The Lord did not know how to pervert a man in his judgment.” The Lord would pervert a man in his judgment if he commanded an innocent person to be condemned. But it is one thing to condemn, and another not to rescue from the punishment of condemnation; one thing to drive people raging into sacrilegious attempts, and another not at all to restrain the madness of an anger that has been admitted.

Therefore the text continues—not by ignorance, but by rejection: “Who is this who has said that it should happen, when the Lord has not commanded it?” He says that the Lord did not command it, though he did not forbid it. God therefore did not command the persecutors to crucify our Savior, because he found nothing in him that deserved punishment. Yet he did not prevent him from being crucified, because he did not in any way free him from the hands of the impious, since he was to suffer for the salvation of the world.

Hence the text immediately adds appropriately: “From the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good things or evil things.” Good things would proceed if he rescued him from the punishment inflicted upon him; evil things would proceed if he found in him a crime for which he ought to be assigned to punishment.

In Christ’s Passion, therefore, neither good things nor evil things proceed from the mouth of the Most High: the Father neither frees him by an exercise of power nor condemns him according to the equity of the law. Although he does not find him a sinner, he nevertheless does not rescue the innocent man placed in his Passion for the salvation of the world. He sees him subject to no sins, yet he does not return him acquitted from the hands of the impious, so that while the innocent man undergoes punishment, the one who is a sinner may return to pardon; and while one who does not owe the debt pays the debts of all, all who were held bound by the interest on the original ancient bond may, once the written bond has been canceled, be restored free under the law.

### CHAPTER X. In the letter to Boniface, that spiritual wisdom should be preferred to external prudence

[Col. 1170A]

Just as heavenly wisdom makes people heavenly and legitimate children of the Church, so earthly prudence makes them earthly and illegitimate. Of these Baruch says: “The children also of Hagar, who sought the prudence that is from the earth—the merchants of the earth, and Teman, and the storytellers and seekers after prudence—did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they remember her paths” (Baruch III).

Those who desire to attain worldly prudence and despise spiritual wisdom are therefore children of Hagar, not of Sarah; and, having become illegitimate, they ought rightly to be judged not Israelites. Since Hagar is interpreted as “stranger,” they are not children of wisdom but [Col. 1170B] strangers and foreigners. They do not belong to those of whom the Apostle said: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II).

[Col. 1169] Here end the testimonies from Jeremiah.

### HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE BOOKS OF THE PROPHETS

[Col. 1169]

### CHAPTER I. In the letter to Bishop V.

[Col. 1169C]

“The whole house of Israel has become dross to me” (Ezek. XXII). The house of Israel is then turned into dross when a sinner, struck by divine punishment, either falls into the abyss of despair or, through impatience, rises up against the authority of the one who is justly raging. Conversely, just as dross flies away from metal under divine blows while the metal remains, so anyone who, chastised by a heavenly stroke, repels from himself the rust of the vices that make him shudder and shines with the whiteness of virtues in bloom and with the brightness of a resplendent life.

### CHAPTER II. In a sermon on Pope Saint Stephen and martyr

[Col. 1169D]

“There is Asshur and his tombs” (Ezek. XXXII). What is understood by Asshur—that is, the proud king—if not the devil, “who, as it is written, is king over all the sons of pride?” (Job XLI.) What are tombs if not the dwellings of the dead?

The devil fell into death when, through pride, he departed from the author of life. Therefore, whoever permits the spirit of wickedness—which is truly dead—to dwell in the lodging of his heart through a perverse will undoubtedly makes a tomb of himself. And it is necessary that he suffer there, together with that spirit, the punishments of torments to which here he had offered himself as a dwelling through the wickedness of a perverse deed.

### CHAPTER III. In the first synodal sermon

[Col. 1170C]

“The earth reaches to the windows, and the windows are closed” (Ezek. XXI). The Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (I Cor. III). The windows of this temple are the priests, who pour the light of holy preaching into the people of the faithful.

But when the earth is heaped up to the windows, the temple is immediately darkened by the closed windows. And when priests entangle themselves in earthly affairs, the temple, as though its windows were closed, is darkened because it loses its light.

We must therefore, insofar as we can, abstain from earthly activities so that we may continually attend to sacred utterances. As the bride says in the *Song of Songs*: “Your eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and dwelling [Col. 1170D] beside the fullest channels” (Song V).

### CHAPTER IV. In the letter to Blanca

“Judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII). Those books are evidently to be understood as the saints, whose merit is now hidden from them through the guardianship of humility and wrapped up like the volume of a book so that it may not be read.

Then, however, their glory is opened to the eyes of all, so that in them transgressors may read, as though in the sections of an arranged document, the commandments of divine law which, while they were alive, they had scorned to observe. There they are compelled to read who here, through arrogant disdain, were unwilling to hear the words of God.

There they perceive that the Lord’s yoke was easy and his burden light to the meek and patient (Matt. XI), although here they had judged it intolerable for the necks of their pride. There every proud person is confounded, and whatever had been exalted is bent beneath the indignation of such great majesty.

Hence Isaiah says: “The eyes of the proud man have been humbled, and the loftiness of men will be bowed down; but the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, because the day of the Lord is against every proud and lofty thing, against every arrogant thing, and it will be humbled; against all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, against all the oaks of Bashan, against all the elevated hills, against every high tower, against every fortified wall, against all the ships of Tarshish, and against everything beautiful to the eye; and the loftiness of men will be bowed down, and the height of men will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and idols will be utterly crushed. And they will enter the caves of the rocks and the hollows of the earth, before the terror of the Lord and the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isa. II).

### CHAPTER V. In the letter to Honestus

“They hated the one who rebuked at the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke with integrity.” To them he says shortly afterward: “You shall build houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them” (Amos V).

He rebukes at the gate who corrects someone blameworthy for the purpose of driving that person toward a return to the heavenly homeland. But the one who hates the rebuker does not dwell in the house he has built; for although he has erected a structure of good works, he will not deserve to dwell in it, because he has scorned to enter through the gate of correction. Whoever was unwilling to enter through the harshness of the narrow entrance will not be able to enjoy the pleasantness of the inner court.

### CHAPTER VI. In a homily on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III). Since this is not read as having happened historically at that time, it is still awaited as something to be fulfilled spiritually.

Nineveh signifies this world; the forty days signify the whole condition of the present life. After forty days, therefore, Nineveh will be overthrown, because after the course of this mortal life, when the number of the elect has been completed, this world will be destroyed.

### CHAPTER VII. In the first sermon on Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist

“The hinges of the earth belong to the Lord, and he has placed the world upon them” (I Kings II). The world is placed upon the hinges of the earth when the holy Church is established as upon foundations by evangelical teachings. Of it, too, it is said elsewhere: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). What are called hinges there are called mountains here.

The number of the evangelists plainly corresponds both to the arrangement of the world and to the course of time, since there are four parts of the world and an equal number of variations of the seasons. It is therefore no wonder if the spiritual world is compared with this visible one, since the two are recognized to possess certain similarities to one another.

### CHAPTER VIII. In the letter to Mainard, abbot

“Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the angel’s face. He answered and said to those standing before him: ‘Take the filthy garments away from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I have clothed you in a change of garments.’ And he said: ‘Place a clean turban upon his head’” (Zech. III).

What is to be understood by Jesus, the great priest, if not the mediator between God and human beings? Just as, through Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who had come from the royal stock of Judah, and Jesus son of Jehozadak, who exercised the office of the priesthood, the Israelite people escaped the yoke of Babylonian captivity for seventy years and rebuilt Jerusalem’s temple, which had been destroyed, in renewed form, so after the times of this life—which proceed through the sevenfold recurrence of days—the number of the elect is rescued from the bondage of mortality through Jesus Christ, who is the true king and priest, and God’s temple, which is the holy Church, is renewed in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Of this bondage the Apostle says: “The creation itself will also be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII).

Then Jesus lays aside the filthy garments in his body, which is the Church; then he assumes the rule of honor and glory, because the whole choir of the elect is freed from the mournful squalor of temporal sadness and clothed in the robe of immortality in the splendor of everlasting happiness.

The Church also sings this most clearly in the psalm for the dedication of a house: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Ps. XXIX).

A clean turban is also placed upon his head, because he is crowned with the glory of eternal happiness.

### CHAPTER IX. In the letter to the cardinal bishops, concerning the dignity of the Roman Church

“Behold the stone that I have placed before Jesus: upon the one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III). This stone is undoubtedly that rock concerning which the true Jesus promises Peter, saying: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

This rock therefore has seven eyes, because the holy Church shines with an equal number of gifts of the Holy Spirit. Like a golden lampstand gleaming unquenchably through these gifts, it drives away the darkness of ignorance and illumines human minds for the contemplation of the Sun of justice.

Concerning this the same prophet says: “I saw, and behold, a wholly golden lampstand, with its lamp above it, and its seven lamps upon it” (Zech. IV). Blessed John also did not conceal that he had learned this mystery in the Apocalypse, where he was told: “The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands” (Rev. I). The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.

### CHAPTER X. In the second sermon on Saint Matthew the apostle and evangelist

Moreover, those chariots that the prophet Zechariah describes when he says: “I turned and saw, and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were bronze.” Concerning them he says shortly afterward: “These are the four winds of heaven, which go forth to stand before the ruler of all the earth” (Zech. VI).

It should be noted that the four evangelists are not called one single chariot; rather, each of them is called a chariot, because one is in four and four are in one. What is written by each is found in all through the intention of the same faith, and what is said by all is found in each.

The two bronze mountains from between which they are said to have come forth are the two Testaments, which are durable and resonant like bronze, because they find no end until the end of the world and produce their sound throughout all the expanses of the earth. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

They are also said to be winds, because it is written of them: “Wherever there was the movement of the spirit, there they went” (Ezek. I). They also go forth to stand before the Ruler of all the earth, because what holy preachers gain from the fruitfulness of the faithful they do not attribute to themselves, but to the author from whom all their gains proceed.

Concerning them it is said to blessed Job: “Will you send forth lightning, and will they go, and returning say to you, ‘Here we are’?” (Job XXXVIII.)

[Col. 1173] Here end the testimonies from the books of the prophets.

### HERE BEGIN THE TESTIMONIES FROM THE BOOK OF THE MACHABEES

[Col. 1173]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 1173B]

“When our fathers,” says Scripture, “were being led into Persia, the priests who were then worshipers of God secretly took fire from the altar and hid it in a valley where there was a deep, dry well, and they concealed it there, so that the place was unknown to everyone. After many years had passed, it pleased the Lord that Nehemiah should be sent by the king of Persia. He sent the descendants of those priests who had hidden the fire to search for it; and, as they told us, they did not find fire but thick water” (II Macc. I).

Among all these words, one point in particular should be noted: fire is first hidden in the deep, dry well of a valley, and afterward those searching find not fire but thick water.

A mind sincere and perfect in its seeking of the Lord is fittingly signified by a deep, dry well in a valley. Such a mind is dry from the fluid pleasures of carnal allurements, deeply excavated beneath the rubble of earthly desire, and founded in the valley of true humility.

Fire from the sacrifice is placed in this well when the flame of divine love is conceived in the mind of any one of the elect and the spirit is first inflamed with heavenly desire. But this fire is changed into water because the fire of divine love produces the compunction of tears.

It should be noted that the water found there is described not simply as water but as thick water. For what is thick water if not the compunction of tears fattened by the richness of divine grace? The prophet was ardent to be fattened by this richness when he said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII). Through another prophet this same richness is promised when he says: “Your soul shall delight in abundance” (Isa. LV).

Nor should it be passed over that those who hid this fire are said to have covered it, but not to have extinguished it completely. The fire of divine love that we kindle in the soul of our heart, so that we may offer to God a sweet sacrifice from the spices of good works, ought indeed to burn secretly within us from the very beginning of our way of life, but it ought not to spread outward through the flames of vainglory.

It is therefore covered with its flames subdued, but it is not deprived of the force of its heat, so that it may not perish altogether but afterward may wonderfully turn from fire into water.

This water—the compunction of tears—both purifies us from the contagion of sins and commends our good works to God, so that they may please him. Every sacrifice of works is made more pleasing in the sight of the heavenly Judge if it is sprinkled with the tears of a contrite heart.

Hence the text appropriately adds: “And the sacrifices,” he says, “which had been placed there, the priest Nehemiah ordered to be sprinkled with that water, and the wood that had been laid upon them.”

The narrative immediately continues: “When this had been done, the time came when the sun shone, which had previously been hidden by clouds, and a great fire was kindled, so that everyone marveled.”

Earlier we heard that water had been found in place of fire; now, conversely, it is said that through the sprinkling of water a great fire was kindled. Thus water is born from fire, and fire is in turn produced from water. For the grace of compunction arises from the fire of divine love, and again the ardor of heavenly desire is increased by the compunction of tears.

Each depends upon the other, and each mutually benefits the other: compunction of tears flows from the love of God, and through tears our mind burns more fervently with love of God. In whatever mind this reciprocal alternation and variation takes place, that mind is undoubtedly cleansed from all the squalor of its guilt.

Hence the text appropriately concludes: “Nehemiah named this place Nephtar, which is interpreted as ‘purification.’”

Our place, then, where sacrifice is offered and where, as has been said, water and fire alternate in their varied forms, is the faithful soul. It is fittingly called purification, because now it is refined by the fire of heavenly love, now inundated by the tears of a contrite heart, and washed as if by the streams of a second baptism.

Isaiah had deeply perceived these alternating successions and variations of spiritual transformations when he said: “Your light shall rise in the darkness, and your darkness shall be as midday; and the Lord will give you rest continually, and will fill your bones with splendor, and will free your soul” (Isa. LVIII).

Behold, the fire hidden in the well. But hear how this fire is changed into water; he immediately adds: “And you shall be like a watered garden and like a spring of waters whose waters shall not fail.”

Finally, so that you may know that this water is again changed into fire, and that through the grace of tears the ardor of divine love is stirred more fervently, he adds a little farther on: “Then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will raise you above the heights of the earth.”

### CHAPTER II. In the letter to Alberic, cardinal

Moreover, concerning what you ask about what became of the Lord’s ark and the tabernacle of the covenant, which were fashioned in the desert: just as ignorance of this matter is almost of no hindrance, so knowledge of it is scarcely proved to provide any benefit.

Nevertheless, as the authority of Scripture transmits, on Mount Abarim, where Moses is recognized as buried, the tabernacle together with the ark and also the altar of incense is found hidden by the hands of the prophet Jeremiah.

This is clearly shown if one carefully considers the beginning of the Second Book of the Machabees: “It was written in the same Scripture,” it says, “how the prophet, having received a divine response, commanded that the tabernacle and the ark should accompany him until he went out to the mountain where Moses had ascended and had seen the glory of God. When Jeremiah arrived there, he found a cave; and he brought the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense into it, and blocked up the entrance” (II Macc. II; Deut. XXXIV).

Jeremiah therefore hid these three sacred objects on the aforementioned Mount Abarim. But whether anything else was afterward done with them, or whether they remained untouched in this condition, since Scripture nowhere records it, our curiosity likewise ought not presume to investigate.

A delicate soldier indeed is one who wishes to triumph before engaging in battle, and to thresh before plowing the fields. When the order of the Scriptures is considered, the sequence of our actions is rightly understood: first comes the law, then judgment, and finally the history of kings.

Now it is fitting for us to observe the commandments of the divine law imposed upon us. Afterward we are compelled to give an account of our works before the tribunal of the dread Judge. Finally, in the glory of heavenly splendor, we shall be granted to reign without end.

Let the person who wishes to avoid Babylon preserve the order. A person confuses the order of his life when he wishes to laugh before weeping, although Solomon says: “A time for weeping and a time for laughing” (Eccl. III).

The person who postpones the Creator of all things in love behind created things also abandons the line of right order. Thus the divine voice says to the perverse person: “You have placed me behind your body.” He places the Lord behind his body who is more concerned to serve the usefulness or pleasure of his flesh than to observe God’s commandments.

Hence the bride says in the *Song of Songs*: “He ordered charity in me” (Song II).

Nowhere, certainly, is a command found in the ceremonies of the Old Testament that honey be mixed with sacrifices. By this it is understood that God wishes those who offer the sacrifice of their life to him to have no carnal sweetness in them, and that nothing should live in them belonging to carnal pleasure.

Oil, however, is frequently added, so that every offering of our work may be presented joyfully. “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

Salt is also commanded to be mixed into everything, so that every sacrifice of a good work may be seasoned with reason, discernment, and heavenly wisdom.

## CONCERNING THE QUESTIONS OF LINCIDARIUS AND THE RESPONSES OF THE SAME AUTHOR

(*Works*, vol. III, short work 3)

[Col. 1175]

[Col. 1175D]

### Question 1. If Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why is a Christian not circumcised in the flesh?

### Response

Rather, this is precisely why a Christian no longer circumcises himself: because Christ fulfilled what was prophesied through circumcision. The stripping away of carnal life, which had been prefigured in the old law, is now seen completed in Christ’s resurrection; and what we expect to happen in our resurrection is already commended in the mystery of holy baptism.

Carnal circumcision is therefore rightly rejected as superfluous, since spiritual circumcision—the reason why the former had preceded as a sign—is now represented.

### Question 2. Why does a Christian omit observing the Sabbath if Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it?

[Col. 1176D]

### Response

We do not observe the Sabbath because what was then set forth in figure we now see fulfilled through the manifestation of the reality. In Christ we observe the true Sabbath of spiritual rest when we place our hope in him alone and rest in him with the whole love and devotion of our heart, so that we cease from every servile work of vice and from ambition for earthly things.

He himself calls us to celebrate this Sabbath when he cries: “Come to me,” he says, “all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XIII).

We therefore call the observance of the carnal Sabbath superfluous, since we already celebrate the true and saving Sabbath for which it was instituted.

### Question 3. If Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian neglect the distinction of foods that the law commands to be observed?

### Response

Rather, this distinction of foods is not admitted by Christians precisely because what it signified is fulfilled by Christ. The impurity that was then avoided in foods is now rejected in human conduct. Just as all the holy and righteous are transferred into the body of Christ, so the wicked and unrighteous are rejected by him as unclean food.

After the Truth itself, which was signified, has arrived, the shadow of the sign has rightly ceased.

### Question 4. If Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian not take care to offer God a sacrifice of the flesh of animals?

### Response

Rather, this kind of sacrifice is not offered by Christians precisely because whatever was performed figuratively in those victims is truly fulfilled in the sacrifice of the Lamb “who takes away the sins of the world” (John III). Since all those things possessed no other purpose of salvation than to point together toward this sacrifice of ours, and since the whole diversity of ceremonies signified this one thing, once the unique victim has appeared, the manifold shadow that preceded it has vanished.

For who does not know that those same sacrifices were imposed rather to restrain that disobedient people, lest it fornicate with idols, than offered to God as though he himself desired them?

### Question 5. If Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, why does a Christian not observe the unleavened bread commanded by the law?

### Response

That visible and bodily unleavened bread is disregarded by Christians precisely because, once the leaven of the old life has been purged, the new dough is spiritually fulfilled. At that time it was a command of the written law; now it is a testimony. After what it signified has arrived, what signified it has passed away.

### Question 6. If Christ came to fulfill the law, why does a Christian not celebrate Passover with the blood of the paschal lamb, since the law itself so emphatically decrees this?

### Response

Here the same response must be given as was already stated above: once that true Lamb which was signified is recognized to have arrived, the one that signified him is judged superfluous. With his blood we no longer anoint wooden or stone doors; rather, we seal the inward parts of the inner person.

## Question 7

If Christ did not abolish the Law, why does the Christian not celebrate the new moon, as the Law commands?

### Answer

For this reason, too, the Christian disdains its celebration: because Christ fulfilled everything on account of which it was formerly celebrated. For the solemnity of the [Col. 1178A] new moon signifies that a new creation is to be brought about in a human being, concerning which the Apostle says: “If anyone is therefore a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5).

## Question 8

If Christ did not come to abolish the Law, why does the Christian not observe those baptisms of washing which the Law prescribes?

### Answer

These things do not deserve the honor of Christian observance because they were then shadows of things to come, whose manifest fulfillment we now possess. “For we were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

## Question 9

If the Law was fulfilled by Christ, not abolished, [Col. 1178B] what justification is offered for the fact that Christians do not honor the solemnity of the Feast of Tabernacles?

### Answer

The tabernacle of God is the fellowship of the Christian people. And because that tabernacle prefigured the holy Church, the sign is disregarded after the thing prefigured has arrived. It would not be called the “tabernacle of testimony” unless it bore witness to someone concerning those things that were to be declared in their own time as truth. Therefore, what was then enacted as a command and presented in figure is now seen as revealed in actuality through testimony; and once what was being signified is observed, what signified it is judged wholly superfluous.

## Question 10

If Christ did not wish to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, why does the Christian neglect to observe the seventh year of remission [Col. 1178C], or even the jubilee?

### Answer

Because the Truth and Wisdom of God, which teaches the angels in heaven, also came to teach human beings on earth. What he had earlier commanded to be observed bodily under the shadow of an enigma, he afterward commanded his disciples to understand spiritually.

Thus the seventh day is commanded to be a day of rest, so that eternal rest might be signified through it. The same applies to the seventh year and to the Jubilee, which, through the cycle of years—seven multiplied seven times and one added to it, producing fifty—announces the secure rest of perpetual blessedness.

At the beginning of the Jubilee, trumpets are sounded, and everyone returns to his own possession. For, as the Apostle says: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God [Col. 1178D]; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Thess. 4). For each person to return to his possessions means immediately to receive his own body incorruptible.

Then Adam will return to the ancient earth of his flesh, in which he had first dwelt. Then Noah, Abraham, Moses, and all the others will be restored to their own possession, when an incorruptible body is re-formed for them.

Therefore our Redeemer, who “opened the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the mysteries of the Scriptures” (Luke 24), did not wish the Jubilee, the seventh year of remission, or the other ceremonies of the legal rite to be observed bodily after he had caused all these things to be understood spiritually. For the legal commandments are truly fulfilled [Col. 1179A] when they are carried out according to the spiritual understanding for which they were instituted. When they were observed bodily, they were empty [Col. 1180A]—namely, a shadow and image of the reality, not the reality itself.

# On the Threats and Promises of God

*(Works, vol. III, opusculum 4.)*

[Col. 1179]

[Col. 1179A] What the pope has granted and established by decree ought in no way to be changed. *(Peter Damian, vol. III, opusculum 4.)*

What wonder is it if human beings change regulations, when almighty God himself also changes things established by him? For sometimes he diminishes what he promises, or even withdraws it altogether; sometimes he threatens evils and does not inflict them.

What is it that [Col. 1179B] God has never promised and then diminished? If it has not slipped your memory, you can recall that the Lord said to Noah: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh; and their days shall be one hundred and twenty years” (Gen. 6). But since Scripture records that Noah was then five hundred years old when the Lord spoke these words to him, and that he was already six hundred when the cataclysm broke out, it is plainly evident that twenty years were subtracted from the span prescribed by that number. Thus God diminished the length of life that he had promised the human race, because their guilt arising from perversity had increased.

The Holy Spirit also promised Judah through the mouth of the patriarch, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. [Col. 1179C] 49). Yet we do not read that, during the period of the Judges, men from the tribe of Judah always held rule over Israel; nor are kings from that same tribe found to have held sovereignty continuously until the coming of Christ. It is therefore clear that almighty God often diminishes what he has promised a human being, because the human being has not fulfilled what he owed to God.

Where has God promised some good and not fulfilled it? Recall that the Lord said to Josiah, king of Judah: “Because you saw the words of the scroll, and your heart was afraid, and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard the words against this place and its inhabitants; and you tore your garments and wept before me, therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace.” [Col. 1179D] Yet shortly afterward Scripture says: “In his days Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria at the river Euphrates; and Josiah went out to meet him, and he was killed at Megiddo when he had seen him” (2 Kings 23).

To Zedekiah, king of Judah, the Lord also says through Jeremiah: “Hear the word of the Lord, Zedekiah, king of Judah. Thus says the Lord to you: ‘You shall not die by the sword, but you shall die in peace; and according to the burnings for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so shall they burn for you; for this word I have spoken, says the Lord’” (Jer. 34). Anyone who examines the course of history will never be able to discover how this could have happened. For after he had once been captured by the king of Babylon and transported to Babylon, he is never again [Col. 1180A] read to have been released from his bonds. Thus, by a just judgment, God sometimes withdraws from a human being the good things he has promised, when the rebellious human being refuses to keep his commandments.

Explain also how God does not inflict what he has threatened.

No one who crosses the threshold of the Church is unaware that Jonah [Col. 1180B], sent by the Lord to Nineveh, cried out, saying: “Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3). But because that city turned to the Lord with its whole heart, it was by no means destroyed by the overthrow threatened in the Lord’s sentence.

Although almighty God is not only truthful but Truth itself, while the purpose of his counsel remains inviolate, he often changes the outward order of his judgment according to the quality of human merit, whether good or evil, so that the person corrected from wickedness may escape what God justly threatens, while the person who has fallen into sin may in no way receive the good things he promises.

Hence he says through Jeremiah: “Make your ways and your practices good, and hear the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against [Col. 1180C] you” (Jer. 17). Hence also the Lord says to Eli through a man of God: “Speaking, I spoke that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever; but now the Lord says: Far be this from me. For whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in disgrace” (1 Sam. 2).

You have rightly strengthened everything you proposed with clear testimonies from Scripture. Now, however, give an account of the injury done to my lord the king.

Far be it from us to have injured the glorious king by choosing a pontiff, since necessity drove us to do so, not plunder. I say that the imminent danger of civil war drew us unwillingly into this action, not the spite of a desire to injure imperial authority.

[Col. 1180D] What does all this matter to me, when it is established that, whatever might happen, you ought in no way to have infringed the judgment of the holy pope? On no account was it lawful to violate the mystery of the synodal decree. For, as Scripture testifies: “It is better that scandal should arise than that the truth should be abandoned.” For if the blessed martyrs had feared this war, they would unquestionably have become deserters from the holy army.

You are not unaware that, among all the holy martyrs, Peter and Paul hold the preeminence at the summit of the apostolic senate. We must follow in their footsteps; their pattern must be impressed upon our actions; under their instruction we must live according to their discipline.

This is certainly clear.

Hear, therefore, Paul truthfully [Col. 1181A] bearing witness concerning his fellow apostle Peter: “Before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Gal. 2).

We therefore see that Peter was not rigid but discerning. For he feared the Jews, lest through the occasion provided by the Gentiles they should withdraw from the faith of Christians. And, so as not to lose the flock that had been lost, he imitated the example of the good shepherd: “He became as a Jew to the Jews, in order to gain the Jews”; just as Christ appeared in the form of sinful flesh in order to free humanity from sins.

Although he did not doubt that the law of Moses was to be abolished, nevertheless, out of concern for brothers who were still inexperienced and weak, he retained the shadow of the Law for a time, so that he might eventually lead them onward to a perfect knowledge of the fullness of truth. In this [Col. 1181B] way blessed Peter gave us a rule of discernment: that at times, where it does not cause very great harm, we should deviate slightly from the path of strictness in order to be able to assist the weak.

You say that Peter at one time observed the Jewish Law. Why do you not also say what is read in the same Epistle—namely, that “Paul opposed him to his face”? “To his face,” he says, “I opposed him, because he was blameworthy; and I said to him: If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

What Peter did out of compassionate mercy, Paul rebuked in the interest of disciplinary instruction. Peter acted in this way as a matter of practical accommodation, to remove a stumbling block from the weak; Paul rebuked it so that any indiscreet person might not everywhere introduce it as an example.

From Peter let us learn to be discerning when danger threatens. From Paul’s words let us be instructed so that, in matters that are sound, our life may rightly devote itself to rectitude.

Hear also what follows from Paul, who places before our eyes the golden line of discernment and likewise presents himself as the author of this compassionate accommodation. For, as the history of the Acts of the Apostles testifies: “Paul passed through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches [Col. 1181C]; and he came to Derbe and Lystra. And behold, there was a certain disciple named Timothy, the son of a faithful Jewish woman but of a Gentile father” (Acts 16).

To come briefly to the point, the Apostle circumcised Timothy because he feared the Jews—rather, the Jewish people who were in those regions. Why, then, did he circumcise a faithful man who was not a Jew but was by nationality a Gentile and had been uncircumcised [Col. 1181D]? It was to serve the purpose of discernment, lest the Jewish faithful should fall into scandal and withdraw from the faith.

This also now comes to mind: at one time, according to the custom of the Nazarenes, he grew his hair in fulfillment of a vow; and after he had sailed to Syria, while he was at Cenchreae, he cut his head according to the commands of the Law (Acts 18).

Luke, the sacred historian, further relates: “When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. And on the following day James and all the elders who were with him, after approving his Gospel, said to him: You see, brother, how many thousands there are in Judea who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealous for the Law. But they have heard about [Col. 1182A] you that you teach the Jews who are among the Gentiles to depart from Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom. What, then, is to be done? The multitude will certainly gather, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you: We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take these men and sanctify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; and everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the Law. Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having been purified with them, entered the temple” (Acts 21).

Let no one be permitted to remain ignorant: Whatever is consecrated to the Lord—whether it is a human being, an animal, a field, or anything else that has once been consecrated—“shall be most holy [Col. 1182B] to the Lord,” and belongs to the rights of the priests. Therefore everyone who demands from the Lord and the Church a citizen/member (*civem*: the reading is uncertain), takes one away, ravages, attacks, or steals one must be judged a sacrilegious person; and, if unwilling to make amends, must be excommunicated.

Whoever takes anything away from a father is an accomplice of a murderer. Without doubt, our father is God, who created us; our mother is the holy Church, which regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever takes away, steals, or defrauds Christ and the Church of money is a murderer and is reckoned a murderer before the Lord. For whoever removes Church property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.

Just as we draw up the battle line of spiritual combat against wicked spirits, so it is exceedingly necessary that we always be found united and bound together by charity, and never [Col. 1182C] severed by discord. For whatever good works there may be in us, if charity is absent, discord opens a breach in the battle line through which the enemy can enter to strike us.

The ancient enemy does not fear chastity in us if it is without charity, because he himself is not weighed down by flesh, whose lust might be dissolved. He does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food and is not driven by bodily necessity. He does not fear the distribution of earthly possessions if charity is absent from that work, because he himself has no need of the support of riches.

But he greatly fears true charity in us, and likewise the humble love that we show to one another; and he is intensely jealous of our harmony, because we possess on earth what he lost in heaven by refusing to preserve it.

Therefore it is well said [Col. 1182D]: “Terrible as an army set in array.” For wicked spirits fear the multitude of the elect insofar as they see them united and gathered together against them through the harmony of charity.

How great, however, is the power of harmony is shown when, without it, the remaining virtues are shown not to be virtues. Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he condemns others for eating and condemns the very foods that God created for consumption with thanksgiving by the faithful, what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt?

Thus the Psalmist also, indicating that there is no abstinence without harmony, says: “Praise him with the tambourine and with the choir.” In the tambourine, dry hide [Col. 1183A] resounds; in the choir, voices sing in harmony. What, then, is signified by the tambourine except abstinence? What by the choir except the harmony of charity?

Whoever therefore maintains abstinence while abandoning harmony praises him with the tambourine, but not with the choir.

Whoever neglects the guardianship of his own life, and fails to examine what he says or thinks, either despises or does not know these things; he does not walk before himself, because he is unaware of what he is like in his habits or actions. Nor is he present to himself, because he is not concerned to examine and know himself every day.

But the person who attends to himself in his [Col. 1184A] actions as though to someone else truly places himself before himself and is present to himself. For we commit many sins, but they do not seem serious to us because, loving ourselves with private affection, we flatter ourselves in our deception with our eyes closed.

Consequently, it often happens that we judge our own grave faults lightly, while judging the slight faults of our neighbors severely. “People will be lovers of themselves”; and we know that private love closes the eye of the heart very tightly. Hence it happens that we do not consider what we ourselves do to be serious, while what is done by a neighbor often appears exceedingly detestable to us.

[Col. 1183] The remainder is wanting.

# To the Reader

Dom Constantine, abbot of Cajetan, to his reader.

We think that you, excellent reader, should be informed that these collections, excerpted from the works of Saint Peter Damian, were sought out by us with great diligence. Nevertheless, what we now bring to light was found to concern only the Old Testament, and even there in an apparently incomplete form.

For the expositions of the New Testament, which the same author—the disciple of the holy Doctor—also compiled, as the old inscription indicates, could not be found at all.

[Note: We have recently reprinted these, edited by the most eminent Cardinal Mai, above, at the end of volume or part III of the works of Saint Peter Damian, together with two other opuscula lacking from Cajetan’s edition. —Editor of the Patrologia.]

Farewell.
